## PR #7996 — Fix marker-path containment and four #7171 survivor rows [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7171-cohort`

Nine rows from the **#7171** survivor cohort (successor to the #5557 audit). Every row was confirmed by re-deriving its **predicate** at current `origin/master`, not by opening the cited line range. Several rows in the cohort do not say what the issue says they say; those are reported on #7171 rather than changed here. **This PR does not close #7171** — 22 rows remain.

## `markerPathIn` did not contain what its comment promised

`Base(Clean(x))` keeps a bare traversal element — `Base(Clean(".."))` is `".."` — so `Join(dir, "..")` returned dir's **parent**, and a name of `"."` or `"/"` returned **dir itself**. The second case is the worse one: the deprovision path calls `os.Remove` on this result, so a name of `"."` aimed a remove at the whole provenance registry directory rather than one marker inside it.

`TestMarkerPathContainment` already claimed to verify this property, and passed. Every input it sampled — `"../../etc/shadow"`, `"/etc/passwd"`, `"a/b/c"` — ends in a real component, so `Base` returns `shadow`/`passwd`/`c` and containment holds under **any** implementation. The fixture varied the right axis and sampled only points that cannot distinguish a correct reduction from a broken one. Extended, it reds on five inputs before the fix:

```
markerPath("..")      = "/var/lib/xpf" escaped "/var/lib/xpf/provisioned-users"
markerPath("../..")   = "/var/lib/xpf" escaped ...
markerPath("a/../..") = "/var/lib/xpf" escaped ...
markerPath(".")       = "/var/lib/xpf/provisioned-users" escaped ...
markerPath("/")       = "/var/lib/xpf/provisioned-users" escaped ...
```

## `UnionHostInboundTokens` rendered one service twice

Dedup keyed on the raw trimmed token, so a zone authoring `ssh` and an interface authoring `SSH` produced both. Downstream membership predicates are case-insensitive, so the two spellings are one admission — the duplicate existed only in the display, which is where this output goes. The **key** is now folded; the **value** keeps the authored case.

Deliberately **not** single-sourced with `junos_host_deny.go` as the issue suggested: that one folds to *match enforcement* (#5557), this one folds only to *dedup* and must preserve spelling. Merging them breaks one of the two.

## Silent HA session-sync drops

`userspaceSessionFromDeltaV4/V6` dropped a delta on an unparseable address or unresolved zone id and returned a bare `false` — `daemon_ha_userspace_convert.go` does not import `log/slog` at all, while the V4 filters one file over log every reason at Debug. A session dropped here never reaches the peer, so after a failover it is simply absent with nothing in the log. Four sites get a Debug line; the two `wireKey == key` returns are left silent because that is "no alias needed", the expected outcome, not a drop.

## CLI stdout swap — and a third site the issue does not list

The filed failure ("a panic between them leaks the swap") is **not reachable**: nothing on either path recovers, so a panic takes the process down. The reachable class is an early `return`, which would leave stdout pointing at an undrained pipe and leak the filter goroutine — live for the in-process CLI, where the process is the daemon and survives it.

The issue enumerates two sites. There are **three**: the pager path in `cli_dispatch.go` performs the identical unprotected swap around `pageStream` and is uncited. All three now restore stdout, close `w` and reap the reader in one deferred block.

## `makeNonce` predictable fallback removed

A fixed `"xpf-ka00"` on `rand.Read` failure would dissolve the anti-spoof property — a reply is matched on Seq + nonce so an off-path forgery cannot pass as a reply to *this* probe, so a predictable nonce lets a spoofed reply hold a **dead tunnel UP**.

The branch was also unreachable: since Go 1.24 `crypto/rand.Read` never returns an error ([go.dev/issue/66821](https://go.dev/issue/66821)). An error-returning variant was written first, gated clean, and discarded — it added an unreachable, untestable branch to callee and caller. **No test is added**; any behavioural guard passes identically before and after.

## Smaller rows

- **Two fail-open twins deleted.** `queryInt`/`queryUint16` had zero callers (handlers moved to the fail-closed `Strict` variants in #2934/#3443/#4926) but sat beside them differing only by a suffix, returning the caller's default — usually a filter sentinel meaning "no filter" — on a malformed value. `RemoveRSTSuppression` had no production caller and swallowed its own teardown result.
- **`wgkey.Generate`** wipes the raw clamped scalar. Scoped honestly in the comment: it clears the rawest copy, it does **not** make the key unrecoverable — the returned `PrivateKey` is an immutable GC-managed string that cannot be wiped.
- **IP-write length preconditions** in `byte_writes.rs` are now `debug_assert`s. A diagnostic, not a safety fix — the indexing is already memory-safe and panics either way; the message now names the helper, length and offset. Release path byte-identical.

## Validation

`pkg/daemon`, `pkg/config`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/nftables`, `pkg/routing`, `pkg/cli`, `pkg/wgkey`, `cmd/...` pass with `-count=1`; `go build ./...` clean. `make test-rust` rc=0, **4973 passed / 0 failed** — the new asserts were live throughout (tests build in debug) and none fired. Both added/extended tests confirmed red before their fix, green after. `docs/host-inbound-service-matrix.md` updated for the dedup change.

## PR #7997 — config/cli: correct two GRE advisories that #7188 cut 1 made false [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7188-stale-accepted-only-advisories`

Found while triaging #7188 for closure. Both operator-facing surfaces still tell an operator that `gre-performance-acceleration` does nothing, after #7188 cut 1 (#7961) made it do something.

## The false claims

| surface | text |
|---|---|
| commit (`validateSecurityFlowAcceptedOnly`) | *"accepted-only … the userspace dataplane keys GRE sessions on the 5-tuple with no tunnel discriminator … independent per-tunnel sessions are not provided"* |
| `show security flow` | *"configured (accepted-only; GRE sessions remain 5-tuple keyed)"* |

Both were accurate when written for #5804. Both became false the moment transit GRE started resolving a discriminator-keyed session flow (`poll_stages.rs` → `gre_keyed_session_flow`, gated on the knob). So an operator who enables the knob is told **at commit and at `show`** that the feature is inert, while it is keying their sessions.

**I gated and merged the PR that made these stale**, and my review of it flagged the upgrade-impact for operators who already had the knob set — but not these two strings.

## The replacement is not "in force" either, and that is measured

`build_synced_session_key` (`userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/session_sync.rs:62`) constructs a peer-synced `SessionKey` with:

```rust
discriminator: Default::default(),
```

So a keyed GRE session that is **independent on the active node ALIASES on the standby**. #7188's acceptance requires such sessions be *withheld* from sync on a peer without the capability, explicitly **"not downgraded"** — and a zeroed discriminator is exactly the downgrade.

That is arguably worse than the feature not existing: an operator gets per-tunnel policy/NAT/counter/timeout separation that silently collapses at the moment of a failover, which is when they are least able to diagnose it. Both surfaces now say **PARTIALLY in force** and name which half is missing.

## The pinning test had to be retargeted, not deleted

`TestGREPerformanceAccelerationAdvisory_5804` required the words `"5-tuple"` and `"one session"`. That pinned #5804's inertness claim — and once the claim went false, **the test actively defended the falsehood**. A test written to hold today's behaviour becomes a test demanding yesterday's.

It now asserts the property that survives — the advisory must name the **remaining** gap — plus the inverse, which is the half a keyword check alone would miss: the advisory must **not** still carry the pre-#7188 sentences, because a message that gains the new words while keeping the old ones reads as self-contradictory and leaves the operator with the wrong model.

Its issue citation moved too. It required `#5804`, which is **closed**; #7188 is the successor carrying the dataplane half. Pinning the closed one sends an operator to a thread whose Problem statement describes behaviour that no longer exists.

## Validation

`go test -count=1 ./...` — **69 packages, 0 FAIL**. The suite caught both stale pins on the first run, which is the guard working correctly on a claim that had genuinely moved.

## PR #7998 — Export the tolerant VRF-overlap/PBR admission as a metric [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7991-vrf-overlap-metric`

Closes #7991

## The gap

#7924 made the **strict** commit path reject cross-routing-instance L3 overlap
combined with a PBR `then routing-instance` term. The **tolerant** load /
peer-sync path still admits it (`lenientVRFOverlapPBR`, the #1960 no-brick
concession) — so the condition is live on exactly the boxes that upgrade *into*
the fix: a config persisted before #7924 and loaded at startup, or one arriving
from a peer.

Until now that state had no queryable surface. #3718 is the **structurally
identical** case — the tolerant path admitted something strict rejects — and it
has a metric. So an operator who knows to look for that one reads its absence
here as the condition being absent, when it means nobody exported it.

**What firing means**, and why the HELP text says it rather than pointing at an
issue: sessions are keyed on the bare 5-tuple with no routing-instance
discriminator, and the established-session fast path runs **before** the PBR
table override with no policy call at all. A colliding 5-tuple in the second
instance is forwarded out the **first** instance's egress, with its NAT, having
never been adjudicated by any policy. That is a cross-tenant forwarding path, not
a configuration-hygiene advisory.

## Two corrections to the issue, both measured

**#3718 has no `show` surface.** The issue proposes "a metric plus `show` state".
Measured, #3718 has a metric and a state-transition log and **nothing** in
`pkg/cli` or `pkg/grpcapi`. Mirroring it therefore means a metric; adding a
`show` command here would be *inventing* a convention rather than following the
one the issue's argument rests on. A `show` surface for tolerant-admitted state
may well be worth having — it should be added for both cases together, by someone
deciding that deliberately.

**It is not "logged once at boot".** `applyConfigLocked` emits the warning for
every `cfg.Warnings` entry on *every* apply path — boot, commit and peer-sync
alike. The substance stands (no queryable state); the log is more present than
that phrasing suggests.

## Single-sourcing was the design constraint

The obvious implementation is a second scan for the metric — the shape that
agrees today and drifts later with nothing to notice. Instead
`validateVRFOverlap` now returns structured `VRFOverlapAdmission` findings
alongside its warnings, and **the warning strings are rendered from the
findings**. One scan, one set of detections, two renderings.

The full `pkg/config` suite passing unchanged is what proves the warning text
survived byte-identical — #2387 and #7924 both pin it.

## PR #8002 — Surface two silent HA fail-open paths (#7171) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7171-cohort`

Two observability rows from the **#7171** survivor cohort. Both are cases where a deliberate, correct fail-open is **invisible**, so the operator cannot tell that a protection is inactive. Neither changes forwarding behaviour. **Does not close #7171.**

## Heartbeat monitor-list truncation was the only silent one in its function

`marshalHeartbeatBody` fits as many monitor entries as the frame allows and breaks on the first that does not, silently — while the group section directly above it has warned through a `sync.Once` since #4434.

The effect is not local: the peer consumes `NumMonitors` to compute weight-based failover, so a node whose monitor list did not fit advertises a **smaller monitored set than it has**, and the peer's arithmetic runs on an incomplete picture with nothing on either side recording the loss.

**No test, and that is a reversal I want visible.** I wrote one — marshal more monitors than fit, unmarshal, assert the count agrees with the entries written and that survivors are the leading ones byte-exact — then mutated the marshaller to see if it earned its place:

| mutation | red |
|---|---|
| count byte over-reports (`len(pkt.Monitors)`) | `TestMarshalHeartbeat_LargeMonitorPayload_RGPreserved` (pre-existing) |
| monitor content corrupted (RGID slot ← Weight) | `TestMarshalUnmarshalHeartbeat_WithMonitors` (pre-existing) |

Both mutations were already owned by existing tests. The new test guarded nothing, so it was removed rather than left to pad the diff. The gap this row names is the missing **warning**, not missing coverage.

## VRRP arrival-interface isolation can be inactive with no indication

`acceptArrivalIfindex` fails open when the platform does not report an arrival interface. That is correct and unchanged — it exists so a kernel/socket combination omitting the interface control message does not lose real advert delivery.

What was missing is any way to know. On such a platform **every** advert takes that branch, so the #2886 per-interface isolation is silently inactive for the life of the process — exactly the configuration #2886 was filed for (two VLAN sub-interfaces of one parent, same VRID), where the symptom is state corruption and BACKUP flapping with nothing pointing at the disabled guard.

Only the platform-side case warns. `expectedIfindex <= 0` also fails open but means an instance with no resolved index — a test construction, not something an operator can act on.

## Why `sync.Once` in both

RETH instances advertise every 30ms and the heartbeat sender runs every heartbeat-interval. CLAUDE.md forbids an unguarded log on a per-packet path, and the group-count warning from #4434 is the in-tree precedent for the instrument. Neither warning is asserted by a test: a process-wide `sync.Once` fires on test *order* within the package binary rather than on the input under test, which is also why the #4434 warning has never been asserted.

## PR #8005 — Key LLDP neighbors on a struct so a peer cannot evict another's entry [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7176-lldp-key-collision`

Refs #7176 (C179-026). Flagged as the first of the security tier.

## The defect

The neighbor table keyed on `fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s/%s", iface, chassisID, portID)`.
Two of those three components are **peer-controlled TLV strings** taken straight
off the wire by `ParseTLVs`, and port IDs legitimately contain `/` (a Junos-style
`ge-0/0/1`), so the join is ambiguous:

```
victim:   chassis "aa"    port "bb/cc"  ->  "eth0/aa/bb/cc"
attacker: chassis "aa/bb" port "cc"     ->  "eth0/aa/bb/cc"
```

**That is not a display collision.** A TTL=0 LLDPDU is an explicit withdrawal
under IEEE 802.1AB and `withdrawNeighbor` deletes **by key**, so a peer choosing
its own ChassisID/PortID could forge the key of a different neighbor and evict an
entry it does not own — remote-input-driven deletion of another peer's state,
from anyone on the same L2 segment.

The cohort filed this as a map-key collision. It is attacker-reachable state
removal.

## The fix, and why not escaping

The key is now a comparable **struct**. That makes the collision
**unrepresentable** rather than escaped: there is no separator to smuggle, so no
escaping rule to get wrong later and no encode/decode pair that can drift apart.
Escaping would have been the smaller diff and the worse fix.

## Two things the change surfaced

**The existing test helper was a copy of the production key.**
`neighborKey(iface, chassis, port) string` re-implemented the `%s/%s/%s` join, so
it would have stayed green through any change to the thing it was testing.
Changing the key type made the compiler find it.

**My own first regression test did not bind the fix.** It built keys with that
helper, so mutating the production construction site left it green. The
collision is created exactly where peer strings *become* a key, so that is the
site a test has to reach — `neighborKeyFor(ifaceName, n)` is now split out of the
receive loop and the test drives it.

## Validation

`go test -count=1 ./...` — rc=0, **0 named FAIL**, 69 packages.

A faithful revert of `neighborKeyFor` to the joined string reds
`TestNeighborKeyCollisionCannotEvictAnotherPeer_7176` by name (3 collected, 1
named FAIL).

## PR #8006 — cmdtree: canonical command spelling + unify the pipe splitter (#7172 cut 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut1-canonicalize`

Cut 1 of #7172, on top of the merged cut 2 (#7974). Two commits, reviewable separately.

Both of the risks flagged for this cut turned out to be **real but latent** — the invariants hold today and nothing asserted them. Neither is a live bypass; both are about to become load-bearing for authorization.

## Commit 1 — unify the pipe splitter

`extractPipe` existed as two copies (`pkg/cli`, `cmd/cli`). I diffed them mechanically rather than by eye: **normalized, byte-identical today**. So this is a drift risk, not a live divergence.

**The repo already paid for this lesson on the other half.** `cliterm`'s own package doc records it:

> "#4968 is the proof: the remote copy lowercased both operands, so `| match Foo` matched `foo` on remote and not on local."

#7210 then moved the *filter* into `cliterm`. The *splitter* was left duplicated — so the half with a documented divergence bug got one implementation, and the half that decides **where the command ends** kept two.

That half is about to matter: #7172 matches deny regexes against the command and Junos counts the pipe as part of it (`show configuration | save /tmp/x` writes a file; `| display set` reformats output a deny may be withholding). If the gate and the dispatcher split a line differently they disagree about what the operator ran, and **that disagreement is the bypass**. Detecting drift is worth less than not being able to have it, so this unifies rather than adding an agreement guard.

**One fixture I predicted wrong, recorded rather than quietly corrected.** I expected `show log | match a | b` to return the truncated command `show log | match a`. It does not — splitting on the last `" | "` leaves `b` as the filter word, `b` is not a filter we implement, and the default arm returns the **original line**. My prediction was the unsafe behaviour; the real one is fail-safe. A separate cell now states that property alone: when `SplitPipe` declines, the command it returns is the whole line, because handing a gate a prefix is exactly how a `| save /tmp/x` suffix goes unseen.

## Commit 2 — `cmdtree.Canonicalize`

`req sys reb` and `request system reboot` are the same command to Junos. A deny regex is written against one spelling and the input has many.

**Not reusing `CompleteFromTree`'s `canonWords` walk**, which computes exactly this and discards it (#5196): that walk is completion-shaped — driven by a trailing `partial`, returning early to yield candidates, and calling `ContextDynamicFn` providers that need a `*config.Config` and exist to enumerate live values. An authorization path should require neither. `Canonicalize` shares `resolveTreeWord` — the actual prefix rule — so the thing that must agree lives in one place.

**The result is not advisory.** On anything but `CanonicalOK` the input comes back unchanged and a caller enforcing a restriction must fail closed: it does not know what command it holds, so it cannot know a deny regex fails to match. Ambiguity and absence are reported separately.

**The dispatcher agreement is pinned.** `pkg/cli`'s flat `operationalCommands` list and `OperationalTree` agree today — same ten names, verified mechanically — and nothing asserted it. The literal is duplicated into the test deliberately: importing it from one side would make the assertion agree with itself.

| 2 | ambiguity reported as OK | 0 | `…FailuresAreDistinguished…` + 2 subtests |

The fixture sat where the distinction did not matter.

- **Cell 6** — every failure fixture failed on the **first** word, where the partially-built output and the input are trivially identical. `req zzzznotasub` fails at word 1 *after* `req` became `request`, so the mutation now returns a spelling the operator never typed.

## PR #8007 — Bind the config-envelope header into the AES-GCM AAD [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7176-cohort`

Refs #7176 (C179-053). Second of the security tier, per the decided posture.

## The defect

The envelope header line — including the **#1922 `committed=` marker that gates
the bootstrap decision** — is plaintext ahead of the ciphertext and was sealed
with a `nil` AAD. Unauthenticated and editable in place.

And it was parsed permissively: `strconv.Atoi` then `n != 0` read `"2"`, `"-1"`,
`"+1"` and `"007"` as committed. **The two halves compounded** — an editable
marker whose parser accepted whatever you edited it to.

## Version-gated AAD, not a fallback

A bare "retry with `nil` AAD" is self-defeating: an attacker strips to force the
weaker path. Instead:

- envelopes at **v2** are sealed with the header line as AAD;
- the **read** side uses `nil` AAD only when the **stored** `v=` is below v2;
- pre-v2 envelopes stay readable and **migrate on their next write** — no flag
  day, no operator step.

So rewriting a v2 header to claim `v=1` makes the reader attempt nil-AAD
decryption against a ciphertext sealed **with** AAD, and it fails. **The
downgrade attempt fails closed rather than succeeding weakly**, and the upgrade
direction cannot be forged because it requires re-sealing.

**`min-reader` is raised only when the body is encrypted.** An unencrypted v2
envelope has no ciphertext to bind, so raising the floor would refuse an older
reader for nothing. Leaving it at 1 always would also be fail-closed, but a
pre-v2 build would report an opaque `decrypt config tree` error instead of the
envelope layer's explicit "too new" — and a confusing error during a rollback is
the worst time for one.

**The AAD is the stored header bytes**, not a re-render from parsed fields. A
re-render would normalise field order, spacing and unknown forward-compat fields
— so any writer difference would silently break decryption — and it would
re-authenticate a header the reader had just rewritten, which is the opposite of
the point.

## The absence default is deliberately unchanged

Present-but-weird values are now canonical (`"0"`/`"1"` only). **Absence still
defaults to committed** (migration rule C3): changing it would alter how existing
envelopes that omit the field are read and risks triggering bootstrap on upgrade.

The AAD binding is what removes the *reason* to want it changed — an attacker can
no longer **delete** the field without breaking decryption — so the default
reverts from a fail-open to a mere compatibility behaviour. Recorded in the
parser comment, so the next reader does not see a half-tightened parser and

## PR #8008 — IPsec selectors: reject identity values, default route-based to 0.0.0.0/0 (#8003, #7171 row 70) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/8003-identity-selector`

Two interacting IPsec traffic-selector fixes, both settled by measurement on **strongSwan 6.0.5** on the cluster under the #1875 lock. The lead asked that they be decided together; they touch the same function.

---

# 1. Identity values rendered as selectors (#8003)

`local-identity` / `remote-identity` are rendered as swanctl `local_ts` / `remote_ts` whenever the VPN declares no `traffic-selector`. **Nothing examined them** — the #4098 walk only descended into `traffic-selector` children.

```
loading connection 'm_fqdnts' failed: invalid value for: local_ts, config discarded
loaded 1 of 2 connections, 1 failed to load
```

**`config discarded` is the whole connection.** The VPN never establishes; commit succeeded, render succeeded, and the only record is a line in charon's log. Same signature `policy.go` documents for #7165 item 2, in the same block.

The trap: `LocalID` is declared `// local traffic selector (CIDR)` but the only statement that fills it is spelled `local-identity`, which **in Junos is an identity** — normally an FQDN or DN.

**Two layers, one predicate.** Commit gate rejects (warns on the lenient load path so a persisted config still boots, #1960); render belt drops the value there, so the key is omitted and the tunnel comes up narrow rather than not at all. Both call `config.IsTrafficSelectorShape` — shared rather than re-derived, since two surfaces enforcing one rule from two predicates is the drift `diagcmd.MaxArgLen` exists to prevent (#6904).

---

# 2. Route-based VPNs carried endpoint traffic only (#7171 row 70)

A route-based VPN — `bind-interface` set, `if_id` emitted — with no `traffic-selector` rendered no selector at all. Measured at the **XFRM policy the kernel enforces**, not a status view. Same connection, same `if_id`, two arms:

| rendered | installed policy |
|---|---|
| *(nothing — today)* | `src 10.99.12.1/32 dst 10.99.12.2/32` — the tunnel **endpoints** |
| `0.0.0.0/0` both sides | `src 0.0.0.0/0 dst 0.0.0.0/0` — wildcard |

Transit traffic does not match a /32↔/32 policy, so it never enters the tunnel. Routing decides what enters a route-based tunnel — exactly why Junos defaults an st0-bound proxy ID to `0.0.0.0/0`.

**This corrects the premise the row was filed under.** It asserted an omitted selector becomes `0.0.0.0/0` — a widening, a security problem. The opposite is true: the default is `dynamic`, which is *narrower*, and the failure is an **outage**. Anyone defending against the filed problem would have defended the wrong direction.

**Scope is deliberately narrow.** The default applies only when `if_id > 0`. For a **policy-based** VPN the selector *is* the enforcement boundary, so widening there would be a real widening — that case still renders nothing. An explicit `traffic-selector`, and a selector-shaped `local-identity`, both still win.

Both families are offered (`0.0.0.0/0,::/0`) since xpf is dual-stack and strongSwan narrows during negotiation. **Flagging the choice**: Junos parity alone would be v4-only, and trimming is a one-line change.

**Interop:** this widens what is *negotiated* on already-committed configs, so a peer expecting narrow selectors could fail where it previously succeeded. Weighed and accepted against a tunnel that silently carries nothing.

## PR #8009 — cluster: replace the session-sync handshake with Noise_NNpsk0 (both admission paths) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7163-noise`

Closes #7163

## What this closes

Vector B of #5078. The session-sync authentication proof carried no role, no node
or endpoint identity and no transcript, and the frame-key derivation canonically
SORTED its two nonces, so both directions of a connection derived one key.

- **The two-connection oracle.** An attacker with no PSK opens a second keyed
  connection and relays a proof computed over connection α's nonce onto
  connection β. The nonces differ per connection, so #7152's equal-nonce
  rejection never fires. Both nodes share one PSK, so the oracle can be the PEER
  NODE ITSELF — no per-node nonce bookkeeping can observe it.
- **Self-fencing.** Because `readKey == writeKey`, a frame the victim SENT
  verifies when echoed straight back on the same connection, and the anti-replay
  counter cannot see it (`verifyFrame` compares against that connection's RECEIVE
  counter, independent of its send counter). The worst reflectable frame is
  `syncMsgFence`: empty payload, and on receipt the victim disables all of its own
  redundancy groups.

Both session-sync admission paths now run **Noise_NNpsk0** (`github.com/flynn/noise`
v1.1.0): the connection-setup handshake and the #6628 in-place upgrade of an
established connection.

## Why both paths, and why the upgrade path could not just be deleted

`sync_auth_upgrade.go` called the same two defective primitives. Converting only
the connect handshake would have left a second admission path with the identical
oracle — and it becomes the one an attacker picks, because it is the one that
still accepts. A partial fix here is not a smaller fix; it closes the door an
attacker will not use.

Deleting the upgrade path instead was not available either. #6628 exists so a
committed key reaches a READ-ONLY secondary, where `EnterConfigureSession`
returns `ErrClusterReadOnly` and config-sync over the established connection is
that node's only writer.

## Where each binding comes from

- **Role** — structural in the pattern. Connect: the TCP *dialer* is the
  initiator. Upgrade: the *lower node id* is. Neither is a field the peer can
  assert; #6628 decided it by comparing the two nonces, which made role a
  function of a peer-supplied value feeding our own key derivation — the same
  mistake vector B exploited.
- **Transcript** — the handshake hash covers every message AND the prologue.
- **Identity** — construction version, a PHASE byte (connect vs upgrade), cluster
  id, ROLE-ORDERED node ids and the fabric index, all inside that hash.
- **Direction** — `Split()` returns two CipherStates. This is the specific
  replacement for the canonical nonce sort.

## PR #8010 — config: validate prefix-list ENTRIES a firewall filter references (#7273) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7273-prefix-list-entry-validation`

Closes #7273

## The gap, verified at master

#6463 closed the partial-list narrowing on the userspace filter wire by marking a term `AddressUnrepresentable` when it carries a malformed address token. That marker is derived from `term.UnknownAddresses`, which is populated from **literal** `from source-address` / `destination-address` tokens only.

A malformed entry arriving by prefix-list **reference** has a different provenance and was covered by neither half:

| validator | what it checks |
|---|---|
| `validateFilterAddressLiteralsStrict` (#3433) | the literals |
| `validateFirewallPrefixListReferencesStrict` | that the name **resolves** — not that its entries **parse** |

So nothing looked at `PrefixList.Prefixes`. The term's `UnknownAddresses` stayed empty, `AddressUnrepresentable` stayed false, and the resolver contributed only the entries that happened to parse: **a term scoped to five prefixes with one typo silently narrowed to four** — fail-open or fail-closed depending on the action, and invisible either way.

## Scope is deliberately the REFERENCED lists

This gate belongs to the firewall family. A prefix-list used only by routing policy has its own consumers and its own tolerance, and rejecting a commit here for an entry no filter reads would change behaviour for configurations this issue is not about. The routing-side equivalent is a separate question and is **not** answered here.

**A test pins that boundary**, and it is the row that distinguishes this implementation from a validate-everything one.

Strict on commit/commit-check, lenient warn on load/peer-sync via `lenientFirewallRefs`, mirroring the reference gate it sits beside so an already-persisted or peer-synced config still boots.

## Fixtures

The malformed-entry fixture puts the bad prefix in the **middle** of three. A list whose only entry is malformed would also be caught by an implementation that rejects any unparseable list, or one that rejects a list resolving to nothing — the partial list is what distinguishes *silent narrowing* from *empty*. A v6 twin exists because the two families are separate maps.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| M1 — neuter the validator | 2 named FAILs |
| M2 — remove the gate call (wiring) | 3 named FAILs, incl. the pre-existing `TestEveryStrictCommitGateIsWired` |
| M3 — widen scope to every prefix-list | 2 named FAILs, incl. the boundary test |

**M3 is worth a note.** My first attempt at it inserted the widening *inside* the referenced-list loop — which never runs when nothing is referenced, so the mutation could not reach the case the boundary test exists for, and the test stayed green for a reason unrelated to its property. Re-run with the widening placed before that loop, it reds correctly. A mutation that does not exercise the property proves nothing about the guard.

## PR #8011 — login class: enforce deny-commands on the operational CLI path (#7172 cut 3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut3-operational-enforcement`

Cut 3 of #7172. **DENY ONLY**, deliberately — the scoping is the substance of this cut, not a limitation of it.

## Why not allow too: the mirror image of the gate-retirement window

The two leaves are in **opposite states** today:

| leaf | today |
|---|---|
| `deny-commands` | **cannot commit at all** — #6838's `validateLoginClassDenyStrict` rejects it |
| `allow-commands` | **commits fine and is deliberately inert** — `compiler_system.go:1241` files it under "Neutral not-enforced knobs" and the advisory says so |

**An allow regex is an allowlist.** Enforcing it here would mean a live class carrying

```
set system login class ops permissions all
set system login class ops allow-commands "show interfaces"
```

abruptly loses `show version`, `request support information` and `configure` **on upgrade** — a restriction its author was explicitly *told* was inert.

That is the mirror image of the window the gate's late retirement exists to prevent. Previously-**rejected** configs must not commit while enforcement is partial; equally, previously-**inert** configs must not become **enforced** while it is partial. Allow lands in cut 6 with the retirement, so both leaves go live in one step with one release note and no intermediate build surprises anyone.

## The chokepoint is `dispatchOperational`, not `dispatch()`

`dispatch()` looks like the entry — it holds the untouched line, pipe included. But **`case "run"` in `dispatchConfig` calls `dispatchOperational` directly**, so a gate at `dispatch()` would leave `run request system reboot` ungated for anyone who can enter config mode — which, until cut 4 exists, is anyone with `configure`. All five entry paths converge at `dispatchOperational`.

Same class as the two `extractPipe` copies from cut 1: the obvious place is not the only place.

## The pipe is part of the command

Junos matches the pipe, and the security argument is independent of parity: `show configuration | save /tmp/x` writes a file, `| display set` reformats output a deny may be withholding. `cliterm.SplitPipe` strips the suffix upstream, so `dispatchWithPipe` hands it back through a field set and cleared around its single recursive dispatch.

## Fail-closed, and scoped

A class whose regex does not compile **denies**; a command that cannot be canonicalized **denies** — "cannot resolve" is not "does not match". Both are **scoped to classes that configured regexes**, so an unrestricted user's ambiguous command still gets its ordinary error rather than a permission denial. Otherwise a typo reports as an authorization failure and operators learn to distrust the message.

## The gate is unreachable end-to-end today, and that shaped the tests

No supported path puts a `deny-commands` class into `ActiveConfig`: strict commit rejects it, and `Store.Load` leaves `ActiveConfig` nil. So a test driving this through a committed config **cannot exist yet**. The decision is split into store-free halves (`loginRegexesFrom`, `checkCommandRegexWith`, `evaluateCommandRegex`) pinned directly. Writing an end-to-end-*looking* test that bypassed commit would have exercised a path no operator can reach.

That reachability fact is also what makes it safe to land now.

## Mutation matrix

All build-clean; `collected == reported == 10` on every cell — the matrix reports **collected** counts because a mutation that *panics* produces neither a FAIL nor a compile error and would otherwise score as an escape.

## PR #8012 — Keep operator-typed comments verbatim in the audit journal (#7171) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-29)

Branch: `fix/7171-comment-trim`

`strings.Trim(desc, "\"'")` strips **any** leading or trailing character in the cutset, balanced or not — so a commit comment ending in a legitimate apostrophe (`fix for users'`) was recorded in the **audit journal** as `fix for users`. An audit record that silently mutates what the operator typed is weaker evidence than one that does not. The property at stake is that the journal is verbatim, not how many characters were lost.

The trim is **not deleted** — it peels the syntactic quotes the CLI tokenizer leaves behind, which is a real need. `Trim` with a cutset is just the wrong tool for "remove surrounding quotes".

## The correct helper already existed

`stripSurroundingQuotes`, written for the #4005 pcap filter, peels exactly one matched pair and has always been right. **Two other call sites in the same package reached for `strings.Trim` instead.** So this is a consolidation, not a new implementation: the helper moves to its own file with a doc covering all three callers, and its regression test moves with it (every #4005 case preserved verbatim — a helper that moves must take its test along, or the test keeps passing while guarding code that no longer lives there).

The issue names **one** site. There are **two**: the commit comment, and the annotate comment in `cli_dispatch.go`, which persists into the stored configuration.

## Two attempts at the guard escaped their own mutation

The second is the instructive one.

1. The first asserted `stripSurroundingQuotes` twice and called itself an anti-drift cell. Reverting **both** call sites to `strings.Trim` produced **zero failures across 968 tests** — a test that calls the helper directly never reaches the site that calls it.
2. The second extracted `commitCommentFromArgs` / `annotateCommentFromLine` so the sites were named units, and asserted those. Reverting the call site to bypass the extracted function **still produced zero failures.** Extracting a function does not bind a call site's use of it; it moves the same tautology one level down.

Only entering through the real path closes it. The commit test drives `handleCommit` against a live store and reads the persisted `JournalEntry.Detail` — the audit journal itself. The annotate test drives `dispatchConfig` and reads the comment back out of the rendered candidate.

**The annotate site needed a different discriminator**, worth recording: its cutset was `"` only, so a trailing apostrophe survives either implementation and cannot tell them apart. An *unterminated* leading quote can — the cutset strips it, the matched pair keeps it.

## Mutation matrix

Full-suite per cell, edit confirmed applied, build verified before the result was believed.

| cell | applied | named FAIL | ran | localises to |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 commit site → Trim cutset | 2 | 4 | 979 | |
| T1b commit site → no strip at all | 2 | 3 | 979 | |
| T2 annotate site → Trim cutset | 6 | 2 | 983 | unterminated-quote case |
| T3 helper strips unconditionally | 2 | 10 | 979 | mismatched-pair cases |
| T4 helper strips all layers | 2 | 7 | 979 | doubled-quote cases |
| control | — | green | | |

## Behaviour note

An unterminated leading quote is deliberately **kept** rather than closed for the operator — preserving it is the same verbatim property as the apostrophe case.

## PR #8013 — cluster: bind where #7163's directional keys are INSTALLED, not just derived [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7163-wrapsyncconn-guard`

Follow-up to #8009 (#7163). **Test-only — no production code changes, no behaviour changes.**

## The gap

#7163's tests bind where the directional keys are **derived**: `performSyncHandshake`
returns two independent keys from `Split()`, and the #6628 in-place upgrade installs
each at its own frame boundary. Nothing bound the connect path's **hand-off** — the two
assignments in `wrapSyncConn` that copy those derived keys onto the `authConn` the frame
layer actually uses.

Found by mutation on the merged tree (`26bf7ea1a`). Changing

```go
ac.writeKey = keys.writeKey   →   ac.writeKey = keys.readKey
```

— the pre-#7163 undirected shape, at the *assignment* site rather than the derivation
site — leaves both `pkg/cluster` and `pkg/daemon` **green, `RC=0`, zero named failures**.

## Why it escaped

Exactly one test called `wrapSyncConn`, and it asserted `wrapped.authed()`. `authed()` is
`readAuthed() && writeAuthed()` — i.e. both keys **non-empty**. An existence check
standing in for a value check passes for every wrong value that is still a value.

## Why it is worth a guard rather than a note

That mutation does not merely produce a wrong key. It makes `readKey == writeKey` on a
connect-authenticated connection, which is precisely the vector-B **self-fencing
primitive** #7163 exists to remove: a frame the node SENT verifies when echoed straight
back at it, and the anti-replay watermark cannot see it because it tracks the RECEIVE
counter, independent of the send counter. The worst reflectable frame is `syncMsgFence` —
empty payload, and on receipt the victim disables every redundancy group it owns.

The cluster smoke covers this end to end (`fw1 has 20 synced sessions` could not happen if
the assignment were wrong). But the smoke is not CI, so a manual cluster run was the only
thing standing between that regression and a merge.

## What the tests assert

`TestWrapSyncConnInstallsKeysDirectionally7163` asserts the **consequence**, not the
assignment: the self-echo is REFUSED, with a positive control that the same frame verifies
at the peer — so the refusal means "wrong direction" rather than "sealing is broken".

That shape is load-bearing rather than stylistic. The obvious guard —
`assert writeKey != readKey` — would be satisfied by the **swapped-directions** mutation,
which leaves two distinct, non-empty, different keys while every frame on the connection
fails verification. That is the same trap as the `authed()` check one level down: a check
that cannot distinguish correct from broken.

## PR #8014 — Report a session-pair mirror that stranded a reverse in the helper (#7179) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7179-error-visibility`

`mirrorSessionPairV4`/`V6` ended in `_ = m.syncSessionPairLocked(reqs...)`. The mirror is best-effort by design and its IPC error is correctly **not** propagated — the periodic session sync reconciles a transient miss — but discarding the whole result also discarded the distinction between a pair the helper **never applied** and one it **half applied**. The first self-heals; the second leaves residue no later transmit necessarily corrects. #7179 invariant 7.

This is the part of #7179 that survived its premise check. The rest is [falsified on the issue](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7179#issuecomment-5465665636).

## The direction that strands state is the opposite of the filed one

Measured against a live `Coordinator`, printed rather than asserted:

```
forward-only import:  forward=true  reverse=true  entries=2
reverse-only import:  forward=false reverse=true  entries=1
forward delete:       forward=false reverse=false entries=0
```

- A forward that **succeeds** never leaves a half pair — the helper synthesizes and publishes the reverse companion itself on every non-reverse import, so one forward upsert yields **two** entries.
- A forward that fails at the **transport** layer aborts the batch (`errSessionHelperUnreachable`), so the reverse is never sent.
- The only way to publish a lone reverse is a forward the helper actively **refuses** — an application error such as a capacity rejection — after which the batch continues and the explicit reverse lands alone.

Hence the asymmetric classifier. `sendSessionSyncBatch` now returns per-half outcomes instead of a bare first error, `orphanedReverse` names that one shape, and both mirror sites report it with a counter and a Warn. Everything else is unchanged: the error is still not propagated, and a wholly-failed pair is still only the existing per-request Debug — warning on it would fire on every transient hiccup and bury the case that matters.

## Two cells escaped, and both found dead code I had just written

- Removing the `r.aborted` guard changed **no** test result. It is unreachable by construction: an abort breaks the batch at the forward, so the reverse is never sent and cannot appear in `applied`.
- `i > 0` when scanning applied indices: if the forward failed it is in `failed`, so it cannot also be in `applied`. Mutating to `i >= 0` changed nothing.

Both read as careful; neither could differ. Both are gone — the classifier is now `forwardFailed && len(r.applied) > 0` — and the reasoning is recorded at each site so they are not reintroduced as defensiveness.

## Mutation matrix

Full-suite per cell, edit confirmed applied, build verified before the result was believed.

| cell | applied | named FAIL | ran |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 wiring removed (V4) | 2 | 1 | 2002 |
| E8 wiring removed (V6) | 2 | 1 | 2003 |
| E2 report ANY error, not orphan | 2 | 2 | 2002 |
| E5 batch stops recording applied | 2 | 1 | 2002 |
| E7 classifier ignores applied set | 2 | 4 | 2002 |
| E4c classifier forces forwardFailed | 2 | 4 | 2002 |
| control | — | green | |

**V4 and V6 are bound separately** — E1 reds only the V4 test, E8 only the V6 one. A fix wired into one call site and not the other is the exact asymmetry this campaign keeps finding (the V6 half of the HA delta-drop logging was silent for precisely that reason), and a single-family test cannot see it.

**E2 is the over-report cell** and reds both negative controls: the wholly-refused pair, and the forward-applied/reverse-refused pair that is a *complete* pair rather than a stranded half.

## PR #8016 — Refuse to append the audit journal through a symlink or into a FIFO [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7176-journal-nofollow`

Refs #7176 (C179-061). Third of the security tier.

## The defect

The journal append opened with `os.O_APPEND|os.O_CREATE|os.O_RDWR` and **no
`O_NOFOLLOW`**, and its only post-open `Stat` read `fi.Size()` for the torn-tail
check — **never `Mode().IsRegular()`**. So the append followed a symlink planted
at the journal path, or wrote into a FIFO/device planted there directly.

**The framing that makes this worth fixing rather than tolerating:** this package
*already* refuses to **chmod** through a symlinked segment — `chmodOwnerOnly`
does `Lstat`, rejects `ModeSymlink`, and requires `IsRegular`. The convention
exists here; the append site just did not follow it. And the audit journal is the
record an operator reads to reconstruct what happened, so writing it into someone
else's file is a worse outcome than the permission gap that convention was
written for.

## Both guards, because neither subsumes the other

- **`O_NOFOLLOW`** refuses when the **final** path component is a symlink, and
  the kernel decides it at open time — no TOCTOU window, unlike
  `Lstat`-then-open.
- `O_NOFOLLOW` happily opens a **FIFO**, device or socket planted directly at the
  path; those are not symlinks. A FIFO is the worst of them: with `O_RDWR` the
  open **succeeds**, the writes land in the pipe buffer, and the daemon
  **blocks** once it fills.

The second check is `f.Stat()` on the open **descriptor**, not `os.Stat(j.path)`
— a path-based stat would be checking a different object from the one just
opened.

**Cost to a legitimate deployment:** an operator who symlinks the journal *file*
now gets a clear error instead of silent indirection. Symlinking the journal
*directory* still works — `O_NOFOLLOW` constrains only the final component.

## Validation

`go test -count=1 ./...` — rc=0, **0 named FAIL**, 69 packages.

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| drop `O_NOFOLLOW` alone | **symlink cell only** |
| drop the regular-file check alone | **FIFO cell only** |
| faithful revert of both | both refusals, control still passes |

Each guard is proven **independently** rather than as a pair, which is the claim
worth holding: a reviewer can otherwise reasonably ask why two checks are needed.

The control cell (a plain regular file still appends) is what stops an open that
refused *everything* from satisfying the two refusals. And the symlink cell

## PR #8017 — api: take a sessionWalkLimiter slot in the metrics session walk (#8001) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/8001-metrics-session-walk-limiter`

Closes #8001

`walkSessionGauges` was the only full-table session walk in `pkg/api` that took no `sessionWalkLimiter` slot. Six siblings do — `sessions.go` ×5 and `nat.go` ×1.

## Why the asymmetry mattered more than the absence

The limiter's guarantee was not the guarantee anyone reading it would assume. Someone reasoning *"full-table walks are bounded, the limiter enforces it"* was **correct about every call site but this one**, and nothing at this site said otherwise.

And it is the worst site to have exempt. Every other walk is driven by an operator request; this one is driven by a **Prometheus scraper on a fixed interval**, so it is the least likely to be noticed under load and the most likely to overlap with something else.

## The fix needs no new error handling

`Acquire()` is **non-blocking** — `ErrBusy` immediately at the cap — so a scrape can never hang behind an operator's session scan. Returning the error takes the caller's **existing** failure path: the cached snapshot and its TTL are left untouched so the next scrape retries, and `scrape_ok` goes to 0. That is the #3345 convention — skip the sample rather than report a misleading one — reached without adding anything.

## The test counts the WALK, not the error

*"Admission refused before walking"* and *"walked, then failed"* are **identical from the return value**, and only one of them bounds the work. So the assertion that matters is that `IterateSessions` was never entered — a counting fake, not an error check.

The firing input is named before the assertion: the limiter saturated by other holders. A negative control on an idle limiter stops an always-`ErrBusy` implementation from passing, and the saturation loop fails loudly if it cannot acquire even one slot, so a cell that measures nothing reports as such rather than passing.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| M1 — remove the acquisition entirely | named FAIL, 1031 collected |
| M2 — acquire but ignore `ErrBusy` and walk anyway | named FAIL, 1031 collected |

M2 is the one worth having: an implementation that consults the limiter and then proceeds regardless *looks* gated at the call site and bounds nothing.

## Validation

`go test -count=1 ./...` — **69 packages, 0 FAIL**.

## PR #8019 — userspace-dp: make the degraded synced-import observable, and bind the sync_session contention (#7209) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7209-observability-and-contention-test`

Two design-independent pieces of #7209, ahead of the published-view change itself. **No production behaviour changes beyond adding one counter.**

Splitting them out deliberately: both are valuable whether or not the published-view fix lands, and having item 4's acceptance criterion in tree **first** is what stops that change's correctness resting on a reading of the lock graph — which is what failed on #7095.

## 1. The degraded synced-import is now observable (#7209 requirement 2)

When a peer-synced import's `(from_zone, to_zone)` pair does not resolve locally, the source-NAT reservation skips #6211's zone narrowing and falls back to the pre-#6211 path — and nothing anywhere says so.

**Severity, driven from the implementation rather than inferred from a comment: LESS NARROW, not incorrect.**

- The translated address and port come off the HA wire and are **never recomputed**, so nothing is mistranslated.
- PASS 2 only books against a rule whose pool **actually owns** that address (`!rule.pool_mode` skipped, membership checked).
- With a single pool-mode owner the two passes agree **exactly**.
- Divergence needs ≥2 pool-mode rules whose pools both contain the address in separate allocators. In-tree invariant: *"Pass 1 can only move a reservation to a better-justified allocator, never remove one."*
- Corroborated independently by the existing `synced_reservation_double_upsert_across_zone_outcomes_frees_both_6211`, which shows the flip's cost is a redundant reservation #6211's teardown already frees.

So a counter suffices — no defer design.

**Wired the full distance, not allowlisted.** `UNSURFACED`'s own doc says adding to it *"means deciding NOT to show it to an operator; prefer wiring it"*, so allowlisting would have answered an observability requirement with the thing the list warns against. `AtomicU64` → `Coordinator::*_total()` → **populate into `ProcessStatus`** (the step #6641's census exists to bind) → Rust `ProcessStatus` field → Go decode → Prometheus `Desc`/`Describe`/`Collect`.

**Counted at the coordinator's once-per-import reservation, not the worker-side twin.** That one runs on *every* worker for the same entry, so counting there would multiply one degraded import by the worker count and make the metric a function of `--workers`.

**Counted only when the unresolved pair actually cost something** — `zones.is_none() && !is_reverse && rewrite_src.is_some()`. The reservation early-returns for a reverse session and for one with no source-NAT rewrite, so for those the zone pair is never consulted and nothing is degraded. Without this the metric would climb steadily on a healthy cluster until operators learned to ignore it.

**The HELP text says what is LOST, and when nonzero is NORMAL** — an in-flight config apply and a standby's first sync both produce it; sustained growth on a settled config means zone drift. A counter an operator cannot interpret is barely better than silence.

## 2. The contention is bound (#7209 item 4)

The issue asks for *"`sync_session` served while `apply_snapshot` reconciles"*. **That test cannot be built as worded.** In this suite the Coordinator is `Coordinator::new()` with no NICs, so reconcile never reaches the 10 s worker-readiness barrier — a timing test built on it would pass whether or not `sync_session` takes the global lock. A fixture that cannot fail.

This holds the `ServerState` mutex **directly** on another thread instead. That binds the *property* — "`sync_session` does not queue behind a `ServerState` lock holder" — rather than one instance of a slow holder; it is deterministic; and it covers all four blocking operations the issue enumerates at once, since they all reach `sync_session` through that one mutex.

`#[ignore]`d and **verified red**, not assumed: `waited 5.0s behind a thread holding the global ServerState mutex`, with `running 1 test` / `1 failed` confirming it *ran* rather than build-broke. Then tightened — the 5 s was my own holder's timeout, released only after the measured request returned, a **circular wait**. The holder is now independently bounded (`HOLD_MS = 1200` against a 500 ms bar), so the red costs 1.2 s and both numbers are named constants.

## Validation

- `cargo test --bins -- --test-threads=1` green (4844 passed) · `go test -count=1 ./...` green, gated on the Rust **terminator and a zero named-failure count**, never on rc alone.
- **Mutation matrix 4/4 RED, tree CLEAN**, run from a committed tree:

| cell | reds | caught by |
|---|---|---|
| counter never bumped | RED(1) | the counter test |
| populate line deleted | RED(1) | #6641 wiring census |
| bumped unconditionally | RED(1) | the counter test |
| precision guard dropped | RED(1) | the counter test |

The discrimination matters: the populate wiring and the bump semantics are guarded by **different** tests, so neither is doing the other's job.

- The counter test carries three legs, because a counter has two ways to be useless and only one is "never fires": unresolved-with-NAT counts, resolvable does not, unresolved-without-NAT does not. Each leg asserts the zone pair's actual resolution state **first**, so a drifting fixture fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. All three register a worker, because `upsert_synced_session` skips the whole reservation when none exists — without one the legs pass by executing nothing, which is how the first draft failed.
- The wire golden gained exactly one key — **1 added, 0 removed, 0 values changed, value zero** — classified *before* regenerating, because a golden regenerated blind greens the suite whether the change was additive or destructive.

## PR #8020 — vrrp: give TestSyncHold_RearmStopsPreviousTimer real margins (#8018) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/8018-vrrp-synchold-timing`

Closes #8018

The test sampled five wall-clock windows at roughly **2x** margin each, and one at **1.25x**. It reds under concurrent-suite load — in `pkg/vrrp`, on changes that cannot reach it, which reads as an HA regression and costs whoever hits it a bisect. A lane lost a run to it today.

## The ratios are the test, not the values

| constant | value | why |
|---|---|---|
| `firstHold` | 100ms | the timer the re-arm must **stop** |
| `rearmHold` | 1500ms | its replacement; must outlast `waitPastFirst` |
| `preRearm` | 10ms | must land **inside** `firstHold` — 10x margin, was 2x |
| `waitPastFirst` | 400ms | must **exceed** `firstHold` or "still held" passes vacuously — 4x past, 3.75x short of `rearmHold` |

## The structural change is the asymmetry between the halves

**"Still held" is a NEGATIVE assertion** — the first timer must not have fired — and absence is only observable by waiting the window out. That half keeps a fixed sleep and buys its safety with margin; there is no polling shape for it.

**"Released" is POSITIVE**, so it now polls against a 6s deadline instead of sampling at a fixed instant. That **removes** the window rather than widening it, which is strictly better than the 1.25x it had.

And the second half is the **control** for the first: it proves the timer mechanism fires at all, so "still held" earlier means the first timer was *stopped* rather than that nothing was ever armed. Without it the first half passes against a manager that never arms anything.

## The property is still bound

Deleting the `Stop()` in `SetSyncHold` reds the test by name at **0.41s** — the first timer firing inside `waitPastFirst`, which is exactly the defect.

Worth noting how that cell was scoped: there are **three textually identical** `m.syncHoldTimer.Stop()` blocks (lines 294, 361, 398). My first mutation asserted its anchor was unique, the assertion fired with count 2, and nothing was edited — so the resulting `FAIL=0` measured nothing. Re-scoped to line 361 by number, it reds correctly.

## Validation

- 5 consecutive runs green
- **3 concurrent full-package runs** green — the condition that produced the original red

## PR #8021 — Write a tombstone marker into a skipped rollback slot [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7176-rollback-tombstone`

Refs #7176 (C179-056). Last of the security tier — completes Batch B.

## The defect, confirmed by probing master rather than by reading

A tombstoned history position left its on-disk slot **untouched**, so the file
kept the **previous generation's** config text. History is most-recent-first and
shifts on every commit, so those bytes then sat under a different index — and on
the next boot `loadRollbackHistory` parsed them as a healthy slot, losing the
tombstone. `rollback N` returned another generation's config with nothing in the
load path able to notice.

Corrupt slot 2 → tombstone at position 1 → commit shifts it to position 2 →
reload:

```
post-commit, in memory:  pos 2 = tombstone     <- runtime correctly refuses
after reload from disk:  pos 2 = HEALTHY       <- another generation's config
```

At runtime **#4810 works exactly as designed** — `rollbackEntry()` refuses the
tombstone. The defect materialises only **across a boot**, which is precisely why
nothing tested it: the suite had no reload cell at all. That reload is the test
that would have caught this, and it is now
`TestRollbackTombstoneSurvivesReload_7176`.

## The marker's content is the whole safety property

Choosing it needed a measurement, not an assumption. The obvious marker is a bare
`# xpf-rollback-tombstone` comment. **Measured, that parses with zero errors into
an empty config** — so a reader predating this change would offer the slot as a
healthy *empty* configuration and `rollback N` would **wipe the config** instead
of returning the wrong generation. The fix making the bug strictly worse.

The marker therefore ends in a stray `}`, which guarantees a parse error. An
older reader tombstones it through the **existing** corrupt-file branch — the
correct outcome there. So it **degrades correctly on every reader**, and this
change needs no format negotiation and no compat gate, unlike C179-053 where the
compat question was real.

## The loader's prefix check is diagnostic, not a correctness guard

The mutation matrix is how I know: **deleting it changes no outcome**, because
the parse error already routes the slot to the corrupt-file branch. What it buys
is the log — an operator seeing `corrupt rollback file` every boot cannot tell a
recorded tombstone from a slot that needs investigating.

The code comment now says that, rather than the "load-bearing" claim I first
wrote, and names the cell that *does* carry the safety. Reported rather than
papered over.

## PR #8022 — Withhold lifeline-shared addresses from real host-inbound drop sets (#7284) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Branch: `explore/7284`

A management address shared onto a second interface was denied by the **real** host-inbound table on an ordinary healthy commit, and the #5566 conntrack reconcile tore down the operator's **established** session with it. No failed install, no fence, no degraded boot.

The lifeline exclusion in the real table was an **interface** exclusion — it answers *"is the snapshot I am walking a lifeline"*, while a host-inbound drop carries no `iifname` (#3718) and poses a different question: *"is this address also reachable as a management address"*. The **fence** has partitioned per address **value** since #6492. The two disagreed, and that divergence is the defect.

## Reproduced at master before fixing

Driving the real builders:

```
(a) zone that ADMITS ssh   view svc=[ssh]  v4=[192.0.2.1]   protected
(b) zone with NO stanza    view svc=[]     v4=[192.0.2.1]   pure drop
(c) UNZONED interface      unzonedV4=[192.0.2.1]            pure drop
    fence (all cases)      v4=[]                            withheld
```

Case (c) only reproduces when the address is **not** also on a zoned interface — `BuildUnzonedHostInboundAddrs` subtracts anything already in a zone view, so a fixture that puts the address everywhere yields an empty unzoned set and proves nothing. That is why the issue's own evidence shows `views=1`.

## Both halves move together — structurally, not as a second fix

`daemon_nft.go` builds **one** `views`/`unzonedV4`/`unzonedV6` triple and passes it to `toNftHostInboundSpec` (the rules) **and** `flushDeniedHostInboundConntrack` (the #5566 reconcile). Withholding at the builders removes the address from the covered set as well as the chain.

Fixing only the rule emission would have stopped *new* management connections being dropped and still killed the operator's *current* session on the next apply — so this is asserted directly rather than trusted: the daemon-side test builds the real views and checks the flush filter's covered set.

## Scoped to empty-admit views, so case (a) is pinned

A view that admits something emits its `accept` before the catch-all drop, so management already survives there and the drop still expresses policy for every *other* service on that address. Withholding it would delete the accept and the deny together, leaving every host service reachable on it — a wider hole than the lockout being fixed.

## This is a widening of a drop set, deliberately

Rows (b) and (c) previously denied the shared address and no longer do. #6492 blessed the same trade for the fence. **The bound is that only an address actually on a lifeline is withheld**, so the #3405 default-deny and the #4420 HI-2 unzoned fail-open are intact for every other address — and that boundary is what the negative controls hold.

The fence and the real table now derive the lifeline address set from **one** walk (`forEachFirewallLocalAddr`), so they cannot drift apart again in the way that produced this bug. The extraction was verified inert before any behaviour change.

Full-suite across both packages, edit confirmed applied, build verified before the result was believed.

| H1 unzoned subtraction removed | 4 | 2 | unzoned test **and the flush test** |
| H2 empty-admit subtraction removed | 5 | 1 | no-stanza test only |

| H4b every iface treated as lifeline | 2 | **22** | both negative controls + 20 pre-existing |

| control | — | green | |

**H1** reds the unzoned test *and* the flush test — the two-halves claim measured rather than argued. **H3** reds the case-(a) pin *and* `TestFenceWithholdsLifelineSharedAddress6492`: over-reaching breaks already-guarded behaviour. **H4b** reds 22 tests — a blanket hole, and the suite says so loudly.

## PR #8023 — host-inbound: withhold lifeline-shared addresses from the real drop sets (#7284) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

## The defect

A management address shared onto an **unzoned** interface, or onto a zone with **no `host-inbound-traffic` stanza**, is denied by the **real** host-inbound table. Both topologies produce a drop with **no accept**, and because the address sits in the #5566 covered set with an empty admit set, `flushDeniedHostInboundConntrack` also tears down the **established** session — an operator's live SSH — on the next successful apply.

The fence already withheld lifeline-shared addresses (#6492). The real-table builders checked the lifeline by **snapshot** rather than by address **value**, so an address on `fxp0.0` *and* another interface was skipped only while walking the lifeline's own snapshot.

## Two things make this narrower than the fence's rule

**The subtraction is scoped to EMPTY-ADMIT views.** A blanket subtraction would strip case (a) — a zone that admits ssh — taking its accept away with its drop and leaving **every host service reachable on a shared management address**. That is a *wider* hole than the lockout it fixes. A view that admits something already protects management with its accept and still expresses policy for every other service; an empty-admit view has no policy to preserve, only a lockout.

**The covered set follows structurally, not by a second fix.** `daemon_nft.go` builds one views/unzoned triple and hands it to *both* `toNftHostInboundSpec` and `flushDeniedHostInboundConntrack`, so withholding at the builders removes the address from both. Measured rather than argued — the daemon-side test builds the real views and asserts the flush filter's covered set directly.

## PR #8024 — Record measured metadata alignment invariant (#7176 C179-019) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7176-meta-align`

Addresses row **C179-019** of #7176. Does **not** close #7176 — the cohort has other live rows.

## The row

The XDP shim writes `UserspaceDpMeta` through a `*mut UserspaceDpMeta` (align 8, from `config_generation: u64`) with a plain aligned store. The userspace consumer reads the same bytes back with `ptr::read_unaligned` and carries a comment explicitly disclaiming any alignment guarantee. The two sides have contradicted each other on paper for as long as both have existed.

## Disposition: record the measured invariant, do not pay to make it explicit

Both code changes were tried and both are rejected on evidence, not preference.

**`write_unaligned` is not free.** It was implemented and measured rather than estimated. The BPF backend lowers it to a byte-wise copy:

| | baseline | `write_unaligned` | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.xdp` section | 48,672 B | 49,824 B | +1,152 |
| instructions | 5,882 | 6,027 | +145 |
| **#1864 headroom** | **19.86%** | **18.73%** | **−1.13 pt** (floor 15.0%) |

That is roughly a quarter of the remaining margin above a hard gate, drawn from a budget every future dataplane change also draws from.

**A runtime alignment check is not implementable at all.** The verifier rejects it:

```
R1 bitwise operator &= on pointer prohibited
```

Both a direct mask and a volatile stack round-trip intended to launder the pointer into a scalar hit the same rejection, and the message names the *operation class* rather than the expression. A BPF program cannot observe a packet pointer's alignment, so neither an in-band probe nor a check-and-refuse variant exists. This is recorded at the site so the option is not re-proposed.

## What was measured

The store's alignment reduces to an identity, with the inputs measured rather than reasoned about:

```
meta_ptr        == xdp->data - size_of::<UserspaceDpMeta>()
size_of == 96, align_of == 8, and 96 % 8 == 0
=> meta_ptr % 8 == xdp->data % 8
```

So the only variable is the driver's `xdp->data` — a kernel property, not an xpf one. Measured out-of-band (zero hot-path cost) with a kprobe on `bpf_xdp_adjust_meta` reading `xdp_buff->data`, at an offset verified against the target's own `include/net/xdp.h` because that kernel ships no BTF:

```
@data_mod8[0]: 5989142
@total:        5989142
```

**5,989,142 samples on the shipped target (mlx5_core VF, AF_XDP native, kernel 7.0.0-rc7+), every one 8-aligned, none in buckets 1–7.** `@total` is retained deliberately: without it, "the kprobe never fired" and "never misaligned" render as the same empty picture.

**Scope, stated rather than hedged:** the histogram was not broken down by ingress path and no fabric traffic was deliberately driven, so the generic-XDP fabric path is unrepresented or under-represented rather than proven clean. Its buffers come from an skb rather than a page-aligned frame, which is the one surface where the answer could differ.

## PR #8025 — Poll the debounce window instead of sampling it at a fixed instant (#7969) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7969-debounce`

`TestDebounceCoalescing` slept a fixed 40ms over a 20ms debounce and read the counter once. Under CPU contention the debounce goroutine had not been scheduled inside that 20ms margin, the counter was still 0, and the test failed on its **lower** bound.

## Reproduced, not assumed

| harness | result |
|---|---|
| default parallelism, 3× oversubscription | 0 / 12 — does not reproduce |
| `GOMAXPROCS=1`, pinned to a core, 4× oversubscription | **2 / 40 failed**, both the lower bound, exact reported message |
| same harness, after this change | **0 / 100** |

That is why it presents as a rare flake: it needs the engine's goroutine to be competing for a single P.

## The lower bound is a setup guard, not the assertion

The property under test is coalescing — the `> 2` bound. `>= 1` only establishes that the sample was taken late enough for anything to have happened. Its old message, *"no actuation after debounce window"*, read as a coalescing failure and sends whoever hits it looking for a defect in the engine. It now names itself as a setup guard, reports the window, and says the coalescing bound was never exercised.

## Why the deadline stays inside the throttle window

This is the case where "poll with a generous deadline" is the **wrong** instinct. The upper bound is scoped to **one** throttle window, so waiting longer admits a second legitimate actuation and breaks the assertion rather than stabilising it. 50ms gives the setup guard 30ms of margin over the debounce (the old fixed sample had 20ms) while staying 10ms below the 60ms throttle.

Polling the whole window also makes the real assertion **stronger** than the single sample it replaces: coalescing is violated the moment a third actuation appears, and one late read could miss a third that came and went. The bound is now checked continuously.

## The second half is deliberately left alone

Its assertion is an upper bound, and every way the machine can misbehave produces *fewer* actuations, not more — the throttle bounds the count regardless of timing. There is no sample to stabilise. That reasoning is now recorded in the test so the next reader does not "fix" it too.

## Two premise corrections

Neither changes this fix; both change what should be done next.

**The clock seam already exists.** The issue's option (2) says there is *"no injected `now`/clock in `pkg/ipmon/ipmon.go`"*. There is — `now func() time.Time` at `ipmon.go:212` — and the test file already has a `fakeClock` and a `newTestEngine` helper that installs it. The tests using that helper are the deterministic ones. `TestDebounceCoalescing` uses real time because it exercises the real timer path end to end, so converting it is a scope decision about what the test covers, not the cleanup the issue implies.

**The coalescing bound is weaker than it looks.** Disabling the debounce entirely (`>= e.debounce` → `>= 0`) does **not** fail this test; only the second half's sustained-flap bound reds under that or a throttle break. The reason is structural — actuation is driven by a dirty flag, and one actuation covers every pending transition regardless of how many arrived, so the storm coalesces by design rather than by the debounce window. The `<= 2` bound cannot distinguish "coalescing works" from "multiple actuations are unreachable here". Pre-existing and out of scope, but worth knowing before trusting it.

## Validation

`pkg/ipmon` passes with `-count=1`; `go build ./...` clean. 0/100 under the harness that produced 2/40 before. Scope check: one file, 53 insertions / 6 deletions, no file with zero insertions.

Closes #7969

## PR #8028 — cluster: make the #7257 race probe reach its window, and stop it waiting on an impossible event (#7663, #7970) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7663-race-probe-reaches-its-window`

Closes #7663
Closes #7970

The `#7257` race probe never executed the code it claims to guard, and its own fail-on-revert contract was false. **This makes it reach the window it probes, proven with both legs.**

## The measurement

At master `b67db1a74`, instrumenting the epoch re-check in `StartHeartbeat`:

```
REACH publish-window entered=0 superseded=60
#7257 race probe: 60 starts against 73384 stops (1223.1 stops/start)
--- PASS (0.00s)
```

**Zero of 60 starts reached the publish.** And the contract in its own doc —

> *"RED on revert: restore the unlocked `m.hbReceiver.start()` / `m.hbSender.start()` pair and `-race` reports `WARNING: DATA RACE`"*

— measured with the #7257 production fix reverted: **0 races, test PASSED.** Both legs green means the probe could not tell a fixed tree from a broken one.

## Why

A stop costs **~226ns**; a start **~61µs** (two socket binds dominate). Both measured here. The teardown loop spun with no pacing, so **~270 stops landed inside every start's entry→epoch-recheck window** and superseded all of them — `StartHeartbeat` returned `ErrHeartbeatStartSuperseded` long before `m.hbSender = sender`, so the unlocked derefs that carry the race never ran.

## The old floor *enforced* the vacuity

`stops >= starts` can only be satisfied by the teardown out-running the starts — exactly the condition under which every start is superseded. Measured both ways:

| teardown | published | stops/start | `stops >= starts` floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| spin (before) | **0 / 60** | 1223 | **PASSES** |
| paced (after) | **59 / 60** | 0.08 | **FAILS** |

The floor and the property are in **strict opposition**, and the floor won every time. That is why two prior fixes (#7650, #7679) left the probe vacuous.

## What replaces it

**The precondition is REACH, not stop volume: at least one start must PUBLISH.**

No production instrumentation is needed. `StartHeartbeat` has a single `return nil` and it sits *below* the publish, so a nil return is an exact witness that the start reached the window. The test already distinguished nil from `ErrHeartbeatStartSuperseded` in its condition — and then **lumped both into one `starts` counter**. That is the specific bug: it reported 60 healthy starts while reaching the publish zero times.

The teardown is paced by a randomised sleep scaled to the measured start cost. **Randomised, not fixed** — a fixed gap phase-locks against the start loop and samples one alignment. It stays **unordered** with respect to any particular start (no channel, no handshake, no happens-before edge), so the race detector still sees unsynchronised accesses; pacing changes how often the probe *reaches* the window, not what it observes there.

## Detection is a measured RATE, not a contract

unified diff in a Go comment gets mangled (see below):
