## PR #8029 — Arm commit-confirmed rollback from the durable never-committed marker (#7291) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `explore/7291`

`commitConfirmedLocked` recorded whether the pending window's rollback target was the empty bootstrap tree from `s.compiled == nil`. That is an incidental proxy for the durable never-committed marker, and the two are **independent state** — so it was wrong in both directions.

## Reproduced at current master

Through the real entry points — `CommitConfirmed`, the rollback promotion, `Store.Load` — with nothing poked directly:

```
phase 2 after Item-1b rollback + restart:
    everCommitted=false  compiled!=nil=true
phase 3 rollback:
    markerWrites(committed)=[]  plainWrites=1  everCommitted=true
```

No `writeActiveMarker(_, false)` at all: **`committed=1` persisted over a never-committed DB holding the empty tree.** That is the operator-committed-empty state, which `computeBootClass` resolves to NORMAL — so the next restart runs the positional claim-all interface rename on an empty config, exactly the #1922 Item 2 case-5 hazard the Item 1b marker exists to prevent.

*(A fixture note: `New()` does not read the DB — `Load()` is the restart path. My first attempt omitted it, `compiled` came back nil, and the defect did not reproduce.)*

## Why the fix is not "treat a nil compiled config as first commit"

The #1960 broken-config load leaves `everCommitted=true` with `compiled==nil` **deliberately**, so the daemon refuses takeover. If the operator repairs the config and commits confirmed, the proxy read that as a first commit and the rollback would write `committed=0` over a box that **has** a committed config.

The fix captures `s.everCommitted` on **entry**, before either of the two `s.everCommitted = true` assignments that precede the arm site, and records `confirmPrevFirst = !everCommittedOnEntry`.

Both readers of the marker — `computeBootClass` (`daemon_run_bringup.go`) and `isApplianceFactoryBoot` (`bootstrap.go`) — already consume the distinction correctly, so the defect was entirely at the writer.

**Interaction check:** #7176 (C179-053) moved the `committed=` marker inside the AES-GCM AAD at envelope v2, so it is authenticated rather than freely editable. That makes the value being *correct* more important, not less — integrity protects a wrong value just as faithfully as a right one.

## My own direction-B test was vacuous, and only the mutation showed it

The correct outcome in that direction is the **non-first** branch, which takes a plain `writeActive` and writes **no marker at all**. So my original assertion — "markerWrites contains no `false`" — was true of an empty slice and would have passed however the code behaved. It did **not** red when the arm site was mutated to always-first.

It now requires `plainWrites == 1` **and** `len(markerWrites) == 0`, which pins that the rollback ran *and* took the branch the test is about.

| C1b revert to the compiled-pointer proxy | 2 | 467 | **both** directions |
| C2 capture moved after the assignments | 1 | 2 | direction B |
| C3b always first-commit | 1 | 2 | direction B |
| C4b never first-commit | 7 | 467 | direction A |
| control | green | | |

**C1b is the cell that matters** — reverting to the proxy reds both directions.

C2 and C3b are reported from a run **scoped to these tests**, because the full-suite run aborted at 73 of 467: the mutation makes the pre-existing `TestConfirmRecovery_*_4577` nil-deref and panic, stopping the binary before these tests execute. ## PR #8032 — test: pin that commit check cannot reach the host-mutating compiler (#7297) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7297-commitcheck-boundary`

Closes #7297

#4960 is about `pkg/dataplane`'s `CompileConfig` mutating the host mid-compile — `compileZones` creates VLANs and reconciles addresses before later phases can still fail. A validate-only path that reached it would mutate the host on a `commit check`, which is a defect independent of #7289's apply-side redesign.

**Today it does not.** `Store.CommitCheck → compileTree → compileTreeStrict` reaches **`pkg/config`**'s `CompileConfig`, the AST-to-typed-structs compiler. But nothing held it that way — and the two compilers **share a name**:

```
pkg/config.CompileConfig(tree)               AST -> typed structs
pkg/dataplane.CompileConfig(dp, cfg, bool)   HOST-MUTATING
```

Two functions of one name, one of which mutates the host, both reachable from a config-compilation context, is exactly the shape where a future refactor routes the wrong one in and **every existing test stays green** — because the mutation is a side effect on the host, not a wrong return value.

## Why an import closure rather than a call path

A call-path assertion pins the **one** route the issue traced and says nothing about a second. Any route from `pkg/configstore` into the host-mutating compiler must pass through an **import**, so asserting the closure excludes `pkg/dataplane` covers every route, including ones nobody has thought of. It is the property itself rather than a proxy for it.

Deliberately **not** a name-based enumeration of forbidden symbols — `pkg/api/drain_scope_6827_test.go` records why those rot: the corpus moves with the toolchain and the claim becomes unkeepable. An import closure is computed from the code on every run.

## Two ways this guard could have been useless, both closed

- **An empty closure** would report the boundary intact while checking nothing. `go list` returning no packages is a hard failure.
- **A wrong package path** would sweep something other than the package it names. The package must appear in its own closure.

A `go list` failure is also a hard failure rather than a skip — this guard is the only thing holding the boundary, so an inability to compute the closure is a failure *of the guard*, not a reason to pass.

## PR #8033 — login class: enforce deny-configuration on the config-mutation path (#7172 cut 4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut4-config-gate`

Cut 4 of #7172. **The first per-command authorization that has ever existed on this path** — please read it as that rather than as a filter added to an existing gate. Until now `configure` was all-or-nothing: once `checkPermission` admitted the verb, every mutation inside config mode ran unchecked, deliberately and documented as such in `compiler_login_deny.go`. There is no prior art here to be consistent with, and nothing upstream narrowing the input.

**One chokepoint**, unlike cut 3 — `dispatchConfig` is a single verb switch, so the gate sits once before it rather than in nine cases that would drift.

## The edit-path bypass is the content of this cut

Junos config mode is hierarchical, and every mutating case builds `append(store.GetEditPath(), parts[1:]...)`. So an operator under `deny-configuration "system root-authentication"` who types

```
edit system
set root-authentication plain-text-password hunter2
```

hands the gate `set root-authentication ...` — which **does not match the deny**.

This is the configuration twin of the abbreviation bypass canonicalization closes on the operational side, and it is **worse**: an abbreviation is a deliberate short form, while navigating with `edit` is simply how operators work. The gate matches the **resolved** path and never the typed fragment.

The test carries **both rows** — the same mutation reached directly, and reached by navigating — because a gate matching the fragment passes the first and fails only the second. A one-row table cannot see it.

## What is not gated, each for a stated reason

| verb | why not |
|---|---|
| `edit` / `top` / `up` | navigation — entering a denied subtree changes nothing, every mutation inside is denied on its own, and gating them would stop an operator merely *looking* |
| `commit` / `rollback` | act on the candidate as a whole; no path for a path regex to match, and denying `commit` would deny the operator's own already-authorized edits |
| `load` | applies arbitrary config whose content is unknown until parsed — enforcing against it means matching every path the loaded content touches, a different mechanism from a verb gate. **Named as a remaining gap**, not quietly assumed covered |

## Deny only, same as cut 3

`allow-configuration` commits today as a documented no-op, an allow regex is an allowlist, and enforcing it mid-series would silently narrow live classes on upgrade. Both leaves go live in cut 6 with the gate's retirement.

## Audit renders the verb and the path's first element only

A configuration path carries operator data **in the path**: `set system root-authentication plain-text-password <secret>` puts the secret there. So the full path must never reach a log line. One element is a deliberate floor rather than a tuned depth — any deeper depends on knowing which level of which hierarchy holds a secret, and that knowledge does not exist here.

Cut 3's `canonicalPrefix` is **not** reused: it walks the operational cmdtree, which config paths do not use. This gate does not canonicalize at all — config paths are not abbreviated the way operational commands are, and edit-path resolution is the normalization this side needs.

## Mutation matrix — all red on the first pass

`collected == reported == 18` on every cell; no panics, no build breaks.

| # | Mutation | named red |

| 1 | match the typed fragment, not the resolved path | `TestEditPathIsResolvedBeforeMatching7172` |
| 2 | gate navigation verbs too | `TestNavigationVerbsAreNotGated7172` |
| 3 | delete the gate call from `dispatchConfig` | `TestDispatchConfigCallsTheConfigGate7172` |
| 4 | compile error skips instead of denying | `TestUncompilableConfigRegexDenies7172` |
| 5 | audit renders the full path | `TestConfigDenialAuditDoesNotLeakTheValue7172` |
| 6 | enforce `allow-configuration` too | `TestAllowConfigurationIsNotEnforcedInCut4_7172` |
| 7 | drop a verb from the mutating set | `TestEveryMutatingVerbIsGated7172` |

## PR #8034 — Retire the unreached NAT write surface from the DataPlane interface (#7268) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `explore/7268`

Removes **23** NAT-family methods from the `DataPlane` interface, their `(*Manager)` eBPF implementations, and the now-orphaned overrides on both compile shims. Scoped by measurement rather than by the issue's list.

## The safety argument is not "nothing calls these"

Zero callers is the weaker half. The stronger one: the maps these wrote — `snat_rules`, `snat_rules_v6`, `static_nat_v4/v6`, `nptv6_rules`, `nat_pool_*`, `snat_egress_ips`, `nat64_*` — are **not declared by the AF_XDP shim** (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`). They don't exist on the deployed dataplane, so the writes have nowhere to land even if a caller returned. #6420 removed the record construction that called them, which is *why* the callers are gone — and a future change could reintroduce one.

## What is NOT retired, and why that's the load-bearing finding

**`SetDNATEntry` / `SetDNATEntryV6` are live.** The shim declares `dnat_table` and `dnat_table_v6` (`lib.rs:375` — *"so dynamic SNAT-return entries are visible here. The Go collection shares the same pinned dnat_table map fd"*), and `PutClusterSyncedV4` calls `SetDNATEntry` on the **HA session-sync receive path**.

That path is unforgiving: it treats the error as fatal and does `errors.Join(err, s.rollbackV4(written))` — a missing map wouldn't degrade the DNAT companion, it would **roll back the whole session install on a standby**.

`DeleteDNATEntry`/`V6` keep their five callers each: `dnat_table` is reaped per-session by the grpcapi companion delete, not a bulk sweep — which is why `DeleteStaleDNAT` has no caller. Those two Manager-only sweepers are **left in place deliberately**: they act on a *live* map, a different judgement from deleting a writer for a map that doesn't exist.

## Scope, measured

The issue names ~7 methods and lists `compileNPTv6`'s writes first — those landed already in **PR #7295**. Twenty-three interface methods measured zero non-test callers, including the NAT pool, SNAT-egress and NAT64 groups the issue never mentions. `SetNAT64Count` looked live at one caller; that caller was `ClearNAT64Configs`, itself dead.

## All four population guards fired — that's them working

Each was re-pointed at the new population, never weakened:

| guard | change |
|---|---|
| `*Manager` exported-method census | 164 → **141**, exactly the 23 removed |
| `registryCallsiteManifest` | rows for the removed callsites |
| `clearArrayEntriesBounds` | the four maps whose clear loops went too — `len(boundsSeen)==0` floor intact |
| #4960 pre-pass fidelity floor | 40/30 → 32/20, lowered to the new population, not deleted |

**One of them caught a mistake of mine.** An early line-level edit removed `"SetNPTv6Rule": "class1", "ReadNATPortCounter": "class1",` as a *whole line*, taking a live method's class entry with it. The census test reported `ReadNATPortCounter` unassigned; the entry is restored. A coarse edit taking a neighbour with it — the same shape as a bad squash, one line lower down.

## The guard

Reflection over the method set, **not** a source scan (a scan can be satisfied by a comment containing the name). It carries an anti-vacuity floor (the interface must reflect ≥ 40 methods) and a **positive control** asserting the four live DNAT methods are still declared — without which the retired-list loop would pass against an empty or misspelled method set.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| re-add a retired method to the interface | **BUILD BREAK** — the shims no longer implement it |
| re-add `SetSNATRule` to `*Manager` only | FAIL=1, the Manager guard |
| remove a live method (`SetDNATEntryV6`) | **BUILD BREAK** — callers |

So the interface surface is compile-enforced, and the reflection test's real work is the concrete-type half, where a method can reappear without breaking anything.

Full `go test ./...` clean with `-count=1`; `go build ./...` clean. Scope check: 10 files, all in `pkg/dataplane`.

Closes #7268

## PR #8035 — Apply deferred-flush output-filter side effects (#7176 C179-001) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7176-deferred-verdict`

Addresses row **C179-001** of #7176. Does **not** close #7176 — the cohort has other live rows.

## The row is real, but it names the wrong filter

The row reads *"deferred neighbor retry reads only `.drop`, so `then reject` loses its reply and `then log` loses its event"*, which sounds like a **security policy** defect. It is not one — policy is evaluated upstream of deferral and a packet only reaches neighbor resolution by having been permitted, so no policy verdict is lost. The loss is in the **egress output filter**, re-evaluated at flush time. Anyone chasing this in the policy code would find nothing and conclude the row was already fixed.

## Confirmation

1. `CoSTxSelection` (`tx/cos_classify.rs:9`) carries six fields: `queue_id`, `dscp_rewrite`, `drop`, `reject`, `reject_message`, `filter_log`.
2. `neighbor_dispatch.rs` bound exactly three: `cos.drop`, `cos.queue_id`, `cos.dscp_rewrite`.
3. The admission path performs **no** output-filter evaluation for a deferred packet — `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` has exactly one occurrence of `resolve_cos_tx_selection_at` and it is inside a comment. So the flush is the sole evaluation, which closes the "something upstream already sent it" escape.

The struct's own doc comment convicts it: `reject` exists so *"the TX/CoS consumer can synthesize the active reject reply (TCP RST / ICMP admin-prohibited) instead of the silent drop a `then discard` or a red policer produces."* The deferred consumer is a TX/CoS consumer and did not.

**Effect:** a packet buffered pending ARP/ND whose output filter resolves to `then reject` was treated as a silent discard, and any `then log` term on that path emitted nothing.

## Approach: extract, don't duplicate

The immediate path's handling (`forward_request.rs`) is ~65 lines carrying four documented subtleties — reply enqueued **before** the log so the logged action is truthful (#3615), a flowless L3 rebuild purely for log attribution (#5467), shared zone resolution for MAC-less interfaces (#6713), and AppID from the hot-path catalog (#2520).

Copying that into the deferred path was rejected: **a divergence between these two paths is what produced this bug**, so duplicating is the same change with a delayed second failure. It is extracted into `apply_cos_drop_side_effects` and both paths call it.

`retry_pending_neigh` gains `event_stream` and `BatchCounters`, which the reply and the log event require. Both production callers already have them in scope.

## Mutation testing

Both cells full-suite, `0 filtered out`, against the committed fix:

| cell | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** | faithful revert of the wiring (restore `if cos.drop { push_back; continue; }`) | **RED** — `deferred_flush_reject_sends_reply_7176`, `deferred_flush_emits_filter_log_event_7176` |
| **M2** | remove reject-isolation (`cos.drop && cos.reject` → `cos.drop`) | **RED** — `deferred_flush_discard_stays_silent_7176`, exactly 1 test |

Stated plainly: **only 2 of the 4 cells are M1-sensitive.** The discard and flowless cells assert *absence* of a reply, which is equally true when the fix is missing; they constrain the fix's shape rather than detect its removal, and M2 is what demonstrates they are not decorative.

**M2 also surfaced a coverage gap:** it mutated the *shared* helper, which both paths use, and reddened **only the new deferred test**. No pre-existing test covered reject-isolation on the immediate path either — that behaviour has been unguarded since #3608.

## Tests bind the wiring, not the helper

The tests drive `retry_pending_neigh` itself. The defect was never in the helper's body — it was that the deferred path did not **call** it — so a test invoking the helper directly would stay green if the call site were deleted again.

Two fixture traps are worth recording, because each produced a convincing false positive that looks exactly like the production defect:

- the stock `build_ipv4_test_packet` is 34 bytes (Ethernet + IP header, **no TCP header**), so the RST builder correctly fails closed;
- the flush reads the packet from **UMEM** (`area.slice(desc.addr, desc.len)`), not from the `frame` Vec the fixture builds — without seeding UMEM the flush parses zeros.

What separated fixture from production was driving `enqueue_filter_reject_reply` directly with the same inputs: it returned `sent=true` while the flush produced nothing, locating the fault on the test's side. The fixture now seeds UMEM and says why.

`RT_FLOW_ACTION_REJECT` becomes visible within `crate::afxdp` so the log assertion compares against the production constant rather than pinning the literal `2`.

## PR #8036 — config: read the packed body on a named instance [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7653-packed-named-instance-body`

Closes #7653

The #2419 class has a shape distinct from the packed LEAF closed by #6818/#6822: **the packed body on a NAMED INSTANCE**. `namedInstances` recognises the instance from `Keys[0..1]`, and the compiler then reads `inst.node.Children` — which is EMPTY when the operator packed the body onto the instance line. The instance is created and everything inside it is dropped.

That is worse than not recognising the instance, because the half-built object then reaches the renderer and the runtime. All three shapes **commit cleanly**: strict `CompileConfig` accepts, and the schema walker ignores leftover keys on a named container by design, so nothing warns.

## Measured live at `9013c7f9d`, before and after

| shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `interface ge-0/0/0.0 authentication simple-password "secret";` | `AuthType="" AuthKey=""` | `"simple"` / `"secret"` |
| `user ops authentication-sha256 authentication-password "s3cret";` | `users=1 AuthProtocol="" AuthPassword=""` | `sha256` / `s3cret` |
| `usm local-engine { user ops { ... } }` | **`users=0`** | `users=1 sha256` |

Each row's expanded spelling was compiled in the same run as the reference.

**Why each row matters, in descending subtlety.** `pkg/frr/protocols_render.go` emits interface activation *unconditionally* while `ip ospf authentication` is conditional on `AuthType`, so row 1 brought the adjacency up with **no authentication** from a config whose text authorises one. Row 2 did not *skip* the user — it installed it with no derived key, and minimum-security enforcement keys on key presence, so a `noAuthNoPriv` request naming `ops` bypassed the authentication the operator authored: a downgrade rather than an outage, and therefore silent. Row 3 is the loudest and the least dangerous — every SNMPv3 user disappears, an SNMPv3 management outage rather than a credential downgrade.

## Implementation — three sites, two mechanisms

Rows 1 and 3 of the *mechanism* split differently from the table. Rows 1–2 are a **dropped body**; row 3 is a **missing intermediate container**, and takes a different fix, as the issue predicted.

- The two OSPF loops route property iteration through `packedBodyChildren`, the same schema-driven expander the #6818/#6821 siblings already use at five production sites, anchored on `schemaForPath("protocols", "ospf"|"ospf3", "area", "interface")`.
- The SNMPv3 user body goes through **`parseSNMPv3UserKeys`** — the function the flat-set path already uses for exactly this key run — rather than a second copy of its table. A divergence between two copies is a silent credential loss either way.
- The packed `usm local-engine` container is recovered through `packedBodyChildren`, whose #6818 behaviour of attaching the nested block **UNDER** the packed node rather than beside it is exactly what this shape needs: the users are `usmNode.Children` and they belong under the synthesized `local-engine`.

## The #2419 inventory drops 18 entries (390 → 372)

Measured as a delta, not assumed: **zero entries were stale at base**, and all 18 became equivalent under this change. They are OSPF-interface rows across `ospf`, `ospf3`, and their `routing-instances` variants, which share the two fixed loops — so the fix reaches further than the three sites named in the issue.

Removing them is required rather than optional. The inventory's own failure text says it: *"a stale inventory is an allowlist that hides the next regression."*

## Why the tests assert absolute values, not `packed == expanded`

Equivalence alone is satisfied when **both** spellings are broken — which is precisely the state a regression here would produce. A future change that stops reading the body on both paths would leave every equivalence cell green. So each cell pins what the packed spelling must COMPILE TO and uses the expanded spelling as a same-run reference rather than as the assertion.

`TestExpandedSpellingsAreUnchanged7653` is the control. A tail-expanding fix can attach rebuilt children in the wrong place — #6818 had to learn to nest rather than sibling — and that shows up as the EXPANDED spelling regressing while every packed cell passes.

## Mutation matrix — four fixes, four paired cells, full-suite per cell

| cell | applied | build | collected | named FAILs | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 revert ospf2 loop | yes | ok | 7107 | 2 | **RED** — `TestPackedOSPFInterfaceKeepsItsAuthentication7653`, `TestCompactBlockEquivalenceInventory2419` |
| M2 revert ospf3 loop | yes | ok | 7107 | 2 | **RED** — `TestPackedOSPFv3InterfaceKeepsItsBody7653`, `TestCompactBlockEquivalenceInventory2419` |
| M3 drop `parseSNMPv3UserKeys` call | yes | ok | 7107 | 1 | **RED** — `TestPackedSNMPv3UserKeepsItsCredential7653` |
| M4 drop the local-engine recovery | yes | ok | 7107 | 1 | **RED** — `TestPackedUSMLocalEngineKeepsItsUsers7653` |

Each cell restores what shipped rather than a paraphrase, asserts the edit reached the tree, confirms `go build` so a build break cannot masquerade as a red, and runs the **full** package suite rather than a `-run` filter — which is what surfaced the #2419 inventory as a second independent guard on M1/M2.

## PR #8038 — syslog: stop advertising two names that are not [edit system syslog] facilities [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7187-facility-advice`

Part of #7187 (its folded-in #5672 half). Does **not** close it — the source-facility envelope, the compiled selector program, and the transport/filter split all remain.

## The defect

The commit-time error for an invalid `system syslog` facility lists the vocabulary an operator may use. **Two of those names were never `[edit system syslog]` facilities** — and this repository had already established that, verified against the documentation, in `pkg/logging/parse_facility_checked_5797_test.go`, while the message went on advertising them:

> `security` names a different hierarchy (`[edit security log]`), `external` and `dcd` do not appear in the configurable set at all, and `ntp` is excluded by the empty-second-column rule.

`junosRemoteFacility` documents the `ntp` exclusion at length and deliberately omits it, ending with: *"a mapping we cannot substantiate must not move a record."* The commit error was substantiating it anyway.

Measured at `d2e4babf1`:

| name | advertised by the commit error | `JunosRemoteFacility` | `ParseFacilityChecked` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `authorization`, `change-log`, `conflict-log`, `daemon`, `dfc`, `firewall`, `ftp`, `interactive-commands`, `kernel`, `pfe`, `user` | yes | **junos** | **known** |
| `ntp` | **yes** | not junos | **unknown** |
| `security` | **yes** | not junos | **unknown** |

## Why it is not cosmetic

An operator reads the error, writes `set system syslog host 192.0.2.10 security info`, and commits. They get **no error, no `security` records, and everything filed silently to local0** — precisely the misfiling #6830 exists to prevent, reintroduced through the help text rather than through the mapping.

This is the "independent transcription from a non-authoritative source" shape: the list was hand-typed into an error string, it agreed with itself, and nothing connected it to the mapping that decides what actually happens.

## The fix

The message is rendered from a named vocabulary instead of a hand-typed string, and `pkg/logging` asserts that vocabulary against the wire mapping in **both** directions:

- **no advertised name the wire cannot deliver** — the defect above;
- **no mapped facility the advice withholds** — the direction that rots silently. Adding a mapping to `junosRemoteFacility` is the natural way to support a new facility, and nothing about that edit makes anyone think of an error string in a different package. The operator then has a facility that works and no way to discover it.

**The agreement is asserted rather than either side pinned to a literal.** A literal encodes which side you trust — and here the side everyone trusted was the wrong one. `pkg/logging` imports `pkg/config`, so the dependency cannot run the other way and the two lists genuinely cannot be single-sourced; asserting agreement is the available correctness, and it is the stronger one anyway.

`any` is the one deliberate exception, documented at the declaration: a selector wildcard valid on the rsyslog-backed file/user destinations, not a numeric facility a host client can stamp.

Both new tests carry an **anti-vacuity floor** (`len(advertised) < 10` → `t.Fatalf`). Without it, a rename or a getter that stopped copying would make every membership check pass over an empty list and certify the agreement while measuring none of it.

## Mutation matrix — three cells, all applied, all building, 281 collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| re-add `security` to the advice | **RED** — `TestConfigFacilityAdviceMatchesTheWireMapping7187`, `TestRemovedNonFacilitiesStayRemoved7187` |
| re-add `ntp` to the advice | **RED** — same two |
| remove `user` (a *mapped* facility) from the advice | **RED** — `TestEveryMappedFacilityIsAdvertised7187` |

The third cell is what proves the second direction is real rather than decorative. `TestRemovedNonFacilitiesStayRemoved7187` names each removed name individually with its own reason, so a regression says *which* one came back and *why* it is wrong rather than just that a list changed.

## PR #8039 — image: fail the pre-sign gate when a leg skips instead of asserting [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7347-validate-skip-ledger`

Closes #7347

`scripts/image/validate.py` is the gate `bake.py`'s `finalize_artifacts` runs **strictly before** `sign_step` (#4017). Scenario Q returned early when `qemu-img` was absent, `main()` ran the scenarios for effect and returned 0 regardless, and `bake.py` reads exit 0 as a pass — so on a host without qemu-utils the entire structural probe was skipped and the artifact was still minisigned `validated: true`.

**A scenario that returns is indistinguishable from one that asserted**, and here the difference was laundered through a signature: `publish.py` and `xpf-deploy.py fetch` verify the signature and read a signed image as a validated one.

## Three changes

**1. A missing `qemu-img` is a hard `fail()`**, matching the posture `assert_image_sealed` took for libguestfs in #6547/#7317 — *"a security gate that skips itself when its tool is absent is the vacuous-gate shape this check exists to remove."* Failing is safe by construction: `bake.py`'s preflight `require()`s qemu-img (`bake.py:805`), so on a real bake host it is present, and the skip could only ever fire where the gate should not have been trusted.

**2. A skip ledger.** Every remaining skip must be recorded, is named in the closing summary, and makes `main()` return non-zero when classified as not survivable. `--allow-skip` is the dev escape hatch, shaped like the existing `--no-verify-sig`; `bake.py` deliberately does not pass it, and a test pins that.

**3. The decision moved out of `main()`** into `_skip_verdict`, a pure function over the ledger, testable without incus, a network, an image import or six VM boots. The bug being fixed was precisely that this decision did not exist.

The module docstring's `(always)` and the code comment's `always runs when qemu-img is present` contradicted each other. The docstring was the claim a reader trusts; the code was the wrong half. Both now state the same posture, and the code makes the docstring true.

## Where this departs from the issue, and why

The issue proposed exiting non-zero **if any scenario skipped**. Applied literally that breaks every bake on a TCG host. Measured in `bake.py`'s own preflight:

| tool | bake.py posture |
|---|---|
| `qemu-img` | **`require()`d** → absence impossible on a real bake → safe to fail |
| `/dev/kvm` | only a **`WARNING`** ("no /dev/kvm access — libguestfs will use TCG (slow)") |
| `qemu-system-x86_64` | **not required at all** |

So a TCG bake host is a *supported* configuration on which the boot leg genuinely cannot run. It is classified **tolerated** — recorded and reported, never silent, but not fatal. The issue's own analysis agrees, calling it *"a genuine partial skip"* with the severity *"concentrated in"* the qemu-img return.

That classification is not a judgement left in a comment. `test_fatal_classification_matches_bake_requirements` reads `bake.py`'s preflight and pins **both** halves, so if qemu-img stops being required or `/dev/kvm` starts being required, the classification goes red rather than drifting from the thing that justifies it.

## Calibrated on known-bad input

The acceptance criteria ask to prove the gate *fails when the tool is absent*, not merely that it passes when present. Both directions, paired:

| PATH | result |
|---|---|
| qemu-img **absent** | `SystemExit(1)`, *"qemu-img not found — install qemu-utils…"* |
| qemu-img **present** | still exits — but on the **image** (*"Could not open …"*), not the tool |

Same exit code, different cause. The positive control matters: without it, a `scenario_qemu` that raised unconditionally would satisfy the first row while measuring nothing.

## Mutation matrix — six cells, all applied, all parsing, all with tests collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| restore the qemu-img skip | **RED** — `test_missing_qemu_img_fails` |
| `_skip_verdict` always returns 0 | **RED** — `test_a_fatal_skip_fails` |
| `skip()` emits nothing | **RED** — `test_a_skip_is_never_silent`, `test_a_fatal_skip_is_recorded_and_named` |
| flip the boot leg to `fatal=True` | **RED** — `test_boot_leg_skip_is_tolerated_not_fatal` |
| drop `qemu-img` from bake's require list | **RED** — `test_fatal_classification_matches_bake_requirements` |

## PR #8041 — cluster: add an installation seam so the daemon's hook wiring can be bound [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7280-cluster-hook-seam`

Closes #7280

`Daemon.startClusterComms` installs fourteen wiring assignments into the cluster Manager and the SessionSync, and nothing bound any of them. #6428 **measured** that rather than assuming it: `go tool cover -func` reported **0.0% statement coverage** for every builder running inside the constructor goroutine, and **nilling all thirty wiring assignments at once left `pkg/daemon` and `pkg/cluster` fully green**.

#6428 bound the seventeen sites that were already observable. The rest could not be, because `cluster.Manager` exposed no way to ask whether a hook had been installed — a production-surface change, correctly out of scope for a code-motion refactor. This is that seam and those tests.

These hooks are cluster failover, fencing and sync-transport selection. A silently dropped assignment there is not a cosmetic defect.

## The seam

| addition | answers |
|---|---|
| `Manager.InstalledHooks() map[string]bool` | is each of the 11 callbacks non-nil |
| `Manager.RemoteTransferOutLease() time.Duration` | did the daemon's computed lease arrive |
| `SessionSync.HasAuthProvider() bool` | is a non-nil PSK provider installed |

It deliberately does **not** assert behaviour. The question is "was this wired", and a behavioural assertion would need a live peer for hooks whose whole job is to talk to one.

**Why the map carries bools and not the funcs.** #6428's first draft of the equivalent test collected the func fields into a table of `any` and compared each against nil — and **fourteen of seventeen mutations stayed green**, because boxing a typed nil into an interface produces a non-nil interface. The nil-ness is destroyed by the boxing, not by the comparison. So the `!= nil` comparisons happen inside `pkg/cluster` against the concrete typed fields, and only bools cross the package boundary. A caller never touches a func value, so the bug cannot be reintroduced from that side.

The map always carries **every** key, so a caller can distinguish "not installed" (present, false) from "no longer a hook" (absent) — a `_, ok :=` lookup of a renamed hook would otherwise silently skip its row. Hook names are exported constants, so a rename breaks at compile time.

## Two corrections to the issue

**The count is fourteen, not thirteen.** #7280 says 13 and enumerates 12; the file carries fourteen wiring assignments across three builders (2 transport refs, 10 failover hooks, 2 fence hooks). Its list was a floor. All fourteen are bound.

**Two were not fully unbound.** Running the matrix full-suite rather than under a `-run` filter is what revealed this: the fence pair already trips `TestWireClusterFenceCallbacksInstallsConfirmFunc_7147`. But that guard is a **source scan** — `strings.Contains` over whitespace-flattened source, comments included — so it proves the call is *written*, not that the setter stored anything, and it would be satisfied by a comment containing the same text. The assertions here are behavioural and strictly stronger; **the scan should not be read as making them redundant.**

## Mutation matrix — one deletion per wiring line, 14/14, zero escapes

Every cell applied, built, and collected **2219** tests, so none is a build-break or an edit-never-applied void.

| # | deleted line | fired |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ss.SetAuthProvider(d.cluster)` | `…TransportRefsInstallsAuthAndTransport_7280` |
| 2 | `d.cluster.SetSyncTransport(...)` | `…TransportRefsInstallsAuthAndTransport_7280` |
| 3–12 | the ten failover hooks + lease | `…PeerFailoverHooksInstallsManagerHooks_7280` |
| 13 | `SetPeerFenceFunc` | `…FenceCallbacksInstallsManagerHooks_7280` **+** `…ConfirmFunc_7147` |
| 14 | `SetPeerFenceConfirmFunc` | `…FenceCallbacksInstallsManagerHooks_7280` **+** `…ConfirmFunc_7147` |

**ESCAPED: none.**

The lease cell asserts the **computed** value (`2*localFailoverCommitTimeout + 20s` = 24s under the fixture), not merely "non-zero". The field is never nil and `SetRemoteTransferOutLeaseDuration` clamps to a floor, so a non-zero check would pass on the clamp alone and bind nothing.

## The negative control comes first

`TestInstalledHooksReportsFalseBeforeWiring_7280` asserts a freshly constructed Manager reports **every** hook uninstalled. Without it the whole file is vacuous in the safe-looking direction: an `InstalledHooks` that returned true unconditionally would satisfy every positive assertion below it. `TestEveryWiredHookHasAReportedKey_7280` additionally reconciles the count, so a hook added to the Manager without a binding test fails rather than passing unnoticed.

## PR #8042 — test: wait for the asserted field, and fix the fixture panic that exposed [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7350-wait-for-the-asserted-field`

Closes #7350

`TestStartClusterCommsWiresBulkSnapshotSource7259` polled for the **object** and then immediately asserted a **field** written two wiring calls later.

`startClusterComms` publishes the SessionSync *before* it wires it — deliberately, because `publishSessionSyncIfCurrent` is the generation check that drops a superseded constructor's object before it touches cluster state. So `getSessionSync()` goes non-nil at `daemon_ha_sync.go:960`, while `BulkSnapshotSource` is assigned inside `wireSessionSyncPeerCallbacks` at `:974`. **Nothing ordered the two.**

The issue measured it: 1 failure in 5 full-`pkg/daemon` runs, 3/3 passing under a `-run` filter — the signature of a window, not of a defect in what it was testing.

## The fix

The wait condition is now the property itself. `published` is tracked separately so a failure says **which** state was reached — "never published" and "published but never wired" are different defects, and collapsing them sends the next reader to the wrong half of `startClusterComms`.

**Acceptance criterion 2 is the one that mattered**: a never-wired field must still *red*, not time out into a pass. A wait-for-the-field rewrite that let the deadline fall through would have converted this regression guard into a no-op — the single way this repair could have gone wrong. Verified by deleting `ss.BulkSnapshotSource = d.userspaceBulkSnapshot`:

```
--- FAIL: TestStartClusterCommsWiresBulkSnapshotSource7259 (15.01s)
    #7259: startClusterComms published a SessionSync with NO BulkSnapshotSource — …
```

Clean red, the original #7259 message, no panic.

Not fixed by wiring before publishing: that inverts the deliberate order and the `Order contract` at `daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:128`.

## Making the test wait exposed a latent fixture panic

This is the more valuable half. Adding the wait turned a clean red into a **SIGSEGV**:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
  daemon.(*wiringExporterDP).HA(...)
  daemon.(*Daemon).startHAWatchdogHeartbeat.func1()
```

`wiringExporterDP` embeds a **nil** `dataplane.RuntimeDataPlane`, so the promoted `HA()` dispatched into a nil interface — and `startClusterComms` launches the HA watchdog heartbeat, whose goroutine calls `rt.HA().SetHAWatchdog` on a ticker. The panic fires roughly **half a second** in.

Nothing ever noticed because the test reached its assertion within milliseconds and tore the daemon down before the first tick. **The fixture was a landmine for anyone who made it live longer** — which is precisely what fixing #7350 requires. And a panic takes the whole package binary down rather than failing one test, so the next person would have gotten an unrelated-looking crash in a package they had not touched.

The double now returns a no-op `HAController`. That is the honest shape: this test is about wiring, not about what the watchdog writes, and a controller that records nothing keeps the goroutine harmless without pretending to model it.

## PR #8043 — ha: guard session-open field parity across both transports [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7194-transport-parity-guard`

Part of #7194 — its **item 1**, the artefact that issue calls load-bearing. Does **not** close it: item 2 (fail-closed capability negotiation) is a protocol change and remains. Item 3 I investigated and believe is **misdiagnosed** — detail below.

## What was missing

Two HA session-open transports, and nothing making them equivalent — only the discipline of remembering to edit both. #5865's evidence is the whole argument: five fields existed on the binary frame and the Go consumer but not on the Rust JSON producer, so the JSON leg installed zeros. And the Go struct's own doc comment asserted those fields were *"mirrored on the JSON RPC-fallback delta"* — **false from the day it was written**, undetected for months, because nothing compared the two transports.

## The parity is currently correct — measured, not assumed

Both sides carry **41 wire fields** and they match exactly. #6949 closed the five-field gap. So this is a **regression guard**, not a fix: it exists so the next field added to one leg reds the suite instead of shipping, which is exactly what did not happen the last two times (#5865, then #6312).

## It compares wire names, not field names

The Rust struct carries **35 `#[serde(rename = "...")]`** attributes; the Go struct carries json tags. Today every rename is an identity rename, so a field-name comparison would also pass — and would keep passing through a future rename that broke the wire while leaving both field names alone. The contract between these two programs is the JSON on the wire, so that is what is compared. Pinning field names would encode the wrong SSOT.

Both extractions carry an **anti-vacuity floor** (35, against a current 41). They are text- and reflection-driven and either can silently come back short — a moved file, a renamed struct, a regex that stops matching — and every comparison would then pass over a near-empty set and certify a parity nobody measured.

## Two defects this file's own mistakes taught it

**The first extraction was truncated and invented a gap.** I read a fixed line range, cut the 139-line Rust struct at line 88, and produced a confident six-field "gap" — `policy_id`, `policy_counter_idx`, `app_timeout`, `nat64`, `nat64_snat_v4`, `rt_flow_session_id` — that does not exist. I nearly reported it. The struct's end is brace-counted now, because **a truncated extraction and a real divergence are indistinguishable in the output**.

**The mutation matrix caught the struct search being a substring match.** Renaming the type to `SessionDeltaInfoRenamed7194` left the test **green**, because the new name still contains the old one as a prefix. A neighbouring `SessionDeltaInfoV2` declared earlier in the file would have been parsed instead of this one, and the parity result would have described the wrong type entirely. It is an exact declaration match now.

## Mutation matrix — 4/4 RED

Each applied, each vetting clean, each collecting both tests.

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| add a Go-only field | **RED** — *"the Go consumer expects session-open field … that the Rust JSON producer does not emit"* |
| add a Rust-only field | **RED** — *"the Rust JSON producer emits session-open field … that the Go consumer does not read"* |
| drift one `serde(rename)` (`queue_id` → `queue_identifier`) | **RED** — fires **both** directions, which is the correct signature of a rename |
| rename the Rust struct | **RED** — *"no longer declares `struct SessionDeltaInfo`"* |

The last cell is the one that found the substring bug; before the fix it was the matrix's only escape.

## Item 3 is misdiagnosed — evidence

#7194 says `export.rs` "binds the fair-drain overflow flag as `_overflow` and discards it, so a ring drop mid-export is silent." The binding is exactly where the issue says it is. **What it means is not what the issue says.**

```rust
let overflow = budget == 0 && bindings.iter().any(|b| b.has_pending_session_deltas());
```

`overflow` is **budget exhaustion with deltas remaining** — not a ring drop. In `wait_and_collect` with `max == 0` the loop drains to empty and overflow is transient; with `max > 0` it means "truncated by the caller's budget", which is the documented, caller-governed behaviour. The existing comment already explains why the latch is deliberately not armed here: *"this export IS the resync/snapshot mechanism … Arming a worker resync from inside a resync export would be circular."*

A genuine ring drop is tracked separately and is **not** silent: `SessionTable::push_delta` increments `delta_drops` (a cumulative counter *"surfaced for health/status telemetry"*) and sets the #2442 loss-of-sync latch, which `take_delta_loss` converts into a full owner-RG resync once per episode.

So "fixing" item 3 as written would mean arming a latch the code explains must not be armed. I have left it alone and will note this on the issue rather than acting on it silently.

## PR #8044 — converge: build the applied-marker driver registry, plan-kill the typed marker [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7343-driver-registry`

Closes #7343

#7343 proposed two mechanisms after #6533 PLAN-KILLED the lint. **Classifying all 42 population sites settles which is worth building — and the answer is not the one the cost estimate predicted.**

## The triage

**19 sites are structurally not markers.** `docs/applied-marker-invariant.md` Measurement 1 anticipated most of it; reading the rest added two categories it did not list — **read-outs into a display view or a returned snapshot** (`cli_show_security_filters.go:490`, `sync_bulk.go:351`, `surface_a.go:2102`) and a **log-dedup memo** (`tunnels.go:212`, which remembers what was last *logged*, not what was applied).

**23 are real markers, and every one is already correct** — by four *different* mechanisms:

| how it is correct | n |
|---|---|
| early return: the error path returned above the stamp | 11 |
| caller contract or explicit guard | 7 |
| status readback or dedup-skip — **no error exists at all** | 4 |
| advances on failure, deliberately (`pkg/dhcpserver`, #6535) | 1 |

**Exactly one site has a live, unreturned error in scope at the stamp**, and it is that declared escape. Checked, not sampled: a scan for enclosing functions accumulating errors (`errors.Join` / `errs = append`) flagged 5 of 42, deliberately over-reporting. Two are zero-resets, two are `manager_worker_arm` where the `errors.Join` sits inside an early `return` **above** the stamp, and one is `dhcpserver`.

## Why item 1 is not built

The issue's own honest test was *"if a third of the real markers need the escape hatch, the guard is not buying much."* The escape rate is **1 in 23** — comfortably under that bar.

**The mechanism still fails, for a different reason.** `Advance(gen, err)` makes the unsafe form unwritable by forcing the caller to hold the outcome — but at **22 of 23** sites there is no error in scope to pass. Every one would migrate to a literal:

```go
m.marker.Advance(gen, nil)
```

> A parameter that is `nil` at every call site encodes no contract. It is a no-op wearing the shape of a guarantee — and worse than nothing, because a reviewer seeing `Advance(gen, err)` would reasonably conclude the invariant is now type-enforced.

That is the same "looks checked, checks nothing" failure #6533 was killed for, relocated from a lint into an API. A single signature also flattens four genuinely different correctness mechanisms: `rg_state.MarkApplied` contains no error *by design*, `process_status`'s readback mirrors bookkeeping the helper has *already confirmed*, and its dedup-skip advances when nothing was published *and that is correct*.

## What is built: item 2, the driver registry

The half #7343 identifies as load-bearing — *"storage without a driver is the bug."* Two tables: real markers, each naming the periodic symbol that re-drives it and **why** its stamp is correct; and non-markers, each with its reason (an unexplained entry is indistinguishable from an unnoticed marker).

Three asserted properties:

1. **Every population assignment is classified.** A new marker added anywhere arrives as an unclassified statement and fails — the recurrence guard, since a marker added without a driver cannot land silently.
2. **Every registered marker names a driver symbol that exists.** Renaming or deleting a converger fails. That is the twelve-times-recurring defect.
3. **`pkg/dhcpserver`'s advance-on-failure is a first-class declaration** naming `ClaimApplyRetry` — not a `//nolint`, which is exactly the suppression #6533 was killed for.

**Keyed on (file, statement, count), not `file:line`.** A line-keyed registry goes stale on any edit *above* a site and would fail for reasons unrelated to convergence; counting identical statements per file is stable under line drift and still fails when a new assignment appears. That distinction matters in `process_status.go`, where the *same* statement appears three times with three different correctness mechanisms.

An **anti-vacuity floor** guards the population scan — it is regex-driven over a directory walk and can silently come back short, after which every comparison would pass over almost nothing.

## PR #8045 — filter: correct the flowless port-term claim, and pin what C19 measures [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7174-c19-flowless-port-except`

Part of the #7174 cohort — row **C19**, measured and resolved. Does not close the cohort.

## What C19 asked, and the answer

Can a non-first fragment reach `evaluate_filter_ref_tx_selection_cached`? **Yes** — and the answer matters because two comments in `cos_classify.rs` assert it cannot.

Driving the real resolver on both arms, differing on **one axis only**:

| arm | result |
|---|---|
| `flow_key = Some`, dst port 22 | `drop=false` — correct, 22 is excepted |
| `flow_key = None` (the fragment) | **`drop=true`** — the term matched |

## Why the stated invariant is false

The flowless arm evaluates the interface output filter with **L4 ports forced to 0**, because the header is absent. The comment's claim —

> Ports are 0, so a port-BEARING term never matches (no spurious drop).

— is **true for a positive port list** (`from destination-port 22` cannot match 0) and **false for an except list**: `from destination-port-except 22` matches everything that is *not* 22, and **0 is not 22**, so the term matches and its `then discard` fires on a fragment of a permitted flow.

**The second line of defence does not cover it either.** The comment relies on the flow-cache declining such filters, via `interface_output_filter_has_per_packet_l4_match`. That reads `Filter::has_per_packet_l4_match`, which tests:

```
tcp_flags_mask · tcp_flags_forbidden · is_fragment · icmp_type · icmp_code · flex
```

**Ports are not in that list.** So the flow-cache does not decline a port-bearing filter, and it reaches this arm.

## Behaviour is deliberately unchanged

Dropping the fragment is **fail-closed**, which is the posture #6055 built this gate to produce. Choosing fail-open for unknown ports would be a security trade, and this change does not make it — it would mean a `then discard` term silently passing fragments.

**What was wrong was the claim, not the code.** A reader relying on *"a port-bearing term never matches here"* would conclude a permitted flow's fragments are safe. They are not. Both comments now state what the code does, and point at the test that pins it.

## The measurement was inert, and now is not

The measurement existed on `measure/7174-c19-reachability` with **no PR** — a print-only test. A test that only prints **cannot fail**, so once in the suite it measures nothing and would have passed forever through any change to this behaviour. It now asserts both arms.

The **control** arm is asserted too, not just the subject: without it the two arms could stop differing on the flow key alone, and the subject assertion would prove nothing. The failure text says which of the two fired and what to do if the behaviour was changed on purpose — update the test *and* both comments together, since they are the pair that went out of step once already.

## One thing the original measurement did not establish

Its title was "reachability", but it drove `resolve_cached_cos_tx_selection` **directly**, bypassing the flow-cache seed path — so it demonstrated the wrong verdict without showing the filter actually gets cached. That gap is closed here by reading the decline gate: `has_per_packet_l4_match` omits ports, so a port-bearing filter is not declined. **That is the step that turns "the resolver would answer wrongly" into "the resolver is reached".**

## Validation

- Full Rust suite: **4,944 passed, 0 failed, rc=0**
- Fail-on-revert cell: restoring the pre-#6055 behaviour (the flowless arm stops honouring the verdict) **reds** with the C19 message
- Scope: `+175/−0` in the test file, `+28/−7` comment-only in `cos_classify.rs`; no file at zero insertions, and no behavioural line changed

## PR #8046 — linksetup: verify live names, and stop phase 2 on a broken premise [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7205-naming-transaction`

Closes #7205

The #5842 remainder. #7203 landed the error channel, so positional naming now fails when it does not converge. These are the three items that channel had nothing to carry — and they share one root: **the positional path had no notion of a naming transaction.**

## 1. Nothing verified the live names

`renamePositional` reports what it **attempted**. A `networkctl reload` that partially applied, a udev race, or a NIC that vanished mid-pass left the box running under names the configuration does not reference — **with a clean return value**.

`verifyPositionalNames` re-reads the interface list after the reload and reports every NIC not wearing its intended name, on the same #5842 channel as a failed rename. The consequence is identical, so the channel must be.

**Why re-enumeration is sound**, stated at the function rather than assumed: `enumeratePCINICs` sorts by `(sortKey, busAddr)` — both PCI-derived and **independent of the interface name** — so index *i* addresses the same NIC before and after a pass. If that sort ever became name-dependent, this check would compare a NIC against another NIC's intended name.

**What it cannot see is stated too.** Positional mode has no stable identity to verify against — the index *is* the identity — so this proves the intended name is worn, not that the right NIC wears it. Device-map's permanent-MAC refusal is the only thing that closes that, and pretending otherwise would be worse than the bounded check.

## 2. `breakNameCollisions` left phase 2 on a false premise

A failed temp rename `continue`d, leaving that NIC still occupying a desired final name — so phase 2's stated premise, *"Collisions are already broken, so no EEXIST here"*, was false for exactly that name. Phase 2 attempted the rename anyway.

Since #7203 that EEXIST is reported rather than swallowed — but **it names the wrong cause.** It points at the rename, and the reader goes looking at udev or the `.link` file instead of at the collision break that did not happen.

The shared function now returns the names it could not free, and **both** callers decline those renames with the real cause:

```
device-map: cannot rename enp9s0 -> ge-0-0-3: the collision break could not free
"ge-0-0-3" (its current occupant failed to temp-rename), so this rename would
EEXIST and phase 2's no-collision premise does not hold for this name (#7205)
```

**Deliberately not a rollback.** Un-renaming the NICs phase 1 moved successfully leaves the box in a third state neither phase understands. Finishing the pass and reporting per name is the discipline phase 2 already chose in #5842. Only the specific unfreeable name is declined; others are unaffected.

## 3. The protected set was accepted and dropped

`applyStartupNamingPolicy` forwarded the #1922 lifeline set to the mapped branch and discarded it on the positional one.

Positional mode **should** have no strand refusal — it claims every present NIC by design, so "the lifeline moved" is the normal case, not an error. But silently dropping the parameter meant a reader could not tell a deliberate non-use from an oversight. The non-use is now explicit, tested, and says so once in the log when a non-empty set reaches the branch that will not honour it. The issue's own framing: *"Either use it or do not take it."*

A **control** test pins that the mapped branch still receives the set — a "fix" that stopped threading it altogether would satisfy the positional test and silently disable device-map's strand refusal, the one place it is load-bearing.

## One existing fixture was unfaithful, and that is how item 1 announced itself

#5842's `stubPositionalRenameSeams` returned a **constant** interface list, so a "successful" pass left the fake box still wearing `enp5s0`/`enp6s0` — a rename that reports success and takes no effect, which is *precisely* item 1's defect. Its success control could not distinguish a converged pass from an inert one, and adding the verification turned it red immediately. The seam now models the rename.

| treat a readback failure as converged | **RED** — `…ReportsAnUnreadableInterfaceList_7205` |

## PR #8047 — fairness-eval: score a stream by the window, not by its own sample count [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7206-fairness-density`

Part of #7206 — row **A1-b5-F3**. Does not close the cohort; my sweep on that issue found 3 of 8 rows already fixed and 5 live, and this is one of the 5.

## The defect

`per_flow_throughputs` divided each stream's summed throughput by `v.len()` — the number of accepted intervals **that stream appeared in** — rather than by the window's accepted-interval count.

So a stream present in **1 of 60** accepted intervals had its single sample taken as its own mean and was scored at its **full instantaneous rate**. A near-total outage produced per-flow throughputs that all looked equal, a CoV near zero, and a **PASS on the CoS fairness gate**.

That is a false PASS that can carry a merge decision — the reason this row is worth more than its LOW severity label.

## The fix

The divisor is `observed_buckets`, so an interval a stream is absent from contributes **0** to its mean. That is the same *"absent == 0, don't drop"* principle `per_flow_throughputs_all` already applies to fully-absent streams: the two are now consistent about what absence **means**, and differ only in *which* absence they cover — the documented V-9 split.

**The `!v.is_empty()` filter is deliberately kept.** A stream absent from every accepted interval is `per_flow_throughputs_all`'s case by that contract, and folding it in here would change the per-flow CoV *population* as well as the divisor — two changes wearing one commit.

`observed_buckets` cannot be zero: the coverage gate above returns `Err` below the steady-state minimum, and the regression asserts the 60-interval precondition rather than assuming it.

## A trap in reading this code

The doc comment immediately above the changed region says *"over EVERY seeded stream, mapping a stream absent from the steady window to 0"* — which reads exactly like the fix already being present. **It is not:** that comment belongs to `per_flow_throughputs_all`, declared a few lines below. The two live adjacent and the *wrong* one carries the reassuring comment. #7206 anticipated this (*"V-9's `per_flow_throughputs_all` zero-fills only FULLY-absent streams, which is the different case"*) and it is worth restating, because it is how this row survives a casual sweep.

## Tests

The regression asserts a **ratio, not a byte count**. What the fix establishes is that a 1-of-60 stream scores about 1/60 of a continuously-present stream at the same instantaneous rate; pinning an absolute number would break on any unrelated change to the window bounds and would not say what went wrong.

A **control** pins that two continuously-present streams at the same rate still score **equally** — without it, a "fix" that scaled every stream down by 1/60 would satisfy the primary cell and destroy every real comparison.

The existing single-socket `interval` helper cannot express *"socket A present, socket B absent"* in one interval, which is the only shape that reproduces this, so a `multi_interval` helper was added.

**Fail-on-revert:** restoring `sum / v.len()` reds the regression with

```
a stream present in 1 of 60 accepted intervals scored 125000000 against the
always-present stream's 125000000 at the SAME instantaneous rate.
```

Exactly equal — which is the defect stated as a number.

## No cluster smoke is owed, and that is checked

#7206's convention is that a `userspace-dp` Rust change moves the helper binary and owes a smoke. This one does not:

$ grep -rn 'fairness_eval' --include=*.rs userspace-dp/src/ \
    | grep -v '^userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/' \
    | grep -v '^userspace-dp/src/bin/fairness-eval.rs'
(no output)
```

## PR #8048 — cluster: stop reporting "No IP monitoring failures" for a demoted RG [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7338-ip-monitoring-status`

Closes #7338

`show chassis cluster ip-monitoring status` printed **"No IP monitoring failures"** for a redundancy group that ip-monitoring had actively **demoted** — and showed nothing about the unreachable targets either. Blank in **both** dimensions, on the primary HA failover diagnostic.

## Why the filter missed it

The renderer filtered by the raw `"ip:"` prefix. Global-threshold mode installs a **single aggregate debt** under `ipAggregateMonitorName`, whose own doc comment says it is *"deliberately distinct from the per-target `ip:<addr>` debts"* — and installs **no per-target debts by design**. So the filter matched nothing and the renderer fell through to the all-clear line.

**This is a false negative on a diagnostic, which is worse than a wrong number.** An operator reads it as *evidence* and rules ip-monitoring out — during the post-mortem of the very failover its global-weight demotion may have caused — then goes looking at, and possibly reconfiguring, the wrong subsystem. And global-threshold mode is the **vSRX-parity mode**: the one an operator following Junos documentation configures.

## The discriminator already existed

`isIPMonitorName` covers both classes, and its doc says in as many words that *any code that reconciles ONE class must use this discriminator to avoid clobbering the other.* The status renderer is such code and never got it.

## What the aggregate renders as now

A **threshold crossing** — the configured threshold and the weight actually applied — not an address:

```
  ip-monitoring        Status: global threshold crossed (threshold 100, weight 120 applied)
  (global-threshold mode installs one aggregate debt and no
   per-target debts, so individual targets are not listed here)
```

Naming an address would **invent a target**: in this mode `desiredRGIPDebts` installs one aggregate debt and returns, so no per-address debt exists to name. A diagnostic that has just stopped lying should not start fabricating instead.

`Monitor.IPGlobalThreshold` supplies the pair and reports `ok=false` for independent mode, so a caller cannot mistake a zero threshold for a configured one.

A per-target debt cannot normally coexist with the aggregate, but any that do are **printed rather than hidden behind the mode** — the two classes share one structure (#5080), and suppressing them would be the same class of blind spot one level down.

| render the aggregate as an address | **RED** — `…RowNamesThresholdAndWeight7338` |

**The first cell is the acceptance criterion verbatim** — *"restoring the `ip:` prefix filter must red the global-threshold case and leave the per-target case green."* That split is what makes the fix attributable to the aggregate class, rather than to "print something for every RG".

A fourth test pins that a **genuinely healthy RG still prints the all-clear line**. Without it, a "fix" that simply deleted that branch would satisfy every other cell while destroying the only positive signal the command has.

## PR #8049 — natshow: render the full NAT rule match, not the back-compat field [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7363-natshow-full-match`

Closes #7363

The rule-detail renderers computed a side's displayed address match from the **singular** field alone, and were wrong in **both** directions:

- A rule scoped only by `match destination-address-name` rendered as **`0.0.0.0/0`** — as matching *every* destination — because the address-book form never touches the CIDR field. **Over-broad**, in the direction an operator reads as "this rule is dangerously wide".
- A rule with a bracket list `[ A B C ]` rendered only **`A`**, because the singular holds the first element for back-compat while the plural holds all. **Under-broad**: the operator is shown a narrower scope than is configured.

**Not a variant of #6534.** That issue is about objects the dataplane did not install being rendered as if it did. Here the rule may be installed perfectly and the surface still misdescribes *which traffic it matches*.

## One helper, both renderers

The source side had the identical shape, so a fix confined to the destination side would have left `show security nat source rule` still rendering a name-scoped rule as `0.0.0.0/0`. The mutation matrix proves the split: reverting only the source side reds only the source test.

**The plural supersedes the singular rather than joining it.** The singular *is* the first element of the plural, so concatenating them prints the first address twice on every bracket-list rule. Reading the plural when populated and falling back otherwise is the only combination correct for both shapes — and it is the one boundary a renderer-level test would not isolate, so the helper carries a table test for it.

**Address-book names render alongside the CIDRs, not in place of them.** Junos permits a rule to carry both, and dropping either half reintroduces the defect for the mixed case.

The wildcard fallback stays with the callers rather than moving into the helper: the two renderers spell it for a different reason and there is no v6 wildcard here, so folding it in would hide which one is being printed.

| drop the name half of the helper | **RED** — 7 named failures |
| join the singular to the plural | **RED** — caught by `…/plural_supersedes_singular` |

**A control pins that a genuinely unscoped rule still renders `0.0.0.0/0`.** Without it, a "fix" that removed the fallback would satisfy every cell above and print a blank exactly where the operator needs to see that the rule really does match everything.

`security policies from-zone X { to-zone Y { ... } }` was accepted at commit and then **silently omitted**. Measured at `e01427aef`, same intent both ways:

| spelling | result |

| `from-zone trust { to-zone untrust { ... } }` (nested) | zone-pairs **0**, policies **0** — accepted |

**An honesty gap, not a parity gap.** Junos documents one combined hierarchy, so the nested shape is not something xpf is missing — it is a shape xpf accepts and does not implement. #4313 supplies the closed-world doctrine; this is its concrete application.

The failure mode is the dangerous one for a security policy: the operator wrote a permit-or-deny rule, the box said nothing, and the pair falls through to the default policy. **The contrast makes it worse** — an undefined zone in the *supported* form already produces a precise commit error, so an operator has every reason to read silence as acceptance.

**Reject-only.** Nothing that compiled before compiles differently; only the refused set changes. A bug here is a loud false rejection caught by the positive controls, never a silently wrong policy.

## The discriminator, and why the obvious alternative is wrong

Four spellings, **dumped rather than reasoned about**:

```
NESTED        Keys=[from-zone trust]                  children=[to-zone]
COMBINED      Keys=[from-zone trust to-zone untrust]  children=[policy]
FLAT-SET      Keys=[from-zone trust to-zone untrust]  children=[policy]
FZ-CONTAINER  Keys=[from-zone]                        children=[trust]
```

Flat-set collapses to the **same node shape** as the combined block form, so `len(Keys)` cannot separate those two. And the fully-nested container spelling `from-zone { X { to-zone { Y { ... } } } }` carries **`len(Keys) == 1`** and is **supported and compiles** — so a gate written as *"reject when `len(Keys) < 4`"* would refuse a valid configuration.

**The mutation matrix found exactly that.** That rewrite passed every test in the file. It only reds now because the escape prompted a positive control for the fourth shape. My own doc comment had also asserted, confidently, that such a gate "would most likely have rejected flat-set" — that was wrong, and it is corrected to name the spelling it actually breaks.

A `to-zone` **child** appears in exactly one of the four.

## Mutation matrix — 4/4 RED, each applied and building, 7112 collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| remove the gate | **RED** — reject + lenient cells |
| make the gate never fire | **RED** — same two |
| swap the discriminator for `len(Keys) < 4` | **RED** — `TestFromZoneContainerSpellingStillCompiles7523` |
| make the tolerant path strict | **RED** — the lenient cell |

## Strict on commit, lenient on load

Lenient on the tolerant Load / SyncApply ingress per the **#1960 no-brick contract**: the shape compiled to nothing before this gate and compiles to nothing now, so a leniently-loaded config enforces exactly what it enforced before, and refusing to boot would cost availability for no enforcement gain. Strict on the operator commit path, where the point is to stop the operator *believing* the policy is in force.

A test pins that the tolerant path **warns** rather than falling silent — downgrading to a warning is the contract; downgrading to silence is the defect.

## Runs on the tree, not the Config

A compiled `SecurityConfig` cannot distinguish *"no policies were written"* from *"the policies that were written were dropped"* — which is the whole defect. The gate therefore joins the tree-taking strict validators beside the #6525/#6735 zone gates.

## PR #8052 — config: reject a policy term naming an undefined as-path [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7471-aspath-reference-gate`

Closes #7471

Split from #6686, which fixes the as-path **regex** widening and deliberately leaves the **reference** direction.

A policy term could name an as-path that was never defined and commit clean — `CompileConfig` nil, no warning, `SchemaValidate` nil.

## Why it is a fail-open

xpf renders `match as-path NOPE` and renders no `bgp as-path access-list NOPE`, because there is no definition to render one from. **FRR accepts that**: `route_match_aspath_compile` merely stores the string, and evaluation-time `as_list_lookup` returns NULL for an undefined list, yielding `RMAP_NOMATCH`.

So the term **never matches**, and nothing anywhere complains — commit, `show configuration` and frr-reload all succeed.

- On `then reject`: **fail-open**. The routes the operator meant to block fall through to the next term or the policy default and are accepted.
- On `then accept`: a silent blackhole of routes meant to be admitted.

## The message deliberately differs from the community gate's

A dangling `match community` makes **frr-reload fail**, which fails the entire FRR config load — loud and self-limiting. A dangling `match as-path` is **accepted** and silently never matches.

Copying `validatePolicyCommunityReferencesStrict`'s wording would tell the operator to look for a load error that never happens, which is why these are two separate walks rather than one. A test asserts the message does **not** claim frr-reload would fail.

Strict on commit, lenient on the tolerant ingress under **its own flag** — not shared with the community one, so the two findings stay independently attributable (#1960 no-brick: a persisted config carrying the typo enforced nothing before and enforces nothing now).

Every `FromASPath` entry of every term is walked — `from as-path` is `multi: true`, and the dangling name is as likely to be the second entry, or in the second term, as the first. Both are pinned.

## Five existing fixtures needed as-path definitions — and two of them mattered

This is the same thing #2881 did to these files for `from community`. One still carries the comment *"Community must be defined (#2881 cross-reference gate)"* directly above the block this change had to extend.

**`routemap_seq_bound_5701` and `routemap_chain_bound_5732` are the ones that mattered.** They build oversized policies to prove a sequence/chain bound rejects them, and 5701's comment explicitly rested on as-path refs *"not [being] definedness-gated"*.

Left dangling, those tests would have gone red — and the naive fix (loosening them) would have left them passing **for the wrong reason**: this gate runs first, so the bound under test would never be reached. Defining the as-paths keeps each test's own property as its subject, and the now-false comment is corrected rather than left contradicting the code.

`TestSlotEscapeCoverage` then demanded a verdict row, because a leaf that no longer commits anything under a synthetic parent path has a rejection to classify. Its base defines the as-path, so the row measures the **slot escape** rather than this gate.

| walk only the first `FromASPath` entry | **RED** — the multi-entry cell |

## PR #8053 — snmp: reject an SNMPv3 user whose protocol has no key material [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7530-snmpv3-key-material`

Closes #7530

An SNMPv3 user configured with an auth or privacy **protocol** but without the corresponding key material committed clean and then **served at a lower security level than configured**. Measured at `3a7be7901`:

| config | commits | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `user ops { authentication-sha256; }` | **yes** | `AuthProto="sha256"`, **no password** |
| `... authentication-sha256 { password } privacy-aes128;` | **yes** | `PrivProto="aes128"`, **no password** |

## Why it degrades silently

`pkg/snmp/v3.go` derives the per-user floor from **key presence**, not configured intent:

```go
if user.authKey != nil && msgFlags&msgFlagAuth == 0 { drop }
if user.privKey != nil && msgFlags&msgFlagPriv == 0 { drop }
```

and `authKey` is derived only when the password is non-empty. So a user naming `authentication-sha256` with no password has `authKey == nil`, **no floor applies**, and a `noAuthNoPriv` request naming that user is answered — unauthenticated, in plaintext. Naming `privacy-aes128` without a privacy-password degrades authPriv to authNoPriv the same way: the scopedPDU is not encrypted.

**That floor is correct as written** — it is the #4897 bypass gate and must stay keyed on what the agent can actually verify. The defect is upstream, so the fix is upstream: the configuration should never have produced a user whose stated protocol has nothing behind it. This is the issue's own design note — *"a user that names a protocol without the material to honour it must fail at commit, not degrade at serve time."*

**Reject-only.** Nothing that compiled before compiles differently. A bug here is a loud false rejection caught by the positive controls, never a silently weaker agent.

## Three positive controls, because the gate must not overreach

| config | must still commit | why |
|---|---|---|
| complete auth only | yes | legitimate **authNoPriv** |
| complete authPriv | yes | the ordinary case |
| **no protocols at all** | yes | a genuine **noAuthNoPriv** user — rejecting it would make the level unconfigurable |

The gate fires on a **named protocol missing its own material**, never on an absent protocol. `M4` mutates exactly that boundary (drop the `!= ""` half) and reds against the noAuthNoPriv control.

## Mutation matrix — 5/5 RED, build **and vet** clean, 7127 collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| remove the gate | **RED** — plus `TestEveryStrictCommitGateIsWired`, a pre-existing census that independently verifies registration |
| drop the auth check | **RED** |
| drop the privacy check | **RED** |
| fire on an absent protocol too | **RED** — the noAuthNoPriv control |
| make the tolerant path strict | **RED** |

**The matrix was re-run after merging master**, because #7471 landed in the same two files while this was in flight and the merge rewrote both — a gate measured against the pre-merge tree would have been stale. Both gates survive the merge distinct and both chains are exercised.

## Strict on commit, lenient on load

Per the **#1960 no-brick contract**: such a config served at the lower level before this gate and still does, so refusing to boot costs availability with no gain in security — while a warning gets the operator to the fix. A test pins that the tolerant path **warns** rather than falling silent.
