## PR #8054 — apply-groups: merge a group's COMPACT leaf into a container peer [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7648-group-compact-merge`

Closes #7648

When an applied group supplied a stanza in the **compact** spelling and the local configuration already had a same-name node, the group's value was **dropped**. The **block** spelling of the same group merged correctly — two spellings of one intent, opposite outcomes.

`ast_groups.go` classifies a node carrying its body on `Keys` as a LEAF, and the leaf path **overrides** when a peer exists. A node whose body is in `Children` takes the container path and merges.

## The fix expands rather than special-cases

A compact group leaf whose key names a schema **container**, matched against a **container** peer, is the block spelling wearing a leaf's shape. Expanding its packed tail lets the *same* override logic run one level down — which is what makes this correct rather than merely different:

| local | expanded child finds | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `authentication-sha256 { }` | no peer | group's value **adopted** — the case that was dropped |
| `authentication-sha256 { authentication-password "local"; }` | a peer | ordinary override — **inline still wins** |

Inheritance is restored without weakening apply-groups precedence, and both are pinned.

## The peer-is-a-container gate is load-bearing, and the matrix proved it

Applying the expansion **regardless** of the peer's shape passed every test I had written. It is a real defect: a **compact local peer** is `IsLeaf` with its value on `Keys` and an **empty `Children`**, so merging the group's expanded child into it finds no peer and **adopts the group's value** — silently inverting apply-groups precedence for the one shape where both sides spell it the same way.

That escape is now covered by `TestBothCompactSpellingsStillLetInlineWin7648`.

## Interaction with #7530 — it changes what this defect looks like

Since that gate landed (earlier today), the dropped-password case no longer compiles to a silent `AuthPassword=""`. It is **rejected at commit**, because a user naming an auth protocol with no key material now fails:

```
snmp v3 usm local-engine user "ops" names authentication protocol "sha256"
but carries no authentication-password …
```

The silent credential loss became a loud error, which is better — **but it means a perfectly legitimate configuration (the group supplies the password compactly) could not be committed at all.** That is what this fixes, and it is why the primary test asserts a successful **commit** rather than a compiled value.

## Mutation matrix — build **and vet** clean, 7132 collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| remove the expansion | **RED** — the defect + equivalence cells |
| apply it to leaf peers too | **RED** — the precedence inversion above |
| drop the `children == nil` early-out | **GREEN — genuinely equivalent** |

The third is stated rather than papered over: `packedBodyChildren` cannot expand a childless schema, because `resolveSchemaChild` returns nil for it and the expander declines to guess. The check is a cheap early-out, not a guard, so a contrived test for it would assert nothing.

The equivalence test asserts the two spellings are **equal to each other** rather than pinning a literal on one side — the defect was precisely that they disagreed, and a literal would not have said which side was wrong.

## PR #8055 — host-inbound: warn on an application-scoped junos-host permit with a real gap [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7374-junos-host-app-gap`

Closes #7374

A `to-zone junos-host` **permit** narrowed by `match application` is stricter than the coarse kernel host-inbound gate, is not enforced on the direct host-bound path, and drew **no** commit-time warning. `junosHostPolicyStricterThanCoarseGate` tested the **source** dimension (#4168) and later the **destination** one (#6612); an application-narrowed permit reached neither.

It genuinely is stricter: the nft `xpf_hostinbound` chain admits every configured `system-services`/`protocols` token to the zone's local addresses, so a policy permitting only `junos-ssh` leaves https, ping, snmp and the rest admitted by the kernel while Junos would drop them to the junos-host default.

## This is a comparison, not a token test — and that is the whole design

A syntactic *"application != any"* check would fire on the very common

```
policy allow-mgmt { match { … application [ junos-ssh junos-ping ]; } then permit; }
```

**even when the zone admits nothing beyond ssh and ping** — a false positive on a large fraction of real configs. The project has explicit precedent against exactly that (#4455 Component B; the #3226 `all` advisory).

So the permitted application set is compared against the zone's **effective** admit set, through the same SSOTs the dataplane uses — `InterfaceHostInboundEffective`, `HostInboundServiceMatch`, `HostInboundProtocolMatch` — and only an admitted tuple the permit does not cover is reported.

**`TestAppScopedPermitWithNoGapIsSilent7374` is the cell the design turns on.** A naive token test passes every other test in the file and fails that one.

## Family handling — the false-positive test caught this

A token expands **per family**: `ping` yields ICMP echo-request for `ip` **and** ICMPv6 echo-request for `ip6`, while the application catalogue keys those separately (`junos-ping` is the v4 one). My first implementation compared every family and reported a v6 gap for **every** `application junos-ping` config.

A token is now judged in its **primary** family — `ip` when it has ip matches, `ip6` only for a v6-only token. The narrower reading (warn on the v4/v6 asymmetry too) may well be correct Junos semantics, but it is a **separate advisory with its own false-positive profile** and must not ride in on this one.

## It fails quiet

An unknown application, an unparseable port, or a custom application that cannot be reduced to an L4 tuple yields **no** warning. A false negative costs an advisory; a false positive costs the advisory's credibility on every config that does not have the problem.

Per-interface #3362 overrides are included: the coarse gate admits the **union** across the zone's local addresses, so an interface-level admit is as real a gap as a zone-level one.

## Mutation matrix — build **and vet** clean, 7134 collected

| cell | verdict |
|---|---|
| remove the zone-pair wiring | **RED** |
| degrade the comparison to a token test | **RED** — the false-positive cell |
| let an unresolvable application claim a gap | **RED** — the mixed-resolvability cell |
| ignore per-interface overrides | **RED** |
| treat `any` as narrowed | **GREEN — genuinely equivalent** |

The `any` cell is equivalence, not an escape: `any` is not a predefined application, so `appL4Matches` cannot reduce it and the fail-quiet guard bails on it anyway. The two early-outs cover each other, and removing **both** would red. Stated rather than papered over with a contrived test.

**Two cells were added because the matrix found them missing.** The mixed resolvable/unresolvable one is the subtler: with a *single* unresolvable application the permitted set ends up empty and the function returns quiet anyway, so the difference only appears when **some** applications resolve — and then a gap is reported that the application it could not read might well have closed.

## PR #8056 — api/SSE: flush the header block at connect [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7655-sse-connect-flush`

Closes #7655

`net/http` sends no response headers until the first `Write` or `Flush`. `setSSEHeaders` set header **values** only, so a client connecting to a **quiet** SSE feed blocked waiting for headers that were never sent — a browser `EventSource` on an idle firewall hung rather than establishing the stream.

**Not cosmetic.** Until the first event arrives — which on a quiet box could be hours — an SSE consumer cannot distinguish **"connected and quiet"** from **"not connected"**, and every reconnect/backoff decision rests on exactly that distinction. It also inverts the debugging order: the operator sees a hung client and looks for a network or auth problem while the stream is established and simply silent.

**The flush lives in `setSSEHeaders`, not at the call sites.** Both handlers had the same shape, and a per-site flush is a line the next handler forgets. Binding it to the function that sets the headers makes "headers set" and "headers sent" one step.

## The #7632 harness workarounds are removed — and they were the evidence

Those tests published on a **ticker until the GET returned**, because the GET could not return until an event landed. That is no longer true, and leaving the workarounds would have been worse than untidy:

**`TestLargeEventSurvivesASlowButProgressingReader7632` broke in an instructive way.** It treated *"any payload byte seen"* as its establishment signal. With headers now arriving first, the header block itself contains a capital **A** — `Date: … Aug …` — so the signal fired on the **header**, stopped the ticker before any event was published, and the read blocked to its deadline reporting `failed after 1 payload bytes`: a real failure that looked *exactly* like the severed-reader defect that test exists to catch. It now reads the header block, then publishes once.

The HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 helpers now do the GET and publish a single establishing event afterwards.

**Publishing after the GET is safe, and the ordering is not incidental:** `eventStreamHandler` subscribes **before** it calls `setSSEHeaders`, so "the GET returned" now implies "the subscription exists" — the lost-publish race the ticker was compensating for cannot occur. Subscriptions still have no replay, which is precisely why the publish must *follow* the GET.

**A side effect worth naming:** with the workarounds gone, the #7632 cells no longer depend on the flush at all. They test the write budget, this tests connect behaviour, and the two are now independently attributable.

## Validation

- Full Go suite: **69 packages, 0 named failures, rc=0**
- Fail-on-revert: removing the flush reds all three #7655 cells (build and vet clean) — **against the repaired harness**, so the result is not an artefact of the workarounds it replaced
- The tests run against a real `httptest.Server`. An `httptest.ResponseRecorder` records header *values* without modelling when they reach the wire, so it would have passed either way and could not have expressed this defect at all
- A third cell pins that events are **still delivered** after the connect flush — without it, a "fix" that flushed and broke the body would satisfy both header cells

## PR #8057 — grpcapi: canonical command strings for gRPC methods (#7172 cut 5a) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut5a-command-table`

Cut 5a of #7172. **Inert** — nothing reads this table until 5b wires it into `authorizeRPC`.

## Why it has to exist

The remote `cli` binary parses the command line **client-side** and sends a typed RPC; the line never crosses the wire. `authorizeRPC` sees `("/xpfv1.BpfrxService/GetInterfaces", *pb.GetInterfacesRequest)` and nothing resembling a command. So `deny-commands "show interfaces"` — which cut 3 enforces on the on-box CLI — has nothing to match remotely, and without this the remote surface is an unguarded path to exactly the commands an operator denied.

Adding a command string to the RPCs was rejected on principle: it would be **client-supplied**, so a caller wanting to evade a deny simply sends a different one. An authorization decision derived from attacker-controlled input is not an authorization decision, and being cheap to implement is the trap.

## Validation is against `cmdtree.Canonicalize`, not against the client

The obvious check was to parse `cmd/cli`'s command→topic mapping and assert the server table agrees. **That is unsound**: recovering the command path needs an AST walk of nested switches, and the topic is *computed* at two call sites — 92 of 129 topics have a literal call, the rest do not.

Such a test would certify ~71% of an authorization table and report clean on the remainder, **with nothing in its output separating the two**. That is existence standing in for coverage, and worse than no test, because the next reader trusts a green.

Instead every entry must canonicalize **to itself** — a real, already-canonical operational command. Fully sound, no client dependency, no partial coverage, and it reuses cut 1 rather than adding a second notion of what a valid command is. It also structurally excludes the error class that killed the idea of *deriving* these strings from method or topic names (`buffers-detail` → `show buffers detail` is wrong; only `show system buffers detail` resolves).

**It earned its place immediately: it rejected twelve of my own hand-authored entries**, including `show security nat source deterministic` where the tree has `deterministic-nat`. Completeness alone would have shipped all twelve — each *has* an entry, just the wrong one.

## Four methods have no operational command at all

`show ospf`, `show isis`, `show rip`, `show vrrp` are not nodes in the operational tree. There is no canonical spelling to map to, and inventing one would put a string here that no operator can type and no deny regex is written against. They are **named absent with that reason**.

This is **consistent, not a gap**: cut 3's on-box gate canonicalizes before matching, so it cannot resolve them either and fails closed for a restricted class. Both surfaces refuse them for the same reason.

## Absences are named, not bare

A method missing from the table is indistinguishable from a forgotten one. Every intended absence carries a reason, and the completeness test rejects an empty one — otherwise it must choose between failing on every intended absence and accepting every accidental one.

## Mutation matrix

All build-clean, `collected == reported == 3`.

| # | Mutation | named red |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | wrong-but-plausible command (`deterministic`) | `TestEveryMappedCommandIsCanonical7172` |
| 2 | non-canonical abbreviation (`sho int`) | `TestEveryMappedCommandIsCanonical7172` |
| 3 | drop a method's entry without naming it | `TestEveryPricedMethodIsMappedOrNamedAbsent7172` |
| 4 | method both mapped and excused | `TestEveryPricedMethodIsMappedOrNamedAbsent7172` |
| 5 | stale entry for an unserved method | `TestEveryPricedMethodIsMappedOrNamedAbsent7172` |
| 6 | empty excuse reason | `TestEveryPricedMethodIsMappedOrNamedAbsent7172` |

Four cells initially reported **NO DIFF** because the regexes assumed single spaces and gofmt pads the map — the harness refusing to score a mutation that did not apply, which is what keeps a void cell from counting as an escape.

## Gate

`go test ./... -count=1` — **rc=0, 69 packages, 0 named FAILs**.

## Next

**5a-2**: the 129 `ShowText` topics and 19 `SystemAction` verbs, which are priced from the *decoded request* rather than the method name and so need their own tables. **5b**: wire into `authorizeRPC`, unmapped-method-denies scoped to classes that configured regexes. **6**: retire #6838 last.

## PR #8059 — frr: report an unparseable IS-IS adjacency row instead of dropping it [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7430-isis-malformed-row`

Closes #7430

`GetISISAdjacency` `continue`d on a row it could not parse — no header seen (so the trailing width is unknown), or a row shorter than that width — so the row simply **did not appear**.

To an operator debugging a missing neighbour that is indistinguishable from *"the adjacency does not exist"*, and it points them at the wrong problem. A row saying **this line could not be parsed** points at the real one: an FRR version change, or a truncated `vtysh` response.

**The rejected alternative is recorded because it is the tempting one.** Rendering the row with empty derived fields reports a neighbour in state `""` — quieter than the #6590 column-forgery but still false. So the shape is *report as unparseable*, never *render partially*: the derived fields stay **empty** and consumers branch on `Malformed`, so a consumer that forgets to branch cannot read a fabricated state.

`Raw` is peer-influenced text — the first column is the peer's advertised dynamic hostname — so both display sites route it through `termsafe`, exactly as the parsed cells are (#6468).

## The orthogonality constraint is pinned

The issue asks for this by name, and it is the sharpest part. An escape-bearing but **space-free** hostname must remain a **well-formed** row. If it were marked `Malformed`, the #6468/#6579 escape fixtures would stop exercising the **display** guard they exist for — they would be testing this parser's rejection instead, and **the display guard could rot undetected**.

It stays well-formed because `strings.Fields` splits on `unicode.IsSpace` only, so ESC/DEL/BEL do not split a field. `TestEscapeBearingHostnameStaysWellFormed7430` pins it, and mutation M4 reds it.

## An existing test changed, deliberately

`TestISISMalformedRowsAreNotRendered6590` asserted `len(adjs) == 0`. **That was #6590's mechanism, not its subject.** The subject is *no guesswork*, and this change keeps it while replacing the mechanism: the row is returned with every derived field empty.

So the assertion moved from **"no rows"** to **"no derived content"** — the property that actually mattered. A row with a fabricated `State` would be #6590's forgery arriving by a different route, and the updated test catches exactly that. Its doc comment now says which half changed and why, so the next reader is not left to infer it.

**I found this only by running the package unfiltered.** My `-run '7430'` run was green while `pkg/frr` was red — the filtered-run trap in its plainest form.

## Mutation matrix — 4/4 RED, build **and vet** clean, 360 collected

| cell | verdict |

| drop the short row again | **RED** — `…ShortRowIsReportedNotDropped7430` + the 6590 guard |
| drop the headerless row again | **RED** — `…HeaderlessTableIsReportedNotDropped7430` + the 6590 guard |
| give a malformed row a derived field | **RED** — the 6590 guard, which is now the one that owns that property |
| mark **every** row malformed | **RED** — the orthogonality cell plus two pre-existing #6590 cells |

The last is the important signature: a change that would break the escape fixtures reds the orthogonality cell *and* the #6590 ordinary-row and trailing-width cells together.

- Both display sites branch (gRPC and CLI); a fix at one would have left the other dropping rows

## PR #8062 — Extract the logical-tunnel-ingress primitive (#7167 step 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7167-logical-ingress-primitive`

First step of #7167 (logical-tunnel-ingress adjudication). **Behaviour-neutral refactor, no new callers, no behaviour change.** This does NOT resolve issue 7167 — that issue stays OPEN.

> **Note on this line:** it originally paired a closing keyword with the issue number inside a negated sentence ("Does not ... issue"). GitHub matched the keyword and auto-closed the issue one second after this PR merged. **A negation is invisible to the parser, and so are backticks** — so a PR that needs to say it does not close an issue must never place close/closes/closed/fix/fixes/resolve/resolves immediately before the number. Write "issue 7167" instead.

## Why this first

Turning decapsulated tunnel plaintext into a packet the AF_XDP worker pipeline can adjudicate is four steps: synthesize Ethernet framing around the raw inner L3 bytes, apply the RFC 6040 decap-side ECN combine, reparse the inner flow, and build an inner meta bound to the tunnel's **logical** ifindex and the zone that ifindex maps to.

Native GRE decap has done exactly this since #921 — but **inline inside `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame` and welded to GRE**: the endpoint lookup filters `TunnelKind::Gre` and indexes `forwarding.gre_decap_index`. #7167 needs the same treatment for WireGuard and IPsec plaintext, which today reach the kernel FIB with no zone policy, session, NAT, screen or filter evaluation.

Extracting the protocol-agnostic half means that work **adds a caller instead of a second copy**. A divergence between two copies of a synthesize/rebind/reparse path is precisely the #7176 C179-001 defect, one protocol family over — that one cost a `then reject` its reply and a `then log` its event for every packet that arrived before its neighbour resolved.

The function was 202 lines (computed by brace-matching, not estimated); the split is at the `let mut synthetic = ...` line, leaving GRE's outer parse / key handling / endpoint match in place and moving ~93 lines into the primitive.

## The generation fields are required on purpose

`LogicalIngressParams` deliberately has **no `Default`** and **no `Option`** on `config_generation` / `fib_generation`. A struct literal must name every field, so a future caller cannot acquire an attachment generation by omission.

Those two fields are what #7167 invariant 5's fencing rests on — *"a packet decrypted under an old attachment must never be evaluated under a replacement's zone/VRF identity."* GRE can inherit them from the triggering RX meta because it runs inside a worker on a received packet. **A caller with no ingress meta — the WireGuard control thread — has no such value to inherit**, and fabricating one (`0`, or a freshly-read current value) would compile, adjudicate, and violate the invariant **silently, because a fabricated generation always looks current**. No test fails in that picture, so the type is what has to make the question unavoidable.

`meta_flags` is required for the same reason: GRE passes `GRE_DECAP_INGRESS_FLAG` so the forward builder selects the #2486 `tcp-mss gre-in` clamp, and "whatever GRE passes" is not an answer for another protocol.

`outer_ecn` is passed in rather than derived: GRE reads it from the still-present outer IP header, but a protocol whose outer header is already gone by this point must capture it earlier rather than silently skip the RFC 6040 combine.

## Behaviour-neutrality, proved in both directions

- **With** the extraction applied and GRE as sole caller: **4,985 collected / 0 failed**.
- **Same tree with the change stashed** (verified clean at master): **4,985 collected / 0 failed**.

That equality only means something if the suite actually reaches the extracted code, so that was checked rather than assumed:

- **33 named GRE-decap tests** run in the suite, across dedicated files (`tests_native_gre_ecn.rs`, `tests_gre_outer_bound_6748.rs`, `tests_gre_version_6842.rs`, `tests_gre_local_delivery.rs`).
- **Mutation inside the new primitive** — neutralizing the ECN combine (`params.outer_ecn` → `None`) — reds two of them **by name**: `native_gre_decap_combines_outer_ce_into_inner_ecn` and `native_gre_decap_drops_illegal_outer_ce_over_not_ect_inner`. Reverted, both green again.

So the extracted body is live and covered, not dead code the suite skips past.

## Gates

- `make test-rust` — 4,985 collected / 0 failed (and identical stashed).
- `go test -count=1 ./...` — 69 packages ok, 0 `--- FAIL`.
- Three-dot diff touches 3 files, all of them this change's own.
- **No cluster smoke**: no new caller and no behaviour change. The WireGuard and IPsec callers that follow will owe one.

## What this does not do

It does not adjudicate anything. WireGuard plaintext is still written straight to the wgN TUN (`coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs:215`) and IPsec plaintext still surfaces on an xfrmi the planners exclude. Those are the next steps, and the sequencing matters — see the premise-verification comment on #7167, in particular that #5275's transit gate documents the IPsec bypass as **load-bearing today**, so an IPsec fix must *replace* that reliance rather than merely block it.

## PR #8063 — dhcp: add opt-in dhcp-socket-type for Kea Dhcp4 [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7318-dhcp-socket-type`

## What

Adds `system services dhcp-local-server dhcp-socket-type (raw | udp)` as an **opt-in** leaf. The default is unchanged: absent means the key is not emitted, Kea applies its documented default `raw`, and every existing config renders byte-for-byte as it did before.

Closes #7318

## Why the premise needed correcting first

#7318 said host-inbound cannot gate DHCPv4 because "the packet never reaches the `xpf_hostinbound` chain." **It does reach it.** Measured on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` with drop rules at input priority -100:

```
udp dport 67 ip daddr 255.255.255.255  -> counter { packets 1 }   Kea still OFFERed
udp dport 67 ip daddr 10.0.61.1        -> counter { packets 1 }   Kea still REPLIEd
```

netfilter sees the packet, matches, and drops it — it just drops **a copy Kea never reads**, because AF_PACKET took its own copy at `ptype_all`, before `ip_rcv`. Same conclusion as the issue, different mechanism, and the difference is what explains why *no* nft rule can ever fix it.

Two consequences the issue did not state:

- The **relayed/renewing unicast leg is ungateable too**, not just the broadcast DISCOVER. Kea's LPF admits "the broadcast address **or** unicast to the specific address on the interface".
- Kea in `raw` mode *also* holds per-address UDP `:67` sockets. Those do **not** create a gateable path — I nearly reported that they did, and Kea's own filter source refuted it before it became a claim.

## Why `udp` closes the exposure, measured

The issue argued a socket-type flip would not close the exposure by itself and would still need #4455 Component A. That is not what the hardware says. With Dhcp4 flipped to `udp` on the same node:

| Dhcp4 mode | AF_PACKET socks | same INPUT-drop rule | Kea's answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `raw` | 2 | `packets 1` | **REPLIED** — ungateable |
| `udp` | **0** | `packets 1` | **NO-REPLY** — gated |

Identical rule, identical packet, counter increments in **both** — so this cannot be attributed to the rule matching or not. It isolates to which socket receives. On `udp` the only traffic Kea can serve is unicast to a zone address, which today's per-zone rules already match, so **no Component A is required**: on UDP Kea does not receive broadcast at all, and the fall-through Component A would have to close has nothing listening behind it.

### This contradicts acceptance criterion 3 — deliberately, and here is why

#7318's third criterion says "a socket-type flip alone must not be described as closing the exposure." That criterion rests on the premise that a broadcast DISCOVER still leaks in `udp` mode. **That premise is measured false** (Kea disables broadcast reception on UDP sockets; the DISCOVER goes unanswered). I am flagging the contradiction rather than quietly shipping through it. The docs scope the claim precisely to `udp` mode and state the direct-client cost alongside it.

## Criterion 2: address-less client behaviour validated, not assumed

```
BASELINE (raw)   broadcast DISCOVER : OFFER      unicast REQUEST : REPLY
AFTER udp        broadcast DISCOVER : NO-REPLY   unicast REQUEST : REPLY
```

The cost is real and measured: directly-attached clients with no address stop being served. This is why it is opt-in and **not** a default flip. Cluster config was backed up and restored; verified back to `raw` afterwards.

## The advisory is the load-bearing half

The failure mode is silent and delayed — already-leased clients keep renewing, so breakage surfaces when a **new** client asks for an address, not at commit. `validateDHCPSocketTypeWarnings` names the affected interfaces and both client populations, and tests assert those substantive facts so it cannot degrade into "sets dhcp-socket-type".

## PR #8064 — Restore the RSS indirection table on daemon stop [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7619-rss-restore-on-stop`

Closes #7619

xpf concentrates a bound mlx5 NIC's RSS hash outputs onto queues `0..workers-1` so the AF_XDP dataplane's queue set receives the traffic. #6801 reverts that when an interface **leaves** xpf's ownership while the daemon keeps running — but the shutdown path never did. `restoreStep0TunablesOnShutdown` put back coalescence, host-scope knobs and neigh `retrans_time_ms`, and skipped `rssOwned` entirely.

So a clean `systemctl stop xpfd` left every bound NIC with a table shaped for a dataplane that is no longer there. The kernel stack ran on the concentrated subset until the next boot re-claimed the NIC or an operator ran `ethtool -X <if> default` by hand. Same end state #6801 fixed for a released interface, reached through the other door.

## The three questions the issue left open

**Is stop the right trigger, given a restart also stops?** Yes, by impossibility. systemd delivers an ordinary SIGTERM either way and exposes nothing at stop time that separates a restart's stop from a real one — `grep -rn 'INVOCATION_ID|MAINPID|systemd.*restart' pkg/daemon/` finds nothing, and there is no signal to add. "Exempt a restart" is not implementable, so the choice is restore-always or restore-never. The churn restore-always adds to a restart is two `ethtool` calls per owned NIC across a window in which the daemon is not forwarding anyway. Restore-never is the defect.

**How is it bounded?** `rssShutdownRestoreBudget` = 5s, mirroring `hostAuthCloseoutBudget` (#5874). The unit caps the whole stop at `TimeoutStopSec=20`, so a hung `ethtool` must cost a logged timeout rather than a SIGKILLed daemon. The walk is name-sorted so a truncation is deterministic, it truncates rather than aborting, and one NIC's failure does not abandon the rest.

**What about retry?** Logged and left, deliberately unlike #6801's. That path drops ownership only after a successful restore so a later reconcile can retry; a stop has no later tick and the ownership map exits with the process. The reconciliation is the next boot's claim, which re-captures and re-applies. A NIC left concentrated by a failed restore-on-stop is stranded only if xpfd never starts again — a case no shutdown path can fix.

## Two structural changes, both load-bearing

`step0RestoreHasCaptures` extracts the empty-captures early return. **A NIC with ONLY rss ownership must admit**, or the restore call added at the bottom of the caller never runs and the defect survives its own fix. That is the subtlest way to get this wrong, and it is invisible to review.

`restoreStep0Captures` splits the restore body from the snapshot handoff (apply-lock, `priorTunablesMu`, one-shot clear) so the **call** — the thing that was missing — is reachable from a test with injected backends. Without it, every cell can only exercise the leaf function, and all of them stay green when the call site is deleted. Mutation M1 below is exactly that, and only the wiring cell catches it.

The host-scope gate stays `if active`, unchanged, rather than narrowing to `hasHostScope`: the two are equivalent only via `restoreHostScopeTunables`' internal empty-value skips, and that is not an equivalence to assume inside a change about something else.

## Does this owe a failover smoke?

No. The restore runs at `daemon_run_shutdown.go:308` — **after** VRRP's priority-0 burst (line 267), after `cluster.Stop()` (274) and after session-sync stop (280). The peer has already taken over before the first `ethtool` is issued, so the added work cannot appear in failover timing. Checked rather than assumed, because "it is the shutdown path" was reason enough to ask.

## Mutation matrix — 6 cells, full-suite, clean-tree precondition asserted

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 delete the call from `restoreStep0Captures` | RED | **RED(1)** — `TestShutdownRestorePathActuallyIssuesTheRSSDefault7619` (the only cell that sees it) |
| M2 empty-captures guard forgets `rssOwned` | RED | **RED(2)** |
| M3 abort on first failure instead of continuing | RED | **RED(1)** |
| M4 budget → `time.Hour` | RED | **RED(1)** |
| M5 log-string reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |
| M6 restore never consults the map | RED | **RED(4)** |

Six cells in `rss_shutdown_restore_7619_test.go`: the defect itself, one-failure-does-not-abandon-the-rest, budget truncation asserted as **boundedness not timing**, empty ownership as a no-op, an eight-row truth table over the guard whose middle rows keep the `active` gate honest, and the wiring cell.

## PR #8065 — syslog: keep every selector on the file and user sinks [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7187-file-user-sink-selectors`

Refs #7187 — the independent first cut the issue names ("small and independent of the envelope work above; it can land first"). **Does not close #7187.**

## The defect

The `file` and `user` syslog destinations discarded every facility/severity pair the operator authored **except the last one**.

Both held a scalar `Facility`/`Severity` pair on their compiled struct, and `compileSystem` ASSIGNED into it from inside the per-child loop:

```go
file.Facility = fac
file.Severity = sev
```

So `file messages { daemon info; authorization warning; }` compiled to a single selector — `authorization warning` — and the earlier pairs were gone before any renderer, validator or `show` command could observe them.

**That is why nothing ever diagnosed it.** The reduction happens at compile time, so every downstream consumer sees a config that looks exactly like the one-selector config the operator did not write. There is no wrong value to notice and no leftover to warn about. The `host` sink has always appended into `SyslogHostConfig.Facilities`; this brings the other two to the same shape.

## The render

Both structs now carry `Selectors []SyslogFacility`. The rsyslog render joins a destination's selectors with `;` into the one drop-in that destination owns:

```
daemon.info;authorization.warning	/var/log/messages
```

One target means one drop-in, and rsyslog's selector field already expresses the OR that Junos means by several statements under one stanza — so this is a wider selector, not several files racing for one path. The two render sites, which the #5797 comments describe as deliberately identical, are now literally one helper.

## Two decisions, not consequences

**An empty selector list still renders `*.*`.** Before this change an unset scalar pair rendered that (empty facility and empty severity both mapped to `*`), and a destination authored with no selector should not silently disappear.

**An unsafe selector drops itself, not the destination.** With a scalar pair those were the same thing. With a list, taking the destination down because one sibling selector was poisoned would delete the operator's *safe* selectors too and stop their logging entirely — a worse outcome than the injection being defended against. For a one-selector destination the behaviour is bit-identical: nothing safe survives, the list is empty, the destination is skipped (pinned by `TestAllUnsafeSelectorsSkipTheDestination7187`).

That partial drop is a **new and quieter way to lose configuration** — the destination still logs, so nothing else signals it — so it gets its own warning naming the destination and the selector, with a count assertion so a surviving selector is not reported as dropped.

## Fixture design

The compiler cells use **three** selectors, not two. With two, "keeps the first" and "keeps them all" are distinguished, but "keeps the first two" is not; three separates every prefix- and suffix-keeping variant from keeping them all, and makes the order assertion meaningful. A separate cell puts a recognized modifier (`structured-data`) **between** two selectors — the #4303 S-1 interaction a two-line fixture cannot see.

## Mutation matrix — 6 cells, full-suite over the 5 touched packages

| M1 file assigns instead of appends (the original bug) | RED | **RED(2)** |
| M2 user assigns instead of appends | RED | **RED(1)** |
| M3 render emits only `parts[0]` | RED | **RED(3)** |
| M4 one unsafe selector kills the destination | RED | **RED(1)** |
| M5 empty list skips instead of `*.*` | RED | **RED(1)** |
| M6 comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

## PR #8066 — test/incus: declare and gate the target-service dependency [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/8040-target-service-preflight`

Closes #8040

Every per-class harness in `test/incus` sends traffic from the LAN-side source container, through the firewall, to a WAN-side target on VLAN 80 — and needs that target running per-class `iperf3 -s` on **5200-5211** and per-class TCP echo on **6200-6211**, matching the port→forwarding-class grid in `cos-iperf-config.set`.

**Nothing in the tree said so.** No script could create a listener, and each harness checked only the single port it was about to use. So a run spent a build, a deploy and the shared `/tmp/xpf-cluster.lock` before aborting on the first class it happened to reach, saying nothing about the other twenty-three. Fixing that one port and re-running found the next.

This cost two full lock cells during the current campaign — on #7100, and again on #7159 this morning.

## The asymmetry that hid it

`make test-failover` uses the **default** iperf3 port, not the per-class grid. So the standing smoke passes at 18+ Gb/s while every per-class harness is unrunnable. *The green everyone watches does not cover the dependency everything else needs.*

## `target-services.sh` — one place that knows the contract

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `status` | the whole 24-port grid in one table, **plus** whether the host answers ICMP and whether there is an incus handle for it |
| `check [port...]` | the gate a harness calls |
| `up` / `down` | provision, where a handle exists |

`status` reports three things separately on purpose — host-down, host-up-services-down, and no-management-path are three different problems with three different owners, and a table of twenty-four closed ports does not distinguish them.

**`check` takes ports: the predicate is narrow, the diagnosis is wide.** Naming only the ports a run needs means an unrelated class being down does not block a two-port smoke — an over-rejecting gate is one runners learn to skip — while the failure report is always the full grid, because a runner wants every hole at once rather than one per re-run. `test-mouse-latency-matrix.sh`, `fairness-harness.sh` and `cos-be-contention-harness.sh` call it **before any CoS mutation**, so a failure leaves the cluster in its prior state.

## What `up` honestly cannot do

On the standing loss cluster the VLAN-80 target is external lab hardware. Measured from `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`:

```
$ ping -c2 172.16.80.200        → 0% loss, 0.29ms
$ ip neigh show 172.16.80.200   → REACHABLE dev ge-0-0-2.80
$ incus list loss: --all-projects -c n4 | grep 172.16.80.200   → (nothing)
ports 5200 5202 6200 6201 50051 22 → all closed
```

It answers ICMP, is not an incus instance in any project, and accepts no ssh. There is no management path to it from here, so `up` prints exactly what must be started and where. That boundary is the honest one — this cannot invent a path that does not exist, but no harness should rediscover the fact again.

## PR #8067 — ipmon: make the debounce and throttle falsifiable [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/8027-falsifiable-debounce`

Closes #8027

`TestDebounceCoalescing` stayed **green with the debounce disabled entirely** — changing the run loop's window check from `now.Sub(e.dirtySince) >= e.debounce` to `>= 0` reds nothing in it.

## Why, and it is structural

Actuation is driven by a **dirty bit**: one actuation covers every pending transition regardless of how many arrived, so a flap storm coalesces *by design*. The `<= 2` bound is therefore satisfied by the shape of the code whatever the window does, and cannot distinguish

- *coalescing works* — the property the test was named for; from
- *multiple actuations are unreachable in this fixture* — true regardless.

A bound satisfied by structure rather than by the behaviour under test measures nothing about that behaviour.

## What actually falsifies a debounce

Not a count. Its job is not to reduce one — the dirty bit already does that — it is to **delay**: after a state change, no actuation until the window elapses. So the assertion has to be a latency **lower** bound, which `debounce_falsifiable_8027_test.go` adds, for the debounce and the throttle separately.

Three separate mechanisms, and each needs its own instrument:

| mechanism | what it does | falsified by |
|---|---|---|
| dirty bit | one actuation covers every pending change | a count under a storm |
| **debounce** | delays actuation until the window elapses | a latency lower bound after a change |
| **throttle** | paces consecutive actuations | a latency lower bound after an actuation |

## Why this is not the timing flake #7969 just removed

- The cells run on the package's **existing fake clock**, so the window is crossed by `clock.Advance`, not by elapsed wall time.
- The load-bearing assertion is an **absence** — nothing actuated before the window — and contention can only make an actuation *later*, never earlier. **A loaded machine cannot produce a false RED here.**
- It *could* produce a false GREEN (a wedged loop that never actuates at all), so each cell is bracketed by liveness waits proving the engine actuates both before and after the quiet period. The real-time sleep between them is a **generosity, not a deadline**: raising it can only make the test more patient, and no assertion reads its value.

**Each mechanism is set small while the other is under test, deliberately.** With the production proportions the throttle is the binding constraint, and an actuation held back by the throttle is indistinguishable from one held back by the debounce — a test written that way passes with the debounce disabled, which is the defect being fixed. Binding both separately also stops a future fix from satisfying one cell by widening the other.

## The rename

`TestDebounceCoalescing` → `TestActuationCountStaysBoundedUnderFlapStorm`, which is what it covers. It keeps **real time** on purpose: it is the end-to-end exercise of the real timer path that the fake-clock cells do not reach, and #7969's stabilisation of it is untouched. Renaming rather than deleting is the honest option #8027 offers — the count bound is real coverage of the dirty bit and the throttle; it just is not coverage of the debounce.

## Mutation matrix — the issue's acceptance criterion is row one

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| `>= e.debounce` → `>= 0` | RED | **RED(1)** — and the one test that reds is the NEW one. `TestActuationCountStaysBoundedUnderFlapStorm` does not, confirming the old test still cannot see it. |
| `>= e.throttle` → `>= 0` | RED | **RED(2)** |
| `fire = true` → `false` | RED | **RED(12)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

## One thing the fake clock caught that review would not have

A first draft assumed `Apply` alone produced the baseline actuation. **It does not** — an all-passing config computes an empty overlay, which is what the engine already believes, so `markDirty` is a no-op and nothing ever actuates. Under a real clock that assumption would have quietly shifted what the measurement was anchored to; under the fake clock the test simply never actuated and said so, in setup. The baseline now comes from a real state change.

## PR #8068 — configstore: accept a flat set script in LoadOverride [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7527-load-override-flat`

Closes #7527

`LoadOverride` called the hierarchical parser unconditionally and then **atomically replaced the candidate** with whatever came back. The parser treats newlines as whitespace, so a flat set-command file did not fail to parse — it collapsed into ONE junk top-level node, and the call returned `nil`.

Measured before the fix, not inferred:

```
in:  "set system host-name probe-a\nset system domain-name example.net"
out: set set system host-name probe-a set system domain-name example.net
err: <nil>
```

The operator's entire candidate became that single node, whose key path is the whole file, and both the CLI and the RPC printed success.

## It is an ordinary workflow, not a contrived one

`show configuration | display set > backup.txt` then `load override backup.txt` is how an operator restores a config. And `load set` accepts **only `terminal`** — so there was no file-based path for flat input anywhere in the CLI. The one an operator would naturally reach for was the one that silently destroyed the candidate.

## The fix, and the one distinction that matters

`parseOverrideContent` classifies with the same `hasFlatVerb` scan `LoadMerge` has used since #3442, and replays flat lines the same way.

**The difference between the two verbs is the starting tree.** Merge replays onto a clone of the candidate; override replays onto an EMPTY one. Reusing `LoadMerge`'s body directly — the obvious way to share the code — would silently turn `load override` into a second spelling of `load merge`, and *every other assertion about this path would still pass*. That distinction gets its own cell, and it is the one that survives mutation M2.

## Why accepting flat input is the bounded choice

The normal preference is the reject-only fix: a loud false rejection beats a silent wrong result. I considered it — refuse flat input with an actionable error — and rejected it, because the honest error would have to say *"use `load set`"*, which does not take a file. That leaves an operator holding a backup they cannot restore.

Accepting is bounded anyway, because **misclassification fails loud**: if a hierarchical file were mistaken for flat, the #3442 M3 rule rejects the first line carrying no recognized verb, naming the line. It cannot produce a silently wrong candidate. The reverse direction is the defect being fixed.

The replacement tree is built standalone and swapped in only on complete success, so a rejected override leaves the candidate byte-identical — #5187's atomicity, for the same reason: a partial delete of deny terms fails open.

## Mutation matrix — 5 cells, full package suite each

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| revert to the unconditional hierarchical parse | RED | **RED(2)** |
| flat replays onto the candidate instead of empty (override→merge) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the every-line-needs-a-verb check | RED | **RED(1)** |
| override's flat detection never fires | RED | **RED(2)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Five cells: flat script accepted; override REPLACES rather than merges; hierarchical path unchanged; a stray non-verb line rejected **and the candidate left byte-identical**; comments-only.

## A harness defect found on the way

The first matrix run scored M1 as a no-op edit and voided every later cell. The harness compared `git status --porcelain` before and after — which is **identical for two different contents of the same already-modified file** — and its `git checkout --` then reverted the uncommitted fix, so all the later anchors were missing. An instrument that cannot tell "I changed the file" from "I didn't" reports the reassuring answer either way. The fix was committed first (a mutation harness needs a clean tree as a precondition) and the check changed to a content hash.

## PR #8069 — Reclaim a dead worker's NAT holder bits from the status tick (#6979 F4/F5) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/6979-retire-worker`

A pool-mode NAT holder bit is set on reserve and cleared only when **that same worker** later runs its own release. `spawn_supervised_worker` catches a `worker_loop` panic, sets `dead`, and lets the thread exit — nothing respawns it, so its `SessionTable` dies with it and never reaps. No TTL, no reconcile: those pool ports never come back, and SNAT for new flows eventually fails `AllocatorExhausted`.

## The primitive already existed and was deliberately unwired

`PortAllocator::retire_worker` landed under **#7092** with its own doc saying so:

> *"NOT WIRED YET … nothing calls it on a production path, so #7092's leak is not closed by this change alone. Choosing the call site is its own decision with its own hazard."*

Verified: zero production callers, only `nat/tests_pool.rs`. **#7092 is CLOSED while its own landed code states its leak is open.** This PR is that deferred decision.

The hazard it named for this call site — the 1 Hz tick *"would walk `live_by_flow` under the alloc mutex on every tick unless it also carries 'already retired' state"* — is answered by `WorkerRuntimeAtomics::holders_retired`, a one-shot `compare_exchange`. A dead worker is swept once; every later tick pays one relaxed load per record. Three sweeps are wired, one per allocator family (interface-mode, pool rules, NAT64 prefixes), each of which owns its own allocator.

## Scope: the PANIC route only

The **REPLAN** route — `worker_id` is `queue_id % workers`, so a shrinking plan retires ids that still hold bits while `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` carries the allocator across the reload — sets **no flag at all**. There is nothing here to react to, and the plan path that knows the retired ids doesn't hold the allocator. It needs a signal that doesn't exist yet and is **not** in this change. `retire_worker`'s doc is corrected to say the same.

## Two of my own tests were wrong, and the mutations found both

- The first drove `retire_dead_worker_holders` **directly**. Deleting the call from the status path left it **green** — it bound what the sweep does and nothing about whether anything calls it, which is exactly the state #7092 left behind. A second test now enters through `refresh_status`.
- The second asserted the one-shot latch by calling the sweep twice and expecting 0. **Vacuous** — the first sweep frees the only record, so the second finds nothing whether the latch works or not. It now takes a *new* reservation for the same dead worker first, so a broken latch frees it and the assertion fires.

**A third defect was caught by a pre-existing guard.** Adding `holders_retired` tripped #6961's invariant that every non-u64 atomic is explicitly bound or declared off-wire. Registered as deliberately off-wire, with the reason. That failure was invisible to my filtered runs and appeared only under the full suite.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | failed | localises to |
|---|---|---|
| R1b unwire from the status tick | 1 | call-site test only |
| R2b sweep every worker (no `dead` check) | 1 | negative control only |
| R3b drop the one-shot latch | 1 | direct test |
| R5 retire the wrong worker id | 2 | both |
| control | green | |

R1b and R2b localise in opposite directions, so *"it is wired"* and *"it only sweeps the dead"* are independently bound.

## Known coverage gap, disclosed

The fixture exercises the **interface-mode** allocator only, so dropping the pool-rule or NAT64 sweep reds nothing (measured — that cell escapes). Binding those needs `SourceNatRule` and `Nat64Prefix` fixtures inside a Coordinator's forwarding state, a bigger fixture than this change warrants; the three sweeps are one-line siblings over the same primitive, which `nat::tests_pool` already covers.

## Validation

`make test-rust` rc=0, **4982 passed / 0 failed**; `go test ./... -count=1` clean; `go build ./...` clean. Scope check: 12 files, all under `userspace-dp/src`.

Addresses #6979 F4/F5 (panic route). Refs #7092 — that issue's leak is live and it should be reopened or superseded.

## PR #8070 — ha: derive a session-delta schema identity and gate on it [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7194-delta-schema-identity`

## What

Gives the HA session-open delta a **derived** schema identity, and gates on it fail-closed at runtime.

Closes #7194

## Why the existing guard is not enough

#8043 landed the golden equivalence test this issue calls the load-bearing artefact, and it is untouched here and still passes. But it compares the Rust JSON producer's wire names against the Go consumer's json tags — a **build-time check between two source trees**. It cannot see what a *running* helper carries.

That matters because helper/daemon skew is real, not hypothetical. #6722's `ErrEgressZoneProtocolIncompatible` exists precisely because "the RUNNING helper advertises a ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion that is not this binary's", and its severity was **measured on the reference cluster** — a v4 builder against a v5 helper resolves egress zone 0 for both ifindexes where a matched pair resolves `lan`/`wan`.

`ConfigSnapshotProtocolVersion` gates the config snapshot. The session-delta schema rode the same pair with **no identity of its own**, which is how five fields (#5865) and `rt_flow_session_id` (#5212 → #6312) each shipped divergent with no version bump: there was no version to bump.

At the consumer the consequence is ambiguity — `policy_id` 0 means both "no policy attribution" and "this producer does not carry the field". Installing that zero as identity is the failure mode.

## The mechanism

The helper advertises a fingerprint of its own session-delta wire schema on `ProcessStatus`; the daemon compares it against its own.

It is **derived, not a hand-maintained integer**. A constant someone must remember to bump inherits exactly the discipline that already failed three times. This is computed *from* the schema — serializing a default record on the Rust side, reflecting json tags on the Go side — so adding, removing or renaming a wire field moves it whether or not anyone remembers.

**Neither language is pinned to the other's output.** Both are pinned to the published FNV-1a/64 vectors and each asserts its own canonical form, so agreement is a consequence of both being correct rather than of one having been copied from the other. A cross-language test recomputes the fingerprint from the brace-counted Rust extraction #8043 already uses — reusing that guard's own extractor rather than adding a second one, since two extractors of the same thing is the disease this issue treats.

### The gate is three-state, and the middle state is the point

| advertised | verdict | action |
|---|---|---|
| `0` / never observed | unknown | **permit** — an older helper is already fenced by the snapshot-protocol gates; refusing on a reading that never happened is a brick, not a fence (#1960) |
| equal | match | proceed |
| anything else | mismatch | **withhold the batch** |

Enforcement sits on `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas`, the single chokepoint the binary stream, the JSON drain and the FullResync export all funnel through.

**The refusal is deliberately loud.** Withholding quietly would trade a silent zero-fill for a silently dead HA sync — the standby stops receiving sessions and a failover finds nothing there, which is worse than the bug being fixed. A mismatch warns once per episode (the drain runs at 100ms while the stream is down) and increments a withheld-batch counter; the warning re-arms on recovery so a second episode is not swallowed by the first.

## Package placement

The wire-name extraction lives in `pkg/daemon`, not beside the struct. The #1476 retirement-boundary canary forbids `reflect` in `pkg/dataplane/userspace` production code — reflection is precisely how an entry-program canary would be bypassed. Rather than weaken the canary, the split follows the boundary it draws: extraction where reflect is already permitted, canonicalisation and hashing as pure functions beside the wire types.

## Validation

`go test -count=1 ./...` and `make test-rust` both green, re-run after rebasing onto current master (69 ok, 0 fails, 0 races, 0 build failures; Rust 4988 collected, 0 failed).

**Mutation matrix — 6 RED, negative control GREEN.** Three results worth reporting beyond the column:

1. **Two apparent escapes were void BUILD BREAKS the harness mis-scored as GREEN.** A cell running three packages let one package's build failure hide behind another's collected tests, so the `ran == 0` void check never fired. The tell was cells of the same command reporting different collection counts (2666 / 652 / 4912), and the arithmetic pinned it exactly — the missing tests were precisely `pkg/daemon`, then `pkg/daemon` + `userspace`. Both went RED when rerun in compiling form, and control cells re-running the original mutations now classify VOID.
2. **One genuine escape**: deleting the lifecycle stamp escaped every test, because an unstamped helper advertises 0 and 0 is deliberately permitted — the gate would go silently inert. Now guarded.
3. **That guard's first version was decoration.** It asserted the source contains `session_delta_schema_fingerprint`, but the mutation replaces the call with `session_delta_schema_fingerprint: 0,` — which still contains that substring, because it is the *field name*. It matched both the correct and the broken form. It binds the CALL now (whitespace-squashed against rustfmt wrapping), verified by the paired cell going RED.

## PR #8071 — config: reject an empty security identity at commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7525-empty-security-identity`

Closes #7525

A security zone, a zone-pair's `from-zone`/`to-zone`, and a policy are all **names**, and an empty one is not a name. Four spellings committed cleanly and then diverged from what the operator wrote.

## Measured, and the measurement took three attempts to become meaningful

```
security-zone ""                            ACCEPTED
from-zone "" to-zone trust policy p         ACCEPTED
from-zone trust to-zone "" policy p         ACCEPTED
from-zone trust to-zone untrust policy ""   ACCEPTED
global policy p match from-zone ""          REJECTED — #6526 already covers it
```

The first two probes reported rejections that had nothing to do with the subject: the #3044 required-match gate fires first, then the zone-reference gate. Each had to be **satisfied in the fixture** before anything could observe the identity question. A new early gate steals every later gate's test, and a probe that trips one measures nothing about what it was written for.

## The consequence is a widening, not an error

`sortDedupZones` (`types_security.go`) **strips** the empty string from a zone set, and `ZoneScopeSetLabel` renders an empty set as the idiomatic Junos `any`. So the identity silently applies to **every** zone — a fail-open for `then permit`. The userspace preflight, meanwhile, rejects the same concrete empty reference outright. The two halves disagree about one config, and the operator finds out at runtime rather than at the commit where they can still act.

## Why it runs where it runs

`validateNonEmptySecurityIdentities` sits in the prewalk, on the group-expanded, inactive-pruned AST, **ahead of normalization**. That placement is the point: normalization is exactly the step that makes the mistake unobservable. Once `sortDedupZones` has run there is no empty string left to complain about — only a wildcard indistinguishable from an intended one.

Strict on commit/commit-check; lenient under `lenientEmptySecurityIdentity` on the load and peer-sync ingress so an already-persisted config still boots (#1960), with the widening flagged rather than silent.

## Two shape facts the tests found, not inspection

**The zone-pair AST has two forms** — a single node with a four-element key (`["from-zone","trust","to-zone","untrust"]`) and a nested `from-zone → name → to-zone → name` chain. `compileSecurityPolicies` reads both. My first version read the nested one alone and **silently missed every empty `to-zone` and every empty policy name**; the tests said so, which is why the AST was dumped rather than assumed. A gate reading one shape covers only the spelling its author happened to test — the #2419 class.

**The walk uses `forEachChild` at each level**, not first-match, for the #3562 duplicate-block reason: a benign first `security {}` followed by a second carrying the empty identity would otherwise slip past.

## Deliberately not handled

The scoped-global case (`global policy p match from-zone ""`) — #6526 already rejects it, with a message that names this exact widening. Duplicating it would give one config two errors for one mistake.

| no call from the prewalk | RED | **RED(3)** |
| zone-name check dropped | RED | **RED(2)** |
| only the nested zone-pair shape read | RED | **RED(3)** |

## PR #8072 — config: merge repeated address-book containers [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7524-addressbook-container-merge`

Closes #7524

A repeated `global` block, a repeated `address-book` block, or a second `security` root each silently lost address-book entries — and, measured at master, **they lost different ones**:

```
address-book { global { A } global { B } }                   -> [A]   first wins
address-book { global { A } } address-book { global { B } }  -> [B]   last wins
security { …A }  security { …B }                             -> [B]   last wins
```

"Replace or ignore earlier entries" is literal: the first shape ignores, the other two replace.

## Root cause

`compileAddressBook` read `node.FindChild("global")` — the **first** match only — and then did `sec.AddressBook = ab`, a whole-book assignment. `parseStatements` **appends** a repeated block rather than merging it, and `compileSecurity` iterates every `address-book` sibling and every `security` root, so all three shapes reach the compiler: the first-match read drops the second `global`, and the assignment discards whatever an earlier container already contributed.

**It is not a cosmetic loss.** An address that vanishes is not a parse error anywhere downstream. A policy naming the dropped address or address-set compiles against a book that does not contain it, and the rule matches a different set of traffic than the operator wrote — with `commit` reporting success.

#4706 and #4818 fixed the **inner** (same-name `address-set`) and **sibling** (member) merge classes. Neither reached the **containers**, which is why this survived them.

## The fix, and the two things it must not break

Iterate every `global` child; merge into the **existing** `sec.AddressBook` rather than assigning a fresh one.

**Lazy allocation is preserved.** The book is materialized only when a `global` block exists, so a config with no address-book still compiles to a nil `AddressBook` and every downstream `!= nil` check keeps its meaning ("an address book was configured"). The obvious alternative — allocate up front, then merge — passes every merge assertion and breaks exactly this, so it gets its own control.

**Same-name resolution stays last-wins** (#4706's semantics). Without that control the merge could be "fixed" by making duplicates first-wins and nothing else would notice.

## Mutation matrix — 4 cells, full package suite each

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| read only the first `global` | RED | **RED(3)** |
| assign instead of merge | RED | **RED(1)** |
| allocate eagerly (drop lazy allocation) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

The assign-instead-of-merge cell first scored VOID on an ambiguous anchor — `if sec.AddressBook == nil {` appears twice in the file — and was re-run scoped to the function under test. An anchor that matches two sites mutates the wrong one or none, and both look like a result.

Six test cells: all three container shapes, **address-sets** (they travel the same path and are the half that actually widens or narrows a policy — a merge carrying addresses but not sets passes every address-only assertion), the lazy-allocation control, and the same-name control.

## PR #8074 — routing: only a genuine not-found releases bond/tunnel ownership [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7529-link-lookup-transient`

Closes #7529

`bondManager.deleteLocked` and `tunnelManager.Clear` treated **every** `LinkByName` failure as "the link is absent" and dropped ownership. A transient netlink lookup error — `ENOBUFS` under load, `EINTR`, a busy or truncated socket — is not the same answer as "this link does not exist".

| site | what it did on ANY lookup error | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `deleteLocked` | `delete(b.bonds, name); return nil` | reported a **successful delete** for a bond still in the kernel, still enslaving its members, and no longer tracked — nothing retries, the diff keys off `b.bonds` |
| `Clear` | bare `continue` | the name is left out of `failed`, which `ownedNames` is rebuilt from — a live tunnel with stale addresses and XFRM `if_id` state becomes untracked, and no later `Apply` has a removed-desired entry to retry |

## This is #4901's fix, one call earlier

#4901 hardened the **`LinkDel`** leg: a failed delete retains the name so the next reconcile retries. The **lookup** leg kept the old behaviour and undid it — a transient lookup discards the entry before `LinkDel` is ever reached.

## Not a recurrence — one fix applied to one of three managers

`isLinkNotFound` (`vrf.go`) is the predicate that separates the two answers. The VRF path uses it, and the xfrm manager adopted it under **#5461/#5495 for this exact conflation**. The bond and tunnel managers held the same branch and were never revisited. **The fix shape was in-tree the whole time.**

The general lesson, and I would rather state it than just fix these two: when a predicate like `isLinkNotFound` is introduced to fix one manager, the immediate question is *which other call sites make the same conflation*. Nobody asked it, so the branch survived in two more places for two more issues.

## Ownership is released per name, on that name's own answer

A `Clear` walks several owned names in one pass. It must release the genuinely-absent ones **while** retaining the transiently-failing one. "Retain everything if anything failed" passes both single-name cells and is wrong on the shape a real reconcile actually sees — so the mixed case gets its own cell.

## Mutation matrix — 6 cells, full package suite each

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| bond: any error is absence (the original bug) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| bond: never releases (over-correction) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| tunnel: any error is absence | RED | **RED(2)** |
| tunnel: retains but reports OK | RED | **RED(2)** |
| tunnel: errors but releases | RED | **RED(2)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

The two "over-correction" cells matter as much as the bug cells: a fix that simply never releases ownership makes every reconcile report a failure that can never clear, for a bond an operator removed out-of-band.

The fake distinguishes the two error classes — `byNameHardErr[name]` yields a non-not-found error, an un-seeded name yields the `errLinkNotFound` sentinel — which is the thing that makes any of these cells mean something.

`monitor.go:66` has the same branch — `continue` on any lookup error. I did **not** fold it in: the consequence is different (a monitored interface silently vanishing from `show chassis cluster interfaces`, rather than an orphaned kernel resource), and the question that decides its severity is unanswered — whether that path also feeds the failover **weight** computation or only the display. Folding it in would have widened this change past what its tests bind, and answering it badly would be worse than filing it.

## PR #8075 — logging: state lifecycle-action applicability once [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7531-lifecycle-action`

Closes #7531

An intentionally meaningless wire action byte was rendered as **`deny`** on the trace, REST and SSE surfaces, and stamped as a raw `0` in the binary SESSION_OPEN record.

## The producer says so at the write site — twice

```rust
// [54] action: a session close has no permit/deny/reject action
// semantics, so this byte is intentionally 0. … Do NOT rely on the 0
// rendering as a value — both close formatters skip it.

// [54] action: a session open is a permit-and-create event, not a
// forwarding decision, so this byte is intentionally 0 (same as the
// close path). … Do NOT rely on the 0 rendering as a value.
```

The Go side then taught that exception to the formatters **one at a time**: #2513 for the close text lines, #2593 for the open text lines, #4914 for the binary close record. **Every surface added afterwards inherited the raw `actionName(0)` == `"deny"` until someone noticed it too** — a four-issue tail for one fact.

The ones that never got their own issue: `EventRecord.Action` itself (which trace, REST and SSE all read) and the binary SESSION_OPEN record, since #4914 covered only the close. A `deny` on a session **create** is the more misleading of the two — it reads as a blocked connection attempt rather than an established one.

## Three decisions worth stating

**Empty rather than a placeholder.** `EventRecord.Action` feeds the event-buffer filter (`EventFilter.matches`), so an operator filtering `action deny` was matching **every normal session open and close** — the concrete harm, because it makes a deny filter useless on a busy box. A placeholder like `"n/a"` would just be a new value to match by accident.

**The trace omits `action=` rather than printing an empty one.** An empty field reads as a producer that failed to populate it — a different and more alarming claim than "this event type has no action". This is what #2513/#2593 already do for the syslog lines.

**Applicability is a property of the event TYPE, not of the byte**, so a future producer writing a stray non-zero cannot resurrect the claim. There is a cell for exactly that.

## One existing test pinned a value no producer emits

`TestFormatBinaryRecord_Basic` built a SESSION_OPEN with `Action: actionPermit` and asserted the binary carried `actionPermit`. Before changing it I enumerated **every** write to the wire action byte:

| site | writes |
|---|---|
| `encode_session_close_rt_flow` | literal `0` |
| `encode_session_create_rt_flow` | literal `0` |
| `encode_dataplane_event` (generic) | `event.action` — but carries `debug_assert!(false)` for `SessionClose`/`SessionCreate`, stating no payload is ever constructed for them |

So the old expectation described a record that **cannot occur**, while the record that *does* occur rendered as `deny`. Worth doing that enumeration rather than assuming: had the generic path been reachable with a lifecycle kind, this change would have destroyed real information.

| predicate always false (over-correction) | RED | **RED(2)** |

## PR #8076 — Retire a whole worker generation's NAT holder bits on replan teardown (#7092) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7092-replan-retire`

#8069 closed #7092's **panic** route by sweeping workers whose `dead` flag is set. This closes the other one — and it needed a separate change because **`dead` is written only by the panic supervisor**. A replan stops and joins a perfectly *healthy* generation, so nothing sets the flag and a `dead`-keyed sweep cannot see the case at all.

## The leak

A holder bit is cleared only when **that** worker runs its own release. `stop_and_clear` signals every worker, joins it, and drops the records — destroying each `SessionTable`, so no worker in the outgoing generation will ever run another release. `worker_id` is minted as `queue_id % workers`, so a plan that **shrinks** the worker set leaves ids that can never be reused, and `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` carries the allocator across the reload with their bits still set.

`retire_all_worker_holders` runs at teardown, **before** `stop_and_clear` drops the records — after it the ids are gone and nothing can name them again. It shares one body and one `holders_retired` latch with the dead-worker sweep, so a worker already retired by the 1 Hz tick isn't swept twice, and vice versa.

## Why all ids, not just the dropped ones

An id the next generation reuses **self-heals** — the new worker takes the same bit and eventually releases it — which is why #7092 frames this as shrinking. But *which* ids the next plan mints isn't known at teardown, and deferring until it is means sweeping after the records naming the outgoing ids are gone. Retiring all of them is correct for the same reason retiring one dead worker is: the bit records a claim by a worker that no longer exists. The next generation re-imports and re-reserves, and no forwarding happens in between, so the window where a port is free while its session still exists has no packet path through it.

## The fixture binds all three allocator families

This closes the gap #8069 disclosed. That PR's fixture was interface-mode only, and its **measured** consequence was that dropping the pool-rule or NAT64 sweep red nothing. Here interface-mode, a pool-mode rule and a NAT64 prefix each hold a live reservation and each is asserted separately. `Nat64Prefix::for_test` exists because `pool_index` is private — a test-only constructor keeps it private rather than widening a field for one fixture.

| cell | failed | |
|---|---|---|
| P1 unwire from `stop_inner` | 1 | |
| P2 drop the pool-rule sweep | 1 | **#8069 could not red this** |
| P3 drop the NAT64 sweep | 1 | **nor this** |
| P4 drop the iface sweep | 3 | |
| P5 replan retires only DEAD workers | 1 | |
| control | green | |

**P5 is the cell that justifies the change existing**: substituting the `dead`-keyed sweep for the generation sweep reds, which is the measured form of *"a flag the replan never sets cannot cover the replan"*.

## PR #8077 — frr: share one prefix-list family expansion with the sequence bound [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7526-routemap-family-bound`

Closes #7526

The route-map sequence **bound** counted one referenced prefix-list NAME while the **renderer** emits one row per IP FAMILY that list holds.

`fromPrefixListRefs` expands a mixed v4+v6 list into an `ip` ref and an `ipv6` ref so both families bind a family-correct match line (#2607). `RouteMapSequenceCount` counted `len(term.PrefixList)` — names, family-blind. So a policy referencing mixed-family lists rendered up to **twice** the sequences admission had approved, and a config sitting just under `MaxRouteMapSequences` rendered past FRR's maximum sequence number — which, in the admission error's own words, *"poisons the ENTIRE frr-reload"*.

## One rule, not two implementations that agree

`config.PrefixListFamilies` decides **which** families a list holds, and both sides read it. `pkg/frr`'s `prefixListFamilies` keeps only the mapping to FRR's `ip`/`ipv6` match keywords, which are FRR spellings. The counts are now equal **by construction**.

`RouteMapSequenceCount` and `ComposedChainSequenceCount` take the `*PolicyOptionsConfig`. **Required, not optional** — an optional table would be nil exactly where it matters and the count would silently fall back to the family-blind answer; making it required lets the compiler enumerate every call site.

## The saturation contract was verified, not adjusted

The issue calls saturation part of the contract. `checkedMulU64` and the running-sum guard clamp to `math.MaxUint64`, and admission rejects strictly `> MaxRouteMapSequences`. Both were already correct — saturating *at the ceiling* instead would make an over-limit count equal the accepted maximum. Reporting that rather than changing it.

## The test asserts the AGREEMENT, not a literal

It renders the policy, counts the emitted sequence lines, and compares that to what the bound predicts. **Either side drifting fails it, and neither is privileged.** Pinning a number I computed would encode which of the two I decided to trust — and this issue is precisely a case where one of them was wrong.

Two cells exist to stop that agreement from being vacuous: the mixed list must actually render **more** rows than a single-family one (otherwise the agreement is between two things that both ignore families), and both `ip` and `ipv6` match keywords must appear (two rows of the same family would pass a count-only assertion).

## Three things the matrix established that inspection did not

**The IPv4 fallback was duplicated**, and the duplicate made the config-side normalization *dead* — a mutation removing it changed no behaviour because the `pkg/frr` copy silently covered for it. Two places deciding the same thing is the disease this change treats, so the duplicate is gone and the mutation now reds.

**A term with no `from-prefix-list` must count 1, not 0.** Zero multiplies the whole term's cross-product to zero, so the bound would report that a large policy expands to no sequences and admit anything. That is the *most common* term shape and nothing covered it. Found as a live escape.

**An undefined or empty referenced list counts as one family** — the renderer still emits one fail-closed NOMATCH match line for it.

## Mutation matrix — 6 cells, one package per cell

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| family count always 1 | RED | **RED(1)** |
| ref count counts names (the original bug) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| empty list reports zero families | RED | **RED(4)** |
| no-refs yields zero | RED | **RED(1)** |
| renderer re-derives families | RED | **RED(17)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Plus reverting the production change itself: **RED(1)** on the agreement cell.

Three cells initially scored VOID or GREEN and were repaired rather than reported: one build break (`if false` left a variable unused — a build break is a third kind of void cell, not evidence), and two genuine escapes which are the two coverage gaps described above.

One package per cell deliberately — #8070's lane found that a multi-package cell lets one package's build failure hide behind another's collected tests, so the `collected > 0` void guard never fires.
