## PR #8078 — daemon: deepen the unarmed transit barrier and gate on attach coverage [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7191-deepen-transit-barrier`

## What

Deepens the unarmed transit barrier beyond the `ip_forward=0` leg, and makes the per-interface AF_XDP attach part of the arm state.

Closes #7191

## 1. The barrier was one sysctl

Verified on a live node before writing any code: `ip_forward=1` and `nft list ruleset | grep -c "hook forward"` returns **0**. A single sysctl — raisable by a `sysctl.d` drop-in, a systemd unit, an operator, or any future code path — was the only thing between an unarmed box and kernel routing.

Adds `xpf_transit_barrier`: an unconditional forward-hook DROP in **both** the `inet` and `bridge` families. The bridge leg is not optional — `ip_forward` does not govern bridged frames at all, and this repo creates bridge domains. Both chain shapes were confirmed creatable on the reference cluster's kernel before relying on them.

### The scoping is the safety argument

Several **armed** paths deliberately rely on the kernel forward hook being open and unfiltered, and `daemon_transit_gate.go` already names them: route-based-VPN plaintext leaving an xfrm interface, SNAT'd frames passed up for kernel routing, and the #7409 slow-path reinject. A forward drop live while armed breaks all three.

So the barrier is scoped strictly to the **unarmed** window — exactly the window in which `ip_forward` is already 0 — and therefore **closes nothing that was open**. It is belt to the sysctl's braces over the same interval, not a new reject surface. That is what bounds the blast radius: the worst case of a bug here is that the barrier fails to install (no worse than today), not that armed transit is dropped.

It is driven from the same `mark*` helpers that drive the sysctls and re-asserted on every apply tail, so a stale barrier self-heals rather than silently black-holing armed transit until a restart. Failure directions are asymmetric on purpose: failing to **install** is a Warn (the sysctl already closed transit); failing to **remove** is an Error (that is the black-hole direction).

Plan §6's flowtable leg is a **deliberate no-op**: xpf creates no flowtable, so there is nothing to flush, and machinery to disable something that never exists would be inert code that reads as coverage. `TestNoFlowtableIsEverCreated7191` pins the assumption — with comments stripped, so the scan cannot be satisfied by the prose documenting it.

## 2. The tracked boundary was `Start`, not the attach

`dataplaneArmed` tracked `rt.Start()`/`LoadUserspaceShim` only. The per-interface attach happens later, inside the first `ApplyConfig`, and neither failure mode reached the arm state: a **native** failure is a warning and the loop continues, and even the **generic** failure — which does return an error — is joined as a deferred commit error rather than an abort. So a box where Start succeeded but an interface never got a shim reported itself **armed** and kept `ip_forward=1` with nothing adjudicating that interface.

The material already existed and was unused: `ProveArmCoverage` computed a per-interface report whose only consumer discarded it. It now publishes from **inside** the proof — so a stashed report cannot be published, the same property the #5275 canary enforces for the logged one — and the daemon consults it on the apply tail, disarming through the **same** `markDataplaneArmFailed` path a Start failure uses. One arm state, one set of side effects.

The gate is **one-way** (it can only disarm; re-arming from a diagnostic would be the second notion of "armed" the issue forbids) and **three-state** (a report never published, or one that could not classify, does not disarm — gating on a reading that never happened is a brick, not a fence).

**Recorded sharp edge:** `coverDirect` collapses "no tracked link" and "identity could not be read" into one uncovered verdict, so a readback fault disarms like a real attach failure. That is the conservative direction and matches the proof's own stance, but it is documented rather than hidden; distinguishing them belongs in `coverDirect`, not at the consumer. The cluster smoke showed zero false positives.

The verdict crosses the package boundary as **primitives**, so `pkg/daemon` does not import `pkg/dataplane` — the #1451 retirement-boundary allowlist exists to shrink, and widening it for a four-number verdict is the wrong direction.

## Validation

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `go test -count=1 ./...` (post-rebase) | 0 fails, 0 races, 0 build failures, 69 ok |
| Mutation matrix | **8/8 RED**, negative control GREEN (2259 collected) |
| Pre-existing #5275 transit tests | all 8 pass unchanged |
| Cluster smoke (deploy + failover) | 17 passed / 0 failed, 22.9 Gbps, IPv6 OK |
| Armed-box posture on hardware | 0 barrier tables, 0 forward chains, 0 remove-failures, 0 coverage disarms |
| Kernel chain-shape probe | inet **and** bridge forward chains both creatable |

The **over-rejection controls are the load-bearing cells**, since a forward DROP fails to a silent black hole rather than a loud error. The matrix leads with them: barrier never removed while armed, gate inverted so complete coverage disarms, and three-state collapsed so "never observed" reads as a hole — all three red.

That last table row exists because the smoke initially asserted something indistinguishable from healthy: "0 barrier tables while armed" is satisfied equally by a correct removal and by an install path that could never create them. The box was armed throughout, so the install path never ran; I probed the chain shape directly, with policy `accept` so the probe could not drop a packet.

Three canaries caught the first cut, and two pointed at better designs than an update: the #5275 AST canary (publish moved inside the proof), and the #1451 boundary canary (import dropped rather than allowlisted).

## PR #8079 — userspace-dp/static-NAT: register a block's usable hosts for proxy-ARP [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7219-static-nat-block-hosts`

Closes #7219

`external_ips()` / `external_ips_scoped()` pushed only a block rule's network **base**, so on a directly-connected external segment the firewall answered ARP/ND for `203.0.113.0` alone. Every other address the block translates was unreachable: peers got no reply for `.1`-`.254`, inbound traffic never arrived to be translated, and the static-NAT match that would have handled it correctly — a prefix-keyed lookup, independent of `local_v*` — was never reached.

**Silent, and indistinguishable from a routing problem.**

## The old comment was right about the wrong thing

It defended base-only emission as *"sufficient parity for the network address without an unbounded blow-up"*. That is a true and sound argument about the DNAT **match** path. It does not address `local_v*`'s **second** role as the proxy-ARP/ND and local-delivery address set, which is the gap.

## The port

`DnatTable::destination_ips` solved this under #3164; this is that port. At or below `MAX_LOCAL_PREFIX_HOSTS` a block expands host-by-host; a larger block contributes only its base and relies on being **routed** to the firewall.

**The bound is `DnatTable`'s constant, not a second copy.** Both tables register into the *same* `local_v*` set, so a divergent bound would mean one NAT family proxy-ARPs a block size the other refuses, for no reason a reader could reconstruct.

**`external_ips()` is implemented on top of `external_ips_scoped()`**, as the DNAT sibling is, so the deduped and scoped views cannot drift on the bound. They were independent implementations before — which is exactly how one could have been fixed and the other not.

## The issue's open question, answered

> *confirm whether static-NAT blocks have an analogous exact-host override that must shadow the expansion the way #6025's `exact_off` does for DNAT*

**They do not.** `off` does not appear in this file's grammar at all — the single match is the word "masked off" in a comment. An exact-host static entry is always a TRANSLATE, so it can only duplicate an address the expansion also yields, which the dedup absorbs. No shadowing to port.

## One escape, and the answer is not "add a test"

Flipping the v6 bound's `is_some_and` to `is_none_or` reds **nothing**. A `/64` does not distinguish them — `host_count_v6(64)` is `Some(2^64)`, too big either way. Only a prefix shorter than `/1` separates them, and there `is_none_or` would enumerate 2^128 addresses: a hang, not a wrong answer.

My first cell for that used `::/0` and asserted `len() <= 1`. **It passed, and it was vacuous** — the count is 0, not 1. A `/0` static-NAT rule produces **no block at all**: #5658 rejects a zero-length block prefix fail-closed before insertion, because an equal-length `/0` pair is an identity translation that would shadow every narrower rule.

So the mutation is **INERT rather than uncovered**, and #5658's rejection is a *stronger* guarantee than the bound check it defeats. The cell now pins that invariant instead, for both families, so if #5658's rejection is ever relaxed this reds and points at the unbounded expansion it would newly expose. The polarity is documented at the site as defense-in-depth rather than the primary guard, so the next reader does not mistake the escape for a coverage gap.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| base-only again (the original bug) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| v4 bound removed | RED | **RED(1)** |
| scoped view drops the block arm | RED | **RED(4)** |
| v6 bound polarity inverted | RED | **INERT** — unreachable via #5658, documented and pinned |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Six cells: block hosts registered (**both** views asserted, so fixing one and not the other fails), the v4 over-bound base-only case, a host-scale v6 block expanding, the v6 over-bound case (its own cell, because the v6 arm returns `Option` and a wrong polarity would expand while the v4 cell stayed green), the exact-host control (registering extra addresses for a `/32` would proxy-ARP for hosts the firewall does not own), and the `/0` invariant.

## PR #8080 — Recycle the backup TX drain's deques instead of reallocating per batch (#7204 A1-b6-F4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7204-hotpath`

The non-CoS backup drain took `pending_tx_local` with `mem::take`, allocated a fresh `VecDeque` for retries, and **on full success skipped the restore and dropped both** — so the common everything-transmitted path re-allocated two deques on the next batch, on a warmed TX path that is supposed to be allocation-free.

Three changes, none of which alter which packets are sent:

- the retry deque is worker-owned (`WorkerTxPipeline::backup_retry_scratch`), parked empty between batches;
- both deques are handed back on **both** paths, not only when a retry remains;
- **the early return for an empty binding also puts `pending_tx_local` back.** `take_pending_tx_requests` `mem::take`s it *before* the emptiness check, so bailing out left the shared deque at capacity 0 and made the producer regrow it — on the idle-binding path that early return exists to make cheap. Not in the issue; found while tracing the lifecycle.

Which deque goes back is **not** interchangeable: `restore_pending_tx_requests` *prepends*, so it must be given the one still holding items or untransmitted requests end up behind newly-arrived ones. `park_drained_deques` encodes that and the test pins it.

## The fixture is the hard part, not the fix

This is a discipline violation, not a wrong result — the drain transmits the same packets before and after — so a test that merely exercises the path passes either way and would tell the next reader the discipline is enforced when it is not. **Capacity is the observable that separates them**: a re-allocated `VecDeque::new()` has capacity 0.

| cell | failed | |
|---|---|---|
| T1 revert to a fresh `VecDeque` per batch | **0** | **ESCAPED — disclosed below** |
| T2 park the WRONG deque | 1 | |
| T3 drop the parked scratch | 1 | |
| control | green | |

**T1 escaped, and that is disclosed rather than papered over.** It reverts the *take* side, a call site inside the drain, while the test binds `park_drained_deques`. Binding it needs a `BindingWorker`, which owns an XSK device and has no in-process constructor — the existing drain tests construct one nowhere and exercise pure helpers only. The handoff was moved onto `WorkerTxPipeline` *because* that type is constructible; the residual gap is the one line that takes the scratch.

## Two of the five items are fixed-since

Separated from *never-true* with `git show 9710cfd13:<path>` against the issue's own base — [full write-up on the issue](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7204#issuecomment-5468981537):

- **A1-b4-F6** — `core::mem::take(&mut *pending)` present at base, absent now. #7201 replaced it with a bounded slice into a recycled buffer, addressing both the capacity **and** the missing service budget.
- **A1-b8-F5** — the gate comment is absent at base, present now. The remaining `statistics_v2()` is the always-on `BindingLiveState` publisher (#802) — deliberate release telemetry, not a residual.

## Still live and unstarted

- **A1-b7-F5** — `canonical_route_table` still returns `Cow<'static, str>`; wants the `TableId` interning.
- **A1-b7-F6** — `SmallVec<[&T; 8]>` spills at ECMP fanout ≥ 9. Cheap *once the supported maximum is decided* — that decision is the blocker, not the code.

## PR #8081 — snmp: bound the v1 successor walk and assert what it depends on [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7433-successor-strict-advance`

Closes #7433

`findNextV1OIDSnap` contains the one unbounded loop over the successor lookup. It advances by `cur = next` and repeats until the lookup returns nil — so it terminated **only** because `findNextOIDSnap` returns a successor that strictly advances past the cursor. Nothing asserted that, and **the property lives in a different function**, so anyone optimising the successor lookup could not see what depended on it.

## The failure mode is a hang, not a wrong answer

Changing the successor's predicate from `> 0` to `>= 0` makes an OID its own successor and the walk spins forever. The mutation cell **hung rather than failing** — no `--- FAIL` line, so a harness gating on named failures scores it as a void or an escape rather than a defect. That is how the issue was found in the first place.

Two callers bounded it incidentally: GETNEXT does one lookup per request OID with no loop, and GETBULK is bounded by max-repetitions plus the #6551 byte budget. But those are properties of the **callers**, which is precisely the fragility. The loop now carries its own bound — the MIB view length, the most steps a strictly-advancing walk can take — and exceeding it returns end-of-view with a warning naming the cursor. Fail-closed: a v1 walk ends early rather than spinning a CPU serving no one.

**The load-bearing assertion is the PROPERTY, not the consequence.** Asserting "the walk terminates" requires running the walk, which is the thing that hangs; asserting strict advance fails in microseconds.

## Three findings that each changed the change

**1. One of my own cells reproduced the hang it was written to prevent.** The first draft called the loop on the test goroutine, so under the `cur = next` mutation it took the whole package down — no attribution, just a suite that never returns. Every cell that calls the loop now goes through a deadline helper. *A test written to make a hang attributable must not itself hang.*

**2. The bound was untestable, so a mutation deleting it escaped.** With the real successor the bound is unreachable — the lookup is correct, so the loop always terminates on its own. `findNextV1OIDSnapWith` takes the successor as a parameter **so the bound can be exercised**, not for production flexibility; there is one production caller and it passes `a.findNextOIDSnap`. A guard whose failure mode is a hang is the one most worth binding.

**3. The fixture for that must return a Counter64 OID.** My first version returned an ordinary one — so the loop returned on its **first iteration** and the non-advancing cursor never mattered. Both the delete-the-bound and widen-the-bound mutations escaped while the cell reported green. It now asserts the successor was consulted at least twice, so a fixture that stops reaching the branch fails rather than passing vacuously.

## Mutation matrix — run under `-timeout` so a hang is distinguishable from a pass

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| successor not strictly advancing (`>0` → `>=0`) | RED | **RED(17)**, 2 mine |
| v1 loop does not advance the cursor | RED | **RED(1)** — *was a HANG; now a named failure, which is the point* |
| remove the step bound | RED | **RED(1)** |
| widen the bound 1000× | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Four test cells: the strict-advance property over an exhaustive probe set, walk termination under a deadline, the Counter64 skip (the control that stops "terminates" being satisfied by a walk that returns nil immediately), and the bound itself against a non-advancing successor.

## Gates

- `go test -count=1 ./...` — **69 packages ok, 0 `--- FAIL`, rc=0**, rebased onto current master.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 3 files, all this change's own.

## On the issue's item 2

The issue asks for "a `-timeout` on the relevant suite, so a future regression fails rather than hangs". Worth recording what I measured: `go test -timeout` **does** attribute a hang — the panic prints `running tests: TestV1GetNext_WalksAndSkipsCounter64 (33s)` before the goroutine dump. It is not a `--- FAIL` line, so a harness must gate on that too, but the information is there. With the production bound in place the hang no longer occurs at all, which is a better answer than making it legible.

## PR #8082 — configstore: fail closed on a wrong-typed encrypted-envelope field [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7454-envelope-type-mismatch`

Closes #7454

#4888's guard fails closed on an envelope-shaped body whose discriminator we cannot support, and its comment names the exact outcome it exists to prevent:

> Treating it as plaintext lets `json.Unmarshal` drop the unknown fields and decode an EMPTY ConfigTree, so `Store.Load` would boot a committed-empty config (loss of policy) instead of failing closed.

**But it sits after the initial unmarshal, and that unmarshal swallowed every error** as *"not the envelope object shape at all — a genuine plaintext body. Pass through."*

That comment is true for a **syntax** error. It is not true for a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`: a perfectly good JSON object, with the right keys, one carrying the wrong JSON **type** — `"salt": 5`, `"format": []`, `"prf": {}`, `"nonce": true` — took the same branch and passed through as plaintext, reaching the empty-tree committed-empty boot that the guard immediately below it exists to prevent.

**The failure was completely silent.** The #4579 plaintext-downgrade warning does not fire either: it keys on `masterPasswordPRF(tree) != ""` and the tree is empty. Contrast the string-valued path, which is correctly fatal all the way to `daemon_run_bringup.go` refusing to start.

## Key presence, not error-type discrimination

The issue suggested discriminating `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`. I used **key presence** instead: strictly stronger (it catches a wrong type, a null, an array, anything) and with **no over-rejection risk here** — which was *verified rather than assumed*.

The plaintext body `writeTreeMarked` writes is `json.MarshalIndent` of a `config.ConfigTree`, and `ConfigTree` is `struct { Children []*Node }`. Its only top-level key is `Children`. **None of the five envelope keys can appear in a genuine plaintext body**, so any body carrying one was *meant* to be an envelope and a decode failure on it is corruption.

## Measured, and it corrects the issue's framing

**JSON `null` is not a type error in Go.** It decodes into any type as a no-op, leaving the zero value — so a null-valued field reaches the envelope's own required-field check (or #4888's discriminator check, for a null `format`) and was **already fail-closed by a different guard**:

```
{"format":"…v1",…,"data":null}   -> "invalid encrypted config envelope"
{"format":null,…}                -> "unsupported encrypted config envelope format"
```

Only a genuine wrong type took the passthrough branch. Both kinds of row are kept, with their **distinct expected diagnoses** — an operator tells a corrupt envelope from an unsupported one by that wording, and the two have different remedies (restore a backup vs. downgrade the reader). A single `wantErr bool` would have hidden the distinction.

## The 13-row table

| group | rows |
|---|---|
| genuine type mismatches | number, array, object, bool — **plus a single wrong-typed key with nothing else**, the row that separates *"was meant to be an envelope"* from *"decodes as one"*; a discriminator-only check lets it through |
| already-fail-closed nulls | `data: null`, `format: null`, each asserting its own diagnosis |
| plaintext must still load | bare `ConfigTree`, populated `ConfigTree`, `{}` |
| non-object unchanged | `null`, array, scalar, garbage |

Plus three controls: the error must **name** the present fields; **#4888's own diagnosis must be preserved** rather than absorbed into the new one; and a well-formed envelope must still be **recognized** — without that last one, every other cell passes for a function that fails closed on everything.

## Mutation matrix — one package per cell

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| revert to swallowing all errors (the original bug) | RED | **RED(2)** |
| key probe finds nothing | RED | **RED(2)** |
| probe treats every object as an envelope | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

## PR #8083 — Select ECMP next hops through a liveness bitmask, not a spilling SmallVec (#7204 A1-b7-F6) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `explore/7204-ecmp`

`select_route_next_hop` collected live candidate references into `SmallVec<[&T; 8]>`, which spills to the heap from fanout 9 up — on the packet-driven session-miss FIB path.

## The collection never needed the references

It is used for exactly two things: **how many** candidates are live, and **which one is the Nth live** in candidate order. A `u64` answers both — `count_ones` and a bit walk — in **8 bytes at every fanout** and an allocation at none of them.

### Why not a bigger inline array, which is the fix the issue implies

The supported ceiling is **64** (`resolveECMP` → `maximum-paths`, and Junos `routing-options maximum-ecmp` is Missing so nothing raises it). `[&T; 64]` would never spill — but it costs **512 bytes of stack on every call**, including the 1–4 fanout that real multi-WAN configs run. That pays the worst case always, to avoid an allocation almost nobody reaches. The mask costs 8 bytes at every fanout, so the trade doesn't have to be made.

### Why not two passes, the other way to drop the collection

`is_live` is not a field read — both call sites reach `tunnel_next_hop_live`, which resolves a tunnel endpoint and consults the neighbour map. The original *"single liveness evaluation"* comment is load-bearing, and the mask preserves it: `is_live` is still called exactly `candidates.len()` times, pinned by its own test.

## Selection is an equivalence, not merely valid

ECMP is flow-consistent — a given 5-tuple must keep landing on the same member — so an implementation picking a *different live* member would satisfy any "the result is live" assertion **while silently repinning every existing flow on upgrade**. The bit walk yields the pick-th set bit in ascending index order, which is the element `live[pick]` named, asserted against the pre-change body verbatim across fanouts **1..=70** and five liveness shapes including all-dead.

Above 64 the original collect remains as a fallback — unreachable through configuration, but a route arriving with more members must still be selected from correctly rather than truncated. The equivalence test spans that boundary in both directions, so **the spill path is asserted to still work rather than pinned as unreachable**.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | failed |
|---|---|
| E1 pick the FIRST live, ignore the hash | 6 |
| E2 hash over candidates, not live count | 3 |
| E4 skip the bit-clear (wrong Nth live) | 6 |
| E3 mask width 64 → 8 | **0 → 1 after the pin** |
| control | green |

**E3 initially escaped, and correctly.** Narrowing the mask changes which *path* runs, not which member is picked, and the two are equivalence-tested — so no behavioural test can see it, and pinning the literal would have pinned an implementation detail. What *is* a real property is that the mask covers the range the control plane can render, so `MAX_SUPPORTED_ECMP_FANOUT` is asserted against the rendered `maximum-paths` ceiling with the derivation in the message. That cell now reds.

## PR #8084 — nat: one prefix-length grammar across Go and both Rust parsers [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7481-nat-prefix-grammar`

Closes #7481

`natMatchPrefixParses` claimed **by comment** to mirror "the Rust NAT match-prefix parser EXACTLY" and named three consumers. One Go predicate, asserted to mirror two structurally different Rust implementations, in prose. It was false.

## Measured all three, and it corrects the issue twice

| literal | Go `ParseCIDR` | `ipnet::IpNet` | `u8::from_str` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `10.0.0.0/024` | accept | **REJECT** | accept |
| `2001:db8::/064` | accept | **ACCEPT** | accept |
| `2001:db8::/0064` | accept | reject | accept |
| `10.0.0.0/+24` | reject | reject | **ACCEPT** |

**1. The open question is answered: `ipnet` rejects `/+24`.** So `source/mod.rs` already agreed with the Go gate — the divergence was `static_nat.rs` alone, one hand-rolled parser against a consensus.

**2. The issue's control value is wrong, and it inverts the severity.** `/024` is listed as a case all ends accept. Go accepts it; `ipnet` **rejects** it. So `/024` passed an **ordinary strict commit** and was then dropped by `parse_match_prefix` — a fail-closed drop via `*_constrained`, so **the rule matched nothing**. A NAT rule the operator committed successfully that silently never fires. `/+24` was never that: the gate already rejected it, so it needed the tolerant load path to arrive at all.

A control that is *assumed* to agree is the one place a differential most needs to actually run — it carries the claim that the rest of the table is a divergence rather than a harness bug.

**3. Found by the corpus itself: `ipnet` disagrees with ITSELF across address families.** It takes a three-digit `2001:db8::/064` and refuses `10.0.0.0/024`. So single-sourcing the Rust side onto `IpNet` — which this change also does, and which is right for the `+` case — **still would not have produced one grammar**.

## Normalize rather than reject — a deliberate reversal mid-change

My first cut narrowed every end to refuse the odd spellings. That is the reject-only direction and normally wins. **#7145's existing test refused it, with the right reason:**

> `match source-address 1.2.3.4/024` … was REJECTED, but the dataplane parses and installs it. A widened validator that refuses a working value bricks the operator's next commit on a box that was forwarding correctly (#1960)

Both spellings are **unambiguous** — `/+24`, `/024`, `/0024` can only mean 24 — so normalizing loses no information and there is no wrong interpretation to pick. **The danger was never the spelling; it was the disagreement**, and agreement removes it whichever answer is shared. Accept is the one that bricks nobody.

One predicate per language (`config.NormalizeNATPrefixLen`, `nat::normalize_nat_prefix_len`), applied at every consumer: the commit gate, the Go DNAT snapshot builder, and both Rust parsers.

## #7215's differential earned its keep, in this PR

Widening the gate without widening `dnatDestinationParts` reproduced — **in the same run** — the exact drift that test was written for:

```
DIVERGENCE on "1.2.3.4/+24": commit gate accepts=true, snapshot builder installs=false.
```

> *"validateDestinationNATAddressesStrict carried a comment promising its acceptance 'MUST match the builder's exactly' and then drifted from dnatDestinationParts for six years' worth of mask spellings … A comment cannot fail; a differential over both predicates can."*

It did, immediately. That is the argument for this PR's own approach, demonstrated rather than asserted.

## The agreement is a SHARED CORPUS, not two lists

`testdata/nat_match_prefix_corpus.txt` is read by a Go test **and** a Rust test. A literal added to it is asserted in both languages; a literal only one side knows about cannot exist. Two hand-maintained lists is this issue's own disease one layer up.

Both sides carry **anti-vacuity floors** — a corpus that failed to load, or one with a single verdict, makes every assertion trivially true — and the Rust side additionally asserts the **two Rust parsers agree with each other**, not merely each with the file.

## PR #8085 — host-inbound: pair the ICMP global accept with the IP family [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7520-icmp-family-pairing`

Closes #7520

`is_icmp_host_inbound_global_accept` switched on the protocol number **alone**, and the two arms mean different things on different families:

| packet | old verdict |
|---|---|
| **IPv4**, protocol byte 58, type 1/2/3/4/133..137 | took the ICMPv6 arm → **globally ADMITTED** |
| **IPv6**, next-header 1, type 3/11/12 | took the ICMPv4 arm → **globally ADMITTED** |

**This predicate returns before the zone lookup.** So a match admits a packet the zone's `host-inbound-traffic` set never permitted — a **fail-open**, not a fail-closed narrowing.

## Why the family, and not just a stricter type list

The type numbers cannot disambiguate it. ICMPv6 destination-unreachable is type **1**, and 1 is a perfectly legal ICMPv4 type number; ICMPv4 time-exceeded is **11**, which is nothing in ICMPv6's error range. A `(protocol, type)` pair genuinely cannot tell the two apart — the family has to be part of the key. That is the issue's own design note, and it is right.

The fall-through is `false`, so a packet whose address family the parser could not determine now stays gated on the zone set rather than exempted.

## Why it survived #3171 and #3292

Those implemented the two halves of this admission and **neither tested their composition**. Each half is correct in isolation; the defect is only visible when you ask what happens to a packet whose protocol byte belongs to the other family.

The nft side was never affected — `icmp type` and `icmpv6 type` are family-scoped matchers by construction — so **the two enforcement surfaces had silently diverged**, which is the kind of gap the host-inbound service matrix exists to make visible.

## The issue's title points one layer up, and that caller is fine

> flowless LocalDelivery passes ICMP type 0 into host-inbound

That caller is **correct**, and its comment says why: a non-first fragment has no readable L4 header, so passing 0 deliberately declines the exemption and the packet stays gated. Measured — type 0 matches neither arm, so nothing was falsely exempted there. The live defect is the family blindness the issue's own **design note** names, one layer down. Reporting that rather than "fixing" a caller that was already right.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| revert to family-blind (the original bug) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| admit everything | RED | **RED(16)** |
| drop the v4 arm | RED | **RED(8)** |
| widen v6 to all types | RED | **RED(3)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Four test cells: both crossed pairs across **every** admitted type; the matched pairs **still admitted** — the over-rejection control, and the one that matters most here, because narrowing too far breaks PMTUD on every configured zone *silently, as a black hole*; the non-error ICMP types that must stay gated on `ping` / `router-discovery` (without which "matched pairs are admitted" is satisfied by a predicate that admits every ICMP type); and non-ICMP protocols across both families.

## PR #8087 — Borrow the route-table name when there is nothing to rewrite (#7204 A1-b7-F5) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7204-f5`

The last of #7204's five. `canonical_route_table` returned `Cow<'static, str>` — and that `'static`, not the rewriting, is what made it allocate on the packet-driven session-miss path.

## Two of the four allocating arms were copying their own argument

Four of six arms allocated, but **two are identity arms**: they hand back exactly the name they were given, and copied it only because a borrow couldn't outlive the call under `'static`. Tying the output lifetime to the input makes those `Cow::Borrowed`, leaving an allocation only where a family rewrite genuinely produces a new string.

**That identity arm is the common case.** A lookup for family F against a table already in family F — `vrf-a.inet.0` asked for v4 — matches neither the default-table arm nor the opposite-family suffix, so *every same-family resolution* paid a `to_string` to get its own argument back.

No caller needed the owned value: **the change compiles with no call-site edits at all**, because every hot-path use is a comparison, a `visited` membership test, or a map lookup — all of which take `&str`.

## Interning wasn't needed

The issue proposes a `TableId` threaded through PBR and next-table recursion with a snapshot-build interning pass. That also removes the allocation, at the cost of a new id type across two subsystems — and it isn't required to make the identity arm free. The question turned out not to be *"how do we represent tables more cheaply"* but *"why is this copying its own argument"*.

## The visited chain is measured and deliberately left

Recorded in a comment at the site. #7204 proposes a fixed `[TableId; MAX_NEXT_TABLE_DEPTH]` stack there too:

- `Vec::new()` **does not allocate** — a resolution that never traverses a next-table (the overwhelming majority) pays nothing.
- The clones happen only on an actual next-table hop, bounded at **8**: bounded work on a configured, non-default path.
- An inline `[_; 8]` stack would cost **~192 bytes on every resolution**, including all the ones that never push — paying the worst case always to remove a cost the common path never incurs, which is the trade #8083 refused.

## A pre-existing test pinned the copy

`canonical_route_table_borrows_default_and_owns_vrf` asserted `matches!(passthrough, Cow::Owned(_))` — pinning **the allocation this item exists to remove**, not a behaviour. Flipped with the reasoning recorded rather than deleted; the value assertion beside it is what that case was really guarding, and is unchanged.

| cell | failed |
|---|---|
| F1 revert the identity arm to `to_string` | 2 |
| F2 borrow unconditionally (wrong table) | 3 |
| control | green |

F1 binds the no-allocation property. **F2 binds the other direction partly through a pre-existing next-table canonicalisation test** — borrowing unconditionally returns the *wrong table* for a genuine rewrite, which no allocation-counting assertion would catch.

## Validation

`make test-rust` rc=0, **5001 passed / 0 failed**; `go test ./... -count=1` clean; `go build ./...` clean. Helper binary moves, so the cluster smoke was run: **17 passed, 0 failed**. Rebased onto current master and re-gated. Scope: 2 files.

## PR #8088 — ddns: withdraw through THIS family's last live backend [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7521-ddns-family-anchor`

Closes #7521

The live-updater-for-withdraw guard substituted `m.updater` — a **single** "last live backend seen" slot, advanced from whichever family happened to be live.

So on a box running **v6 DDNS only**, `m.updater` holds the v6 backend. When v4 became **backend-less** while still owning records, the guard substituted it and sent **v4's withdrawal to the v6 endpoint**. The wrong server is asked to delete a record it never published: the delete is refused or lands in the wrong zone, and the real A record is **orphaned live while the manager believes it withdrew**.

The trigger is narrow, and narrower than the source report said — the family must become backend-*less* (both blocks disappearing, or backend construction failing) while a withdrawal is needed. The ordinary disable path resolves to a nop with the anchor intact and was never affected.

`lastLiveUpdater` is the per-family anchor **#5814 already added** for the endpoint-transition path. It sat directly beside this guard, unused by it.

## The nil check is load-bearing, and it is not paranoia

`isNopUpdater` is a type assertion against `nopUpdater`, so it answers **false for a nil interface** — and `lastLiveUpdater` starts as two nils, which is exactly the post-restart state. `m.updater` was never nil (it is seeded), so swapping the anchor without the check substituted nil and **segfaulted the restart path**. `TestRestartNoBackendKeepsOwnershipNotOrphan` caught it.

Declining to substitute there is also the *right* answer rather than merely a safe one: after a restart with no backend there is no evidence which endpoint published the owned records, so the withdrawal waits for a live one rather than guess. **Guessing is the defect this fixes.**

## I bound the data first, and the matrix said so

My first version kept the two conditions inline and wrote cells against the **anchor array** — asserting `lastLiveUpdater[0] != lastLiveUpdater[1]` and so on. The matrix showed **both** the cross-family substitution and a wrong-index read escaping every one of them:

```
M1-revert-to-cross-family-anchor | GREEN   <- the defect itself, unbound
M3-v6-reads-the-v4-anchor        | GREEN
```

I had bound the data structure, not the wiring that reads it. Extracting `applyWithdrawAnchors` — reachable only through a full reconcile with DHCP leases, policies and a state file otherwise — turned both into reds. **Burying a one-line selection under that much machinery is how the defect survived in the first place.**

## Mutation matrix, after the extraction

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| cross-family anchor (the original bug) | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the nil check | RED | **RED(1)** — a panic |
| always read index 0 | RED | **RED(1)** |
| ignore ownership | RED | **RED(1)** |
| overwrite live arms | RED | **RED(2)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

Six test cells: the defect, **its mirror** (so a fix hard-coding index 0 is caught — "v4 uses v4's anchor" is otherwise satisfied by a function always returning `anchors[0]`), ownership gating the substitution, a live arm never overwritten by its anchor (without which the function could return the anchor unconditionally and every other cell still passes), the nil anchor, and the nop anchor.

## The file split

With its reasoning attached the method took `manager.go` to **2001 LOC**, one line over the 2000 `[REFACTOR]` floor the modularity audit measures against the merge base. Splitting is right rather than an accepted-list entry — the withdraw-anchor selection is a cohesive unit and the growth was mine. `manager.go` is now 1950.

## PR #8089 — config: redact archive-site URLs and the archival inline password [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7511-archive-sites-redaction`

Closes #7511

Two credentials rendered **verbatim** on `show configuration` and the raw-AST REST surfaces. Measured at master:

```
in : set system syslog file audit archive archive-sites "scp://user:pw@host/dir"
out: set system syslog file audit archive archive-sites "scp://user:pw@host/dir"

in : set system archival configuration archive-sites "scp://host/dir" password "s3cr3t"
out: set system archival configuration archive-sites scp://host/dir password s3cr3t
```

## Why #7510's fix could not reach them

#7510 fixed the **typed** half — a marshaller per owning type plus a reflective census that fails when a new URL-shaped field renders a planted credential. Neither sees these: the syslog `archive-sites` URL lives only in the raw AST and is never promoted to a typed field, so no `MarshalJSON` touches it; and the generic `password` key was masked only under `api-auth` or `dynamic-dns`, so a password nested under `archive-sites` matched neither scope. Same name-keyed limitation #6733 documented, on the other surface.

## Two different treatments, on purpose

The **URL** goes through `urlLeafIndices` → `RedactURL`, which strips userinfo and keeps the host and path. An operator needs to see *which* archive site is configured; only the credential is secret.

The **inline password** is masked outright by `secretIndices`, because all of it is.

## The `archive-sites` arm stops at `password`, and that is not incidental

The flat path is `archive-sites <url> password <secret>`. Marking every trailing token would hand the **secret** to `RedactURL` — and `RedactURL` is a no-op on input that is not a URL, so the password would render **verbatim while looking like it had been processed**. The two rules must not overlap.

If another sub-keyword is added under `archive-sites` it needs adding to that stop list, or its value is fed to `RedactURL`: a no-op rather than a corruption, but also an unredacted leaf. That is stated at the site.

## Asserted on the rendered output

The issue's acceptance criteria call this out and they are right — *"an existence check is what let the typed half hide"*. Every cell renders and greps.

| cell | what it stops |
|---|---|
| both URL spellings | the leak |
| inline password, asserting the **placeholder is present** | a render that merely dropped the secret, indistinguishable from one that masked it |
| the URL beside the password survives | the two rules overlapping |
| five credential-free values render unchanged | over-redaction — and the raw side needs its **own** check, because the values reaching this pass are lexer tokens, not typed strings |
| an `api-auth` password still masked, exactly two placeholders | the widening becoming "mask every password", which would silently remove the context gate that keeps a future non-secret `password` unmasked |

Every URL cell also asserts **the host and path survive** — a redaction that dropped the whole value satisfies "the credential is absent" and makes the leaf useless to the operator it is rendered for.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| drop the archive-sites URL arm | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the password scope | RED | **RED(2)** |
| no `password` stop (feeds the secret to RedactURL) | RED | **RED(2)** |
| URL pass always redacts (over-redaction) | RED | **RED(4)** |

## PR #8092 — vrrp: self-frame check consults the interface's address SET [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7334-self-frame-addr-set`

Closes #7334

`resolveLocalIPv4` selects **one** address — the lowest non-VIP IPv4 — and stores it as the snapshot. The four receive-path self-checks compared a frame's source against that single value.

So the self-check **also failed with a non-nil snapshot**: a self-advert sent from address A bypassed the comparison once the selected source had become B. `resolveEqualPriorityMaster` then compared `peerCmp` (our own **old** source A) against `localCmp` (our own **new** source B) and stepped down whenever `A > B` — **a coin flip, and a self-inflicted master-down.**

#6560 fixed the two delivery paths and named this residual explicitly. The comparison is the last line of defence if a delivery path is ever re-opened.

## The selection and the set are different things, deliberately

| | purpose | shape |
|---|---|---|
| `localIP` / `localIPv6` | the **send** source | one deterministic address (the lowest), so it does not flip on unrelated secondary-address churn — #2528's whole point |
| `localAddrSet` / `localAddrSetV6` | the **self-check** | every address we might have sent from, *including one the selection has since moved off* |

Both are recomputed from a single `reresolveLocalAddrs` read, so the set can never lag the selection — with a cell asserting they clear together.

## It fails open, and that bounds the risk

An unresolved set means *not ours*, so the frame is accepted. That is the #2528 RETH-MAC flush window, when `programRethMAC`'s link DOWN has removed every kernel address. **A frame we cannot classify must still be able to be a peer's advert** — dropping it would be the self-inflicted master-down this change exists to prevent. The fix's failure direction is bounded by the same rule as the bug's.

## The MAC alternative was not taken

The issue offers comparing the frame's source MAC against `vi.iface.HardwareAddr`. That covers only the AF_PACKET path, whereas the address set covers **all four** call sites including the raw-socket receivers — and it would introduce an L2 identity the package currently does not use at all (`grep HardwareAddr pkg/vrrp/*.go` non-test is still zero hits).

## The matrix caught my tests binding the wrong thing

My first ten cells called `isLocalAddr` directly. Unwiring a receive call site escaped **every one of them** — and "the check exists but consults the wrong thing" is the shape of this very defect. Four cells now drive the real `parseAfPacketIPv4`/`IPv6` and assert on `rxCh`, which is what an admitted advert actually reaches.

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| revert to the single selected address | RED | **RED(3)** |
| fail CLOSED on an unresolved set | RED | **RED(7)** |
| set not recomputed with the selection | RED | **RED(1)** |
| families cross | RED | **RED(1)** |
| v4 parse site unwired | RED | **RED(1)** |
| v6 parse site unwired | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

One mutation is **INERT rather than uncovered**: removing the explicit `To4()` from `canonicalVRRPAddr` changes nothing, because `net.IP.String()` performs the same check internally. Kept so the intent is visible at the call site rather than inferred from the standard library — with a comment saying *why* the mutation is inert, so the next reader does not delete it, see nothing red, and conclude the canonicalisation is untested.

## PR #8093 — nat: warn that a pool-utilization alarm cannot fire on an address-only pool [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7361-addr-only-alarm-advisory`

Closes #7361

**The defect is real and confirmed.** `used_ports` is a popcount over the allocator's occupancy bitmaps; `reserve_address_only` never touches occupancy — it records ownership in `live.address_only_owners`. So for a `port no-translation` pool `UsedPorts` is permanently 0, the utilization percentage is permanently 0, and the raise-threshold cannot be crossed.

**The harm is not the missing percentage.** The configuration reads as *working*: `show` renders the alarm, and 0% utilization is indistinguishable from a healthy pool. The alarm's silence looks exactly like the silence of a pool with plenty of headroom.

## I did not implement the fix the issue asks for, deliberately

#7361 proposes `capacity = AddressCount`, `used = distinct addresses currently allocated`. That models an exhaustion mode this pool class does not have.

Addresses are handed out round-robin (`reserve_address_only_roundrobin`) and freely **reused** across flows with different destination tuples — an address-only pool exhausts on **reverse-identity collision**, not on running out of addresses. So:

> **A one-address pool would report 100% utilization after its first flow and stay there while serving thousands more.**

That is not a warning. It is an alarm that fires on the first packet and never clears — worse than the current silence, because it trains operators to ignore the alarm that *does* work on port-bearing pools. On a two-address pool it would sit at 50% or 100% with no relation to headroom.

This replaces a never-fires alarm with a **statement that it cannot fire**, which fixes the stated harm, invents no percentage, and cannot false-positive. If a genuine early warning is wanted for this class, the signal is the **denial rate** (the `AllocatorExhausted` / collision path) — a different mechanism with its own threshold semantics, deserving its own specification.

The issue's acceptance criterion *"an address-only pool crossing raise-threshold RAISES"* presumes the percentage model and is not met, on purpose. Flagging that rather than shipping through it.

## Warn, never reject

The combination is valid — `port no-translation` and a global `pool-utilization-alarm` are each legitimate, and the alarm applies correctly to every other pool. #4316 accept-with-advisory, and the tolerant load / peer-sync path must keep booting (#1960).

## The monitor side

It stops evaluating such a pool and records the reason (`InapplicableReason`). **No syslog** — this is not an alarm transition, and raising one would be a permanent alarm on a healthy pool, exactly the failure mode the proposed denominator would produce. A pool raised while port-bearing and later switched to `no-translation` has its latched state dropped **without a clear syslog**, because a CLEAR would claim utilization fell below the threshold and that is not what happened.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| never warns | RED | **RED(2)** |
| warns on every pool | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the threshold gate | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the referenced gate | RED | **RED(1)** |
| deterministic not skipped | RED | **RED(1)** |
| unwired from `ValidateConfig` | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

**Two escaped first, and both were fixture problems worth naming.**

The threshold gate was uncovered because the only fixture without a raise-threshold had **no alarm stanza at all** and returned one line earlier at the nil check. I measured that the in-between state is reachable — `clear-threshold 50` with no raise compiles leniently to `RaiseThreshold: 0` — *before* writing the cell.

The deterministic fixture used a bare `deterministic ...` path that never populated `pool.Deterministic` (it lives under `port deterministic`), so it asserted the skip against a pool that was not deterministic. It failed **loudly** rather than passing vacuously, which is the good direction — but it is the same class as any fixture that does not reach the condition it names.

## PR #8094 — grpcapi: the #8057 validity check was weaker than its PR claimed [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7172-5a-validity-check-was-too-weak`

**Self-reported defect in merged code**, found while authoring cut 5a-2. Test-only; no shipped mapping was wrong.

## The overstated claim

#8057's body says every entry is checked to be "a real, already-canonical operational command". **That is too strong.**

`cmdtree.Canonicalize` returns `CanonicalOK` for `show interfaces zzbogus`, because `interfaces` carries a dynamic child and **value slots absorb arbitrary words**. So an entry naming a command nobody can run passed the check — provided the garbage landed in a value slot rather than at a keyword position.

The mutation run against #8057 (`show zzbogus nonexistent`) reds because nothing under `show` matches. That is why the hole did not surface: **the top level has no value slot to absorb anything. One level down it does.**

## `Canonicalize` is not wrong and is not changed

Absorbing operator data into value slots is exactly what it must do for a command an operator typed — `show interfaces ge-0/0/0` has to canonicalize. The mismatch is that *this table* holds argument-free command paths, so the stricter rule belongs to the table's validity check, not to the shared canonicalizer where it would break the callers cut 1 exists for.

## The fix

Every word must name a real node. Verified as a **paired result**:

- rejects `show interfaces zzbogus` and `show route zzbogus`
- accepts **all 40 current entries unchanged** — so no shipped mapping was wrong

Mutation: `GetInterfaces` → `show interfaces zzbogus` now reds `TestEveryMappedCommandIsCanonical7172` by name (build-clean).

## How it surfaced

The candidate-generation pass for 5a-2's 98 topics produced obvious nonsense that *resolved* — `show interfaces address book`, `show route alarms`. That is the tell, and I would not have seen it by re-reading the check. Generating a large batch of candidates against a validator is a cheap way to find out what the validator actually accepts, as opposed to what its author believes it accepts.

## Gate

`go test ./... -count=1` — **rc=0, 69 packages, 0 named FAILs**.

Refs #7172, #8057.

## PR #8095 — ddns: state the fingerprint's no-credential claim precisely [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7405-fingerprint-credential-claim`

Closes #7405

`BackendFingerprint`'s doc comment claimed the persisted digest "carries NO credentials", justified by listing the four `config.Secret`-typed fields that are excluded. The list is right; the headline is broader than the list supports. It is a claim about field *types*, and it reads as a guarantee about the hashed *values*.

`Server` is documented as accepting a full base URL, so `https://user:pw@host/` is a legal value, and it is hashed. `Server` is a plain `string`, not a `Secret`, so nothing redacts it on the way in.

### What I measured before deciding

| question | answer |
|---|---|
| is the digest persisted? | yes — `/var/lib/xpf/dhcp-ddns-state.json` |
| is it logged? | **no** — zero call sites |
| is it exported off-box? | no — not on any API or proto surface |
| which hashed inputs can hold userinfo? | **only `Server`**. `UpdateServer` is host/host:port, no scheme. `URLTemplate` handles credentials via its `%u`/`%p` placeholders |
| is a userinfo-bearing `Server` secret elsewhere on disk? | **no — it is already cleartext** in the config store, same root-only directory |

The issue's premise was that the digest is "persisted **and logged**". The logged half does not hold.

### Disposition: accept and document

The FNV-64a brute-force concern is real in the abstract and non-additive in practice. An attacker holding the ownership store also holds the config store beside it, where the same credential sits in cleartext — attacking an unsalted 64-bit digest is strictly harder than reading the neighbouring file.

Option 1 from the issue (fingerprint `RedactURL(Server)`) is the wrong trade here, and the reason is worth recording: it moves **every existing fingerprint**, and a moved fingerprint is indistinguishable from an endpoint change. On the first reconcile after upgrade that raises the #3735 ownership alarm for every record — a real upgrade hazard incurred to close a non-additive exposure.

So this changes only the comment. It states the enforced property, names the test that enforces it, states the `Server` caveat plainly, and records the condition under which the acceptance lapses (if the store ever ships off-box — a support bundle, telemetry, a peer sync) so that change is not made without revisiting this.

### No test added, deliberately

The property was already bound by `TestBackendFingerprintStableAndSecretFree` (#3735), which is **stronger** than anything this issue would have prompted — it also covers `Username`, `TSIGKeyName`, `AWSAccessKeyID`, `SourceAddress` and `Name`. I had written a replacement before finding it; it was strictly weaker, so I deleted it rather than ship redundant coverage.

Worth noting how it surfaced: my first mutation cells were run filtered to the new issue number and would have reported the new test as the only guard. Running them against the **whole package** is what showed the #3735 test reddening on both mutations.

### Validation

Two arity-preserving mutations of `backendFingerprint` (add/drop breaks `authorityFingerprint`'s signature and yields a build break, not a red — my first attempt did exactly that and scored two void cells):

| cell | mutation | build | collected | `--- FAIL` | reds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `p.URLTemplate` → `p.URLTemplate+string(p.Password)` | 0 | 536 | 2 | secret-invariance half |
| M2 | `p.Server` → `""` | 0 | 536 | 2 | endpoint-identity half |

Each localises to one half. `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` clean, zero `--- FAIL`. Diff is one file, comment-only.

## PR #8096 — config: redact the per-feed path on the AST config-read route (#7406) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `docs/7406-feed-url-secret-placement`

Closes #7406

## What #7406 asked, and what measuring it turned up

#7406 argues its residual is unsatisfiable: a secret that **is** a host label or a path segment cannot be redacted by any string rule, because `https://SECRET.dyn.example.com/upd` and `https://api.example.com/upd` are indistinguishable strings. **That is correct** — all four rows reproduce at HEAD, and this PR does not try to close them.

But the reachability question underneath it had not been asked, and asking it found a live leak of the *satisfiable* class on a surface the issue never checked.

## Which leaves can actually carry a secret in the host or path?

Exactly one family. The issue treats all five as equivalent; they are not.

| leaf | credential leaf available? | host/path secret reachable by construction? |
|---|---|---|
| DDNS `server` / `update-server` | YES — `password` / `api-token` | No |
| DDNS `url-template` (generic) | YES — `password`; template carries `%u`/`%p` **specifiers**, not literals | No |
| DDNS `checkip-url` | n/a — public IP echo, no auth | No |
| `archive-sites` | YES — sibling `password` leaf; userinfo handled | No |
| **`feed-server` `url` / `hostname` / `feed-name <f> path`** | **NO — the schema has none** | **YES** |

A `feed-server`'s complete leaf set is `url`, `hostname`, `update-interval`, `hold-interval`, `feed-name <n> path` (`pkg/config/schema_security.go:1293`). With no credential leaf, a subscription key has nowhere to go but the URL — and the provider, not the operator, picks the URL shape. Every DDNS backend by contrast has a dedicated `config.Secret` leaf, which is why `pkg/ddns/README.md` (`f329e0d12`) can tell operators to use the userinfo or query. **That advice does not transfer to feeds**, and the feeds README had no mention of redaction, tokens, credentials or secrets at all.

## The defect this fixes

`feed-name <f> path` is URL-bearing: `resolveBaseURL` joins it onto the feed-server's `url`/`hostname`, so the leaf carries a URL tail. `FeedEntry.MarshalJSON` has redacted it since #6703 — its own doc comment says a `?token=SECRET` query "is the common shape".

The AST route did not. `urlLeafIndices` had no `path` case. Measured before the fix, same config, two surfaces:

```
feed-server et url                 https://feeds.example.com/base?<redacted>   <- agree
feed-server et feed-name bad path  /sub/list.txt?token=SECRETPATHQ             <- AST VERBATIM
```

`RedactedClone` backs the on-box CLI `show configuration` (`pkg/cli/cli_show.go`), the gRPC config RPCs (`pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go`) and the REST config reads (`pkg/api/config.go`), so the token that the REST JSON route redacted was printed in cleartext on all three. This is the **query-string class** — the class #6703's acceptance criteria explicitly cover and `RedactURL` handles correctly — not the unsatisfiable host class.

## The fix

One `case "path"` gated on `feed-server` ancestry, following the doctrine already stated in the `urlLeafIndices` doc block: distinctive leaf names (`url`, `url-template`, `checkip-url`) match unqualified; generic ones (`server`, `update-server`) are context-gated. `path` is generic, so it is gated.

## Tests assert the agreement, not a literal

The two surfaces must agree, so the tests assert *that*, rather than pinning either side to an expected string — a literal would encode which surface is trusted, and here the AST side was the wrong one.

- `TestFeedPathQueryTokenIsRedactedOnBothSurfaces7406` — the token survives neither surface, and both render identically.
- `TestFeedPathWithoutCredentialIsUnchanged7406` — over-reach control: a credential-free path is still rendered verbatim on both. Without it, "redact the whole leaf" would pass the test above while destroying the value operators read.
- `TestFeedPathSegmentSecretIsRenderedOnBothSurfaces7406` — pins the boundary this deliberately does not cross, so a later one-sided "fix" of the path-segment case reproduces exactly the two-surface disagreement being closed here.

## Validation

- `go build ./...` clean.

## PR #8097 — nat: release the replaced synced session's reservation (#6979 F3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/6979-f3-release-on-replace`

Part of #6979 — closes **F3** only. F1 and F7b remain open, so this deliberately carries no close keyword.

## The row, and why it survived

F3 reads: *"`upsert_synced_with_origin` removes the previous session and discards `_previous`; the handler then reserves only the new decision. The replaced session's reservation is not released."*

The predicate still holds at the call site (coordinates drifted: the two `_previous` discards are now `install.rs:139` and `:324`). But taking it at face value produces the wrong fix, because **#6528 moved the release inside `reserve_flow`**, keyed on `SourceNatFlowKey` — the ORIGINAL 5-tuple, with no translated field. A same-key re-decision therefore finds the incumbent under the same flow and retires it with RELEASE semantics. Its own comment names F3's defect: *"retire the stale reservation first so we do not leak the old port's bit."*

So a NAT → different-NAT replacement already self-heals. Adding a release at the call site for that case would **double-free the port the new decision legitimately owns**.

## What actually leaks

The retire only runs if the replacement reaches `reserve_flow`. The reserve is gated twice — on `is_peer_synced() && !is_reverse` at the call site, and on `nat.rewrite_src.is_some()` inside `reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation_with_holder`. Three shapes route around it:

1. **NAT → no-NAT** — the active re-evaluates a reused 5-tuple after its NAT rule is withdrawn.
2. NAT → a reverse entry.
3. peer-synced → local-origin (HA activation, `allow_replace_local`).

Each installs the new session while the old port stays reserved with nothing left to free it: delete-sync releases the *current* decision, which no longer names that port. The port is held until the process exits.

## Measurement

Through the real `handle_upsert_synced`, reading `source_nat_pool_statuses().used_ports`, with the installed decision as an **anti-vacuity discriminator** — `used_ports` alone cannot separate "freed" from "the upsert was REJECTED so nothing changed":

| replacement | `used_ports` | installed `rewrite_src_port` | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| NAT → port 20001 | 1 → 1 | `Some(Some(20001))` | #6528 retires; correct |
| NAT → no-NAT | 1 → **1** | `Some(None)` | **leak** — landed with no NAT, port still held |
| NAT → no-NAT *(fixed)* | 1 → **0** | `Some(None)` | freed |

## The fix

Capture the previous `(decision, metadata)` before the upsert discards it; when the new entry will not re-reserve the flow, run the same teardown pair `handle_delete_synced` uses (`release_source_nat_allocation_for_worker` + `release_nat64_allocation_for_worker`, same holder id). The release sits **above** the `is_peer_synced()` gate so it also covers shape 3.

`new_entry_reserves` is load-bearing in **both** directions:
- Skipping the release when the new decision *does* reserve is what keeps `reserve_flow`'s own eviction from being double-freed.
- Releasing *unconditionally* — the obvious simplification — would drop this worker's holder bit and re-take it on a same-tuple refresh (HA sync reconnect, periodic re-upsert), opening a window for another worker's local allocation to steal the port.

## Tests

Three, all driving the real entry point so deleting the wiring reds them — testing the release helper directly would not. Each asserts a *different* value, so no cell can pass for another's reason:

- `synced_replace_dropping_nat_releases_the_old_reservation_6979_f3` — fail-on-revert; pins `installed == Some(None)` **first** so a rejected upsert cannot make it pass vacuously.
- `synced_replace_changing_nat_port_keeps_exactly_one_reservation_6979_f3` — over-reach control for the #6528 path. `0` here would mean this release double-freed the new decision's port.
- `synced_refresh_with_identical_nat_keeps_its_reservation_6979_f3` — over-reach control for the unconditional-release regression described above.

## Validation

- Rust: `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` → **rc=0, 5014 collected, 0 FAILED**.
- Go: `go test -count=1 ./...` → **rc=0, 0 `--- FAIL`, 0 package FAIL, 0 races**.

## PR #8098 — session: give SessionKey a routing domain (#2387 Track B-P0, phase 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `feat/7160-vrf-session-key`

Phase 1 of the Option-B decision on #7160. **Does not close it** — this is the structural half; the field is not yet populated.

### The defect

Two flows in different routing-instances sharing a 5-tuple collide in the conntrack map. Live under PBR `then routing-instance`: the established-session fast path short-circuits before `ingress_route_table_override`, so tenant B's flow inherits tenant A's cached egress, NAT and **policy** decision — a cross-tenant policy bypass.

### What this does

`SessionKey` gains `routing_domain: u32` (`0` = default instance, so single-VRF identity is byte-identical). All five key transforms **preserve** it rather than defaulting it. That symmetry is what makes the field legal on the key, and is the axis on which it differs from #6928's `ingress_ifindex`/`ingress_vlan_id` — those sit on the session *value* because the reply ingresses on the forward flow's *egress*.

### What this deliberately does NOT do

Nothing populates the field. Every value in the tree is `0`, so **the defect is still live in production** and the commit-time overlap warning remains the operator's only signal. Phase 2 threads `StableRoutingInstanceTableID(name)` through the control plane and onto the wire.

### Correction: phase 2 does not need an HA protocol bump

#7160 says Option B "bumps the HA wire, which makes a release non-rolling-upgradable", and I repeated that in my implementation contract on the issue. **Both quote plan §4d, which plan v5 §0a corrected** — and the correction is already in this repo, in the section directly below the one this PR edits:

> The HA session-sync wire does NOT need a version bump […] it rides as a length-gated trailing **value** field, exactly like #2170 `Generation` […] Interning **domain 0 = the default routing-instance** makes an old peer's omitted field decode to the default VRF […] and `CurrentHAProtocolVersion` never moves.

Acting on the issue text would have broken rolling upgrade for nothing. My first draft of the README section asserted the bump and **contradicted the wire bullet twenty lines below it**; that is fixed, and the guard's failure message now warns the phase-2 implementer by name.

### The doc guard was inverted, not deleted

`vrf_session_identity_doc_guard.rs` asserted `!key_rs.contains("routing_domain")` and fired on this change — which is exactly why the docs are in this PR. Deleting a guard that has just done its job would retire it silently, so instead it now:

- pins that the field **exists** (a revert re-opens #2387);
- **counts** the five preserving transforms — fixing four and missing one is the plausible partial revert, and a search rather than a count would not see it;
- fires when `routing_domain` reaches `src/protocol/`, so phase 2 cannot land without revisiting the docs.

### Validation

`make test-rust` and `make test-go` both clean, zero failures.

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `reverse_wire_key` zeroes the domain | 4882 | 0 | 1 — transform cell only |
| M2 | field excluded from `Hash`/`Eq` | 4882 | 0 | 2 — the two identity cells only |
| M3 | a third transform zeroed | 2 | 0 | 1 — guard, *"found 4, expected 5"* |

Each localises to the cell that owns the property.

### Two process notes worth recording

**`cargo fmt` must not be run in this repo.** Pristine `origin/master` has **3054 rustfmt hunks** under rustfmt 1.9.0, so formatting produces thousands of lines of unrelated churn. My first attempt did exactly that: 307 collateral files, which broke the #6592 runtime-view canary and made the diff 3674/2104 instead of 557/23. `git diff origin/master --name-only` against the set of files actually containing my change is what caught it — a scope check is the only gate that is scope-independent.

**The 241 construction-site updates came from rustc's own E0063 spans**, re-run to zero remaining, with indentation copied from the preceding field line so no formatter was needed.

The 6 deletions outside my additions are a pre-existing 12-space misindent on `discriminator:` normalized to 8 in the five transform bodies this PR edits.

## PR #8099 — cli: record why the egress FIB hit cannot be zone-corroborated (#7240) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7240-comment`

Comment-only. Does not close #7240 — it records the measured reason that issue cannot be done as filed, so the next reader is not sent at a change that does not work.

The existing comment said the symmetric check awaited "the egress zone's own value … enumerated across the fabric/tunnel override paths". I did that enumeration, built the check on all three surfaces, and **four pre-existing tests went red**. They are right.

```
--- FAIL: TestInterfaceFilterEgressArmMakesColumnNameAnotherInterface6928
    `interface lo.80` must select both sessions through the egress arm, got 0: []
--- FAIL: TestInterfaceFilterReachesRowViaEgressArm6928
--- FAIL: TestMatchesV4_InterfaceFilter
--- FAIL: TestSessionEntryEgressIfaceParity_4650
```

### Why it is structural, not a pending enumeration

**Ingress** — the zone and the `{ifindex, VLAN}` are stamped at the *same instant from the same observation*: the packet arrived on that interface, and that interface's zone is the one policy used. They must agree, so a disagreement is positive evidence of a recycled ifindex. That is the whole mechanism of #6987.

**Egress** — the FIB result and the security zone are *two different derivations*. One answers "which netdev does this route leave by", the other "what zone did policy assign". They legitimately differ for any egress interface that is not a zone member: `lo`, and by construction the tunnel and fabric paths. A disagreement is the normal case, so it cannot adjudicate a recycle.

I had enumerated where `egress_zone` is **written** and concluded it was safe. That was the wrong half — the hazard is that a *correct* egress interface need not belong to the recorded egress *zone* at all. The tests found what the enumeration missed.

### No partial landing is available

- **Filter**: the row becomes unreachable by a filter naming the interface it actually left on. The failing test documents selecting on either direction as intended — *"not a defect"*.
- **Display**: the same row prints `""` instead of `lo.80` — suppressing a **true** name to remove a hypothetical wrong one. Strictly worse.

A real fix needs a datum recorded at the same instant as the FIB ifindex: an interface generation compared at query, or the resolved egress *name* carried on the session. Both are larger than #7240 as filed; full reasoning is in the issue.

Validation: `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` clean, zero failures. One file, comment only.

## PR #8100 — cos: make the residual-surplus reset linearizable against refill (#7206 A1-b5-F4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7206-f4-residual-linearizable`

Part of #7206 — closes **A1-b5-F4** only. A1-b1-F6 is the other survivor, so no close keyword. (I re-measured the cohort today: [6 of the 8 rows are already fixed](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7206#issuecomment-5470687073).)

### The race

`reset_residual_surplus_budget` published `tokens = 0` and `last_refill_ns` as two independent stores. `refill_residual_surplus_budget` claimed the timestamp CAS and then added tokens in a **separate** loop. A reset interleaved between those two steps left non-zero tokens after a completed reset — residual surplus that the reset had just cancelled.

### Why the check runs after the CAS, and only after

A pre-CAS check is the intuitive placement and is what I wrote first. It cannot be the guarantee: a reset can land between that check and the CAS, and **the CAS cannot detect it** — a reset stores `0`, so if the expected `tokens` is also `0` the compare *succeeds* and writes the stale `added` on top of a completed reset. That is exactly the reported failure.

### Mutation testing removed half the fix

I implemented both checks. Each turned out **redundant given the other** — deleting either one alone left the full suite green, because the survivor caught the case:

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `reset` no longer bumps the generation | 4890 | clean | 2 |
| M2 | pre-CAS check removed (both present) | 4890 | clean | **0 — escaped** |
| M3 | post-CAS check removed (both present) | 4890 | clean | **0 — escaped** |
| M4 | post-CAS check removed, now the sole guard | 4890 | clean | 1 |

Two guards where only one is load-bearing read as defence in depth while actually being an untested branch beside a guard nobody could tell was doing the work. So the pre-CAS check is **removed**, and M4 shows the remaining one is bound.

This is the compound-mutation blind spot in miniature: neither single deletion could fail, so only mutating each *in the presence of the other* revealed that my test could not distinguish them.

### Testability

`commit_refill_tokens` is extracted from the refill loop so the guard is reachable from a test **without winning a race**. That matters more than usual here: a threaded probe that simply fails to hit the interleaving returns the same green as a correct implementation, so it cannot be the primary evidence. The concurrent test is kept for livelock and bound checking only, and its doc comment says exactly that.

The positive control is load-bearing too — a `commit_refill_tokens` that never added anything would satisfy the "adds nothing" assertion perfectly.

### Accepted trade-off

Restoring `0` rather than retrying is deliberate: the reset is the newer intent and declared the budget empty as of its own `now_ns`. A legitimate post-reset refill running concurrently can have its tokens dropped — transient (the next refill re-adds them) and erring toward granting *less* surplus, which is the safe direction. Documented in the code.

### Validation

`make test-rust` and `make test-go` both clean, zero failures. Scope is 2 files, zero collateral.

`session_install_stale_ignored_total`, `session_delete_stale_ignored_total` and `synced_import_reserve_refused_total` were computed, unit-tested, and **never assigned into `ProcessStatus`** — so they reached no operator through status, gRPC or Prometheus. A counter nobody can interpret is barely better than one nobody can see, so each descriptor says what a nonzero value means:

- the two **stale-ignored** counters are the helper-side back-stop for #2170's generation guard (the authoritative half is the Go cluster apply layer). Nonzero = a delayed peer install/delete arrived after a newer generation was committed and the helper declined to regress it. Expected 0 outside config churn.
- **synced_import_reserve_refused** is #6600: peer-synced imports refused because this node could not reserve the translated NAT port. Sustained growth means the standby cannot hold the primary's translations, so those flows **will not survive a failover** — the pre-failover warning, not the post-mortem.

## PR #8102 — dataplane: run the input filter before the embedded-ICMP reversal (#7359) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7359-icmp-reversal-filter-order`

Addresses the **input-filter half** of #7359. No close keyword — the PBR half is deliberately not done; see below.

The flowless embedded-ICMP NAT reversal reverse-translated an ICMP error, queued it toward the internal client, and `continue`d — skipping the interface input filter further down the same arm. A `discard` term did not drop it, a `count` term did not advance, a policer did not meter it.

### Hoisted, not duplicated

The L3 identity and the filter evaluation move **above** the reversal so both consumers share one evaluation. Adding a second call site inside the reversal arm would double-count every counter and re-fire every log term on the flowless path — a worse defect than the one being fixed, and one no single-path test would catch.

### PBR is not in this PR, and that is a decision rather than an oversight

The issue's title covers PBR too, but the two are not the same change. The input filter is an **admission** question and the hoist answers it. `then routing-instance` steers a route lookup that the reversal *replaces* with its own resolution toward the client — threading an override in changes **where the reversed error is routed**, not whether it is admitted. It wants its own review and its own test, so I have left #7359 open for it rather than folding it in quietly.

### Two things about the test

**The fixture nearly produced a false negative.** My first version left `flow_src_addr`/`flow_dst_addr` zero in the metadata. `l3_session_flow_from_meta` returns `None` for an unspecified address — the *reachable* #7055 leg — so `l3_ctx` was `None`, the filter block was skipped on **every** path, and the test failed **against the fixed code**. That reads exactly like "the fix does not work", and I was one step from recording it as one. What separated a fixture defect from a production finding was instrumenting the hoisted block to print whether it was reached and whether `l3_ctx` was `Some`:

```
PROBE7359 reached hoist, l3_ctx.is_some=false
```

Reached, but empty — so the ordering was right and the input was wrong.

**The absence assertion needs a fixture guard.** The ordering cell asserts *no queued forward*, and an absence is satisfied just as well by a fixture that configures nothing. So `the_7359_fixture_actually_attaches_its_input_filter` is kept **permanently** rather than deleted after use: if a renamed snapshot field, a changed family string or a moved ifindex ever stopped the filter attaching, the ordering test would keep passing while measuring nothing.

The ordering test also reuses the #5690 reachability fixture unchanged except for the filter, so the pair shows the filter is what changed the outcome.

### Validation

`make test-rust` and `make test-go` clean.

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | move the filter evaluation back below the reversal | 4892 | clean | 1 — `input_filter_discard_drops_the_embedded_icmp_reversal_7359`, and nothing else |

Cluster smoke on the loss userspace cluster under `/tmp/xpf-cluster.lock` (hot-path ordering change): **17 passed, 0 failed at 22.7 Gbps**.
