## PR #8106 — session: populate SessionKey.routing_domain from the ingress interface (#7160 phase 2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7160-phase2-routing-domain`

Closes #7160

## What this does

#7160 phase 1 (PR #8098) put `routing_domain: u32` on `SessionKey`. Nothing set it, so every value in the tree was 0 and the defect was still live in production: two flows in different routing instances that share a 5-tuple collided in the conntrack map, and because the established-session fast path short-circuits before `ingress_route_table_override`, tenant B's flow inherited tenant A's cached egress, NAT and **policy** decision.

**This is phase 2. It populates the field.**

## The number, and where it is decided

`StableRoutingInstanceTableID(name)` — a pure FNV-1a of the routing-instance NAME into `[100000, 999999]`, already gated at commit against collisions — is computed in **Go** (`routingInstanceDomain`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go`), shipped per interface on the config snapshot as `InterfaceSnapshot.routing_domain`, and never re-hashed in Rust. Two implementations of one hash in two languages is exactly the "when two spellings must agree" trap, and this number has to mean the same thing on the HA peer.

The band starts above 0, so a named instance can never collide with the 0 that means "the default instance". That is what lets 0 do triple duty: an interface in no instance, a snapshot from an older Go binary, and a peer ingress identity this node cannot resolve.

## The stamp

One site — the poll path's **stage 9b**, immediately after fabric-ingress classification — from the **LOGICAL** (VLAN unit) ingress ifindex, the same identity the zone, filter and pre-routing-NAT paths already use. Every key the descriptor derives (lookup key, installed forward key, reverse companion, index entries) therefore carries one consistent domain.

It runs *after* stage 9 because that is an input, not a detail: a frame that arrived over the fabric link did not arrive on the flow's real ingress interface, so the fabric link's own membership would be a **wrong** answer rather than a missing one. A peer-zone-encoded frame resolves its domain from that zone (`zone_routing_domain`), which is **absent** for a zone straddling two instances — the #6722 "identify exactly one, or nothing" discipline.

`has_routing_domains` is a single-bool gate, false for every deployment with no routing-instance interface membership (including the smoke cluster), which keeps session identity there bit-identical to pre-#7160.

## The correction phase 2 had to make — please read this part

Phase 1's field doc and plan v5 §0a both assert *a flow's routing domain is the same in both directions*, and all five key transforms preserved it on that basis. **Measured against this dataplane, that is false**, and §3 of the plan already says why: the transit route lookup is **not** VRF-isolated — it uses the DEFAULT table unless a PBR term overrides it. So a flow that ingresses on a routing-instance member interface and egresses out of the default instance is a real, *working* configuration whose reply resolves a different domain. Keying the reverse-match index on the forward domain would have blackholed every such flow's replies: a forwarding outage, not a hardening.

The maintainer flagged exactly this on the issue — *"config-derived guarantees the two NODES agree; it does not guarantee the two DIRECTIONS do"*. This is the answer.

So the transforms split, and **both halves are load-bearing**:

| transform | domain | why |
|---|---|---|
| `forward_wire_key` | preserve | another key of the same direction |
| `translated_session_key` | preserve | a reverse entry's own translated alias |
| `reverse_session_key` | preserve | navigates between the two halves of one flow |
| `reverse_wire_key` | **zero** | builds the index a REPLY is looked up under |
| `reverse_canonical_key` | **zero** | same |

The isolation the zeroing would otherwise cost is recovered one layer up: `find_forward_nat_match` walks the (1:N) reverse bucket in **two passes**, preferring a candidate whose forward session carries the reply's own domain and falling back to a domain-agnostic match only when none does. Two contained tenants demux exactly; a non-contained flow keeps forwarding as it did before the field existed. `reverse_match_key` is the one name for the zeroing convention so the index side and the probe side cannot drift. The shared NAT map, being 1:1 rather than 1:N, expresses the same preference as two probes.

**The forward direction — which is where the bypass lives** — is exact: forward lookups go through `key_to_handle` on the full key, so two tenants hold two entries and neither can reach the other's.

## HA: no protocol bump, and no new wire field either

The issue text says Option B "bumps the HA wire"; that quotes plan §4d, which v5 §0a corrected. §0a's finding stands, and phase 2 is cheaper than §0a needed it to be: **the domain does not ride the wire at all.**

It is a pure function of the flow's ingress interface and the config; both nodes run identical config; and #7095 already resolves the peer's cluster-stable ingress NAME into the importing node's own ifindex/vlan. So the importing node **derives** it (`Coordinator::synced_routing_domain`) instead of reading a second number that could disagree with the first. `CurrentHAProtocolVersion` and `SessionSyncWireVersion` both stay put; rolling upgrade is unaffected.

A session whose ingress identity the peer could not name (fabric-redirected, #7096) imports at domain 0 — the pre-#7160 identity — and re-adjudicates through policy after a failover instead of being taken over. A correctness-preserving degradation, not a bypass, and it is stated in the docs.

## PR #8107 — config: hard-reject dangling class-of-service interface references (#7337) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7337-cos-iface-ref-strict`

Refs #7337 — the **Go strict gate** the issue says must land *before* a Rust backstop. No close keyword; the backstop is now unblocked but not done.

The seven `class-of-service interfaces` reference fields were warn-only at commit and then failed OPEN in the dataplane: `forwarding_build/cos.rs` resolves each name with a bare `.get(...)` yielding `None`, with no `Missing*Ref` and no error. The interface materializes no scheduler queues, or a classifier arm contributes nothing — QoS silently degrades to best-effort while the committed config still says the interface is shaped and classified. The operator's only evidence is a warning they saw once at commit time.

### The population is seven, not four

The issue names four. At master there are seven — `scheduler-map`, `output-traffic-control-profile`, the `dscp` / `ieee-802.1` / `inet-precedence` classifiers, and the `dscp` / `ieee-802.1` rewrite-rules. The two added since it was filed leak the same way.

### Why the existing gate did not cover this

`validateClassOfServiceSchedulerMapRefsStrict` validates the **scheduler-map → scheduler** link. This is the **interface → scheduler-map** link. They are the outer and inner halves of one reference chain and only the inner one was gated, so an interface naming a scheduler-map that does not exist at all committed cleanly. Easy to mistake one for the other when grepping — I nearly closed this issue on that basis.

### The no-brick half is load-bearing, and the matrix proves it

Strict on commit, lenient on load/peer-sync per #1960. That is not a formality here: **the mutation that ignores the lenient flag reds five tests besides the one written for it**, because several existing fixtures legitimately load dangling-reference configs. A gate that rejected on both paths would brick an upgrading node carrying a config its previous binary accepted.

### Two judgement calls, stated rather than buried

**`Level` is checked as well as `Units`.** `applyCoSInterfaceLevelBindings` folds an interface-level binding into each *configured* unit before the gates run, so for an interface with units this is redundant — but an interface-level binding on a stanza with **no** configured units is folded nowhere and would otherwise be invisible. It has its own cell; removing the check reds exactly that cell.

**A dangling `ieee-802.1` rewrite-rule is rejected even though that feature is documented inert here.** The gate is about whether the NAME resolves, not whether the resolved rule has a runtime effect. Gating only the enforced references would make commit behaviour depend on an implementation detail the operator cannot see from their config.

### Three existing tests were repointed, not loosened

They asserted the warning these references used to produce. They now compile on the **tolerant** path, where a warning is still the outcome. I did not loosen the shared strict helpers: that would have silently removed the strict check from every other test in those files, which would keep passing while proving nothing about commit behaviour. Two files get a lenient *sibling* helper used only by the fixtures that dangle on purpose.

### Validation

`make test-go` clean; `make test-rust` clean at 5023 collected (no Rust touched).

| cell | mutation | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | gate unregistered | clean | 3 |
| M2 | lenient flag ignored — the #1960 brick | clean | 6 (mine + 5 pre-existing) |
| M3 | `Level` check removed | clean | 1 — exactly its own cell |

Scope checked against the **merge-base**, not the moving `origin/master` ref: 7 files, zero collateral.

One process note: I lost this implementation once mid-work by running `git checkout --` inside a mutation cell while the fix was still uncommitted — the applied-check is meaningless there, and the restore wiped the subject rather than the mutation. Re-applied, then committed *before* mutating.

## PR #8109 — userspace-dp: revalidate established sessions against a changed static input filter (#7212) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7212-static-filter-revalidation`

Implements the mechanism #7212 decided: lazy per-tuple revalidation of an
established session's interface INPUT filter, stamped by config generation.

Does NOT close #7212 — one acceptance bullet remains, tracked as #8108 and
stated below.

## The gap

A purely STATIC address/protocol/port `then discard` attached or tightened after
a session was created was never rechecked, so that flow forwarded until it idled
out. The session-hit fast path re-evaluated an input filter only when its verdict
genuinely varies per packet (a DSCP match, #1430, or a per-packet L4 match,
#2362), and the rotation purge is gated on the same predicate, so a static filter
change matched neither. Junos firewall filters are stateless and evaluated on
every packet, so this was a parity gap as well as a revocation gap.

The obvious symmetry — an interface-keyed clear, mirroring the policy
invalidation that runs at commit — was rejected in #5858 with evidence and is not
re-proposed: it drops PERMITTED flows, and a purged permitted SNAT flow
reinstalls on a DIFFERENT translated port.

## Mechanism

For a static filter the verdict is a pure function of `(ingress interface,
family, 5-tuple)`, all constant for the life of one direction of a session:

* `SessionEntry::filter_revalidated_gen` records the
  `ValidationState::config_generation` this direction's verdict was computed
  under. `install` stamps the generation the worker published for the pass;
  `upsert_synced` stamps `0`, which is never a live generation.
* On an established-session hit whose stamp is stale, the static verdict is
  re-derived ONCE and the entry re-stamped.
* The session is revoked only if the new verdict is DENY.

The re-derivation is side-effect free. `NonRoutingCountPolicy::Never` runs the
SAME walk the counted evaluator runs with counting suppressed on both of its
arms, so the action it returns is that walk's action by construction — there is
no second walk to drift. Counting here would inflate every matched `then count`
term by one packet per PERMITTED session per commit, which is the common case and
would be silent. Only on a DENY does the ordinary counted evaluator run, so the
one newly-denied packet is counted, logged and rejected exactly once.

It evaluates on the flow's 5-tuple ALONE (`TermMatchExtra::default()`), not on
the triggering packet — see "Two defects found in review" below for why that is
load-bearing rather than an optimisation.

Which is why this lands as one PR rather than a multi-PR feature. Each verified

## PR #8110 — userspace-dp: carry the tunnel discriminator on the HA session-sync wire [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7188-session-sync-discriminator`

Closes #7188

## The defect

Two RFC 2890 GRE tunnels between one pair of outer endpoints are two sessions
on the active and **one aliased session on the standby**.

GRE is IP protocol 47 and carries no L4 ports, so the two tunnels share a
5-tuple. The helper's own `SessionKey` separates them on a typed
`TunnelDiscriminator` — that is #7188's landed half. The sync path did not carry
it: `build_synced_session_key` hardcoded

```rust
discriminator: Default::default(),
```

and `Default` for `TunnelDiscriminator` is `None` — the *"no discriminator
concept for this protocol"* class, not even `Unkeyed`. So a keyed GRE session
did not merely lose its key across sync; it arrived in the class reserved for
non-tunnel protocols, and **both** records rebuilt to the same key. `install.rs`
opens with an unconditional `remove_entry`, so the second install evicted the
first. After a failover the two tunnels shared one policy decision, one NAT
state, one counter set and one timeout — the exact collapse #7188 exists to
prevent, restored silently by the failover.

## Why this is 30+ files and not a one-line receive-side fix

**Go collapsed the two tunnels BEFORE the wire.** `snapshotDeltaSink` — the
cold-prime bulk window — deduped into `map[dataplane.SessionKey]`, and protocol
47 has no ports, so two same-endpoint tunnels are one Go key. The later delta
silently overwrote the earlier, and the standby was primed with one session for
two tunnels regardless of what the wire carried. A value-only wire field would
**not** have satisfied the acceptance bullet on its own. The dedup key is now
`(session key, discriminator)` and the sink's delete arms take the converted
value, so a close in the same batch retracts only the tunnel it names.

The discriminator itself crosses six hops, each an independent place to drop it:
the helper's JSON delta producer, both binary HA delta frames (**open AND
close** — a close names the session to retract, and for protocol 47 the 5-tuple
names two tunnels at once), Go's `SessionDeltaInfo`, `SessionValue{,V6}`, the
`pkg/cluster` wire (v4 and v6), `SessionSyncRequest`, and the peer helper.

## `0` is RESERVED for "not carried", and is NOT the encoding of `None`

This is the load-bearing detail, and it is a correction to the obvious design.

`serde(default)` and a short length-gated record both yield `0`, so `0` is the
one value a peer produces **without meaning to**. A build that has the field
always states a class, `None` included. Without that separation a peer that
predates the field is indistinguishable from a new peer with

## PR #8111 — nat: refuse a source-NAT identity a peer pool already owns (#6979 F6) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/6979-f6-pool-address-overlap`

Part of #6979 — **F6 only**, and nothing else on that issue. F1, F7b and F3 are already disposed
(measured in the issue's own re-measurement comments); F4 and F5 stay open.

## What actually reproduces, and what does not

F6's second half says a **match-only** rule edit "strands a reservation in an
allocator that can no longer match the flow, while the rule that now owns it is
free to reissue the tuple". Before designing anything I drove three probes
against `origin/master`. Single-address pools, one-port range, so a duplicate is
unambiguous:

| probe | construction | master |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | pools `a` and `b` both `[203.0.113.1]`; a **match-only edit** narrows r1's `source-address` so flow 2 matches r2 | flow 2 gets the **identical** `203.0.113.1:20000` flow 1 still holds |
| **P2** | the same two pools, **no edit at all** | the same duplicate |
| **P3** | **ONE** pool, the same match-only edit | `Unavailable(AllocatorExhausted)` — **no defect** |

**P3 is what decided the design, and it corrects the finding.** The key's
ignorance of match criteria and zone scope is harmless on its own: a match-only
edit changes none of `(pool name, addresses, port range)`, so the allocator is
reused by `Arc` and its live reservation keeps refusing the tuple. **F6's own
fix suggestion — add match criteria to the key — would have fixed nothing and
broken exactly that carryover**, which is the stranding `drain_allocator_key`
(#7717) exists to prevent. P2 says the edit is not load-bearing either.

What is left is the real defect: **two distinct allocator keys can cover one
pool address**, so that address carries two independent occupancy bitmaps and
neither can see the other's reservations. The comment #7858 left on
`carry_renamed_pool_reservations` names the hazard exactly — "keeping them apart
would give one address two independent occupancy domains, which is the collision
the key exists to prevent" — while two differently-named pools on one address
are that state, live on master.

## Severity, not oversold

- The config is **rejected at strict commit** by the Go #5144 gate
  (`validateNATPoolExternalTupleOverlapStrict` — on address overlap alone; it
  does not consult port ranges). It reaches the dataplane only from a tolerated
  lenient load, a peer sync, an older control plane, or a handcrafted snapshot:
  the same population #6812's aggregate-budget gate exists for.
- The consequence is a duplicate translated identity — two live flows on one
  `(pool address, port)` toward one remote, replies the reverse index cannot
  attribute. Mis-delivery, not a leak.
- What the issue calls "protection in the wrong place" is real but **benign on a
  valid config**: teardown sweeps every pool rule without running its matcher,
  so a stranded reservation is still released. P3 measures that. **This PR does
  not claim to fix a stranded release, because there is not one to fix.**

The test is right and the code is wrong. `reverse_wire_key` builds the **reverse-match index** — the bucket a reply is looked up under — and this dataplane's transit route lookup is not VRF-isolated (default table unless a PBR term overrides). ## The finding

Phase 2 resolves a peer-synced session's routing domain from the #7095 cluster-stable ingress identity rather than carrying it on the wire. That is right for every session whose ingress the sender could *name*. It was wrong for the ones it could not — #7096 fabric-redirected sessions, and any session with no cluster-stable ingress name. Those imported at **domain 0**, and phase 2's own docs called it *"a correctness-preserving degradation, not a bypass"*.

**That claim was wrong.** 0 is not a neutral placeholder on a node that runs routing instances — it is the **default routing instance**. An import filed there sits at exactly the key the domain-agnostic fallback probe in `lookup_shared_forward_nat_match` reaches:

```rust
if let Some(exact) = map.get(reply_key).cloned() { return Some(exact); }
let probe = crate::session::reverse_match_key(reply_key);   // domain -> 0
map.get(&probe).cloned()
```

So a reply that *did* resolve its own domain can match a session that was only keyed at 0 because nothing knew its domain. That is the HA half of the collision #7160 exists to close, and no single-instance test can see it, because there every key is legitimately 0.

The fallback probe is **not** the defect — it is what keeps a non-contained flow's reply resolving at all. Manufacturing wrong domain-0 keys on the sync path was.

## The fix: three states, not two

`Coordinator::synced_routing_domain` now returns `Option<u32>`:

| state | meaning | upsert | delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Some(0)` | the default routing instance — and the **only** domain on a node with no routing-instance membership | import | delete |
| `Some(n)` | a tenant's instance | import | delete |
| `None` | routing instances exist and the request named nothing to resolve one from | **refuse** | proceed at 0 + per-domain sweep |

The two verbs answer `None` differently on purpose: a refused **delete** *leaks* a session, while an over-broad sweep removes nothing the 5-tuple did not already name.

The refusal is `SyncedImportOutcome::RejectedUnknownRoutingDomain`, carrying its own stable reason token (`unknown-routing-domain`) so Go can tell it from a transport failure and from the other semantic refusals, and counted by `synced_import_unknown_routing_domain_total`.

**What refusing costs, stated plainly:** on a VRF deployment a synced session with no cluster-stable ingress name is not taken over, so its flow re-adjudicates through policy after a failover. That is the *same* outcome the old behaviour produced for those flows, minus the cross-domain reachability.

## Tests

A cell that asserted the OLD behaviour by name (`an_unnamed_peer_ingress_imports_at_the_default_domain`) is **rewritten rather than deleted**, and records why its previous claim was wrong.

The new cells drive the real control-socket dispatcher:
- refused, **nothing published**, and counted — on a node with routing instances;
- **still imports** on a single-instance node (the half that keeps this from being a fail-closed regression for every cluster today);
- a **named** ingress still imports at its own domain, so the refusal is scoped to the unresolvable case rather than turning off HA sync for VRF deployments.

## Not done here, and why

Carrying the domain on the sync wire is the *complete* fix — it removes the degradation as well as the reachability. It is not in this PR because Go's `SessionValue` takes its ingress identity from the **BPF conntrack mirror struct**, so a wire-carried domain is a shared C struct change with its own alignment rules. That belongs in its own cut. This change removes the reachability now.

## Observability

The refusal is counted and **exported**: `xpf_userspace_synced_import_unknown_routing_domain_total`. It is the only signal that a VRF cluster is silently not taking over a subset of its peer's sessions, and it is always 0 on a single-instance node — so sustained growth is actionable and a 0 is a real "every synced import resolved its domain" answer.

## Three cost sites, one shape

#8111 rebuilt the pool-overlap index per **distinct allocator** rather than per
rule, because rules are not bounded by #6812's aggregate budget and pool
addresses are. That fixed the counting pass and the owner pass. Three sites with
the same shape survived:

| # | site | before | after | found by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the **assignment** pass — deciding which rules get the index — scanned every pool-mode rule's full address vector | 1024 rules over two overlapping `/16` pools: **67,108,864** hash lookups at apply | 131,072; the address scan runs once per distinct allocator and the per-rule step is a pointer compare | my own re-check |
| 2 | the **`distinct` dedup** was documented as bounded by `max_pools`. It was not: `PortAllocator::default()` builds a **fresh `Arc` per rule** and every failed pool rule carries one, so D could equal R | **R(R−1)/2** `same_allocator` comparisons | rules whose allocator has zero occupancy slots are skipped — such an allocator can never answer `holds_port` true, so it is not an occupancy domain | Codex round 2, finding 1 |

slots, so the case that actually matters is still indexed by site 2's skip.

Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: a rule receives the index exactly when its
allocator covers an address another **real** allocator also covers.

## PR #8118 — cluster: show when a peer's RG state was substituted locally (#7367) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7367-peer-override-visible`

Refs #7367 — the **second** acceptance criterion only. No close keyword; the first criterion is not addressed and I say why below.

`show chassis cluster status` renders the **post-override** `peerGroups` map, so a peer state *this node substituted* was indistinguishable from one the peer actually reported.

`applyTransferCommitOverridesOnPeerStateLocked` rewrites a peer group's `State` to `secondary-hold` in the **same map that feeds both the election and the operator's view**. One write corrupts both.

That is how #6656 presented as a healthy cluster **on both nodes at once**: node0 printed node1 as `secondary-hold` because node0's own override forced it, node1 printed itself `primary`, and neither render carried anything anomalous — while one node held 33 sessions and 4.6M packets against the other's 1 session and 4.7K.

### The change

`PeerGroupState` gains `StateOverriddenLocally` and an `OverrideReason`. The reason is not decoration: a transfer-out override stays armed until cleared, a commit-grace window expires on its own, and the operator's response differs. **`State` and every election consequence are unchanged** — this only lets the render say which of the two it is.

```
node1    100      secondary-hold                     ...   <- peer reported
node1    100      secondary-hold (local: transfer-out override)  ...   <- this node substituted
```

### What this does NOT do

Criterion 1 — surfacing `rg_active`, VIP presence, or a per-RG session count to distinguish *"primary and carrying traffic"* from *"primary and carrying nothing"* — is **not** addressed. That data lives in `pkg/daemon`, and the only thing comparing RG ownership against VRRP mastership (`CheckVRRPPosture`) is gated off entirely under `private-rg-election`, which is the compiler default. It needs a design across a package boundary, not a render change. The issue stays open for it.

### The test is a pair, and that is the point

A single case cannot show a *difference*. Asserting only the override case passes equally well against a render that appends the suffix unconditionally; asserting only the reported case passes against one that never appends it. Both managers are driven to the **same** `NodeState` first, with that asserted, so the comparison is about the substitution being visible rather than about two different states.

| cell | mutation | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | render annotation removed | clean | 1 |
| M2 | override site stops marking | clean | 2 |
| M3 | annotate **unconditionally** | clean | 1 — via the over-reach assertion |

M3 is the one that matters: it shows the fix does not simply mark every row, which a test asserting only the override case would have missed.

## PR #8123 — userspace-xdp: assert the two facts #5192's residual decision rests on (#7464) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7464-xdp-align-asserts`

Closes #7464

#5192 item 2 measured the aligned-store fix at **+14,047 processed insns (+1.81%), −1.40 pp of verifier budget** and declined it — in a file with a documented outage, where `08a0bbd7f` blew the 1M cap and took both cluster dataplanes down. That decision is sound. It rests on two facts nothing asserted.

1. **`size_of::<UserspaceDpMeta>() % 8 == 0`.** The store does `bpf_xdp_adjust_meta(ctx, -meta_len)`, so `data_meta = data − 96`, and the whole *"the UB is unreachable on the zero-copy fast path because that path is in fact aligned"* argument needs that offset to **preserve** 8-alignment. The existing size assertion happens to imply it, and the implication was nowhere stated — grow the struct to 100 bytes, update that assertion to 100 (an ordinary, reviewable edit), and the UB moves silently from a generic-XDP portability concern onto the **primary forwarding path** with nothing failing.
2. **`align_of::<UserspaceDpMeta>() == 8`.** The layout block pins the size and six offsets and **no alignment**. The residual is scoped to an 8-byte demand from `config_generation: u64`; a future field raising it widens the residual on every path with no signal.

### The `.o` does not move — and the control is what makes that claim mean anything

```
CONTROL regen (before any edit):  f576dfef5644337fc6f614c35c4555e2  == tracked
AFTER regen (assertions added):   f576dfef5644337fc6f614c35c4555e2  == tracked
```

I ran the control **first**, deliberately. Without it, "byte-identical afterwards" would be consistent with a build that never reproduces the tracked object at all, and would prove nothing about this change.

Exactly **one of eleven** manifest sha entries moves, and it is `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` — the source I edited. The object entry does not.

### Gate

| cell | mutation | assertion 1 (`size % 8`) | assertion 2 (`align == 8`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| M-A | `config_generation: u64` → two `u32` (size preserved, demand drops to 4) | holds | **FAILS by name** |
| M-B | `#[repr(C, packed)]` | **FAILS** | **FAILS** |

**Recording the coupling honestly rather than implying two independent guards:** under `repr(C)` the size is always a multiple of the alignment, so **no mutation can fail assertion 1 while assertion 2 holds**. Assertion 1 is not independently falsifiable here. Its value is that it *states* the implication the size assertion only implies — which is exactly what #7464 asks for — and that the two decouple if the `repr` ever changes. I would rather say that than present a matrix that looks stronger than it is.

## PR #8124 — nat: release the NAT reservation a dropped synced delete strands (#6979 F4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/6979-f4-dropped-delete-strands-reservation`

Part of #6979 — **F4 only**. F5 is measured and dispositioned here but
deliberately NOT fixed; see below.

## The finding's prediction is right about the route it names, and that is the trap

#6979's closing note expects the #6211 holder-set to bound F4 to "that worker's
bit is cleared". Constructed rather than re-read, **it does** — for the route
the finding describes. A worker that passes its command stage and then **stops**
is covered twice: `retire_dead_worker_holders` (#8069, panic) and
`retire_all_worker_holders` (#7092, generation teardown).

The unbounded route keeps the worker **alive**. `push_bounded` DROPS the command
at `MAX_PENDING_WORKER_COMMANDS`, and its return was ignored. Probe at the
parent:

```
PROBE-F4 queue_drops_delta=1      occupied_after_delete=true
PROBE-F4 dead=false               retire_dead_freed=0
PROBE-F4 occupied_after_sweep=true
```

Shared authority is already gone so no replay re-delivers, and no sweep selects
a live worker. The port is held for the life of the allocator — F4's "until
process restart", by a mechanism the finding does not describe.

## The repair

A dropped push runs `release_source_nat_allocation_for_worker` for that worker
id: byte-for-byte the call the worker makes when it processes the command, so
the holder mask empties on the same last-release rule and the port is returned
exactly once.

It cannot **over**-release: the command was dropped, so that worker will never
run this teardown itself, and `release_flow` no-ops unless
`live_by_flow[flow].translated` equals this exact tuple, so a worker whose own
`UpsertSynced` is still queued is untouched.

Only the **forward** key is repaired — the reverse companion's NAT teardown
returns immediately on `is_reverse`, so repairing its drop would call a no-op
and count a repair that did not happen. Measured: it made the counter read 2 for
one stranded reservation.

`session_delete_dropped_released` counts the repairs, wired through
`ProcessStatus` (additive, `serde(default)`; wire fixture regenerated, one
line). **Not repaired:** the same dropped command also costs that worker its
local session-table and BPF map teardown. Shared authority governs which
sessions exist and the process-wide session-map delete already ran, so the NAT
reservation is the part with no other owner.

**Master is red.** #8123's doc comment wrote `bpf_xdp_adjust_meta(ctx, -meta_len)`, and the #5173 shim-index census is a **textual walk** counting occurrences of `ingress_ifindex`, `rx_queue` and `ctx` per file. The bare `ctx` in prose took `lib.rs` from 17 to 18 and failed `shim_index_path_has_one_construction_and_one_lookup`.

Reworded to name the helper without the token. The census keeps the count it asserts — it exists to pin how many places construct and look up the shim index, and moving its expected number to accommodate a comment would spend a real guard on prose.

### How it reached master — my error

#8123 was a **Rust source** change and I gated only `make test-go`, on the reasoning that the compiled object does not move so the dataplane is unaffected. The object genuinely did not move. A source-scanning gate does not care whether the object moved.

Second appearance of this hazard: the #6641 status-wiring gate had to strip comments before scanning because its own doc comment quoted the assignment it greps for. Any source-scanning gate can be tripped by prose — satisfied by it there, broken by it here.

## PR #8130 — test: resolve the #5173 tally collision at 17 (master red) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/master-red-census-collision`

**Master is red.** Two independent fixes for #8123's one red landed in **opposite directions**, each green against a master that lacked the other:

- **#8127** (`f5c174437`) reworded the #7464 comment to name `bpf_xdp_adjust_meta` without its first argument — source back to **17** `ctx` mentions.
- **#8126** (`e11433476`) moved this tally row from 17 to **18** to accommodate that same comment.

Source says 17, row expects 18, `shim_index_path_has_one_construction_and_one_lookup` fails again.

### Resolved at 17, keeping the reword

Both fixes were defensible, and the row-move carries the stronger argument *about the tally's design*: it counts comment and doc mentions **on purpose**, because a version that ignored them could be paid off by moving a binding into a macro-generated doc string, and moving a row for a legitimate mention is an action its own failure message explicitly describes.

But that argument is about whether the tally should count prose — not about whether *this* comment needed the token. It didn't; the sentence reads no worse without it. So the tighter bound is free and the row stays where the #5173 measurement put it.

### The collision is the lesson, not either fix

A red master invites more than one agent to fix it at once. "Green separately, red together" applies to two fixes for the **same** red at least as sharply as to two unrelated features — arguably more, because both authors are staring at the same failing test and neither expects a second repair to exist. Checking whether a red is *already being fixed* is now part of fixing it.

## PR #8131 — flow: enforce the tcp-session initial/closing/time-wait timeouts (#7342) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7342-tcp-session-timeouts`

Enforces `security flow tcp-session initial-timeout`, `closing-timeout` and
`time-wait-timeout`, which #6539 recorded as accepted-only. Closes #7342.

## The split had to come first, and the issue was right about that

`session_timeout_ns` split a TCP close only two ways — RST onto the 2s abort
window, everything else onto ONE post-FIN window described in-source as "the full
30s TIME_WAIT-style window". Junos distinguishes CLOSING (after the first FIN)
from TIME_WAIT (after the close completes), so that single window had to stand
for both leaves. Mapping `closing-timeout` onto it was a guess, mapping
`time-wait-timeout` onto it was an equally arguable guess, and mapping both was
impossible.

The discriminator is a FIN per DIRECTION. Forward and reverse are independent
entries, so each knows whether its own direction FINed;
`propagate_tcp_state_to_companion` already mirrors close state between them and
now mirrors that bit as the companion's peer-side FIN. One FIN is CLOSING, two is
TIME_WAIT, and a RST short-circuits both — an abort has no close handshake to
complete, so the bits are gated on FIN specifically rather than on `is_closing`,
which is FIN **or** RST.

### The field that looks like the answer and is not

`SessionEntry.observed_tcp_flags` appears to give this for free, and building on
it would have been wrong in a way no test would have shown. `account_packet`
OR-folds BOTH directions' flags onto the FORWARD entry **on purpose** (#2749, so
NetFlow's `tcpControlBits` reports the whole flow), so `observed_tcp_flags &
TCP_FIN` is already true after ONE fin. A TIME_WAIT detector built on it puts
every half-closed session straight into TIME_WAIT — **and every single-FIN test
still passes.**

That is also why the load-bearing cell drives TWO FINs from opposite directions.
After the first, both halves are already `closing` (#4109 F17 pulls the companion
onto the close window), so a fixture that stops there shows CLOSING and proves
nothing: the pre-split code produces exactly that. The negative control is a
RETRANSMITTED FIN from one direction — an implementation that counted FINs rather
than tracking direction passes the first cell and puts half-closed flows into
TIME_WAIT whenever a FIN-ACK is lost.

## Why all three, in one PR

"Carry three, enforce two, flip the third later" is not available, and it is
closed **by design rather than by oversight**:
`TestTCPSessionTimeoutsHaveNoWireCarrier_6539` asserted the table and the wire
agree in BOTH directions, so an unenforced leaf that reaches the wire snapshot
reds it. #6539 deliberately made carrier and enforcement equivalent. One additive
wire bump is therefore also one protocol change, one cluster smoke and one
release note rather than two of each.

### Measured before writing it down

- `resolveECMP` (`pkg/frr/config_render.go`) reduces the one named policy to **two booleans**: any term carrying `load-balance` sets `ecmpMaxPaths = 64`, and `consistent-hash` selects the hashing mode. No per-route evaluation, no composition rule — because there is no per-route forwarding-policy model to compose into.
- A list carrying more than one policy is **hard-rejected at commit** (`compiler_validate_strict_routing.go`, *"forwarding-table export declares N policies"*), with the error stating it renders as a single ECMP policy, and downgraded to a warning on the tolerant path per #1960.

So the contract is **enforced**, not merely documented, and an operator cannot silently receive chain semantics they did not get. "Nothing is broken today" is accurate.

### The note records why the shortcut is refused

Because it is what a future reader will reach for: OR-ing several policies' terms together would accept the Junos spelling while computing a **different answer than Junos**. That is worse than the current rejection precisely because it is silent — a loud refusal tells the operator their config means something else here; a quiet reinterpretation does not. The issue says the same thing and it deserves to survive the close.

## PR #8134 — nat: a synced import must not fall through to a sibling allocator (#6979 F1 half 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/6979-f1-pass1-refusal-is-final`

Part of #6979 — **F1 half 1**, the last row.

## The ruling was right in direction and one level too high

You ruled: *a PASS 1 `Refused` returns without falling through to PASS 2; a
`NothingToReserve` must still fall through.* I implemented exactly that and
**re-ran the reproduction. It still reproduced.**

PASS 1 never returned `Refused`. `reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` iterates
its candidate set and, on a pool-owning rule whose allocator declines,
`continue`s to the **next rule**. Both overlapping rules are in PASS 1's *own*
filtered set — so A refused, B accepted, PASS 1 returned `Reserved`, and the
PASS1→PASS2 seam was never reached at all.

The fall-through is **inside the scan**, which is what F1's original text said:
*"it reserves on the first candidate whose allocator currently accepts; a
refusing rule falls through to the next."*

## Both levels ship, because each is inert without the other

- **`reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` takes `stop_at_first_owner`.** PASS 1
  passes `true`: its candidate set is already "rules the active could have
  matched" in snapshot order, which **is** the Junos specificity precedence
  (#4161) the active resolves with. So the first candidate whose pool owns the
  translated address *is* the active's rule, and its refusal is the answer.
  Walking on answers a different question — "who will accept?" — and books the
  reservation in an allocator the active never used.
- **PASS 1's `Refused` returns without falling through.** `NothingToReserve`
  still falls through, so interface-mode SNAT (#6751) and genuine config drift
  keep today's behaviour.

**PASS 2 is byte-identical** — the un-narrowed pre-#6211 fallback for an
unresolvable zone pair or drifted config, where "first rule whose pool contains
the address" is the only question available. Refusing there would reject every
import on a standby that has not yet applied a snapshot.

## The counter is bound, not assumed

Your fourth requirement. A coordinator-level cell drives the real import and
asserts `synced_import_reserve_refused_total` increments. If that path did not
reach the counter, the reasoning the whole trade rests on would be false while
every unit-level cell still passed.

## PR #8135 — harness: refuse a definitive TX-kick OUT from a capture with no evidence (#7424 row 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7424-step3-insufficient`

Refs #7424 — **row 1 only**. Row 2 (validate.py reading a transport error as "absent") is not addressed; no close keyword.

step3 printed **"the TX-kick hypothesis is ruled out"** — a definitive negative about the dataplane — from a file in which nothing was measured. An empty or truncated capture reduces to 12 all-zero blocks, every one of which satisfies `t1_out_block` (`retry_delta` 0 is below `RETRY_OUT`, then `count_delta == 0` returns `True`), so `t1_out_holds` is **vacuously** true and `main()` returned 0 regardless. `grep -c INSUFFICIENT` over step3 was **0**; over its sibling step2 it is **6**.

Reachability is real: step1 emits `shape = np.zeros(16)` on an empty capture and its K2 no-evidence guard is traffic-gated (`if c == 0 and txp > 10_000`), so it stays silent when `txp == 0`. This is the only downstream place that can catch the shape.

### The choice the issue said to make deliberately

I took the **narrow / step2-faithful** option, and on the merits rather than to avoid test churn.

**The two-condition guard is load-bearing.** Zero *kicks* alone is a legitimate OUT — a valid capture in which the dataplane simply never kicked is real evidence, and refusing it discards a true negative. What is not evidence is a capture with no *histogram* either: a normalised block sums to 1.0, so a zero sum means the block was never populated. Requiring both separates **"measured, and there were no kicks"** from **"nothing was measured at all"**.

The broad option (INSUFFICIENT whenever all 12 `count_delta == 0`) would report INSUFFICIENT for a valid capture with a real zero result — a false negative in the other direction.

### Three cells; the two controls are the point

| cell | asserts |
|---|---|
| all-zero capture | `INSUFFICIENT`, not a definitive OUT |
| **valid capture, zero kicks** | still `OUT` — without this, a guard keyed on `count_delta` alone passes the first cell while breaking every real OUT |
| **zero histogram, kicks present** | not `INSUFFICIENT` — fails if the guard is keyed on the histogram alone |

Verified by **running**, since pytest is not installed here — a driver exercising `classify()` directly returns OUT / INSUFFICIENT / OUT across the three shapes.

### Worth knowing: this file's test suite runs in no gate

`test/incus` holds **21** `*_test.py` files. The Makefile runs exactly **one** (`host_inbound_probe_test.py`, via `test-host-inbound-lib`). The other 20 — including this one — are pytest-style and are not run by any target. That is how a vacuous verdict survived in a file that *has* a test suite. Filed separately.

`Enforced`, but left the surrounding comments describing the old world.

They are **deleted, not corrected**. The table is the authority; sentences
restating it are places to be wrong the next time it moves, and correcting them
only resets the clock. This applies #6539's own doctrine — shared authority,
not copies — one level up, to the prose *about* the table rather than to the
table's consumers.

Comments only — no behaviour change.

## The sharpest one

`TCPSessionTimeoutDataplaneDefault`'s doc comment said:

> time-wait-timeout returns false: the dataplane has no TIME_WAIT state, so
> there is no window to report as its default

…four lines above the switch arm that returns `true`. A reader trusting the
comment over the code concludes the opposite of what ships.

## All six

| Site | Claimed |
|---|---|
| `flow_tcp_timeouts_6539.go` header | "only established-timeout actually reaches the dataplane" |
| same, continued | the other three "stop there", no wire field, no live consumer |
| `TCPSessionTimeoutDataplaneDefault` doc | time-wait "returns false" / "no TIME_WAIT state" |
| `TCPSessionConfig` type doc | the #6539 split paragraph |
| `InitialTimeout` field | `// NOT enforced` |
| `ClosingTimeout` field | `// NOT enforced` |
| `TimeWaitTimeout` field | `// NOT enforced; the dataplane has no TIME_WAIT state` |

## Why the existing guard did not catch it

The `pkg/dataplane/userspace` test binds the **wire carrier** to the **table**
in both directions — add a carrier without updating the table and it fails.
That is a real guard and it worked; it simply says nothing about prose, so
these comments drifted freely while the table beneath them stayed correct the
whole time.

I deliberately did **not** add a phrase-absence test for this. A guard keyed on
"NOT enforced" is defeated by the next paraphrase while looking like coverage,
and the next reader would trust it more than it deserves. The gap is recorded
in the type doc instead.

## PR #8140 — nat: rebuild persistent-NAT leases on the HA standby [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7360-persistent-nat-lease-standby`

Closes #7360

## The defect, and it is worse than the issue was filed for

Persistent-NAT lease state is not reconstructed on the HA standby, so after a
failover a client that held a stable translated port gets a different one.
Measured through the real import path:

```
ACTIVE   203.0.113.13:40000   persistent_leases=1  live_flows=1
STANDBY  after import                          0              1
STANDBY  new flow             203.0.113.13:40001
```

The synced reserve inserted `LiveAllocation { persistent_key: None, .. }` and
never touched `persistent_by_source`. Both lease-creating sites are reachable
only from the LOCAL admission path.

**It also drops sessions.** Two flows from one client under persistent NAT share
ONE translated tuple — that is what a lease is for — but on the standby they are
two different `SourceNatFlowKey`s, so `reserve_flow` missed its `live_by_flow`
early-return, fell through to `occupancy.reserve(port)`, and failed on the bit
its own lease already held. That refusal returns `RejectedReserve` **before**
`publish_shared_session`. So a persistent client's 2nd..Nth sessions were not
merely un-leased on the standby — they were never imported at all. They are not
degraded across the failover; they were never there to degrade.

The two are **one change**. A lease-aware synced reserve both reconstructs the
lease and stops refusing the client's other sessions, because it takes the reuse
path instead of competing for the occupancy bit. They also cannot be validated
apart: adding lease creation on top of the old reserve would still drop every
session after the first, leaving `active_flows` stuck at 1 — a green fixture
measuring a broken thing.

## Nothing crosses the wire

Enumerating `PersistentLease` against what the receiver already reaches: the
translated tuple is on the wire as `nat_src_ip`/`nat_src_port`, `addr_index`
resolves from it, `timeout_ns` comes from the rule's `timeout_secs`, and
`PersistentSourceKey` is the session key plus the rule's permit shape. Only
`expires_at_ns` had no local source — and it turns out not to need one:

```
flow1 t=1ns          : 203.0.113.10:40000   (1-second persistence timeout)
flow2 t=5s (EXPIRED) : 203.0.113.10:40000   REUSED
```

The predicate is `active_flows > 0 || expires_at_ns > now_ns`, so while any flow
is active the expiry is never consulted, and `complete_persistent_lease_locked`

## PR #8141 — docs: carry the #7415 ARI residual into critical-patterns and close it [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/7415-ari-residual`

Closes #7415

#7415 recorded a divergence that **could not be reproduced on available hardware**: systemd's `net_id` reinterprets the PCI slot and function fields as one 8-bit function number when ARI is enabled (`func += slot * 8`); `pciAddrToEnp` does not. Reproducing it needs an ARI-enabled, **non-VF** network function at a **non-zero** PCI slot, and no such device exists here.

**The issue was the record, and the doc merely pointed at it.** That is the wrong way round for something nobody can action — an issue blocked on hardware that may never appear is noise on a board being driven down, while the mechanism and the discriminator are exactly what `critical-patterns.md` exists to carry.

Moved in full: the arithmetic, the sysfs discriminator script for anyone who *does* have the hardware, the reason it was not implemented, and precisely what to change if the divergence is confirmed.

### The reason it wasn't implemented is the part worth preserving

It is an argument, not an omission. #6677 made udev authoritative — `deriveKernelName` reads `ID_NET_NAME_PATH` from `/run/udev/data/n<ifindex>`, which already accounts for ARI, the VF parent and the port suffix — so `pciAddrToEnp` runs **only when udev data is absent** (early boot before settle, or a container). The residual is reachable only on a host that simultaneously has an ARI non-VF NIC at a non-zero slot **and** no udev data for it.

Adding arithmetic that cannot be demonstrated, to a nearly unreachable path, in a function that silently renames network interfaces, is risk without measurable benefit. **A naming fix that guesses is worse than none.**

If someone confirms it on real hardware, the doc now names the change: `func += slot * 8` gated on `ari_enabled`, which requires the helper to take the device *path* rather than the address string since ARI is a property of the device, plus a fixture from that hardware's real `udevadm` output, keeping udev-first primary.

## PR #8142 — scripts: add a mutation harness that refuses cells it cannot observe [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `tools/mutation-harness`

## The defect this exists to prevent

A mutation runner that gates in **one** language scores every mutation in
another language as an **ESCAPE** — because nothing it ran could possibly have
failed. An escape is a claim that the code under test is unguarded, so this is
not a missing feature; it is the harness manufacturing evidence for a
conclusion it never tested. It cost a false escape verdict on a Go-side cell
during #7342, where the runner only ever invoked cargo.

`scripts/mutate.sh` derives the language set from each cell's touched paths and
**refuses** to emit a verdict when a touched language has no configured gate,
naming the uncovered language.

## Scoring is four facts, never rc

    infrastructure -> applied -> built -> collected -> named failures

Order matters: each earlier condition makes the later numbers meaningless.

`rc != 0` is not "the tests failed". A build break, a panic before collection,
and a full disk all exit non-zero with no failing test. A harness keying on rc
calls them kills; one keying on "no named FAIL" calls them escapes. They are
VOID — and both wrong answers are the ones that end an investigation.

## Four pinned misreads, each of which has produced a wrong verdict

| misread | why it wins |
|---|---|
| `-race` failure | emits **no** `--- FAIL` line — only `WARNING: DATA RACE` plus a package-level FAIL, so a `^--- FAIL` counter scores a genuine race red as a PASS |
| `collected` counting result lines | makes collection move with the failure count, so a package that failed to **build** hides behind another package's extra failures |
| full disk | reds **named** tests and reads exactly like a real regression |
| `make`'s echoed Makefile comments | recipe-region comments start with `#`, so a detector keyed on `^# ` scored a healthy `make test-go` run as VOID(build break) |

That last one was found by **running** this harness against a real cell, not by
reading it — which is the argument for landing it with tests rather than
keeping it in scratch. The detector now matches a compile diagnostic
(`file.go:line:col:`) or go's explicit `[build failed]` marker, neither of
which appears in prose.

## The self-test is mutation-checked

A self-test that cannot fail would be the same defect one level up. Two checks,
both verified to red and then green:

- breaking the refusal gate so it treats every language as covered → reds 2
  named checks
- restoring the `^# ` build detector → reds the Makefile-comment cell

## PR #8143 — docs: a -race failure is a kill, not a VOID verdict [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/mutate-lib-verdict-wording`

## What

The `make test-mutate-lib` entry added in #8142 (mine, merged an hour ago)
listed a `-race` failure among "the three verdicts that are neither kill nor
escape". That is wrong, and it inverts the point of the pin.

**A race failure IS a kill.** The harness counts `WARNING: DATA RACE` alongside
`--- FAIL` precisely so a genuine red is not lost. What it shares with the VOID
cases is only that a naive `^--- FAIL` counter misreads it — and it misreads it
as a **PASS**, which loses a kill, rather than as an uninterpretable cell.

The VOID cases are a build break, a run that collected nothing, and a full disk.
Separating those two groups is the whole distinction `mutate-lib.sh` encodes, so
a summary that merges them teaches the reader the opposite of what the code
does — in the file most likely to be read *instead of* the code.

Also folds in the fourth pinned misread from the same PR (`make`'s echoed
Makefile comments are not a build break), which the entry predated.

## PR #8145 — slowpath: surface the worker's TUN failure from the constructor [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7820`

`SlowPathReinjector::new` returned `Ok` the instant it spawned the worker
thread. `slow_path_worker` opens the TUN as its first act, and on failure it
records the cause, clears `active`, and returns — so the caller held a
reinjector whose worker had already exited and whose receiver was dropped.
Every subsequent enqueue failed with the downstream symptom "slow-path worker
is not running", while the actual reason sat unread in `last_error`.

The one production caller, `afxdp/coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs`, already
has an `Err` arm that publishes the cause into `last_slow_path_status`. It
simply could not be reached, because the constructor never failed.

## The reported symptom vs. the defect

The issue's hypothesis — a constructor/worker startup race — is not what was
happening. The error was `Disconnected`, not a not-yet-started worker: the
worker had run, failed, and gone.

Six tests built a real reinjector purely to exercise logic that needs no
device (the #2471 live-MTU admission gate, the day-2 reconcile — both driven
entirely by `status.live_mtu`). Wherever the suite runs without CAP_NET_ADMIN,
which is everywhere it currently runs, `open_tun` fails with
`TUNSETIFF: Operation not permitted`, so the worker exited immediately. Those
tests passed only when they won the race to enqueue before the disconnect
landed, and lost it under load. One documented the dead worker in a comment
and asserted around it, accepting either outcome — a test that could not fail
for the reason it was written. They now use `new_without_worker`.

## Validation

`cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp` — 5001 passed, 0 failed. Both suites via
`make test-go` and `make test-rust`.

Mutation matrix, full-suite cells, scored on applied / build / collected /
named-FAIL:

| cell | result |

| delete the handshake | KILLED — 1 named failure, the regression test, nothing else |
| handshake observes the error but `break`s instead of propagating | KILLED — same single test |
| over-reach control: return `Some` for the empty initial string | KILLED — on the non-empty assertion |

The third cell is the one worth noting: it confirms the "error is non-empty"
assertion is load-bearing rather than decorative.

The regression test uses a device name longer than `IFNAMSIZ` so it fails on
every machine. Relying on the suite being unprivileged would make it pass for
an environmental reason and silently stop testing anything under
CAP_NET_ADMIN — the class of vacuous green that produced this issue.

## PR #8146 — session sync: carry the routing domain instead of deriving it on import (#7239) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7239-install-stamped-domain`

Closes #7239

## The defect

#7160 phase 2 had the importing node **derive** a peer-synced session's routing domain from the #7095 cluster-stable ingress fold. `stampIngressIfaceFold` runs on the **send** path and folds against the **current** config, so an ifindex recycled onto a sibling between install and sync folds to the sibling's name, the peer resolves it to its own sibling, and the derived domain files the session in the **sibling's routing instance**.

If the two interfaces sit in different instances, that is a cross-tenant mis-file — in the field #7160 added to prevent one — and a **confident** one: `find_forward_nat_match`'s two-pass preference matches a reply in the wrong tenant's domain on pass 1.

**#8116's fail-closed does not cover it.** That refuses an *absent* ingress identity. A recycled ifindex resolves fine, just to the wrong interface, and absent vs mis-resolved are indistinguishable downstream.

The domain is now stamped at **install** — it is already on the session key — and carried, so no later recycle can move it.

## A cost estimate I got wrong, corrected

I previously scoped this as "a shared C struct change with its own alignment rules", and that deferred it. It was wrong: `grep -c "IngressIfaceFold" pkg/dataplane/bpf_session_value.go` → **0**. `SessionValue` carries userspace-sync-only trailing fields that never touch the BPF ABI, populated from the session **delta**. This rides the same route #5212 and #7095 took — **no C struct, no `SessionSyncWireVersion` bump**.

## The wire encoding: #7188's reserved zero

The first cut preferred a non-zero carried domain and otherwise derived. But 0 was ambiguous — both "the default routing instance" and "a peer predating the field" — so a legitimately-default-instance session from a **new** peer still fell through to the derivation, which is the exact case this issue is about. The fix missed its own motivating scenario in that corner.

Per #7188's merged precedent: **reserve 0 for ABSENT and make every real state encode non-zero**, including the one meaning "nothing special here" (`TunnelDiscriminator::None` rides as `WIRE_NONE = 1`, not 0). Here `WIRE_DEFAULT_INSTANCE = 1`, and a tenant domain rides as itself — the reserved `[100000, 999999]` band keeps it clear of both.

Decoding returns three states, dispositioned #7188's way:

| state | disposition |
|---|---|
| `Present(d)` | used, including `Present(0)` = default instance **stated** |
| `Absent` | pre-#7239 behaviour, incl. #8116's unresolvable-domain refusal |
| `Unrecognized` | **refused**, not coerced — filing under an identity this build cannot reproduce is the failure that arm exists to stop |

Go carries the value **opaquely** and never interprets it.

## The close frame — a near-miss worth recording

**I nearly shipped this without the close frame**, and the next person adding a field to this path will make the same omission.

A close names the session to **retract**. Two routing instances sharing a 5-tuple are two sessions, so a close without the domain retracts the wrong tenant's session — or none. #7188's own comment is the argument, and it is sitting four lines above where the field had to go:

> A close names the session to RETRACT, and for protocol 47 the 5-tuple names two tunnels at once — so a close that could not carry the discriminator would retract the wrong one.

Both frames carry it. Both delta transports carry it, because a field on one leg and not the other reads as "not carried" rather than as an error — the #6949 lesson on this exact struct.

## PR #8147 — test: wait for the cold-path writer instead of sleeping 20ms [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8139`

`snapshot_under_concurrent_writer_never_tears` slept a fixed 20ms to let its
writer spin up, then asserted the reader observed a non-zero sample. Under load
the writer can be starved through both that sleep and the reader loop, so the
reader takes 1000 perfectly coherent all-zero snapshots and the assertion fires.

The old failure message named the tell without acting on it — `0
retry-exhausted` means the seqlock behaved flawlessly. The test was asserting
**writer progress**, a property of the scheduler, not of the histogram. Since
`cargo test` aborts at the first failing binary, that took the whole
`make test-rust` gate down with it.

## The change

- Replace the sleep with a bounded wait for the writer's first publish, failing
  with the file's existing "OBSERVABILITY PRECONDITION FAILED, NOT A TEAR"
  idiom (#7650 already drew this distinction for the coherence floor). Deadline
  10s — ~500x the old literal.

## PR #8148 — routing/monitor: carry a monitored interface through a transient lookup [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8073`

`monitorManager.Apply` treated every `LinkByName` error as absence. The comment
was right about the intended case — a monitored interface living on the peer
node genuinely is absent — but `err != nil` also catches ENOBUFS under load,
EINTR, and a truncated netlink socket.

## Answering the issue's first question: it reaches the weight

The issue says the first step is establishing whether this path feeds the
failover weight or only the display. **It feeds the weight** —
`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go` calls `SetMonitorWeight` once per status
returned here, under a comment that says exactly that.

The consequence is more specific than "contributes no weight": a dropped
interface is absent from the slice, so `SetMonitorWeight` is never **called**
for it and its weight is not recomputed — it **persists stale**. If the
transient error coincided with the link actually going down, the interface kept
its last-known `Up` weight and the RG did not demote.

## The fix

Mirror the sibling bond/tunnel managers (#5461/#5495/#7529), which branch on
`isLinkNotFound` and **retain** on the transient arm. Here that means carrying
the previous pass's status forward. The configured weight is re-read from
current config, so a weight change in the same commit is still honored while
only the link state is stale.

Deliberately **not** synthesizing `Up=false`: demoting an RG because a netlink
lookup hiccuped is a worse failure than briefly stale state.

## A fixture defect found on the way

`monitorFakeOps.LinkByName` returned `net.UnknownNetworkError` for an absent
link — which `isLinkNotFound` reports **false** for. The fake's "absent" case
was indistinguishable from a transient failure. Harmless while every caller
treated the two identically; it would have made the new test pass for the wrong
reason. Fixed here.

## Validation

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| revert `monitor.go` (78 deletions, applied-check confirmed) | KILLED |
| `if !isLinkNotFound(err)` → `if true` (over-reach) | KILLED, on pass 3 |

The test runs three passes plus a weight-change pass. Pass 2 alone is
insufficient: a fix that carried **every** failed lookup forward would satisfy
it while breaking the peer-owned case. Pass 3 is that control.

Docs updated in `pkg/routing/README.md` — its `monitor.go` row already specifies
the link-health semantics this extends. (An earlier revision of this PR body

## PR #8149 — natshow: give the NAT session walks one cancellable authority [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7315-natshow-walk-cancellation`

## The defect, confirmed live at `c0003252f`

`#6553` gated the four gRPC `ShowText` NAT topics for **admission** but could
only do half the job: `pkg/natshow`'s `Render*` helpers took no
`context.Context` and are shared with `pkg/cli`, so the admission lease could
not reach the walk. It disclosed the cancellation half as a residual — this
issue.

Verified still open at today's head: none of `RenderPersistentDetail`,
`RenderSourceRuleDetail` or `RenderDestRuleDetail` took a context, and
`acquireNATShowWalk` used the plain `Acquire`. `#7294` (the structural
admission redesign) is still open and has landed no mechanism, so there was no
newer authority to adopt instead.

Admission bounds **concurrency**; the lease bounds **duration**. They fail
independently — a handler can hold its slot correctly and still walk the whole
table for a client that has hung up. That is other surfaces' problem because
REST and gRPC alias ONE 4-slot `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter`: the slot a
departed client's walk keeps is a slot the REST surfaces that *do* honour
cancellation are queueing for. These topics are also on the FABRIC listener,
unlike the loopback-only NAT RPCs.

## One authority, not three copies

The obvious fix — add a `ctx` parameter and paste
`if ctx.Err() != nil { return false }` into each callback — recreates the shape
that produced the bug: three hand-copied `IterateSessions`/`IterateSessionsV6`
pairs, each with its own scan-error precedence, and the check absent from all
three.

Instead the three pairs collapse into a single `walkSessionValues`
(`pkg/natshow/walk.go`) whose per-renderer visitors take the session **value**
and **return nothing**. A renderer physically cannot decide to keep walking, so
the cancellation check is inherited rather than remembered, and a renderer added
later gets it for free. Same shape `#6553` gave the gRPC NAT RPCs via
`countNATSessions`.

`acquireNATShowWalk` switches `Acquire` → `AcquireCtx` and returns the lease
context alongside the release, making these topics consistent with
`GetNATPoolStats` / `GetNATDestination`. There is no in-process delegation under
`ShowText` today, so the lease-*reuse* arm of `AcquireCtx` is not exercised from
here — it is the cancellation propagation that is load-bearing, and the comment
says so rather than implying a guarantee that is not being used. `pkg/cli`
passes `context.Background()`: a local render has no request to cancel and does
not draw on the shared limiter.

## Premise correction: the count is THREE, not four

The issue names four walking topics and cites `persistent.go:85` / `:102` for
`RenderPersistent`. **Both of those lines are inside `RenderPersistentDetail`.**

## PR #8150 — grpcapi: map ShowText topics and SystemAction verbs to commands (#7172 cut 5a-2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut5a2-topic-verb-command-tables`

## What this is

**#7172 cut 5a-2.** Cut 5a (#8057) mapped every gRPC **method** to the
canonical operational command it performs, so `deny-commands` — a regex
matched against a *command string* — has something to match on the remote
surface, where the `cli` binary parses the line client-side and only a typed
RPC crosses the wire. It deliberately left out the two methods that are
**multiplexed**: `ShowText` serves 129 topics and `SystemAction` 19 verbs, so
one string for either would be a lie. Both are already priced for coarse
permissions from the **decoded request**; this maps them to a command the same
way.

`authz_command_table_topics.go` adds `showTextTopicCommand` (129) and
`systemActionVerbCommand` (19). Values are transcribed from `cmd/cli`'s
dispatch, which is where the topic or verb is chosen.

**Count note:** 129, not the 98 a `grep -oE 'case "[a-z0-9-]+"'` reports. The
dispatcher branches on a topic in three shapes and only one is a `case` label;
`showTextTopicsFromDispatcher` — the AST extraction the #5278 topic guard
already uses — collects all three, and it is the enumeration this cut is
pinned to. Re-measured at my head rather than carried from the handoff.

## What is verified — and what is not

The guards prove **canonicality** (every value resolves against
`cmdtree.OperationalTree` to *itself*, with every word a real command KEYWORD
so garbage absorbed by a value slot cannot pass — the #8094 rule) and
**completeness** (each key set pinned to production source in both
directions).

**Attribution is NOT verified, and cannot be here.**
`chassis-cluster-status` mapped to some other real canonical command passes
every test in the package. That is *measured*, as an over-reach control in
the matrix below, not asserted. The file and the README say so in those words.
Reasons, all measured rather than assumed:

- Deriving the command from the topic name reproduces **35 of 111** exact-keyed
  topics (**31%**) — the rest drop intermediate hierarchy (`alarms` →
  `show system alarms`, `tunnels` → `show interfaces tunnel`), so the exemption
  list would be the larger half. A test measures and logs this rate so the
  rejected design stays falsifiable instead of resting on prose.
- The server's handler name is `camelCase(topic)`, so it restates the topic and
  agrees with it **by construction** — zero information about which *command*
  reaches it.

The only sound source is `cmd/cli`, which is not mechanically walkable today
(computed topic strings, nested switches). #8058 tracks making that mapping
declarative, which would turn the cross-check into a table comparison.
**Until then, a reviewer checking these entries IS the check.**

## PR #8152 — image/validate: distinguish an absent path from an unobserved check [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7424-row2`

Scenarios A and C assert that the factory boot installed no config and that a
rejected day-0 drive wrote nothing. Both ran an in-guest existence probe through
`guest(...)` and treated a zero return code as "the path is there".

`incus exec` exits non-zero both when the in-guest `test -e` finds nothing **and
when incus could not run the command at all** — instance not running, agent not
up, connection refused. Only the zero case was tested, so a transport failure
was indistinguishable from absence and scored as PASS. Those are the central
negative claims of both scenarios.

**The asymmetry that hid it:** the sibling positive assertions compare `!= 0`,
so a transport failure makes them fail **closed**. Only the four negatives were
exposed, which is why the file reads as uniformly careful.

## The fix

`guest_absent(inst, path)` makes the guest say which it is — the probe echoes an
explicit `XPF_PRESENT`/`XPF_ABSENT` token, and anything else (non-zero exit,
empty output, unrecognised output) is reported as an *unobserved check* rather
than as absence. A token can only be produced by a shell that actually ran.

This is the pattern the file already uses three times, at `:384` ("a probe that
silently produced nothing cannot be mistaken for a clean run") and `:704-706`
("a gate that could not observe the property it exists to assert has not
asserted it").

## Validation

`scripts/image/test_validate_guest_absent_7424.py`, auto-discovered by
`run-selftests.sh`'s `scripts/image/test_*.py` glob.

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| revert one call site to the return-code form | KILLED (census cell), applied-check 2 lines |
| helper returns `True` on an unrecognised token | KILLED (transport cell), applied-check 2 lines |

Two notes about the guard rather than the fix:

**The middle row is the one that matters.** Cells for PRESENT and ABSENT alone
would leave the fail-open exactly as it was — the old code got both of those
right. The cell that earns its keep is the one asserting that a check which
*could not observe* its property does not report that the property holds.

**The census cell is deliberately narrow, and my first draft was wrong.**
Forbidding the literal `"test", "-e"` idiom red on five sites that are
**correct** — they compare `!= 0` and fail closed. Only the `== 0` comparison is
the fail-open shape. The broad version would have warned on valid inputs and
pushed five correct sites to churn to satisfy a test. A second cell now pins
that the fail-closed form stays permissible, so a future tightening cannot
quietly re-create that.

## PR #8154 — configstore: clear both holder fields on ExitConfigure [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7635-exitconfigure-configholder`

## What

`ExitConfigure` cleared `exclusiveHolder` but left `configHolder` set. Its three siblings — `ExitConfigureSession`, `ForceExitConfigure` and the `reclaimStaleLockLocked` re-acquire — all clear both, so the asymmetry was in this one function rather than in the contract. This makes the release complete on all four paths.

## Why it mattered, and how little it mattered

Stated honestly in both directions, because the issue's own framing is "safe today only by an accident of check ordering" and that is exactly what I found.

The stale string escaped the package through the **public** `ConfigHolder()` accessor, which returns `effectiveHolderLocked()` and so reported the dead holder alongside `locked == false`.

It was **never operator-visible**: all three consumers check the `locked` bool first and take the "No configuration lock held" branch —

- `pkg/cli/cli_clear.go:77` (`clear system config-lock`)
- `pkg/api/system.go:431` (REST `clear-config-lock`)
- `pkg/grpcapi/server_diag_system_action.go:219`

It was also **not exploitable**: `ensureHolderLocked` short-circuits on `!s.configDir`, and every in-tree caller of `ExitConfigure` pairs it with the unsessioned `EnterConfigure`, which sets `configHolder` to `""` on the way in.

Neither of those is a property of `ExitConfigure`. That is the whole point of the issue — the field was clean by accident of check ordering and caller pairing, not by construction.

## What is deliberately unchanged

The `#6808` holder-epoch bump. It is independent, and it is what makes this path safe **without** depending on the field being clean: a commit authorized before the exit still fails verification after it.

The stale note above `ExitConfigure` — which claimed the asymmetry was deliberate and "tracked separately" — is **deleted rather than amended**. It restated a contract that is no longer true, and a corrected copy is one more place to drift.

## Test, and why its fixture is spelled out

`TestEveryConfigModeExitClearsBothHolders_7635` is a table over the three public exits, asserting `ConfigHolder()` returns `("", false)` after each.

The fixture is the load-bearing part. The state that makes the bug observable is a **non-empty** `configHolder`, and only `EnterConfigureSession` with a non-empty session id produces one. A fixture built on `EnterConfigure()` — which is what every in-tree caller of `ExitConfigure` actually pairs with — sets `configHolder` to `""` on the way in, so the post-exit assertion reads `""` whether or not the fix is present and the cell passes **vacuously**. Each row therefore enters with a session id and asserts the entered state first, so a green result means the clear happened rather than that the field was never dirty.

The assertion is on the public accessor rather than the private field, because that accessor is where the staleness escaped.

A paired control (`TestExitConfigureClearsHolderAfterExclusiveEnter_7635`) covers the exclusive-enter shape, which would pass even before the fix — it keeps the sibling row honest by distinguishing "the clear works" from "this accessor always returns empty after an exit".

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE` lines, 0 "no space left".
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 3 files, all intended.
