## PR #8155 — userspace-dp: guard CoSSchedulerSnapshot literals against re-enumerating [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7689-cos-snapshot-literal-guard`

## What

#7689's second acceptance bullet. The first half landed in `85e5ea721` (the 71 exhaustive literals #6846 broke were given `..Default::default()` tails); this is the cell that stops the pattern coming back, since the habit is what regrows it.

Measured at this base: **83 literals, 0 exhaustive.**

## A correction to the numbers I reported during triage

I earlier reported "0 of 87 literals lack a `..` tail". The exhaustive count was right; **87 was wrong** — it counted 4 non-literal matches (`-> CoSSchedulerSnapshot {` return types). The real literal population is **83**. The figure came from a naive `..`-substring scan, and building the real detection rule is what surfaced the error.

## The detection rule, and the three false positives that shaped it

Each of these produced a wrong answer on this tree while the rule was being built, so each is recorded at the site rather than left for the next reader to rediscover:

1. **A substring search for `..` scores `foo: 0..3` as a struct-update tail.** The tail occupies the position a *field name* would, so the test splits the body on **depth-0 commas** and asks whether a segment *starts* with `..`.

2. **`-> CoSSchedulerSnapshot {` matches the identifier-then-brace shape.** An unguarded scan brace-matches a constructor helper's whole **function body** as a literal body, finds no depth-0 `..` segment, and reports it exhaustive. Four such helpers exist here — this was the false positive that first flagged the naive rule.

3. **A trailing `// comment` before the tail** puts the comment at the head of the final depth-0 segment, so an unblanked scan reads a *guarded* literal as exhaustive. One such literal exists here (`forwarding_build/tests.rs`).

(3) is why the guard reuses `blank_comments_and_strings` and `afxdp_rs_files` from `afxdp::worker_queue::tests` rather than re-deriving them — which is the reason `worker_queue.rs` itself gives where it widens their visibility: *"a second copy of comment-blanking is exactly where a source-scanning gate quietly stops seeing what it is meant to."* That turned out to be literally true here.

## Non-vacuity

The assertion is an **absence**, so it passes for two very different reasons: every literal carries a tail, or the scan found nothing. A rename, a file move, or a regression in the match shape would each silently produce a clean report.

Two populations are floored so a scan that reached nothing **fails** instead: files read (`>= 200`) and literals matched (`>= 70`).

The scan is rooted at `src`, not `src/afxdp`: `src/protocol/` holds 15 of these literals, and a scan rooted at the afxdp subtree would report a clean tree while never reading them.

## Not `#[non_exhaustive]`

Per the issue, and it is correctly absent today. It would force the tail at compile time but also block exhaustive construction outside the defining crate, changing the type's public contract to solve a test-hygiene problem.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`, 0 "no space left".
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`, 0 `test result: FAILED`.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 3 files, all intended.

**Mutation cells** (committed first, then mutated; full-suite, not `-run`):

| cell | applied | built | collected | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** — add a compiling exhaustive literal | yes | yes | yes, 5018 filtered | `...carry_an_update_tail_7689`, naming `protocol/tests.rs:2875` |
| **B** — narrow the scan root to `src/event_stream` | yes | yes | yes, 5017 filtered | same test: `scan read only 24 .rs files under src — the walk is broken, so the exhaustive-literal assertion below would pass vacuously` |

**A first attempt at cell A was a VOID cell and is reported as such**: simply deleting `..Default::default()` from an existing literal is a *compile break* (E0063 missing fields), not a test failure, so it proves nothing about the guard. The valid mutation is a literal that enumerates every field and therefore **compiles** — which is also the real-world shape the guard exists to catch.

## PR #8156 — selftest: run mutate-selftest.sh with bash, and census the interpreter [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8153`

`make selftest` was **red at master**. `run-selftests.sh` registered
`scripts/mutate-selftest.sh` with `run_shell`, which forces `sh` regardless of
the script's shebang. The script declares `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and resolves its
library through `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, so dash reported "Bad substitution", line 12
sourced a nonexistent path, and **nothing the self-test tests ever ran**.

The contract already existed — `run_bash` is there for exactly this, and the doc
comment on `run_shell` names the failure ("fails under dash with 'Bad
substitution' — a syntax error, not a real result"). This was a registration that
did not follow a written contract, so the repair is one word.

## The census is the part that prevents the next one

The #7296 self-test census asks *"is every self-test **invoked**"*. It globs
`test/incus/*-selftest.sh`, so this script was outside it twice over — wrong
directory, and wrong question. A script can be listed, be invoked, and still
execute none of what it tests. **"Invoked" and "invoked with the interpreter it
declares" are different properties.**

The new census asserts no `run_shell` leg declares a bash shebang, reusing
#7296's swept-nothing guard: matching zero registrations reports a broken census
rather than a clean pass.

It is written in **strict POSIX shell**, because this runner is itself invoked
with `sh` — a bash-ism here would break the whole harness with the same class of
error it exists to catch. `sh -n scripts/run-selftests.sh` is the check.

## Validation

`sh scripts/run-selftests.sh`: **passed=96/failed=1 → passed=98/failed=0**, with
`PASS: scripts/mutate-selftest.sh` and `PASS: interpreter census (7 run_shell
legs, none declaring bash)`.

Fail-on-revert cell, applied-check confirmed at 2 lines: restoring `run_shell`
reds **both** the leg and the census, and the census names the offending script.

## Three notes, two of them about my own mistakes on this PR

**The script exits 0 in the broken state.** It surfaced as FAIL only because the
runner reports its stderr — a gate keyed on the return code alone would have
scored it as a pass. That is how it survived.

**An earlier revision shipped the census without the one-word fix.** The
three-dot scope check caught it: 40 insertions and *zero deletions*, when the
registration swap should have shown a deletion. That combination — a guard
landing without the repair it guards — reds on the defect it was written for and
reads as the guard being wrong.

**A revision after that committed git conflict markers**, left by a `git stash
pop`, which dash reported as `line 245: Syntax error: redirection unexpected`

## PR #8158 — smoke: point the failover throughput gate at the unshaped CoS class [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7673`

`make test-failover` reported **~92-94 Mbits/s against a 1.0 Gbps floor**, with
all 13 failover assertions passing, and reproduced on master. It reads as a
forwarding regression. It is a misdirected probe.

The CoS output filter classifies by **destination port**, and the iperf3 client
was invoked with no `-p`, so it used the 5201 default:

| port | filter term | forwarding class | scheduler |
|---|---|---|---|
| **5201** (old default) | term 1 | `iperf-100m` | `transmit-rate 100m exact` |
| **5211** (new default) | term 11 | `iperf-uncapped` | no transmit-rate |

The gate was measuring a deliberately 100-Mbit-shaped class against a 1 Gbps
floor. It could only fail, and ~92 Mbits/s is the shaper working correctly.

**Why it was intermittent, which is what made it read as a regression:** the
classification applies only once `apply-cos-config.sh` has run, and that config
survives on the cluster until the next deploy wipes it. The gate passed or
failed depending on what the previous agent left behind, so the same tree gave
different answers on different days.

## The guard asserts an agreement, not a literal

`iperf-throughput-selftest.sh` now reads the `IPERF_PORT` default out of
`test-failover.sh`, resolves it through `cos-iperf-config.set` in two steps
(port → filter term, term → forwarding class), resolves the class to its
scheduler, and fails if that scheduler carries a `transmit-rate`.

Pinning the port to 5211 would encode which side is trusted — and the side that
was wrong here is the one nobody suspected. Each step also fails loudly when it
resolves nothing, so a renamed filter or a moved term reports "matches no term"
rather than passing having checked nothing.

## Validation

`iperf-throughput-selftest.sh`: **24 passed**, hermetic. Two mutation cells,
applied-check confirmed at 2 lines each:

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| restore the 5201 default | KILLED — names the resolved chain: "port 5201 lands in `iperf-100m`/`scheduler-100m`, which HAS a transmit-rate" |
| drop the `-p` flag | KILLED — separately, on the flag cell |

**Cluster run in progress.** This changes the smoke script itself, so the
hermetic test covers the port/class resolution but not that 5211 actually
carries traffic. I am running `make test-failover` on the loss userspace cluster
and will post the measured throughput here.

Closes #7673

## PR #8159 — docs: correct the host-inbound dhcp token's stated mechanism [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/8060-host-inbound-dhcp-mechanism`

## What

Two in-tree documents told operators that a zone's `host-inbound-traffic system-services dhcp` / `dhcpv6` token is what lets a client's DISCOVER or SOLICIT reach the firewall's DHCP server. That is **the one path the token provably does not gate**, so the project's own reference configuration was pointing an operator at the wrong knob.

## The true mechanism, taken from the in-tree authority rather than paraphrased

`validateDHCPServerHostInboundBypassWarnings` (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn_dhcp_hostinbound.go`, #6460) already states this correctly, and it is what the operator sees at commit. The corrected comments now use its language:

- A **DHCPv4 DISCOVER** is addressed to `255.255.255.255`, which the XDP shim hands to the kernel without entering the userspace dataplane, and Kea receives it on an AF_PACKET raw socket delivered **before** the netfilter input hook — so neither host-inbound plane sees the request.
- A **DHCPv6 SOLICIT** is addressed to the `ff02::1:2` multicast group, and every per-zone host-inbound rule is scoped to the zone's **unicast** addresses, so the request matches no rule and falls through the input chain's accept policy.

I verified this against the validator's own text rather than transcribing the issue, because an independent transcription from a non-authoritative source agrees with itself.

## The non-goal, which is the important half

**The tokens stay, and are verified intact in all five reference configs after the change.** They are inert for the server request path but **load-bearing for the firewall's own DHCP client renewals**: a RENEWING client unicasts udp/68 to a zone address, which *is* daddr-matched, so withdrawing a token costs that interface its **address** rather than merely refusing a service.

```
docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf             6
docs/ha-cluster.conf                       6
docs/ha-cluster-loss.conf                  6
test/incus/xpf-cluster-fw0.conf            5
test/incus/xpf-cluster-fw1.conf            5
```

A fix that deleted `dhcp;` would be strictly worse than the wrong comment.

## Population: the issue's two sites are the whole set, checked rather than assumed

The issue named two sites. Treating that as a floor, I swept every reference config and every doc for the same claim in other wordings. `grep -rn "MUST admit dhcp|DISCOVER to the firewall is denied" docs/ test/` now returns **empty**, and the surviving DISCOVER/SOLICIT mentions are each correct in context (`host-inbound-service-matrix.md:1494` on the relay role, `phases.md` on router discovery, `install-images.md` on `AUTODISCOVER`). Two sites is the census here.

## No claim-guard test, deliberately

The issue asks whether the reference configs deserve one. The obvious guard — assert the false phrase is absent — is **defeated by paraphrase**, which is precisely the failure mode it would exist to prevent. A guard that looks binding without being binding is worse than none, so this is left as an open question on the issue rather than answered with a weak test.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`.

## PR #8160 — wg-interop: gate all four config sessions on the CLI success markers [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7792`

`wg-interop.sh` drives four config-mode CLI sessions through a piped heredoc and
gated none of them on the #6440 markers. The piped-stdin CLI is a REPL: a failed
command prints `error: ...`, the loop advances, and the process exits 0 — so no
gate on the session's exit status can fire.

## The gap is sharper than "ungated"

Each session did have an ad-hoc `grep -q "commit complete"`. That grep is
**unanchored**, so it is also satisfied by:

```
error: commit failed: ... commit complete ...
```

`cos_transcript_has_marker` matches `^${marker}` for exactly this reason,
documented at its definition — the marker must match `commit complete` and
`commit complete: <summary>` while **not** matching an error line quoting it. So
the previous check could report success on a commit that failed.

## The teardown session is the interesting one

It legitimately accepts **either** `commit complete` **or** `path not found` —
removing an already-absent stanza is a success. `cos_require_markers` requires
*all* its markers, so that session uses the single-marker predicate twice as a
disjunction: line-anchored, without forcing an AND that would fail every re-run.

The `"wg-interop.sh": "#7792"` exemption is deleted. An allowlist entry is a
claim, and that census checks entries for staleness, so leaving it would now
fail in the other direction.

## Validation

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| control (fix in place) | PASS — 5 config-committing smoke scripts scanned |
| revert `wg-interop.sh`, exemption stays deleted | KILLED by name, applied-check 2 lines |

The kill message is the census's own: *"wg-interop.sh commits configuration
through the piped-stdin CLI but never references the #6440 marker gate"*. So the
guard fails in **both** directions, which is what makes deleting the exemption
safe rather than merely tidy.

## PR #8162 — ha: count a synced import that had no session map to publish into [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7209-unpublished-import-counter`

First slice of #7209. **This is the instrument, not the fix** — it changes no
locking and does not close the window it measures. What it does is make a
currently-invisible condition observable, so the lock change that follows can be
*shown* to be correct rather than argued from a reading of the lock graph, which
is what failed on #7095.

## The defect: one `&&` conflating two opposite meanings

`upsert_synced_session` published a peer-synced row to the kernel session map
behind one conjunction:

```rust
if synced_entry_allows_local_replace(..) && let Some(fd) = ..session_map_fd
```

The **first** operand failing is correct behaviour: the peer owns the redundancy
group, so this node must not take the redirect. The **second** failing is a gap:
the entry is recorded in the shared `synced` map and answered to Go as installed,
while no kernel row exists. `SyncedImportOutcome::Applied` is returned — its own
doc comment says *"The entry was published"* — `refusal_reason()` is `None`, so
`response.ok` stays true and Go keeps its BPF mirror row.

All three publish sites (`ha/session_import.rs:403`, `:438`, `:519`) are
`if let Some(..)` with no `else`: no refusal, no counter, no log.

`bpf_maps.session_map_fd` is `None` before the first successful reconcile and
again between `stop_inner` (`coordinator/mod.rs:733`) and `reconcile::bringup`
(`bringup.rs:394`). **An HA standby taking bulk session sync before its first
snapshot apply — the ordinary failover-preparation sequence — lands there for
every session in the batch.**

## This is not a loss today, and the counter is deliberately not an alarm

I checked this rather than assuming it, because it decides whether the work is a
bug fix or a prerequisite.

Every `reconcile` opens with `teardown::tear_down` (`reconcile/mod.rs:337`),
which calls `snapshot_shared_session_entries()` (`coordinator/mod.rs:837`). That
**clones** the whole shared map — it does not drain it — and
`replay_preserved_sessions` republishes it once the new map is up. So an entry
recorded while the fd was absent is published by the next reconcile. The
standby-before-first-apply case self-heals.

The only genuinely lossy interval is an entry arriving **between** that capture
and the replay, and the snapshot-wide `ServerState` mutex closes it: `handlers/mod.rs`
dispatches `apply_snapshot` and `sync_session` under one `state.lock()`, so they
cannot interleave.

**That mutex is what #7209 removes.** Filed separately as **#8157** so it is not
carried in a PR body: once `sync_session` runs off the mutex, an import in the

## PR #8165 — docs: a gate and a mutation cell pull opposite ways on rc [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/gate-vs-cell-rc-scoring`

`docs/engineering-style.md` already names a panic as a VOID cell and already
warns that `rc != 0` is not "the tests failed". I checked that before writing
anything, precisely so this would not become a second place for an existing
authority to drift.

That rule is written for scoring a mutation **cell**. The **gate** case is the
inverse and is nowhere stated, and it is the one that bit on #7209.

## The measurement

When the question is "is this change shippable", `make test-go` / `make
test-rust` is the instrument, and there `rc` is the ONLY signal that catches a
panic — a panic emits no `--- FAIL` line anywhere in the log.

A new Prometheus emit landed in `emitUserspaceDynamicBufferMetrics`, which

initialised collector ("the rest stay nil and are not exercised by this test").

```

--- FAIL lines: 0
packages ok:   71
```

Every FAIL-line heuristic scores that as a pass. Only the exit code does not.

So the two rules do not substitute for each other, and the doc now says so:
**gate on the exit code AND on packages-collected; score a cell on the four
facts.**

## Placement

One bullet, beside the existing `-race`-has-no-`--- FAIL` and
count-collection-in-packages bullets it belongs with — not a new section. The
surrounding text is the authority; a restatement elsewhere would be a second
place to drift.

## PR #8166 — show forwarding-options: list instances in a stable order [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7357-render-order`

Every `show forwarding-options` renderer iterated its instance map with a bare
`range`. Go randomises map iteration per run, so two calls against identical
config produced different orderings — an operator diffing captures sees churn
that is not there, and any golden or transcript over these surfaces is unstable
for a reason unrelated to the config.

## The census was a floor

#7357 names two port-mirroring renderers and says so itself. Measuring the tree
found **six sites across three files**, spanning *both* the port-mirroring and
sampling families:

| file | families affected |
|---|---|
| `pkg/grpcapi/server_show_forwarding.go` | sampling + port-mirroring |
| `pkg/cli/cli_show_routing.go` | sampling + port-mirroring |
| `pkg/cli/cli_show_flow.go` | sampling |
| `pkg/cli/show_services_mirror.go` | port-mirroring |

The helper is generic over the value type (the two instance families have
different types) and extracted rather than inlined, so the ordering is one
decision with one name — two inlined sorts are two things to keep in step,
which is how these drifted into sharing a defect. It is duplicated once per
package because `pkg/cli` and `pkg/grpcapi` do not import each other; each
package's test asserts the same property, so changing one without the other
reds its own package.

## Why the assertion is "equals sorted", not "two runs agree"

Comparing two runs is weaker **and** flakier: two randomised iterations can
coincide, so it passes by luck at a rate set by the fixture size. Comparing
against sorted order fails deterministically the moment a sort is reverted.

The fixtures use **eight** instances for the same reason. An unsorted render
matches sorted order with probability 1/n!; at n=4 that is 1/24, which would let
a mutation cell escape ~4% of the time and leave the test quietly flaky *in the
direction of passing*. At n=8 it is 1/40320. Names are inserted in an order that
is neither sorted nor reverse-sorted, and both helpers fail loudly on an empty
render rather than passing vacuously over an empty slice.

## Validation

| revert `cli.showPortMirroring` | KILLED — its own test only |
| revert `cli.showForwardingOptions` port-mirroring | KILLED — its own test only |

## PR #8167 — cli,grpcapi: say when a hit-count 0 means "not measured" [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7776-policy-stats-disabled-note`

## What

`show security policies hit-count` renders a well-formed `0` for every row whose counter was never read. An operator reads that as "this policy has not matched"; the truth is "this view was never asked to look".

#7776 was filed after that misread cost an investigation: localizing a live deny, the reporter read all-zero hit counts on a node that was **demonstrably denying packets**, and the answer had to come from the `POLICY_DENY` journal line instead. Same class as the AF_XDP capture blindness in `docs/testing.md` — an instrument that answers "nothing" when it means "I cannot see".

Both text renderers now emit a trailing note, mirroring the #7016 unpublished-counter note already sitting beside it, and naming the remedy.

## The note counts rows; it does not claim "every count reads 0"

A rule carrying `count` **is** read even when the system-wide knob is off, so the blanket wording would be false for a mixed config. Both cells therefore use a deliberately **mixed** fixture — a uniform one cannot tell the two wordings apart — and each asserts the **number**, not merely that a note appeared.

## The two guards are asymmetric, and a mutation escape is why

I originally wrote the same explicit guard in both files. Dropping `!pol.Count` then **escaped every cell**, which is the measurement: the term was decoration in one file and unbound in the other.

- **gRPC**: the read condition also carries `readPolicy != nil`, so the else branch is reachable a second way — an unloaded dataplane. Both terms are load-bearing there. Without `!statsEnabled`, an unloaded dataplane with stats **enabled** prints a note claiming stats are disabled. Without `!pol.Count`, a `count`-bearing rule is blamed on a knob that does not gate it. Both now have cells.
- **CLI**: `showPoliciesHitCount` early-returns unless the dataplane is loaded, so those terms are **tautological**. It keeps a bare `else` with a comment saying why that is sufficient — a guard that cannot fail reads as protection and is not.

The two note strings are byte-identical so the renderers cannot drift into saying different things.

## Scope, held deliberately

Six functions gate on `statsEnabled`; this changes two. Not changed:

- `showPoliciesDetail` (both surfaces) has the same gap but **no trailing-note mechanism**, so covering it is new mechanism rather than this fix. **Flagging it as a real, separate row.**
- The structured gRPC `GetPolicies` and REST `policiesHandler` need an availability **field**, not a line — the wire-surface shape deferred in #7473.
- Prometheus already does the right thing and **skips** the metric.

Also unchanged: the cell still renders `0` rather than `n/a`. Switching would be more correct under the #3345 counter-unavailable-is-not-zero contract, but `policyCountCell` is shared and it changes every row's output — a much larger blast radius than this issue scopes.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`.
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 5 files, all intended.

| A | delete the CLI note block | CLI cell RED, gRPC green — independently guarded, not cross-covered |
| B | delete the gRPC note block | gRPC cell RED, CLI green |
| C | make both notes unconditional (`if true`) | both ENABLED **controls** RED — the note is genuinely conditional |
| D | drop `!pol.Count` from the gRPC guard | **ESCAPED at first.** Reported as an escape; produced two new cells, and now REDs |
| E | drop `!statsEnabled` from the gRPC guard | RED on the unloaded-dataplane cell |

## PR #8168 — test: probe target services from the traffic source, not the firewall [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `measure/7100-canonical-shape`

Closes #8164

`test/incus/target-services.sh` is the #8040 gate that exists so a per-class
harness stops rediscovering the target-service dependency after it has already
spent a build, a deploy and the shared cluster lock. It defaulted to probing
from `xpf-userspace-fw0`.

The firewall **forwards** VLAN-80 traffic; it does not originate it. Its own
host stack cannot open TCP to the target even when every service is up, so the
gate reported every port closed — a value indistinguishable from the target
host having died, and the value a runner acts on.

## Measurement

One instrument (`bash /dev/tcp`), the same 24 ports, the same target, at the
same moment:

| probed from | result |
|---|---|
| `loss:cluster-userspace-host` — the container every harness SENDS from | **OPEN: 23 / 24** (only 6200 closed) |
| `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` — the old default | **OPEN: 0 / 24** |
| `loss:xpf-userspace-fw1` | closed (spot-checked 5205, 6205) |

Not an L2/L3 failure and not a primary/secondary artifact — both nodes behave
alike. From the firewall, `ping` is 0% loss at 0.18 ms with the neighbour
REACHABLE, and `ip route get 172.16.80.200` resolves `dev ge-0-0-2.80 src
172.16.80.8` — but that interface carries only `169.254.1.1/32`; `172.16.80.8`
is a RETH/VRRP VIP, not an address available to locally-originated traffic.

After the fix, `target-services.sh status` against the live cluster reports the
truth: 23 of 24 up, 6200 down.

## What it cost

#7100 and #7159 were both parked as blocked on lab hardware with "every TCP
port is closed", recorded explicitly as *"Probed from `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`"*.
The service set was never gone. Across that whole period exactly **one** of the
24 listeners was down — 6200, the best-effort TCP echo — which blocks the
canonical mouse-latency mouse and nothing else.

The earliest #7100 comment had probed from `cluster-userspace-host` and
recorded the right answer (`iperf3:5201 OPEN, echo:6200 closed`); the later
firewall-vantage probe overwrote it with a worse one and both issues were
re-scoped around it.

## The fix

```
-PROBE_FROM="${PROBE_FROM:-xpf-userspace-fw0}"
+PROBE_FROM="${PROBE_FROM:-${CLUSTER_LAN_HOST_NAME:-${LAN_HOST:-cluster-userspace-host}}}"

## PR #8169 — cli: sanitize streaming command output before it reaches the terminal [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7389-streaming-termsafe`

`handleMonitorTraffic` (tcpdump), `handlePing` and `handleTraceroute` wired
`cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout` directly, so there was no string for the #6584 sweep to
sanitize and all three were exempted as "needs a shape change".

They are the **highest-taint sites in that class**: tcpdump renders packet
*bytes* as ASCII, so the payload is chosen by whoever sends the packet; ping and
traceroute resolve PTR records, so displayed hostnames come from DNS an attacker
may control. All three stream straight to an operator's terminal, where a
control sequence can drive an OSC clipboard write or CSI cursor/erase.

## `termsafe.SanitizingWriter`

A line-wise `io.Writer` between the command and the terminal. Buffered capture
was rejected for #6584's stated reason — unbounded for tcpdump, and it breaks
Ctrl-C and the incremental output that is the point of `monitor traffic`.

Two design points that each have a test:

- **Line-at-a-time, not chunk-at-a-time.** A read boundary can fall mid-rune;
  sanitizing such a chunk would escape the split halves as invalid UTF-8 and
  corrupt legitimate output — making the *sanitizer* the thing that mangles the
  text. Asserted at every split offset of a multi-byte string.
- **The buffer is bounded at 64KiB.** Waiting for a newline is an
  **attacker-controlled allocation** here: whoever sends the packets decides
  whether a newline ever arrives. Emitting a partial line is a cosmetic wrap;
  holding it is a memory defect.

The three CLI exemptions are deleted — an allowlist entry is a claim, and that
census checks entries for staleness in both directions. The gRPC twin
`streamDiagCmd` is a different shape (per-line protobuf sends) and stays exempt.

## An escaped mutation decided the shape of the fix

My first version wired the two streams inline and separately. Reverting **only**
`cmd.Stdout` then left the function still mentioning `termsafe.` via
`cmd.Stderr`, so the census's relative count still passed and the mutation
**escaped**. That was measured, not hypothesised — the census is function-level
and cannot see *which* stream is wired.

Routing both streams through one named helper makes the partial revert
inexpressible: the only way to unwire a site is to delete the call. That
required teaching the census the wrapper's name, since the body no longer says
`termsafe.` at all. The relative-count property is preserved — deleting the call
still reds.

## PR #8170 — upgrade: bound waitPredicate's poll sleep by its own deadline [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7424-rolling-bounded-sleep`

## What

`rolling.go`'s `waitPredicate` checked its deadline and then slept a full `rc.PollInterval`, overshooting the deadline by up to one interval.

Because the deadline check sits **before** the sleep, this is a wrong **answer**, not merely a late one:

1. a predicate that first became true **after** the deadline was accepted as satisfied within it;
2. a genuine timeout was reported up to one poll interval late.

## Reuse, not a third shape

This was the last raw `time.Sleep` in `pkg/upgrade`. The same bug has already been fixed twice in this package — `kernel_drain.go`'s two drain loops via `sleepBounded`, and `HelperHealthProbe` in #5808, which carries a fail-on-revert pin — so this calls that helper rather than inventing a third pattern.

`sleepBounded` now takes the interval as a **parameter**: its two kernel-drain callers pass `drainPollInterval` and are unchanged in behaviour, while `waitPredicate` passes the caller-supplied `RollingConfig.PollInterval`.

## The fixture is the load-bearing part

**Every pre-existing fixture in this package uses `PollInterval: 1ms`**, which is exactly why none of them could catch this — the overshoot is 1ms and invisible. The new cells invert the ratio: a **50ms deadline against a 5s interval**. That is the smallest shape in which removing the bound changes an outcome.

The primary cell asserts an **outcome, not a duration**: a predicate that first turns true 1s in must be **refused** against a 50ms deadline. A paired control runs the same predicate under a deadline long enough to contain it and requires **success**, so the primary cannot pass merely because the predicate never fires or because `waitPredicate` always errors.

A third cell exercises `sleepBounded`'s own contract directly at both boundaries — clamping to the remaining time, and returning immediately on an already-elapsed deadline.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`, 0 "no space left".
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 4 files, all intended.

**Mutation cell** (committed first; full `pkg/upgrade` package run, not `-run`):

|---|---|
| applied | yes — 1 line, `git diff --stat` confirms |
| built | yes |
| collected | yes — whole package |
| named FAIL | `TestWaitPredicateRejectsAPredicateThatOnlyTurnsTrueAfterTheDeadline_7424` |

Message on revert, which is the diagnostic the cell exists to produce:

```
waitPredicate returned nil for a predicate that first became true at 1s,
950ms past its own 50ms deadline — the sleep overshot the deadline and the
post-deadline result was accepted as satisfied within it (elapsed 5.000968313s)
```

## PR #8171 — reconcile: replay synced sessions from the live map, not a stale clone [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8157-replay-reads-live-map`

`teardown::tear_down` cloned `snapshot_shared_session_entries()` before
`stop_inner(false)`, and bringup replayed that clone. An entry landing in the
shared synced map between the clone and the replay was therefore absent from the
replay, never published to the new kernel session map — `bpf_maps.session_map_fd`
is `None` for the whole reconcile and the three publish sites are
`if let Some(fd)` with no `else` — and never replayed, while
`upsert_synced_session` still returned `SyncedImportOutcome::Applied` and the
handler answered Go `ok`. A split truth with no signal.

The replay now derives its entries from the **live** map at replay time, so an
arrival in that window is included by construction: the read happens after
everything the reconcile could race.

## Why that is sound

`tear_down` calls `stop_inner(**false**)`, and the shared-map clear is gated on
that parameter — only full shutdown passes `true`. So `sessions.synced` survives
a reconcile intact. #6652's own regression note is the load-bearing premise and
already says it:

> *"stop_inner(false) replaced the workers and bring-up replayed nothing, **while
> the shared map still held them**."*

## The filter moved with the set — this is what makes the obvious version wrong

The captured `Vec` was **not** a passive snapshot. `apply_snapshot` mutated it:

```
snapshot.rs  filter_replayed_synced_sessions(preserved, &tunnel_purge_ids)
```

dropping sessions whose tunnel the new snapshot remapped **and their derived
reverse companions**, "so the replay cannot resurrect them, whole or as half-dead
pairs". Reading the live map without carrying that filter across would
re-publish exactly those — and as half-dead pairs, which is worse than either
extreme.

So `tunnel_purge_ids` is threaded from the snapshot phase to the bringup replay,
which calls the **identical** predicate. Not a paraphrase: if the late-arrival
path re-implemented "is this tunnel purged", the two sites would disagree
silently and rarely.

For every entry predating `purge_remapped_tunnel_sessions` the filter is now
redundant — that purge has already removed them from the live map. It is
retained for the one case it still covers: an entry for a purged tunnel arriving
**after** the purge.

I found this by grepping every use of the captured `Vec` rather than only
reading the seam I was changing. The seam looked clean; the filter was one file

## PR #8172 — feeds: pre-size the SnapshotForBindings union instead of regrowing it [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7174-c12b-presize`

`SnapshotForBindings` unions a binding's prefixes across feeds from
`make([]string, 0)` and an unsized `seen` map, regrowing across every prefix of
every feed. A per-feed cap exists (`maxFeedPrefixes`, at fetch time), but
nothing bounded the union **across** feeds and bindings — the spike #7174 C12b
describes.

Establish readiness **and** the upper bound in one pre-pass, then allocate both
containers at that size. The sum of constituent lengths is an upper bound
because dedup can only shrink the result, so this never under-allocates and the
output is byte-identical.

Moving readiness into the pre-pass is the second half: a binding with any
unready constituent is OMITTED (#5645 fail-closed), and the old shape discovered
that only *after* merging every prefix of every feed ahead of the unready one.
That work was always discarded.

## Why the allocation and not the data

Per the ruling on the issue. These feeds drive security policy, so truncating a
deny-list fails **OPEN** while truncating an allow-list fails **CLOSED** — the
same code with opposite failure directions depending on how the operator uses
the feed. An aggregate data cap deserves its own issue where the failure
direction is the subject, not a side effect of a row about allocation.

## Validation

Byte-identical output means no assertion over the returned data can fail for the
reason the fix exists. The observable property is the allocation count, and it
discriminates cleanly on a 4-feed × 2000-prefix fixture:

| version | allocations |
|---|---|
| pre-sized (this change) | **36** |
| unsized (before) | **98** |

The bound is 60 — between them with margin either way, so Go-version drift in
constant overhead does not red it while a revert to unsized regrowth does. The
test says as much, and says that a failure near 36 rather than near 98 means the
regression is elsewhere and the bound should be **re-measured, not raised**.

The alloc test carries a **premise check** that the binding actually resolved:
an omitted binding allocates almost nothing, so without it the cell could pass
having measured the empty path.

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| revert to unsized containers | KILLED — allocation cell |
| drop the unready-omission | KILLED — fail-closed cell |

Branch: `fix/7804-retire-nat64-pool-write-surface`

## What

Finishes the surface `089a61d4f` (#7268) started. `DeleteStaleNAT64` and `ZeroStaleNATPoolConfigs` are removed from the `DataPlane` interface, their `(*Manager)` implementations, and the orphaned stubs on `discardingDataPlane` and `userspaceShimCompileDataplane`.

## The safety argument is not "nothing calls these"

Re-measured here rather than inherited. Zero production callers is the weaker half. The stronger half is that the maps they wrote **do not exist on the deployed dataplane**:

```
nat64_configs          shim-hits=0
nat64_prefix_map       shim-hits=0
nat_pool_configs       shim-hits=0
nat_pool_ips_v4        shim-hits=0
nat_pool_ips_v6        shim-hits=0
--- positive control ---
dnat_table             shim-hits=9      (the shim DOES declare this one)
```

The control is what makes the zeros mean something rather than proving my grep was broken. So the write had nowhere to land even if a caller returned.

## Answering the issue's second question rather than leaving it open

#7804 also asks whether the three sweepers that **do** have callers (`DeleteStaleZonePairPolicies`, `ZeroStaleScreenConfigs`, `ZeroStaleFilterConfigs`) are worth running on the commit path at all.

Measured: `zone_pair_policies`, `screen_configs` and `filter_configs` are equally shim-undeclared (0 hits each), so those writes are inert for the same reason. **But the cost is already nil, which is the part the issue could not see.** Each opens with `lookupMapLocked`, which reads `m.maps` — populated only by `publishShimRegistryLocked` from the shim's own collection. On the deployed dataplane the name is absent, `present` is false, and the function returns before constructing a key. The commit-path cost is one mutex-guarded map miss, not a write.

And retiring them is **not this change**: they have live callers, so it edits the **compile path** rather than deleting an unreferenced declaration — a different blast radius and its own review. Recorded in the guard's doc comment; out of scope here.

## The population guard fired, which is it working

The `*Manager` exported-method census went **142 → 140**, exactly the two removed, and is **re-pointed to the new population rather than weakened** — the same treatment #7268 gave it going 164 → 141. The armed-gate class table and the registry callsite manifest lost the rows for the removed methods. The #4960 pre-pass fidelity floor did not move and was left alone.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`, 0 "no space left".
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 10 files, all in `pkg/dataplane` plus its README.

**Mutation cells**, and they show the work is split across two enforcement mechanisms:

| cell | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| A | re-add `DeleteStaleNAT64` to the `DataPlane` interface | **BUILD BREAK** — `*Manager does not implement DataPlane`. The interface half is compile-enforced |
| B | re-add `DeleteStaleNAT64` to `*Manager` **only** | **compiles**, then FAILs the census: `inventory = 141, want 140`. This is why the concrete-type half needs a test at all |
| C | re-add `ZeroStaleNATPoolConfigs` to the interface **and** every impl, so it compiles | FAILs `TestRetiredNATWriteSurfaceStaysOff`: *"DataPlane declares ZeroStaleNATPoolConfigs again"* — binds the list I extended |

Cell A is a legitimate result rather than a void cell: a build break *is* the guard, and it is stronger than a test. Cell C exists because A short-circuits before the reflection guard ever runs, so without it the line I added to the retired list would be unbound.

## PR #8174 — flowexport: exclude a collector that can never receive a record [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8163-flowexport-collector-exclusion`

Closes #8163

A `flow-server` whose port is absent or outside 1-65535 was carried all the way
to `dialCollectors`, which treats a dial failure as fatal for the whole group.
`NewExporter` propagates that out of the constructor, and
`Daemon.reconcileFlowExporter` builds the replacement set in a loop that
`return`s on the **first** constructor error. So a single unusable
`flow-server` disabled NetFlow **and** IPFIX export for **every**
template/family group, not just its own siblings.

Under the #3742 build-before-swap design the previously-running exporters were
kept, so a reload left stale export up; on a boot with nothing running it
published the empty bundle and export was simply off. The only record was a
`slog.Warn` and `Daemon.FlowExportError()`, which no show surface, REST field
or metric reads.

## This is reachable from an ordinary config, and that is the severity

Nothing validates a flow-server port at commit —
`validateSamplingTemplateRefsStrict` checks template references only — so

```
set forwarding-options sampling instance s1 family inet output flow-server 10.0.0.2
```

with no `port` **commits cleanly**. This was an operator typo silently
disabling flow export, not a drift-only malformed state reachable through the
lenient load path.

## The fix, and why it goes where it does

`collectInstanceVersionCollectors` drops such a collector where the list is
**built**, using the shared `config.FlowServerExcludedReason` — the same
predicate `show security flow monitoring` and `show forwarding-options`
annotate `NOT INSTALLED` with (#7422). One spelling, so the exporter and the
renderers cannot disagree about which collectors are live; two would drift in
opposite directions — an exporter skipping what the renderer calls active lies
to the operator, and one dialling what the renderer calls dead cries wolf.

Two nearby behaviours are deliberately **not** changed, and the fix is placed
where it is precisely so they need not be:

- **`reconcileFlowExporter` still returns on the first constructor error.**
  That is the #3742 availability design for a TRANSIENT failure (a pinned
  source-address bind before its interface is up, collector DNS): keeping the
  old exporters running beats swapping in a degraded set.
- **`dialCollectors` still fails the group on a dial error**, so a well-formed
  but unreachable collector stays fatal at construction and is handled
  afterwards by the #2464 write-health path.

## PR #8175 — test(ha): pin the worker-set gate on the synced-import path [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7209-pin-worker-gate`

Test-only. It pins a fact that is currently **folklore** and is about to become
load-bearing.

## The gate

`upsert_synced_session` reaches the source-NAT reservation through a
short-circuiting conjunction (`ha/session_import.rs`):

```rust
if entry.origin.is_peer_synced()
    && !entry.metadata.is_reverse
    && !self.workers.records.is_empty()          // <-- this operand
    && !self.reserve_synced_translation(&entry)
```

`reserve_synced_translation` is the **only** reader of `forwarding` on the
peer-synced import path. `stop_inner` clears `workers.records` in the **same
teardown** that sets `self.forwarding` to `ForwardingState::default()`. So this
operand is why an import arriving mid-reconcile never resolves against the empty
table.

## Why it needs pinning now

That fact is what **retired a proposed #7209 slice**. The plan was to give the
import path a "last-good" forwarding handle, published from the same seam as the
worker-visible `RuntimeView` but skipping the teardown reset. It was built, then
measured: the read it serves cannot happen, because the gate short-circuits
first. Nothing in the suite would have said so — the change would have merged as
a plausible-looking improvement that changed no outcome.

**Today the gate reads as an optimisation**, and its in-tree comment justifies it
as one:

> *"Skipped when NO worker is registered: nothing polls, so there is no racing
> local allocation to guard against, and an `Untracked` reservation that no
> worker ever adopts has no one to release it."*

A reviewer looking at it now sees a redundant-looking conjunct and may reasonably
propose hoisting the reservation out. **After #7209** takes `sync_session` off
the snapshot-wide `ServerState` mutex, it becomes part of why a *concurrent*
import is safe. The pin is what makes that refactor red instead of silent.

## The two legs

| leg | fixture | expected |
|---|---|---|
| A | no worker registered | counter must **not** move — the reservation is never reached |
| B | a worker registered | counter **must** move |

## PR #8176 — grpcapi: give persistent-nat its own budget, not the session-scan one [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8151-snapshot-budget`

`ShowText{persistent-nat}` took a `diagcmd.SessionWalkLimiter` slot. **It does
not walk.** `natshow.RenderPersistent`'s only dataplane read is
`PersistentNATTable.All()` — an O(bindings) snapshot copy of an in-process Go
map under that table's own RWMutex. It touches no conntrack bucket and contends
with nothing the session walks contend for. #6553's own line cites for this
topic point into `RenderPersistentDetail`, a different function.

**That is exploitable, not merely inaccurate.** `MaxConcurrentSessionWalks` is
4, REST and gRPC alias ONE limiter, and `ShowText` is on
`fabricAllowedUnaryMethods` — so a cluster peer polling `persistent-nat` could
hold all four slots and make genuine scans (`GET /api/v1/sessions`,
`GetSessions`, `GetStatus`'s `SessionCount`) start refusing.

## The bound is moved, not dropped

New `diagcmd.SnapshotReadLimiter` with its own cap. ShowText is peer-reachable
and an O(bindings) allocation is still worth bounding — and removing a bound
from a fabric-reachable surface is a security-shaped change that should not be a
side effect of correcting which budget applies. The caps are sized
independently because they bound different costs (a map copy versus per-bucket
BPF-map locks held across the whole v4+v6 table).

The #6553 cell asserting `persistent-nat` IS refused over the session cap
**moved** rather than being deleted or loosened — its subject is still live, it
just belongs to the other budget now.

## An escaped mutation rewrote the test

My first independence test substituted a fresh single-slot limiter for each
budget. A mutation aliasing `SnapshotReadLimiter = SessionWalkLimiter`
**escaped** it: the substitution destroyed the aliasing before the assertion
could observe it. The test was structurally incapable of failing for the reason
it existed.

It now drains the **real** limiters to their real caps — read from `diagcmd`
rather than hardcoded, so a cap change moves the drain with it — and asserts
`InFlight()` equals the cap before proceeding, since an under-filled drain would
admit on a free slot and pass having tested nothing.

Both directions are asserted. Saturating one budget and checking only that the
other's topic still works would pass on an implementation that had merely
renamed the shared limiter.

## PR #8178 — test: retry the policer contention cell instead of failing a serial run [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7841-policer-contention-retry`

`concurrent_refill_under_contention_neither_over_nor_under_grants_6307` ends with
a non-vacuity guard — `interleaved > 0` — asserting the eight threads actually
raced. **That is a property of the scheduler, not the policer.** On a loaded box
(this repo routinely runs ten-plus concurrent gates) the threads degenerate to
serial execution and the guard reds a test whose subject is fine, taking the
whole `make test-rust` leg with it since cargo aborts at the first failing
binary.

**The guard is right and is not weakened.** A serial run genuinely proved
nothing about the refill *race*, so accepting one would leave a cell reporting
coverage it does not have — precisely what the guard exists to prevent. A start
barrier cannot fix it either: it releases all eight threads but cannot give them
CPU.

So the run is retried, and **only the contention precondition is retried**. A
serial run still proves the refill *arithmetic*, so the over-grant and
under-grant assertions run on **every** attempt and a real defect fails on the
first one.

Failing after five attempts is deliberate and is not a flake: eight threads
failing to interleave five times running is a real signal (a single-core runner,
or a policer that serialises internally), and the panic reports per-attempt
contention rates so the reader can tell which. A loaded box normally measures
99.4–99.7%; this run measured 89.9%.

## Validation — the second cell is the load-bearing one

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| halve the refill window (`elapsed_ns / 2`) | **KILLED on attempt 1** — *"starved under concurrent refill: admitted only 132800 B green against a 225000 B budget"* |
| double `added_full` | **VOID** — panics on an arithmetic underflow in the remainder computation rather than failing an assertion |

The first is the property this change had to preserve: the retry must not
swallow a genuine defect. The second is reported as void rather than as a kill,
since a panic produces no assertion failure.

## A finding about the existing test, reported not fixed

Making the losing side of the `last_refill_ns` `compare_exchange` credit its
window anyway — the exact double-refill hazard the over-grant assertion names —
**escapes**. It is *inert* rather than uncovered: the committed bucket caps at
CBS, so the duplicated credit overflows into the excess/peak bucket, which this
fixture's own comment says never binds. The over-grant assertion is weaker
against that specific mechanism than its comment implies.

Not changed here — tightening it means re-deriving the ceiling arithmetic, which
is a different change from fixing the flake.

Closes #7841

## PR #8179 — afxdp: publish the coordinator BPF map set behind an ArcSwap [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7209-arcswap-bpf-maps`

Groundwork for #7209 (a). It changes no behaviour today and is deliberately
staged before the `Arc<Coordinator>` rather than after it.

## The problem

`Coordinator.bpf_maps` held `Option<OwnedFd>` fields that `stop_inner` set to
`None` — dropping them, and `OwnedFd::drop` calls `close(2)`. A reader that took
a raw `fd` out of one of those fields could have it closed underneath it by a
concurrent teardown.

Safe Rust prevents that today, **for exactly one reason**: every mutator takes
`&mut self`, so no `&self` reader can run concurrently. #7209 removes that
guarantee by putting the Coordinator behind an `Arc` so `sync_session` can be
served off the snapshot-wide `ServerState` mutex. This is the field-level
replacement for it.

## The refcount is the guarantee, not the swap

This is a **lifetime** failure, not a stale read, so republishing a "current"
value cannot fix it. The distinction matters because the obvious simplification
— a `Mutex<BpfMaps>`, or a plain field with the mutex taken elsewhere —
serialises access **without extending any lifetime**, and every test in the tree
would still pass, because nothing reads these concurrently yet.

That sentence is on the **field declaration**, which is what someone proposing
that simplification is looking at; the long-form rationale is on `BpfMaps`
itself.

## Whole-set stores

Writers replace the entire set in one `store` — teardown to `BpfMaps::default()`,
bringup to the newly opened descriptors — so a reader can never observe a
half-updated generation (a live `session_map_fd` beside a stale
`dnat_table_fd`). Both write sites were *already* whole-set updates spelled as
seven field assignments; this makes that atomic rather than incidental.

Readers bind the loaded set to a local for as long as the raw descriptors are
used. That is load-bearing at the two `DnatTableFds` sites, which copy raw fd
numbers out: extracting the number and dropping the guard would reintroduce the
window this closes.

## Not a hot path — measured before starting

Packet workers copy raw descriptors into their own `WorkerBpfMaps` at spawn and
never load this. The coordinator's field has **23 non-test sites across four
files**. An `ArcSwap` load per packet would have been a hot-path regression under
the allocation rules in `docs/engineering-style.md`; this is not one. That census
decided feasibility and was taken first.

## PR #8180 — host-inbound: withhold zone-level dhcp from a DHCP server (#7490 option 2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `feat/7490-zone-level-dhcp-server-flip`

## What this is

**#7490 ruled option 2 on #6519's parity gap: flip enforcement for the
server/relay role only.** A zone-level `host-inbound-traffic system-services
dhcp` / `bootp` no longer authorizes udp/67-68 on a member interface that runs a
DHCP **server or relay**. It still does on the firewall's own DHCP **client**, on
an interface that is **both**, and on one running **neither**.

## Read this first: #8060 landed mid-implementation and changes the risk story

I caught it because the rebase conflicted on the very stanza I was migrating.
#8060 measured on hardware that a zone-level `dhcp` token **does not gate a
DHCPv4 server's request path at all**: DISCOVER/REQUEST is addressed to
`255.255.255.255`, the XDP shim hands that destination straight to the kernel,
and Kea's `Dhcp4` runs in `raw` mode so it receives on an **AF_PACKET** socket
delivered *before* the netfilter input hook — an nft INPUT drop **counted** the
packet and Kea answered anyway. Kea's LPF admits unicast-to-own-address the same
way. DHCPv6 SOLICIT is `ff02::1:2` and every per-zone rule is unicast-daddr
scoped.

Three consequences, all handled here:

1. **My advisory originally said "client DISCOVER to the firewall on that
   interface is DENIED."** That is false, and it is the *exact sentence* #8060
   was filed to delete from this repo's reference config. I would have put the
   deleted claim in front of every operator instead of one config. Rewritten to
   the measured mechanism, with a guard test keyed on the **claim**
   (`discover` + `denied` co-occurring), not on a word a paraphrase would slip
   past.
2. **The flip is therefore expected to be inert on a `dhcp-local-server`'s
   request path.** Its value is parity plus removing a real over-authorization —
   a zone-level token opening udp/67-68 on the firewall-local addresses of every
   member — not preventing a live exposure. The advisory now names what the
   bypass argument does **not** cover: a relay's unicast leg, and the firewall's
   own client, whose RENEW **unicast** to a zone address *is* daddr-matched.
3. **#8060's non-goal says deleting `dhcp` from that zone would be worse than the
   wrong comment.** So the migration **keeps** the zone-level tokens and only
   *adds* the per-interface stanza. `reth1` resolves from its own stanza
   (effective set bit-identical), the zone level still covers a future member
   with no stanza, and the advisory goes quiet because `reth1` declares one.

**One correction to freshly-landed text, flagged rather than slipped in.**
#8060's new comment says the tokens are there "for the firewall's OWN DHCP
CLIENT renewals on this interface". `reth1` carries a **static** address
(`10.0.61.1/24`) and runs no DHCP client — checked against master's own file. The
reason is right in general, and it is `fxp0` in that file that actually runs one.
I kept #8060's mechanism paragraph verbatim and corrected only that clause, in
the stanza this change was editing anyway.

## PR #8181 — test/vrrp: capture only the subject's own log record [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8091-subject-only-slog-capture`

`captureSlog` installed a Debug-level handler as the **process-global** default
logger, so every record emitted anywhere in the process while
`TestArrivalIfindexDetector` ran landed in the buffer its negative control
asserts is empty. The named intruder is `runAddrWatcher`'s `slog.Info("vrrp:
address watcher started ...")` (`addrwatch.go:68`), emitted from a goroutine
another test starts — so the cell red on test **order**, not on its subject.

## Level-scoping was measured and rejected

The obvious fix is to capture `Warn+`, since the subject emits a warning and the
intruder is `Info`. But `pkg/vrrp` has **26 `slog.Warn` call sites**, several on
goroutines and timers — link-subscription closed, address-subscription closed,
sync-hold timeout. That fix would have excluded the one intruder named in the
report and stayed open to all of those: a fix shaped to the symptom.

Filtering on the subject's own message is immune to every foreign record
regardless of level or origin.

**The trade-off is stated at the helper** rather than left implicit: the negative
control now means *"the subject stayed silent"* rather than *"nothing logged at
all"*, so a regression warning with some **other** message would not be caught
here. That was never what this cell bound — the previous formulation only
appeared to bind it while actually being a coin flip on goroutine timing.

## The flake is bound deterministically, not hoped away

The test now emits **both** intruders — the exact `Info` record from the report,
and one of the `Warn` records that level-scoping would have missed — immediately
before the negative control reads the buffer. If the capture ever stops
filtering, the very next assertion fails, instead of failing once a week on a
loaded box.

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| revert to the unfiltered global handler | KILLED — negative control, with both injected records quoted |
| over-reach: filter matches nothing | KILLED — the **positive** assertions |

## PR #8184 — userspace-dp: bind the flow-cache replay reject message-type [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7678-flow-cache-hit-reject-fixture`

## What

The fourth of four hops carrying a filter term's `then reject <message-type>` to the ICMP builder. #6854 bound three; this one had **nowhere to stand**, so hardcoding `cached_descriptor.tx_selection.reject_message` to the default left the entire suite green — an operator's `then reject host-unreachable` would silently revert to administratively-prohibited on flow-cache-replayed traffic.

## The blocker was not where the handoff thought

The prior attempt measured `tallies=(0,1,0)` — a cache **miss** — and read it as the UDP frame and the re-keyed entry disagreeing on what `FlowCacheLookup::for_packet` derives.

It is simpler and elsewhere. **`stage_flow_cache_hit` does not derive its key from the packet** — it takes `flow.forward_key` as a parameter, and this harness hardcoded that to `test_key()` (`PROTO_TCP`) at the single site `forward_key: test_key()`. Re-keying only the *cached entry* therefore made `entry.key != *key` in `lookup_with_observed_bytes`, and the lookup could never hit however the frame was built. Both sides have to move together, which `StageSeed.flow` now does.

## Three more things had to be true, each failing silently

1. **The frame must not be TCP.** `reject_reply.rs` branches on `PROTO_TCP` and synthesizes an RST, never consulting `reject_message`.
2. **The ICMP source comes from the LOGICAL ingress ifindex, not the physical one.** `enqueue_reject_reply` resolves `resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex` *before* the egress lookup, and this fixture maps `(6, VLAN 80) → 20080` — so an egress entry keyed on `PHYS_INGRESS_IFINDEX` is never consulted and the builder returns `None`.
3. **The stock TX pipeline can never admit a reject reply.** `syn_cookie_reply_budget_available` needs `free_tx_frames.len() > TX_BATCH_SIZE` (64) *and* `admitted < max_pending_tx - 64`. The fixture carries **8** free frames with `max_pending_tx: 64`, so both fail: `8 <= 64`, and `0 < 64 - 64` is false. The reply was **built and then dropped at the budget gate** — indistinguishable from the reject branch never running. Found by instrumenting, not by reading.

Each was diagnosed by asserting in **cost order** — cache hit, then reply enqueued, then the code byte — so an earlier failure names itself instead of masquerading as the later one. For an issue whose subject is a wired-but-unasserted hop, a cell that read an empty queue and passed would have been the worst possible outcome.

## Two additive seams, no existing cell moves

`StageSeed.flow` and `StageSeed.tx_headroom` both default to today's behaviour. Three existing `StageSeed` literals enumerated every field and needed `..StageSeed::default()` — **the same #7689 shape, in a second struct**.

## The second user the issue asks for

A paired cell drives the identical fixture with the **default** message-type and requires code 13. The two together show the wire byte **tracks** the cached field rather than being constant at either value — the code-1 assertion alone would pass for a builder that ignores `reject_message` and a fixture that coincidentally agrees.

## Validation

- `make test-go` — `GO_RC=0`, 0 `FAIL` / `WARNING: DATA RACE`.
- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`, 0 `test result: FAILED`.
- Rebased onto `90c28431e` and **re-gated on both suites after the rebase**, since master moved while this was in progress.
- `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` — 1 file, test-only.

**Acceptance mutation** — the issue names this as the test *of the fixture itself*: "if it does not red, the fixture is not reaching the consumer."

| | |
|---|---|
| mutation | `flow_cache_hit.rs`'s `reject_message` read → `RejectMessage::ADMIN_PROHIBITED` |
| applied | yes, 1 line |

## PR #8186 — test/api: hold the peer lookup so the occupancy check is an observation [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7882-peerdone-occupancy-window`

`TestPeerDoneMeansTheSlotIsBack_6977` fills the pool to capacity-1, opens a
connection so the lookup takes the last token, then asserts the pool is full
while that lookup is in flight — with an instantaneous `select`/`default`
**sample** of a window the test does not control.

`connContext` takes the token synchronously, but the goroutine releases it with
a defer, so the window closes as soon as the injected resolver returns — which
for a resolver that does nothing is essentially immediately. When the lookup
wins that race, a free slot exists and the cell reports *"the lookup did not take
one"*, which is the opposite of what happened. On a loaded box the ordering is a
coin flip.

## The fix

`peerLookupFn` is already injectable, so the test can make the in-flight window
last exactly as long as it needs: signal on entry, block until released. It
waits for that entry signal before asserting occupancy, so reaching the
assertion means the token **is** held and cannot yet have been released — the
release is deferred past the point the test is standing at. The sample becomes
an observation.

The entry wait carries its own bound and says what a timeout means: the lookup
never entered the resolver, so the occupancy assertion would be sampling a
window that never opened. That is a different failure and should not be reported
as the one the cell is about.

## Validation — cells against production, because the point is the cell still binds

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| remove the goroutine's `defer func() { <-pool }()` | KILLED — this test; the token never comes back |
| swap the defers so `close(p.done)` precedes the release | KILLED — `TestPeerDoneIsClosedAfterTheSlotIsReturned_6977`, the structural cell the file names as the detector |

The second is the more interesting result: the ordering invariant keeps its own
guard, and my change does not weaken it.

## Stated plainly

**The determinism this buys is structural, not demonstrated by a mutation.**
There is no cell that reds on the old form, because the old form is correct
whenever it wins the race — which is most of the time, and is exactly why the
flake was hard to attribute. The argument is the mechanism: the release is
deferred past the assertion point, so blocking in the hook makes the window
explicit rather than hoped for.

Closes #7882

## PR #8187 — test/eventengine: bound waitFor for real commit latency, not idle latency [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7931-waitfor-commit-latency`

`TestQueue_ConcurrentProbesSerialize` times out under parallel suite load — and
the timeout is **not** a scheduling hiccup. The conditions `waitFor` waits on
are driven by real config **commits**: atomic DB persistence plus a JSONL audit
journal, serialized through the event engine's single worker. That test waits
for **eight** of them, so the 3s deadline was ~375ms per commit — comfortable
idle, not on a box running ten-plus concurrent gates. The work genuinely takes
longer; the condition is not failing to happen.

## Why raising the shared deadline is the right fix, not a papering-over

The issue flags exactly the right risk: the helper has **16 call sites**, so
relaxing it moves every one. That is true, and it is benign for a reason worth
stating rather than assuming:

**A wait-for-condition deadline is not a performance budget.** When the
condition holds, `fn()` returns true on an early poll and the deadline is never
reached — so **no passing test gets slower**. Measured: `go test
./pkg/eventengine/ -count=2` still completes in **2.6s**, unchanged.

The cost is paid only by a test that was going to fail anyway, which now takes
longer to say so. A slower *true* failure is a better trade than a *false* one,
because a false failure sends someone chasing a defect that is not there —
which is precisely what this issue is.

All 16 sites wait on the same class of condition (engine statistics advancing
after real commits), so one bound is right. Sixteen per-site deadlines would be
sixteen independent bets on the same scheduler.

## The message now distinguishes two failures that look identical

Elapsed time and poll count are reported. A timeout that polled **thousands** of
times over the full window is a condition that never became true; one that
polled a **handful** of times spent the window descheduled — a different
diagnosis, pointing at the box rather than the code. #7931 itself would have
been classified in one glance.

## Validation

- package passes at `-count=2` in 2.6s, unchanged — the passing path is
  genuinely unaffected;
- a probe with the constant temporarily lowered confirms a genuinely never-true
  condition **still fails** rather than hanging, so the raised bound did not
  convert a failure into a hang.

Closes #7931

The local CLI and the gRPC text surface rendered `show forwarding-options port-mirroring` from **two byte-identical copies with no shared formatter**. - **#8166** had to fix the nondeterministic instance order in *both*.

Every future edit paid the same tax and could silently pay only half of it.

## Tests moved with the code

This is the part single-sourcing most easily gets wrong. The two #6534 surface tests still pass — but they now exercise two thin wrappers around one function, so they bind the **wiring** and no longer the behaviour. A guard that passes while guarding nothing is worse than no guard.

- `make test-rust` — `RUST_RC=0`.

## PR #8190 — nat: stop reporting live port usage for a pool the dataplane refused [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7473-live-port-usage`

Three operator surfaces published a source-NAT pool's **live port-usage** figure
for a pool the userspace snapshot builder REFUSED to install.

## One wrong premise, three surfaces

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_nat.go` assigns `ApplyResult.PoolIDs` without consulting
any disarm predicate — `grep` for `Unusable|DisarmedReason|OverBudgetPools`
across the non-test `pkg/dataplane/*.go` returns nothing — so `cr.PoolIDs[name]`
succeeds for a refused pool, `ReadNATPortCounter` returns 0, and every surface
treats that 0 as observed.

| surface | what it published |
|---|---|
| `pkg/api/metrics_nat.go` | `xpf_nat_pool_used_ports` emitted |
| `show security nat source pool` | `Ports allocated` / `Ports available` |
| `show security nat source` (summary) | the `used` column |

**A missing series says "not installed"; a `0` says "measured, and nothing is
used".** The #5046 comment three lines above the metrics site already refuses
exactly this zero on the counter-*read-failure* path, for the same reason. The
refused-pool case reaches the same fake zero by a different route.

#7000 fixed the **capacity** half of all three. The **usage** half was never
gated: the pool view printed `Unusable: <reason>` and then `Ports allocated: 0`;
the summary rendered `N/A` in Ports/Available/Utilization and a bare `0` in the
used column, directly above its own `NOT INSTALLED` line.

## Reachability — narrower than "any config", and more specific

This cannot arise from a freshly committed config. #5877's strict gate rejects a
rule referencing an empty pool and #7640's rejects an actionless destination
rule, so the disarmed state is reachable **only through the tolerant ingress** —
`Store.SyncApply` / lenient load, i.e. HA peer-sync, boot and rollback. That is
the #1960 no-brick shape: strict refuses, tolerant warns and carries on so a
persisted or peer-synced config still boots.

That narrows the blast radius and sharpens it. The population is a **standby that
took a config its own strict gate would have refused** — which is exactly where
nobody is looking, and exactly where a monitoring gap costs the most.

It also decides the test design: a cell built through strict commit would be
testing a state production cannot produce.

## No new predicate

I wrote one, then deleted it. Every site already had the verdict in hand and
threw it away: the metrics loop computed `ports, _ := SourceNATPoolReportable
Ports(..)` and discarded the reason into `_`; the pool view already bound it as
`unusable` to print its Unusable line; the summary already bound it as
`poolDisarm` to print NOT INSTALLED. Each now gates its usage output on the value

## PR #8191 — grpcapi: enforce deny-commands on the gRPC listener (#7172 cut 5b) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `feat/7172-cut5b-enforce-deny-commands`

## What this is

**#7172 cut 5b.** Cuts 5a and 5a-2 built the tables answering "what command is
this RPC" for all 52 methods, 129 `ShowText` topics and 19 `SystemAction` verbs.
They were **inert**. This reads them: `authorizeRPC` now evaluates the calling
class's `deny-commands` regexes against the mapped command, **after** the #5278
coarse permission check and never instead of it.

`TestCommandTableIsNotYetConsumed7172` is deleted in the same change, since it
asserted the tables were still dead and this falsifies it.

## The constraint I wrote for this cut, and how it is discharged

My handoff comment on #7172 says 5b must **either accept the argument-free gap
explicitly or narrow it**, and must **not read a populated table as meaning the
two surfaces match the same thing**. Both halves:

**Accepted, and asserted rather than described.** `pkg/cli` matches the full
canonicalized line — argument values and output pipe included. This gate matches
the command **path**, because the remote CLI parses the line client-side and
`ping 10.0.0.1` arrives as `Ping{Host:"10.0.0.1"}`. So a deny written against a
*path* (`request system reboot` — the shape Junos' own examples use) is enforced
identically on both, while a deny written against *argument text*
(`show route table secret-vrf`) is enforced on the box and **not** here.
`TestArgumentLevelDenyIsOnBoxOnly7172` asserts **both directions with the same
compiled rules object** — the on-box call denies the full line, this gate allows
the path — so the asymmetry is a fact the suite carries, not prose.

**Narrowed, by telling the operator which of their patterns it affects.**
`unenforceableDenyPatterns` asks whether a pattern matches **any** command this
listener can produce; one that matches none can never fire here, and is logged
once per class (deduped — it is a property of the config, not of a request, and
the check sits on a per-request path).

## The design I rejected, and the measurement that killed it

The obvious version inspects the pattern: `regexp.LiteralPrefix`, flag a literal
that extends a mapped command. I built a probe before trusting it:

| pattern | `LiteralPrefix()` |
|---|---|
| `show route table secret-vrf` | `"show route table secret-vrf"` |
| **`^show route table secret-vrf`** | **`""`** |
| `.*secret-vrf` | `""` |

The anchored form yields nothing — and **anchors are what Juniper's own guidance
tells operators to use** for anything complex. That heuristic would cover the
unanchored spelling and silently miss the anchored one. A guard that covers one
spelling of the same intent reads as coverage and is not. Matching against the
actual command set has no such dependence.

## PR #8192 — test/daemon: wait for the OUTER gate check before flipping the probe [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7617-outer-gate-ordering`

`TestReassertRechecksTheGateInsideTheSemaphore6793` is about the **inner** gate
re-check — the one `reassertDeadRASendersOnce` performs *after* acquiring
`applySem`. It constructed that state by starting the tick, flipping the probe,
and releasing the semaphore, synchronised only on a `started` channel closed as
the goroutine **begins**.

That is one instruction before the thing it needs to order against. The tick
checks the gate twice and the flip has to land **between** them. If it lands
before the outer check instead, that check sees a healthy sender,
short-circuits, and the tick never acquires the semaphore at all — `applies`
stays 0 and the cell passes green whether or not the inner re-check exists.

## The fix

Signal from the probe closure itself. Its first call **is** the outer check, so
waiting on that signal means the check has run and returned true, the tick is
committed to acquiring the semaphore, and the flip lands strictly between the
two. The wait carries its own bound and says what a timeout means — the tick
never consulted the gate — which is a different failure from the one the cell
asserts.

## Stated plainly: the vacuous pass does not reproduce here

Deleting the inner re-check from production kills the **original** test 10 times
out of 10 on this box. Its non-vacuity currently holds — it wins the race every
time. The same mutation kills the rewritten test too.

So this is **not** backed by a demonstrated escape. What it removes is the
*dependence*: the old cell is non-vacuous only while it keeps winning a race it
does not control, and nothing in it makes that true. The rewritten one
constructs the state it names regardless of timing.

## The title's other clause is stale

The data-race half of #7617 is **already fixed** — `85bab7cc4` (PR #7838),
landed under **#7075**, not under this number. Verified: `go test -race -count=5`
on this test at master is clean. Only the vacuous-pass clause was live.

| cell | result |
|---|---|
| delete the inner `if !d.raHasDeadSenders()` after `defer d.applySem.Release(1)` | KILLED — by name, applied-check confirmed |

Closes #7617

A text renderer is repaired by appending a line. A structured object cannot be: a
consumer parsing `{"type":"pool","pool":"p1"}` has nowhere to learn the rule
translates nothing, and `hit_packets: 0` reads as "no traffic matched" rather
than "not armed".

`not_installed` / `not_installed_reason` are added to four protobuf messages and

older client decodes them as `false`/`""` and behaves exactly as before.

The *predicates* already lived in `pkg/config`. What did not was the two lines
around them — which pool map to look a rule's pool up in, and what to answer when
it is absent. `pkg/cli` held that privately; `pkg/api` and `pkg/grpcapi` were each
about to grow a copy. **Three copies of "which map, and what if it is missing" is
three chances to answer it differently for the same rule.**

So it is exported once (`SourceNATRuleNotInstalledReason`,
`DestinationNATRuleNotInstalledReason`) and all three call it; `pkg/cli` now
delegates rather than duplicates.

It is the only getter under both families in the census, because it has two
