## PR #8223 — Scope the failover rejoin assertions to every redundancy group [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7368-rejoin-scope`

**The phase's own regression detector was dead in exactly the case it was written for.**

The post-reboot rejoin check in `test-failover.sh` is an `if`/`elif`: it tried `grep -q "node0.*secondary"` first and `grep -q "node0.*primary"` second, both unscoped over the whole `show chassis cluster status` output. A cluster that auto-preempted for RG1 while staying secondary for RG0 matched the **first** branch and reported PASS — so the `elif` that exists to name the auto-preempt regression was **unreachable in precisely the mixed case it was written for**.

That is not "an assertion that can pass on a partial state". The phase exists to catch auto-preempt, and on a partial auto-preempt its detector could not fire at all.

This is the shape #7368 retired from the preflight primacy check at `:178`, which survived here. The adjacent `grep -q "node1.*primary"` three lines below is the same defect in the same phase and is fixed in the same change — splitting it would leave the phase still passing on a mixed node1 state, which is the hole being closed.

**Deliberate?** No. I checked before changing it: the failback loop at the end of the file is already per-RG (`grep -A1 "Redundancy group: $rg"`), the preflight is per-RG since #7368, and this phase sat in the gap with no comment claiming a node-global intent. Note the `:178` comment's claim that "the post-failover phase below already asserts all three" is **true** — it refers to that failback loop, not to this site.

## Change
`deploy_reassert_node0_primary_ok` is generalised to `deploy_node_role_every_rg_ok <node> <role>`, and both rejoin assertions go through it. The old name is kept as a thin alias for `(node0, primary)` — it is the vocabulary the deploy path and #6591 use, and keeping it means its four existing cells still bind rather than being silently decommissioned.

## Mutation scoring (by failing cell name)
| cell | result |
|---|---|
| revert the rejoin site to the unscoped grep | **KILLED** — `rejoin: test-failover.sh wiring incomplete`, message quotes the offending line |
| weaken the predicate's "every RG" to "any RG" | **KILLED by 3 named cells**, two of them *pre-existing* (`reassert verify: ... RG0-ok/RG1-inverted`, `primacy: node0 is SECONDARY for RG0`) — direct evidence the alias refactor did not decommission the old tests |
| over-reach control: a **legitimately scoped** `grep -A1 "Redundancy group: $rg" \| grep -q "node1.*primary"` | **caught a defect in my own guard** |

**The control found a bug in the guard I wrote, not in the code under test.** My first wiring guard banned the retired substrings outright, so a legitimate future *scoped* use of `grep -q "node1.*primary"` reddened it — a false positive that would have forced correct code to be written incorrectly. Mutation A had already shown the positive check alone catches the realistic revert, so the blanket ban was contributing false positives **and no detection power**. The fix was to remove capability rather than add an exemption: the guard now tests **scoped-ness, not the substring**, firing only on a role grep with no `Redundancy group:` scoping on the same line. Re-verified afterwards — control green, mutation A still killed.

The consequence is the proof it is aimed correctly: `grep -q "node0.*primary"` at `:440` stays legitimate, which a substring ban would have made unfixable without loosening the detector.

Following the existing cell's discipline, the mixed-state cell first asserts the fixture *still reproduces the retired grep's false accept*, so it cannot quietly stop testing what it was written for.

- `make test-go` — green
- `make test-rust` — green, 0 failed across all crates

## PR #8224 — wg: put the endpoint resolver counters on the status wire (#7936) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `feat/7936-wg-endpoint-resolver-counters`

## What this is

#7158 added a per-tunnel WireGuard endpoint resolver with four counters —
`resolve_ok`, `resolve_fail`, `family_mismatch`, `endpoint_changed` — plus a
retained last-error string. They were **in-process only**: an operator whose
tunnel was stale because DNS broke could see it in the journal and nowhere else.

## Why this is not a field addition

**The resolver is a local of the WG control thread.** It is spawned after the
UDP bind because it needs `socket_is_v6` to filter answers to the family the
interface's single socket can send from, and it is dropped when the thread
returns — which is exactly the lifetime it should have. The coordinator held no
handle, so the 1 Hz status path had nothing to read, and the two `pub(crate)`
accessors #7158 added had **zero callers**.

The fix is the shape `recent_exceptions` already uses for the same reason: the
**coordinator** owns an `Arc` and clones it into the thread. A new
`WgEndpointResolverTelemetry` hangs off `WgControlEntry`, and `spawn` takes it
rather than creating its own. Held **across restarts** deliberately — a
self-heal respawn reuses the Arc, so the counters do not reset at the moment an
operator is most likely to be reading them.

## `family_mismatch` gets more than a number

It means the name resolved but to no address of this socket's family: **DNS
looks healthy and the peer simply never initiates**, which is indistinguishable
from a dozen other causes. So the surfaces split by what each can carry:

- the four **counts** become one Prometheus metric with an `outcome` label —
  they are alternatives of the same event, and "which outcome dominates" is the
  operator's question; four separate series would make that a join;
- the **last-error string** has no Prometheus home (an unbounded label would be
  worse than useless) and is rendered on `show security wireguard detail`, along
  with a line saying what the condition *is*.

The count says how often, the text says which name — only the pair is
actionable.

## Skew, extended in the same change

Rust fields carry `#[serde(default)]`, the Go mirror carries `omitempty`, so an
old helper decodes to zero and an old Go binary emits nothing a new helper can
misread. **Both** existing ladders are extended with matching values (51..54),
so a swapped pair of json tags shows up as a wrong *number* on both sides rather
than as two green suites — that is mutation cell m2.

**The wire specimen is unchanged, and I checked rather than regenerated.**
`wg_tunnels` is `skip_serializing_if`-empty, so it is absent from the default
`ProcessStatus` and a `WgTunnelStatus`-only change cannot move the fixture.

## PR #8226 — mutate: the FAIL-counting instrument is itself unsound (#8213) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `tools/8213-fail-count-unsound`

## The instrument, not a sixth shape

`scripts/mutate-lib.sh` encodes five ways a mutation cell produces no usable
verdict. **All five are detected by counting `^--- FAIL`, and that instrument is
unsound under the conditions the harness actually runs in.**

Parallel `go test -v` interleaves the output of concurrently running tests
**mid-line**, so a real `--- FAIL: TestX` can be spliced into another test's
failure text and no longer start at column 0. The anchored grep misses it and
the cell scores as an **ESCAPE**.

**The direction is the damaging one.** An escape reads as *"the fix is not
bound"*, which points a reviewer at the **test** as the thing to weaken. It does
not merely lose a signal — it manufactures an argument for deleting a guard that
works. And one spliced cell inverts a row without announcing itself, so the whole
matrix becomes untrustworthy rather than one line of it.

## Two halves, only one of which counting can fix

**Counting is now splice-tolerant.** Unanchored; matched on `--- FAIL: ` with the
colon and space so prose *about* the marker does not register; and counted per
**occurrence** rather than per line, because `grep -c` counts lines and two
markers can share one spliced line.

Measured, not assumed — the previous expression against the two new fixtures:

```
FAIL a SPLICED --- FAIL is still a kill
     want: yes 2 1 KILLED
     got:  yes 2 0 ESCAPED
FAIL two markers on one spliced line count as two
     want: yes 2 2 KILLED
     got:  yes 2 0 ESCAPED
```

So the cells bind the change rather than restating it.

**Attribution cannot be fixed by counting at all**, and that is the sharper half.
If a cell's `--- FAIL` is spliced but another test in the same package fails
cleanly, the count is still ≥ 1 — so the cell scores **KILLED for the wrong
test**, with rc and the count in agreement and *nothing looking wrong*. A count
cannot distinguish "my cell's test failed" from "something failed".

Only a name can, so the library gains `mutation_go_failed_names_json` (parsing
`go test -json`, where a name cannot be spliced by construction) and
`mutation_verdict_for_target`, which refines a counted `KILLED` to
`ESCAPED(other tests failed: …)` when the intended test is not among the
failures. It refines **only** a `KILLED`: a `VOID` has no trustworthy names to
compare, and refining one would repeat the score-the-prefix error the timeout
ordering exists to prevent.

## PR #8227 — Pin the raw reinject primitive's caller set and fix its doc [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7480-reinject-caller-pin`

`maybe_reinject_slow_path_from_frame` hands any parseable L3 frame to the kernel slow path **without** consulting `is_slow_path_eligible`. Its own doc block is what a caller reads before deciding it may bypass the predicate, so that enumeration is a security-relevant claim — and it was wrong.

#1946 wrote "the **ONE** INTENTIONAL unfiltered caller". #6664 discovered a second — the host-terminated IPsec passthrough in `poll_stages.rs`, which calls the primitive with a synthetic `LocalDelivery` decision — and corrected the architecture doc **and** the sibling comment at the `handle_forward_build_failure` call site, while leaving the primitive's own doc block saying "ONE". Two spellings of the same fact in one file, disagreeing, and the stale one sat on the item a caller actually reads.

## Measured, not trusted
Neither text is evidence, so I counted the call sites. Four production sites:

| site | filtered? |
|---|---|
| `tx/dispatch/slow_path.rs` — `maybe_reinject_slow_path` wrapper | filtered (via `slow_path_admit`) |
| `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` — #1913 trailing chokepoint | filtered (via `slow_path_admit`) |
| `tx/dispatch/slow_path.rs` — `handle_forward_build_failure` | **unfiltered**, resolved `ForwardCandidate` |
| `poll_stages.rs` — IPsec passthrough | **unfiltered**, synthetic `LocalDelivery` |

I read the last one to confirm it never consults the predicate: it calls the raw primitive with `ipsec_passthrough_decision()`.

## The fix is a pin, not a comment
A comment cannot be kept true by review — this one demonstrably wasn't. The set is now pinned in the existing #6664 source guard, so **any new production call site reds**, forcing the new caller to be classified filtered/unfiltered and reflected in the doc in the same change.

The restatement on `is_slow_path_eligible` loses its count and points at the authority instead. It had accumulated its own stale copy of the same number, which is what a restatement does.

## Mutation scoring (by failing test name)
| cell | result |
|---|---|
| a third production call site appears | **KILLED** — `raw_reinject_primitive_caller_set_is_pinned_7480 ... FAILED`, and only that test; the two pre-existing guards stayed green |
| control: the same call in a **test-named** file | **GREEN** — correctly not counted |
| control: the primitive named in a **comment** | **GREEN** — prose cannot satisfy or trip the guard |

**Stated limitation:** the pin guards the caller *set*, not the doc *text*. Reverting the doc block to "ONE" would not red anything. That is deliberate — a phrase-match on prose is defeated by paraphrase, and the enforceable property is the set. What the pin guarantees is that the list cannot go stale *silently*: the event that invalidated it (a new caller) is now the event that reds.

## Scope
No behaviour change. This is the **guardedness** half of #7480, deliberately separate from the `NoRoute` adjudication, which is a forwarding-behaviour change requiring the HA cluster smoke gate.

- `make test-go` — green

## PR #8228 — dataplane: test the AttachXDP/DetachXDP serialization claim [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7547-attach-detach-concurrency`

Closes #7547

The issue asks for a test that either reproduces the race or proves it cannot
happen. **Both halves are here, and the answer is "it cannot happen today, for a
reason that lives entirely in the callers."** No behaviour change, no fix, and
the lock is deliberately not widened.

## The three things established before writing anything

**1. Can the callers run concurrently?** Not through anything in
`pkg/dataplane`. Neither `Compile` nor `CompileUserspaceShim` takes `m.applyMu`
— that mutex guards `apply.go`'s generation bookkeeping, not these sequences —
so there is **no in-package serialization at all**. The whole safety is the
daemon's applySem around `applyConfigLocked`, plus the userspace Manager's own
`m.mu` held for the duration of `applyCompiledSnapshot` on that path. Exactly
the claim the issue was filed to test.

**2. What a double `Close()` does** — checked in cilium/ebpf v0.20.0 rather than
assumed. `FD.Close` is idempotent **sequentially** (`if fd.raw < 0 { return nil }`),
but `Disown()` writes `fd.raw` with no lock and no atomic:

```go
func (fd *FD) Close() error {
    if fd.raw < 0 { return nil }
    return unix.Close(fd.Disown())
}
func (fd *FD) Disown() int { value := fd.raw; ...; fd.raw = invalidFd; return value }
```

So two concurrent closes are a **data race on `fd.raw`** *and* two
`unix.Close(N)` calls on the same fd number. The second either fails EBADF or,
if that number has been reused in between, **closes an unrelated file**. This is
a correctness hazard, not a noisy one — conditional entirely on (1).

**3. The lock is not widened.** Holding `m.mu` across `Close()` would
reintroduce exactly the syscall-under-lock #6740 removed.

## What ships

**`TestDetachXDPIsNotSelfSerializing7547`** — the hazard as a measurement rather
than prose. Two concurrent `DetachXDP` calls for one ifindex through a fake
`link.Link` yield `closes=2 unpins=2 overlapped=true`: both goroutines inside
`Close()` on the same handle. A deliberate tripwire pinning today's behaviour,
in the spirit of #6790's misclassification cell — **if it ever reds, per-ifindex
exclusion was added, which is a good change**, and its comment says so with
instructions.

**`TestEveryAttachDetachCallerIsSerialized7547`** — the census. A property of
call sites stops holding *silently* when a new call site appears: the new caller
compiles, passes vet, and passes every existing test. So every call site must be

## PR #8229 — docs: retire the #6749 armed-state plan with its trigger [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7546-binding-arm-identity`

Closes #7546

## Decision: retire, with a trigger

#7546 lists two "remaining" items from #6749 as though they were small and independent. **They are the two halves of the plan's option C**, and the plan says a half-C is worse than none. This records the decision so the 89-commit research branch is *parked with a reason* rather than stranded — which the issue itself asks to avoid.

The outage half shipped in #7544 and is unaffected.

## Why the two items are not separable

**Item 2** — "make Go's convergence check include each registered binding" — is **option B**, whose §5-B verdict is verbatim **"REJECT B-as-Go-converger."** The plan answers this issue's exact wording rather than by implication:

> *"The issue's third fix-direction leg … is answered in detection form by option D below — whose predicate the marker now makes exact (`!Armed && !ActivationPending` = genuine drift, not pending activation)."*

D's predicate is exact **only because of** C's `activation_state` wire field. Built without C, it reports every pending activation as drift — a false positive on every expansion commit.

**Item 1** — "preserve arm state by stable identity" — has a safe form (**R3**) which also carries `activation_state`, so it is not standalone either.

## The counterexample that settles it

#7546's own "Before building" section warns that hardcoding `armed: true` for a **new** slot is a forwarding fail-open. True, and guarded.

Nobody had noticed that preserving `armed` **by identity** has the same failure mode **through a different door**:

> *"a post-teardown `WorkerSpawn` failure returns WITHOUT `stop_inner` — already-launched workers KEEP their records — and the reconcile refreshes actual partial state before returning `Err`. An arm-at-replan model therefore reports `enabled=true` against a partially-dead worker set … and Go can publish READY rows for the surviving subset."*

A future implementer will reach for the identity-preserving shape **precisely because it looks like the careful option**. That paragraph leads the record.

## A trigger, not a shrug

The record states a condition a later reader can test, rather than a judgement to re-litigate. Take C+D when **either**:

1. provenance drift produces an **operator-visible wrong answer** (today it is internal), or

## PR #8230 — userspace: assert the ingress gate precedes the binding lookup (#7588) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `test/7588-binding-gate-ordering`

## The hazard, and why nothing catches it today

`programBootstrapMapsLocked` zeroes stale `userspace_bindings` rows via
`clearAllBindingRowsLocked`, which iterates `m.lastBindingIndices` — an
in-process field that is **nil on a freshly constructed Manager**. The array is
`PinByName`-pinned under `/sys/fs/bpf/xpf`, so its rows **outlive the process**.
On the first apply after an xpfd restart the bootstrap clear zeroes nothing, and
rows written by the previous process survive.

Nothing bad happens — because the shim consults `USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES` and
**returns early** before it ever reaches the binding lookup, so a stale row for a
de-configured interface is never read. That ordering is stated nowhere and
asserted nowhere. Reorder the two statements, or add a path reaching
`USERSPACE_BINDINGS` without passing the ingress test, and inherited rows become
live routing state **with nothing going red**.

## Verified at HEAD, not taken from the issue

The issue's measurements are from `c54d4b918`. At HEAD the gate is
`lib.rs:478` and the lookup `:502`, in one function.

**The enumeration you asked for — every reader of the pinned rows:**

| Reader | Gated? |
|---|---|
| shim `lib.rs:502` — the only one | yes, by `:478` |
| Go `verifyBindingsMapLocked` ×2 | n/a — iterates the **helper's live bindings**, not the map |

Both Go reads key off queues the helper currently reports, so a stale row for a
de-configured interface is invisible to them too. **There is no second consumer
bypassing the ordering.**

## That enumeration also settles the issue's alternative fix — it does not work

#7588 offers: reconstruct the occupied-slot inventory from the helper's reported
bindings at first status. The helper reports the queues it is *currently
serving*; the stale rows that matter are exactly those for interfaces the config
no longer has, which the helper **does not report** and such an inventory cannot
name. It would let the Manager name rows that `applyPrimaryBindingRowsLocked`
rewrites on the next ~1/s poll anyway, and still leave the de-configured ones
behind.

A blanket sweep is the other alternative, and the issue already measured it out
at 1,048,576 rows per apply.

So the dependency stays and is asserted instead.

## PR #8232 — mutate: say that bypassing make would NARROW the gate (comment-only, follows #8226) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/8231-do-not-bypass-make`

## One comment, landed on its own so the window is bounded

#8226 made the driver print its attribution limit on every `KILLED` line — its
verdicts are count-based, so they say *something* failed, not that the cell's
target failed. Naming the gap at the point of use was right. The comment
explaining it then ended:

> A JSON-capable driver should use `mutation_go_failed_names_json` +
> `mutation_verdict_for_target` instead.

Read cold, that is an **invitation to make this driver JSON-capable** — to
bypass `make` — which is the repair that must not happen.

**An honest limitation pointing at the wrong remedy is worse than a bare one.**
It converts "someone might do the wrong thing" into "someone will do the wrong
thing and cite this comment as authority."

## Why bypassing `make` is the wrong repair

Gating through `make` is *why* a cell carries `go vet`, the targeted `-race` runs
with `-count=2`, and on the Rust side `--release` and `--test-threads=1`. A bare
per-package `go test -json` driver would buy better attribution and pay for it in
**coverage** — and a narrower gate that agrees with the old one is
indistinguishable from a sufficient one until the day it isn't. Trading gate
strength for verdict precision is the wrong direction for a harness whose only
job is to say whether a guard is real.

The comment now says that, names the legs that would be lost, and points at
**#8231** — make the *gate targets* emit machine-readable results alongside their
normal output, so attribution costs no coverage — rather than at bypassing them.
The two name-based helpers are documented as being for a caller that **already
has** such a stream.

## Scope

Comment text only, inside the branch that was already printing the warning. No
behaviour change; `git diff --numstat` is `16 2 scripts/mutate.sh`.

## PR #8234 — test: decap an IPv6-outer GRE frame through the #6748 bound [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7541-gre-v6-outer-decap`

Closes #7541

## First: fixture gap or code gap?

The issue does not say which, and they are different results. **It is a fixture gap.**

The decap path is family-generic throughout — `parse_outer_addresses` and `outer_datagram_end` both branch on `meta.addr_family`, and `match_tunnel_endpoint` keys on `(outer_family, dst, src)`. The hardcoded 20-byte constants in `gre.rs` are inner-packet parsing or the encap side, not the outer decap path. A well-formed v6-outer frame decaps today; nobody had written one.

`gre_decap_accepts_a_plain_v6_outer_frame_7541` is the cell that establishes this, and it exists so the other three are **not vacuous**: if a v6 outer never resolved its endpoint, every bound cell would pass by refusing for the wrong reason, and the file would assert nothing while looking thorough.

## The fixture arithmetic is not the IPv4 one

This is why these are separate builders rather than a parameterised v4 one. The v6 outer end is `l3 + 40 + Payload Length`, and **Payload Length excludes the 40-byte header** where IPv4's Total Length includes its own 20.

A premise check copied from the v4 cells would compare the wrong quantity — and because the frame is self-consistent either way, it would **pass while asserting nothing**. `assert_v6_fixture_premises` states the v6 form once.

`write_gre_v6_outer` is shared by both v6 builders so the Payload Length rule is written once. The issue's acceptance criterion is that the two families cannot drift into testing different things; two copies of that arithmetic is how the drift starts.

**Only the outer family varies.** The inner stays IPv4 in every cell, exactly as in #6748, so any difference in outcome isolates the outer family.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | remove the #6748 bound (`outer` = whole frame) | **2 of 4 v6 cells RED** — the primary and checksum-present, i.e. exactly the two that assert the bound. Both acceptance cells stay green. |
| M2 | v6 arm of `outer_datagram_end` forgets the 40-byte header | **3 of 4 v6 cells RED, and all four #6748 IPv4 decap cells stay GREEN.** |

**M2 is the measurement that justifies this issue.** It reproduces exactly the regression class #7541 names — a fault in the v6 arm reaching the bound — and shows that before these cells it was visible **only** to the direct unit test of `outer_datagram_end`, with every decap-level cell blind to it.

### One honest note, recorded in the file

Under M2 the v6 **refusal** cell still passes, because a shortened outer end refuses for a different reason. That is precisely why each family carries an **acceptance control**: a refusal cell can pass for the wrong reason, and only the honest-inner cell distinguishes "bounded correctly" from "refuses everything".

## Vacuity discipline

- All four cells confirmed **registered by the runner** (`cargo test 7541 -- --list`) rather than inferred from a green summary — an unregistered module compiles to nothing and reports success.
- Results **counted**, not read off the tail: `4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored`.
- No cell needs elevated privileges or a real BPF map, so none can skip silently.

`make test-rust` RUST_RC=0, `make test-go` GO_RC=0. Tests only; no production code touched.

## PR #8235 — nat: count and report the persistent leases a pool change drops [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7560-partial-overlap-leases`

Closes #7560

A partial-overlap SNAT pool change drops **every** persistent-NAT lease —
including leases on addresses the change **retained** — and said nothing about
it.

Carry-over is keyed on the whole `SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey` (pool name + both
full address lists + port range), so **any** address change misses the reuse
lookup and rebuilds the allocator for the whole pool. #6765 added
`reseed_retained_from` to carry live *port* ownership onto retained addresses;
it deliberately does not carry `persistent_by_source`.

**Whether it should is the open policy question, and this does not decide it.**
What it fixes is that the drop was invisible.

## What "partial overlap" means, and who survives

| pool change | what carries |
|---|---|
| **identical** address list | everything — the exact key match shares the whole `Arc<PortAllocatorShared>`, so leases, expirations and occupancy all carry |
| **partial overlap** | live **port ownership** for flows on retained addresses, via `reseed_retained_from`. **Not** `persistent_by_source`, `lease_expirations`, `lease_expirations_by_addr`, or address-only tokens |
| **disjoint** | nothing (the index map is empty and the pass returns early) |

So on a partial overlap a source with a live flow on a retained address keeps
*that flow* working and loses its *persistence guarantee* — its next new flow
may land on a different address.

## Was the drop silent? Half of it, in the worse half

`skipped_address_only` was counted and printed. **Persistent leases were counted
nowhere and mentioned nowhere.** The operator-facing line accounted for what the
rebuild carried and what it skipped, and leases appeared in *neither* column.

The message was **true**, and the shape of a carried/skipped accounting implies
it is complete — so an operator who added one address read a reassuring
"carried N live translation(s)" and found out about the leases when subscribers
re-mapped. That implied completeness was the defect, not a missing log.

## Two counts, not one

Only one is a surprise. A lease on a **removed** address cannot be honoured. A
lease on a **retained** address was dropped only because the key includes the
whole address list. Reporting one number buries the actionable half inside the
expected one.

Counting runs inside the **same lock acquisition** as the existing live-set
snapshot, so it adds no second lock/release to a config-apply path and both
counts describe one consistent instant.

## PR #8236 — Adjudicate NoRoute against the zone pair before kernel reinject [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7480-noroute-adjudication`

> [!WARNING]
> **Availability-visible on upgrade — release-note candidate.** On a Junos-default deny box, traffic to a destination the kernel knows but the helper does not will now **drop** where it previously forwarded. That is the fix — those frames were bypassing zone policy — but an operator who meets it cold will read it as a regression. See "What changes for an operator" below.

A `NoRoute` frame is slow-path eligible, so it was reinjected to the kernel FIB with no zone policy, session, NAT or screen. Nothing downstream re-checks it: there is no nftables `hook forward` chain at all, `ip_forward` is force-enabled while armed, and `rp_filter` is deliberately 0 on the TUN. The **destination is chosen by the sender**, which is what makes this the attacker-steerable half of #6664.

## This is an adjudication, not a drop — and that was not a free choice
#7480 presents "adjudicate before reinjecting" vs "stop reinjecting" as open. It is not: `pkg/routing/fibimport.go:42-53` already settles it. #7409's importer **bounds** the kernel/helper FIB divergence without closing it — the snapshot is pushed on operator commit and ip-monitoring actuation only, and I verified there is no netlink route subscription anywhere in the tree (`RouteSubscribe` occurs exactly once in the repo: in that comment). So a route the kernel learns between pushes must still reach it. Dropping `NoRoute` outright would black-hole every learned destination for the width of that window, and on a fresh boot until the first push.

## Shape: follow #4024, don't invent a second convention
`poll_descriptor/mod.rs:3806` documents the precedent by name — `MissingNeighbor` already enforces this same zone policy on its cold-path arm, including the flowless branch (#4024). So this evaluates, then **downgrades the disposition to `PolicyDenied`** and lets the existing #1913 chokepoint refuse it fail-closed with the accounting that already exists.

That keeps **one** authority for "may this reach the kernel" (#6664) rather than two that agree today, and it needs no change to the shared gate's signature.

**The both-paths constraint is satisfied by a fact, not by placement.** `maybe_reinject_slow_path` — the other documented refusal point — has **zero production callers** (nine non-test mentions: comments, the definition, one unused re-export). The `poll_descriptor` chokepoint is the only live gate a `NoRoute` frame can reach, so a single arm covers transit and WG-decap by construction.

## What changes for an operator
Both `NoRoute` constructors set `egress_ifindex: 0`, so the to-zone is always the #3110 unzoned sentinel and **every evaluation falls through to the DEFAULT action**. Consequences:

- default-deny box → NoRoute frames now drop;
- **an explicit zone-pair `permit` does NOT rescue them** — #3110 makes an unzoned flow ineligible for zone-pair *and* `junos-global` rules, so no rule is consulted. Someone will otherwise "fix" the reported drop by adding a permit and find it changes nothing. There is a cell pinning exactly this;
- affected traffic is destinations learned between snapshot pushes, plus everything before the first push after a boot — the **first-boot case** being the one most likely to be hit and least likely to be attributed.

## Testability — the part that needed structure
The call site is inside `poll_binding_process_descriptor`, which no test in this crate can drive (live binding, UMEM, descriptor ring — the same reason #6664 used a source guard). **Every existing cargo test passed both before and after the behaviour change**, which is the demonstration, not an assumption. So the decision is extracted as `noroute_policy_denial` and tested directly, with a source guard for the wiring.

## Mutation scoring (by failing test name)
| cell | result |
|---|---|
| helper always returns `None` (pre-#7480 always-delegate) | **KILLED** — `noroute_is_denied_on_a_default_deny_box_7480` +2 |
| helper always returns `Some` (the black-hole) | **KILLED** — `noroute_is_delegated_when_the_default_permits_7480` +2 |
| revert the arm to pre-#7480 (compiling) | **KILLED** — `noroute_arm_adjudicates_before_reinjecting_7480` |
| evaluate but discard the verdict (no downgrade) | **KILLED** — same guard; a policy check whose result is dropped |

Both directions are covered: the security direction *and* the availability direction.

**A fixture bug worth recording:** the flowless cell first used `applications: ["junos-https"]`, but `parse_policy_state` takes no application definitions, so the name never resolved and the rule became `match_any` — which short-circuits the L4-presence check. It would have passed for the wrong reason. It now uses an inline port-bearing `application_terms` entry, and the helper documents why.

**Instrument note:** my first mutation scorer treated cargo's `error: test failed` as a build break and reported two real kills as VOID. Corrected to key on `could not compile` / `error[E`, then validated against a known-green baseline before trusting any result.

## Docs updated in the same change
The comment at `poll_descriptor:3806` said "NoRoute is **NOT** adjudicated here and does **NOT** drop" — this change made that false, which is the same stale-claim defect #8227 just fixed one file over. Corrected, along with the `is_slow_path_eligible` eligibility doc, the architecture doc, and `fibimport.go`'s description of the bypass (still accurate for permitted frames, now scoped).

## Validation
- `cargo test 7480` — 4 passed, 0 failed; `--test slow_path_admit_single_site_6664` — 4 passed
- `make test-rust` — green, 10/10 binaries
- `make test-go` — green

## PR #8237 — cluster: do not raise the boot epoch above a LIVE sibling's (#7501) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7501-boot-epoch-live-sibling`

## The defect

`refineBootEpoch` raises whenever the persisted value is at or above what this
node published — that is how a backward clock step is carried across a restart.
But **"a predecessor wrote it after a backward step" and "a concurrent newer
incarnation wrote it" leave the identical file**: a bare decimal.

So with two overlapping `xpfd` instances — reachable, since there is no pidfile
and the gRPC listener sets `SO_REUSEPORT` — the **older** one reads the newer
one's value, treats it as its predecessor's, and raises **itself** above it. The
peer latches that higher epoch from the process about to exit and refuses the
**survivor** for the life of its process.

`withEpochFileLock` cannot close this: it serializes by lock **acquisition**, and
there is no happens-before edge from daemon start to that acquisition.

## Criterion 2 rules out the option the issue recommends first

#7501 calls single-instance enforcement "the only one of the three that removes
the precondition". Its own criterion 2 forbids it as written, and the reason is
structural rather than a matter of care.

Criterion 2 is met **for free** by anything on the refine worker —
`heartbeat_epoch.go:589`: *"the wall-clock value is published **synchronously**,
with no file access, and every frame carries it from the very first send.
Persistence is a **refinement**, not a prerequisite."* Single-instance
enforcement runs at **daemon startup, upstream of publication**, so a node that
cannot take its lock has not emitted anything yet:

- **refuse to start** → a storage fault takes a healthy node off the air;
- **start anyway** → it is not single-instance enforcement.

An errno split complies by reintroducing the overlap window exactly when storage
is faulted. Filed as **#8233** with its own criteria, along with whether
`SO_REUSEPORT` is load-bearing at all.

**And options 1 and 2 are not independent.** An identity says *who* wrote the
value, not whether they are running, and predecessor-vs-live-sibling is a
**liveness** question; a lifetime lock needs an identity to attribute. This is
the two fused.

## A sidecar, not a new field

The epoch file is written as `FormatUint(epoch)+"\n"` and read with `ParseUint`
over the whole trimmed contents, so **any** added field makes an older binary
read it as unreadable and lose backward-clock-step protection. `<path>.owner`
leaves the epoch file **byte-identical**, satisfying criterion 3 in *both*
directions rather than the one it asks for: an older binary reads exactly what it
always did, a missing sidecar means "owner unknown" — today's behaviour — and
#6711's preserve branch never learns the sidecar exists.

## PR #8238 — nat: make an ungated reseed population fail to compile [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7560-lease-drop-visible`

Refs #7560 — **complementary to #8235, not a competing implementation.** That shipped the lease counters and a note for them; this fixes the report **gate** that swallows them at two of three call sites. Rebased onto master; everything #8235 shipped has been dropped from this branch.

## What #8235 left behind

`git grep 'skipped_address_only\|needs_report' master -- 'userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs'` returns nothing. The gate was already wrong at two of three `reseed_retained_from` sites, and both are still wrong at its merged head:

- **`nat64.rs`** gated on `reseeded || skipped_out_of_range || refused` and omitted `skipped_address_only` **entirely** — a pass that skipped only address-only tokens counted them and then printed nothing.
- The **#6979 rename** site always printed a line but left that count out of the message.

Both are one shape: the condition **and** the text are restated at each caller, so a field added to `ReseedOutcome` must be added in three places — and was not, twice, independently.

## Not "fix the two sites"

Two corrected conditions are still three places to forget next time. `needs_report()` derives the gate from the struct, so a silently-ungated population becomes **unrepresentable** rather than merely fixed.

**Scope:** the gate covers the populations *that line* accounts for. Dropped leases are deliberately **not** in it — they have their own note and condition (#8235's), and folding them in would print a `0 not carried, 0 skipped, 0 refused` line on a lease-only drop, which is the noise that teaches an operator to skip the line. A cell pins that separation in **both** directions, so a later simplification can neither merge the conditions nor drop the population between them.

## Also wires the lease note at the other two sites

The counters live in the allocator, so they are populated at all three; #8235 wired the note at one.

**The rename site is the sharp case.** A rename builds its index map as an **identity over every address** — same addresses, same range, which is what makes it a rename — so *every* dropped lease lands in `dropped_persistent_on_retained`: 100% of the pool's leases, in the bucket #8235 identifies as the actual operator surprise, and nothing printed.

The `nat64` site is wired too and is **latent**: nothing in `nat64.rs` allocates through the persistent-lease path, so the note should always be `None` there. Wired anyway — *"the counter exists but nobody prints it"* is the defect.

## Mutation matrix

Control: 4 collected, 0 failures.

| cell | site | applied | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | drop `address_only` from the derived gate | 1/1 | 2 |
| R2 | gate always true | 1/1 | 2 |
| R3 | fold leases into this gate | 1/1 | 1 |
| R4 | drop `refused` from the derived gate | 1/1 | 1 |

**R1 reproduces the `nat64` omission exactly** and is why this change exists.

**R4 is why the populations are asserted one at a time** rather than in a single fixture with all three set: a combined fixture stays green when two of the three disjuncts are missing, so it cannot catch a *single* omission — the only kind that has actually happened here.

R2 and R3 are the noise controls; without them the gate is satisfied by `true`.

## The modularity gate forced a better shape

`nat/source/mod.rs` sits at **1499** against a 1500 `[WATCH]` floor, and my additions crossed it. #8235's own note records hitting the same wall and answering it with *"a new concern gets a small file"* rather than dodging into `allocator.rs`.

So the emit moved into `lease_note_7560.rs` as `report_dropped_leases`, called identically by all three sites: **which sites report dropped leases is now one line of code instead of a convention three callers have to remember** — and that convention is exactly what produced the gap. File is back at 1499, and `dropped_persistent_lease_note` stays exported because #8235's tests bind it directly.

## PR #8240 — config: rescue the security-log-stream leaves and say what the rest are [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7492-unreachable-leaves`

Closes #7492

Two things, and the second is worth more than the first.

## 1. Rescued, measured

A `security log stream` with no `host` compiles to **nothing** —
`cfg.Security.Log.Streams["s"]` stays nil — so every stream-level leaf varied
its value against an absent object and looked inert. One host materialises the
stream.

Measured the way the existing BGP row was: that parent's unreachable count goes
**7 → 0** and its compared count **1 → 8**. All seven rescued; none was a flag
in disguise.

The ratchet did its job — adding the row turned the coverage gate **red** with
*"COVERAGE IMPROVED — TIGHTEN THE RATCHET (this is a good failure)"* and the
exact numbers. Floor **692 → 699**, unreachable ceiling **144 → 137**.

## 2. Said what the rest are — this changes how the issue reads

The ceiling reads as a debt to pay down. **Most of it is not debt.**

Measured: the residual spans **66 parents** (67 before this change — the
security-log-stream parent is fully rescued and drops out) and is at least two
populations.

- **Rescuable** — the parent compiles to nothing without a sibling. These come
  in *clumps*, which is why hand-written rows work: one row rescued 13 (bgp
  group), this one rescues 7.
- **Declared inert** — the leaf is accepted for Junos compatibility and nothing
  reads it, so "varying it changed nothing" is **the truth, not a gap**. The
  schema says so in its own descriptions: `system dataplane cores` is *"Legacy
  DPDK core count (retired, ignored)"*, `socket-mem` likewise, and every
  unreachable leaf under `dhcp-local-server group <*> interface <*>` is
  *"(parsed, not implemented)"* — all ten of them, checked individually rather
  than sampled. No prerequisite can rescue these; only implementing the feature
  would, and that is not gate work.

  Worth noting that this is a **two-source agreement**, not one claim twice.
  `classifyGateBlindLeaf` is purely behavioural — it lands a leaf in
  `unreachable` because naming it bare changed no compiled output, and it has
  never read a `desc` string. So three of those ten (`exclude`, `overrides`,
  `trace`) take no value at all and *still* do not classify as `flag`. The
  schema's prose and the compiler's behaviour were written independently and
  say the same thing.

That distinction is recorded **on the ceiling constant**, where the next reader
looks, rather than only in an issue comment.

## PR #8242 — userspace-xdp: stop pinning an absolute verifier baseline in prose [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7494-headroom-baseline-prose`

`Refs #7494` — this does not close it. #7494 is the fragment-consumption
work; this is the measurement its plan rests on, which had gone stale.

## What was wrong

Two normative texts stated the shim's processed-insn count as a
present-tense fact:

- `pkg/dataplane/README.md` — "at a 777,901-instruction baseline (22.21%
  headroom under the 1M cap)"
- `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` — "from this object's 777,901 baseline"

Measured at `9e28d1c25`. At `35399d2b3`, 1836 commits later, the object is
**801,448 insns / 19.86% headroom**. Neither sentence was ever edited.

**The bigger error is the ceiling, and it predates the drift.** Both texts
frame the budget against the kernel's 1,000,000 cap. `shimverify` exits
**4** — a hard failure, not a warning — below the 15% floor, and
`build-userspace-xdp.sh` admits only exit 0 as a measured pass. The
install-blocking ceiling is therefore **850,000**. Two effects compound:

| | |
|---|---|
| wrong denominator alone, at HEAD | 198,552 vs 48,552 = **4.09x** |
| plus the stale baseline | 222,099 vs 48,552 = **4.57x** |

Someone sizing the fragment fix against the documented figure budgets
~4.5x the room that exists. That is the number they would plan against,
which is why it is worth correcting ahead of the fix.

## The repair is not a fresher number

The count moves with every change to the crate, so any absolute figure in
prose is stale by the next merge, and a tracked constant would red on
unrelated edits and invite updating it without re-measuring. The prose now
carries only the relationships that do not move — carrying the sighting

## PR #8243 — docs: plan for consuming the #6704 non-first-fragment sighting [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/7494-fragment-plan`

`Refs #7494`. Plan only — one new file, no code, no behaviour change.

#7494 was filed as "blocked on verifier headroom (measured)". That measurement
was taken at `9e28d1c25`, **1836 commits** ago. Re-measuring changes the
conclusion for one of the two families.

## Measured at HEAD, against a control

Real kernel verifier via `make generate` → `shimverify`, toolchain
`nightly-2026-05-23` / `bpf-linker 0.10.2`. **No `XPF_SHIM_ALLOW_LOW_HEADROOM`
override anywhere** — rc=6 would not be a measured pass.

| shape | insns | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| control — unmodified master | 801,448 | PASS — 48,552 slack |
| carry the flag as a `ParsedPacket` field, **never read** | 1,000,001 | REJECT (`total_states 54787`) |
| **re-derive at the branch point, IPv4** | **805,941** | **PASS — 44,059 slack** |
| …the same, plus IPv6 (second ext-header walk) | 1,000,001 | REJECT (`total_states 47128`) |

**The IPv4 half is not blocked: it costs 4,493 instructions** against 48,552 of
usable slack.

## The reusable lesson

Carrying one **unread** `bool` costs ≥198,552 instructions. Re-deriving the same
bit at the point of use costs 4,493. Same information, three orders of magnitude
apart — one widens long-lived state across every downstream branch, the other is
a leaf the verifier folds.

The state counts are carried per row deliberately: the insn figure alone invites
a budget reading, and `total_states 54787` for a field **nothing reads** is what
refutes it. That is state explosion, so "recover headroom elsewhere" cannot work
— a linear saving does not pay down a superlinear one. The tree already paid for
this at `lib.rs:560`, where `saturating_sub` lowering into a materialised-boolean
re-branch defeated pruning and **took both cluster dataplanes down**.

## Two rejected shapes, recorded with reasons

Both **pass the gate**, which is the point.

- **Declining in `parse_ipv6`** lands on `drop_degraded_transit` — a **DROP**
  that blackholes every legitimate fragment. It reads as the cheapest option on
  the board and is the shape most likely to be independently reinvented.
- **Hoisting the IPv4 guard** into `if !native_gre && !frag` routes every
  non-native-GRE fragment into the **native-GRE inner classifier**. Measured
  805,394, verifier PASS. Correct nesting costs 547 more.

The verifier gate is a headroom instrument, not a correctness one.

## PR #8245 — docs: make the throughput invocation canonical, re-home the orphaned HA validation row [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `docs/cluster-measurement-protocol`

Three protocol gaps, each found by getting it wrong on #7480.

## The orphaned row is the most consequential
The validation table in the shared-cluster section had **four rendered rows and a fifth stranded** underneath 17 lines of #7610 prose. Markdown does not resume a table across a prose block, so that row rendered as literal pipe-text.

The stranded row is the one requiring **`make test-failover` + `make test-ha-crash` for HA / VRRP / session-sync / fabric changes.** A reader of the rendered document — which is how a doc is normally read — saw a complete-looking four-row table with no HA line, for exactly the class of change where skipping the cluster smoke is most expensive. A four-row table does not announce that it should have five.

Re-homed into the table. This is the `1 deletion` in the diffstat.

## `-P 16` is canonical, not illustrative
A flag appearing in an example reads as someone's habit. Dropping this one costs **4.4x**. Measured on the same port in the same CoS state, minutes apart:

```
iperf3 -P 16 -t 30 -p 5211  →  23.1 Gbit/s
iperf3        -t 10 -p 5211  →   5.23 Gbit/s
```

So a lane that improvises the invocation reads 5.23 against a `≥ 23` bar and owns a regression created entirely by its own command. #7480 did exactly that, then spent a lock cell and two hypotheses on the gap — auditing `cos-iperf-config.set`, `scheduler-uncapped` and `afxdp/cos/admission.rs`, and concluding from single-stream numbers both that CoS state made figures incomparable and that a 24g class "delivers 6.11" — before reading the row. **Both conclusions were retracted.**

The note ends on the general rule, with the scar attached because a rule stated abstractly is skimmed: *a number that disagrees with a documented threshold is evidence about the INSTRUMENT before it is evidence about the system*, and a mechanism hunt feels like rigour while being structurally unable to detect a wrong invocation.

## Omitting `-p` is worse than substituting a port
iperf3's default is **5201 → `iperf-100m` → `transmit-rate 100m exact`**, so a bare `iperf3 -c 172.16.80.200` silently measures a 100 Mbit shaper (~96 Mbit/s observed). The existing #7610 note covers *substituting* a port; nothing covered *omitting* the flag — and a warning about choosing the wrong port cannot help someone who never chose one.

## A worktree with a live cluster cell is off-limits
The cell verifies the **tree** it finds when the lock is granted, not the branch it was launched from, and a lock wait can be tens of minutes. Amend during that window and you smoke-test one tree while shipping another, with logs identical to a correct run. #7480 amended during a ~20 minute wait; the cell recorded a different HEAD than the PR carried, and the result transferred only because that diff happened to be comments-only (`git diff <tested> <head>` → zero non-comment lines). That is luck, not method. Adds: echo the tested HEAD from inside the cell, so the comparison is possible at all rather than reconstructible.

## Deliberately not included
A restatement of the port→class mapping. The #7610 note already carries "the port IS the class", the 5203/5211 mapping and 23.1 for 5211; repeating it would create a second authority for one fact. Only the default-port clause was genuinely missing.

Also retracted and therefore absent: the CoS-state comparability rule and the "a class's nominal rate is not a measurement" rule. Both rested on single-stream measurements.

## Validation
`make test-go` and `make test-rust` both clean. `git diff origin/master...HEAD --stat` → 1 file, 32 insertions, 1 deletion, with the deletion accounted for as the orphan row moving — the check that matters on a docs edit, since a stray deletion is the one thing a docs diff can hide.

Refs #7480

## PR #8250 — harness: run all 21 test/incus test files, and keep them running [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8136-harness-discovery`

Closes #8136

## The defect, and why widening the pattern is half a fix

The only target running any of `test/incus`'s Python tests passed a **literal filename** as the discovery pattern, so 1 of 21 files ran.

Two separate mechanisms make a file contribute **zero** tests while the run reports success:

1. a **hyphenated filename** is not a valid module identifier, so `unittest discover` cannot import it and skips it silently — **six files, 77 tests**, including the 260-line `step3` file the issue notes had failed to catch #7424 row 1;
2. a **pytest-style module** has module-level `def test_*` and no TestCase, so unittest imports it and collects nothing.

Neither is a failure. The suite prints `OK` and a smaller number, and nothing compares that number to the files on disk — the same fails-to-a-healthy-value shape the suite exists to catch.

So this adds **`harness_discovery_test.py`**: every `test/incus/*_test.py` must contribute at least one collected test, with hyphens called out **separately** so the failure says what to do rather than only what is wrong.

**Counts, measured at each step:** 291 (pattern widened alone) → 339 (after the six renames) → 368 (after the pytest port) → **370** with the guard. Zero failures.

## The six failures were not test rot — one assertion changed

**Five were one cause.** The tests invoke the *real* harness against a *fake* target, and #8040 later added a live target-service precheck that probes for CoS-port listeners and an incus handle. A fixture has neither, so the harness aborts. **The harness already defines `SKIP_TARGET_PRECHECK` for exactly this case**; the tests predate the precheck and had been failing invisibly since, because nothing ran them. Setting it fixes all five **without touching an assertion** — the tests were right, the environment declaration was missing.

**The sixth** asserted `sleep.call_count == 2`. `mock.patch.object(fairness_multi_sample.time, "sleep")` patches the attribute on the **shared stdlib `time` module**, so the count includes every sleep anywhere in the process. The module has exactly one `time.sleep` — the cooldown — and the observed total was **178–230, varying per run**, which is the tell that it isn't the module's own. It now counts calls whose argument is the cooldown. Pinning 230 would have pinned noise.

## The pytest port uses a shim, deliberately

~840 lines of mechanical re-indentation into TestCases, over tests nobody has run in months, is where a silently-inverted assertion hides. `unittest_shim` provides exactly what those files use — `raises`, `approx`, and the two **built-in** fixtures they request by parameter name — and **fails loudly** on any fixture it does not implement, so a half-emulation cannot quietly change what a test asserts.

Its fixture set came from reading the signatures: grepping `@pytest.fixture` finds *definitions* and reports zero here, because a built-in fixture is requested by parameter name and defines nothing.

## Mutation matrix on the guard

| cell | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | reintroduce a hyphenated filename | **both** guard cells red, count 370 → 356 |
| M2 | drop `load_tests` from a pytest-style module | contributes-check reds, **hyphen cell stays green**, count 370 → 356 |

**M2 is the discrimination check.** Both causes produce the same symptom — a file contributing nothing — and the guard reports the one that actually happened. Without the separate hyphen cell, M1 would report "contributes no tests", sending the reader to look for a missing TestCase.

## The guard found a bug in the shim it guards

`FunctionTestCase` wrappers reported `unittest_shim` as their origin, so the ported files read as contributing **nothing** even while their tests ran and passed. `functools.wraps` carries the origin through. The guard caught that on its first run, before any of this shipped.

## Gate

`make test-go` GO_RC=0, `make test-rust` RUST_RC=0, `make test-incus-lib` 370 tests OK. Touches the Makefile, so no disjointness exception.

## PR #8251 — userspace-xdp: stop reading fragment payload as an L4 header [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7494-fragment-no-l4`

Closes #7494. Closes the **IPv4 sibling**, which is what remained actionable
there; the **IPv6** half — issue 7494's headline subject — is blocked on
headroom and tracked in **#8249**, with a cell in this PR asserting it is still
broken.

Closing rather than re-scoping is deliberate: issue 7494's comment history is
the IPv6 channel exploration, and #8249 is a purpose-built successor carrying
the measured four-channel table. Retitling would file that history under the
half that is done.

This closes the **IPv4** half. IPv6 is blocked on headroom and tracked as
**#8249**, with a cell here asserting it is still broken.

## The defect

A non-first fragment has no L4 header, but `parse_ipv4` handed the bytes at the
resolved offset to `parse_l4` anyway. Both exposures are **demonstrated by
running packets through the real program** (#8247's harness), not argued:

- **Exposure 1** — `live_userspace_session_action` is keyed on ports, so a fragment was
  adjudicated on a tuple taken from its own payload. A collision with a live
  `PASS_TO_KERNEL` session handed it to the kernel instead of the helper.
- **Exposure 5** — `parse_l4`'s TCP arm returns `None` when the payload byte it reads as
  a data-offset nibble is below 5, and the caller turns `None` into
  `drop_degraded_transit`. **The same fragment of the same flow was dropped or
  forwarded depending on its own content** — a disposition an off-path party
  selects. Not in the issue's original list, and sharper than the four that
  were: the others mis-classify, this one silently discards traffic.

## The fix, and why it is 92 instructions

Substitute `PROTO_FRAGMENT_NO_L4` for the upper-layer protocol on a non-first
fragment, routing it into `parse_l4`'s **existing** unknown-protocol arm, which
returns zeroed ports and **cannot fail**.

`801,448 → 801,540`, **+92**, 48,460 slack. Real gate, exit 0, no
`XPF_SHIM_ALLOW_LOW_HEADROOM`.

Cheap because it adds no information the program has to carry — it changes the
value of a variable the match already branches on. Every rejected shape tried to
add state; an **unread** `bool` field on `ParsedPacket` cost ≥198,552.

**A guard beside the session lookup cannot do this.** Built and measured:
+4,493, closes exposure 1, and **cannot** fix exposure 5 — `parse_l4` runs inside the parser,
so exposure 5's drop happens before any later consumer sees the packet. A second
candidate (per-CPU scratch sideband) came in **23,419 instructions cheaper than
master** and still left exposure 5 live.

## PR #8253 — snmp: measure GETBULK cost in allocations, and write down the rule [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8211-8218-test-time-discipline`

Closes #8211
Closes #8218

## #8211 — a port, not a design change

`TestGetBulkCostDoesNotScaleWithMaxRepetitions_6551` asserted on a ratio of two
wall-clock measurements. Its v3 twin has always measured allocations and
`pkg/snmp/README.md` already stated the intent, so only the instrument changes:
the `> 10` threshold and the failure text are untouched, and a reviewer can diff
the two tests and see one expression differ.

Also in that file, as requested: the best-of-both-orders mitigation is deleted
(four measured runs to narrow a noise band that no longer exists), and the
degeneracy guard goes from `t.Skip` to `t.Fatal`.

**Validated against a known answer rather than trusted because it passed.** A
green on a new instrument is indistinguishable from a dead one, so I reproduced
the defect:

| `handleGetBulk` budget | M=1 | M=100 | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| the real ceiling | 8,965 allocs | 8,965 allocs | **1.0x** |
| `math.MaxInt` (pre-fix expansion) | 19,488 allocs | 1,009,349 allocs | **51.8x** |

It still sees the defect it exists for, with an order of magnitude of headroom
on each side of the threshold — and bounded, the two readings are now *identical
integers* rather than a ratio near one.

**The rationale is rewritten, not just the code.** The comment claimed *"a ratio
between two measurements of the same magnitude on the same machine, so machine
load cancels out."* That is false — the readings are taken at different moments,
so a hiccup landing on one moves the ratio and nothing else does — and it is why
the test looked safe. Porting the instrument while leaving that sentence would
have preserved the reason nobody questioned it.

## #8218 — the rule, with the clause that was missing

Written into `docs/engineering-style.md` as its own section, because a policy
that lives only in a tracker is not read before the next test is written, which
is how this reached four packages.

1. a pass criterion is never a duration or a ratio of durations — measure work;
2. a degeneracy guard **fails, not skips**, and observes the state rather than
   inferring it from timing;
3. **a deadline bounding a wait is legitimate and must be generous.**

Clause 3 is the one that keeps the rule from damaging the half of the population
it does not govern. Applied literally, "assert on work, not wall-clock" says
delete the deadline in #8182 / #8031 — converting a flake into a hang, which
prints nothing, has no `--- FAIL` line, and eats the budget for every later test.

## PR #8254 — cluster: assert FormatStatus's positional layout contract [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8206-formatstatus-layout-contract`

Refs issue 8206 — this is the early-detection half. The other half (generating the `deploy-lib-selftest` fixture from real `FormatStatus` output instead of a captured sample) is **not** done here, so that issue stays open.

## The contract nothing asserted

`FormatStatus` has a layout contract that two shell smokes parse positionally:

- `test/incus/deploy-lib.sh` awks on `$1 == "node0"` inside a `Redundancy group: N` block and reads `$3` as the status — node token must be field 1, state field 3;
- `test/incus/test-failover.sh` does `grep -A1 "Redundancy group: $rg" | grep -q "node0.*primary"` — the node row must be the **first** line after the header, because the `-A1` window is exactly one line wide.

`status.go` documents both in three separate comments (the `Held secondary:` placement, the #7367 `Forwarding:` placement). Nothing enforced them.

## The existing tests cannot see it — measured, not argued

`TestFormatStatus` and its three siblings are entirely `strings.Contains`: token presence, not structure. With a sub-line inserted one line too early in `status.go`, **all four pass**:

```
--- PASS: TestFormatStatus
--- PASS: TestFormatStatus_WithMonitorFails
--- PASS: TestFormatStatus_WithPeer
--- PASS: TestFormatStatus_InsideHoldWindowIsNotTakeoverReady
```

The three sub-lines added so far passed under them because they happened to be placed correctly, not because anything checked.

## What breaks if it drifts

`deploy_rolling_secondary_node` defaulting to the wrong node makes a rolling cluster deploy **restart the PRIMARY first** — the #4009 regression that function exists to prevent. It would ship with `make test-deploy-lib` green, because that self-test runs the real parsers against **frozen captured fixtures** which a renderer change does not touch. Only the cluster would notice.

## The guard is extracted so it is itself testable

`statusLayoutViolations` is a function, not an inline assertion, so a second cell feeds it a synthetic bad render and requires it to complain — plus a correct render it must not reject. **A contract check that has only ever run against correct input is indistinguishable from one that always returns nil.**

## PR #8256 — config: reject a unit whose device name collides with an authored one [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7795-vlan-ifname-collision`

Closes #7795

## The gate

Third pass in `validateInterfaceNameCollisionStrict`, modelled on #6964's second pass. An interface authored `<base>.<n>` and a unit resolving to the same `<base>.<n>` are two config objects on one kernel device, with no commit-time signal.

**The device name comes from `ResolveKernelIfName`, not a local `fmt.Sprintf`.** Pass 2 binds to `unit.Tunnel.Name` — the value the compiler assigned — so the gate cannot drift from the scheme it polices. There is no equivalent stored field here (a sub-interface device name is never assigned, only computed), so calling the resolver is the closest form of the same constraint.

**That is not stylistic.** The issue describes this as the VLAN derivation, `base + "." + vlan-id`. Re-deriving it literally polices **half** the shape: `types.go` also resolves a non-zero unit with **no** vlan-id to `base + "." + unit-number`, so `ge-0/0/0 unit 100` collides with an authored `ge-0/0/0.100` just as surely. Mutation **S2b** reproduces the literal reading and reds exactly the unit-number cell.

## ⚠️ A scope correction to the issue: RETH aliasing is not a defect

#7795 treats every shared `<base>.<n>` as a collision. **For a reth it is not.** A reth's units resolve onto the *physical member's* device, so `reth1 unit 100 vlan-id 100` lands on `ge-0-0-1.100` — exactly where an authored `ge-0/0/1.100` lands — and **#6722 established that aliasing as legal** and built the resolution for it:

> *"the dotted name is a real, separate configured interface AND an alias of a reth unit … Resolving the AUTHORED binding through the aliasing does"*

Rejecting it here would un-ship that decision, so reths are skipped **entirely** rather than exempted from part of the check.

## I did not find that by reading, and would have shipped the opposite

- **Version 1** rejected a reth against its own member. Caught by `TestReconcilePassUsesOneDataplaneSnapshot` in `pkg/daemon`.
- **Version 2** fixed the collapse and still rejected the VLAN alias. Caught by three **#6722** cells in `pkg/dataplane/userspace`.

A scoped `go test ./pkg/config/` was **green for both**. Worse, I had written a cell *asserting* the rejection — so my own suite would have defended the over-rejection. Both versions would have broken every HA cluster config in the tree.

## Cross-product reachability, stated honestly

Three name sources means three pairs; pass 3 runs last and checks both prior registries. But the sub-interface-vs-tunnel branch **cannot fire**: a sub-interface device is `<base>.<digits>` and a tunnel device is `<base>u<digits>`, so the character before the trailing digit run is `.` in one and `u` in the other — one position cannot be both. Retained for the same reason pass 2 retains its own unreachable branch: the argument rests on the separator characters. The pairwise structure is at its limit at three sources; a fourth needs a single owner map, and the comment says so.

## Mutation matrix

Control: 7 collected, 0 failures.

| cell | site | applied | built | FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1b | neutralise pass 3's authored-collision check | 1/1 | yes | 2 |
| S2b | re-derive from `VlanID` (the issue read literally) | 4/1 | yes | 1 |
| S3b | drop the unit-0 collapse skip | 2/1 | yes | 1 |
| S5 | drop the reth skip | 1/1 | yes | 1 |

**S2b and S5 justify design decisions rather than confirming code.**

## Several of my own cells failed their first scoring

Recorded because they were mine, not the code's: a first S1 disabled only the sub-vs-sub registry and scored as an escape; a first S3 left `base` unused so the package didn't build and the cell collected **zero** tests (a compile void, not a pass); a first cross-product cell asserted only `err != nil` and passed by catching **pass 2's** error; two reth cells were rejected by *unrelated* strict gates (a missing cluster PSK, then a reth member configuring unit 0) and now assert **which** rejection they got.

The tunnel-skip cell carries **no** fail-on-revert claim and says so — deleting the skip does not red it, because pass 2 returns first. Measured, not assumed.

## Two live leaks, found by building the census

|---|---|---|

`feed-server hostname` is literally one leaf over. All authenticated surfaces,
so a privilege-boundary defect (an operator who may read config and may not see
credentials) rather than an unauthenticated disclosure.

## The first leak was predicted in writing, by the fix that created it

`FeedServer.Hostname`'s redaction comment, from #6733:

> Hostname is the other credential-bearing slot on this struct. It is named for

That fix covered the REST surface, named the exact leak shape, and nothing
carried it to the AST route. **Nothing existed to notice**, for the years since.
That is the issue's thesis with the author's own words as the evidence.

> **A leaf is URL-shaped iff the typed route runs its field through a
> URL-redaction helper inside `MarshalJSON`.**

Checkable, stable, and it asserts the **agreement between two surfaces** rather
than trusting either. A heuristic encodes which side you believe; the defect
here is precisely that the two sides disagreed.

It also **maintains itself**: adding a `RedactURL` call on the typed side enrols
the leaf automatically. `urlLeafIndices` could only ever grow by someone
remembering — which is how three leaves were missed.

**A name heuristic was measured and rejected, not argued away.** Copying the
JSON census's patterns selects **18** of the schema's **2,171** leaf paths and
includes NetFlow `version9-template` — template *names*, not URLs — reproducing
the exact false-population failure that census's own comment records from its
first draft. The agreement predicate selects **12**, with no judgement in it.

## PR #8260 — dataplane: decide one desired state per netdev, then write it once [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8119-8120-iface-reconcile-coalesce`

Closes #8119
Closes #8120

Two defects, one root: **the same physical netdev was reconciled more than once
in a single apply, with a different desired state each time, and the last writer
won.**

## The witness comes first, because it is what makes the rest worth anything

A single apply is self-consistent, so a single-apply assertion passes on **both**
defects whichever way the zone map happened to iterate. The assertion spans two
applies. On the pre-fix tree:

```
after apply 1:
ge-0-0-0 mtu=1400 addrs=[10.0.2.1/24]

after apply 2:
ge-0-0-0 mtu=1500 addrs=[10.0.2.1/24]
```

Both defects visible at once — the MTU alternating between two configured values
(#8119), and only one of the two units' addresses present because the other was
deleted by whichever unit the map yielded second (#8120).

The host fake models the **one** netlink property #8119 depends on: `LinkSetMTU`
sends `RTM_SETLINK` and never writes back to the caller's `Link`. A fake that
refreshed it would hide the defect and every cell here would pass on the broken
code.

## The fix

`planPhysDesired` merges every zone interface reference resolving to a netdev
into one `physDesired` — the **union** of the untagged units' addresses, one
MTU, and a `skipAddrs` flag folding in DHCP / RETH / fabric-parent ownership —
and `mapZoneInterface` actuates it once. That removes #8120's second writer by
construction and leaves #8119 a single comparison against a cache that is still
fresh.

Sorting the zone map would have made the outcome **stable and still arbitrary**.
Stability is not correctness here: the union is the only address set that both
survives a second apply *and* keeps both units' addresses. Between units naming
an MTU the lowest unit number wins — arbitrary, but *decided*, which map
iteration order was not.

## PR #8261 — dataplane: census verifier-headroom figures for a commit or a floor [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8241-headroom-figure-census`

Closes #8241

A verifier-headroom figure must carry either the **commit** it was measured at or the **floor** it is measured against. Bare figures satisfying neither rot silently — three independent recurrences, per the issue.

## The census found a site the issue's instance list did not

`pkg/dataplane/README.md`'s #6884 block said **"Re-measured 2026-08-27"** with 784,175 / 21.58%. Commit `eaf589bac` landed **the same day** and moved the object to 801,448 / 19.86%.

**So a date is not a commit** — that date names two different budgets and a reader cannot tell which. It now cites `3cfca758e`.

The two 21.58% derivation sites are **dated, not renumbered**, as the issue asks: renumbering would silently re-derive a JUDGEMENT those blocks are at pains to mark as judged rather than measured.

## Two escapes, both found by mutation

**1. A ±8-line evidence window passed the exact site the issue names.** `verify_userspace_shim.go`'s block *discusses* the 15% floor at length (*"a floor set too high is an announced detour"*), so the bare figure inherited a "floor" from prose eight lines away and the guard reported healthy on the defect it was written for. The property is an attribute of the **figure**, not of the paragraph — window is now ±1.

**2. Removing bare `headroom` from the context pattern made the real site invisible.** Removing it was necessary (ECN/WRED and CPU senses were matching), but that block says *"insn change"*, singular, so it fell out of scope entirely. The **cap number** is the discriminator present at every real site and absent from the unrelated senses.

Neither would have been found by re-reading. Both were green.

## Scope — narrow on purpose

A naive scan over "headroom" flags **47** sites, almost all session-count caps, bps conversions and review archives. This walks the **normative** texts only — the ones a reader consults to learn the current budget. Archives (`docs/log`, `docs/reviews`, `docs/pr`, `docs/research`, `_Log.md`) are dated by construction.

The figure pattern excludes `1,000,000` and `1,000,001`: the kernel's cap and its reject boundary are **constants, not measurements**, and including them flagged a #7494 matrix row recording which shapes the verifier rejected. A constant cannot rot.

## The accepted-list is keyed on substrings, not file:line

**Line numbers rot exactly like the figures this census catches** — pinning them would reproduce the defect inside the guard. Each of the six entries carries its reason, and **dead-entry rejection** makes it a queue rather than a permission slip: an entry that stops matching a real line fails the gate.

The three exclusions the issue lists get **green control cells** rather than silent skips.

## Validation

- 32 figures across 9 normative texts; all six accepted entries match a real line.
- Reverting either dated site to its shipped text **reds** the census, naming file and line.
- A synthetic bare figure reds; the same figure **with a commit**, and **with a named floor**, both pass.
- ECN/WRED headroom, a session-count cap and a bps conversion are all correctly ignored.
- A degeneracy guard **fails** (not skips) if the census scanned nothing.
- `go vet` and `go test ./pkg/dataplane/` pass.

Docs and a test only — no production behaviour changes, so no cluster smoke is owed.

## PR #8264 — policy hit-counts: cover the surfaces #7776 left, and put the knob on the wire [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/8177-policy-hitcount-surfaces`

Closes #8177

All four open rows, plus a tripwire on the one that was already correct.

## Rows 3 and 4 — the same gap at two different costs

Row 3 (CLI `brief`) already had the #7016 trailing-note mechanism, so it is the
edit #7776 made, with the wording reused verbatim.

Row 4 (gRPC `detail`) had **no note mechanism at all** — with the knob off it
omitted the `Session statistics` block entirely, which #7016's own comment *two
lines away* calls indistinguishable from policy-stats being off. Covering it
meant introducing the mechanism.

## Rows 5 and 6 — the knob, not a new availability field

The issue's correction to #7776 holds, and I re-verified it: `hit_counters_unavailable`
already exists and is already populated by both surfaces. What was missing is
that eligibility has **two** inputs — `statsEnabled || rule.Count` — and only the
second was on the wire:

| | gate | counter read? | emitted |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** stats ON, `count=false` | true | yes | `count=false`, `unavailable=false`, `hits=0` |
| **B** stats OFF, `count=false` | false | **no** | *byte-identical* |

`policy_stats_enabled` is **added** to `GetPoliciesResponse` and to each REST
`PolicyInfo`. Setting `hit_counters_unavailable` for case B needs no new field
and does make the two states differ, which is exactly what makes it tempting —
and it would contradict the proto comment reserving that flag for
counter-*eligible* rules, lying to the consumer that implemented the documented
split. On an older binary the new field reads false, the conservative direction:
treating an unmeasured zero as unmeasured loses nothing, the reverse invents a
measurement.

**The REST field is repeated per zone-pair block**, and that is a considered
trade rather than sloppiness: the handler's payload is a bare `[]PolicyInfo`
inside the generic envelope, so there is no per-endpoint place for a system-wide
field. Adding one to the envelope puts it on every endpoint; turning the payload
into an object changes `data` from array to object and breaks every existing
consumer.

## Row 7 — untouched, and now pinned

`collectPolicyCounters` skips the series rather than emitting a zero, which is
right for a time series and the *opposite* of what the other six needed. The risk
is a later audit "fixing" the inconsistency the wrong way, so the skip has a
tripwire — with a control proving the collector does emit when the knob is on,
without which a collector that emitted nothing at all would pass.

## PR #8265 — Close orphaned shim registry FDs at Teardown [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7755-teardown-close-registry-fds`

`publishShimRegistryLocked` overwrites `m.maps`/`m.programs` without closing the
displaced handles, and `Teardown` never closed them either — `Close()` handles
only the XDP/TC links, and the cleanup sweep unpins without closing. Every
registry FD survived the bootstrap cycle that created it, keeping its kernel
object and locked memory alive, once per `enterBootstrapMode` and once per
standalone first-commit timeout.

Closing is also the **mutation-time half of #6741 AC1**. AC1 refuses handles
obtained *after* the Teardown boundary; one obtained just before and held across
it was neither refused nor counted, and the check that would cover it cannot be
written under `m.mu` because #6740 forbids holding the lock across a BPF
syscall. A closed FD *is* that check, enforced by the kernel with no lock held:
the mutation returns `EBADF` instead of silently succeeding against an orphan
nothing forwards through.

**Closing is not clearing.** The entries stay, so `classifyRegistry` still reads
a non-empty `m.maps`, `registryObsoleteLocked` still refuses and counts, and
injected test fixtures are untouched. Only the FDs go.

### Canary refinement, and why it is not a hole
The snapshot goes through a named `takeRegistryHandles` helper rather than
adding `Teardown` to `registryAccessAllowlist`, which would widen exactly the
surface the canary defends. Ranging the registry to build a snapshot is not an
aliasing escape, so an `*ast.RangeStmt` over the registry inside an allowlisted
function is now an accepted shape.

Proven load-bearing in **both** directions:
- removing the `RangeStmt` arm makes the well-formed fixture report
  `m.maps escapes as a non-indexed reference` — the arm does work;
- a new `bad_rangenolock.go` negative (the identical range with the lock
  removed) must still violate — "range is permitted" did not become "range is
  permitted *anywhere*".

Every pre-existing alias negative (assign, struct field, return, argument,
paren, two-hop, method value, cross-object, cross-file) still fails.

### Also corrected here
Two comments that asserted the opposite of the code: the helper was named
`...Locked` and documented as "caller must hold m.mu" while its body locks
itself (a self-deadlock trap, since `sync.Mutex` is not reentrant), and a claim
that the snapshot was taken "in the SAME hold" as the obsolescence publish when
it is a second hold. What closes that window is **order**, not atomicity.

Closes #7755
