## PR #8267 — Bound the gRPC EADDRINUSE retry and fail the daemon on a duplicate [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8233-bounded-addrinuse`

A second `xpfd` used to start silently. `supervisePrimaryListener` treated every
bind failure as transient — log, mark Failed, back off to a 30s cap, retry
forever — and `Run` returned nil, so the daemon came up with a permanently dead
management listener while the dataplane, config store, FRR and the cluster state
machine all started normally. Every gRPC-driven surface was gone with no
external signal.

**The issue's attributed mechanism is wrong and is corrected here.** It blamed
`SO_REUSEPORT` on the gRPC listener. The primary listener is a plain
`net.Listen` with no `ListenConfig` and no `Control` hook, and the second bind
genuinely fails with `EADDRINUSE`. The mechanism was the unbounded retry.

### Bounded, not fatal on sight — and the unit is why
`xpfd.service` sets `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=1`, `TimeoutStopSec=20`,
so a restart routinely overlaps a legitimately-exiting predecessor. Fatal on
first `EADDRINUSE` would make the fatal exit re-trigger the start: a restart
loop for the whole shutdown window, and no convergence at all if the
predecessor is wedged. The grace window is derived from `TimeoutStopSec`
rather than being a magic number.

### Test soundness
The fatal-path test ran on `context.Background()`. Since the defect it guards
is *retries forever*, an unbounded context made the test inherit the hang — with
the fatal branch disabled it ran until the CI timeout killed the package, which
reports a **void**, not a diagnosis. It now runs under a 10s context (~400x the
20ms grace; the clean run is 0.029s), and the deadline is not the pass
condition — expiry returns something that is not `ErrManagementPortHeld`, so the
assertion still fails, just with a message. Verified by mutation: `false &&` on
the fatal branch previously hung past a 120s kill and now yields
`--- FAIL: TestPersistentAddrInUseIsFatal_8233 (10.00s)`.

### Provenance
Rescued from a lane that died mid-mutation-test with the `false &&` mutant still
applied to its working tree. Only the commit was taken; the mutant was
discarded and its absence checked with a positive control on the guarded line.

Closes #8233

## PR #8268 — mouse-latency: stop the elephant where it actually runs [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7159-cos-p999-remeasure`

## What

`test-mouse-latency.sh` stopped its elephant generator from the EXIT trap
with `kill "$IPERF_PID"`. `IPERF_PID` is the **local** `incus exec` client;
killing it does not terminate the remote process. Measured directly against
`loss:cluster-userspace-host` — a backgrounded
`incus exec ... -- sh -c "sleep 137"` was still running 8 s after its local
client was killed, and 8 s later again.

The consequence is not a leaked process, it is a **corrupted cell**. The rep
script re-enters ~8 s after an early INVALID while the orphaned 90 s iperf3
keeps sending, so the next rep's elephants share the 1 Gb/s exact class with
the previous rep's, miss the cwnd-settle floor, exit early themselves, and
orphan another. One marginal rejection guarantees every later rep in the cell
fails, and the cell reports zero valid reps with a plausible
`cwnd-not-settled` reason and no trace of the cause.

## Evidence it already bit

The 2026-08-31 surplus leg on this issue, re-read from its artifacts:

| rep | elephant aggregate | utilization | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 00-02 | 1017 / 1047 / 1014 Mb/s | 0.93-0.99 | settled |
| 03 | 1083 Mb/s | 1.00 | INVALID (window spread 0.187 > 0.15) |
| 04 | 398 Mb/s | 0.36 | INVALID (aggregate too low) |
| 05-14 | 232-269 Mb/s | 0.22-0.27 | INVALID (aggregate too low) |

1 Gb/s divided by the ~3.5 concurrent 90 s runs a 28 s rep cadence sustains
is ~285 Mb/s — the observed plateau. The strict-exact control in the same
session ran 10 reps at 954 +/- 3 Mb/s because it never rejected a rep, so
the artifact presented as a clean dichotomy between the two CoS fixtures.

`git log -S IPERF_PID` puts the defect in the harness's first commit
(`840d5545d`, 2026-04-25), so it predates every measurement in this lineage.
It only corrupts reps that FOLLOW an early-INVALID rep in the same cell.

## Fix

The elephant gets an identity on the remote side that a kill can address:
`echo $$ > <pidfile>; exec iperf3 ...` makes the remote shell's pid become
iperf3's own, and the EXIT trap reads it back over incus. Both halves are
load-bearing — without `exec` the pidfile names a wrapper shell whose death
orphans iperf3 again.

A rep also refuses to start when an iperf3 client is already running on the
source container, which converts a silent halving of the offered rate into a
named `stale-elephant-client` INVALID.

## PR #8269 — Adjudicate the #7167 tunnel-ingress shape; bind the WireGuard dispatcher arm [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7167-tunnel-ingress`

Issue 7167 asks for a single bounded logical-tunnel-ingress abstraction, on
the premise that WireGuard and IPsec are one defect wearing two costumes so
the hard part should be solved once. **That premise is wrong at the level of
mechanism**, which is the level a fix is built from. This PR records the
adjudication, corrects two premises that have rotted under the issue, and
closes the one measurement gap that let the central claim rot unnoticed.

**Issue 7167 stays open** — the gap is real and the remaining work is a
genuine multi-PR build. Nothing here adjudicates a packet. (Deliberately not
spelling a keyword before that number: the negated sentence in #8062 is what
auto-closed the issue last time.)

## The finding that re-shapes the work

**WireGuard's two directions are asymmetric, and only one is broken.**

- **Encap already runs in the AF_XDP worker, post-adjudication.**
  `frame/mod.rs` dispatches `TunnelKind::WireGuard` to `wg::wg_encap_frame`
  from inside the forward-frame builder — i.e. on a packet that has been
  through screen, flow cache, session, route, policy and NAT. It reads the
  live engine from `ForwardingState.wg_engines`, runs its own AllowedIPs
  longest-prefix match, and resolves the physical underlay into
  `resolution.tx_ifindex`.
- **Decap runs in the control thread, adjudicated by nothing.**

So the worker already holds every input decap needs — the engine
(`try_decap` takes `&self`), the tunnel's `logical_ifindex`, and #8062's
`build_logical_ingress_packet` — and it holds the outer ECN bits *better*
than the socket path does, because the outer IP header is still in the frame
rather than having to be recovered via `IP_RECVTOS`.

The WireGuard fix is therefore **"move decap to the side that already does
encap"**, which needs **no bounded cross-thread packet handoff at all**.
Invariants 1, 5 and much of 8 are satisfied by not creating the thing they
constrain.

## Why IPsec does not share the hard part

Its plaintext is produced by the kernel XFRM stack, which the issue
correctly forbids duplicating. The xfrmi ingress-binding sub-option is
**refuted** here on four independent measured grounds:

1. **Framing** — the shim's `parse_l2` is Ethernet-only and runs *before*
   the ingress-set check, so a raw-L3 frame is PASSed without the set ever
   being consulted; and for an inner source of the form `8.0.x.x` the shim
   misparses an IPv4 header 14 bytes into the real one.
2. **Queue collapse** — `planning.rs` takes a global minimum RX-queue count
   over all candidates, so admitting a 1-queue xfrmi collapses **every**
   physical NIC to one queue and one worker.
3. **Bind fragility** — exactly one copy-mode attempt, no fallback; failure

## PR #8272 — mouse-latency: stop every remote job where it runs, not just the elephant [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8270-mpstat-remote-orphans`

## What

#8268 fixed one of three backgrounded `incus exec` jobs in
`test-mouse-latency.sh` and left two with the shape it had just diagnosed.
Killing the local client of a backgrounded `incus exec` does not terminate the
remote command, so `SETTLE_MPSTAT_PID` and `MPSTAT_PID` kept sampling on the
source container after any rep that exited early.

| var | backgrounded from | before | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IPERF_PID` | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` | remote stop (#8268) | remote stop |
| `SETTLE_MPSTAT_PID` | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` | **local kill only** | remote stop |
| `MPSTAT_PID` | `incus_exec "$SOURCE"` | **local kill only** | remote stop |
| `RG_POLL_PID` | local subshell `) &` | local kill | local kill — **unchanged, and pinned** |

## Severity, stated honestly

This is **not** #7159 severity. An orphaned mpstat is a monitor, not a load
generator; its count is bounded (`mpstat 1 <N>` exits on its own); and it
cannot move the throughput column the way an orphaned iperf3 did. The #7159
determinations and the in-flight re-measurement are unaffected.

It is worth fixing for narrower reasons: the harness measures p99.9 mouse
latency **on the source container**, and an orphan is unaccounted CPU on
exactly that container, one per early-exit rep; both samplers write
`/tmp/mpstat[-settle]-<tag>.txt`, so an orphan outliving its rep can still be
writing the file a later same-tag reuse reads; and leaving two call sites with
a shape the file itself documents as wrong invites the next backgrounded job —
which may well be unbounded — to copy it.

## `RG_POLL_PID` is the discriminator

It has the same `kill "$VAR"` spelling and is correctly unaffected, because
its `$!` is a local subshell. Routing it through the remote path would add a
round-trip per rep that stops nothing. A test pins it as local, so the next
reader does not "finish the job" by making it uniform.

## Also folded in

The stop command now confirms `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` still names the expected
program before signalling. That makes it safe to run unconditionally, which
removes the `IPERF_DONE` bookkeeping and, with it, the pidfile a completed rep
used to leave behind — a pid recorded for a job that has since exited can
belong to an unrelated process by the time the EXIT trap fires.

## Tests — verified by mutation

A test asserting "the pidfile exists" would pass on the broken version, so the
guard is split: behavioural cells prove the **leaf** is reaped, and wiring
assertions catch a site regressing to a local-only kill, which no library test

## PR #8273 — nat: bound the recycle FIFO's length and per-claim cost (#7174 M13) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7174-m13-nat-recycle-fifo`

## Summary

- An out-of-band `reserve()` — HA session sync, persistent NAT, deterministic NAT — sets a pool port's occupancy bit without removing the port's queued token from the per-address recycle FIFO, so after HA role churn the ring holds tokens that can never be claimed.
- **The churn case is not the target.** `claim`'s recycled phase re-queues a collided token at the BACK (062-10), so K reserved tokens ahead of the free ones cost O(K) *once* and then sit behind them. What does not amortize is the **exhausted address**: with the free tokens gone the ring is K reserved tokens and nothing else, so every claim popped all K, retained all K, allocated a K-element retain buffer and returned `None` — and `None` is the *correct* answer there, so nothing self-corrected. O(K) per FAILED claim, forever.
- **Cost bound**: `claim` returns `None` immediately when `occupied == range`, a live counter maintained by the only two sites that transition a bit.
- **Length bound**: `RecycleRing` pairs the `VecDeque` with a per-offset "already queued" bitset, so a port holds at most one token and the ring is bounded by the address's port range. The bitset is allocated lazily on the first push.
- Neither bound changes **which** port is handed out.

## Why an exact test and not a scan budget

The analysis already recorded on the issue rejected a bare scan budget: `None` on budget exhaustion is read by callers as "this address is full", so under exactly the condition this row describes it converts a slow allocation into a **spuriously dropped NAT translation**. That analysis said a budget needs a way to tell *"scanned enough"* from *"genuinely full"*.

`occupied == range` **is** that discriminator — every set bit is an offset below `range`, so the equality holds iff no port is free — and once you have it the budget is unnecessary for the case that motivated it.

It is exact rather than a hint because `free_recycle` now clears the bit **and** queues the token under the same per-address mutex `claim` holds: a free that has not taken the lock has not pushed a token either, so a full scan would miss it identically. The critical section grows by one `fetch_and` on a path that already took that mutex to push.

## Why not eager removal at `reserve()`

Two counts. It moves a one-time cost onto the HA-sync path to delete tokens that are not the recurring cost; and a port released through the deterministic `free_no_recycle` path pushes no replacement token, so removing its token eagerly would strand the port — the same pool-shrink 062-10's retain policy exists to prevent.

## The duplicate-token source

Named in the issue's analysis as "a second accumulation source the row does not name". A retained token means the bit was set at pop time; when that occupant later releases through `free_recycle` the `1 -> 0` transition queues a **second** token for the same port. Growth per churn cycle, past `range`, forever — unbounded memory, and every duplicate is one more pop for every later claim.

## Hot-path shape

Per successful claim: one extra relaxed `fetch_add` (in `claim_offset`) and one relaxed load. Per free: one extra relaxed `fetch_sub`, plus the bit clear moving inside a mutex the path already took. Per **failed** claim on a full address: one mutex acquire and one relaxed load, replacing a full ring walk plus a `Vec` allocation. The scan-pop instrumentation is `#[cfg(test)]`.

Memory: one lazily-allocated `range/64`-word bitset per address that has ever recycled a port. Eager sizing was rejected — a pool may declare up to `MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS` addresses, each already carrying a `words` bitmap.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-rust` — 5052 passed, 0 failed, 5 ignored.
- [x] Four fail-on-revert cells in `nat/tests_pool.rs`, each mutation-checked:
  - delete the short-circuit → exhausted-address cell RED (96 pops against an asserted 0)
  - delete the dedup → duplicate-token cell RED (`[1025, 1025]` against `[1025]`)
  - move the gate one port early (the false-exhaustion direction) → **three** cells RED, including the partially-occupied control
  - drop the counter's decrement → counter/bitmap agreement cell RED
- [x] The cost assertion reads a `#[cfg(test)]` scan-pop seam, not the return value. An exhausted address returns `None` with or without the short-circuit, so a cell asserting only the outcome would be satisfied by no fix at all — and the fixture contains a genuinely EXHAUSTED address, not a merely churned one.
- [x] The control cell (`..._partially_occupied_address_still_scans_...`) fails on the most nearly-correct mutant: a gate one port early passes the exhausted-address assertion and would silently turn a working pool into spurious exhaustion.
- [x] Docs updated in the same change: `userspace-dp/README.md` (the #3011 FIFO bullet gains the two bounds and their fail-on-revert cells); `docs/log/7174-m13.md`.

## Deferred

Rust change ⇒ the helper binary moves ⇒ a cluster smoke is owed before merge (`make cluster-deploy` + `make test-failover`), and this touches the HA reserve path specifically.

Refs #7174 — this is part 1 of 2 for that issue's two remaining survivors; the journal half is a separate PR against `pkg/configstore`.

## PR #8275 — configstore/journal: defer rotation while an append is being fsynced (#7174 C06) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7174-c06-journal-rotation-defer`

## Summary

- `Log` releases `j.mu` before its fsync (#4829), so a writer can be parked between its `f.Write` and its `f.Sync` while another writer rotates.
- The **renames** are harmless — a rename preserves the inode, so the parked writer's bytes move with it into `.1`. The **unlink** is not: rotation destroys the oldest kept segment, and once that inode is gone the parked writer's fsync still succeeds and `Log` still returns `nil`.
- `maybeRotateLocked` now checks the inode of the segment it is about to destroy against a `Journal.inflight` registry — appends registered under `j.mu` from their write until their fsync completes — and **defers** the rotation when they match.

## Why it is worth closing an edge case this narrow

Reaching the destroyed slot takes `maxSegments+1` rotations — three full segments of appends at the defaults — so this is not a routine loss. It is worth closing because of **how** it fails, not how often:

- the fsync on an unlinked inode **succeeds**, so `Log` returns `nil`;
- `Store.journalLog` only warns when `Log` returns an error, so it warns about nothing;
- the audit record is simply absent.

There is no signal anywhere. This is the commit audit trail.

## Why deferring cannot starve

The condition names **one old inode**. Later appends land on the current segment — a different inode — so nothing that arrives afterwards can extend the deferral; the next append after that writer's fsync rotates. The cost of deferring is a current segment that overshoots `maxSegmentBytes` by one record. The control test pins this: a guard that deferred forever would satisfy the main cell while silently disabling retention.

## The other half of this row is deliberately unchanged

The audit row is written as one item but names two things: the off-lock fsync and the unguarded rotation unlink. **The off-lock fsync stays.** `journal.go` documents it as a reviewed choice with the durability contract it preserves, and `TestTailNotBlockedByLogFsync` pins that a `Tail` does not stall behind a writer's fsync; moving it back under `j.mu` would undo #4829. What the off-lock fsync *does* create is the in-flight window this change guards — which is why the two belong in one row and only one of them is a code change. Both halves are scoped, one as code and one as a recorded decision (`pkg/configstore/README.md`, `docs/log/7174-c06.md`).

## Implementation notes

- Exactly one inode dies per rotation: the oldest kept segment removed at the top. The shifting renames only replace paths whose inode that `Remove` already unlinked, so one lookup covers the whole operation.
- **`Lstat`, not `Stat`.** A symlink planted at a segment path must be identified by its own inode; following it would compare against a target inode that is never ours and silently defeat the guard. The package already refuses to follow a symlinked segment elsewhere (`chmodOwnerOnly`'s `Lstat`, `appendLocked`'s `O_NOFOLLOW`).
- Inode `0` is a sentinel for "could not be determined" — no real inode is 0 — and an outstanding sentinel defers, because nothing can be proven about it.
- The registration happens under `j.mu`, before the lock is dropped: doing it after would leave a window for a rotation to slip between the write and the registration.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-go`.
- [x] `TestRotationDoesNotDestroyInflightAppend7174C06` — `maxSegments=1` plus a `syncFile` hook parks the first writer between its write and its fsync for exactly the two rotations it takes to destroy its inode. This is the minimum shape in which the loss is reachable.
- [x] `TestRotationResumesAfterInflightAppendDrains7174C06` — the control.
- [x] Mutation-checked four ways: removing the guard, removing the registration, and removing the release each red the correct cell; a guard that always defers reds the control **plus four pre-existing rotation tests**.
- [x] A test asserting only "`Log` returned nil" would pass on the broken code — on the broken code `Log` *does* return nil. The assertion is on the record's presence in `Tail`.
- [x] Docs updated in the same change: `pkg/configstore/README.md` (a rotation bullet for the guard, and the durability bullet now records the off-lock fsync decision explicitly).

Refs #7174 — this is part 2 of 2 for that issue's two remaining survivors; the NAT allocator half is #8273.

eighth *shell* self-test could not accumulate unreached, and the census globs
`test/incus/*-selftest.sh`, so the python files were outside it from the start.

`make selftest` report 105 passed / 0 failed. Both observations were correct.

## Two of the files were lying

`step1_histogram_classify_test.py` and `step3_tx_kick_classify_test.py` are
pytest-style modules collected by the #8136 `load_tests` shim:

| file | `python3 <file>` | `unittest discover` |
|---|---|---|
| step1 | **NO TESTS RAN** | 17 |
| step3 | **11** | 14 |

Both exited successfully. The cause is **ordering**, not style:
`unittest.main()` collects at call time and never returns, so anything below
the `__main__` block does not exist yet when collection happens — the
`load_tests` assignment in both, and in step3 three `_7424` cases someone
appended after it. So step3 silently ran 11 of its 14 tests for anyone running
it the obvious way, **including the three added for the specific defect the
file is named for**. Both `__main__` blocks now sit last.

## Why the existing guard did not catch it

`harness_discovery_test.py` already asserts *"every file contributes at least
one test"*. That is a lower bound, and a lower bound cannot see a file that
collects **most** of its tests — 11 of 14 satisfies it, and so does 0 of 17.

The new cell asserts the **agreement** between direct execution and discovery
rather than pinning either count: pinning one would encode which of them we
trust, and the defect is precisely that they disagree while both look healthy.
Verified by mutation — reverting step3 to its master ordering fails it with
`0 != 14`.

## PR #8282 — Correct the #7167 adjudication: a raw-L3 TUN is already in the ingress set [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8279-adjudication-correction`

Docs-only. Corrects two errors in `docs/research/7167-tunnel-ingress/adjudication.md`
(merged in #8269, which I wrote) and one premise in
`docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md`. The security finding itself is **#8279**.

## How the error was found, because the mechanism generalises

The adjudication refuted Option B1 partly on the shim's Ethernet-only `parse_l2`
running before the ingress-set lookup. **That ground was written about the
hypothetical interface B1 would introduce — but the parse ordering is a property
of the CURRENT code.** Asking "is that ground live today?" is what found this.

## Correction 1 — the misparse's consequence was stated without saying what it DOES

`try_xdp_userspace` runs `parse_l2` -> `parse_ipv4`/`parse_ipv6` ->
`let Some(parsed) = parsed else { drop_degraded_transit(...) }` -> and only THEN
tests `USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES`. `drop_degraded_transit` is `XDP_DROP`.

So the branches differ:

- **ifindex not in the set** — the shifted parse's RESULT is discarded at the
  gate, but a shifted parse that FAILS is dropped *before* the gate.
- **ifindex in the set** — the garbage 5-tuple feeds binding and session lookup.

On a raw IPv4 packet, bytes `[12..14]` are `src[0..2]`, so a source in
`8.0.0.0/16` reads as `0x0800`; `parse_ipv4` then reads `src[2]` as the
version/IHL byte and **241 of its 256 values fail and drop**. Remote-selectable,
and `8.0.0.0/16` is allocated space.

## Correction 2 — recommendation 5 is already violated

It said *"do not admit a tunnel netdev to the ingress set"* as forward-looking
advice. One already is:

- `interfaces.go:371` — the BASE row is `Tunnel: iface.Tunnel != nil`,
  **interface-level only**; the unit row at `:446` is the OR.
- The zone fans UP from unit to base (`host_inbound_effective_view.go`).
- So `set interfaces wgN unit 0 tunnel mode wireguard` — the spelling this repo
  calls canonical — yields a base row with `Tunnel = false` and a Zone, matching
  no exclusion class.
- On a userspace-dataplane box that netdev is an anchor TUN
  (`daemon_run_routehelpers.go:63` `anchorOnly`, applied to the unit-level
  tunnel at `:106`; `routing/tunnel.go:503-512` creates
  `netlink.Tuntap{Mode: TUNTAP_MODE_TUN}`) — **ARPHRD_NONE, raw L3**.

Pinned green at HEAD by
`TestRefusedNetdevNeedsEveryOwnerToAgree/canonical_wireguard_spelling`, which
asserts `wantIngress: []uint32{10, 40}` / `wantRSS: [ge-0-0-0 wg1408]` where 40
is the WireGuard TUN. The #6691 round-9 unanimity rule was added specifically to
re-admit it — long-standing and deliberate, not a regression.

Every abort between `CompileConfig`'s Phase-2 host mutation and that tail returned first, leaving the cell describing a **different apply**. `evaluateArmCoverage` then had two reachable states, neither of which disarmed.

| when the abort happens | what the gate reads | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| a box's **FIRST** apply | cell never published → `armCoverageUnknown` | the switch has **no case** for unknown — nothing |
| **any later** apply | the **previous generation's** report, `Ran=true Uncovered=0` → `armCoverageComplete` | logs `arm coverage complete` — nothing |

The apply tail then writes `writeTransitForwardSysctls(d.DataplaneArmed())` with the box still armed. On a fresh boot the runtime is armed *before* the first per-interface attach, so this is an **armed, open kernel transit path over an interface carrying no XDP shim** — the policy-free-router state #7191 exists to prevent. `removeUserspaceShimXDPLinkPins()` runs immediately *before* the attach, so after a failed attach the interface really can carry no program.

**The issue names only the first state.** The second is the one a box in service actually reaches, and it is the sharper of the two: `armcoverage_publish.go` states as its own invariant that *"a stale report answering for a previous generation is worse than no report"*, and the abort path is where the implementation did not honour it.

`CompileUserspaceShim`'s post-`CompileConfig` aborts now route through `abortAfterHostMutation`, which runs the **real** proof and returns the caller's error unchanged.

## Why the real proof and not a synthetic verdict

Publishing a hand-built "everything uncovered" report on abort is the obvious implementation and it is **wrong**: a re-attach can fail while the **previous shim is still attached** and still adjudicating that interface's transit, and disarming there bricks a box whose forwarding was never unadjudicated — a brick, not a fence (#1960). `ProveArmCoverage` reads live kernel and bpf state, so it answers both directions correctly using the same classification the success path uses.

It is also the only way to publish at all: `publishArmCoverage` is deliberately reachable only from inside the proof, so a stashed report cannot be published. That guard is left intact, as is the #5275 canary — the top-level `ProveArmCoverage(...).LogArmCoverage(...)` statement is untouched and the new call is nested, so `TestArmProofIsInvokedFromCompileUserspaceShim` still anchors on the success path.

## Scope, and what this deliberately is not

Covers the aborts that hold a `CompileResult`: the two bpffs cleanups and `runPostMutationSteps` (`preflightCheckIfindexCaps`, `attachUserspaceShimXDP`). `CompileConfig`'s own later phases return a **nil** result on every phase error, so there is no `pendingXDP` to prove against — consistent with the issue classing those as "effectively unreachable post-#6894". The wiring guard exempts that one abort explicitly and asserts its shape rather than skipping an index on faith.

**This is not an undo, and not a re-drive.** PR #7288 makes the host/dataplane divergence *visible*; this makes the forwarding surface it leaves *adjudicated*. An undo for live host state is itself fallible, and one that fails mid-rollback leaves a third state worse than the two it was reconciling. The issue's own r1 also established that converge-forward cannot terminate here: the reachable trigger is a driver refusing an XDP attach, which is **persistent**, while #5679's self-heal is scoped to *transient* errors in its own sentence.

## Premise checks

The issue hedges four reachability claims. Verified by property at `origin/master` `9baa81bf5`, not by opening the cited line ranges:

- **`preflightCheckIfindexCaps` cannot be hoisted — TRUE.** `pendingXDP` has exactly one production writer, `compiler_iface.go:501`, inside `compileZones`. (Positive control: the test-only writers in `armproof_5275_test.go` did turn up, so the search works.)
- **`CompileConfig`'s later phases** return `nil, err` for the result on every phase error — which is what bounds this PR's scope.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-go` — 78 packages, 0 FAIL.
- [x] `make test-rust` — 5052 passed, 0 failed (no Rust change; run as the gate).
- [x] Three cells, each mutation-checked:
  - delete the publish → republish cell **and** the control both RED
  - unwire the attach abort in `loader.go` → AST wiring guard RED, naming the line
  - **synthetic "everything uncovered" report** → the republish cell still **passes**, the control RED. This is the control that decides the fix is *aimed* right rather than merely powerful.
- [x] The publish→disarm link is already bound by `transit_barrier_7191_test.go` (`{"ran, one uncovered", 1, true, true, armCoverageIncomplete}` plus a fail-on-revert on the `evaluateArmCoverage` call), so this change completes an already-tested chain rather than adding an untested one.
- [x] Docs in the same change: `pkg/daemon/README.md`'s #7191 arm-state section, `docs/log/7289.md`.

## The rest of the issue's slice

The issue's last comment defines a four-item slice. R1 is here. The others, with evidence:

- **R2** — its stated mechanism does not work: an aborted apply never constructs an `ApplyResult` at all, so threading `hostMutations` through `ApplyResultFromCompileResult` would surface it only on the applies where it is always empty. The want is real; filed as #8285 with the verification.

## PR #8287 — userspace-xdp: fix the raw-L3 misparse — order the ingress test, and refuse the shim on non-Ethernet netdevs [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8279-shim-raw-l3`

The shim parses a 14-byte Ethernet header unconditionally, and it is attached to
netdevs whose frames carry none. Two bugs with one root, **both fixed here**.

**Closes #8279.**

## The root

`parse_l2` reads bytes `[12..14]` as the ethertype. On a raw IP packet those are
the first two octets of the **source address**, so the packet's own source
selects what the shim does:

| inner `src[0..1]` | `eth_proto` read | then |
|---|---|---|
| anything else (the vast majority) | not a handled type | `pass_non_ip_l2_direct` → `XDP_PASS`. **This is why tunnels work today** |
| `8.0` with `src[2]` in `0x45`–`0x4f` | `0x0800` | shifted `parse_ipv4` **SUCCEEDS** → garbage 5-tuple |
| `8.0` otherwise (241/256) | `0x0800` | `drop_degraded_transit` → **XDP_DROP** |
| `134.221` | `0x86dd` | same two arms via `parse_ipv6` |

`8.0.0.0/16` is allocated, routable public space.

## Blast radius

The attach set is strictly **larger** than the ingress set: `compiler_iface.go`
puts **every zoned netdev** into `st.xdpIfindexes`, tunnels included ("Tunnels
need XDP for ingress"), and `syncInterfaceAttachments` reconciles the difference
away only at the two post-acceptance points — **indefinitely if the apply fails
first** (#5485). On a userspace-dataplane box every tunnel is an anchor TUN
(ARPHRD_NONE). And the **canonical WireGuard spelling** is not even excluded
from the ingress set: the base row's flag is `iface.Tunnel != nil`
(interface-level only) while the zone fans up from the unit.

## Measured on a live kernel, not reasoned about

| device | ARPHRD | XDP attaches? | runs on userspace writes? | byte 0 | bytes `[12..14]` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TUN | NONE | **yes** | **yes** | `0x45` (IP ver/IHL) | `0a4d` — **the IP source octets** |
| TAP (control) | ETHER | yes | yes | `0x86` (dst MAC) | `0800` — the real ethertype |

Same harness, same kernel, only framing differs. A first attempt used a
verdict-*changing* program; the Ethernet control showed the same effect, so that
reading was **void** and was replaced with an *observing* one.

## Commit 1 — order the ingress test before the L3 parse (the DROP)

Deliberately **not** hoisted above the non-IP arm: ARP/LLDP must keep taking
`pass_non_ip_l2_direct` (plain `XDP_PASS`) on every interface, because
`cpumap_or_pass` would route them to a remote CPU that does not drive the local
L2 state machine — and the gap contains real NICs during a failed apply. As
placed, it alters the fate of no packet except the one it fixes, and it leaves
the #5173 tallies exact (`ingress_ifindex` 22, `rx_queue` 3).

## PR #8290 — afxdp: publish the worker runtime records behind an ArcSwap (#7209) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7209-syncsession-lock`

## Summary

- `WorkerManager::records` becomes `Arc<ArcSwap<BTreeMap<u32, Arc<WorkerRuntimeRecord>>>>` and private, readable through `&self`. It is the **last** piece of `Coordinator` state the peer-synced import path reaches that a `&mut Coordinator` was required to read — everything else it touches is already `Arc`/`ArcSwap`-shared (`sessions`, `bpf_maps` via #8179, `ha.rg_runtime`, `neighbors.dynamic`).
- The worker `JoinHandle` moves out of `WorkerHandle` into a private `WorkerManager::joins`. Consuming it needed `&mut` on the record, and that was the only thing standing between the record and being publishable behind an `Arc`.
- `upsert_synced_session` takes **one** records snapshot for the whole import instead of three independent loads.
- No lock moves and no behaviour changes. `sync_session` still dispatches under the snapshot-wide `ServerState` mutex; this is the ownership prerequisite, not the fix.

## Why `ArcSwap`, and why this is not the projection that was already rejected

#7209's fan-out projection (comment 5475077474) was built and discarded because it published an `ArcSwap` **beside** `records`, refreshed by calling a helper at each mutation site with nothing enforcing the call. 17 test sites inserted directly and it silently went short — drift demonstrated, not hypothesised.

There is no second structure here. The `ArcSwap` **is** the map, so a site that mutates without publishing does not compile.

`ArcSwap` rather than `RwLock` deliberately — and the reason needs stating precisely, because the first version of this rationale was falsifiable. The fan-out loop takes only the per-worker command mutex, **not** `sessions.synced`. The hazard is the other direction: an `RwLock` read guard covering the whole import would be held **across** `publish_shared_session`'s acquisition of `sessions.synced`, inventing a records-before-sessions ordering nothing else observes. That is a lock-graph change — the #7095 category, which a green suite cannot see because every test calls in from outside the lock.

`records_reader()` returns a `WorkerRecordsReader`, not the `Arc<ArcSwap<..>>`. Handing out the `ArcSwap` hands out `store`/`rcu`/`swap` through `Deref`, and `register`'s read-clone-store is a non-atomic RMW that would silently drop such a write. `RuntimeViewChannel::reader` took the same decision for the same reason.

## The two-map invariant, and the bug that hid in it

`records` and `joins` must agree on their key set: `stop_and_clear` signals over the published records and joins over `joins`, so a join whose record is gone is a thread **joined without ever being signalled** — a hang, not an error. `clear_records` is therefore private and asserts `joins` is empty. `assert!`, not `debug_assert!`: `make test-rust` builds the cargo legs in **release**, where a debug assertion is compiled out and the guard would exist only in the profile nobody gates on.

## What is and is not bound by a test

**Bound.** Six cells, each shown to fail against a targeted mutation:

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| `records_reader` returns a detached copy (the projection shape) | the aliasing cell only |
| collapse `stop_and_clear`'s two passes into one | the #6242 ordering cell only |
| `register` does not publish | all cells |
| `clear_records`'s guard deleted | its control cell only |
| `records.len()` inside `synced_import_cap_for` replaced by a constant | the cap formula cell |

**NOT bound, stated plainly because an earlier revision of this body claimed otherwise.** The PR's headline property — that one snapshot sources the cap, the reservation gate and the fan-out — **has no test.** Mutating `upsert_synced_session` to pass `&BTreeMap::new()` to the cap, or reverting to three independent `records()` loads, leaves all 5060 tests green (measured). The map parameter on `synced_import_cap_for` binds the *formula*, not the *call-site sourcing*, and every `upsert_synced_session` cap test sets `synced_import_cap_override`, which returns before `records.len()` is read.

This is not fixable here: the property is genuinely unobservable while dispatch is single-threaded, because no mutation can interleave. It is inert today and its instrument lands with the dispatch change. Recording it rather than leaving a stronger claim standing.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-rust` / `make test-go` — see the checks on this PR
- [x] `cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp` — 5060 collected, 0 failed, 0 `Terminated`/`Killed`
- [x] `make cluster-deploy` + CoS re-apply on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`
- [x] `make test-failover` — **17 `PASS` lines counted** against the summary's "17 passed", 0 FAIL, `rc=0`, zero `Terminated|Killed|Timeout` in the log; 21.3 Gbps
- [x] `make test-ha-crash` — 42 passed, 0 failed (earlier run, same code)
- [x] `sync_session_is_served_while_the_state_lock_is_held_7209` re-run to confirm it did **not** go green: still 1.2034s, still `#[ignore]`d

### What the cluster smoke actually exercised

`xpf_userspace_synced_import_reserve_refused_total` moved **2 → 12** on fw0 and **0 → 2** on fw1. That counter has exactly one `fetch_add` site (`ha/session_import.rs`), inside a block whose `&&` chain includes `!worker_records.is_empty()` — the snapshot this PR introduces. `&&` short-circuits, so each bump proves the changed line ran and took its live branch. Corroborating: `worker_active_seconds` 0 → ~38s across workers 0-5, `fw1 has 10 synced sessions`, and iperf3 surviving an unclean sysrq reboot without re-handshake (which requires fw1's workers to already hold the synced sessions — the fan-out loop).

## PR #8293 — dataplane: keep an aborted apply's host-divergence evidence across the retry (#8285) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8285-abort-evidence`

## The issue's premise was wrong, and enumerating the path exposed a sharper defect

#8285 (which I filed) said abort evidence has **no carrier that exists on the abort path**. The sub-finding it rested on was correct — an aborted apply never constructs an `ApplyResult` — and my generalisation from it was not. Traced hop by hop instead of assumed:

```
annotateHostMutationOnAbort   wraps with %w
  -> abortAfterHostMutation   returns unchanged
  -> CompileUserspaceShim     return nil, err
  -> manager_compile.go:246   return nil, err
  -> manager.go:496           return nil, err
  -> daemon_apply_dataplane.go:176  recordCompileFailure(err)   <- BEFORE the abort-class branch
       -> compileLastError -> CompileHealthSnapshot -> /health
       -> and the same err is joined into the commit the operator sees
```

**The carrier exists and already has two live consumers.** So this PR plumbs and renders nothing new. Building the typed carrier the issue asked for would have added a field with no reader — inert code, whose tell is that every test still passes.

## What is actually broken: the evidence does not survive the retry

`CompileResult.hostMutations` is per-**COMPILE** and fires only on a real change (`if vlanCreated`; `reconcileInterfaceAddresses` returning true). `annotateHostMutationOnAbort` returns the error unchanged when nothing moved — and its own doc gives the reason, which is right: *"a converged re-apply records nothing and the message stays worth reading"*.

Both correct alone. Together:

| | what happens | what the operator sees |
|---|---|---|
| **apply #1** | creates the VLAN child, reconciles addresses, aborts at the attach | the full *"this apply ALREADY changed live host state … and there is no undo"* annotation |
| **apply #2** (the retry) | Phase 2 is converged, so it records nothing | a bare `attach userspace shim XDP: …` — **no mention that the box is still diverged** |

The divergence is identical across both attempts. Only the evidence disappears — and it disappears on the attempt the operator is most likely to be looking at. Retrying is the expected response to a failed commit, and #7289's r1 established the reachable trigger (a driver refusing an XDP attach) is **persistent**, so the un-annotated retry is the *steady state* after the first failure, not an edge case.

## The fix

`Manager.hostDivergence` — sticky, per-**BOX**. `hostMutations` answers a per-compile question ("did this compile move anything"); the operator's question is per-box ("is this box diverged"). Conflating the two is what produced the gap; both are wanted.

- `recordHostDivergence` **merges** on the abort path — two aborts moving different classes leave the UNION, so the operator is not sent to look at one of the two things that moved.
- `inheritHostDivergence` stamps the retained classes onto the next compile's result, before any abort site can fire.
- Only the compile **success** tail clears them. Clearing on an abort, or at the head of an apply, drops the fact while it is still true.

Stamping the result rather than adding a second annotator keeps exactly one renderer, so the operator cannot read the same fact twice in two formats, and a step added to the post-mutation window keeps inheriting the contract from `runPostMutationSteps` unchanged.

## Modularity gate

`pkg/dataplane/loader.go` crossed the 1500 LOC [WATCH] floor (1490 → 1508) and `TestTouchedFileCrossedModularityThreshold` caught it. Resolved by **shrinking this change's footprint** to 1498 rather than by an accepted-list entry — the rationale belongs in `hostdivergence_8285.go`, which owns the mechanism, and `loader.go` keeps only what a reader of that line needs. Nothing was lost, it moved to where it is the source of truth.

- [x] `make test-rust` — 5052 passed, 0 failed.

## PR #8294 — Refuse to attach the XDP shim to a non-Ethernet netdev [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8279-nonether-attach`

Follow-up to #8287, which merged **before this commit reached the branch** — so
the ordering half is on master and the misparse half is not. #8279 has been
reopened; this closes it.

**Closes #8279.**

## What #8287 left open

Ordering stops a **non-adjudicated** ifindex reaching the parser, which closes
the DROP. Two paths still reach the **misparse**, and neither depends on
ordering:

1. A raw-L3 netdev that **is** in the ingress set passes the gate, so the shifted
   parse survives into binding and session lookup with a 5-tuple read 14 bytes
   into the real header. Reachable through the **canonical WireGuard spelling**:
   the base row's flag is `iface.Tunnel != nil` — interface level only — while
   the zone fans up from the unit, so it is not excluded.
2. The **ctrl-disabled** path (`degraded_ctrl_disabled_action`) never consults
   the ingress set at all, by design — a disabled ctrl must fail closed on every
   attached interface — so its local/control exemption is evaluated against the
   misparse. That direction is **fail-OPEN**: a transit packet whose shifted
   parse yields a configured local destination is PASSED where it should drop.

## The fix

`compileZones` no longer puts a netdev into `pendingXDP` unless its link layer is
Ethernet. If the shim is never attached, neither path exists — one change, both
paths, rather than patching each.

**Keyed on `EncapType`, not the link kind — measured, not assumed:**

```
xpf8279t  kind=tuntap  EncapType="none"    (TUN: raw L3, no Ethernet header)
xpf8279p  kind=tuntap  EncapType="ether"   (TAP: Ethernet)
```

Both are `Type() == "tuntap"`. A kind-keyed predicate would have refused the TAP
too and still said nothing useful about the tunnel case.

## The polarity of the unknown case — I had it backwards first

The **predicate** refuses an unrecognised encap type: an Ethernet parser must not
be pointed at framing it does not recognise. The **gate must not**, because the
failures are asymmetric:

- attaching on unknown framing risks a misparse, and only on the rare class that
  is actually raw L3;
- **refusing** guarantees an UP, zoned netdev with no XDP at all, whose traffic
  is then forwarded unadjudicated — a *certain* hole on what is almost always a
  healthy Ethernet NIC whose netlink lookup failed transiently.

## PR #8295 — configstore: decide envelope-ness by key presence, not four of five fields [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8288-envelope-prf`

A `{"prf":"sha256"}` config body passed `unmarshalEnvelope` as **plaintext**, and
the daemon then booted an active firewall with **no security policy**, reporting
success.

**Closes #8288.**

## Reproduced by execution before touching anything

At this HEAD, with `{"salt":"x"}` refused in the same probe as a control so the
result is not vacuous:

```
body={"prf":"sha256"}                 -> ok=false err=<nil>   (PLAINTEXT passthrough)
body={"prf":"sha256","Children":null} -> ok=false err=<nil>
body={"salt":"x"}                     -> refused
body={"Children":{}}                  -> passthrough (correct)
null / [1,2] / 42 / garbage           -> passthrough (correct)
```

Downstream `json.Unmarshal` drops the unknown field, an **empty `ConfigTree`**
decodes, `Store.Load` compiles it. Silently — the #4579 plaintext-downgrade
warning keys on `masterPasswordPRF(tree) != ""` and the tree is empty.

## It is a gap BETWEEN two guards, not a missing one

- **#7454's key-presence guard** lists all five keys including `prf`, but
  `envKeys` is consulted **only inside** the `json.Unmarshal` error branch.
  `{"prf":"sha256"}` is well-formed JSON that decodes cleanly, so that branch
  never runs.
- **#4888's fail-closed discriminator** then tests
  `Format || Salt || Nonce || Data` — four of five, **omitting PRF** — so the
  body satisfies "no format AND no AES-GCM fields", which the comment directly
  above it defines as a genuine plaintext body.

## The fix, and why not the obvious one

`len(envKeys) > 0`, **not** `|| env.PRF != ""`.

The obvious fix works — I verified `env.PRF` binds (`json:"prf"`). But the
**defect IS** a five-field struct guarded by a hand-maintained four-field list,
and adding a fifth item reproduces the shape that caused it. `envKeys` is derived
from the body and answers the question #7454 already answers, so it cannot drift
out of sync with the struct.

It is also **strictly stronger, intentionally**: `{"format":""}` carries the key
with an empty value, which the field test passed through and key presence
refuses. A body that *names* an envelope key was meant to be an envelope. The
refusal now also reports which keys it saw, so an operator is not sent looking
for a `format` field the body does not have.

## PR #8299 — afxdp: de-flake the #6242 teardown-ordering cell and fix its neighbours (#7209) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7209-review-followup`

## Summary

Repairs seven defects a hostile review found in #8290 **after** it merged. No production behaviour changes — every edit is a test instrument, an assertion, a rustdoc, or prose.

The headline one: **#8290 shipped a flaky test, and I wrote it in the same session I filed #8291.**

## The flake, and why it is the worst kind

`d_stop_and_clear_signals_every_worker_before_joining_any_7209` had each worker spin on its **own** stop flag, then immediately count how many of the three were set. `stop_and_clear` sets those flags with three sequential relaxed stores, so a deschedule between two stores lets worker 0 wake and count 1 — yielding `[1, 2, 3]`.

That is **exactly** the signature the failure message attributes to a collapsed one-pass teardown ("a leading 1 or 2"). A scheduling hiccup and a real #6242 regression were indistinguishable in the output, which is the property that makes a flake corrosive rather than merely annoying: whoever hits it cannot tell which they have.

It did **not** reproduce here — 0/40 unloaded, 0/40 under 8-core load. That is not evidence against it; the window is narrow, not absent, and the review demonstrated it with forced preemption.

**The fix removes the timing assumption rather than widening a margin.** Each worker now waits for **every** peer's flag, bounded:

- under the correct signal-all-then-join-all order, every worker's condition is already true when the joins begin — the scheduler cannot change the outcome;
- under a collapsed signal-one-join-one order, worker 0 is joined while its peers are unsignalled, so its condition can *never* become true and it runs to the deadline.

That second case is what makes the bound load-bearing rather than a hang guard: it converts a deadlock into a recorded sentinel. The same bound still covers a `register` that never published, and the message now names both causes instead of only the second.

**Measured:** collapsed-teardown mutant reds deterministically at 10s with `[MAX, MAX, 3]`; **25/25** clean runs pass.

## A vacuous cell deleted

The snapshot-outlives-clear cell could not fail. In safe Rust there is no implementation of `records_snapshot()` whose return breaks the keep-alive claim, and even a detached deep copy satisfies both its `get` and its `Arc::ptr_eq` — a `BTreeMap` clone clones the inner `Arc`s. Its one live assertion (that `clear_records` clears) is already made by another cell.

It read as coverage of the refcount guarantee and provided none, which is worse than no cell. Removed, with a comment recording why it should not be helpfully restored.

## A rationale that was falsifiable as written

The field doc justified `ArcSwap` over `RwLock` by saying a lock would collide with `sessions.synced`, *"which `upsert_synced_session` takes while iterating this map"*. **It does not** — the fan-out takes only the per-worker command mutex, and `publish_shared_session` acquires and releases `sessions.synced` earlier in the call.

The hazard runs the other way: a read guard covering the whole import would be held **across** that acquisition, inventing a records-before-sessions ordering nothing else observes. The conclusion was right and the argument was checkable and false — the shape where a future reader disproves the argument and discards the conclusion with it.

## The rest

- `remove_record_for_test` gains the un-joined-thread assertion `clear_records` already carries. Latent today (both callers pass `join = None`), same invariant.
- The #8157/#8171 doc correction **contradicted the paragraph directly beneath it**: the `.md` sibling was rewritten to past tense and the rustdoc was not, so the two spellings of one claim disagreed. The `.md` also said "#7209 **removes** that mutex" in the present tense, which #8290 did not do and this does not either. Both now cite the issue **and** the PR, because in-tree comments cite #8157 and a grep for one was missing the other.
- `coordinator/tests.rs`'s fail-on-revert recipe still said "make the spawn-fail arm also `coord.workers.records.clear()`" — which stopped compiling when `records` became private. **A fail-on-revert recipe whose instructions do not build is a guard nobody can run.**
- Unused `WorkerRecordsReader::load_full` dropped rather than carried with an allow-attribute, and the reader's doc no longer claims to be "the seam the peer-synced import path reads through" — false at this head; that path still uses `records_snapshot()` because it still runs under the `ServerState` mutex.

Prose that merely *names* `workers.records` is left alone deliberately: the field still exists, so those references are accurate rather than broken.

## PR #8300 — test/incus: give the cluster smoke pool-mode NAT coverage (#8280) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `test/8280-pool-nat-smoke`

## The blind spot

Every `source-nat` rule on the loss userspace cluster was `interface;` mode, which is **address-only**: `match_rules.rs` takes the `interface_mode` branch, rewrites the source to the egress interface's own address, and returns **before any port allocation**. It never reaches `PortAllocator` or `AddressOccupancy::claim`.

Measured on #7174 M13: a change to the NAT port allocator passed the full cluster smoke **17/17** while the smoke never executed a line of it. The run looks identical whether such a change is correct, reverted, or actively broken — so every past and future allocator change has shipped with zero hardware coverage, and the next person would not be looking for it.

## Non-interference — proven, not asserted

The rule matches `10.0.61.240/28`, which nothing is assigned (LAN host `.102`, VIP `.1`, DHCP `.100-.199`), and is listed **before** the catch-all `snat` rule so first-match-wins leaves every current flow on the interface path. `POOL_NAT_SMOKE=0` disables the phase entirely so the config change can be measured on its own:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| `POOL_NAT_SMOKE=0` (config change only) | **17 passed, 0 failed** — exactly the pre-change count |
| full run | **20 passed, 0 failed** |

37 PASS artifacts collected across the two runs, 0 `Terminated`/`Killed`/`VOID` tells. Both in one lock cell on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/fw1`.

## What the three assertions ENTER

Stated explicitly, because a cell that passes without entering the state buys nothing — which is exactly the trap the first version of this work fell into.

| assertion | state entered |
|---|---|
| fw0 translated to `172.16.80.7` | `allocate_translation -> AddressOccupancy::claim`. The assertion is on the **translated address**: only the allocator can put `.7` in the `Out:` line, so "a session exists" would have passed on interface mode and measured nothing. |
| fw1 imported it | `handle_upsert_synced -> reserve_flow -> occupancy.reserve() -> claim_offset` — the HA import side, and the exact call #7174 M13 changed. |
| allocation after a full role-change cycle | fw0 primary → secondary (crash) → primary (manual failback). A **fresh** claim then walks the recycle FIFO in the post-churn state: ports fw1 imported as reservations, then owned as primary, then handed back. Sessions are **cleared first**, so a survivor from before the failover cannot satisfy it vacuously. |

The third asserts the **allocation**, not data-path liveness — see below.

## Two bugs found on the way

- **#8296** — the first version of the `proxy-arp` stanza sat under `security` instead of `security { nat }`. It **committed clean, rendered back verbatim** through `show configuration`, and was completely **inert**: no `NTF_PROXY` entry, pool return traffic blackholed, no error anywhere. With a control, `CheckText` also accepts `flooby { wibble 42; }` under `security`.
- **#8297** — both cluster nodes install the `NTF_PROXY` entry for a NAT pool address **regardless of RG ownership**, so the upstream sees one IP at two RETH virtual MACs and pool-mode TCP never completes a handshake. Discriminating control: same host, same second, `.230` (interface mode) reaches 5.95 Gbit/s while `.240` (pool mode) times out; ICMP through the same pool works 3/3, clearing translation, routing and the reverse path.

**#8297 is why the traffic-survival assertion is not here.** Asserting it today would fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the allocator. It is owed once #8297 lands, and the code says so at the call site.

## Design notes

- The pool address is `172.16.80.7`, distinct from reth0.80's own `.8`, because the **#6751 commit gate rejects** a pool sitting on an interface-mode SNAT egress address — both would mint the same `(address, port)` tuple with no shared occupancy (#5144). A distinct address then needs proxy-ARP or return traffic blackholes, the lesson `xpf-cluster-fw0.conf` already records.
- `pkg/configstore/ha_cluster_conf_8280_test.go` runs the **real commit-check** over the shipped cluster config offline, so an edit to it cannot be discovered by half-applying it to a shared cluster. Its proxy-ARP assertion reads the **parsed** `cfg.Security.NAT.ProxyARP`, not the file text — the first version checked text and passed on the misplaced, inert config.

## Test plan

- [x] Two cluster runs as above (17/17 and 20/20), one lock cell, artifacts counted.

  - a pool on the interface address → commit-check cell RED, with the #6751 reverse-index error
  - `proxy-arp` moved back under `security` → parsed-config cell RED, **while the text-based version it replaced passed**
- [x] Docs in the same change: `docs/log/8280.md`.

## PR #8303 — docs: a green cluster smoke owes a witness that your change ran [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `docs/counter-witness-smoke`

## Summary

Adds a subsection to step 8 of "Workflow for every change" in `docs/engineering-style.md`: how to establish that a cluster smoke actually reached your change, using a counter, **forward** rather than by reading the config afterwards.

## Why now

Two runs of the same target this week differed in the only way that matters, and nothing in the protocol distinguished them:

- **#8280** passed **17/17 while never executing the change it was owed for.** The cluster carries no pool-mode source-NAT rule, so the run would have looked identical had the change been correct, broken, or reverted. Established only afterwards, by reading the cluster config.
- **#8290** established the opposite forward. `xpf_userspace_synced_import_reserve_refused_total` moved 2 → 12 on fw0 and 0 → 2 on fw1; that counter has exactly one `fetch_add`, behind an `&&` chain whose third clause is the read the change introduced. `&&` evaluates left to right, so each bump proves the changed line ran **and took its live branch** — a statement about which branch executed, not merely that the process stayed alive.

## What the section says

Three steps: find a counter whose **only** increment site is downstream of your change (verify "only" by grep **with a positive control**, so a wrong pattern surfaces as the control coming back empty rather than as your counter looking unique); prefer one behind a short-circuit your change participates in; diff `/metrics` per node across the run.

And the other half, which is worth as much: **say what the run did not reach.** In that same #8290 run the cap's refusal branch never fired, so a wrong cap magnitude would have looked identical, and the property the change existed for was inert under a still-single-threaded dispatch — the green was the same for the change and for its absence. An unexercised dimension that goes unmentioned is read as covered.

## PR #8305 — cmdtree: end the canonical walk at a leaf instead of at its siblings [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8289-canonicalize-trailing`

`Canonicalize` `continue`d when a node had no children, leaving `current` at the
**parent** map, so the next word resolved against the leaf's own **siblings**:
`show version configuration` canonicalized OK as a three-word command.

**Closes #8289.**

## §3 settled — and the audit's bypass claim is REFUTED, not confirmed

The issue asked what the dispatcher does with the trailing word. **It never
executes it.** `case "version"` in `pkg/cli/cli_show.go` and
`pkg/grpcapi/server_show.go` each call a no-argument `showVersion` and drop
`args[1:]`, so `show version configuration` runs as `show version` — *not* as
`show configuration`. The audit's specific claim does not hold.

## But there IS a bypass, in the other direction — demonstrated, not asserted

The hazard is the one the issue named regardless of which side is lenient: **the
authorizer and the dispatcher disagree about what the command is.**
`evaluateCommandRegex` decides on `strings.Join(canon, " ")`, so it judged three
words while the box ran two:

```
deny="^show version$"  line="show version"                -> denied
deny="^show version$"  line="show version configuration"  -> ALLOWED   (pre-fix)
deny="^show version$"  line="show ver conf"               -> ALLOWED   (pre-fix)
```

Appending **any** sibling keyword ran the denied command.

**Matching is unanchored partial by default**, so a plain
`deny-commands "show version"` matched inside the longer string and never had
the hole. **The operator who followed Junos's own advice to use anchors is the
one who was bypassed.** That is why the regression cell uses the anchored form —
an unanchored-only test passes on the broken code, which is the shape of test
that let this survive.

## The fix

Descend unconditionally, including into a leaf's nil child map. The next word
then falls into the not-a-keyword arm, which still admits the legitimate
consumers of a following word — a typed leaf's value, a dynamic node, a
placeholder — and refuses anything else as `CanonicalUnknown`, which callers
fail closed on per the function's own contract.

## Over-rejection was the real risk, and it was measured differentially

Failing closed on `CanonicalUnknown` means refusing a **lawful** command for
every operator with a restricted class, so a too-strict fix here is an outage.
Verified against master rather than by inspection: of a dozen real commands
exercised, **three already returned not-OK before this change**

## PR #8306 — api: make a failed peer fetch visible on the session list surface [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7294-peer-list-refusal-visible`

Second prerequisite for #7294 item 3, landing ahead of it for the same reason
#8301 did: the thing that would make this reachable shouldn't also be the thing
that fixes it.

## The defect

`writeSessionList` discarded the peer fetch error:

```go
if pr, err := svc.PeerSessions(...); err == nil { ... }
```

A failed or refused fetch returned **HTTP 200 with the peer table simply
absent** and nothing saying why. An operator could not distinguish *"the peer
has no sessions"* from *"we never asked"*.

The summary and zone-pair surfaces have always classified this. The list
surface was the one that did not — the shape that survives review because two
of three places look right and nobody checks the third.

| surface | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| summary | `peer_status` + `peer_error` | unchanged (+ refusal wording) |
| zone-pairs | `peer_status` + `peer_error` | unchanged (+ refusal wording) |
| **list** | **error discarded, 200, no signal** | `peer_status` + `peer_error` |

## Why now, and why it is independently correct

The path is currently **unreachable**: the REST handler stamps the session-walk
lease before delegating, so `PeerSessions` takes `AcquireCtx`'s reuse arm and
never returns `ErrBusy`. #7294 item 3 gives peer-directed work its own budget,
at which point the REST caller arrives with no *remote* lease, takes a real
slot, and can be refused for the first time.

**It is fixed because it is wrong, not because item 3 needs it.** "Unreachable
today" is a property of the current call graph, not a guarantee, and the next
change to that graph gets no warning.

## A refusal is not a partition

All three surfaces reported any fetch error as `unreachable`. An admission
refusal means the peer **is** reachable and this node declined to ask — calling
that a partition sends an operator debugging a fabric problem after a network
fault that does not exist. Refusals (`codes.ResourceExhausted`, which is what
`peer_only_5968.go` already returns) now report `busy`; genuine failures still
report `unreachable`.

## PR #8307 — cargo: enforce the single-threaded test requirement the suite already has (#8291) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8291-enforce-single-threaded-tests`

## Summary

`cargo test` in `userspace-dp` reds about **one run in three**, with a different test each time. Setting `RUST_TEST_THREADS = "1"` in `.cargo/config.toml` makes the single-threaded execution the suite **already requires** automatic rather than conventional.

## This is not a latent defect — it is an unenforced requirement

Single-threaded execution is deliberate and documented **twice**:

- the Makefile's own `--test-threads=1` note: *"some dataplane socket tests can wedge in `__skb_wait_for_more_packets` when run concurrently; single-threaded execution avoids the intermittent hang"*;
- `afxdp/checksum.rs`'s #6872 canary: the process-global DNAT counters are bumped by `publish_dnat_table_entry` / `delete_dnat_table_entry` — **production functions on the DNAT path that must not take a lock** — and dozens of tests call them unguarded. That comment states the consequence outright: *"the reason the unguarded writers do not corrupt a sample today is that this crate's suite runs `--test-threads=1`"*.

The requirement lived only in the Makefile recipe. So `make test-rust` was **always sound** — the gate is not and never was affected — while a bare `cargo test`, the command everyone runs while iterating, silently violated it.

## Measured

Each family run **alone**, 20 runs, pristine worktree:

| family | tests | default threads | `--test-threads=1` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tests_gre_version_6842` | 4 | **19/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `tests_decap_dnat_table` | 21 | **14/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `io_uring_write` | 29 | **8/20 fail** | 0/20 |
| `afxdp::wg::engine` | 28 | 0/20 | 0/20 |

Three families collide with their own **siblings**, not with other modules. The fourth is deliberately **excluded rather than folded in**: `wg::engine` already carries a `wg_engine_test_serial()` guard (#6157), which makes it the precedent, not a member of the population.

Full bare `cargo test`: **2 of 6 runs red before, 6 of 6 green after.**

## Why guarding the tests does not work — built, measured, discarded

The obvious fix is a serialization guard on the cells that sample each global. It took `tests_decap_dnat_table` from 14/20 to 2/20, left `tests_gre_version_6842` at **17/20** (from 19), and made `io_uring_write` **worse**.

The reason is a mistake worth recording: I identified the affected cells by which ones **reference** the counter symbol, when what matters is which ones **change** it. The other cells in those files bump the counter as a *side effect* of calling the production path, without ever reading it. **Serialising readers against readers cannot exclude a writer**, and the writers are production functions that must not lock.

That attempt also tripped #6872's canary — which is exactly what it exists for. A function-local `static` lock reads as a guard and serializes nothing, and the canary named the guard that already existed (`checksum::dnat_counter_guard`) rather than letting a second parallel one land.

## What this does NOT do

It does not remove the race; it enforces the configuration under which the suite is sound. **The flake is still reachable with explicit parallelism, demonstrated rather than asserted:**

- `cargo test tests_gre_version_6842 -- --test-threads=4` → **8 of 8 fail**
- `RUST_TEST_THREADS=4 cargo test tests_gre_version_6842` → **6 of 8 fail**

Both are deliberate escape hatches: cargo's `[env]` is non-forcing so a caller's environment wins, and libtest's CLI flag beats the variable. Anyone hunting concurrency bugs can still ask for parallelism and get the honest answer. #8291 stays open for the underlying isolation work.

## Cost

A bare `cargo test` goes from **~16s to ~75s** on this machine. `make test-rust` is unchanged — it already passed `--test-threads=1`, which is now belt-and-braces rather than the only thing between a developer and a flaky suite. If a reviewer would rather pay the flake than the 4.7x, that is a legitimate call and the numbers are here to make it.

## PR #8309 — daemon: make proxy-ARP for a NAT pool address follow RG ownership (#8297) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8297-proxyarp-rg-ownership`

> **Stacked on #8300** (`test/8280-pool-nat-smoke`), because the cluster acceptance needs a pool-mode NAT rule on the cluster and that is #8300's contribution. Review/merge that first; this PR's base retargets to `master` once it lands.

## The defect

Both nodes installed the `NTF_PROXY` entry for a source-NAT pool address regardless of redundancy-group ownership:

```
fw0  node0 200  primary         ->  172.16.80.7 dev ge-0-0-2.80 proxy
fw1  node1 100  secondary-hold  ->  172.16.80.7 dev ge-7-0-2.80 proxy
```

A WAN capture showed both answering, with their distinct per-node RETH virtual MACs. The upstream sees one IP at two MACs and pool-mode TCP never completes a handshake.

**The discriminating control**, because "pool NAT is broken" has many possible causes — one host, one second, same target and port:

| source | matching rule | result |
|---|---|---|
| `10.0.61.230` | `snat` — interface mode | **5.95 Gbit/s, iperf Done** |
| `10.0.61.240` | `pool-snat` — pool mode | **connect timed out** |

ICMP through the same pool worked 3/3, clearing translation, routing and the reverse path.

**It was only reachable because of #8280.** Before that work no cluster config had a pool-mode source-NAT rule at all, so the question could not be asked.

## The fix

Answering proxy-ARP for a pool address is claiming a VIP-adjacent identity — the question VRRP already answers for the VIPs themselves, and it answers it by **not holding the address** rather than by filtering replies. `proxyARPOwnsInterface` mirrors `relayMasterGateOpen` (#2456) and the DDNS per-RG writer gate exactly:

- standalone (`d.cluster == nil`) → always answers;
- interface with no redundancy group → always answers;
- RG-owned → answers only while this node is MASTER for that RG, from the live `rgStateMachine`.

**The first two arms carry the wider blast radius**, so they are checked before ownership and each has its own cell: gating a box with no RGs breaks pool-mode NAT on every standalone deployment — the larger population — while passing every cluster test.

**No removal path was needed.** Losing ownership is expressed as "no longer desired", and `reconcileProxyARP` already sweeps orphans out of the desired set (#4955) and drives the per-interface sysctl down. Gating the input buys install *and* removal.

**The 2s convergence poll is not a tuning constant.** The 30s reassert beat alone leaves a demoted node answering long enough for an upstream to cache its MAC and steer pool return traffic at a node that no longer owns the address. The poll is one config lookup and one `rgStateMachine` read per entry — no netlink, no apply semaphore — and only a *change* costs a reconcile.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-go` — 73 packages, EXIT 0.
- [x] Four cells, three mutations, each red on the right one:

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| gate removed (the shipped defect) | the standby cell |
| standalone gated | the **standalone control** |
| unit suffix not stripped — every sub-interface resolves to RG 0, gate silently inert | the resolution cell |

That last mutation is the dangerous one: an inert gate looks exactly like a working fix.

## PR #8310 — diagcmd: give peer-directed session work its own admission budget [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7294-remote-walk-budget`

**#7294 item 3** — the last of the three. Items 1 and the two prerequisites are
merged (#8292, #8301, #8306).

## What

The peer-only entry points (`PeerSessions`, `PeerSessionSummary`,
`PeerZonePairSummary`) drive **no local walk** but took a slot from
`SessionWalkLimiter` anyway. On a 4-slot budget shared across REST and gRPC,
with `ShowText` fabric-reachable, a burst of peer-directed requests could refuse
genuine local scans while the local conntrack table was untouched.

They now take `diagcmd.RemoteWalkLimiter` — same capacity, same fail-fast
semantics, same lease-aware `AcquireCtx`, its own budget.

## Not a loosening

The question worth settling before writing it, and the answer is measurable
rather than a matter of taste:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| bound on an unleased peer call | 4 slots (`SessionWalkLimiter`) | 4 slots (`RemoteWalkLimiter`) |
| scope | global | global (**not** per-peer — a per-peer bound would fail to bound N peers) |
| consumers | shared with every local scan surface | those three methods only |

What changes is *which* budget, and therefore that saturating one can no longer
refuse the other. A shared budget bounds the **sum**, so adding a consumer here
tightens it for the existing ones; the constant's doc says so.

#5880's lease-propagation property moves with the path rather than being
retired: `AcquireCtx` is still the acquire, so nested in-process delegation
within one request graph still reuses the ancestor's slot.

## The escaped mutation is the part worth reading

Independence is asserted in **both** directions per #8151, plus a direct
statement that a peer fetch moves the local limiter's in-flight count by zero.

**All three of those cells passed** on a mutant that pointed
`remoteWalkLimiter` at `SessionWalkLimiter` — a "separate" budget that is the
same instance under a different name, which is precisely the failure #8151's
own test warns about.

They passed because each cell substitutes **both** package aliases with fresh
`NewLimiter` instances so it can drain one safely — and that substitution
destroys the property it is trying to observe. #8151 answers this by draining
the *real* limiters. The census for this issue surfaced that fact and I did not
apply it until the mutation forced it.

An instance-identity cell now closes it and reds at both levels:

## PR #8311 — io_uring: give the retained-buffer accounting an injectable sink (#8291) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8291-isolate-counter-families`

## Summary

#8291 part **1 of 3**. `io_uring_write`'s two #7106 cells sampled the process-global `RETAINED_BUFFERS` / `RETAINED_BYTES` and asserted a **delta**; the module failed **8 of 20** runs under a parallel `cargo test`. The counters now live behind a `RetainedCounters` reached through an `Arc`, so a test can hand a registry a **private sink** and assert absolutes.

## Why a serialization guard cannot fix this — built, measured, discarded

The obvious repair is a guard on the cells that sample the counters. It left this module **worse**.

The accounting is written by `InflightRegistry::drop`, so **every test that drops a non-empty registry is a writer — 28 of this module's 29 tests construct a registry** — while only two read. You cannot serialise two readers against twenty-eight writers, and the writers sit on a production `Drop` path that must not take a lock.

The mistake that produced that attempt is worth naming: the cells were chosen by which ones **reference** the counter symbol, when what matters is which ones **change** it.

## The original rationale is preserved, not overruled

The global's doc says *"a registry that leaks is being dropped, so a per-registry counter would be destroyed with the thing it describes."* That is exactly right, and it is why the counters are **not** simply moved into `InflightRegistry`.

An `Arc` satisfies the constraint: the sink outlives the registry because its holder keeps it alive, so `Drop` records into something that survives the drop. Production still has exactly one instance — `process_retained()` — which is what the status surface reports. The comment now says this rather than being deleted, because the constraint it states is still load-bearing.

Same shape as **#6819**, which moved the session counters off process globals for the same reason: as globals, every assertion about them depended on what every other test happened to do.

## Measured

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `io_uring_write` @ `--test-threads=8`, 20 runs | **8/20 fail** | **0/20** |
| the two `_7106` cells, 30 runs @ `--test-threads=8` | — | **0/30** |

**Fail-on-revert re-verified rather than assumed:** deleting the accounting from `Drop` still reds `unproven_buffers_are_retained_not_freed_7106` with its original message. Each cell also asserts its fresh sink starts at `(0, 0)`, so an absolute assertion cannot pass on state the test did not create.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp` — 5060 collected, 0 failed
- [x] family at `--test-threads=8`, 20 runs — 0 failures (was 8/20)
- [x] fail-on-revert mutation still reds the subject cell
- [x] `rustfmt` deliberately **not** run: all three files were already unformatted at master, so formatting them would widen this diff with unrelated churn

## Not done here — and both need a different fix

- **`tests_gre_version_6842`** (19/20) shares this non-atomic read-act-read sub-shape over `GRE_DECAP_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION_REFUSALS`, but its writer set spans **five test files**, and the bump sits on the packet decap path where threading a sink is not free. A file-scoped guard would be incomplete for the same reason it was here.
- **`tests_decap_dnat_table`** (14/20) is the *other* sub-shape: it clears the **entire** `DNAT_STEERING_HOLDERS` global and then asserts absolute counts, so siblings wipe each other's setup. Its assertions are already keyed, so per-test key uniqueness looks tractable — to be measured, not assumed.

#8307 keeps all three from reddening a bare `cargo test` in the meantime. It suppresses rather than fixes, so **#8291 stays open** until all three are isolated.

Refs #8291.

## PR #8313 — Refresh the shim manifest after the .cargo/config.toml change (master is red) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8307-shim-manifest-buildinput`

**master is currently RED.** `TestUserspaceXDPShimObjectMatchesSourceManifest`
fails on plain `origin/master`.

## Cause

#8307 added `RUST_TEST_THREADS = "1"` to `.cargo/config.toml`. That file is one
of the shim manifest's tracked **build inputs** (manifest entry
`".cargo/config.toml"`), so its content hash moved and the lockstep check fired:

```
build input changed: .cargo/config.toml
  manifest 61e88aad...
  actual   26c894f8...
```

## Why this is bookkeeping, not a rebuild

`make generate` re-ran the full pinned-toolchain build and kernel-verifier gate
(PASS, 686919 insns against the 1,000,000 limit, 31.31% headroom). The resulting
object is **byte-identical** to the tracked one:

```
$ git diff origin/master -- pkg/dataplane/userspace_xdp_bpfel.o
(empty)
```

So the only change in this PR is the manifest's recorded hash for that input.
`RUST_TEST_THREADS` is a test-runner setting and does not reach codegen.

`make test-go` on this branch: **73 packages, 0 FAIL.**

## How it got in — my error, recorded so the general form is usable

I gated #8307 with `make test-rust` alone, reasoning that a `.cargo/config.toml`
change is Rust config. **The manifest lockstep guard is a Go test**, so the Rust
leg could not see it.

The general form: *choose the gate by what the change can BREAK, not by what
language the changed file is written in.* A config file at the repo root is an
input to everything that reads it, and this repo deliberately hashes build inputs
precisely so a change to one cannot slip past.

## Follow-up worth filing, deliberately not fixed here

The manifest hashes `.cargo/config.toml` **wholesale**, so any test-only or
lint-only setting added there reds this guard while the object is provably
unchanged. Narrowing the tracked input set — or hashing only the
`[build]`-relevant keys — would remove a recurring false positive without
weakening the staleness check. The guard is doing its job; its input set is just
broader than its subject.
