## PR #8314 — daemon: make proxy-ARP for a NAT pool address follow RG ownership [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8297-proxyarp-rg-ownership`

**Replaces #8309**, which GitHub auto-closed when its base branch
(`test/8280-pool-nat-smoke`) was deleted on #8300's merge. Same head commit
`e3ac9f145`, unchanged; only the base differs. Closing a stacked PR by deleting
its base is a merge-hygiene mistake on my side, not a problem with the work —
the original discussion is on #8309.

## The defect

Both nodes installed the `NTF_PROXY` entry for a source-NAT pool address
regardless of redundancy-group ownership:

```
fw0  node0 200  primary         ->  172.16.80.7 dev ge-0-0-2.80 proxy
fw1  node1 100  secondary-hold  ->  172.16.80.7 dev ge-7-0-2.80 proxy
```

A WAN capture showed **both answering, with their distinct per-node RETH virtual
MACs**. The upstream sees one IP at two MACs and pool-mode TCP never completes a
handshake.

## The discriminating control

"Pool NAT is broken" has many possible causes, so the report isolates it — one
host, one second, same target and port:

| source | matching rule | result |
|---|---|---|
| `10.0.61.230` | `snat` — interface mode | **5.95 Gbit/s, iperf Done** |
| `10.0.61.240` | `pool-snat` — pool mode | **connect timed out** |

ICMP through the same pool worked 3/3, which clears translation, routing and the
reverse path and leaves ARP identity as the remaining explanation.

## Why it was only reachable now

Before #8280 no cluster config carried a pool-mode source-NAT rule at all, so
this question could not be asked on hardware. The coverage work created the
fixture that exposed it — which is the argument for that work rather than an
accident of it.

## Gate

Merged onto current master (`2bbb1a481`): `make test-go` **73 packages, 0 FAIL**.
Previously gated green in a combined tree with #8300/#8310/#8311
(`make test-go` 73/0, `make test-rust` 5193/0, `make selftest` 128/0, no void
tells).

`Closes #8297` is deliberately NOT used here — see the acceptance discussion on
#8309; the standby-does-not-answer assertion is the criterion that closes it.

## PR #8316 — cluster: pin that a promoted RG0 authority has a LIVE config-epoch guard [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7323-config-epoch`

Settles the one fact #7323 was waiting on. **Docs + one test cell; no production
code changes.**

This does not close the issue — it establishes the fact the design turns on, and
the answer rules out the "no protocol bump" half of the proposal. The remaining
five open questions are untouched.

## The question

> In which direction and deployment does a tagged stamp reach a receiver whose
> guard is currently **LIVE**?

## The answer: a PROMOTED RG0 authority — measured, not reasoned

`lastAppliedConfigGen` is written only by `recordAppliedConfigGen`, and cleared
only by `initGenState` (construction) and `resetRecvGen` (the peer's bulk
re-prime). **Nothing clears it on a role transition.** So a node that was the
secondary, applied the authority's config, and was then promoted to RG0 carries
that high-water into its authority life.

Same receiver, opposite verdicts, decided only by the top bit:

| receiver | barrier | untagged epoch 3 | top-bit-tagged epoch 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| never-applied authority | 0 | admitted (inert) | admitted |
| **promoted** authority | 10 | **REFUSED** | **admitted** |

## What that does to the design

The claim licensing the skipped `ProtocolVersion` bump is:

> "A legacy receiver reads a tagged value as a very large generation, which its
> unsigned `epoch < barrier` comparison admits — fail-OPEN, **i.e. exactly
> today's behaviour**."

The bolded clause holds only where the barrier is 0. Against a live barrier
today's behaviour is **REFUSE**, so the tag does not preserve the status quo — it
converts a working fail-CLOSED guard into fail-OPEN, on a receiver that cannot
report that it did.

**And a rolling upgrade necessarily involves a failover**, so "promoted
authority" is the normal path through one, not an exotic state. This is exactly
the `epoch == 0` escape hatch's opposite: 0 disables the check explicitly,
`tag | small` disables it accidentally while looking like a very fresh epoch.

## Why "scope the tag so it cannot fire where the guard is live" is not available

The stamping side is the non-authority. It has **no way to know whether the
receiver's barrier is live** — that depends on the receiver's own role history.
So the sender cannot scope around it, which makes this a **negotiation** problem

## PR #8319 — port-mirroring: render the runtime drops the config predicate cannot see [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7357-flowexport-mirror-remainder`

#7357 §2 — the last of the #6534 remainder.

## Most of this issue was already done

Verified by symbol at master `236568b42` before scoping, per the "check the
remainder is still the remainder" discipline:

| section | state |
|---|---|
| §1 flow-export, three renderers | **already done** under #7422 — `config.FlowServerExcludedReason` exists and the builder plus all three named renderers consult it |
| §3 duplication + sort | **already done** under #8166 |
| §2 runtime port-mirroring drops | **open** — this PR |

A near-miss worth recording, because the method matters more than the result:
grepping for `FlowServerExcludedReason` returns **no hit** in
`cli_show_routing.go`, and I was one step from reporting *"two of three
renderers annotate, the third still lies"* — the exact shape this issue is
about, and confidently wrong. The call is one indirection away behind
`flowServerNotInstalledSuffix`. An absence claim from a symbol grep needs a
positive control; the cheap one was *"does that renderer emit an annotation at
all?"*

## The defect

`buildMirrorConfigSnapshots` drops entries for three reasons that depend on the
**runtime interface table**, which the shared config predicate cannot evaluate:

| condition | drops | issue body |
|---|---|---|
| output interface has no ifindex | the whole **instance** | counted |
| an input interface has no ifindex | that **input** | **missed** |
| an input's ifindex already mirrored | that **input** | counted, but as instance-level |

## Applied verdict, not a fresh derivation — a deliberate departure from the body

The body prescribes threading *"the resolved ifindex map"* to the surfaces.
That invites the renderer to **re-derive**, and a re-derivation against a live
interface table answers a different question: `show forwarding-options
port-mirroring` asks what **is** installed; a re-derivation reports what
**would** be installed if the builder ran again now. An ifindex moves across a
netdev recreate, so the two genuinely differ.

Where they disagree the applied answer is the true one, and the disagreement
means a **missed rebuild** — a bug in a different component that a re-deriving
renderer would silently paper over. That is this issue's own failure mode
reintroduced one layer up.

## PR #8320 — afxdp: give each DNAT steering cell a row nothing else touches (#8291) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8291-decap-key-isolation`

## Summary

#8291 part **2 of 3**. `tests_decap_dnat_table` failed **14 of 20** runs under a parallel `cargo test`; it now fails **0 of 20**.

## The mechanism — the other sub-shape

The steering row is keyed by `(protocol, snat_ip, snat_port)`, and all but the protocol come from the **NAT decision**, not the session key. `dnat_snat_decision()` pins port 54321, so every cell in this file that publishes lands on **one shared row** in the process-global `DNAT_STEERING_HOLDERS`.

Six cells then asserted **absolute** holder counts over that row, and each opened with `reset_dnat_steering_holders()` — which clears the **whole registry**, not one row. Run in parallel they saw each other's publishes and wiped each other's setup.

## Isolation, not serialisation

Each cell now publishes under its own `rewrite_src_port`, so it asserts over a row nothing else touches and the absolute counts are true **by construction** rather than by scheduling. Every cell also asserts its row **starts empty** — the control that the isolation is real rather than assumed, and the thing that reds if the port band ever stops being unique.

That ordering matters. A guard was the obvious repair here too, and #8311 recorded why it cannot work for this class: the writers are production functions on the DNAT path that must not lock, and they outnumber the readers. Isolation removes the shared subject instead of trying to schedule around it.

## `reset_dnat_steering_holders()` is removed, not left unused

A test-only "clear all shared state" helper **looks like isolation and is the opposite** — it isolates its caller by destroying everyone else's, which is exactly how these six cells broke each other. Deleting the capability is what stops it coming back; a comment asking people not to call it would not. Its last caller went with this change.

The no-SNAT cell keeps no unique port and needs none: with no source rewrite `dnat_steering_key` yields `None`, so it touches no row at all. Stated at the cell so the asymmetry does not read as an oversight.

## Measured

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `tests_decap_dnat_table` @ `--test-threads=8`, 20 runs | **14/20 fail** | **0/20** |

**The #6745 properties are re-verified rather than assumed to have survived isolation:**

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| `add_dnat_steering_holder` records nothing | 4 of the 6 cells |
| `release_dnat_steering_holder` always reports the row unheld | `a_shared_steering_row_survives_the_first_close_6745` — the cell that exists for that bug |

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-rust` — 5193 collected, 0 failed
- [x] `cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp` — 5060 collected, 0 failed
- [x] family at `--test-threads=8`, 20 runs — 0 failures (was 14/20)
- [x] both fail-on-revert mutations above
- [x] `rustfmt` deliberately **not** run: both touched files were already unformatted at master, so formatting would widen this diff with unrelated churn

## Remaining

`tests_gre_version_6842` (19/20) is the last family and the only one with a real design trade: **five test files** can bump `GRE_DECAP_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION_REFUSALS` and the bump sits on the packet decap path, so neither a file-scoped guard nor cheap sink-threading is obviously right. **#8291 stays open** for it.

## PR #8322 — cluster: bound the redundancy-group id by the array it indexes [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8315-8317-ceilings`

An RG id has two ceilings and only one was enforced. **Closes #8317.**

**#8315 is already closed as not-a-defect** — see below; the two were filed as
one defect in two costumes and only one has a body in it.

## The defect (#8317), confirmed by execution

| constraint | value | enforced at commit? |
|---|---|---|
| heartbeat per-group id field is one byte | 255 | yes, with a precise message |
| `rg_active` / `ha_watchdog` array length | 16 | **no** |

`validateChassisClusterStrict` accepted RG **1, 15, 16, 17, 200, 255**.

**The runtime failure mode was the issue's open question, so I measured it.**
A real BPF array with `max_entries` 16:

```
Update(key=  0) -> nil        <- control
Update(key= 15) -> nil        <- control
Update(key= 16) -> update: key too big for map: argument list too long   (E2BIG)
Update(key= 17) -> E2BIG
Update(key=255) -> E2BIG
```

`UpdateRGActive` returns that error **before** recording the group in `haGroups`
or syncing HA state to the helper, so such an RG never activates and its RETH
interfaces never forward, while the reconcile loop retries forever (#757). **Loud
and permanent, not silent** — but a failure the operator was allowed to commit.
The audit's `-E2BIG` claim is confirmed.

## The fix: single-sourced, not a second literal

The constant moves to `pkg/config` — the only package both the commit gate and
the map sizing can share, since `pkg/dataplane` already imports `pkg/config` and
the reverse is a cycle — and `dataplane.MaxRedundancyGroups` becomes an **alias**.

That makes "the commit bound equals the array length" a **compile-time identity**
rather than a test someone must remember, and keeps every existing reference
working, including the #7465 array-declaration cell. A duplicated `16` in
`pkg/config` would have re-created the drift that produced the gap.

The new check runs **second**, so the wire-truncation message still wins for an
id violating both — it names the more surprising consequence (a silent collision
with another group) and renumbering fixes both.

## PR #8324 — afxdp: move the GRE decap refusal counter onto ForwardingState (#8291) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8291-gre-counter-on-forwarding`

## Summary

#8291 **part 3 of 3** — the last flaky family. `tests_gre_version_6842` failed **19 of 20** parallel runs; it now fails **0 of 20**, with every assertion still an **exact equality**.

Two commits: the fix, and a one-line test-classifier refinement the fix surfaced (flagged below — a reviewer would not expect it otherwise).

## Why the cheaper fixes do not work — measured, not reasoned

**A lower bound (`>= before + 1`) does not fix it.** The cell is a **three-row table** and two rows are *"must NOT count"*. Those are **upper bounds**, and a process-global counter under concurrent writers cannot provide an upper bound at all — there is no relaxation of them. Converting the one countable row took the family from 19/20 to **3/20 and no further**; the survivor was `gre_version_refusal_counter_ignores_a_non_gre_row_with_the_same_outer_tuple`.

The cell's own doc already said the countable row does not stand alone:

> *the interesting failure is a counter bumped unconditionally at the version check: **that reads identically to a correct one on the first row***

A lower bound also **trades a false RED for a false GREEN** — `>=` cannot distinguish this test's refusal from a sibling's.

**A serialization guard** fails as it did for the other two families: five test files reach the decap path, so a file-scoped guard is incomplete.

**"Accept that these cells are single-threaded-only"** cannot be enforced. libtest does not expose the effective thread count, and `-- --test-threads=4` beats the `RUST_TEST_THREADS` the cargo config sets — so a cell asserting the variable would pass **exactly when the condition it guards is violated**.

## What this does

The counter becomes `GreDecapCounters` on `ForwardingState`, `Arc`-backed so `Clone` shares the cell.

**It adds no parameter to any packet-path function.** `note_unsupported_gre_version` already takes `&ForwardingState`, and it is `#[cold] #[inline(never)]`. Each test builds its own forwarding state, so each gets its own counter and the exact assertions become true by construction.

The carry follows **#3651** rather than inventing a second mechanism, at the same call site as its two siblings — for the reason the flood half already gives there: a separate attach function could be moved or dropped independently. `attach_zone_counters` **keeps its name** though the new store is not per-zone: renaming would have broken ten rustdoc intra-doc links across five files this change does not otherwise touch. Its doc now describes the third store.

## Two guards, both mutation-verified

| guard | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| the total **survives a config apply** — driven through the real decap path, not a direct bump, and asserting the `Arc` is **shared** not copied | delete the carry line in `attach_zone_counters` | **reds**, with the operator-facing message |
| the **status surface** reports the forwarding state's total | — | reading through `self.forwarding` instead of a static is a behaviour change on the operator path, so it gets its own assertion rather than riding on the isolation work |

The carry guard matters because its failure is otherwise **invisible**: a cumulative operator-visible metric that silently resets on every commit looks exactly like a quiet network, since a fresh box reads zero anyway.

## Second commit — please look at this one separately

`is_fixture` recognises `tests.rs`, `*_tests.rs` and `*/tests/` but **not the `tests_<topic>.rs` prefix** this tree uses for most per-subject suites. Every canary built on `afxdp_production_sources()` was therefore scanning 21 top-level (plus nested) **test** files as production.

It surfaced here: my status-surface test assigns `coordinator.forwarding` and tripped `forwarding_publish_population_is_pinned_7015`, whose message asks whether a new *apply path* appeared. It had not. That canary offers an allowlist for non-apply sites, and taking it would have **recorded a misclassification as intentional** in a list the next reader trusts — so the predicate is refined instead.

**Sound by construction, not merely by a green suite:** every `tests_*` module is declared `#[cfg(test)]` (`afxdp/mod.rs:528+`), so the compiler guarantees no production path reaches them. (An earlier check — "do these files contain `#[test]`?" — was too weak to support that: production files contain test modules too, and `gre.rs` matches it.)

## This is a production change made for test isolation

Stating it plainly because a reviewer will reasonably ask why a counter moved for a test. It is the **lesser evil**, not a free choice — the alternatives were a hot-path parameter (a precedent), an undetectable single-threaded-only dependency (folklore), or relaxing an upper bound (a false green).

## PR #8327 — policymatch: deny an unzoned ingress, as the dataplane does [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8318-unzoned-from`

The simulator collapsed both unknown-zone sides into one branch returning
default-policy. The dataplane does not.

**Closes #8318.**

## The divergence — FROM side only

| case | dataplane | simulator (before) | agree? |
|---|---|---|---|
| unknown **ToZone** | falls through to default | default-policy | yes |
| unknown **FromZone**, `deny-all` | Deny | Deny | yes, **coincidentally** |
| unknown **FromZone**, **`permit-all`** | **Deny** | **Permit** | **NO** |

The runtime denies `from_id == 0` unconditionally (#6682) — Junos does not pass
transit on an interface in no zone, and screens were already skipped for it. It
deliberately does **not** do the same for the egress side: denying on `to_id`
*"would risk black-holing a correctly-configured path to fix a case that has not

after that exclusion**.

A regression row pins the eligibility half explicitly, so a "fix" that merely
made an unknown zone *eligible* cannot pass by matching a wildcard permit and
then being denied for some other reason.

cause of a deny it did not produce. On a `permit-all` box that is **actively

## PR #8328 — cos: render every transmit-rate form, and correct the doc that hid two [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/7422-show-surface-rows`

#6565 **row 4** of #7422. The row names one site; there are two, and the
unnamed one is the worse of them.

## The defect

The three Junos transmit-rate forms are **mutually exclusive**
(`validateClassOfServiceStrict`), so a scheduler authored as `transmit-rate
percent 30` has `TransmitRateBytes == 0`. Reading that field alone didn't make
the percent form render *badly* — it made it invisible **by construction**,
always:

| site | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `format/cos_show.go` (named in the row) | `-` — reads as "no guarantee configured" for a shaped queue | `percent 30` / `remainder` |
| `format/cos_sections.go` (**not** in the row) | `guaranteeEnabled=false` → the runtime merge **discards the dataplane's resolved rate** | resolved rate rendered |

The second one is worse: `show class-of-service interface` had the true
absolute rate in hand, from the dataplane, and threw it away.

## The doc is the third half

`pkg/config/types_cos.go` said `TransmitRatePercent` was **ACCEPTED-BUT-INERT**
and that *"xpf does not yet resolve the percent against the interface's
shaping-rate"*.

Verified against the Rust side rather than taken on trust: percent resolves in
`cos_effective_transmit_rate_bytes` (#4228 Gap 2), remainder through #6846's
sibling pre-pass. **Both forms are live.** The comment was true when written,
was invalidated by the work that implemented it, and nothing re-read it — and
it had gone on to justify the renderer's dash.

The two mechanisms are now recorded as **different**, because they're easy to
assume shared and aren't: percent is a function of the scheduler and its
interface so it resolves per-scheduler; remainder means *"whatever the shaping
rate has left after every sibling resolves"* and needs a pre-pass.

## Why render the authored form

The absolute value a percent resolves to depends on the interface, so it
belongs on the interface view — which is the second site this change also
fixes. The scheduler table renders what was authored.

## Tests

A control on each side, because every assertion here is "something renders":
the formatter's control is a scheduler with **no** guarantee form, which must
still render `-` — without it, "percent renders something" is satisfied by a
formatter that never returns a dash. The second site additionally **binds the
wiring**, since a copy of the predicate in a test proves nothing about the call
site.

(shell self-tests), #8278 (test/incus python) — and every one of them exists
because a test accumulated on disk that **nothing ran**. One layer up, at the

thing had already happened at scale:

**28 of the 41 runnable harnesses under `test/incus/` and
`scripts/userspace-*.sh` are invoked by no Makefile recipe.** 15 of them are
gates the tree built, unit-tested, documented, and then ran zero times — the
#4800 new-flow ceiling among them, whose own doc opens *"the code ships; the
measurement is OWED"*.

Reached today (13): the 8 HA smokes, `test-connectivity.sh`,
`test-host-inbound.sh`, `setup.sh`, `cluster-setup.sh`, `with-cluster.sh`.

## What the gate does

`make harness-census` asserts that every runnable harness is **invoked by a
Makefile recipe** — directly, or transitively through another invoked harness —
or **declared in `test/incus/HARNESSES.unreached` with a one-line reason**. It
lands green with all 28 declared, which is the deliverable: it is the first
time anyone has had to say, once, which of these the project intends to keep
running. Each entry is tagged GATE (15), COMPOSED (3) or DIAGNOSTIC (10).

That list is **only allowed to shrink**. The census fails if an entry becomes
reached, stops existing, or carries no reason — so it cannot be used to re-hide
a harness later.

Reachability is **transitive** and rooted only at Makefile recipes, because the
interesting cases are clusters that call each other while nothing calls the
cluster: `cos-simul-load-smoke.sh` → `cos-gate1-small-four-alone.sh`, and the
whole `step1`/`step2` capture chain. A census that merely asked "does anything
reference it" scores every one of those green.

All four are real instances in this Makefile. Each is a cell in
`test/incus/harness-census-selftest.sh`, asserted **twice** — once by a fixture
that must score UNREACHED, and once by a **mutation of the census** that must
make that same fixture flip:

## PR #8334 — nat: a rule naming an undefined pool is not armed [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8329-nat-missing-pool`

`SourceNATRuleNotInstalledReason` returned `""` — the value meaning *"this rule
is installed"* — for a source-NAT rule naming a pool that does not exist. The
snapshot builder does the opposite: it marks that rule unusable with the reason
token `missing_pool` (`dataplane/userspace/nat_source.go:98-102`).

A surface disagreeing with the builder is the #6534 defect, and this one
occurred **inside `pkg/config/nat_not_installed_7473.go`** — the composition
exported specifically so the three #7473 surfaces could not answer *"which map,
and what if it is missing"* differently. They agreed with each other, and all
three were wrong.

## The fix is a deletion

The right answer was already in hand: `SourceNATPoolUnusableReason` returns
`"missing_pool"` for a nil pool, and a map miss yields exactly that nil. The
early return discarded a correct verdict the predicate was about to produce,
in favour of the single value meaning *nothing is wrong*.

Removing it makes the renderer and the builder share the **token**, not just
the intent — one vocabulary for one verdict.

## Reachability is the finding, and it's asserted in the test

| path | commit | reason returned |
|---|---|---|
| `CompileConfig` (strict) | **refuses** | branch unreachable — which is why it survived |
| `CompileConfigLenient` | **accepts** | `""` — rendered **armed** |

Lenient is the stored-config load and HA peer-sync path: a node that booted
from disk, or took a config from its peer. Precisely where a config arrives
without strict re-validation, and where the operator has no other signal that
the rule is dead.

**So the fixture compiles leniently.** A strict fixture cannot construct the
state at all and would pass on the broken code by never reaching the branch —
the fixture-cannot-enter-the-state trap, *guaranteed* here rather than merely
likely. The test also asserts that strict still refuses, so if that ever
changes the lenient-only framing fails loudly instead of quietly going stale.

## The empty-pool-name arm is unchanged, and pinned

It shares an exit with the fixed branch and means the **opposite**:
interface-mode source NAT has no pool to be unusable and *is* armed.
Conflating them would disarm every interface-mode rule in the tree — a much
larger population than the one being fixed, and a regression that renders
working NAT as dead.

The over-budget case from the original report is **not** a defect and is
untouched; it reaches `SourceNATPoolUnusableReason` and reports correctly.

## PR #8335 — screen: reject IHL < 5 in extract_screen_info (#8298) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

Branch: `fix/8298-ihl-floor`

## Verdict on the open question: it is a LIVE bypass, not defence-in-depth

The issue proved the mechanism and left **reachability** open, noting that the answer decides the severity. Traced per call site, and then bound with a test: a teardrop fragment reaches the live screen path without ever passing an `ihl < 20` rejection.

## The trace

`extract_screen_info`'s two fail-closed checks both guard the header being **longer** than the capture. `ihl_bytes` of 0..16 is *smaller* than the 20 bytes already asserted present, so `IHL < 5` passes both. `check_teardrop` then computes `hdr_len = ip_ihl * 4` and subtracts it from `ip_total_len`, so `IHL = 0` makes the payload read as the **whole** total length — and the canonical teardrop (a non-first fragment whose real payload is under 8 bytes) clears the `< 8` test written to catch it.

**It is reachable because of the fragment path specifically.** `parse_session_flow_from_bytes` returns `None` for a non-first fragment (#2344) — a **flowless classification, not a drop** — taken *before* any header-length validation. The packet then reaches `stage_screen_check`'s flowless branch, which calls `extract_screen_info`.

Neither `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` nor `poll_stages.rs` contains an `ihl` check at all. **Positive control:** `ihl < 20` rejecters *do* exist elsewhere (`nat64.rs`, `gre.rs`, `frame/generated.rs`, …), so the empty result means absence, not a bad pattern.

So the frames that skip flow parsing are exactly the non-first fragments this screen exists for.

**The issue named three call sites; there are four.** `poll_stages.rs:936` (`stage_screen_syn_cookie_ack_on_session_miss`) was missing from its enumeration — a floor, not a census.

## Tests: bound end-to-end, and aimed

Reachability is the claim, so the guard is **end-to-end through the real `stage_screen_check`**, not a `check_teardrop` unit test.

| cell | role |
|---|---|
| `flowless_teardrop_fragment_with_ihl_zero_is_still_dropped_8298` | **RED before this change.** Drives the live stage pipeline. |
| `flowless_teardrop_fragment_dropped_3064` (existing) | **control** — the same frame *without* the IHL mutation, passing throughout, proving the two differ by the IHL nibble alone |
| `flowless_legitimate_ihl5_fragment_is_not_dropped_8298` | **aimed-right control** — minimal legal header, 8-byte payload (the first size `< 8` admits) |

Measured in both directions: deleting the floor reds **only** the bypass cell; widening it to `< 6` reds **only** the control. A guard that fires on the mutant proves it has power; a control on the most nearly-correct input proves the power points the right way.

## Why the extractor, not `check_teardrop`

This is the documented fail-closed boundary — its own comment frames the contract as *"a runt/malformed capture shorter than the base header its own layout requires"*, which is exactly an IHL below 5, **declared rather than measured**. A clamp inside `check_teardrop` would leave every other consumer of `ip_ihl` believing the bogus value.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-rust` — 5198 collected, 0 failed
- [x] `make test-go` — 73 packages, 0 FAIL
- [x] `cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp` — 5064 collected, 0 failed (so the fail-closed floor rejects nothing legitimate across the suite)
- [x] both mutations above
- [ ] **cluster exercise — attempted twice, VOID both times. Reporting it as void rather than as evidence either way.**

### On the void cluster lane, in detail

The validation table wants screens exercised end-to-end. Two things went wrong, and both are mine:

1. **The standard smoke cannot see this change at all.** `stage_screen_check` is gated on `has_screen_state()`, and the cluster has no `security screen` config — so `extract_screen_info` is never reached. Running the standard smoke and reporting it green would have been exactly the #8280 failure: a pass that measures nothing.
2. **So I armed a teardrop profile on zone `lan` and sent crafted fragments with scapy — and the instrument was blind by construction.** I sampled `xpf_screen_drops_by_reason_total`, but a parse-error drop surfaces as `ip-malformed`, which bumps only the **aggregate** (`afxdp/mod.rs`: those reasons "are surfaced only through" it). The aggregate stayed 0 as well, and my arrival control failed to produce output — so I could not distinguish *"never arrived"* from *"arrived and was not dropped"*. That is a third state, not a result.

Config was removed on both nodes and verified (`grep -c ihl8298` → 0 on fw0 and fw1); nothing was left on the shared cluster.

What a real cluster reproduction needs, for whoever wants it: a working **arrival witness** (a counter or capture proving the crafted frame reaches stage 10) plus the **aggregate** drop counter rather than the per-reason one. Without the first, a zero is unreadable.

## PR #8342 — Revert #8314: the RG-ownership gate silences proxy-ARP on BOTH nodes [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-02)

**neither** node for an RG-owned interface, where before it was on both.

## Measured on the cluster

Acceptance run at `9417667ee`:

```
FAIL  the RG OWNER does not answer proxy-ARP for 172.16.80.7 (fw0=0 fw1=0)
FAIL  a pool-mode TCP flow could not connect after the role change
```

again after the smoke. The failure moved from two answerers to zero.

## Cause

The fix borrowed `isRethMasterState`, whose own doc says it *"returns false if no
instances exist for the RG"*. For the DHCP relay it was copied from, "no
instances -> don't relay" avoids a duplicate — **failing closed is safe there**.

`redundancy-group 1`, so the gate consults `isRethMasterState(1)`, and whatever
makes that false on a node reporting primary for every RG closes the gate on
both.

**A predicate's fail DIRECTION belongs to its consumer, not to its name.**

Fixing forward was arguable — pool-mode TCP was already broken before #8314
(measured in the same second: `.230` interface-mode 5.95 Gbit/s, `.240`
pool-mode timed out), so the revert buys nothing *for the pool case*.

It is the **other** entries that decide it. The gate applies to every proxy-ARP
entry on an RG-owned interface, and:

- `docs/feature-gaps.md:292` records Proxy ARP for NAT as a shipped, **"Done"**,
  **High**-priority feature — *"Required when SNAT pool, DNAT, or static-NAT
  external addresses are on same L2 segment."*
- `test/incus/xpf-cluster-fw0.conf:171` carries exactly the affected pattern —
  a `proxy-arp` block on `reth0`, which is in RG 1.

So this is working-to-broken for any config using a documented feature in the
supported way, in exchange for nothing on the case it was meant to fix. That is
the wrong side of the trade, and it is live on master now.

## PR #8343 — cluster: key peer redundancy groups by the local config id (#8337) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8337-rg-id-wire-key`

## Summary

**#8322 did not fix this** — it tightened the *strict* commit gate; the wire cast and the runtime were untouched.

The defect is a **key disagreement**, not a wrong number. `buildHeartbeat` narrowed the RG id with a bare `uint8(...)` — directly beside a `clampWireWeight` that saturates, so the hazard was known at that line — and `handlePeerHeartbeat` keyed `peerGroups` by whatever byte arrived, while **every reader indexes that map by the raw config id** (`election.go`, `status.go`, `failover.go`, `upgrade_drain.go`, `group_state.go`). For any id whose low byte differs the two keys never meet, and `election.go` turns the miss into `peerAlive && peerGroup == nil -> electLocalPrimary, "Peer has no RG info"`.

A node receiving and parsing its peer's heartbeats concludes the peer has no RG info and **elects itself primary**. Where the peer has done the same, that is a second primary reached through *successful* heartbeat exchange.

## The fix is on the producer — the ~8 consumers are untouched because they were right

`peerGroups` is now keyed by the local config id the wire byte resolves to, which is how every reader already indexes it.

Both directions go through **one function**: `wireRGID` narrows an id onto the wire, and `localRGIDForWireByte` matches a received byte by asking `wireRGID(local id) == byte` — the same computation the sender performed. They cannot drift without changing `wireRGID` itself. That is what "agree by construction" has to mean; a comment asserting agreement is the shape that has failed repeatedly here.

**The issue named one unsaturated cast; there were two.** The monitor path's `RGID: uint8(ls.RedundancyGroup)` sat beside its own `clampWireWeight` with the identical defect. Peer monitors are resolved back the same way. Re-deriving the set rather than taking the named one is what found it.

**Saturate, not refuse.** Declining to advertise an out-of-range group leaves the peer with no entry — the same `peerGroup == nil` the wrap produces, so the "fix" would reproduce the bug. Two ids above the ceiling do collapse onto 255; that is inherent to a single-byte field, not introduced here, and it is documented at the function.

## Reachability, and the pattern behind it

Strict refuses these ids; `Store.Load` and `Store.SyncApply` compile **leniently** and admit them with warnings — persisted-config boot, and HA peer sync.

This is the second instance of that shape today after #8329, and the generalisation is worth stating: **a strict gate is not a bound on the value, it is a bound on what an operator can type.** Any invariant enforced only at strict commit should be assumed reachable through the lenient paths.

## Tests

The fixture is built through **`CompileConfigLenient`**, deliberately: a strict fixture cannot construct the state, so a test built on one would pass against the broken code **by never entering it**.

The heartbeat is produced by the **peer's own `buildHeartbeat`**, not hand-written. Writing `GroupID: 255` would encode this fix's own output as the fixture and pass even if the sender were wrong — what must hold is that the two sides *agree*.

Both cases run; the in-range id is the **over-correction control**, and getting that wrong breaks every working cluster while not showing in the 300 case.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|

## PR #8344 — test/incus: assert the proxy-ARP owner set and the pool data path (#8297, #8341) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `test/8297-acceptance`

The harness that found #8297, #8314's over-correction and #8341 — landed rather than left on a branch.

## Two cells the pool phase could not see

**1. The standby must not answer (#8297)** — read from the **kernel** (`ip neigh show proxy` on both nodes), not from config. The config said the same thing on both nodes throughout; it was the installed `NTF_PROXY` entry that differed from what RG ownership required, so a config-derived assertion would have been **green on the shipped defect**.

Three outcomes, because a one-sided assertion ships the opposite failure:

| observed | verdict |
|---|---|
| both answer | the defect — **KNOWN #8297** |
| owner only | **FIXED** — `known_gap` fails, demanding promotion |
| neither | **hard FAIL** — the #8314 over-correction, strictly worse than the defect it replaced, never a tracked gap |

**2. The pool data path — pointed at #8341, not #8297.** Measured: with the proxy-ARP entry installed on the **RG owner only**, the exact state a correct #8297 fix produces, a pool-mode TCP flow still times out while an interface-mode control from the same host in the same run reaches 6.29 Gbit/s. The duplicate responder was not the cause. Labelling this cell #8297 would make it go green the day #8297 is fixed and **read as validating a fix it does not touch** — the same "one dimension read as validation of another" shape this harness exists to prevent.

## Why `known_gap` and not `fail`

A plain `fail()` makes every lane's `make test-failover` red for bugs none of them touched, and a smoke that is red by default is a smoke people stop reading.

But a gap that merely prints and passes is worse: the day it is fixed, nothing says so, the cell keeps reporting a gap that no longer exists, and the real assertion it should have become is never written.

So it asserts in **both** directions — still broken is `KNOWN` and uncounted; no longer broken is a `FAIL` naming the promotion now owed — and the summary carries the open issue numbers every run:

```
Failover test: 20 passed, 0 failed, 2 known-gap (#8297 #8341)
```

## Verification

- Helper **control-tested in both directions** before any cluster run: `broken=1` → KNOWN, no FAIL; `broken=0` → FAIL demanding promotion.
- Cluster run on reverted master `3e20f3b18`: **20 passed, 0 failed, 2 known-gap**, with `fw0=1 fw1=1` independently confirming the revert restored both answerers.

## A discarded run, recorded rather than quietly re-run

A first landing run reported `fw0=0 fw1=0` and was **discarded, not reported**. The branch had not rebased — an earlier attempt failed on unstaged changes and I did not re-run it — so `cluster-deploy` built the **pre-revert tree** and the run measured this branch's own reverted-away gate, not master. Had I reported it, it would have read as "the revert did not work".

It is evidence for exactly one thing: the third assertion branch fires correctly on the over-corrected state.

## PR #8347 — applications: a dangling leaf on the direct body is not a permit-all [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8339-dangling-application-leaf`

A recognized value-taking leaf left with **no value** on an `applications
application <name>` **direct** body committed on the **strict** path and then
matched every port.

`applicationDirectLeaves` synthesises a 1-key childless node, `nodeVal` returns
`""`, `resolveAppPort` passes it through, and `portInSpec("")` returns `true`
for **every** port. So `protocol tcp destination-port` — one token short, an
ordinary typo — turned a single-port application into an all-TCP permit, and
the config renders exactly as the operator typed it.

The guard has existed for inline `term` bodies since #6564. It had no direct
twin.

## Extended, not duplicated — and the split matters

The obvious "share everything" is wrong here:

| | term path | direct body |
|---|---|---|
| **detection** | consumes `keys[i+1]` → dangling is `i+1 >= len(keys)` | reads the node's own value → dangling is `nodeVal(prop) == ""` |
| **contract** | *which keywords require a value* | **the same question** |

The grammars park the value in different places, so the detection cannot be
common. But *which* keywords require one is a property of the Junos statement,
not of the shape it was typed in — so `valueTakingTermLeaves` became
**`valueTakingApplicationLeaves`**: one set, both switches, a coverage gate per
switch. Two sets would have drifted apart exactly the way the two guards did,
which is the defect being fixed.

The existing #6564 coverage test **moved with the rename** rather than being
left pinning a symbol that no longer exists.

## The exclusions are derived from the switches, not assumed

- **`description`** consumes a value, but a dangling one drops a cosmetic field
  and widens nothing. Refusing it adds commit failures with no security
  benefit.
- **`term`** is a container whose name is consumed by descending.

Both stay out, **pinned by an over-correction control** — a guard that refuses
working configs on upgrade is worse than the fail-open it replaces: the
fail-open widens one application, the over-correction bricks a commit.

## The branch that discards the parent struct

Term-bearing bodies throw `app` away (#6524 documents this one line above the
carry it already needed for `UnknownDirectLeaves`). The new verdict is carried
onto each generated term for the same reason — without it, a dangling direct
leaf on a term-bearing application escapes the gate entirely **while every
other test here still passes**.

## PR #8349 — test: catch a ledger row a merge dropped, which lint cannot see (#8346) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8346-ledger-merge-completeness`

## The gap

`ledger-lint` checks the rows that are **present** — a repeated `run_id` with a differing payload, a malformed row, an empty file. A row that is simply **missing** leaves a well-formed, internally consistent, perfectly lint-clean file. Nothing in the surviving rows says anything is gone.

That is the *fails-to-a-value-indistinguishable-from-healthy* shape, and it is not hypothetical.

## What happened

`.git/config` contains **`merge.union.driver = true`** — a custom merge driver named `union` whose command is a no-op. A custom driver **shadows git's built-in `union`**, so every `merge=union` file silently resolves to "ours": no conflict, no warning, not even a line in the merge summary, while `git check-attr` reports `merge: union` throughout.

**Three real gate records were lost this way**, and were noticed by hand. `ledger-lint` was green the entire time.

| same two commits, merged | rows |
|---|---|
| in this repo | **5** — three dropped |
| in a fresh clone (no local config) | **8** — correct union |

**The config is not changed here.** It is the shared repo's, so that is the maintainer's call — and it is worth knowing *why* it was added before removing it. If the suppression was deliberate, the correct shape is a differently-named driver, not shadowing a built-in.

## The guard

`lint_merge_completeness` compares the merge **result** against its **parents**: the ledger must retain every `run_id` present in either.

**Validated against the actual incident, not a synthetic one.** Run on the real merge commit it names all three dropped ids and exits 1; the same two commits merged in a clean clone report `8 run_id(s), none dropped`.

**A set check, not a count**, and the difference is load-bearing: a merge that drops one row and adds another leaves the count identical, so a count-based guard passes on exactly the corruption it exists to catch. `test_a_count_preserving_swap_is_still_caught` pins that, and mutating the set check into a count reds it.

**Mechanism-independent on purpose.** It never asks *why* a row vanished, so it survives the config being fixed, the storage moving to one-file-per-run, or a future driver regressing — and a `git rm` of a shard under `ledger.d/` is just as invisible as a dropped line.

On a non-merge HEAD it prints `nothing to check` rather than a bare pass, because "checked nothing" and "checked and clean" must not look alike in a runner whose other legs already guard against the empty-set pass.

## A comment that overstated its guard

`lint_ledger`'s docstring claimed it was *"what catches that reasoning being wrong rather than trusting it"*. It is not — it cannot see a drop. The docstring now says so and points at the check that can. **A comment overstating a guard's reach is how the gap stayed invisible.**

## The control, and its first draft being wrong

`test_lint_ledger_is_blind_to_the_same_drop` runs the **row** linter over the damaged result and asserts it reports **clean** — the argument for this check existing at all.

Its first draft failed for a *schema* reason instead: hand-rolled fixture rows omitted required keys, which made it look like lint had detected the drop. Fixtures now build through the module's own `row()` helper. **A control that passes for the wrong reason is worse than no control**, and this one nearly shipped that way.

## Test plan

- [x] `bash scripts/run-selftests.sh` — **145 passed, 0 failed**, including the new `ledger-merge-completeness` leg
- [x] `python3 test/incus/ledger_compare_test.py` — 38 tests OK (34 existing + 4 new)
- [x] guard run against the **real** dropped-row merge → exits 1, names all three ids
- [x] matched control: same commits in a clean clone → `none dropped`
- [x] mutations: set-check → count reds 2 cells; guard deleted reds 2 cells

## PR #8350 — cluster: the interface-monitor reconciler owns only non-reserved debts (#8338) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8338-reserved-monitor-debts`

## The defect

`reconcileMonitorDebtsLocked` builds its desired set solely from `rg.InterfaceMonitors`, so a reserved monitor key is never in it, and the delete loop exempted only `isIPMonitorName`. **Every config commit that reached monitor reconciliation deleted the `__dataplane-arm__` election debt.**

`applyDataplaneArmTrack` is edge-triggered — called only from the three arm-transition helpers — so a commit taken while the dataplane was **already** unarmed reinstalled nothing. The node kept forwarding no transit and lost the penalty that said so, and could then win an election and hold the redundancy group as a blackhole, with cluster status reporting an ordinary election.

## The fix inverts the default rather than adding a second exemption

`monitor.go` described this reconciler as owning *"the rest"* — **that phrasing is the fail-open**: any debt class that is not an interface monitor falls into "the rest" and is deleted. Ownership is now positive (skip every key it does not own), so a third reserved class is safe by default instead of requiring the next author to remember an exemption.

That sentence is corrected **at its source**, not just at the call site, because it is the claim a future reader builds on.

The category is named once: `reservedMonitorNames` is a single list read by both `isReservedMonitorName` and the guard test, so predicate and test cannot disagree about what is reserved.

**Why not fully structural (separate storage):** the shared `monitorWeights`/`MonitorFails` layout is deliberate, documented where `isIPMonitorName` is defined, and the IP class already depends on it. A third storage location would give the weight computation two places to read — a worse shape than the one being fixed.

## The tree already documented this trap, and one feature dodged it

`status.go:113-116` records that #6387 used a **dedicated manager field** for the config-sync failure *"so `reconcileMonitorDebtsLocked` cannot wipe it on the next UpdateConfig."*

The trap was written down, #6387 sidestepped it, and #7178's arm-track walked straight in. That is the argument for inverting the default rather than adding a third exemption — the next one will walk in too.

## Operator-visible change, called out so it is not read as a leak

`__dataplane-arm__` now **persists** in the `Monitor-failures` column while the dataplane is unarmed, instead of vanishing at the next commit. That is the operator seeing *why* the node is penalised. A penalty with no visible cause is worse than a noisy column.

## Tests

**The fixture enters the unarmed state before committing**, which is the whole difficulty: a cell that commits while ARMED passes against the broken code, because in that state there is no debt to delete.

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| revert to the ip-only exemption | **only** the `__dataplane-arm__` subtest, at weight 1 → 255 (the blackhole condition itself); the ip subtest stays green as the discriminating control |
| make the reservation exempt everything | **only** the ordinary-monitor cell, at 155 — an over-broad reservation would strand real monitor debt and reintroduce #5080 |

Three cells: the reserved debt survives an unrelated commit (driven over `reservedMonitorNames`, so the IP class rides along as the control); the arm transition that legitimately **clears** the debt still clears it (over-correction — getting it wrong pins a node penalised forever after one arm failure); an ordinary interface-monitor debt is still reconciled away when its monitor leaves the config.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-go` — 73 packages, 0 FAIL
- [x] `make test-rust` — 5198 collected, 0 failed
- [x] `go test -race ./pkg/cluster/` — ok, 53s (a real run, not a skip)
- [x] both mutations above
- [x] `make test-failover` — **20 `PASS` lines counted** against the summary's "20 passed", 0 FAIL, 0 `Terminated|Killed|Timeout`; 21.1 Gbps, IPv6 5/5, fw1 took 11 synced sessions; the two tracked `KNOWN` gaps (#8297, #8341) present and correctly not counted as assertions

## PR #8353 — docs: record two verification rules from the union-driver incident [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `docs/8348-verification-discipline`

Two rules earned by the `merge.union.driver` incident (#8348), added to `docs/engineering-style.md` as a new **Verification discipline** section.

**1. A check you had to manufacture to pass is measuring your setup, not the system.**
The key was residue from PR #1582 (rejected, May 2026), whose checklist asserted `git config --get-all merge.union.driver` returns the built-in. The built-in has no such key — a healthy repo returns nothing — so the check could only pass if someone set it. Passing the verification *required creating the defect*, and the residue outlived the rejected PR by four months. Usable test: **would this step pass on a fresh clone with nothing done to it?**

Corollaries recorded: never name a custom merge driver after a built-in; and a detector docstring is a claim about what it can see (the ledger lint overstated its reach, which is how a dropped row stayed invisible).

**2. Tell a peer what baseline to expect, so their green becomes falsifiable.**
A smoke reported `20 passed, 0 failed` from the *older* cell set, which coincidentally also totals 20. Caught only because a peer named the two `KNOWN` lines to expect. A summary line is a count of whatever ran — naming the expected signal is a property of the brief, not the reader.

Docs-only, no code paths touched. Credit to lane-7209 and lane-7174, who found the mechanism, reproduced it with independent controls, and sharpened both rules.

## 1 — `test: give the ledger one file per run` (#8346)

`test/results/ledger.d/<run_id>.json`, one shard per gate run, replacing the
single appended `ledger.jsonl`. Two writers never touch the same path, so the
conflict is removed **by construction** rather than by a rule people must
remember under merge pressure. The emitter writes under a temp name in the same
directory and renames — `rename(2)` is atomic where the old append needed
`flock`, and a reader globbing while a gate finishes never sees a half-written
shard.

`.gitattributes` **loses** its `merge=union` rule rather than retargeting it.
One file per run needs no driver, and #8348 is why that matters: a custom driver
*named* `union` whose command was the no-op `true` shadowed git's built-in for
months, so every `merge=union` path silently resolved to "ours" and three real
gate records were lost. A rule whose driver can be disarmed from a file nobody
reads does not belong in the path of a data file.

### Keeping #8349's guard armed across the move — the sharpest thing here

`lint_merge_completeness` compares the merge result's run-id set against each
**parent's**, and a parent predating this change has no `ledger.d/` at all. A
source reading only the new layout returns the **empty set** for it, `missing`
is empty, and the guard passes **vacuously** — loudest on the one merge most
likely to drop rows: *this change's own*, whose other parent is legacy-only.

So `run_ids_at_rev` reads **both layouts at every revision**: the legacy file
via `git show`, and the shard directory via `git ls-tree --name-only`, where the
run_id **is the filename** and nothing has to parse. The second source is
strictly the more robust — a shard whose *content* was damaged still contributes
its id — and `lint_shard_names` keeps it trustworthy by pinning filename ==
payload id.

The set logic moved to `lint_merge_completeness_ids`; the text-taking signature
was **kept** as the public door, so #8349's cells still drive the guard through
the path they were written against rather than being quietly decommissioned.

* **The guard validates this migration.** 10 ids in the pre-migration parent

## PR #8360 — routing: drive the helper FIB from kernel route events [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7437-route-listener`

#7409's importer made the helper FIB agree with the kernel FIB, but the snapshot
was only republished on an operator commit or an ip-monitoring actuation. A
route the kernel learned in between stayed absent, so traffic for it resolved
`NoRoute` and took the unadjudicated reinject #7409 exists to stop — forwarded
by the kernel with **no zone policy, session, NAT or screen**. The window was
"time to the next commit", unbounded in practice on a quiet box with a flapping
peer.

## The listener marks; it does not publish

Every publish is a full snapshot replace over a control socket whose deadline
scales with payload size, and CLAUDE.md is explicit that a new caller above 1/s
starves session installs during bulk sync. Under BGP churn a per-event push is a
control-plane brownout whose failure mode is **not a visible error**.

Its imported-table predicate calls `routing.LearnedRouteTableIDs` — the
importer's *own* function — so the two cannot disagree about which events
matter.

## Why `pkg/coalesce` is new rather than extracted (shape 3)

`ipmon.Engine` entangles the same loop with policy state, next-hop resolution
and `publishEnabled`, the HA-standby publication gate. Refactoring an HA-gated
engine inside a feature PR would surface any regression on the cluster rather
than in review, and attribute it to the route listener.

So it is written **as the type ipmon would adopt**, its adoption is filed as
**#8354**, and `pkg/ipmon` is untouched here — verified, the diff against master
is empty. Two implementations of one discipline is a real cost; tracking it is
what keeps it time-boxed rather than structural.

It is ipmon's discipline exactly: `dirtyGen` bumped on every mark so a change
arriving *during* an actuation is not swallowed; `lastActuation` advanced when
the attempt **starts**, so a failing actuation retries once per throttle window
instead of hot-looping; dirty cleared only when converged **and** the generation
is unchanged. Four mutations, each red.

## The rate is asserted, not that a push happened

A naive per-event implementation passes "a push occurred" trivially. Against an
injected clock, numbers fixed **before** the run:

| scenario | expected | measured |
|---|---|---|
| 50 marks inside 100 ms | exactly 1 actuation | 1 |
| 200 events over 10 s | ≤ 4 | ≤ 4 |

A rate assertion written with sleeps races wall time and gets widened until it
proves nothing.

## PR #8361 — config: warn at commit when a chassis cluster has no NTP server (#8357) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8357-cluster-ntp-advisory`

## Summary

Split out of #7487, which closed as **operationally closed**. This is the **prevention** half; #6708 closed the diagnosis half at runtime.

Cross-node fabric RPC authenticates with `HMAC(PSK, unix_time / 30)` and the verifier accepts ±1 window, so beyond ~a minute of skew every inbound fabric RPC rejects — permanently, because skew does not self-correct without NTP. #6708 measured it: **141 s of skew, `NTPSynchronized=no` on both nodes, every cross-node RPC dead.** The symptom the operator saw named **sessions**; the cause was the clock.

**The cluster simply had `system ntp` unset — and that is a product gap, not operator error.** The appliance ships chrony installed and enabled with every default source deliberately commented out (`scripts/image/bake.py:543`), `set system ntp server` is a config leaf, and xpfd renders `/etc/chrony/sources.d/xpf.sources` itself. A cluster with no `system ntp server` therefore has **no time source by construction**, and the first thing that tells the operator is a dead control plane.

## Three decisions worth reviewing

**It names fabric RPC, not "the clock."** #6708's whole finding was that the symptom and the cause were far apart. An advisory saying only "no NTP configured" recreates that gap one layer earlier — the operator would have to already know fabric RPC depends on the clock. Saying what *breaks* is what makes it actionable where it is emitted.

**Warning, never an error.** An operator legitimately configures a cluster before NTP is reachable — off-net staging, a box being built. Hard-rejecting that would be worse than the fault it prevents.

**Strict path only**, and this is the half most easily got wrong. `CompileConfigLenient` / `CompileConfigForNodeLenient` back `Store.Load` (persisted-config boot) and `Store.SyncApply` (HA peer sync); without suppression this fires on **every boot and every peer sync of a config committed long ago**, which trains operators to ignore warnings. `compileOpts` has no single "is lenient" predicate — it is a bag of named per-feature flags — so this gets its own, matching the file's convention. Unlike its neighbours it suppresses an *advisory* rather than downgrading an *error*, and the comment says so.

One helper shared by both compile entries rather than the condition written at each: the two carry near-identical warning blocks, and a duplicated condition drifts.

## Tests — five cells, three mutations, each killing its own

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| remove the emit | **only** the strict cell |
| remove the lenient suppression | **only** the tolerant cell — *both* subtests (`Store.Load` and `Store.SyncApply`) |
| drop the cluster-only guard | **only** the standalone cell |

The tolerant cell is the **discriminating control** and the one a strict-only fixture cannot see.

The keyed fixture also matters: the strict path hard-rejects a cluster with no `authentication-key`, so an unkeyed fixture fails for an unrelated reason and reads as *"the advisory is absent"*. It cost three red cells before I noticed, which is exactly how a fixture passes for the wrong reason.

## Golden

`TestCompileGolden4406` reds on this change, correctly, and the baseline is regenerated.

**Verified the delta rather than regenerating on faith:** 6 insertions, **all on STRICT cells**, across two cluster configs (`ha-cluster-userspace` and `ha-cluster`), **zero on lenient cells**. Worth recording that the test's failure message lists every case in a group, so it initially read as though the lenient cells had changed too — attributing each insertion to its case key is what showed they had not. Regenerating without that check would have hidden a broken suppression behind a green golden.

## Test plan

- [x] `make test-go` — 73 packages, 0 FAIL
- [x] `go test ./pkg/config/ -count=1` — ok
- [x] all three mutations above
- [ ] **no cluster smoke, and why:** this adds a warning string on the strict compile path and changes no runtime behaviour — `stage_screen_check`-style "the smoke cannot see it" applies. `make test-go` is the gate that can observe it. Stating that rather than running a green that would measure nothing.

Refs #8357, #7487, #6708.

Closes #8357

## PR #8362 — frr: deny an emptied BGP policy chain [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7625-emptied-policy-chain-deny`

Implements the #7625 decision: **emptied chain → bounded deny; narrowed chain → unchanged, pending measurement.**

## The hole

`filterDefinedPolicies` returns the surviving subset of an authored chain. When *every* member names an undefined policy-statement the chain empties, and an empty chain resolved to `""` — so no `route-map ... in|out` line was emitted at all.

Under the FRR semantics established in #6807, that is backwards. A named-but-undefined route-map **denies**; only an **absent** attachment **permits**. So the direction whose filter failed hardest ended up unfiltered. Confirmed empirically before the fix — the rendered section for a neighbor with `import [GHOST]`:

```
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 10.0.2.1 activate
 exit-address-family
```

No route-map line. Permit-all on a direction the operator explicitly filtered.

## The fix

The four neighbor attachment sites now resolve through `bgpNeighborImportRef` / `bgpNeighborExportRef`, which map the emptied case onto a bounded explicit deny under a reserved name — the same shape #6807 uses for the adjacent oversized-expansion case. Reference and definition are emitted **together**, so #6807's property (every referenced route-map name is defined in the same managed section) holds **by construction** rather than by the reference being dropped, as the decision required.

The definition is emitted *outside* the `PolicyOptions != nil` guard that wraps the other route-map renderers: a nil `PolicyOptions` makes every authored name a ghost, which is exactly when the deny is referenced and when skipping its definition would leave it dangling.

## The direction asymmetry (found while verifying, not assumed)

A bare protocol token (`static`, `direct`) in an `export` list means `redistribute <proto>` on a separate path, so such a list **also** filters to empty — but attaching a deny there would withdraw every route to the peer, a worse outage than the bug. Inbound has no redistribute construct, so the same token is a name that resolves to nothing and **must** deny (`config.TestBGPNeighborImportProtocolTokenRejected` is the strict path saying so).

My first implementation had this exclusion direction-agnostic, which would have preserved the permit-all on a leniently-loaded `import static`. Reading that sibling test is what caught it. Both directions are now pinned by cells that fail on each other's mistake.

## Scope held

**Narrowed chains are unchanged.** Whether a surviving-subset chain should instead deny depends on how FRR evaluates a chain whose earlier member accepts — the measurement #7625 tracks separately. Not assumed here.

**No commit-time surface was added, because none is reachable.** Strict commit already rejects an undefined policy reference in either direction (`TestBGPNeighborImportTypoRejected`). These configs reach the renderer only on the lenient load / HA peer-sync / rollback path (#1960) — committed on an older binary, or arrived from a peer. That is the population the renderer fix serves.

## Fail-closed belt

A render-side collision guard refuses the apply if an operator policy-statement carries the reserved deny name — FRR merges same-named route-maps, so a merge could fuse permit sequences into the deny and reopen the hole. Same posture as `bgpComposedChainCollision` (#5277) and `redistAliasCollision` (#5116).

## Two stale rationales corrected

Rather than left to drift:

- `routing_export_ref_test.go` claimed *"the render path then drops the dangling route-map in (no permit-all leak)"* — wrong in both halves, and now wrong in a second way.
- `filterDefinedPolicies`' comment described the drop as deliberately left as is.

## PR #8364 — Cap binding plans at the slot-keyed map capacity [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7497-binding-slot-capacity-cap`

## What this is

Prerequisite work for #7497, not a fix for a defect reachable today. Stated plainly up front because an earlier revision of my analysis on the issue claimed otherwise and was wrong; that claim is [retracted](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7497#issuecomment-5519592764).

The shim addresses binding rows two different ways, and only one was bounded:

```
lib.rs  USERSPACE_BINDINGS.get(ifindex * 16 + queue)   1,048,576 entries   guarded (#814)
lib.rs  USERSPACE_HEARTBEAT.get(binding.slot)              4,096 entries   unguarded
lib.rs  USERSPACE_XSK_MAP.redirect(binding.slot, 0)        4,096 entries   unguarded
```

`slot` is assigned **densely** by the helper planner — a plain `slot += 1` counter over the bindings it planned (`replan_bindings_from_candidates`) — so it is a ceiling on the **total number of bindings**, not on any ifindex or queue id. The `#814` write-side guards check the composed index against a bound **256x larger** than the maps that actually get indexed by `slot`, so a slot they admit can still be unaddressable.

Nothing capped the binding count at plan time. The one clamp in the area, `effectiveWorkers`, bounds the **worker** count (`heartbeatMapCap / heartbeatSlotsPerWorker` = 128) — a different quantity from the one that indexes these maps.

## Changes

- **`userspace-xdp/src/binding_index.rs`** — `BINDING_SLOT_MAP_MAX_ENTRIES`, replacing the two bare `4096` literals the map declarations carried.
- **`userspace-dp/.../planning.rs`** — refuse a plan whose `queue_count * interfaces` exceeds the cap, naming the interface count, the queue count and the limit. Modeled on the `#6211 F2` refusal in the same function, which already establishes the fail-closed precedent.
- **`pkg/dataplane/`** — `BindingSlotMapMaxEntries` pinned against the **compiled** shim in `validateUserspaceShimSpecWith`.
- **`docs/afxdp-packet-processing.md`** — that document bounded the queue/ifindex axis in detail and never mentioned the slot axis; it does now.
- **`pkg/dataplane/userspace_xdp_manifest.json`** — refreshed via `make generate`, because the manifest hashes shim sources by content and both changed. `TestUserspaceXDPShimObjectMatchesSourceManifest` caught this on the first full run — the same source-vs-object boundary the Go ABI pin exists to cover.

  Note that `userspace_xdp_bpfel.o` itself is **unchanged**: the rebuilt object is byte-identical, because the named constant equals the literal it replaced. That is worth stating rather than glossing — it is direct evidence the shim edit is codegen-neutral, and the verifier gate re-passed at 31.31% headroom.
- **`docs/log/7497.md`** — action log (`_Log.md` has been closed to new entries since #6874).

## Two deliberate properties

**Plan time, not registration.** `register_xsk_slot` (`afxdp/bpf_map/ha.rs`, called from `worker/mod.rs:904`) runs during bringup, after the previous bindings have been torn down. Failing there takes forwarding down instead of declining to change it — which is what acceptance criterion 4 on the issue forbids.

**Refuse, don't truncate.** Capping to the first 4,096 would leave the surplus RX queues unbound, and an unbound queue does not reduce throughput: the shim takes `drop_degraded_transit` on `BINDING_MISSING`, so every transit packet arriving there is dropped while the interface still reads up and most traffic still flows. That is an availability failure indistinguishable from a healthy one. A refusal is loud and diagnosable.

## Three spellings, each boundary asserted

The value appears in the shim, the helper and Go. Rather than pinning any one of them to a literal — which would encode which spelling is trusted and stay green when the others moved — each boundary is asserted:

| boundary | mechanism |
|---|---|
| shim source ↔ helper | host test `#[path]`-includes `binding_index.rs` and compares the two constants |
| shim **object** ↔ Go | `validateUserspaceShimSpecWith` checks the embedded map's `max_entries` |

These are genuinely different boundaries: the shim `.o` is git-tracked and rebuilt only by `make generate`, so source and object can drift independently.

`make test-go` and `make test-rust` both green.

## PR #8365 — frr: measure narrowed-chain evaluation, and make narrowing visible [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `measure/8363-narrowed-chain-eval`

The #7625 remainder, measured. **The stated objection is refuted — and the measurement found a different, worse hazard that changes what the fix can be.**

Expected result was recorded before running: *an accepting earlier member terminates evaluation, so the deny catches only the fall-through and the objection dissolves.* Half right, and the half I got wrong is the important half.

## Fact 1 — the objection is refuted

xpf emits `on-match next` only for **non-terminating** terms, so a `then accept` term renders as a bare `permit` and FRR stops there. Composed `[ACCEPTER, SYNTH-DENY]`:

```
route-map C-xpf-chain permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list PL      <-- no on-match next: STOPS here
exit
route-map C-xpf-chain deny 20         <-- fall-through only
exit
```

A route the surviving member accepts is permitted at seq 10 and never reaches the deny. The argument that a synthesized deny would take a works-but-narrowed config to deny-all, *as stated*, is wrong.

## Fact 2 — position is the real hazard

A synthesized deny is a chain member with a terminating **default** action, and `renderComposedRouteMap` does `terminated = true; if terminated { break }`. So a deny at a non-final ghost position doesn't shadow the rest of the chain — it **deletes** it. Composed `[SYNTH-DENY, ACCEPTER]` renders in full as:

```
route-map C3-xpf-chain deny 10
exit
```

Deny-all. It is the outcome the objection feared, reached by a mechanism nobody had named, and it is invisible in the rendered output because there is nothing left that looks wrong.

**Consequence:** a synthesized deny is safe **iff the undefined members form a SUFFIX** of the authored chain. Ghost-last (a policy appended and never defined, or since removed) is safe. Ghost-first or ghost-middle must keep the surviving subset, because the "fix" there is a routing outage.

## What this PR does

**Commit 1 — the measurement, bound as cells.** No behaviour change. Includes the control fact 1 requires: a non-terminating member must be shown to *do* continue into the deny, or "no `on-match next`" is only measuring a renderer that never emits it. A future attempt at the narrowed fix now trips over the position constraint instead of rediscovering it in production.

**Commit 2 — visibility.** Behaviour still unchanged; what changes is that narrowing is no longer silent. `warnNarrowedChains` logs each site with what was authored, what is applied, and what was discarded. A test asserts the narrowed render is **byte-identical** to its surviving subset, so visibility cannot silently become a behaviour change.

Three shapes are deliberately not reported, because each resembles narrowing and is not: an **emptied** chain (already warned by the #7625 deny path — reporting it here would describe one config error twice), an **intact** chain, and an **export** chain naming a bare protocol token (`static` is a redistribute verb, not a failed policy reference — the same asymmetry the emptied path encodes, and why the detector takes a direction flag rather than one rule).

**Commit 3 — operational carriage.** The signal has to be operational, not commit-time: strict already rejects an undefined reference in both directions, so the entire affected population arrives via `Store.Load` / `SyncApply` on a reboot, peer sync or rollback, and a commit warning would reach nobody in it. Two gauges, both rebuilt per render with an explicit 0:

| gauge | meaning |
|---|---|
| `xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed` | attachments filtered by less than authored. Alert on > 0. |
| `xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed_deny_safe` | the suffix-shaped subset — where a deny *would* be safe |

Deliberately **separate** from `xpf_frr_route_maps_quarantined`: that gauge's documented meaning is that every route on those neighbors is being *withdrawn*, with "alert on > 0". A narrowed chain withdraws nothing, so folding it in would fire a withdrawal alert for a non-withdrawal and make the existing alert rule wrong. Same carrier pattern, separate series.

The `deny_safe` split records the safety condition while behaviour is still unchanged, so the decision on whether to ever synthesize a deny is sized on how often the safe shape occurs rather than on the kind of argument this measurement just overturned.

## PR #8366 — frr: refuse a composed chain that forges the reserved deny name [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8362-forgeable-deny-name`

**A live defect in merged #8362.** Found while confirming, at the lead's request, that Fact 2 of the #8363 measurement (a synthesized deny at a non-final chain position *deletes* every later member) does not affect the emptied-chain deny.

It does not — an emptied chain has no surviving members by definition, so the deny is always the sole member and there is nothing after it to delete. That reading is confirmed. But the check surfaced a different collision, and #7625's own comment is what was wrong.

## The defect

The comment justifying the reserved deny name claimed `ReservedChainSuffix` made it unforgeable, because strict commit bars operator policy-statements from that namespace. Strict rejects a name that **ends** in `-xpf-chain`. It does not stop several legally named policies from **joining** into it:

```
composedChainName(["xpf","emptied","chain"]) == "xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain"
emptiedChainDenyName                         == "xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain"
```

Rendered end to end — a composed chain on one neighbor, an emptied chain on another — three definitions land under one name and **both existing guards return `nil`**:

```
emptiedChainDenyCollision = <nil>
bgpComposedChainCollision = <nil>

route-map xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain permit 10   <- composed chain
route-map xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain permit 20   <- composed chain
route-map xpf-emptied-chain-xpf-chain deny 10     <- emptied deny
```

FRR merges same-named route-maps into one object, so the emptied neighbor — the one that **must** deny — acquires a `permit 20` catch-all and **the unfiltered-direction hole #7625 closed reopens**. The damage is bidirectional: the legitimate chain's seq 10 collides with the deny's seq 10, corrupting that neighbor's filter in the same merge.

`emptiedChainDenyCollision` only looks for a policy-statement *literally named* that. `bgpComposedChainCollision` checks composed names against policy-statements and against other chains — never against the reserved deny. Each guard's blind spot is exactly the other's case.

## Why a guard and not a structural fix

I looked for unforgeability first. Policy-statement names have no banned character set, so every prefix of the reserved name is a legal `-`-join of legal names, and a doubled suffix is forgeable the same way. So this takes the posture already established for the sibling collisions (#5277, #5116): fail the whole apply **closed**, and FRR keeps its last-good config rather than loading a fused route-map.

Reachability: the config passes strict commit, and several spellings derive it (`["xpf-emptied","chain"]`, `["xpf","emptied-chain"]`, …). Contrived, but precisely the class the two sibling guards exist for.

## Validation

- The **derivation itself** is asserted, not assumed — so a future change to either name construction fails there rather than silently making the guard unreachable.
- Mutating the guard to `if false`, **verified landed by md5 before the verdict was read**, reds the fail-closed cell; restored green.
- A **negative control** asserts an ordinary composed chain still renders — a guard that refused every chain would satisfy the fail-closed assertion and be indistinguishable from a correct one.
- `pkg/frr` suite green.

The false comment is corrected rather than deleted, and `pkg/frr/README.md` — which implied the same protection — now states which guard covers which spelling and that both are required.

Refs #7625
