## PR #8403 — daemon: gate proxy-ARP on a three-state RG ownership answer [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8297-ownership-gate`

Closes #8297

## #8314's bool gate turned a two-answerer bug into a zero-answerer outage

#8314 gated proxy-ARP on `isRethMasterState -> AllVRRPMaster -> allMasterLocked`, which returns **false when the RG has no known VRRP instances**:

```go
if len(s.vrrpInstances) == 0 { return false }
```

For the DHCP relay that predicate was written for, *"nothing known -> do not relay"* avoids a duplicate and failing closed is right. **For proxy-ARP it is an outage**, and #8342 measured exactly that: `fw0=0 fw1=0`, the entry installed on **neither** node, so nothing answered for the NAT pool address and every documented use of a shipped High-priority feature went dark.

**The failure moved from two answerers to zero.**

## A bool cannot carry the distinction this needs

*"We are not the owner"* and *"we do not know who is"* must be treated **oppositely** by proxy-ARP, and a boolean has nowhere to put the difference. The answer becomes three-state, and the gate suppresses only on an **affirmative** not-owner:

| state | proxy-ARP |
|---|---|
| not owner | **suppress** — #8297: the standby must stop |
| owner | answer — #8342: the owner must keep answering |
| unknown | answer — the exact #8314 failure |
| rg 0 / unresolvable | answer — no ownership question to ask |

It is a **named type rather than a bool** so a later caller cannot silently re-collapse the unknown case into either verdict — which is how the two states got conflated in the first place. Same forcing function as an exhaustive `match` with no `_` arm.

## The detail that decides whether the gate works at all

A SUPPRESSED entry is dropped from every return set and specifically **not** added to `unresolved`. Unresolved means *"the netdev did not resolve, retain its responder state as debt"* (#6536). Conflating the two would leave the standby answering — **green tests, unchanged behaviour, and a closed issue**: the fix would measure as no fix.

## Gate

Merged onto `76a3a09c4`, no conflicts. `go build ./...` rc=0; `go test ./pkg/daemon/` ok.

Mutation-verified in **both** directions, each redding a different subtest — so the table can tell the two opposite bugs apart rather than merely detecting that something is wrong:

| mutation | red |
|---|---|
| `!= rgOwnershipOwner` (unknown suppresses — reintroduces #8314's outage) | `TestProxyARPSuppressesOnlyOnAffirmativeNotOwner8297/unknown_->_answer` |
| `return false` (never suppress — reintroduces #8297's two answerers) | `.../not_owner_->_suppress` |

Both with `build rc=0`, so both genuine reds rather than voids.

## One question left open, deliberately

**Does suppressing the standby correct an upstream that has already cached the standby's binding?** Removing a responder does not invalidate a cache entry, so an upstream may keep sending to the old target until it ages out. Two readings are live: both nodes may answer with the same RETH virtual MAC (in which case the ARP entry was never wrong and the mechanism is switch-port MAC learning), or the window is short enough not to matter in the measured scenario.

**This PR is strictly better than master either way** — master currently carries the #8314 zero-answerer outage — so it should not wait on that question. If a GARP on ownership change turns out to be required, it is an addition, not a correction.

## PR #8404 — session: run the PPTP association expiry once per GC interval [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7699-expiry-placement`

**A defect in #8399, which I merged this morning.** The association expiry was hooked into `expire_stale_entries_ha` but placed **above** the gc-interval gate, so it ran on **every** call instead of once per interval.

## Why that matters

`expire_stale_entries_ha` is called from the **worker poll loop**, and the gate is what makes it periodic:

```rust
if self.last_gc_ns != 0
    && now_ns.saturating_sub(self.last_gc_ns) < SESSION_GC_INTERVAL_NS
{
    return Vec::new();
}
```

Above it, `expire_idle` scanned the whole association map at **poll frequency** — per-poll work in a tree whose discipline is specifically not doing per-poll work. It is cheap while the map is empty and gets worse **exactly as PPTP gets used**. Moved below the gate, it runs once per `SESSION_GC_INTERVAL_NS` (1 s), like the session expiry it rides on.

## Why no existing cell caught it

Every cell in that file asserts what the table ends up **containing**, and the placement changes only **how often** that is computed. All of them passed either way. The defect is invisible to any assertion about final state — which is why the new cell binds the placement by its *observable consequence* instead.

## The cell

A sweep the gate short-circuits must not expire anything, **even something already stale**. Three steps, and the third is what makes the second mean anything:

1. at the bound — not yet stale, survives, and the gc clock is set;
2. half a second later — it **is** stale, but the gate short-circuits, so it must survive;
3. past the interval — the gate opens and the same association goes.

Without step 3, step 2 would pass against a timeout that never fires.

## Validation

Restoring the original placement — the code exactly as #8399 merged it, **verified landed by md5**, 0 build errors — reds `the_association_expiry_respects_the_gc_interval_gate_7699` and **nothing else**.

Full cargo suite green: **5118 passed, 0 failed**.

## How it was found

Reading `SESSION_GC_INTERVAL_NS` to state the dispatch's latency budget — not by a test, not by review. Which is the argument for checking **what a hook lands next to**, not only that it lands: I verified the call was production-wired and built a cell proving it, and both were true while the placement was wrong.

Refs #7699

## PR #8406 — Move the fragment-association cache into fragment_assoc/ [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `refactor/7899-fragment-assoc`

Closes #7899

Two commits: **motion**, then **renames**. Neither changes logic.

## The seam was verified before anything moved

The issue's justification for the split is a checkable claim, and it is the *whole* justification, so it was checked first rather than assumed.

**Confirmed as stated:** `FragKey` is family-agnostic — `addr_family`, `src`, `dst`, `ident`, `protocol`, `authority`, nothing NAT64-specific. And the entry's only NAT64-typed field is `reverse: Option<Nat64ReverseInfo>`.

**The stated reason is wrong, and correcting it strengthens the case.** The issue says the field is optional *"precisely because the same-family NAT arm leaves it `None`"*. Measured: **both** arms leave it `None`. There is no `Some(..)` in any `frag_assoc.install(..)` call anywhere in the tree, production or test, and **both** `lookup` consumers bind `_reverse` and discard it. The field is optional because the reverse (v4→v6) direction is a *documented deferred increment*.

So the entry carries no **live** NAT64-specific content at all. The move concentrates a property that was already true and mislabelled — the test a split has to pass — more cleanly than the issue argued.

**A false comment was load-bearing for that argument.** `frag_assoc.rs` claimed cross-family NAT64 *"has its own install (which also stamps the reverse info)"*. It does not and never did. That sentence is where the issue's premise came from, so a stale comment had been propagating into a design decision. Corrected, with the measurement recorded beside it.

**The `reverse` field is kept.** It is a placeholder for deferred work, not dead code to reclaim: `Nat64ReverseInfo` is live in session sync, and #6386 — where the consumers acquired their underscore — was itself a pure move that decommissioned nothing.

## The exact non-motion delta

The lead asked that anything beyond motion be called out rather than ride inside the relocation. In full:

**Eight visibility widenings, all private → `pub(crate)`, none wider.** `FRAG_SHARDS`, `FRAG_CAP_PER_SHARD`, `FRAG_TTL_NS`, `frag_shard_index` in the new module; `Ipv6FragInfo`, its four fields, and `ipv6_fragment_header` in `nat64.rs`. They exist because `nat64_tests.rs` reached these through `use super::*` while they lived in `nat64.rs` and now sits in a sibling module. `ipv6_fragment_header` stays in `nat64.rs`, which still has four other uses of it.

Plus: the `//` section narrative became the `//!` module doc.

## Renames

Only the misleading token is dropped. `frag` is kept where the bare name would collide — `shard_index` and `SHARDS` already name unrelated sharded structures in `flow_cache.rs`, `sharded_neighbor.rs` and `cos/token_bucket_tests.rs`, and taking those names would be legal per-module while making a grep for either ambiguous.

Three names deliberately kept, per the issue's *"or explicitly decide to keep them and say why"*:
- `FragAuthority` — already family-neutral.
- `NAT64_FRAG_CROSS_DOMAIN_MISSES` / `NAT64_FRAG_PROTOCOL_ALIAS_MISSES` — these **are** the shipped Prometheus series `xpf_userspace_nat64_frag_{cross_domain,protocol_alias}_misses_total`. The identifier is the grep path from an alert to the code that moves it; renaming them would break a real workflow to make one module read tidier. Recorded at the definition site so it reads as a decision, not an oversight.

## Deliberately not done

- **The cache instance stays on `Nat64State`** (`forwarding.nat64.frag_assoc`). Re-homing it is a lifecycle change, not motion — the Arc is threaded across config reloads in `from_snapshots_with_previous` so in-flight datagrams keep translating. Mixing that in is what makes a relocation unreviewable.
- **The 55 fragment tests stay in `nat64_tests.rs`.** They are interleaved with 119 non-frag NAT64 tests across 7000 lines, and extracting them has its own failure mode — an insertion between a doc comment and its `fn` steals the `#[test]` attribute and silently decommissions the guard.

## Validation

"Pure move" is exactly the claim that gets taken on trust, so it was measured.

- **The moved text was diffed against the original region at `origin/master`.** `key.rs` is **byte-identical** (100/100 non-blank lines). The cache body differs on exactly **8 lines** — the widenings listed above, enumerated by the diff rather than by memory.
- **The full test inventory (`cargo test -- --list`, 5257 entries) is byte-identical** before and after both commits: no test lost, added, renamed, or duplicated. Post-rebase it differs by exactly one entry, a test master added in its own commit.
- Scoped duplicate checks on `fragment_assoc::` and `nat64` are both **0** — *scoped*, because the unfiltered form reports 22 false positives from modules compiled into two binaries.

## PR #8407 — dataplane: refuse the zoned-vs-zoned ifindex contest instead of guessing (#7509 partial) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7509-contested-ifindex-unzone`

> **Refs #7509 — this is a PARTIAL fix and no part of it should be read as resolving that issue.** It addresses the zoned-vs-**zoned** contest only. The reported zoned-vs-**unzoned** case remains unaddressed; see "What this deliberately does not address".
>
> (The verb is dropped on purpose: GitHub's parser does not read negation, so "this does not fix #N" contains a live close token. That happened in a sibling PR's first draft.)

## The defect

A parent ifindex whose units carry **different** zones got one of them by an arbitrary, order-dependent pick — first-wins on the fan-UP arm, last-wins on the same-ifindex arm. A packet was then adjudicated under a **sibling unit's** policies: a policy set the operator never wrote for that unit, chosen by walk order.

The dataplane sees an ifindex, not a unit, and nothing on the wire distinguishes them. When it cannot know which zone a packet belongs to, a firewall must decline to pick one — so a contested parent is left unzoned and its traffic falls to the default policy.

This **collapses an asymmetry** rather than adding a mechanism: the egress half already resolves a contested ifindex to nothing (`EgressZoneClaim::Conflicting` → `resolve` → `None`). Ingress now matches it — the #6727 symmetry.

## Scope is wider than the issue's framing

#7509 describes interface-level **tunnel** units sharing a netdev. The condition is **any parent whose units span different zones**, including an ordinary VLAN trunk. The affected traffic stays narrow: a tagged frame resolves to its own logical unit ifindex first (#3021), so only traffic resolving to the **raw parent** changes — untagged traffic on a mixed-zone trunk.

That traffic has no principled unit attribution today: `native-vlan-id` is accepted-only and unenforced (#4308) and already carries its own commit advisory. This removes a coin flip, not a working feature. **The change site records what would invalidate that rationale** if #4308 is ever implemented.

## The eight reds, characterized before anything was touched

The full gate red eight cells across #5802, #3021, #4983, #6965. The [characterization table](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7509) is on the issue. Two findings shaped the retarget:

**They are four assertion sites, not eight dependencies.** Five fail on **one shared line** in a test driver asserting the parent carries its first sub-interface's inherited zone; the other three are file-local copies of the same claim.

| classification | cells | treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **incidental** | 5 (#4983 ×3, #6965 ×2) | subjects are numeric and zone-independent — `ingress_ifindex == 11`, `vlan_id == 50`, `owner_rg_id == 0`, publish count/direction. Two have **no zone assertion at all**. One retarget of the shared driver line fixed all five. |
| **load-bearing** | 3 (#3021 ×2, #5802) | assertions **re-expressed, not deleted** — their subjects compare the logical unit's zone against the parent's, so the contrast is the point. |

## The re-expressed assertions are STRICTLY STRONGER

Worth stating plainly, because three changed assertions otherwise read as three weakened ones.

The old claim was *"the logical unit resolves to `lan` while the parent resolves to `wan`"* — satisfied by **any two different values**. A contested parent now resolves to **no zone**, so the claim becomes *"the logical unit resolves to `lan` while the parent resolves to nothing"*, which additionally distinguishes **"resolved correctly"** from **"resolved to some other zone"**. The old form could not make that distinction.

## The uncertain row was traced, not assumed

The table marked one row uncertain: `poll_descriptor_reverse_companion_carries_no_ingress_identity_4983` pins the reverse companion's `ingress_zone == wan`, and I could not say whether that read the parent. **It does not.** `reverse_metadata.ingress_zone = to_zone_id`, and `to_zone_id` comes from `zone_pair_ids_for_flow_with_override(.., ingress_logical, .., resolution.egress_ifindex)` — the **egress unit's own ifindex 12**, never parent 11. Incidental. Nothing left uncertain.

## What this deliberately does not address

**The reported zoned-vs-unzoned case.** `st0.1` in `vpnb`, `st0.0` deliberately in no zone, one base ifindex. The rule here sits under `row_zone_id != 0`, so an unzoned row contributes nothing and no disagreement is seen.

It **cannot** simply be widened: *"zoned + unzoned on one ifindex is contested"* also fires on a trunk parent legitimately inheriting its single child's zone (#921/#3618), because that is the **same shape** — one row with a zone, one without, one ifindex. Separating them needs the authored-vs-inherited fact, which is not on the wire. That is the provenance-field argument, recorded in #7509's body.

`unzoned_macless_unit_does_not_inherit_a_zoned_siblings_zone_6722` keeps its original subject and is **not** retargeted: it asserts the **to-zone** and passes, because egress already refuses to inherit. The defect is direction-asymmetric and only ingress has it.

## PR #8408 — Guard the sweep replay and correct what the sweep is for [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `docs/7842-sweep-comment-accuracy`

Refs #7842 — **does not close it.** The volume question stays cluster-blocked; this lands what was decidable from code, and the guard that decides it.

## What was asked

Is #7842's option 2 ("skip the mirror walk when the dataplane streams authoritative deltas") costed correctly? Its stated cost is *"removes the backstop entirely, so a dropped delta is never recovered"*. If the delta stream had its own recovery, that cost would be overstated.

## The answer: understated, not overstated

**The delta stream has no recovery path of its own for a daemon→peer drop. The sweep is that path.**

1. Both producers share one bounded `sendCh` — `queueUserspaceSessionDeltas` → `queueDeltaSink.openV4` → `QueueSessionV4` → `queueMessage`, and the sweep calls the same `queueMessage`.
2. That function's overflow branch arms `syncBackfillNeeded` and logs **"enabling sweep replay"**. The counter #7842 says to measure (`stats.Errors`) and the walk it proposes to delete are two halves of one mechanism.
3. `syncBackfillNeeded` has exactly three consumers, all in the sweep. *(Positive control: the same search shape returns 35 test refs plus the arm and declaration sites for the sibling flag `forceResync`.)*
4. The recovery is not a message retry — an overflowing sweep **declines to advance `lastSweepTime`**, so the next sweep re-walks the identical `Created >= threshold` window and re-sends what was dropped, including dropped *deltas*.
5. The helper's `FullResync` is a **different failure domain** — helper→daemon loss when the replay buffer is trimmed past the daemon's ack. By the time a delta reaches `queueMessage` the daemon has already consumed and acked it.

Full analysis posted on the issue.

## The guard that was missing

`syncBackfillNeeded` had **zero** test references; `forceResync` had 35. The path that makes the walk load-bearing was entirely unguarded — an implementation of option 2 would have deleted it with a **green suite**.

Two cells:
- **`TestSweepOverflowArmsBackfillAndReplaysTheWindow_7842`** — pins the arm, the held window, and the re-send.
- **`TestDeltaStreamOverflowArmsTheSweepReplay_7842`** — deliberately about the *delta* path, not the sweep. This is the cell that decides option 2: a delta dropped on the shared queue must arm the *sweep's* replay.

**The first draft was vacuous and the mutation caught it.** The fixture used `now` for both `lastSweepTime` and `Created`, so a mutation letting the sweep advance the window on overflow **escaped** — advancing *to* `now` is indistinguishable from holding *at* `now`, and a session with `Created == now` still satisfies the advanced filter. The fixture now opens the window strictly behind the sweep's clock. Re-run after the fix, that mutation reds both assertions, including `replay re-sent 0 sessions, want 2`.

| mutation | expected red | result |
|---|---|---|
| disable the sweep's `if overflow { … return }` early return | window + replay assertions | RED (escaped before the fixture fix) |
| drop the `syncBackfillNeeded` arm from `queueMessage` | the delta cell | RED |

## Two comments that were load-bearing and wrong

**`SessionSyncSweepProfile`** said the walk keeps *"a periodic refresh for long-lived flows"*. It does not and structurally cannot — `Created >= threshold` sends only sessions created *since* the last sweep, and `sync_conn_sweep.go` says so itself: *"every session that existed before the sweep started is permanently invisible to it"*. **That sentence is cited as the justification for option 3**, so a false comment was setting the price of a design choice. Option 3 is therefore not "narrow the walk to its stated purpose" but "build a refresh capability the sweep never had".

**`sync_conn_sweep.go`** said the arm holds the sweep *"at the 1s active cadence"* — the eBPF default; under userspace the profile makes it 15s.

The profile comment now also records that **`enabled` is not an on/off switch**: `sweepIntervalsForDataPlane` consults it only to decide whether to adopt the profile's intervals, and `false` falls through to the 1s/10s defaults. Returning `false` to "disable" the sweep would run it at **1s instead of 15s** — fifteen times more of the duplication #7842 is about, silently. Anyone implementing option 2 from the issue text is one plausible edit from that.

## Scope

**Production changes are comments only** — verified, zero non-comment lines changed. `go build ./...` and the full `go test ./...` pass.

## What is still cluster-blocked, with one note for the run

Choosing between option 1 and a redesigned option 3 remains a volume question and the `SessionsSent`/`Errors` run stands.

The metric is **not linear in connection rate**: an overflowing sweep does not advance `lastSweepTime`, so the next sweep replays the same window — grown by everything created meanwhile — while the arm holds it at the active cadence. Pressure feeds pressure. Sampling one "realistic" rate can land below the knee and report a clean `Errors == 0` that says nothing about the rate just above it. The run should **bracket** the overflow threshold rather than sample one point, and record `queue_len`/`queue_cap` from the warn line alongside the counters.

## PR #8409 — coordinator: correct the neigh-monitor "no spawner leaks" claim [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7810-monitor-leak-claim`

Closes #7810

## The contradiction is real, and the counterexample was already in the tree

#7810 filed a contradiction rather than a diagnosis: 7 live `neigh-monitor` threads in a wedged test binary against the doc claim that *"none of them LEAKS one (every spawner stops it), so the contamination is concurrent overlap and nothing else."*

**The refutation was sitting in a different file the whole time.** `coordinator/tests.rs`, on `rejected_spawn_apply_does_not_prune_live_rule_counters_7010`:

> a cell that PANICS skips the trailing call and leaks its neigh-monitor thread into the process-wide #6637 gates, which then red alongside it

And it is **measured**, not hypothesised — the first #7010 mutation matrix showed that cell's red carrying two collateral #6637 failures unrelated to the mutation.

So the claim holds only on the normal path, and **the contamination has two sources needing different remedies**: concurrent overlap, which the serial lock fixes, and panic leakage, which `StoppedCoordinator` fixes. The blanket *"and nothing else"* is the load-bearing error — it sends a reader looking for one cause.

## Not a production leak, and the doc now says so

`stop_inner` signals **and joins** the monitor (#5165), and bringup installs `monitor_stop` + `monitor_join` together only when the thread actually spawned. This is a test-hygiene property. #7810 said it *"may still turn out to be benign"* — for production, it is.

## Census, and one exposed cell converted

At `3961adbee`, **12** guard-taking cells in `coordinator/tests.rs`. Ten already panic-safe via `StoppedCoordinator::{new,wrap}`. Two were not:

| cell | disposition |
|---|---|
| `committed_reconcile_prunes_zone_counters_for_removed_zones_6832` | plain trailing `coordinator.stop()`, no panic handling — **converted** |
| `coordinator_bringup_does_not_leak_a_neigh_monitor_thread_6637` | **left as-is, deliberately** |

**Why the leak gate is left alone:** it already calls `stop()` before its one explicit panic branch, so its residual window is a panic in setup or in `reconcile`. And it asserts process-wide thread **counts** at specific points — wrapping it would add a second `stop()` after the measurement it exists to take. Recorded in the doc rather than changed.

Worth noting the shape: **the leak gate is the more exposed of the two**, and its own precondition message would blame a predecessor — *"a previous test leaked one"* — for a monitor it leaked itself.

## The mechanism is already bound, and bound well

I looked for a guard before writing one. The existing cell asserts the spawn happened **inside** the scope (`before + 1`, *"the guard must not suppress the spawn — it must clean up AFTER one"*) before asserting the count returns after the drop. **A guard that "worked" by suppressing the spawn cannot pass it** — the middle assertion is what makes the outer one mean something.

| `cargo test coordinator::tests` | 139 passed, 0 failed |

A first pass using grep looked only for `StoppedCoordinator::new`, missed `::wrap`, and produced a false "exposed" row for `teardown_quiesce_fires_when_live_workers_and_snapshot_rebinds` — corrected before acting on it. ## PR #8410 — test/incus: wait for the transfer before clearing the pin it drove [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7771-reassert-pin-race`

Closes #7771

## The pin that drives the transfer was cleared on the next line

`deploy_reassert_primary_node0` drove each RG as **reset → transfer → reset**, with the second reset issued immediately. But `request chassis cluster failover redundancy-group $rg node 0` **is** a manual pin, and it is the only thing driving the transfer — so clearing it races the transfer it just started.

When the reset won, the RG fell back to the natural election and stayed on node1. That is **correct behaviour** for a non-preempting cluster (`Preempt: no` on every row, failover counts 0) and exactly the state the deploy must not leave. The failure surfaced as *"node0 is not primary for every redundancy group after 15 verification attempts"* — indistinguishable from an HA regression in whatever branch deployed next.

**The reporter's manual repro is the evidence**: the same commands by hand, with a wait between them, fixed it on the first attempt.

## Three phases, mirroring the repro

Every RG gets its peer pin cleared, its local pin cleared, and its transfer issued. Then **one** bounded poll waits for `show chassis cluster status` to report node0 primary for every RG. Then every pin is cleared.

**The wait is not a settling heuristic.** Once the transfer has committed, clearing the pin is safe for the same reason the race was fatal: a non-preempting cluster leaves the new primary in place. The wait is the **precondition that makes the reset non-destructive**.

**The pins are cleared whether or not the poll converges.** A left-behind pin is #7688's failure and is not traded away for this one; the verify loop after it is still the verdict.

## The self-test cell pinned the race as the expected answer

It asserted the literal byte sequence `reset|transfer|reset` per RG — **the race, written down as correct** — and it `grep -v`'d the status reads out of the log first, so it could not have expressed the new property even if someone had thought to ask. It discarded the evidence before looking.

It now asserts two orderings instead of a literal: a transfer is issued per RG (#6591 — a reset alone clears the flag and never moves ownership), and the **first** reset after each transfer is separated from it by a status read (#7771).

## My first version of that assertion was insensitive, and the mutation caught it

Worth stating plainly because it is the whole argument for running the mutation rather than reading the test.

The first draft took the **last** reset for the RG (`tail -1`). Restoring the race adds a reset immediately after the transfer — but the later phase-3 reset still satisfied *"the last reset comes after a status read"*, so **the cell passed the mutation it was written for**. It was caught only by the #7688 reset-**count** cell next door, which noticed `node0 resets=6 (want 4)`.

Taking the **first** reset after the transfer binds it. The reason is recorded at the assertion so the next editor does not revert to the weaker form.

## Validation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `bash -n` (both files) | clean |
| deploy-lib selftest | **55 passed, 0 failed** |
| mutation — restore the race, md5-verified | **53 passed, 2 failed** |

The mutation reds the new ordering cell with `the FIRST reset after the transfer (line 4) has NO status read between it and the transfer (line 3, of 11)`, alongside the #7688 count cell. Restored, md5 back to baseline, 55/0 again.

## On closing

#7771 filed its cause as *"Hypothesis (NOT established)"*. What **is** established is the reporter's manual repro — the wait fixes it, first attempt — and this implements that wait as a bounded poll rather than a sleep. The remaining confirmation is a `make cluster-deploy` observing a clean reassert, which is the same standard as any deploy-tooling change and does not need this issue held open.

## PR #8411 — Clamp io_uring write SQE length instead of truncating [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7751-sqe-len-clamp`

Row 12 of #7751 is real and worse than reported. The other three rows are
declines with reasons — recorded below and in a comment on the issue, since
"if a row turns out to be right as written, that is a result".

## Row 12 — SQE length truncation (FIXED)

`write_all` described each `Write` SQE with `buf.len() as _`, narrowing a
`usize` to the `u32` that `io_uring_sqe.len` carries. The sweep reported a
silent truncation. It is not a short write:

- For a remaining length that is an exact multiple of 2^32 the cast yields **0**.
- The kernel completes a legitimate 0-byte write.
- `offset += 0`, and `while offset < slot.bytes.len()` (`:654` / `:716`) never
  advances — **a livelock**.

The value looks healthy at every layer: valid SQE, successful completion,
non-negative result. Fixed by clamping to `MAX_SQE_WRITE_LEN` instead, which the
existing partial-write loop already handles (both targets are byte streams, so a
split write is indistinguishable from the short counts it already resumes from).

Reachability: the production caller is the state-snapshot writer, whose buffer is
data-dependent rather than MTU-bounded — a volume convention, not a structural
invariant. That is materially weaker than row 14's impossibility, which is why
this row is fixed and that one is not.

## Rows 08 / 14 / 17 — declines

**Row 08 (`zone_counters.rs`, poisoned-mutex `.expect`) — decline, and a count
correction.** The sweep said seven; the earlier triage corrected it to six; the
count that matters is **four**. Two of the six are `#[cfg(test)]`
(`tracked_zone_ids_for_test`, `lock_totals_for_test`) and never ship. The four
shipping critical sections are `entry().or_default()` + `Arc::clone`, an
iterate/collect, a `values()` reset, and a `retain` over `u16 -> Arc<atomics>`.
None can panic — no indexing, no unwrap, no user closure, no arithmetic — and
allocation failure aborts rather than unwinds. A `Mutex` is poisoned only by a
panic *inside* its own critical section, so the poison these `.expect`s describe
is unreachable. They document an invariant that cannot fire, which is the
correct use of `.expect`.

**Row 14 (`filter/compiler.rs`, `unique_runtime_id` probe loop) — decline,
unreachable.** `used_runtime_ids` is created empty (`:68`) per compile and the
loop's own `insert` (`:406`) is its **only** writer, so its size equals the
policer count. The probe therefore terminates in at most `|used_ids| + 1` steps
and non-termination needs 2^32 - 1 policers in one config. Adding a bound
counter here would be a claim written into inert code — unfalsifiable until
something populates it.

**Row 17 (`csrc/xsk_bridge.c`, prod/cons cancel asymmetry) — decline, right as
written.** This is the row the previous triage could not verify. The asymmetry
is real — `bridge_xsk_ring_prod_cancel` writes `ring->cached_prod -= nb` while

## PR #8412 — test/ra: make the #8031 goodbye assertion attributable [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `test/8031-attributable-goodbye`

Refs #8031 — **does not close it.** This is an instrument, not a fix.

## The evidence does not survive the failure

#8031's central limitation is *"the detailed failure output is lost."* But even the output that **did** survive would not have identified the emitter:

```
restart timeout emitted a goodbye (1 conns / 3 writes)
```

`goodbyeStats` iterates `fl.allConns[name]` — **every conn generation** for the interface — counting writes with `lifetime == 0`. That is the correct property for the invariant being asserted (*"nobody emitted"*), and it is useless for diagnosis. `1 conns / 3 writes` is byte-identical whether:

- **the wedged owner emitted on the timeout path** — the defect the assertion is named for (#2033 round-4 MAJOR 1);
- **a replacement sender emitted**;
- **the reclaimer's legitimate post-close goodbye was observed early** — and the test's own #5094 comment says *"exactly one goodbye is emitted"* after `close(wedge)`, so **that signature matches the observed failure precisely**.

Three different causes wanting three different fixes, and one number that cannot tell them apart.

## What this adds

`goodbyeAttribution` renders, per conn generation, how many writes and how many goodbyes it carries, and marks the wedged owner. Forced:

```
per-conn attribution (#8031):
  conn[0]: 1 writes, 0 goodbye <-- the WEDGED owner
```

The invariant is unchanged. Only the failure message grows.

## Deliberately not done

**No fix, and no timing change.** The test's precondition — that the racing `Withdraw()` lands inside the 150 ms `claimWaitTimeout` window — is **assumed by timing and never asserted**, which is a real weakness and a plausible contributor. Widening that window or gating on it would change what the test measures, so it belongs with whoever reproduces the failure.

Guessing at a fix for a race I could not reproduce is how a flake becomes a silently weakened assertion.

## Negative result, recorded so nobody repeats it

**25 runs** of the test under a concurrent `go build ./...` plus a two-package test run: **0 failures.**

Consistent with the issue's own negatives (10/10 idle; 12/12 under six CPU hogs at loadavg 15.8) and it **tightens the envelope**: moderate concurrent load is not enough. The reported reproduction needed three concurrent full suites, and that distinction — CPU saturation does *not* reproduce it, a real gate does — is itself a clue worth preserving.

## Validation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `gofmt -l pkg/ra/` | clean |
| `go vet ./pkg/ra/` | rc=0 |
| `go test ./pkg/ra/ -run TestRestartTimeout... -count=3` | ok |
| forced-failure probe (md5-verified, restored) | attribution renders, wedged owner marked |

## PR #8413 — Copy the inner DS byte on the WG host-originated encap [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7758-wg-host-encap-dscp`

Closes #7758

## The premise was wrong in a way that made this bigger, not smaller

The issue says WireGuard "implements only the decap half". **WireGuard has TWO encap paths**, and the transit one (`frame/wg.rs:516`) has copied the inner DS byte since #2303, using the same `gre::inner_tos_byte` helper GRE uses.

What was actually missing is narrower and sharper: `wg_control::encap_and_send` — the **host-originated** path, inner read from the wgN TUN — ended at a bare `send_to` with no per-datagram control message, so its outer DS byte stayed 0.

**So the two WG encap paths disagreed.** The same inner marking produced a different outer DSCP depending on which path a packet took — an internal routing detail no operator can see, while a downstream classifier sees WG traffic marked or unmarked accordingly.

That matters for how the issue was framed. It held on "harm reachability is unmeasured — does any deployment classify on WG outer DSCP?", a question about deployments that no measurement in this tree could answer. The real harm is an **internal inconsistency, provable from the tree**, and the posture question dissolves: #2303 already made this exact decision for GRE *and* for WG transit, unconditionally, with no config gate. This is a consistency fix, not a new posture.

## Shape

`wg_send_to` takes the outer TOS as an explicit `Option<u8>`. `None` is the pre-existing `send_to` path byte-for-byte; `Some` goes through `sendmsg` with `IP_TOS` / `IPV6_TCLASS` ancillary data — per-datagram, because the value is the inner packet's and varies packet to packet.

**The cmsg level follows the destination's WIRE family, not the socket family.** A v4-mapped destination on the dual-stack AF_INET6 socket emits an IPv4 datagram and takes `IP_TOS`, mirroring the receive side whose own doc says `IP_RECVTOS` *"governs both native v4 and the v4-mapped datagrams the dual-stack v6 socket delivers"*. **This is asserted, not trusted** — the test reads the DS byte back off a loopback round trip, so a wrong level choice reds instead of silently sending unmarked.

**Exemptions are explicit at the call site.** Handshake initiation, handshake response, cookie reply and keepalive carry no inner packet and pass `None`. The parameter is explicit rather than defaulted so a new send site has to decide instead of inheriting either answer.

**No fallback on cmsg rejection.** The error returns; the existing caller already counts `transport_send_errors` and records a tunnel exception carrying the errno, so a rejecting kernel is diagnosable as `wg_socket_send:EINVAL`. A silent fall back to an unmarked send would be a safety net no test can reach.

## Tests

Two cells, each mutation-verified, each mutation redding **only** its own:

| mutation | expected red | result |
|---|---|---|
| `encap_and_send` passes `None` (the pre-fix tree) | the copy cell | RED |
| a keepalive passes `Some(0xB8)` | the exemption cell | RED |

The copy cell asserts the DS byte **as received on the wire**, not the helper's return value — the helper was never the missing part, and a cell calling `inner_tos_byte` directly would have stayed green through the entire defect. Its second assertion pins the **agreement** between the two paths (`got == inner_tos_byte(&inner, AF_INET)`) rather than a literal, so it still fails if either path later changes what it means by "the inner DS byte".

The exemption cell drives the real `send_keepalive` rather than `wg_send_to`, because the claim is about the call site's choice; a cell that only checked data packets could not see a change that started stamping keepalives.

`wg::tests::established_pair` and its module widen to `pub(crate)` so the wg_control tests can drive a real session — test-only visibility.

## Docs

`docs/wireguard-interop.md` reported this as **"DSCP/ECN encap DONE (#2303)"**, which was half true for two years — #2303 wired the transit path only. That row and the DSCP/ECN section now record both paths and which one was unmarked. `wg/dscp.rs`'s note said "the production WG/GRE encap path", singular; it is plural, and that was load-bearing.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` green (5122), `go build ./...` rc=0. Rebased onto `a04057800` and re-verified after master moved mid-work; zero file overlap with what landed. Touched Rust files carry the same rustfmt-diff count as master (the tree at large is not rustfmt-clean and was left alone).

## PR #8414 — Bound the io_uring in-flight registry with a capacity refusal [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7944-inflight-registry-cap`

The accumulation is real, but the issue's two callers do not share its exposure —
and the scariest column is not a reachable production quantity. Both halves are
below, since the discriminator you asked for ("bounded, or bounded by something
the caller guarantees?") splits this issue rather than settling it.

## What is bounded, and by what

**State writer — bounded at ONE entry by the caller.** `IoUringPersist::Deferred`
constructs `PersistOutcome { io_uring_failed: true, .. }`, and `apply_outcome` is
the demotion chokepoint: on `io_uring_failed` it sets
`*mode = WriteMode::SyncFallback` **permanently** (no cooldown, explicitly to
avoid flapping). So the FIRST deferral retires the ring; there is never a second
parked buffer.

That matters for how this issue reads. The `state-ring bytes (256 KiB)` column —
16 MB at 64 deferrals — is not reachable: that measurement drives `write_all` and
`FakeRing` directly and never passes through `apply_outcome`. The fixture even
labels its case "state-ring shape after 32 deferred writes", which is where the
attribution comes from. The registry-layer numbers reproduce exactly (I re-ran
`measure_teardown_residual_7106`: `inflight_len=32` with `SQ depth is 8`, and
`64 -> 0` after the storm); it is the *caller* attribution that does not hold.

**Slow path — genuinely unbounded, and deliberately so.** `classify_io_uring_write`
sets `ring_terminal: fatal_ring`, and the documented contract is that a bare
retry-ceiling storm (`fatal_ring = false`) **keeps io_uring** because the ring is
otherwise healthy. Nothing else bounds it: `inflight` is a plain `Vec`, `defer` is
its only writer, and the only fail-closed limit is the `u64` id space (~584 years
at 1e9 ids/s). So this is the half worth fixing — with MTU buffers, not 256 KiB
snapshots.

## Disposition — why refusing is safe here

Capping at 256; past the cap `write_all` returns `NothingWritten` with the buffer
handed back, having submitted nothing.

**`NothingWritten` is not a drop — it is the rescue arm on both callers**, which
is the whole reason a cap is safe on this path:

- slow path: `WriteResult::NothingWritten(bytes, _)` → `sync_fallback(bytes)`, and
  the ring is explicitly *not* demoted ("transient, not a demotion");
- state writer: → `IoUringPersist::Retry(bytes, msg)`, which rewrites synchronously.

So the data is still written; what is refused is the io_uring *submission*, not
the I/O. Refusing the write outright — dropping a host-bound packet while the ring
is otherwise healthy — would have been the damaging reading of "fail closed", and
it is not what this does.

The cap is checked **after** `reap_ready`, which makes it self-healing: once
completions surface the registry drains and io_uring resumes, so a transient storm
costs sync writes rather than the ring. Permanent demotion was the other candidate

*(truncated — 80 lines total)*

## PR #8415 — afxdp: split the session-identity question from the enforcement one [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7890-enforcement-addresses`

`l3_session_flow_from_meta` returns `None` for an unspecified source, and **that judgement is correct** — a session keyed on `0.0.0.0` aliases every other unspecified-source flow. Nothing here changes it.

**But the call sites were not asking that question.** A per-packet interface filter, a PBR `then { routing-instance X; discard; }` term and a zone policy do not need a *session* — they need the packet's **addresses**, and those parsed fine. `0.0.0.0` is a perfectly well-defined value to evaluate a `from`-clause against.

One resolver answering two questions, and the call sites reading a refusal of the first as *"nothing to enforce"* for the second. That is why every site has the identical shape: **one misuse repeated, not N oversights.**

## Two resolvers, not one

`ForwardPacketMeta::l3_addrs` carries the identical refusal — its own doc said it *"Mirrors"* the other. Its two callers are both flowless **egress output-filter** evaluations gated on it inside an `&&` chain, so an unspecified source skipped the operator's `filter output` entirely, **`then discard` included**.

Fixing only the `poll_descriptor` sites would have left that live while the issue read as closed.

## Why not "drop on `None`"

It substitutes a **disposition** for the verdict the operator configured — right only when that verdict happens to be `discard`, and silently contradicting it otherwise.

The cells are written so the two repairs are **distinguishable**: they assert the returned **addresses**, which a drop-on-`None` implementation cannot produce, because it leaves the resolver refusing.

## Sites changed

Four in `poll_descriptor` (`:3422`, `:3593`, `:4684`, `:5052`), two in `forward_request` (the flowless filter-**log** attribution and the post-NAT wire tuple), and the mirrored resolver itself.

The witness counter now means *"an unspecified address was seen here"* rather than *"a lookup was refused"*, and is bumped on both paths — so it stays usable as the thing a per-arm fixture asserts to prove it entered the arm **before** asserting what enforcement did.

## Validation — and the mutation that escaped

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| restore the refusal in the enforcement resolver | 2 cells |
| restore the refusal in `l3_addrs` | **nothing, on the first run** |

Both **verified landed by md5**.

The escape is the useful half. Every cell I had written bound resolver **A** only, so the egress half was **fixed and unguarded** — the two-correct-halves-and-no-join shape, one resolver over. A cell for it now exists and the mutation reds it.

Full cargo suite green: **5124 passed, 0 failed**. Duplicate-`#[test]` check **0 across 5130 tests** (`--bin … -- --list | grep ': test$'`; the count is the anti-vacuity half).

## Not in this change

**Per-arm integration fixtures** for the four `poll_descriptor` arms, and a **dedicated cell for the filter-log site** — a skipped `discard` fails open, a skipped `log` fails *silent*, and you cannot test that by checking a packet was forwarded.

The resolver split is bound; what an individual arm does with it is not. The four arm shapes are derived and recorded on #7890, so those fixtures can be built from each arm's own class rather than from the issue's stated shape, which belongs to `:3422` alone.

Refs #7890

## PR #8417 — Record that a directed broadcast is never locally delivered [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `docs/8061-directed-broadcast-verdict`

Closes #8061

The issue was filed as *"a latent asymmetry to check, not a confirmed defect"*, so the deliverable is a **verdict**, not a fix. **No production code changed** — this is the verdict, the recording, and the guard that keeps the recording true.

## Verdict, on the issue's own three questions

**1. Does it resolve to `LocalDelivery`? No.**

The asymmetry itself is real: `should_fallback_early` hands `255.255.255.255`, multicast and link-local to the kernel, and a subnet-directed broadcast is none of those, so unlike the limited broadcast it enters the AF_XDP dataplane.

But the consequence chain is conditional on `LocalDelivery`, and none of the six production sites that return it is reachable for this class:

| site | gate | reachable for `192.168.1.255`? |
|---|---|---|
| `forwarding/fib.rs:275` (v4) | `owned_here` — `local_tables_v4` / `local_nat_any_table_v4` | **no** |
| `forwarding/fib.rs:336` (v6) | v6 path | n/a — IPv6 has no broadcast |
| `forwarding/local_delivery.rs:168` | `iface.primary_v4 == Some(ip)` | **no** |
| `poll_stages.rs:1030` | IPsec passthrough — not address-derived | n/a |
| `forwarding/nat.rs:159`, `:178` | DNAT-to-local | only if configured as a DNAT external |

Those membership sets are built from each interface's **host** address (`forwarding_build/interfaces.rs`, `local_v4.insert(v4.addr())`), so the broadcast is never a member. **The packet is dropped before the host-inbound gate is consulted** — so the L2-less write to `xpf-usp0`, the invisibility to `AF_PACKET`, and the fail-closed gate asymmetry all do not occur.

**2. Is there a consumer? No.** The product's three `AF_PACKET` consumers each take a different class — DHCP client → limited broadcast (early fallback), VRRP → multicast (early fallback), HA ARP probe → EtherType 0x0806, which never reaches the `AF_INET` arm.

**3. What is the repair? Does not arise** — and that is where the cost was. No shim change means no `make generate`, no pinned toolchain, no kernel-verifier gate.

## Why a recording rather than a fix

The product already has a stated position: `family inet targeted-broadcast` is a real config leaf that is **ACCEPTED-ONLY and not enforced** (#4308), with a commit-time advisory telling the operator so, guarded by `TestInterfaceParityKnobsAdvisory_4308`. The dataplane's non-handling is the *advertised* state of a knob deliberately left unimplemented.

What was missing is a pointer from the **dataplane** side — someone reading `should_fallback_early` had no way to reach that answer. `docs/host-inbound-multicast.md` gains a row in its destination-class table (the doc #8061 itself names) with the disposition and the reasoning.

## The guard

The verdict rested on *reading gates*, which is the shape that has gone wrong repeatedly, so it is now measured. `subnet_directed_broadcast_is_never_locally_delivered_8061` builds a real `ForwardingState` from a `192.168.1.1/24` snapshot and asserts the disposition for `192.168.1.255`.

**The positive control is inside the cell**: the interface address is asserted to resolve `LocalDelivery` *first*, so the negative assertion cannot pass merely because nothing in that state resolves locally.

**Mutation-verified against the exact future hazard**, not an arbitrary one: adding the broadcast to `local_v4` + `local_tables_v4` in the builder — which is how someone would naturally implement #4308's dataplane half — compiles and reds the cell. (Compilation confirmed *before* reading the verdict; a build failure is a VOID, not a red. The first attempt at this mutation didn't compile and was correctly discarded rather than counted.)

That is the point of the guard: this class turns dangerous exactly when someone makes the directed broadcast a recognised local address, and that is the change most likely to happen next.

## Method note

My first search for the issue's named identifiers returned nothing, because it was scoped to `userspace-dp/` and the shim is a separate crate, `userspace-xdp/`. Same boundary error as #7758 — verifying inside a boundary cannot audit the boundary — caught in one step here by widening the corpus and re-running with a control (`ForwardingDisposition`, 510 hits) that proved the search worked.

## PR #8418 — daemon: restart cluster comms when a teardown owes one [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7901-rollback-comms-recovery`

Closes #7901

## The gap, measured

`bootstrap.go`'s rollback teardown is a genuine **stop-without-start**: it calls `stopClusterComms` and **returns**. It is one of only two production `stopClusterComms` call sites; the other (step 20) restarts on the next line. So recovery depended entirely on step 20, whose condition required a transport **change**:

| corrected commit | restarts |
|---|---|
| transport key **differs** | **1** — comms recover |
| transport key **identical** | **0** — comms stay DOWN |

An operator who bootstrap-rolls-back and then commits a correction that does not happen to move an endpoint holds a valid cluster config with **no heartbeat, no session sync and no fabric refresh** until the process restarts — and nothing about the corrected config tells them which row they landed on.

## The fix, and why it is one-shot

The teardown now **marks** an owed restart; step 20 **consumes** it.

**The one-shot shape is the design, not an implementation detail.** I built the obvious alternative first — a live `clusterCommsRunning()` predicate — and **the full suite refuted it.** It fires on *every* apply in that state and breaks two deliberately asserted properties:

- **#5078** — a key commit must not restart comms: that *"drops the established session-sync connection at the moment the primary becomes keyed, and it is the ONLY path by which the key can reach a config read-only secondary — the rollout then deadlocks."*
- **#6878** — an unchanged transport must not restart: step 20 firing on every apply *"would make the completion assertion above pass for the wrong reason."*

**Measured: the predicate form reds three cells across those two issues.** Both properties are older than this change and neither is discoverable from #7901, so the reasoning is recorded at the accessor rather than only in this diff.

`active != zero` is **unchanged** and still load-bearing — the boot `applyConfig` runs before `daemon_run.go`'s `startClusterComms`, so step 20 runs during boot with the field still zero, and `TestStepTwentyIgnoresANeverStartedNode_7072` brackets it.

## Modularity

The canary fired: `daemon_ha_sync.go` 1471 → **1509**, crossing the 1500 WATCH floor. The flag and its accessors are **extracted to their own file** rather than entered in `refactoring-audit-accepted.txt` — this is a natural seam, not one of the documented "when NOT to refactor" cases. `daemon_ha_sync.go` is back to 1471.

## The new cell fills the row the #7072 pair does not cover

Those two **bracket** step 20's `active != zero` conjunct — must act after comms have run, must not before — and both either move the transport or never start comms. **The defect fell exactly between them.**

Its fixture commits a change that is **not** a transport change and asserts the key is identical **as a precondition**, so a repair that merely widened the key comparison cannot pass it. Its second assertion binds the one-shot property.

## Validation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `gofmt -l pkg/daemon/` | clean |
| `go build ./...` | rc=0 |
| `go test ./...` | **70 ok / 0 FAIL** |
| all 5 cells in the file | verified to **run by name**, not by count |
| mutation A — disjunct removed | reds **exactly** the new cell's **first** assertion |
| mutation B — `take` → `read` (flag not consumed) | reds the **same cell's second** assertion: `a SECOND apply restarted comms again (restarts=2, want 1)` |

Both md5-verified, placement confirmed by grep, `build rc=0` in each — so real reds rather than voids.

**Method note:** mutation A's first attempt left a variable declared and unused, so the package failed to **build**. A build failure is a void, not a red; I re-ran with the binding removed before reading a verdict.

## PR #8419 — Extend the §5.7 drain mint quarantine to the NAT64 path [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7799-nat64-drain-quarantine`

The gap is real. It is also **wider than filed**, because the claim that bounds
its severity does not hold — and that claim is what made this a "narrow, named
deferral."

## The bounding claim is false

The issue's "what is already covered, so nobody rebuilds it" says:

> Config-time foreclosure for NAT64 is done. The Go snapshot builder emits an
> overlapping NAT64 rule with an **EMPTY pool** … So a NAT64 pool that overlaps
> an interface egress address does not get to mint at all once the snapshot lands.

Measured at master, **there is no such emptying**. `buildNAT64Snapshots`
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat64.go:66`) copies `pool.Address` + `pool.Addresses`
verbatim, with no overlap check of any kind. The only way its `poolAddresses` is
empty is an unset or unresolvable `SourcePool`.

The real foreclosure is `validateNATPoolExternalTupleOverlapStrict`
(`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:3989`), which collects NAT64
rule-set pools *and* interface-SNAT egress addresses as owners and, via
`emitNATOverlap`, **rejects at strict commit** — but on the tolerant-load /
peer-sync path it only warns. `compiler_opts.go:1003-1017` states the
consequence outright:

> Unlike lenientNPTv6 / lenientNAT64Prefix the dataplane does **NOT** reject the
> overlapping snapshot — the config installs with a **LATENT reverse-index
> collision** that persists until corrected.

So an overlapping NAT64 pool **does** get to mint, for the whole tolerant-load
lifetime of such a config — not merely "in the window before the snapshot
lands". The runtime quarantine is the only thing standing there, and it was
absent.

## The fix

NAT64 mints from `Nat64Prefix`'s own `PortAllocator` — a **third** occupancy
domain, disjoint from both the interface registry and the source-NAT pool
allocators. Thread the live source-NAT rules to
`Nat64State::allocate_source_for_worker` and refuse when any address in the
prefix pool carries draining occupancy, reusing the same
`address_has_draining_pool_occupancy` scan the interface path uses.

Two design points worth stating rather than leaving to be re-derived:

- **The gate tests the whole pool, not the address about to be picked.** The pick
  happens inside `allocate_translation`, and `occupancy` is indexed by the
  address's POSITION in `pool_v4` — filtering the slice would shift every index
  and corrupt the bitmap. Refusing is also #7717's settled posture for a mint
  colliding with a domain it cannot enumerate, and it is self-limiting.
- **It sits before the deterministic branch, so both mint paths are covered.**

## PR #8421 — Classify the empty-alternate-slot peer reboot on the boot epoch [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/7762-peer-boot-epoch`

Closes #7762

Built on the narrow shape, not the one the issue proposed. **Cluster smoke run** — required by CLAUDE.md for session-sync changes.

## Shape: an injected callback, not a `clusterRuntime` method

Extending `clusterRuntime` is a **category error**, not merely broad. It is the dataplane-backend surface — `Sessions()` + `Telemetry()`, implemented by `*dataplane.Manager` and `*userspace.LegacyDataPlaneAdapter` — and the boot epoch is cluster-Manager state on a different axis (`d.cluster`, not `d.dataplane()`). No dataplane backend can answer it: **every implementor would return 0, and 0 is exactly the silent fail-open this classification must not have.** 19 implementors, 17 of them test doubles — 17 new sites defaulting to "no reboot".

`SessionSync` already carries six injected callbacks, two wired by the daemon as closures over `d.cluster`. `PeerBootEpochFn` joins them, at the same site, over the object that holds the state.

## Two values, not one

An unlatched floor reads 0, and 0 is a *legal* floor ("none accepted yet"). A single `uint64` collapses "the peer has not proved it emits epochs" into "no reboot happened" — silently, which is what makes a broken fix here indistinguishable from a working one. With the nil check there are **three** states and the code names each:

| state | meaning | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `Fn == nil` | not wired | exactly pre-#7762 |
| `latched == false` | reboot race window | no reboot **and record nothing** |
| `latched == true` | ordered floor usable | classify on a strict raise |

## Promoting a diagnostic to a classification input

Answered on the evidence rather than the label. `peerEpochFloor`/`peerEpochLatched` are "Diagnostics and tests only" — a statement about consumers, not a ceiling. The update path is safe for a correctness consumer:

- both writes happen in `admitAuthed` under `s.mu`, and the read takes the same mutex;
- the floor is **monotonically non-decreasing** (sole assignment guarded by `epoch > s.highEpoch`; the `<` case writes nothing);
- the latch is **one-way** — `epochSeen = true` is the only production assignment, nothing sets it false, and `hbAuth` is an embedded value surviving heartbeat restart, VRF rebind and `UpdateConfig`.

New `peerBootEpoch()` reads both under **one** acquisition: two separate locks could interleave with `admitAuthed`'s single critical section and return `(floor=0, latched=true)` — an incoherent pair a classifier would misread as a reboot.

`peerEpochLatched`'s warning that it is *"A FACT ABOUT THIS STATE, NOT ABOUT CURRENT ENFORCEMENT"* is respected: it is used only as a validity flag for the floor.

## A second defect, found by reasoning and confirmed by a red test first

The #6910 boot-id prime path retires an incarnation **without** going through `installConn`. Left alone it keeps the old floor as the baseline, so the peer's **second fabric** coming up afterwards reads a raise already consumed, advances again, and **evicts the connection the prime just established** — a healthy second fabric evicting the first, the exact case `installConn`'s comment says must not clear.

The cell was written first and **failed** before the fix. Both signals now share one baseline: whichever observes the reboot consumes it.

## Guards, including one that was wrong

The headline cell asserts the **chosen fabric** (the issue's acceptance criterion — the stamp is the mechanism, the choice is the property). A nil-source control proves the fixture does not retire the corpse by itself.

**The middle-state cell was wrong first and a mutation caught it.** Its first draft drove behaviour with a third install — but with both slots occupied any third install *supersedes* a live connection and retires the incarnation on its own. It passed, then survived the mutation that records the unlatched floor: it was measuring the supersession path. It now asserts the baseline directly, with the reason recorded in the cell so nobody "fixes" it back.

| mutation | red |
|---|---|
| drop `\|\| epochReboot` from `installConn` | headline fabric cell |
| record the unlatched floor | baseline cell |
| remove the rebase from the boot-id switch | interaction cell |
| delete the daemon wiring | **daemon cell only — every cluster cell stays green** |

part 2. The trailer below is deliberately `Refs` rather than a closing keyword —
and this paragraph avoids writing one next to the issue number at all, because
GitHub does not parse negation and would act on it.

## The two questions, answered before building

**Reachable?** Yes, and verified rather than assumed:
`reuse_existing_lease_locked` admits a lease on
`active_flows > 0 || expires_at_ns > now_ns` (`allocator.rs:1932`), with an
explicit idle-reactivation arm at `:1935-1940`. So on the active node an idle
lease inside its timeout really is reused. The cost is bounded and worth stating
plainly: the client gets a *working* translation after failover, just not its
previous port. Not an outage, not a fail-open — a silent loss of the stickiness
the operator configured, for a window exactly as wide as the configured timeout.

**Wire gap or rebuild gap?** A **wire gap**. #7360's rebuild is entirely local —
it derives the lease from a synced flow plus locally-known rule config — and
nothing lease-shaped crosses the wire: the only lease-adjacent thing on any
status surface is a COUNT (`persistent_by_source.len()`). `pkg/cluster` has no
persistent-NAT lease code at all. (`lease_sync_wire_test.go` there is *DHCP*
leases — a name collision I checked rather than assumed.)

## What this lands

Export selects exactly the population #7360 cannot reach; import installs one
record. Three constraints come from the issue; the fourth does not, and it is
the one that could have made this fix worse than the bug:

| must not | why |
|---|---|
| carry `active_flows` | the standby installs a strict SUBSET, so a carried count never reaches zero, never enters `lease_expirations`, and no GC path reclaims it |
| carry `expires_at_ns` | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, boot-relative — a node up ten days reads a value from a node up one hour as long expired. Carry REMAINING, compute locally |
| carry `addr_index` | it is a POSITION in the pool list. Carry the ADDRESS, resolve the index locally, refuse an address this pool lacks |
| **install without claiming the port** | **not in the issue.** An idle lease still HOLDS its occupancy bit — freed on the EXPIRY path, not when the last flow closes, which is *why* the tuple is reusable. Installing without it lets a local flow mint the same identity, and then has the lease's own expiry free that other flow's bit |

## PR #8423 — nat: refuse an address-only identity a peer pool already owns (#8115 R1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8115-r1-address-only-peer-identity`

Refs #8115 — closes **R1 only**. R2 (the HA synced reserve) and R3 (NAT64
prefixes) stay open on that issue; R2 in particular needs a decision, not a
patch, and folding either in here would undo the split #8111 made deliberately.

## The defect

#6979 F6 (#8111) made a LOCAL, port-translating mint refuse a
`(pool address, port)` another pool's occupancy bitmap already holds. **The
bitmap is only one of the two ownership tokens this allocator issues**, and the
check asked about only that one.

A `port no-translation` flow, or a port-less protocol, takes the ADDRESS-ONLY
path: no occupancy bit, an `address_only_owners` entry keyed by the full reverse
identity instead. The two spaces never met, so both directions were open:

- a peer pool preserving `X:P` toward a remote did not stop a PAT mint of `X:P`
  toward it;
- two address-only flows in different pools collided whenever protocol and
  remote matched.

Both mints now ask both questions through one predicate over the index #8111
already builds. No overlapping pools ⇒ no index ⇒ one `Option::is_none`.

## The precision asymmetry, and why it is deliberate

| query | keyed on | over-rejects? |
|---|---|---|
| `peer_holds_identity` (bitmap) | `(address, port)` — **remote-agnostic** | yes, by design — F6's posture; costs a PAT mint one port rotation |
| `peer_holds_address_only_identity` | `(proto, addr, port, dst_ip, dst_port)` — **remote-specific** | no |

Two control cells hold that line: a peer identity toward a *different* remote
must still translate. Overlapping pools are a shape this dataplane deliberately
supports, so nothing may stop translating that is not an actual duplicate.

The key is built by `AddressOnlyReverseKey::for_flow` — the same constructor the
reserve paths insert with — rather than from three literals. That is precisely
the #6751 defect that constructor exists to prevent: a check keyed differently
from its insert finds nothing, every mint "succeeds", and no behavioural test
can see it.

## Verified rather than assumed

The issue's central population claim is the one sentence its whole scope rests
on, so I checked it. It holds, and is **stronger** than stated: the tolerant
path is real (`lenientCompileOpts`, wired at `configstore.Store` load and
SyncApply), and unlike its `lenientNPTv6` / `lenientNAT64Prefix` siblings the
dataplane does **not** reject the overlapping snapshot — the compiler's own doc
says it "installs with a LATENT reverse-index collision that persists until
corrected".

## PR #8425 — Sync idle persistent-NAT leases across the cluster (#8121 part 2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `feat/8121-part2`

Part 1 (#8422) landed the helper core and nothing called it. This is the channel
that does, so the inert window closes. **#8121 stays OPEN** — see "What is still
owed" at the bottom; the trailer is `Refs`, and this paragraph avoids putting a
closing keyword next to the number because GitHub does not parse negation.

## The gap

An IDLE persistent-NAT lease has zero flows but is still inside its persistence
timeout, so on the active node it is live and reusable while being invisible to
session sync — a lease is learned FROM a session, and this one has none. A client
that went quiet within its timeout keeps its translated port on the active and
loses it across a failover.

## Four layers, each carrying identity rather than position

**Coordinator** — answers what the per-allocator operations cannot: *which*
allocator. A lease with live flows resolves to a rule through its flow; an idle
lease has none, so the record carries `pool_name`. Not a rule index — that is the
same identity-versus-position hazard part 1 avoids for `addr_index`, one level
up. Export dedups by pool, because several rules can share one allocator and
exporting per RULE would send one lease as many times as there are rules pointing
at that pool.

**Control verbs** — `export_idle_leases` / `import_idle_leases`. Both take the
clock from the coordinator rather than the request, which makes *"the receiver
computes expiry from its own clock"* **structural** rather than a convention: no
caller can hand the lease path a peer's `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` value. Conversion
refuses rather than defaults — a `0.0.0.0` fallback would be a plausible address
the receiver could resolve to a real pool slot, turning a malformed record into a
wrong binding instead of a dropped one. In particular **a non-empty remote that
does not parse is malformed, not `permit-any-remote-host`**; collapsing those two
would silently widen a lease's reuse scope on the standby.

**Cluster message** — `syncMsgPersistentNatLease = 38`, with the full-set
sequence trailer and both refusals the DHCP full-set arms make: a stale sequence
or a truncated payload retains previous state rather than installing a prefix,
because a full set REPLACES.

**Daemon push loop** — gated on RG master. **The gate is not an optimisation**: a
standby holds leases only because it IMPORTED them, so exporting those would
bounce the same set between the nodes forever, and each bounce re-derives the
remaining lifetime from the receiver's clock — a lease could be refreshed
indefinitely by the echo rather than expiring.

## The cadence, as a number

**30 seconds — 0.033/s.** CLAUDE.md is explicit that a new control-socket caller
at **>1/s** starves session installs during bulk sync; this is a 30× margin under
that. It is also slow relative to what it protects: at most the last 30s of
newly-idle leases are missing on the peer, against a persistence timeout

## PR #8431 — Ship policer bandwidth as bits, not bytes, on the wire [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8429-policer-bandwidth-units`

Closes #8429

A configured `bandwidth-limit 8m` was metered at **1 Mbit/s — 12.5% of the configured rate**, because the unit chain divides twice:

```
parseBandwidthLimit          = parseScaledDecimalUnit/8  = BYTES/sec
wire `bandwidth_bps`         = that byte value, under a BITS name
filter/compiler.rs  bps / 8  = one eighth of the configured rate
```

With `then discard` that drops **conforming** customer traffic, and the policer counters attribute it to the customer — so the surface an operator checks to diagnose it confirms the wrong story.

## Direction confirmed from the body, not the comment

Verified before writing anything, since if the comment were the stale half the fix would invert. It is not — the function is literally `parseScaledDecimalUnit(s) / 8` and does return bytes.

## Fixed at the single crossing emitter

`BandwidthBps: pol.BandwidthLimit * 8` in `buildPolicerSnapshots` — **not** by removing the divisor from the shared parse. Three-color policers call the same `parseBandwidthLimit` and are correct, because they emit into `committed_rate_bytes_per_sec`, a byte-**named** field the helper does not re-divide; the eBPF leg's `RateBytesSec` is byte-named too. The single-rate userspace leg is the only one that crosses units.

No overflow: the value is `scaled/8` for a `scaled` that already fit a `uint64`.

## A second surface, mislabelled in the same direction

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_filter.go` logged `"rate_bps", pol.BandwidthLimit` — a **bytes** value under a bits key, on the eBPF leg whose *enforcement* is correct. Only the label lied, and it lied the same way: an operator reading that line to check a policer saw a rate 8× too low. Corrected to `rate_bytes_sec`.

Checked and clear otherwise: no `show` command and no Prometheus descriptor renders policer bandwidth, and `filter/compiler.rs:488` is the only wire consumer of `bandwidth_bps`. No third surface, nothing further to file.

## The guard binds the CHAIN, because neither side alone was wrong

Both sides were internally coherent — Go consistent in bytes, Rust consistent in "divide a bps field by 8" — so a Go-side pin and a Rust-side pin **both passed while the product was wrong**. That is the class no single-side test can see.

So the cell asserts the wire value **and** the result of applying the consumer's own formula to it, which makes a change on *either* side that breaks the agreement fail here.

The three-color cell is a control in the strict sense — it must be **unchanged** by this fix — and it is mutation-verified as having power:

| mutation | red |
|---|---|

## PR #8432 — config: reject a firewall filter defined twice under one family [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8426-same-family-filter-dup`

Closes #8426

## The gap

`compileFirewall` writes `dest[filter.Name] = filter` **unconditionally**, so a second `filter F` block under the **same** family replaces the first whole — terms and `then discard` included. Strict commit accepted it silently.

**The #3884 gate next door cannot see it, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight.** `filterFamilies[name]` is documented as *"the ordered set of **DISTINCT** non-inet6 families"*, and `record` returns early on a family it has already recorded — *"same family already recorded — not a cross-family reuse"*. #3884 is about cross-family reuse, so discarding the within-family repeat is **correct for it**. The consequence is that two `family inet filter F` blocks give `len(fams) == 1`, the `len(fams) < 2` guard skips them, and nothing downstream can notice: filters are referenced by NAME within the inet/inet6 buckets, so there is no dimension left to disambiguate on.

## The fix

A per-`(family, name)` count beside the existing distinct-family set, refusing a repeat — following the convention #3884 and the #5180 duplicate-named-block gate share: **reject at strict, warn on the lenient load / peer-sync path** so an already-persisted config an older binary accepted still boots with its historical result.

Same-family duplicates report **before** the cross-family loop: a name repeated under one family is a strictly more local error and gives the operator the smaller edit.

## The inet6 half is not a freebie

inet6 filters live in their own `FiltersInet6` pool and cannot collide cross-family, so **the inet6 branch `continue`s before `record` ever runs** — and it recorded names into `inet6Names`, a **bool** set, which cannot count. The write into that pool is the same unconditional last-write-wins.

**A fix that guarded only the non-inet6 branch would have left it open and passed every inet-side cell.**

## Scope — so nobody rebuilds it

| gate | covers |
|---|---|
| **#3884** | cross-family reuse |
| **#4287** | `family any` colliding with inet6 in the inet6 pool |
| **#5180** | duplicate `groups` / `interfaces` / `screen ids-option` top-level blocks (scope list verified) |

This is the remainder outside all three.

## Validation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `gofmt` | `pkg/config` debt unchanged at **6 = 6**, and `compiler_firewall.go` not among them (baseline compared against a master worktree, not remembered) |
| `go build ./...` | rc=0 |
| `go test ./...` | **70 ok / 0 FAIL** — so no existing fixture carried a duplicate this now refuses |
| all 5 new cells | verified to **run by name**, not by count |

**Two mutations, full-suite (never filtered):**

- **same-family loop removed** → reds the three duplicate cells, **both controls stay green**
- **inet6 `noteDup` call removed only** → reds **only** the inet6 cell

So the two halves are **independently bound** rather than one covering for the other — the asymmetry that let a mutation escape on #8415.

## The two controls are deliberate

A **single filter must still compile**, or a gate that rejects every filter passes the duplicate cells. And the **#3884 gate must still fire and still be reported as #3884** — this change edits `record`'s neighbourhood, and a new early return there could silence the older gate while every new cell stays green.

## PR #8439 — nat: make NAT64 prefixes members of the pool overlap index (#8115 R3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-03)

Branch: `fix/8115-r3-nat64-overlap-index`

Closes #8115 — R3, the last of the three routes. R1 landed in #8423, R2 in #8424.

## The defect

A `Nat64Prefix` owns its own `port_allocator`, keyed by `(prefix_bytes, pool_v4)`.
A source-NAT pool sharing one of those addresses — or a second prefix over the
same pool — is a **second occupancy domain over one address**: both mint the same
`X:P` for two live flows and the reverse (1:N) index cannot attribute the replies.
#5144 names exactly these as distinct collision owners at commit, which is the
evidence the dataplane treats them as independent.

## A registry gap, not a missing caller — and that decides the guard

R2 was a missing **call**: the query existed and the code did not reach it. R3 is
a missing **member**: the query works fine, the domain was absent from the
population it searches.

`wire_overlap_peers` runs inside `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous`, where
`state.nat64` does not exist yet — a prefix could never have been added there.
`wire_nat64_overlap_peers` is the second pass, from `forwarding_build` once both
are assigned. It **replaces** the source-only index with a combined one (a strict
superset, so no rule loses coverage) and hands it to both features, closing both
directions.

So **every cell goes through `build_forwarding_state`**, the real path that
populates the index. A cell that built a `PoolAddressOwners` by hand would prove
the query works and stay green with the registration deleted — which is exactly
the defect.

## Three mutations, and they are distinguishable

That distinguishability is the point: it shows registration and query are
separately bound.

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| delete the `wire_nat64_overlap_peers` call | the registry cell **and** all three direction cells |
| keep registration, delete the mint-side check | only the two NAT64-side cells — registry cell and source-NAT direction stay green |
| keep both, delete the rollback | **only** the deterministic cell, on its stranded-reservation assertion |

Each run against the full suite.

## Structure

`build_owner_index` now takes an already-deduped `OwnerView` list and both passes
use it; two copies of the counting/owner-list logic would be free to drift, and a
drifted copy still answers — just about a different population. Same reasoning
put the composed query behind one `peer_owns_identity_in` reachable from both a
`SourceNatRule` caller and an allocator-only one. **The refactor was verified
neutral on its own before anything was added.**
