## PR #8491 — Refuse the unimplemented login-class *-regexps family [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/7971-regexps-reject-at-commit`

## The finding: the family is not refused — it commits clean and vanishes

#7971 asks whether to implement the Junos `*-regexps` login-class family or close it won't-do. Before answering that, the current posture needed checking, because both the issue **and** the shipped `docs/system-login.md` record it as safe — and record it *as the safety argument*:

> "There is no schema leaf, so a `-regexps` statement is rejected at commit as an unknown leaf rather than accepted and ignored — the safe posture for a control that is not implemented."

**That is false.** Measured on the real commit path, with the supported `deny-commands` as the accept-side control:

```
deny-commands-regexps       "^set system"  ->  ACCEPT, nothing retained
allow-commands-regexps      "^show"        ->  ACCEPT, nothing retained
deny-configuration-regexps  "^system"      ->  ACCEPT, nothing retained
deny-commands (CONTROL)     "^set system"  ->  ACCEPT, DenyCommands retained
```

Both families commit clean; only one does anything. The single warning emitted is the generic `"custom RBAC recognized"` line, which fires **identically for the control** and never names the dropped leaf.

**The inference is the part that was wrong.** `closedWorld` is opt-in per subtree (`schema.go`) and `system login class` does not set it, so `SchemaValidate` leaves an unmodeled keyword to the compiler, which drops it. *Absence of a schema leaf does not imply rejection; only `closedWorld` does.*

For an **access control** that is the fail-open direction: the operator authors a restriction, sees a clean commit, and is not restricted. It is strictly worse than the missing feature, because the missing feature is at least visible — so it is a live defect, fixed here ahead of the feature question the issue actually asks.

## What this deliberately does NOT do

It does not implement the family. The four leaves are modeled **solely so they are refused**, and nothing in the new file consumes `LoginRegexFamily`.

The two families have **opposite** allow/deny precedence (plain: allow wins; `-regexps`: deny wins) and different matching subjects (`-regexps` matches the command's full path). Reusing the plain family's logic yields a `deny-commands-regexps` that loses to an `allow-commands-regexps` — a privilege escalation delivered by what looks like reuse of tested code. The refusal message carries that inversion, so an operator hitting it learns why it is not a spelling variant.

Strict commit rejects; the tolerant Load/SyncApply path downgrades to a warning like every schema validator (#1319 PR 2 / #1960), so a persisted or peer-synced config does not brick the daemon.

## Two existing guards fired — both satisfied, neither worked around

- **#5831's classification inventory** requires every login-class schema leaf to carry an explicit row in `loginClassLeafRestrictive` *and* `loginClassLeafAllowRegex`. Added as explicit `false` in both, with a note that `deny-*-regexps` will need `true` in the restrictive table if the family is ever implemented — those rows are where that decision belongs.
- **#7484's spelling-gate ratchet** moved `136 → 140` in the "unreachable (leaf changed nothing)" class. Raised **deliberately**: a leaf whose every value is refused has no output for a spelling to move, so the blindness is a property of the leaf's purpose rather than slack. The comment records the condition for lowering it again.

## Docs

`docs/system-login.md` is corrected in the same change, with the measurement inline and the reasoning error named, so the next reader does not re-derive rejection from the absence of a leaf.

## PR #8492 — config: range-gate the packed vrrp-group timer one-liners [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8483-vrrp-advertise-interval-strict`

Closes #8483

`vrrp-group <id>` is a named-instance container, and the packed hierarchical
one-liner spelling packs its properties onto the instance node's `Keys`, which
`walkInstanceChildren` consumes as unvalidated identity tokens. #5184 closed
that hole for `priority`. It was still open on the timer leaves.

## Census of the class, not just the reported member

One `*ConfigTree` per row, handed to both `SchemaValidate` and `CompileConfig`,
with a braced control that must REJECT and an in-range packed control that must
ACCEPT. Four validated leaves under `vrrpGroupSchemaNode`, two uncovered:

| leaf | schema bound | packed bypasses `SchemaValidate` | backstop before this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `virtual-address` | `ValueCIDR` | yes | yes — VIP re-parsed at compile |
| `priority` | 1..255 | yes | yes — #5184 |
| `advertise-interval` | 1..40 | yes | **no** |
| `preempt hold-time` | 1..3600 | yes | **no** |

The issue reported one. The gate closes both, and the PR states their severities
separately rather than lumping them:

**`advertise-interval` is the sharp one.** Seconds at the config layer,
converted seconds→ms then ms→centiseconds (`uint16(cfg.AdvertiseInterval / 10)`)
into the VRRPv3 Max Advert Int field, which `packet.go` writes under a 12-bit
mask (`p.MaxAdvertInt&0x0FFF`). 4095 cs is the largest interval that survives
the wire, so 40 s is the last whole-second value that encodes and 41 s aliases
to 4 cs. The aliasing is silent and **asymmetric**: the local advert timer uses
the un-narrowed value while the peer's master-down calculation uses the narrowed
one, so a packed `advertise-interval 256;` advertises as 10.24 s and the two
nodes disagree about how long silence must last before a takeover. A negative
survives `strconv.Atoi` into the same `uint16` arithmetic.

**`preempt hold-time` is a consistency gate, not a wire-safety one.** It reaches
the runtime un-narrowed (`time.Duration(PreemptHoldTime) * time.Second`), so
nothing corrupts; the bound exists so the packed spelling obeys the same range a
structured spelling of the same config already does.

## The row a naive mirror of #5184 would fail

Zero is **not** out of range for either field — it is the compiler's "unset"
sentinel (`pkg/vrrp` substitutes the 1 s default for `AdvertiseInterval == 0`
and treats `PreemptHoldTime <= 0` as preempt-immediately). A gate without that
exemption refuses every `vrrp-group` that does not configure a timer, which is
nearly all of them. There is a cell for it, and dropping the exemption kills 4.

## PR #8494 — Record the login-class *-regexps family as won't-do [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `docs/7971-regexps-feature-gap`

## The decision #7971 asks for

#8491 fixed the live defect underneath the question — the four `*-regexps` leaves committed clean and were silently discarded, which for an access control is fail-open. It deliberately did **not** answer the question the issue actually asks. This does.

**Won't-do for now**, with a `docs/feature-gaps.md` §22 row.

## Why won't-do is the honest call

Implementing is neither small nor routine, and it is security-sensitive: the family needs its own precedence (**deny wins**, against the plain family's allow wins), a different matching subject (each pattern matches the command's **full path**, not partially), compiled fields, and wiring into both enforcement points #7172 established. A mistake in any of that is a privilege escalation rather than a bug.

It is not required for the parity #7172 closed, and the leaves are now refused with a message naming the inversion and the supported alternative — so an operator following Juniper's documentation is told what to write instead of being silently ignored.

## What the row has to say — and why it is not just a parity note

The obvious framing, *"xpf implements one of Junos' two restriction families"*, understates it.

**The family xpf lacks is the deny-precedence one.** So xpf has **no** deny-wins restriction family at all — and `pkg/config/login_regex.go` already documents that the plain family's allow-over-deny, combined with unanchored partial matching, lets a wide allow silently re-permit a narrow deny. The absent family is the one whose precedence fails safe.

The row says that outright, because a reader who takes this for a syntax gap will reach for the plain family as an equivalent, and it is not one.

It also records the precedence inversion as the reason reuse is unsafe, points at `LoginRegexFamily.IdenticalPatternWinner` (#7172) so an implementer has somewhere correct to put the second rule, and names the test shape the issue specifies: a config carrying **both** families with one command matching an allow in one and a deny in the other — a single-family fixture cannot distinguish a per-family rule from a shared one.

## Counts — verified for the row I touched, deliberately not "fixed" globally

The System Enhancements summary row was **recounted directly against that section's own rows** before being incremented: 5 Missing + 1 Parse-Only beforehand, matching what the table already claimed. So its `5 → 6` / `6 → 7` is verified, not assumed.

The TOTAL row takes the same +1 and **no further**. The 23 category rows already summed to **121** against a TOTAL of **120** — a pre-existing off-by-one I did not cause. That is recorded in a note beside the table rather than silently absorbed: correcting a global quantifier would mean recounting all 23 sections, and a re-count over a population nobody has verified is worse than a known-stale number, because it reads as audited.

(My own whole-document recount returned 111, which I am *not* reporting as a finding — a crude status-prefix classifier over rows I selected is exactly the unverified population the note is about.)

## Validation

Docs-only; no behaviour change, so no suite or cluster gate applies. Both scope halves clean.

Closes #7971

## PR #8495 — test,docs: pin the fabric RETURN direction and correct its residual (#7770) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `work/7770`

**`Refs #7770` — this does NOT close it**, and the reason is the issue's
own: the remedy is a design decision about *where* the return-path
authorisation record lives (get the session to the LAN node before the
reply, versus have the redirecting node keep a punt record). Two of the
four options are dead by measurement; the thread deliberately leaves the
other two open. Picking one here would be picking it in a PR body.

What this lands is the part that is true whichever is chosen, and that is
wrong or missing today.

## 1. The disposition, established from running code

`docs/fabric-cross-chassis-fwd.md` attributed the post-#6478 residual to
*"the return direction's resolution on the receiving node is HAInactive
until the RG converges"*. Driving a session-less `wan -> lan`
fabric-ingress return frame through the real poll loop (LAN RG local, WAN
RG remote — the split placement in which the #6458 stamp validates), with
a reachable LAN neighbour so the MissingNeighbor confound is out:

```
w2l ICMP echo reply  sessions=0 forwards=0 recycle=[128] policy_deny=2 missing_neigh=0
  event kind=PolicyDeny action=0 reason=5 ingress_zone=wan egress_zone=lan
        policy_id=4294967295
w2l TCP SYN-ACK      sessions=0 forwards=0 recycle=[128] policy_deny=2 missing_neigh=0
l2w CONTROL (lan)    sessions=2 forwards=1 recycle=[]    policy_deny=0   (no event)
```

**It is a policy default-deny, not HAInactive.** `reason=5` is the TRANSIT
policy deny (6 would be host-inbound — a different arm, different fix);
`policy_id=4294967295` is the no-match default. The LAN node evaluates and
denies; it does not forward unevaluated.

That distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic: an HAInactive drop
resolves itself when the RG converges and a default-deny does not, so the
two attributions imply different remedies. It also means the posture is
already fail-**closed** — the design question is how much to safely
*relax* it, not whether to tighten it.

## 2. "Confined to the race window" is wrong when the window does not close

The same paragraph described the loss as bounded by RG convergence. A
LAN/WAN redundancy-group split is a legitimate steady state reached by two
supported `request chassis cluster failover` commands, with nothing warning
that the groups are now split. There the RGs never converge, so every new
flow re-enters the race — 12.5% of an 8-packet probe in both families,
unchanged on a fresh probe 45 s later.

## 1 — OSPF interface `authentication` (#8443)

#8473 closed the IS-IS and RIP half, where `authentication-type` is a real
free-form leaf and an unrecognised value downgraded md5 to plaintext. OSPF's half
is a **different grammar** and was left open deliberately: OSPF has no
`authentication-type` leaf at all, and `compiler_protocols.go` assigns
`AuthType` only from a matched `md5` / `simple-password`, so there is no
free-form value to type-check and #8473's instrument could not reach it.

Measured before the change, **every row committing clean**:

| authored | compiled | rendered |
|---|---|---|
| `authentication { md5 1 { key "SEKRIT"; } }` | `AuthType="md5"` | correct |
| `authentication { md5-typo 1 { key "SEKRIT"; } }` | `AuthType=""` | **nothing — UNAUTHENTICATED** |
| `authentication { md5 1 { keyy "SEKRIT"; } }` | `AuthKey=""` | nothing |
| `authentication-type md5;` | `AuthType=""` | **nothing — UNAUTHENTICATED** |

The failure direction is the point: the operator believes the adjacency is
protected and every surface they can check agrees with them.

Two mechanisms, because those are two shapes. The first three are unmodeled
keywords *inside* a modeled subtree → `closedWorld: true` on `authentication`
(which, inheriting down, also catches the misspelled `key` child of `md5`). The
fourth is a leaf that does not exist under OSPF at all → modeled solely so it is
**refused**, in the shape #7971 established (`ValueEnumOf` + unconditional
validator; `ValueAny` would leave the validator uninvoked).

**Scope was a decision, not an omission.** Closing the whole OSPF `interface`
world would also catch the fourth row — measured, and the `pkg/config` suite
stayed green with all eight `protocols … interface` nodes closed. Not done here:
it converts every unmodeled protocol leaf from inert to refused, which is the
#8296 class. `TestOSPFAuthGateDidNotCloseTheInterfaceWorld8443` reds if a later
change makes that flip incidentally.

## PR #8497 — test: record which BUILD a cluster cell measured [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/cluster-cell-build-identity`

The #1875 lock serialises **access** to the shared loss userspace cluster. It says nothing about what is **running** on it. Those are different guarantees, and the gap between them silently invalidated two of my measurement runs tonight.

## The incident

I waited ~5 minutes for the lock, never touched the holder, acquired cleanly — and then measured a binary another lane's deploy had installed moments earlier. Its subject was `fix/7209-prewarm-index-never-drop-underivable`: the session prewarm/replication path, which was *the very code path I was testing*. Every lock-level check said clean.

The only tell was a CLI banner reading `uptime: 1m46s` for a daemon I believed I had deployed hours before. The build then changed under me a **second** time in a later cell (`89d2eec0…` → `a7414a5d…`). Two runs of careful, plausible-looking numbers described the wrong binary, and one of them had already been reported as a finding before I caught it.

That is a confound that survives every discipline this board has. It should not be left to be re-derived per lane.

## What this adds

`with-cluster.sh` samples the deployed `xpfd` sha per node at acquire, exports the baseline path so a **long** cell can re-assert it before each measurement rather than only at the boundaries — the originating incident took both of its measurements inside **one** cell — and reports a change at release naming **both** shas. Knowing *which* build was measured is what let me trace mine to a specific sibling branch.

Three surfaces, deliberately different in severity:

| surface | severity | for |
|---|---|---|
| `xpf_cluster_build_report` | **advisory** (fatal under `XPF_CLUSTER_BUILD_STRICT=1`) | the cell boundary |
| `xpf_assert_cluster_build_unchanged` | **fatal** | a measurement, called immediately before it samples |
| `xpf_cluster_rebaseline_build` | — | a cell that deployed on purpose |

**Why the boundary is advisory and the assert is fatal.** A cell that deploys legitimately changes the sha. The sanctioned deploy path re-baselines, but an image roll, an `xpfd upgrade`, or a path nobody wired would trip a fatal boundary check and break a working target for a diagnostic. A measurement is the opposite case: it is where a wrong answer is expensive *and* the caller knows it is not deploying. So that is where the hard failure goes.

The assert fails on **"cannot tell"** as well as on a change. A measurement that cannot name its subject is not evidence — and "I could not sample" must never read as "unchanged", which is the failure-to-a-healthy-looking-value shape this whole file exists to close.

**Re-baseline is wired into `cluster-setup.sh`'s deploy.** Without it every deploy cell cries wolf and the warning gets trained away — the exact failure mode the check exists to prevent.

**Sampling is best-effort and bounded** (10s/node, overridable). A node that is off or mid-reboot yields `unknown`. This is a diagnostic; it must never become a new way for the cluster to be unusable.

## Tests

`cluster-build-identity-selftest.sh` — **9 cases**, mocked `incus`, mocked `cluster-env.sh`, private paths, no cluster. Registered in `run-selftests.sh` and `make test-cluster-lock-lib`.

Five mutations, **all killed, each by a different case**:

| # | mutation | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | treat an `unknown` sample as a clean bill | case 5 (unsampleable → UNKNOWN) |
| P2 | diff always reports "unchanged" | case 2 (changed build) |
| P3 | assert lenient about "cannot tell" | case 5 |
| P4 | `STRICT` no longer promotes the boundary report | case 7 |
| P5 | **delete the re-baseline call from the deploy path** | case 9 only |

P5 is the one worth noting: cases 1–8 all stay green without that call, because they exercise the helpers directly. Case 9 binds the **call site**, with a negative control so the search can actually fail.

Two things the repo's own guards caught in intermediate revisions, both fixed here:

- the **self-test census** in `make selftest` failed because my new self-test was not invoked by the runner — exactly what that census is for;
- the two existing lock self-tests were reaching a **real cluster** through the new probe. `XPF_CLUSTER_BUILD_PROBE=0` keeps them hermetic.

## PR #8498 — test,docs: separate the four #7209 blocking calls by what forwarding holds [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `work/7209-item2`

`Refs #7209` — **this does not close it, and it does not take anything off
the lock.** It is the STEP-1 result for scope item 2, and the result is a
negative one that changes the plan.

## The four blocking calls are not interchangeable

I went in expecting item 2 to be uniformly blocked by the derived-state
work item 1 needs. **It is not.** Two of the four can be taken off the
lock today; two cannot. The discriminator is what `Coordinator.forwarding`
holds at that instant — not how long the call blocks.

Phase order inside `Coordinator::reconcile`, read rather than inferred:

| # | phase | `forwarding` there | blocking call | releasable today |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `snapshot::preflight_map_fds` | previous table, still installed | BPF map-pin opens | **yes** |
| 2 | `tear_down` → `stop_inner(false)` | **emptied** | worker `join()` (unbounded) | no |
| 3 | `tear_down`, after `stop_inner` | **emptied** | mlx5 quiesce, 500 ms | no |
| 4 | `snapshot::apply_snapshot` assigns `coord.forwarding = new_forwarding` | new table installed | — | — |
| 5 | `bringup::bring_up_workers` | new table | readiness barrier, **10 s** | **yes** |

`apply_snapshot` installs the new table and `reconcile` calls it **before**
`bring_up_workers`, so **the 10 s barrier runs with a populated table.**
That is the call that matters — the one that can exceed the Go side's 3 s
session round-trip budget and take the rest of a #5380 bulk batch with it —
and it is releasable without item 1.

## Why phases 2 and 3 are blocked — three executable legs, not prose

* `stop_inner(false)` empties the table but deliberately **keeps** the
  shared synced map, so an import landing in the window persists;
* `synthesized_synced_reverse_entry` has exactly one early return, on
  `is_reverse` — no forwarding-dependent `None` arm — so the companion is
  built from nothing and published;
* `replay_synced_sessions` publishes `entry.decision` **verbatim** and
  re-queues the entry. It never re-synthesizes, so the reconcile that would
  have to repair it does not.

Latent today: the only way to reach it without a lock move is a standby
taking bulk sync before its first apply, and RG activation re-derives the
companion (measured: `NoRoute`/ifindex 0/owner 0 before,
`ForwardCandidate`/ifindex 6/owner 2 after). A mid-life `apply_snapshot` on
an already-**active** node reaches no activation, so a lock release is
exactly what turns it into a permanent wrong reply-path row.

The three cells are **characterization** cells. They pin what the code does
now so the prerequisite is a red rather than a paragraph, and each carries
in its failure message what a reader should do when it flips.

`make test-go` target — every other package's result lost with it. The cost is
not the lost run: it trains re-running a red reflexively until it goes green, and
a genuine intermittent regression here would be waved through by the same reflex.

Two changes, **proven to different degrees**, and saying which is which is the
point of this PR.

---

## The retry — this is the part that closes both issues

A single degenerate attempt no longer fails the test. The contended run moves
into `runHeartbeatRaceProbe7257`, which returns what it reached; the caller
retries up to 3 times and fails only if **every** attempt reached the publish
window zero times.

Its correctness does not depend on *why* an attempt went degenerate, which is
what makes it the right instrument: calibration measures the load at calibration
time, and a full-suite run's load is not stationary. It does not hide a
structural degeneracy — a probe that cannot reach its window by construction
reaches it zero times on every attempt and still fails, with per-attempt data in
the message. It only distinguishes *"this machine was busy"* from *"this probe is
broken"*, which is the distinction one attempt could not make.

**Mutation-tested both ways:**

| mutation | observed |
|---|---|
| force every attempt degenerate | retries 3×, fails with the all-attempts message + per-attempt data |
| force only the **first** attempt degenerate | retries once, **passes on attempt 2**, log says so |

## PR #8500 — dataplane: do not let a zero replica erase a session's volume (#7919 hardening) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/7919-session-counters`

**Refs #7919 — this is a HARDENING, not a fix for the reported defect, and it should not be read as one.** #7919 stays open.

(The verb is dropped deliberately: GitHub's parser does not read negation, so "this does not fix #N" contains a live close token.)

## What happened, in order

1. The issue's standing diagnosis was **pacing** — the mirror refresh being up to ~6.4s behind. That is refuted by the issue's own recorded data: three samples at t=8/22/38s, and **exactly one** live row out of many, which a cursor sweep cannot produce. Retracted on the issue.
2. I proposed a replacement: every worker refreshes its **own** session table into the **same** BPF row, and the replication types carry **no counters field at all** (`SyncedSessionEntry` at `worker/mod.rs:391`, `SessionInstall` at `ctx.rs:31`), so a non-owning worker's copy is created at zero and can never advance. Five of six writers publishing zero over the owner's volume.
3. I built the gate, measured it on the cluster, and it looked like it worked.
4. **Then I ran the control, and it refutes step 2 as the cause.**

## The control

Same box, same workload, deployed sha verified at deploy **and** re-checked at end of cell:

| build | control conn | data conn A | data conn B |
|---|---|---|---|
| with the gate (`d5cd426c…`) | 6 pkts | 24865 → 107202 | **0** |
| gate reverted (`89d2eec0…`) | 6 pkts | 20073 → 102417 | **0** |

Identical. Master already mirrors live counters for one data flow and zero for another; the gate changes **nothing observable**. My earlier "the fix works" came from comparing against a *different lane's binary* and is discarded — see #8497, which exists because of that.

## So why keep it

The hazard is real and **structural**, not incidental — it cannot be argued away by timing or ordering, only by a change to which workers hold the entry. `a_sibling_workers_replica_carries_zero_counters_for_a_live_session_7919` drives the **real** `synced_replica_entry` + `upsert_synced_with_origin` fan-out and shows the owner's table yielding `(5000, 7500000)` while the sibling's yields `(0, 0)` for the same key, with a positive control on the owner so the sibling's zero is not "the walk found nothing".

And the write it prevents is never desirable: a zero-counter entry has nothing to contribute to a row that has volume.

**What is NOT established** is that a sibling's refresh reaches that row in production — `handle_upsert_synced`'s HA re-resolution is bypassed by the pin, and the control suggests it does not. The rationale at the change site says exactly this, in those words. That was the point of the second commit: the first one's comment claimed the clobber was why counters read zero, which would have written a false cause into the tree.

## The predicate: there isn't one, deliberately

An origin predicate gets this wrong twice:

- skipping `is_peer_synced()` entries **entirely** also stops refreshing `last_seen`, which drives idle/expiry — on a **standby** every entry is `SyncImport`, so it expires synced sessions early;
- excluding `is_peer_synced()` from just the **counter** write covers `SharedMaterialize`, which is exactly the origin a worker takes when it *receives* traffic for a shared session (`materialized_shared_hit_origin`) — freezing counters for post-failover traffic specifically, which no test written before a failover can see.

So the rule is **"an all-zero entry does not overwrite"** — origin-agnostic, no new state, correct across promotion and materialization. `last_seen` and `policy_id` are still refreshed unconditionally; only the four counter fields are gated.

Two checks it rests on, both **verified in-tree rather than assumed**: a legitimate zeroing goes through `publish_bpf_conntrack_entry` with `BPF_ANY` (which creates/overwrites) and never needs to propagate through the refresh, which is `BPF_EXIST` and cannot create — stated at `publish_conntrack.rs:302-303`, and those are the only two writers of the maps. And a session whose owner genuinely has zero counters keeps its published zero, which is the correct value; that limit is written at the change site.

The choice is **extracted** into `mirrored_counters` because the refresh does raw BPF syscalls a unit test cannot observe, and four inline assignments cannot be bound.

| N2 | narrow to `fwd_packets == 0` alone | **only** `a_reverse_only_session_is_still_mirrored_7919` |

## PR #8501 — dataplane: stop filing a VLAN bring-up failure as a creation failure [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8122-vlan-adopt-observability`

Closes #8122

**#8122's body premise was already falsified on the issue** — the create path
does not fail the apply either. This implements what the thread converged on
instead, and records the one residual it decided not to implement, with the
measurement behind that decision.

## 1 — The record said a creation failed that had not

The caller's soft-skip labels its `UnarmedSurface` `"create failed"` for any
error that is not `errVLANAdoptRefused`. Two of `ensureVLANSubInterface`'s error
returns happen **after** `netlink.LinkAdd` has already succeeded — the created
link could not be found again, or `LinkSetUp` refused. Both were filed as
creation failures for a link that **was** created.

That is the #6916 harm one branch over: *"a false statement in the operator's own
record … the statement that would send them looking for a creation error that
never happened."* `errVLANBringUpFailed` marks those two and the label becomes
`"created but could not be brought up"`.

It deliberately **does not change the disposition**. `errVLANCreateFailed` stays
the only sentinel that fails the apply, for the reason its own comment gives: the
link exists, `compileFirewallFilters` resolves it, and the #6893 harm does not
arise. A cell pins that, and the mutation that widens the gate reds 3.

## 2 — `accept_ra` was applied on one path because of where the line sat

The write sat below `netlink.LinkAdd`, so the adopt branch returned before
reaching it and a VLAN child that **pre-existed the daemon** with `accept_ra=1`
kept it. Both paths now call one `disableAcceptRA`.

Narrow, and stated as such: `pkg/networkd` emits `IPv6AcceptRA=no` for every
managed interface and daemon bring-up sets `default/accept_ra=0`. But it does
**not** self-heal on an aborted apply — `d.networkd.Apply` is guarded on
`applyResult != nil`, so the re-assertion is skipped precisely when the abort
leaves the child adopted. Taken here only because this change already touches the
create/adopt symmetry.

An adopted child whose `LinkSetUp` nudge fails stays in the dataplane, is armed,
and is DOWN. A fourth record type was considered and **rejected on measurement**:

| `UnarmedSurface` | consumed by the arm-coverage proof, which is about attachment — a down-but-attached child is legitimately `CoverageDirect`. `StillForwarding` documents the opposite condition. |
| a new type, following `UnappliedFilterBinding` | that precedent has **no production consumer** outside its own tests. A record nothing reads is not observability. |

## PR #8503 — userspace: say why forwarding was disarmed [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8447-instrument`

## The cause is not in NAT

On a chassis cluster, a source rule pointing at a pool carrying `persistent-nat`
sets `ForwardingSupported=false` (`capabilities.go`, verbatim:
`cfg.Chassis.Cluster != nil && userspaceConfigUsesPersistentSourceNAT(cfg)`).
That makes `disarmBeforeUnsupportedPublishLocked` send
`set_forwarding_state{armed:false}` **before** the snapshot publish;
`desiredForwardingArmedLocked` then keeps it disarmed and the 1 Hz reconcile
short-circuits because desired == actual. Disarmed bindings stop counting RX,
which is #8447's reported `rx=0`.

**That boundary is deliberate and documented** — #1449, written up in
`docs/ha-failover-status.md` and `docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md`.
Persistent-NAT leases are helper-local allocator state that is not
HA-synchronized, so the dataplane declines to forward rather than forward with
semantics it cannot honour. **This PR does not touch it.**

## What was actually wrong: it was silent

The commit succeeds. Nothing logs. There is no metric. The only surface is
`Forwarding supported: false` inside a `show` nobody runs when the symptom is
"the link went down".

The smoking gun is in the function itself: `reason` was computed and used
**only** to decorate an error string on the FAILURE path, so the success path —
the one that actually stops traffic — emitted nothing at all.

#8447 took five rounds of cluster measurement (counter deltas, arm-order
controls, log-line censuses) to rediscover a documented contract whose reason
the daemon already had and threw away. So this is an **observability defect**,
and the fix is scoped to that: log it at WARN, with the reasons and the
consequence, once per publish.

## A hypothesis I held and had to abandon

I suspected the finding was an instrument artifact. Every number in the issue's
table comes from one `curl -s --max-time 8 .../metrics`, and
`test/incus/pnat-upstream-stage-8447.sh` prints only non-zero deltas with **no
emptiness guard** — so an empty scrape produces a byte-identical table.

**Refuted, by the newer harness.** `pnat-wedge-recovery-8447.sh`'s `rx_now()`
prints the literal `ABSENT` when the series is missing, and the landed run
reported numeric `6 / 0 / 0 / 6`, never `RX-ABSENT`. The endpoint answered and
carried the series; the counter was present and flat.

Recorded because the older harness's table still is not evidence on its own —
it cannot distinguish absence from flatness, and anyone re-running it should
know that.

## PR #8504 — cluster: make the #5303 buffer-sizing observation per-SessionSync [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8182-per-instance-configure-hook`

Closes #8182

`TestPreAuthDefersBufferSizingUntilAuth` reds under full-suite load and passes in
isolation, as a full package, and on a clean re-run.

## The mechanism is a shared global, and the failure was a FALSE NEGATIVE

The test swapped the package-level `configureConnFn` and restored it with
`defer`, and the assertion built on it is a **negative** — *"this must not have
been called"*. `pkg/cluster` has 36 `t.Parallel()` calls and seven test files
that reach `handleNewConnection`, so a parallel sibling completing a
**successful** handshake while the swap was installed satisfied the hook and
reddened the assertion. The #5303 deferral was intact the whole time.

That is why this is fixed rather than retried. A negative assertion over shared
global state cannot distinguish *"the deferral was reverted"* from *"a neighbour
ran"* — so a real revert of #5303 would have been indistinguishable from the
noise, and waved through by the same re-run reflex the noise trains.

## The fix

`configureConnFn` becomes a per-instance `SessionSync.configureConn` with a nil
default, reached through a `configureSyncConn` method. A test binds its own
sync's hook; another `SessionSync` running concurrently cannot reach it.

The field is deliberately **not** under `mu`: it is written only before the
connection goroutines that read it start, so the `go` statement supplies the
happens-before edge — and `mu` is already held by the connection paths when they
reach the call site.

## The isolation is proven, not argued

A new cell runs the neighbour **deliberately**: a second `SessionSync` completes
a real successful handshake — the path that legitimately sizes buffers — while
the first sync's observation is installed, and the first sync's counter must stay
false. It carries its own vacuity control asserting the neighbour actually
sized, because without it the cell passes when the neighbour silently does
nothing (and that control fired for real during development, twice).

## Two wrong mutations before the right one

Reverting to a package-wide hook must make the new cell red. Getting that
mutation right took three tries, and the two failures are worth recording
because each would have been read as a result:

| attempt | outcome | why it was wrong |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **ESCAPED** (green) | deleted the vacuity control along with the mechanism, so the cell passed vacuously |
| 2 | red, but on the **wrong assertion** | made the shared hook take priority instead of chaining, so the neighbour's own hook never ran and the cell reported "vacuous" rather than "isolation broken" — a reader would have misdiagnosed it |
| 3 | **red on the isolation assertion**, with the message naming the defect | chains, which is what the old test actually did: `configured.Store(true)` then `orig(c)` |

## PR #8506 — userspace-dp: report the session's own window in the Timeout column [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8125-session-timeout-column`

Closes #8125

`show security flow session` printed `Timeout: 1800` for every session regardless
of the window in force. Measured on the cluster, with the **reap behaviour**
proving the windows differed:

```
closing-timeout UNSET (30 s window):   Timeout: 1800s   session alive at +8s
closing-timeout 3     (3 s window):    Timeout: 1800s   session GONE  at +8s
```

…and 1800 for ESTABLISHED sessions too, whose window is 300 s unless configured.
1800 is the JUNOS default for `established-timeout`.

## The source is one constant in the publisher

`publish_conntrack.rs` stamped `timeout: 1800` at install for v4 and v6, and
nothing filled it in afterwards. `pkg/cli/cli_show_flow.go:371` prints
`val.Timeout` verbatim, and `SessionValue.Timeout` has **no assignment anywhere
on the local read path** — its only Go writers decode a *peer's* wire payload. So
the column was exactly what the helper stamped, every time.

Worse than an unimplemented column: a wrong number is indistinguishable from a
right one at the point of reading, and #7342 gave operators a reason to look at
this column to confirm which window a session is on.

## Fixed on both paths, because either alone leaves a lying window

| path | what it does now |
|---|---|
| **install** | the window is resolved from the session table (`SessionTable::timeout_secs_for`, mirroring the #5213 `session_id` plumbing) at all four `poll_descriptor` sites and threaded to both builders |
| **refresh** | `iter_with_idle_budgeted` now delivers each entry's `expires_after_ns`, and the refresh re-stamps `value.timeout` beside the `last_seen` and `policy_id` it already re-stamps |

Fixing only the install would leave every already-open session on the constant;
fixing only the refresh would leave a new session reporting 1800 for up to a full
refresh cycle. **1800 survives only as the documented fallback for a publish with
no live entry** — the pre-#8125 behaviour for exactly the case that has no window
to report.

The refresh reads the window **from the walked entry**, not by looking it up
again by key: the walk already holds it, and a second lookup could observe a
different entry than the one being refreshed. Zero is never written — it would
render as an immediate expiry the session is not on.

`expires_after_ns` is the field the expiry wheel itself uses, so this reports
what actually governs the session rather than a re-derivation that could disagree
with it.

## PR #8508 — Treat a mid-token bracket as a literal, not list sugar [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8453-mid-token-brackets`

## The defect

An unquoted value whose domain legitimately contains `[` / `]` had its brackets stripped by the bracketed-list lexer before any validator saw it, and the result was a **different value that was still valid**:

```
as-path ap1 .*65000[0-9]*   ->  stored ".*65000 0-9 *"
community c1 members a[b]c  ->  ["a", "b", "c"]
```

The regex still compiles, so #6686's `ValidASPathRegex` passes it — what that gate checks is *compilability*, and the mangled form is compilable. It matches the literal text `65000 0-9`, which no real AS path contains, so the term never fires. The community case is worse: **one authored member becomes three**, and the route-map now matches `a` OR `b` OR `c` where the operator wrote one community.

The quoted spelling was preserved byte-for-byte through the same path, which is what made the diagnosis unambiguous.

## It is not the #2419 class, and that decides where the fix goes

#2419 is "the compiler reads `Keys[1]` and drops the rest", repaired by accumulating `Keys[1:]` **and** `Children`. The AST dump shows the opposite:

```
unquoted  Keys=["as-path" "ap1" ".*65000" "0-9" "*"]
quoted    Keys=["as-path" "ap1" ".*65000[0-9]*"]
```

Stored is **exactly `Keys[2:]` joined** — the compiler already accumulates correctly, and **the accumulation is the mechanism of the damage, not the fix**. `isIdentChar` excludes both brackets, so the scanner terminates at one and `Next`'s skip loop consumes it as a delimiter. The characters are gone before the AST exists, so no compiler change and no commit-time gate can recover them. Reconstruction fails too: `grouped` records that a token came from inside brackets, but not whether the bracket was *adjacent*, so a rebuild's best effort is `.*65000 [0-9] *`.

## The rule

> **A `[` or `]` met mid-token, outside any open bracket list, is a literal character of the value.**

The discriminator is **position, not shape**: a Junos list opener always *begins* a token, so a bracket met after a character has already been consumed cannot be one. That is the principle #5182's `tryBracketedEndpointLiteral` already established for `[<addr>]:port`, narrowed further — that one looks *forward* from a leading `[` and needs a `:port` suffix to stay unambiguous, while this never fires on a leading `[` at all.

Gating on `bracketDepth == 0` is what keeps a genuine list intact: inside `[ a b ]` the depth is 1, so the closing `]` still terminates `b` and closes the list.

## The residual — stated, not hidden

**A *leading* bracket is not fixed.** `as-path ap1 [0-9]+` is genuinely indistinguishable from a one-element list by any local rule and still requires quoting. It is stated in the code, pinned by a cell asserting it is **still** tokenized as a list, and named here — a fix that silently leaves one case unfixed is how the next reader concludes the class is closed.

## The matrix

| authored | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.*65000[0-9]*` | `.*65000` `0-9` `*` | `.*65000[0-9]*` | **fixed** |
| `a[b]c` | `a` `b` `c` | `a[b]c` | **fixed** |
| `65000:[100` | `65000:` `100` | `65000:[100` | **fixed** |
| `[ a b c ]` | `a` `b` `c` | `a` `b` `c` | unchanged |
| `[a b]` | `a` `b` | `a` `b` | unchanged |
| `[tcp]` / `[ ]` | `tcp` / — | same | unchanged |
| `[2001:db8::1]:51820` | whole (#5182) | whole | unchanged |
| `[ 65000:100 65000:200 ]` | two members | two members | unchanged |
| `[0-9]+` | `0-9` `+` | `0-9` `+` | **residual — quote it** |

## PR #8509 — mutate: emit the machine-readable stream from the GATE, not a bypass [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8231-machine-readable-gate`

Closes #8231

The mutation driver's `KILLED` verdicts are **count-based**: they say *something*
failed, not that the cell's target failed. If another test in the package was
already red, a cell that changed nothing scores `KILLED` with rc and count in
agreement and nothing looking wrong. That is a false claim of coverage, and only
a **name** refutes it.

`make test-go GOTESTJSON=<path>` now appends the `go test -json` event stream to
that file while leaving stdout byte-identical — `scripts/go-test-json.sh`
reconstructs the human stream from the `.Output` fields, which carry every byte
the text formatter would have written. `scripts/mutate.sh` sets it per cell and,
when a spec row names a target test in an optional **5th TAB column**, refines
the verdict with `mutation_verdict_for_target`. Four-column specs keep working.

## This is deliberately not the obvious repair

Converting the driver to `go test -json` would buy attribution and pay for it in
**gate coverage**. Gating through `make` is why a cell carries `go vet`, the
targeted `-race` runs with `-count=2`, and on the Rust side `--release` and
`--test-threads=1`. A narrower gate that agrees with the old one is
indistinguishable from a sufficient one right up until the day it is not.

## The mechanism produced a wrong attribution on its own first outing

Worth leading with, because it is the failure this PR then fixes. `test-go` has
two legs and both **append** — required, they must land in one stream. Without a
truncate at the top of the target, a second `make test-go GOTESTJSON=x`
attributes over the **union of two runs**.

The first full gate run reported `rc=0` while the attribution named
`TestMakefileRunsAuditPackageUncached` — a test that failed in the *previous* run
and passes in this one. A reader taking the name at face value would have chased
a test that was already green. The target now truncates once before the first
leg; `mutate.sh` already truncated per cell. Both halves of that contract —
*the wrapper appends*, *the caller truncates* — are pinned by their own cases,
because it spans two files and either side changing silently breaks attribution.

Proof: a truncated run over the refactoraudit leg yields **243 events and an
empty failing-name set**.

## Two properties, each with its own case

- **Default path** (`GOTESTJSON` unset) execs `go test` unchanged. The shared
  gate must not acquire a `jq` dependency or a new failure mode; the selftest
  asserts stdout and exit code match a direct run.
- **A set `GOTESTJSON` with no `jq` REFUSES** rather than falling back. A caller
  that asked for attribution and silently got a stream it cannot attribute over
  would read an empty file as "no failing tests" — the
  indistinguishable-from-healthy value this exists to prevent. It also leaves no

## PR #8511 — dataplane: report per-worker session-volume high water (#7919 instrument) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/7919-session-counter-query`

**Refs #7919.** Adds the measurement the issue has been missing, and nothing else. It does not fix #7919 — it makes the remaining question answerable.

## Why this, and why it is not the per-session query I was authorised to build

#7919 narrowed to one question no surface could answer: **does the owning worker's own session table hold the volume, or does it not?** The two answers point at different defects — a mirror losing a value it was given, versus accounting that never produced one — and every derivation on the issue so far, mine included, reasoned about the *mirror* rather than the source of truth behind it.

I was cleared to add a per-session control-socket verb. I built something smaller instead, because the axis turned out to be per-**worker**, not per-session:

> Measured on the reference cluster with three transit flows — `xpf_userspace_worker_session_table_entries` reads **6 on all six workers** (3 flows × fwd+rev) while the conntrack map holds **3** rows, against a **0-across-the-board baseline** with no transit.

So every worker holds a copy of every session, but only the worker whose packets land accounts for one — the replication types carry no counters field. *"Which workers' tables ever hold volume"* is therefore the whole discriminator, and it needs one number per worker, not a query per session. That is an added status field rather than a new verb, a new round-trip, and a new blocking wait.

The per-session verb stays available if this does not discriminate. **Ping me and I will build it** — I am not closing that option, just not spending it yet.

## What it does

`WorkerRuntimeCounters::session_volume_high_water` — the largest `fwd_packets + rev_packets` this worker has ever seen on a **forward** entry of its own table.

Sampled on the conntrack-mirror refresh walk, which **already** iterates the table on a budgeted slice: one compare per walked entry, **no new iteration**, nothing on the packet path. `refresh_bpf_conntrack_last_seen` now returns a `RefreshSliceOutcome` carrying the cursor it always returned plus the observed max; the cursor contract is unchanged and its existing budget test still binds it.

**A high-water, not a per-cycle max**, deliberately: the walk is budgeted, so one cycle may miss a busy session, and a per-cycle value would read 0 for a worker whose one busy session was simply not in that slice — a zero indistinguishable from *"never accounted"*, which is the exact confusion this exists to resolve.

## Absent is not zero

This is the part that makes it usable as evidence rather than decoration.

The field is **ADDED, never a redefinition** — in a rolling HA upgrade the two nodes run different binaries on one wire, so the new concept takes a new key. An old helper omits it; Go decodes it as `*uint64` and **nil means "this helper does not report it"**. A missing answer read as `0` would assert that a worker has never carried traffic — manufacturing exactly the evidence being gathered.

The helper also skips the key while the value is 0, so a genuine never-observed reading and an old helper are indistinguishable. That is correct: both mean *"no positive evidence of volume"*, and neither is a measurement.

## The consumer ships with it

A record nothing reads is not observability. `xpf_userspace_worker_session_volume_high_water` is emitted per worker and **only when the helper reported it** — no series is the honest encoding of "cannot answer".

## Tests

**Rust** — the slice reports the busiest walked session's volume, with a control that an *unaccounted* table reports 0 so the value cannot be an artefact of walking rather than of volume; plus the wire contract both directions, including an old payload without the key still decoding.

**Go** — the metric carries the value when reported; is **absent** when unreported, with a positive control that sibling worker series *are* emitted for the same status so the absence assertion cannot pass vacuously; and the decoder pins absent→nil with a control that the old payload really decoded.

### Mutations — 5, all killed, each by the intended cell

| # | mutation | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | delete the metric's **CALL SITE** (not its function) | `...IsEmittedWhenReported7919` |
| Q2 | emit unconditionally, so absent becomes a measured 0 | `...IsAbsentWhenUnreported7919` |
| Q3 | rename the JSON key | `...AbsentDecodesToNil7919` |
| Q4 | remove the Rust sampling | `a_refresh_slice_reports_the_largest_session_volume_it_walked_7919` |
| Q5 | drop `skip_serializing_if`, so a 0 reaches the wire | `an_unobserved_session_volume_high_water_stays_off_the_wire_7919` |

## PR #8513 — Warn at commit when a deny pattern cannot fire on a surface [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8189-commit-time-unenforceable-advisory`

## What lands

The unenforceable-deny finding moves from the **authorization path** (logged once per class when someone first makes a restricted call) to **commit output**, where every other #7172 advisory speaks.

Measured on the real commit path before this change, an unenforceable pattern and an enforceable one produced **identical** output — one warning each, the generic `recognized (custom RBAC)` line, no advisory of any kind. Nothing distinguished them.

## Why a registry and not a moved table

The three command tables live in `pkg/grpcapi`, which imports `pkg/config` and not the reverse. Relocating them is not available either: `showTextTopicCommand` is **derived** from `cmdtree.ShowTextTopicCommands()` (#8058), and `pkg/cmdtree` imports `pkg/config` too — so no package holding all three can be imported from `pkg/config`.

Inverting the dependency is the only direction available: a surface registers what it can produce, `pkg/config` reasons over whatever registered. It also makes the honest wording literally accurate — this **is** the registered command set.

`unenforceableDenyPatterns` now **delegates** to the shared predicate instead of keeping its own loop. Two implementations of "can this pattern ever fire" would be two things to keep in agreement, and a commit-time answer disagreeing with the runtime one is the confusion this advisory exists to remove.

The delegation is **scoped to grpcapi's own surface name**, not "any registered surface" — those are the same set only while gRPC is the sole registrant, and an unscoped check would quietly start answering a different question the moment a second appears.

## Every ambiguous case resolves to silence

This is the load-bearing decision, and it follows from the failure direction. If a command is reachable but missing from a table, a pattern matching only it is reported unenforceable — telling the operator **at commit** that a restriction which actually works does nothing. They then remove it or broaden it, and both are worse than the silence being replaced. Moving the finding into commit output *raises* the cost of it being wrong.

So: **no registered surface, or a surface reporting zero commands, emits nothing.** An empty set makes every pattern vacuously unmatched, which would fire the advisory on every config in the field.

## The wording is scoped to what the guards actually bind

It says **"the REGISTERED command set"**, never "the commands this surface can present".

Each of the three tables *is* guarded against its own source in **both** directions. What is **not** guarded is server-table vs client (`cmd/cli/show.go`) — #8058's subject, single-sourced for one of three: `showTextTopicCommand` is derived from `cmdtree`, while `methodCanonicalCommand` and `systemActionVerbCommand` are still hand-maintained literals. The narrower phrase is true of what is checked; the wider one would claim the correspondence nothing checks.

## No fourth drift guard — and that is deliberate

#8189 asks for one, on the premise that *"only the first one currently has a guard"*. **That is false at `origin/master`.** Both named tests carry the reverse direction, and say so in their own comments:

```
authz_command_table_topics_7172_test.go:162  "...does not serve — a stale entry hides an unmapped real verb"
authz_command_table_7172_test.go:109         "Stale direction: an entry for a method that is no longer served."
```

A fourth guard would be a second list of the same fact, and two lists of one fact drift apart. The correction is posted on the issue.

## Validation

`go build ./...`, `go vet`, and the `pkg/config` (97s) + `pkg/grpcapi` (14s) suites green at the rebased head. Both scope halves clean — five files, all mine.

`go test ./...` reports one failure, **`pkg/memlockcensus/TestMemlockCensusMatchesTheTree`, which is PRE-EXISTING and not from this branch.** Verified by running that package on a clean detached worktree at `origin/master` `d3fefa473` with none of these changes present: identical failure, same two rows. It appears to be self-referential — the census flags `census_8371_test.go`'s own `TestMemlockGuardsAreInertHere` and `scanTree` as unregistered memlock-gated guards — and it arrived with #8512, which merged shortly before this branch rebased. Flagged separately; master is currently red on it.

## PR #8514 — test: stop the memlock census matching its own scanner [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8371-census-self-match`

**Master is red from #8512 and this fixes it.** Reproduced on a clean worktree at
`origin/master`:

```
--- FAIL: TestMemlockCensusMatchesTheTree
    #8371: 2 memlock-gated guard(s) exist in the tree but are NOT in the registry:
      pkg/memlockcensus/census_8371_test.go -> TestMemlockGuardsAreInertHere
      pkg/memlockcensus/census_8371_test.go -> scanTree
```

The scanner was censusing itself. Neither row is a guard whose protection is
conditional — the first **calls** `rlimit.RemoveMemlock` to report whether the
privilege exists, the second **greps for the literal**.

## Why the pre-merge suite was green, which is the part worth keeping

`git grep` reads **tracked** files only, and `census_8371_test.go` was still
untracked when `go test ./...` ran in the authoring worktree. **The scanner could
not see itself until the commit landed.**

So the green was real, and it was measuring a tree that stopped existing the
moment the file entered the index. A pre-merge verdict that cannot hold
post-merge, from an instrument whose input is the index rather than the working
tree.

**Generalises:** a scanner reading `git grep`, `git ls-files`, or any
index-backed source must be exercised against a tree where its own files are
**committed**. Run on a dirty worktree, it measures a different population than
CI will.

## The exclusion is pinned in both directions

An exclusion is a hole, and a hole widened by one character stops the census
seeing an entire package — which would leave it trivially satisfied and reading
exactly like a clean tree. `TestTheScannerExcludesItselfAndOnlyItself` asserts:

- the constant names a file that **exists** — an exclusion naming a missing path
  excludes nothing and would go unnoticed;
- it is a single `_test.go` file, not a prefix or directory;
- the scan still finds the tree's guards afterwards;
- no censused row is the scanner itself.

Widening the constant to the directory **reds 2 cells**.

## PR #8516 — afxdp: re-derive the synced reverse companion at reconcile replay (#7209 item 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `work/7209-barrier-offlock`

`Refs #7209` — **does not close it.** Both acceptance cells stay
`#[ignore]`d and `sync_session` is still under the snapshot-wide mutex.
This is item 1, shape (ii), which unblocks two of the four blocking calls
scope item 2 wants off that mutex.

## The defect

`synthesized_synced_reverse_entry` has exactly one early return — on
`is_reverse`. There is **no forwarding-dependent `None` arm**, so an import
taken while `Coordinator.forwarding` cannot resolve the reply path does not
degrade gracefully: it builds a companion carrying `NoRoute`, ifindex 0 and
owner RG 0, publishes it into all four shared surfaces, and into the kernel
session map whenever the local-replace guard holds.

Nothing re-derived it. The replay republished `entry.decision` verbatim, and
the only mechanism that ever rebuilt a companion was
`prewarm_reverse_synced_sessions_for_owner_rgs` at RG **activation** — which
a mid-life `apply_snapshot` on an already-active node never reaches. The
wrong reply-path row was permanent for any node that did not subsequently
fail over.

Reachable today on a standby taking bulk sync before its first apply, where
activation repairs it before it matters. It becomes permanent the moment a
reconcile releases the lock — which is why it is item 2's prerequisite.

## The fix, and why the replay is the right place

`reconcile` reaches the replay **after** `snapshot::apply_snapshot` has
assigned `coord.forwarding = new_forwarding`, so the table read there is the
new generation's rather than the emptied one `stop_inner` left. That
ordering is what makes the replay a repair point at all, and it is the same
shape #8171 established for the entries themselves.

## The shape was chosen on measurement, not taste

#7209 left item 1 open between *refuse the companion* and *defer to the
replay*. Implemented as mutations against the full binary suite:

| shape | cells red |
|---|---|
| (i) refuse when the table cannot resolve it | **8** — incl. six pre-existing |
| (ii) re-derive at replay | **1** |

Shape (i)'s extra reds are structural: `synced_import_cap_for`'s `2x` is
load-bearing **because** the companion is returned for every non-reverse
import, so the cap counts ENTRIES at two per admitted forward. Refusing
changes that accounting.

## PR #8519 — cmdtree: let a node declare it accepts free-form arguments [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8304-freeform-arg-nodes`

## The premise, verified from the code first

The issue names three commands that "should canonicalize but don't". Measured at
`origin/master a5f2f94a4`, with resolving controls in the SAME run so the absence
result is not vacuous:

| command | `Canonicalize` at master | dispatcher actually serves it? | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `show log messages` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **yes** — `showDaemonLog` reads `/var/log/<name>` for a non-numeric first arg | valid defect |
| `show configuration security zones` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **yes** — `cli_show.go` `case "configuration":` joins every remaining word into the config path | valid defect |
| `clear security flow session all` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **no** | **not a defect — see below** |
| *controls:* `show route 10.0.0.0/8`, `show security policies`, `show version` | `CanonicalOK` | — | instrument works |

**Two of the three are real.** And the class is wider than the issue's sample:
**every** `show configuration <stanza> <deeper>` fails — all 16 stanza children,
at more than one depth — and so does **`show log 50`**, the `[N]` form that
node's own `Desc` string advertises.

## Why this is a security bug, not a cosmetic one

`Canonicalize`'s result is not advisory. `evaluateCommandRegex` (`pkg/cli`) fails
closed on anything but `CanonicalOK`, so a legal-but-unresolvable command is
**refused to every login class carrying `allow-commands` / `deny-commands`** —
while an unrestricted class runs it fine. The operator sees a permission error
for a correctly spelled, fully implemented command.

`pkg/cmdtree/README.md` already predicted this exact failure:

> Over-rejection is the risk to watch when touching this, because a caller MUST
> fail closed on anything other than `CanonicalOK`: refusing too much REFUSES a
> lawful command for every operator with a restricted class.

#8304 is that warning coming true.

## The third command is not a defect, and modelling it would be the mirror bug

`clear security flow session all` **is refused by the box.**
`parseClearSessionFilter` delegates to `parseSessionFilterMode(args, true)`
(`pkg/cli/session_filter.go`); its token switch has `case "zone"`, `"protocol"`,
`"source-prefix"` … and **no `all` arm**. The `default:` at `:242` sets
`unknown session filter "all"`, and `hasFilter()` (`:356`) counts
`parseErr != nil` as its **first** term — so the parse error never falls through
to a clear-all.

would assert a command that does not exist — the mirror defect of #8304, and
exactly what #8057's canonicalize-to-self check exists to catch. A test pins it
unresolved so a later "finish the issue" pass cannot quietly add it.

## PR #8520 — firewall: reject a valueless `from` leaf in a filter term [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8480-valueless-from`

Closes #8480

`set firewall family inet filter F term T from protocol` — value omitted — parses
to `Keys=["protocol"]` with no tail and no children. `firewallMatchValues` skips
`""` and returns an empty slice, so `term.Protocols` is empty, and the term reads
an empty match set as **match-ANY** rather than as an error. A stateless
first-line filter widens: `then discard` discards every protocol, `then accept`
opens every protocol.

Security policies have rejected this since #6526 and NAT since #8430. **#8430's
title covers "NAT `match` AND firewall `from`" and only the NAT half shipped** —
this is its unshipped remainder, a consistency gap in an area already hardened
twice.

## Scope is the whole risk, because this gate's failure mode is over-reach

Not every `from` leaf is value-bearing:

| leaf | why it must NOT be flagged |
|---|---|
| `is-fragment` | a presence-only **flag** — `compileFirewall` sets `term.IsFragment = true` and reads no values. The likeliest over-reach, precisely because it *looks* valueless. |
| `flexible-match-range` | carries its operands in **children**, with their own `match-start` / `byte-offset` grammar |

Both have their own control. The gate reads through `firewallMatchValues` — the
same helper `compileFirewall` uses — so gate and compiler cannot disagree about
which leaves carry semantics in their operands.

A leaf written more than once is valueless only if **every** occurrence is: Junos
merges duplicate blocks, so `from { protocol; }` beside `from { protocol tcp; }`
is constrained.

Strict rejects at commit; lenient warns so an already-persisted config still
**boots** (#1960). It walks the AST rather than the compiled `*Config` because
the defect is the *absence* of values — afterwards a valueless leaf and an
omitted one are byte-identical empty slices.

## Validation — the two escapes are the instructive part

| mutation | |
|---|---|
| gate never fires | killed |
| `is-fragment` added to the value set | killed — the over-reach control |
| last-occurrence-wins duplicate handling | killed, **after a fixture fix** |
| prefix-list read via the general helper | **equivalent mutant — branch removed** |

**The duplicate mutation escaped** because the fixture tested only
`protocol; protocol tcp;` — an order that *ends* on the valued occurrence, so
last-occurrence-wins passes either way. The reverse order discriminates; its
absence made the case a fixture that varies the right axis and samples only the
passing point.

## PR #8521 — dataplane: add a read-only per-session counter query (#7919 instrument) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/7919-session-counter-verb`

**Refs #7919.** Adds the read-only per-session counter query — the instrument that separates the two remaining explanations. It does not fix #7919; it makes the question answerable.

## Why a verb, after I argued against one

I previously talked the reviewer out of this in favour of a per-worker aggregate (#8511, merged). That aggregate was the right *axis* and the wrong *instrument*, and building it is what proved so: `session_volume_high_water` is **monotonic over the process lifetime**, so a large value on a worker whose current flow reads 0 may be residue from an earlier flow that worker owned. **Axis and attribution are different properties.** Only a per-session read supplies the second.

Two other candidates were ruled out before adding wire surface:

- **The shared session table can't** — `SyncedSessionEntry` has no counters field. Positive control: `Packets` occurs **0** times in `protocol_ha.go` against **8** and **12** in two sibling files, so the search term is right and the field is genuinely missing.
- **`export_idle_leases` isn't a template** — it returns *data* rather than deltas, but only because idle leases aren't worker-owned. It's a near-miss that would have been adopted by analogy and quietly answered a different question.

## What it does

`session_counters` takes one 5-tuple and reports what **each** worker's own table holds. Broadcast, because every worker holds a copy of every session (measured: `session_table_entries` reads 6 on all six workers for three flows) while only the worker whose packets land accounts for one.

| condition | how |
|---|---|
| **ADD, never redefine** | one new request key, one new response key. The **wire-invariant golden confirms it** rather than my asserting it: the diff is a single added `"session_counter_query": null`, nothing renamed or removed. The response and status fields don't appear in the default specimen at all — both are skipped while empty. |
| **Read-only** | `counters_with_replica_flag` looks the key up without touching the table. Nothing installs, refreshes or expires. |
| **Unsupported ≠ zero** | an older helper's `unknown request type <verb>` maps to `ErrSessionCountersUnsupported`, never to an empty result. |
| **Not hot-path, not periodic** | diagnostic-triggered only; two-phase like `kick_owner_rg_export` (#2962), with the bounded 3 s wait **outside** the `ServerState` lock. |

**The sequence is the ack.** A worker writes its answer fields, then its sequence with `Release`; the reader loads the sequence with `Acquire` before reading the answers. There is no second completion flag that could disagree with it.

## Three states, and none may collapse

- `answered = false` — did not reply before the deadline. **Not an answer.**
- `answered && !found` — replied: it does not hold this session.
- `answered && found` — holds it; counters are its copy's, and `replica` says whether that copy is a peer-synced origin.

A row flattening these into "counters or zero" would answer neither question the verb exists to separate. `replica` is carried because **a replica reporting volume would falsify the premise the whole investigation rests on** — so the answer carries what it would take to notice.

## Why "unsupported ≠ zero" is the load-bearing part

In a rolling upgrade the two nodes run different binaries on one wire, so an old helper refusing this verb is **normal operation**, not a test path. Returning `nil, nil` there would tell the caller *no worker holds this session* — one of the two states the query exists to distinguish. **The failure would look exactly like a finding.**

The Go match is against wording produced by binaries **already released**, whose text cannot be changed retroactively — so it's a wire contract in everything but name, and the helper's exact wording is **pinned on the Rust side** so a reword breaks a test instead of silently downgrading "ask a newer helper" to a generic error.

The classification is **extracted** into `sessionCountersFromResponse` / `isUnknownVerbError`, because the request path has no test seam and an inline choice cannot be bound.

## Mutations — 6, all killed, attribution checked

| # | mutation | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | predicate matches **nothing** | `TestUnsupportedVerbIsAnErrorNotAnEmptyResult7919` |
| R6 | predicate matches **everything** | `TestAnExecutionFailureIsNotReportedAsUnsupported7919` |
| R2 | return `nil, nil` for unsupported | the unsupported cell |
| R3 | reword the helper's refusal | the wording pin |
| R4 | drop the missing-query refusal | the refusal cell |
| R5 | zero the accessor's counters | the accessor cell |

## PR #8522 — api: export each management listener's state, address and surface [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8195-grpc-listener-visibility`

Closes #8195

The gRPC management listener's state has exactly one consumer,
`show system services` — and that is reached **over the gRPC listener**. When it
fails, the surface that would report the failure is the surface that is down.
That circularity is what this issue is about, and it is why the fix is a metric
scraped over the **separate HTTP listener** rather than another CLI verb.

## Correction to the issue, which shrinks it

The body says the state is on neither REST nor Prometheus. A gauge already
exists: `xpf_management_listener_down`, landed in `ffddaa69d` on 2026-08-27 —
**four days before the issue was filed** — plumbed through a `func() bool` seam
rather than via `sysservices`, which is presumably why the original grep missed
it.

It does **not** satisfy the acceptance, and this is not a "you already have it"
note:

| gap | why it matters |
|---|---|
| bare 0/1, **no address** | an operator cannot tell *which* endpoint failed to bind — the first question asked |
| **HTTP leg only** (`mgmtListenerDown` → `effectiveHTTPListener`) | the gRPC listener is absent entirely |
| **three states collapsed into two** | `StateDisabled` — deliberately turned off — is indistinguishable from `StateListening` at 0 |

So `xpf_management_listener_down` is left **exactly as it is** (dashboards and
alerts reference it) and `xpf_management_listener_state` **adds** what it cannot
express. Add, never redefine.

## Two design choices that carry the weight

**Same snapshot as the CLI.** It is emitted from the `sysservices.Listeners`
snapshot `show system services` renders — deliberately, so the metric and the CLI
cannot disagree about a listener's state. That is the one-renderer-fixed-the-
other-forgotten shape #8258 tracks and #8183 was an instance of.

**Every state gets a series, not only the current one.** A collector emitting
just the active state would make an alert on `state{state="failed"} == 1`
silently un-evaluable while the listener is healthy — the series would not exist,
and an **absent series is indistinguishable from a healthy one** at the point an
alert reads it.

The seam is optional and emits **nothing** when unwired: a zero-value
`Listeners` renders both legs as `StateDisabled`, which is a *claim* (the
operator turned them off) rather than the truth (we do not know), and it reads as
healthy. Same absent-vs-zero doctrine as the #6828 sibling gauges.

## PR #8523 — test(worker): give worker_loop_setup its first test caller [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `test/worker-setup-harness`

`Refs #7209` — the prerequisite that was hiding behind a one-line change.
**No production diff**; this lands the test substrate only.

## `worker_loop_setup` had no test callers. At all.

`worker_loop` and `worker_loop_setup` were reachable only from
`reconcile/bringup.rs`, and the spawn seams that exercise the #5143
readiness barrier substitute **stub threads** rather than the real body.
Verified with a positive control: worker-level fixtures do exist, but they
construct a `BindingWorker` directly and bypass setup entirely.

The consequence is not thin coverage — it is coverage that **cannot fail**.
Every cell over worker setup was green *by construction*.

**Measured on the branch that prompted this:** deleting a load-bearing line
from `worker_loop_setup` passed the **entire suite — 5214 cells, zero
failures** — because nothing ran it. A guard that cannot reach the mechanism
it names is not a guard on it.

## Two design constraints, both forced rather than chosen

* **The harness runs on its own thread.** `worker_loop_setup` opens with
  `pin_current_thread(worker_id)`; pinning a cargo test thread would outlive
  the cell and follow whatever test that thread is next reused for. It also
  matches production, where setup always runs on a freshly spawned worker.
* **It returns observations, not the setup.** `WorkerLoopSetup` owns an
  `Rc<WorkerUmemInner>` and is therefore not `Send`, so it cannot cross the
  thread boundary. The facts a cell wants are reduced inside the closure.

## The positive control is the point

A harness that ran setup but returned *before* the bind partition would look
exactly like coverage while testing nothing — the same failure mode the stub
seams already have. So the first cell asserts something **only the real body
produces**: an explicit per-slot `BindingSetupFailure` for a plan whose map
fds are all `-1`. If it ever goes empty, the harness stopped reaching the
bind and everything built on it is vacuous.

The second cell is its complement, and it exists because the first has a way
to pass for the wrong reason: a body pushing a failure **unconditionally**
would satisfy it. With no plans to bind, setup must report neither a binding
nor a failure.

#8484 reports that the #7509 and #8402 advisories are produced and then dropped

## PR #8525 — afxdp: saturate the two computed IP length casts in TCP segmentation [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-saturate-seg-len`

#8321 findings 19 and 20: the two bare `as u16` casts on computed IP length fields in the TCP segmentation path.

**Reachability — the question the issue said was next, now answered.** `total_ip_len <= mtu` identically (chunk_len is bounded by `segment_payload_max = mtu - headers`). The config layer places no upper bound on mtu (`ValidateIntegerMin(1)`, and its own valueDesc defers to the kernel), which is what made these look reachable. But the mtu reaching the dataplane is **read back from the kernel** — `buildLinkSnapshot` sets it from `link.Attrs().MTU` — so it is whatever the driver accepted, far below 65535 on every interface this dataplane forwards on. Findings 19/20 are mechanism-real and consequence-refuted, the same shape as finding 17.

**The casts change anyway, for an independent reason.** `saturate_len16` already exists with its own test, and these were the only two computed-length casts not using it. A wrap forges a plausible small length; a saturation is wrong on the wire but never mistakable for valid. Uniform costs nothing on any reachable input, and the derivation is recorded in the code so nobody re-derives it a fourth time.

The cell binds the helper at the boundary rather than driving the segmenter, and says why: a segmenter-driven cell could only exercise lengths the MTU permits, so it would pass identically against a bare cast. A control asserts every in-range length passes through byte-identical.

Validation: build clean, new cell passes, 5229 other cells unaffected.

## PR #8528 — harness: let the mouse-latency gate FAIL on a concentrated tail [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8277-concentrated-tail`

#8277. The degenerate-coroutine validity rule is a **fairness** predicate used as a **validity** predicate, which made the gate incapable of returning FAIL on the one shape it exists to detect.

When the tail is *concentrated* — a minority of flows starved while the rest are fine — the starved flows necessarily complete far fewer transactions, so `min < 0.5 * median` fires on exactly the reps that demonstrate the phenomenon. On master `d8a876042` a cell whose loaded p99.9 was 740–1349 ms against a 6.66 ms idle baseline (**111×–202× against a 2.0 gate**) reported `INSUFFICIENT-DATA`, 0 of 15 valid. A *uniform* slowdown still failed correctly — the median moves with the min — so only the concentrated shape was unreachable.

## A narrowing, not a deletion

The rule was written against a real client-side artifact, and deleting it would re-admit that. So the distinction comes from data the run already emits — `attribute_starvation` takes the largest of the three per-coroutine phase maxima:

| dominant phase | meaning | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `read_us` | the echo path — the thing being measured | **RESULT**, rep admitted |
| `sleep_overshoot_us` | timer wake delay in the probe's own loop | client-side, still invalid |
| `drain_us` | local socket backpressure | client-side, still invalid |

Threshold-free on purpose: an arbitrary cutoff is what put this rule in the position of invalidating its own phenomenon, and the separation is two orders of magnitude, not a judgement call.

A rep is admitted only when **every** starved coroutine is echo-attributable — one client-side or unattributable coroutine invalidates it. `coroutine_diagnostics` has **no default**, so a caller that cannot supply it must choose the pre-#8277 behaviour explicitly; making it required broke 11 call sites loudly, which is the point.

## Tests

Every fixture shares one `attempts_per_coroutine` and varies **only the attribution** — the acceptance criterion, and the only shape that can tell the versions apart. Five mutations, all killed:

| mutation | killed |
|---|---|
| unconditional invalidation (old behaviour) | the phenomenon cell |
| delete the rule | 4 client-side/unattributable cells **+ the pre-existing** `test_degenerate_coroutine_min_attempts` |
| drop the unattributable arm | 3 cells |
| wrong phase named server-side | 4 cells, both directions |
| rename the probe.json key format | the schema pin |

**That last one was found by mutation.** Routing the key names through `phase_max_key` moved producer and consumer together, so every behavioural cell stayed green while `probe.json` silently emitted different names — single-sourcing working internally and losing a guarantee externally. The three names are cited in #8277's acceptance and appear in `docs/log/`, so they are now pinned as literals in the test while staying single-sourced in the code.

## Docs

`docs/fairness-regimes.md` gains the section the issue asks for: which tail shapes the gate can and cannot verdict on, how the two starvation causes are separated, and what this does **not** fix — #8259's attribution defect (neither subsumes the other), the `error_rate >= 0.01` rule (same shape, left alone deliberately, with the reason), and the historical `INSUFFICIENT-DATA` cells that are candidate masked FAILs.

**Not cluster-validated.** This changes a pure decision function and its unit tests; a live re-measurement of the surplus fixture is the separate confirmation the issue wants. 36 cells green (27 pre-existing, 9 new).

Closes #8277
