## PR #8529 — afxdp: parse the DECAPPED frame in both ICMP-error arms [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8271-icmp-decap-frame`

#8271. `poll_binding_process_descriptor` substitutes an owned decapped inner frame at `stage_native_gre_decap` and rebinds `meta` to it. Two arms then **classified** on `packet_frame` (correctly, at the inner `meta.l4_offset`) and handed their helper `raw_frame` + `desc` — the still-encapsulated **outer** frame — with the **inner** meta. The helper parsed outer bytes at inner offsets.

This is the #1885/#1902 class, not a novel reading: two sibling arms of the same function were fixed for the identical pairing and carry comments stating the rule verbatim. These two were never brought along, and they are reachable on exactly the input those fixes were about.

Both helpers now take the frame they **parse**. `desc` stays the outer descriptor in both — that use (queue/recycle the original UMEM frame) was always correct.

## The wrapper is deleted, not left unused

`try_embedded_icmp_nat_match` existed only to slice the UMEM frame at `desc.addr`/`desc.len` and call its `_from_frame` twin. Its single behaviour was to pair whatever frame `desc` points at with whatever `meta` it was handed, and after the fix it had zero callers. Removing it removes the ability to make the mistake; every caller must now name the frame it means.

## Two cells, because there are two defects — measured, not assumed

With arm 2 fixed and **arm 1 reverted, the entire 5230-cell suite was green** — including arm 2's own new cell. One cell proves one arm. Reverting either arm now reds exactly its own cell and no other:

| revert | red |
|---|---|
| arm 2 (embedded ICMP) | `gre_decapped_embedded_icmp_reversal_reads_the_inner_frame_8271` only |
| arm 1 (NAT64) | `gre_decapped_nat64_icmp_error_reads_the_inner_frame_8271` only |

**The fixtures use a VLAN-tagged underlay deliberately**, which the issue asks for by name. On an untagged underlay the mis-paired read lands on the outer L3 header — a valid version nibble — so the parse proceeds and fails as an ordinary miss. The 4-byte dot1q tag is what turns the same defect into a misaligned slice, so an untagged fixture would pass under the defect for the wrong reason.

**The fail-on-revert result is also the control that the fixtures reach decap.** If the tunnel endpoint did not match the frame's outer destination, `stage_native_gre_decap` would never fire, `packet_frame` would equal `raw_frame`, and both cells would pass against both versions — silently degrading into duplicates of the #5690/#6472 originals they are adapted from. They go red on revert, so decap is firing.

Both arms were verified live at `origin/master` before anything changed; the issue recorded them at `e0748d0c2` and master has moved.

## Scope

Reachability is narrower than #1885's. Arm 2 needs native GRE decap AND an ICMP-error inner AND `allow-embedded-icmp`. Arm 1 needs decap AND an ICMP-error inner AND a configured NAT64 prefix — it is otherwise **ungated**, so its reachability is the wider of the two.

Validation: **5226 cells green** (5224 before + 2 new), build clean. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/README.md` updated — it named the deleted function.

## Measured before and after, through `configstore.CheckText`

| authored under `security { flow { … } }` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `aging { early-aegout 10; }` (typo) | REJECTED | REJECTED |

## Why the typo matters, and why the fail direction decides it

The render-back is the trap: `show configuration` is how an operator confirms a
commit took, and it confirms the **text was stored**, not that anything consumes
it. What the typo then does is not uniform:

- `rst-invalidate-sesion` — a **hardening** flag. The typo silently drops a
  protection the operator explicitly asked for. **Fail-open.**
- `timout` / `inital-timeout` — the session falls back to the **default**, which
  is usually **longer** than the value being tightened.
- `no-syn-check`, `no-sequence-check` — relaxations, so a typo fails **safe**.
  Reasoning from those makes the class look benign; they are the wrong examples.

`security flow aging` has rejected its unknown options since #4313. These three
siblings are the same shape and were left open — a partial hardening that
stopped, not a compatibility posture.

## MODEL BEFORE FLIP — the measurement changed the scope

The obvious change is "flip `closedWorld` on the three subtrees". **That is
unsafe as stated**, and the audit is what caught it.

`schemaNode.closedWorld`'s own contract permits a flip only once a subtree is
**leaf-complete**, "otherwise it false-rejects a valid-but-not-yet-modeled
config" — and it names the #2078/#4231 accept-with-advisory knobs as exactly
what a blanket flip breaks.

`security flow tcp-session strict-syn-check` **is** such a knob, documented in
`docs/feature-gaps.md`. It was modelled by **nothing**: absent from `setSchema`,
absent from the compiler, and — contrary to that doc's claim that *"Commit emits
an accepted-only advisory"* — carrying no advisory either. Verified with a
**count**, not a truncated listing: the only Go file mentioning it was a scratch
test I had just written.

So a real Junos keyword committed clean, rendered back, and reached no consumer
— **this issue's own defect, for a keyword the tree documents as supported.**
Flipping `tcp-session` first would have rejected it.

## PR #8531 — config: census the SECOND route by which a leaf redacts [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8258-secret-coercions`

#8258 starting point 3 — and the hole it found in starting point 1, which landed an hour ago in #8527.

## Measured first: point 3 was mostly closed already

All ten custom `MarshalJSON` implementations in `pkg/config` were classified. **Eight** transform by calling `RedactURL`/`redactURLSlice` and are already covered by #8104's URL census. **One** (`SNMPConfig`) is a field-shape alias with no value transform. **One** is covered by nothing, and it is the interesting one.

`SNMPCommunity.Name` is declared `string`. It becomes a `Secret` only inside `MarshalJSON`/`MarshalYAML`:

```go
return json.Marshal(alias{Name: Secret(c.Name), ...})
```

So the typed route redacts it exactly as if the field were declared `Secret` — and **#8527's reflection census cannot see it**, because at the type level it is a plain string. The SNMP v1/v2c community string is the v1/v2c authenticator, so this is not an obscure corner.

## The error, stated plainly

#8527's commit argued reflection beats a source scan because "the population is a TYPE, so reflection enumerates it exactly. No wrapper can hide from it." Reflection is exact about the question it answers; the error was believing that question was the whole population. It is the identical trap #8104's own census comment warns about, arriving from the other direction:

> defining a set as "things that call X" is a CLAIM that X is the only route to the behaviour.

Defining a set as "things whose **type** is X" is the same claim. A conversion is a route the type does not record. I quoted that warning in #8527 and then walked into it.

## The fix

A second census enumerates the conversion route with `go/ast` rather than a regex — `Secret(x.F)` inside a method is a syntactic fact, so it is extracted rather than pattern-matched — and feeds the **same** `astLeafForSecretField` map, so a leaf enrolled by either route gets the same behavioural verdict. The reflection census's reverse check now runs against the **union**; it fired on the new row when the second route was added, which is that check correctly measuring the wrong population.

## The result: still no divergence

`snmp community <name>` **is** redacted on the AST route (`secretIndices` masks the token after `community` under an `snmp` parent). The surfaces agree here too. What changed is that the agreement is now asserted for a leaf no instrument could previously see.

## Sensitivity — four mutations, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop the `snmp` ancestor gate from `secretIndices` | kills **exactly** the `SNMPCommunity.Name` behavioural row — proves the new row guards a real redaction |
| break the `go/ast` scan | trips the known-instance guard (the assertion #8527 lacked, and why it shipped blind) |
| remove the mapping row | coercion census fails by name |
| drop the union | reverse check fails by name |

The scan also carries a positive control on itself: fewer than 20 non-test files parsed means it did not read this package, and everything downstream would pass vacuously.

`docs/architecture.md` corrected — its #8258 bullet, written an hour ago, claimed reflection was the population. True when written, incomplete by the time this landed.

Validation: `pkg/config` green (100s), 26 cells across the three census tests, gofmt/vet clean on the new files. (`gofmt -l pkg/config/` flags six other files; all pre-existing on master and untouched here.)

Addresses #8258 starting point 3. Point 2 — drop/permit verdicts across the shim and the userspace helper, the #6534 family — remains, and the issue stays open for it.

## PR #8532 — test: build the session key and its probe by their two production routes (#8262) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `test/8262-key-route-harness`

**Closes #8262.**

## The gap, verified from the code

`cached_entry()` sets `key: test_key()`; the session installs from `entry_for_session.key`; the probe uses `flow.forward_key`, defaulting to `test_key()`. **Both operands of the comparison came from one literal**, so they agreed by construction. That harness could vary every other axis — TX headroom, admission, mirror sampling, validation state — and never touch the axis a key-mismatch bug lives on. Invisible to review, because the tests around it are real and passing.

## What it does now

The key comes from the **frame**: `parse_session_flow_from_bytes`, then the poll loop's own post-parse mutation (`forward_key.routing_domain` from `ingress_routing_domain`). Nothing is copied out of `test_key()` into the probe.

Two seams were missing:

- **`StageSeed::install_key`** — the key the session installs under, when it must differ from the cached entry's. Without it the operands cannot diverge at all.
- **`StageRun::session_lookup_miss_counts`** — the harness computed `lookup_miss_counts()` nowhere, so the counters that distinguish "probe key ≠ installed key" from every other miss were unreadable from a test.

Two cells, because a harness that can only show agreement proves nothing about its own power: a **control** asserting the routes agree (whole `(0,0,0)` tuple, so it is a real baseline) and a **red cell** installing under one route's key and probing with the other's.

## Proof it can fail — the only thing separating it from the old harness

Three mutations, all red:

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | **revert the `install_key` seam — i.e. restore the pre-#8262 harness** | **red cell FAILS** |
| S2 | route helper stops applying the poll-loop mutation | both cells fail on preconditions |
| S3 | fixture loses its routing domain, so the mutation is a no-op | both cells fail |

**S1 is the issue's claim demonstrated rather than argued**: with the old fixture's behaviour restored, the harness cannot express this mismatch.

S3 is worth its own note — without a non-zero domain the two routes cannot diverge, and the cells would **pass while testing nothing**. That is precisely the failure this file is being fixed for, so it is asserted as a precondition rather than assumed.

## A measured result that contradicts the obvious guess

A plain divergent key does **not** bump `lookup_miss_key_mismatch`. It misses with **no handle** — the two keys hash to different slots, so the probe never resolves a handle whose key it could compare. `key_mismatch` is for a *resolved* handle whose stored key disagrees (slab-handle reuse), a different defect.

Measured: `(0,0,0)` when the routes agree, `(2,0,0)` when they diverge.

**This matters beyond the file.** #7919's cluster reading found `session_lookup_miss_key_mismatch_total` at 0 on every worker, and it would be easy to read that as "no key divergence anywhere". It is not evidence of that. The cell records the reason where the reasoning lives, with an assertion that reds if the counters ever behave differently.

## Correction to the issue's motivation

The body says this is *"the reason [#7919's] confirmed mechanism cannot be exhibited below the cluster"* and calls #7919 *"a confirmed key mismatch"*. **#7919 is not a key mismatch** — key-mismatch counters read 0 on every worker, and the mechanism confirmed there (10/10 against a pre-registered protocol) is a multi-worker mirror clobber, which this harness would not exhibit. Recorded on #8262.

The test gap is **independently real** and is what this PR closes; it just is not unblocking a live fix. Flagged so nobody re-derives the link.

## PR #8533 — dataplane: retain helper crash history across a recovery [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8397-crash-history`

#8397. Nothing kept helper crash history once the helper came back. `restartHelperAfterCrash` wipes the whole record on success, so a helper that crashed four times in the last hour and is healthy now presented a **completely clean crash surface** — and nothing else retained it either, since there was no crash or restart metric.

That is the worst shape a diagnostic can have: the failure is a *disappearance*, and a clean crash surface is also exactly what a healthy helper is supposed to look like. No assertion about the current record can tell the two apart.

## A separate store, not more fields

The wipe is not incidental — the record's contract is "the current crash episode", and that is what makes `LastExitWasCrash`, `RestartPending` and `CrashLooping()` mean what they mean. Keeping some fields across the clear would put two lifetimes in one struct. Preserved as-is.

## The two questions the issue asked to be decided

- **Where it lives:** on the Manager, lost on daemon restart. A daemon restart is a far louder event and already journalled, and the counter crosses that gap monotonically. Persisting diagnostic history adds a durability surface for data whose audience is an operator answering "is this recurring?" in session.
- **Rendered or queryable:** both, minimally. The block is dense, so history contributes **one** summary row; per-episode detail is reachable through `HelperCrashHistory()` for a future verb.

## The row's placement is the load-bearing detail, and I got it wrong first

The crash block returns early on `!LastExitWasCrash && !RestartPending` — correct for every current-episode row, fatal for this one. History exists for the helper that crashed repeatedly and is running **now**, and at that moment both flags are false. A row after the guard renders in every case *except* the one it was written for, and the failure is invisible.

It is emitted above the guard, and `TestCrashEpisodeRowRendersForAHealthyHelper8397` fails if it is moved back — verified by making that move.

## The counter is a counter on purpose

`xpf_dataplane_helper_crash_episodes_total` is monotonic within a daemon lifetime, because every gauge-shaped view reads clean the moment the helper is healthy. `rate()` is the alert; the ring is the follow-up. Emitted **before** the dataplane gate — "has this helper been crashing?" is most worth answering when the dataplane is *not* loaded — and extracted into its own collect method so its three-way distinction is drivable:

| source | emits |
|---|---|
| 4 episodes | 4 |
| 0 episodes | **0**, not omitted — an absent series reads as healthy to an alert exactly as a zero does |
| no source wired | **nothing** — a daemon with no dataplane accessor knows "unknown", not "never crashed" |

The **total is not bounded by the ring**: a daemon that recovered from 40 crashes reports 40 while holding the last 8. "8 crashes" and "at least 8 crashes" are different answers to the question this exists to answer.

## Tests

History survives the wipe (with a control asserting the wipe *actually happened*, or the file would be measuring the wipe not occurring); the ring bounds and drops the **oldest** while the total does not cap; the accessor returns a copy; **no phantom episode before a recovery** — a ring appending on the *crash* would satisfy every other cell while reporting an episode that may still be looping; the row renders healthy **and** crashed, and not at all with no history or unknown crash state; the metric's three-way distinction; and the daemon accessor is nil-safe on both receiver and dataplane, since it is handed over as a method value and called from the collector goroutine on every scrape.

`pkg/fwdstatus/README.md` records the new accessor and why the row sits above the early return.

Validation: `pkg/fwdstatus`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace` all green; gofmt and vet clean on every touched file.

Closes #8397

## PR #8534 — proto: add BUSY and carry peer_status on the session list [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8308-peer-status-list`

#8308 — both of #7294's scoped residuals. Each was left open because it is a wire change with its own rolling-upgrade question, and neither should have ridden along inside a rendering fix.

## Two additions, never a redefinition

`PeerFetchStatus` gains `PEER_FETCH_STATUS_BUSY = 4`; `GetSessionsResponse` gains `peer_status` (8) and `peer_error` (9) — the fields the two summary responses have carried since #5320.

The tempting alternative was to narrow `UNREACHABLE` to mean "unreachable or refused" and let the error string carry the difference. That is a **redefinition**, and in a rolling HA upgrade the two nodes run different binaries against **one wire**: the older binary keeps its old reading of the same number, so the nodes would report different things about one event while agreeing on the bytes. The additive choice costs an older client rendering BUSY as the raw integer `4` rather than a word — visibly odd rather than quietly wrong. That is the trade, and it is the right one, because the alternative's failure is invisible.

## Why BUSY

`peer_only_5968.go` returns `codes.ResourceExhausted` when this node declines to ask the peer on admission. **The peer is reachable.** Calling that a partition sends an operator debugging a fabric problem after a network fault that does not exist — and since #8306 fixed the REST wording, REST said `busy` while gRPC said `unreachable` about the same event.

## Why the list surface reported nothing

Not a discarded error — the discarded error was *downstream of a gap in the message*. There was nowhere to put an outcome, so #8306 worked around it by setting `peer_status: "ok"` locally, which meant only "the fetch succeeded". Every arm of `fetchPeerSessions` now records its outcome through the same helpers the summary surfaces use; a list and a summary disagreeing about one peer fetch would always be a bug, so it is single-sourced rather than bound by a test. The page-token arm is `NOT_APPLICABLE`, not `UNREACHABLE` — nothing was attempted and nothing failed.

## Both upgrade directions tested, through real encode/decode

A new-against-new test proves nothing about the window, so these round-trip the wire:

| direction | asserted |
|---|---|
| new server → old client | BUSY crosses as `4`, and explicitly **not** as `3` — which an older client renders "unreachable", the exact misreport this fixes, invisible to that client |
| old server → new client | a response omitting fields 8/9 decodes as `UNSPECIFIED` / `""`, with a control that the older fields still decode so the cell cannot pass against an empty marshal |

**The member numbers are pinned.** Renumbering BUSY to 3 does not fail a test — it fails to *compile* (`duplicate key 3 in map literal`), which is the strongest available form of that guard.

REST reports what the **server** classified, keeping the local `"ok"` only for an `UNSPECIFIED` response so an older peer does not regress below #8306 during the window. The REST cell asserts the two routes **agree** on the word rather than pinning either to a literal — the literal encodes which side you trust, and the defect was that the sides disagreed.

## Validation

`pkg/api`, `pkg/grpcapi`, `pkg/cli`, `cmd/cli` green; `go build ./...` clean. Three mutations killed: a refusal classified UNREACHABLE, BUSY rendered "unreachable" on REST, BUSY renumbered to 3. The regenerated `xpf.pb.go` was checked to be purely additive — no exported method removed, exactly two added.

`pkg/api/README.md`'s #7294 paragraph is corrected; it recorded both of these as open residuals.

Closes #8308

## PR #8535 — test/cluster: a reusable crafted-frame screen probe with an arrival witness [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8336-screen-probe`

#8336. #8298 was a live security bypass whose cluster reproduction was **not achievable with the obvious tooling** — two measurement attempts came back VOID, both for reusable reasons. This turns those two failures into a procedure.

## The three traps

| trap | why it bites | what the probe does |
|---|---|---|
| **The standard smoke exercises no screen code** | `stage_screen_check` is gated on `has_screen_state()`, and the loss cluster carries no `security screen` config — so a deploy + failover against a screen change is green for unrelated reasons | arms a profile first, disarms on **any** exit, verifies removal on **both** nodes (shared cluster, config syncs to the peer) |
| **The per-reason counter cannot see a parse-error drop** | `extract_screen_info` failing closed yields `ip-malformed`, which — with `syn-cookie` and `icmp-fragment` — is surfaced **only** through the aggregate. There is no label to sample, so a fail-closed drop is invisible **by construction** and the zero reads exactly like "nothing happened" | samples `xpf_screen_drops_total` |
| **Without an arrival witness a zero is unreadable** | a flat aggregate means either the frame never reached the firewall or it arrived and was permitted — only the second is a finding | sends a **witness** frame crafted to trip a per-reason check; its counter moving proves the path is live |

## The verdict is three-valued, and the order matters

VOID is decided **before** the subject is read, in dependency order: an unarmed profile makes the witness meaningless, and a flat witness makes the subject meaningless. A layer evaluating the subject first would report `PASSED` — not dropped — for a frame that **never arrived**. That is the exact false finding both earlier attempts were one step away from.

Four mutations, each red on the cells aimed at it: reordering the witness check, treating an unreadable sample as zero, skipping the armed gate, and summing the two nodes in the disarm check.

## The self-test found a hole in my own layer

Its totality check — *every input class yields exactly one verdict* — caught that an unquoted empty variable at a call site word-splits away, so the function arrives with fewer arguments than its signature and under `set -u` aborts and emits **nothing**. A verdict layer that can emit nothing is the missing-cell defect this file exists to prevent, wearing the file's own clothes. Parameters are now defaulted and short-argument classes are in the totality list.

"Did not move" and "could not be read" stay distinct throughout — an absent metric, a failed scrape and a helper restart mid-probe (a counter that went **backwards**: the two samples describe different processes) all render as "no number", and treating any as zero turns a broken instrument into a clean result.

A VOID run exits 2 and a dirty cleanup exits 3, so a caller checking only the status cannot read "we did not measure" as "nothing was wrong".

**Hermetic**: the selftest feeds literal counter samples — no incus, cluster, network or crafted frames. Wired into `make test-screen-probe-lib` and `scripts/run-selftests.sh` beside its siblings. `docs/engineering-style.md` gains the technique.

**Not cluster-validated**: the driver needs the shared lock and a crafted-frame sender, which is the caller's half. What *is* validated is the decision layer — which is where both earlier attempts actually failed.

Closes #8336

## PR #8536 — nat: release the import-time reservation when the tunnel-remap purge deletes a session [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8138-nat-purge`

## The leak, reproduced on the purge path

The #1873 R-D tunnel-remap purge deletes peer-synced sessions whose stored
`tunnel_endpoint_id` was remapped. It never released the NAT reservation the
coordinator took when it **imported** those sessions.

Measured before the change: **`purged = 1`, `occupied_after_purge = true`.**

`reserve_synced_translation` takes that reservation as `NatHolder::Untracked`,
which contributes **no holder bit**. Every teardown sweep frees by *clearing
bits*, so none can see it, and `delete_synced_session` frees one only on the
#6979 F4 dropped-command route (with a worker id). A session purged before any
worker adopted the reservation has nobody to release it — the `(pool_addr, port)`
is held for the life of the allocator.

## Where the release must be aimed — the part that isn't obvious

`purge_remapped_tunnel_sessions` now takes the forwarding to release against as
a **parameter** instead of reading `self.forwarding`, because the two production
callers hold different states and **one holds nothing**:

| call site | state at the purge |
|---|---|
| `coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs` | `stop_inner(false)` has already **DEFAULTED** `coord.forwarding` — no rules, no allocators |
| `coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs` | purge runs *before* `self.forwarding = new_forwarding`, so it is the live previous state |

Both pass `&new_forwarding`, which is correct for both because `forwarding_build`
carries `iface_nat_allocators` across a rebuild by **`Arc::clone`**
(`mod.rs:657-658`) — the new state's allocators *are* the objects the reservation
was minted against. That is also why the leak is observable at all.

**This is the #8124 hazard.** Driving the release against the reconcile caller's
defaulted state frees nothing *and* increments a repair counter — a repair that
did not happen. That is why it was removed before merge rather than shipped.

## It cannot over-release

`drop_holder_locked` returns early — *keeping* the record — whenever any holder
bit remains, and `Untracked.bit()` is `0`. So a reservation a worker **has**
adopted is left for that worker's own teardown; only a record with `holders == 0`
is freed. The allocator documents this as the deliberate direction: an
under-release leaks a bounded, observable port, an over-release hands a live
worker's `(pool_addr, port)` to a new flow.

## Honest counting

`release_source_nat_allocation` now **returns whether it actually freed
anything** — `release_flow`/`rollback_flow` already computed it and the value was
discarded — so `tunnel_purge_reservations_released` counts *outcomes, not
attempts*. Surfaced as `xpf_userspace_tunnel_purge_reservations_released_total`.

## PR #8538 — userspace-dp: bound the peer-supplied owner_rg_id before filing it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8486-owner-rg-bound`

#8486. `metadata.owner_rg_id` arrives from the peer as a raw `i32` and was filed into the shared owner-RG indexes for **every positive value**.

The buckets are not the cost. The authoritative un-file uses `HashMap::retain`, which is **O(capacity)** and visits empty slots — so removing N keys filed under N distinct ids is **Θ(N²)** of outer-capacity work on the session-control thread.

The Go side bounds RG ids to 0..15 on the *strict* path and downgrades that to a WARNING on the tolerant peer-sync path. The helper is the last line, and it did not hold one.

## Clamp the filing, not the import

The issue's second candidate, and it is the right one. Refusing the import would decline a takeover this node is otherwise fit for — the tolerant path exists precisely because a peer may legitimately run an older or looser config, so a hard refusal trades a bounded memory cost for a **blackhole on failover**. The session is kept and stays usable; only the index entry is skipped.

**The remove path stays permissive (`> 0`) deliberately**, and the asymmetry is the point: anything ever filed can always be un-filed, including under a future tightening. A symmetric bound would strand entries filed under the old one — turning a hardening change into a leak.

## The counter is surfaced, and the tree caught me not surfacing it

An internal counter nothing reads is a claim written into inert code. #6641's `every_counter_accessor_is_wired_into_process_status` failed until the accessor was assigned into `ProcessStatus` — the instrument doing its job on exactly the change that needed it.

**Only out-of-range ids are counted.** The ordinary "no redundancy group" case (id 0, carried by every standalone session) is not a decline; counting it would make the metric read as an attack on every non-clustered box and bury the signal. That distinction has its own cell.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| remove the bound (pre-#8486) | all four |
| reject **everything** — the over-rejection that would silently disable owner-RG indexing and stop a takeover finding the peer's sessions | all four |
| count the no-RG case too | only the counter cell |
| off-by-one on 15 | only the boundary cell |

## One process note

The test module was first registered under an existing `#[path]` attribute, which aliased it to a **different file** — so the new cells never ran and a duplicate registration of the embedded-poll-filter tests passed under the new name. The output said "ok" for tests I had not written. Caught by reading *which* cells ran rather than that something ran.

The status field is additive: `#[serde(default)]` so an older helper decodes 0 rather than failing the whole status parse, and the wire fixture diff was inspected before regenerating — one new key, nothing changed or removed.

Validation: **5232 cells green**, build clean.

Closes #8486

## PR #8539 — nat: make the persistent-NAT forwarding disarm visible at commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8447-visible-disarm`

#8447. Adding `persistent-nat` to a rule-referenced source pool on a chassis-cluster member stops the dataplane forwarding transit entirely — rx goes to 0.

**The behaviour is deliberate and documented (#1449)** and nothing here changes it: persistent-NAT leases are helper-local and not HA-synchronized, so the dataplane declines to forward rather than forward with semantics it cannot honour.

**The defect is that it happened invisibly.** Interfaces stay up, the config commits cleanly, and the failure presents as a *connectivity* problem rather than a NAT one. The only surface was `Forwarding supported: false` inside a `show` nobody runs when the symptom is "the link went down" — and this issue spent five rounds of cluster measurement rediscovering a contract the daemon already knew the reason for and threw away.

#8503 fixed the disarm-time silence. This fixes the other two surfaces.

| when | surface |
|---|---|
| **at commit** | a `ValidateConfig` advisory naming the **consequence** — that forwarding stops, that it will look like a link failure, and where to look |
| at disarm | the #8503 WARN (already merged) |
| **continuously** | `xpf_dataplane_forwarding_supported` — what an alert keys on |

An **advisory, not a rejection**: the config is valid, the behaviour is the documented contract, and `chassis cluster` and the NAT stanza commit independently — rejecting would make the standalone case unreachable through a shared config.

The metric reads the **same field** `desiredForwardingArmedLocked` gates on, so it cannot disagree with the arm/disarm decision. Three-way, and the third value is the point: forwarding → 1, disarmed → 0, **no source → no series**. A daemon with no dataplane accessor does not *know* whether forwarding is live; emitting 1 there would turn "we cannot see" into "everything is fine" — the exact reading this issue is about. Reasons are deliberately not labels (unbounded, operator-facing, a cardinality problem).

## The predicate is single-sourced, not mirrored

It moved to `pkg/config` (which `pkg/dataplane/userspace` already imports, not the reverse) and the capability gate now **calls** it. The tree's habit for this shape is to mirror with a comment saying it mirrors — see `deterministicIPv4Enforced`. A mirror is a drift surface whose failure mode is an advisory that stops firing for a config that still disarms forwarding: **silence that reads exactly like safety.**

Both are keyed on the **rule**, not the pool table — an unreferenced `persistent-nat` pool translates nothing, so it neither disarms forwarding nor warns, and the two agree by construction rather than coincidence.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| drop the cluster condition | the standalone cell — warning on every persistent-NAT config would train operators to ignore it |
| key on the pool table | the unreferenced-pool cell |
| remove the consequence wording | the actionability assertion |

## PR #8540 — protocol: stop counting path-qualified type positions as struct literals [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8537-literal-guard-paths`

## The defect

`exhaustive_literal_count` finds a struct name followed by `{`, then excludes
non-literals by inspecting the text immediately **before the name** (`->`,
`struct`, `impl`, `for`, `enum`). A path-qualified occurrence defeats every arm:

```rust
fn f() -> crate::ConfigSnapshot {   // pre ends with "::", not "->"
```

so a **return type** was counted as an exhaustive struct literal. Found on the
#8138 branch, where a test helper with that signature — containing no literal at
all, it builds one with `::default()` — tripped the ratchet.

## The fix, and the repair that looks right but isn't

Strip the path qualifier, then apply the **same** arms to what precedes the whole
path.

The obvious alternative — *skip any hit preceded by `::`* — is wrong in the other
direction: `crate::Name { .. }` in **expression** position is a real exhaustive
literal and must still count. That alternative is mutant **G2** below, and the
qualified-literal rows in the fixture are what catch it.

## Why it wasn't cosmetic

The guard is a **ratchet**, so the natural response to a red is to raise the
ceiling — which writes the miscount permanently into the baseline and leaves the
ceiling holding room for a *real* literal nobody will notice. Its failure text
("Add `..Default::default()`") also sends the reader hunting for a literal that
does not exist.

## Seven ceilings tightened — and the headline number is measured, not inferred

| struct | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `ConfigSnapshot` | 15 | **0** |
| `FabricSnapshot` | 8 | 7 |
| `InterfaceSnapshot` | 2 | 0 |
| `MapPins` | 2 | 0 |
| `NAT64RuleSnapshot` | 4 | 3 |
| `SourceNATRuleSnapshot` | 1 | 0 |
| `ThreeColorPolicerStatus` | 2 | 1 |

A 15 → 0 swing is too large to accept on faith, so I checked it against the
source rather than the guard:

- the tree contains **exactly 15** `-> crate::ConfigSnapshot {` return types —
  matching the old ceiling one for one;
- **control:** 60 bare `-> ConfigSnapshot {`, which the pre-fix arms already

## PR #8541 — config: a reversed integer range must not silently disable the check [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8358-range-footgun`

#8358's one real residue. `ValidateInteger`'s body guards its comparison with `min <= max`, so `ValidateInteger(1, 0)` — the shape a caller reaches for when they mean "at least 1" and mis-order the arguments — returned a validator that **accepted every integer**, and nothing said so.

That is the worst shape a check can have: it fails to a value indistinguishable from a healthy one. The leaf has a validator, review sees a validator, `?` completion shows a typed leaf, and the gate does nothing. It would be found the way this class is always found — by an operator committing something absurd that works.

## A panic at construction, not an error at validation

This is a *programming* error, not an operator one. `setSchema` is a package-level var built at init, so a reversed range fails every test in every package that imports `pkg/config`, immediately and unmissably. It cannot reach an operator because it cannot get past a build.

Measured before adding it: all 35+ literal call sites and every named-constant site are well-ordered, so nothing relies on the disable. `ValidateIntegerMin` is the documented "no upper bound" spelling and its own comment says so.

The `min <= max` term in the closure is **kept** rather than simplified — it is what made the case silent, and leaving it beside the panic documents the pairing.

## Mutations

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove the guard | the panic cell reds |
| panic **unconditionally** | the whole package fails at init with `ValidateInteger(0, 255) has min > max` — demonstrating both that the guard runs at initialization **and** that its message renders correctly against a real call site |

Boundary covered both ways: a well-ordered range still validates (without which an unconditional panic would satisfy the first cell while disabling every numeric leaf), and `min == max` is allowed and exact — a leaf with one legal value is well-ordered, and panicking on it would be an off-by-one in the guard itself.

## How this was found

#8358 asks for a `ValidateIntegerRange` constructor, on the measured premise that `ValidateIntegerMin` is the only numeric bound the schema can express. **That premise is wrong.** `ValidateInteger(min, max)` is exactly that constructor — **109 sites** against 32 for the Min-only form — already carrying `(1, 65535)` for ports, `(0, 255)` for octet fields, and `(1, 4094)` for VLAN ids, the last being the issue's own worked example of a justified constant.

The search was for the *name* `ValidateIntegerRange`; the conclusion was drawn about the *capability*. Full reasoning is on the issue, including why the 32 Min-only leaves are Min-only deliberately under the reviewed `no-schema-only-caps` doctrine (PR #1845) — which means the issue's item 3 would delete a design decision rather than consolidate a duplicate.

Validation: `pkg/config` green (120s), `go build ./...` clean, gofmt clean.

## PR #8542 — ipmon: adopt pkg/coalesce so one debounce/throttle discipline exists [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8354-ipmon-coalesce`

#8354. The debounce/throttle/dirty-generation discipline existed **twice** — once in `ipmon.Engine`'s run loop and once in `pkg/coalesce`, which #7437 wrote as the type ipmon would adopt rather than extracting it from an HA-gated engine inside a feature PR.

A discipline whose entire purpose is to be obeyed identically, implemented twice, is a divergence with a delay fuse: whichever copy is edited first is right, and nothing tells the other.

## What moved, and what did not

The engine keeps what is genuinely ipmon's — policy evaluation, next-hop resolution, recovery hold-downs, and the `publishEnabled` HA-standby gate. **The loop owns *when* to actuate; the engine owns *what* is published.** That split is the reason the extraction was deferred, and it is preserved rather than blurred.

## The seam is two hooks, because the condition is not one an adopter can compute

`OnConverged` fires on `ok && generation unchanged`. Both halves live in the loop, and the second is **invisible to an actuator**, which sees only its own return. ipmon records its *applied* overlay under exactly that condition (#3761 H8) — "the actuator published what it read" is true only when no newer change landed mid-actuation. Without the hook the adopter must either duplicate the generation tracking (the duplication this removes) or widen to plain `ok` and record a **desired** state as an **applied** one.

`OnFailed` is deliberately narrower than "did not converge": a non-convergence from a concurrent re-dirty does not fire it. Nothing failed — the work is simply not finished, and counting it would make a flap storm look like an outage.

Three small additions to the shared type, each because recomputing it outside would be the same duplication moved one function along: `NextWake` (ipmon combines it with its own hold-down expiries), `SetActuateTimeout` (**found by a test failing**, not by inspection — ipmon's timeout is operator-visible and a cell drives it down), and `Dirty`.

The loop is constructed in `New`, not `Start`: `Apply`/`HandleTransition` can mark the engine dirty before it starts, and Go compiles a nil-pointer method call happily — a loop built later is a runtime panic with no compile-time sign.

## All 29 pre-existing ipmon cells pass UNCHANGED

That was the acceptance condition, and they are the real guard on the relocated behaviour. Three new cells cover what they cannot:

- **that the adoption happened.** Without it, a future "simplification" reinstating a local dirty bit passes all 29 — they assert the *behaviour*, which both implementations have. That is exactly how the two copies came to exist.
- **the HA gate**, the interaction the extraction risked: gated off, the published overlay must be the *baseline*, with a control proving it becomes non-empty on takeover — without which the cell passes against an engine that publishes nothing at all.
- a mark landing **during** an actuation must produce a second one.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each by the right cells

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| clear the dirty bit on plain `ok` (generation ignored) | the concurrent-mark cell |
| advance `lastActuation` *after* the actuation | the throttle and flap-storm cells it paces |
| drop the `OnConverged` wiring | `TestRoutesAppliedReflectsActuationNotDesired` — precisely the applied-vs-desired contract the hook exists for |
| never push the timings into the loop | eleven cells |

The cross-reference in `pkg/coalesce`'s package comment (*"ADOPTION IS TRACKED AS #8354 … if you edit one, the other is the copy that will not follow"*) is removed — there is now one implementation.

**Timings unchanged.** `DefaultDebounce` 1 s / `DefaultThrottle` 3 s are ipmon's values and `pkg/coalesce` already mirrored them, which is what makes this a refactor.

Validation: `pkg/coalesce`, `pkg/ipmon`, `pkg/daemon` green; `go build ./...`, gofmt, vet clean.

Closes #8354

## PR #8543 — daemon: give the fabric reassert loop the reaping half it lacked [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8372-fabric-reaper`

#8372. `reassertFabricIPVLANOnce` only ever **created**. It had zero deletes, so a fabric IPVLAN the active config no longer names persisted for the daemon's lifetime — and past it.

**The route in** is the deferred `OnXSKBound` callback: it iterates a closure-captured slice and calls the ensure *unconditionally*, with no re-derivation from the current config and no stopping fence. Apply A registers fab0 → apply B drops it and the stale-overlay sweep correctly tears the link down → the XSK binds → the stale closure puts it back. The dispatch is `go m.OnXSKBound()` and nothing joins it, so the **shutdown variant needs no second apply at all** — reachable on a plain restart.

## Why it did not self-heal

Two mechanisms look like they should reap it, and neither does:

- `CleanupFabricIPVLANs` is reachable only from the `xpfd cleanup` subcommand — **the daemon never removes these links when it exits**;
- the stale-overlay sweep inside `applyInterfaces` runs on the next interface apply, i.e. the next **commit**.

So the end state was healable by an *operator action* rather than a timer, while the link carries the fabric / session-sync address — possibly on a parent the config no longer designates.

#6791 designated this loop the persistent recovery owner. It owned only the create half.

## The cheap-path gate is the part most likely to be got wrong

The loop returned early on `len(missing) == 0`. **A stale overlay is an extra device, not a missing one** — so that condition is precisely the state a stale overlay produces. A reaper added below the gate is unreachable in the only case it exists for, and *invisible*, because every unit test of the reaper function itself still passes. It has its own cell.

## The race

The reap runs after the ensure, same pass, same semaphore. That does not prevent a racing `OnXSKBound` goroutine from recreating a link mid-reap — nothing can, without joining a goroutine nobody joins — but it makes the outcome **convergent** rather than oscillating. The cell drives the race (recreating the link from inside the delete callback, asserting convergence across three passes) rather than a steady state, which the issue specifically warns would pass under a broken implementation.

Two guards on blast radius: only an `*netlink.IPVlan` is ever considered (a same-named device of another type is not ours, and deleting it would be this reaper causing the outage it prevents), and the candidate names are single-sourced with `CleanupFabricIPVLANs`.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each by its own cell

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| cheap path keys on `missing` alone | the gate cell + the race cell |
| reap regardless of config | the configured-overlay control |
| drop the IPVlan type check | the non-IPVLAN cell |
| remove the reap loop | the gate cell + the race cell |

**Not fixed here:** fencing `OnXSKBound` itself (re-derive from current config, abandon on the stopping fence) — that is #7675's H2. This converts the end state from "persists until the next commit, possibly indefinitely" to "converges within 30 s", which is the change that does not need the G+H+H2 plan.

Validation: `pkg/daemon` green (54s), `go build ./...` and gofmt clean.

Closes #8372

## PR #8544 — cluster: purge every per-RG authority map at the incarnation boundary [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8435-rg-incarnation`

#8435 filed one gap and predicted the shape of the guard that would find the rest. **The guard found eight.**

## The filed defect

`UpdateConfig`'s RG-removal loop purged `holdTimer`, `degradedTimer`, `monitorWeights`, `garpCounts` and `groups` — but not `peerTransferOutOverride`. A stale override survived an RG being removed and re-added under the same id, and the subject **self-promoted to primary**. Reproduced at master with a control (identical remove + re-add without the override stays secondary).

## What the issue actually asked for

> a guard binding that an RG's incarnation boundary purges every per-RG authority map, **enumerated from the struct** — not a test naming the maps someone remembered. A cell naming three maps cannot see the fourth. That is precisely how this one survived #5990 and #6027.

Both of those added a map to the loop *and a test for that map*. This adds neither.

## Seven more, found on the guard's first run

```
peerTransferCommitGraceUntil   localTransferOutHoldUntil
peerTransferOutPrevious        remoteTransferOutLeaseUntil
remoteTransferOutLeaseReqID    failoverInProgress
failoverGen
```

**`failoverInProgress` is sharper than the filed defect.** It exists so "a second request for the same RG is rejected immediately" — so a stale `true` on a same-id re-add makes that RG **permanently un-failoverable**. A wedge, not a 20 s window.

**`failoverGen` needed the opposite argument**, because resetting a generation counter usually is *not* safe. The supersede check is `gen != captured → abandon`, so deleting the entry makes a later read return 0 and an operation that captured a non-zero generation on the old incarnation sees a mismatch and abandons. *Keeping* the counter is what would let it match and clobber. The comment says why, so the next reader does not "fix" it back.

## One exclusion, and it owes its justification

`peerGroups` is an **observation**, not local authority: the heartbeat handler replaces the whole map (`m.peerGroups = newPeerGroups`) every 200 ms and it carries what the *peer* reports. Purging one entry on a local config change would be overwritten within one heartbeat and would misrepresent the map as ours to reset. The exclusion list is deliberately tiny — an exclusion is how a map stops being checked.

## Why the guard is worth more than the eight deletes

- a **positive control on its own enumeration**: the four known RG-keyed maps must be found *by name*, so a scan that silently stops matching fails instead of reporting a clean census over an empty set;
- it **fails on a key shape it cannot classify** rather than skipping it — a per-RG map the guard cannot check is a per-RG map nobody is checking, which is how this class kept recurring;
- a **retained-RG control**, without which everything passes against a loop that purges unconditionally and drops live state on every commit.

Struct keys need `reflect.NewAt` because reflect refuses to write an unexported field even inside the declaring package. Confined to the test — the alternative, an accessor per map, would reintroduce the hand-maintained list this exists to remove.

Three mutations, all killed: dropping the filed override delete; dropping `failoverInProgress`; purging unconditionally (which reds the retained-RG control too).

Validation: `pkg/cluster` green (49 s) including every existing failover, election and heartbeat cell; `go build ./...` and gofmt clean.

Closes #8435

## PR #8545 — bench: price the in-process half of the #8276 IPsec capture bridge [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `research/8276-b2-pricing`

Adds the pricing instrument #7167's adjudication says B2 lacks. **No production
code changes** — one bench and its `Cargo.toml` entry.

The adjudication narrows the IPsec half to Option B2 and records it as
**unpriced**. This prices the half that can be priced without hardware, so the
design argument rests on a number rather than an estimate.

## The two halves, and which one this covers

| half | what it is | measurable here? |
|---|---|---|
| **kernel** | getting plaintext out of the XFRM stack and an authoritative verdict back (nfqueue round trip, or AF_PACKET capture + re-inject) | **no** — needs a box where XFRM SAs and netfilter can be configured against real traffic |
| **in-process** | handing a captured frame to a worker to adjudicate — Option E's "bounded packet-bearing `WorkerCommand` + owned-frame adjudication entry point", which the adjudication names as B2's cost | **yes**, it is pure userspace |

Nothing here implies a number for the kernel half.

## What it measures

The in-tree shapes, recreated directly per the `tx_kick_latency.rs` convention
(the daemon is a bin crate): the worker command queue
(`Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<WorkerCommand>>>`, bounded at 4096) and the slow path's
existing kernel-facing handoff (`mpsc::sync_channel(16384)` → the dedicated
`xpf-slowpath` thread).

Four rows: the irreducible 1500-byte copy; an owned-`Vec` handoff same-thread; a
pooled-slot handoff same-thread; and the cross-thread round trip that is the
shape a capture source actually needs, since a capture thread and a worker are
not the same thread.

## Two things stated in the file rather than left to the reader

**The pooled row is not a clean isolation of allocation cost.** It takes an extra
per-slot mutex the owned row does not, so the near-equality between them must
**not** be read as "allocation is free" — the extra lock may simply be paying
back what the allocation saved.

**The queue-size figures are arithmetic, not measurement.**
`size_of::<WorkerCommand>()` is **264 bytes** at this HEAD, so a full 4096-deep
queue is ~1.03 MiB per worker. A `Vec<u8>` payload is 24 bytes inline and does
**not** grow the enum; an inline `[u8; 1500]` payload would take the variant to
~1504 and a full queue to **~6.16 MiB per worker** — paid by every queued command
of every kind, not only captured frames.

## Validation

- `cargo build --benches` clean; the bench also compiles as a test target.
- Both scope halves pass — two files, no production code.
- Rebased onto current `origin/master`.

The measured figures and what they imply for B2's viability are written up on

## PR #8546 — cluster: a new RG owner announces its pool proxy-ARP addresses [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8405-pool-garp`

#8405. #8297 landed the ownership gate — the standby no longer *answers* proxy-ARP for a pool address on an RG it does not own. Necessary, and **not sufficient**: removing a responder does not invalidate a binding already cached upstream. The target keeps transmitting to the standby's MAC until its own entry re-resolves, so the symptom persists on exactly the path the fix was meant to repair.

## The measurement that makes this a defect rather than a theory

The seven misdelivered SYN-ACKs carried the **standby's** MAC (`02:bf:72:16:01:01`) on a NIC with `IFF_PROMISC` clear — so they were *addressed to it*, so the upstream had the pool address bound to the standby. A witness flow in the same cell recorded **zero** on the standby, which is what makes the seven mean something.

It also rules out the switch-port MAC-learning alternative: that mechanism delivers frames carrying the *owner's* MAC to the wrong port, and a non-promiscuous NIC drops those at the wire rather than counting them received.

## Design points, each with its reason

- **One GARP per address, not a burst.** The burst survives loss where a single VIP must be re-bound; here the job is *breadth*, and depth × breadth is what turns this into a storm on a large pool. A missed announce falls back to upstream ARP ageing — the pre-#8405 behaviour for every address.
- **Bounded at 64.** A proxy-arp statement expands to ≤256 hosts and an interface may carry several; unbounded, this recreates the exact CPU/socket-exhaustion vector `GratuitousARPBurstClamp` exists to prevent, through a different door. 64 is chosen against the fault's shape: an address needs announcing only if an upstream has it *cached*, which requires it to have been used for translation. Truncation warns once and keeps the first 64 **in configured order**, so the same addresses go out on every failover rather than a subset that changes between events.
- **The RG filter is #8297's own predicate.** This announces exactly the set the standby stops answering for, so the two cannot disagree about which addresses belong to which RG. A divergence would announce an address this node does not own — telling the upstream to send us traffic the **peer** is primary for, which is worse than the stale binding being fixed. Same reasoning for honouring `stillValid` and stopping mid-announce.
- **IPv6 is deliberately not announced here.** It needs an unsolicited NA; pushing a v6 address through the v4 burst would be silently wrong rather than merely absent.

## Mutations — five, all killed, each by its own cell

drop the RG filter · remove the bound · burst instead of one-per-address · ignore the ownership fence mid-announce · announce v6 through the v4 path

## What this does not close

Carried from the issue rather than papered over: an earlier run removed the standby's responder, went quiet 90 s, and pool-mode TCP **still** failed. Two readings the issue could not separate — 90 s was not enough (a stale ARP entry is still *used* for transmission while the kernel re-resolves, which would make this announce even more clearly required), or something else also contributes. **This change makes the first reading no longer matter; it does not settle the second.** Confirming that needs the cluster.

Validation: `pkg/daemon` green (54 s), `go build ./...` and gofmt clean.

Closes #8405

## PR #8547 — userspace-dp: measure the delta buffer's occupancy, not just its overflow [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8108-delta-highwater`

#8108 item 1. The acceptance is *"a measured ring-occupancy figure from a revocation burst large enough to matter — not a computed bound"*, and it explicitly allows the issue to be **closed** if the measurement shows the ring is not reached.

**Neither outcome was available, because there was no instrument.** `pending_session_deltas.len()` was read only for the cap check and nothing retained it; `delta_loss_pending` is a **boolean** — "we overflowed at least once", never "we reached 90%". A buffer running comfortably and a buffer surviving on luck were the same observation.

## A high-water mark, not a depth gauge

This buffer **drains**. A depth sampled at 1 Hz sees a revocation burst only if the sample lands inside it, and reports a comfortable small number otherwise — for exactly the event being measured. A high-water mark cannot miss a burst it observed. `the_high_water_survives_a_drain_8108` drains *before* asserting for that reason; a cell that only pushed and read would pass against a plain gauge.

Paired with `session_delta_dropped` it separates three states:

| state | high water | dropped |
|---|---|---|
| comfortable | well under cap | 0 |
| **surviving on luck** | at/near cap | 0 |
| lossy | — | > 0 |

Only the third was observable before, and only as a boolean. **The middle one is what decides whether item 2's denied-set-scoped BulkSync fallback is worth building** — precisely the question the acceptance says the measurement must answer.

The mark tops out **at** the cap rather than counting the overflow, so "reached the cap" and "lost deltas" stay distinguishable.

Surfaced end to end — binding snapshot, worker record, coordinator refresh/reset, the wire, the Go struct — with `#[serde(default)]`. A counter nothing reads could not answer the acceptance question.

## Three pinned-layout guards fired, all re-measured

The two compile-time `offset_of` consts (2176→2184, 2304→2312) and the #6304/#6114 runtime pin. Re-measuring is what their own comments prescribe for an **unconditional** field, and the discriminator they give is that both build configurations must be green on **one** set of literals — which a `#[cfg(test)]` field could not achieve. Both are.

`size_of` did **not** move (still 2368) — the second time the "tail padding is now full" prediction has failed to hold, which is exactly why those guards pin the offsets separately from the size. Both comments record this pass.

Wire fixture diff inspected before regenerating: one new key, nothing changed or removed.

## Mutations — three, all killed, each by its own cell

`store` instead of `fetch_max` (a depth gauge wearing a high-water name) · recording depth **before** the push · counting the overflow as depth.

## What this does not do

**It does not take the measurement** — that needs a revocation burst on the loss cluster, which is what the acceptance asks for and what this makes possible. It also does not build item 2's fallback, correctly: the issue's own acceptance makes that conditional on what the measurement shows.

#8436. The census landed in `77e9d2a79` and did the hard part — it enumerated the population from `setSchema` and classified every non-conserving container as **rejected-at-commit** (conservation by refusal, acceptable) or **SILENT** (configuration discarded with no error).

Its own comment says what comes next: *"What the census supplies is the enumeration, so the next fix is chosen from a list rather than discovered."* This takes three from that list.

**Why the issue's "do not add a registry row" warning does not apply:** that is about the *guard*, and the guard is already the general one. A per-site fix is now chosen from an enumeration rather than reacting to a review — exactly the difference the issue draws.

| site | was | consequence |

| `security ike policy` | construct-and-overwrite | a second `policy P {}` discarded the first's mode, PSK and proposals — crypto-relevant, and the direct sibling of #8433's proposal wipe |
| `security ipsec vpn` | same shape, same file | same |

All three become **find-or-create** — the disposition the census names as correct (it is what dhcp-relay already does), and the one that makes the hierarchical spelling agree with the flat-set spelling. `mapJunosPermissions` now runs over the *merged* permission set rather than one block's half.

Census moves **25 → 22**, and `TestDuplicateBlockConservationIsPinned8436` **demanded** the three lines be removed from the inventory — *"a stale entry hides the next regression at that site"*. Fix and inventory cannot drift apart, because leaving a fixed site listed fails.

**Two mutations, both killed by the pin rather than by a bespoke cell** — reverting ike policy to construct-and-overwrite, and login class to append-both. That is the census doing what a per-container test could not: neither mutation needed a test written for it.

Reachability, unchanged: through a hierarchical config file, `load merge` or `load override` — **not** through `set`, which merges correctly today.

## Fourteen SILENT sites remain, and they are listed

class-of-service interfaces / schedulers / traffic-control-profiles, protocols isis interface, ospf and ospf3 area interface, router-advertisement interface, security dynamic-address feed-server, security nat source pool, both flow-monitoring template containers, system ntp server. ## PR #8549 — daemon: name IPv6 static next-hop interfaces by VLAN ID, not unit [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-f07-vlan-netdev`

#8321 finding 07, validated and fixed.

`inferIPv6StaticNextHopInterfaces` formatted the next-hop netdev as `base.<unit>`. For an 802.1q sub-interface where unit and VLAN ID differ — `set interfaces ge-0-0-1 unit 10 vlan-id 100` — networkd creates `ge-0-0-1.100`, so the FRR static route named an interface that **does not exist**. Zebra flags such a route inactive and blackholes every destination behind it.

## What made this decidable without a box

The tracking issue is explicit that the source review *"asserts consequences it never established"* and that each remaining finding is *"a location plus a hypothesis, not a verdict"*. So the question was not whether the trace sounded right — it was whether the tree has a convention.

It does, and it is unanimous. **Five** other sites resolve the same name the other way:

| site | uses |
|---|---|
| `daemon_dhcp.go:311-315` | `VlanID`, with a unit fallback |
| `daemon_ha_vip.go:327 / 393 / 678` | `VlanID` |
| `daemon_neighbor.go:130` | `VlanID` |

This was the one site that did not. An asymmetry against five siblings is evidence in a way a plausible trace is not — and it supplied the exact shape to copy, fallback included.

## The fallback is not decoration

A unit with **no** vlan-id is not a tagged sub-interface, and there `base.<unit>` is correct. That is why this is a conditional and not a substitution — and it is measurable: replacing `unitNum` with `VlanID` outright reds **seven** tests, six of them pre-existing.

That same fact is why the defect survived. `TestInferIPv6StaticNextHopInterfaces` sets no `VlanID` anywhere, so it exercises only the fallback and passes identically against both implementations. The new cell uses unit 10 / vlan-id 100 — the one shape where the spellings disagree — because a fixture that cannot distinguish them is not a test of this change.

## Mutations — two, opposite directions, both killed

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| revert to `unitNum` only | the new VLAN cell |
| substitute `VlanID` with no fallback | the new fallback cell **+ six pre-existing** |

## PR #8550 — test/cluster: gate the screen probe's commits on the CLI transcript [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8336-marker-gate`

**Fixes master, which I broke with #8336.**

`TestEveryConfigCommittingSmokeUsesTheMarkerGate_6936` scans every config-committing smoke script for the #6440 marker gate. `screen-probe.sh` commits configuration (arm/disarm a screen profile) while gating on the piped CLI's **exit status**.

## The guard is right and the bug is real

The piped-stdin CLI is a REPL: it prints `error: ...` for a failed command and **still exits 0**. So `if arm; then armed_state="armed"` set that flag whether or not the commit landed — and the probe would then measure an **unarmed** box and render a verdict about it.

That is **trap 1 wearing the script's own clothes**: trap 1 is precisely *"the screen stage short-circuits and the run is green for reasons unrelated to the change"*. The one thing the file exists to prevent, in the file itself.

Both commit sites now verify the transcript with `cos_require_markers`. `arm` returns non-zero on a missing `commit complete`, so the verdict layer reports **VOID** rather than a measurement. `disarm` stays best-effort — it runs from an EXIT trap, including after a failure — but reports loudly when it did not commit, because a silent disarm failure leaves the **shared** cluster armed for every other lane.

## Why I missed it

I ran `make test-screen-probe-lib`, the hermetic selftest, shellcheck and `go build ./...`. I did **not** run `go test ./cmd/cli/`, because the change was a shell script and shell scripts do not belong to a Go package. But the guard is a *Go test that scans shell scripts* — it lives in a package the change never touched.

The general form, worth more than this fix: **a merge gate scoped to "the packages this diff touches" cannot see a guard that scans by content rather than by ownership.** #6440's gate, #6641's counter-wiring gate and the layout-offset pins are all this shape.

## PR #8552 — api: emit control-plane metrics when the dataplane is not loaded [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-f14-controlplane-metrics`

#8321 finding 14, validated and fixed.

`collectDHCPMetrics`, `collectDDNSMetrics`, `collectSurfaceADDNSMetrics` and `collectSystemMetrics` sat **after** `if dp == nil || !dp.IsLoaded() { return }`. So on a config-only boot or a degraded dataplane, daemon uptime, DHCP lease and DDNS metrics vanished from monitoring — at exactly the moment an operator is trying to work out what happened.

**A metric that disappears during the incident it would explain is worse than one that was never added:** its absence reads as "nothing to report" rather than "I cannot see".

**Verified dataplane-independent before hoisting.** None of the four references `c.srv.dp`, `IsLoaded` or the dataplane package — they read the config store, the DHCP client and DDNS state. That check is what makes this a hoist rather than a behaviour change: on a loaded dataplane the emitted set is identical, just earlier in the scrape.

Two configurations, because there are two paths to that early return and operators hit them for different reasons: `dp == nil` is a config-only boot; a non-nil dataplane reporting `!IsLoaded()` is a wedged helper. Reverting the hoist reds both.

## A negative result worth recording

I tried to ship a control that could not fail. I wrote a cell asserting *"the gate still suppresses dataplane families"* — and it **survived deleting the gate outright**. So I measured it: removing the gate changes the emitted set by **zero families** in either configuration, because every downstream collector already guards itself.

The gate is therefore a **cost** boundary (it skips a control-socket status round-trip and a good deal of wasted work per scrape), not a correctness boundary for the metric set. No cell can distinguish its presence from its absence by looking at output — so this file has no "the gate still gates" assertion, and says why.

A cell that looks like a control and cannot fail is worse than no cell: it certifies a property nobody checked.

## PR #8553 — grpc: report destination-NAT rule-set sessions instead of nothing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-f16-dnat-sessions`

#8321 finding 16, validated and fixed.

`GetNATDestination`'s `RuleSetSessions` was **empty on every call**, whatever the traffic.

`countDNATSessions` keys its map `{ingressZone, egressZone}` from the session's *real* zones. A **destination** rule-set has no `to` clause — the compiler calls only `applyNATFromScope`, so `rs.ToZone` is always `""` — and a real session's egress zone is never `""`. The `{FromZone, ""}` lookup could not match any entry.

With no egress zone to match on, the count is every session entering the from-zone, summed across egress zones. **The pair lookup is kept** for a rule-set that *does* name one, so a future to-bearing destination rule-set gets the tighter key rather than silently widening — which a blanket "use the from-zone aggregate" fix would have done.

Absence stays distinguishable from zero: an unknown from-zone reports not-ok, so the handler appends no row rather than fabricating a `0`.

## The resolution rule is single-sourced

`ruleSetSessionCount` is called by the handler **and** by the tests, rather than the tests reimplementing the two-step lookup. Deliberate, given what the defect was — a lookup key that no longer matched what the writer produced. A test carrying its own copy would pass against a production copy that had drifted: the same failure wearing the test's clothes. The first draft of this test did exactly that and was changed.

## Mutations — three, all killed, each by its own cell

drop the from-zone fallback (the defect) · always use the from-zone total (the over-widening) · fabricate a `0` for an unknown from-zone

## PR #8554 — measure: the learned-route publish cost, and what actually bounds it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8355-route-size-measurement`

#8355 acceptance item 1: *"A measurement relating learned-route count to serialized publish size and to the resulting control-socket deadline, with the fixture stated — not a cap asserted."*

## Measured — single next-hop, no ECMP, so every number is a **floor**

| routes | bytes | bytes/route | deadline |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 106 | 106.0 | 3s |
| 1,000 | 111,205 | 111.2 | 3s |
| 10,000 | 1,119,656 | 112.0 | 4s |
| 100,000 | 11,266,078 | 112.7 | 13s |
| 500,000 | 56,386,908 | 112.8 | **56s** |

~113 bytes/route, stable to within 1.5% across three orders of magnitude — which is what makes a route-count cap derivable from a byte budget at all, and is asserted rather than assumed.

## The measurement sharpened the premise

The issue frames the problem as **size**. But 500k routes serialize to ~56 MiB, which **fits** under the 64 MiB `MaxControlRequestBytes` ceiling — the size cap is not what stops it. That ceiling admits ~595,000 routes.

**What stops it is time.** At `3s + 1s/MiB` that publish carries a **56-second** control-socket deadline, on a socket CLAUDE.md already flags as contended: *"shared by status poll (1/s), HA sync, session installs, snapshot sync, and forwarding sync … a new control socket request at >1/s will starve session installs during bulk sync."* A minute-long publish does not starve that socket at the margin — it owns it. And #7437 makes publishes more frequent.

So the assertion is written against **duration**, not bytes. My first version asserted a full table exceeds the size ceiling and **failed** — correctly, and that failure is the finding.

## The number a cap decision needs

| publish-time budget | allows |
|---|---|
| 5s | ~18,600 routes (~2 MiB) |
| 10s | ~65,100 routes (~7 MiB) |
| 30s | ~251,300 routes (~27 MiB) |

## The fixture is stated in the file

The issue names how this measurement goes wrong — *"a table of near-identical routes that compresses or serializes unrepresentatively produces a confident wrong number"*. So the file states what it models and why: destinations spread across the /8 space with varying prefix lengths (a table of `10.0.N.0/24` understates the destination field); **256 distinct next-hops cycled**, because a real table has far fewer next-hops than routes *and JSON does not deduplicate*, so every route carries its next-hop in full; one next-hop per route, making the result a floor any ECMP table exceeds. What is deliberately *not* modelled is stated too.

**This does not choose a cap.** Acceptance items 2 and 3 — the loud degraded diagnostic, and degrade-to-no-import versus bounded-subset — are policy questions with different security postures, and the issue is right that they should be decided rather than inherited from a number. What they lacked was the number.

## PR #8555 — protocol: pin the idle-lease wire and assert Go and Rust agree [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `test/8121-verb-driven-sync`

#8121. `IdleLeaseWire` exists **twice** — `pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol.go` and `userspace-dp/src/protocol/control.rs` — and they meet over the control socket in `export_idle_leases` / `import_idle_leases`. **Nothing asserted they agree.**

## The wire fixture would normally cover this, and could not

`wire_invariant_default_specimens` dumps `::default()` specimens, and `idle_leases` carries `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"` — so an empty vec is omitted and this payload's field names **never appeared in the fixture at all**. Four of the type's own fields are `skip_serializing_if` too, so even a non-empty vec of *default* records would have hidden them.

That gap is not specific to this type, and the comment says so where the next reader will find it: **any field that is `skip_serializing_if` on its default value is unpinned by a default specimen.** Whether the tree's other such fields need populated specimens is a separate census; this one is pinned because two languages have to agree about it.

So the Rust side contributes a **populated** specimen — all eleven fields set — and the Go side asserts its own serialization matches that specimen, read from the fixture file both languages share.

## Assert the agreement, never pin one side

A literal encodes which side is trusted, and the failure being guarded is precisely that the two sides disagree: **a field named differently on one side decodes to its zero value on the other.** For this payload that is a persistent-NAT binding that survives on one node and not the other — what #8121 exists to prevent, arriving through the mechanism built to prevent it. On a rolling upgrade the two nodes run different binaries against one wire, so it is not hypothetical.

## Mutations — three, all killed

| mutation | covers |
|---|---|
| rename a field on the **Go** side | one direction |
| rename a field on the **helper** side (via the fixture) | the other |
| **delete the specimen entirely** | the guard's own premise — a cell that silently passes when its reference disappears is not a guard |

The Go cell also carries a positive control on its own serialization (a field-count floor), since an empty map would make the comparison vacuous.

## PR #8556 — nat: rebuild the persistent lease on the ADDRESS-ONLY synced path [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8132-addr-only-lease`

Closes #8132

#7360 taught the HA standby to reconstruct a persistent-NAT lease from the sessions it imports — but only on the PORT-TRANSLATING arm of `reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner`. The address-only arm (`port no-translation`, or a port-less protocol such as GRE/ESP) reaches a different reserve function a few lines above and was untouched: `reserve_address_only` minted the #5269 reverse-identity token and nothing else, so the standby held **zero leases** for every such client.

Measured on `origin/master`, four-address pool, `address-persistent` OFF, decoys interleaved:

```
ACTIVE   addr=203.0.113.2   persistent_leases=1  live_flows=1
STANDBY  after import       persistent_leases=0  live_flows=1
STANDBY  new flow           addr=203.0.113.4     SAME=false
```

## The assertion axis inverts, and that is the whole fixture

Under `port no-translation` the client keeps its own source port on the wire, so there is no translated PORT to lose. What the lease pins is the **ADDRESS**, and the address is what moves across a failover. #7360's cells call the address "the axis that survives for free"; here it is the entire property.

So the fixture must be a multi-address pool with `address-persistent` **OFF**. With one address, or with the flag on — where `sticky_pool_index` is a pure function of `(src_ip, pool_len)` and the standby recomputes the same slot — the assertion passes by construction. That claim is **tested rather than asserted**: `the_address_assertion_is_vacuous_under_address_persistent_8132` shows the two nodes agreeing with no lease at all, and it passes on the unfixed code, which is its job.

## Why a third variant, not a call-site swap

The local `reserve_address_only_persistent` also creates the lease, but it **CHOOSES** the pool address. A synced reservation must not choose — the active already did. `reserve_address_only_maybe_persistent` mints the token AND joins-or-creates the lease **at the address the wire named**, mirroring #7360's `reserve_flow_maybe_persistent` parameter for parameter. `reserve_address_only` becomes a delegate, so both local callers are unchanged.

#7360's session-DROP half has no counterpart here, structurally: an address-only allocation claims no pool port, and its `AddressOnlyReverseKey` folds in the remote, so two flows from one client to different servers never collide.

## A second defect, found by writing the join, present on BOTH arms

`rollback_flow` decides whether an activation *created* a lease from two recorded facts — has it seen a completion, and did the activation record a previous state. Both false means "this lease did not exist before this flow", so rollback **deletes** it, and on the port-bearing arm frees the pool port with it.

The local reuse path sets those fields on the 0→1 edge. Both **synced** joins omitted it, #7360's included. Harmless for a lease that went idle the ordinary way (`activation_saw_completion` is already true). #8121's `import_idle_lease` installs a lease that has completed **nothing**:

```
import an idle lease (#8121)    -> leases=1
a synced flow joins it          -> leases=1  flows=1
the flow is rolled back (#8115) -> leases=0
```

It needs BOTH changes present, which is why neither landing noticed. Fixed on both arms, one cell each; each reds only for its own arm's mutation.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` green — 5249 passed / 6 ignored, plus every integration target. `go build ./...` and the tree's content-scanning packages (`cmd/cli`, `pkg/config`, `pkg/cluster`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace`) green, including `fence_timeout_doc_drift_7147_test.go`, which asserts on the doc edited here.

**Seven mutations, each killed by the cell that names it:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| pass `None` for `persistent` (the whole revert) | 5 of 6 red; the vacuity control correctly stays green |
| delete the lease-drift refusal | only the drift cell |
| drop the idle-index removal on join | only the rejoin cell |
| mint the lease but do not join the flow | the refcount cell |
