## PR #8557 — Measure what a bind failure leaves for recovery (#8388) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8388-per-binding-rebind`

## What this is

Not the per-slot `rebind_slot` verb #8388 asked for. #8388's premise is
false, and this lands the measurement that shows it, the guard that keeps
it shown, and the corrections to the two places the premise had already
been written down as fact.

## The premise, and what actually happens

#8388: *"with `Sum min(rx, 16)` bindings the realistic failure is PARTIAL
— fifteen bind and one returns EBUSY"*, so recovering one wedged queue
tears down fifteen healthy sockets.

A bind failure never produces that shape. The helper's reconcile is a
transaction. The #5143 startup readiness barrier requires
`bound == planned` for **every** spawned worker, and on any shortfall
`bring_up_workers` calls `stop_inner(false)`, which stops and joins every
worker — the fifteen that bound included — before `reconcile`'s closing
`refresh_bindings` publishes anything. One EBUSY reaches the Go manager
as `bound == 0` with every registered+armed slot wedged. There are no
healthy siblings for a targeted rebind to spare, and the global rebind is
exactly proportionate to a globally-down dataplane.

The shape that **is** partial is the other post-teardown failure class: a
#4952 worker-thread SPAWN failure at worker K returns *without*
`stop_inner`, so workers `0..K-1` stay live and bound while worker K's
slots are registered, armed and unbound. What is missing there is a
worker THREAD, not a socket — a per-slot socket rebind cannot
`pthread_create` — so the targeted verb would not repair the one case
where the mixed shape is real. The global rebind re-runs the whole plan
and spawns the missing worker.

That is why the expensive prerequisite the issue's own follow-up analysis
identified (per-slot worker lifecycle + per-slot zero-copy quiesce, then
the verb) is not built here.

## What landed

- **Two cells** in `afxdp::coordinator::tests`:
  - `bind_incomplete_leaves_no_bound_sibling_8388` — measures the
    operator- and Go-visible `BindingStatus` surface (what
    `hasBusyBindingsWedgeLocked` actually reads) after a THREE-worker
    reconcile in which one worker binds short and two bind fully. The
    reported bound set is empty; every registered+armed slot is wedged.

## PR #8559 — dataplane: mirror one session upsert, refuse a standalone reverse [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8015-explicit-reverse`

Closes #8015

## What the issue actually was

A simplification, and the issue's own deciding question — "what does a
reverse-only entry admit?" — resolves to *tidying, not a security fix*, which is
what the last comment on the issue concluded and what this change is judged on.

The local session mirror sent **two** upserts to the Rust helper: a forward and
an explicitly built `is_reverse=1` companion, added under #310 so the worker
would hold the reverse before RG activation. The second was redundant.
`upsert_synced_session` calls `synthesized_synced_reverse_entry` for **every**
non-reverse import — a total function on forwards, its only `None` arm being
`is_reverse` — and publishes both halves. A single forward upsert already leaves
a complete pair; the #5674 aggregate ENTRY cap is sized at 2× the logical
ceiling *because* of it. Synthesis happens **at import**, earlier than the Go
pre-install ever was, so #310's invariant is satisfied by the request that
remains, and the helper's companion is the better one (#5698: it resolves
egress/FIB, fabric/tunnel and owner-RG against live node-local state).

Worth being explicit about, because it changes what "delete the second request"
means: the explicit reverse was never *additive*. The helper had already
published a companion for that forward by the time it arrived, so the second
request either **overwrote** it (when `val.ReverseKey` and the helper's
`reverse_session_key(forward, nat)` name the same tuple, which is the ordinary
case) or published a **third** entry (if the two derivations ever disagreed).
Either way, removing it cannot leave the reply direction uncovered — and the
version that survives is the one resolved against live node-local state.

What the second request added was a failure mode. On a *semantic* refusal of the
forward (`RejectedCapacity` and friends — a transport failure aborts the batch)
the explicit reverse still went out and published alone. It admits nothing the
requester did not already hold — its tuple and decision are the forward's own —
but it can **outlive** its forward, because `delete_synced_session_gen` derives
the companion to remove from the *stored* forward and after a refusal there is
none.

## What landed

**Go** — `mirrorSessionPairV4`/`V6` → `mirrorSessionV4`/`V6`, one `upsert` each.
With one request the #5007 single-snapshot build and the #5698 contiguous
transmit are vacuous, so `syncSessionPairLocked`, `sessionPairMaxRequests`,

## PR #8560 — userspace: bound control round trips at daemon stop [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8526-policy-schedule-lock`

Closes #8526

## What the issue actually was, and where it was wrong

The body's mechanism and arithmetic are correct: `m.mu` is held across a
control-socket round trip whose **reachable** bound is `3s + 64s = 67s`
(`controlBaseDeadline + 64 * controlDeadlinePerMiB` at the
`MaxControlRequestBytes` ceiling), against `TimeoutStopSec=20` — a 3.35x
overrun. `TestControlRoundtripBoundExceedsUnitStopBudget7675` measures the
constraint; nothing enforced it.

The comment on the issue is right that this is a class, not a site — and it
undercounted. Recomputing the census over the package finds **21** `*Manager`
methods that take `m.mu` and then round-trip under it, not sixteen: the hand
list missed the #8121 idle-lease pair (`ExportIdleLeases` / `ImportIdleLeases`)
plus `QuerySessionCounters`, `DrainSessionDeltas` and `ExportOwnerRGSessions`.
That is the last time anyone should hand-count it —
`TestEveryControlCallerHoldsTheManagerMutex8526` recomputes and logs the list
on every run.

**Where I disagree with the comment**, and it changes the fix: `m.mu` is *not*
the de-facto serializer of control traffic. The Rust helper's control-socket
accept loop is strictly sequential — `listener.accept()` then `handle_stream()`
inline, on one thread (`userspace-dp/src/server/lifecycle.rs:430`), with only
the *session* socket getting its own thread (#452). So the helper already
serializes control traffic; a second Go caller queues in the listen backlog.
What `m.mu` actually provides at these sites is **atomicity of (build snapshot
from state, publish, commit state)** — a state invariant, not a transport
ordering one. That kills the two-mutex split as the fix: the "channel lock" it
would preserve is redundant with the helper, and the state lock is the half
that must not be released.

## What landed

Nothing narrows a critical section. `m.mu` keeps exactly the scope it has;
what changes is that the **I/O performed under it becomes short once a stop is
in progress**. All 21 sites reach the socket through `requestDetailedLocked`,
so one site fixes the class.

- `BeginControlShutdown()` pulls every **in-flight** round trip's connection
  deadline in to `controlShutdownCutover` (500ms) and caps every round trip
  started **afterwards** at `controlShutdownCeiling` (= `controlBaseDeadline`,
  a no-op for every small request the teardown itself issues; it binds only on
  a large `apply_snapshot` that slipped past the daemon's apply fence).
- `ctrlIOMu` is a **leaf**: nothing holding it acquires `m.mu`, the only legal
  order is `m.mu -> ctrlIOMu`, and `BeginControlShutdown` takes `ctrlIOMu`
  alone — which is the entire reason it can cut a round trip that is itself
  holding `m.mu`. Registration and `SetDeadline` happen under one acquisition,
  so a cut cannot be overwritten by an arm already computing its deadline. The
  #7930 `Locked`-suffix analyzer is unaffected and green.

## PR #8561 — userspace-dp: require the post-NAT tuple on the cached flowless CoS arm (#8367) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8367-postnat-flowless-filter`

## What the issue actually was

Not what the title says, and the difference is worth stating before someone
re-derives it. The issue names two arms; they turned out to be different in
kind.

**Arm 1 (fresh flowless) was already correct at master — and untested.**
`forward_request.rs` builds `flowless_wire_flow` with
`l3_wire_session_flow_from_meta(meta, decision.nat)`, and the `forward_wire_key`
inside it rewrites `src_ip`/`dst_ip` **unconditionally**; only the address family
and the ICMP↔ICMPv6 swap sit behind `if nat.nat64`. So #7656 fixed plain
SNAT/DNAT on this arm as a side effect the day it landed. But every #7656 cell is
NAT64, so the behaviour was right *by side effect* with nothing to notice it
regressing. **Measured:** narrowing `l3_wire_session_flow_from_meta` to
`if nat.nat64 { forward_wire_key(..) } else { pre.forward_key }` — the exact
scope boundary the issue body draws — left **5251 of 5252 cells green** before
this PR.

**Arm 2 (cached flowless) was stale, and unreachable.**
`resolve_cached_cos_tx_selection_impl`'s flowless arm read the ingress `meta` in
all three places (`is_v6`, `l3_addrs()`, `meta.protocol`). But it could not be
reached with a wrong tuple: `flow_cache.rs:537` always seeds with
`Some(&tx_selection_wire_key)`, and `mirror/resolver.rs`'s `mirror_cos_queue_id`
— the only caller that reached the flowless arm — consumed `.queue_id`, which is
computed *before and independently of* the filter block. So the staleness was a
trap armed for the next caller, not a live defect. That confirms the reachability
analysis in the issue's last comment.

## What landed

A **type change**, not three patched reads, because the shape problem the
reachability analysis exposed is that the caller reaching the flowless arm has no
`NatDecision` to synthesize a tuple from:

- `CachedTxTuple::{Flow{egress_wire_key, ingress_flow_key}, Flowless{wire_l3}}` —
  both variants carry a **required** post-NAT on-wire key. The three entry points
  (`resolve_cached_cos_tx_selection`, `_prenat`, and the new `_flowless`) take
  `&SessionKey`, not `Option`. There is deliberately no entry point that lets the
  key be omitted, because "no tuple" and "the pre-NAT tuple" are not the same
  answer and only one of them is honest.
- The flowless arm moves into `cached_cos_tx_selection_flowless`, which reads
  family, addresses and protocol from that one key — the property #7656
  established on the fresh arm. A mixture (egress family, ingress addresses)
  selects the right filter and then cannot match any address-bearing term in it,
  which no address-less fixture can see.
- `mirror_cos_queue_id` asks for what it consumes: `resolve_cached_cos_tx_queue_id`.
  For a flowless clone that is the behaviour-aggregate lookup alone (5-tuple
  independent), so the queue is byte-identical to before.
- `#6055`'s fail-closed intent is preserved rather than reversed: emptying the
  fields would restore exactly the fail-open it removed.

## PR #8562 — Carry the bind-failure cause past the fail-closed teardown (#8558) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8558-wedge-cause-survives-failclose`

## The defect

`hasBusyBindingsWedgeLocked` gates auto-rebind recovery on
`(busyErr || repaired)`. Neither disjunct could be satisfied by the state a
bind failure actually leaves, so the recovery built for that fault never
fired for it — silently, and without even the `auto-rebind GAVE UP` log,
which lives inside the same predicate.

- **`busyErr`** is a substring match on the per-binding `LastError`. The
  helper's fail-closed bring-up erases it: the `BindIncomplete` arm calls
  `stop_inner(false)`, which empties `workers.live`, so `refresh_bindings`
  routes every slot through `zero_unbound_slot`, whose last act is
  `last_error.clear()`. Measured on the real sequence with the failing
  slot's `BindingLiveState` carrying `"Device or resource busy"`: the
  published rows came back `last_error = ["", "", ""]`.
- **`repaired`** needs a forwarding-live (`Ready`) binding from
  `verifyBindingsMapLocked`, and a fail-closed reconcile leaves none.

This is the dominant outcome of a bind EBUSY, not an exotic one — per #8388
a single-queue bind failure fails the whole reconcile closed and leaves the
entire dataplane unbound. And for a link-cycle `rebind`, or any path where
the snapshot generation does not advance, auto-rebind is the *only* recovery
the status loop has: `syncSnapshotLocked` returns early on
`publishedSnapshot >= lastSnapshot.Generation`.

## The fix

`Coordinator::last_bind_failures` (slot → reason) carries the terminal
per-slot causes across the teardown that erases them.

- `stop_inner` **clears** it; the `BindIncomplete` arm **repopulates** it
  from the #6245 explicit `BindingSetupFailure`s **immediately after**
  calling `stop_inner`. That ordering *is* the fix — recorded before the
  teardown, the teardown clears it again (mutation 2 below).
- Clearing in `stop_inner` rather than at the top of `reconcile` covers the
  teardowns that never enter `reconcile`: `Coordinator::stop` (the disarm
  branch of `reconcile_status_bindings`) and the `no_snapshot` path. A
  legitimately unbound slot never inherits the retired generation's error.
- `refresh_bindings` restores the cause after `zero_unbound_slot` has zeroed
  the slot. It has to live there, not in a one-shot write into `bindings`:
  `refresh_status` runs the refresh on **every** control response, so a
  cause restored anywhere else is erased within one ~1 Hz status poll — well
  inside the 5s dwell the Go predicate requires before acting. The map is
  consulted only where a slot has **no** `live` entry, so a bound slot can
  never pick up a stale cause.
- Scope is the **explicit** per-slot failures only. The barrier-TIMEOUT
  shortfall (`bound: None`) carries no cause to attribute, and inventing one
  would put a reason on slots that may well have bound. Recovery still does
  not fire for it; widening the predicate to act on a wedge whose cause is
  unknown is a separate decision, because the `maxConsecutiveAutoRebinds`

## PR #8563 — server: serve sync_session without the ServerState mutex [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/7209-session-domain`

Closes #7209

The HA session socket has had its own socket and its own thread since #452, but it dispatched through the same `Arc<Mutex<ServerState>>` as every main-socket verb. **The socket split never split the critical section.**

`apply_snapshot` holds that mutex across a 10 s worker-readiness barrier, a 500 ms mlx5 teardown quiesce, worker `join()`s and BPF map-pin opens. Go budgets 3 s for a session round-trip and #5380 **aborts the remainder of a bulk batch** on the first transport failure. So the contention never cost latency — it cost up to 255 dropped session mirrors, during exactly the failover the path exists to serve.

## What the verb actually needs

The handler reads nothing but `guard.afxdp`. Six methods, all `&self`. The whole `impl` block they live in referenced exactly `sessions`, `forwarding`, `bpf_maps`, `workers`, `ha.rg_runtime` and `dynamic_neighbors_ref` — no coordinator-only dependency anywhere in the subgraph, and the type system had already proved it `&self`-only, since `upsert_synced_session(&self)` compiled.

So the import domain moves to a `SessionDomain` handle and the coordinator delegates. Delegating rather than leaving a second copy behind keeps the **87 existing call sites** pointed at the code that now runs, instead of quietly becoming tests of a decommissioned path.

**Not `Arc<Coordinator>`:** 42 `&mut self` methods. The handle needs six things and five were already shared. `SessionManager` becomes **one** `Arc` — it has zero `&mut self` methods, zero `&mut self.sessions` sites, and is never reassigned. That subsumes the abandoned `724ebb5bc`, which Arc-ified six of its eleven counters individually; re-deriving it would have been work spent reaching a worse design.

## Forwarding moves, and it moves to something better

The import path read `Coordinator::forwarding`, an owned field. It now reads the **published `RuntimeView`** — the one the packet workers hold. A session resolved against the published forwarding agrees with the tables that will actually carry its packets; `self.forwarding` mid-apply is a state no worker is using. `republish_runtime_validation` already prefers the published forwarding for the same reason and says so.

They cannot diverge in production — both sites that assign `self.forwarding` publish on the next lines. That was checked specifically, because if any site mutated without publishing this would have been a silent behaviour change rather than a refactor.

One view per request, **structurally**: `SessionDomainView` holds the guard, so a handler cannot resolve its domain against one generation and its zones against another — the pairing defect #6592 closed, reintroduced one layer up.

## No status attach on this verb

An earlier draft kept the `!suppress_status` attach. That left the verb **starvable by any caller that omitted the flag**, and the acceptance cell asserts the property unconditionally. Measured before removing it: nothing consumes `status` on a `sync_session` response — both daemon senders set `SuppressStatus`, no Go caller reads the field, none of the 18 Rust cells asserts on it.

## This is the consumer several increments were built for

`bringup.rs`'s replay reads the live shared synced map (#8157) so a mid-reconcile arrival is included; its comment read *"NOT REACHABLE TODAY… #7209 is what makes it reachable, and this is its prerequisite — landing it afterwards would mean shipping the race first."* That is now reachable, and both that comment and `teardown.rs`'s sibling are updated rather than left describing a world that moved. `synced_import_cap_for` already takes the records **map** for the straddle this makes possible, and `synced_import_unpublished` already exists to make the window observable.

**Two pre-arranged `#[ignore]`d acceptance cells are un-ignored here.** The second is the one that matters: it drives a real upsert *and* a real delete and asserts each got past the payload guard, so a fix that moved only the dispatch and re-took the lock inside the verb body would leave the first green and this one red.

## What it costs if wrong

Data races are excluded by construction. The residual is semantic: a mid-reconcile import resolves zones against the previous published generation. Its reverse companion is re-derived under the live tables at replay; its NAT reservation is against the previous generation's allocators, which is **not a new class** — every pre-existing session's reservation is in the same position across a reconcile, which #6765's retained-address carryover already handles. The degraded case is counted, so it is observable rather than silent.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` green — **5265 passed, 0 failed**. `go build ./...`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace` and `cmd/cli` green.

Two guards fired during development, both correct, neither near the changed code:

- `every_shared_session_lock_in_production_recovers_from_poison_6653` caught a bare `.lock()` in the new accessor, from another module, by **content** — the class of guard a package-scoped run cannot see.
- `forwarding_publish_population_is_pinned_7015` caught the new test seam entering production source, which is why `set_forwarding_for_test` lives in a fixture file: adding a test-only exception to that pin would have raised `coordinator/mod.rs` from 1 to 2 and masked the third apply path it exists to catch.

A third red was checked rather than patched. `a_dropped_deletesynced_releases_the_workers_reservation_6979_f4` fails because the release path now resolves allocators through the published view — safe only if the published clone **shares** allocator state. It does (`PortAllocator` derives `Clone` over an `Arc<PortAllocatorShared>`). A deep-cloning allocator would have made that a real port leak rather than a fixture that forgot to publish.

## PR #8567 — configstore: key the confirm-removal debt to its own record (#7675 item 4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/7675-commit-confirmed-hazards`

Delivers **item 4** of #7675 — the hazard census over the G+H+H2 seed's §4-mirror work-item bodies — and lands the one hazard it turned up that is fixable without any of the disputed durability machinery.

## The census result, in one line

**The residue was not one row. It is five**, and only one of them is the G/H ordering hazard the tracker's last comment expected to be alone. Full table, dispositions and measurements are on #7675; the short version:

| hazard | status |
|---|---|
| unkeyed removal debt destroys a FRESH window's crash-recovery file | **FIXED HERE** |
| hash basis is not canonical → a LIVE record is stale-dropped on restart | filed #8564 |
| a resolution with no error channel reverts an already-CONFIRMED config on boot | filed #8565 |
| a boot `ReadConfirm` error silently discards the rollback window | filed #8566 |
| G/H dispatch ordering | stays residual — it is the one that genuinely needs the unit |

Three of the four new rows are peelable, which is what the tracker's own comment predicted would decide it: *"the next question is whether that is itself peelable — fixable on master without the durability machinery, as three hazards already were."*

## What this PR fixes

`resolveConfirmRemovalLocked` retains a debt when a resolved window's `confirm.json` cannot be durably deleted (#5835), and the persist-retry loop re-drives the delete. That re-drive was **unconditional** — it deleted whatever `confirm.json` was on disk, not the record the debt was taken for.

An operator who arms a **brand-new** `commit confirmed` while a debt is outstanding therefore has the **new** window's crash-recovery file deleted by a retry that believes it is clearing the old one. Deterministic on the next backoff tick, not a race. And invisible: the in-memory timer stays armed and `IsConfirmPending()` is true, so the window looks healthy. The damage shows only after a restart, when the record is absent and the UNCONFIRMED config stands permanently with no rollback — the #4577 failure the record exists to prevent.

**Measured on master before the fix** (hermetic, existing `installConfirmDeleteSeams` seam):

```
debt taken: ConfirmRemovalDegraded=true
fresh window C armed; record on disk = true
INFO stale pending commit-confirmed record removed after earlier failure   <- deleting a LIVE one
after retry: C's crash-recovery record on disk = false
timer still armed in memory = true
```

#5473 had recognised this exact shape for the **other** debt it introduced, and drains it at every arm site before `writeConfirmState` writes the fresh record — the reason is stated verbatim in `CommitConfirmed`'s post-rename branch: *"so the stale flag does not survive to make the degraded retry's heal delete E's OWN fresh record."* #5835 then added a second debt and did not extend that drain. This **keys** the debt rather than extending the drain, so the property holds for an arm path that forgets to drain.

## Implementation

`resolveConfirmRemovalLocked` captures the on-disk record's identity (GuardedHash + deadline + FirstCommit — `writeConfirmState` is the sole production `WriteConfirm` caller and makes it distinct for every arm and re-arm) **before** attempting the delete, and retains it as `confirmRemoveDebtID` on failure. The retry consults `confirmRemovalSupersededLocked`: a **different** record on disk means a newer arm's `WriteConfirm` (temp+fsync+rename+dir-fsync) already durably replaced the one the debt was owed for, so the debt is satisfied by construction and clears without deleting.

Absent or unreadable is deliberately **not** superseded — an absent record still owes the #4864 directory barrier, and an unreadable one cannot be a fresh arm — so both still re-drive the delete and #5835's self-healing is untouched.

Deliberately **not** done: the sibling deferred-resolution path. Every commit and sync path already drains it before arming (#5473), so a guard there would be unreachable and unbindable. I wrote it, could not bind it, and removed it.

## Mutation matrix

The two cells are a **discrimination matrix**, not two views of one property. `..._StillHealsItsOwnRecord_7675` exists specifically to fail on the OVER-BROAD fix: a supersession predicate that always answered yes would satisfy the defect cell while silently disabling #5835's self-healing and leaving a genuinely stale rollback on disk for the next boot to resurrect.

| mutation (applied alone, reverted) | eat-fresh | still-heals |
|---|---|---|
| remove the supersession branch | **FAIL** | pass |
| supersession predicate always `true` | pass | **FAIL** |

## PR #8570 — dataplane: resolve the PPTP data channel against its association [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/7699-pptp-data-resolve`

Closes #7699

#7699's stages landed the identity substrate, the TCP/1723 control-channel parser and the packet-path dispatch that feeds it. **Nothing read the associations.** Every hit on `resolve` / `resolve_and_touch` / `note_unassociated` was a test, and `gre_discriminator` refused the class outright (`TunnelDiscriminator::Pptp(_) => return None`), so a GRE version-1 packet never consulted the table.

That is this issue's own subject. A version-1 packet is `Unparseable`, which is fail-closed **across** classes but equal to **itself** within one — so two simultaneous PPTP calls between one endpoint pair share a `SessionKey` and alias, with the policy, NAT, counter and timeout state hanging off it. **Acceptance criterion 2 could not be met by the dispatch alone: the associations existed and nothing read them.**

## Why version 1 needs its own extractor

The 32 bits after the flags word are `Payload Length | Call ID`, not an RFC 2890 Key. `gre_transit_discriminator` refuses version 1 for exactly that reason: reading the word with RFC 2890 field order promotes a **per-packet-varying length** as if it were a stable tunnel identity, giving one call a new session per packet. `pptp_call_id` is the other half of that refusal, not a relaxation — it reads the low half only, and the fixture gives the two halves different values so a cell can tell a correct extractor from one reading the wrong one.

## Why the join is in the descriptor loop

`stage_parse_flow_and_learn` takes `&WorkerContext`, and the association table is per-worker state on `SessionTable` — deliberately per-worker, broadcast at install, so the packet path reads it without a lock. `poll_descriptor` is the one point in the loop where the frame and `&mut SessionTable` are both in scope.

Gated on `flow.is_none()` and on `gre_acceleration`, so it is purely **additive**: a packet that already has an identity is untouched, a version-1 packet is flowless today, and with the knob off the expression does nothing. The only reachable change is flowless → identified.

## Direction symmetry is the whole reason for the handle

RFC 2637 §4.1 call ids are per-direction, so the two directions of one call carry **different** values on the wire. No symmetric reverse-key transform can pair them, which is why stage 1 put a locally derived handle in the discriminator rather than the id off the packet — a packet-derived discriminator would make a reply match *no session at all*, worse than the aliasing it replaces. The cell uses ids 100 and 200 rather than equal values, because equal ids would let it pass under an implementation that keyed on the raw id.

## `resolve_and_touch`, not `resolve`

Refreshing on use makes the idle timeout mean "no traffic" rather than "old". Without a data-path caller the clock advanced only at install, so a long-lived call carrying traffic aged out on its **learn** time. That is worse than a leak: PPTP call ids are 16 bits and reused, so expiring a live call frees an id whose next taker mis-attributes onto the dead handle.

## Unassociated is forwarded and counted

A call already up before this node started resolves to `None`, is counted, and gets no session — the same flowless treatment as today, so this can only add identity and never remove forwarding. The counter is not decoration: it is documented as expected non-zero during startup, and until now nothing called `note_unassociated`, so it read **zero forever**. A lone counter at zero cannot distinguish "nothing happened" from "this code is unreachable" — which is what it was reporting.

## Validation

`cargo test` green — **5274 passed** — plus `go build ./...`, `cmd/cli` and `pkg/config` (needed here because this edits a Go advisory and a doc).

**Four mutations, each killed by exactly the cell that names it:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| **delete the production call** from the descriptor loop | **50 of 51 #7699 cells stay green; only the wiring guard reds** |
| read the payload length instead of the call id | 5 cells, including both aliasing cells |
| `resolve` instead of `resolve_and_touch` | only the idle-clock cell |
| drop `note_unassociated` | only the counter cell |

The first is not hypothetical. **This issue already shipped exactly that failure once** — deleting the drain call survived the whole suite, because every cell drove the drain directly. The new guard follows the sibling added for that, reusing its matcher and needle discipline so the two cannot drift, and carries its own over-reach control proving it rejects a commented-out call and a prose mention.

## Docs

The commit advisory said transit GRE is keyed on the RFC 2890 discriminator on this node and does not survive a failover — accurate, and now incomplete: it did not mention that PPTP calls are separated too, nor that a call whose reply this node did not see stays unkeyed. Both are stated now. `docs/feature-gaps.md`'s M-item recorded the aliasing sentence as retired by #7188; it now says the PPTP half is retired here, failover half still true for both.

## The premise, checked first

`fabric_ingress_return_traffic_is_denied_on_the_lan_node_7770`, which drives a

reaches **neither** the policy call nor the install — for every new flow, for as
long as the split lasts. That is both "first packet of EVERY new flow" and "does
not self-heal", in one place.

## The design question, and why B/C/D collapse

The thread left three options and ranked D (a punt record) over B (synchronous
sync), naming two unestablished things. Both resolve against the code, and
together they collapse the set to one answer:

**1. The verdict bit cannot ride a `META_FLAG` — this corrects the last
comment.** It proposed stamping the peer's verdict on the return frame using a
spare `META_FLAG_*` bit and flagged "whether the fabric redirect path preserves
meta flags across the fabric hop" as the thing that would make or break it. It
does not. `meta_flags` is a field of `UserspaceDpMeta` — the XDP metadata area
the shim writes for the LOCAL userspace pass. The fabric hop transmits an
Ethernet frame and the receiving node's shim writes fresh meta. The only
wire-carried metadata on that hop is the synthetic source MAC, and all six bytes
are spoken for (`[0x02,0xbf,0x72,MAGIC,zone_hi,zone_lo]`). A second `MAGIC` value
*would* be additive room, so the idea is implementable — just not by the proposed
carrier.

**2. It is not needed, because the record does not have to be bespoke.** D's cost
was "adding a record adds per-flow state on a node that deliberately holds none,
and its lifetime, cap and eviction are exactly the kind of thing that turns into
its own issue". The session table already answers all three. So the punt record
**is** a session — which is option C, ruled dead because the redirecting node
"never evaluates policy for the flow, so it would be minting sessions for traffic
it never authorised". That is a statement about the current code, not a
constraint on it. Add the evaluation and C's objection is answered, D's state
question disappears, and the peer's verdict stops mattering: the authorisation is
this node's own.

## PR #8572 — nat: bind the persistent-lease population to its sync routes [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8121-idle-lease-acceptance`

Closes #8121

#8121's mechanism is complete and **wired end to end** — allocator verbs, control handler, Go manager, cluster-sync payload, daemon hook — with the Go/Rust wire pinned by a populated specimen (#8555) and the acceptance property itself covered in-process: a client idle inside its persistence timeout keeps its translated port across a failover, on a multi-address pool with an interleaved decoy so neither half of the identity is true by construction.

What was **not** covered is the claim the three landed pieces make *together*.

## The claim, and why it needs binding

| lease | route to the standby |
|---|---|
| live flows, port-translating | rebuilt from the synced sessions (#7360) |
| live flows, address-only | rebuilt from the synced sessions (#8132) |
| idle, inside its timeout | exported and imported (#8121) |

That is an **exhaustiveness claim about a population**, and defining a population by a mechanism is a claim that the mechanism is the only route. The way it fails is not that one of the three breaks — each has cells — but that a **sixth creation site lands later and nobody classifies it.** At that moment the argument is quietly false, every existing cell stays green (each tests a route; none tests the *set* of routes), and anything resting on the claim inherits the error.

Something does rest on it. **The #1449 capability gate disarms forwarding for every HA persistent-NAT configuration, and its stated reason is that these leases are not HA-synchronized.** On this census, that reason no longer describes the tree.

## What this adds

A census over `src/nat` production source pinning every site that inserts into `persistent_by_source`, **by enclosing function rather than by count**, each annotated with the route that carries it. Five sites: two that create a lease on the ACTIVE (local PAT mint, #6041 address-only mint) and three on a STANDBY (the two session-rebuild arms, the idle import). A new one reds until someone says which route carries it — and if it creates a lease on a *standby* it is a new **route**, so the exhaustiveness argument must be re-made rather than inherited.

It carries a **positive control**, deliberately: a scanner whose pattern has rotted finds nothing, compares empty to empty, and passes forever while measuring no population at all.

## What this deliberately does not do

**Re-decide the #1449 gate.** Removing a gate's premise and removing the gate are different changes: the second re-arms forwarding for a configuration class that has been disarmed, which is a user-facing availability change wanting its own verification rather than arriving as a side effect of the work that removed its premise. Filed separately, with this census as its evidence.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` green — **5280 passed**. `go test ./pkg/cluster/` green, including `fence_timeout_doc_drift_7147_test.go`, which asserts on the doc edited here.

**Mutations:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| add a sixth creation site | the census reds **and names it** — the failure mode it exists for is an unclassified addition, not a regression in an existing route |
| delete one entry from the expected list | the census reds **and the positive control reds** — correct, since a trimmed list is exactly how this degenerates into comparing empty to empty |

## Docs

`docs/ha-failover-status.md` said the idle lease was "still not rebuilt" and that #8121's acceptance run was blocked by the gate. The first is now wrong — the chain is wired — and the second read as though the issue were stalled rather than complete. The section now states the three routes as a table, says the exhaustiveness claim is bound by the census rather than asserted, and says plainly that the gate's stated reason no longer describes the tree while the decision to lift it is not taken here. Its closing "a future change must add full lease sync or replay" now notes all three parts exist, so what remains is the decision, not the mechanism.

## PR #8574 — configstore: fix three silent commit-confirmed boot-recovery failures (#8564, #8565, #8566) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8564-8566-confirm-recovery`

The three defects the #7675 hazard census turned up, fixed together. Three commits, each independently reviewable and revertable.

**Why one PR and not three:** all three live in the same two functions — `recoverPendingConfirmLocked` and `resolveConfirmRemovalLocked` — and the #8565 tombstone needs the record that #8564's identity capture already reads. Split across three PRs they would conflict on every rebase and the second and third would each be reviewed against a base that no longer describes the code. Split across three *commits* they stay separable: each carries its own guards, its own mutation matrix, and its own `Closes`.

**What they have in common, and what it demanded of the fixtures:** all three are failures of a RECOVERY path on the BOOT path, and all three fail silently — a stale-dropped live record, a revert of an already-confirmed config, a discarded window with no timer and no degraded health. A fixture that exercises a clean boot passes under an implementation that never recovers anything, so every cell here **enters the failure state**: an invalid UTF-8 byte actually present, a `confirm.json` removal that actually fails, a `ReadConfirm` that actually errors. Each fix also has a control that fails on the OVER-BROAD version of itself, because for all three the over-broad fix deletes #4577's safety hatch and looks like a pass.

---

## 1 · `Closes #8564` — hash the guarded config on its canonical text

`GuardedHash` is computed at ARM time over the IN-MEMORY tree and re-computed at BOOT over the tree DECODED FROM DISK. Any value the JSON encoding normalizes makes them differ, so recovery drops a **live** record as stale — and logs *"a later commit/confirm superseded it"* when nothing did, which is a false diagnostic describing a benign situation.

Reachable instance: `hasControlChars` rejects only C0/DEL, so a raw `0xff` in a free-text leaf commits, and `json.MarshalIndent` coerces it to U+FFFD. Measured: arm a window on `interfaces eth0 description "lan\xffside"`, restart, `IsConfirmPending()` is false and the record is gone.

Fixed by hashing the tree's text after one JSON round trip, so the two bases are equal **by construction** rather than by the absence of any normalizing value — rejecting `0xff` at commit would close this instance and leave the class open. No versioned-basis field is needed: for every config the encoding does not normalize the canonical basis is byte-identical to the plain one, and that claim is a **cell**, not a sentence.

| mutation | normalized | clean | stale | legacy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| revert the ARM site | **FAIL** | pass | pass | pass |
| revert the RECOVERY site | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| `guardedConfigHash` → constant | pass | pass | **FAIL** | **FAIL** |
| `canonicalizeTree` → identity | **FAIL** | pass | pass | pass |
| canonical basis prefixed | pass | pass | pass | **FAIL** |

**The recovery-site mutation escapes, and that is reported rather than papered over:** `s.active` there was decoded from disk by `Load` immediately above, so canonicalizing it again is idempotent by construction. The call is written anyway so both ends name the same function, and the code comment says exactly that so it is not "simplified away" later on the grounds that it is provably a no-op.

## 2 · `Closes #8565` — tombstone a resolved record

"Window pending" and "window RESOLVED but the deletion failed" were the same bytes on disk. #5835's binding separates them only when the resolution CHANGED the active config, and a confirmation changes nothing — `store_commit.go` says so directly. So the hash matched, recovery treated the record as live, and past the deadline **reverted a config the operator had explicitly confirmed**; inside the window it re-armed the rollback, which reverts it a minute later.

On two of the three resolution paths nobody is told: `ConfirmPendingOnDemotion` returns a bool, the plain-commit/HA-sync paths discard the error. The README recorded this as a residual that *"fails SAFE … consistent with `ConfirmCommit` having returned an error"* — a rationale covering only the one path with an error to return. That sentence is **replaced**, not extended.

**Which way it errs, since the campaign has twice found the conservative-sounding choice to be the damaging one:** a tombstoned record is IGNORED, so the CONFIRMED config stands. #4577 is untouched — an UNRESOLVED record carries no tombstone and still reverts, which is the control cell. The tombstone is written only where the removal is actually reached, which #5473 already defers until the resolving write is durable, so it can never mark a window whose resolution did not take effect; and a tombstone write that itself fails degrades to exactly the pre-fix behaviour, so this can only shrink the window in which a resolved record looks pending, never widen it. **Transient and permanent removal failures get the same answer deliberately** — both mean the window is resolved — and differ only in how long `ConfigPersistDegraded()` keeps reporting the undeleted record, which the fixture asserts so the state becomes recoverable *without* becoming silent.

| mutation | resolved-not-resurrected | unresolved-control |
|---|---|---|
| recovery ignores the tombstone | **FAIL** | pass |
| never write the tombstone | **FAIL** | pass |
| recovery ignores EVERY record | pass | **FAIL** |
| tombstone written at ARM time | pass | **FAIL** |
| `Resolved` dropped from the wire | **FAIL** | pass |

Both over-broad mutations — the two that delete #4577's hatch outright — are caught **only** by the control.

## 3 · `Closes #8566` — report a boot read failure

`Load` succeeded, no timer, no debt, `ConfigPersistDegraded()` false → /health 200 and the gauge 0, while an UNCONFIRMED config stood permanently with no rollback. Every other unsafe boot outcome raises degraded health; this one did not, so nothing could alert on it.

Now: ERROR log, `confirm_recovery_read_error` journal entry, `confirmRecoveryReadFailed` folded into `ConfigPersistDegraded()` (→ 503 + gauge) with `ConfirmRecoveryReadFailed()` exposed on its own. The gauge HELP and the `ConfigPersistDegradedFn` contract comment both named only #1799 and were already stale after #5835; both now name all three causes. That widens what the gauge fires on, deliberately — the condition was previously unreportable through any channel.

## PR #8575 — docs: re-measure the #7494 v6 fragment shapes, and refute the hypothesis [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `measure/8249-loop-correlation`

Refs #8249. Docs only — no source change.

#8249 blocks the IPv6 half of the non-first-fragment fix on headroom, records four rejected channels, tells the reader **"do not re-derive these"**, and names one unmeasured experiment as the right opening move. This runs that experiment. The result changes the direction of the fix.

## The baseline moved, so the matrix had to be re-derived

| | plan §0 | now |
|---|---|---|
| processed insns | 801,448 | **686,919** |
| headroom vs the 1M cap | 19.86% | **31.31%** |
| usable slack vs the 850,000 ceiling | 48,552 | **163,081** |

Second time this issue's ground has moved — the plan itself records the first (777,901 → 801,448). The instruction not to re-derive was reasonable when written and is now the thing standing between a reader and a correct decision.

## Re-measured: +114,529 of headroom bought nothing

| shape | result | signature |
|---|---|---|
| sentinel at the CALL SITE | **REJECT** 1,000,001 | `53311 / 3637` |
| sentinel INSIDE the walk, where flag and protocol are already the same loop-carried state | **REJECT** 1,000,001 | `53311 / 3637` — **identical** |
| SKIP `parse_l4` on the fragment arm (removes a call rather than adding a value) | **REJECT** 1,000,001 | `53221 / 3595` |

The cost is not additive, and **placement is irrelevant** — moving the substitution inside the walk gives a bit-identical verifier signature, which kills the intuition that the call site is what creates a new correlated pair.

## The hypothesis is refuted by two controls

#8249 hypothesises that correlating an L4 value with a **loop-carried** predicate is what explodes, and names the isolating build: take the v4 shape and derive its bit from a loop instead of a fixed-offset read.

| control (in `parse_ipv4`, same value, same consumer) | insns | delta | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| loop-carried flag, bounded loop, flag set inside an arm | 711,603 | **+24,684** | **PASS** 28.84% |
| the same + an offset advancing by a packet-derived length, as the walk does | 742,420 | **+55,501** | **PASS** 25.76% |

The second control has **every property the hypothesis names** and costs +55,501 with 107,580 slack left. The same structural shape is cheap in one parser and impossible in the other, so the mechanism is not loop-carried correlation.

## What it actually is

The constraint is the **IPv6 parse region's state budget** — not the derivation, the placement, or the consumer. That is the only reading consistent with the one datum that never fitted the hypothesis: the channel where a new `ParsedPacket` field is **never read** also cost ≥198,552. A never-read field cannot be correlated with anything; it can only add state to a region that has none left.

So the candidate #8249 proposes — restructure the walk so the sighting is not loop-carried — is measured here as **fixing a problem that does not exist**. What has to come first is a reduction in IPv6 parse-path state large enough to move a region three structurally different shapes all fail against at one signature.

## Validation

The measurements were taken by editing `userspace-xdp/src`, building, and reverting; the tree here carries none of them. **The instrument is reproducible:** after reverting every experiment, a rebuild from clean source returned 686,919 again and emitted an object byte-identical to the tracked one, so `git status` showed only this file. That is the zero noise floor the plan claims, re-established at the new baseline rather than inherited from the old one.

## PR #8576 — Release the reservation a refused DeleteSynced strands (#8114 item 4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8114-item4-dropped-delete`

## The defect

`replicate_session_delete` fans a `DeleteSynced` out to every sibling
worker's queue and **discarded `push_bounded`'s return**, so at
`MAX_PENDING_WORKER_COMMANDS` (4096) the command was dropped silently.

That is not a missed optimisation. `handle_delete_synced` is what a worker
*does* with the command, and it drops **that worker's** source-NAT and
NAT64 holder bits; the port is freed by whichever worker drops the last
bit. A worker that never receives the command never drops its bit — and it
is **alive**, so neither the dead-worker sweep (#8069) nor the
generation-teardown sweep (#7092) can see the bit. The reservation is held
for the life of the allocator.

So item 4 is a **port leak** as well as the stale-forwarding window the
issue describes, and it is the same stranding
`Coordinator::delete_synced_session_gen` already repairs on the
control-plane side (#6979 F4).

## The blocker, and how it is resolved

The coordinator's repair releases **for a named worker**. The worker-side
fan-out could not name one: `peer_worker_commands` is built in
`reconcile/bringup.rs` as `.filter(|(id, _)| **id != worker_id).map(|(_,
queue)| queue.clone())` — the ids are gone by the time the fan-out sees the
slice, and its order relative to any id-keyed structure depends on which
worker was excluded. (This is the structural fact flagged in #8569's PR
body.)

Changing that slice's element type reaches ~190 references. Instead
`WorkerContext` gains `worker_commands_by_id` — the same queues, keyed —
and the repair asks it *"which id is THIS allocation?"* by `Arc::ptr_eq`.
That cannot desynchronise the way a parallel `&[u32]` would: the two
structures hold the same `Arc`s, not the same fact written down twice. The
lookup is O(workers), on a path taken only when a push is refused.

**Why the id cannot be skipped.** Releasing for a worker that *will* still
process its delete is harmless (idempotent); releasing for one still
**forwarding** the flow hands its port to another flow — the direction of
error `PortAllocator::drop_holder_locked` forbids. So "release for every
worker" is not a substitute, and an unresolvable id is **counted, not
guessed**.

## Deliberately not repaired

The refused sibling also never deletes its **local session-table entry**
and never invalidates its **flow-cache slots**, so it can keep serving the
revoked session until the entry ages out. Neither is reachable from the
deleting thread — both live behind that worker's `&mut SessionTable` and
its own per-binding caches — and the signal that would have to reach it

## PR #8577 — dataplane: assert the shim/Go degraded-reason agreement instead of a list [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8258-verdict-agreement`

Closes #8258

Point 2 — drop/permit verdicts across the shim and the helper — has a surviving pair, joined by an **index**, with nothing but a comment asserting the two sides agree.

The shim records a degraded-path disposition by index into a per-CPU array (`USERSPACE_FALLBACK_REASON_*`). Go reads that array and renders each slot under a name from `degradedPathReasonNames`. Three slots are literally drop/permit verdicts — `transit_drop`, `strict_drop`, `pass_to_kernel` — so an operator asking *"why is traffic disappearing"* reads this mapping and nothing else. What held it together: *"Must stay in sync with USERSPACE_FALLBACK_REASON_* in userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs."*

## The existing guard is the thing #8258 warns about

`TestDegradedPathReasonNamesCoverRetainedShimActions` looks like the guard for this. It pins the **Go** side to a hand-written list of eleven names and a length of 16, and never reads the shim — a heuristic on one surface, which encodes which side you trust, when the failure being guarded is that the sides disagreed.

**Measured, not argued — both failures leave it green:**

- **ADD** a reason (index 16, MAX→17): the Go array stays at 16, its length check passes against its own literal 16, and `readDegradedPathStatsLocked` — which loops to `len(...)` — never reads the new counter. The disposition exists, fires, and is invisible.
- **RENUMBER**: swap `strict_drop` and `pass_to_kernel`. All eleven names present, length still 16, no empty slot, existing test **passes** — and every affected slot now renders under the **wrong name**. An operator reading `transit_drop` is shown a different disposition's count.

The second is the #6534 shape exactly: a surface presenting a value it did not compute, with no way to notice it is presenting someone else's.

## What lands

The agreement predicate: read the shim's constants, require the Go table to match **index for index**, and require `len(degradedPathReasonNames) == USERSPACE_FALLBACK_REASON_MAX`. Self-maintaining in the direction that matters — adding a reason in Rust enrols it here automatically and the build stays red until Go carries it. A duplicate index is refused too, since two dispositions counting into one slot are indistinguishable at every surface.

It extracts a **constant list — a syntactic fact** — and models no behaviour, which is the distinction the #4555 parity corpus draws after five successive source-text models each leaked to a more ordinary edit.

**A positive control on the scan itself**: a regex that has stopped matching finds nothing, compares nothing to nothing, and passes forever. Fewer than ten constants found is a failure. That is the assertion #8527 lacked and precisely why that census shipped blind.

## Two accepted entries, with reasons and a dead-entry check

The second cell (separate, so one failure can be told from the other) found two dead reasons — residue whose use sites were removed: `icmp` (`13241e75e`) and `no_session` (`324d6b9d1`).

They are **recorded, not deleted, deliberately**: removing them renumbers every constant above, which is the exact hazard the first cell exists to catch — a change to make *with* the guard in place, not a tidy-up folded into the guard's own landing.

The allowlist carries a dead-entry check **in both directions**: an entry whose reason becomes used again reds as stale, and an entry naming a reason the shim no longer defines reds as overstating the population. An allowlist entry is a claim and this is the test it owes.

*A correction:* the first draft of that cell said a dead reason lets an operator read a disposition the shim cannot produce. `readDegradedPathStatsLocked` omits zero-count entries, so it never reaches an operator — it misleads the *reader* of the table. Overstated, and fixed.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/ ./cmd/cli/` green. Four mutations, all killed:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| renumber two reasons | both slots named with the direction of each mismatch — **and the existing guard passes on this same mutation** |
| add a 17th reason | the length disagreement is named — **existing guard passes** |
| break the scan pattern | the positive control fires rather than passing vacuously |
| wire an allowlisted reason back up | the stale-entry check fires |

## PR #8578 — userspace: derive the NAPI probe count from the queue count [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8377-napi-binding-cohort`

Closes #8377
Closes #8378
Closes #8384

Three siblings in one bring-up path. They turned out to share one root question — *what actually makes a bound AF_XDP queue's fill ring get consumed* — and the answer decides all three.

## #8377 — the arithmetic is right, and it matters more than it looked

The comment said "~2× the queue count"; the code sent a hard-coded **30**. Neither is right, and the disagreement is the dangerous half: an editor implementing the *prose* rule would have cut 30 → 12 on a 6-queue NIC and made coverage **worse**.

Queue selection is by RSS hash, so this is coupon-collector, not linear — covering `n` queues needs ≈ `n·(ln n + ln(1/ε))` draws. Verified the issue's table independently; it is exact:

| queues | E[uncovered] | P(all covered) |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 0.025 | 0.975 |
| 8 | 0.146 | 0.864 |
| 16 | 2.308 | **0.099** |
| 32 | 12.345 | 0.000 |

**Does 16 queues occur?** Not on the loss cluster — its mlx5 VFs expose **6**, where 30 probes gives 97.5%, which is exactly why this has never been seen in-fleet. #8374 raised the per-interface binding count from the global minimum to `min(rx, BindingQueuesPerIface)`, so 8- and 16-queue interfaces are now reachable on a PF. The fix is therefore the "derive it" shape rather than "raise the constant": `napiProbeCount` takes the interface's own queue count, floors at the historical 30 so nothing already-covered regresses, and clamps at `BindingQueuesPerIface` — because covering queues that can hold no binding buys nothing and would make a 64-queue NIC send ~500 packets per bring-up. The clamp *is* the bound, so there is no separate magic maximum.

## The part worth reading: a draft of this fix was wrong, and I withdrew it

I found that two per-socket wake paths look like they make an uncovered queue self-heal — the bind-time kick in `drive_fill_prime_loop`, and `maybe_wake_rx`'s `poll(POLLIN)` on every empty RX poll — and I had written that into three places as the reason all three issues were premise-failures. I dispatched an agent specifically to falsify it, and it did.

Reading the kernel **does not settle it**, in either direction:

- `xsk_poll` forwards to `ndo_xsk_wakeup` only when `pool->cached_need_wakeup` is set — and it *is*, seeded `XDP_WAKEUP_TX` at pool creation (`xsk_buff_pool.c:191`), precisely so "drivers that do not implement this feature … will always have to call sendto() or poll()". So the agent's "the gate is closed on a cold queue" is wrong.
- But `mlx5e_xsk_wakeup` (`en/xsk/tx.c:10`) then returns 0 **without triggering NAPI** when the channel NAPI is already scheduled (`napi_if_scheduled_mark_missed`) or an XSK-TX NOP is pending (`MLX5E_SQ_STATE_PENDING_XSK_TX`). So my "poll always kicks it" is wrong too.

Three readings, each inverting the last. **The only measurement is in this tree's own history, and it points at the probes:**

- `ffe0b5520` — *"Known: mlx5 zero-copy fill ring consumer (frC) stays at 0 after daemon restart despite correct XSKMAP registration. XDP_REDIRECT succeeds but packets are silently dropped."* Recorded **with the `poll(POLLIN)` wake already in the tree.**
- `e0c01ac2b` — added `SO_BUSY_POLL` because *"ndo_xsk_wakeup's ICOSQ NOP mechanism **fails** when NAPI is already scheduled from other sources"*, and observed the failure mode directly: *"The ARP/NDP reply for the egress next-hop **may hash to an XSK queue that hasn't been bootstrapped yet**."*

So the probes are **load-bearing**, #8377 is a real defect class, and the comments now say so — including an explicit "do not delete these on the strength of a source reading", because the trap is easy to fall into twice.

## #8384 — closed on the instrument, which is the part that holds

Its own last comment already established two inversions and I verified both independently: `fill_prime_is_total_failure` fails the bind closed (`bind.rs:356`, propagated at `:536`, sole caller always passes the frames at `worker/mod.rs:489`), so a never-populated ring never reaches `bound`; and in the #8377 state the ring is **full** — primed and never consumed — so a fill-ring-emptiness term and `rx_fill_ring_empty_descs` both read healthy in exactly the failure they would be added for.

I checked the tempting cheap alternative and it is the **same mistake one level over**: `rx_wakeups` is already per-binding and already on the wire (unrendered), but it counts wake *attempts*, and the whole difficulty above is that an attempt can be inert. Rendering it would have shipped a third signal blind to its own fault, so this PR deliberately adds **no detector**.

And a runtime liveness term does not belong in `binding.ready` regardless — forwarding admission (`maps_sync.go`) and HA standby fitness (`manager_ha.go`) both read it as "may I use this binding", so a term that can go false under load sheds capacity exactly when it is needed and declares a busy node unfit to take over. The root fault is remediated where it belongs, in #8377's coverage.

## #8378 — documented (option 3), which is where its own analysis landed

The concentration is #785's deliberate 1:1 worker-to-queue mapping; the idle bindings are its price, and they are *owned* (`worker_id = queue_id % workers`), not orphaned. Option 1 (`min(rx, 16, workers)`) is not taken because `handlers/rebind.rs` clears every binding and `tear_down` stops all workers — there is no per-slot path — so it would turn `set system dataplane workers N` into a full dataplane teardown. The docs now carry the arithmetic (~160 MB/binding at ring=16384; `workers=2, hwq=6` → 4 idle → ~640 MB) and, importantly, that the sizing term is **BOUND** bindings, not workers.

## PR #8579 — Compose the static verdict for a PBR-bearing filter (#8114 item 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8114-item1-pbr-static`

## Why it was declined, and why the reason does not force the decline

`evaluate_input_filter_on_session_hit` returned `None` for any filter with
`affects_route_lookup`. The reason was sound: the static verdict runs the
NON-ROUTING walk, which **defers** on a matched `routing-instance` term —
returning the default `Accept` before that term's own action is examined —
and #4392 established that `then { routing-instance X; discard; }` is a
DROP. Reading the deferral as an Accept would have preserved *and stamped*
a session the routing-aware evaluation drops.

That is a fact about **one walk**, not about the question. The verdict is
now composed the way the packet path composes it:

- Ask the routing-instance walk first. `Some(r)` means a matched
  **terminating** term carried a routing-instance — exactly what
  `ingress_route_table_override` acts on: it drops on `Reject`/`Discard`
  and otherwise applies the table override and forwards. So `r.action` **is**
  the verdict, deny or permit.
- `None` means no PBR term terminated the walk. Production returns
  `RouteOverride::None` there and the packet's verdict comes from the
  ordinary non-routing walk — so that is what is asked.

The **only** case where the two walks differ is the matched
routing-instance term carrying a drop action. Composing rather than
replacing is what keeps the revalidation and the miss path from drifting.

## Implementation notes worth reviewing

- **`evaluate_filter_ref_routing_instance_uncounted` is a separate entry
  point, not the counted one with `packet_bytes = 0`.**
  `record_filter_counter` bumps the PACKET count even with zero bytes, so
  zero bytes is not a substitute for not counting. Both family walks take a
  `count` flag; the counted wrapper passes `true` and is otherwise
  unchanged.
- **The DENY arm replays the counted routing walk once**, so the newly
  denied packet is charged and logged exactly once — the routing-aware twin
  of the existing `evaluate_non_pbr_input_filter` replay. Both walks get the
  same `TermMatchExtra::default()`, so the verdict and the charge cannot
  reach different terms.
- **A plain `routing-instance` term does NOT revoke.** It is a permit that
  changes the route table. #7212 revokes on DENY; revoking on a route
  *change* is a separate question with a different blast radius, and an
  established session keeps the route it was built with.
- **The log source is now a parameter.** A verdict from a routing-instance
  term is logged as `Pbr` — what `ingress_route_table_override` stamps on
  the same term for a session-MISS packet. Getting this wrong does not
  change what is dropped; it mislabels the record an operator correlates
  against.

## PR #8582 — test/incus: provision the second VLAN-80 target so a verdict can be attributed [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8259-mouse-target`

Closes #8259

**The blocker was never the check.** #8467 already made the mouse-latency gate return `VOID-NOT-ATTRIBUTABLE` rather than a PASS or FAIL it could not support, and recorded that it *"passes the moment the two targets differ"*. Making them differ was impossible:

- the standing target is external lab hardware — answers ICMP on `ge-0-0-2.80`, is not an incus instance in any project, accepts no ssh, and `target-services.sh` says outright that *"there is no handle to run a command on it from here"*;
- the firewall's WAN neighbour table held **exactly two entries**, the target and the upstream router. There was nowhere to move a flow to.

**There is now.** `test/incus/mouse-target-setup.sh` creates a third: an incus container with an SR-IOV VF on the WAN PF **tagged into VLAN 80**, pinned at `172.16.80.201`, running the grid `target-services.sh` documents as the contract — iperf3 5200-5211, echo 6200-6211, plus port 7.

**Why a tagged VF:** the firewall's own WAN interface is a VF on the same PF, *untagged* — the firewall does the VLAN 50/80 tagging itself. A VF tagged 80 by the hypervisor lands on the same L2 as `ge-0-0-2.80`, which puts the new host in the firewall's neighbour table *beside* the existing target rather than behind another hop. Capacity checked rather than assumed: the PF exposes 32 VFs, the two firewalls use two.

## Measured on the standing cluster

Built by hand, then the script written from it, then the script run **against** the host to prove it reconciles rather than merely creates. Verified while the cluster was forwarding:

- the new host reaches the firewall (`.8`), the existing target (`.200`) and the router (`.1`);
- the firewall's WAN neighbour table now shows **four** entries, `172.16.80.201` carrying its **own MAC** — a genuinely separate host, not a second address on the old one;
- from `cluster-userspace-host`, the container the harnesses actually send from, **all seven sampled ports** answered through the firewall.

A later re-probe returned nothing, and that is recorded because it nearly became a false conclusion about this change: **the original target was equally unreachable at that moment**, and fw0 was in a readiness hold (`userspace XSK liveness not proven`) with RG election blocked. Cluster-wide, from concurrent work — not a property of the new host, which reached everything on its own VLAN throughout.

## Wiring

`loss-userspace-cluster.env` defaults `MOUSE_TARGET_V4`/`V6` to it — a **default**, not a hard-wire, so a run reproducing an older measurement puts both flows back on one host by overriding it, and every harness that never mentions the knob keeps its behaviour except that the gate can now attribute the result. `target-services.sh`'s "no second host" note is corrected in place; everything it says about the *original* target stays true and is now scoped to it.

## The census caught the new script — and a pre-existing red

`harness-census.sh` fails a runnable harness no Makefile recipe invokes. It flagged the new script, which is the guard working: provisioning nobody can find is provisioning nobody runs. Three recipes added (`mouse-target-up` / `-status` / `-destroy`).

It also flagged `screen-probe.sh` and `screen-probe-lib.sh`, which are **not new** — **the census has been failing on master since #8336 landed them, and that is my own earlier debt from this campaign.** The library is declared as a LIBRARY; the probe is declared unreached *with a reason* (it arms a screen profile on a live cluster and needs the shared lock, so `make selftest` cannot run it — while its analysis layer *is* reached via `make test-screen-probe-lib`). The census refuses a declaration without a reason — *"a declaration without a reason is a suppression"* — which is correct, and is why my first attempt failed.

## What this does not do

Make the earlier numbers attributable. **#7100's FAIL, #7159's PASS and the 2x2 that followed were all measured with both flows on one host and stay void** — they have to be re-taken, not reinterpreted. The docs say so rather than leaving a reader to assume the new host retro-validates them.

## Validation

`harness-census.sh` **OK** (FAILED before this, on master). `target-services-selftest.sh`, `mouse-elephant-selftest.sh` and `make test-cluster-env-lib` pass. `go test ./cmd/cli/` green — this adds a shell script, and that package holds the guards that select subjects by **content** rather than ownership. shellcheck clean on both touched scripts.

## PR #8583 — Drive the gemini-review-048 validation tracker to zero (#8321) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-gemini-048-validation`

Drives the gemini-review-048 validation tracker to completion. **Every remaining finding now has a verdict**, and the tracker closes.

## Where the tracker actually stood

The body says "6 of 20 checked" and the handover said 03, 04, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18 and the cohort remained. Both are stale — comment 1 resolved 03/04 (already filed and fixed by another route), comment 2 resolved 11/12/13, comment 3 resolved 15/17/18. What was genuinely undone: **the grouped cohort (8 items, never opened)**, and turning the already-validated 11/12/13/15/17/18 verdicts into dispositions.

## Verdicts on everything remaining

| item | verdict | disposition |
|---|---|---|
| 15 — REST VRRP omits RETH instances | **REAL**, mechanism and consequence both hold | **fixed here** |
| 17 — VRRP priority `uint8` truncation | **consequence REFUTED** | no change, evidence below |
| 18 — parser lacks the RFC 5798 §5.1.1.4 discard rule | **mechanism real, consequence refuted, and fixing it would be a net risk** | rationale recorded at the call site |
| 11/12/13 — NAT surfaces bypass `pkg/natshow` | REAL, one root | filed **#8580** (needs a design decision first) |
| cohort 1 — lo0 filter-log zone on VLAN ports | **REAL**, at a *different site* than named | **fixed here** |
| cohort 2 — `ingress_ifindex as i32` truncation | **UNREACHABLE** | no change, evidence below |
| cohort 3 — `write_ipv4_*` `debug_assert` | **not a defect** — already reasoned and documented as a diagnostic (#7171); the indexing is memory-safe either way | no change |
| cohort 4 — `pkt_len` is the inner length | mechanism real, **no consumer wants the L2 length** | filed **#8581** (a convention question) |
| cohort 5 — duplicate `recordChildExtras` | **REAL**, and at **two** sites, not the one named | **fixed here** |
| cohort 6 — script hardcodes a pre-split path | **real but INERT** | no change, reasoning below |
| cohort 7 — sub-zero Celsius | **REAL** | **fixed here** |
| cohort 8 — no terminal-escape sanitization | **REAL**, and the sharpest item in the cohort | **fixed here** |

### The three refutations, with what decided them

**17.** Both priority leaves that reach VRRP are bounded at commit: `vrrp-group … priority` by `ValidateInteger(1, 255)` *plus* the #5184 semantic gate `validateVRRPGroupPriorityStrict` backstopping the packed one-liner, and the chassis node priority by `ValidateInteger(1, 254)`. The schema comment at that leaf names the very `uint8` cast the finding points at. Both production callers of `UpdateRGPriority` pass a literal `200`. The residual needs an `active.json` that never passed a validator — root-level tampering, where the wire priority is the least of the operator's problems. No clamp added: choosing between clamp-to-255 (unintended takeover) and wrap-to-0 (resignation) is inventing policy for an unreachable input.

**Cohort 2.** Three independent bounds, none an argument from plausibility: the kernel field is populated from `net_device->ifindex`, a C `int`; the shim only steers packets whose ifindex is present in a control-plane-populated map; and the binding array is indexed as `ifindex * 16 + q` over `MAX_INTERFACES` = 65536, so anything ≥ 65536 is never redirected. The one remaining gap is already reasoned in-tree at `binding_index.rs` and sits far below `i32::MAX`. The cast is consumed only as a map key, where `u32 as i32` round-trips losslessly, and the one place the value crosses a wire already saturates.

**Cohort 6.** The script's subject path no longer exists, so the mechanism is real — but it is not wired into the Makefile or any CI (positive control: `run-selftests` **is** found there), it is a one-shot artifact of a completed split, and running it by hand fails loudly on `git show` rather than silently. It misleads nobody.

## What this PR changes

**`Closes #8321`.**

### 1 · REST VRRP reports RETH instances (finding 15)

`/vrrp` collected only generic per-interface `vrrp-group` instances, so on a chassis cluster — where the VIPs live on RETH instances — it returned an **empty** list. The gRPC `GetVRRPStatus` has appended `CollectRethInstances` all along; the collector was never what was broken. Threaded as an optional `Config` hook, the way every other daemon-owned fact reaches `pkg/api`.

### 2 · CLI terminal sanitization + sub-zero temperatures (cohort 7 & 8)

`show system core-dumps` printed the core-dump **filename** raw. That name is not root-controlled — systemd-coredump derives it from the crashing process's `comm` — so an ANSI escape in it is interpreted by the operator's terminal and can overwrite what the CLI already wrote. Sanitized with the same shape `lldp.sanitizeTLVString` already uses, applied to the sysfs-sourced siblings too.

`show chassis environment` rendered sub-zero readings as `-12.-5 C`, and `-0.5 °C` as `0.-5 C` — losing the sign entirely.

### 3 · lo0 filter-log zone, duplicate extras, and the finding-18 rationale

The lo0 log attributed its ingress zone from the raw **physical** ifindex while `ifindex_to_zone_id` is keyed by the **logical** unit, with the physical parent only an inherited fallback that #7509 removes on a zone contest. Decided by an asymmetry, not a trace: three sibling sites in the same file resolve the logical ifindex, and the enclosing wrapper already holds it and already documents why the physical one is wrong (#3609). Consequence is log-only — `ingress_zone_id` has exactly one consumer and it emits an event.

## PR #8584 — routes: bound the learned-route import, and decline rather than truncate [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8355-route-cap`

Closes #8355

Acceptance items 2 and 3. Item 1 — the measurement — landed as #8554 and **moved the premise**: the binding constraint is time, not size. Neither of these needed another measurement; they needed that one first.

## The cap is derived, not picked

A learned route serializes to **~113 bytes**, stable to within 1.5% from one route to 500,000. That stability is what makes a route *count* derivable from a byte budget at all, and it is pinned by the #8554 cell rather than assumed here.

500k routes come to ~56 MiB — comfortably under the 64 MiB `MaxControlRequestBytes` ceiling, which admits ~595,000 routes. **So the size cap is not what stops this.** `controlRoundtripDeadline` grants `controlBaseDeadline` + `controlDeadlinePerMiB` per mebibyte, so that publish holds the control socket for **56 seconds** — a socket CLAUDE.md describes as shared by the 1/s status poll, HA sync, session installs, snapshot sync and forwarding sync, where *"a new control socket request at >1/s will starve session installs during bulk sync"*. A minute-long publish does not starve it at the margin; it owns it. #7437 makes publishes more frequent, which is what turns a slow publish into a persistent one.

So the policy input is `learnedRoutePublishBudget` — how long one publish may hold the socket — and the route cap falls out of it **through the same constants the deadline uses**. 10s: above that is hard to justify against a 1/s poll (ten polls of head-of-line blocking); below it the cap starts excluding table sizes a real eBGP edge carries.

Deriving it is the point, not a nicety. A hardcoded route count would be *a number wearing the shape of a budget*, which is what this issue was filed about.

## The decision: decline the whole import, never a bounded subset

Both options leave some destinations resolving `NoRoute` and taking the slow-path reinject, so neither is an outage — the kernel still forwards. They differ in **predictability**:

- **No import** is uniform. Every learned destination behaves the same, the box is in one describable state, and one diagnostic explains it.
- **A bounded subset** is per-destination, and which destinations make the cut is decided by the **emission sort order** — table id, then family, then destination string. That is arbitrary with respect to anything an operator cares about: two prefixes to the same peer land on opposite sides of the cut because of where they sort. Some traffic takes the fast path and some does not, with no rule anyone can state, presenting as intermittent performance rather than as a limit being hit.

The second is the shape this project keeps being bitten by: a degraded state that looks healthy from every surface. A partial FIB reports a plausible route count, forwards traffic, and gives no signal that it is a *prefix* of the intended table.

**Loud**, because the issue is right that silently importing a prefix is the failure that reads as healthy. The WARN names the count, the cap, the budget, the consequence, why a partial import was not chosen, and the remedy. `LearnedRouteCapHits` makes the state readable without log scraping.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/ ./cmd/cli/` green. **Three mutations, each killed by the cell that names it:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| **truncate** instead of declining — the rejected option, implemented | the "nothing is imported" cell reds and reports the 64,956 routes that got through |
| **hardcode** the cap at 5,000 | the derivation cell reds: a table at the cap leaves 6.46s of the 10s budget unused, *"so the cap is not derived from the budget but from something else"* |
| drop the counter | the visibility half reds while the behaviour is still correct — which is why they are separate cells |

The over-cap cell asserts **zero**, not "fewer than N" — the latter would pass for the truncating implementation. The under-cap control is not decoration either: without it, an importer that returned nothing at all would satisfy the over-cap cell. And the derivation cell asserts the **relationship**, not the value, so a deliberate budget change still passes while a broken derivation does not.

Also fixed: `degraded_reason_agreement_8258_test.go` was not gofmt-clean when it landed an hour ago. Formatting only.

## Docs

`docs/multi-wan.md`'s #7409 section described the import as gap-fill and window-narrowing **with no bound at all**. It now carries the bound, the measurement it rests on, why the constraint is time rather than size, and the decline-vs-truncate reasoning — an operator reading that section to decide whether a DHCP or eBGP uplink is viable needs to know the import has a ceiling and what happens at it.
