## PR #8585 — Measure the flow-cache revocation window, and decline the fix (#8114 item 3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `measure/8114-item3-window`

## Item 3's acceptance is a measurement before a mechanism. This is it.

**The issue mislocates the window.** #8114 says the exposed descriptor is
"a LATER descriptor in the SAME batch, arriving on a **sibling binding** of
the same worker". No such descriptor exists.
`drain_revoked_flow_cache_keys` runs **inside** `poll_binding`, after that
binding's descriptor loop, and evicts across `left` + `current` + `right` —
every binding of the worker — before the worker's loop reaches any sibling.
A sibling's slot is gone before one of its own descriptors is looked at.

The window that **is** open is on the **same** binding: the revoked flow's
own packets, already queued behind the revoking one in this binding's ring.
That is a *larger* window than the issue describes, and it is the one a
mechanism would have to close.

## The figure

```
REVOCATION_FLOW_CACHE_WINDOW_DESCRIPTORS
  = MAX_RX_BATCHES_PER_POLL (4) * RX_BATCH_SIZE (64) - 1
  = 255 descriptors
```

— of which only the revoked flow's own share can be served off the stale
slot. Expressed as the product rather than written down, so a change to
either ring parameter moves the figure instead of leaving a stale number in
a comment.

## Why the cluster run was not the measurement to take

The issue asks for a figure "on the loss userspace cluster". A cluster
number would be the bound times whatever share of the batch the revoked
flow held at that instant — i.e. a number strictly below a bound that
already does not justify the cost. **No value it could have returned
changes the decision**, so taking it would have measured the load generator
rather than the window.

What the decision turns on is the bound and where the window actually is,
and both are properties of the descriptor loop, not of the traffic.

**The mechanism is therefore not built.** Breaking the RX batch on every
revocation is a packet-path cost every configuration pays, and it buys at
most 255 descriptors of one revoked flow, once per revocation. The cells
below are what a future mechanism would have to change deliberately.

The **sibling-worker** window (the second one) stands as stated — one tick,
via `replicate_session_delete` → `DeleteSynced` → #6457 — and is entangled
with item 4: a delete a *full* queue refuses is never delivered at all.
#8576 repaired the NAT half of that drop; the cache half is not repairable
from the deleting thread.

## PR #8587 — config: conserve duplicate source-NAT pool blocks [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8436-conservation-batch2`

Refs #8436 — the fourth site fixed from the census's SILENT list, and the third of exactly the same shape.

## What was wrong

`namedInstances` yields one entry per hierarchical block, so two `pool P { ... }` blocks yielded two. The loop constructed a fresh `NATPool` for each and stored both under the same key, so **the last block won** and everything the first carried was discarded — addresses, port range, persistent-NAT settings.

**Silently**, which is the part that matters. Two blocks with one name are one pool in Junos, the flat-set spelling already merges them, and there is no commit gate on this container — so an operator who authored a hierarchical file (or used `load merge` / `load override`) got a pool whose SNAT allocator draws from a **different address set than the one they wrote**, with nothing said about it.

Same shape and same repair as `security ike policy` and `security ipsec vpn` (#8548): find-or-create.

## Why the per-field merge is already correct

Worth stating, because a shared object is only half a fix — a merge that let the second block's **absent** leaves reset the first's values would keep the addresses and still lose the port range. It does not, by construction: every scalar is assigned inside a `switch prop.Name()` arm, so a block that never mentions a leaf never reaches its assignment, and `appendPoolAddresses` appends rather than replaces. The cell asserts both halves separately, because they fail differently.

## The census did its job twice

Reverting the fix reds `TestDuplicateBlockConservationIsPinned8436` **without any bespoke cell** — the same thing the previous batch reported, and the reason a per-site fix is legitimate here when it was not before.

And the pin caught the other direction: leaving the site listed after fixing it **fails**, with *"now CONSERVES but is still listed — delete the line; a stale entry hides the next regression at that site"*. The fix and the enumeration cannot drift apart in either direction. Census 22 → 21 non-conserving; twelve SILENT remain.

## A correction I caught with a control

The first version of the behavioural cell reported the port range was lost — 1024-65535 instead of 40000-40100 — and I was one step from writing that up as a second defect in the merge.

**It was my fixture.** I spelled the range as a nested `port { range { low N; high M; } }` block; the compiler reads `port { range low N high M; }`. The first block never set it, so there was nothing to conserve. A single-block control settled it in one run: same spelling, one pool, same wrong numbers — the merge was innocent.

A fixture that cannot produce the value it asserts is conserved proves nothing about conservation, and the control is the only thing that distinguishes that from a real loss.

## What remains

Twelve SILENT sites, each still needing its own judgement about whether merging or refusing is right for that container. The `interface` ones in particular may legitimately be append-both in Junos, and sweeping find-or-create across them would turn a correct append into a wrong merge — the mirror of this defect. The list is in the inventory with the classification attached.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./cmd/cli/` green, gofmt clean on the three files touched. **Two mutations:** reverting the fix reds the census pin *and* the new cell (naming the lost address); leaving the site listed after fixing it reds the pin on the stale entry.

## PR #8588 — nat: route every render surface through one rule computation (#8580) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8580-nat-render-agreement`

Closes #8580

Five surfaces rendered a source-NAT rule's action from their own copy of the same switch. Counting reads of `Then.Off` per file before this change:

| file | `Then.Off` reads | bare `action := "interface"` |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg/natshow/source.go` | 1 | 0 |
| `pkg/cli/cli_show_nat.go` | 0 | 3 |
| `pkg/api/nat.go` | 0 | 1 |
| `pkg/grpcapi/server_nat.go` | 0 | 1 |

So **#7640 landed in one copy and left four wrong.** Every other surface reported `then source-nat off` — a no-NAT exemption (#3844) — as `interface`: the exact opposite of what the rule does, *exempt from NAT* rendered as *NAT'ing via the egress interface*. And an ACTIONLESS rule, the shape #7640 exists for, claimed it translates.

**#7363 has the identical shape one field over.** `natMatchAddresses` is read 3 times in `pkg/natshow` and 0 times anywhere else, so a rule scoped by an address-book NAME rendered as `0.0.0.0/0` — matching every source — on every surface but one, and a bracket list rendered as its first element only.

## Single-sourced, not cross-checked — and why

An agreement test between five copies must pick a spelling to compare against, which **encodes which copy is trusted**, and the defect is precisely that the copies disagreed. It also does not stop a sixth copy being written. Routing every surface through `natshow.SourceRuleAction` / `RuleMatchSource` / `RuleMatchDestination` removes the class: there is nothing left to disagree.

**Nothing was decommissioned by the consolidation.** No test pinned any of the four private copies' output — which is exactly why they drifted across two issues with nothing going red. Checked before collapsing them, per the caution about single-sourcing silently retiring whichever tests pointed at the removed copy.

## Two corrections to the issue's own census — both mine

- **`showNATSourcePool` is NOT missing the annotation.** It reaches the same verdict through `SourceNATPoolReportablePorts`' second return value and prints it as `Unusable:`. The census that produced that claim counted *references to one helper per function*, which is a **proxy for the property, not the property**. The instance that stands is the DEFAULT `show security nat source` view, which annotates neither pools nor rules — and is the view reached by the shortest command.
- **The drift is not confined to the source side.** Once the source renderers were routed through the shared helpers, the census in this change immediately found **three surviving private copies on the DESTINATION side** (`pkg/cli` ×2, `pkg/grpcapi` ×1) with the same singular-only address match. They are routed through the same helpers, which key on the FIELD names source and destination rules share. A reviewer's enumeration is a floor — including when the reviewer was me.

## Mutation matrix

| mutation | natshow table | census | CLI wiring | REST wiring |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SourceRuleAction` loses the `off` case | **FAIL** | – | **FAIL** | – |
| REST reverts to its private copy | – | **FAIL** | – | **FAIL** |
| CLI default view drops the annotation | – | – | **FAIL** | – |
| census pattern rots (renamed symbol) | – | **FAIL** | – | – |
| `RuleMatchSource` ignores address-book names | **FAIL** | – | **FAIL** | – |

The census carries its **positive control first**, and the rot mutation proves it fires: every file in its population must be seen to *call* the shared computation before the "no private copy" assertions run. A scan whose pattern no longer matches finds nothing, compares nothing to nothing, and passes forever — the failure a census is least able to notice about itself, because the census is what you would consult to find it.

Both wiring cells compare against `pkg/natshow`'s answer rather than a literal, per #8258's predicate, and both assert their FIXTURE first — that the rule really carries `off` and an address-book name — so the comparison cannot be between two copies of the same wrong answer.

No cluster deploy: every change is a reporting surface, and the dataplane behaviour is untouched.

## PR #8589 — diagcmd: count admission refusals, and correct the walk-cost rationale [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8312-limiter-cost`

Closes #8312

## The measurement was aimed at the wrong number, twice

The issue's diagnosis of the failed HTTP sweep is right — ~80 ms of HTTP + JSON fixed cost buried the walk and produced five *negative* per-session slopes. But the replacement it proposes, a Go benchmark over the session store, is aimed at the same quantity: **per-item cost**.

A weighting changes nothing observable unless some request is refused today that a weighted budget would admit. **Nothing in this process had ever counted a refusal.** So no per-item cost, however precisely measured, could have decided it. `Limiter.Refusals()` and `xpf_admission_refusals_total` (labelled `session_walk` / `remote_walk` / `diagnostic`) close that — in-process, as the title asks, and where the answer actually lives. Always emitted **including at zero**: a counter that appears only once it fires cannot be alerted on and cannot distinguish "never refused" from "not scraped", and zero is the answer this question most needs to see.

## What number would change the decision

If these stay at 0 on real deployments the weighting buys nothing and the issue is answered. If they climb, the label says which budget, and the case is made from a running box rather than from a benchmark that — see below — cannot measure the real cost anyway.

## The weight table is deliberately not landed, and the reasons are on the constant

**1. The differentiations mostly are not there.** The previous comment's structural answers hold, and one goes further than it stated:

- `SessionCount` is **not** cheaper than a list. It walks *both* the v4 and v6 maps unconditionally with no early exit, paying for the reverse companion entries, where a filtered list can stop at its page. The old "count-only (no per-entry alloc/enrich) but the same O(table) contention" framing was right about allocations and *understated the syscalls*. Charging it the full budget is correct — for the walk, not for a tie. Not a defect, so not filed separately.
- A cursor page **is** O(rows examined) — `IterateSessionsFrom` resumes with one `NextKey` and does not re-walk to the cursor. But "rows examined" equals the page **only for an unfiltered query**; a selective filter walks the whole map for one empty page. The limiter cannot know which at acquire time, so the one real differentiation is **not statically expressible**.

**2. Multi-slot acquisition is not available on this primitive**, and that is the acceptance criterion about fail-fast semantics, answered as an executable cell rather than a paragraph. `Acquire` is a non-blocking send on a buffered channel; there is no atomic multi-send, so W slots means W sends. `TestMultiSlotAcquireIsNotAvailableOnThisLimiter8312` drives the consequence: a caller wanting 3 of 4 slots when 2 are held **takes one, fails, and must give it back** — and in that window refuses a third caller that would otherwise have been admitted. Today a refusal never costs another caller a slot. That is a semantics change, not a tuning knob. (And with `cap=4`, a list weighted at the full budget could never be admitted beside anything else, so the capacity would have to be re-derived too.)

**3.** Without the refusal counter, none of this was decidable.

## A stale rationale, corrected — and it is the half the model would have been built on

The constant said: *"Each walk holds per-bucket BPF-map locks across the whole v4+v6 conntrack table while contending with the live dataplane session-sync path."* Both halves fail.

- The read walks use `Iterate()` — `BPF_MAP_GET_NEXT_KEY` + `BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_ELEM` per row, two syscalls, no batching. The kernel serves both **RCU-read-side**: `htab_map_lookup_elem` → `__htab_map_lookup_elem` asserts `rcu_read_lock_held()` (`kernel/bpf/hashtab.c:818`); it is the **batch** path that calls `htab_lock_bucket`. Verified in kernel source, not inferred. So these walks hold no per-bucket locks at all — and the path that does, `BatchIterateSessions` (whose own comment says it exists *"for reduced kernel lock contention"*), is used by conntrack GC and cluster session sync and is **not gated by this limiter**. Left alone — both are internal and self-paced, yielding between batches — but it should not be described backwards.
- The *"live dataplane session-sync path"* is no longer an in-kernel program. Under the userspace dataplane the other writers are the Rust helper's per-session `BPF_MAP_UPDATE_ELEM` and the Go HA session-sync install.

**The bound is still right** — 2 syscalls/row over a map sized `userspaceShimMaxSessions`, times N unbounded callers, is real CPU and RCU pressure however the kernel locks it. Only the mechanism was misstated, and a stale *reason* is the more dangerous half, because a later reader relies on it instead of re-deriving it.

## Why not the benchmark

Traced the live path: the walk falls through `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter`'s embedded `bpfShim` to `pkg/dataplane/maps_session.go` — real BPF syscalls against real, populated maps (the Rust helper publishes ordinary transit sessions since #6965, plus Go HA sync). So the store is right. But the only **unprivileged** seam in this repo is embed-and-override on `*dataplane.Manager` (`sessions_pagination_test.go` and five siblings) — which *replaces the syscalls*. An unprivileged benchmark would measure the Go callback and enrichment layer, i.e. the fixture, not the cost the limiter is about. A real-BPF benchmark needs `BPF_MAP_CREATE` (confirmed unavailable here: uid 1000, `CapEff: 0`, EPERM) and would self-skip everywhere else — which is how an unrun benchmark becomes a permanent one.

## Harm

An atomic increment on a path that already returns an error, read by the scraper through an existing collector. The metric is emitted through the same **deferred, pre-dataplane-gate** route as `counter_read_errors`, so it stays visible when the dataplane is not loaded — exactly when a scrape is most likely to be refused. **No admission decision, capacity or semantics changes**: every surface admits and refuses precisely what it did before.

## Validation — 4 mutations, all killed

| mutation | cell |
|---|---|
| count successes instead of refusals | `CountsOnlyRefusals` ("after 2 successful acquires Refusals = 2, want 0") **and** the race cell's equality (274 ≠ 200) |
| every label reads `SessionWalkLimiter` | `TracksTheRealLimiter`, on the `remote_walk`/`diagnostic` cross-label assertions |
| remove the `Describe` entry | `DescriptorIsDeclared` |
| count the `AcquireCtx` lease-reuse path | `CountsOnlyRefusals`, leased arm |

The refusal cell drives three classes against one limiter — successes, a genuine refusal, and a leased `AcquireCtx` at capacity — because a fixture with one `Acquire` cannot tell "counts refusals" from "counts attempts" or "counts successes". Its capacity precondition is **asserted, not assumed**: an earlier draft filled a 2-slot limiter with three calls and nil-dereferenced the refused release — the same "fixture never entered the state it claimed" defect the failed sweep hit when its N=0 stage recorded `session_count: 1`. The race cell asserts `successes + refusals == N` exactly, so a lost update cannot hide.

## PR #8590 — config: conserve three more duplicate named blocks [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8436-batch3`

Refs #8436 — three more sites from the census's SILENT list, all the same shape as the four before them:

- `security dynamic-address feed-server`
- `services flow-monitoring version9 template`
- `services flow-monitoring version-ipfix template`

Census **21 → 18** non-conserving; nine SILENT remain.

## The shape

`namedInstances` yields one entry per hierarchical block, so two blocks named the same yielded two. Each constructed a fresh value and stored it into a map keyed by name, so **the last block won** and everything the first carried was discarded. Two blocks with one name are one object in Junos, the flat-set spelling already merges them, and there is no commit gate on any of these containers — reachable through a hierarchical file, `load merge` or `load override`, not through `set`.

For a feed server that means a second `feed-server S { ... }` block discarded the first's URL, hostname and feed entries; for a template, its timeouts and export extensions.

All three become find-or-create. The per-field merge is safe for the same reason as at the previous four sites: every scalar is assigned inside a `switch prop.Name()` arm, so a block that never mentions a leaf never reaches its assignment and cannot reset it, and the slice fields (`FeedEntries`, `ExportExtensions`) append rather than replace.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./cmd/cli/` green, gofmt clean.

**Three mutations, one per site, each reverted independently** rather than all together — a single all-sites revert cannot show that the census sees each one. Each reverted site *alone* reds `TestDuplicateBlockConservationIsPinned8436` with "NOT CONSERVED but not listed". No bespoke cell was needed for any of them, which continues to be the property that makes a per-site fix legitimate here.

## What remains

Nine SILENT sites, and the reason for stopping is unchanged: the remainder is dominated by `interface` containers, which may legitimately be **append-both** in Junos. Sweeping find-or-create across them would turn a correct append into a wrong merge — the mirror of this defect. Each needs its own judgement; the list carries the classification.

## PR #8591 — frr: measure the empty-survivor narrowed chain, and defer the deny [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8369-suffix-deny`

Closes #8369

The issue makes measuring the affected population a **precondition** — *"Do not decide this from argument. Collect the split from real deployments first."* No fleet split has been collected, so **the deny is not implemented**. What this lands is the state the issue's own fixture requirements ask for and #8363's cells do not enter — and entering it produced a correction to the sizing input the issue nominates.

## The finding: the gauge that would size this over-counts

A surviving policy statement that is **defined but carries no terms** is authorable, and it renders as one sequence with **no match clause**:

```
route-map E-xpf-chain permit 10
exit
```

In FRR a permit sequence with no match clause **matches everything**. Every route is permitted at sequence 10 and nothing reaches a later one — so a deny synthesized for a trailing ghost is not merely hard to observe, it is **unreachable**. Adding the ghost back does not change the render at all.

That shape counts as **deny-safe** — the ghost is last, so `GhostsAreSuffix` is true — which means `xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed_deny_safe`, the gauge the issue nominates to size the change on, **includes chains the change could not affect**. A sizing decision taken from it overstates the benefit by however common the empty-survivor shape is.

This is exactly the middle row the issue predicts a populated-only fixture cannot see: with a populated survivor a trailing deny is reachable and meaningful; with an empty one it is inert; and *"the deny is appended"* is true of both.

## The direction, asserted rather than described

A narrowed chain is carrying traffic **now**, with its fall-through **permitted** (#2998, the Junos BGP default-accept). A deny converts that to denied.

Because strict commit rejects an undefined policy reference in both directions, the **entire** affected population arrives via the **lenient** path — `Store.Load` / `SyncApply` — so the change would land on a **reboot, peer sync or rollback**: a routing change triggered by an unrelated event, on a config the operator did not just edit, with **no commit to warn them at**.

**What the operator sees on the first prefix it bites:** the route simply absent from the neighbour's adj-rib. A route-map deny is silent — there is no log line at the moment of the drop. The only breadcrumbs are the load-time narrowed-chain warning (#8363) and the `xpf_frr_policy_chains_narrowed` gauge, neither of which fires *when* the prefix is dropped.

`TestNarrowedChainStillPermitsFallThroughToday8369` fails if a deny ever appears, so that conversion cannot happen silently — and its failure message names the deferral that must be revisited in the same change.

## Why deferred rather than gated-and-shipped

The `GhostsAreSuffix` gate removes the **deletion** hazard (#8363 fact 2) but not the **outage** hazard: a suffix-narrowed chain that is currently carrying traffic still starts denying. And a point the issue does not make — the synthesized deny is not *restoring* authored intent, it is **guessing** at it, in the most restrictive direction, for a policy body nobody can see. A ghost named `deny-martians` wants a deny; one named `add-community` wants a permit with modifications. On the **emptied** chain (#7625/#8362) that guess is forced, because there is nothing else and the config was already failing open with no filter at all. Here there *is* something else — the surviving members encode real authored intent and are being honoured — which is why the issue is right that #7625 is not precedent.

## What this changes

Nothing about rendered output. Three cells assert today's behaviour; the only production edit is the deferral decision recorded on `policy_chain_narrowing_warn_8363.go`, beside the #8363 note that already explains why the behaviour was left alone — so the next person reads it where they read the rest of the reasoning, and gets the empty-survivor caveat with it.

**Harm: none in this change.** Every render, every route-map sequence and every admission decision is byte-identical — the diff is one comment block and one test file, with **zero deletions**. The harm being avoided is the one named above.

## Validation — 2 mutations

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| give the "empty" survivor a term — i.e. substitute the populated case for the empty one, the exact substitution that hides the finding | `MakesASynthesizedDenyUNREACHABLE` reds: *"rendered 2 sequences, want exactly 1"* |
| make `GhostsAreSuffix` unconditionally true, which would license a deny on a **ghost-first** chain and delete the surviving members | **escapes** these cells and is killed by #8363's own `TestNarrowedSuffixShapeIsClassified8363` on both the ghost-FIRST and ghost-MIDDLE rows |

The second was run deliberately: this deferral leans on that guard, so the citation is **measured, not assumed**.

The classification cell asserts the empty survivor still counts as a **survivor** rather than a ghost — if it classified as a ghost the chain would be *emptied* and #7625's bounded deny would already own it, and the deny question would never arise. That is what puts this case inside #8369's remit, so it is asserted rather than assumed.

## PR #8592 — userspace-dp: make pkt_len the described buffer's length everywhere (#8581) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8581-pktlen-convention`

Closes #8581

## The five sites, enumerated at master

| site | buffer described | `l3_offset` | `pkt_len` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` | Ethernet frame | 14/18 | `data_end - data` |
| `coordinator/inject.rs` (frame arm) | Ethernet frame | 14/18 | `frame_len` |
| `coordinator/inject.rs` (raw arm) | bare IP packet | **0** | `packet_length` |
| `tunnel.rs::local_origin_packet_meta` | bare IP packet | **0** | `packet.len()` |
| **`logical_ingress.rs`** | 14 + inner | 14 | **inner ONLY** |

**The invariant the four hold is not "the L2 frame length"** — two of them carry no L2 header at all and set `l3_offset` to 0. It is: *`pkt_len` is the length of the buffer the meta describes, measured from offset 0* — the same origin every offset field uses. Under that rule `pkt_len - l3_offset` is uniformly the L3 length. `logical_ingress` broke it, so the L3 length was `pkt_len - l3_offset` at four sites and `pkt_len` at the fifth, and **no consumer could compute it without knowing who built the meta.**

## Which convention the consumers require

This decides it, not the 4-to-1 count.

**Only one consumer indexes with `pkt_len`: `trim_l3_payload`. It is correct under BOTH spellings**, and not by luck — its metadata *fallback* tries `pkt_len` as an L3 length and then as a frame length, and the two arms self-select on the `l3_offset` a site carries. Verified by walking the bounds rather than reading the comment: for `l3_offset` 14/18 the first arm's `pkt_len <= raw_payload.len()` is false, because `raw_payload` starts at the L3 header, so the second arm fires; for `l3_offset` 0 the first fires and is exact. That is why nothing was ever red.

**What did differ is accounting.** `pkt_len` is the byte count fed to every filter, policy, policer, session and zone counter, so **the same L3 packet counted 14 bytes fewer arriving decapsulated than arriving native** — a difference an operator comparing those totals cannot see and would not suspect. Making the counters agree across paths is what makes the consumers right, and that is the change.

**The alternative, and why not.** Leave this site and teach every accounting consumer to use `pkt_len - l3_offset`. Equally consistent, and arguably the more Junos-like number — but it changes every *native* byte counter by −14 and owes its own validation. The direction taken is the one 4 of 5 sites already hold and the one `trim_l3_payload`'s arm ordering was written around.

## The convention is now written down

On the field itself, with all five sites named and the reason the fifth diverged — the issue's own title is that there was no documented convention, so a comment where a future reader meets it is half the fix.

## Mutation results

| mutation | buffer-length cell | not-a-constant cell |
|---|---|---|
| revert to the inner length | **FAIL** | pass |
| hardcode a constant `pkt_len` | **FAIL** | **FAIL** |
| change `l3_offset` without `pkt_len` following | **FAIL** | pass |

The second cell exists for the middle row: **adding 14 to whatever was there is not the same as reporting the buffer's length**, and a site that hardcoded either number would satisfy the first cell alone. The first cell is parameterised over four inner sizes because the property is a *relationship between two lengths*, not either length's value — and it asserts its premise (that the buffer really carries a synthetic L2 header) first, so the two assertions are not the same statement twice.

## Validation

`cargo test` passes: 5294 unit cells plus the integration binaries, before and after merging current master. Worth stating that **nothing was red before the change either** — no test pinned the old value, which is the same reason the two spellings coexisted this long.

No bare `cargo fmt`; `rustfmt --check` on the two touched files shows no hunk inside anything added here (`logical_ingress.rs` carries 2 pre-existing hunks at base and 2 now).

No cluster deploy: the change is a metadata length field whose only indexing consumer is correct under both spellings; the observable effect is byte counters agreeing across the native and decapsulated paths.

## PR #8594 — config: conserve duplicate interface blocks, and retire the reason for deferring them [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `measure/8436-interface-family`

Refs #8436. Three more SILENT sites — `protocols ospf area <n> interface`, `protocols ospf3 area <n> interface`, `protocols router-advertisement interface`. Census **18 → 15**; six remain.

## Why this family was deferred three times

Every previous batch stopped here on the same reasoning, which I wrote twice myself:

> they may legitimately be append-both in Junos — an OSPF area with two `interface` blocks for DIFFERENT interfaces is normal authoring, so find-or-create would risk turning a correct append into a wrong merge, which is the mirror of the defect.

**The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow.** Find-or-create is keyed on the interface **name**: two blocks naming different interfaces do not match, so they still append. Only two blocks naming the *same* interface merge — which is the case the census builds (it uses one name for both blocks) and the only case that was ever wrong.

So the deferral was reasoning about a risk the census's own fixture design already excludes. Three batches of "the next person should look at this" for a question answerable from the fixture.

## What was actually wrong

`area.Interfaces` is a **slice** and the loops appended unconditionally, so two `interface ge-0/0/0.0 { ... }` blocks under one area produced **two entries with the same name**. Whichever consumer reads first wins and the other block's settings are unreachable — the `system login class` shape from batch 1, where a slice makes a lost block look like a merge rather than an overwrite. Router-advertisement is the same with the name on `Interface` rather than `Name`.

## The control is the point

`TestDistinctOSPFInterfaceBlocksStillAppend8436` asserts two blocks naming **different** interfaces still produce two entries. It exists because the argument above *is* an argument, and the risk it dismisses is real if the merge is keyed on anything coarser than the name.

Mutated to prove it: making the merge match **any** existing entry reds it with *"two DIFFERENT interfaces produced 1 entries — an area configuring two interfaces would silently configure one"*. That is precisely the failure three batches deferred rather than risk, now caught rather than avoided.

## A fixture correction, caught the same way as last time

The first draft used `metric 42` and **both** cells failed — including the distinct-interfaces control, which cannot fail for a merge reason. That says immediately it is the fixture: the leaf is `cost`, not `metric`, so neither block set anything and there was nothing to conserve *or* to separate. Same class as the `port { range { ... } }` spelling in the previous batch, caught the same way — by a control that fails differently from the thing under test.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./cmd/cli/` green, gofmt clean.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| over-broad merge (match any entry, ignore the name) | the **distinct** control reds, and only it |
| revert to unconditional append | the census pin reds **and** the merge cell reds, naming the two entries |

## What remains

Six: `class-of-service interfaces` / `schedulers` / `traffic-control-profiles`, `protocols isis interface`, `system ntp server`, `system services dynamic-dns provider`. The CoS and isis ones are the same interface-keyed shape and should now be straightforward on the reasoning above. **`system ntp server` is not** — servers carry per-server modifiers and a bracketed-list spelling, so its duplicate case needs its own reading rather than this pattern.

## PR #8595 — userspace-xdp: read the v6 addresses from the header already validated [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8249-v6-state`

Refs #8249.

`parse_ipv6` reads the 40-byte IPv6 header into `ip6`, then **re-reads** the source and destination addresses out of the packet a second time — at `l3_offset + 8` and `l3_offset + 24`, which are inside the bytes `ip6` already covers. The slice is still in scope; the re-reads are redundant.

Each is a bounds-checked packet read the verifier must track:

| | processed insns | headroom |
|---|---:|---|
| before | 686,919 | 31.31% |
| after | **686,201** | 31.38% |
| delta | **−718** | |

Correctness is structural rather than tested-into: `ip6` spans `[l3_offset, l3_offset+40)`, source at +8, destination at +24, so `ip6[8..24]` and `ip6[24..40]` are the same bytes. The removed reads could not fail independently either — they addressed a range whose bounds the first read had already proven — so no packet's disposition can change.

## What this is not

**It is not a fix for #8249, and the number is why.** Consuming the non-first-fragment sighting costs at least **313,000** instructions — three structurally different shapes all reject at 1,000,001 from this baseline with near-identical verifier signatures (~53,000 `total_states`). 718 is four orders of magnitude short, and the shim shrinking by 114,529 instructions since the plan was written already showed that linear headroom does not move it.

Recorded explicitly so the next person does not read a saving in this file as progress toward that fix. #8249 needs a structural reduction in the IPv6 parse region's **state**, not instructions — see `docs/pr/7494-non-first-fragment/plan.md` §0b.

## Validation

Kernel verifier PASS via `build-userspace-xdp.sh` (real verifier, `shimverify`, no `XPF_SHIM_ALLOW_LOW_HEADROOM`). Full `cargo test` for userspace-dp green — **5294 passed** — including the #4555 shim/helper extension-header parity corpus that executes the shared walk on real buffers. `go test ./pkg/dataplane/` green. The regenerated object and manifest are committed, as the build script installs them.

## PR #8596 — cluster: construct the RETH virtual MAC in one place (#8340 K18/K105) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8340-muse-004-batch1`

Closes #8340

First and, as it turns out, only code batch from the muse-spark-review-004 tracker. It fixes the one member of the RG-id byte-cast family that was neither already covered nor refuted, and the tracker's remaining balance is dispositioned in a comment on the issue.

## The census the tracker was owed

The last comment left "the RG-id byte-cast census" explicitly undone, with the warning not to assume #8343's `wireRGID` saturation generalised. It did not, and it did not have to:

| finding | sink | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| K100 | `RequestPeerFailover` → wire RG byte | **already fixed** — `validateFailoverProtocolRGID` rejects `<0 \|\| >255`, and all **5** wire sites in `sync_failover.go` call it |
| K104 | heartbeat monitor `RGID` | **fixed by #8343** — `wireRGID(ls.RedundancyGroup)` on send, `localRGIDForWireByte` on receive |
| K102 | `rg_active` / `ha_watchdog` E2BIG | commit vector closed by #8317; residual is lenient-path log volume |
| K18 | `RethMAC` / `StableRethLinkLocal` | mechanism real, **unreachable from a committed config** — see below |
| K105 | inline MAC in `compiler_iface.go` | **REAL, and this PR fixes it** |

`wireRGID` has exactly **two** call sites, both in `heartbeat_manager.go`. It never reached the MAC constructors, which is what the warning was about.

## What this PR changes

`02:bf:72:CC:RR:NN` was built from two copies of the same literal — `cluster.RethMAC`, which the daemon **programs** onto the interface, and an inline `net.HardwareAddr{0x02, 0xbf, 0x72, ...}` in `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go`, which **searches** for that MAC to recover a RETH member whose `.link` rename was lost.

A search key and the thing it searches for, written twice. A drift in either makes the recovery find nothing and drop the RETH member silently — the failure that path exists to prevent, with no diagnostic, because "no interface matched" is indistinguishable from "no interface is missing".

They had not been merged because **`pkg/cluster` imports `pkg/dataplane`**, so the dependency can only go the other way. The constructor now lives in `pkg/config` — the leaf both already depend on, and where the "this id is one octet" fact already lives as `MaxRethRedundancyGroupOctet`.

## On the casts themselves: an agreement, not a clamp

All three ids are bounded to one byte **at commit**: cluster id by `ValidateInteger(0, 255)` on a leaf whose own description reads *"one byte of the RETH virtual MAC"*; redundancy-group id twice over by `validateChassisClusterStrict` (255, then `MaxRedundancyGroups` = 16); node id is 0 or 1. `byte(id)` is therefore **exact for every configuration that passed commit**, and the aliasing K18 describes needs a tolerantly-loaded config that never did.

**The prescribed saturating clamp would not deliver what the finding asks.** Two out-of-range ids collapse onto 255 *and* onto a legitimate id 255 — three groups sharing a MAC instead of two. It makes the aliasing deterministic, not absent. What holds the invariant is the commit bound, so the commit bound is what the guard asserts: widen it without widening the MAC and the test says so.

Contrast `wireRGID`, where saturation **is** right, because declining to advertise a group reproduces the `peerGroup == nil` the wrap produces. Same family, opposite answers, and both comments now say why.

## Mutation results

| mutation | agreement | census | bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| dataplane rebuilds the literal inline (K105 regression) | pass | **FAIL** | pass |
| commit ceiling widened past the MAC octet | **FAIL** | pass | pass |
| the MAC format itself changes | pass | pass | **FAIL** |

One mutation per cell, each cell with its own subject. The census carries its **positive control first** — it fails if it scanned too few files or found no construction at all, because a census that scanned nothing finds nothing and passes forever.

## PR #8599 — tree: make gofmt -l an empty set, and keep it that way [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `check/master-health`

Twenty-two files under `pkg/` and `cmd/` had drifted out of gofmt. None was *wrong* — and that is the point. **The cost was never the formatting; it was that `gofmt -l` printed twenty-two names on every run.**

A check whose output is dominated by accepted noise cannot report the one thing that is new. I filtered those twenty-two mentally, and an hour later **shipped an unformatted test file of my own without noticing** (`degraded_reason_agreement_8258_test.go`, corrected in a follow-up). The new name was indistinguishable from the backlog I had already decided to ignore — the same shape as every other *"a check that fails to a value indistinguishable from healthy"* defect on this board, wearing style clothes.

So the repair is not to look harder. It is to make the expected output **empty**, so any name at all is a result.

## The guard

`TestTreeIsGofmtClean` walks `pkg/` and `cmd/` and asserts every `.go` file already is what the formatter would produce.

- **It uses `go/format`**, the package `gofmt` is built from, rather than shelling out to whatever `gofmt` is on PATH — making the verdict a property of the toolchain in `go.mod` instead of the developer's installation. Shelling out would let someone with a newer Go red this on a file their binary formats differently: a different question, and a flaky one.
- **Positive control:** fewer than 500 files walked is a failure. A walk that matched nothing would compare an empty set to an empty expectation and pass forever — the failure mode a scanner is least able to notice about itself, because the scanner is what you would consult to find it.
- A file that does not **parse** is reported as its own error rather than counted as clean; otherwise the scan starts agreeing with itself on exactly the files most likely to be broken.

## No allowlist, deliberately

#8258 landed an allowlist earlier today with dead-entry checks in both directions, and that was right *there*: each entry encoded a decision somebody made for a reason. Formatting encodes no decision. Every entry would mean "not yet run through a command that takes one second", and a list of those institutionalises precisely the noise this removes.

## Validation

`gofmt -l pkg/ cmd/` is now empty. `go build ./...`, `go vet` on the reformatted packages, and `go test ./cmd/cli/ ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/upgrade/... ./pkg/logging/` all green. gofmt is semantics-preserving, so the 90/92-line diff cannot change behaviour — the suites establish that rather than assert it.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| append an unformatted function to `pkg/upgrade/version.go` | caught, and it **names the file** |
| point the walk at a nonexistent root | the positive control fires rather than passing over an empty set |

Checked before touching anything that **none of the twenty-two files is being modified by any in-flight branch**, so this creates no conflict for work already underway.

Also confirms master is healthy after today's merges: 5294 Rust cells green, `harness-census.sh` OK, `go build ./...` clean.

## PR #8600 — config: conserve duplicate CoS and IS-IS interface blocks [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8436-remaining-six`

Four more sites from #8436's SILENT list — `class-of-service interfaces`, `class-of-service schedulers`, `class-of-service traffic-control-profiles`, `protocols isis interface`. **Census 15 → 11; two SILENT remain** (`system ntp server`, `system services dynamic-dns provider`, both in a follow-up).

Refs #8436

## The shapes

The three class-of-service containers are name-keyed maps whose loops constructed a fresh object per hierarchical block and stored it under one key — a second block discarded everything the first set. `protocols isis interface` is the slice-backed variant: it appended a **second entry with the same name** rather than overwriting, which *looks* like a merge until the entries are counted; whichever consumer reads first wins and the other block's settings are unreachable. That is the `system login class` (#8548) / #8594 OSPF-interface shape.

All four become find-or-create, the disposition the census names as correct.

## Every merge cell is paired with a different-names control

Find-or-create is keyed on the authored **name**, so two blocks naming different schedulers, profiles or interfaces still produce two entries — ordinary Junos authoring. Only two blocks naming the **same** one merge.

The control is the load-bearing half: **a merge that matched any entry rather than the same-named one passes every merge cell** while silently configuring one interface where the operator wrote two. Measured, not argued — that mutation reds `TestDistinctISISInterfaceBlocksStillAppend8436` with *"two DIFFERENT interfaces produced 1 entries, want 2"*.

## `class-of-service interfaces` needed three levels, not one

A shared map entry is only the first third. Two objects hang inside it that a fresh construct still wipes wholesale:

- the **per-unit bodies** — two blocks both naming `unit 0` must merge their leaves rather than the second's fresh object replacing the first's (the #8433 per-field wipe, reached through a container fix);
- the **interface-level body** (the `unit -1` pseudo-unit carrying bindings authored directly under the interface).

Both are now found-or-created, and **each fails differently**: reverting only the per-unit half reds the dedicated field cell while the census passes; reverting only the interface-level half reds the census while the field cell passes. Reuse is safe by construction for the same structural reason previous batches relied on — `parseCoSInterfaceUnitBody` assigns only inside `if node.FindChild(...) != nil` guards, so a block that never mentions a leaf cannot reset it.

## Fixture spellings verified before the assertions were written

Single-block compiles first: `metric 42` → `Metric=42`, `transmit-rate 100m` → `12500000` bytes, `shaping-rate 1g` → `125000000`, `unit 0 shaping-rate 500m` → `62500000`. #8587 shipped a fixture whose nested `port { range { low N; high M; } }` set nothing and nearly reported an innocent merge as a second defect. The probe also surfaced a constraint worth knowing: a `scheduler-map` reference must be **defined** or the compile fails, so the profile and interface fixtures carry one.

## Modularity

The comment triplication this would otherwise add pushed `compiler_class_of_service.go` past the 1500-LOC WATCH floor. The shared find-or-create rule is now stated **once** at the schedulers loop and cross-referenced twice, and the code-point token parsers moved to `compiler_cos_code_point_tokens.go`. That split follows a real seam, not a line count: those six functions turn classifier/rewrite-rule *tokens* into numeric points and share one alias/range expander, nothing else in the CoS compiler parses code points, and none touch the container structure the rest of the file builds. Pure relocation.

## Harm

Merging is **strictly additive** for the same-name case: nothing that compiled before compiles differently unless two blocks named one object, and then the first block's settings stop being discarded. The different-names case is byte-identical — asserted by four controls. A duplicate `unit N` inside **one** block keeps the last-write-wins it always had. Reachability unchanged: flat-set `set` already merged, so none of this is reachable through `set` commands, only a hierarchical file / `load merge` / `load override`.

## Validation — 7 mutations, all killed

| mutation | cell |
|---|---|
| ISIS merge matches ANY entry | `DistinctISISInterfaceBlocksStillAppend` |
| revert ISIS to append-both | `DuplicateISISInterfaceBlocksMerge` **and** the census pin |
| revert schedulers | its merge cell + census pin |
| revert traffic-control-profiles | its merge cell + census pin |
| revert cos interfaces | `DuplicateCoSInterfaceBlocksMerge` + the same-unit field cell |
| per-unit body still wiped (entry shared) | the same-unit field cell **only** — the census cannot see it, which is why that cell exists |
| interface-level body still wiped | the census pin **only** |

## PR #8601 — api/grpcapi/daemon: bracket IPv6 endpoints, reject a null Origin (#8597 batch 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b1`

First batch of the muse-spark-review-004 residual (#8597). Two findings fixed, two verified already closed, and the running tally goes on the issue as batches land.

Refs #8597

## IPv6 endpoints — K29, plus two siblings the review did not name

`fmt.Sprintf("%s:50051", ip)` yields `2001:db8::2:50051` for an IPv6 literal. That is not an address: `grpc.NewClient` and `net.Listen` both parse it as a bogus host:port. On an IPv6-only fabric **the peer dial silently fails and the fabric gRPC listener silently never binds** — and both present as "the peer is unreachable", not as a formatting bug.

**#4909 already fixed this shape once**, in `pkg/cli/peer.go`, and that fix's comment names the failing string verbatim. What it did not do is sweep the class:

| site | kind | named by the review? |
|---|---|---|
| `grpcapi/server_diag.go:57` | **dial** | yes (K29) |
| `daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:160` | **listen** | no |
| `daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go:164` | **listen** | no |

A reviewer's enumeration is a floor — and here the two it missed are the listener, so the finding as filed understated which half of the fabric was affected.

**The census is precise rather than over-broad**, and the discriminator is worth stating: it keys on a **hardcoded port literal** in a `%s:` format. A literal port means an endpoint; rendering a packet's port for display uses `%s:%d` with a *variable*, and there are ~15 of those in the tree that are legitimately not endpoints (session tables, log lines, flow output). Matching only the literal-port form separates the two exactly.

## Null Origin — K89

`crossSiteRejectReason` carried `!strings.EqualFold(origin, "null")` on its Origin arm, so a mutation request with `Origin: null` **skipped the host check entirely**.

`null` is not a neutral value. It is what a browser sends specifically from the contexts an attacker controls — a sandboxed iframe without `allow-same-origin`, a `data:` or `file:` document, a cross-origin redirect. **The one Origin value that names an opaque provenance was the one value waved through.**

It also contradicted the file's own stated policy, three paragraphs above the code: *"Origin ... Rejected when present and its host:port differs from the target."* `null` differs from every host. A carve-out the policy does not mention is the shape review cannot see, because the prose reads correct.

**What failing closed costs**, since a security tightening owes that answer: nothing reachable. A non-browser client (curl, the CLI, a scraper) sends no Origin at all; the management UI is same-origin. Both are asserted as controls, not assumed.

## Verified already closed — no change needed

**K26 and K27** (gRPC `GetNATRuleStats` reporting `then source-nat off` as `"interface"`, and collapsing address-book matches to `0.0.0.0/0`) are already fixed by **#8588**, which routed `pkg/grpcapi/server_nat.go` through the shared `pkg/natshow` computation — as a *sibling* of the REST surface that review had named. Two Mediums closed by a sweep done for a different issue.

## Mutations

| mutation | null-origin | endpoint-census |
|---|---|---|
| restore the null-origin carve-out | **FAIL** | pass |
| reject EVERY present Origin (over-broad) | **FAIL** | pass |
| the named dial site regresses | pass | **FAIL** |
| a **sibling listener** regresses | pass | **FAIL** |

The over-broad row is caught by the **same-origin control alone** — a guard that rejects every Origin passes both subject rows and breaks the only browser client that must work. The census carries two controls: one on the walk (fails if it scanned too few files) and one on the **pattern itself** (fails if the regex no longer matches the string it exists to find).

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/api/ ./pkg/grpcapi/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./cmd/cli/ ./pkg/config/` passes, before and after merging current master. `gofmt -l pkg/ cmd/` empty.

## PR #8603 — config: conserve duplicate NTP server and dynamic-dns provider blocks [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8436-ntp-ddns`

The last two SILENT entries in #8436's census — `system ntp server` and `system services dynamic-dns provider`. **Census 11 → 9, and the SILENT section is now EMPTY**: everything remaining is conservation by *refusal*, where an operator is told rather than quietly given a different config.

Refs #8436

## Neither is the shape the previous batches fixed

`system ntp server` especially. It already iterated every `server` node and already appended to a slice, so it **looked** merged. Measured before writing the fix:

```
server 1.1.1.1 { key 5; }   server 1.1.1.1 { version 4; }
  -> NTPServers=[1.1.1.1 1.1.1.1]   opts={Key:0 Version:4}
```

Two defects that fail differently: the address is appended **twice** (a duplicate chrony `server` directive), and the per-address option entry is **replaced** rather than merged, so `key 5` is gone. Both are fixed and asserted separately — an option-only fix leaves the duplicate directive; a dedupe-only fix still loses the key.

**The bracketed spelling is why the dedupe is per ADDRESS, not per node.** `server [ a b ]` collapses onto one node's Keys (#2419) and `ntpServerValues` returns both addresses from it, so a node-level "already seen" check would keep only the first — turning a conservation fix into a config loss. That mutation is run, and reds with one server where the operator wrote two.

The option merge is field-wise and depends on zero meaning unset — the **declared contract** of the type, not an assumption: `Key int (0 = unset)`, `Version int (0 = chrony default)`, `RoutingInstance string ("" = default)`. `Prefer` is a bool with no unset state, so it is a logical OR: neither statement can un-prefer the other, which is the conservative direction.

## dynamic-dns merges by walking, not by folding structs

`DDNSProvider` carries ~21 leaves. A field-wise merge would be a second enumeration of them that every future field has to be added to, and forgetting one is a silent loss of exactly the kind this census exists to find. Walking both blocks into one property map and materialising once has no such list.

## And that surfaced a second defect the census cannot see

Once the two blocks shared a property map, a leaf named by **both** resolved to the **first** block's value. The census fixture uses two *different* leaves, so first-vs-last never differs there and it passes either way. The flat-set oracle was measured directly:

```
set ... update-server first.example.com
set ... update-server second.example.com   ->  "second.example.com"
```

So hierarchical first-wins is a conservation violation — and it is the duplicate-**leaf** instance #8436's own comment already recorded (*"provider first; provider second; → hierarchical keeps 'first', flat-set keeps 'second'"*), reached through the container fix.

The repair keeps **both** orderings, because they answer different questions: **within** one block the first occurrence wins (the walker descends children, so one leaf can appear at several depths and the outermost statement is authoritative); **across** blocks the later block wins (what flat-set does). A single shared map would have silently inverted the second.

## Harm

Strictly additive for the same-name case: nothing compiles differently unless two statements named one server or one provider, and then the first's settings stop being discarded. The different-name case is byte-identical, asserted by a control for each. The NTP dedupe can only remove a duplicate **address**, never a distinct one — the bracket cell pins that. Reachability unchanged: flat-set already merged, so none of this is reachable through `set` commands, only a hierarchical file / `load merge` / `load override`.

| mutation | cell |
|---|---|
| NTP option entry replaced, not merged | merge cell (*"Key = 0, want 5"*) **and** census pin |
| NTP address dedupe reverted | merge cell (*"[1.1.1.1 1.1.1.1]"*) **and** census pin |
| NTP dedupe keyed per **node** instead of per address | different-address control **and** bracket cell — the census does **not** see it, which is why both exist |

## PR #8604 — docs: record the B2 capture-bridge pricing residual in the adjudication [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `docs/8276-b2-pricing-residual`

## What this issue asked, and where each part landed

#8276 is explicit that it is **a pricing task first and an implementation
second**, and that a PR which starts implementing before its pricing question
is answered is doing the thing the split exists to prevent. So this closes it
on the pricing, and lands no production code.

The pricing question has four parts. Three are answered; the fourth is
recorded as hardware-gated.

### 1. How does plaintext get from the kernel to a worker? — PARTIALLY, and the part that decides is measured

The in-process half is measured and the instrument is committed (#8545,
`userspace-dp/benches/b2_capture_bridge.rs`). Budget: #5275's appliance
measurement of the very path B2 would intercept — 4.29 Gbit/s v4 through
kernel forwarding = 357,500 pps = **2,797 ns/packet**.

| shape | time | % of budget |
|---|---|---|
| 1500-byte copy alone (the floor any capture pays) | 25.4 ns | 0.91% |
| same-thread queue handoff | 111 ns | 3.97% |
| **cross-thread round trip** | **12,648 ns** | **452%** |

The **kernel half** — nfqueue round trip, or AF_PACKET plus an authoritative
re-inject — is **not** priced, cannot be inferred from a userspace channel
benchmark, and needs a box where XFRM SAs and netfilter can be driven against
real traffic. This PR records it in adjudication §5.3 next to the three
reachability questions already waiting on that same hardware.

### 2. Which worker receives it, and how does it enter adjudication? — ANSWERED, and it is a refusal

**Option E as a per-packet cross-thread mechanism is priced out.** One-way the
handoff is ~2.3x the entire per-packet budget on its own, before the capture
syscall, before adjudication, before re-inject — a sustainable ~158,000 pps
against the 357,500 pps the kernel path already delivers. That is the issue's
literal ask and the answer is negative.

What survives: **same-thread adjudication** (4% of budget — the capture thread
adjudicates rather than handing off), or a **batched handoff at B >= 3** frames
per wake, where the wake amortizes below budget.

### 3. Ordering with the outbound direction — ANSWERED

`noroute_policy_denial` is present at this tree
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/forwarding/mod.rs:126`, with
`tests_noroute_adjudication_7480.rs` pinning it). It runs in the `NoRoute` arm

## PR #8605 — Surface the delete-replica drop split, and correct a hollow claim (#8586) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `measure/8586-queue-drop-rate`

## Why an instrument PR, and why it is not the fix

#8586 puts its question 2 first — *how often does the worker command queue
actually reach 4096* — because a mechanism sized against an unmeasured
window is a cost paid for nothing. **This PR does not build the epoch.** It
makes the measurement takeable, which is the same shape #8547 took for
#8108.

The counters #8586 names are `WORKER_COMMAND_QUEUE_DROPS` (already on the
wire) and the gap between `SESSION_DELETE_REPLICA_DROPPED` and
`SESSION_DELETE_REPLICA_DROP_REPAIRED` — process-wide statics #8576 added
and did not surface. The DELETE-specific half of the question could not be
read off a running box at all.

## Two fields, not one, and not folded into the aggregate

`worker_command_queue_drops` says a producer found a full queue. It cannot
say **what** was lost, and the two possibilities are not comparable:

- a dropped `UpsertSynced` is a replica whose content the shared map still
  holds;
- a dropped `DeleteSynced` leaves a sibling worker serving a session that
  no longer exists **and** holding its NAT reservation for the life of the
  allocator (#8576).

#8586 is about the second. `dropped - repaired` is the **unattributed
remainder** — a refused delete whose queue could not be resolved to a
worker id, so nothing ran the teardown on its behalf. That is a
subtraction of two independently carried fields, which is exactly why they
must not alias: one number, or two that serialize onto one key, reports
**0** for a box that is losing deletes and repairing none of them.

## A hollow claim, corrected

`worker_command_queue_drops`' own doc said:

> The expected steady-state value is 0, because the consumer drains the
> whole deque in one `core::mem::take` and so cannot be outrun by a
> sustained producer. A rising value therefore does not mean "busy"; it
> means some worker has stopped draining.

## PR #8608 — userspace-dp: decapsulate WireGuard transport data in the AF_XDP worker [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8274-step3-worker-decap`

Moves WireGuard type-4 decap into the AF_XDP worker so an authenticated peer's
inner plaintext is adjudicated under the tunnel's zone instead of being written
to the `wgN` TUN for the kernel to route with no policy at all.

Step 2 (#8598) built the shim classifier and was deliberately inert. This is the
step that moves packets.

## Direction of the change

**A tightening. It can deny traffic that flows today.**

Before this, `allowed-ips` was the only check in the path — and `allowed-ips` is
a cryptographic check on the inner SOURCE address: no destination, no zone pair,
no application, no direction. It is not a security policy.

**What an operator sees on the first packet after the change:** WireGuard inner
traffic that flowed yesterday is denied unless a policy admits it from the
tunnel's zone. An operator with no policy from that zone loses transit over the
tunnel at once. This is not a corner case and it belongs in a release note.

`poll_loop_denies_wg_inner_plaintext_with_no_permitting_policy_8274` is that
sentence as a test: same record, same fixture, policy removed, no session.

## Two edits, one change

The worker gains a decap stage **and** the shim stops handing type-4 records to
the kernel. Either alone is broken — the first leaves the stage unreachable, the
second breaks every tunnel. They land together.

| Piece | Role |
|---|---|
| `wg/decap.rs` → `try_wg_decap_from_frame` | outer parse under the #6748 bound → type-4 gate → endpoint by listen port → `try_decap` → inner reparse → `build_logical_ingress_packet` under the TUNNEL's `logical_ifindex` |
| `poll_stages.rs` → `stage_wg_decap` | stage seam, shaped like `stage_native_gre_decap` |
| `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` | **the wiring** — stage 6b, after GRE, guarded on `owned_packet_frame.is_none()` |
| `worker/mod.rs` → `wg_scratch` | per-worker decap buffer; no per-packet allocation |
| `wg/peer.rs`, `wg/engine.rs`, `wg_control/mod.rs` | worker reports the observed endpoint, control thread drains it on its timer pass — decap leaving the control socket would otherwise take away its dominant endpoint-learning signal |
| `userspace-xdp/` → `wg_worker_claims_record` | the `is_local_destination` arm declines a claimed record so it reaches AF_XDP |

Generations are **inherited** from the RX meta (#7167 invariant 5) — fabricating
them makes every packet look current and silently defeats attachment fencing.
`meta_flags` is deliberately `0`, not `GRE_DECAP_INGRESS_FLAG`.

## What is NOT closed

The control thread's plaintext TUN write is **unchanged**, and this is
deliberate, not an oversight:

- It is unreachable for type-4 on any shim-covered ingress (`userspaceCtrlFlagWgRx`
  is set iff a listen port is configured).
- On an ingress the shim does **not** cover, it is the only path. Failing closed

## PR #8609 — config: pin the conservation census's SKIP set, and fix what it hid [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8436-rpm-test-and-skips`

Closes #8436

Asked to determine whether #8436 could close, I ran the census. It reported **SILENT = 0** — true, and not the whole answer.

## The census had a hole exactly the shape of the class it guards

Of 49 named containers: **29 CHECKED, 20 SKIPPED** — and the skips were reported as two integers. *A site the census cannot check is not a site that conserves.* That is the same "opt-in discovered one review at a time" shape #8436 was filed against, one level up.

Checking all five *"a spelling did not parse or compile"* skips by hand found a real defect:

**`services rpm probe <p> test <t>`** — two `test T { ... }` blocks overwrite each other. The **probe** level had already been fixed by an earlier issue (`compiler_services.go` says so: a second `probe P` used to *"silently REPLACE the first, discarding ALL of its tests"*); the **test** level one layer down had not. It is the #8587 "a shared object is only half a fix" shape, and it survived **seven batches** of #8436 because the census's synthesized fixture omits the required `target`, so the compile failed and the site was *counted* rather than checked.

## So the skip set is pinned too

`dupConservationSkipped8436` lists every unprobed container; a **new** skip fails `TestDuplicateBlockConservationIsPinned8436`, and a **stale** skip fails too. "The census could not probe this" is now a decision someone records rather than the one place a defect can hide from the guard #8436 asked for.

The other four nocompile skips were checked with complete configs, verdicts recorded per line:

| site | verdict |
|---|---|
| `security policies from-zone … policy` | **REFUSED** at commit (#3473 — duplicate policy name shares a hit counter) |
| `security policies global policy` | **REFUSED** at commit (#3473) |
| `class-of-service fairness rss-expectation … queue` | **REFUSED** (*"duplicate expectation \"any\" conflicts with \"balanced\""*) |
| `services ip-monitoring … preferred-route route` | **CONSERVES** (fixture omitted the required `match rpm-probe`) |

The 15 *"second leaf not observable"* skips are the census's own vacuity guard and are structurally uninteresting — the merged form compiles identically to a block carrying only the first leaf, so no loss can show either way. Listed anyway so the set is **bounded**: a container that newly becomes unobservable is a change worth noticing, not a silent drop in coverage.

## Why this closes #8436

The issue's acceptance is *"bind the CONSERVATION property, as one rule across call sites"* and explicitly *"do not bind 'the registry has a row for X'"*. That is now true in both directions:

- **No container is silently reduced.** SILENT = 0 across 29 checked; all 9 non-conserving are conservation by **refusal**, where the operator is told; and all 20 skips are individually accounted for above.
- **A new site fails as a regression without anyone adding a row.** Demonstrated repeatedly by mutation across the batches — whole-site reverts red the pin with *"NEW non-conserving container"* and no bespoke cell. And now a new **unprobeable** site fails too, which was the residual hole.

The two lists stay as the enumeration the issue asked for; the guard is the general one.

## Harm

The rpm fix is strictly additive for the same-name case: nothing compiles differently unless two `test` blocks named one test, and then the first's settings stop being discarded. Two blocks naming **different** tests are different map keys and both survive — asserted by the control, because an over-broad merge there would collapse two configured probes into one and a monitored target silently stops being monitored. The census change is test-only. Reachability unchanged: flat-set already merged, so none of this is reachable through `set` commands.

## PR #8610 — Reconcile a worker whose DeleteSynced was refused (#8586) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8586-delete-drop-epoch`

## The half #8576 could not repair from the deleting thread

`replicate_session_delete_repairing` releases the refused worker's NAT
holder bit on its behalf, because nothing else ever will. It cannot delete
that worker's **local session entry** or invalidate its **per-binding
flow-cache slots** — both live behind its own `&mut SessionTable` and its
own caches. So the refused worker keeps serving a session that no longer
exists until the entry ages out.

The signal cannot travel through the queue that refused the command — that
is the whole condition — so it goes out of band:

- `SESSION_DELETE_DROP_EPOCH[worker_id]` is bumped at the refusal, beside
  the NAT repair and for the same `Arc`-identity-resolved worker id.
- The worker loop compares it once per pass (one relaxed load) and on a
  change runs `reconcile_peer_synced_against_shared` plus the flat
  flow-cache eviction. A burst raises **one** reconcile per pass however
  many refusals it caused — the epoch is compared, not counted down.

## Why the trigger is the DELETE drop and not queue pressure

This is the measurement from #8586's own acceptance, and it is what makes
the trigger choice a fact rather than a preference:

| arm | queue drops | **delete replicas dropped** |
|---|---|---|
| establishment (32,768 creates) | +85,668 (queue pinned at the 4096 cap) | **+0** |
| `clear` (32,770 entries) | +30,841 | **+30,786** (all attributed, `dropped − repaired = 0`) |

Establishment saturates the queue and loses **only upserts**, whose content
the shared map still holds. A trigger on queue depth — or on
`WORKER_COMMAND_QUEUE_DROPS`, which counts both kinds — would run a
whole-table walk continuously through normal traffic and reconcile nothing.

The cell asserts that **separation**, not the mechanism: same queue, same
cap, same `push_bounded` refusal, only the command kind differs.

## Why `is_peer_synced()`, and the trap inside it

The exclusions are the safety property:

- **`SharedPromote` is excluded** and is the one a reader expects to be in.
  It is synced-*derived* but no longer peer-*authoritative* — the origin an
  entry receives **after** local traffic promoted it — so this node owns it
  and its absence from the shared map is not evidence it should die.
  `loop_body`'s "synced-derived, never create-counted" arm **does** include
  it; that classification answers a different question and is correct for
  it. Using it here would be the bug, so the cell makes the choice
  explicit rather than an implicit consequence of which predicate got
  typed.

## PR #8611 — nat: report pool occupancy from the helper, not a random seed [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8606-nat-port-counter`

Closes #8606

## The number was random, not merely mis-converted

`show security nat source pool all` printed `Ports allocated: -2147483648`
(exactly `INT32_MIN`) for a pool that was translating correctly into
`172.16.80.7:30000/30001`, inside its configured `30000-30999` window.

The chain:

1. `SeedNATPortCounters` (`pkg/dataplane/maps_nat.go:166`) seeds
   `nat_port_counters` with **`rand.Uint64()`**. That is deliberate and right
   for what it was for: it makes the map a randomly-offset rolling allocation
   CURSOR, so a restarted daemon does not re-issue ports a peer still holds in
   ESTABLISHED state. It was never an occupancy count.
2. **Nothing advances it any more.** The eBPF programs that did were deleted in
   #1476. `nat_port_counters` appears **0** times in `userspace-dp/src` and
   `userspace-xdp/src` (positive control on the same grep: `sessions_v6` 6 hits,
   `rg_active` 9 hits). So a read returns the seed unmodified.
3. `used64 = int64(cnt)` is unchecked; ~half of all uint64 seeds exceed
   `MaxInt64` and convert negative.
4. `clampInt32` saturates that to `math.MinInt32`.

**This also explains the clue in the report.** `Ports allocated` was
bit-identical across two runs while `Utilization` differed — because utilization
is computed from the **unclamped** `used64` and so tracks each restart's fresh
seed, while the clamped integer sits pinned at the saturation constant. Two
symptoms, one cause.

The existing clamp is not broken. #2282 added it for a real reason and it works;
it is simply placed **after** a narrowing that has already destroyed the value.

## Why the arithmetic fix would have been the wrong fix

Guarding `cnt > MaxInt64` yields a stable, plausible, still-meaningless number —
`4611686018427387904` presented as occupancy on a 1000-port pool. That is
strictly worse than `-2147483648`, which is at least visibly broken.

**The product already computes this correctly.** The helper reports per-pool
`UsedPorts` over the control socket and has published it as
`xpf_userspace_snat_pool_used_ports` all along. Four other surfaces read the
dead map:

| surface | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `xpf_userspace_snat_pool_used_ports` | correct | unchanged |
| gRPC `GetNATPoolStats` / remote CLI | `INT32_MIN` | helper |
| REST `pkg/api/nat.go` | helper, **falling back** to the seed | helper |
| `xpf_nat_pool_used_ports` | seed | helper |
| local CLI | huge positive (`%d` on the raw `uint64`, unclamped) | helper |

## PR #8613 — ha: clear the tunnel-endpoint flag with the value it describes [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8612-scrub-tunnel-flag`

Refs #8612 (first half — the invariant. The failover measurement stays open.)

## The defect

`ScrubNodeLocal` zeroes `FibGen` on a peer-owned row, correctly — it is a
node-local field. But `FibGen` is **overloaded**:
`daemon_ha_userspace_convert.go:409-411` stores the tunnel endpoint id in it and
sets `LogFlagUserspaceTunnelEndpoint` to say so, because a non-zero `FibGen` is
otherwise a FIB generation and the two are not distinguishable by value.

The scrub did not touch `LogFlags`. So a scrubbed row asserted it carried a
tunnel endpoint it no longer carried.

## Nothing is fooled today — stating that plainly, because the first reading was wrong

Both read sites (`manager_sessionsync_request.go:54` and `:162`) test the flag
**and** a non-zero `FibGen`:

```go
if val.LogFlags&dataplane.LogFlagUserspaceTunnelEndpoint != 0 && val.FibGen != 0 {
    req.TunnelEndpointID = val.FibGen
}
```

so a scrubbed row declines and the peer's id is never adopted. It fails **safe**.
The finding was originally reported to me as "the peer's tunnel id is adopted
verbatim", and verifying it is what showed that it isn't.

What is wrong is that *"flag set implies value present"* held only by that
convention. A consumer testing the flag alone — which is what a flag is for —
reads a tunnel endpoint id of `0` as meaningful. Clearing the bit with the value
it describes makes the invariant true instead of customary. Only that bit;
`LogFlags` carries unrelated userspace sync metadata the peer legitimately owns.

## The larger half: the census could not have seen this

#7097's scrub census states that it verifies the helper *"zeroes the declared
node-local set and NOTHING else"*. That guarantee was weaker than it reads.

It is built on `zeroedFields`, which reports a field only on a **non-zero → zero**
transition. Any PARTIAL mutation was invisible to it — clearing one bit of a
multi-bit field, or setting a field to a different non-zero value, passed both
directional checks while doing something nobody declared. Concretely: with
`fillNonZero` seeding `LogFlags = 0x5A`, clearing bit 6 leaves `0x1A`, still
non-zero, so the census would have accepted this very change silently.

`changedFields` is the strictly stronger companion, and
`partiallyScrubbedSessionFields` declares which bits of which field the scrub may
clear. The stated guarantee is now the one the test actually makes.
