## PR #8651 — Stop enabling the IPv4 proxy_arp sysctl [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8637-narrow-proxy-arp-sysctl`

Closes #8637

## The sysctl's entire justification was false

`reconcileProxyARP` set `net.ipv4.conf.<if>.proxy_arp = 1` on every interface with a `proxy-arp` entry. #2160 added it, reporting that with the sysctl at 0 the firewall would not answer ARP for a proxy-ARP'd static-NAT external address.

**#2160's own example is `proxy-arp ge-0/0/1 address 10.0.2.50/32`, and `ge-0-0-1` carries `10.0.2.10/24`** — the proxied address is inside that interface's *own connected subnet*. So `rt->dst.dev == dev`, and every arm of `arp_process`'s proxy branch declines:

- `arp_fwd_proxy` returns 0 on its **first line**, before it ever reads this sysctl
- the `pneigh_lookup` arm is guarded by `rt->dst.dev != dev`
- only `arp_fwd_pvlan` could answer — which #2160 names parenthetically and nothing sets

**Setting `proxy_arp` cannot have answered #2160's ARP.** The issue was closed on a change that could not fix it; that case was genuinely fixed only by #8621's userspace responder.

## Measured

NTF_PROXY entry installed **manually** rather than through config, so the #8621 responder could not confound the reading:

| target | `proxy_arp=1` | `proxy_arp=0` |
|---|---|---|
| different device, **entry present** | answered | **still answered** |
| different device, **no entry** | **answered** | silent |
| the interface's own address (control) | answered | answered |

Row 1 is the pneigh arm — no sysctl term, needs none. **Row 2 is the sysctl's only distinct contribution: answering ARP for addresses nobody configured.** That is the over-answer #2197 item 3 asked to remove, on by default in every config using `proxy-arp` at all, including WAN and untrust interfaces.

A **void first attempt** is recorded on the issue: the probing host routed the target *via a gateway*, so it never emitted an ARP and proxy ARP was never exercised. It would have read as "the pneigh arm does not answer". The tell was that the **positive** row was empty too.

## What changes

`proxyResponderSysctlEnabledFor(family)` — false for AF_INET, true for AF_INET6.

**v4 is driven to 0, not skipped.** Skipping leaves a stale `proxy_arp=1` on every interface an older build already set it on, so the over-answer would survive this change on exactly the deployments that have it today.

**IPv6 keeps `proxy_ndp`, and the asymmetry has a reason.** `ndisc_recv_ns` gates on `forwarding && proxy_ndp && pndisc_is_router(...)` — a **required conjunct**, not an alternative path — so clearing it breaks v6 proxy NDP entirely. v4's pneigh arm has no sysctl term; v6's does.

Per-address behaviour is unaffected and now comes only from mechanisms that answer for configured addresses: pneigh entries (different-device) and #8621's responder (same-device).

## Two pre-existing cells inverted/retargeted, not deleted

- **`TestEnableProxyResponders_IPv4`** was the #2160 regression. Inverted: the write must still *happen* and must be a *disable*. Its comment records why #2160's premise was false, so the next reader does not restore it.
- **The #6536 fallback cell** recorded only `enable == true` writes. Its subject is that the fallback *re-asserts* the sysctl rather than merely preserving the inventory entry — the interface must be **written**; which value is a different question. Filtering on `enable` conflated the two, so it went red on a change that left its own property intact.

## Mutations — four, all killed

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| v4 sysctl enabled again | enable-pass cell + predicate cell |
| **v6 sysctl no longer enabled** | both — the row that stops this silently breaking IPv6 proxy NDP |
| v4 skipped instead of written to 0 (×2 forms) | the enable-pass cell — the assertion that makes the upgrade path work |

## PR #8652 — userspace-dp: resolve or refuse a domain-0 session delete, never fan out [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8636-refuse-ambiguous-delete`

A delete built from a bare 5-tuple resolved routing domain 0 and was then retried in **every** configured routing domain. Routing instances exist to carry **overlapping address space**, so two tenants holding the same 5-tuple is the normal case — and the retry tore down the other tenant's live session.

Closes #8636

## The rationale was true on a different axis

*"A refused delete leaks a session while an under-matching one removes nothing the 5-tuple did not already name"* is sound for #7188's tunnel **discriminator**, where the alternatives really are match-too-little or refuse. It does not carry to the routing-domain axis, where the fan-out removes sessions the 5-tuple names **in other tenants** — precisely removing something it did not name.

## Resolve, or refuse

The handler now probes before acting — the same loop over the same handful of domains on the same slow path, a lookup instead of a delete:

| matches | action |
|---|---|
| none | the exact delete above it was the whole job |
| exactly one | delete **that one**, scoped — strictly better than the fan-out: same session removed, no other domain touched |
| more than one | refuse, with its own reason token |

## Why refusing is cheap now and was not this morning

The objection to failing closed is that a session survives a policy invalidation. **#8356 changed that**: zone policy is re-derived on the established-hit path once per `config_generation`; a commit bumps it, invalidating the flow cache, so the next packet is judged and revoked if the live policy denies. And **every** reason the Go side invalidates for is a zone-policy change (`PolicyDeleted` / `PolicyModified` / `DefaultPolicyChanged`) — the populations coincide exactly. A refused delete leaks for **one packet**, not until idle timeout.

The re-derivation is also a *better* answer than the delete: it revokes only if the policy actually denies, so a session the deleted rule admitted but another still permits **survives**. The fan-out gets that wrong in the other direction.

## The residual, with its direction

Refusal leaks until timeout only where the re-derivation **declines** — ICMP under a type-constrained permit (#8618's gate 1b), an unresolvable zone (`to_id == 0 || from_id == 0`), `NoLocalEntry` — **intersected** with "the tuple is ambiguous", since a unique tuple deletes exactly as before. Every member of that intersection fails toward **keeping a session too long rather than tearing down another tenant's**. The direction is what makes it acceptable, not the size.

## Details worth noting

`SYNCED_DELETE_REFUSED_PREFIX` is deliberately distinct from the import prefix — an import refusal means this node declined to *take* a session, a delete refusal means it *kept* one it was asked to remove. One token would make a cross-tenant guard firing look like an import problem. Go already tolerates a per-key refusal without aborting the batch (#5881).

`synced_session_contains` reads through `lock_shared_recover` for the same reason `delete_synced_session_gen` does (#5154): with `.lock().ok()` a poisoned mutex reads as `None`, and an ambiguity probe that silently answers "no matches" resolves to "delete nothing" — quiet, and indistinguishable from a clean miss.

## Validation

`cargo test` **5341 passed / 0 failed**; `go test ./pkg/dataplane/...` clean; `gofmt -l` clean.

Three cells. **The first decides safety rather than care** — refusing is the new behaviour, so the risk is that it fires on ordinary deletes and turns every policy invalidation into a session leak:

- `an_unambiguous_bare_tuple_delete_still_removes_the_session_8636`
- `an_ambiguous_bare_tuple_delete_is_refused_and_touches_nothing_8636`
- `a_bare_tuple_delete_matching_no_instance_still_succeeds_8636`

Fixtures assert **doubled** entry counts (2 per session: forward key + reverse companion) rather than relaxing to `> 0`, so a domain that silently failed to install is still caught by the setup check.

## PR #8653 — Bound config duration knobs at the overflow point, and guard the class [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8642-duration-overflow-sweep`

Closes #8642

## The most severe site was not in the filed census

**`pkg/vrrp/instance_timing.go:75` and `:92` — the VRRP advertisement interval.** Found by re-running the census rather than inheriting it.

- config-derived: `vg.AdvertiseInterval`, set by a bare `strconv.Atoi` with **no range check**
- schema ceilings exist and are irrelevant on the tolerant path
- runtime guard was `ms <= 0`
- **milliseconds**, so the residue floor is **64ns**, not 512ns

A wrapped value is a **64ns advertisement timer on the RETH interfaces** — the 30ms heartbeat HA failover timing is built on, at ~1.5e7/s. That is CLAUDE.md's own control-path starvation warning, and worse than the LLDP site the filed census rated the closest sibling of #6769.

## Why the existing guards could not see this

The residue is small and **positive** — `gcd(1e9, 2^64) = 512`, `gcd(1e6, 2^64) = 64`. Every swept site guarded with `<= 0` or `> 0`. **A guard asking "is it nonsense in the obvious direction" cannot see wrap, because a wrapped value is not nonsense — it is a plausible fast interval.** A post-multiply check has the same blindness: `dhcprelay`'s own `w > pendingTTL` would not have caught it either.

A schema ceiling is not the fix: `compileTreeLenient` downgrades typed-leaf violations to warnings on the tolerant ingress, so a persisted or peer-pushed config never meets it.

## The census, verified rather than inherited

The filed positive control — *"the fixed packages no longer show a raw site"* — does not hold as a grep predicate; all five still match. Every match is a comment, the multiply **inside** the hardening helper after its bound, or a non-config operand. Right in substance, wrong as a predicate — and load-bearing, because a scanner on the literal pattern flags five already-fixed packages on day one.

Also: `ra/sender.go` carries **8** sites not 7, and two filed line numbers are off by one.

## 11 sites fixed, 13 verdicts recorded

Two worth naming: **`compiler_nat.go:461`'s guard is `timeout == 0`** — *weaker* than `> 0`, so a wrapped value never even reaches the 300s default and every persistent NAT lease expires in ~512ns. And **`ra/sender.go:1032`**, where #4525's floor covers the *storm* half of overflow but not a wrap landing **large** positive, which stretches the RA interval and costs hosts their default route.

**Seven RA wire-field lifetimes deliberately not fixed**, with a verdict: same arithmetic, different harm — they encode into wire fields rather than arming a timer, so the ceiling is the field width and the fallback must be argued per field. `RouterLifetime = 0` means *"not a default router"*. Guessing seven fallback directions in an unmeasured subsystem is how a sweep becomes a defect.

The **LLDP neighbour TTL** is the only *attacker-influenced* operand in the census, safe only because the TLV is 2 bytes clamped to `[0,0xffff]` — an incidental bound now load-bearing for arithmetic safety, recorded so whoever widens that field knows.

## The guard — `pkg/durationaudit`

An AST census; a site is safe when bounded, or inside a function that bounds — the #8629 fixpoint, which accepts the shared converters and each package's helper **by construction** rather than by an exemption list that could later bless a helper that stopped bounding.

**My first draft had a hand-listed set of bounding constants and it rotted on the first run** — the census flagged `withinWindow` (#8597, already fixed) because it bounds against the domain-specific `MaxEventWithinSeconds`. Recognition is now by shape, and because a name pattern alone is a heuristic, a companion cell checks **every accepted ceiling is at or below its unit's overflow point**. Recognition by name, soundness by value.

It **parses rather than greps**, and both reasons were measured: a regex counts the `valueDesc` string describing this hazard, and the multiply inside every hardening helper.

| M1 ceiling dropped | two converter cells |
| M2 seconds bounded at the **millisecond** ceiling (1000× loose) | both, incl. the cross-unit cell |

| M4 census calls everything bounded | degenerate guard 2 |

## PR #8654 — Bound the top-talkers scan and lock the VRRP send paths (#8597 K05/K20) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b7`

Batch 7 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K05 and K20. Both confirmed by execution before anything was changed.

## K05 — a show command that OOMs the process it is diagnosing

`show security flow session sort-by bytes|packets` built one formatted row per **session**, sorted the whole slice, and printed twenty. The console runs *in* xpfd with no recover, `MaxSessions` is dynamic and large by design (#5323), and each entry holds six freshly allocated strings. A legitimate, unprivileged diagnostic OOM-kills the control plane on a busy box.

The REST side has treated a full conntrack walk as an admission decision since #5318 (`sessionCountCap`). The console path had no equivalent. The other CLI session views stream (`count++` and print), so this really was the only local accumulator — the population is the two append sites the finding named.

The bound is on **collection**, not print: a `topTalkerLimit`-sized min-heap of raw session key/value copies, formatted only for survivors.

### The measurement rejected my first fix

Two properties are load-bearing. **The scan allocates nothing per session** — not less, nothing. **The output is unchanged**, including `(of N total)`, which still counts every admitted session rather than rows kept.

The first property is here because the first draft did not have it. That draft deferred formatting behind a closure per candidate: bounded-looking, and still O(N), because the closure heap-allocates on every session and the address/zone work ran before it.

| version | 100 sessions | 20,000 sessions | ratio (table ratio 200x) |
|---|---|---|---|
| closure-deferred draft | 53,952 B | 6,757,040 B | **125x** |
| raw key/value heap | 39,904 B | 39,456 B | **0.99x** |

That is why the cell measures a **ratio between two real runs** rather than asserting the design, and why it carries a positive control that deliberately builds the unbounded shape and checks the probe can see the growth. A design assertion would have passed on the draft.

The print cap stays explicit and independent of the collection cap. Deriving it from `len(entries)` makes the two one bound — and the mutation removing the collection bound then **hangs** a test on a full stdout pipe instead of failing it. Found by running that mutation.

## K20 — VRRP send-path data races

`updateConfig` writes seven mu-guarded fields on the **manager** goroutine (the #5087 day-2 path). Every reader in `instance_preempt.go`, `track.go`, `manager.go` and `instance_timing.go` snapshots under the lock — the #6230/#5718 discipline. Four statements on the send paths did not.

**Reproduced before fixing**: `go test -race` fires at `instance_send.go:46` against `instance.go:378`, and `instance_garp.go:154` against `instance.go:379`.

### The property the race detector cannot see

`sendAdvert` takes **one** snapshot for both arms, not one per arm. A read per arm silences `-race` completely and is still wrong: a dual-stack instance sends its v4 and v6 adverts from one call, and a writer landing between them makes the two families advertise different `MaxAdverInt`. The peer derives its master-down interval from that field, so the families would disagree about the failover horizon — the flapping shape gemini-048 finding 06 describes.

That needed a different instrument. `TestOneAdvertCallUsesOneIntervalSnapshot_8597` drives the write from **inside** the v4 arm through a new `sendPacketFn` seam, so the forbidden interleaving is deterministic rather than raced for. The near-miss mutation — one locked read per arm — escapes every other cell in the file and dies to that one.

`advertiseIntervalMS` returns the raw milliseconds rather than reusing `advertInterval()`: that helper substitutes the 1000 ms default for a non-positive value, and folding the default into the wire field would make a misconfigured instance advertise a cadence it is not sending at.

## PR #8655 — config: expand a v4-mapped proxy-ARP block under v4 rules [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8631-proxyarp-4in6`

Closes #8631

`expandProxyARPPrefix` asked `addr.Is4()` — **false for a 4-in-6 address** — so `::ffff:10.0.0.0/126` expanded under v6 rules. The installer (`pkg/dataplane/proxyarp.go`) asks `addr.Is6() && !addr.Is4In6()` and classifies the identical literal as **v4**. Two layers, one literal, opposite answers.

So the expansion skipped no network address and emitted a `/128` suffix, and the installer then programmed those entries as `AF_INET` — including the network address no host ARPs for.

## Why this is not `Unmap()` and done

A prefix length on a 4-in-6 address is in **v6 bit-space**. `::ffff:10.0.0.0/126` describes four addresses; the v4-equivalent mask is `126 - 96 = 30`. Unmapping the address while keeping `Bits()` at 126 builds a v4 address with a /126 mask — not a narrower answer, an **invalid** one.

That near-miss is recorded in the issue, and here it is **mutation-tested** rather than left as a warning.

## Single-sourced

`proxyARPUnmap4In6` is called from all three sites that classify a prefix — the expansion, the host count, and the commit gate — so the count and the expansion cannot disagree about what a `::ffff:` block is. That disagreement is the shape of the original defect, one layer down.

`Bits() < 96` is left alone: such a prefix does not denote a v4 block (`/64` → `-32`), and it already fails closed via the over-cap gate. `/96` converts to a v4 `/0`, still far over the cap, so the conversion cannot smuggle a block past the gate either.

## Two things established before writing the conversion

**Reachability** — the issue asked for this first, and it decides fix-versus-document. A `::ffff:` block **does** reach commit: `validateProxyARPAddressesStrict` rejects only what fails `netip.ParsePrefix` and what is still multi-host after expansion. A mapped block parses, and the v6-rule expansion turns it into single-host `/128` entries that pass. So this is a change.

**A correction to the issue**, measured rather than reasoned: it states a v4 `/30` yields **3** hosts. It yields **2** — `proxyARPPrefixHostCount` subtracts the network *and* the broadcast address. A cell asserting 3 would have failed against correct code.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/...` clean (0 failures across all packages); `gofmt -l` clean; **zero deletions** in the diff.

Four cells. **The counts are the assertion, not the suffixes** — checking only `/32` vs `/128` passes on a half-fix that unmaps the address and keeps the v6 host count, which is the likelier wrong repair.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert the normalization | two cells **RED** |
| the **naive unmap** (unmap address, keep v6 mask) | the same two **RED** — the repair the issue records trying first is bound, not just described |
| drop the `Bits() < 96` floor | **escaped — and equivalent**, not a gap |

On the third: `netip.PrefixFrom` returns an invalid prefix for a negative length, so the `IsValid` backstop catches the same inputs. Both are kept — the floor states the *intent*, `IsValid` the *mechanism* — and the comment records that deleting either leaves the other holding, so the next reader learns it from the code rather than from a green suite.

## PR #8658 — docs: record the merge-gate step a scoped gate cannot cover [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `docs/content-scanning-guard-gate`

## Why

A merge gate scoped to the packages a diff touches **cannot see a guard that selects its subjects by content** — a census that walks the whole tree looking for a shape rather than checking the files you changed.

The failure signature is what makes it expensive: **the lane that breaks it stays green** (its diff does not touch the guard's package), and **every other lane inherits the red** on its next merge, then investigates a failure it did not cause.

Three instances in one day, across two guards:

| guard | lives in | broken by a diff touching |
|---|---|---|
| `TestTreeIsGofmtClean` | tree-wide | one package's formatting |
| `TestOperatorPackagesOnlyUseDocumentedLegacyDataplaneImports` | `pkg/dataplane` | a new file in `pkg/cli` |
| `TestRetirementBoundaryDocsMentionLegacyImportAllowlist` | `pkg/dataplane` | an allowlist entry with no docs row |

The third is the one that argues hardest for writing this down: it was the *fix* for the second, and applying the obvious one-line remedy would have traded one red for another.

## What

Adds a subsection to **Verification discipline** recording:

- the gate step that is deliberately **not** scoped to your diff — `gofmt -l .` tree-wide plus `go test ./pkg/dataplane/`, run regardless of what you changed;
- the corollary that satisfying a guard via its allowlist means you should look for **the guard that guards the allowlist**;
- the distinction between the two kinds of allowlist entry, since only one is legitimate — a **new capability** gaining an exception is *weakening the guard*, while a **relocation** out of an already-allowlisted file is *keeping the guard accurate* (the allowlist is keyed by filename, so splitting code trips it while the import boundary is unchanged);
- that a reason string is a **claim about the import boundary**, not a description of the change that moved the code, so it stays true after that rationale is rewritten.

Recording it here rather than repeating it per-dispatch — `CLAUDE.md` already directs every agent to read `docs/engineering-style.md` before non-trivial work, so this removes the decision instead of adding a step to remember.

## Validation

Docs-only; no code touched.

- diff carries nothing outside `docs/engineering-style.md`, and no deletion lines
- `gofmt -l .` — clean tree-wide
- `go test ./pkg/dataplane/ -run 'Canary|Retirement|Operator'` — `ok`

The gate step this PR documents was run against this PR.

## PR #8661 — Pair a supersession bump with responsibility, bound a shutdown wait (#8597 K19/K23) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b8`

Batch 8 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K19 and K23. Both reproduced by execution before anything was changed.

## K19 — a withdraw that SKIPPED an interface still cancelled its restart

`claimWithdrawOnceLocked` bumped the per-interface supersession epoch in a loop over **every** named interface, running before the busy check — so it bumped the ones it then skipped.

The invariant this package runs on is that a supersession bump accompanies real superseding **responsibility**. `Withdraw` flips the global fence and owns every drain. `WithdrawInterfaces` bumps and then flips `goodbyeWanted` on the entry it supersedes, so even its already-draining path takes over the goodbye. The skip path did **neither**: it emitted nothing, claimed nothing, and reported `Skipped`.

`finishDrainDecision` starts a changed-config replacement only while `m.ifaceEpoch[name] == e.startIfaceEpoch`, and `applyDeferred` aborts a deferred start on the same comparison. So a stray bump made the replacement silently not happen, released the tombstone anyway, and returned nil from **both** error paths.

The first run of the new cell printed exactly the consequence: *"lo is senderless and every caller was told it succeeded"*. Hosts behind that interface keep the router until Router Lifetime (1800 s default) expires.

The trigger is routine — the daemon runs `runStartupGoodbye` on its own goroutine, so a cold-boot `WithdrawOnce` runs concurrently with `Apply`'s changed-config restart.

**The bump moves into the claim branch; it is not deleted.** On the claimed path this call takes the interface over and emits the goodbye, so a deferred `Apply` start that captured the epoch must still be superseded. The over-broad mutation — delete rather than move — has its own cell.

The contrast is the invariant, written as a test whose two halves differ only in which entry point is called: a `WithdrawOnce` that skips must **not** cancel a restart, and a `WithdrawInterfaces` naming the same interface still **must**.

## K23 — the one shutdown acquire that was not bounded

`stopPolicySchedulerLoop` acquired `applySem` with `context.Background()`. `daemon_run_shutdown.go` states the rule at its own drain — *"bound it defensively anyway so a wedged apply cannot block the whole shutdown past the drain budget"*.

With an apply wedged the acquire never returned: the scheduler was never cancelled, shutdown never reached HA relinquish, and systemd's `TimeoutStopSec` SIGKILLed the process — no `rg_active` clear, no priority-0 advert, no RA goodbye. A contained degradation the bounded drain right above it was written to survive became a blackout.

**Bounding an acquire has a second half: do not release a permit you did not take.** The original released unconditionally, safe only because the acquire could not fail. On a weight-1 semaphore, releasing without acquiring raises the count above capacity and admits a second holder alongside the wedged apply — from the very path whose purpose is to serialise against it.

On timeout the call proceeds to the cancel anyway, because bounding the wait is only worth something if the call still does its job (#5308 orders this before the dataplane teardown so no late tick runs against a closed runtime).

### The prescribed fix's safety argument is false

The finding says the join is already safe because *"the tick blocks on applySem acquire with the daemon ctx, which is cancelled"*. `daemon_run.go` says twice that `d.daemonCtx` is the **raw parent** and stays **production-uncancelled**, so cancelling the scheduler's child ctx does not release a tick parked on it.

This is therefore a **partial** fix, and the code and `pkg/daemon/README.md` both say so rather than implying otherwise. It removes the case where the stall happens with no tick in flight at all. The rest needs the scheduler's own ctx to reach its `updateFn` — a signature/ownership change, not a bound — filed as **#8660** with three candidate shapes and what each costs.

## Population

| finding | claimed | actual |
|---|---|---|
| K19 | one bump loop | **correct as filed** |
| K23 | one unbounded shutdown acquire | **correct as filed** — 7 acquires use `context.Background()`, but only one is reachable from the shutdown sequence, and it is the named one |

K19's more useful census result is negative: `WithdrawInterfaces` has the same unconditional-bump shape and is **not** defective, because `claimGracefulLocked` takes responsibility for every name it is given. The thing to check is the invariant, not the shape.

## PR #8665 — dhcp,nftables,nat64: bound the IA_PD prefix-length hint at the point of use (#8597 Lows) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-lows-k51-k53-k54-k62`

The four #8597 Low findings in my slice. Two were real, two were not — and the pair that looks identical is the useful part, because which one is real turns entirely on **where its range check lives**.

## K51 — real, and the half that mattered was still open

`net.CIDRMask(n, 128)` returns a **nil** mask for any `n` outside `[0,128]`, and `net.IPMask(nil).Size()` is `(0,0)`. So an out-of-range `preferred-prefix-length` never failed — it silently became an IAPREFIX on the wire with **prefix-length 0**. The operator asked for a /56 delegation and we SOLICITed a degenerate hint instead, which is worse than sending none: a 0 is a positive statement to the upstream server, not an absent preference.

The schema already bounds this leaf (`2e02fc995`), and that closes the operator-facing half — a strict commit rejects 999. It does not close this one:

| path | verdict |
|---|---|
| strict `SchemaValidate` | rejected: `integer out of range [0..128] (got 999)` |
| tolerant `Store.Load` / `Store.SyncApply` | **reaches the runtime as 999** → nil mask → wire prefix-length **0** |

`compileTreeLenient` downgrades the violation to a `slog.Warn` and continues (#1319 — deliberately, so a stale persisted config cannot blackout-boot a node), and `parseIntLeaf` only rejects non-integers. **A schema ceiling is a commit gate, not an invariant.**

What settled it: **#6531 already fixed this exact nil-mask defect on the inbound path of the same file** — it rejects a degenerate IAPREFIX arriving *from* the upstream server. Line 637 was its unguarded outbound twin. Same file, same class, same tolerant provenance, one direction guarded.

Fixed at the consumption point, falling back to "no hint" rather than clamping (#8642 doctrine): a clamp invents an intent we cannot know, while 0/absent is the sentinel this leaf already documents.

## K53 — state the invariant `stableSubnetID` silently relies on

Its modulo can produce any value in `[0, keaSubnetIDMax)`. On a 32-bit `int` every result above `0x7FFFFFFF` — about half of all subnets — wraps **negative**, and a negative Kea subnet-id is not a diagnosable error: it lands in the generated Kea config and the daemon rejects or misfiles the subnet, on a hash nobody can predict from the config.

That cannot happen today, and the reason is not a check — it is that this tree builds only amd64 and arm64. The arithmetic is correct because of a **build-target property nothing stated**. `const _ = int(keaSubnetIDMax)` states it, and reds at build time the day someone adds a 32-bit target. A range check would have been the wrong remedy: dead code on every target we build.

## K54 — refuted, verdict recorded in the code

`uint8(v)` does truncate, but its only inputs come from `resolveICMPTypeToken`/`resolveICMPCodeToken`, which accept `0..255` and divert the rest to `UnknownICMPTypes` (#3205/#6806). The difference from K51: **that bound is in the compiler, not in `setSchema`, so it runs on the tolerant path too.** Recorded at the function with the K51 contrast, so nobody adds the guard that is not needed.

## K62 — a real divergence, in the safe direction, unreachable

The nat64 `/96` backstop is strict but not identical to the Go gate it backs. Go uses `strconv.ParseUint` (**no sign permitted**); Rust's integer `FromStr` **permits a leading `+`**. So `64:ff9b::/+96` is rejected at commit and accepted by the dataplane.

Swept exhaustively — all 7,240 strings of length ≤3 over `[0-9 + - _ space x X . e E]`:

| direction | count |
|---|---|
| Rust accepts, Go rejects | **110** — every one a leading `+` |
| **Go accepts, Rust rejects** | **0** |
| both accept, different value | 0 |

Rust's accepted language is a strict superset, so **the dangerous direction is empty**. That inverts the obvious fix. nat64.rs says the backstop "must be strict" — but the invariant worth holding is not that the grammars are equal, it is that *the backstop never rejects what the gate accepted*. Tightening Rust to reject `+96` would trade a harmless divergence for the exact failure this code exists to prevent: a cleanly-committed rule silently skipped, NAT64 off. It is unreachable anyway — no xpf version can persist a `/+96`, because ParseUint has never accepted a sign. So this is recorded, with an explicit "do not tighten", rather than changed.

## Populations established, not assumed

Per #8597's standing instruction, with the count found beside the count claimed:

- **Prefix-length consumption**: 46 `net.CIDRMask`/`netip.PrefixFrom` sites; 16 take a variable length; exactly **1** is config-sourced and unbounded (K51). The rest derive from `.Bits()`/`.BitLen()` of an already-parsed prefix — in range by construction.
- **Cross-language numeric parses**: 14 Rust `.parse::<uN>()`; **3** read a config token — the two nat64 sites plus the WireGuard endpoint port. I checked the third rather than assuming: its Go mirror uses `Atoi`, which diverges the *other* way (110 leading-`-` tokens Rust rejects), but Go's `port < 1 || port > 65535` rejects every one, so that mirror agrees on verdicts across the corpus. Not a finding.

## PR #8666 — config: build flat-set modifiers as siblings, not nested under each other [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8657-setpath-modifier-siblings`

Closes #8657

`SetPath` nested each successive modifier under the previous one, so the compiler — which scans **siblings** — reached only the first:

```
set system ntp server 1.2.3.4 prefer version 4
  [server 1.2.3.4]
    [prefer]
      [version 4]        <- a CHILD of prefer
```

Exactly one modifier survived, and **which one depended on authoring order**. The hierarchical spelling of the same config produced siblings and kept both — one configuration, two compiled results, on the `set` path that is also the cluster config-sync path.

## Which side is the datum

A disagreement can be resolved either way, and resolving it toward the wrong side erases information. The **hierarchical** shape is correct: it yields siblings and the compiler reads all of them, so the compiler's read is right for the shape it is handed. This moves the **shape** and leaves the read alone.

## The scope was measured twice, and the obvious rule was wrong

*"A node declaring no sub-structure cannot be a container, so never descend into it"* is true in the abstract and **breaks 23 cells** across `pkg/api`, `pkg/cli`, `pkg/config` — the `applications`/`application-set` bodies rely on that descent for repeated childless keywords, and flattening them turns one definition into several duplicates.

Scoped to *modifiers of a `valueList` node*: 23 → 1. And that one was **this repo's own #2419 differential gate**, reporting a new shape-dependent drop on `static route … next-hop <gw> interface a b` — a site that agreed across all six spellings before. The arm emitted `1 + args` tokens and orphaned the rest; adding the trailing-value absorption the multi-leaf arm already performs took it to **0**. The gate found that, not reasoning.

## Population — 6 sites across 4 leaves, not 2

Established as a schema **walk**, not a grep:

| site | modifiers |
|---|---|
| `system ntp server` | 4 |
| `system services dhcp-local-server group interface` | **10** |
| `system services dhcpv6-local-server group interface` | **10** |
| all three again under `groups <*>` | |

Both omissions have one cause: the DHCP pair is generated by a **single helper**, so a `valueList: true` grep sees one source line; the apply-group variants never appear as their own declaration.

**The omitted leaf exhibited the same broken shape** (`interface <if> trace exclude` → `[trace] → [exclude]`). Its modifiers are parsed-and-ignored today, so no compiler-visible harm — but it inherits the defect the moment one is implemented. That is the argument for a shape-keyed guard, made concrete.

## Cells — the observable named before the control

Agreement between the two spellings **alone cannot distinguish "both keep it" from "both lose it"**, so it is paired with an explicit `Prefer && Version == 4` check.

- `..._ModifiersAreSiblingsNotNested8657` — flat-set vs hierarchical compile to the same struct (agreement, not a literal, so it cannot go vacuous if a default changes) plus that degenerate-failure control.
- `..._ModifierOrderDoesNotChangeTheResult8657` — the defect kept whichever modifier came *first*, so a single-order cell would pass on a fix that still drops the second.
- `..._EveryMultiModifierValueListLeafBuildsSiblings8657` — keyed to the **shape**: walks the schema for `valueList` leaves with ≥2 modifiers, so the next such leaf is covered on arrival. Fails **degenerately** if the walk finds nothing.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert the arm | two behavioural cells **RED** |
| emit the modifier but still descend | all three **RED**, including the shape guard |

## PR #8668 — Reject a statement that declares a value and gives none (#8597 K15) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b10`

Batch 10 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K15.

Every arity gate in the schema walker is about a token too **many**. `validateScalarValueLeaf` has rejected a trailing token since #3332, with the reasoning *"the extra token would be silently dropped"*. A token too **few** is silently dropped in exactly the same sense, and was accepted everywhere.

Measured at HEAD:

```
next-hop fe80::1 interface       -> commits clean, Interface: "" — an UNSCOPED IPv6 link-local next-hop
system host-name                 -> commits clean, the system carries no host-name
family inet address              -> the same
policy p match source-address    -> the same
```

The finding names the static-route `interface` modifier, and that is the instance with the sharpest consequence: a link-local gateway is meaningless without its egress interface, so the route an operator can least afford to mis-scope is the one that commits unscoped.

## Two sites, and they are the two-copy shape

The scalar half is one line — the #3332 check now runs in both directions.

The walker half is where the shape is interesting. `walkSchemaNode` computes `missingArgs := declaredKeyTokens - consumed` and, when positive, delegates to `walkInstanceChildren` — the dual-AST path, where a hierarchical spelling supplies the missing name/arg levels as nested AST children. **With zero children it iterates nothing and returns nil**, so a valueless statement fell out of the gate through a branch written to handle a different shape.

**The discriminator is the AST node having no children**, not the schema node being a leaf. A container legitimately takes its missing name level from nested children, and so does a leaf with modifier children (`address 10.0.0.1/24 { primary; }`). Rejecting on `missingArgs` alone condemns the dual-AST shape, and that mutation dies to its own control.

## Measured before landing, because the sibling did not survive it

K16 in this same review prescribes a gate of the same family. I built that one first: it rejects **the project's own shipped HA cluster config** plus four existing over-reach controls — 16 cells. It is filed as **#8662** with the measurement instead of a patch.

This gate was run against `pkg/config`, `pkg/configstore`, `pkg/cli` and `pkg/daemon` **before** being kept — zero failures — and carries its own explicit list of spellings it must NOT reject: a zero-arg flag leaf, a multi-value leaf, a correctly-authored modifier, and the hierarchical container shape.

## Population

| finding | claimed | actual |
|---|---|---|
| K15 | the `interface` modifier and a qualified `preference`/`metric` | `preference` was **already rejected**; the real population is **every `args > 0` leaf authored with no value**, in a different place entirely |

It is not a next-hop-modifier defect. Four instances are in the cells, which is why the gate is at the walker rather than per-leaf.

**One shape found while measuring is NOT fixed here**, stated so it is not mistaken for covered: `next-hop fe80::1 interface preference 7` compiles to `Interface: "preference"` — a modifier keyword installed as another modifier's value, with `preference 7` dropped. Catching that needs the #8437 sibling-token discriminator applied one level in, which is a separate gate with its own over-reach risk. Bundling it would put two unmeasured changes in one commit.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/configstore/ ./pkg/cli/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./cmd/cli/` — all pass. `gofmt -l` clean.

**4 mutations, each killed by a named cell:**

| mutation | killed by |

| container-path gate disabled | `ValuelessLeafIsRejected` — 3 of its 4 subcases |
| scalar-leaf gate disabled | `ValuelessLeafIsRejected` — the 4th |
| **over-broad**: reject on `missingArgs` alone | `ValuelessLeafGateIsScopedToLEAVES` |

## PR #8669 — nat64: correct the #8597 K62 note — /+96 is reachable and fails open [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-k62-correct-unreachability-claim`

Corrects a claim I landed in #8665. The K62 note there called the Go/Rust `+96` grammar divergence **unreachable**. It is reachable, and it fails open.

The claim was: no xpf version can persist a `/+96`, because `ParseUint` has never accepted a sign, so the value cannot survive the commit that would persist it.

That is a **commit-path argument** — and the headline finding of the very same PR is that a commit-path argument does not bound what reaches the runtime. K51 was real *precisely because* `Store.Load`/`Store.SyncApply` compile leniently and a violation becomes a warning. I applied that rule to K51's leaf and not to this one. Credit to @team-lead for catching it rather than endorsing it back.

## Measured end to end

| stage | result |
|---|---|
| strict commit | **REJECTED**, as documented |
| `Store.Load` / `SyncApply` | `emit()` warns and the loop `continue`s — rule **not dropped, not zeroed**; prefix reaches the helper **verbatim** |
| `Nat64State::from_snapshots` | **rule INSTALLED** — `prefix_bytes = 00:64:ff:9b:00…` (`64:ff9b::`), active and translating |
| same path, `/64` (**control**) | `is_active=false`, `0` prefixes |

The control is what makes (3) mean something: the loader *does* reject a bad length, so acceptance of `/+96` is the `+` specifically and not a broken probe.

## Why this is worse than a silent divergence

The warning emitted on the lenient path says the helper *"rejects the whole forwarding snapshot"* and that this rule *"will not reach the dataplane until it is corrected."* **Every clause is false for this input.** A warning asserting non-delivery while the rule is live is worse than no warning — it steers the operator away from the config that is actually running.

So the end state is: **the dataplane is running a NAT64 rule the control plane believes is inert, and says so out loud.**

## What is unchanged

The note's *conclusion* — **do not fix this by tightening the Rust parse** — was not the part that was wrong, and it stays exactly as written in both files. A backstop stricter than its gate silently skips cleanly-committed rules, which is the failure that code exists to prevent. The divergence is on the Go side of the lenient path, which is also where the false claim is made.

Filed as #8667 with three candidate directions (normalise the token into the snapshot; make the lenient *warning* predicate mirror Rust; reject on the Go side of the lenient path). This PR does not pick one — it only corrects the record, so the next reader is not misled by my own note while that is decided.

## Gate

Comment-only on both sides — **0 non-comment lines added** to either file. Scope is exactly those 2 files; all 6 deletions are the false paragraph being replaced.

Worth noting: the gate caught a **stale base**. My first run diffed against a `master` that had moved, and showed this branch deleting `pkg/config/ast_edit.go` and the `#8657` sibling-modifier test — someone else's landing. Merging current master first turned a 300-line phantom deletion into the 6 real ones. That is step 3 of the gate doing exactly its job.

`pkg/config` suite green, dataplane content-scanning canaries green, tree-wide `gofmt` clean, `userspace-dp` builds. The Rust probe used to produce the measurement ran against the real loader and was removed before commit.

Part of #8597 — no close keyword: the Lows landed in #8665, lane-8367 holds the Mediums plus K19/K23, and the defect this uncovers is tracked separately as #8667.

## PR #8671 — Fail closed on an unlistable images dir, gate the printed install (#8597 K07/K08) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b11`

Batch 11 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K07 and K08. Two fail-**open** shapes on the libvirt golden path in `scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py`.

**These are not the out-of-scope class K56–K61 was dispositioned into.** That call was about `scripts/` and `test/incus/` tooling with no product consequence. This file is driven by `make test-deploy`, ships as the deploy toolchain, and both of these end in a corrupted golden image under live HA overlays. The scope question was re-asked, not inherited.

## K07 — the guard passes when it could not look

`_dependent_overlays` swallowed an `OSError` from `os.listdir` and returned two **empty** lists. The caller reads that as *"nothing backs onto the golden"*, so the guard passes and `_atomic_install_golden` overwrites the golden under live overlays — #5043's HA-pair disk corruption, arrived at through the guard written to prevent it.

The state is not hypothetical: the non-root `fetch --install-libvirt` flow is a supported path where **this process cannot read the images directory and the `sudo install` fallback can still write the golden**. The guard's inputs and the write's privileges are different, so "I could not look" must not mean "there is nothing there".

Two things in the same file already said so, which is what makes this a straightforward call rather than a judgement:

- the function's **own docstring, three lines above the swallow** — *"`unknown` exists because an unprobeable file is not evidence of safety"*;
- its sibling `_golden_lock`, which reports its analogous `OSError` **loudly** (*"proceeding WITHOUT serialization"*) rather than proceeding silently.

Reported through the existing `unknown` channel rather than a new `die` site: the caller already refuses on any unknown with an actionable message, and one refusal path is easier to keep correct than two. The caller's text is widened from "sibling qcow2 file(s)" to "path(s)" and names the unlistable-directory case, so the message matches what can now appear in the list.

## K08 — a verification that already happened is not a gate

The `--no-import` / `--qcow2-only` path printed

```
sudo install -m 0644 -D <public path> <golden>
```

for the operator to run **later**. The two importing paths beside it stage into a private directory (`_verified_private_artifacts`, #5817) and re-verify the staged copy, precisely so *"a post-verify swap in `--out` cannot poison the golden"*.

This path cannot stage — it hands over a command to run at an unspecified later time — so the gap between the verify and the install is unbounded, and it is exactly the window `_verified_private_artifacts`' own docstring names: *"The public `--out` dir may be writable by another local process."* The golden is never re-verified downstream.

The printed command is now `sha256sum -c` on the computed digest, joined to the install by `&&`, so the check happens at the **moment of the write**. This is not the cwd-relative `sha256sum -c` that `sign.py` warns about: the digest and the path are on one line, so the file being hashed is the file being installed.

## Validation

Every `scripts/deploy/test_xpf_deploy_*.py` passes. The new file is picked up by `scripts/run-selftests.sh`'s existing glob — no wiring needed, verified rather than assumed.

**3 mutations, each killed by a named cell:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| `OSError` back to the silent empty return | `test_unlistable_images_dir_reports_unknown` |
| printed hint back to a bare `sudo install` | `test_printed_install_is_gated_on_sha256` |
| **over-broad**: report every images dir as unknown | `test_listable_dir_is_unaffected` |

The K08 cell binds the **shape** of the emitted command rather than its execution — driving the fetch subcommand needs a signing key and a network — and its docstring says so rather than reading as stronger than it is. What it catches is the regression that would actually happen: someone simplifying the hint back to a bare install.

## PR #8672 — ipmon: stop TestNotifyNextHopChangeGate racing the scheduler [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8664-ipmon-flake`

Two sightings of an intermittent failure under full-suite load, twice costing a
lane a diversion, and **never once with its assertion text captured**. The issue
carried a symptom and a hypothesis, and those were not the same thing.

## Made it deterministic instead of chasing it

Rather than stress and hope, perturb the timing budgets in **both** directions:

| budgets | result |
|---|---|
| **lengthened** to 400ms | 20 runs clean |
| **shortened** to 4ms | **fails every run**, at `probe failure did not actuate` |

That settles which of the test's four `t.Fatal` sites is fragile without waiting
for another sighting.

**It also refuted a competing model I held.** I had argued that sleep *overshoot*
under load would make the "must happen" assertions more robust and the "must not
happen" ones fragile — which inverts the reading in the issue. The experiment says
the opposite. The issue's reading was right and mine was wrong.

## The defect

The test mixes two waiting idioms:

- **"something MUST happen"** — fixed sleep, then assert it did. This is a race
  against the scheduler: it fails when the actuation is merely *late*, a property
  of the machine and not of the engine.
- **"nothing MUST happen"** — fixed sleep, then assert it did not. This genuinely
  needs a fixed wait; an absence cannot be polled for.

The "must happen" assertion now **polls to a deadline**, matching the idiom this
same test already uses correctly one assertion further down.

The absence windows are **unchanged in duration** — still 40ms — but expressed as
`4 * (debounce + throttle)` so they track those timings if either is retuned.
Enlarging them was rejected: it converts a fast flake into a slow one, makes the
next occurrence rarer and more confusing, and leaves the racing assertion racing.

## A second site, found by re-running the squeeze after the first fix

The literal-only arm captures its baseline `b2` after a fixed sleep — and **that
baseline is a "must happen" step in disguise.** If the transition's own actuation
has not landed when `b2` is taken, it lands during the next window and is
attributed to `NotifyNextHopChange`.

Squeezed, it failed with `literal-only policy actuated: 0 -> 1` — **a false
accusation rather than a missed event**, which would have sent the next reader
hunting a spurious-actuation bug that does not exist. It now waits for the
transition's actuation before baselining.

## PR #8673 — daemon: hand the scheduler tick its own context, so shutdown can join it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8660-scheduler-join`

Closes #8660

`stopPolicySchedulerLoop` ends in `schedulerWg.Wait()`. The goroutine it joins runs the scheduler tick, whose `publishPolicyScheduleState` acquired the apply semaphore with `d.daemonCtx` — the raw, production-uncancelled parent — falling back to `context.Background()` when nil. **Both branches are uncancellable**, so there was no configuration in which a parked tick could be released.

`schedulerCancel()` cancels a *child* of that parent, so with a tick mid-publish behind a wedged apply the cancel released nothing and the join blocked: shutdown never reached HA relinquish and systemd SIGKILLed the process — no `rg_active` clear, no priority-0 advert, no RA goodbye.

## The ctx was already in the caller's hand, three frames up

`startPolicySchedulerLoopLocked` does `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(d.daemonCtx)` and passes it to `sched.Run(ctx)`. `Run` held it and dropped it — `Run → evaluate → updateFn` did not carry it, so the closure reached for `d.daemonCtx`. This threads a value that already existed.

## Why option 1

Its stated cost is mostly not there: **two** production construction sites (one a no-op closure, so one real updateFn), and **`Scheduler.Update` — the only other path that fires `updateFn` without a ctx — has no production caller at all.** Residual churn is test sites, compiler-enforced.

**Option 3 rejected on the issue's own terms** — it makes a publish droppable, touches the #3780 latch and #5669 fail-closed, and owes a proof that a dropped publish converges, which is a claim about a *timer*. **Option 2** works but leaves the coupling implicit, and *a reader reaching for the wrong ctx is the defect itself*. A parameter makes it a type obligation. **The timeout was not widened** — a longer bound is still a stall and would satisfy a wall-clock cell while leaving the join blocked.

## Two findings worth more than the fix

**The pre-existing cell was green while testing a configuration production never has.** `TestPublishPolicyScheduleStateUsesDaemonContext` asserted that cancellation releases the parked publish — a real property — by cancelling `d.daemonCtx`, a field that is never cancelled in production and whose nil fallback is uncancellable. It verified a release path no running daemon could take, beside the one it actually took. It is re-aimed at the supplied ctx and now leaves `d.daemonCtx` **uncancelled as a control**: if the publish reads that field again, it times out.

**My first new cell claimed to bind a chain it did not.** It called `evaluate` directly and said it bound `Run → evaluate → updateFn`. A mutation making `Run` pass `context.Background()` — *the defect, one frame up* — left it **green**. A cell that calls the function under the defect cannot see its caller handing it the wrong argument. It now drives `Run` through a `tickInterval` seam, and that mutation kills it.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/...` **0 failures**; `gofmt -l` clean tree-wide; `go test ./pkg/dataplane/ -run 'Canary|Retirement'` ok (step 7).

| cell | binds |
|---|---|
| `TestRunHandsItsContextToUpdateFn8660` | Run's ctx reaches updateFn, and cancelling it cancels what updateFn got |
| `TestPublishPolicyScheduleStateReleasesOnSuppliedContext8660` | the publish releases on the ctx it is handed |
| `TestStopPolicySchedulerLoopJoinsATickParkedOnAWedgedApply_8660` | **the end-to-end join** — a real tick parked in the real scheduler goroutine behind a wedged apply, and stop still returns |
| `TestPublishPolicyScheduleStateWaitsWhenItsContextIsLive8660` | **the over-reject control** — a live ctx must WAIT for the permit |

The observable is named rather than assumed: a non-nil ctx proves nothing, since passing `Background()` down satisfies that and reinstates the defect. The join cell asserts the tick **actually entered** the publish and fails if it did not — "stop returned quickly" is also what a fixture that never parked a tick produces.

**The over-reject control exists because a mutation proved nothing else could see it.** Every other cell asserts something *releases* or *returns*, and that whole family is satisfied by a publish which never does its work: acquiring with an always-cancelled ctx **reds nothing** in `pkg/daemon`. Those cells were pinning *"returns fast"*, not *"returns correctly"* — the exact difference between bounding a stall and silently dropping the enforcement snapshot.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `Run` passes `context.Background()` | scheduler cell **RED** — and it **escaped** the first, evaluate-level version |
| publish re-reads `d.daemonCtx` | release cell + join cell **RED** (join at 15s vs 5s green) |
| publish always acquires with a cancelled ctx | **escaped everything** until the wait control was added; now **RED** |

Two seams added in the repo's existing `test_seams.go` form: `SetTickIntervalForTesting` (production is a fixed 60s) and `LatchRepublishForTesting` (which reaches the same #3780 latch the production error path sets, rather than inventing a second way to force a notify).

`stopPolicySchedulerLoop`'s residual comment is rewritten rather than deleted: what remains true is that the **order** matters — `cancel()` before `Wait()`, of the ctx the tick is parked on.

## PR #8674 — Omit the interval end for a prefix that reaches the top (#8597 K06) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b12`

Batch 12 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K06.

An anonymous nftables interval set encodes each prefix as a start key plus an `IntervalEnd` key at the first address the prefix does **not** cover. For a prefix whose last address is the top of the key space — `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, `128.0.0.0/1`, `255.255.255.255/32` — there is no such address, and `prefixNext` fell back to the **unspecified** address, which is the bottom.

## Verified against the real kernel, not argued

The set was installed in a private netns and read **back**; the kernel stores exactly what it is sent:

```
{0.0.0.0/0, 10.0.0.0/8}
  00000000, 00000000!end, 0a000000, 0b000000!end
  -> the /0 member is a ZERO-WIDTH interval. A term that must match
     everything matches nothing.                       Fail-CLOSED.

{128.0.0.0/1, 10.0.0.0/8}
  00000000!end, 0a000000, 0b000000!end, 80000000
  -> the wrapped end sorts to the BOTTOM as an end marker with no start
     before it; 128.0.0.0 is left open to the top anyway.  Fail-OPEN.
```

Two wrong encodings, in opposite directions, from one fallback.

**The kernel accepts both.** `Flush` succeeds either way — which is why this survived a package whose kernel-gated tests check that every construct *loads*. Loading was never the problem, so the guard reads the elements back rather than asserting an install succeeded.

`prefixNext` now returns `(addr, ok)` and the builder omits the end element when `ok` is false — the representation for an interval running to the end of the range. After the fix the same readback shows the stray `00000000!end` gone and `128.0.0.0` open to the top, with `10.0.0.0/8`'s closed interval untouched.

## Population

The finding names `/0` and "max-ending prefixes". Both are the same predicate — `lastAddr(pfx).Next()` invalid — and the helper's new boolean makes that one condition rather than a family-specific fallback per branch. `prefixNext` has one call site.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/nftables/` passes, and passes again under `unshare -rn env GOFLAGS=-mod=mod`, where the kernel-gated cells actually run rather than skip.

**2 mutations, each killed by a named cell:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| wrapped-`Unspecified` fallback restored | `TopOfRangePrefixHasNoEndElement`, `PrefixNextReportsWhetherAnEndExists`, `KernelStoresTheIntervalSetAsEmitted` |
| **over-broad**: drop the end element for EVERY prefix | `OrdinaryPrefixesStillGetTheirEnd` (plus the two above) |

The over-broad mutation matters more than usual here: dropping every end turns each interval open-ended from its lowest member upward — a total fail-open that looks like a simplification.

Docs updated: `pkg/nftables/README.md`.

## PR #8675 — config: correct the NAT64 prefix gate's stale failure-mode claims (#3888 hollowed #3886) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8667-nat64-stale-failure-mode-claims`

Four operator- and reader-facing places said a malformed NAT64 rule-set prefix makes the dataplane **reject the whole forwarding snapshot** and freeze at the last-good state, so *"this rule — and every later config change — will not reach the dataplane"*.

That was true when the gate was written (**#3886**). **#3888**, two issues later, made NAT64 fail *scoped*. Nothing re-checked the Go side.

## What #3888 actually changed

`Nat64State::from_snapshots*` is now **infallible**: it skips the offending rule with a loud log line and publishes the remaining NAT64 rules plus the rest of the forwarding snapshot. The fallible `try_from_snapshots` and its `Nat64UnparseableRule` variant were **removed** — `Nat64State` has no `try_from_snapshots` at all today, which is the method three of these comments name. That name and its whole-snapshot semantics belong to `Nptv6State`, which *is* still fail-closed; its own references in this file are correct and untouched.

**Measured, not read** — a snapshot with a malformed `64:ff9b::/64` alongside a valid `64:ff9b::/96`:

```
P1 mixed(bad /64 + good /96): is_active=true prefixes_installed=1
```

The bad rule is skipped, the good one publishes. Nothing freezes.

## Why fix the words rather than note them

The messages are what an operator acts on, and they point the wrong way. Told that *every later config change* is silently not reaching the dataplane, the reasonable response is to hunt a wedged control→dataplane pipeline and consider rolling back good config — when the truth is one missing NAT64 rule-set and everything else applying normally. **A false failure mode costs more than a vague one.**

The gate itself still earns its place on the narrower consequence: a malformed prefix silently disables NAT64 *for that rule-set*, with no operator-visible signal beyond a helper log line. Only its stated justification was hollow, so the #3886 rationale is rewritten rather than the gate weakened.

## Second defect on the same leaf

The lenient **warning fired on inputs the dataplane accepts**. #8597 K62 established that Rust's integer `FromStr` permits a leading `+` where Go's `ParseUint` permits none, so `64:ff9b::/+96` is rejected at commit and accepted by the helper — measured as installed, active, and **byte-identical to a canonical `/96`**:

```
P2 '/+96' alone:            is_active=true prefixes_installed=1
P3 '/96'  alone (reference): is_active=true prefixes_installed=1
P4 '/+96' bytes == '/96' bytes ? true
```

The old code warned anyway, telling the operator a live rule was inert. The warning makes a claim about the dataplane, so it now uses `dataplaneAcceptsNAT64Mask`, which mirrors the Rust mask parse exactly. **The strict gate still demands the canonical `/96` spelling** — that asymmetry is deliberate and is the invariant the file now states: *a backstop laxer than its gate is the safe direction, and the warning must mirror the backstop even where the gate is stricter.*

## Deliberately not done

**Tightening the Rust parse to reject `+96`.** A leniently-loaded config carrying `/+96` reaches the dataplane either way, and Rust's laxness is what makes that case *work* — it parses to 96, the correct value. A strict Rust parse would reject it at the dataplane instead, silently disabling NAT64 for that rule-set, which is the exact failure this gate exists to prevent.

## Validation

Three cells, each mutation-tested with a **compiling** mutant:

| mutation | killed by | observed |
|---|---|---|
| restore "aborts the entire forwarding rebuild" | message cell | quotes the stale phrase back |
| remove the lenient mirror | mirror cell | `prefix "64:ff9b::/+96": lenient warned=true, want false` |
| make the mirror stricter than the gate | safety sweep | `token "96": the commit gate ACCEPTS it but the dataplane would REJECT it` |
| remove the `+` laxness | sweep's degeneracy control | `no dataplane-only acceptance found … this cell proves nothing` |

The sweep runs 7,240 tokens and reports 1 dataplane-only, all leading `+`. The message cell asserts on **text**, because the message *is* the defect here — there is no behavioural symptom to observe — and it checks both that the stale claims are absent and that the true one is present, so a merely vague rewrite does not pass.

## PR #8676 — nat64: make the K62 note coherent and correct its "do not tighten" reason [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8667-k62-note-coherence`

Three revisions (#8665, #8669, #8675) edited the same note and it stopped being coherent. Four lines apart it said the divergence was *"a harmless, **unreachable** divergence"* and that it is *"**REACHABLE**, and the consequence is a fail-open."* #8669 corrected the second half and left the first standing, so the file carried both readings at once and a reader would believe whichever they reached first.

## Three corrections

**1. The stale "harmless, unreachable" sentence is gone.** Reachability was measured; nothing in the note may still assert otherwise.

**2. "active and translating" narrowed to what was actually observed.** The measurement is `is_active=true`, one prefix installed, `prefix_bytes` byte-identical to the state a canonical `64:ff9b::/96` produces. **No packet was driven through it.** The claim that matters survives — the installed rule *is* the canonical rule — but it is loader state, not a datapath observation, and the note now says which.

**3. The reason not to tighten the Rust parse is replaced, because the one given was wrong even though the instruction is right.**

It argued a stricter backstop would strand a cleanly-committed rule. It would not: the Go gate rejects **every one** of the 110 divergent tokens at commit, so no such rule can exist and that hazard is vacuous over exactly this set. The sweep recorded in the same comment says so — the refutation was sitting four paragraphs above the claim.

The real reason is that tightening converts a **fail-open into a fail-closed**. Today a leniently-loaded `/+96` translates with the correct prefix; tightened, it would be rejected at the loader and NAT64 would be off for that rule-set — a defensible posture, and arguably *better* than the current one. That is a behaviour decision belonging to #8667, which weighs it against normalising the token when the snapshot is built or accepting the spelling at commit. Doing it in the Rust parse alone would also paper over the live defect, which is on the Go side.

So the instruction is now **"do not tighten unilaterally"**, with a reason that does not overclaim.

## Also

The note described the lenient warning as falsely telling the operator the rule would not reach the dataplane. #8675 fixed that, so the description is now historical rather than current, and the note says the Go side mirrors this parse today.

Added the requirement that any eventual binding test must red on divergence in **either** direction — a one-directional cell would let the next drift through on the other side.

## Gate

Comment-only on both sides — **0 non-comment lines added** to either file. Scope is exactly those 2 files; all 42 deletions are superseded note text. `pkg/config` suite green, #8667 cells green, dataplane content-scanning canaries green, tree-wide `gofmt` clean, `userspace-dp` builds.

## PR #8677 — Bound the AST the parser builds (#8597 K14) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-muse-residual-b13`

Batch 13 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K14. **The last Medium.**

#5827 capped the retained **diagnostics** and said so precisely — *"only the parser's RETENTION is capped"*. The tree itself was not capped, and a **valid-syntax** payload produces zero diagnostics, so it passes that cap by construction.

## Measured

`runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc` after GC, tree kept alive:

```
stmts=10000    live heap  1,824,960   -> 182 B/statement
stmts=100000   live heap 18,589,296   -> 185 B/statement
stmts=500000   live heap 92,647,960   -> 185 B/statement
```

Linear, roughly **60x the input bytes** for a minimal `a;` statement. The 16 MiB `MaxConfigSize` ceiling therefore admits ~5.6M statements and about a **gigabyte** of live AST — built before any gate runs, on entry points that take untrusted input. `configstore.CheckText` validates a day-0 config-drive blob on first boot with no operator involved; the same parser sits behind load/commit and HA config-sync.

Both of the finding's refutations were re-checked rather than taken: `maxParseDepth` bounds **stack**, and a flat `a;a;a;…` payload never nests (confirmed by the linear measurement on flat input); the group-expansion budget runs **after** the tree exists.

After the fix, 2M statements retain the same 37 MB as 500k.

## The number is chosen against real configurations, not the input ceiling

`maxParseNodes = 200_000`. The largest configuration in this repository (`test/incus/xpf-test.conf`) is **250 statements**; the largest shipped one (`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf`) is **120**. The cap is ~800x the former, bounds the live AST to about 37 MB at the measured 185 B/node, and sits in the same order as the existing 100,000-unit group-expansion budget.

Deriving it from `MaxConfigSize` would defeat the purpose: 16 MiB of minimal statements **is** 5.6M nodes.

## Two details a naive implementation gets wrong

**The counter is parser-wide, not per-block.** A per-block counter bounds nothing — a payload of many small nested blocks builds an unbounded tree while no single block exceeds anything.

**The budget diagnostic is appended directly, bypassing `maxParseErrors`**, for the same reason #5827's suppressed-count summary is. A hostile payload can exhaust both caps; if the budget error went through `addError` it would be dropped as the 65th, and the caller would receive a **truncated tree whose error list says nothing about truncation** — silently accepted as the whole configuration.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/configstore/ ./pkg/cli/ ./cmd/cli/` — all pass, zero failures, measured **before** keeping the cap.

**4 mutations, each killed by a named cell:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| node budget removed | `ParseHeapDoesNotScalePastTheBudget`, `BudgetErrorSurvivesTheDiagnosticCap`, `NestedStatementsCountTowardTheBudget` |
| budget diagnostic routed through the capped `addError` | `BudgetErrorSurvivesTheDiagnosticCap` |
| **over-broad**: budget of 100 nodes | `RealConfigurationsAreFarBelowTheBudget`, `ParseHeapProbeCanSeeUnboundedGrowth` |
| counter made **per-block** | `NestedStatementsCountTowardTheBudget` |

**The diagnostic-cap mutation escaped the first version of its cell.** That fixture used unterminated strings — measured afterwards to produce **zero** parse errors, so the cell was asserting something about an error list that was never capped. It now uses stray bytes (64 errors + the #5827 summary) and asserts the cap was actually exhausted *before* asserting what survives it.

The heap cell measures a **ratio between two real parses** and carries a positive control that measures the same two sizes *below* the cap, where growth must still be visible — a ratio near 1.0 is also what a probe measuring nothing returns.

Docs updated: `pkg/config/README.md`.

## PR #8678 — Bound two config values before they reach a narrow wire field (#8597 K68/K72) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-lows-b14`

Batch 14 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual, and the first of the **Low** tier: K68 and K72.

Both are the family this tracker has now met six times — a config value reaching a narrower consumer with the bound enforced only on the strict commit path, while the tolerant Load / peer-sync ingress downgrades it to a warning (#1960).

## K68 — a mirror rate that wraps onto a SENTINEL

`Rate: uint32(inst.InputRate)` is the port-mirroring wire field, at **two** sites. `rate 4294967296` wraps to exactly **zero**, and zero in that field means **mirror every packet**. An operator asking for the sparsest possible sample gets a full traffic duplicate onto the output interface.

That is worse than the negative case #6534 wrote this predicate for. A negative rate mirrors nothing while the screen reads *"Input rate: all packets"* — the screen lies. **A wrapped zero makes the screen and the behaviour agree, and both are the opposite of what was asked for.**

The sibling knob already had the bound: `forwarding-options sampling` caps its own `InputRate` at `math.MaxUint32` (#1977). Port mirroring was left out of that sweep.

The fix goes in the **shared predicate**, not at the two cast sites, because `PortMirroringInstanceExcludedReason` is what the snapshot builder *and all three show surfaces* consult (#6534). Fixing the casts alone would drop the instance while three screens still rendered it as armed.

Excluding rather than capping, unlike the sampling sibling: it matches the negative case three lines up so one knob does not have two out-of-range behaviours, and a value this far out is a typo or a hostile config rather than a request for the sparsest mirror the wire can encode — capping would invent an intent (#6769).

## K72 — RA header timers wrapping to the MAXIMUM

Measured on the wire (`ndp.MarshalMessage` of `buildRA`):

```
DefaultLifetime = -1  ->  Router Lifetime 65535   (~18 hours)
ReachableTime   = -1  ->  4294967295 ms           (~49 days)
RetransTimer    = -1  ->  4294967295 ms
```

**A negative router lifetime advertised this box as a default router for the maximum the field can express.** `pruneUnmarshalableOptions` probes only the *options* for a marshal abort; the header fields marshal without complaint precisely because they wrap silently.

Flooring at 0 invents no intent: 0 is the documented neutral for all three — *"not a default router"* for the lifetime, *"unspecified"* for the other two — and is what the RA carried before these leaves existed. Above the field width the value **saturates**, which is monotone where wrapping is not: 70000 s used to marshal as 4464, a lifetime an order of magnitude *shorter* than asked for.

Both clamps bind `config.RARouterMaxLifetimeSeconds` / `config.RAReachableRetransMaxMillis` — the constants the commit gate uses, exported for this — rather than a local literal, so the gate and the sender cannot disagree about the ceiling. #4525 put a runtime floor on the advertisement **interval** for exactly this ingress; the header timers were not covered.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/ra/ ./pkg/dataplane/ ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/ ./cmd/cli/` — all pass. `gofmt -l` clean.

**6 mutations, each killed by a named cell:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| K68 upper bound removed | `OversizedMirrorInputRateIsExcluded`, `MirrorRateBoundaryIsTheWireWidth` |
| K68 **over-broad**: boundary off by one (excludes `MaxUint32` itself) | the same two |
| K72 negative floor removed | `NegativeRAHeaderTimersDoNotWrapToTheMaximum` |
| K72 upper saturation removed | `OversizedRAHeaderTimersSaturate`, `RAHeaderClampsBindTheSchemaConstants` |
| K72 millis floor off by one (`-1` still wraps) | `NegativeRAHeaderTimersDoNotWrapToTheMaximum` |
| K72 **over-broad**: lifetime clamp always returns 0 | `OversizedRAHeaderTimersSaturate`, `ValidRAHeaderTimersAreUnchanged`, `RAHeaderClampsBindTheSchemaConstants` |

The K68 boundary cell asserts the **rule** rather than the number: an admitted rate must survive the `uint32` cast unchanged and an excluded one must not, checked across the boundary. That is what makes the off-by-one mutation fail rather than merely shifting a literal.

The K72 cells marshal through `ndp` and re-parse rather than reading the struct back, because **the defect is the marshal** — a negative `Duration` is visibly negative in the struct and only becomes 65535 on the wire.

## PR #8679 — config: census the compact/block sites whose folded token declares children (#8662) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8662-census-children-bearing-folds`

The #2419 compact/block census excluded every folded token that **declares children** — and excluded them *silently*. Those sites were never enumerated, so they appeared in no skip bucket and the census's own *"this is a FLOOR"* note did not account for them. The gate reports its unruled sites honestly (252 not-observable, 44 uncompilable, 17 unsynthesizable); this class was in none of those tallies.

Relaxing the predicate adds **97 divergent sites and removes none**: checked 547 → 654. Two independent probes agree on the 97 — a standalone walk written before touching the gate, and the gate's own regeneration.

## Why the exclusion was wrong, not merely narrow

Declaring children says nothing about whether the compiler reads a folded tail. `transmit-rate` declares `exact`/`percent`/`remainder` — per its own comment, *"purely so `set ... transmit-rate ?` surfaces them"*. The census was excluding sites for a reason unrelated to the property it measures.

Both of #8662's hand-verified members sat in the hole, and both reproduce exactly:

```
class-of-service { schedulers be { transmit-rate 1g; } }  -> 125000000
class-of-service { schedulers be transmit-rate 1g; }      ->         0

security { zones { security-zone trust { interfaces ge-0/0/0.0; } } } -> [ge-0/0/0.0]
security { zones { security-zone trust interfaces ge-0/0/0.0; } }     -> []
```

The zone case is the worse of the two: **the elided form walks past the strict gate that rejects the braced form** for an undefined interface, so the zone commits clean and boots with no members.

## Scope, deliberately

The CoS member is now censused and tracked. **The zone member is not**, and a cell pins that rather than leaving it ambiguous: `security-zone <z> interfaces <if>` names its instance with a **wildcard**, not an `args` token, and this census's site model assumes the instance name is an arg. Covering it is a model change, not a predicate relaxation.

I probed that shape and am **not quoting the number**: my probe varied two things at once (wildcard *and* `args <= 1`), so it is confounded and not trustworthy. It goes to a follow-up done properly rather than bolted on here.

## What this is NOT

**It rejects no configuration.** The census is an inventory, not a gate on config. #8662 records that the prescribed blanket rule reddened 16 cells including the shipped HA config, because `redundancy-group 0 node 0 priority 200` is brace-elided **and read correctly**. Verified here — `TestShippedHAClusterConfigPassesCommitCheck8280` passes, as do the four over-reach controls that ruled the blanket rule out.

It also does not widen `packedTail`, which would validate a tail the compiler still ignores — a silent drop with a certificate.

## Second defect, found while fixing the first

**The regenerator destroys hand-written prose.** The inventory's #6940 note — explaining that a blind-spot count *rising* after a fix is the fix working — had been written into the generated file and was silently erased by the next regeneration. I only noticed because my own regen diff showed 21 removals I could not account for.

Prose in a generated file is not durable unless the generator emits it, so it now lives in `inventoryNotes`. The #6940 note is restored, and the #8662 findings including the uncovered wildcard shape are recorded beside it.

## Validation

| cell | asserts |
|---|---|
| class | the population is non-empty **and** contains the specific member #8662 verified — a count alone would be satisfied by any 97 sites |
| divergence | on the **compiled config**, not the inventory file, with a positive half that fails if the braced spelling stops carrying the rate (otherwise it compares two zeroes) |
| gap | the wildcard-named shape is still uncovered, and **reds if it becomes covered**, so the note cannot go stale silently |

**Mutation**: restoring the `children == nil` exclusion is killed by the class cell (*"the class #8662 measured is invisible again"*) **and** independently by the existing inventory gate.

Whole tree green (69 packages); tree-wide `gofmt` clean; dataplane content-scanning canaries green.
