## PR #8714 — config: report the duplicate-block loss that six containers hid (#8704) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8704-report-dup-block-loss`

A repeated hierarchical block for the same named instance loses configuration on a **strict commit that reports success**, with no warning on either path, for six containers. The worst:

```
security { ipsec { vpn v1 {
    traffic-selector ts1 { local-ip  10.0.0.0/24; }
    traffic-selector ts1 { remote-ip 10.1.0.0/24; }
} } }
  -> local-ip "", remote-ip 10.1.0.0/24, COMMIT ACCEPTED, zero warnings
```

A traffic selector decides **which traffic enters the tunnel**. It renders into `swanctl.conf` with the local side missing, so the SA is negotiated against a selector the operator did not write — on the path we tell operators is authoritative. The merged spelling keeps both halves, which attributes the loss to the re-opening rather than to the fixture.

## Why nothing saw it

`namedDupRules` reaches `<stanza> [<inner>] <keyword>` — two container levels, neither a named instance. These six sit deeper.

And #8436's conservation census, which *does* record them, binds **"conserved, refused, or listed"**. It does not bind **"conserved, refused, or reported"**. A listed exception is permitted to be silent, so every future silent site is compliant by construction — **an exception mechanism that does not require the exception to be visible turns a guard into a registration desk.**

## The fix

`deepDupRules` locates a container by explicit path. Duplicates are scoped to the **immediate holder**, not the rule: two VPNs may each carry a `traffic-selector ts1`, and a rule-wide map would reject that valid config (measured — two VPNs give two selectors).

Effects are **measured**, because `dupEffectStrict`'s own comment is right that a wrong effect sends the operator to delete the wrong block. traffic-selector is last-wins, established by authoring **both orders**: local-then-remote loses local, remote-then-local loses remote. One order alone would not have distinguished last-wins from "the local side is dropped".

## I tried to gate all six and the existing suite refuted two

That is the over-reach control working, and the result is in the code rather than in my head:

- **`protocols bgp group <g> neighbor` rejects valid config when gated** — it fails `TestSlotEscapeTable`'s control `set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2 import PS`, because flat-set authoring produces sibling nodes at this depth and the gate reads them as a repeated block.
- **the dhcp/dhcpv6 `static-binding` containers already have a better diagnosis** — a generic duplicate message pre-empts the duplicate-MAC rejection `TestDHCPStaticBindingRejectsDuplicateMAC` asserts, replacing *"this MAC is already bound"* with *"this block is repeated"*.

Both are recorded in `deepDupUnreportable` **with the measurement**. That is not the allowlist this issue was filed about: an entry must say what breaks, the binding fails for any container neither reported nor listed, **and it fails for a container that is reported AND listed** — a stale exemption is a standing claim of a hazard that no longer exists.

**I also lumped the five non-traffic-selector containers together and condemned them as a set on two failures.** Testing them individually showed three of the five were fine — the same probe-one-member error the whole finding came from, committed again inside the remedy.

Merging (Junos semantics) stays deferred: on a reload it would add content that has never been in effect on nodes running with the split, trading a silent loss for a silent gain.

## Validation

| cell | asserts |
|---|---|
| binding | every not-conserved container is reported **or** reasoned, with a degeneracy control that fails when nothing is not-conserved |
| traffic-selector | strict rejects and lenient warns; **positive half** fails if the merged control stops carrying both halves; the message must say **LAST** — what was measured — not something inferred |
| over-reach | two VPNs sharing a selector name still commit, with its own positive half requiring the fixture to really produce two |

**Mutation**, each mutant proven to have run: emptying the registry kills the binding and the traffic-selector cell; sharing the `seen` map across holders kills the over-reach cell.

Whole tree green (69 packages); shipped HA config green; tree-wide `gofmt` clean; dataplane content-scanning canaries green.

## PR #8715 — Bound the source-NAT pool numbering and seed the whole counter map (#8597 K75) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-lows-b29`

Batch 29 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K75.

The finding is *"`nat_port_counters` has 32 slots against a 256-wide PoolID space; the boot seed covers 0..31"*, with the fix direction *"size the seed loop and the shim spec from one constant tied to the pool-ID space"*. **Measured at this head, both halves are a different shape.**

## The 32 is not arbitrary

`MAX_NAT_POOLS` in `bpf/headers/xpf_common.h` is the **shared C/Go ABI** for that map: `xpf_maps.h` declares `nat_port_counters` with the C constant and `loader_userspace_shim.go` creates it with the Go mirror. *"Size it from the pool-ID space"* would desync Go from the header rather than resolve an incoherence.

What the seed loop actually owed was to stop repeating the number as a literal — it read `poolID < 32` next to a map declared with `userspaceShimMaxNATPools`: **the same number twice, with nothing to notice if one moved.** It now reads the constant, and a cell pins the Go/C agreement the way `TestMaxInterfacesMatchesCHeader` does.

The seeding loss the finding grades is also smaller than stated: `nat_port_counters` has had **no writer since #1476** deleted the eBPF pipeline, and #8606 moved every reader to the helper's live pool status keyed by pool *name* — precisely because the map reported a `rand.Uint64()` seed as occupancy.

## The pool-ID space is *unbounded*, not 256-wide

Nothing limited the numbering at all. `poolID uint8` increments per named pool and per anonymous interface-mode pool, `result.NextPoolID` likewise, and both wrap silently. Measured:

```
260 pools -> 256 distinct IDs, 4 colliding IDs, NextPoolID=4
pool ID 0 is shared by [pool256 pool000]
```

A wrapped `NextPoolID` then hands `compileNAT64`'s auto-assign branch an id another pool already holds.

The numbering now **saturates** at the `uint8` range and warns, mirroring `assignNATCounterID`'s exhaustion contract for the sibling identifier space — that one has a guard and this one did not. It saturates rather than rejecting because nothing indexes a live structure by this id, so 256 pools forward correctly today and a commit-time refusal would be a regression dressed as a fix.

**The cap is the `uint8` range, not `MAX_NAT_POOLS`.** Capping the allocator at the legacy map's 32 slots would reject working configs, and a cell at 40 pools fails if anyone does.

## A stale docstring, corrected

`compileNAT`'s header claimed `result.PoolIDs` is *"the source-NAT pool numbering the operator surfaces read back through ApplyResult (`show security nat source pool`, the REST/gRPC pool views, the Prometheus pool metrics)"*. They do not, and have not since #8606. Outside `pkg/dataplane` the only mentions of `PoolIDs` are the two `maps.Clone` calls in `apply.go`, and nothing reads it there.

That is *why* the aliasing is invisible today — and why it needed a guard rather than being left for a future consumer to inherit.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/dataplane/... ./pkg/daemon/ ./pkg/api/` pass; `go build ./...`, tree-wide `gofmt`, dataplane `Canary|Retirement` clean.

**7 mutations, each killed:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| the wrap guard removed (the defect) | `SaturateRatherThanWrap` |
| the **SNAT** allocation site unguarded only | both saturation cells |
| the **NAT64** auto-assign site unguarded only | `NAT64AutoAssignAlsoSaturates` |
| **over-broad**: the cap lowered to the legacy map's 32 slots | `PoolIDsAreDistinctAtNormalScale` |
| the seed loop's literal restored | `SeedNATPortCountersCoversTheWholeMap` |
| the Go cap drifted from the C header | `ShimNATPoolCapMatchesTheCHeader` |

**The NAT64 mutation escaped the first cell set** — guarding only the SNAT site passed everything I had written. Two allocation sites share one cursor, and a cell that drives one of them says nothing about the other.

## PR #8716 — config: ask the pass, not a model of it, in the #8690 partial-site guard [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8690-partial-guard-behavioural`

## The partial-site guard was checking a model of the normalizer, not the normalizer

This is the guard that prevents the **destructive** failure in #8690: normalizing
a site whose drop shape is `partial` truncates a tail that something **reads**,
and the config still commits clean.

It reconstructed the pair from the inventory path:

```go
head := fields[len(fields)-1]
kw   := fields[len(fields)-2]
if compactNormalizeInScope(kw, head) { ... }
```

Production doesn't pass that. It passes `node.Keys[0]`:

| shape | example | production sees |
|---|---|---|
| wildcard container | `interfaces { ge-0-0-0 mtu 1500; }` | `("ge-0-0-0", "mtu")` — the **instance name** |
| named child w/ args | `system { login { user u1 class X; } }` | `("user", "class")` — the **keyword** |
| plain child | `term t1 { then metric 5; }` | `("then", "metric")` |

The inventory path carries the schema **arg placeholder** in that position, so
for the ten `interfaces/bridge-domains xpfname <leaf>` partials the guard asked
`("xpfname", …)` while production asks `(<instance name>, …)`.

**It was sound — by accident, not by construction.** Production's keyword there
is an arbitrary instance name no static rule can match, and a head-only rule
matches both spellings, so the two questions happened to agree.

**The accident ends** the moment a partial site appears under a
named-child-with-args container: production asks `("user", "uid")`, the guard
asks `("xpfarg", "uid")`, matches nothing, and reports a clean scope for a
widening that truncates a tail something reads. Not hypothetical —
`system login user <u> uid` became a live site during #8697, and the identical
`("user","class")` shape already caused a real miss in #8708.

The guard now builds each partial site's elided spelling, runs
`normalizeCompactStanzas`, and requires the pass to leave it **alone** — the same
admission technique `TestCompactNormalizeScopePreservesCompiledResult8690`
already uses and documents. No model, no drift.

## The new degeneracy control is not decoration

The old loop iterated the inventory and **could not skip**. The new one drives a
real parse and **can** — an unsynthesizable value, an unparseable spelling, a
site absent from the census walk — and every skip is silent.

**A partial site the guard did not examine is not a site it found safe.** It is
precisely the one a widening can cross into unobserved. So the examined count is

## PR #8717 — Give the DHCPv6 dynamic-DNS policy the commit warnings it never had (#8597 K66) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-lows-b30`

Batch 30 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K66.

`validateDDNSBackendWarnings` read exactly one policy — `System.DHCPServer.DynamicDNS` — so the independent v6 policy #2691 P1b added got none of its diagnostics. The v6 stanza is committable through the **same** schema tree (`dhcpDynamicDNSSchema` is returned fresh per call for both parents), so this is a coverage gap, not a reachability one. Measured:

```
v4 `enable`, no update-server                        -> 1 warning
v6 `enable`, no update-server                        -> 0 warnings
v6 update-server + hmac-md5 + key without secret     -> 0 warnings
v6 `backend kea-d2`                                  -> 0 warnings
```

The silence covered the security-relevant halves too: the #4483 unsigned-UPDATE warning and the #2666 TSIG-tuple warning.

The body is now a per-policy helper called once per family. The label leads each message with the stanza the operator has to edit — and **the v4 strings are byte-identical to before the split**, which matters because every existing v4 pin matches on the substring `"dhcp dynamic-dns"` and would otherwise have started matching v6 input too.

## The inheritance note

This is worse than a one-family gap. `pkg/ddns` `ReconcileScoped` keeps the pre-#2663 compatibility rule that a family with **no block of its own inherits the other's**:

```go
if ddns4 == nil && ddns6 != nil { ddns4 = ddns6 }
```

so a broken v6-only block silently governs v4 as well. A warned single-family block now says so. The note is **attached to warnings** rather than emitted on its own, so a healthy single-family config — the historical and by far the most common shape — stays quiet.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/ddns/ ./pkg/dhcpserver/` pass; `go build ./...`, tree-wide `gofmt`, dataplane `Canary|Retirement` clean.

The v6 cells drive the real `set` → `SchemaValidate` → `CompileConfig` → `ValidateConfig` pipeline, mirroring the v4 pins, because the row is about what an operator sees at commit.

**8 mutations, each killed:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| the v6 policy not inspected (the defect) | all four class cells, the label cell, the inheritance cell |
| the v6 warnings carrying the v4 label | the label cell **and** the both-families cell |
| **over-broad**: the v4 wording changed by the split | seven **pre-existing** subtests of `TestDHCPDDNSBackendWarnings` |
| **over-broad**: the v6 note fires without a v6 warning | the healthy **v6-only** cell |
| **over-broad**: the v4 note fires without a v4 warning | the healthy v4-only cell + the pre-existing absent-or-disabled cell |
| **over-broad**: the note fires when both families have a block | the both-families cell |
| a **disabled** policy warned about | the pre-existing absent-or-disabled cell |

**The v6-note mutation escaped the first cell set.** The only healthy single-family fixture was a v4 one, and the v4 note has its own guard, so nothing exercised the v6 guard's quiet case.

> A quiet-when-healthy claim needs a fixture on each side.

**Docs:** `docs/config-schema.md`'s #1387 block claimed these warnings for the subtree shared by both parents. It is now accurate rather than aspirational, and records the per-family split plus the inheritance note.

**That choice has a cost the cell did not acknowledge.** Unlike a loop over a static list, it can **skip** a site — and a site it skipped is not a site it found safe. It reported only the admitted count, so skips were invisible and read as a clean scope.

@lane-8015 found this shape while making the partial-site guard behavioural (#8716) and added an examined-against-population reconciliation. The same gap arrived here for the same reason; this is the same fix.

## Three buckets, separated because they carry different weight

**19 skipped before scope can be determined** (17 unsynthesizable, 2 unparsable) — whether the pass touches them is unknown, so they are reported as unknown rather than counted clean.

**18 ARE normalized by the pass but cannot be examined**, because a reference spelling does not compile in isolation. **This is the dangerous bucket: production rewrites them and the cell says nothing.** Asserted for **equality** against a checked-in list — the same shape as the #2419 inventory. A new member reds because a widening admitted something invisible to the guard; a member that becomes examinable **also** reds, so the list cannot outlive its reason. A threshold would permit both.

**22 have unmeasurable gate status** (the third state from #8719).

## Why the 18 are not merely unfixtured

Every entry needs a required sibling *inside* the stanza that the synthesized fixture cannot supply — a `three-color-policer` with no rate block, an `ip-monitoring policy` with no probe. That is the **#8436 duplicate-block dependency** @lane-8526 measured: the compact spelling cannot carry the sibling, and re-opening the instance does not merge. They are unmeasurable by this method until #8436 lands. Recorded at the list so the next person does not try to fixture their way out of it.

## Scope

**No production code changes, no scope change.** This only makes the cell say what it does not know. The 18 are pre-existing and were being counted clean.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop an entry from the list | **red**, names it `NEW (pass normalizes it, cell cannot see it)` |
| add a bogus entry | **red**, names it `GONE (now examinable, drop from the list)` |

## PR #8723 — Serve the two console-only request verbs from the remote cli (#8597 K47) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8597-lows-b31`

Batch 31 of the #8597 muse-spark-review-004 residual: K47 — the last of the sixteen rows this lane claimed.

The remote `cli` dispatcher rejected two `request` verbs the SSOT command tree advertises and the local console implements:

```
request security policies check
  -> unknown request security target: policies
request system configuration rescue save|delete
  -> unknown request system command: configuration
```

Tab completion is served by that **same** cmdtree, so completion offered a command the dispatcher then refused. Fail-closed, hence Low — but the remote binary is the surface most operators use, and for `policies check` it withheld the shadowed-policy lint from remote incident response.

## Why two different RPCs

`policies check` is a pure config lint that produces **text** and mutates nothing — which is what `ShowText` is. Rescue save/delete are store mutations with a one-line result — which is what `SystemAction` is. Inventing a third RPC for a `request` verb would have added a method the #5278 authz map, the #7172 command table and every completeness guard each need a new case for, to express what two existing methods already express.

## Single-sourced, rendering included

`pkg/grpcapi` cannot import `pkg/cli` (`pkg/cli` imports `pkg/grpcapi`), so a server-side policy lint had to be either a second copy of the analysis or a move. It moved to `pkg/policymatch` — the package that exists because #3042 collapsed three hand-written shadow matchers into one after all three diverged from the runtime evaluator.

**Both the analysis and its rendering moved.** Sharing only `AnalyzePolicyShadowing` would leave each surface owning its own header line, empty-result sentence and nil-config wording — three strings that must agree for the command to mean the same thing on either surface, with nothing to notice when one changed.

The cells assert **agreement** between the surfaces rather than pinning either to a literal — the #8183 lesson, where the copy three golden files trusted was the broken one.

## Authorization parity, in both directions

`pkg/cli` charges the `request` family's `PermControl` for both verbs; neither is in `requestSubcommandIsMaintenance`'s destructive set. So:

- the `policies-check` topic is priced `PermControl` **explicitly** — left to the `show` family's view tier it would make the remote surface **looser** than the console;
- `rescue-save` / `rescue-delete` are listed **explicitly** — absent, they fall to `systemActionPermission`'s `PermMaint` default and make the remote surface **stricter**, the same parity defect this row is about, in the other direction.

The tier agreement is **two halves, not one test**: the CLI's resolver is unexported and the packages cannot import each other, so each half pins its own side and names the other in its failure message.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/cli/ ./pkg/grpcapi/ ./cmd/cli/ ./pkg/policymatch/ ./pkg/cmdtree/ ./pkg/api/ ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./pkg/showaudit/ ./pkg/docsref/` pass; `go build ./...`, tree-wide `gofmt`, dataplane `Canary|Retirement` clean.

**12 mutations, each killed:**

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| the remote security-policies case removed (the defect) | the remote dispatch cell + the help cell |
| the remote system-configuration case removed (the defect) | three rescue cells |
| `delete` mapped onto the `save` verb | the distinct-verbs cell |
| the rescue stray-argument refusal removed | the malformed-forms cell |
| the remote verb pointing at the wrong topic | the dispatch cell |
| the server topic dispatch removed | the agreement cells **and** the pre-existing #7172/#5278 completeness guards |
| the server handling only `rescue-save` | both pre-existing verb guards |
| the topic losing its explicit price | #7172 key-agreement, #5278 completeness, the parity cell |

## PR #8724 — config: anchor the compact/block positive control to a PARTIAL site (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8690-partial-anchor`

#8690 follow-up. #8721 withheld `interfaces <if> aggregated-ether-options lacp periodic` from normalization because it was one of the census's two hand-verified known-true anchors, and normalizing it blinded the instrument. **Right call for that increment, wrong shape for the problem.**

## Why it kept recurring

The anchor was an `empty` site — and an `empty` site is **by definition a candidate for the next widening**. It was consumed the moment its own family was normalized, and any `empty` replacement would be consumed by whoever takes the next family. The control needs a fresh hand-verification every increment, and the increment that forgets is the one where it silently stops proving anything.

@lane-8015 hit the same wall twice and diagnosed it: **re-anchor to a `partial` site**, which `TestNormalizerScopeNeverCoversAPartialSite8690` forbids *any* scope from covering. The control becomes structurally immune to the sweep rather than needing replacement.

## The new anchor, hand-verified by reading the compiler

Membership here requires reading the compiler, not trusting the inventory — my last candidate (`applications application <a> destination-port`) failed exactly that check.

`compileInterfaces` skips `if child.IsLeaf { continue }` at `compiler_interfaces.go:31`, and the compact `ge-0/0/0 mtu 9000;` **is** a leaf (Keys `["ge-0/0/0","mtu","9000"]`). So the whole **instance** is dropped, not merely the value.

```
braced   interfaces { ge-0/0/0 { mtu 9000; } }   -> mtu=9000
compact  interfaces { ge-0/0/0 mtu 9000; }       -> no interface at all
```

It also preserves the property the earlier swap established: a different compiler file from the surviving anchor in `compiler_protocols.go`.

With the anchor no longer depending on it, **`lacp periodic` is normalized** and the withholding note is retired. The site cost one increment; the structural fix ends the recurrence.

## Not the same trap one level up

An `empty` anchor is protected by nothing. A `partial` anchor is protected by a guard whose entire purpose is to forbid covering it — and by the inventory's own positive control. **Two independent mechanisms**, which the mutation shows.

## Mutation

Adding the pair `("interfaces","mtu")` does **nothing** — production passes the *instance name* there, so that pair is never asked. **A mutation that changes no behaviour is not a survival**, so it was redone as the realistic dangerous shape.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| pair `("interfaces","mtu")` | no-op — not a valid test |
| head-only `head == "mtu"` | **killed twice**: the positive control names the anchor, and the partial-site guard reds independently |

## PR #8727 — config: scope every #8690 normalizer rule by (container, head) pair [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-qualify-credential-heads`

Three rules in `compactNormalizeInScope` matched on a **single token**: `head == "authentication-key"` and `containerKeyword == "match"` (#8689), and the credential head map (#8708). Each was correct for the inventory as it stood, and for no stronger reason than that. Refs #8690.

**That is the defect.** A head-only rule is safe only while no container acquires that head with a tail somebody reads; a container-only rule is safe only while no head appears under it that somebody reads. Both make the predicate's correctness contingent on the **current inventory** rather than on the rule — and this sweep moves the inventory, so such a rule fails when a family lands, inside someone else's merge conflict. @lane-8526 raised this against the credential rule; it applied equally to the two older ones.

**Both directions were real, not hypothetical.** `containerKeyword == "match"` was written for security policies and NAT rule-sets, and also admitted `services ip-monitoring policy <p> match rpm-probe` — a different feature in a different subtree, reached only because it spells its criteria block `match`. It stays in scope because it **measured** safe, not because the rule meant it.

## This is a restatement of scope, not a widening

The 35 pairs are exactly what the three rules admitted:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| admitted sites | 351 | **351** |
| empty-equivalent | 269 | **269** |
| inventory lines | 186 | **186** |

## The pairs came from the schema, and my first attempt used the census and was wrong

`TestCompactNormalizeRunsAtBothCompileEntryPoints8690` red on its own fixture. `security ike policy <p> pre-shared-key` is a **real site** the head-only rule admitted, is **not a census site**, and so never appeared in a census-derived pair list.

**The admitted-site count did not move either** — because that count is taken over the same census. The check meant to prove behaviour preservation was structurally unable to see the narrowing. A schema walk found three such pairs: `policy pre-shared-key`, `match source-address-excluded`, `match destination-address-excluded`.

## The property is now permanent, not the state

`TestNormalizerScopeIsPairScopedNotTokenScoped8690` re-asks, for every admitted pair, with the container replaced by a sentinel no schema contains — and again with the head replaced. If either still says yes, the rule was reading one token.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| reintroduce `head == "authentication-key"` | **red**, names 20 head-only rules |
| reintroduce `containerKeyword == "match"` | **red**, names 58 container-only rules |
| walk admits nothing | **red** (degeneracy control) |

A future single-token rule reds by being *written* the old way, rather than depending on someone noticing it in review.

## One documented cost

The #6662 `authentication`/`user` exclusion is kept and now documented as **pre-empting every pair below it**. With pair scoping it is no longer load-bearing for the credential heads, but it remains the explicit record of that decision — and a future pair naming those containers would silently never fire. A rule that cannot match reads like coverage, the same trap as the wildcard-container site in #8719, so the escape hatch is stated at the site.

This takes the smallest bucket. Every one of the ten sites it resolved turned out to be a verdict about `synthPair`, not about the leaf.

## Three declared value types the switch never covered

`ValueHostname`, `ValueDate` and `ValueUnixSocketPath` fell through to the one-example bailout, so six leaves were recorded *"no two distinct synthesizable values"* while their own declared type says exactly what they take.

## Five enum leaves whose second value the schema already knew

`system services {dhcp,dhcpv6}-local-server dynamic-dns backend` (rfc2136 | kea-d2), `system services dynamic-dns provider <p> backend` (six backends) and `system services ssh protocol-version` (v1 | v2) each declare **one** `valueExamples` entry with the accepted set inside a `ValidateEnum` closure.

**The set does not have to be duplicated here.** `ValidateEnum` *names* it when it rejects — `invalid value %q (expected one of: a, b, c)` — so a deliberately invalid probe makes the schema state its own answer. The alternatives are worse: parsing `valueDesc` prose invents a grammar over free text that would silently produce **wrong** values as the wording drifts, and copying the sets into the test duplicates the schema, which is the failure mode every census note in this package is about.

> The parse cannot produce a wrong answer, only no answer — every candidate is re-verified by calling the same validator with it.

```
checked         677 -> 685
divergent       186 -> 191
no-pair          17 -> 7
not-observable  234 -> 236
removed           0

> A blind-spot count that rises after a fix is the fix working.

They land in `schedulers` and `system`, both held by **lane-8388**, so that family's count grows by five — flagged on the issue.

Three became **equivalent**, and two moved to the not-observable bucket — still unruled, but now for the *fixture* reason a `contextFor` entry addresses rather than for a missing synthesiser.

Seven remain in the no-pair bucket and **six are declared inert by their own `valueDesc`**: `authentication-type` (*"not an OSPF leaf; use `authentication { md5 ... }`"*) ×2 and the four `system login class` regexp leaves (*"not implemented by xpf"*). ## PR #8730 — config: classify what remains in the #2419 inventory, and retire the zero target (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-exclusion-artifact`

## #8690 is essentially finished — and the artifact it leaves behind was the wrong one

**47 lines remain; 42 must NEVER be normalized. Two are genuinely available work.**

A bare remaining-count reads as remaining **work**. The only way to drive this
one down is to normalize sites the guards exist to protect — so the number would
eventually argue against the guards. That pressure is not hypothetical: the
file's own plan of record said *"the PR 2 normalizer should drive this file to
zero data lines, and the diff is the evidence for that claim."* True when every
line was a compact-blind reader awaiting a fix; **false now, in the direction
that costs the most.**

## The register

`testdata/compact_block_permanent_exclusions_8690.txt` classifies every
remaining line with its class and the measurement behind it:

| class | n | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `partial` | 20 | something already **consumes** part of the tail |
| `gate` | 17 | normalizing makes a config the box **refuses today** start committing clean |
| `unclassified` | 3 | in another lane's family, **not measured here** |
| `open` | 2 | genuinely available |
| `hazard` | 2 | breaks documented shipped behaviour |
| `unreachable` | 1 | no `(container, head)` rule can express it |
| `unmeasurable` | 1 | the fixture cannot produce a type-valid value |
| `gate-collateral` | 1 | shares a pair with a `gate` site |

**`unclassified` is deliberately distinct from `open`.** Three `system` lines are
in another lane's family and were not measured here; recording them as available
would assert a measurement nobody took. *Nobody has checked* is a third state.

## It is a gate, not a registry

A file that only accumulates is a place to hide defects. Set-equality is asserted
against the inventory in **both** directions:

- **a listed site that LEFT the inventory reds.** A site leaves when compact and
  block compile the same — so for these it means a widening normalized something
  the register says must never be normalized. Either a gate was disarmed or the
  classification was wrong. Both need a human; both are otherwise silent.
- **an inventory site ABSENT from the register reds**, because an unclassified
  remaining line is exactly what reads as work.

Two cross-checks keep the classification honest: a site classed `partial` must be
marked `partial` by the inventory and vice versa — that class is the one
`NeverCoversAPartialSite8690` actually enforces, so a wrong entry is a protection
nobody is applying. And **a class with no reason is rejected at parse**: the
reason is the part a future reader cannot reconstruct.

## PR #8731 — config: normalize `policy proposal-set`, the two sites a gate had blocked (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-policy-proposal-set`

@lane-8015 landed the security family in `950df1331` while I was measuring the same 47 sites, so **45 of them were already done** — my pair list for those is dropped rather than landed redundantly. Two remained:

```
security ike   policy <p> proposal-set
security ipsec policy <p> proposal-set
```

They share one `(container, head)` pair, and they were left **not because of anything about the fold** but because a commit gate blocked them. The disarm arm flags them REJECTED without the pass and ACCEPTED with it — a red until a person classifies it, so no widening could take them without doing that first.

## Classified benign, with the gate saying so itself

```
elided, pass disabled  -> REJECTED "ipsec policy p1 has no resolvable ipsec proposal ...
                          the configured perfect-forward-secrecy group would be
                          SILENTLY DROPPED"
elided, pass enabled   -> accepted
braced (the reference) -> accepted either way
```

The config was always legitimate; only the elided spelling lost the proposal-set. **That gate exists to catch this exact drop**, which makes the pass repairing the drop and the gate then passing the intended interaction rather than a disarm. Same classification as `snmp trap-group <t> targets` in #8726, and the second entry in that map.

## Consequence

A `proposal-set` names the crypto proposals an IPsec policy offers. Brace-elided it compiled to nothing — so the policy negotiated with a different proposal set than the operator wrote, **and the gate that would have said so was itself suppressed by the drop.**

## Cells

The consequence cell carries a positive half that fails if the *braced* spelling stops carrying the proposal-set, and a **non-vacuity guard** asserting the two spellings actually differ — an earlier draft of a cell in this family had them byte-identical and compared a config to itself. The scope cell asserts the pair stays a pair.

| mutation | killed by |

| drop the pair | consequence cell |

## PR #8733 — config: scaffold the fixtures the compiler was rejecting (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8690-lane8367-b2`

Second increment of the #8690 unruled-fixture sweep. The first took the smallest bucket (no synthesizable pair, 17 → 7); this takes the next, **"a spelling did not parse or compile": 45 → 31**.

```
checked      685 -> 699
divergent    +12
removed        0
```

Every one of the fourteen was a fixture the **compiler** rejected — and the compiler said why:

```
services rpm probe <p> test <t>: target is required
services ip-monitoring policy <p>: match rpm-probe is required
firewall three-color-policer <n> requires positive committed-information-rate
security nat source pool <p>: deterministic host address required
policy <p> references undefined scheduler <s>
```

Each scaffold is the smallest addition that turns that rejection into a compiled config. **None was guessed.**

## Two mechanisms, because the requirement is not always inside the parent

`contextForStanza` widens `contextFor` with the **stanza under test**, because a three-color-policer's `single-rate` and `two-rate` are *mutually exclusive*: the right scaffold depends on which is being probed, and a fixture carrying both is rejected outright.

`preambleFor` is new — a top-level prefix for a requirement **outside** the site's container tree. An ip-monitoring policy must name a probe under `services rpm`, a sibling of `ip-monitoring`; a policy's `scheduler-name` must name one under the top-level `schedulers`; a deterministic NAT pool needs an address range on the *pool*, a sibling of `port`.

Both are additive because **a re-opened block merges** — measured before being relied on, at both the inner and the top level.

## `contextFor` keeps its signature and its answers

Five other censuses call `contextFor(parent)`. Every new entry is gated on a **non-empty stanza**, so those five get byte-identical fixtures. Widening a shared helper under several in-flight guards is how a census starts measuring something nobody asked it to — and the mutation that removes that gate reds one of *those* guards, not just mine.

The depth census is the deliberate exception: its own premise is *"depth 1 IS the base census's spelling"*, so it takes the same two calls. `TestCompactDepth1AgreesWithTheBaseCensus7653` **went red** the moment the base census learned a scaffold that walker did not have.

> That cross-check working is how this landed correctly rather than as two disagreeing accountings.

## What remains, and why none of it is a missing scaffold

- **13** whose own leaf *value* is synthesized as `xpfaaa` and rejected by the leaf (a burst size, a rate, an IP). The `synthPair` gap again, surfacing in this bucket rather than the no-pair one because the fixture got far enough to be rejected for the value instead of the shape.
- **6** under `class-of-service fairness rss-expectation interface <i> queue <n>`, whose *instance name* must be 0..255 and is synthesized as `xpfarg` — a site-model gap, the same shape #8662 fixed for the wildcard container.
- `system services ssh ciphers` / `macs` (an example containing `@` that needs quoting) and `system dataplane-type`, where **the validator accepts a value the compiler then rejects** — a finding about those two disagreeing, not about this census.

## One thing removed rather than shipped

A first attempt added nine more `ValueType`s to `synthPair` for the value class above. **It moved nothing** — the leaves in question are untyped, so the switch never reached them — and it was removed.

> Inert code that looks like a fix is worse than the gap it does not close.

## PR #8734 — config: record what arm 2 cannot see, and keep the claim executable [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-arm2-reach`

**A green arm 2 does not mean a widening is safe**, and until now nothing in the file said so. Refs #8690.

The arm compiles **one well-formed elided spelling** and compares acceptance against rejection. Any gate whose predicate needs something that spelling cannot express is invisible to it **by construction**, not by oversight. Three kinds are known — and every one was caught by an ordinary cell in the full suite *after* arm 2 passed:

| blind spot | example | why arm 2 can't see it |
|---|---|---|
| gate fires on a **duplicate** | `chassis … ip-monitoring global-weight` — *"specified 2 times with different values"* | one spelling cannot be two occurrences |
| gate fires on a **trailing token** | `security ike gateway <g> dynamic hostname <fqdn> <extra>` | the fixture supplies a well-formed value and no extra |
| **content survival** across a multi-statement packed body | `redundancy-group` losing `preempt` | a wrong compiled *result*, not a wrong verdict — an acceptance comparison never looks |

**So the operative instruction now sits in the arm: run the full `pkg/config` suite after a widening. It is not redundant with this cell.** All three were found that way, by @lane-8015, on families where arm 2 was green.

## The duplicate case is circular, and that is worth keeping

Those chassis sites are **absent from the census precisely because the gate rejects their packed spelling** — so an inventory-based over-reach analysis cannot see them either. **Absence caused by the very gate the widening would disarm.**

## The claim is executable, not prose

`TestArm2CannotSeeATrailingTokenGate8690` pins the one kind isolable in a fixture: the well-formed spelling compiles, the extra-token spelling is rejected, so the arm reports "no gate here" for a site a gate governs. **If the arm later learns to vary token count, this cell reds** and the limitation note shrinks with it rather than outliving its reason.

The other two are **described and attributed but not asserted** — I could not isolate them in a fixture, and asserting a shape I have not measured is the defect this file exists to catch. My first duplicate fixture had *both* the single and the duplicate spelling rejecting, which demonstrates nothing.

## Visibility is not a verdict

The fixture-limited bucket's message now instructs **hand-measurement before an entry is added**. Reporting the third state is necessary and **not sufficient**: `security dynamic-address feed-server <n> url` sat in that bucket reported as merely unmeasured, and hand-measuring it with a real URL showed it **rejected without the pass and accepted with it**. lane-8015 found that; no guard in the tree would have. **The bucket is where a disarm hides.**

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope. Mutation-tested — swapping the demonstration's fixtures so it asserts the wrong direction reds it.

Third increment of the #8690 unruled-fixture sweep. The first two drove the two small buckets down (no-pair 17 → 7, uncompilable 45 → 31). **This one does not move the largest — it says what is in it**, which turns out to matter more.

`leaf value not observable in the typed config` holds **236** sites, and the census's own note described every one of them as *"a site whose synthesized fixture was too thin to observe the value (as #6821 was before its required-sibling context line)"*.

Measured, that describes **five**:

```
nothing registered (fixture too thin)          5
stanza registered, leaf contributed nothing  219
registered, but the value did not vary        12
```

**The 219 are not a fixture backlog.** Their stanza compiles, their own empty skeleton compiles, and the two are **equal** — so the compiler reads the stanza and does not read the leaf, under *either* spelling. That is why they cannot be compact/block divergences, and it makes them a question about the **compiler** (a leaf that commits and does nothing, a leaf consumed elsewhere, or one needing an in-stanza sibling) rather than about this census.

Recording the split is the point. **236 reads as one backlog and would have been worked as one**; the three numbers are three different pieces of work, and only the first is the one the note described. The classification is computed by the census itself and reported beside the counts, so nobody needs a scratch probe to see it.

|---|---|
| the residual arm stops counting | the partition check (the classes must **sum** to the bucket) |
| the two arms **swapped** | the reachability check |

The swap is the one worth recording. Every nothing-registered site also satisfies the leaf-ignored test — its skeleton compiles to empty too — so testing leaf-ignored first silently absorbs all five, **and the partition check still passes** because the total is unchanged.

> A sum over classes cannot see a class going empty; only asserting each arm is *reachable* can.

#8730's message said a `gate-confirmed` entry with a reason under 80 characters
is rejected at parse. **It was not.** The edit adding it used a silent string
replacement whose anchor stopped matching after gofmt, and I described the guard
as broader than it was — the same failure mode this register exists to prevent,
committed against the register.

Both checks are now present, mutation-tested, and the replacement that adds them
**asserts its anchor**.

## `owed-own-change` — a class for "the fix is right, the vehicle is wrong"

`security policies {from-zone <a> <b> <c> | global} policy <p> scheduler-name`
was classed `unmeasurable`, which is false — it *can* be measured — and it must
not be swept into a family widening. Two consequences, and the second is what a
commit-time reading misses:

- **commit-time**, in lane-8526's words: *"it would start rejecting configs that
  pass today"*;
- **forwarding**: today the dropped `scheduler-name` leaves the policy with **no
  schedule at all**, so normalizing converts a **permanently-active** security
  policy into a **time-limited** one. That changes what traffic is permitted and
  when, so it owes `make test-failover` v4+v6, not a commit-check alone.

Neither `open` (sweeping it would be wrong) nor permanent (normalizing it is
right). Without the class such a site can only be recorded as an exclusion —
false — or as available, which invites the sweep.

**An `owed-own-change` entry whose reason names no owed verification is
rejected.**

## UNKNOWN must say WHY, not just THAT

The twelve sites that entered after `fa7d18502` carried their *provenance* —
which lane, which sweep made them visible — which reads as an explanation while
explaining nothing about measurability.

Admitting them produces no disarm from arm 2, **but it also moves them into the
set arm 2 cannot examine** — so arm 2's silence is the **absence of evidence**,
not evidence of absence. Every UNKNOWN reason now says so, held by two checks: a
length floor, and a requirement that the reason actually state the measurement
was not or cannot be taken.

**A long, plausible reason that never states absence passes the first and fails
the second** — and that is precisely the shape that would otherwise read as
cleared.

scheduler DEFINED    skipNorm=false  err=<nil>   pol[p1].SchedulerName="S"
scheduler DEFINED    skipNorm=true   err=<nil>   pol[p1].SchedulerName="S"
scheduler UNDEFINED  skipNorm=false  err=policy "p1" references undefined scheduler "S"

with the pass on and off; the hierarchical sibling-elided form is rejected by

## PR #8745 — config: separate an unread leaf from a sibling wall, and record a heuristic not to fix (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8690-lane8367-b4`

Fourth increment of the #8690 unruled sweep, and it starts with a correction to my own #8735 wording.

I split the 236 not-observable sites into three classes and described the largest — **219** whose stanza registers and whose leaf adds nothing — as *"the compiler does not read the leaf"*. **That was stronger than the instrument.** The classifier cannot distinguish it from a leaf read only once a required sibling is present, which is #6821's case and is structurally unreachable from the fixture side.

This is the experiment that separates them.

## The method

For each site: add the **other children of the same stanza**, each with a value the schema itself declares, and re-compare the two probe values. If the leaf starts contributing, it is a sibling wall; if not, it is genuinely unread.

With a **positive control**: the sibling fixture must itself have changed the compiled config. Without that, *"still unread with a sibling"* is a conclusion drawn from a fixture that did not actually change.

## The measurement

```
sibling-wall                                   6/219    3%
genuinely-unread                              41/219   19%
inconclusive: the siblings were unread too   135/219   62%
inconclusive: no sibling declared             36/219   16%
inconclusive: sibling fixture did not compile  1/219    0%
```

Of the **47 determinable** the split is **41:6** — but **79% is not determinable**, and that is the headline rather than the ratio.

All six sibling-wall sites are `security log stream <s>`, the container #6821 wrote the required-sibling mechanism for. **The case the census already knows needs a sibling is the case this classifier finds** — a coherence check on the whole experiment.

## Two fixture hypotheses tested, both refuted

- **Container siblings** as well as leaf siblings (the generator emitted only `args == 1` children): moved **4 of 137**.
- **A parent-chain preamble**, measured by hand on `class-of-service interfaces <i> unit <u> scheduler-map` — declaring the interface under `interfaces {}`, declaring the scheduler-map, and both: **still not observable in every combination**.

So this is a **wall, not a backlog**. The remaining work per site is not "add a fixture entry"; the two mechanisms that could add one have been tried and do not move it.

## A heuristic *not* to fix, recorded where it will be found

`synthPair`'s numeric-placeholder test matches `id` as a **substring**, so `<provider-name>` (prov·**id**·er), `<identity>` and `<bandwidth>` get numeric probes alongside `<uid>`. That reads as a defect. Bounding it to a whole token made the census measure **less** — checked 699 → 697, not-observable 236 → 238: two sites are observable *only* because the loose match hands them a number.

> A heuristic that is wrong for the right reason can be right in effect.

The note is in the census file rather than only in an issue comment, because the next reader finds the substring match before they find the measurement.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./pkg/cli/` pass; `go build ./...` and tree-wide `gofmt` clean.

| the sibling-wall arm can never fire | the reachability cell |

Every entry now carries a verdict **a person reached**, with a type-valid value and the siblings its validator needs. 22 were marked "nobody has looked"; the count is now **zero**. Refs #8690.

@lane-8015 established why this matters — it hand-measured three sites and one was a would-be gate disarm no guard in the tree would have caught. The bucket had been growing on the strength of visibility alone.

All trip the same #8430 gate for the same reason. Without the pass the elided spelling drops the criterion and the gate refuses an empty match set (*"the dataplane reads an EMPTY match set as UNCONSTRAINED — this rule would translate EVERY packet reaching it"*); with it the criterion survives. **Benign** — and the decisive evidence is not the acceptance flip but that elided-with-pass compiles to a config **identical to the braced spelling's**, verified directly.

They share **one verdict constant** rather than thirteen copies: thirteen restatements would read as thirteen independent confirmations of something established once.

#3044 requires all three of `source-address`, `destination-address`, `application`, and the elided spelling carries only **one** criterion — so both spellings are rejected however good the fixture is.

```
pass OFF -> "missing required criterion source-address, destination-address, application"   (three)
pass ON  -> "missing required criterion destination-address, application"                   (two)
```

The criterion that survives is the one that was folded.

**Two BGP `neighbor {export,import}`** — safe; both spellings compile cleanly, no gate involved. The arm read them as undecidable only because its minimal fixture lacked the referenced policy.

Four `-name` leaves reported undecidable *again* on my first pass, because I put the address-book inside a **zone** and NAT resolves address names against the **global** book. With the book moved they measure benign like the rest.

**A fixture that is wrong in a new way produces the same "undecidable" output as a site that genuinely is** — which is exactly the confusion this bucket exists to prevent, reappearing one level up.

## Validation

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope. The cell now reports how much of the bucket is measured, so a widening that adds an undecidable site without measuring it is visible rather than absorbed — reported rather than failed, since whether such an entry may land is a policy call across lanes.

`target` is the benign pattern: the gate refuses the CONSEQUENCE of the
drop ("target is required") and the pass repairs it. The other nine are

the site -- a wildcard-named container. These mean the rule names it

required sibling cannot ride along in the compact spelling. Same
conclusion, different wall, and collapsing them would lose which wall a
future reader is standing at. Its parse rule requires the reason to
state the measurement was taken with the pair ADMITTED: for an excluded
pair "nothing changes" is true by construction, so the qualifier is the
entire claim.

Nine of the ten would have inherited `target`'s verdict under any
family-level judgement. That is the v4/v6 static-binding lesson reached
from the opposite direction -- there the twins differed in whether the
INSTRUMENT could see them, here in whether the PASS changes anything.

## PR #8748 — config: pin the flat-set vs hierarchical merge difference as a guard [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/flat-set-merge-guard`

CLAUDE.md states the rule outright -- "Testing flat set syntax: ALWAYS
use ParseSetCommand() + tree.SetPath() loop, NEVER NewParser()" -- and
three separate people broke it on one issue in one day, each writing
hierarchical text through NewParser as a stand-in for what a CLI `set`
session produces, and each drawing a conclusion the flat spelling does
not support. One lane listed it as error 1 of a withdrawn consequence
class; I did it in my first probe on `policy <p> scheduler-name` and
retracted a decision because of it; a lane then did it again in the PR
correcting that retraction, attributing a duplicate-policy shape to two
`set` lines that in fact merge.

Prose lost three times, so this pins the difference instead.

Measured, and asserted here on BOTH compile paths because the whole
confusion was that they can disagree:

  flat set, either ordering  -> ONE policy, scheduler-name preserved,
                                match criteria intact
  hierarchical duplicate     -> TWO policies: the operator's, with its
                                schedule LOST, plus a match-less
                                duplicate defaulting to deny

The hierarchical shape is the one that reaches production -- through a
hand-edited file, a config written by an older build, or an HA peer push
-- which is precisely the population Store.Load and Store.SyncApply
exist to accept. It is not what the CLI produces.

The cell identifies the operator's policy by its match criteria rather
than by index, so a reordering cannot silently invert the assertion, and
each failure message says what a change in that direction would mean
rather than only that a number moved.

Why prose was not enough, recorded in the cell: hand-written
hierarchical text LOOKS like a faithful rendering of a CLI session, the
merge behaviour is the entire difference, and a fixture that gets it
wrong does not fail -- it produces a different, plausible config and
confidently answers a question nobody asked.

Validation: both mutants killed, each in its own subtest, by making each
subtest use the OTHER spelling -- the exact error the cell exists to
catch. `go test ./...` green tree-wide, 77 packages, 0 failures;
`gofmt -l` clean.

## PR #8749 — config: hard-fail unmeasured bucket entries, and catch cross-switch duplicate pairs [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-hardfail-unmeasured`

Two changes, both enforceable **only because of measurements that just landed**. Refs #8690.

## 1. An unmeasured bucket entry is now a hard failure

Possible only because the backlog reached zero in 27aed7c9e — with entries outstanding it would have had to grandfather them and would have been **born weak**.

A reported count starts at zero and grows one individually-defensible entry at a time, and the entire history of this bucket is that **visible-but-unmeasured reads as clean**. @lane-8015 measured three of its entries by hand and one was a would-be gate disarm no other guard in the tree would have caught.

The escape hatch is not a threshold but a person: record what you found, the same shape as `benign`.

## 2. No pair may be admitted by two family switches — a safety property, not tidiness

Each family added its own `switch containerKeyword + " " + head` block; nothing stops two listing the same pair, and **52 currently do**.

Harmless while the answer is "admit" — but when somebody needs to **remove** a pair because a measurement showed it disarms a gate, they delete it from the family they're working in and **the other switch still returns true**. The exclusion looks applied, the diff looks right, and the site is still normalized.

**Found by a mutation, not by reading:** deleting `"match source-address"` from one switch left the pass admitting it from the other, and the mutation reported a clean escape when it was an incomplete edit.

**The compiler already covers the other half**, which is why the cell is scoped this way: a duplicate case *within* one switch is a build error. Only cross-switch duplication is invisible — and that's precisely the shape here, because each family is a separate switch written by a different lane. Establishing that took a mutation that turned out to be a build failure (a **void**); reading it as an escape would have left the cell claiming ground the toolchain already holds.

The 52 are **pinned, not endorsed**: they came from several lanes' landed families, and redding them would block work for a hazard this assertion exists to stop growing. A new duplicate reds; a *resolved* one reds too, so the list shrinks as families are tidied.

## 3. The strongest evidence on this issue is now executable

The #3044 policy gate requires three match criteria and **names the ones it cannot find**. On a site that can never be a disarm:

```
pass OFF -> missing source-address, destination-address, application   (three)
pass ON  -> missing destination-address, application                   (two)
```

**The criterion that stops being missing is the one that was folded.** A direct observation of the tail surviving, from an instrument with no stake in the question — different in kind from an assertion this lane wrote about its own pass. `TestTheGateCountsTheSurvivingCriterion8690` asserts the **difference** between the two readings rather than literal error text, so a reworded #3044 message doesn't red it for the wrong reason.

## Validation

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope.

|---|---|
| remove the witness cell's pair from **both** switches | **red** |
| break the `skipCompactNormalize` seam | **red** |
| add an unmeasured bucket entry | **red** |
| introduce a cross-switch duplicate | **red**, names it |
| resolve an existing duplicate | **red**, names it |

Every edit was **verified by occurrence count before its result was read**. Two first came back as false results — one incomplete edit, one build failure — and both would have read as escapes.

## PR #8750 — config: print the admission state beside every #8690 gate verdict [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-scope-in-verdict`

## What

A gate verdict from the #8690 compact-normalizer scope cell reads identically whether the pass was in scope at that site or not:

```
passOFF=REJECTED passON=accepted
```

With the site admitted, that means "the pass disarms a gate". With the site **not** admitted, the same two compiles produce the same line and mean nothing of the sort — the pass rewrote no node, so the difference came from elsewhere and the line is evidence about the fixture. The reader supplies the missing half from memory.

That failed three times in one day, once as two fixture-limited sites reported as live disarms because the probe that produced them had those sites admitted and the report did not say so.

Asking authors to *state* the scope does not fix it: an author can restate it from a probe run under different conditions, which is exactly how that misreport happened. A printed value cannot be copied forward wrongly — the instrument recomputes it at the moment it prints.

## How

`gateVerdict8690` runs the pass-off/pass-on pair and logs the verdict with `touched=N` **on the same line**, returning the count so callers can assert on it.

`touched` is the *measured* admission state and is strictly stronger than the `compactNormalizeInScope` predicate: a pair can be admitted and still touch nothing here when the fold is absent from the fixture, and a verdict about a text the pass never rewrote is not a verdict about the pass. `touched=0` prints an explicit note voiding the comparison beside it. The `(container, head)` pair may be passed to also print the predicate, which distinguishes the two reasons `touched` can be 0.

The scope cell's own per-site probe is routed through the helper, so it is exercised every run rather than sitting inert for the hand probes it exists to discipline.

## Also: the one-clause addition

The unexaminable-bucket failure message gains the clause for the shape where the standing advice ("give it a compilable fixture") is impossible to follow:

> **unless the leaf under test is itself the stanza's validity condition**, in which case the control cannot be built and the site needs a hand measurement.

Any fixture that makes such a site compile must supply the very value the control exists to omit. `services rpm probe <p> test <t> target` is the worked case; `bgp group <g> neighbor <n> peer-as` and both `three-color-policer <p> {single,two}-rate committed-information-rate` are the same shape.

The **weaker variant is kept distinct**: `feed-server {url,hostname}` and `device-map interface {pci,mac}` are satisfiable by an alternative leaf, so their control *is* constructible and the existing advice is correct for them. The clause is written not to over-apply to those.

## Validation

- **Mutation-tested, each mutant asserted to have actually run** before its verdict was read: hard-coding `touched=1` and `touched=0` are both CAUGHT (2 executed markers each, 0 residual).
- The control observes the helper's **own returned count** rather than re-deriving it alongside. An earlier draft re-derived it and would have stayed green against exactly the constant it was written to catch — reproducing inside the control the vacuity it exists to prevent. That draft was discarded, not shipped.
- The new clause was rendered through the **real failure path** by removing a `knownUnexaminable8690` entry (1 FAIL marker, restored after) — not asserted from the source text.
- Full `pkg/config` green at the merged head (114s), dataplane content-scanning canaries green, `gofmt` clean tree-wide.

No docs change: the discipline governs how a verdict line is *read*, and it is carried in the line itself plus the cell's comments — where the reader of a verdict already is. No prose doc describes the normalizer scope cell.

Part of #8690.

## PR #8751 — config: the duplicate-pair cell was reading 521 of 532 pairs (#8690) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-dup-cell-reach`

TestNoPairIsAdmittedByTwoFamilySwitches8690 scans the predicate's source
for admitted (container, head) pairs and reports those listed by more
than one family switch -- a latent silent-non-exclusion, since removing
such a pair from one family leaves the other switch returning true.

It matched only `^\t\t"..."`. gofmt puts the FIRST pair of a `case`
clause on the `case` line itself, so the cell missed exactly one pair per
clause: 11 pairs unread, and two of them are genuine cross-switch
duplicates -- `address-book address-set` and `dataplane control-socket`
-- each precisely the hazard the cell exists to catch.

Why it survived, which is the part worth recording. The cell reported 52
duplicates. 52 is a plausible-looking number, so nothing in its output
suggested it was reading 521 of 532 pairs. Its degeneracy check
(`len(counts) == 0`) is sound and could never have fired here, because
the first pattern matching 500+ entries masks the second matching zero.
A healthy total says nothing about whether every SHAPE of entry is being
read.

So this adds the second pattern AND a positive control specific to it: if
the `case`-line pattern matches nothing, the cell fails saying the first
pair of every clause is unread, rather than quietly reverting to its
original reach on some future reformat.

The two newly-visible duplicates are pinned on the same terms as the
other 52 -- they came from landed families and redding them would block
work for a hazard this assertion exists to stop growing. Now 478 distinct
pairs, 54 listed twice.

Validation: both mutants killed. Dropping the `case`-line pattern from
the scan reds with GONE entries naming both newly-visible duplicates,
reproducing the exact gap the cell shipped with; breaking that regex so
it matches nothing fires the new control. `go test ./...` green
tree-wide, 77 packages, 0 failures; `gofmt -l` clean.

family inet { filter input f1; }      -> filter input ""     , 0 warnings

The brace-elided spelling **commits clean and emits fewer warnings than the correct one**, because there is no binding left to warn about. The compiler's own message for an *undefined* filter names the hazard — *"the security hook would otherwise be silently disarmed and the interface would forward unfiltered, a fail-open on a firewall filter"* — and a **defined** filter dropped this way walks straight past it.

The flat-set `set` form is unaffected. The loss is the hierarchical elided spelling a config file, a `load override` or a peer-sync payload carries — the ingress this issue exists for.

## The key stays canonical

Only the fixture **text** renders real names. The site **key** keeps `xpfarg`: it is an identity — the inventory, every per-site verdict and three lanes' family lists are keyed on it — and re-rendering identities to fix a fixture would rewrite the whole inventory for a reason unrelated to what it records.

`contextForStanza` / `preambleFor` stay keyed on the canonical path with their text rendered to match, **element-wise**, so a scaffold naming a different container does not move.

The depth census takes the same rendering, because its own premise is *"depth 1 IS the base census's spelling"*. It went red the moment the base census learned something it had not — **the second time that cross-check has caught me improving one walker and not the other**.

## How it was found

I flagged `class-of-service interfaces <i> unit <u> scheduler-map` as possibly *"a config subtree that commits and does nothing"*. The first falsifier — re-run the fixture with a **real** interface name and unit number — showed it compiles correctly. The finding was about my fixture.

> A finding whose fixture uses an invented value is a finding about the fixture until it is re-measured with a real one.

That rule is lane-8526's, and it applies to a lane's own claims as readily as to a review's. **Retracting the claim is what exposed the model defect underneath it.**

## Register

The 24 are added to the #8690 permanent-exclusion register as `open` — ordinary brace-elided drops with nothing protecting them — **except** `interfaces <if> unit <u> tunnel routing-instance destination`, whose drop shape is `partial` and which is therefore forbidden to every scope by construction. Its register guard caught me classing all 24 by their common origin, which is the family-level judgement error that register exists to prevent.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./pkg/cli/ ./pkg/dataplane/` pass; `go build ./...` and tree-wide `gofmt` clean.

## PR #8754 — config: read the #8690 predicate with a parser, not a pattern [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-dup-cell-ast`

The duplicate-pair cell scanned the source with a regex and read **521 of 548** case strings. Refs #8690.

**Nothing in its output said so.** It reported 52 duplicates — a plausible number — and its degeneracy check was `len(counts) == 0`, which could never fire, because a pattern matching 500+ entries masks the fact that a whole *shape* matches zero. **A degeneracy check on the TOTAL cannot see a gap in the SHAPES.**

## What was invisible

gofmt writes a multi-entry clause as `case "a",` / `\t\t"b",` / `\t\t"c":` — so the **first** pair sits on the `case` line and the **last** ends in a colon. A pattern anchored to `\t\t"..."` with an optional comma missed **both ends of every clause**:

| shape | count | seen by the regex |
|---|---|---|
| `\t\t"X",` | 521 | ✅ |
| `\t\t"X":` | 15 | ❌ last pair of each clause |
| `\tcase "X",` | 11 | ❌ first pair of each clause |
| `\tcase "X":` | 1 | ❌ single-entry clause |

**Six of those 27 were real cross-switch duplicates** — the exact silent-non-exclusion the cell exists to catch — and **two of the six are pairs this lane added** in the system-arrivals increment. The guard was blind to duplicates its own author introduced.

## Why a second regex isn't the fix

A `case`-line pattern was landed first; it closes the 11 and leaves the 16. **Two patterns is still a set of spellings somebody enumerated by looking.** This walks the file with `go/parser` and reads the case expressions, which covers every shape by construction and cannot be broken by a future gofmt change — which is what caused this in the first place.

True count **548**, distinct **490**, duplicates **58** rather than 52.

## The control is now made of evidence

The degeneracy check is **replaced by a reach control**, not strengthened: two pairs only reachable through the `case`-line shape must be present, and they are the two real duplicates the regex missed. Plus a total-against-source floor, which is the shape-independent form — with a parser there are no patterns to assert, so the equivalent question is whether the walk read as many pairs as the file holds.

Both totals are reported, so a future reach gap shows as **a total that disagrees with the source** rather than as a plausible duplicate count.

## Validation

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| skip the first expression of each clause (reproduces the regex gap exactly) | **red** — reach control names the pair it lost |
| introduce a cross-switch duplicate | **red**, names it |
| resolve an existing duplicate | **red**, names it |

Each edit verified by occurrence count before its result was read.

## PR #8756 — config: require a pasted touched= line, not the word ADMITTED [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8690-touched-parse-rule`

## What

The `sibling-blocked` register class asserts a measurement taken **with the pair ADMITTED**, and that qualifier is the whole content of the class: for an *excluded* pair the pass touches 0 nodes, so "the pass changes nothing here" is true by construction and says nothing about the site.

The rule enforcing it required the reason to contain the word `ADMITTED`. That asks the author to assert what they already believe — and a belief can be carried forward from a probe run under different conditions, which is exactly how two fixture-limited sites were once reported here as live disarms. **Restatement is the step that fails, and a rule asking for a restatement cannot catch it.**

The rule now requires a **pasted `touched=N` line from `gateVerdict8690`** — evidence an author cannot produce without running the instrument.

## Why the count is sufficient — measured, not assumed

| pairs | probe reports |
|---|---|
| at master (**excluded**) | `touched=0` for all nine |
| temporarily **admitted** | `touched=1` for all nine |

A non-zero count is therefore not a restatement of the admission — it is **the admission's only obtainable signature**. The nine reasons now carry `touched=1 admitted=true passOFF=REJECTED passON=REJECTED`, which reproduces the existing family-7 table exactly.

`no-drop-measured` gets the same clause. It currently holds **zero entries**, so it guards future ones only — deliberate, because a rule added after the first entry has to argue with an entry instead of a blank sheet. Its zero case gets its own message: an admitted pair can legally report 0 there when the fold is absent from the fixture, so 0 means the pasted run cannot be the evidence, rather than that the claim is false.

This is **one mechanism with an enforcement clause**, not two mechanisms for one property. The printed state removes the error where a verdict is *read*; this rule keeps the prose channel from publishing a verdict that was never read off the instrument at all. Different artifacts, so neither replaces the other.

## Validation

Three mutants, each asserted to have actually run (2 executed markers each, 0 residual) — all CAUGHT, **each by its intended branch**:

1. strip the pasted line → missing-evidence branch
2. paste `touched=0` → zero branch
3. replace with a prose restatement (*"I measured this with the pair ADMITTED and it was rejected both ways"*) → missing-evidence branch

**The first draft of the regex was wrong and the mutation caught it — but by the wrong branch.** It matched a bare `touched=(\d+)` anywhere in the reason, and all nine entries contain the sentence *"the same probe reports touched=0"* explaining why a non-zero count is meaningful. So the guard read its count out of its own explanatory **prose** rather than the pasted evidence, passing only because `touched=1` appeared earlier in the string than `touched=0`. A reordered sentence would have flipped it. Checking *which* branch fired is what exposed it; the regex now requires the instrument's following `passOFF=` field, which prose does not carry.

Register edits are **reason-only**: site and class columns byte-identical to master for all 45 entries. The scope predicate was temporarily widened to take the measurement and restored — byte-identical to master. Full `pkg/config` green, dataplane canaries green, gofmt clean tree-wide.

## PR #8757 — config: a conservation exemption cannot rest on a strict-path-only refusal (#8752) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8752-duplicate-instance-fold`

## Two of three exemptions are unjustified on the path that loads what is on disk

`dupConservationSkipped8436` exempts three containers with the reason **"REFUSED
at commit"**. That is true, and it is a fact about the **strict** path. The census
governs both, and `Store.Load` / `Store.SyncApply` compile **leniently** — the
entire point of them, since they read configurations the operator did not just
author.

| container | strict | **lenient** | objects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `security policies from-zone <a> <b> <c> policy` | REJECTED | **ACCEPTED** | **2** |
| `security policies global policy` | REJECTED | **ACCEPTED** | **2** |
| `class-of-service fairness rss-expectation interface <i> queue` | REJECTED | rejected | 0 |

On that path the **duplicate wins**: the operator's policy keeps its match
criteria while the spurious one contributes a match-less deny. #8752 tracks the
fold itself; this change is only about the exemption.

`security policies global policy` had not been named anywhere — found by
**censusing the class rather than the reported instance**, the same method that
found the third site in the #8690 K84/K85 family.

## The entries stay; the reason is annotated

The census genuinely cannot synthesize these, so skipping is right. What was
wrong is the **reason** — and a skip with a stated reason reads as settled:
nobody re-derives it, and the next reader trusts it.

The third entry is annotated too, recording that it was re-checked and **is**
correctly skipped because it refuses on both paths. The negative result is what
makes the group readable — two were wrong, one was not, and a reader needs to
know which without re-measuring.

## The general form

**A census governing two compile paths cannot take an exception justified on only
one.** "REFUSED at commit" is unanswerable for the tolerant path *by
construction*, so an entry carrying that reason is **unexamined**, not settled.

## A guard, not prose

The annotation would rot the moment any answer changed, so the three lenient-path
behaviours are **pinned by measurement**. The cell also asserts the strict-path
premise still holds, so if a container stops being refused at commit the stated
reason reds rather than silently becoming false.

| mutation | reddens |
|---|---|
| the fold starts **merging** (2 objects → 1) | object count — with a message saying that's the good direction and the annotation moves with it |
| the lenient path starts **refusing** | the accept assertion — the operational-blackout direction |

## PR #8759 — config: state the duplicate-policy consequence as measured [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8752-skip-reason-consequence`

## What

lane-8015's #8757 correctly established that two `dupConservationSkipped8436` entries were exempted on a **strict-path** fact in a census governing both paths. Its annotation then described the consequence as: the duplicate **wins** — *"the operator's policy keeps its match criteria while the spurious one contributes a match-less deny."*

First half exact. Second half wrong in a way that would misdirect the fix. Measured on the tolerant path:

```
policy[0] src=[10.0.0.0/8] dst=[any] app=[any] permit  dropped=false
policy[1] src=[]           dst=[]    app=[]    deny    dropped=TRUE
```

The spurious policy sits **second**, so it never wins a first-match evaluation. Its all-empty match reads as match-ANY, putting a deny-all exactly where the zone pair already has an implicit default-deny — close to inert on its own.

## The operative harm is `LenientContentDropped`

`compilePolicy` sets it (`compiler_security_policy.go:413`) because the tolerant path accepted the policy only by dropping a required match dimension. `policies_lower.go:194` then poisons the rule with the `__unsupported__` sentinel **so that the Rust integrity preflight rejects the whole snapshot** — previous-good retained, fresh-boot default-deny.

So the consequence is not an altered policy set an operator could read in `show`. It is that **the operator's entire configuration does not load**. On a fresh boot that is a blackout.

## Why the wording matters

The two readings prescribe different fixes. *"The duplicate wins"* invites making the **first occurrence authoritative** — which leaves `LenientContentDropped` set and the snapshot still poisoned. The duplicate object would be gone and the outage would not.

Folding the occurrences into one policy carrying the operator's criteria is what clears the flag, and clearing the flag is what makes the config load.

**So the new cell is also the acceptance criterion for the #8752 fold:** after the fold, `LenientContentDropped` must be **false** for the folded policy. An implementation that removes the duplicate *object* but leaves the flag set has not fixed what operators feel — and counting objects cannot tell those two apart.

Landed as a guard rather than corrected prose because the claim is exactly the kind that rots: it spans two packages (flag set in `pkg/config`, consumed in `pkg/dataplane/userspace`) and nothing else asserts the pairing.

## Validation

Mutation-tested, each mutant asserted to have run **and checked for the right branch**, not merely for a red:

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| invert the poison assertion | CAUGHT, via the `LenientContentDropped` branch |
| invert the match-empty assertion | CAUGHT, via the match-tokens branch |
| **production**: `LenientContentDropped = false` at `compiler_security_policy.go:413` | **CAUGHT** — the regression the guard exists for |

2 executed markers each, 0 residual; the production file was restored and verified clean. Full `pkg/config` green, dataplane canaries green, gofmt clean.

The skip entries themselves are unchanged — the census still cannot synthesize these, so skipping remains correct. Only the reason moves, which is what #8757 established and what this makes exact.
