## PR #8812 — config: fan out bracketed groups for device-map and OSPF interfaces [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/device-map-interface-group`

## The defect

`chassis device-map interface [ ge-0/0/1 ge-0/0/2 ] { pci … }` compiled to **one** entry — `namedInstances` takes `Keys[1]` and discards `Keys[2:]`. The second NIC vanished and was governed by `unmapped-interface-policy` instead. Under `manage-down` that brings it **down**, and on bare metal (#1956 §9.6) the console is the only fallback.

## The remedy is NOT "map both NICs", and that correction is the point

A grouped statement shares **one body**, and a device-map body must carry a per-NIC stable identity (`pci` or `mac`). Two NICs cannot share a PCI address, so the grouped spelling **can never be valid**.

```
BEFORE  interface [ a b ] { pci X }   ACCEPTED, entries=1
AFTER   same input                    REJECTED: "PCI address … is bound to both
                                      ge-0/0/1 and ge-0/0/2 — one NIC cannot be
                                      two interfaces"
```

**The fan-out converts a silent misconfiguration into a commit rejection**, by letting the existing duplicate-identity validator *see the second name at all*. Before it, that name did not exist, so no conflict could be detected — the validator was not broken, it was blind.

**My first guard demanded two entries and failed against the correct behaviour.** Reading *why* it failed — the message named both NICs and the shared PCI — produced the right remedy. Adjusting the cell until it passed would have driven the compiler to accept a config that cannot be meant.

## The same syntax wants opposite outcomes on the two containers

OSPF interfaces legitimately share a body (`metric`, `passive`), so `area <a> interface [ a b ] { metric 10; }` must **create** both — and now does (1 → 2).

> Create-N where the body is shareable, **reject** where it must carry a per-instance identity. A fan-out is right in both cases; only the container's semantics say what happens next.

## Scope, deliberate

Five `namedInstances(...FindChildren("interface"))` sites exist. The other two — `nat proxy-arp` and `router-advertisement` — have the same mechanism and **unmeasured** severity, so they are named rather than fixed blind. Unlike #8794's zones, the five enumerate **disjoint stanzas**, so a partial fix cannot produce the compiler-vs-validator disagreement that made the partial #8802 worse than the bug. Checked, not assumed.

Helper renamed `zoneGroupInstances8794` → `bracketedGroupInstances8794`: named for the shape now that zones are not its only caller.

## Validation

| mutant | fails |
|---|---|
| revert the chassis site | device-map cell **alone** |
| revert the OSPF site | OSPF cell **alone** |

0 residual. Guards assert **absolute outcomes** — the grouped device-map is rejected *and the rejection names both NICs*; both OSPF interfaces are created — never grouped == longhand. **The `manage-down` arm is asserted explicitly**, since a cell exercising only the default policy measures the mild half.

Closes #8810

## PR #8813 — docs: the dual AST shape is a BRACING choice, not flat-set vs hierarchical [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8808-ast-shape-docs`

Part of #8808.

Three project docs taught that flat `set` produces a different AST shape from the
hierarchical spelling, using `family inet dhcp` as the example:

```
Hierarchical `family inet { dhcp; }` -> Node{Keys:["family","inet"]} with children
Flat `set … family inet dhcp`        -> Node{Keys:["family"]} with child Node{Keys:["inet"]}
```

**The second line is false, and it is false for the example it uses.**

## Measured

```
FLAT  "set interfaces eth0 unit 0 family inet dhcp" ->
  [interfaces] [eth0] [unit 0] [family inet] [dhcp]
HIER  interfaces { eth0 { unit 0 { family inet { dhcp; } } } } ->
  [interfaces] [eth0] [unit 0] [family inet] [dhcp]
```

**Byte-identical.** `SetPath` descends a `compoundKey` container exactly as the
parser does (`ast_edit.go:506`, `:850`, `:999`).

Checked across four shapes — the compound `family`, a **non-compound** chain
(`bgp group neighbor peer-as`), nested containers (`security policy match`), and a
bracketed list — and flat and hierarchical agree in **every one**.

That last point matters. The obvious repair is *"keep the general dual-shape point,
it still holds for non-compound containers."* **It does not.** Flat and hierarchical
agree there too, so correcting only the `family inet` example would have left a
second false statement behind.

## The real axis is bracing — three shapes, not two

| spelling | tree | |
|---|---|---|
| `family inet { dhcp; }` | `[family inet]` + child `[dhcp]` | COMPOUND |
| `family { inet { dhcp; } }` | `[family]` → `[inet]` → `[dhcp]` | SPLIT |
| `family inet dhcp;` | `[family inet dhcp]` | PACKED (#2419) |

A compiler must handle all three. The **SPLIT** form is where a bare
`Node{Keys:["family"]}` with an `inet` child actually comes from — an operator
bracing the family separately, never a `set` command.

## Why a doc line is worth a change

It is false **in the direction that makes people skip a measurement.** It says the
flat surface has a different shape, so a defect proven against the compound shape
reads as inapplicable to `set` input. That inference was drawn during #8763 and the

## PR #8816 — config: NAT pool address must be groupReplace, not leaf-list UNION [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8804-groupreplace-union`

**Fixes a regression that is live on master right now.** Follow-up to #8800 / #8804.

#8804 declared `address` under the source NAT pool with `multi: true`, which made the leaf **leaf-list eligible** — `isLeafListSchema` requires `multi` — so apply-groups switched it from scalar **OVERRIDE** to token **UNION**. An inline `address` then merges with the group's instead of replacing it, and a NAT pool carries an address the operator believed they had replaced.

```
group  address 10.0.0.9/32;   inline  address 10.0.0.1/32;

before #8804   addresses=1 [10.0.0.1/32]   OVERRIDE, correct
after  #8804   addresses=2 [both]          UNION, regression
master today   addresses=2 [both]          still live
```

## The fix is `groupReplace`, and the alternative was measured rather than argued

`groupReplace`'s own contract describes this leaf exactly: *a multi leaf that packs a SEPARATOR onto its value list is not a set, so token-level union/dedup would corrupt it* — citing a port range packing `to`. The NAT pool address leaf packs `to` for a `<low> to <high>` range. Setting the flag reverts it to the safe pre-#4070 OVERRIDE, which is precisely the pre-#8804 behaviour.

The obvious alternative — drop `multi` — is wrong, and three states were measured on master to establish that rather than reasoned about:

| | union regression | existing NAT cells |
|---|---|---|
| master as-is | `addresses=2` **broken** | 0 failing |
| drop `multi` | `addresses=1` fixed | **14 FAILING** |
| add `groupReplace`, keep `multi` | `addresses=1` fixed | **0 failing** |

`multi` governs **flat-set token absorption**, not validation: it is why `set ... address <low> to <high>` and the bracket-list form reach the compiler as ONE leaf. Dropping it leaves `SchemaValidate` accepting every spelling identically — validation is not the property `multi` governs — while silently changing the compiled result, redding #4521, #4422, #5144, #6812 and the deterministic-NAT flat-set family.

**Reasoning from "SchemaValidate is unchanged" to "multi is unnecessary" is the specific mistake this change's comment exists to stop being repeated.** I made it, and the full suite was the only thing that caught it — a targeted run over the cells I had just written passed.

## Why `groupReplace` rather than dropping `multi`, stated for the history

Keeping `multi` and adding `groupReplace` is not merely the smaller change — it is the one that preserves behaviour in both directions. Dropping `multi` would have fixed the merge semantics **by giving up the multi-value spellings**: `address <low> to <high>` and `address [ a b ]` stop reaching the compiler as one leaf. `groupReplace` keeps both working and restores only the scalar-override merge behaviour.

## Reviewer arms attempted, and the scope of the exception

Recorded rather than summarised as "reviewed", because a record that reads stronger than its evidence is the defect class this change belongs to:

- **Codex** — worked on the third attempt (the first hung on stdin; the forwarder subagent returned a job id with no entry in the local state DB). **It found this regression.**
- **AGY** — failed all three attempts on a documented plugin bug (`--print took "--print-timeout" as its prompt`), including with a short focus and with no timeout argument. An infra outage, not a review outcome.
- **Claude SMR** — my own arm; on the parent change it found the destination-pool half.

So: two working arms and one infra outage. Not a clean triple, and this body says so.

## Guard

`TestNATPoolAddressGroupOverride8804` asserts the override **and** carries a degeneracy control: with no inline address the group's value must still be inherited, so the cell cannot pass by apply-groups failing entirely. Its failure message names `groupReplace` and warns off the multi-removal fix, since that is the plausible-looking wrong repair.

Mutation-checked: removing `groupReplace` (i.e. master today) reds the cell; restoring it greens.

## PR #8817 — config: declare `address` under the DESTINATION NAT pool [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8800-destination-pool-address`

Follow-up to #8800, which fixed the **source** NAT pool only. The destination pool has the identical defect and it is **still live on master** (confirmed at `7bff3b595`).

```
braced        addr=10.0.0.5/32 port=0     strict accepts
packed        addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
braced-port   addr=10.0.0.5/32 port=8080  strict accepts
packed-port   addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
```

`compileNATDestination` reads `address` here — `parseDNATPoolAddress` deliberately walks every token so `address <ip> port <n>` captures both — but the pool declared `children: nil`. The head was therefore not a schema child, the brace-elision pass was never *asked* about it, and the packed spelling compiled to an empty address. After the declaration all four agree, with `packed-port` correctly carrying both the address and port 8080.

## Severity is LOW and it fails LOUD

The packed spelling is **rejected at commit**, with a message naming the pool and the consequence, so an operator gets a clear error rather than a silent misconfiguration. That is the opposite of the source-pool case as originally reported, and it should not be ranked against the #8781-class fail-opens.

## What made this half invisible — the generalisable part

The scope predicate is **pair-keyed**, so the `("pool","address")` entry added for the source pool *already* covered this path: `inScope("pool","address")` returned **true** here while the path was still broken. **Checking the scope list would have shown the pair present and looked correct.**

That is a blind spot distinct from the pass-driven and position-blind ones in this family, and nastier than either, because the instrument returns **true** rather than zero. A missing entry is visible; a *satisfied* predicate over a still-broken path is not. No test failing would have surfaced it.

It was found by asking which other container the same compiler-arm shape appears in. The cheap general form, which has now caught three defects:

> **When the code names one member of a declared pair, the other is a candidate by construction** — `source`/`destination`, `ike`/`ipsec`, `inet`/`inet6`, `input`/`output`.

## `groupReplace`

Set for the same reason as the source leaf (#8816), and this leaf needs it more: its value list packs `port`, so apply-groups token UNION corrupts the **address** outright rather than merely over-collecting. Measured — inheriting `address 10.0.0.2/32 port 8080;` over an inline `address 10.0.0.1/32 port 80;` compiled the address as `"8080"`. Pinned by `TestDestinationNATPoolAddressGroupOverride8800`.

## Guard changes

- Two packed-vs-braced cells (`address`, `address-port`) plus the group-override guard.
- **#8690 scope arm** gains one entry, hand-measured as that bucket's failure message requires: with a valid value the pass makes packed agree with braced; with a **malformed** value the single-host-address gate still **rejects** under the pass and only the reason changes — so no gate is disarmed. The verdict and its measurement are stored **with the entry**, not only in the commit message, because a hand measurement that lives in a commit message is invisible at the point someone next reads the bucket.
- **#7484 floor 702 → 703**, re-measured at this head rather than derived by adding one, with blind holding at 364.

Validation: `go test ./pkg/config/` green; `go build ./...` clean.

Same standing as #8816 and recorded rather than summarised: Codex working (it found the `multi`/apply-groups regression on the parent change), AGY infra-blocked on the documented `--print-timeout` plugin bug, Claude SMR (which found this destination gap in the first place). Two arms and one outage — not a clean triple.

## PR #8818 — config: the NAT address-range cap rejected on the LENIENT path, so a persisted config could not boot [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8814-nat-range-lenient`

Part of #8814.

`address <low> to <high>` in a NAT pool expands to one address per IP and is
capped at 256. The cap was raised as a **compiler** error inside
`expandAddressRange`, so it fired on the lenient path as well as the strict one:

```
braced, 257 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> FAILS TO LOAD
braced, 256 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> loads
```

`CompileConfigLenient`'s own doc says it exists *"so an upgraded node boots
through"*. A braced oversized range **could not boot through, on master, before
any recent change** — #8800 only removed the accident that hid the same failure
for the packed spelling.

The chain is `compileSecurity → compileNATSource → appendPoolAddresses` and carries
no `compileOpts`, so there was no seam at which to downgrade it.

## Why the cap is NOT moved out of the compiler

The issue proposed moving it into a strict validator. Measured, the widest legal
spelling is:

```
address 0.0.0.0/32 to 255.255.255.255/32   ->  4294967296 IPs
```

An expansion with no bound would try to allocate **4.29 billion strings on the
lenient path — the boot path.** That trades a load failure for an OOM.

So the bound **stays** in `expandAddressRange` and only the **error** becomes a
recorded fact — the shape `NATPool.PortRangeInvalidSpec` and
`FirewallFilterTerm.UnknownFrom` (#3307) already use in this package, and the
narrower of the two options you named: **no signature change to `compileSecurity`.**

| path | behaviour |
|---|---|
| strict (commit / commit-check) | REJECTS, naming the cap |
| tolerant (load / peer-sync) | warns; the pool loads **without** that range |

A size failure is separated by sentinel from a **malformed** one. Size has a safe
fallback — omit the range — and malformed input does not, so `low > high`, a
non-IP endpoint, and IPv6 endpoints still fail on **both** paths. A sentinel that
swallowed parse errors would turn this into a silent-acceptance bug, the class the
NAT gate family exists to prevent.

## PR #8820 — config: land the arity census as a ratchet with its blindness stated (#8807) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/8807-census-guards`

Lands the arity census (#8787's predicate A) as a **ratchet with its own blindness in the failure text and its mutation control in the cell**, rather than as a one-off report. Partial progress on #8807; the positional predicate itself is not built and this says so.

## Why an instrument at all

#8787 ran this census once, fixed some rows, and left nothing behind — so the class can reappear silently. Worse, it recorded the predicate as *"control-validated"* using `pre-shared-key`, a row that **kept firing after #8777 fixed it**, because a *correct* `args: 1` sibling at `security ipsec vpn` matched by name.

> **A control that still fires after its own fix cannot distinguish fixed from broken.**

That is nastier than a control that never fires, because a firing control looks like diligence.

## Container-keying: 12 hits → 6

Each compiler `case` clause is now paired with the innermost enclosing `range ... FindChildren("X")` container and compared only against schema declarations under a node of that name.

**The validation is not the reduction — it is the agreement.** The six rows removed were `preempt`, `inet6`, `match`, `local-identity`, `remote-identity`, `pre-shared-key`: **exactly** the false-pairing and already-fixed sets from the hand adjudication, with no overlap error in either direction. A mechanical predicate independently reproducing a human adjudication is a much stronger result than "it found fewer things".

And `pre-shared-key` dropping out is the specific point: the successor **fixes a named defect in the predecessor**, so the control goes quiet when the defect is fixed.

## Result: 12 hits, ZERO defects

`reject` and `then` were the last two genuine candidates. lane-8015 measured both with an absent baseline and a reachability check: every spelling delivers, a bogus `reject` message-type is a **loud commit rejection** via the `UnknownActions` path rather than a silent drop, and both values reach real consumers.

So the arity-contradiction class is **empty at this head**. That is a result, not a null — and it cost four false-pairing adjudications to establish. The ratchet fired for real to record it:

```
genuine arity candidates FELL to 0 ([]) -- THIS IS A GOOD FAILURE.
Set arityGenuineFloor8807 = 0. Leaving it at 2 gives the next regression that much room to hide.
```

One real residue: **completion under-offers** for both leaves, because the compiler is *ahead* of the schema — the mirror of the #8773 rule. lane-8015 is landing that separately.

## The three properties this guard has to keep

**1. Ratchet, not equality.** The hit set is asserted against a hand adjudication, because a hit is a *candidate* and not a defect — a new one reds with instructions to confirm the site and the declaration are the same path **first**, then measure braced-vs-packed. The genuine count is ratcheted in **both** directions; a drop is a good failure that must tighten the constant.

**2. The blindness is in the failure text, and it has been seen to render.** I forced a real red to confirm it appears — a failure message is only correct if you have watched it fail. It states three limits:

- **Name-keying.** It localises a site only when the container is lexically recoverable; the four remaining false pairings are all sites where it is not.
- **Existence.** In *either* mode it is blind to a leaf undeclared at its own position while declared elsewhere, because it can only pair with declarations that exist. That is the #8800 shape, and **no arity predicate can see it** — it is an existence question.
- **Constant index only.** Found by lane-8015 while checking a row here: `parsePolicyTermInlineKeys` (`compiler_routing.go:1269`) consumes a following token via a *variable* index and is invisible. So a keyword can have sites this predicate reports **and** sites it cannot see, and a row's recorded evidence may describe only the visible half — which is exactly what the `then` row did before it was corrected.

So green means *"no new arity contradiction this predicate can localise"*, never *"the class is covered"*.

**3. The mutation control lives in the cell and asserts both halves in one run.** It re-breaks #8796 by narrowing both `gateway local-identity` declarations and requires the row to appear; requires silence on the unmutated tree; and requires the restore to have restored. **Either half alone is satisfiable by a dead instrument** — one by something that always fires, the other by something that never does. Verified by a meta-mutation: blinding the census reds both cells.

## Residual blindness, stated beside the ratchet

The four unlocalisable sites are unlocalisable for two concrete reasons — a bare `range node.Children`, where the container is whatever the caller passed and is not written at the site (`count`, `reject`, `then`), or a variable bound further up the function (`from-zone`, `interface`, `pool`, `match`). Recovering those needs the **call path**, not a lexical walk, which is the positional predicate #8807 exists to build and the reason it is separate work rather than a bigger regex.

## PR #8826 — config: declare what the compiler already reads, so completion stops under-offering [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/completion-reject-then`

Part of #8807 — the residue its census surfaced. Not a close: that issue is about building the positional predicate.

Two leaves the **compiler reads more of than the schema declared**:

| leaf | compiler | schema |
|---|---|---|
| `firewall … term then reject` | reads a message type from `Keys[1]` **or a child** | declared neither |
| `policy-options policy-statement then` | **iterates this node's children** for the policy default action | declared a bare leaf |

Nothing was dropped, because neither compiler path consults the schema. The symptom went to the other surface — completion and `?` help offered nothing where the compiler accepts something:

```
then reject <TAB>                 n=0  ->  n=14
policy-statement <p> then <TAB>   n=0  ->  n=2   [accept reject]
term <t> then <TAB>  (control)    n=12 ->  n=12
```

### This is the #8773 docs rule running backwards

`docs/config-schema.md` records that adding a schema leaf is a *compiler-behaviour* change, because the packed reader resolves its tail through the schema and an undeclared-but-compiled leaf drops **silently**. Here the compiler is **ahead** of the schema instead, so nothing drops and completion **under-offers**. Two directions, two very different symptoms, one relationship.

### Declared as children rather than `args:1` + enum — on a measurement

The args form adds no leaves and is tidier by the numbers. It was tried: every compiled spelling survives it, and `then reject <TAB>` still offers only `<[Enter]>`, so **it does not fix the defect**. The children form was chosen because it works, and because the compiler already reads the child shape (`then { reject { tcp-reset; } }` compiles today).

### A schema declaration is not monotone, so compilation was measured

Nine spellings captured **before** the change and byte-identical after: bare / packed / braced / child-form `reject`, all three policy-statement spellings, the typo rejection (`then reject nonsense` still refused — that gate is the compiler's `UnknownActions`, not the schema's), and **apply-groups inheritance** of a reject message type, which is the surface where an earlier schema change caused a live regression.

### The guard asserts both halves in one cell

The newly declared paths offer their values **and** the untouched control still offers twelve. A completion guard asserting only `n>0` on the fixed paths is satisfied by a completer that matches everything; one asserting only the control is satisfied by a completer that regressed the fix. **Either alone is satisfied by a stuck answer.**

### Two ratchet movements, both deliberate and explained at the constant

- **`valueMoves` 1 → 0 (tightened).** Its single member was `policy-options policy-statement <*> then` — a leaf whose value demonstrably reached the compiler while the gate could not compare its spellings. Declaring the children emptied the class. A zero here is a claim, not an absence.
- **`flag` 179 → 209 (raised).** The 30 new members are the reject message types (14 per family) and the two default actions. They are enum **values** modelled as child keywords, not configuration leaves: `tcp-reset` *is* the value, so there is no second spelling for a differential to compare, and they can never leave this class however the gate improves — unlike the other 179, where "make them compare" is a real option.

### And the #8807 census ratchet

It landed mid-flight and correctly fired: declaring the `then` children removes that row. The cell asks that a vanished hit be distinguished from a broken instrument, so — **`reject` is still reported by the same run.** Had the glob or schema walk broken, both would have vanished together. `arityGenuineFloor8807` stays 0: `then` was measured *benign*, so resolving it moves the hit count, not the defect count.

## PR #8831 — config: read a packed `security alg <proto>` stanza [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8823-alg-packed`

`security { alg ftp disable; }` compiled to `FTPDisable=FALSE` on a **clean commit**. All four wired protos measure false in that spelling — an operator disabling an ALG gets a success and an ALG still **enabled**.

## A fourth spelling nobody listed is worse than the reported one

Testing the adjacent shape found `alg ftp { disable; }` — proto packed onto `alg`, body as a child — and it does not merely drop:

```
alg ftp disable;          ftp=false  unsupported=[]            silent drop
alg ftp { disable; }      ftp=false  unsupported=[disable]     WRONG advisory
alg h323 { gatekeeper; }             unsupported=[gatekeeper]  WRONG name
```

The #4232 advisory exists to report a proto the dataplane does not wire. In the mixed spelling it named `disable` and `gatekeeper` — a keyword and a sub-statement — **as protocols**. A reader acting on that goes looking for an ALG that does not exist. **An advisory built to catch silent drops was itself silent in one spelling and misleading in another.**

## The remedy was measured, not reasoned

I have twice reached for a remedy without checking what the codebase already does with the shape, so both candidates were run:

| remedy | dns/ftp/sip/tftp | h323 |
|---|---|---|
| schema-side: admit `("alg",<proto>)` | **fixed** | **NOT fixed** |
| compiler-side packed read | **fixed** | **fixed** |

Admitting the pair **cannot** reach an undeclared proto: the pass asks *nothing* for `h323` (measured `asked=[]`) — the #8800 signature — and declaring unsupported protos so it would ask defeats the advisory those declarations exist to preserve.

**So the site is both classes at once** — unadmitted-pair for the four declared, #8800 for the rest — and only a compiler-side read covers both. It mirrors `algDisabled`, which already reads a packed tail one level down, and matches #8795.

The **early return** matters as much as the read: children of a packed `alg <proto>` belong to the *proto*, and letting the old loop also see them is what produced `unsupported=[disable]`.

## Validation

Three mutants, each caught with a **distinct blast radius** rather than a shared red:

| mutant | fails | branch |
|---|---|---|
| revert the packed branch | 10 subtests | value: *"ALG is still ENABLED"* |
| drop the children check | exactly the 4 mixed-spelling protos | value |
| remove the early return | exactly 1 — the mixed advisory | `UnsupportedProtos=[h323 gatekeeper]` |

0 residual. Guards assert the **value**, never that the commit succeeded — every broken cell committed cleanly (`CompileConfig` returned nil for all twelve), so a commit-succeeded assertion is vacuous here **by construction**. Four protos × four spellings, plus the advisory in all three h323 spellings.

**Touches no schema file**, so it is disjoint from the `schema_security.go` region work in flight (#8824, #8825).

Full `pkg/config` green, canaries green, gofmt clean.

Closes #8823

## PR #8833 — config: build the positional predicate, both directions (#8807) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/8807-positional-predicate`

Builds the positional predicate #8807 specifies and #8787 explicitly deferred — **both directions, with both acceptance controls passing**.

**No close keyword, deliberately.** team-lead owns #8807 and is closing it with a caveat in the closing comment. See "What this does not establish" below — there is a real soundness gap and it should be read before the issue closes.

## Direction 1 — read at P, undeclared at P

The class every keyword-anywhere check passes silently: a head declared *somewhere* but missing at the path the compiler reads it. A head declared **nowhere** is #8787's predicate B and is excluded by design.

**Control (#8800): passes.** Removing the `address` declaration from both NAT pools makes the predicate report `pool / address`; restoring silences it; the restore is asserted so a later cell cannot inherit a broken tree.

5 hits: 3 are **#8825** (a packed `application-set` loses its members), 2 are **benign** — `vpn / gateway` and `vpn / ipsec-policy` compile identically in both nestings. **A candidate is not a finding: assuming would have over-reported by 40%.**

## Direction 2 — declared at P, unread at P (the converse)

The predicate that defeated #8787's predicate C five times. **Control (#8785): passes**, and both halves run — it must report `proposal / description`, and must *not* report `proposal / dh-group`, which the same compiler does read.

9 hits: one is #8785; **eight are pinned as `unmeasured`** under a ceiling that ratchets down and must never rise. "Not measured" is a third state, not a pass.

## Three earlier versions failed, and the failures are in the file

1. **Reusing the arity census's site collector** — the #8800 control **failed**. That collector records only clauses containing a constant `Keys[i]`; the #8800 site reads `prop.Keys[1:]`, a slice. The control caught a predicate that otherwise looked like it worked.
2. **Nearest enclosing `FindChildren`** — 104 hits with obvious noise (`ids-option / ping-death`), because a switch often iterates a *nested* child and the nearest container is then an ancestor.
3. **Requiring the immediate range to iterate that container's DIRECT children** — 5.

Plus a bug in the schema walk: keying `seen` on the node alone meant a node reached under a second container name recorded no children, so that name looked like a container declaring nothing. Keyed on `(node, name)` now; it had manufactured three false hits.

## The filter I rejected, recorded because it is tempting

An **unambiguous-container** filter cuts the converse from 60 hits to 2. It also **excludes the #8785 control itself**, because `proposal` has two schema paths. A filter that kills its own control invalidates everything downstream of it — #8787's recorded lesson about predicate A. The 60→2 reduction looks like a win and is not.

The coverage gate used instead is **not tuned to save the control**: it passes at 50%, 60%, 70% *and* 80%. The threshold was chosen for signal-to-noise (26 hits at 50%, 9 at 70%), and the sweep is in the file so that stays checkable.

## What this does NOT establish

**The #8785 control proves sensitivity, not soundness** — that the instrument fires when it should, never that it fires *only* when it should. Blindness item (5) states the specific hole:

The converse marks a head as READ if any `.Name()` clause at that container names it. **It never checks the clause does anything with the value.** A clause reading into nothing is scored as a read and the row goes quiet — which is #8785's own defect with a clause in front of it. `description` under `security ike proposal` is caught **only because no clause exists**.

That is the same mistake one level up from the `then next` retraction: #8787 called it clean by checking `Action` when the value lands in `NextTerm`. **Checking for the existence of a read rather than for where the value lands.** Answering "unread" properly needs whole compiled results compared with and without the statement, warnings included — behavioural, not AST. **Filed as #8830.**

And the sharper form of the same point: the #8785 control passing is **partly luck about which form #8785 took**. Had it been the clause-that-drops variant, the control would have failed and that would have been visible. A control whose success is contingent on an incidental property of the case it was built from is not measuring what a green run reads as measuring.

All five blindnesses are in the **failure text**, not comments, and were confirmed to render by forcing a real red.

Validation: `go test ./pkg/config/` green; `go build ./...` clean. Every control mutation-checked in both directions.

## PR #8834 — config: refuse an unparseable tcp-mss child instead of silently clamping nothing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8824-tcp-mss`

Part of #8824 — the half that is not in dispute. See below for the half I deliberately did **not** fix.

`security flow tcp-mss all-tcp { mss notanint; }` committed clean, clamped nothing, and warned nobody.

`selectMSSToken` prefers the `mss` child only when it parses, then falls through to the flat token. That fall-through is correct for the **mixed** shape `gre-in 1400 { mss bogus; }` — the #1979 precedence, where the flat 1400 is what the compiler uses. With **no** flat token there is nothing to fall through to, and returning "no value selected" reported *nothing configured* for a config that plainly configures one. No gate ever saw a token, so nothing refused it.

The asymmetry is what makes it a defect rather than a policy:

```
all-tcp notanint;            REFUSED   (same bad token, flat)
all-tcp { mss 70000; }       REFUSED   (same braced shape, out of range)
all-tcp { mss notanint; }    ACCEPTED as 0    <- only this vanished
```

MSS clamping exists to stop PMTU blackholes on tunnels. A clamp that silently does not happen is indistinguishable from one that was never configured — which is the state the operator believes they have left.

### What I did not fix, and why it is escalated

#8824 also reports that `set security flow tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350` is refused. Whether that is a defect turns entirely on whether inline `mss` is a **typo** or the **flat-set flattening** of the braced child.

`TestCompactLeafTCPMSSKeywordStillRejected6564` pins the rejection on the former reading — deliberately, with a stated acceptance criterion ("identical in both AST shapes **or** rejected at commit") that "both reject" satisfies. #8824 asserts the latter reading.

I implemented that change, measured it working across every spelling, **and then reverted it.** Nothing in this tree settles the premise: the only in-repo support for either reading is #6564's own reasoning and the copy of it in `docs/config-schema.md` — one source cited twice. A lane that cannot produce evidence for its premise should not overturn a numbered, tested decision on it.

The comment on `tcpMSSOptionNodes` now records the dispute instead of asserting either side, and the new cell deliberately does not cover that spelling.

### What must not change, asserted alongside the fix

Widening acceptance could have taken these with it, so they are pinned: the #1979 mixed-shape precedence (`gre-in 1400 { mss bogus; }` still selects 1400), typo detection (`all-tcp msss 1350` still refused), every previously-working spelling, and `ipsec-vpn` still refused **for its own unrelated reason** — which is also the control proving these refusals are attributable to the value rather than to a blanket rejection.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| fix removed (silent zero returns) | killed |
| unparseable child **always** wins (breaks #1979) | killed |

The second is the one worth having: it is the *over-fix*, and it passes every assertion about the defect while breaking the behaviour the original fall-through existed for.

## PR #8835 — config: fold a doubly-elided tcp-mss so the clamp stops silently vanishing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8824-double-elision`

Part of #8824 — the SILENT half, which the issue body does not name. The loud half is PR #8834; the disputed `mss`-inline question is escalated and untouched.

`security { flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350; }` **committed clean with MSS clamping OFF.** The operator configured a clamp, the commit succeeded, and forwarded TCP went unclamped — a PMTU blackhole on tunnels with no diagnostic.

The same stanza failed **loudly** at one elision depth and **silently** at the next, which is why one symptom was reported and this one was not:

```
security { flow { tcp-mss { all-tcp 1350; } } }       1350   worked
security { flow { tcp-mss { all-tcp mss 1350; } } }   —      REJECTED (loud)
security { flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350; }               0      COMMITTED (silent)
```

### Cause

`inScope("flow","tcp-mss")` was **false**, so the doubly-elided run `[flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350]` never folded, `compileFlow` walked an empty child list, and nothing refused it. Admitting the pair folds the tail and the value reaches the compiler — the #8763/#8690 class, where an unadmitted pair means nothing folds and a compiler reading `Children` sees an empty body.

The fix is one scope entry. Its effect on the `mss`-inline spellings is to make them refused at **every** depth rather than accepted-and-discarded at one — which *is* the repair. Whether those should instead be accepted is the separate #6564-vs-#8824 dispute, escalated and deliberately not settled here.

### Wider than reported

The fail-open is **not** specific to the `mss` keyword. `flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350` — the spelling that works at every other depth — was also silently zero, as were `gre-in` and `gre-out`.

### The guard asserts "arrives OR is refused", never "commits"

A commit-success assertion is **vacuous by construction** on this defect: the broken spelling committed with `err=nil`. So every row checks the compiled **value**, and the rejected rows check that they are *rejected* rather than merely that the value is absent — because absent-and-accepted is the bug itself. Three affected kinds × three depths, with `ipsec-vpn` as the control that would catch a blanket rejection satisfying the rejected rows.

### Provenance

Found by lane-8526 working an adjacent region; measured independently here. The blind spot is #8832: `compact_leaf_cohort_6564_test.go` builds every member with the container braced, so double elision is outside its model by construction and the cohort certified this stanza green throughout.

### Mutation

Removing the scope entry restores the fail-open and kills the cell. ## PR #8836 — config: declare application-set members so the packed spelling works (#8825) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8825-application-set-members`

Closes #8825

`applications application-set <n> application <m>;` — the brace-elided spelling — compiled to a set with **zero members** while the braced form carried them, and the member was not even recorded in `UnknownMembers`, the field that exists to catch unrecognised member statements.

Found by the #8807 positional predicate. This is the class a keyword-anywhere check passes silently: `application` and `description` are declared under many other containers.

## Cause and remedy — the #8800 shape

`application-set` was declared `args: 1, children: nil`, so its members were not schema children, `isBody` was false, the brace-elision pass was never *asked* about the pairs, and no scope entry could have named them.

Two parts, and **declaring alone is not sufficient** — #8800 measured that. This also admits `("application-set","application")` and `("application-set","application-set")` in `compactNormalizeInScope`.

Measured with a masked-pair baseline plus `skipCompactNormalize`, so the tree the compiler sees is the one the probe normalised:

```
application    BASE []  ->  FIXED [a1]
application-set BASE []  ->  FIXED [inner]
bracket-list   BASE []  ->  FIXED [a1 a2]
```

## Scoped to TWO heads, not three — `description` was measured, not inherited

The compiler reads three heads under this node. The third is **benign**:

```
description    braced=[]  packed=[]   IDENTICAL
```

`compileApplications` accepts `description` deliberately — *"without adding a member and without flagging it"* — and `ApplicationSet` has **no `Description` field**. The value lands nowhere by design, so no spelling can lose it. Declaring it would move completion and validation and change no compiled result, which is a different change.

I originally marked all three as defects by inheriting the verdict from `application`. A guard now pins that `description` stays inert, so if that assumption is ever made again the cell catches it.

## No new rejection — the binding constraint

`UnknownMembers` exists *because* `application-set` was opaque: the #3890 typo guard depends on `SchemaValidate` never reaching inside. Declaring children could therefore have started **rejecting typos**, which would be a new rejection on the load path.

Measured: `SchemaValidate` returns nil for every spelling above **and for a typo'd member**, before and after. The node is not `closedWorld`, so declaring children does not begin refusing undeclared ones.

## A typo'd packed member is unchanged, and pinned as such

It does not reach the #3890 `UnknownMembers` arm — the fold only fires for admitted pairs and a typo is not one — so the set stays **empty** and the #3146 empty-application-set gate rejects it **loudly** when referenced. Baseline `[]` both before and after, so this is pre-existing rather than introduced here.

It is pinned because without the guard, a later change that made typos fold would silently convert a loud rejection into a populated set.

## `groupReplace` deliberately NOT set, and the rule is now written down

These are pure single-token value lists, which is exactly the leaf-list UNION case apply-groups exists to serve (#4070) — unlike the NAT pool `address` leaf, which packs `to` and `port` and **needed** the flag (#8816, #8817).

That distinction is load-bearing in two places now, so the deciding question is recorded at the `groupReplace` field itself where someone setting it will read it. **Getting it backwards is silent in both directions**: a dropped inherited member, or a spliced value that still looks like a value.

## PR #8837 — config: accept inline `mss`, reversing #6564 on evidence from its own instrument [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8824-inline-mss`

Closes #8824

`set security flow tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350` was refused, along with the half-packed and fully-packed hierarchical forms. #6564 pinned that refusal **deliberately**, on the premise that `mss` is the hierarchical keyword and "legitimate only as a child", so inline it is a typo.

### The disconfirming row was always in the same instrument

It had simply never been put beside the others:

```
all-tcp { mss 1350; }           ACCEPTED, compiles to 1350
tcp-mss { all-tcp mss 1350; }   was REJECTED
tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350;       was REJECTED
set … all-tcp mss 1350          was REJECTED
```

If `mss` were a typo the braced form would refuse it too. It does not — so `mss` is a real keyword in this grammar, and CLAUDE.md's contract is that a hierarchical form and its flat-set flattening compile the same, because flat `set` **is** the hierarchy written inline. The old premise was half right: `mss` is legitimate as a child, which is precisely why it is legitimate flattened.

### How a correct-looking criterion produced the wrong answer

Recorded because the criterion is still in use elsewhere. #6564's acceptance was *"compile identically in both AST shapes **or** be rejected at commit"*. It found the half-packed form rejecting and satisfied the criterion through the **OR** branch — propagating the rejection so the two shapes would agree — without checking the third shape, which already **accepted**.

That is consistency by **levelling down**: two forms made to agree by matching the broken one, with a working form a single spelling away. **An "identical OR rejected" criterion is satisfiable by making everything wrong.**

### The cell is replaced, not deleted

`TestCompactLeafTCPMSSKeywordStillRejected6564` → `TestCompactLeafTCPMSSKeywordIsAcceptedEverywhere6564`, asserting all four spellings deliver 1350 **and** that the shipped short form (`tcp-mss { all-tcp 1396; }`, `docs/ha-cluster.conf:140`) still delivers 1396 — widening acceptance must not cost the spelling the project itself ships. Both halves in one cell, with the reversal and its evidence recorded there rather than left to read as drift.

A genuine typo is still refused: `all-tcp msss 1350` and `all-tcp mss` (no value) both fail. Only the exact keyword followed by a value is consumed — and the mutation that consumes *any* second keyword is killed by those rows.

### The #4406 golden moved, and the movement is the fix working

Nine diffs, one root: a lenient fixture carrying `tcp-mss all-tcp mss 70000`.

```
before  "invalid tcp-mss value: not an integer: \"mss\""   -> 0
after   "integer out of range [0..65535] (got 70000)"      -> 70000
```

The old diagnostic named a **phantom** problem — it blamed the token `mss` because the packed form mis-selected it — and the value became 0 by accident. The new one names the actual problem; the lenient path keeps the value per its documented contract (the dataplane coerces out-of-range to 0) and the strict path still rejects. Diffed field-by-field before regenerating.

### Provenance

Adjudicated by team-lead on the measurement above, after I implemented this, measured it working across every spelling, and **reverted it** for lack of in-tree evidence for the premise. The evidence existed — one row away in my own baseline table — and I did not recognise it as evidence.

### Validation

Full `go test ./...` green tree-wide — 72 packages ok, 0 FAIL, counted; `gofmt -l` clean; both mutations confirmed to apply and build before their verdicts were read.

## PR #8840 — config: refuse a malformed braced tcp-mss body, as the packed spelling already does [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8838-braced-typo`

Closes #8838

The **same typo** was loud in one spelling and silent in the other:

```
packed  all-tcp msss 1350;      REJECTED
braced  all-tcp { msss 1350; }  ACCEPTED, clamp silently 0
packed  all-tcp mss;            REJECTED
braced  all-tcp { mss; }        ACCEPTED, clamp silently 0
```

`selectMSSToken` returned "no token" for a braced body that yields no usable value, and every caller reads that as *nothing configured* — so a **malformed** body was indistinguishable from an **absent** one. That is the #8824/#8835 shape with the token *misnamed* or *absent* rather than unparseable: same path, same end state, different kind of mistake.

The fix returns the offending keyword so the braced form inherits the **exact** refusal the packed form already gives, rather than adding a second gate that could drift from it. An empty body (`all-tcp { }`) still yields no token and stays accepted-as-unconfigured — the line the fix walks is between a body that says something unusable and a body that says nothing.

### This exists because my own report was wrong

#8837's summary claimed *"typo `msss`, `mss` with no value → still refused"*. I measured that on the **packed** spelling and generalised it to the braced one.

team-lead caught it by running the controls I had **asserted rather than measured**, and bisected first to establish the behaviour was pre-existing rather than a regression from #8837 — which it is: identical at `6d2b0a7c4` and `0b25be04c`.

The failure is the one I had just described in the opposite direction: **I varied the axis under dispute (which keyword? which value?) and held the undisputed axis (which spelling?) at whatever value was in hand.** Both of us hit it on this same stanza within an hour, from opposite sides. The comment above the #8824 branch now carries that correction, so the over-general sentence is not left standing next to the code it describes.

### Mutations

|---|---|
| fix removed (braced typo silent again) | killed |
| empty body refused too (**the over-fix**) | killed |

The second is the one that matters: refusing everything satisfies every assertion about the defect while breaking `all-tcp { }`, which is legitimate to write.

Branch: `fix/8832-double-elision-cohort`

Closes #8832

The cohort built every member as braced / singly-elided / flat-set, with the **container braced in all three**. So a config eliding two levels was outside its model *by construction*:

```

security { alg { dns disable; } }       d1  the shape it was built for
security { alg dns disable; }           d2  OUTSIDE THE MODEL
```

That gap was not hypothetical. Member 7 (`alg`, #8823) and member 4 (`tcp-mss`, #8835) were both **live at d2 while this file was green**, and both were found by other means. **A cohort that certifies a stanza has to say at what depth**, or its green is a claim about one spelling wearing the name of the class.

### What changed

Every member now carries d2, asserted as a **shape under test** rather than folded into the setup references — a regression there is a defect and must not read as a broken fixture. The distinction matters: the setup maps hold the forms the member is compared *against*, and d2 is the form being compared.

**Measured before writing:** all four members pass d2 today, because the two that were live there are already repaired. This is coverage that locks in existing fixes rather than a change that repairs anything — and the mutation confirms it has power: **removing the #8823 packed-proto read reds the new ALG d2 assertion**, which nothing else in the file covers.

Eliding the **top-level stanza keyword** too — `security alg dns disable;`, `routing-options static route 10.9.0.0/16 next-hop 192.168.1.1;`, `security flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350;` — **commits and loses the statement**, for every member that has such a form. Measured, consistent across all four.

It is the same fail-open one level further out, it is a separate defect, and fixing it means admitting top-level pairs to the normalizer rather than extending a test. So it is written into the cohort's model statement as a stated limit rather than left for the next person to rediscover — **a stated boundary is a claim and is as falsifiable as the coverage around it.**

## PR #8843 — config: parse the dash-form FPC name so node 1 picks its own RETH member [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8829-reth-member-slot`

`InterfaceSlot` parsed only the config spelling `ge-0/0/0` and returned -1 for
`ge-0-0-0` — the OPERATIONAL spelling, which is what `pkg/daemon/linksetup.go`
emits (`ge-%d-0-%d`) and therefore what an operator reads off a running box and
is likely to paste back into a config. Three silent defects followed, all from
that one parse.

## The three defects

**1. RETH resolution picked the wrong node's member.** `RethToPhysical` scores
2=local / 0=peer / 1=slot-unknown. In the dash spelling every member scored 1,
the tie broke alphabetically, and node 1 resolved `reth0` to node 0's member:

```
node 0  SLASH reth0=ge-0/0/0   DASH reth0=ge-0-0-0
node 1  SLASH reth0=ge-7/0/0   DASH reth0=ge-0-0-0   <-- node 0's member
```

**2. The alignment gate skipped the spelling that needed it.** Every such gate
is `InterfaceSlot(...) >= 0`, so a name it could not parse bypassed validation
entirely — a peer-slot interface the slash form correctly rejects was accepted:

```
CONTROL slash LOCAL slot 0   ACCEPTED
CONTROL slash PEER  slot 7   REJECTED
        dash  PEER  slot 7   ACCEPTED   <-- gate blind
```

**3. Both cluster members demoted themselves (found while enumerating callers).**
`pkg/cluster/monitor.go` decides whether a missing interface is the PEER's
before treating its absence as a local failure:

```go
slot := config.InterfaceSlot(im.Interface)
if slot >= 0 && config.SlotToNodeID(slot) != mon.mgr.NodeID() {
        continue // peer's interface
}
```

With the dash spelling that guard is **unreachable by arithmetic** — `-1 >= 0`
is unconditionally false — so control falls through to `up = false` /
"local interface missing, treating as down", feeding the RG weight dampener.
One config text describes both nodes and is synced verbatim, and each RG
monitors both nodes' interfaces at weight 255
(`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf`), so node 0 demotes itself by 255 for node 1's
link while node 1 does the same for node 0's — both members demoted over
interfaces neither ever owned. The shipped config uses the slash spelling, which
is why this stayed latent.

## PR #8846 — security: declare `keys` under perfect-forward-secrecy — packed spelling silently disabled PFS (#8844) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8844-pfs-keys`

Closes #8844

`security ipsec policy <p> perfect-forward-secrecy keys <group>;` — the brace-elided spelling — **silently disabled PFS**.

```
braced   perfect-forward-secrecy { keys group14; }   PFSGroup=14
packed   perfect-forward-secrecy keys group14;       PFSGroup=0   <- identical to ABSENT
absent   (no stanza)                                 PFSGroup=0
```

## Why this one is different from the rest of its family

Every other member of the #8800 class fails **closed** or **loud**: a zero-address NAT pool (#8800) is rejected at strict commit; an empty application-set (#8825) is caught by the #3146 gate.

**This one fails open and is undetectable afterwards.** `PFSGroup == 0` is a legitimate value meaning *deliberately disabled*, so no downstream gate can distinguish "operator chose no PFS" from "operator configured PFS and we dropped it". The tunnel comes up, traffic flows, forward secrecy is off — and the operator has positive evidence it worked: the stanza is in the file, the commit succeeded, `show configuration` displays it.

The consequence is exactly what PFS exists to prevent: a later compromise of long-term keys retroactively decrypts recorded traffic from every session negotiated while this was in effect.

## Cause — the #8800 shape

`perfect-forward-secrecy` was declared `children: nil` while `compileIPsec` reads a `keys` **child** of it. So the head was not a schema child, `isBody` was false, the brace-elision pass was never *asked* about the `("perfect-forward-secrecy","keys")` pair, and no scope entry could have named it.

The schema's own `desc` — *"Perfect forward secrecy (keys group<N>)"* — **documented the child it failed to declare.**

Two-part remedy, both required as measured on #8800: declare `keys` so the pass asks, and admit the pair in `compactNormalizeInScope` so it says yes. Both halves mutation-checked — dropping either reds 2 subtests.

## No validator on `keys`, deliberately

`parseDHGroup` accepts `group<N>` or a bare integer and leaves `PFSGroup` at 0 otherwise. `keys` is now reachable on the tolerant path, so validating it would newly **reject** a value `Store.Load` accepts today — the binding constraint.

That leaves a **second route to a silent disable**, by bad value rather than by spelling:

```
perfect-forward-secrecy keys nonsense;   ->  PFSGroup=0
```

It is **pinned as known-and-unchanged** in the guard, so nobody reads this fix as closing the whole silent-disable surface. It is a different question and wants its own decision.

## Guard

- packed ≡ braced at `group14` and `group19`;
- a **baseline arm** — the pair masked *and* `skipCompactNormalize`, because the pass also runs inside `compileConfigWithOpts` and a pre-normalised tree is not a baseline on its own;
- a **degeneracy control**: `absent` must still be 0. Without it, a fix that hard-coded a non-zero default would satisfy every other assertion while turning PFS on for operators who never asked — the same fault inverted, and equally undetectable;
- the bad-value route pinned as unchanged.

## Ratchet

Both constants tightened to measured values, with the delta **attributed** — the only schema edit here is the #8844 declaration and `enumerated` is unchanged at 1098, so both movements are from this change:

- `gateCoverageFloor` **705 → 706** (`keys` now compares)

Branch: `fix/8842-top-level-elision`

Closes #8842

Eliding the **top-level stanza keyword** lost the statement, in every member, with a clean commit on both compile paths:

```
security alg dns disable;                                       ALG stayed ENABLED
security flow tcp-mss all-tcp 1350;                             clamp at 0
routing-options static route 10.9.0.0/16 next-hop 192.168.1.1;  NO route installed
```

Reachable exactly where the already-fixed shallower cases were: the parser accepts it and `CompileConfigLenient` — the `Store.Load` and `SyncApply` ingress — returned nil while dropping the value. Same severity as #8823 and #8835, one elision level further out; the static-route case is a routing blackhole with no diagnostic.

### One mechanism, not three — and the data carried its own control

`policy-options prefix-list PL 10.0.0.0/8;` is the identical shape and **already worked**, because `("policy-options","prefix-list")` was the one such pair already admitted to the normalizer. Three pairs were missing; admitting them is the whole fix. Had the working member needed something else, the uniformity would have been coincidence rather than a lever.

### What this does to acceptance

Measured on both paths and with a typo variant, because **a new refusal on the load path is the failure mode that matters most**:

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SchemaValidate` | accepts all | accepts all | unchanged |
| `CompileConfigLenient` | accepts all | accepts all | **unchanged** |
| strict commit | accepts all | one new refusal | `tcp-mss all-tcp notanint` |

**Nothing that loads today stops loading**, and the cell asserts that directly rather than assuming it — three typo'd configs go through `CompileConfigLenient` and must still be accepted. The single new refusal is on the **strict** path for a typo previously swallowed: folding the tail makes it visible to gates that were already watching, and those gates disagree with the load path only where an operator is present.

### Scope, bounded rather than implied

80 top-level pairs exist, 26 were admitted, 54 were not; this admits three. **The remaining 51 are an upper bound on the class, not a defect count** — a pair only fails open if its compiler reads `Children`, and `alg` at d2 works with *no fold at all* because `compileALG` reads its own packed `Keys` (#8823). Each is a candidate needing the same braced-vs-elided measurement these three got.

Every pair is load-bearing — each removed separately, each kills the cell. d0/d1/d2 asserted alongside d3 as the regression half, with the shipped braced spelling from `docs/ha-cluster.conf` as the control a widened normalizer must not cost.

## PR #8848 — config: validate the VRRP group identity slot (#8839 increment 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/8839-increment1`

#8839 **increment 1**, scoped to the slots whose absence is *measured* to break something. The rest of the census is deliberately untouched and gated on this landing.

## The defect

A non-numeric `vrrp-group <id>` commits cleanly and the group then does not exist. `parseVRRPGroups` calls `strconv.Atoi` on the instance name and `continue`s on error, discarding the whole group silently.

```
vrrp-group 1     strict accepts, 1 group compiled     correct
vrrp-group foo   strict ACCEPTED, 0 groups compiled   <- the defect
vrrp-group 300   strict REJECTS                       already gated elsewhere
vrrp-group -5    strict REJECTS                       already gated elsewhere
```

**The validator therefore checks integer-ness ONLY.** Range and sign already have a gate; only the non-numeric case was unguarded, and it is the one that fails silently rather than loudly. Adding a 1–255 range here would create a **second source of truth** for a rule that already has one, which is how two gates drift apart.

`keyValidator` runs on the strict/commit path only — the tolerant `Load`/`SyncApply` ingress does not call `SchemaValidate` — so this rejects an operator edit **without changing what `Store.Load` accepts**. The guard asserts the tolerant behaviour is unchanged, and carries a **degeneracy control**: a validator that rejected everything would satisfy "foo is refused" just as well, so the numeric case is asserted alongside it.

## Increment 1 shrank 7 → 2 during this work, and every reduction was a CENSUS defect

Recorded because the census, not the schema, was wrong each time:

| | |
|---|---|
| **7 → 5** | `args:1 with children` also matches a **value leaf with sub-options** — `transmit-rate percent <n>` is a value, not an instance name. `valueType` discriminates. (census 121 → 117) |
| **5 → 3** | **"no `keyValidator`" is not "unvalidated"** — `chassis cluster redundancy-group` is already hard-rejected at strict commit by #5694's identity gate. A census keyed on the presence of one mechanism cannot see another doing the same job. |
| **3 → 2** | `services rpm probe` / `probe test` have empty placeholders but are **free-form names**. Their gap is self-description, not validation; a validator would invent a constraint that does not exist. |

Scoping to the measured-harmful subset is what made each of these visible — at 34 the remedy would have been applied across the population, writing validators onto two slots that must not have them.

## Census discipline this produced

Three separate properties, and a census can pass any two:

- **stability** — a node-keyed `seen` plus a path filter is non-deterministic under Go's randomised map order; two runs gave 79 and 112. Path-keyed, groups skipped at root: stable at 121 across three runs.
- **correctness of definition** — 121 was *stable and wrong*; value leaves were being counted as identity slots.
- **correctness of remedy** — 117 was definitionally right and still wrong about what to *do*, because already-validated and free-form slots do not want validators.

All three are in #8839's body for whoever writes the wider census.

## PR #8849 — config: split an `advisory` blind class out of `unreachable`, and correct the gateParentPrereq attribution [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/7484-advisory-bucket`

Two in-place corrections to landed guards, both **claim defects** — a guard that says something false about what it measured. Neither earns a board entry; both are fixed with their evidence here.

## 1. A new `advisory` blind class (#7484)

Seven leaves sat in `unreachable (leaf changed nothing)` while **demonstrably changing the compiled output** — via `cfg.Warnings`.

The cause is a helper whose normalisation **encodes a question**. `gateMarshal` nulls `cfg.Warnings`, and its rationale is written down and correct: for the **differential**, comparing two spellings, an advisory about a rejected value would make it look installed. But `classifyGateBlindLeaf` asks a different question — *"did the leaf reach the compiler at all"* — and for that an advisory is **evidence that it did**.

> **The same channel is signal for one question and noise for the other.**

Inheriting the helper inherited the differential's question silently, with no diagnostic. That is the shared-fixture hazard one layer down, in a marshal rather than a builder.

The seven are **read and deliberately ignored**: `system dataplane cores` compiles to *"retired DPDK-era knob (#1525), accepted for config compatibility but ignored"*. That is the **loud** form of dropping a value and it is #8785's documented remedy shape — *read it AND say it does nothing* — so it must not sit in a bucket asserting the leaf changed nothing.

`gateLeafChangesWarnings` is deliberately a **separate probe** rather than a flag on `gateMarshal`: the differential must keep nulling warnings, and a shared helper that sometimes does and sometimes does not is exactly how this arose.

**Reclassification, not regression, and the arithmetic shows it** — blind totals are conserved.

### The near-miss, recorded

My first version classified correctly but did **not add the class to the `classes` enumeration**, so the seven vanished from the blind total *and* the per-class report **while the test still passed** — every remaining bucket was at its ceiling. **A class that is classified but not enumerated is strictly worse than one in the wrong bucket.** Caught only by printing the buckets rather than accepting the green.

## 2. The `gateParentPrereq` attribution (#7492)

The header recorded that `vrrp-group` with a `virtual-address` prerequisite *"still lose the value"*, concluding those rows were **"not a parent-path problem"**. The observation is right; the **attribution** is wrong, and the attribution is the harmful half — read as written it says *"no prerequisite can help, stop looking"*, which is what a reader will do.

The prerequisite is fine. What defeats it is the synthetic **instance name**:

```
synthetic names + virtual-address    priority moves output = FALSE
real names      + virtual-address    priority moves output = TRUE
real iface + SYNTHETIC vrrp id       priority moves output = FALSE
```

The third row isolates it to the group id, not the interface name. A VRRP group id must be numeric; the gate synthesises `xa60`, the compiler discards the group, and every leaf under it reads inert regardless of prerequisite.

So an unknown fraction of #7492's 228 "not a parent-path problem" leaves is this instead, and is fixable. #7492 has a comment saying so, because a closed issue's body is what the next person reads when they arrive from a commit.

*(Note: the root cause — `args: 1` identity slots with no `keyValidator` — is filed as #8839, whose increment 1 has since landed.)*

## Ratchet resolution

This branch and #8844 both moved `gateBlindUnreachable`, in **different ways**, so the merged value is **re-measured**, never reconciled from the two:

- **#8830** (this branch): seven leaves to `advisory`. A pure **reclassification**; nothing about them changed, the measurement did.

**Predicted before measuring**, so the number is falsifiable rather than confirmatory: `perfect-forward-secrecy` is not among the seven, so the changes are disjoint and **140 − 7 = 133** was expected. ## PR #8851 — security: type the PFS `keys` leaf so its DH group is validated (#8845) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8845-pfs-values`

Closes #8845

#8844 closed the **spelling** route into a silently-broken PFS. Three **value** routes remained, all silent, and they are not the same defect:

```
keys group14    PFSGroup=14   correct
keys nonsense   PFSGroup=0    silently DISABLED
keys            PFSGroup=0    silently DISABLED (empty value)
keys group99    PFSGroup=99   PFS nominally ON with a group that does NOT EXIST
```

The first two repeat #8844's property — indistinguishable from never configuring PFS, because `0` is a legitimate "disabled" value. **`group99` is the opposite failure sharing one line of code**: not disabled, *misconfigured*, failing later and elsewhere with a diagnostic that never names this stanza.

## The remedy, and a correction to the issue's stated constraint

The issue rules out a validator because *"`keys` is now reachable on the tolerant path, so validating it would newly REJECT a value `Store.Load` accepts today."* **Right question, wrong answer** — measured:

```
                 SchemaValidate (commit)              CompileConfigLenient (Load)
keys group99     REJECTS "unsupported DH group 99"    accepts
keys nonsense    REJECTS "not a valid DH group"       accepts
keys (empty)     REJECTS "missing value"              accepts
keys group14     nil                                  accepts, PFSGroup=14
```

`validator` runs inside `SchemaValidate`, which is the **commit** path. The tolerant `Load`/`SyncApply` ingress does not call it — by documented #1319 design, and for exactly the hazard the constraint invoked: a persisted config from an older binary must not blackout-boot the node.

So all three routes reject at commit while `Store.Load` keeps accepting exactly what it accepts today. That constraint is **asserted in the guard**, not assumed.

## No second source of truth

`ValidateDHGroup` already exists and is shared with the proposal-level `dh-group` leaf and — through `config.DHGroupKeyword` — with `ipsec.formatDHGroup`. **#8597 removed that renderer's own fall-through for precisely this reason.** The list existed; this wires to it rather than writing one. Same reasoning that kept a 1–255 range off the VRRP identity validator when `strconv.Atoi` already owned that rule.

## A validator without a `valueType` is SILENTLY INERT

This cost a full diagnostic pass and is the most reusable thing here. `walkSchemaNode` gates on:

```go
if childSchema.isTypedLeaf() && (childSchema.validator != nil || childSchema.treeValidator != nil)
```

Wiring `validator: ValidateDHGroup` **alone changed nothing** — `SchemaValidate` still returned nil for `group99` and `nonsense` — while the declaration read as perfectly correct. It compiles, it looks wired, it never runs.

**Caught only by a positive control:** the proposal-level `dh-group` leaf carries the same validator, so it was run through the identical fixture shape and *did* reject. That exonerated the fixture and forced the difference into the declaration.

So the guard asserts the **arming** (`keys.isTypedLeaf()`), not merely that a validator is present — a cell checking `validator != nil` would have passed against the inert version.

## Guard

- all three broken routes rejected at commit, each **naming its own reason** (a rejection for the wrong reason reads as a working guard);

## PR #8853 — config: ratchet against INERT validator declarations (0 today) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/inert-validator-ratchet`

A `validator` on a leaf that is **not a typed leaf never runs**. `walkSchemaNode` gates on:

```go
childSchema.isTypedLeaf() && (childSchema.validator != nil || childSchema.treeValidator != nil)
```

and `isTypedLeaf()` is `valueType != ValueAny`. So a declaration carrying a validator with no `valueType` compiles, reads as correct, and is **silently inert** — the schema asserts a check that does not happen. That is a **claim defect** before it is a behavioural one: even where nothing depends on the check, the declaration is a lie about what is enforced.

## The class is empty today — 311 armed, 0 inert — and that is the argument FOR the ratchet

The failure is silent and self-consistent; nothing about the declaration looks wrong. It already cost a full diagnostic pass on #8845, where wiring `validator: ValidateDHGroup` onto the PFS `keys` leaf **changed nothing** and surfaced only because a sibling leaf carrying the same validator *did* reject in the same fixture shape.

Precedent: the arity census landed at 12 hits / 0 genuine defects for exactly this reason.

## The control is synthetic, deliberately

**A natural control was tried first and was worse than useless.** Running the census at the commit before #8845 also returned 0 — which looks exactly like a broken walk. It was not: at that commit the leaf carried no validator at all, because the inert state existed only in an uncommitted tree between two edits. **The natural control was measuring a state that never existed.**

So the cell injects a validator onto an untyped anchor and requires **exactly one hit at that exact path**, then **zero after removal**, then asserts the restore actually restored. Either half alone is satisfiable by a dead instrument — one by something that always reports, the other by something that never does.

It also **refuses to run if the anchor has since become a typed leaf**, because injecting there would *arm* the validator and the control would silently test nothing.

## Two further self-checks, both from cheaper failures earlier today

- The walk is **path-keyed**. A node-keyed walk combined with a path filter is non-deterministic under Go's randomised map order and gave 79 / 112 / 121 on an unchanged tree.
- The cell **fails if `armed == 0`**, since a walk reaching nothing would report zero inert as a property of itself rather than of the schema.

## Blindness, in the failure text

It compares `validator`/`treeValidator` against `isTypedLeaf()` and nothing else. It says nothing about a validator that is **armed but wrong**, one never reached because its parent path cannot compile, or a rule enforced outside the schema — `chassis cluster redundancy-group` is gated at strict commit by #5694 with **no schema validator at all**, so *"no validator" has never meant "unvalidated"*.

Green here means *"no declaration promises a check it cannot run"*, never *"the values are validated"*.

Validation: `go test ./pkg/config/` green (127.8s, 0 fail); `go build ./...` clean.

## PR #8855 — test: red when a scope widening lands with nothing adjudicating it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8852-blind-scope-pairs`

A widening admitted to `compactNormalizeInScope` whose pair yields **zero census
sites** is indistinguishable from one the guard fully adjudicated. Both are
green, and nothing in the output separates them.

## The mechanism

`TestCompactNormalizeScopePreservesCompiledResult8690` (arm 2) adjudicates the
sites `collectCompactSites` generates, and that census emits a site only for a
**single-arg valued leaf** or a **named-instance container**:

```go
wildcardNamed := ch.args == 0 && ch.wildcard != nil
if (ch.wildcard == nil && ch.args == 1 || wildcardNamed) && len(path) >= 1 {
```

Admitting a pair whose HEAD is a plain container, a zero-arg leaf, or a
multi-arg node produces no site at all. It does not even reach a skip bucket —
`unsynthesizable`, `unparsable` and `inScopeUnexaminable` are populated per
SITE, and there is no site to bucket.

## Measured

**503 admitted pairs, 489 with at least one adjudicated site, 14 with none.**

The whole of #8847's widening is in the blind set — `security alg`,
`security flow` and `routing-options static` were adjudicated by nothing here.
The set is security-weighted: `policy pre-shared-key` is the IPsec PSK, and
`policies global`, `policies from-zone`, `security-zone address-book` and
`security-zone host-inbound-traffic` are the policy and zone surfaces.

| shape | pairs |
|---|---|
| plain-container | `policies global`, `policy then`, `routing-options static`, `security alg`, `security flow`, `security-zone address-book`, `security-zone host-inbound-traffic` |
| multi-arg | `gateway local-identity`, `gateway remote-identity`, `policies from-zone`, `policy pre-shared-key` |
| zero-arg-leaf | `flow tcp-mss`, `match destination-address-excluded`, `match source-address-excluded` |

**Blind means UNMEASURED, not broken.** Registering a pair is not a claim that
its folding is correct; it records that this arm does not measure it. I have not
checked whether any of the 14 actually mis-folds.

## Attribution by removal

No static predicate over the output can attribute a site to the pair that
admitted it. **A site's path prefix is not its pair**: the arm derives
`stanza := container[len-1]`, so `routing-options static route` has the pair
`("static","route")` and exercises `("routing-options","static")` not at all. A
substring test and a path-prefix test both misattribute it — the first count of
this gap said one pair of three, on a prefix match.

## PR #8856 — config: fold a packed tail even when the node has a braced body (#8850, zones + screens) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8850-elided-security-containers`

Partial fix for #8850 — **zones and screens; `filter` is diagnosed and deliberately left for a second change.**

## The defect

An elided **container** brace dropped the entire stanza, with no error on either path:

```
security { zones { security-zone z1 { ... } } }   zones=1
security { zones security-zone z1 { ... } }       zones=0
security { screen { ids-option s1 { ... } } }     screens=1
security { screen ids-option s1 { ... } }         screens=0
```

## It is not a scope-admission problem

The pass asked **nothing** — `asked=[]` for every case — so no pair entry could have reached it. `normalizeCompactNodes` gated on:

```go
if len(node.Keys) > identity && len(node.Children) == 0 {
```

and the elided form is *precisely* a node with a packed tail **and** a braced body: eliding the container brace leaves the inner stanza's own braces intact, giving `Keys=["zones","security-zone","z1"]` with `Children=[the zone body]`. Every such node was declined silently.

**`Children == 0` was not the discriminator.** The comment immediately below it states the real one: a tail reads as an elided *body* only if its first token **names a child of this container**; otherwise it is the node's own multi-value payload and is left alone. That check — `head := node.Keys[identity]` plus `childSub.children[head]` — is what separates a body from a bracketed list. `Children == 0` excluded a whole *shape* wholesale, and that shape is what this issue is about. So this removes a **redundant conservatism**, not the discriminator.

## The naive version is worse than the defect, and I nearly shipped it

Dropping the guard alone makes every **count** go green while the body is lost:

```
BRACED  zone="z1" hostInboundTraffic=[ping]
ELIDED  zone="z1" hostInboundTraffic=<nil>
```

The zone **exists with an empty body**, because the braced body is left as a *sibling* of the packed statement. **That converts a missing zone into an empty zone — strictly worse**, since an absent zone is detectable as absent while a zone named `z1` with no body reads as configured. It is the sibling-attachment trap #6821 documents for readers.

So the body is re-attached **under the deepest packed statement** — the rule `packedBodyChildren` already applies, because they spell one path. It attaches to the **last** statement only; attaching to the container, or to every statement, invents structure the operator did not write.

## Guards

- **Contents, never counts.** `TestElidedContainerBraceKeepsBody8850` compares the zone *body*, and its failure message names the sibling-attachment failure explicitly, because a count-based version of this cell passed against the broken fix.
- **Negative control.** `TestElidedBraceLeavesPayloadsAlone8850` covers five nodes carrying a packed multi-value payload *alongside* braced children — a bracketed `from protocol`, a policy application list, `authentication md5 7 { key }` (the #6821 case where both genuinely coexist), a static route body, a vrrp virtual-address. Their compiled fingerprints were **byte-compared against master** before this landed and were identical; the cell pins determinism thereafter.

## `filter` is diagnosed, not fixed here

```
before this change   asked=[]                     unreachable by any scope entry
after this change    asked=[[firewall family]]    asked, and NOT admitted
```

node is fully packed with no children, so it passed the gate, was asked
about, and was refused. The within-container control that isolated it:
same container, same depth, two heads, one folds and one loses.

    d1  address-book address a1 10.0.0.1/32;   asked, REFUSED -> 0

complete on a single-entry fixture:

    scope entry only     one address -> 1 (fixed)   two addresses -> 1 (a2 LOST)

entries produces a policy referencing an address that does not exist. The
policy still exists and still reads as correct — only the reference
resolves to nothing — so it is *less* visible than an empty zone.

The naive relaxation turned a missing zone into an EMPTY zone. Counts
went green; `hostInboundTraffic` went `[ping]` -> `<nil>`. A braced body
must be re-attached UNDER the deepest packed node, never as a SIBLING of
it. That is why every cell here asserts on CONTENTS, never on "commit
succeeded".

A node can carry a packed tail AND a braced body. Attaching the body to

root-authentication -> <credential>    <- admitted since #8690, unreachable
