## PR #8870 — test: compare a leaf against ITSELF in the packed opt-in guard [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8867-same-leaf-pairs`

STACKED ON #8866 — base is `fix/8850-filter-scope`, not master. The two
address books are only opted in there, and they are 2 of the 6 containers
this touches. Retarget to master once #8866 merges.

## The hole

`TestPackedOptInHoldsForEveryLeafPair8768` iterates ordered pairs of
admitted leaves and opens with:

```go
for _, a := range leaves {
    for _, b := range leaves {
        if a == b { continue }
```

So a leaf was never compared against a second instance of itself. One
instance proves a statement is REACHABLE; only two prove the RUN IS
SPLIT. The guard was only ever measuring the first.

## Population, measured not estimated

Leaves that are `multi: true` or `args >= 2` — where a one-instance
fixture cannot distinguish a split run from a swallowed one. **10 leaves
across 6 of the 10 opted-in containers, out of 46 admitted leaves.** A
leaf in that population with no `second` fixture now reds, on the same
terms as a missing `stmts` entry, so the population cannot silently
shrink to whatever someone remembered.

## PR #8877 — config: a repeated ssh-key `set` line must ADD a key, not revoke the first [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8863-ssh-key-accumulate`

Part of #8863.

`set system root-authentication ssh-ed25519 "K2"` after `"K1"` compiled to `[K2]`.
The commit succeeded, nothing warned, and `applyRootAuth` writes the compiled set
as the **whole** of root's `authorized_keys` — so the operator who added a second
key **revoked the first**, and that administrator lost root access at the next
apply. Same shape under `system login user <u> authentication ssh-rsa`.

Fails **closed** — access lost, not granted — so it is a lockout, not a permissive
leak. Severity argued from what the daemon does on the next apply, not the config diff.

**The hierarchical spelling was already correct**, so this had a ground truth
rather than an invented expectation:

```
root-authentication { ssh-ed25519 "K1"; ssh-ed25519 "K2"; }   [K1 K2]
set … ssh-ed25519 "K1" ; set … ssh-ed25519 "K2"               [K2]
```

## Two parts, and either alone is wrong

`multi: true` on the six leaves makes repeated `set` lines accumulate onto one
node. But the compiler read `nodeVal` — `Keys[1]` only — so **with the schema
change alone the second key would be dropped instead of the first**: the #2419
multi-value defect pointed the other way, and it would have looked like a fix.
`sshKeyValues` reads the whole Keys tail *and* the children, so flat, bracketed
and hierarchical spellings all land the same set.

A real key contains spaces and arrives quoted; the lexer keeps a quoted string
whole, so `multi` never splits one key into several. Asserted.

## The duplicate-block fold (#6992)

#6992 cleared `SSHKeys` when a later `user` block re-declared `authentication`,
justified from `applySystemLogin` rewriting `authorized_keys` per entry. **That
justification is about scalars** — uid, class, password — and is untouched.

The key half of that reset was **derived, not decided**: #6992 matched the flat
spelling, and the flat spelling was the defect above. With flat corrected, the
derivation is stale, so the reset goes and both spellings land `[FIRST, SECOND]`.
#6992's equivalence **property** survives; only the expectation it was derived
from moves.

Keys are a **set** and are unioned. Scalars are replaced. uid/class still take the
last authored value — asserted, so a future change cannot quietly make everything
accumulate.

## A direction change this trades for, stated plainly

Before, `set NEW` silently revoked OLD — a lockout, but also an implicit rotation.

## PR #8884 — config: decline a fold that would strand the rest of the run [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8880-fold-strands`

`security { policies from-zone a to-zone b {…} from-zone c to-zone d {…} }` compiled
to **one** zone pair where the braced spelling gives two. Clean commit, zero
warnings, on the product's primary enforcement surface.

## The mechanism is STRANDING, not a failure to split

The parser splits a run packed onto an elided container's line into **siblings**,
and only the first carries the container keyword:

```
[policies from-zone a to-zone b]{…}   folds into `policies`
[from-zone c to-zone d]{…}            left behind
```

The fold built `policies { from-zone a … }` and left the second block as a sibling
— a `from-zone` node directly under `security`, a position the schema does not
model, which the compiler ignores without a word.

## `packedStatements` is not the fix, and that was measured

Setting `packedStatements: true` on `policies` left the packed arm at one zone
pair. That flag splits a packed **tail**; this is a sequence of **braced bodies**
after an elided container brace — different code path. **The remedy proposed on
the issue was wrong**, and testing it before claiming the issue is what caught it.

## Why decline rather than absorb

Absorbing means rewriting the **parent's** child slice, and `normalizeCompactNodes`
receives a slice plus the parent *schema*, not the parent node. Declining is the
established response for a run the fold cannot take whole.

The check is "the next sibling's head is a declared child of the container", not
"the continuation is unambiguous". Measured: **348 of 384** (parent, container)
pairs share no child name, but **36 do** — `class-of-service > interfaces` shares
`classifiers` with its own parent — and there a continuation cannot be told from a
sibling. Declining covers both.

## Blast radius, measured

**62 folds** across the shipped `.conf` corpus with this change; **62** without.
It suppresses none of them — the decline fires only where stranding would have.

## What this closes, and what it does not

Closes the **stranding**: the fold no longer produces a tree the compiler cannot
represent. It does **not** make the packed spelling work and does not make it loud
— an unknown child of `security` still commits clean, tracked separately as the
closed-world coverage gap. After this the packed form applies **nothing** rather
than half, and half-applied security policy is the worse of the two.

## PR #8893 — config: memoise nested application-set expansion [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8889-appset-memo`

Issue 8889. Expanding a nest of application-sets was **quartic** in the
branching factor and re-ran in full for every referencing policy.

### The severity is the lock, not the latency

`CommitCheck` holds the store's **read** lock across the whole compile
(`store_commit.go:70`), and `mu` is a `sync.RWMutex` — so a long read-hold
blocks **writers**: Commit, Load and the HA `SyncApply` path queue behind it.

Qualifier for the record: this needs **configuration authority**, nothing is
mis-compiled, and concurrent readers are unaffected because it is a read lock.

### Both factors, not one

A per-call memo removes the within-policy B⁴ factor; sharing **one** memo across
the strict policy validation also removes the `N_policies` factor that made 8
policies cost 8× a single one. This does both.

### The key carries the depth, deliberately

A set that expands cleanly at depth 0 may exceed the cap when reached at depth
3. A **name-keyed** memo would serve a shallow success into a deep context and
silently satisfy the depth check — the very guard that makes this cost bounded.
Keying on `(name, depth)` reuses a result only in the identical depth context,
so cap behaviour is unchanged bit-for-bit, and the memo is still at most 4
entries per set.

**The depth cap is not the defect and is untouched.** It is a working guard, and
it is what makes "quartic" a derivation rather than a guess.

### The guard asserts the curve, not a stopwatch

A wall-clock threshold is flaky and tells the next reader nothing. The cells
count expansion **bodies** and assert both that the count is bounded by 4 per
set and that bodies-per-set does not grow with breadth. A separate naive
recursion in the test computes the replaced curve, so the failure text prints it
rather than citing a remembered number:

```
breadth= 4 sets= 16 memoised= 13 naive=   85
breadth= 8 sets= 32 memoised= 25 naive=  585
breadth=16 sets= 64 memoised= 49 naive= 4369
```

Removing the memo reds it with **85 and 585** — the naive counter's own numbers,
which cross-validates both.

Liveness assert fails if the fixture reaches no expansion or yields no members,

## PR #8894 — dataplane: bump the snapshot protocol version for routing_domain [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8892-snapshot-version`

Issue 8892. `routing_domain` was added to the config snapshot in `9472a66fd`
**without bumping the protocol version**, so a helper built before it advertises
the same 8, passes the exact-equality gate, ignores the field, and resolves every
interface to domain 0 — the cross-tenant session aliasing #7160 exists to close.

The compatibility note on the field was **true and pointed one step the wrong
way**: the field *is* additive and an old helper *does* degrade to pre-#7160
behaviour. What fails is treating pre-#7160 behaviour as an acceptable fallback —
`afxdp/tests_routing_domain_7160.rs` asserts that exact state is a defect.

**Additive-and-degrades-to-old-behaviour is sound for a feature and unsound when
the old behaviour is the defect the field was added to fix.**

### Bump, not a new compatibility gate

The gate is already exact equality and is the right design — it didn't fire
because both sides said 8.

**Rolling upgrade:** daemon and helper are a **node-local** pair over the control
socket, deployed together, so a mismatch is same-node deploy skew, not
cross-node. The helper then refuses the snapshot (`unsupported snapshot protocol
version`) and does not arm the dataplane — loud and fail-closed instead of
silently enforcing weaker isolation. In an HA pair mid-upgrade each node runs its
own matched pair; the cross-node config-sync wire carries its own version
(`sync_wire_version_7990.go`) and is unaffected.

**ADD, never REDEFINE**: no field changed meaning. `MinProtocolSecureTunnelRefusal`
(7) is a production floor gating real behaviour and is deliberately **not** moved
— a v8 helper still handles `secure_tunnel` correctly.

### The guard is a shape pin, because a lockstep pin would not have caught this

The obvious defence — assert the Go constant equals the Rust one — **passes
straight through this defect**: both sides stayed at 8 and therefore *agreed*.
The drift was between the snapshot's **shape** and its version.
`TestSnapshotShapeIsPinnedToProtocolVersion8892` digests the wire structs'
exported fields and demands the version move when the digest does. It can't tell
a compatible addition from an incompatible one and doesn't try — it forces the
decision when it's cheap. The existing `TestSnapshotProtocolVersionLockstepWithRust`
is kept, not duplicated; it answers the other question.

### Two existing cells pinned the version at 8 — read, not edited away

Both use a **test-only** constant documented as *"the version this PR must ship
at"*: a development-time pin from #6691, which has shipped. Its live invariants
(planes agree; version exceeds the pre-secure-tunnel value) survive a bump. Only
the literal moved, with the reason recorded beside it.

## PR #8895 — userspace-dp: fail closed on NAT64 egress through a native tunnel (#8890) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8890-nat64-tunnel-plaintext`

A NAT64-translated packet whose route resolved through a native GRE or WireGuard endpoint was emitted on the physical NIC **unencapsulated**. It is now dropped, counted, and surfaced to the operator.

## What was measured

The TX copy path selects its frame builder on `is_nat64` **exclusively**, and only the branch it skips carries the tunnel post-pass. `enqueue_pending_forwards` refuses direct TX when `is_nat64 || uses_native_tunnel`, so the combination is routed *into* that path rather than away from it.

At `c2e0a9ecb`, varying only `resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id`:

```
P8890 tunnel_endpoint_id=7 -> Some(len=58)  control_len=58
P8890   ethertype=0x0800   ipproto@23=0x06  IDENTICAL_TO_PLAINTEXT=true
```

Byte-identical to the no-tunnel control — plain IPv4, no encapsulation, **no drop**. Of the three possible outcomes this was the worst: encapsulating would have refuted the finding, `None` would have been fail-closed. Traffic an operator routed through WireGuard left as plaintext on the underlay, with no counter to see it by.

## Why drop rather than encapsulate

Dropping is the posture this codebase had already chosen for the sibling cases: #1873 R-E drops a tunnel-marked decision whose outer next-hop is unresolved rather than let a later in-place rewrite *"TX PLAINTEXT"*, and #2327 — in the very function this builder is selected against — drops rather than emit for an unknown tunnel mode, because a fail-OPEN default in a security appliance is the defect.

**Writing the dispatch cell surfaced something worth stating: #1873's gate on the slow-path REINJECT exit was already correct for this case.** It simply never ran, because the build exit returned a frame and the packet was enqueued for TX. The two gates are siblings on the two ways out of a failed forward, and only one of them existed. Both exits are now pinned closed by the cell.

Encapsulating is the better end state and is deliberately **not** done here. The tunnel post-pass wraps a finished inner frame, so it looks composable — but `wg_encap_frame` parses that frame using `inner_meta.addr_family` in three places (`packet_trimmed_len`, `inner_dst_ip` for AllowedIPs peer selection, `inner_tos_byte`). After NAT64 the frame is IPv4 while `meta` still describes the IPv6 *ingress*, so passing `meta` through would parse an IPv4 packet as IPv6: wrong length, destination read past the header into the TCP payload. Composing needs a corrected meta plus a re-derivation of the outer identity (#2680/#3992/#5292) — separately reviewable, and shipping it wrongly reintroduces exactly this failure. Filed as its own issue.

## Review notes

- **The gate is in the BUILDER, not the dispatch site.** It is the only production caller today, but an inert gate on a second path would be indistinguishable from a working one by inspection.
- **The attribution is checked FIRST**, mirroring the builder's own guard order. A frame that is also ext-header-ineligible or a fragment must not be attributed to those: the real signal is "this NAT64 + tunnel route is not forwarded at all", and the other reasons send an operator chasing a translation fault that does not exist.
- **The untunnelled control is the first assertion of the builder cell and is load-bearing.** Asserting only `is_none()` is satisfied by a builder failing for any unrelated reason — the cell would stay green while measuring nothing.

## Validation

| mutation | reds on |
|---|---|
| remove the production gate | `is_none()`, reporting `control 58 bytes, Got Some(58)` — the original measurement reproduced inside the cell |
| force the builder to always return `None` | the control's non-vacuity message (not the subject) |
| swap the attribution order | the tunnel-counter assertion |
| Go aggregation `+=` → `=` | `want 7 = 2+5` (2 and 5 across two bindings, so only 7 distinguishes summing from reading one worker) |

The dispatch cell drives the real dispatcher because the builder cell cannot answer reachability, and reuses the #6922 AH-fragment fixture so all three attribution reasons are live at once and the order is observable.

**Layout guards.** Adding an `AtomicU64` moved `offset_of(pending_tx_admitted)` 2192 → 2200 and `offset_of(delta_loss_pending)` 2320 → 2328, `size_of` unchanged at 2368. The compile-time asserts and the #6304 runtime guard were re-measured **only after building both configurations and confirming they shift identically** — that agreement is the discriminator those guards exist for, since a `cfg(test)` field would move the test build alone and one set of literals could not make both green.

Full Rust suite **5354 passed / 0 failed**; `go test ./pkg/dataplane/...` ok.

## Docs

Recorded in `docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md` (the authoritative gap doc) as a mixed-boundary row plus a dedicated section, and in the NAT64 row of `docs/feature-coverage.md`. A non-zero `NAT64 tunnel encap unsupported drops` is an unsupported-configuration signal, not a capacity or fragmentation one.

Closes #8890

## PR #8897 — test: make the sweep's WARNS verdict mean what it claims [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8895-warns-soundness`

`gated()` in the brace-elision sweep asked *"does the elided spelling produce ANY
warnings?"* and scored **WARNS** — which the #8859 criterion reads as **HANDLED,
the operator is told**. That is a different question from "is the operator told
about **this drop**", and any container carrying a standing advisory answered it
for free.

Measured on `aggregated-ether-options -> lacp` — the identical #6544 notice in
both arms:

```
braced  warnings=1   "aggregated-ether-options configured but
elided  warnings=1    accepted-only — xpf does not implement 802.3ad"
```

The operator is told LAG is unimplemented. They are **not** told their `lacp
active` was discarded.

### Fix

Compare the warning **sets**: only a warning present in the elided arm and absent
from the braced one is about the drop. The liveness rule applied to the warning
channel — a warning in both arms is standing and proves nothing, exactly as a
value absent from both proves nothing.

**Error direction**: this could only score a real drop as HANDLED, never the
reverse. It under-reported, which is the direction that looks clean.

### The branch had no control, which is why the rule survived

The sweep's own header already recorded that the WARNS branch has no member and
that *"nothing here proves it still fires"*. An unexercised branch is exactly
where an unsound rule lives undisturbed. The new cells supply both controls the
sweep structurally cannot:

- a standing warning present in both arms must **not** score WARNS
- a warning unique to the elided arm **must** — so the fix cannot trade an
  unsound branch for a dead one

### No published row changes

The WARNS branch had no members, so totals stay: 55 pairs / 31 SILENT / 2
STRICT-REJECTS / 0 WARNS / 21 SAME / 1 NO-REFERENCE. `pkg/config` green.

## PR #8900 — dataplane: restart the helper when process identity changes during XSK startup (#8899) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8899-process-identity-restart`

A config changing only the helper's binary, its sockets, its state file or its poll mode was **acked without restarting the helper** during the pending-XSK-startup window. The apply succeeded, the desired config was recorded as running, and the live child kept its original argv and socket.

## Why the trigger could not fire

That window's restart trigger compared binding **plan keys**. `snapshotBindingPlanKey` covers workers, ring entries and interface/fabric topology; process identity is not in it. Measured on #8899, with controls:

```
base plan key: "workers=4;ring=2048;"
Binary A->B                  plan key unchanged = true
ControlSocket A->B           plan key unchanged = true
StateFile A->B               plan key unchanged = true
PollMode busy->interrupt     plan key unchanged = true
CONTROL Workers 4->8         plan key unchanged = false
CONTROL RingEntries          plan key unchanged = false
```

`m.cfg = ucfg` in that branch is what makes it non-self-repairing: a later **identical** apply compares against the desired config, sees no change, and does not restart either. **The obvious operator recovery — reapply the same config — is exactly the one that cannot work.**

## The fix consults the predicate that already exists

`configEqual` is what `ensureProcessLocked` uses on the normal path, and it covers exactly the seven process-identity fields. This branch simply never asked it.

**Widening the plan key instead would have been wrong.** It also gates the same-plan refresh exception that lets FIB-only updates through during XSK startup, and it must not churn when a tunnel appears or moves (the four-call-site note in `ingress_exclusions.go`). Each predicate still answers the question it is named for.

## The population is five fields, not four

The issue measured four. **`EventSocket` is equally absent from the plan key and equally argv-adjacent** — derived from the control socket's directory when empty, and the event stream is dialled on it. The cell derives the count from the two predicates rather than transcribing it, so it cannot drift.

## My first completeness guard asserted the wrong policy

It required every exported field of `config.UserspaceConfig` to be compared by `configEqual`. Seventeen exist, seven are compared, so it failed on ten — and "fixing" that would have **restarted the dataplane on a cpu-governor change**. Running the blanket rule is what showed it was more dangerous than the bug.

The ten are applied by the **daemon** out of band (sysfs/ethtool, `daemon_apply_tail.go`), travel inside the snapshot (`SharedUMEM`), or are diagnostic (`RetiredKnobsSeen`). The guard now asserts **classification, not membership**: every field must be in exactly one set, exempt entries carry their reason, and a newly added field fails until someone decides which it is. That decision is the one never made for the seven.

## The fourth cell exists because the first three were not enough

Removing the `|| processIdentityChangedDuringStartup` disjunct left **all three green** — they exercise the predicate, `configEqual` and the plan key, so the predicate is correct and the dispatcher just would not consult it. That is the same defect I held #8897 for earlier today, reproduced in my own work, so it gets a guard rather than a note.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop `ControlSocket` from `configEqual` | reds all three predicate cells |
| remove the production disjunct | reds the wiring guard |
| delete the call entirely | **fails to compile** |
| add a field without classifying it | reds the classification guard |

The wiring guard is a comment-stripped source scan — the weaker instrument, and the one this codebase already uses for this problem (`nat64_never_reaches_the_in_place_rewrite_path_6922`). Driving the real branch needs a live child, and the existing startup-window harness fakes it with `os.FindProcess(os.Getpid())`, so a cell reaching `stopLocked` would signal the test runner. **It cannot prove the branch behaves correctly; it proves the call was not deleted, which is the failure that happened.**

`go test ./pkg/dataplane/...` all green.

## PR #8902 — config: keep the master-password PRF when the system brace is elided [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8898-master-password-elision`

Issue 8898. `system master-password pseudorandom-function <p>;` resolved to **no
selector**, so configstore fell back to `defaultMasterPasswordPRF` and the config
DB was encrypted with a KDF the operator did not choose — while `show
configuration` rendered the one they wrote.

**Display and enforcement disagreeing silently is what makes this a security
defect rather than a config-loss defect.**

### Two fixes, and the first alone did nothing

**1. Admit `system master-password`** to `compactNormalizeInScope` — the #8858
shape exactly. The inner pair `master-password pseudorandom-function` had been
admitted all along and **inert**, because the fold reaches a child only after
`system -> master-password` creates the container.

**2. Fold at the scan site.** That first fix repaired the *compiled* config and
changed nothing here, because **this consumer does not read the compiled
config**: `effectiveMasterPasswordPRF` walks the **raw tree**, so it never sees
the normalizer, which runs inside the compiler. The selector still resolved to
nothing after the scope entry landed.

This is #8867's shape with a different consumer — `SchemaValidate` walked the
un-normalized tree and *validated* nothing; this reader walked it and *resolved*
nothing. **The fold is a property of the compile path, and every reader outside
it has to opt in.** Both halves are proven necessary: unwiring either reds the
cells.

### The fixture value is deliberately not the default

The first measurement of this defect used `sha256`, which **is**
`defaultMasterPasswordPRF` — so losing the selector produced the same effective
value as keeping it. The braced arm was live, the comparison was real, and the
row measured clean while fully broken. `TestFixtureIsNotTheDefault8898` reds if
the constant ever becomes the default or an unsupported value, because the next
person will reach for the default exactly as I did.

### Validation

All three depths resolve the authored selector, asserted on the **enforced**
value rather than on compile success. A display/enforcement cell asserts the
rendered configuration and the enforced PRF agree, with a liveness check that the
render mentions the selector at all — without it the cell compares two blanks. A
mutation cell asserts the scan does not mutate the caller's tree, which
configstore persists. The new pair is registered in the #8852 blind list
(zero-arg plain container) with a pointer to the cells that do measure it.
`pkg/config`, `pkg/configstore`, `pkg/daemon` green.

## PR #8908 — test: a sweep verdict must not be a single-leaf sample [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/sweep-leaf-contingent`

Closes #8907.

`TestSweepFull` deduped by `(stanza, child)` and kept the **first site it reached**, so every published verdict was a property of whichever leaf `collectCompactSites()` enumerated first — an order no reader of the table can see.

Found by lane-8526 on `interfaces <name>`, which published `STRICT-REJECTS` while a hand-written leaf compiles strictly clean on both arms.

## Before and after, same commit `7813df3db`

| verdict | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| CANDIDATE-DROP/SILENT | 22 | 19 |
| CANDIDATE-DROP/STRICT-REJECTS | **2** | **1** |
| SAME | **21** | **18** |
| NO-REFERENCE | 1 | 1 |
| **LEAF-CONTINGENT** | — | **7** |

```
class-of-service classifiers    SILENT(via inet-precedence) | SAME(via dscp)
class-of-service rewrite-rules  SILENT(via exp)             | SAME(via dscp)
class-of-service fairness       NO-REFERENCE(via queue)     | SAME(via interface)
interfaces <name>               SILENT(link-speed) | STRICT-REJECTS(periodic) | SAME(bandwidth)
services ip-monitoring          SILENT(via policy)          | NO-REFERENCE(via hold-down)
services rpm                    SILENT(via probe)           | NO-REFERENCE(via destination-interface)
system services                 SILENT(dhcp-socket-type) | NO-REFERENCE(ciphers) | SAME(error-backoff-max)
```

## The direction of the error is the harmful one

**Four of the seven mix `SAME` with `CANDIDATE-DROP`.** Under first-site-wins those pairs could publish **SAME — no defect —** while a different leaf under the same pair silently loses its value.

This column decides admit-vs-decline for anyone working the population, so a genuinely silent drop that drew a strict leaf reads STRICT-REJECTS and gets skipped as *"already loud"*. That is the `system login` trap **inverted** — there a handled row looked like a defect; here a defect row looks handled.

`system login`, the other published STRICT-REJECTS, is unaffected: #8859 batch 1 asserts its rejection with a hand-written fixture rather than through `synthPair`.

The guard's first draft compared configs with `fmt.Sprintf("%v")`. The Config graph is full of pointers, so `%v` prints **addresses** — every site read CANDIDATE-DROP, every pair agreed, and it reported **zero** contingency against the sweep's seven. It marshals to JSON now.

## PR #8912 — config: key the sweep skip on re-split tokens, and land a Config compare helper [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/sweep-leaf-contingent`

Continuation of #8908, which I merged at `0cd91606b` while its author was still working. This carries the two commits that were left stranded when that PR closed — **opened by the gate, not the author, so the work is not blocked on a round-trip.**

## 1. The population defect (found by a second lane, verified independently by the author)

`TestSweepFull` skipped already-admitted pairs with `compactNormalizeInScope(stanza, child)` where `child = s.container[1]`. For a named-instance container **that element holds two tokens** — `"policer xpfarg"` — so the predicate, keyed on the bare keyword, never matched and admitted pairs stayed in the un-admitted population.

Measured independently by both lanes, matching exactly: **16 pairs, 108 sites.**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| population | 46 | **30** |
| SAME | 18 | **3** |
| SILENT | 19 | 19 |
| silent fraction | 41% | **63%** |

**Those 16 rows read `SAME` because the fold already handles them**, not because the two spellings are naturally equivalent — so the `SAME` column was conflating *"no defect here"* with *"already fixed"*. That is the fold-does-the-work distinction surfacing in a third instrument today. **The correction moves in the worse direction**, and was held to a higher bar for that reason: all 16 enumerated, all 16 located in the published table, causal claim controlled two-sided rather than asserted.

This is the same keying bug the #8852 census already fixed, which is the argument for the helper below landing once rather than per-instrument.

## 2. `ConfigFingerprint` / `ConfigsIdentical`

The mechanical form of a lesson that bit its own author today: their first draft of the #8907 detection compared configs with `fmt.Sprintf("%v")`, which on a pointer-laden `Config` prints **addresses** — so every site read CANDIDATE-DROP, every pair agreed, and it reported **zero** contingency against the sweep's seven. They had documented that exact trap hours earlier and sent it to another lane as a time-saver.

**Having written the warning is not protection against the thing.** The helper makes the trap unavailable instead of documented, and its cell *demonstrates* the need rather than asserting it: two compiles of one text, `%v` says DIFFERENT, the helper says identical — and it still separates two configs that really differ, so "always equal" cannot pass.

## Gate note

The binding half of #8908 was gated and merged separately at `0cd91606b`; M3 and M4 were both re-run there by the gate and kill on independent assertions. **This PR needs gating only for the two items above** — I will re-derive the 46→30 numbers rather than check the arithmetic, since two instrument fixes have now landed against one baseline.

## PR #8913 — test: key the sweep skip on re-split tokens, and land a Config compare helper [CLOSED] (closed 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/sweep-population-and-compare-helper`

Re-lands the two changes stranded when #8908 merged at `0cd91606b` (the binding fix only). Same commit, cherry-picked onto current master — **not rebased or re-derived**, except the published numbers, which I re-measured because master moved.

## 1. The sweep was still sweeping 16 ALREADY-ADMITTED pairs

The un-admitted filter keyed on `s.container[1]`, but a container **element** can hold two tokens — `"policer xpfarg"`, `"community xpfarg"`, `"three-color-policer xpfarg"` — because a named-instance container carries its placeholder in the same element. `compactNormalizeInScope` is keyed on the bare keyword, so `("firewall", "policer xpfarg")` never matched and the admitted pair stayed in the population.

Found by lane-8526, who had the identical bug in #8852's census and fixed it the same way. **Verified independently before fixing: 16 admitted pairs across 108 sites**, matching their count exactly.

It is silent in both directions — a two-element slice one of whose elements contains a space prints exactly like a three-element one.

### Numbers RE-DERIVED at current master `9e1bd2ac4`

My earlier report said 46 → 30 / SAME 18 → 3. **Those were measured at an older base and no longer hold** — #8909 and #8911 landed admissions in between. At the current base:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| population | **38** | **22** |
| SAME | **17** | **2** |
| CANDIDATE-DROP/SILENT | 14 | 14 |
| silent fraction | 37% | **64%** |

The 16-pair delta is the same; the totals moved underneath it. Two instrument fixes have now landed against one baseline, so an adjustment carried across both would have agreed with itself while being wrong — the numbers above are a fresh measurement, not arithmetic.

**Those 16 rows read `SAME` because THE FOLD ALREADY HANDLES THEM**, not because the two spellings are naturally equivalent. The `SAME` column was conflating *"no defect here"* with *"already fixed"*. The corrected population is substantially less benign than the table reported, and **the correction moves in the worse direction.**

## 2. `ConfigFingerprint` / `ConfigsIdentical`

So the `%v` trap is **unavailable rather than documented**. The Config graph is full of pointers, so `%v` prints addresses: two structurally identical configs render differently on every compile, and **the failure is stable**, which is why re-running confirms it.

Three wrong measurements in this campaign came from it — a sampling row filed as a defect, a contingency guard reporting zero against the sweep's seven, and the same trap committed hours after its author documented it and warned another lane.

`TestConfigFingerprintBeatsPercentV8908` **demonstrates** the need rather than asserting it:

- two compiles of one text → `%v` says DIFFERENT, the helper says identical;
- **and** the helper still separates two configs that really differ, so *"always equal"* cannot pass it.

That second half is what makes it a helper rather than a way to stop comparisons failing.

The sweep now uses it instead of a local renderer.

## PR #8917 — test: a STRICT-REJECTS verdict requires the BRACED arm to be accepted [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/gate-strict-rejects-braced-arm`

The gate reported `STRICT-REJECTS` whenever the **elided** spelling failed strict commit, without asking whether the **braced** one compiles. If both arms are refused, the rejection is about the fixture — an undefined reference, a missing required sibling — and says nothing about the elision.

**This is the WARNS unsoundness of #8897 in the other operator-facing channel.** One defect, two costumes:

| channel | the fix |
|---|---|
| `WARNS` | compare warning **sets** between arms — a warning in both is standing |
| `STRICT-REJECTS` | require the **braced arm to compile** — a rejection in both is about the fixture |

Both are the liveness rule aimed at an operator-facing channel rather than at a value. **The error is in the under-reporting direction**, which is the one that looks careful: a row the census has cleared as *"already loud"* is one nobody re-opens.

## Measured on my own filed rows — two of three flip

```
interfaces -> classifiers     braced=REJECTS  elided=REJECTS  -> NOT about the elision
interfaces -> rewrite-rules   braced=REJECTS  elided=REJECTS  -> NOT about the elision
policy -> match               braced=accepts  elided=REJECTS  -> HOLDS
```

Leniently neither of the two loses anything, so they are **non-defects with a wrong gate reading**, not defects filed as handled. That is luck rather than method — the exposure being audited was a real drop wearing a HANDLED badge, and only the lenient measurement rules it out.

## And the sweep's own positive control was resting on an artifact

With the check wired, the single published `STRICT-REJECTS` row — **`system login`, the row #8859 cites as proof the gate arm fires** — reclassifies to `BOTH-ARMS-REJECTED`. Its synthesized fixture fails strict on *both* spellings, so the sweep was never demonstrating that the elision is loud.

**The underlying fact is true**, verified separately with a hand-written fixture:

```
system { login { user alice { class super-user; } } }   accepts, 1 user
system login user alice { class super-user; }           REJECTS
```

Which is exactly what lane-8526 said when they noted #8859 batch 1 asserts that rejection directly rather than through `synthPair`. **The claim was independently established; only the sweep's evidence for it was an artifact.** The positive control was real, and the instrument was not the thing establishing it.

`BOTH-ARMS-REJECTED` is published as its own verdict rather than folded into `SILENT` or `?`, on the same principle as `LEAF-CONTINGENT`: a fixture that cannot answer the question is a third state, not a quiet member of one of the other two.

## Validation

`go test ./pkg/config/ -count=1` green (117s). `./pkg/refactoraudit/` green. Sweep counts deterministic across repeat runs.

## PR #8926 — test: ratchet the #8876 latent rows, with membership by measurement [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `test/8876-latent-ratchet`

Closes out the brace-elision census (issue 8876) with the agreed durable artifact: a ratchet over the rows adjudicated LATENT.

## What a latent row is, and why it needs a guard

An edge filed NOT A DEFECT on a premise with an expiry date — the edge is unadmitted so the fold never fires, but nothing is lost *today* because no leaf under the container carries a value worth losing. **Add one tomorrow and it is dropped silently.** The row is a prediction nobody was watching.

## Membership is by MEASUREMENT, not by the census's own label

Five rows were filed LATENT. **Two survive.** The premise — "a future leaf is lost SILENTLY" — is a claim about a leaf the compiler does not yet know, and that is directly measurable:

| row | unknown leaf under it | latent? |
|---|---|---|
| `ip ip-sweep` | STRICT-REJECTS + warning | no |
| `icmp flood` | STRICT-REJECTS + warning | no |
| `interfaces oversubscription-policy` | warning | no |
| `pool persistent-nat` | **SILENT** | **yes** |
| `firewall family inet` | **SILENT** | **yes** |

The two screen rows are not latent at all: their family reader normalises packed tails through the **generic, schema-driven `packedBody`**, so a new leaf reaches the switch, lands in `default:`, and #3318's `validateScreenUnknownStrict` refuses the commit fail-closed. It cannot vanish quietly — it is refused until someone adds compiler support.

Keeping those three would have made the guard assert something **false** in its own failure text ("drops values SILENTLY"). A wrong diagnostic is worse than a missing one: the reader trusts it and stops looking.

## Two corrections carried in the file so they are not re-learned

- **Counts are unioned across every site.** A container reachable by several paths is a different node at each, and first-seen-wins made the set depend on Go's map order. `family inet` is the live example — 4 leaves across 2 sites, recorded by the census's own running list as **1** because it was measured at one.
- **`policy-statement -> then` is a DEFECT, not latent.** It was filed LATENT from a fixture using `accept` — one of exactly two `args:0` survivors out of ten children. All eight value-carrying routing actions are dropped. It must not be re-added here.

`chassis -> cluster` is **deliberately excluded** despite adjudicating LATENT: 17 value-carrying leaves on an actively-developed container would fire on ordinary work, and a guard that fires on ordinary work gets worked around. Recorded rather than dropped silently, so the exclusion is a decision someone can reverse rather than an omission to rediscover.

## The failure text refuses to offer the easy fix

It does not say "update the expected count". Editing the constant without adjudicating the new leaf converts a caught defect into a filed one, which is the single thing this guard exists to stop.

## Validation

    clean                                  PASS  2 edges, 6 leaves
    M1 leaf added to pool persistent-nat   FAIL  "GAINED a value-carrying leaf: expected 2, found 3"
    M2 container renamed                   FAIL  "reached NO SITE in the schema walk"

Each mutant killed on its **own** branch with its own message — asserted, not just the failure. Full `pkg/config` green, gofmt clean, counts re-derived at this base.

## PR #8930 — fix: admit ssh ciphers and macs to the brace-elision fold [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8922-ssh-algorithm-lists`

Fixes the defect filed as issue 8922.

## The defect

`system services ssh` declares three algorithm allowlists. They are **schema-identical** — `args:1, multi:true, validator ValidateSSHAlgorithm, children nil` — read by the same loop over `firewallMatchValues` into three parallel fields, each rendering one line of the same sshd drop-in.

Only `key-exchange` was admitted to the brace-elision fold:

    system { services { ssh { ciphers aes256-ctr; } } }   ->  [aes256-ctr]
    system { services { ssh ciphers aes256-ctr; } }       ->  []    silent

An empty list writes **no `Ciphers` line at all**, so sshd keeps its permissive built-in default. A config hardening all three applied `KexAlgorithms` and silently ignored `Ciphers`/`MACs` — **partial application, which reads as success**, because the drop-in visibly carries the operator's key-exchange line.

The comment above the `key-exchange` reader describes this exact failure — *"a hardening change that appears applied and is not"* — and was written while fixing one leaf of three.

## Measured, both sides

|  | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `ssh ciphers X;` | `[]` | **`[aes256-ctr]`** |
| `ssh ciphers [ a b ];` | `[]` | **`[a b]`** |
| `ssh ciphers X; macs Y;` | `[]` and `[]` | `[]` and `[]` — unchanged |

The multi-statement run stays broken and is **not made worse**: #8850's decline branch already refuses to fold an ambiguous run, so everything was dropped before this change too.

## Scope, stated honestly

**The CLI is unaffected.** `set system services ssh ciphers X` builds a nested tree through `SetPath`, so the compiler never sees the elided shape. The loss is reachable through a config **file** using the compact spelling. Real, and a real inconsistency — but not the operator's normal path, and worth saying so plainly rather than letting a reader rate this a live CLI bypass.

## #8921 check done BEFORE landing

`compactNormalizeInScope` is keyed `(containerKeyword, head)` with **no parent context**, so an admission leaks to every same-named container. Enumerated first: `ssh` names exactly one container (reached directly and through the `groups` mirror of the same node), and `ciphers`/`macs` are declared by no other container. The admission cannot leak.

## The guard derives the family from the schema

A literal list would need editing by the same person who forgets the siblings. The predicate — a multi-value identifier list under `ssh` — makes a **fourth** algorithm list fail the test the day it is declared. It also binds the derivation itself, so a predicate that stops selecting the three is a visible failure rather than a silent pass over an empty set.

## The #8880 ratchet moved, and the delta is attributed rather than absorbed

95 → 97 / 460 → 462: exactly these two pairs. The constant's comment carries the before/after measurement and **the residual that stays open** — `ciphers`/`macs` are `multi`, so they land in the group where the `packedStatements` opt-in is known insufficient. The ratchet's warning is not waived, it is answered.

    M2  only `macs` removed      ->  FAILs naming macs alone — the ORIGINAL

## PR #8937 — fix: admit the eight policy `then` actions to the brace-elision fold [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8933-policy-then`

Fixes the defect filed as issue 8933 — the last live row from the issue 8876 census, and the highest-consequence one.

## The defect

A brace-elided `policy-statement <p> term <t> then <action>` clause lost every value-carrying routing action **and** corrupted the term's terminal action:

```
braced:  then { metric 50; }   ->  Action=""        Metric=50
elided:  then metric 50;       ->  Action="metric"  Metric=0
```

`policy_render.go` branches on exactly that field:

```go
nonTerminating := term.Action != "accept" && term.Action != "reject"
```

so the term renders as `permit` + `on-match next` with no `set` clauses — it loses its attributes **and stops terminating**, falling through to later terms and the default action. A term written to accept-with-metric does neither.

The fall-through half is invisible to a fingerprint comparison, which is why the census that found this row could tell that something was lost but not what the loss did.

## Scope, measured

The predicate is keyed on a `(container keyword, head)` pair with no parent context, and **fourteen** containers are named `then`. I walked the schema: exactly one declares any of these eight heads, so the admission cannot leak (issue 8921). All eight are admitted together — a partially admitted family is the issue 8922 shape, where partial application reads as success.

## Why this overrides a prior decision

Issue 8690 classed these eight `partial` and excluded them, on the rule that a partial site has a reader consuming its tail, so folding truncates a value that is READ.

That rule contains two claims. **Something consumed the tail** — measured. **It was entitled to** — inferred, never measured. Here the consumer was the defect itself. Removing it makes both spellings agree, verified across all eight heads including the multi-token tails the original single-value fixture never exercised:

| tail | result |
|---|---|
| `community add BLUE` | preserved |
| `community delete [ LA LB ]` | both names preserved |
| `as-path-prepend "65001 65001"` | both ASNs preserved |

Filed separately as issue 8936, because it invalidates a control. The 2419 `filedStillOpen` anchor was deliberately re-anchored to a partial site on the recorded premise that a partial site is *"structurally immune to the sweep"*. That anchor was `then local-preference`; this change normalizes it — the **third anchor in a row** consumed by the next family to land, and the only one chosen expressly to end that churn.

Re-anchored to `bridge-domains xpfname routing-interface` on the property that actually holds and that nobody had written down: **its container slot is an arg placeholder**, so production asks the predicate with an arbitrary instance name and no static pair can ever match it — a permanent bound of a pair-keyed predicate, not a classification a later fix can dissolve. Third compiler file too, preserving the two-different-files property that anchor exists to provide.

## Reachability

**The flat-set path is not affected and never was.** Measured through `ParseSetCommandGrouped` + `SetPathQuotedGrouped`: identical output with and without this change, across six multi-statement cases. The defect is confined to the hierarchical brace-elided spelling, reached via `load merge` of an operator-authored file. I had been about to claim the wider severity.

Each recorded the same false claim:

## PR #8941 — fix: split packed runs in tunnel and policer if-exceeding containers [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8904-packed-run-truncation`

Fixes the defect filed as issue 8904.

## The defect

A packed run of two statements keeps the first and silently discards the rest.

    tunnel { source 10.0.0.1; destination 10.0.0.2; }   src=10.0.0.1  dst=10.0.0.2
    tunnel source 10.0.0.1 destination 10.0.0.2;        src=10.0.0.1  dst=""

    if-exceeding { bandwidth-limit 10m; burst-size-limit 100k; }   bw=1250000  burst=100000
    if-exceeding bandwidth-limit 10m burst-size-limit 100k;        bw=1250000  burst=0

`warnings=0`, no strict rejection, on both.

This is the sibling mode of #8883's **injection**: there a `multi` leaf absorbed a repeated keyword as one of its own values and produced a phantom extra member; here the container carries the first statement correctly and drops everything after it.

**A GRE tunnel that keeps its source and loses its destination is worse than one that fails to compile.** The interface exists, `show configuration` renders both endpoints because the config is stored as authored, and the tunnel points nowhere. Missing becomes *wrong* rather than missing becomes *absent*. The policer is the same mechanism on an enforcement surface.

## The remedy is the one the docs already prescribe

`docs/config-schema.md` documents three decisions that must agree. Two were already right — the pairs are admitted and every leaf carries `args: 1` — and only `packedStatements` was missing, so the tail became a chain instead of siblings.

## The elided arm was checked for LEGALITY before the divergence was believed

A two-statement container has no elided spelling unless the grammar admits one, and a fixture that invents one measures nothing. `ParseSetCommand` accepts `set … tunnel source A destination B`, so this is a form the grammar takes rather than a fabricated arm.

## Scope, measured rather than assumed

**Hierarchical spelling only.** The flat-set CLI reaches the same symptom by a **different mechanism**: `SetPath` builds the tokens as a nested chain (`tunnel > source 10.0.0.1 > destination 10.0.0.2`) before any pass runs, so there is no packed tail to split and `normalizeCompactStanzas` correctly folds nothing (measured: `folded=0`). It affects at least four unrelated stanzas and is filed as issue 8939.

Fixing it here would mean changing the flat-set grammar under cover of a compact-normalize change.

## The #8768 guard required the work it exists to require

Opting a container in is a claim that **every** admitted leaf survives the packed spelling. So all six admitted tunnel leaves and both `if-exceeding` leaves get fixtures at **both** declaring sites, each with a **second** instance — one instance proves a statement is reachable, only two prove the run is split.

`keepalive` and `routing-instance` are not admitted, so fixtures for them would be inert and the guard's reverse check rejects them.

## PR #8944 — config: reject community literals FRR cannot parse (#8934) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8934-narrow-reject`

Closes #8934

`members "@evil"` commits clean today and renders `bgp community-list standard
C1 permit @evil` into frr.conf. FRR rejects a malformed standard-list literal at
config load, and one `CMD_WARNING_CONFIG_FAILED` exits the whole vtysh
add-batch non-zero — **failing the entire frr-reload and leaving every dynamic
routing change stale.** The lexer blocks a bare `@` only in the *unquoted*
spelling, so quoting reaches it with no lexer change needed.

## Narrow on purpose — and narrow is the ceiling, not a compromise

Enumerating FRR's accepted literals would be **a claim about another program's
grammar that nothing in this repo can verify**; get it wrong and it
false-rejects working configs, which is worse than the defect. The original
author declined to enumerate for exactly that reason and the reasoning still
holds.

So this rejects **characters, not names**: a NON-REGEX member containing
anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9:_-]`. Every literal FRR accepts — `ASN:VALUE`,
large-community `A:B:C`, the well-known names — is spelled from that set, so a
member outside it is not one of them. Strictly weaker than an enumeration, and
it leaves the enumeration available to whoever has FRR's grammar in hand.

**Limited to non-regex members deliberately**: in an `expanded` list the same
`@` is an ordinary literal inside a POSIX ERE and regcomp accepts it.

## Two decisions I did not take over

Control characters and space are excluded — the #1798 gate rejects control
characters and `sanitizeFRRValue` collapses them at render time (#4097).
Claiming them here would not add protection, it would **replace** that
behaviour (an omitted definition instead of a sanitized rendered one). #4097
asserts the sanitized line and **went red when I first over-reached.**

## Upgrade path — measured, not reasoned about

A persisted config may already carry such a member; a reject firing on LOAD
would turn a running-but-broken node into a non-starting one. Measured on the
function `Store.Load` actually calls:

| path | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `CheckText` (strict commit) | accepted | **REFUSED**, naming the character |
| `compileTreeLenient` (Load, rollback) | accepted silently | **accepted WITH a warning** |

The guard pins **both** halves — the fix is only safe while they stay different.
Booting through is correct; doing it silently is not.

## PR #8947 — userspace-dp: compose NAT64 with native GRE / WireGuard egress [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8896-nat64-tunnel`

Fixes the capability gap filed as issue 8896. A NAT64-translated packet routed through a native GRE or WireGuard endpoint is now translated, encapsulated and forwarded. Issue 8890 had made the combination fail closed — correct, but a black hole for anyone who configured it.

## The two questions 8890 left open, both measured

Issue 8890's doc comment named these as the reason composing "is not a drop-in". Neither turned out to be the obstacle it looked like.

**Which `meta` fields the encapsulators read — exactly two, and both read the same two.** `addr_family` at three sites each (`packet_trimmed_len`, `inner_dst_ip` for WireGuard AllowedIPs peer selection, `inner_tos_byte` for the 2303 DSCP copy) and `l3_offset` as one fallback. `l3_offset` is self-correcting because `frame_l3_offset(inner_frame)` is consulted first, so `addr_family` is the field that actually has to be rebuilt.

**Whether the outer identity survives a family change — it does.** Neither encapsulator derives the outer from the inner family:

| | outer L3 | outer L2 | outer MTU |
|---|---|---|---|
| native GRE | `endpoint.outer_family` / `endpoint.destination` | `decision.resolution.{neighbor_mac, src_mac, tx_vlan_id}` | `tunnel_outer_mtu` |
| WireGuard | `peer_endpoint.is_ipv6()` | physical underlay egress | physical underlay (2680/3992/5292 SSOT) |

The only inner-dependent inputs are `inner_dst` and `inner_tos`, both correct once `addr_family` is. Issue 8896 called this "the harder one"; it needed no work.

## A third edit site the plan did not list

`post_transform_inner_mtu` **selected rather than composed**: its `is_nat64` arm returns before any tunnel arm can run, and the `egress_mtu` it adjusts resolves `decision.resolution.egress_ifindex` — the tunnel *logical* ifindex, not the physical underlay the outer header egresses.

Composing the frame builders without this ships a PTB too large by the whole encapsulation overhead. **Measured by mutation, not asserted: 1420 where 1396 is correct** at a 1400 transport MTU — 24 bytes over, exactly outer IPv4 (20) + GRE (4). Packets would satisfy the clamp, encapsulate, then exceed the underlay: an intermittent failure that reads as a path problem rather than a configuration one, and so **worse than the black hole it replaced**.

## What did not change

The 2327 fail-closed posture is preserved verbatim — an endpoint id resolving to no row, or to a mode that is neither GRE nor WireGuard, is dropped rather than emitted. A fail-open default in a security appliance is the defect. What changed is that a *known* mode is no longer in the unsupported set, and `nat64_tunnel_encap_unsupported` narrows to that residue: attributing every tunnel-marked NAT64 `None` to "unsupported" would now send an operator hunting a missing capability instead of reading the ext-header (5625) / fragment (2562) signal the next arms carry.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` green — 10 binaries, 0 failures. `go build ./...` and `go test ./pkg/dataplane/...` green.

**Mutations, each killed by a different cell**, so no cell is redundant:

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| pass `meta` through unrebuilt (the precise 8890 defect) | 2 cells |
| narrow the family rebuild to `AF_INET6` | **only** the reverse cell |
| drop the 2327 fail-closed arm | only the fail-closed cell |

**The reverse (v4→v6) cell exists because my first three cells all drove forward ingress**, and a forward-only composition survived every one of them. That is the same gap 8890's own reverse cell was written to catch, and I reintroduced it before catching it.

`nat64_8896_encap_ignores_every_meta_field_but_family_and_l3` poisons every meta field *other* than the two named above and asserts the emitted bytes are unchanged — so the two-field claim reds if a third is ever read, rather than going quietly stale.

## Docs

`docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md`: capability row and gap section rewritten. The 8890 upgrade WARNING is replaced rather than edited — it described an availability regression that this change reverses.

## Note for reviewers

This diff is formatting-clean by hand. Running `cargo fmt` on this crate rewrites ~380 files and breaks the 6592 runtime-view canary in an unrelated file; filed as issue 8945. It had inflated `tx/dispatch/mod.rs` here from 38 changed lines to 665 before I reverted it.

## PR #8949 — dataplane: agree with the Rust binding-plan hash on what a plan change is [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8901-plan-key`

Fixes issue 8901.

`snapshotBindingPlanKey` (Go) and `update_snapshot_binding_plan_key` (Rust, `planning.rs`) are two independently-maintained answers to one question — *did the AF_XDP binding plan change?* — and they disagreed about six inputs.

The Go key gates the **same-plan refresh exception**: the rule that lets a FIB-only update publish during the pending-XSK-startup window, because blocking it deadlocks (XSK liveness needs RX traffic, transit traffic needs FIB data). A field Rust hashes and Go does not means Go classifies a real plan change as "same plan" and publishes it straight through — while the helper, whose hash *does* include it, rebuilds its AF_XDP bindings. Back-to-back reconciles in the window whose entire purpose is to prevent them.

## The population, which the issue said nobody had run

The issue filed `shared_umem`. Diffing the two functions field by field found it is **one of six**, and one runs the other way:

| input | Rust | Go | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shared_umem` | ✓ | ✗ | Rust only — as filed |
| iface `vlan_id` | ✓ | ✗ | **Rust only** |
| iface `parent_linux_name` | ✓ | ✗ | **Rust only** |
| iface `logical_only` | ✗ | ✓ | **Go only** |
| iface `rx_queues` | effective (sysfs-resolved, 3007) | raw | value differs |
| refused-row filter | ✓ both loops (6691) | ✗ neither | population differs |

The three Rust-only inputs are added. `logical_only` is **adjudicated, not fixed**: it is a Go-side admission concept and Rust drops those rows upstream via `include_userspace_binding_interface`, so hashing it is how Go reaches the population Rust reaches by filtering.

**`vlan_id` deserves more attention than the field this was filed for.** Issue 3091 records why Rust hashes it: `replan_queues` dedups a VLAN-child netdev onto its physical parent using exactly `vlan_id` and `parent_linux_name`, so a re-parent or VLAN re-tag moves the layout. Both are ordinary config edits — far more routine than a SharedUMEM change.

## The guard is cross-plane by construction

A Go-side cell asserting "the key covers X" re-derives Go's own opinion and passes whatever Rust hashes. The failure being guarded is a *disagreement*, so the guard reads both sides — and **parses both rather than transcribing either**, because a transcribed list is a second copy that agrees with itself and drifts silently, which is this defect one level up.

It **states its own scope**: it compares field *names*, and is structurally blind to the value-level (`rx_queues` effective vs raw) and population-level (refused-row filter) differences the census found. Both are recorded in the file with their directions, because a guard that reports agreement on a set it never examined is worse than no guard.

The directions are not symmetric, and the file says so: Rust-hashes-more means Go **under**-detects and publishes through the window (dangerous); Go-hashes-more means Go over-detects and blocks where the helper would not (wasteful, safe).

## Validation

`pkg/dataplane/...`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace` and `pkg/config` green; `gofmt` clean.

Mutations: removing each of the three added inputs reds the guard naming that input alone; removing the `logical_only` adjudication reds the **Go-only direction**, which is the half a one-sided guard cannot have at all.

**The first version of the `shared_umem` assertion was vacuous, and mutation is the only thing that could have found it.** It searched the function body for the identifier `SharedUMEM` — and the explanatory comment beside the fix names SharedUMEM three times, so it passed on the prose and survived deleting the code it guards. Green before and after. It now asserts the emitted key literal `"shared_umem=`.

## PR #8950 — daemon: force a FIB refresh when the netlink subscription errors [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8915-netlink-overflow`

Fixes issue 8915.

The route listener's update channel is bounded at 256. On overflow the kernel drops route messages and reports `ENOBUFS` to `ErrorCallback`, which only `slog.Debug`d it — and `loop.Mark()` has exactly **one** other call site, the `case upd := <-updates` arm. So the dropped messages *are* the refresh edges: nothing else in the daemon can produce one, and the helper FIB stayed stale until the next route event that happened not to be dropped.

Which, on a churning box, is precisely when it is least likely to arrive promptly — the same churn that overflowed the queue is what delays the next event.

## Why nothing recovered it — the link that reads wrong

The coalescer runs a 100 ms ticker, which looks like a periodic refresh. It is not: `Tick` fires only `if !l.dirtySince.IsZero()`, so an unmarked loop sweeps forever and actuates never.

Measured rather than read. `TestCoalescerTickIsASweepNotAPeriodicActuate8915` drives 50 sweeps with no mark and requires **0** actuations, then one mark and requires exactly **1**. Without that control, "the error callback marks" is satisfied by a loop that would have actuated anyway, and the cell would be measuring the coalescer instead of the fix.

**That control earned its place by catching a defect in its own harness first.** The first version asserted that one `Mark` plus one `Tick` actuates — it does not, because `Tick` requires the debounce and throttle windows to elapse. Read as a failing fix rather than a failing instrument, that would have sent the investigation somewhere else entirely. The cells now inject a clock.

## The mark is unconditional, not ENOBUFS-only

This callback's contract is *"something went wrong with the subscription"*. Every such condition can leave a gap in the update stream, and a refresh is idempotent because the coalescer decides whether to actuate.

Discriminating on the errno would make recovery depend on matching a string the netlink library does not promise, and **the failure mode of guessing wrong is a silently stale FIB**. `TestEveryNetlinkErrorMarks8915` pins it: a mutant marking only on `"no buffer space"` reds on three of its four errors.

The callback is extracted as `routeListenerErrorCallback` rather than left inline **so the cells drive the function production installs**. A hand-rolled `func(err error)` in a test would pass whatever production does — the failure the extraction exists to prevent.

## Observability

`RouteListenerErrors()` makes the recovery visible. Before this the overflow was a Debug line, so a stale FIB had no counter pointing at it and read as a routing problem rather than a dropped-edge one. A non-zero value means the 256-deep queue is being outrun and some of the marks beside it are recovery rather than route churn.

## Validation

`pkg/daemon`, `pkg/coalesce`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/routing` green; `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean.

Mutations, each killed distinctly:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert to Debug-only (the defect) | reds 5 assertions |
| mark only on the `ENOBUFS` text | reds the three other errors by name |
| drop the counter alone | reds only the observability assertion |

## PR #8952 — config: make the fail-open control a required field, and screen the class (#8943) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8943-control-rule`

`TestElisionSuppressedAValidation8879` asserted **two** rows per instance and
described a third in prose that was not actually there. The third is the one
everyone reaches past:

    braced, BAD  reference  ->  REJECTED   (the validator exists)
    elided, BAD  reference  ->  ACCEPTED   (the finding)
    braced, GOOD reference  ->  ACCEPTED   (the CONTROL)

Without the control, "elided accepts" is equally consistent with **the validator
never firing on that path at all** — in which case there is no fail-open, just a
validator that does not apply. Not hypothetical: `class-of-service
forwarding-classes` looked exactly like a fourth instance until its
no-definition control came back ACCEPTED too, and it would have been filed
wrong.

**The control is now a required field of the table**, not a note in the doc
comment — a fourth row cannot be added without one, because the struct literal
will not compile. A rule that lives only in a comment is a rule the next person
reads *after* they have already written the row. Mutating a control to name an
undefined policy fires the new assertion.

## The mechanism is narrower than "elision suppressed a validation"

    REFERENCE-side elision  ->  FAILS OPEN.  The elided container holds the
                                statement that NAMES something; dropping it
                                removes the reference before the check runs.
    DEFINITION-side elision ->  FAILS LOUD.  The elided container holds the
                                DEFINITION; dropping it makes a reference
                                elsewhere dangle, and the check fires.

All three known instances are reference-side.

## Screening the remaining population — the class is closed at three

Of the 16 un-admitted #8943 rows, only `flow-monitoring version9` and
`flow-monitoring version-ipfix` are named by **any** cross-reference validator.
Both are **definition-side**, and both measured **fail-loud**: eliding the
templates makes the flow-server's reference dangle and strict commit refuses,
matching the no-definition control exactly.

So the class needs **no** further per-row adjudication in that population —
three instances, screened rather than assumed.

## A near-miss kept on the record

The first version of that screen elided `(services, flow-monitoring)` — a pair
admitted in #8879 batch 9, which folds correctly — and produced an apparent
**fourth instance**. Checking *which pair* a fixture actually elides is the same
discipline the #8938 correction turned on, and it caught itself here rather than
in review.

## PR #8955 — userspace-dp: refuse a prepared offset on a binding that does not share the UMEM [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8916-neighbor-umem`

Fixes issue 8916.

`dispatch_pending_neighbor_frames` built a `PreparedTxRequest` carrying `rewrite_result.offset` — an offset into the **ingress** binding's UMEM — and pushed it onto a **different** binding's `pending_tx_prepared` whenever the egress resolved elsewhere.

`WorkerBindingLookup::target_index` resolves purely by `(egress_ifindex, ingress_queue_id)` with a `first_by_if` fallback. No UMEM, sharing-group or ownership term, so a target on another NIC with its own allocation is an ordinary result. Under `shared_umem` mode `off` — a supported configuration — that offset does not address the same frame in the target's UMEM, or any valid frame.

The normal dispatcher already refuses exactly this. The guard appears **three times** in `tx/dispatch/mod.rs` and **zero times** in `neighbor_dispatch.rs`; this deferred retry path was the one exit without it.

## Fall back to a copy, not a drop

The frame is already rewritten and its neighbor has just resolved, so it is deliverable. Copying it into the target's local queue costs one memcpy on a path that is already off the fast path; recycling it to fill would discard a packet the dataplane went to some trouble to hold.

Uses `shares_allocation_with` rather than comparing `allocation_ptr()` — the codebase already expresses this question, and re-deriving it would be a second implementation of one predicate that can drift from the first.

`neighbor_retry_cross_umem_copies` makes the fallback observable: without it, a deployment crossing a UMEM boundary on every retry is indistinguishable from one that never does, and the fallback cannot be told apart from dead code.

## What the existing mirror cell revealed

`retry_pending_neighbor_mirrors_original_frame_before_rewrite` went red. `new_for_mirror_test` gives each binding its own allocation, so the cross-binding forward it reads off the prepared queue now takes the copy path. **Its subject is mirror identity, not UMEM ownership** — the prepared-queue read was an unstated assumption this change made load-bearing. The fixture now shares the forward target's UMEM explicitly.

**Only the forward target.** Sharing the mirror target too reds the same cell *differently*: it reads the mirrored frame back out of that binding's UMEM and asserts **pre-rewrite** L2 bytes, so a shared allocation has it reading the memory the in-place rewrite just mutated. Measured, not reasoned — the failure prints the rewritten MACs. An over-broad repair would have kept the cell green on mirror identity while silently ending its pre-rewrite check.

## Validation

Full `cargo test` green — **5363 passed, 0 failed**. `go build ./...` clean.

Mutations, each caught by a **different** cell and in opposite directions:

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| remove the guard (the defect) | the fix cell; control **passes** |
| invert it — every cross-binding forward copies | the **control**; fix cell passes |
| drop the packet instead of copying | only the copy assertions |

## Severity, unchanged from the issue's own bound

The offset is submitted into a UMEM it does not belong to. The drain-side handling of a foreign offset was not traced, so no claim is made about memory safety — only that the guard the sibling path applies was absent here.

## Note for reviewers

Formatting is by hand. Per issue 8945, `rustfmt` cannot be run on this area: `neighbor_dispatch_mirror_tests.rs` is `#[path]`-included inside a `mod` block and indented for its parent, so rustfmt de-indents all 48KB of it.

      -> ControlLinkAuthKey="A"   ControlLinkAuthKeyAlt=""
      strictErr=false   warnings=0

The dropped value is the **alternate control-link PSK**. An operator rotating cluster keys writes both, sees the command accepted, and gets one — so the rollover they staged does not exist, and the peer presenting the new key is refused.

**A silently absent second key is worse than a rejected command, because the rollover looks staged.**

## The hierarchical spelling already worked, and that identifies the mechanism

    chassis { cluster { authentication-key A additional-authentication-key B; } }   both keys — OK
    set chassis cluster authentication-key A additional-authentication-key B        second key LOST

In the hierarchical form both statements land on **one node's Keys** and `splitClusterKeys` separates them. The flat-set command instead builds a **chain**:

    [authentication-key A]
      [additional-authentication-key B]

Nothing is packed onto `Keys`, so `clusterBodyNeedsSplit` said no and the entire normalization was skipped for that shape. Both halves are fixed — the gate now recognises the chain, and `splitPackedClusterChild` hoists it — and **each half is bound by its own cell**.

## Promotion is gated on the schema, not applied blanket

A nested body is legitimate under a container that declares children — `redundancy-group 1 { node 0 priority 100; }` — and hoisting that would flatten the shape `clusterBodyStatements` depends on. Only a leaf the schema says holds **nothing** can have something nested under it by the chain, so that is the discriminator. Recursive, because one `set` command can chain three or more leaves.

## The remedy follows #6524 rather than rejecting the spelling

The chain is a **supported** form — `set applications application a1 protocol tcp destination-port 80` is tested behaviour in `TestChainedAppDirectLeavesCompile` — and #6524 recorded why a schema reject is the wrong shape:

> a schema-only reject would leave the LENIENT path — boot load and HA SyncApply

which is exactly where already-stored configs are. A reject **was** built for issue 8939 and withdrawn on that evidence; this is the compiler-side remedy that issue's own precedent prescribes.

## Validation

    M1  gate clause removed    ->  chain cell FAILS ("lost the ALTERNATE control-link
                                   key: got 0 bytes, want 16"), container cell passes
    M2  schema gating removed  ->  CONTAINER cell FAILS ("redundancy-group 1 has 0
                                   node-priority entries ... its body was flattened"),
                                   chain cell passes

Each half killed by its **own** cell, so neither is carried by the other. The reference arm is asserted — a two-command build with no alternate key fails the cell rather than passing it — and both previously-working spellings are asserted so the fix cannot be bought at their expense.

Full `pkg/config` green, gofmt clean.

## PR #8958 — docs: userspace-dp is not formatter-managed, with a guard for the worst case [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8945-rustfmt-doc`

Fixes issue 8945, taking resolution option 2 (document that the tree is not formatter-managed) plus a guard for the one variant that silently destroys a file.

## Why option 2 rather than option 1

Option 1 was "pin rustfmt and make the tree clean under it". That cannot be done without a decision about `#[path]`-included files that live inside a `mod` block in their parent: their contents are indented four spaces by convention while the braces live in the parent, so **they cannot be simultaneously rustfmt-clean and correct in their parent's context**. Documenting the tree as unmanaged sidesteps that entirely.

## What happens today

| what you run | what you get |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt` on the crate | ~380 files rewritten, **suite fails** — the 6592 canary counts `RuntimeView` constructions by scanning lines, and the failure lands in `worker/loop_body/mod.rs`, a file you never touched |
| `rustfmt <file>` | walks the module **subtree** — five files in, sixteen out |
| `rustfmt` on an indented `#[path]` include | **every line de-indented**; `neighbor_dispatch_mirror_tests.rs` is ~48KB rewritten end to end |

Beyond the wasted time, formatting hides the change. On PR 8947 the same six files went from **1349/593** insertions/deletions to **669/114** once formatting was reverted, and `tx/dispatch/mod.rs` alone from **665 changed lines to 38** for a three-hunk edit.

## Why a guard and not only prose

**The de-indented file still compiles.** Nothing in the build objects, the diff is enormous but uniform, and a reviewer skimming it sees whitespace. A rule in a doc is one you read *after* reaching for the formatter — so `indented_include_guard_8945` detects the de-indent directly, by finding top-level items at column 0 in a file that should carry its parent's indentation.

The file list is **enumerated, not discovered**. A discovery pass would have to model which `#[path]` includes sit inside a `mod` and which are bare — and a model of the include graph is the same second-implementation drift that issue 8946 is about.

## Validation

The mutations are the **real failure**, not a simulation:

- running `rustfmt` on the file reds the guard, naming the column-0 items
- emptying the file list reds the non-vacuity assertion

The `rustfmt` mutation also silently modified a **third** file (`xfrmi_6710_tests.rs`) — demonstrating the subtree cascade from inside the mutation that was testing for the de-indent.

Runtime-view canary passes (31 tests) at this head.

`collectCompactSites` models two site shapes: a single-arg valued leaf, or a wildcard-**named** container. `system syslog file <name>` is neither — `args:1` for the file name, **plus** a wildcard for the open-ended facility keyword, **plus** modifier children. A third shape, with no clause for it.

**The blindness was silent and it disarmed a different guard.** Those pairs produced no census site at all, so when #8943 admitted `syslog file` / `host` / `user`, the standing empty-equivalence verification — the rule the pass requires before **any** admission — passed over all three **by examining nothing**.

    sites for pair (syslog, <leaf>)     before 0     after 6

#8852 offers two remedies: *"fix the census or the classifier"*. #8943 took the classifier branch and registered the three as explained-blind. **That is legitimate by the guard's own text** — and it leaves the verification vacuous.

This takes the census branch, which removes the blindness rather than naming it, and drops the three registrations. That is the removal the registry exists to force: a registration outliving its reason is a recorded blindness nobody re-opens.

## Bounded, and measured before widening a shared instrument

Exactly **six** schema nodes carry the arg-named-with-wildcard-body shape — the three syslog destinations and their `groups` mirrors. No other container in the schema has it.

So this is three containers wide, not a re-baselining of every lane's population. Had it been broad it would have gone to the board first rather than landed in flight.

#8943 landed the admission, the bookkeeping and a docs log. This asserts the drop is actually gone:

    braced   files=1 hosts=1 users=1
    elided   files=0 hosts=0 users=0     strictErr=false  warnings=0

**A firewall that silently logs nothing.** Security logging that is *absent* produces exactly what security logging that is *quiet* produces — an empty file — so there is nothing to notice until an incident, at which point the evidence for the incident is the thing that was missing.

Each destination is measured in its **own arm**. One fixture packing all three is a multi-statement **run**, which #8850 makes the pass decline *by design*; measuring that shape reports a correct fix as broken, because it tests the decline policy rather than the fold.
