## PR #8961 — config: ratchet the admissions that are live at more than one schema site [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8921-multisite-guard`

Issue 8921, **item 3 and only item 3**.

`compactNormalizeInScope(containerKeyword, head)` takes no parent context. An admission is live at **every** site where a container of that keyword declares that head — not at the site it was adjudicated on. **163 admitted pairs are effective at more than one declaring site**, and every one was adjudicated by measuring a single fixture at a single site.

This does **not** adjudicate those extra sites (item 2) and does **not** parent-qualify the predicate (item 1). Both are large, and both are honest costs of a keyword-keyed predicate. Neither is a reason to let the debt grow unmeasured meanwhile — this makes a new multi-site admission impossible to land silently, which is the difference between a known debt and an unknown one.

**The failure it prevents already happened once without consequence.** Issue 8933 admitted eight `then <action>` pairs against 14 `then` containers. Nothing collided because the firewall `then` declares none of those eight names — *safe by coincidence of naming, not by construction*. That check was done by hand because someone remembered to.

## Two things about the measurement

**My first walk called every pair multi-site: 575 of 575.** `groups` mirrors the entire schema, so every pair appears at least twice through it. Excluding `groups` is what makes the distinction exist at all.

**Issue 8921's headline is not reproducible; its per-row data is.** It reports 223; this instrument measures 163, at 575 admitted pairs where it had 547. The difference is the criterion, not drift:

| criterion | count |
|---|---:|
| declaring sites > 1 — *the admission is actually effective* | **163** |
| container keyword occurs > 1, head may not be declared | 327 |

223 falls between the two, so it used a third variant — and its probe was a throwaway file, run and removed. What **does** reproduce is 8921's per-pair table: all ten named rows match this walk exactly (bfd `minimum-interval` 8, `multiplier` 8, `forwarding-class loss-priority` 7, `loss-priority code-points` 7, `route next-hop` 6, `match destination-address` 5, `match source-address` 5, `then log` 5, `interface cost` 4, `hello-interval` 4).

The argument in that issue rests on the per-row data, which holds. Only the aggregate is unreproducible, and the registry header says so rather than quietly adopting a new number.

The criterion chosen is the behaviourally meaningful one: an admission is effective where the container **declares** the head. Where the container exists and does not declare it, the predicate is never consulted for a pair that cannot form.

## Validation

Full `pkg/config` green; `gofmt` clean.

Mutations, each killed by a **distinct branch**:

| mutation | branch |
|---|---|
| new genuinely multi-site admission (`interface passive`, 6 sites) | ADDED — names the pair and its sites |
| delete a recorded row | ADDED |
| drift a recorded count | CHANGED |
| break the wildcard descent | REMOVED — the traversal defect 8880 documents having had |

A stability cell runs the walk three times and requires identical per-pair counts, because Go randomises map iteration and the 8880 census recorded a per-pair property that drifted between runs on one unchanged tree.

Registry lives in `testdata/` rather than the Go file: `compact_normalize_8662.go` is 8 lines from its modularity floor (issue 8954) and a 163-row list has no business there.

## PR #8970 — daemon: correct a deferral comment that outlived its work (#8942) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8942-stale-2501`

`daemon_flowexport_session_close_test.go` said its fixture's volume counters are
zero because *"the userspace dataplane does not yet maintain per-session
byte/packet accounting (tracked in #2501)"*.

**That stopped being true.** `userspace-dp/src/event_stream/codec/rt_flow.rs`
writes offsets 56 and 64 from *"real per-session forward volume harvested from
the closing entry's worker-owned counters"* — tagged `#2501` in that file — and
#2501 is closed. The zeros are still correct (the fixture exercises the *decode*
path, where zero is a legitimate wire value); its stated **reason** was false and
told a reader a capability is missing when it exists.

## Why this is one half of #8942, not a typo fix

Sweeping every deferral spelling (`tracked on|in`, `deferred to`, `follow-up
in`, `left to`, `handled by`, `TODO … #N`) finds **21 citation sites over 17
distinct issues — and all 17 are closed.** So *"the cited issue is closed"*
carries no information and cannot be the filter. What discriminates is what is
true of the code now, and it splits two ways with opposite harms:

| | meaning | harm |
|---|---|---|
| **HOLLOWED** | residual LIVE, tracked nowhere | the work never gets done — nothing says it is outstanding |
| **FALSE-ABOUT-CODE** | residual DONE, comment still defers | a reader designs around an absence that is not there |

Verified so far: **3 hollowed** (#4234, #8058, #8449), **1 false-about-code**
(this one), **8 unclassified**. Not extrapolated — classification is per-site
work and the interesting cases are unevenly distributed.

## A correction to my own first pass, recorded on the issue

I initially classified `#2330` as false-about-code because `EmitPacketTooBig`
exists in the Rust dataplane. It does — on the **general egress path**. Both
#2330 comments are about the **GRE-encap-DF-oversize** case specifically, which
that does not establish. Matching a symbol name and inferring the specific
capability is the substitution I had just declined to make for the other rows in
the same comment, made in the row I happened to check first. #2330 is
unclassified.

The asymmetry that fell out is worth keeping: **HOLLOWED is cheap** to establish
(the evidence usually sits in the same function — #4234's live *"partially
enforced"* advisory is four lines below its own deferral note), while
**FALSE-ABOUT-CODE is expensive** and owes a citation to the implementing line
rather than to a symbol name.

`pkg/dataplane/compiler_filter.go` branches on the dropped field, and the branch below it is a **fallback**:

```go
if term.DSCPRewrite != ""   { base.DSCPRewrite = <explicit> }
if term.ForwardingClass != "" && base.DSCPRewrite == 0xFF {
                              base.DSCPRewrite = <derived from fc> }
```

Dropping `then dscp` does not disable the rewrite — it hands the decision to the forwarding-class derivation, and **the packet goes out remarked with a DSCP the operator never configured.**

    separate commands     dscp=af11  fc=EF   ->  EXPLICIT af11
    packed, fc first      dscp=""    fc=EF   ->  FORWARDING-CLASS DERIVATION

A missing value is eventually noticeable because something is unconfigured. A **wrong** one is not, because nothing is. It is also **order-dependent**: the run keeps the first action, so which survives depends on the order typed — a signature `docs/config-schema.md` already names for this trio.

## Two mechanisms, two commits, one test table

    packed tail   the run lands whole on the node's Keys   -> packedStatements
    flat-set      SetPath NESTS the actions into a chain   -> the reader walks it

The remedy follows #6524 rather than rejecting the spelling — the chain is **supported** (`set applications application a1 protocol tcp destination-port 80` is tested behaviour), and that issue recorded why a schema reject is wrong: it leaves the **lenient** path (boot load, HA SyncApply) untouched, which is exactly where already-stored configs are.

The chain flatten is **schema-gated**: `then reject <message-type>` legitimately carries a body, so only an action the schema says holds nothing may be flattened.

## Validation — no arrangement lands a green half

    M1  packedStatements reverted  ->  cell FAILS naming `packed-hier`
    M2  chain flatten reverted     ->  cell FAILS naming `packed CLI`
    M3  schema gate removed        ->  reject-body cell FAILS

Each mutation names its **own** mechanism. The three spellings are asserted in one table with a positive control on the braced reference arm.

## The gate cost is recorded, not absorbed — and my first reading of it was wrong

`packedStatements` moved eight leaves **out of** the value-less-flag blind bucket, making them comparable to the #7484 spelling gate for the first time. Once comparable, 22 sites reported a `#2419` shape-dependent drop, and registering them in `notAValueList` — which that gate's own text prescribes — removed them from enumeration.

    master   1098 enumerated  706 compared
    after    1076 enumerated  692 compared      NET -14

**Measured, correcting the claim this was nearly justified on:** the divergence is **pre-existing**, not introduced. `then { count c1 c2; }` and `then count c1 c2;` compile **identically, before and after** the opt-in. The change *exposed* a divergence among other spellings; it did not cause one.

Branch: `fix/8936-tunnel-ri`

Closes #8936

The brace-elided `tunnel { routing-instance destination vrf1; }` compiled

routing-instance that does not exist and discarding the operator's actual
instance name.

    braced   routing-instance { destination vrf1; }   -> "vrf1"
    elided   routing-instance destination vrf1;       -> "destination"   <- defect
    bare     routing-instance vrf1;                   -> "vrf1"

The braced spelling gives `routing-instance` a **child** named `destination`;

**Worse than a drop.** A missing value leaves the tunnel visibly unbound; a
wrong one produces a plausible binding that silently resolves to nothing. Same

plausible value* rather than an absent one.

The #8690 register classed the site `partial` because *"something consumed the

not. The consumer was this defect. Fixing it makes the spellings agree; **no
scope admission is involved**, and the site has left the divergence inventory
and the register entirely.

One branch at each of the two call sites, through a shared helper, so the
pre-existing braced and bare-name paths are byte-for-byte unchanged and the two
sites cannot drift.

The regression cell asserts **all three** spellings — a repair that fixed the
elided form by breaking `routing-instance <name>;` would pass a two-spelling
cell.

## PR #8975 — cluster: guard BulkStart's epoch the way BulkEnd's is guarded [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8966-bulkstart-epoch`

Fixes issue 8966, found by lane-8367 adjudicating issue 8791 finding 11.

`BulkEnd` refuses a message whose epoch does not match the in-progress bulk. **`BulkStart` compared nothing** — it assigned `bulkRecvEpoch` unconditionally and reset the accumulators, so a delayed or reordered BulkStart carrying a *lower* epoch discarded the in-progress bulk's receive set, after which the newer stream's BulkEnd failed the comparison at the bottom of the same function.

Two handlers disagreeing about which epoch is authoritative, and only one of them checking. **Two fabric streams is the normal configuration**, so reordering between them is the expected case rather than an exotic one.

## The 2198 rationale is true and covers a different case

The comment above the reset explains that a re-priming peer's `genCounter` restarts lower and must be accepted, or the standby is stranded. That is correct **for a reboot**. The code could not tell a rebooted peer from a late BulkStart on the other stream, and applied the reboot treatment to both.

**`switched` — already computed two lines above for issue 6910's fabric preference — is exactly that discriminator.** The information needed to separate the two cases was in hand and simply not consulted by the code that needed it. Across an incarnation change the behaviour is unchanged; within one incarnation a BulkStart must now be strictly newer.

## The generation reset moves to the accepted path, and stays outside the lock

Running `resetRecvGen` for a stale BulkStart discarded the generations of a bulk that was still valid, so it belongs after the guard. It stays **outside** `bulkMu`, where it has always been: pulling it inside would add a `bulkMu → recvGenMu` edge to the lock graph as a side effect of a correctness fix. No inversion exists today — checked — and the point is that nobody would look for one introduced this way.

## Validation

`pkg/cluster` and `pkg/dataplane/...` green; `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean.

**Mutations, and the matrix found a real gap:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove the guard | reds the stale cell, naming the clobbered epoch |
| drop the `!switched` term | reds the **reboot** cell — a blanket epoch guard breaks 2198, which is what makes the discriminator load-bearing rather than decorative |
| `<` instead of `<=` | **survived the first three cells** |

That third mutation is why there is a fourth cell. An **equal** epoch is the retransmit/reorder case with the identical consequence — accumulators reset for the bulk already in progress, which then fails its own BulkEnd. The new cell seeds the accumulator, replays the same epoch on the other stream, and asserts the entry survives; it now kills that mutant naming the count.

## PR #8976 — fix: give #8768 an existence-requirement field, and split the log-stream run [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8768-always-field`

Closes the #8768 capability gap handed over on issue 8932, and fixes the row that exposed it.

## The defect, and it FAILS OPEN

    stream s1 { host 192.0.2.1; category policy; }   category="policy"
    stream s1 host 192.0.2.1 category policy;        category=""

`daemon_system.go` sets `Categories` only when the field is non-empty, and `logging/syslog.go` documents `Categories == 0` as **ALL**. A stream the operator scoped to `policy` silently carries **every** category — **more data leaving the box than was configured.**

That is the **fallback** shape rather than the missing shape: the consumer has a default, the default fires, nothing is unconfigured, and the value is **wrong** rather than absent.

## An admission could not have worked — this is the third node-vs-pair case

`stream <s>` is **arg-named**, so production calls the scope predicate with the operator's actual stream name — `("s1", "category")`, never `("stream", "category")`. Every pair up that chain was already admitted and **every one of them inert**, which presents as *"the pair is admitted and the fold still does not fire"* and sends the reader hunting a bug in the pass.

For an arg-named container a pair-keyed admission is not merely collision-prone, it is **structurally unreachable**. The remedy had to be a node opt-in. (That case is documented in `docs/config-schema.md` alongside the other two.)

## #8768 correctly refused, and the refusal was not satisfiable

A stream with no `host` does not compile, so a same-leaf fixture for any other leaf had **both arms at ABSENT** and the non-vacuity check rejected it — a comparison of two nothings cannot tell a split from a swallow. No better fixture exists: **the requirement is the container's, not the fixture's.** The workaround fails too — two `stream s1` blocks do **not** merge (measured: the second block's `category` is discarded).

So the guard gains an **`always`** field: a statement the container cannot compile without, appended to **both arms of every comparison**. It goes *inside* the body, so the packed arm packs it into the run exactly as an operator would write it. Every existing case carries `always: ""` and is byte-identical to before.

A leaf supplied as the existence requirement is **exempt** from the per-leaf fixture demand — it is already in both arms and observed by `read`, so it *is* compared, just not with a varying value. Demanding a second fixture would put the statement in twice, testing duplicate-leaf handling rather than the split. It is still exercised where it matters: if the run fails to split, the existence statement is lost with everything else and every arm diverges at once.

`stream` is the **first** container to need this, so the capability ships with exactly one caller — and the guard's own per-leaf check will say if a second container silently needed it all along.

## Validation

    M1  stream opt-in reverted  ->  regression cell FAILS naming the category loss
    M2  `always` neutered       ->  #8768 FAILS, so the field is load-bearing

17 opted-in containers, 470 ordered leaf pairs, 85 same-leaf comparisons, 53 three-statement runs. Full `pkg/config` green, gofmt clean.

The #8880 ratchet SHRANK 460 → 452 at `args>=1`, holding at 100 for `args>=2`. Re-derived at this base, twice, not computed. **This member is a third cause its remedy advice does not fit** — which is what that cell's new membership-vs-advice note exists for.

## Also: the diffstat rule, in the contract doc

`docs/engineering-style.md` gains it. Read **both** forms before every push:

    git diff --stat origin/master HEAD      # catches a real DELETION
    git diff --stat origin/master...HEAD    # says whether the change is YOURS

Neither alone is the check. A stale base made two-dot report eighteen files including a `pkg/daemon` test nobody had opened; three-dot alone would not have caught the 413-line guard file a stale base was about to delete — **while the suite stayed green, because a deleted guard cannot fail.** It caught a third stale base while this very PR was being committed.

## PR #8978 — daemon: let the IPsec SA sync publisher be enabled by a later commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8967-ipsec-sa-hotenable`

Fixes issue 8967, found by lane-8367 adjudicating issue 8791 finding 17.

`startClusterSyncAuxLoops` launches four comms-scoped loops. Three handle being enabled by a later commit; the IPsec SA publisher read its boolean **once at comms start**:

```go
if cc.IPsecSASync && d.ipsec != nil { go d.syncIPsecSAPeriodic(...) }
```

So enabling `ipsec-sa-synchronization` on a running cluster **committed successfully and started nothing**, until an unrelated comms restart. The operator sees a clean commit and no SA advertisement, with nothing naming the gap.

## What made this a finding was the siblings, not the absence

*"IPsecSASync has no apply-path presence"* alone is consistent with correct-by-design — plenty of things are start-time only on purpose. **Three siblings in the same function that do handle it, with the reasoning written out beside them**, is what converts an absence into a defect:

```
IPsecSASync    comms-wiring=2  apply-path=0   <- the only zero
DHCPLeaseSync  comms-wiring=2  apply-path=2
ConfigSync     comms-wiring=0  apply-path=8
SessionSync    comms-wiring=6  apply-path=1
```

## The remedy is 4647's, deliberately

`ensureDHCPLeaseSyncLoop` already solved this for the sibling knob: an idempotent starter called from **both** comms start and the apply tail. This mirrors it rather than inventing a second shape — a second shape here would be a second thing to keep in step.

The starter is comms-gated: the apply path can run before comms exist, and the comms-start call re-runs it once they do, so a knob-ON state committed early is not lost.

## Validation

`pkg/daemon` and `pkg/cluster` green; `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean.

**Mutations, and the matrix found a gap:**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| revert the apply-path call | reds the **sibling** cell — the assertion that every knob-gated aux loop is also reconciled on apply, which is the cell that would have caught the original |
| drop the comms gate | reds the no-comms cell |
| drop the idempotence guard | **survived** |

That third is why `launches` exists. `loopCancel != nil` is true both when the second call was a no-op **and** when it started a second publisher and overwrote the first one's cancel — leaking that goroutine to advertise in parallel with its replacement. A counter makes idempotence observable rather than inferred, and the mutant now dies naming `launches=2`.

The sibling cell is written about the **set** rather than about IPsec: a fifth aux loop added start-time-only reds it.

## PR #8979 — deploy: order tilde pre-releases and fail closed on unorderable versions [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8969-tilde-sort`

Closes #8969

## What was wrong

`_ver_key` split a version on the first `-` only, so Debian's tilde pre-release spelling never produced a suffix. `1.2.3~rc1` parsed as the single non-numeric release token `3~rc1`, and because a non-numeric token ranked ABOVE every numeric one, it sorted AFTER `1.2.3` — passing an anti-rollback watermark that the semantically identical `1.2.3-rc1` is correctly refused by.

## The tilde was one instance, not the defect

Measured against a `1.2.3` watermark before the change, all of these ranked NEWER and passed:

| candidate | old verdict | new verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `1.2.3~rc1` | passes (newer) | refused (older) |
| `garbage` | passes (newer) | refused (older) |
| `1.2.x` | passes (newer) | refused (older) |
| `1.2.3_rc1` | passes (newer) | refused (older) |
| `1.0.0+build.7` vs `1.0.0` | passes (newer) | equal |
| `1.2.4`, `1.3.0`, `2.0.0` vs `1.2.3` | passes | passes (unchanged) |

Any version the comparator could not order was treated as the newest thing it had ever seen.

## The two open columns from the issue, settled

**Reachability.** The BUILD path cannot reach it: `git check-ref-format refs/tags/1.2.3~rc1` is REJECTED while the hyphen form is accepted, so `git describe --tags` cannot emit a tilde version. The OPERATOR path can: `validate_version` ACCEPTS `1.2.3~rc1`, `1.0.0+build.7`, `1.2.x` and `garbage`, and **two of the three spellings its own docstring advertises as supported were exactly the ones that bypassed the watermark**. Latent via bake, live via `fetch --version`.

**Which way it fails.** Chosen deliberately: **fail-CLOSED**. For an unparseable candidate the outcomes are a refused upgrade (loud — the operator sees it and has `--allow-rollback`) or a bypassed anti-rollback watermark (silent — an older image replaces a newer one). Fail-closed matches the discipline `validate_version` states a few hundred lines above.

## One row differs from the issue's table

`wm=1.2.3~rc1, cand=1.2.3-rc1` now PASSES (the issue recorded it blocked). This is correct: the two spellings denote the same version, they now compare equal, and the call site uses `>=`, so a same-version redeploy passes exactly as `1.2.3` over `1.2.3` does. The issue's row documented the buggy inflation.

## Validation

4 new cells in `VersionKeyOrderingTests`, deliberately placed beside the existing hyphen cases so those act as the control for the tilde ones — no argument about what a pre-release *should* do is needed.

Mutation matrix — reverting each part of the fix reds its own cell:

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| revert the `~` split | 1 failure |
| revert the `-1` fail-closed rank | 3 failures |
| drop the `+build` strip | 1 failure |
| **rank EVERY release token below the watermark** | **4 failures** |

The fourth is the levelling-down control: a fail-closed change is trivially satisfiable by refusing *every* upgrade, and that mutant would pass every other assertion here. It reds the upgrade controls, so it cannot.

`python3 -m unittest test_xpf_deploy_correctness` 16/16 · `make test-deploy-lib` 55/55.

Docs: `docs/distribution.md` gains the fail-closed ordering contract and the `--allow-rollback` escape hatch next to the existing watermark paragraph.

## PR #8981 — frr: give DHCP-learned routes the routing instance that learned them [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8963-dhcp-vrf`

Fixes issue 8963, found by lane-8367 adjudicating issue 8791 finding 13.

A DHCP-learned default or classless route was emitted once, in the default FRR context, **even when the interface that learned it belonged to a routing instance**. The instance did not get the route it learned, and the default context got one it should not have.

## What made this a finding was the sibling, not the absence

*"`renderDHCPDefaults` emits no vrf clause"* alone is consistent with correct-by-design. **The same file, for the same kind of object, threading `vrf <name>` for static routes since 5557 and not for DHCP-learned ones** is what converts it into a defect.

## Reachability — the column the issue left open, now settled

Measured at `configstore.CheckText`:

```
control: dhcp iface, no instance      ACCEPTED
control: instance, static iface       ACCEPTED
subject: dhcp iface IN an instance    ACCEPTED
```

Nothing upstream refuses the combination, so this is **live, not latent**. Both single-sided controls are there because "the subject is accepted" alone would not distinguish a reachable combination from a fixture that accepts anything.

Leaving that column open and named — rather than filling it with the plausible answer — is what made it one command to settle.

## Two defects, two remedies

**The clause.** The route carries the instance of its learning interface, and the renderer emits it through `sanitizeFRRValue` — the same 5557 property the static renderer has, for the same reason: the tolerant load / HA config-sync paths only warn, so a control character reaching here could otherwise inject a second vtysh line into the managed `frr.conf`.

**Suppression is now per-VRF.** It read only the top-level static lists, so a static default *inside* an instance neither suppressed nor was suppressed by the DHCP-learned one — an instance could install both, and a default-context static could suppress a default belonging to an instance. The `""` key is the default context, so pre-existing top-level behaviour (5519) is unchanged.

## Validation

`pkg/frr`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/configstore` green; `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop the vrf clause | reds the main cell, naming the table the route lands in |
| append the clause **always** | reds the **control** |
| revert suppression to top-level only | reds both suppression cells, in opposite directions |

**The second is the one worth having:** a fix that gives every DHCP route a vrf clause passes the main assertion and breaks every default-context route. The obvious wrong fix passes the obvious right assertion.

## PR #8983 — fix: class-of-service bindings lose every statement after the first [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8939-cos-bindings`

Third family of issue 8939, after `chassis cluster` (#8956) and `firewall <f> term <t> then` (#8973).

## The defect

    classifiers { dscp c1; ieee-802.1 c2; }    both bound
    classifiers dscp c1 ieee-802.1 c2;         ieee-802.1 LOST
    set … classifiers dscp c1 ieee-802.1 c2    ieee-802.1 LOST

## The loss is the FALLBACK shape, and that sets the severity

`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go` records what an unpublished binding means:

> the dataplane sees no classifier and every packet falls through to the **default queue**

Traffic is still classified — into the **wrong** queue — so nothing is unconfigured and the result is plausible. And the **first** binding survives, so the interface visibly carries a working classifier while the second silently does nothing. **Partial application reads as success:** an operator checking that classification works will find that it does.

## Two mechanisms, and the flatten is now generic

    packed tail   the run lands whole on the node's Keys   -> packedStatements
    flat-set      SetPath NESTS the bindings into a chain  -> the reader walks it

This is the **second** container to need the chain flatten, so it moves into `compact_chain_flatten.go` rather than being written twice. `flattenThenChain8939` is its firewall-specific predecessor; both are gated on the schema — only a leaf the schema says holds **nothing** may be flattened — and they should converge when a third caller appears.

Applied to the **four binding sites** (unit-level and interface-level × classifiers and rewrite-rules), not to the top-level classifier/rewrite-rule **definitions**, which are a different shape.

## The #8768 guard corrected three over-generalisations of mine

Each an instance of claiming a family where only some members qualify:

1. Fixtures for all four containers with the same leaf set — but **the two levels do not have the same children**, and a fixture for a leaf the container does not declare is silently unused.
2. `inet-precedence` registered as unobservable at sites where it is genuinely **distinguishable** — the registry's reverse check refused five such entries, and they were deleted rather than re-justified.
3. `exp` fixtured under containers that do not declare it.

The same-leaf comparisons that **are** registered unobservable are so for a measured reason: these bindings are **scalar** fields, so a repeated statement overwrites rather than accumulating and one instance reads identically to two. The **ordered-pair** comparisons remain live and are the ones that do the work — `dscp c1 ieee-802.1 c2` is exactly the shape that was losing the second binding.

    482 ordered leaf pairs (up from 470)
     94 same-leaf comparisons (up from 85)

## PR #8984 — deploy: a failed virsh probe must not read as "domain absent" [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8977-virsh-probe`

Fixes issue 8977, found by lane-8367 adjudicating issue 8791 finding 08.

`_virsh_domain_exists` returned `False` for *"no such domain"* and for *"could not reach libvirtd"* alike. Both teardown paths guarded the **destroy** on it and left the disk **unlink** unguarded — so with libvirtd unreachable and a domain live, teardown skipped the shutdown and **removed the running VM's overlay anyway**, in one path escalating to `sudo rm -f` when the unlink was refused.

## One function, two operations, one guarded

That asymmetry is what identifies this as a defect rather than a design choice, and **the guard was on the wrong half**: skipping a shutdown is survivable; deleting a live VM's backing store is not.

Comparing the two *probes* would have shown nothing — `_incus_exists` and `_virsh_domain_exists` are the same shape and both conflate error with absence, so there's no odd one out. The peer set that carries the finding is the two operations **inside each caller**.

## The tolerance is deliberate, for a different case

The sibling's docstring states it: *"tolerant of a missing incus binary (returns False)"*. Tolerating a **missing binary** is correct — the tool isn't installed, so the object can't exist. That tolerance was then extended to a tool that **is** installed and **failed to answer**, where existence is simply unknown. `returncode == 0` cannot tell them apart.

## The fix: three states

`_virsh_domain_state` returns PRESENT / ABSENT / UNKNOWN, reading libvirt's stderr wording rather than the exit code. A missing binary still maps to ABSENT — genuine absence, and the case the original tolerance was for.

**An unrecognised failure maps to UNKNOWN rather than ABSENT, deliberately:** the cost of a wrong ABSENT is deleting a live VM's disk; the cost of a wrong UNKNOWN is refusing a teardown the operator can retry.

`destroy_libvirt` refuses on UNKNOWN, naming the file it declined to remove. `_cleanup_libvirt` warns and returns rather than raising — it runs on the failed-deploy path, where re-raising would replace the caller's diagnosis with this one. `_virsh_domain_exists` is retained for the non-destructive preflight caller.

## Validation

Deploy suite passes (237 tests). Mutations, each killed:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| collapse UNKNOWN back to ABSENT | reds the refusal cells |
| refuse on ABSENT **too** | reds the **control** — an over-broad fix passes the main assertion and breaks every ordinary teardown |
| leave the cleanup path unguarded | reds the cleanup cell |

The ABSENT control catches `SystemExit` explicitly so it fails with its own message. Without that it died as an unexplained `SystemExit` — killed by the wrong branch, which reads as a crash rather than as the control it is.

**The first matrix run was measured against a stale `__pycache__`** and had to be re-run with the cache cleared; the numbers above are from the clean run.

## PR #8985 — scripts: census real #[ignore] cells, not prose that mentions one [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8980-census-prose`

Closes #8980

## The defect

`scripts/ignored-cell-census.sh` scanned with `grep -rn '#\[ignore'` — unanchored, no comment exclusion. `userspace-dp/src/server/tests.rs` contains **no `#[ignore]` attributes at all**; two of its doc comments read:

```rust
/// UN-`#[ignore]`d by the change that satisfies it. It was written
/// before the fix so the fix had a red to work against
```

Those were reported as two undeclared cells, reddening `make selftest` for **every lane**.

## Why it was urgent rather than cosmetic

The prose arrived with a change that *removed* two `#[ignore]`s and documented having done so. **The guard fired on the correct behaviour**, so the cheapest route to green was to delete the explanation — the incentive pointed at erasing the record the guard exists to protect.

## The control is the point, not the pattern fix

The census already **had** a control for the scan — the ZERO-hits check ("found zero cells, the pattern is wrong"). It cannot see this class:

> **A non-zero-hits control detects a pattern that is too TIGHT. It is blind BY CONSTRUCTION to one that is too LOOSE.**

So the new control bounds **both** directions against synthetic probes:

| bound | probes | required |
|---|---|---|
| LOOSE | doc-comment mentions in `//`, `///`, `//!` styles; a tab-indented one; `#[ignored_by_some_other_tool]` | **0 of 5** |
| TIGHT | bare; tab-indented; space-indented; **one whose reason cites a URL** | **4 of 4** |

Two design points that were found by mutating, not by planning:

- **It drives `scan_ignores` itself** through a stdin arm rather than calling the pieces. An earlier draft tested `grep` and the filter separately, so removing `| drop_comment_lines` *from the composition* survived the control. Both arms now feed one filter.
- **The URL probe** exists because `grep -v '//'` — dropping any line *containing* `//` rather than one in comment *position* — passes every other assertion here while silently discarding every cell whose reason cites a link. That mutant survived until the probe was added.

It uses **no temp files**: checks (1) and (2) are documented as hermetic, and an earlier draft using `mktemp` broke the deliberately-minimal no-gh environment (`PATH` carries only `sh grep sed cut sort awk wc`) in the census selftest. That was my regression, caught by the existing selftest.

`-H` is now explicit too: with a *single file* argument grep omits the filename and emits `line:content`, which misaligns both the filter and the pre-existing `cut -d: -f1,2`.

## Mutation matrix

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| drop the comment filter from the composition | `too-loose(4 of 5 non-cells)` |
| require a column-zero attribute | `too-tight(0 of 4)` |
| drop the `\b` word boundary | `too-loose(1 of 5)` |
| filter on `//` anywhere | `too-tight(3 of 4)` |
| filter on `.*//` (position-blind) | `too-tight(3 of 4)` |

Two of these are landed as permanent selftest cells (7a loose, 7b tight), so the matrix is a guard rather than something I ran once by hand.

## PR #8986 — fix: refuse a live cluster control-endpoint move at commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8965-control-endpoint-preflight`

Fixes issue 8965.

## The defect

Applying a control-link peer-address move restarts this node's cluster comms on the **new** address and only then pushes the config to a peer still listening on the **old** one. The peer never receives the change, and the two nodes are durably partitioned.

**A commit whose purpose was to preserve HA is what removes it.**

## Nothing heals it — verified, not inherited

The issue marked this checked-not-executed because it rests on the reconciler's *trigger*, a different site from the one quoted. Executed:

- `QueueConfig` no-ops on a nil connection, so the push fails **silently** rather than erroring the commit.
- `reconcileConfigSyncToPeer` returns early on `!syncPeerConnected` (`daemon_ha_sync.go:546`), and that flag is set true in **exactly one place** — the session-sync connect callback. It cannot bootstrap a mismatch in which nothing is connected.
- Both config-delivery paths funnel through `QueueConfig`. Heartbeats carry no config.

**No third path — so this is a durable partition, not a window.** Retry and reboot reproduce it, the standby eventually promotes on the stale tuple, and fencing cannot traverse the severed channel either.

## Refuse rather than make-before-break, and the argument is structural

**Three** apply paths reach `applyConfigLocked` — `commitAndApply`, `syncAndApply`, `commitConfirmedAndApply`. A stage-and-ACK would have to be correct at each, and a version landed at one would leave the others silently broken: the partial-fix shape on a row where the missing half is invisible.

A preflight runs **before all three** and covers them by construction. It is wired at all three call sites alongside the existing topology and identity gates.

It is also the answer this file already gives twice — for mode changes and identity changes — to exactly this class: a change that cannot be re-keyed live from one side. **You cannot move both ends of a point-to-point control link atomically from one end of it.**

## The refusal names the procedure

A refusal without a path is worse than the defect for someone mid-maintenance: they will find the way around it, and the way around it — committing on each node separately while both run — **is the same partition by hand**. The message gives both addresses, the both-nodes-then-restart procedure, and an explicit warning off that workaround. A cell asserts each.

## Scope, recorded rather than papered over

This gates the peer **address**, which is what the node dials and therefore what decides whether the push can land. `control-interface` is **not** gated — the manager keeps no running value to compare against without further plumbing, so a gate on it would compare config-to-config and could fire on a peer-synced text. **An interface-only move has the same shape and is not covered here.**

Peer-sync is safe: `PeerAddress` is per-node and a synced text compiles for the local node, so in steady state candidate equals running and the gate is a no-op — the same reasoning the identity gate documents for itself.

## My first test for this was vacuous, and the mutation caught it

It exposed only the message builder for testing, so the cell asserted the operator-facing **text** while the **decision** went unexercised: neutering the gate to `return nil` left it **green**. A seam that bypasses the thing under test is worse than no seam, because it reads as coverage. The decision is now split out and tested directly.

    M1  decision neutered           ->  FAILS ("must be REFUSED")
    M2  procedure removed from msg  ->  FAILS naming both the missing guidance
                                        and the missing workaround warning

Four decision cases asserted: a real move refused; unchanged allowed; no running endpoint yet allowed; candidate unset allowed.

`pkg/daemon`, `pkg/cluster`, `pkg/config` all green; gofmt clean.

## PR #8988 — fix: the retired-dataplane rewriter could not see a packed value [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8964-packed-retired-rewrite`

Fixes issue 8964, raised by lane-8015 while censusing raw-AST readers.

## The mechanism, narrower than "runs on the un-normalized tree"

    braced   Keys=[system]                       Children=[[dataplane-type ebpf]]
    packed   Keys=[system dataplane-type ebpf]   Children=[]

**`systemBlocksOf` finds the stanza in both** — measured, `systemBlocks=1` either way. So this was never a walk that missed the node. `rewriteRetiredLeavesIn` walks `Children`, and the packed spelling carries the value on the stanza's own `Keys`.

**The consequence is a boot failure, not a dropped setting.** The compiler hard-rejects a retired value (`ErrEBPFDataplaneRetired`), which is why this rewriter exists — to neutralise the token *before* the compiler sees it. A token left behind fails `Store.Load` and the node comes up with `ActiveConfig()==nil`.

Inert today only because `system dataplane-type` is not an admitted compact pair, so the compiler drops the packed tail anyway. **One line in `compactNormalizeInScope` ends that** — which is why it was filed before the campaign arrives rather than after.

## Fixed in the lookup, not by reordering the pipeline

The deciding measurement is lane-8015's, not mine: **the naive fold-before-rewrite is a silent no-op.** `config.NormalizeCompactForScan` returns a **clone** when it folds while this function mutates **in place**, so the rewrite lands on the clone, the caller keeps the original tree, and the count still reports `1`. A cell asserting `rewrites == 1` passes while the retired value survives into the compile.

Beyond that, pre-folding changes **which tree continues down** `Store.Load` and `SyncApply` for every config — measured at 10 of 11 shipped configs rendering differently after folding. That is a decision about which tree survives, not a reordering.

The lookup-local fix needs no such decision, has a blast radius of one function, and is **correct whether or not the pair is ever admitted**. The general question stays with #8903, where it can be answered once with the whole raw-AST reader population in view rather than from one container.

The value is **removed** from `Keys` rather than blanked, so the result matches the braced path: a `dataplane-type` with no value would reach the compiler as a different malformed input rather than as an absent statement.

## Validation

    M1  packed-tail call removed        ->  FAILS on both the count AND the tree
    M2  counted but Keys not mutated    ->  FAILS on the TREE only

**M2 is the one that matters.** It is lane-8015's silent-no-op shape, and it is caught by the assertion that reads *the tree the caller keeps* rather than the count. The count is not the property.

Controls: a non-retired leaf, a **live** `userspace` value, and a live value in the **packed** spelling all rewrite 0 — so the zeros are a measurement rather than a claim about the walk. *A zero from a rewriter is a claim about the rewriter until something in the same run makes it fire.* A sibling statement is asserted to survive the removal.

`pkg/configstore` and `pkg/config` green, gofmt clean.

## PR #8999 — config: ratchet the flat-set chain-walk split, and refute #8939's remedy [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-flat-set-chain-ratchet`

#8939 reports that a flat `set` command naming two leaves under one container builds a **nested chain** rather than siblings, so the second leaf is silently dropped. **The report is correct. Its proposed remedy is not**, and this PR lands the measurement that says so plus the ratchet that bounds the real population.

## The remedy is wrong because the chain is not the discriminator

The chain is built identically for **every** container. What differs is whether the container's **compiler** walks below the first leaf. Same grammar shape, one command each:

```
applications application myapp protocol tcp destination-port 8080
   packed  proto="tcp" dport="8080"     <- compiler WALKS the chain (#6524)
   split   proto="tcp" dport="8080"

interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 0 tunnel source A destination B
   packed  src="10.0.0.1" dst=""        <- compiler does NOT walk
   split   src="10.0.0.1" dst="10.0.0.2"
```

Identical nesting, opposite outcome. So "reject at parse time" would reject a spelling a large minority of containers handle **correctly today** — `applications` among them, which has an entire test file devoted to the chained form working (`compiler_application_chained_leaves_6524_test.go`).

## The population, measured with the compiler as the oracle

| outcome | containers |
|---|---:|
| **LOSE** the second leaf | **40** |
| **WALK** the chain | **41** |
| vacuous (both forms empty) | 2 |
| unmeasured (synthetic values don't compile) | 50 |

All 40 losers lose the second leaf **entirely** — total silent loss, never partial corruption.

## Two controls make those numbers mean something

- **Vacuity control on the WALK side.** Two equal-but-empty compiles prove nothing about walking; this cut 43 to 41.
- **Total-loss discriminator on the LOSE side.** Does the packed form equal leaf-A-alone? This is immune to whether leaf B takes a value — which the schema cannot answer, since `schemaNode` has no such field.

## Why the obvious instrument was discarded

The first predicate written for this was a schema-shape one, and **its own positive control killed it**: it detected **2 of the 4 examples #8939 itself names**, while flagging hundreds of working lines across the suite. Its headline "0 of 711 shipped set-lines affected" was a real measurement of a predicate answering the wrong question. The differential instrument replaced it because it uses the compiler as the oracle rather than a claim about shape.

## The ratchet

Fails in **both** directions and names which: a container entering the list is a silent configuration-loss regression on an accepted spelling; one leaving it is a fix that must be recorded (`UPDATE_8939=1`). Mutation-tested — dropping a fixture row reports `+ NEWLY LOSING (regression)`, adding one reports `- no longer losing (fixed)`, and mutating **production** so `applicationDirectLeaves` returns only immediate children kills the WALK control and its vacuity check together.

The file states its own blind spots inline: one pair per container, unmeasured rows are not cleared, depth capped, `groups` not traversed. The count is a **lower bound** and is deliberately not reconciled to the issue title's figure, which came from a different instrument — two instruments disagreeing is a fact about the instruments until someone reconciles them.

Test-only. `go test ./pkg/config/` green.

Refs #8939, #8904, #6524, #2419.

## What was measured

`TestSitesThatCannotBeSeparatedShareAClass8690` says of itself: *"It measures ONE spelling per site — the census's synthesized packing… a red is a definite hazard, a green is 'not at this packing'."* Honest, and never measured. Over all 50 register sites:

"Measure every site, collapse only on agreement, publish the disagreement" assumes the measurements being collapsed are **valid and merely disagree**. Collapsing `{some keys}` against `{}` would publish CONTINGENT, which reads as *"the answer depends on the spelling"* when the truth is *"the second probe observed nothing at all."* **A vacuous measurement is not a dissenting one.** That is a distinction #8946 does not currently draw, and it means the issue's "three instruments, one remedy" is a claim about a subset.

The value-axis result matters too, in the other direction: the remedy has **nothing to collapse** here, so applying it would have been motion without effect. Reading the instrument would have suggested otherwise.

The cell reds if the braced form starts recording keys (#8763 fixed — the census must then be re-derived across both packings, and the #8859 remedy finally *does* apply) or if the flat form stops (census vacuous). ## PR #9001 — docs: fix CLAUDE.md's dual-AST example, which showed no difference [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8808-ast-example-doc`

The "Parser Dual AST Shape" section exists to teach that flat `set` and hierarchical braces build different trees. Its only example was `family inet`, for which **they do not**:

```
FLAT  set interfaces eth0 unit 0 family inet dhcp
HIER  interfaces { eth0 { unit 0 { family inet { dhcp; } } } }
  -> both: [interfaces] > [eth0] > [unit 0] > [family inet] > [dhcp]
```

`family` is declared `compoundKey`, so `SetPath` consumes the sub-key into the same node the hierarchical parser does. Being the **only** example, it is the one readers generalise from — and it is wrong in the direction that makes people skip a measurement: a compiler exercised only against `family inet` looks shape-agnostic while being blind to every non-compound container.

The replacement is `protocols bgp group g1 neighbor <ip> peer-as <as>`, where flat `set` builds a **chain** and the hierarchical spelling of the same configuration builds **siblings**.

## One correction to the issue's own wording, and it changed the design

#8808 phrased the claim as *"byte-identical"*. The accurate claim is **structurally identical**. `reflect.DeepEqual` reports the two trees **unequal** — and the difference is not structural:

```
flat  {Keys:[family inet] … Line:0 Column:0}
hier  {Keys:[family inet] … Line:1 Column:42}
```

Measured as the only difference at every node. That is not pedantry, because it decides how the guard has to compare. A `DeepEqual` assertion here fails for a reason that has nothing to do with AST shape, and the natural way to make it pass is to loosen the comparison until it stops discriminating at all. So the cells compare structure explicitly, and a separate assertion proves position metadata is the *only* thing ignored.

## The guard

`pkg/config/ast_shape_doc_8808_test.go` holds the documented strings verbatim and asserts three things: the old example's shapes converge, the new example's diverge, and the convergent pair differs in nothing beyond `Line`/`Column`.

Both mutations kill:

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| `family` no longer compoundKey (production, `ast_edit.go`) | converge cell reds |
| replacement example rewritten as nested braces | divergence cell reds — *"this example teaches nothing"* |

**That second mutant is not hypothetical — it was my first attempt.** I replaced the example and wrote the hierarchical form as `neighbor 10.0.0.1 { peer-as 65001; }`, which is a chain in both spellings: an example illustrating nothing, exactly like the one being removed. Committing this issue's own defect inside its fix is what the divergence assertion exists to catch, and it caught it.

Closes #8808

## PR #9002 — grpcapi: exercise show vlans through the grammar it actually reads [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8990-vlans-fixture`

Closes #8990

## The red

`TestShowTextGolden` committed a top-level `vlans v100 vlan-id 100` stanza. There is no `vlans` top-level keyword in `pkg/config` and there never was — `git log -S'"vlans"' -- pkg/config/` is empty — so that line was **silently discarded on every run**.

The proof is the golden baseline itself: it recorded `"No VLANs configured"` for the `vlans` topic. The fixture asserted the renderer's **empty branch** while believing it had configured a VLAN.

The #8965 unmodeled-stanza gate turned that silent discard into a commit rejection. **The gate is right; the fixture was wrong.** An operator now learns at commit that the stanza reaches nothing, rather than discovering it in production.

## Fixed by writing what the renderer reads, not by deleting the line

`showVLANs` renders from `cfg.Interfaces` — `unit.VlanID` and `ifc.VlanTagging`. The fixture now carries `vlan-tagging` plus a tagged unit, so the topic exercises the real table:

```
Interface        Unit   VLAN ID  Zone         Mode
ge-0-0-1         0      native                trunk
ge-0-0-1         100    100                   trunk
```

Deleting the line would have left the golden asserting `"No VLANs configured"` for a topic the product supports — locking in a row with **zero coverage of the renderer**, which is the vacuous-cell class this campaign keeps finding. The red was an opportunity to add coverage, not just to remove an error.

**Not** fixed by modelling a `vlans` stanza: that adds a leaf which validates and is read by no compiler — the accepted-but-inert class #8903/#8939 are cataloguing.

## Reachability of the documented feature — checked, because the remedy depended on it

README/CLAUDE.md claim *"VLANs: 802.1Q tagging, trunk ports"*. Both are reachable through the modelled grammar:

| claim | grammar | reaches |
|---|---|---|
| 802.1Q tagging | `interfaces <if> unit N vlan-id <id>` | compiled (`compiler_interfaces.go:375`) → the wire (`process_napi.go` builds the `base.<vid>` netdev) |
| trunk ports | `interfaces <if> vlan-tagging` | compiled (`compiler_interfaces.go:73`) → `showVLANs` renders `Mode=trunk` |

**The docs claim does not outrun the grammar**, so there is no second defect and nothing further to file. That was the open question in #8990's body; this settles it.

## Golden audited rather than trusted

Regenerating rewrites every topic, so the diff was compared programmatically: **exactly one topic changed (`vlans`), none added, none removed.** `show interfaces` is not in the golden topic set at all, which is why adding a unit moved nothing else.

## PR #9015 — config: state the census unit in the output line, not in a comment [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8946-units`

Closes #8946 — the last of its three suggested items. Context in the issue.

## What this lands

A count is meaningless until it says whether it counts **sites** or **pairs**, and this codebase has burned three measurements on exactly that: the 320-sites / 95-pairs reconciliation, #8921's 223-of-547, and #8938's population reported as 51 by counting a slice that double-counted `family inet6`.

Surveyed the census family. **Most outputs already name their unit** — `%d pairs swept`, `%d site(s)`, `%d published rows`. Two published a bare count; both are now explicit where a reader meets the number rather than in a comment three screens up.

| census | output now says |
|---|---|
| depth-2 population | `got N PAIRS, want N PAIRS (unit: distinct (mid, head) pairs — NOT sites; one pair reached under two stanzas is ONE)` |
| #8755 unmeasurable | `N/N SITES unmeasurable (unit: sites, not pairs — several sites can share one (container, head) pair)` |

**The two units differ in opposite directions, which is why each line says which way.** The depth-2 population *collapses* sites into pairs, so its number is smaller than a site count; #8755 measures sites, so several of its rows can belong to one pair. A reader carrying either convention across is wrong half the time — which is how the 51-vs-50 error happened.

Verified by **forcing the failure**, not by reading the format string: the depth-2 message renders as `population GREW: got 24 PAIRS, want 23 PAIRS (unit: ...)`.

## Why #8946 closes here

Its three items are now settled, and one of them dissolved on inspection rather than being done:

1. **The remedy across instruments** — measured in PR #9000, and it **partially falsified the issue's own claim**: `sweepPairVerdicts8859` collapses only where several *valid* measurements disagree, and does not apply where the alternative measurement is vacuous. That split (contingent vs bounded instruments) is recorded on the issue.
2. **Instrument 3 has no live code left.** The depth-2 sweep was a throwaway harness; its 26 DROPS were all admitted, and no live cell publishes SAME verdicts from it. The nearest candidate, `arity_census_8807_test.go`, is a different family — hand adjudication over a name-keyed predicate, not a one-value synthesiser — and already states its own bound.
3. **This change.**

## PR #9076 — test: close two gates that reported success without measuring [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9045-9046-gate-gaps`

Two unrelated gates, one shape: each returned a passing result from a path that had not examined its subject.

## #9045 — the `pkg/dataplane` race leg

`test-race-dp` raced `./pkg/dataplane/ -run 'ArmedGate|PreArm'` — 15 of the package's 463 tests, and **not one** of its goroutine-driven probes. The decisive measurement is on one of them:

**`TestPersistentNATTable_AllConcurrentSaveNoRace` contains zero `t.Error`/`t.Fatal` of any kind in 47 lines.** Its only possible failure is the race detector firing. Outside the race leg it is not a weak test — it is a test that *cannot fail*, and it was green for exactly that reason.

`pkg/daemon` and `pkg/cluster` each already carry a canary that fails when their leg narrows. `pkg/dataplane` had none, so the exclusion was invisible.

**The canary keys on the test's own body launching a goroutine, not on the file.** The originating report swept test *files* containing `go func` and counted 33 tests — but `persistent_nat_test.go` holds fifteen ordinary table tests beside one probe, so a file-level predicate would demand the race leg run 24 tests that exercise no concurrency. Body-level gives **9**, and the widened pattern covers all 9.

It reads the Makefile line by **package path** rather than position. `pkg/daemon`'s canary reads "the FIRST `-run` line", which forced a Makefile comment warning that this leg *"must stay BELOW the pkg/daemon one"* — a positional coupling a harmless reordering breaks silently.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| restore the narrow pattern | reds, naming **3 of 9** excluded |
| delete the `./pkg/dataplane/` race line | reds — "no longer race-gated" |

Two positive controls cover the two ways the cell could pass having measured nothing: zero tests found, and zero tests classified as probes by a broken predicate. **The widened leg itself runs clean — `ok 35.7s`, 0 data races.**

## #9046 — the merge-completeness lint

It inspected **HEAD only**. A merge that dropped a ledger shard was catchable only while HEAD was exactly that merge; one commit later it is permanently invisible, because plain `ledger-lint` structurally *cannot* see a missing row — a deleted shard leaves a lint-clean directory. Now walks the last 25 merges (`--lint-merge-count`).

**The accounting half is the subtler defect.** On a non-merge HEAD it returned 0 and the caller printed `PASS: ledger-merge-completeness (… nothing to check)`. The author was aware — a comment says the words are in the label so that "checked nothing" and "checked and clean" do not look the same. But a PASS line still increments `passed=157`, and **the total is what anyone actually reads**. A disclosure that does not survive aggregation is not a disclosure. Exit 3 now means "we could not look" and maps to SKIP.

```
before:  PASS: ledger-merge-completeness (lint-merge: HEAD is not a merge commit — nothing to check)
after:   PASS: ledger-merge-completeness (lint-merge: OK — 25 merge(s) checked, 25 run_id(s), none dropped)
```

Both new exits exercised: rc 0 with 25 merges checked, rc 3 in a synthetic repo with no merges.

## Validation

- `go test -count=1 ./...` — **zero failures**
- `make selftest` — **157 passed / 0 failed**
- widened race leg — **green, 0 data races**

Closes #9045
Closes #9046

`security ike gateway` and `security ipsec gateway` share the `IPsecGateway` struct and **duplicate the reader**: `compileIKE` and `compileIPsec` each carry their own `for … range inst.node.Children` loop, forty lines apart in one file. *"They share a struct so probably a reader"* was plausible and **false** — a fix applied to one would have left the other silently broken with a green suite.

    two    [address A]

    three  [address A]
             [external-interface E local-address L]  <- ONE node, a FLAT RUN

`SetPath` models only the **first** link; every remaining token packs onto **one** node's `Keys`. A recursive descent reads the second leaf and silently drops the third. The scan follows #6524's `parseApplicationTerms`, which took that form for the same reason.

`expandFlatRun` is **shared rather than inlined twice**, because that loop shape is what the remaining #8939 containers have — writing it inline here would be the first two instances of a repetition that wants continuing.     - security ike gateway arg1    [address | external-interface | ike-policy]

Worth recording why: the two-leaf ratchet witnessed this fix, the three-leaf one that briefly replaced it **could not** — both gateway containers dropped out of the measured population at three leaves, so a real fix to two real defects moved the acceptance signal by nothing. #9079 emits both widths: **two leaves carries the coverage, three carries the discrimination.**

That is why `gateway_flat_run_8939_test.go` carries its own three-leaf assertion and stays load-bearing: a cell asserting the contract at the site and a census asserting a population property are different claims.

## PR #9078 — config: make the #8939 ratchet discriminate a recursive descent [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-ratchet-three-leaf`

lane-8388 showed the ratchet I landed in #8999 **could not distinguish the correct fix from the obvious wrong one**, and fixing that exposed an error in the numbers that file published.

## The instrument defect

At two leaves a flat-set chain is indistinguishable from ordinary nesting:

```
two    [address 192.0.2.1] > [external-interface ge-0/0/0]
three  [address 192.0.2.1] > [external-interface ge-0/0/0 local-address 10.0.0.1]
```

At three the remainder packs onto **one** node's `Keys`, so a recursive descent recovers leaf B and silently drops C. The ratchet tested the two alphabetically-first leaves — so it would have recorded that fix as *"no longer losing"*. **The acceptance signal I handed a lane would have certified a wrong fix.**

It now synthesizes three leaves wherever a container declares three, and classifies each loser `total` / `partial(descent-shaped)` / `differs`.

## What that exposed in my own numbers

Moving to three leaves shifted containers from LOSE to **WALK** — `schedulers scheduler <s> friday` among them — which **cannot happen if the measurement is sound**, since a third leaf can only expose more loss. The cause: the two spellings compared equal because the **last leaf is not observable in the typed config at all**. The existing vacuity control only caught a wholly-empty config.

| | losers | walked | vacuous | unmeasured |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| published (2-leaf) | 40 | **41** | 2 | 50 |
| corrected (3-leaf) | 34 | **5** | 42 | 52 |

**So "41 containers genuinely walk the chain" — which I published in PR #8999 and in the #8939 comment — was wrong.** 40 of those 41 were vacuous rows.

Worse: **`applications`, the witness the whole argument rests on, was never in this population.** Its match leaves are `multi` or carry children, so the eligibility predicate excludes them. The count never had anything to say about the claim it was quoted to support.

The argument against #8939's parse-time rejection is **unchanged** — it rests on the `applications` control, which drives a real value through a real compile and asserts it (`dport == "8080"`). The census corroborated nothing. The `walked < 20` floor I wrote into the file fired and said exactly that, so it now guards the control instead of the count.

## Mutation

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| revert to two leaves | reds — fixture moves |
| drop the observability control | **survived at first** |

The second is the interesting one. Removing that control only shuffles rows between `vacuous` and `walked`, which a **loser-only fixture cannot see** — a control deletable in silence. The four counts are now part of the fixture, which is what makes it a control rather than a comment, and the mutant now reports:

```
! counts moved, now: losers=34 walked=45 vacuous=2  unmeasured=52
! counts were:       losers=34 walked=5  vacuous=42 unmeasured=52
```

Test-only. Sequenced ahead of lane-8388's `security ike gateway` fix so they build against a signal that discriminates.

## PR #9080 — harness-census: tell an UNTRACKED file apart from an unregistered one [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9006-census-untracked-diagnostic`

`make selftest` reported **155 passed / 2 failed** on my checkout where another lane had measured **157/0** on a fresh one. The offender was `test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh` — **untracked**, a scratch file in my own working tree.

```
$ git ls-files --error-unmatch test/incus/per-stream-diag.sh
error: pathspec ... did not match any file(s) known to git
```

## The scan is right; the diagnostic is the defect

Scanning the filesystem is correct — a harness you've added and not committed is exactly what the census should catch. But the message asserts *"a harness was added or a recipe removed"*, which points at recent commits, and offers two remedies of which **neither fits a local scratch script and one is actively wrong**:

> - add a Makefile recipe that runs it, or
> - add a line to `HARNESSES.unreached`

`HARNESSES.unreached` may only name **committed** paths, and a declaration for a path not in the tree is itself a FAIL — so following the printed remedy produces a *second, different* failure. I spent a cycle hunting recent commits before checking `git ls-files`.

It also means a shared gate's verdict depends on untracked files in the runner's tree, with nothing explaining why two people at one SHA disagree.

## Hermeticity was the constraint, not an afterthought

This script promises *"a pure file scan … it either scans the tree or fails to start"*, and a hard `git` dependency is what broke that promise once before — a `mktemp` added to the census died in the restricted-PATH leg, where `PATH` holds only `sh grep sed cut sort awk wc`.

**Git here refines the remedy TEXT only** — never the verdict, never the exit status, never whether the scan runs. With no git, or outside a repository, every path falls through to the original message and the census behaves bit-identically. Verified by running it outside a git repo: no UNTRACKED text, generic message, scan completes.

## Two cells, because one direction does not bound the branch

| case | must say | must NOT say |
|---|---|---|
| untracked | `UNTRACKED harness` | `UNREACHED and undeclared` |
| tracked, undeclared | `UNREACHED and undeclared` | `UNTRACKED harness` |

A branch that fired for *both* would satisfy either cell alone. They are git-**gated** rather than git-dependent, so the suite skips them instead of acquiring a dependency.

| mutant | killed by |
|---|---|
| collapse the branch (generic text always) | the **untracked** cell |
| invert it (untracked text always) | the **tracked** cell |

## Validation

- `make selftest` — **157 passed / 0 failed**
- census selftest **25 → 27** cells
- `go test -count=1 ./...` clean

Closes #9006

## PR #9083 — userspace: stop defaulting the helper control socket into /tmp and prove the peer (#9003) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9003-control-socket-perms`

## Mechanism (confirmed, not assumed)

The daemon puts the **WireGuard local private key and every per-peer preshared key** into the
`apply_snapshot` body in cleartext — `pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:139,149`. The **on-disk**
half was already handled: `snapshot.rs:775,814` mark both fields `skip_serializing` with a
redacting `Debug` impl and a test at `:917` pinning it, so `state.json` cannot carry them. The
**socket** half was gated by nothing except the mode the socket inherited from the ambient umask,
which no code, no unit file and no test asserted.

Three defects composed, each individually idiomatic:

1. **The compiled-in default was under `os.TempDir()`.** `capabilities.go:20,33` defaulted to
   `${TMPDIR}/xpf-userspace-dp/control.sock`, so any deployment that omits
   `set system dataplane control-socket` binds inside world-writable `/tmp`. The shipped reference
   configs *do* pin `/run/xpf` (`docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf:391`,
   `docs/ha-cluster-loss.conf:310`) — which is exactly the shape where "the shipped config is fine"
   stops being a defence, because the defect is in the default.
2. **`os.MkdirAll(dir, 0755)` adopts.** `process.go:125`. It returns `nil` for a pre-existing
   directory of **any owner and any mode**. An unprivileged local user who wins the race to
   `mkdir /tmp/xpf-userspace-dp` owns the directory the root helper then binds inside, and can
   unlink that socket and bind their own.
3. **Neither end identified its peer.** `handlers/mod.rs:179-181` dispatches `ping` / `status` /
   `apply_snapshot` / `set_forwarding_state` / `update_ha_state` with **no caller check**, so a
   connectable socket is dataplane *takeover*, not merely key readback. The earliest reachable
   instance is `boot_probe.go:94`, which dials **before any helper spawn**
   (`pkg/daemon/bootstrap.go:221`) — so `removeStaleUnixSocket`'s fail-closed guard has not run, and
   a squatter can **lie** about `Enabled` / `ForwardingArmed` to the #1993 fail-closed boot decision
   and the #5286 upgrade-readiness gate. That is an integrity defect independent of the keys.

Two framing corrections, so the fix is not aimed at the wrong place. A Unix socket's mode gates
**connect**, not reading bytes in flight — a third party can never read AF_UNIX traffic regardless
of mode, so "eavesdropping in transit" is not the exposure; **impersonating the endpoint** is. And
under the documented `/run/xpf` config with systemd's default umask the socket lands 0755 and an
unprivileged `connect()` gets EACCES today — the safety there rests entirely on an inherited umask
nothing asserts, and a `UMask=0000` in the unit silently converts it with no signal anywhere.

## The fix

- **Defaults moved to `/run/xpf` on both sides** (`DefaultControlSocket` / `DefaultStateFile` in Go,
  `DEFAULT_CONTROL_SOCKET` / `DEFAULT_STATE_FILE` in Rust), matching the shipped configs. They are
  pinned to each other by a lockstep test, because the #1993 probe dials the path the **daemon**
  derived while a surviving helper listens on the path the **helper** chose.
- **`ensureTrustedRuntimeDir` creates and then proves.** The directory must be root-owned (or owned
  by this daemon, so a non-root test binary can drive the real path) and must not be world-writable
  without the sticky bit; and no **ancestor** may be world-writable without sticky, since such an
  ancestor lets a non-owner rename the whole subtree aside.
- **SO_PEERCRED on every dial and every accept.** `dialTrustedHelperSocket` verifies before writing
  a byte on the control socket, the session socket and the boot probe. `EventStream.acceptLoop`
  verifies before letting a connection **displace** the current helper (that block closes `es.conn`
  and installs the connector as the event source — so an unprivileged connect was both a disconnect

## PR #9084 — userspace-dp: a capped learned-route import must not black-hole the FIB (#9054) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9054-learned-route-cap-blackhole`

## Mechanism (both halves read at master, not inferred)

**The Go half.** `learned_route_cap_8355.go:113-129` declines the **entire** learned-route import
above `maxLearnedRoutes()` — derived, not picked, through the control deadline constants, and
landing at ~64,968 routes. Its own operator-facing WARN line says:

> `"consequence": "…every LEARNED destination resolves NoRoute and takes the slow-path reinject, so`
> `traffic still forwards through the kernel but not on the AF_XDP fast path"`

The gate sits at `routes.go:745`, and the importer is unconditionally enabled in production
(`EnableLearnedRouteImport()` in `New()`).

**The Rust half.** `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:4883-5010` (#7480) adjudicates the zone pair **before**
the trailing #1913 chokepoint. The egress is unresolved by construction, so `to_zone_id` is the
#3110 unzoned sentinel `0`; `forwarding/mod.rs:171-185` refuses to match any rule against zone 0 and
falls through to the default action; `noroute_policy_denial` returns `Some` for anything that is not
`Permit`, and the frame is downgraded to `PolicyDenied` and dropped. The Rust comment says so
outright: *"On a Junos-default deny box that means a NoRoute frame now drops."* And
`tests_noroute_adjudication_7480.rs::a_zone_pair_permit_does_not_rescue_noroute_7480` already pins
that no operator permit can rescue it.

**The composition.** On a default-deny box carrying more than ~65,000 learned routes and no
config-derived covering route, the cap converts every learned destination from "kernel slow path" to
"dropped in userspace" — a **total blackhole of the dynamic FIB** — while the diagnostic tells the
operator the opposite. The deployment that exceeds the cap is a full-table or large-partial eBGP
edge, which typically has no static default to mask it.

## Why it survived two closed issues, and what that decides about the tests

#8355's own regression cells check the cap **message** and the imported route **count**, and both are
still perfectly correct — a capped import does import zero routes. Neither cell can see what the
helper then does with a frame for one of those destinations, and no cell in either language spanned
the boundary. That is what the new cells are shaped around: the disposition-bearing fact and the
wiring between the two languages, not the count.

## The fix — at the composition, not at either half

#7480's adjudication is sound only while `NoRoute` **carries information**: while the helper FIB is a
near-complete mirror of the kernel's, so a destination missing from it is genuinely unroutable. Its
own justification says exactly that ("#7409 bounds the kernel/helper FIB divergence without closing
it"). A wholesale declined import suspends that premise: `NoRoute` stops meaning "there is no route"
and starts meaning "the daemon did not tell you". Dropping on a signal that carries no information
is not fail-closed; it is just closed.

So:

- `buildRouteSnapshots` / `addLearnedRouteSnapshots` now **report** whether the cap declined the
  import. Deliberately distinct from "nothing was imported": an empty kernel table and a refused
  100k-route table both add zero routes, and only the second leaves the FIB deliberately incomplete.
- `ConfigSnapshot.LearnedRouteImportCapped` carries it, set at **both** publish sites. The route-only

## PR #9085 — docs: an anchored deny-commands narrows, and only the allow half was written [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9022-anchored-deny-doc`

#9022 reports `deny-commands "^show log$"` permitting `show log 100`. **Reproduced independently** through the real path (`cmdtree.Canonicalize` → `CompiledLoginRegexes.Evaluate`):

```
deny "^show log$"   show log denied · show log 100 ALLOWED · show log messages ALLOWED
deny "show log"     show log denied · show log 100 denied  · show log messages denied
                    show version configuration -> FAIL-CLOSED  (in every case)
```

## This is documented parity — but only half of it was documented

`docs/system-login.md` states matching is partial and illustrates it with an **allow**:

> `allow-commands "show interfaces"` admits `show interfaces terse`

That is the direction operators notice, because it is permissive in an obvious way.

**The deny direction is the one that bites, and it was never stated.** An anchored deny is *narrower* than operators generally intend, and the command still runs — `show log 100` invokes the same `journalctl` the denied form invokes. A restriction that does not restrict is exactly what the pre-#7172 commit refusal existed to prevent.

## The remedy is measured, not asserted

The unanchored spelling denies all four forms, works today, and needs no code change. The note says so and shows it.

It also records what is **not** affected: appending a sibling *keyword* rather than an argument still yields an unresolvable canonical command and fails closed, so **#8289's property is intact** and the hole is confined to nodes that legitimately accept arguments. That distinction matters — without it a reader would conclude the whole family is bypassable.

## What I deliberately did not do

A commit-time advisory when an anchored deny pattern names an `AcceptsArgs` node. I think it is the right shape — additive, catches configs already committed, changes no enforcement — and xpf already deviates from pure regex parity by failing closed on unresolvable commands (#8289; the docs call this *"Tier 3 is ours, chosen fail-closed"*), so an advisory would be consistent with the stated posture rather than a new deviation.

But it is an access-control surface and the choice is not mine to make unilaterally. The reasoning is on #9022, which stays open for it.

Docs only; no behaviour change.

Refs #9022, #8289, #7172.

## PR #9089 — config: record which #8939 rows an OPERATOR can actually type [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9089-census-admission-channel`

This census calls `config.CompileConfig`. **The operator path is `Store.Commit → compileTree → compileTreeStrict`, which runs `schemaValidateExpandedTreeForNode` FIRST.** So every row has been measuring the *tolerant* channel while being reported as the operator channel — conflating two defect classes with different severities.

I had already written this rule down (*`configstore.CheckText` is the commit gate, not `CompileConfig`*) and built the instrument on `CompileConfig` anyway.

## Measured

```
tcp-session PACKED   STRICT REJECTED: closing-timeout: unknown modifier "established-timeout"
tcp-session SPLIT    STRICT ACCEPTED  tcp{close=10 est=20 init=30}
```

**An operator cannot type the command #9086 fixed.** That compiler defect is real, but reachable only through `Store.Load` (boot from the persisted DB) and `Store.SyncApply` (HA config sync from the peer) — both of which use `compileTreeLenient` and downgrade the same gate to a `slog.Warn`.

So for a fully-declared container the flat run is **rejected from the keyboard, warned-then-silently-truncated on boot and on HA sync.** Arguably the worse channel, since nobody is watching it.

## The discriminator is the schema being behind the compiler

A container whose leaves `setSchema` declares catches the packed run on its own arity check. One whose leaves the compiler **reads** but the schema never **declared** has no closed-world check to fail, so the run passes admission.

#9088 files the instance — measured against a complete IPsec preamble so no rejection could be an undefined reference:

```
CONTROL split   gw="G"  ipsec-policy="P"  bind-interface="st0.1"   STRICT ACCEPTED
PACKED          gw="G"  ipsec-policy=""   bind-interface=""        STRICT ACCEPTED
```

## The split

Each loser row now carries `OPERATOR` or `lenient-only`. **24 / 31** — and the OPERATOR set contains rows nobody had flagged:

```
protocols isis  [authentication-key | authentication-type]  total  OPERATOR
protocols rip   [authentication-key | authentication-type]  total  OPERATOR
```

An operator-typed command that silently drops routing-protocol **authentication**.

## `unmeasured` is not neutral

Recorded because it changes how every count in this file should be read. A row leaves the population **precisely when a strict validator rejects the synthetic placeholder** — so the census is blind exactly at the containers someone cared enough about to gate. `unmeasured=75` is *enriched* for high-stakes sites, and this file has been reporting it as a boring remainder.

That is the fourth generator defect in this instrument and the first that is **biased rather than random**.

## Implementation note

Calls `SchemaValidateWithDefinitions` directly rather than `configstore.compileTreeStrict`, because `configstore` imports `config`. The fixtures carry no `groups` and no `inactive:` nodes, so the expansion and stripping that wrapper performs are identity here; the comment says what stops being true if a fixture ever gains either.

| force the predicate `true` | reds, 62 changed rows |
