Branch: `fix/8939-ipsec-vpn`

Six readers under `security ike` / `security ipsec` dropped every leaf after the first of a flat `set` command. All six are in `compiler_ipsec.go`; they were found by compiling each container by hand, and **three of them are not in the #8939 ratchet fixture at all**.

    set security ipsec vpn v1 ike gateway G ipsec-policy P
      -> gateway="G"  ipsec-policy=""

Every site uses the shared `expandFlatRun` from #9077 — no new implementation.

| site | leaves |
|---|---|
| `vpn <V>` | the VPN's own leaf set |
| `vpn <V> ike` | gateway / ipsec-policy |
| `vpn <V> vpn-monitor` | destination-ip / optimized / source-interface |
| `vpn <V> traffic-selector` | local-ip / remote-ip |
| `<ike\|ipsec> gateway <G> dead-peer-detection` | one **shared** reader, both containers |

## `dead-peer-detection` read as already-walking and was not

`parseDeadPeerDetectionNode` does scan `node.Keys` — but that is the **hierarchical** spelling (`dead-peer-detection interval 10;` on one line). The flat spelling nests ONE node under `always-send` carrying `["interval","10","threshold","4"]`, which the child switch never reached. A container can carry a correct scan for the wrong shape and read as covered.

`validateIPsecTrafficSelectorsStrict` walks the same children. On the flat spelling the `remote-ip` node nests UNDER `local-ip`, so `trafficSelectorValues` counted `remote-ip` as a second `local-ip` VALUE and the gate rejected the command **naming the wrong problem**:

A wrong diagnostic sends the operator to inspect a prefix that is fine. The #5692 duplicate-prefix rejects this gate exists for are unchanged and still asserted — `expandFlatRun` only splits a node whose Keys carry a further schema sibling.

Its container recovery matches `range <v>.Children`, so every `expandFlatRun`-wrapped loop this campaign produces turns the range into a `CallExpr` and makes the container unrecoverable. Measured:

    without the call case:  187 localised sites, 22 containers
    with it:                225 localised sites, 25 containers

The ratchet reported the loss as unmeasured converse rows FALLING to 7, labelled `GOOD FAILURE. ## PR #9092 — test: key the #8876 latent ratchet on MEMBERSHIP, not a count [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8876-latent-set-not-count`

The table held an INT per edge, and I justified that in the file itself:

> "a set literal invites `add the new name and move on', which is precisely the non-adjudication this guard is for."

**That argument does not survive being stated next to its alternative.** Bumping `4` to `5` is exactly as cheap as appending a name. What actually resists a lazy edit is the failure TEXT and the adjudication it demands, not the data type — so the count bought nothing on the axis it was chosen for.

## And it paid for that nothing with a blind spot: a SWAP

Lose `filter`, gain `policer`, and the count is still 4. A new value-carrying leaf appears under an edge `compactNormalizeInScope` does not admit — **exactly the event this ratchet exists to catch** — and it passes in silence. A rename is the ordinary way that happens.

Demonstrated rather than argued. The same mutation, both assertions:

    membership:  FAIL  LATENT ROW "family inet" SWAPPED (lost policer, gained filter)
    count:       ok

The count-keyed form does not report a substitution worse. **It does not report it.**

## Where this came from

Found while repairing a *different* ratchet (the #8807 positional predicate, in the #8939 IPsec PR #9090), whose good-news branch — `unmeasured rows FELL, tighten the constant` — would have banked a coverage loss as progress. The generalisation is what sent me back here:

> **A ratchet keyed on a COUNT cannot see a SUBSTITUTION**, and the direction that looks like nothing happened is the one nobody audits.

The falsified argument is kept in the file **as a falsified argument** rather than quietly rewritten. The next person to prefer a count over a set deserves the counterexample, not just the conclusion.

## No expectation changed

The two edges carry the same six leaves they did, now named — `family inet` {address, filter, mtu, unnumbered-address} and `pool persistent-nat` {inactivity-timeout, permit}. The failure text now names GAINED / LOST / SWAPPED members explicitly, and the "DO NOT simply edit the table" instruction is unchanged.

Full `pkg/config` green; gofmt clean; both diffstat forms agree.

## PR #9093 — daemon: anchor the #8967 scraper so a moved apply tail is not a knob finding [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9090-scraper-anchor`

**Reading a source file BY NAME survives the change that breaks it.** The file still exists, `ReadFile` succeeds, the match returns false, and the cell reports a finding about the wrong subject.

## Prompted by a sibling lane losing an entire census to the silent form

Their scraper read the elision predicate's file by name. The campaign split the predicate into `compact_normalize_scope.go`. **The old file still existed**, so the read succeeded, the regex matched nothing, and the census reported a stable, confident `edges=0 ADMITTED=0 MISSING=0`.

**Re-running never catches that — the zero does not vary.** What caught it was a positive control comparing the scrape against the predicate itself:

```
scraped pairs                          = 0
control (policies from-zone) in scrape = false
predicate says admitted                = true
```

Two sources for one fact, disagreeing.

## Blast radius, measured before fixing anything

```
in-tree references to the split file BY NAME : 3, all PROSE (comments)
in-tree tests reading a source file by name  : 27
  WITH a zero/vacuity guard                  : 21
  WITHOUT                                    : 6
```

Nothing committed is silently zero on that file, and the guard practice is established in-tree — that lane's probe was a worktree instrument that had not acquired it.

## One of the six unguarded is mine

`applyTailMentions8967` reads `daemon_apply_tail.go` by name and returns `Contains(src, "d."+starter+"(")`. If the apply tail is split out, every starter reads absent.

**This is the weaker form** — the caller asserts `!applyTailMentions8967(...)`, so it fails loud rather than passing silently. The anchor therefore buys a correct **diagnosis** rather than a caught defect: without it the message reads *"knob X is gated at comms start but its starter is not called from the apply tail"*, which is **false**, and sends the next reader to the knob rather than to the move.

Same class as #9006's untracked harness and #8992's `container "system" does not exist` — loud, and pointing the wrong way.

## Mutation

Pointing the scrape at a real `pkg/daemon` file carrying no `Daemon` methods (`cli_rbac.go`):

```
daemon_apply_tail.go no longer contains any Daemon method, so it is not the apply
tail any more. This cell scrapes it BY NAME; the file was renamed, split, or
emptied. Repoint the scrape -- do NOT read the result below as a finding about any knob.
```

A first attempt mutated the receiver type instead and only broke the build, which tested nothing.

Test-only. `go test -count=1 ./...` clean.

Refs #8967, #9006.

## PR #9094 — test: make the duplicate-block census count what it cannot see [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

The census reported `SILENT (no commit gate at all): 0` and the inventory
declared the silent set **EMPTY**. Both read as "this class is handled". The
census was examining **9 containers out of 139 eligible**.

### The ratchet guards the population; the population was filtered first

`collectDupSites8436` appended a site only when `twoLeaves8436` could pick two
scalar leaves. A container whose children are all containers has no scalar pair,
so the **collector discarded it before the census ran** — reaching neither the
population nor `dupConservationSkipped8436`.

The named-skip ratchet (added after `services rpm probe xpfname test` hid in a
skip *count* for seven batches) works correctly and **could never have caught
this**, because it guards sites that entered the census and these never did.

```
139 eligible containers
 85 dropped by the pre-filter (61%)
  9 examined  ->  "SILENT: 0"
```

Among the dropped: `forwarding-options sampling instance`, `security policies
from-zone`, both `security nat … rule-set`.

### What changed

An eligible container with no constructible fixture is now a **recorded skip
with its reason**, and the two reasons are kept apart because they have different
futures — *container-only children* is structural and will not change, *no two
synthesizable leaves* may resolve when the schema grows one. All 85 are pinned,
so the ratchet fails on a new one **and** a stale one.

**Both confirmed drops from #9023 are now visible** as named unprobed entries.
Honest state: the census still cannot *check* them, and now says so by name
rather than by omission.

The census prints its **denominator** — `SILENT: 0` over 9 reads identically to
`SILENT: 0` over 139, and that difference is the whole finding.

### The header hedge

*"EMPTY … Every container the census could reach"* was **true**, and the
qualifier carried 130 containers. A hedge doing that much work reads as a
limitation rather than a scope; it now states the reach in numbers.

### One filed claim was stale

The skip buckets are **not** count-only — that machinery already exists. The
blind spot sat upstream of it. Corrected on the issue.


**63% discarded before the census ran.**

Both exclusions are defensible — a leaf with children is a container, and a `multi` leaf absorbs a trailing run **by design** (#2419 bracketed lists). But defensible is not the same as visible, and every count this file has published was a fraction of 133 presented as though it were the world.

## Why it goes in the fixture rather than the log

The reach line lives **in** the fixture, so it ratchets like the loser set instead of being a comment that drifts. It is also rendered under its own diff branch — a header line reported as `NEWLY LOSING (regression)` would be a wrong diagnostic in a cell whose entire subject is wrong diagnostics.

## Mutation

Widening eligibility to admit `multi` leaves:

```
! COLLECTOR REACH moved, now: 363 containers walked, 162 reached the census (110 dropped: no eligible leaf, 91 dropped: only one)
! COLLECTOR REACH was:        363 containers walked, 133 reached the census (134 dropped: no eligible leaf, 96 dropped: only one)
```

Test-only. No row's verdict changes and no container newly loses. `go test -count=1 ./...` clean.

cluster run that validated it — and no record of the run that did not.

afterwards returned 3/3 at `ttl=63` — i.e. through the firewall — so the abort was transient settling
after the deploy's RG re-assert, not a forwarding defect. The gate was then re-run on a fresh deploy
and passed.

## Why the VOID row is kept rather than quietly dropped

"The measurement did not happen" is a **third state**, neither pass nor fail, and it is only useful if
it is visible. A ledger that omits its inconclusive runs reports a cleaner board than the cluster
earned, and `harness-compare`'s baseline is drawn from what the ledger holds.

This is also the one thing `ledger-lint` structurally cannot catch, by its own docstring's logic: it
keys on a repeated `run_id` with a **differing** payload — corruption — and a silently dropped row is
well-formed and lint-clean by construction. So it has to be a habit, not a check.

## PR #9098 — daemon: policy-rematch extensive re-evaluates on a referenced-object change [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8993-rematch-extensive`

Closes #8993

## The gap

`policy-rematch` clears the live sessions of a policy whose own match/action changed. Junos' `extensive` also re-evaluates sessions of an **unchanged** policy when a referenced object's *definition* changes — tighten `trusted-hosts` to drop a host and that host's established sessions must be re-evaluated, though every policy's text is byte-identical.

xpf accepted `extensive`, warned it was "only partially enforced", and left those sessions forwarding until idle timeout. `policyMatchOrActionChanged` compares address-book **names**, so it cannot see it.

## The fix

`changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` gains a third arm comparing the **resolved** form — `PolicyResolvedFingerprints`, a hash of the very `PolicyRuleSnapshot` the dataplane is sent. Gated on the sub-mode: with plain `policy-rematch` the maps are never built and the path is bit-identical to before.

### A third of the fix was deleted by its own mutation test

The first version *also* hashed the address-book table, justified in its own doc comment by *"a rule carries book IDs, and an ID is stable while its CONTENTS change."*

**Two mutants removing that contribution changed no result.** Probing why refuted the premise outright:

- `SourceAddresses` in the snapshot is already the **resolved prefix list**, not names.
- Book IDs are **content hashes** (`addressBookContentHash64`) — dropping a set member moves `trusted-hosts` from `1949101590` to `834444897`.

So the extra machinery was inert and is gone. That was a wrong rationale written into a comment — **#8942's own defect, inside the change closing one of #8942's residuals** — caught only because the mutants survived. Hashing exactly what ships is also what stops this drifting from the dataplane's view.

## Validation

Six cells, **four of them controls**:

| cell | guards |
|---|---|
| set membership tightened | the defect |
| address value redefined under a stable name | the defect, with nothing else moving |
| **identical config clears NOTHING** | the levelling trap — a fingerprint that always differs passes both defect cases while clearing every session on every commit |
| stable across repeated builds | non-determinism (map order in snapshot or book table) |
| plain `policy-rematch` unaffected | the sub-mode gate |
| real match/action change still fires | #4234's shipped behaviour |

Mutation matrix, each killed by the cell that names its failure:

| mutant | failures |
|---|---|
| remove the arm (pre-#8993) | 3 |
| constant fingerprint | 3 |
| arm always fires | 3 — named by the nothing-changed control |
| sub-mode gate removed | 2 — named by the plain-rematch control |

An earlier attempt at the first mutant **did not compile** and so reported nothing, reading as "survived". The harness now refuses to score a mutant that did not build.

**`make test-failover`**: 21 passed / 0 failed, iperf3 **17.8 Gbps** across a manual failover of both redundancy groups, under a lock cell against a deploy of this working tree (build tag `…-dirty` confirms it). Required because these invalidations propagate to the peer via the #2468 delete-sync. `go test` green on daemon, config, dataplane/userspace, refactoraudit.

## PR #9099 — docs: `git stash` is a shared stack and has already cost work twice [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `docs/shared-stash-protocol`

Every worktree of one repository shares **one** stash stack. `git stash pop` with no argument takes whatever is on TOP, which during a campaign is very likely another lane's work.

## This is not hypothetical, and the evidence is on the stack itself

Measured 2026-09-05: **32 entries, oldest 2026-05-28** — two of which exist *because it already went wrong*:

```
RESCUE-2026-08-21-foreign-stash-accidentally-popped-into-wt-close-cohorts
                                    (icmp_embed/nat64/wg WIP, NOT mine)
RESCUE-2026-06-17-displaced-1635wip-from-errant-pop
```

Somebody popped someone else's work into their worktree, **twice**, and had to stash the displacement to get it back. Those recoveries are themselves on the shared stack, where the next bare `pop` can displace them again.

Raised by lane-8526, who needed a stash to take a clean `git merge origin/master`, handled it correctly — push, pop immediately, verify the restored files were theirs — and flagged the hazard rather than moving on.

## Where it goes, and why there

Beside the diffstat rule, deliberately: **a stale base is what usually prompts a stash, and merging master is the better answer to it.** The two failures travel together — the same lane hit a 70-file / 3478-deletion diffstat from a stale base in the same hour.

## Also recorded in that section

`git diff --stat` alone **understates** a change: an un-added new file is invisible to it. #8993 landed with two new files its diffstat did not mention. The existing rule covers the two-dot/three-dot pair; this is a third way the same command misleads.

## What I did not do

**Nothing was popped, dropped, or cleared.** Several of the 32 look like real stranded work — a `1635-wip`, an `snmp-trap-batch` pair, a `2419-spelling-differential-gate` WIP. Entries that look like abandoned debris from outside are exactly how stranded work looks from outside, and tidying the stack is the destructive move it already documents.

## PR #9100 — fix: walk the flat run in system login class (#8939) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-login-class`

An `OPERATOR` row from the #9089 channel column, on the RBAC surface.

    set system login class ops allow-commands "a" allow-configuration "c"
      -> allow-commands="a"  allow-configuration=""

## The lost value is not the whole loss

`compiler_system.go` also records leaf **presence** into `LoginClass.AllowLeavesPresent`, and #7172's `loginRegexesFor` keys enforcement on presence, not value:

```go
if !allowSet && !denySet { return CompiledLoginRegexes{}, false, nil }
```

with that file's own caller contract — *"callers MUST skip evaluation entirely"*. An allow regex is an **allowlist**. So dropping `allow-configuration` does not narrow the class to an empty allowlist; it **removes the family's rule altogether** and the class keeps everything `permissions` grants. #7172 cut 6 turned allow enforcement on, so this silently discards a live control. **The loss direction is toward more authority.**

## Acceptance is unchanged — measured, because it was a landing condition

Eight packed spellings through the strict pair (`SchemaValidateWithDefinitions` then `CompileConfig`, which is what `compileTreeStrict` runs), with and without the fix: **identical verdicts 8/8** — including `allow-commands + deny-commands`, which I expected might newly reach `validateLoginClassDenyStrict` and does not. **The fix makes a declared restriction *reach* the compiled class; it adds no rejection.**

## Reachability is a property of the LEAF the run starts at, not of the container

Same container, same two statements, **opposite verdicts by order**:

    ike gateway:  address A external-interface E      ACCEPTED
    ike gateway:  version v2-only address A           SCHEMA-REJECT
    login class:  allow-commands "x" idle-timeout 30  ACCEPTED
    login class:  idle-timeout 30 allow-commands "x"  SCHEMA-REJECT

> A flat run is rejected iff the leaf it **starts** at declares a type/validator. A validated leaf routes to the typed-leaf branch, whose modifier-child check rejects the trailing tokens; an untyped `args:1` leaf falls through to the container branch, which by #3332's compiler-faithful contract **deliberately ignores leftover Keys**.

This **corrects** the container-level reading I gave earlier ("`class` is `args:1` with children and no wildcard, therefore nothing under it is validated"). That is false — `idle-timeout` is validated. What *is* container-level is unknown-keyword blindness, a separate property: `bogus-token 5` admits under `class` and under `user`, and is rejected under the closed-world `security flow tcp-session`.

**A measurement error, corrected.** I first checked this by transcribing the run into **hierarchical** text and calling `configstore.CheckText`. That rejects — but via #8437's fused-statement guard, which reads trailing tokens off the leaf's *own* `Keys`, while the flat-set spelling nests them as a *child chain* #8437 cannot see. `CheckText` parses text and so cannot express the flat spelling at all.

## This PR also repairs a regression it introduced — caught by the shipped spelling gate

`expandFlatRun` hoisted **every** child of a terminating leaf, reasoning that a leaf declaring no schema children can have no body. **False for a `multi` leaf**, and #2419 had already said so: in `permissions { view; configure; }` the children are VALUES. Hoisting them turned a READ leaf into an unread one:

    system login class <*> permissions
    spellings : A=keep B=inert C=keep D=keep E=keep F=drop

**The loser fixture could not have seen it.** This container was *already* on the loser list, so the row leaving reads as the fix working — a container that starts walking and simultaneously stops reading a *different* leaf produces the same fixture delta as a clean fix.

> **An aggregate ratchet cannot see a fix that breaks a neighbour inside the same row.** `TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate` caught it because it reports per-spelling verdicts, so "read here, inert there" surfaces as a disagreement instead of an aggregate.

## PR #9101 — config: the OPERATOR column must take the union over leaf ORDERS [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9100-operator-any-order`

Two corrections, both to claims **I** published in #9089.

## 1. The column tested one leaf order

lane-8388 established the real rule, and it is **leaf-level, not container-level**:

> A flat run is rejected iff the leaf it **starts at** declares a type/validator.

A validated leaf routes to the typed-leaf branch, whose modifier-child check refuses the trailing tokens; an untyped `args:1` leaf falls through to the container branch, which by #3332's compiler-faithful contract *deliberately* ignores leftover Keys. Verified independently through `compileTreeStrict`:

```
ike gateway   address A external-interface E       ACCEPTED
ike gateway   version v2-only address A            SCHEMA-REJECT
login class   allow-commands "x" idle-timeout 30   ACCEPTED
login class   idle-timeout 30 allow-commands "x"   SCHEMA-REJECT
```

**Same container, same leaves, order swapped, opposite verdicts.**

So `lenient-only` meant *"not reachable in the alphabetical order this generator happened to synthesize"* — and an operator types whichever order they like. Measured: **21 rows flip to OPERATOR** once every first-leaf position is tried, among them `chassis cluster redundancy-group` and `protocols bgp`.

The column now takes the union. OPERATOR is the dangerous verdict: a false `lenient-only` **hides** an operator-reachable silent drop, while a false OPERATOR only over-warns. Split moves **24/29 → 30/18**.

And the *explanation* I published — "the schema being behind the compiler is what makes a site operator-reachable" — is **one of three causes**, not the cause. The others are an arg-modelled instance container and this first-leaf rule.

## 2. An admitted blind spot, now stated in the file

lane-8388's login-class fix hoisted the children of every terminating leaf — wrong for a `multi` leaf whose children are **values** (#2419: `permissions { view; configure; }`). The container began walking and `permissions` went inert **in the same change**, and this fixture reported `53 → 52` with no other row moving.

> **An aggregate ratchet cannot see a fix that breaks a neighbour inside the same row.**

`TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate` caught it because it reports **per-spelling** verdicts, so "read here, inert there" surfaces as a disagreement instead of collapsing into one number. Same shape as #9077 deleting the #8807 predicate's container recovery while every aggregate stayed green.

A green delta here is **necessary and not sufficient**, and the file now names the instrument that is.

## PR #9103 — docs: a WRONG INSTRUMENT and a WRONG POPULATION need different remedies [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `docs/instrument-taxonomy`

Two ways an instrument can be wrong that **look identical in its output** and are not fixable by the same move.

## Wrong instrument — right subject, wrong layer

Four cost real numbers on one class in a single day:

| # | error | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `CompileConfig` where the commit gate is `CheckText` | a census reported the tolerant channel as the operator one |
| 2 | a schema walk where a later compiler gate also runs | 246 blind, 205 actually accepted |
| 3 | counting `groups`-rehosted paths as distinct | 205 collapsed to 102 |
| 4 | hierarchical text where the subject is a flat run | would have measured #8437's guard and reported it as the walk |

Every one is found by **a control at that layer**, and each was.

## Wrong population — the subject was never admitted

No control at any layer can reach it, because **a control interrogates what the filter passed.**

The instance, measured: the #8939 collector admits a leaf only when `children == nil && wildcard == nil && !multi`, discarding **63% of containers** before the census runs. A fix to `system login class` turned `permissions` from read to inert — and `permissions` is `multi`, so **the census could not have measured that leaf under any outcome.** The row left the loser list, which reads as the fix working.

> **An aggregate ratchet cannot see a fix that breaks a neighbour inside the same row. A ratchet cannot see anything its filter removed at all. The first needs the dimensions kept separate; the second needs a SECOND INSTRUMENT.**

`TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate` caught it — per-spelling verdicts rather than one number per subject, over a differently-filtered population.

## Four practices from the same day

- **Publish the denominator.** `SILENT: 0` over 9 and over 139 are the same string.
- **Print a per-prefix breakdown.** Nearly free; a `groups` double-count was caught this way by someone who had personally written the note warning about it.
- **An accurate load-bearing hedge is worse than a wrong claim** — it survives review, because the reviewer checks it and it holds. *"EMPTY, every container the census could reach"* was true, and the qualifier carried 130 containers.
- **Validate an instrument change against a known-good fix**, not against the population it measures — which is what moved.

Distinction drawn by lane-8388 from lane-8015's pre-filter finding and lane-8526's four-layer count. Docs only.

## PR #9104 — config: pin the one place the interface-name resolvers actually disagree [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8994-resolver-guard`

Refs #8994. Lands the measurement its closure condition asks for; does **not** attempt the fix (reason below).

## Measuring the resolvers instead of the note

`pkg/config/types.go` asks in a NOTE that three resolvers be "kept in sync". Measuring them narrows the claim a lot:

| resolver | finding |
|---|---|
| `resolveJunosIfName` | **not a third derivation** — literally `config.LinuxIfName(cfg.ResolveReth(ifName))`, an alias that cannot drift |
| tunnel units | **one value, not two** — `snapshotLinuxName` reads `cfg.TunnelNameMap()`, populated from `unit.Tunnel.Name`, which is what routing keys on. #8995 closed as refuted |
| dotted declared name + tunnel collision | **genuinely diverges** |

## The divergence

`ResolveKernelIfName` picks its arm by splitting the ref on `"."`, so a ref that *names a declared interface* containing a dot is parsed as a unit ref. With a tunnel unit publishing a `TunnelNameMap` entry under the same string, the dotted arm consumes the **tunnel's** device:

```
interfaces "gr-0/0/0.0"  +  gr-0/0/0 unit 0 carrying a tunnel
  ResolveKernelIfName("gr-0/0/0.0") -> gr-0-0-0     (the tunnel device)
  snapshotLinuxName(..., ifc, nil)  -> gr-0-0-0.0   (the interface itself)
```

Two subsystems name one configured interface differently, and **the config compiles**, so an operator can author it. A dotted name with *no* colliding tunnel entry (`ip-0/0/9.0`) agrees — the control showing the collision, not the dot, is the cause.

## A known-bad ratchet, mutation-tested BOTH ways

The divergence set is pinned to exactly that row. A ratchet that can only fail one way is half a guard, so both directions were mutated:

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| **apply the fix** (declared interface outranks the dotted parse) | set SHRINKS → cell reds |
| drift `snapshotLinuxName` further | set GROWS → cell reds |

So the one-line fix is **known to work**, and the cell is known not to be vacuous — which matters here, because the guard I wrote for #8995 passed, was found vacuous under mutation (both sides moved together), and was deleted rather than landed.

## Why the fix is not applied

`ResolveKernelIfName` has **15 non-test callers**, including `daemon_ha_vip.go` and `daemon_cluster_bind.go`. Changing its precedence touches VIP and cluster binding, so it is a staged change owing the cluster gate — not a drive-by inside a measurement PR.

## Method note kept in the cell

Only refs naming a **declared** interface are compared. Handing `snapshotLinuxName` a nil iface makes it return `LinuxIfName(ref)` on its first line, manufacturing a divergence the dataplane can never produce (it always iterates real `(ifName, iface, unit)` triples). An earlier draft reported two such rows as findings.

## PR #9106 — fix: walk the flat run in protocols isis / rip authentication (#8939) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-protocol-auth`

> **Stacked on #9100** (`fix/8939-login-class`). Base is that branch, not master — see "Why this is stacked" below; it is not a convenience.

    set protocols isis authentication-key secret1 authentication-type md5
      -> authentication-key="secret1"  authentication-type=""

## This is not a lost setting. It is a silent cryptographic downgrade

The proof is at the rendered FRR config, not in the typed struct:

    split   area-password md5 secret1     domain-password md5 secret1
    packed  area-password clear secret1   domain-password clear secret1

    rip split   ip rip authentication mode md5
    rip packed  ip rip authentication mode text

**The operator's key goes out in cleartext in every IS-IS PDU and RIP packet.** Authentication is not lost — it stays ON and downgrades, which is worse, because an operator verifying that adjacencies are authenticated sees exactly that.

**Alphabetical order picked the worse of the two outcomes.** `authentication-key` precedes `authentication-type`, so the run keeps the KEY and drops the TYPE. Reversed, authentication would have switched off — noisy, adjacencies would fail. This way it silently succeeds in plaintext.

## And the one diagnostic built for this does not fire

#8443 added `slog.Warn("rendering PLAINTEXT authentication")` for an **unrecognized** authentication-type. Measured:

    AuthTypeUnrecognized("") = false      <- #8443 stays silent
    AuthTypeIsMD5("")        = false      <- renderer emits plaintext

> Two predicates that disagree about the empty string, and the defect lived in the gap. An **absent** type is not *unrecognized* and not *md5*. #8443 reasoned about a WRONG value and never about a MISSING one — and a missing one is exactly what a flat run produces.

`TestProtocolAuthEmptyTypeIsNotUnrecognized8939` pins that, and skips itself if `AuthTypeUnrecognized("")` ever becomes true, so the note cannot outlive its premise.

## Why this is stacked

Cut against master, this change **reds the spelling-differential gate** at `protocols isis export` and `protocols rip neighbor` — both `multi:true`, both `A=keep B=inert C=keep D=keep E=keep F=drop`, the **identical signature** to the `permissions` break fixed in #9100. That is not this change: it is the old `expandFlatRun`, whose multi guard and sibling-gated hoist live in #9100's commit. Rebasing onto it turns the gate green, which is what **confirms** the diagnosis rather than assuming it.

> **Three casualties now, at three unrelated containers, every one a `multi` leaf.** One could have been a property of `permissions`; three cannot be. It is a property of the helper — and every casualty sits in the class the #8939 collector's `!multi` eligibility filter discards, so the loser fixture reported nothing at any of them. A wrong-**population** blind spot does not fail once; it fails silently every time the same helper meets the same excluded class.

Cherry-picking `flat_run_scan.go` into both PRs would put one edit on two branches and make merge order load-bearing, so it stays in #9100 alone.

## The wire assertion lives in `pkg/frr`, deliberately

*"authentication-type is empty"* and *"the key goes out in cleartext"* are not obviously the same statement, and the second is what sets the severity. A cell asserting only the first would let a future renderer change make the finding stale without reddening anything. It asserts the two spellings render **identically** — stronger than checking for `md5`, and not satisfiable by a renderer that stops emitting authentication altogether — behind a reference arm that fails if the split arm renders no auth lines, because otherwise the comparison would pass against silence.

## A second validator bypass, recorded and NOT closed here

`authentication-type bogus` is schema-rejected as its own statement and **accepted inside a flat run** — the same shape as #7971's refusal in `system login class`. The walk never descends, so a compiler fix cannot reach it. This change does move that case from *silently* plaintext to *warned* plaintext, because the compiler now reads `bogus` and `AuthTypeUnrecognized("bogus")` is true.

## Fixture: 47 → 41

Six rows, **all six `OPERATOR`**. `vacuous` 51 → 52, attributed rather than banked: the `rip [… | group]` 3-leaf row went vacuous because `group` is a container and the generator synthesizes a bare `group arg1` with no body, so nothing observable lands and vacuity control 2 correctly fires. That is the control working, not a row broken.

## PR #9107 — config: a fully elided stanza must be deletable (#8992) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8992-elided-delete`

```
system master-password pseudorandom-function hmac-sha2-256;
  -> ONE node, Keys = [system master-password pseudorandom-function hmac-sha2-256]

delete system master-password
  -> path not found: container "system" does not exist
```

`deletePath` descends by looking for a **container** whose Keys equal the path segment. In the elided spelling `system` is not a container — it is the first token of a leaf carrying the whole statement — so the descent finds nothing and reports the container absent **while `show configuration` renders it on screen.**

## Four of the five rows are controls, each ruling out a different wrong explanation

| row | rules out |
|---|---|
| fully braced — already worked | "delete is broken" |
| **child** elided — already worked | "elision breaks delete" |
| genuinely absent — *different* message | "this is the generic not-found path" |
| **elided beside a braced sibling** | **placed the fix** |

That last one matters: there the descent **succeeds** into the sibling and fails deeper, so the error changes to `no node matching "master-password"` and the elided node is never examined. A fix in the not-found branch would have missed it entirely.

## The bound matters more than the fix, because this is the delete path

A node's Keys can carry a packed **run**:

```
system master-password pseudorandom-function hmac-sha2-256 host-name fw1;
```

Whole-node removal would silently take `host-name` — the #3846 fail-wide. Splitting the run is `consumeNodeKeys` work #8932 records as unfinished. So a run is **refused**, with a message naming the situation and the workaround rather than the "container does not exist" misdirect (#9006's shape). Asserted: the run is left intact and `host-name` survives.

## My first fixture was not a config, and it read as the fix not working

I probed with `master-password ascii-text "x"` — but that container declares only `pseudorandom-function`. The schema walk stopped at an unknown token and returned false for the right reason about the wrong input, so I measured "#8992 is still live" **against an invalid fixture** and nearly concluded my own fix had failed.

Fourth instance this campaign of *a synthetic config that is not a config*; the other three were in the #8939 generator. It generalises past generators to hand-written probes.

Mutation: disabling the new branch reds the fully-elided row and leaves the packed-run row correctly refused. `go test -count=1 ./...` clean.

Closes #8992

## PR #9108 — fix: walk the flat run in policy-statement `then` (#8939) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-policy-then`

> **Stacked on #9106**, which is stacked on #9100. Base is `fix/8939-protocol-auth`.

Two census rows, and they are **not equally interesting** — a distinction the census cannot draw, because it synthesizes the alphabetically-first eligible leaves and cannot know whether the pair it built is a command anyone writes.

    policy-statement <p> then            accept | reject
    policy-statement <p> term <t> then   TEN children, including load-balance,
      local-preference, metric, next-hop, origin, as-path-prepend, community

## The policy-level row is a consistency fix, not a security one

`accept` and `reject` are **mutually exclusive**, so the pair the census built is the only one that exists there and is not a command an operator writes. It is still fixed — the spellings disagreed about which action won (split last-wins `reject`, packed `accept`), and a spelling difference on a contradictory input is still a spelling difference — but the severity is *"the spellings disagree"*, **not** *"a control was lost"*.

An earlier "a dropped `reject` is a routing-policy fail-open" reading of this row was mine and is **withdrawn**. It was made from shape rather than measurement.

## The term-level row is the one with an operator behind it

    set … term t1 then accept load-balance per-packet local-preference 200
      -> action="accept"  load-balance=""  local-preference=0

`then { local-preference 200; load-balance per-packet; accept; }` is ordinary Junos. And `accept` is alphabetically **first**, so it is the token that survives: **the route is still accepted and installed without the attributes the operator attached to it** — default local-preference, no ECMP. Not a fail-open; a route present with the *wrong attributes*, which `show configuration` renders exactly as authored. A traffic-path change, not an admission change.

## The placeholder defect is also in `vacuous` — found by attributing this fix's own delta

The 3-leaf term row moved from LOSER to `vacuous`. The generator hands every `args:1` leaf the placeholder `xpfval`; for a leaf whose compiler does `strconv.Atoi` that lands nowhere, so `split(3)` equals `split(2)`, vacuity control 2 fires, and the row is filed as *"the last leaf is not observable in the typed config at all"*.

Controlled — the real-value arm is what settles it:

    lldp   placeholder   third-leaf-observable = false
    lldp   REAL VALUE    third-leaf-observable = TRUE
    aging  placeholder   third-leaf-observable = false
    aging  REAL VALUE    third-leaf-observable = TRUE

The compiler reads those leaves perfectly well.

> **`unmeasured` is honest about being a non-result. `vacuous` reads as a VERDICT** — nothing here to fix, the leaf is unobservable — and it is a confident claim about the compiler produced by a defect in the harness.

And the consequence lands on exactly what #9078 → #9079 was built for: a `vacuous` row is **excluded from the loser list**, so a container whose third leaf is **typed** can never produce a three-leaf loser row, and the two-versus-three discrimination is silently unavailable there. A descent-shaped fix at one of those containers would clear the two-leaf row with nothing left to catch it.

Three confirmed instances reported to the generator's owner (`protocols lldp [transmit-interval]`, `security flow aging [low-watermark]`, and this term row); my schema-path walk was crude so treat 3 as a **lower bound**. Not fixed here — it is not this file's defect.

## Fixture: 41 → 38

Three rows, all `OPERATOR`. `vacuous` 52 → 53 is the mislabel above, attributed rather than banked.

## Validation

- **2/2 per-site mutations killed**, each by its OWN subtest.
- Three leaves where a third exists — the width a recursive descent fails.
- Reference arms assert the split build is complete, so no comparison can pass against a term carrying nothing.
- `pkg/config` + `pkg/frr` + `pkg/configstore` + `pkg/daemon` green; gofmt clean.

## PR #9112 — docs: hand over a MECHANISM not a count; gate a shared helper differently [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `docs/handoff-rules`

Two rules from one afternoon, both about **what a finding does to whoever receives it.**

## A count invites a fix scoped to the counted rows

A lane found three census rows mislabelled `vacuous` and — rather than filing *"3 rows are wrong"* — handed over the **mechanism** plus an explicit lower bound, because their schema walk was crude.

The real cause sat one level above where either of us was looking: the generator derived every value from the leaf's **name** while the schema already carried an example.

```
530 leaves · 57 typed · 42 handed a placeholder their validator rejects
```

**"3 rows are mislabelled" makes three special cases the plausible remedy and leaves 39 typed leaves still guessed.** The mechanism invited a fix where the mechanism lived: one lookup. Six rows recovered, not three.

This does **not** contradict *"publish the denominator"* or *"an aggregate count is not reviewable"* — those govern a **claim**. This governs a **handoff**: a number tells the recipient how big the problem is and simultaneously tells them where to stop looking.

## A change to a shared traversal helper needs a differently-filtered gate

An edit to `expandFlatRun` broke three leaves at three unrelated containers — **every one of them `multi`**, and `!multi` is the #8939 collector's own eligibility filter, so its fixture reported nothing at any of them. `TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate` caught all three because it sweeps a differently-filtered population and reports per-spelling verdicts.

The full-package gate enforces this **by accident** today. The reason it works is not that it is bigger, it is that it is **differently filtered** — so a future scoped gate would look like a reasonable optimisation and would silently remove the only instrument that can see this class. That is why it is written down rather than left to package scope.

> A wrong-population blind spot does not fail once. It fails silently every time the same helper meets the same excluded class.

Both rules are lane-8388's. Docs only.

## PR #9148 — config: the flat-run reachability rule is a CONJUNCTION, not the leaf half [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9113-conjunction`

I published, in #9101's comment and onward in routing decisions, that *"a flat run is rejected iff the leaf it **starts at** declares a type/validator."* **That is half.** Measured through `compileTreeStrict`:

```
container                    unknown-kw   run@untyped   run@typed
system login class           ACCEPT       ACCEPT        REJECT
security ike gateway         ACCEPT       ACCEPT        REJECT
security ipsec proposal      REJECT       REJECT        REJECT
security flow tcp-session    REJECT       --            REJECT
```

> **A flat run is ACCEPTED iff the container is OPEN-WORLD *and* the leaf it starts at is UNTYPED.** Either condition alone rejects it.

`security ipsec proposal` falsifies the leaf-only form: its starting leaf is untyped and the run is rejected anyway, because #4313 made that container closed-world.

## The column was never wrong

It calls `SchemaValidateWithDefinitions` — the real gate — so every row's verdict is **measured**, not derived from this rule. Only the explanation was wrong, which is the third time this file has carried a correct measurement under a wrong account of why.

## The failure mode is new, and it is recorded in engineering-style.md

lane-8526 held the container half. lane-8388 found the leaf half **while correcting them**, and named their own half as *the* discriminator rather than conjoining the two — in their words: *"I shipped a rule with the exact defect I had just diagnosed in theirs, in the same message."*

That is not ordinary over-generalisation. **Correcting someone puts you in a frame where their account is the thing being replaced**, and a newly-measured half arrives feeling like the whole — you have just demonstrated their claim was incomplete, which is the worst state in which to test your own for the same property.

The rule landed: ask explicitly whether what you measured is a **replacement** or a **conjunct**. A replacement needs the old account to be *false*, not merely partial.

## Routing consequence

**lane-8526's 102 stands and its title is right** — it measures the open-world half directly. It is a *necessary* condition for flat-run reachability, not the reachable population; the reachable set is a strict subset gated per-leaf.

Comment and docs only. `go test -count=1 ./...` clean.

Refs #9101, #9091, #4313.

## PR #9149 — routing: decide the WireGuard question Clear was deferring, and pin it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8996-wg-clear-decision`

Closes #8996

## The question

`clearLocked` carried an open question — *"whether ClearTunnels should also flush WG addresses is deferred to #1434 (full teardown grammar)"* — behind a tracker that is **closed**. It read as a design choice nobody had made, which is why I filed #8996 as the one of the four that was a **decision rather than a measurement**.

**That triage was wrong.** The answer is derivable from the code beside it.

## The decision: NO, and why

The WG link is kept by #1432 S2a precisely because tearing one flaps the device and destroys the live peer/session and the FRR routes over it. **Flushing the addresses destroys the connected route and the address that live session is using** — the same harm S2a exists to prevent, one level down — while leaving the device up to imply it still works.

A link that is up but stripped of its address is worse than either flushing both or keeping both: it looks configured and carries nothing.

Address hygiene on config **removal** is already handled by a mechanism that can tell removal from teardown: Apply's #1919 WG-removal diff prunes a WG name that *disappeared from config* while keeping its link. `Clear` is not a removal and must not borrow that behaviour.

## What dropping the map costs, recorded rather than rediscovered

A WG tunnel removed from config **across** a Clear boundary is not in `oldWG` at the next Apply, so the #1919 prune cannot see it. That is the **same** restart-adoption limitation this manager already documents ("a WG tunnel removed while the daemon was DOWN is not in `wgConfigured` on the next start") reached by a second route — not a new gap. The manager prunes only what it tracked applying.

## Pinned, not just written down

`TestClearTunnelsKeepsWireguardAddresses8996` asserts `Clear` keeps the link **and** its addresses, so the decision is falsifiable instead of being prose that the next reader can quietly reverse.

**Mutation-tested:** teaching `clearLocked` to `AddrDel` the tracked WG names reds it with `flushed the WG address` — it fails for the reason it names rather than incidentally. (The first mutant attempt did not compile, against the wrong `pruneAppliedAddrsLocked` signature; a mutant that does not build is not a mutant that survived, so it was rewritten before being scored.)

## Scope

**No production behaviour changes** — a comment and a test. The `make test-failover` gate is not triggered because nothing executable in the tunnel/teardown path moved. `go test ./pkg/routing/ ./pkg/refactoraudit/` green.

## PR #9180 — fix: walk the flat run in router-advertisement interface (#8939) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-ra-interface`

    set protocols router-advertisement interface ge-0/0/0 \
        managed-configuration default-lifetime 0
      -> ManagedConfig=true  DefaultLifetime=0  DefaultLifetimeSet=FALSE

## This re-creates #4119 by a different route

`DefaultLifetimeSet` is the entire point of that issue, and `pkg/ra/sender.go` keys on it:

```go
lifetime := defaultRouterLifetime          // 1800
if s.cfg.DefaultLifetimeSet { lifetime = s.cfg.DefaultLifetime }
```

So an **explicit** `default-lifetime 0` — RFC 4861 §6.2.1's *"this router is NOT a default router"* — reaches the wire as **1800**. #4119's own comment says what that costs:

> xpf could never advertise `not a default router' and **hijacked host default-route selection on multi-router LANs**.

**#4119 removed a `lifetime <= 0` coercion in the sender. This reaches the identical wire outcome by never setting the flag at all.** A fixed defect is not fixed against a second route into the same state.

Measured end to end through `buildRA`: packed marshals `RouterLifetime 1800`, split marshals `0`.

The wire assertion lives in **`pkg/ra`**, beside #4119's own cells — the consequence is observable there and not in the compiler — with a reference arm that fails if the *split* spelling stops reaching the wire as 0, so a `buildRA` regression cannot make both arms wrong and let the comparison pass.

## Operator-reachable only in the ordering an operator would type

    default-lifetime 600 link-mtu 1400 managed-configuration  SCHEMA-REJECT
    link-mtu 1400 default-lifetime 600 managed-configuration  SCHEMA-REJECT
    managed-configuration default-lifetime 600 link-mtu 1400  ACCEPTED

Flag-first admits because `managed-configuration` is `args:0` and untyped and the container is open-world — the #9148 conjunction. **And flag-first is the natural way to type it.**

A first probe that tested only the alphabetical ordering said `SCHEMA-REJECT` and would have filed a false correction against the census's `OPERATOR` tag. The census takes the **union over first-leaf orderings** and was right; my narrower instrument was not.

The fixture shows the conjunction incidentally:

## PR #9182 — fix: walk the flat run in protocols bgp (#8939) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8939-bgp`

> The remedy for issue #9184, which carries the severity write-up. Split out of the #8939 series because the failure is categorically different: not a lost field, an entire routing protocol absent.

    set protocols bgp graceful-restart cluster-id 1.1.1.1 local-as 65001
      -> GracefulRestart=true  ClusterID=""  LocalAS=0

## A packed run does not degrade BGP. It deletes it.

`pkg/frr` gates the **entire stanza** on the AS number:

```go
if bgp != nil && bgp.LocalAS > 0 { fmt.Fprintf(&b, "router bgp %d…") … }
```

Rendered, both spellings:

    split    router bgp 65001 / bgp cluster-id 1.1.1.1 / bgp graceful-restart
    packed   <NO BGP CONFIG RENDERED AT ALL>

**The operator's entire BGP configuration commits clean and reaches FRR as nothing** — no sessions, no routes, no protocol — while `show configuration` renders exactly what they typed.

> A dropped leaf that happens to be a **guard for everything downstream of it** does not lose a setting; it removes the feature.

Found by **rendering**, not by reading the struct: the typed config looked like an ordinary two-leaf loss. The wire cell asserts the two spellings render **identically** — stronger than grepping for `router bgp`, and not satisfiable by a renderer that stops emitting BGP altogether — behind a reference arm that fails if the *split* arm renders nothing.

## Operator-reachable only in the flag-first ordering

    cluster-id 1.1.1.1 graceful-restart local-as 65001  SCHEMA-REJECT
    local-as 65001 cluster-id 1.1.1.1 graceful-restart  SCHEMA-REJECT
    graceful-restart cluster-id 1.1.1.1 local-as 65001  ACCEPTED

`graceful-restart` is `args:0` and untyped and the container is open-world — the #9148 conjunction. **Second container running (after #9180) where the only admitted ordering is the natural one**, which is why the census's union over first-leaf positions is the instrument that matters and a single-ordering probe is not.

## The census cannot see this row's severity — a fourth placeholder sub-cause

    cluster-id  validator=true valueType=10 valueExamples=[10.0.0.1 1]   -> fine
    local-as    validator=true valueType=6  valueExamples=[]             -> "xpfval"

`local-as` is **typed with an empty `valueExamples`** (its `placeholder` is `"<as-number>"`, a help string, not a value), so it still falls back to `xpfval`, fails the integer validator, lands nowhere — and the 3-leaf row is filed **`vacuous`**, the label that reads *"nothing to fix here"*, **on the leaf whose loss deletes the whole configuration.**

Reported to the generator's owner with a suggested **type-directed fallback** rather than a per-leaf `valueExamples` entry, and deliberately without a sweep count: an entry for `local-as` fixes one row, a type-directed default fixes the class, and a number would scope the fix to the number. ## PR #9185 — nftables: stop emitting a wrapped interval end for a port range at 65535 [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9004-expandaddrset-guard`

`portEnd` returned a **wrapped 0x0000** for a range reaching the top of the key
space, and the caller emitted it as an interval-end element. That is not an end
marker at the top — it is an end marker at the **bottom**, and the kernel stores
it as such.

This is the port twin of #8597, which measured the identical encoding for
addresses and fixed it by emitting **no** end element for a top-of-range prefix.
`portEnd` becomes `portNext(hi) ([]byte, bool)`, matching `prefixNext`'s shape
and contract so a caller cannot forget to check.

### Measured on the emitted ruleset, not the helper

A unit assertion over `portNext` would pass against a caller that ignored its
second return value, and the defect lives in what reaches the kernel:

```
ports 80/80 + 1024-65535   ->  [0050 0051!end 0400 0000!end]
after                      ->  [0050 0051!end 0400]
```

### A reachability detail the fixture depends on

A **single** port range compiles to an `expr.Range`, not a set, and emits no
elements at all — the set path is taken only with two or more entries. The first
version of this measurement used one range, returned an empty list, and **would
have read as "no defect"**. The cells therefore carry a second port and a
liveness assert that fails on an empty dump, so a fixture that stops reaching the
set path says so rather than passing.

### Validation

Restoring the wrapped end reds the golden cell with the bottom-of-key-space
message. A non-vacuity cell asserts an **ordinary** range still gets its end, so
the fix cannot pass by suppressing every end — which would open the interval to
the top and match far more than configured. Full `pkg/nftables` green.

**#9004 is handled separately**: measured unreachable and recommended for
closure on the issue, not fixed here.

## PR #9186 — config: a ref naming a declared interface is that interface, dot or not [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8994-dotted-precedence`

Closes #8994

## The defect

`ResolveKernelIfName` picked its arm by splitting the ref on `"."`, so a ref that **names a declared interface** containing a dot was re-read as a unit ref. With a tunnel unit publishing a `TunnelNameMap` entry under that same string, the dotted arm returned the **tunnel's** device:

```
interfaces "gr-0/0/0.0"  +  gr-0/0/0 unit 0 carrying a tunnel
  ResolveKernelIfName("gr-0/0/0.0") -> gr-0-0-0     (the tunnel device)
  snapshotLinuxName(..., ifc, nil)  -> gr-0-0-0.0   (the interface itself)
```

Two subsystems named one configured interface differently, and **the config compiles**, so it is operator-reachable. A dotted name with *no* colliding tunnel entry agrees — the control showing the collision, not the dot, is the cause.

## The fix

A precedence arm placed **first**: an explicit declaration outranks a parse — the same rule the secure-tunnel arm already applies when an authored `bind-interface` outranks the tunnel-name map.

## Why this is safe despite 15 callers

#8994 deferred this fix on that count, **and the count was the wrong measure.**

> A caller total is a property of the **call graph**. Risk is a property of the **input distribution through the changed branch**.

A ref with no dot already took the bare arm. A genuine unit ref (`ge-0/0/0.0` where only `ge-0/0/0` is declared) is not a key in `Interfaces`. **Only a config that declares a dotted interface name reaches the new arm at all** — which is the defect case itself. Fifteen callers all supplying inputs that take the unchanged arm is fifteen callers of zero exposure.

## The guard moved rather than loosened

`TestResolverAgreement8994` landed earlier as a **known-bad ratchet** pinning the divergence to that one row, mutation-tested in both directions. The mutant that *applied* this fix is what proved it worked before it was written for real: it shrank the set to empty and reddened the ratchet **exactly as designed**.

So the expectation is moved to empty, not relaxed — and the cell is re-confirmed non-vacuous in its new form: reverting this arm reds it with `disagree on 1 declared`.

> A ratchet that goes green because its population emptied is indistinguishable from one that went green because it stopped looking — unless you run that second step.

The corpus deliberately **keeps** the collision case, since removing it would leave a green cell measuring nothing.

## Docs

The `types.go` NOTE asked readers to keep three resolvers in sync and named #8994 as tracking the residual. The obligation is now **enforced rather than requested** — and two of the three turned out not to be independent derivations at all (`resolveJunosIfName` is literally `LinuxIfName(ResolveReth(x))`; a tunnel unit's name comes from `TunnelNameMap` on both sides).

## Validation

`go test` green on config, dataplane/…, daemon, routing, api, cli, refactoraudit — **10 packages**.

**`make test-failover`**: 21 passed / 0 failed, iperf3 **23.0 Gbps** across a manual failover of all three redundancy groups, under a lock cell against a deploy of this working tree (build tag `…-dirty` confirms it). Required because this function feeds `daemon_ha_vip.go` and `daemon_cluster_bind.go`.

## PR #9187 — Gate ipsec proposal lifetime-seconds on the tolerant path [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9008-ipsec-lifetime-tolerant-path`

Part of #9008

## The defect, with its channel named

Both `security ike proposal <n> lifetime-seconds` and its Phase-2 sibling
`security ipsec proposal <n> lifetime-seconds` carry
`validator: ValidateIntegerMin(1)` in `setSchema`. But `SchemaValidate` is
invoked **only** from `compileTreeStrict`, so that floor was enforced on the
`Store.Commit -> compileTree -> compileTreeStrict` channel and nowhere else.
`compileTreeLenient` — which backs `Store.Load` (daemon boot, reading back the
persisted active config) and the HA `SyncApply` path — downgrades schema
findings to `slog.Warn`, and the compiler then dropped the offending token with
no diagnostic at all.

Measured at master `b8b0636a1` before the fix, both channels named:

| channel | `lifetime-seconds -5` |
|---|---|
| `SchemaValidate` (Store.Commit runs it first) | **REJECT** — "integer must be at least 1" |
| `CompileConfigLenient` (Store.Load, HA SyncApply) | **ACCEPTED, 0 warnings**, compiled `lifetime=-5` |

A negative was worse than dropped: `strconv.Atoi("-5")` succeeds, so it was
**stored** as `LifetimeSeconds` and carried on into the swanctl renderer.

## The fix

The compiled int cannot express either failure mode — a non-numeric token
leaves the field at `0`, indistinguishable from "not configured" — so both
compiler loops now **record** the raw token in `LifetimeSecondsInvalidSpec`,
and `validateIPsecProposalLifetimesStrict` reads it. The recorded floor mirrors
the schema's `ValidateIntegerMin(1)` so the two channels *agree* rather than
merely both erroring.

Wired through `opts.lenientIPsecProposalLifetime`: hard reject on commit,
`cfg.Warnings` on the tolerant path. That asymmetry is the #1960
fail-closed-on-load doctrine — `Store.Load` may gain a new WARNING but never a
new REJECTION, or a downgraded binary strands the box on an active config it
cannot read. The only non-test caller of the strict `config.CompileConfig` is
`compileTreeStrict` itself, which schema-rejects first, so **no tolerant path
gains a rejection** from this change.

## Validation

The guard drives all three channels (`SchemaValidate`, `CompileConfig`,
`CompileConfigLenient`) × both phases × `{3600, -5, 0, abc}`, with `3600` as an
accepted-control so the gate cannot pass by rejecting everything.

mutant that *reaches* it — dropping the recording (M1) and removing the gate
wiring (M2) both die on the strict-compiler arm and so never exercise the

## PR #9188 — config/daemon: read the node-local posture in every spelling (#8997) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/8997-elided-node-local`

Closes #8997

`chassis cluster strict-session-auth` is node-local (#7441): config-sync must
neither clear it nor set it, because an admitted-but-unauthenticated
session-sync stream reaches `handleConfigPayload` and a STANDBY accepts a push.

`chassisClusterFlagSet` walked the raw tree with `FindChild`, which matches only
a node whose Keys are exactly one segment:

```
chassis { cluster { strict-session-auth; } }   found
chassis { cluster strict-session-auth; }       MISSED
chassis cluster strict-session-auth;           MISSED
```

**A miss here is not a false negative, it is an AGREEMENT.** Misreading the local
node as not having the flag makes both sides `false`, the sides agree, the hook
`continue`s — so the branch that logs and the branch that fails closed are both
downstream of a difference that is never detected. The correct fail-closed
handling was unreachable in exactly the case it guards.

Both of #7441's directions were affected, which matters because its own rationale
says preserving one direction leaves the other as a lever: a peer could also SET
the posture on a node that had not chosen it.

## Two bounds in #8992 that nobody could see

Found by the *strip* direction of this fix failing — the hook now detects the
difference (it never did before) and then `DeletePath` could not act on it.

1. `findElidedNodeForPath` required `len(Keys) > len(path)`. #8992 was written
   against a VALUED leaf, where the value makes Keys longer, so the guard read as
   a description of the elided shape rather than a restriction to valued leaves.
   **A bare flag elides to a node whose Keys are exactly the path**, so every
   valueless leaf was excluded.
2. The check ran only at `i == 0`. An elided node can sit at any depth.

## Extending it red four existing cells, and they were right

A `multi` leaf absorbs a bracketed value list onto its Keys (#2419), which is
**indistinguishable from a packed statement run by key count and has the opposite
correct answer**:

| node | shape | correct answer |
|---|---|---|
| `protocol tcp udp icmp` | one multi leaf, trailing tokens are VALUES | member delete is legal — #3846/#3872 own it |
| `cluster strict-session-auth foo` | two statements packed by the flat-set chain | must be REFUSED (#3846 fail-wide) |

`elidedPathIsMultiLeafValues` makes that distinction. The top level has no multi
leaf, which is why #8992 never met the ambiguity and nothing recorded it existed.

## PR #9190 — daemon: refresh the FIB when a route subscription is re-established [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9010-route-catchup-marker`

Closes #9010

A gap between route subscriptions was invisible to the daemon. The subscription
is opened with `ListExisting:false`, so a **new** subscription replays nothing —
the outer loop's resubscribe closed the *socket* gap without closing the *data*
gap. Every route that changed while there was no subscription stayed lost, and
the helper FIB remained stale until the next route event that happened to
arrive.

### The reader was established before the fix

Per the dispatch — a marker set at the wrong moment is only a defect if
something reads it to decide. `loop.Mark()` sets `dirtySince`/`dirtyGen`, and the
coalescer's run loop reads them to decide whether to **actuate**. #8915 measured
**0 actuations across 50 sweeps with no mark, 1 after a single mark**, and the
periodic-floor alternative that would otherwise recover this was considered and
**deliberately declined** there. So a missing mark is a missing FIB refresh.

### Why #8915 does not already cover it

That fix marks from the `ErrorCallback`, which exists only for a fault during a
**live** subscription. A subscribe that **fails** never installs a callback — the
2-second retry path marks nothing — and a subscription that simply ends returns
before any error is raised.

### The route listener was the outlier

`docs/bugs.md` records the **link-state** listener doing exactly this since
#3950: *"each fresh subscription runs `resyncLinkState` right after it goes live
and emits catch-up traps for any transition missed during the overflow."* This
mirrors an established, documented pattern in the same daemon rather than
inventing one, and the doc now carries the route entry beside it.

Marking on the **first** subscription too is deliberate: a refresh is idempotent
and the coalescer debounces, so the cost is one actuation at startup, and
special-casing "not the first" would make recovery depend on counting rather than
on the invariant.

### Validation

The cell drives the function **production calls** (`routeListenerCatchUp`, the
seam — exactly as the #8915 cell drives `routeListenerErrorCallback`) and asserts
the **actuation**, not the counter: removing the mark while *keeping* the counter
reds it, because the count is not the property. A non-vacuity sweep runs first so
the assertion cannot pass against a loop that actuates freely, and a nil-loop cell
keeps a refresh helper from crashing the daemon it exists to help.

`pkg/daemon` green. Docs updated in the same change (`docs/bugs.md`).

## PR #9191 — Reject one BGP neighbor address in two groups [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9007-bgp-duplicate-neighbor`

Part of #9007

## Reproduced at the current head, not inherited

The issue was probed at `9bb0e8f11`, and #9182 (the #8939 BGP flat-run series) landed on `compiler_protocols.go` in between — so it was re-measured at `2f80dc085`. It still reproduces exactly:

| channel | result |
|---|---|
| `configstore.CheckText` (the real commit gate) | **ACCEPTED, 0 warnings** |
| `generateProtocols` | two `remote-as`, two `timers`, two **divergent `password`** lines, two `peer 192.0.2.1` BFD blocks |

Which line FRR honours is decided by render order, while `show` keeps displaying both groups as authored. The other divergences are misconfigurations an operator can eventually observe; the authentication key is not.

## The fix

`validateBGPDuplicateNeighborStrict`, following the house pattern of the peer-as-0 gate (#2963): hard reject on commit/commit-check (Junos rejects this too), downgraded to a `cfg.Warnings` entry on the tolerant load and peer-sync paths via `opts.lenientBGPDuplicateNeighbor` — the #1960 fail-closed-on-load doctrine, where `Store.Load` may gain a WARNING but never a REJECTION.

The check partitions by **BGP instance**: the same address in two routing instances is legitimate, since separate VRFs peering with one address is ordinary.

## The first version was wrong, and an existing cell caught it

It keyed on the address alone and paired the gate with a first-wins dedup at the renderer's `validNeighbors` construction. `TestSlotEscapeTable` went red reporting a collision **"(G and G)"** — the same group twice.

The compiler emits one `*BGPNeighbor` **per AST node**, and one authored neighbor can occupy several:

```
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2 import PS
```

— ordinary flat-set authoring, and the shape `pkg/config`'s own slot-escape fixtures use — yields **two entries for one peer**, both in group G, one carrying the import policy. Measured against the pristine renderer that shape emits a redundant but *correct* stanza:

```
neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001
neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001      <- redundant, FRR accepts it
neighbor 10.0.2.2 activate             <- only the SECOND entry carries these
neighbor 10.0.2.2 route-map ... in
```

The first-wins dedup dropped that second entry and **silently deleted the route-map**. So the render change was reverted in full and the gate narrowed to *different* groups. The renderer is deliberately left alone: the commit gate is the defense, and the tolerant path warns.

The per-AST-node duplication is a separate, broader defect (a plain two-line authoring sequence renders a redundant `remote-as`) and is filed on its own rather than folded in here.

Five **production** mutants, all killed, one per assertion arm:

| # | mutation | arm it reds |
|---|---|---|
| M9 | same-group repeats no longer exempt | same-group control **+ both slot-escape fixtures** — proves the narrowing is load-bearing |

## PR #9193 — Refuse symlinked factory-reset erase targets [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9013-zeroize-symlink-targets`

Closes #9013

## Measured, not reasoned

`os.Remove` and `os.RemoveAll` act on the **link** when a path's final component is a symlink — they unlink it, return `nil`, and the real bytes stay on the target volume. Measured at `f37079b8e` as surviving bytes:

| shape | reported | surviving |
|---|---|---|
| archive dir symlink | `nil` | 83 bytes, IKE PSK **intact** |
| `.configdb` symlink | `nil` | `master.key` **destroyed**, `active.json` 97 bytes, PSK **intact** |

Encryption is conditional on `system master-password` (`maybeEncryptTreeJSON` returns plaintext when unset — the default), so on an ordinary box that surviving body is the full cleartext config and the key-first cryptographic-erasure guarantee buys nothing.

## Censusing the remedy found seven shapes, not two

Every erase target leaks identically. Beyond the two reported: the live config, the rescue config, the audit journal, the numbered rollback slots, the **inverse** `master.key`-as-symlink (the real key survives while the ciphertext is erased — against a backup of the DB, a surviving key is the whole secret), and — only on the production path — **`tls/key.pem`, the device HTTPS private key**, which the issue never mentions. A control with no symlink anywhere confirms the probe discriminates.

## The reachability check changed the fix

`configstore.FactoryResetConfigDir` — where the issue points — has **no non-test caller**. `pkg/grpcapi`'s `zeroizeConfigDir` is a near-identical twin and is what production runs, via `PerformZeroizeWipe` (the gRPC path, and the console through the `zeroizeFullWipe` seam). **A guard written only against the configstore copy would have been an inert security fix.** The predicate is therefore exported as `configstore.SymlinkTarget` and shared by both, so it cannot land on one of the pair again.

## Why refuse rather than resolve-and-erase

A link may point at a shared, remote or compliance volume that is not xpf's to destroy — so the reset fails **closed**, matching `ValidateFactoryResetRoot`'s stated doctrine, and hands the operator the exact paths **and their targets**. A skipped erase outranks a failed one (#7173 already states that an erasure which did not happen at all is strictly worse, since only a failure announces itself); the two are `errors.Join`ed so neither is swallowed. The `.configdb` check precedes every removal in that block because the key deletion resolves *through* the link — checking afterwards would still have destroyed the key first.

## Validation

Eight **production** mutants, all killed, one per assertion arm:

| # | mutation | arm it reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | predicate always false | refusal |
| M2 | `Stat` instead of `Lstat` | refusal |
| M3 | skips collected but never returned | refusal |
| M4 | predicate always **true** | **CONTROL, in both packages** — proves the guard didn't just break ordinary zeroize |
| M5 | skip recorded without its link target | operator detail |
| M6 | `master.key` checked *after* its removal | ordering |
| M7 | #7173 ownership skip returning the new type | distinct type |
| M8 | console returns `%v` instead of `%w` | CLI wrapping (`errors.As` must reach the type) |

M4 is the one that matters most: every other mutant would pass a guard that simply refused everything.

Gates, all green: `go test ./pkg/configstore/ ./pkg/grpcapi/ ./pkg/cli/ ./pkg/refactoraudit/` · `go vet` · `go build ./...`.

Docs: `pkg/configstore/README.md` carried the promise "`zeroize` must remove EVERY on-box generation of config secrets" — now qualified with the symlink refusal, both twins, and the reachability note.

## PR #9194 — Correct the multi-port WireGuard advisory: unsteered is not dead [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9016-wireguard-multiport-advisory-text`

Advances #9016 — the claim half only. Multi-port steering (#1434 Increment 2) is not implemented here, and the issue stays open for it.

## Reachability first, because it gates the severity

Measured at `e10d4c28f`: the schema **does** express two wireguard tunnels on distinct listen-ports, `configstore.CheckText` (the real commit gate) **accepts** the shape, and `WireGuardListenPorts()` returns **both** ports.

## The report's headline is overstated; the wording defect is real

The issue frames the second port as "the #8274 bypass" — inner plaintext forwarded with no zone adjudication. Measured across four topologies, that is **not differential**:

| topology | ports | #5618 adjudication advisory |
|---|---|---|
| single tunnel | `[51820]` | fires (unzoned heading) |
| two tunnels | `[51820 51821]` | fires (unzoned heading) |
| single tunnel, zoned | `[51820]` | fires (**acute** heading) |
| two tunnels, both zoned | `[51820 51821]` | fires (**acute** heading) |

No WireGuard tunnel's decapsulated plaintext is zone-adjudicated — one tunnel or two, zoned or unzoned — and the product already says so loudly for every tunnel. The steered tunnel is not policed either.

*A measurement error I made and caught, since it nearly became a finding:* my first probe grepped only for the `NOT ZONE-ADJUDICATED` heading and I read its absence on a zoned tunnel as "zoning suppresses the safety warning". There are **two** headings — a zoned tunnel gets the acute `ASSIGNED A ZONE THAT IS NOT ENFORCED` variant. The absence was an artifact of my predicate. An absence claim from a grep needs a positive control.

## What is actually wrong: one false claim in three places

All three said the unsteered tunnel is **dead** — no transport reaches it, no handshake ever completes:

- `pkg/config/compiler_validate_wireguard_multiport.go` — the commit warning, which reads as authoritative
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go` — *"that second rule is currently a no-op at the kernel"*
- `docs/wireguard-interop.md` — the paragraph **and** a verbatim copy of the warning

All false the same way. The host-inbound filter admits **every** configured listen-port (`config.WireGuardListenPorts` feeds `emitHostInboundWireGuardAcceptNetlink`, the production *netlink* installer, not just the nft text renderer), and the helper binds a socket per wireguard endpoint. The unsteered port receives transport and decapsulates — on the **kernel** path. "Unsteered" means *not on the fast path*, not *inert*.

Nothing in the tree bound any of these strings, which is how a false claim survived in a warning operators are meant to act on.

## Coupling, so the three cannot drift again

- `snapshotWgListenPort` cell pins that only the **first** port is steered — it reds if multi-port steering lands, sending whoever lands it to the advisory text.
- `emitHostInboundWireGuardAccept` cell pins that **every** configured port is admitted.

The corrected warning also states explicitly that steering is not adjudication — omitting that would imply the steered tunnel is policed, the same false reassurance in the other direction.

## Validation

Five **production** mutants, all killed, one per arm:

| # | mutation | arm it reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | advisory reverts to the "dead" wording | retracted-claim |
| M2 | advisory drops the not-adjudication sentence | false-reassurance-in-reverse |
| M3 | advisory fires for a single port | control |
| M4 | steering picks the LAST port | mechanism the wording depends on |

Branch: `fix/9017-firewall-family`

Closes #9017

```

set firewall family any filter BLOCK term T1 then discard
```

committed clean through `configstore.CheckText`, rendered in `show`, and minted
**zero filters**. A deny-everything-not-matched filter that enforced nothing —
no counter, no warning, and no difference in output between "installed" and
"does not exist". The hierarchical spelling worked, which kept it invisible.

## Two defects shared one symptom

1. **`any` was not declared**, so the flat-set path never delivered the token to
   `compiler_firewall.go`'s existing `case "any": dests = {Inet, Inet6}`.
2. **Any undeclared token collapsed identically** — `family inett` also committed
   clean and minted zero filters. That is the fail-open half, and a fix aimed
   only at `any` leaves it live.

| spelling | strict compile | FiltersInet | FiltersInet6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `family inet` | ACCEPT | 1 | 0 |
| `family inet6` | ACCEPT | 0 | 1 |
| `family any` | ACCEPT | 1 | 1 |
| `family inett` | **REJECT**, naming the token (WARN on the tolerant path) | 0 | 0 |

## Two designs tried and backed out — both look obviously right

**`closedWorld: true` on the compound key INHERITS.** Arming it at `family` closed
the entire filter grammar beneath it and began rejecting `from source-prefix-list
trusted` — valid config that ships in the CLI tests, which is how it was caught.
Replaced by `validateFirewallFilterFamilyTokensAST`, a prewalk gate beside the
#3884 collision gate with the same strict-rejects / lenient-warns split (#1960).
Its permitted set is read from the schema, so a fourth family needs no second list.

**`any` sharing `inet`'s children map** is wrong for a reason specific to this
tree: a dozen schema censuses walk it and several **dedup by node identity**, so
one node at two paths is attributed to whichever is reached first and the other
silently stops being covered — observed as #8768 reporting
`firewall/family/inet/filter/term/then` "no longer opts in" while nothing about
inet had changed. Now a deep copy: trades invisibility for drift, and drift is
the failure a test can see.

## Declaring the leaf was necessary and NOT sufficient

The compact spelling `family any filter F { … }` stayed packed until `any filter`
joined the compact-normalize scope, **reproducing the exact zero-filter outcome in
a spelling the original probe did not use**. Caught by the #2419 census flagging a
new compact-blind site, not by review.
