## PR #9196 — config: the duplicate-block skip set gave a false reason for three entries [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9181-false-skip-reason`

Refs #9181, #8436.

## The false justification

`dupConservationSkipped8436` justified three skips with one sentence:

> the merged form compiles identically to a block carrying only the first leaf, so the second leaf **is invisible to the typed config and the site cannot show a loss either way**.

The first clause is a true observation about **the fixture**. The second is a claim about **the site** — and it is false for all three entries it covers.

## Measured — and each needs a DIFFERENT thing

| entry | what the fixture could not supply | result |
|---|---|---|
| `protocols bgp group` | a **sibling** (`neighbor`) *plus that sibling's own prerequisite* (`peer-as`, required by the compiler, absent from the schema) | **DIFFERS** |
| `class-of-service interfaces … unit` | the referenced object **DEFINED** — a `scheduler-map` reference to an undefined map is rejected outright, so the fixture never compiled | **DIFFERS** |
| `protocols router-advertisement … prefix` | a **third leaf** — its first two are booleans that collapse identically, so two leaves cannot separate the spellings at all | **DIFFERS** |

That is why one shared sentence covered three entries and was wrong about every one: their causes are unrelated, and the sentence described only the symptom they had in common.

## What changes, and what does not

The entries **stay skipped** — the fixture still cannot express those prerequisites. What changes is the stated reason: from a false claim about the site to a true one about the instrument.

That distinction is #9181's whole subject. *"Not measured"* and *"nothing to measure"* had the same spelling here, and the wrong reading had hardened into a justification a reader would not re-check. Two independent censuses recorded the same site as structurally unobservable, for the same wrong reason.

The BGP row was falsified in one line on #9181 by team-lead. The shared sentence covers three entries, so **the other two were tested rather than assumed to behave the same way** — and both turned out false for reasons the BGP case would not have predicted. Fixing only the row that was reported would have left two false justifications behind, each looking freshly confirmed by the edit next to it.

## PR #9197 — dataplane: fail closed on an unrepresentable flexible-match-range [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9020-flexible-match-range`

Closes #9020

An unrepresentable `flexible-match-range` shipped to the userspace filter as a
**defaulted live match**. The compiler records the offending tokens in
`UnknownFlexMatch` and assigns `term.FlexMatch` anyway, so the term reached the
dataplane enforcing something the operator never wrote — a `discard` term then
dropped traffic it should not and admitted the traffic it was written to drop.

### Which layer — measured before choosing

The **strict commit gate already rejects** every unrepresentable form, so no new
commit-time gate is needed. The defect is reachable only on the tolerant load /
peer-sync path (#1960) — the path that *cannot* reject, because it exists to boot
a config already on disk. Its only correct option is to fail **closed**.

### The nftables sibling was already right

`daemon_nft.go:2248` and `daemon_nft_netlink.go:231` both check
`FlexMatchRangeNames > 1 || len(UnknownFlexMatch) > 0`. The userspace builder
checked only the first — so one plane poisoned the term and the other shipped it
live. This adds the missing condition to the **existing** fail-closed channel
rather than inventing a second mechanism.

### Reproduced against a live control

A representable range ships `offset:4 value:4660`. The three unrepresentable
forms shipped:

```
byte-offset 999       -> offset:0   enforced at offset 0, not 999
match-value 0xZZZZ    -> value:0    enforced "equals zero"
match-start payload   -> offset:4   evaluated at the layer-3 base
```

### Sentinel renamed

`unrepresentable-multi-range` → `unrepresentable`. It reaches `show firewall …
effective` and now covers two causes; telling an operator with **one** range that
their term names several is the misdirecting-diagnostic shape this tree keeps
hitting. No wire contract on the string — Rust matches `layer-3`/`layer-4` and
lowers everything else to `Unsupported` — and nothing pinned it.

### Fixture note

Recorded because it cost four attempts and **every wrong one looked like "no
defect"**: the compiler expects a nested `range <name>` level. Without it nothing
compiles and each row reads `flexMatch=nil`. The cells lead with a liveness
control, and each defect row asserts the compiler actually recorded the token
before checking the snapshot.

## PR #9198 — configstore: raise degraded health on a failed commit-confirmed arm (#9014) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9014-confirm-arm-degraded`

Closes #9014

`commit confirmed` arms its rollback by writing `confirm.json`. When that write
failed, `writeConfirmState` logged one `slog.Warn` and returned — no flag, no
journal, no retry — and `CommitConfirmed` still returned `(compiled, nil)`. A
crash or reboot inside the window then found no record, the unconfirmed
configuration stood permanently, and /health returned 200 throughout.

## The asymmetry is the evidence

The invariant it broke is written down in the same package, in #8566's own
rationale: *"Every OTHER way the store ends a boot unsafe raises degraded
health; this one did not, so nothing alerted on it."*

| failure | flag | journal | retry | health |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| confirm **read** at boot | `confirmRecoveryReadFailed` (#8566) | yes | — | degraded |
| confirm **removal** | `confirmRemoveDegraded` (#5835) | yes | yes | degraded |
| confirm **arm** (before) | **none** | **none** | **none** | **200 OK** |

## The commit is deliberately NOT failed

Matches both neighbours and the #1960 no-brick posture: the configuration is
applied and correct, only its crash-recovery record is missing. Refusing the
commit would turn a durability problem into an availability one.

## The retry is generation-pinned — the half that is easy to get wrong

If the window is confirmed, superseded or rolled back while the write is still
owed, re-driving it would write a crash-recovery record for a window that **no
longer exists** — a restart would then resurrect a rollback the operator already
resolved. That is the exact mirror of #7675 on the removal side.

Removing the guard reproduces the resurrection **deterministically**, which is
how the cell was written:

```
--- FAIL: TestArmWriteDebtIsNotResurrectedAfterResolution9014
    the retry RESURRECTED a crash-recovery record for a window that was already
    confirmed — a restart would now revert the operator's confirmed configuration
```

A successful arm (first try or a later re-arm) discharges outstanding debt,
because the record on disk is then current.

## Testability was part of the defect

`DB.WriteConfirm` now goes through the `rbWriteFileDurable` seam rather than
calling `fsatomic` directly. **Until this change there was no way to fail the arm
write in a test at all** — which is part of why this was the leg with no guard:

## PR #9200 — Roam the peer endpoint on the worker's authenticated decap arms [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9018-wg-worker-roam-authenticated-arms`

Closes #9018

## The defect

`try_decap` returns two errors carrying the **proven** peer public key — `DecapError::Keepalive` (#7230) and `DecapError::MalformedInner` (#7686), both given a `[u8; 32]` payload precisely so the identity would stop dying with the error. The AF_XDP worker collapsed every arm with `.ok()?` and threw both away.

The keepalive case is the one that matters: it's a type-4 transport record, so `wg_worker_claims_record` claims it for the worker and the shim declines `cpumap_or_pass`. The socket path in `wg_control/dispatch.rs` — which *does* map both arms to `Authenticated(pk)` — never sees it. So a keepalive from a NAT-rebound or roaming endpoint, the exact case WireGuard keepalives exist for, moved nothing.

Both arms now observe the endpoint through the same `note_worker_observed_endpoint` the success arm uses, then decline the frame exactly as before. Cold path, no fast-path cost, and the "no TUN write" contract is unchanged.

## Severity — bounded, and measured rather than asserted

The identity is not recoverable at that site: `.ok()?` returned `None` and the frame continued as opaque outer UDP, so nothing downstream saw the pubkey. But the *consequence* self-heals — handshake records are still steered to the kernel (`wg_steer_to_kernel_on_port_match` = `local_destination && !is_transport_data`) and the socket path learns from them. With `REJECT_AFTER_TIME_NS` at 180s the roaming stall is bounded at **roughly 120–180s: degraded, not an outage** — the same bound `docs/wireguard-interop.md` had already reached for the pre-#7230 socket-path version of this defect.

**One correction to the framing:** the Keepalive/MalformedInner *counters* do not need the identity. `count_decap_err` matches both as `(_)` and bumps a single engine-wide counter. Endpoint learning is what needed it.

## A hollowed doc claim, found on the way

`docs/wireguard-interop.md` said endpoint learning "now holds on **any** interface for both the keepalive and malformed-inner arms." True of the **socket** path when written — and hollowed by #8274 step 3, which moved transport-data decap into the worker where `.ok()?` discarded exactly the two arms #7230/#7686 had just created. Nothing re-checked the sentence. Corrected here.

Also corrected: `decap.rs`'s `inner.is_empty()` branch is **unreachable** (`try_decap` returns `Err(Keepalive(..))` before it can produce an `Ok` with zero-length plaintext) and carried a comment saying the control thread's endpoint learning "still wants it" — describing, *on dead code*, the very work the `.ok()?` above was discarding. The branch stays as a defensive guard; the false claim is gone.

## Deliberately not changed: T7

The report suggests not clearing `t7_armed_send_ns` when the endpoint could not be applied. With the endpoint now applied, "the peer is alive" is accurate, and the no-reply reinit arm is the wrong mechanism to compensate for a stale endpoint — changing it is a protocol-timing change with a far wider blast radius. A cell **pins the pairing** instead (T7 cleared *and* the endpoint moved in the same pass), arming T7 first so the assertion isn't vacuous.

## Validation

Four **production** mutants killed, one per arm:

| # | mutation | arm it reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | revert to `.ok()?` | both roam cells |
| M2b | AEAD failure reported as identity-carrying `MalformedInner` | **the unauthenticated control** |
| M3 | only `Keepalive` matched | malformed-inner |
| M4 | records `dst_port` instead of `src_port` | both — which is why the fixture roams the port *and* the address |

M2b is the one that matters: a roam hoisted above the crypto would let anyone who can reach the listen port redirect a tunnel's egress, and every other cell would still pass.

A fifth attempt is recorded **VOID, not survived** — it called a `single_peer_pubkey` helper that #7686 deleted, so it never compiled, and a filtered result line made that indistinguishable from a clean pass until it was re-run unfiltered.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` green post-merge (5375-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed), and `go test ./pkg/refactoraudit/` since it scans by content rather than by package.

## PR #9201 — config: enumerate the vacuous rows hiding a loss behind an undeclared sibling [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9181-vacuous-enumeration`

Refs #9181. Answers the part the issue left unmeasured.

## The answer

Measured at master `c0e7b1221` — census `losers=36 walked=68 vacuous=44 unmeasured=76`, population `369 containers walked, 135 reached`:

| | count |
|---|---|
| vacuous rows via the **last-leaf** control | **42** |
| ...with a child container to declare at all | **21** |
| ...showing a loss once the child is declared | **2** — both `protocols bgp group` |

**The shape is real and rare.** It is not one row, and it is not widespread. The 21 rows with no child container cannot be this shape, which bounds the answer without measuring them individually.

## A correction to the issue's framing

`vacuous` is **two controls sharing a bucket**: 2 rows land there because `packed == split == EMPTY`, and 42 because the **last leaf** is unobservable. `protocols bgp group` is the *second* kind, not the first — the issue's wording ("no struct for the values to land in") reads like the first.

## The instrument reported 0 until two things were fixed

Both mutation-verified as load-bearing — reverting either reds the positive control:

1. the child's prerequisite leaf must be on **one line** with the instance. `neighbor <ip>` followed by `neighbor <ip> peer-as N` does not merge, so the fixture never compiles;
2. leaves must be tried **smallest-addition-first** — adding all of them lets one invalid leaf sink the child while the error names a *different* missing prerequisite.

Both failures produced a fixture that did not compile, which the loop skipped, **which reads as "no loss"** — #9181's own defect inside the instrument built to measure it.

The positive control is what caught it: `protocols bgp group` is a *measured* instance (lane-8388 fixed its compiler and the census moved **zero rows**), so an enumeration that cannot find it is reporting a property of itself.

## One change kept and recorded as NOT load-bearing

Reading `placeholder` for an instance value *looks* necessary — bgp `neighbor` declares `placeholder:"<address>"` with no `valueExamples`/`valueHint`, so `synthPair` invents `xpfaaa`. Mutation shows reverting it changes no result: the compiler accepts a non-address neighbor name on this path.

It stays for robustness, and the comment **says it is not why this reports 2** — because the honest version of a comment is the mutation result, not the order in which I found things. I would have shipped that claim as fact otherwise.

## Ratchet behaviour

The cell asserts the count, so a new container hiding a loss behind a vacuous label reds it — and a compiler fix that makes one observable reds it too, asking for the number to be re-derived rather than silently absorbed.

## PR #9202 — Derive the NAPI probe target from both families, and count the skip [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9019-napi-probe-target-family`

Advances #9019. Two of the issue's three fix items land here; the issue stays open for the rest, so this PR carries no close keyword.

## The defect

`bootstrapNAPIQueuesLocked` derived its probe target from IPv4 only — `RouteList(link, FAMILY_V4)` and `NeighList(idx, FAMILY_V4)`, each additionally filtered through `.To4() != nil` — then `continue`d on an empty target with **no log, no counter, no status field**. An interface with no v4 gateway route and no v4 neighbour was skipped unconditionally: a v6-only segment always, and plausibly a cold-boot LAN segment where this firewall *is* the gateway.

The silence is what made it expensive. A skipped interface is indistinguishable from a probed one, and nothing else covers it — the binding wedge recovery keys on `Registered && Armed && !Bound` (a bind *failure*, and its own give-up message says binding readiness cannot see a bound-but-dead queue), and the XSK liveness gate is box-wide, so one live queue sets `xskLivenessProven` for the whole box and masks a cold one.

## The fix

Both lookups now ask for `FAMILY_ALL`, and the derivation moved into a pure `deriveNAPIProbeTarget(routes, neighs)` applying **v4 gateway → v4 neighbour → v6 gateway → v6 neighbour**.

**Order is part of the contract**: an interface that derived a target before derives the *same* one now, so this widens the probed set and changes the target for no existing box. A remaining skip is counted (`NAPIProbeTargetSkips`, mirroring the existing `LearnedRouteCapHits` pattern) and logged with the interface name; the other silent `continue` — a link-lookup miss — is counted too.

## The seam exists for the measurement

"The v6 path is silently skipped" is an **absence** claim, and an absence observed against a harness that was never wired up measures the harness. Extracting a pure function lets the v6 rows run beside v4 rows that demonstrably **do** derive a target in the same run, so a broken fixture reds the v4 controls instead of quietly passing the v6 ones. The table asserts a floor on how many rows returned a live target for exactly that reason.

## One mutation survives, and it is EQUIVALENT — not a gap

Dropping the `To4() == nil` clause from the v6 arms changes nothing: the v4 arms run first and return for any `To4() != nil` address, so the v6 loops cannot see a v4 address however they are written. The clause is defensive redundancy that becomes load-bearing only if the arm *order* changes — which the ordering rows do red.

My first version of that code comment claimed the cell made the discriminator "falsifiable". It does not and cannot; the comment and the cell's doc now say so. Verified by re-running the mutation **unfiltered** after it produced no output, since a build failure and a clean pass are indistinguishable through a filtered result line.

| # | mutation | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | v6 arms removed (the original defect) | killed |
| M2 | `To4() == nil` dropped from the v6 arms | **survives — equivalent, verified applied + compiled** |
| M3 | v6 arms hoisted above v4 | killed (ordering rows + the v4-in-v6 cell) |
| M4 | NUD_FAILED exclusion dropped from the v6 neighbour arm | killed |
| M5 | the skip stops incrementing the counter | killed |

## What is NOT in this change

- **The last-resort probe target** the issue suggests for a segment with neither a gateway nor a neighbour. A datagram to this box's own address is handled locally and generates **no hardware RX event**, and a multicast probe's efficacy is unmeasured in this tree — this file's entire history is a warning against adding or weakening a probe path on a source reading rather than a measurement. Such a segment is now *counted* as unprobed, which is the actionable part.
- **A per-interface status field.** The counter is queryable and the log names the interface, but there is no `show` surface. Worth stating plainly: the precedent this follows, `LearnedRouteCapHits`, also has no non-test consumer — "exposed so the condition is visible to something other than the log" is aspirational for both.
- **Per-queue liveness** replacing the box-wide `xskLivenessProven` (the issue's item 3, already scoped as longer-term).

## PR #9203 — cli: an anchored deny-commands regex now covers argument forms (#9022) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9022-anchored-deny`

Closes #9022

With `deny-commands "^show log$"` the bare form was denied and every
argument-bearing form **ran**:

```
show log            DENIED
show log 100        ALLOWED   -> journalctl -u xpfd -n 100
show log messages   ALLOWED   -> tails a syslog file
show log FOO extra  ALLOWED   -> `extra` dropped, tails a syslog file
```

`Canonicalize`'s `AcceptsArgs` arm passes trailing tokens through (#8304,
deliberately), so the string the rule matched carried them and `$` stopped
matching.

## The fix is NOT "deny if either form matches" — that breaks the idiom

```
deny-commands  "^show log$"
allow-commands "^show log 100$"
show log 100   -> "deny if either" denies the form the operator explicitly allowed
```

Instead **each side** takes its longest match across the full canonical string
and the argument-free command prefix, and the documented precedence tiers are
untouched: deny matches 8 chars on the prefix, allow matches 12 on the full
string, tier 2 gives it to allow. Safe by construction — a side's match length
can only grow, and growth on the *allow* side requires a pattern the operator
wrote that matches the bare command.

## One half of the issue's evidence was wrong, and is corrected on it

`show configuration system` is **not** this mechanism. Measured:

```
show log            AcceptsArgs=true   children=0
show configuration  AcceptsArgs=false  children=16   (`system` IS a declared child)
```

It is a distinct command node with its own handler, so an anchored rule not
matching it is the same property as `^show version$` not matching `show route`.
Denying it would mean an anchored rule silently covers a subtree — the
over-denying direction.

That distinction is what the fix rests on: **`show log 100` runs the very handler
`show log` runs**, while `show configuration system` runs another. Hence the
widening uses the resolved keyword run (`canonicalPrefix`), not "the first two
words".

## PR #9207 — config: measure the population a multi leaf's closed-world defeat reaches [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9206-absorption-population`

Refs #9206. Answers the part the issue asked for — the population, not the RIP instance.

## The answer

Measured at master `efdfc786c`:

| | count |
|---|---|
| structural sites (multi leaf, closed-world ancestor) | **19** |
| ...of which are `groups`-rehosted duplicates (#8921) | 2 → **17 distinct** |
| absorb at the **schema walk** (all controls reject without the multi leaf) | **19** |
| survive the **compiler** and reach the config | **1** |

**The mechanism is general; the exposure is singular** — the same shape #9181 turned out to have, where a known mechanism had a population of one. That is exactly why the issue asked for the count before a remedy.

## The discriminator is not the container

It is whether the absorbing leaf's **value type has a downstream validator**.

`protocols rip group neighbor` takes free-form interface names and nothing checks that an interface exists — so the absorbed tokens become two non-existent interfaces named to FRR. Every other multi leaf in the set validates its values (`export` requires a known policy; the NAT match leaves require parseable addresses) and each **rejects the absorbed token by name**.

That is what turns 19 into 1, and it points the remedy at **value validation** rather than at closed-world enforcement.

## Two measurement corrections, each of which alone gave a wrong number

1. **The fixture path must carry an instance name for every node that takes one.** `protocols rip group` is `args:1` with no wildcard, so a path without one makes the undeclared keyword the *group name* — the control then wrongly ACCEPTS and the row is discarded. **That silently removed 15 of 19 sites, the RIP instance among them.**
2. **Every compiler row needs a baseline omitting the absorbed token.** Three rows initially rejected for unrelated reasons — a missing `then`, an undefined pool, an unknown policy — which is indistinguishable from the absorption being caught without the baseline beside it.

## Mutation matrix

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| drop the instance-name arm | reds — `control ACCEPTED` |
| ignore `closedWorld` | reds — population collapses to 0 |
| **drop the `multi` filter** | **SURVIVES — and that is the evidence** |

The third is not a gap. Widening the filter to *every* leaf under a closed-world container leaves the count at 19, so **no non-multi leaf absorbs** — the mechanism's own prediction, measured rather than restated. Had the filter been doing the work, widening it would have added sites.

`go test ./pkg/config/` green. `TestRipGroupMultiLeafStillAbsorbs9151` continues to pin the instance; this pins the population.

## PR #9210 — config: merge duplicate blocks at four more containers (#9209) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9209-more-dup-blocks`

Closes #9209

Writing the same named block twice at four containers silently lost
configuration. The worst is the policer, because a policer is a **control** and
this one quietly became a no-op:

```
policer p1 { if-exceeding { bandwidth-limit 1000000; } }
policer p1 { if-exceeding { burst-size-limit 15000; } }
  -> bw=0 burst=15000        a rate limiter with no rate
```

`protocols ospf area` is a **different shape** — nothing is discarded, the area is
DUPLICATED: two `area 0.0.0.0` stanzas reach the FRR managed section, where one
rejected line costs the whole reload.

**These are not new defects.** They were never inspected — the #8436 census could
not fixture a container whose children are all containers, so all four left the
population before any verdict was formed and it reported `SILENT: 0` over a set
that excluded them. #9024 widened it and they appeared at once.

## Each site checked for an existing gate first

Merging first destroys a diagnostic where one exists (the reason #8752 folds only
on the tolerant path). Three accept the duplicate silently. **`security ipsec
policy` does reject** — and is the `snmp trap-group` shape again: it says `ipsec
policy "p1" has no resolvable ipsec proposals`, a true statement about the SECOND
block the operator never meant to exist alone, describing a *symptom* of the
duplication. Merging first lets that gate see the policy actually described. No
diagnostic is lost; a misdirecting one is.

## The site list alone was not enough — and the partial state was worse

Folding appends the second block's children, so the merged node carried **two**
`if-exceeding` blocks and the compiler read the first: the policer recovered its
bandwidth-limit and **lost its burst-size-limit instead**.
`mergeSiblingContainers9209` folds identical container heads within one block.

It is scoped to the node a duplicate was just folded into, and **leaves leaves
alone** on purpose: two leaves with the same key are a value-level question
already answered per leaf by `multi` and the compilers, and re-answering it from
a layer that cannot see those decisions would override them.

## Validation

`pkg/config`, `pkg/configstore`, `pkg/frr`, `pkg/cli` green. **Mutation-checked in
two independent halves**: dropping the four sites reds all four cells; dropping
the sibling merge reds *only* the policer, at exactly the `burst=0` partial state.
A negative control pins that two distinct policers are not merged into each other.

## PR #9212 — config: stop expandFlatRun cutting a leaf's VALUE (#9124) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9124-flatrun-value-cut`

Closes #9124

The flat-run scan split a node's Keys at every token the container declares as
another leaf, testing every index from 1 and **never consulting `leaf.args`**. So
index 1 of an `args: 1` leaf — its value slot — was a cut candidate whenever the
value happened to spell a sibling keyword:

```
security ike gateway gw1 { ike-policy address; address 198.51.100.1; }
```

With an IKE policy legitimately **named** `address`, `ike-policy address` was cut
into `ike-policy` + `address`. The gateway compiled with `IKEPolicy=""`, committed
CLEAN at `configstore.CheckText` with zero warnings, and swanctl generated a
gateway with no IKE policy.

Measured:

```
policy named `address` (defect)   ikePolicy=""      addr="198.51.100.1"
policy named `pol1`   (control)   ikePolicy="pol1"  addr="198.51.100.1"
```

The fix starts the scan at `1 + leaf.args` and skips each sibling's own `args`
after a cut. **The schema already carried the arity** — the scan simply never
asked for it, and it is the same information the `SetPath` walk uses.

The trigger is a naming *coincidence*, not an ordinary spelling: the operator's
own object name has to equal a sibling keyword. That is why it survived, and it
bounds the severity — no attacker input, no enforcement bypass.

## Validation

`pkg/config`, `pkg/configstore`, `pkg/ipsec` green.

**Mutation-checked, and the control is the load-bearing half.** Restoring the
arity-blind loop reds both colliding rows with `IKEPolicy = ""`. The third row
(an ordinary policy name, which always worked) and
`TestFlatRunStillExpandsPackedChains9124` are what stop a "fix" that simply
stopped cutting — `expandFlatRun` **exists** to split packed chains, and
`set applications application a1 protocol tcp destination-port 80` is tested
behaviour such a fix would break while clearing every defect row.

## PR #9214 — config: refuse an absorbed statement at the rip neighbour leaf [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9206-rip-neighbor-validation`

Closes #9206.

## What this fixes

The population measurement (PR #9207) found **one** site of the multi-leaf absorption defect that reaches the compiled config: `protocols rip group <g> neighbor`. The discriminator was never the container — it is whether the absorbing leaf's **value type has a downstream validator**. `export` requires a known policy, the NAT match leaves require parseable addresses, and each rejects the absorbed token *by name*. Interface names were free-form, so nothing did:

```
set protocols rip group g1 neighbor ge-0/0/0 authentication-key secret1   -> ACCEPTED
  ifaces = [ge-0/0/0 authentication-key secret1]      # two non-existent interfaces to FRR
```

## The shape was censused BEFORE it was chosen

The ordinary risk in tightening a name validator is rejecting a name someone actually uses. Across **every interface-name value in the repo**, a hyphen is the media-type separator and is always followed by the FPC digit — `ge-0/0/0`, `xe-1/0/0`, `gr-0/0/0`, `ip-0/0/0.0` — with **zero counterexamples**. Junos keywords hyphenate the other way (`authentication-key`, `route-timeout`, `update-interval`), so the rule separates them.

A 35-name corpus is asserted to survive, including every name you flagged: `ge-7/0/1`, `reth0.100`, `fab0`, `em0`, `fxp0`, `st0.1`, `lo0`, plus `irb`, `enp101s0f1np1`, `vlan100`, `ae0`.

## What it does NOT catch is pinned, not omitted

A **bare** single-word keyword — `export`, `metric`, `passive` — is shape-indistinguishable from a bare interface name, because **`irb` is a real one this repo configures** (`set interfaces irb`). No shape rejects the first without rejecting the second.

`TestRIPNeighborBareKeywordStillAbsorbs9206` asserts those **still absorb**, so a partial fix cannot be mistaken for a complete one and the marker cannot go falsely green. A landed partial fix removes the reason anyone looks again; this one carries its own reason.

## `ValidateInterfaceName` alone would have been the trap you named

It is reused here for the **character allowlist** — the security half, since the name reaches a systemd `[Match] Name=` where whitespace and globs claim other devices, and this slot had none at all. But it is a character allowlist by design and **accepts `authentication-key` cleanly**, so wiring it alone would have been a validator that only *appears* to discriminate.

## A validator alone does not run — and that cost the first attempt

The walk's typed-leaf branch is a **conjunction**: `isTypedLeaf() && validator != nil`, where `isTypedLeaf()` is `valueType != ValueAny`. The validator was wired, the absorbed token was still accepted, and nothing said why — **a leaf with a validator and no valueType is silently never checked**.

Hence `ValueInterfaceName`, and `TestNoLeafCarriesADeadValidator9206`, which censused **zero** other leaves in that state and exists to keep it so. The next person to wire a validator is told here rather than shipping one that does nothing.

## Mutation matrix — both directions, which is what a name validator needs

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| remove the validator | reds — `still accepted as a neighbour` |
| remove the valueType (validator left **dead**) | reds **twice** — absorption cell *and* the dead-validator guard |
| neuter the shape rule (char allowlist only) | reds — `still accepted as a neighbour` |
| over-tighten to "ends with a digit" | reds — `legitimate interface name "irb" was REJECTED` |

The last is the false-rejection risk the census existed to avoid, reproduced deliberately.

`go test` green on config, frr, daemon, refactoraudit. Not a cluster/VRRP/session-sync path, so `make test-failover` is not triggered.

## PR #9217 — api: close the HEAD read-authorization bypass (#9134) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9134-head-authz`

Closes #9134

`isSafeHTTPMethod` admits HEAD, `readAuthz` keyed its lookup on
`r.Method + " " + r.URL.Path`, and `restReadPermissions` holds **40 `"GET "` keys
and zero `"HEAD "` keys**. An unknown key is the deliberate fail-**open** arm (so
/health and /metrics keep serving), so every HEAD landed there and went straight
to the mux — which routes HEAD to the GET pattern directly, no redirect.
**No authorization decision ran at all** on any of the 40 guarded read routes.

Measured on the production middleware chain, with a local account that has no
`system login user` entry (class `""`):

```
GET  /api/v1/config         403  permission denied ... class ""
HEAD /api/v1/config         200  handler executed
HEAD /api/v1/config/export  200  clen=168   exact body SIZE disclosed
HEAD /api/v1/routing/ospf   200  clen=55    the FRR handler ran
HEAD /api/v1/config/set     405  mutating routes correctly NOT aliased
```

A HEAD response carries no body, which is why this reads as harmless and is not:
Content-Length is the body's **exact** size, and the status code separates
"exists and you may not see it" from "exists". Both are read access to
information the same caller was refused on GET, by the same server, in the same
second.

## Fixed at the resolver, not by adding 40 keys

A second table entry per route clears the symptom and keeps the shape that
produced it — two edits per route forever, and a hole reopening for the next safe
method the mux learns to alias. `readPermissionFor` resolves the alias once, so
a route added with only a GET entry is guarded under **every** safe method that
can reach its handler.

The fall-through for a genuinely unknown path is unchanged, and that bound is
asserted: /health and /metrics must keep serving — the in-tree incus harnesses
read /metrics.

## Validation

`pkg/api`, `pkg/grpcapi` green.

The defect cell asserts **HEAD and GET agree** rather than a status code for HEAD
alone — "HEAD is 403" is also satisfied by a server that refuses everything — and
each row checks the GET is genuinely refused first. **Mutation-checked**:
removing the alias resolution reproduces `HEAD 200 while GET 403` on every row.
The completeness gate is keyed on the mechanism (every safe method × every
registered route), so it fails for OPTIONS and TRACE too.

## PR #9218 — configstore: encrypt at rest for every master-password spelling (#9152) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9152-masterpw-q1`

Closes #9152

Two supported spellings of `system master-password` made the store decide "no
master-password configured", so `active.json` and `confirm.json` were written in
**cleartext** — including IKE pre-shared keys — on a clean commit, with no warning
at any level, while `show configuration` rendered the stanza back.

## The two questions disagreed about the same tree

```
                  Q1 configured   Q2 effective PRF   result
braced            true            juniper-prf1       encrypted
stanza elided     FALSE           juniper-prf1       PLAINTEXT
fully elided      FALSE           juniper-prf1       PLAINTEXT
```

`masterPasswordPRFOfNode` reads `pseudorandom-function` as a **child** of
`master-password`; in a packed spelling the token is on the parent's Keys. #8898
fixed Q2 — and its own comment says exactly why the fold is needed — while Q1 was
left raw-scanning. So Q2 understood the operator's selector and Q1 reported there
was no master-password at all.

**This is not "the wrong KDF was chosen". It is no encryption at all**, and the
only observable is reading the raw DB file. HA config sync ships `Format()`,
which preserves the packed spelling, so a standby inheriting this config writes
its own DB in cleartext too — both nodes, one operator action.

## The broad fail-closed scope is unchanged

This folds spellings; it does not strip inactive nodes or restrict to applied
groups, so a dormant or wildcard master-password still forces encryption (#4705,
#5231). That bound is asserted, not assumed.

## Validation

`pkg/configstore`, `pkg/config`, `pkg/api` green.

Cells assert **the secret is not on disk**, not merely that a PRF resolved, and
each requires the config to **read back** — an "encryption" that cannot
round-trip would satisfy the first two checks and brick the node. Two controls:
a config with no master-password must still persist in plaintext (or the fix is
"encrypt everything"), and an inactive one must still force encryption.
**Mutation-checked**: restoring the raw scan reds exactly the two defective
spellings and leaves the braced control green.

## PR #9219 — frr/config: an ABSENT authentication-type is not a plaintext choice (#9105) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9105-authtype-absent`

Closes #9105

`authentication-key` with no `authentication-type` rendered the key in
**plaintext on the wire**, silently. At the three `pkg/frr` render sites an
absent type and a chosen plaintext type are the same state:

```
AuthType=""        Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=false  -> CLEAR  (SILENT)
AuthType="simple"  Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=false  -> CLEAR  (SILENT)
AuthType="md5"     Unrecognized=false  IsMD5=true   -> md5    (SILENT)
AuthType="bogus"   Unrecognized=true   IsMD5=false  -> CLEAR  (warned)
```

Look at the `simple` row: it renders clear, silently, and **that is correct** —
the operator asked for plaintext. The empty string takes the identical path, so
no care at the render site could have caught this; the information needed to
separate them was destroyed before the renderer ran.

## It is a downgrade, not a loss

Authentication stays **on**. The area/domain password is still emitted,
adjacencies still come up and still authenticate — with the key in cleartext in
every PDU — and `show configuration` echoes back the `md5` the operator wrote. A
dropped-authentication defect is noisy because adjacencies fail. This one
succeeds.

## The fix is split, following the doctrine already in auth_type.go

> "The commit gate stops every NEW instance; the warning at the render site tells
> the operator about the existing one."

- **Strict commit refuses** a key with no type, naming the remedy.
- **All three render sites warn** when rendering plaintext for an absent type —
  covering a config already persisted or arriving over HA sync.
- **Lenient warns rather than refusing** (#1960): refusing would turn a silent
  downgrade into a failure to load, on the path whose purpose is that it does not.

`authentication-type simple` **stays legal** and is asserted so. This gate asks
for a decision; it does not forbid plaintext. Without that row, "reject when it
would render clear" satisfies every defect case and quietly removes a supported
configuration.

`AuthTypeIsMD5` is deliberately **unchanged** and pinned: promoting an absent
type to md5 would flip a box running plaintext against a peer expecting it,
dropping the adjacency on upgrade — a silent downgrade traded for a silent outage.

## Validation

`pkg/config`, `pkg/frr`, `pkg/configstore` green. Mutation-checked: forcing the
gate lenient reds three rows.

## PR #9220 — config: split a packed firewall-filter `then` run (#9153) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9153-then-run`

Closes #9153

A `then` clause written on one set line lost every action past the second, and
when the lost one was the **terminating** action the term fell through:

```
then count c1 discard              action="discard" count="c1"           OK
then count c1 log discard          action=""        count="c1" log=true  FAIL-OPEN
then discard log count c1          action="discard" count=""             modifier lost
then count c1 dscp af11 policer p1 policer=""
```

Clean commit, zero warnings.

## The tree explains it

`SetPath` builds the #8939 flat chain, and the **last link carries a packed run
on one node's Keys**:

```
then > [count c1] > [log discard]
```

`flattenThenChain8939` hoists each nested node out of the chain, but a node whose
Keys are `[log discard]` is still one node, and `compileFilterThen` reads its
first key and drops the rest. **The chain fix was necessary and not sufficient**
— it moved the run without splitting it.

`expandFlatRun` splits a node's Keys at every token the container declares as
another leaf, which is exactly the missing operation, so this **composes the two**
rather than adding a third mechanism. Applied on both arms (a single node can
carry a run with no chain to hoist), and arity-aware since #9124 — which the
four-action row depends on: `count c1` must not be cut at its value.

## Every case is asserted against the split spelling

Not against a hand-written expectation, and each row checks the split form
**actually produced the terminating action** before comparing. A compiler that
dropped the action in both spellings would satisfy an equality check and fail
that reference arm.

Case C changed from "policer silently empty" to a compile **error** naming an
undefined policer until the fixture defined one — the reference is now *read*, so
its definedness gate finally sees it. That is the fix working, and it is asserted
with the policer defined.

## PR #9221 — fix master: three breakages I landed by gating per-package [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/master-red-9125-9105`

**Master was red and all three are mine.** The common cause is one mistake made
three times: I gated each change against the packages it *touched*, and all three
have effects that are not package-local.

| # | failure | why a package-scoped gate could not see it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `TestTreeIsGofmtClean` (cmd/cli) | #9014 left `pkg/configstore/store.go` unformatted; the cell scans the **whole tree** |
| 2 | `TestSnapshotShapeIsPinnedToProtocolVersion8892` | `ConfigSnapshot` embeds the entire typed `Config`, so #9125's `StaticRoute.HasPreference` landed on the **helper wire** |
| 3 | two `pkg/grpcapi` fabric tests | #9105 added a **new commit-time rejection**, which can red any package holding a config fixture |

**The rule: a change to a config type, or one that adds a commit-time rejection,
needs a repo-wide gate.** Its blast radius is not the packages it touches; it is
every package that constructs a config or reflects over one.

## HasPreference is now `json:"-"`, not a ProtocolVersion bump

The #8892 cell offers both arms — bump, or *"explain why the change is invisible
to a helper"* — and this is the second. The bit is compiler-internal: it exists
so the merge of two `route <p> { }` blocks can tell an authored `preference 5`
from an absent one, and the helper reads `Preference`. **Bumping the protocol for
a field nothing transmits would spend the one signal that tells a helper the wire
really changed.** Nothing is lost by not persisting it — the config DB stores the
TREE and the compiler recomputes the bit on load. Same choice #9008's
`LifetimeSecondsInvalidSpec` made.

The digest still moved because the walk records the json **tag** deliberately —
adding `json:"-"` to an *existing* wire field would be a silent removal and the
cell must see that. Verified against the #4406 golden as a pure reversal: **36
deletions, all HasPreference, zero other changed lines.**

## PR #9222 — authz: enforce the configuration regexes on all three surfaces (#9154) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9154-config-regex-surfaces`

Closes #9154

A login class's `allow-configuration` / `deny-configuration` was evaluated on
**exactly one** dispatch surface — the on-box CLI. The gRPC listener the shipped
`cli` binary speaks to, and the REST API, both performed config mutations
without ever consulting them.

So an operator who gave someone broad `permissions` while withholding specific
configuration authority had that withholding enforced **only if the person
happened to log in at the console**. #7172's own acceptance says this must not
happen: *"Both dispatch surfaces must use it — pkg/cli and pkg/grpcapi — and
neither may be gated alone."*

The actor is an ordinary authenticated non-superuser in a supported class. No
peer compromise, no administrative access.

## Sharing the resolver was necessary and not sufficient

#7172 cut 6 moved the **resolution** into `pkg/config` for exactly this reason —
*"so this gate, the operational gate and the gRPC gate all read one
implementation"* — and the **decision** stayed behind in `pkg/cli`, where the
other two surfaces could not reach it. It now lives in
`config.AuthorizeConfigMutation`, which all three call.

Both new gates sit in the **existing** authz middleware, after the coarse
permission bits and never instead of them. REST reads the already-buffered body,
so the line gated is the line the handler will apply.

The edit path is empty on both remote surfaces, deliberately: the remote CLI
prepends its own cursor before sending, so the server receives the **resolved**
path — which is what it acts on. A cell pins that `edit system` +
`set root-authentication …` still matches a deny on `system root-authentication`.

## My first gRPC cell bound the function, not the wiring

A mutation removing the interceptor's **call site** left it green — the gate
correct and unreachable, which is the state this whole issue is about.
`TestConfigMutationGateIsWiredIntoTheInterceptor9154` is the repair.

## The docs were a live overclaim

`docs/system-login.md` said all four regexes "are evaluated on every dispatch
surface" and then enumerated two. An operator reading it had no way to discover
the restriction was not in force. Corrected — with the shape of the error kept
rather than quietly deleted.

`load` remains a stated gap on every surface (arbitrary content, paths unknown
until parsed), as do `commit`/`rollback`, which carry no path to match.

## PR #9223 — config: refuse a multi-value run that repeats its own keyword (#9027) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9027-apikey-injection`

Closes #9027

A missing semicolon in a multi-value run injected the leaf's own keyword as a
**value**, and at one site that value is a **credential**:

```
api-auth { api-key AAA api-key BBB; }
  key[0] = "AAA"
  key[1] = "api-key"      <- authenticates
  key[2] = "BBB"
```

The braced spelling yields two keys. The injected credential is a **predictable,
publicly-known English literal** — anyone who can reach the management listener
can present `X-API-Key: api-key`.

## The two readers guessed opposite ways

| reader | behaviour | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `firewallMatchValues` | SKIPS the repeat (#8883, an *experiment*) | silently DROPS a legitimately-named object (#9029) |
| `multiLeafAuthoredValues` | ACCEPTS it as a value | INJECTS |

Both are guesses, and they are opposite because the input is **genuinely
ambiguous**: two statements missing a semicolon, or one statement listing a value
named after the keyword.

**So this refuses rather than guessing.** The operator is the only one who knows,
the question is cheap for them, and both guesses are wrong in a way invisible
from `show configuration` — which renders what was typed under either reading.
The message offers both readings rather than saying "ambiguous".

Lenient **warns** (#1960). That residual is asserted, in a cell that skips itself
with an instruction if a later reader fix removes it.

## The walk's descent nearly shipped wrong

My first version handed a compound-key node's children the schema of the compound
**keyword**, advancing one level where the node advanced two — so it never visited
anything beneath `family inet`. That is #8763's finding, reproduced. The firewall
row was ACCEPTED and looked like a scoping decision rather than a broken walk.

## Validation

**`go test ./...` green across the repository** — which is also the census: this
is a new commit-time rejection over **403 multi leaves**, and the suite's config
fixtures are the population. Nothing in the tree trips it.

**Mutation-checked twice**: neutering the predicate reds two rows; reverting the
compound-key descent reds exactly the firewall row.

## PR #9224 — config: let a legitimately-named object through the self-repeat gate (#9029) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9029-quoted-self-name`

Closes #9029

#8883's `k == self` skip could not tell *"the packed run injected the keyword"*
from *"the operator named an object after the keyword"*, so it over-dropped,
silently. #9027's gate replaced the guess with a refusal — and **my first version
of that gate made the same over-reach in the other direction**, refusing the
legitimately-named object instead of dropping it.

Both mistakes treat the spelling question as unanswerable when the AST already
answers it, twice:

- **Arity.** `Keys[1..args]` is the leaf's first value — or, for a leaf that names
  an object, its NAME. `address address 10.0.0.0/8` *defines* an address called
  "address"; flagging `Keys[1]` refused a definition rather than a repeat.
- **Quoting.** `address "address"` says in the grammar itself that the token is a
  name. `KeysQuoted` is exactly that bit (#6673: *"the one bit about a key that
  its TEXT cannot carry"*). The refusal now offers quoting as the **remedy**.

## The pair that matters produces identical Keys

```
address-set AS1 { address ADDR-A "address"; }   ACCEPT
address-set AS1 { address ADDR-A address; }     REJECT
```

`[address ADDR-A address]` in both — the verdict comes from `KeysQuoted` and
nothing else.

## The quoting branch was inert until that row existed

A mutation found it: disabling `KeyQuoted` killed **zero** cells, because arity
scoping already covered every other case in the file. **A branch nothing can fail
is a claim, not a guard.** The row was added and the mutation now kills it.

The security case is unchanged and asserted: the bare `api-key AAA api-key BBB`
run is still refused, so quoting does not reopen #9027.

## Validation

`go test ./...` green across the repository — this widens a commit-time
rejection, so its census is every config fixture in the tree. **Mutation-checked
on both branches independently**: ignoring arity reds two rows, ignoring quoting
reds the row above.

Every arm of the children walk reads `child.Keys[1]` and ignores `Keys[2:]`.

The **leaf** path already recorded an unrecognised token in `UnknownActions`

already warns. Reusing it keeps **one** answer to "the operator typed something we

The arity is **read from the schema**, not listed — a hand-kept table would be a
second place to remember. A cell pins the six arities the scan depends on.

The issue asked whether the A–F spelling divergence at these sites matters, and
recorded that it should be *decided* rather than absorbed. The divergence was only
ever over **malformed** input — a two-element value at a leaf that takes one — and
that input no longer commits, so the six spellings can no longer disagree about it
on the operator path. The sites stay out of the gate's population, now for a

## PR #9226 — rpm: hold, not fail over, on an unscopeable link-local tcp-ping (#9026) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9026-probetcp-scope`

Closes #9026

`probeICMP` resolved an IPv6 link-local scope and `probeTCP` did not, so the
**same** unscopeable target held the test on one probe type and counted as **path
loss** on the other.

The consumer distinction is load-bearing: `pkg/rpm` treats `ErrProbeSetup` as
"this probe never ran" (no counters, no transition) and any other error as a path
signal that increments `SuccFail` and can trip a state change. `services
ip-monitoring` drives preferred-route injection off that state — so a tcp-ping to
an unscopeable `fe80::` address, **a probe that never left the box**, could fail
over a WAN.

## The guard is shared now, not copied

#2494 wrote it once for ICMP and the TCP path was never given it. Copying it
would leave the same drift available a third time at `http-get`. One function
called by each probe is what makes "both probe types agree about scope" a
property rather than a coincidence.

The deliberate **non-fallback** is preserved verbatim: `opts.BindDevice` can hold
the routing-instance VRF device, which is *not* an egress link for `fe80::`.
Defaulting to it would let the probe SEND — counted as path loss — instead of
HOLDING.

## My first cells bound the helper, not the wiring

A mutation removing the **call** from `probeTCP` left all of them green — the
guard correct and unreachable, which is exactly the state this issue reports.
`probeTCP` is now driven directly, and the assertion is the **sentinel** rather
than "an error" — "probeTCP returned an error" is satisfied by the defect itself.
With the guard removed the cell reports
`TCP connect failed: dial tcp [fe80::1]:80: connect: invalid argument`.

Two controls keep it narrow: a global v6 and a v4 target are not scoped, and a
link-local **with** a destination-interface must reach the dial rather than hold.

`transfer-on-commit transfer-interval 30` set only the first — an archive that
uploads on commit but never on a schedule. **A backup that silently stops
happening is discovered when it is needed.** Census: losers 23 → 22.

## rpm probe test — a new operation

```
set … test T target address 10.0.0.1 probe-type icmp-ping probe-count 5
  [test T] > [target] > [address 10.0.0.1] > [probe-type …] > [probe-count …]
  -> target=10.0.0.1  probe-type=""  probe-count=0
```

A probe running with the wrong **type** does not detect what it was configured to
detect, and `services ip-monitoring` drives preferred-route injection off these
results.

`expandFlatRun` cannot see this, and neither could a copy of
`flattenThenChain8939`: the trailing statements are not on the container's
children at all — they hang off a leaf that legitimately **owns a body**
(`target { address X; }`), which every existing bound deliberately declines to
touch.

`hoistAndSplitRun8939` is that operation, written **once** rather than a ninth
time: it lifts, out of a body-owning leaf's subtree, exactly those descendants
whose head resolves as a leaf of the **enclosing** container. That predicate is
the whole safety argument — `address` resolves under TARGET and stays put;
`probe-type` resolves under TEST and is hoisted.

## The census cannot measure the rpm fix

It builds fixtures from **eligible** leaves (childless, non-multi), and `target`
owns a body — so it can never generate the nesting that loses the properties. The
row it *does* carry there, `target [address | url]`, is an **artifact**: those two
are alternatives that both write `test.Target`, so a fixture setting both is
malformed input rather than a loss. Recorded as such rather than "fixed" —
levelling them into agreement would mean accepting two targets.

That is the #9181 shape again: a real loss the instrument's own population filter
excludes.

## PR #9240 — grpcapi: derive the peer clear's deadline from the caller, not Background [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9041-clear-peer-ctx`

Refs #9041 — **part 1 of two. Does not close the issue**; part 2 is untouched and `docs/log/9041.md` says why.

## Reachability, established before writing anything

A `context.Background()` peer leg only matters if something cancels, and "nothing cancels" would have been a **close**, not a fix. Two independent cancellers, found in the callers rather than assumed from "gRPC cancels contexts":

- `pkg/api/sessions.go` calls `svc.ClearSessions(r.Context(), …)` — an in-process call carrying the HTTP request context, which `net/http` cancels when the client disconnects;
- `cmd/cli/shared.go` supplies `cmdCtx`, declared `// per-command context, cancelled by Ctrl-C` and built with `context.WithCancel`.

So an operator's Ctrl-C on a clustered clear returned immediately while the **peer** clear ran to completion.

That is not merely untidy: #5882/#2468 built the `clearErrors` / partial-success apparatus precisely because partial clears are normal and must be **reported**. A ghost clear is the one outcome it cannot represent — the work happens after the reporter is gone.

## The fix

`clearPeerSessions` gains a `ctx` parameter and derives its 5s deadline from it; both call sites pass the handler's context. The site now matches its five siblings.

## The guard is structural, and its third check is the load-bearing one

Binding this behaviourally needs a live `cluster.Manager` with `PeerAlive()` plus a real authenticated peer dial — the limit `peer_fanout_attach_6851_test.go` already states for its sibling. So the **wiring** is bound, which is the half a behavioural test could not reach.

| check | why it is not redundant |
|---|---|
| the function TAKES a `context.Context` | before this it did not, so no call site could fix it |
| its timeout is not rooted at `Background()` | the body half |
| **call sites pass a ctx AND not `context.Background()`** | arity alone is satisfiable while the cancel is still dropped |

**Mutation-verified, each by its own branch:**

| mutant | message |
|---|---|
| revert the body to `Background()` | `roots its peer-RPC timeout` |
| remove the parameter | `takes no context` |
| call site passes `context.Background()` | `passes context.Background()` |

The third is why the call-site check was strengthened from a bare arity test — **the first version let that mutant through.**

## What is NOT fixed

Part 2: four handlers hold the `sessionWalkLimiter` slot across the peer RTT (up to 4s dial + 3–5s RPC against `MaxConcurrentSessionWalks = 4`), bounding *local* walks while doing no local walking. Releasing before the peer leg is a concurrency change across four handlers touching a DoS bound, and owes its own reasoning about double-release and limiter re-entry. Landing this alone is not a close.

`go test` green on grpcapi and api.

## PR #9241 — Reach #3112's DNAT ICMP reversal: widen the SNAT-only gate [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9030-dnat-icmp-reversal-reachable`

Closes #9030

## The defect

The already-closed issue #3112 landed the destination-side ICMP-reversal builders, their struct fields and their regression cells. **The production caller could not reach any of them** for the scenario it was filed about.

The gate in `try_reverse_embedded_icmp_error` tested `icmp_match.nat.rewrite_src.is_none()`. A pure-DNAT decision is `rewrite_dst: Some(_), rewrite_src: None`, so it returned `NotHandled`. `build_nat_reversed_icmp_error_v4/v6` have exactly one production caller each, below that line.

The comment the gate carried — *"a flow with no source translation leaves the inner quoted source unchanged, so no reversal is required"* — is true of the **source** and says nothing about the destination, which is what a DNAT flow moved.

## This touches no builder, and that was checked before widening

A gate that admitted a case the builder could not serve would turn a *missing* reversal into a *corrupted* one. The builder is already complete for the widened set:

| restore | guard |
|---|---|
| destination address | `had_dst_nat` (`rewrite_dst`) |
| destination port | `rewrite_dst_port \|\| rewrite_dst` (`builders.rs:150`) |
| source address/port | `rewrite_src_port \|\| rewrite_src` |

Each arm tests its own field, so admitting DNAT-only, port-only or static-NAT cannot half-restore a quote — an arm whose field is `None` does not fire.

*A correction to my own reading:* a narrow `sed` window over `builders.rs` showed no destination-port arm and I nearly widened only to the address case. `original_dst_port` is read three times in that file, including the restore at :150. The windowed read was the error, not the code.

## HA wire: nothing moves

No `SessionKey` field and no wire struct changes. The reversed error carries `flow_key: None` and seeds no session — asserted in the cell — so it is not a session-sync participant.

## Validation

The regression drives the **real call site** (`poll_binding_process_descriptor`), not the builders — bypassing the caller is exactly what let this survive with green #3112 cells.

| # | mutation | arm it reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | gate reverted to `rewrite_src.is_none()` | "must reach the reversal" |
| M2 | `had_dst_nat = false` | "inner destination restored to the VIP" |

So the cell binds the gate **and** the destination-restore arm, not just the former.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` green post-merge (5376-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed) · `go test ./pkg/refactoraudit/` (scans by content).

Branch: `fix/8928-ip-monitoring-elision`

#8928 records **both** of its named instances as fixed. Measured at master, only
one is:

```
braced  bad rpm-probe -> REJECTED, naming the probe
elided  bad rpm-probe -> committed clean
```

A typo'd rpm-probe therefore reached production and **probe-driven WAN failover
silently never armed** — no value and no complaint, the shape the issue calls the
worst the campaign produced.

The elision suppressed a **second** validation too, which is how we know the
whole policy is dropped rather than just its reference check: the braced GOOD
control is rejected for *"at least one then preferred-route route is required"*,
and the elided GOOD control commits clean.

The pair was already admitted and **inert**, because the fold reaches a child
only after the link above it has created the container:

```
services      -> ip-monitoring   ADMITTED
ip-monitoring -> policy          MISSING     <- the break
match         -> rpm-probe       ADMITTED    (unreachable below it)
```

Only the missing link is added.

`policy match` is **not** admitted. Measured, it is effective at **three** schema
sites — `security policies from-zone <n> policy`, `security policies global
policy`, `services ip-monitoring policy` — so admitting it would change how
**security policies** compile in order to fix an ip-monitoring defect. It is not
needed: the body from `match` inward is already braced. A cell pins that it stays
unadmitted, so a later change cannot acquire that blast radius silently.

Each re-derived by running the cell at this base, never by adjusting the old

## PR #9243 — grpcapi,api: bound the authorization-denial log without deleting the signal [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9042-denial-log-bound`

Closes #9042.

## The defect

Five denial sites emitted an unconditional `slog.Warn` **per request**, two on the network-exposed fabric listener, with no limiter, no dedup, and **no counter**. The rate is attacker-controlled — `principalForPeer` returns `Unauthenticated` for any unattributable peer and `PrincipalForUID` returns an empty-Class principal for any resolvable UID that isn't a configured login user, so **every local non-root UID** can drive the line at one `Warn` per unary call. `Warn` always ships, fans out to remote syslog, and journald's 10000/30s cap then suppresses xpfd's *other* lines.

| site | surface |
|---|---|
| `grpcapi/authz.go` `denyRPC` | `grpc_login_class` |
| `grpcapi/fabric_auth.go` `checkFabricAuth` | `fabric_auth` |
| `grpcapi/server.go` `fabricAllowlistUnaryInterceptor` | `fabric_method_allowlist` |
| `grpcapi/server.go` `fabricAllowlistStreamInterceptor` | `fabric_stream_allowlist` |
| `api/crosssite.go` `mutationCrossSiteGuard` | `rest_cross_site` |

## The counter is the load-bearing half

There was no denial metric anywhere and the audit journal records no authorization events, so **a bare demote to Debug would have deleted the only signal that a denial happened** — worse than the flood.

`xpf_authz_denials_total{surface}` is **always emitted, including at zero** (#3464), because zero is the normal state here and "never denied" must be distinguishable from "not scraped". The counter advances on *every* denial including suppressed ones, and each emitted line carries `suppressed_since_last`.

## The key space is fixed, and that is a security property

A per-principal map keyed by attacker-supplied identity grows without bound — **the same defect class being fixed, one level down**. 64 fixed buckets keep memory constant.

The cost is accepted deliberately and stated at its real strength: two principals can share a window, so under an attacker occupying every bucket a new principal's *first* denial may be suppressed. That trade cannot be avoided, only chosen — guaranteeing otherwise makes the line count grow with an attacker-controlled key count, which is the flood. The test asserts the guarantee that **is** made (prompt logging while free buckets remain), not one the design cannot keep.

## Three of my own bugs, and what caught each

1. `resetForTest` assigned `bucket{}` **while holding that bucket's mutex**, replacing the mutex so the unlock hit a fresh one — fatal.
2. **The metric was described but never emitted.** The neighbouring call site reads `defer c.emitAdmissionRefusals(ch)`, and my pattern written without `defer` matched nothing — so the counter that justified demoting the logs **scraped as absent**, and nothing about either file looked wrong.
3. The site guard **brace-counted** function bodies, and `interface{}` in the two fabric signatures closed its depth inside the *parameter list* — reporting that two sites which **do** route through denyaudit did not. A guard that reads the wrong bytes fails in the direction that looks like a real finding. Replaced with `go/parser`.

## Mutation matrix

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| revert one site to a bare `Warn` | reds the site **and** count guards |
| counter advances only on emission | `counter advanced by 1` (want 500) |
| remove `emitAuthzDenials` from `Collect` | `never calls emitAuthzDenials` |

The second is the *bounding must not hide the volume* property; the third is bug 2 above, pinned so it cannot recur.

`go test -race` green on denyaudit, grpcapi, api.

## PR #9244 — daemon: force the full apply when the LAST delegated prefix is withdrawn [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9239-pd-withdrawal`

Fixes the finding filed as #9239 (muse-spark-007 finding 14).

## A transition detector written as a state test

`dhcpLeaseChangeRequiresRecompile` asked:

```go
if d.dhcp != nil && len(d.dhcp.DelegatedPrefixesForRA()) > 0 {
        return true
}
```

The callback runs **after** `commitLease` has removed a withdrawn prefix, so this
reads the post-state. "The last IA-PD was just withdrawn" and "this box never had
PD" are the same empty set — and the event that most needs RA re-applied is the
one classified as needing nothing.

## Why nothing else recovers it

On the supported composition — standalone, the only DHCPv6 client is the `fxp0`
management lifeline, its PD mapped to a downstream RA interface — *every* DHCP
client is a lifeline, so the classifier takes the management-only branch. That
branch refreshes routes, DNS and IPsec, and never RA. Meanwhile:

- `reconcileClusterRAServices` is a no-op off-cluster, by its own doc comment.
- The mode-agnostic 30s loop retries only **dead** senders. This one is alive and
  merely holding stale desired state.

So the sender keeps refreshing a withdrawn prefix until an unrelated apply or a
restart, downstream hosts keep autoconfiguring from it, and their traffic is
dropped **off-box** — far from the daemon responsible.

`ra.Manager.Apply` with an empty set was already the graceful path (removes the
sender, emits a router-lifetime-zero goodbye so the last PIO ages out). This only
had to reach it.

## Shape of the fix

The predicate stays **pure** and takes the previous pass's answer as a parameter;
`onDHCPAddressChange` — the single production caller, which runs once per
lease-change event — owns the transition with one atomic `Swap`.

A config commit that removes the DHCPv6 client can leave the memo set with no
callback to clear it: one conservative full apply on the next lease change, which
then clears it. Deliberate asymmetry — the failure being guarded is advertising a
prefix the upstream withdrew.

## Validation, and two traps worth reading

Three cells. **The third is the only one that matters.**

## PR #9245 — monitoriface: say when the rate had to drop the userspace component [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9047-rate-userspace-note`

Closes #9047.

## The gate is right; the silence was not

`snapshotTrafficDeltas` drops the userspace component when either sample lacks a traffic source. **That is correct** — the counters are cumulative, so folding a missing side in as zero attributes the helper's whole lifetime to one window and renders a spike that never happened.

What was wrong is that declining was **silent**.

## The same render disagrees with itself

`displayTrafficCounters` gates on **`curr` alone**; `snapshotTrafficDeltas` gates on **both**. So in any window where `prev` lacks a source and `curr` has one, the displayed **total includes** userspace bytes while the displayed **rate excludes** them — with no indication.

**The gates are deliberately not reconciled to match.** They answer different questions and are both right: a total is a single-sample fact; a rate needs two samples. Forcing the total to drop userspace whenever `prev` lacked a source would make **the total wrong** to fix a cosmetic disagreement. The honest reconciliation is to report it.

## This is #7422's own doctrine, applied to the path that undid it

#7422 row 10 decided a counter group that could not be contributed must carry a **note** rather than silently render 0, since 0 is indistinguishable from a genuinely idle interface — and it fixed the two sibling groups **on the strength of the userspace group already having one**. The rate path then kept dropping that same group in silence.

## The note fires only on a real gap

Reporting whenever the gate declines would put a permanent note on every **kernel-only** interface, which has no userspace source to drop and never will. A note that appears on every window is one operators learn to skip — disarming it for the window that matters. So it is raised only when `curr` has a source and `prev` does not: helper start, helper restart, or a failed status read (which sets `Userspace` to a struct carrying only a `StatusNote`, so the gate declines).

## On the dismissal

The external review was **right on the mechanism** and wrong only that "no coherent distinct fix exists". Its correct half is preserved and pinned — `TestDroppedComponentIsNotFoldedInAsZero9047` asserts the delta stays kernel-only, and the mutant that folds the missing side in as zero reds two cells. **Auditing the dismissal is what found the rest.**

## Mutation matrix

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| never report the drop (pre-#9047) | `dropped from the rate and NOT reported` |
| report **always** on decline | `kernel-only interface reported` |
| fold the missing side in as zero | **2 cells red** — the spike the dismissal warned of |

## PR #9247 — cluster: a superseded remote failover must ACK failed, not applied (#9036) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9036-superseded-ack`

A remote failover **superseded by a concurrent `ResetFailover`** performs no demotion and was ACKed `applied`, so the peer promoted while this node was still Primary — #5640's invariant, reintroduced by #8000's barrier disarm.

## Four correct steps composing into a two-owner window

1. `pkg/cluster` returns `FailoverSuperseded` before the SecondaryHold write — **correct** (#5246): the reset is the operator's newer intent.
2. The daemon wiring **disarmed** the fence barrier — **correct in isolation** (#8000): nothing will ever actuate it, and leaving it armed makes the applied-ack burn the fence timeout and blame the fencing path.
3. `waitFailoverActuated` returns nil when no barrier is armed — **correct**, and the reason step 2 chose disarming.
4. `sync_failover.go` sends `failoverAckApplied` when the wait returns nil — **correct** (#5640): a clean fence means the peer may promote.

> **#8000 removed the only thing on the wire that distinguished "fenced" from "never happened"**, and the typed `FailoverSuperseded` that could have carried the distinction was collapsed to `nil` at the callback boundary.

## The fix

`failFailoverActuation` resolves the barrier with `cluster.ErrFailoverSuperseded` and **leaves it for the waiter to consume**, so the ack downgrades to `failed` and the peer holds. The operator still gets the true reason rather than #8000's misleading fence timeout.

**Per-request, not per-RG.** `resolveFailoverActuation` fans a demotion *event* out across every in-flight request for the RG because the event answers all of them. A supersede is a fact about **one** request's generation check; failing a sibling's barrier with it would discard the identity discipline #6177 exists to enforce.

## Wiring matrix — the call site deleted, the named cell red

    M1  DELETE the singular call site
        -> TestSupersededRemoteFailoverAcksFailedNotApplied9036/singular   RED
           TestRemoteFailoverDisarmsSupersededBarrier8000                  RED

    M2  DELETE the batch call site
        -> TestSupersededRemoteFailoverAcksFailedNotApplied9036/batch      RED
           TestRemoteBatchFailoverDisarmsSupersededBarrier8000             RED

    M3  revert BOTH to disarmFailoverActuation (the pre-fix behaviour)
        -> all four                                                        RED

**M1 does not red the batch subtest and M2 does not red the singular one** — the two closures are independently bound, which is exactly the property a cell driving `failFailoverActuation` directly would have missed. Verified with before/after grep counts, not exit status.

**Mutant that must SURVIVE:** `TestUncontestedRemoteFailoverStillFences9036`. Without it, a "fix" that resolved *every* barrier as superseded — defeating #5640 entirely and making no failover ever complete — passes the cells above.

## It redded #8000's own two cells, and that was a prior decision speaking

Those cells assert #8000's **mechanism** (disarm → nil), not its **goal** (don't burn the fence timeout, don't blame the fencing path). Re-anchored to **PROMPT + SUPERSEDED**, with **#8000's timing assertion kept verbatim** — dropping it would hand back what #8000 bought while claiming to fix something else. Both FAIL-ON-REVERT comments now name two directions.

## `make test-failover`: PASS, and the three VOIDs before it are committed too

    verdict            PASS
    exe_check          MATCH
    build_git_sha      913b754c8
    build/running sha  bbfd037f… == bbfd037f…
    cells              21 passed, 0 failed      throughput 22.9 Gbps

The first attempt reported **`20 passed, 1 failed`** with the #8297 proxy-ARP cell red — and the harness voided it: `exe_check=UNAVAILABLE`, `build_exe_sha256=<none>`. **No deploy had run; it tested an unknown build.** On the verified re-run that same cell passes. All four ledger rows are committed, VOIDs included, because a ledger whose value is three states stops having it if lanes record only their greens.

## PR #9249 — api: export the two dataplane counters that nothing could read (#9019) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Completes #9019. The derivation half already landed in `575973541`; this is the
observability half, which had not.

## The measurement that prompted it

#9019's acceptance asked for a counter **and** a status surface. Grepping for the
consumer:

```
NAPIProbeTargetSkips  -> its own file, its own test, one comment
LearnedRouteCapHits   -> its own file, its own test, one comment
                         (and that comment lives in napi_probe_target_9019.go,
                          which copied its shape)
```

**Zero consumers outside their own package.** Not in Prometheus, not in a status
field, not in a CLI command. Two exported counters, added by two separate fixes
that were each asked to make a silent skip observable, and neither could be
observed by anything.

That is worse than no counter, because the counter *reads as* the remedy. The
visible half of the acceptance was satisfied — something increments — while the
box stayed exactly as silent as before. Both were found by grepping for the
reader, not by reading either fix, and that is the general shape:
**adding the producer is the part that gets reviewed; adding the reader is the
part that gets forgotten, and from inside the producing file the two states look
identical.**

## What landed

`xpf_napi_probe_target_skips_total` and `xpf_learned_route_cap_hits_total`, both
always emitted including at zero (#3464 / #8312 convention — a counter that
appears only on first fire cannot be alerted on, and cannot distinguish "never
skipped" from "not scraped"; zero is the normal state for both, so it is the
reading that has to be trustworthy).

Both emit **before the dataplane gate**. For the admission-refusal and
authz-denial counters beside them that is convention; here it is load-bearing —
these describe a dataplane that came up *incompletely*, so gating them on a
healthy dataplane would hide them in exactly the case they exist for.

## Validation

The cells drive the collector's real `Describe`/`Collect` and never call
`emitDataplaneSilentSkips` directly — calling the emitter would reproduce the
original mistake exactly, proving the emitter works while the collector still
never calls it. The harness leaves `srv.dp` **nil on purpose**, so `Collect`
takes the early return at the dataplane gate and the counters must still arrive.

## PR #9250 — config: state the WireGuard steered/unsteered security asymmetry (#9016) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9016-wg-multiport`

The multi-port WireGuard commit advisory told operators:

That is false at HEAD, and it erases the one difference the advisory exists to
convey.

## How it got there

`921028959` correctly retracted this advisory's earlier claim that the unsteered
tunnel was *"dead while appearing configured / no handshake ever completes"*. The
replacement sentence then made a **new** claim pointing the same direction:

| claim | reads as |
|---|---|
| retracted: "the tunnel is dead" | nothing to worry about |
| added: "steered or not, equally unadjudicated" | nothing to choose between them |

Both stop a reader from finding the bypass. The second was inherited in good
faith — it cites the #5618 advisory, which still **opens by describing the
pre-#8274 world**: *"The XDP shim deliberately steers inbound UDP on the
configured WireGuard listen port to the KERNEL (#5582)."* #8274 replaced that for
transport-data records, and nothing re-checked the advisory built on it.

Three independent in-tree statements, all at HEAD:

1. `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`, the #8274 step 3 arm — *"a WireGuard
   TRANSPORT-DATA record for a configured local listener is NOT local delivery
   any more — the worker decaps it and adjudicates the inner packet under the
   tunnel's logical ingress zone."*
2. `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` at the `stage_wg_decap` call — *"Everything
   downstream then sees the INNER packet — flow parse, screen, session, policy,
   NAT, forward build ... instead of being written to the wgN TUN for the kernel
   to forward with no zone policy at all."*
3. `maps_sync.go` — `userspaceCtrlFlagWgRx` is set iff at least one WireGuard
   tunnel is configured, so that gate is armed exactly when this advisory fires.

`wg_worker_claim` compares the destination port against a **single scalar**, so a
second listen-port never matches:

```
steered port    transport data -> worker decap -> zone/session/policy/NAT
unsteered port  transport data -> kernel -> control thread -> wgN TUN
```
