`TestFabricShowTextAllowlistCoversEveryProxiedTopic_9059` reads the two call
sites' **source** and requires every literal topic to be allowlisted — so adding a
proxied topic and forgetting the allowlist cannot pass, which would otherwise make

## PR #9282 — grpcapi: let the legacy session walk be cancelled (#9060) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9060-getsessions-cancel`

The legacy `GetSessions` walk had **no cancellation** — both iterate callbacks
returned `true` unconditionally, so once started it ran to EOF.

It holds one of `MaxConcurrentSessionWalks = 4` slots, and **that limiter is
shared with REST**. Four abandoned legacy calls block every REST *and* gRPC
session scan until each finishes on its own: a poller that times out keeps
paying, on a surface it did not call.

**Both shipped clients take this path** — `cmd/cli/show_flow.go` sends `Limit:100`
with no `PageSize`, `pkg/cli/session_filter.go` sends `Limit:10000`, and only
`PageSize > 0` reaches the bounded cursor walk. Ordinary
`show security flow session`.

## Only one of the three missing guards is fixed here

Per the issue's own analysis, they are not equal:

| guard | disposition |
|---|---|
| offset ceiling | **inert** — `Total` counts every matching row, so the walk runs to EOF regardless of offset |
| count cap | **cannot be fixed here alone** — a `capped` flag needs a field absent from `proto/xpf/v1`, and truncating silently is worse than not truncating |
| cancellation | **the live defect**, fixed |

The contention is real (the map is the shared conntrack hash the Rust helper
writes on session *install*), but the report's per-packet claim is refuted and is
**not** made here.

## A partial result is not a success

A cancelled walk yields a truncated list **and** a `Total` that understates the
table — a client reading it as an answer concludes sessions disappeared. Same
reasoning as the iterator-error arms beside it (#2469). It returns the *context*
error rather than `Internal`, so a caller can tell "you went away" from "the walk
broke".

## A survivor that is correct, documented rather than papered over

Deleting the sampler's `if cancelled { return true }` early return **survives** —
and that is right. Latching comes from the captured flag never being reset
(`ctx.Err()` cannot go back to nil), so that line is a **fast path guarding
nothing**. Both the code and the cell now say so, instead of carrying a comment
claiming it is the latch.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| v4 callback stops checking | killed |
| return the partial result as success | killed |
| probe every entry instead of sampling | killed |
| drop the early-return fast path | **survives, correctly** — documented |

## PR #9283 — cluster: bound the peer IPsec SA full set and stop it aliasing the frame (#9061) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9061-ipsec-sa-payload-bound`

`decodeIPsecSAPayload` split a peer-supplied frame with **no element-count or
name-length bound**. The only bound in the chain is the 16 MiB frame ceiling.
Measured there:

```
16 MiB of "\n"    -> 16,777,217 parts, 272.1 MB transient, 0 names retained
16 MiB of "a\n"   ->  8,388,609 parts, 674.8 MB transient, 128 MB RETAINED
```

**The retained set is the sharper end, twice over.** Every one-byte name from
`strings.Split` is a substring sharing the payload's backing array, so the whole
16 MiB stays reachable while any name does — and `reinitiateIPsecSAs` iterates
the retained set **on takeover**, calling `InitiateConnection` per name. Millions
of exec-shaped calls on the failover path: the cost lands exactly when the
cluster is least able to absorb it.

## Three parts

1. **Bounds** — 4096 names, 256 bytes each. The second is not redundant: without
   it a single enormous "name" stands in for the element bound.
2. **Copy, don't alias** — scan and convert each name individually, so retained
   size tracks the *names*, not the frame.
3. **Refuse, don't truncate** — the arm beside this one already states the
   doctrine: *"a full set REPLACES, so installing a stale or truncated one is
   worse than installing nothing."* A truncated SA set makes the standby
   reinitiate a **subset** on takeover and look like it succeeded.

## Two gaps found by mutation, not by reading

**The receiver wiring was unbound.** Three cells tested the decoder; a mutation
making `handleMessage` install a malformed set anyway **killed zero of them** —
the defect restated one layer up, because a bound only matters if the caller acts
on it. A cell driving `handleMessage` and asserting the held set is unchanged now
kills it.

**My first aliasing mutant was not one.** `string(b)` in a helper still copies, so
it survived and proved nothing. The honest mutant is the *actual original* —
`strings.Split(string(payload), "\n")` — which aliases, and which the aliasing
cell kills. A mutant that cannot express the defect reports coverage it did not
test.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| drop the element bound | killed by 3 cells |
| drop the name-length bound | killed |
| receiver installs a malformed set anyway | killed (after the wiring cell) |
| **the real original `strings.Split` decoder** | killed by **all 4** |

`go test ./...` green.

## PR #9284 — dataplane: refuse a peer delete that would kill a live local session [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9048-sync-gen-guard`

The report said both HA session-sync generation guards fall through when the local stored generation is 0 — which it is for every locally-created session, since `recvGenV4` is populated only by prior *peer* installs — leaving a second primary free to overwrite and delete. Following that to ground gives a **different answer on each verb**, and neither is the one the issue proposed.

## The guards are not broken

`installGenGuardV4` / `deleteGenGuardV4` are per-key **reordering** guards for one sender's stream (#2170): *"is this delta older than the last one I applied for this key?"* `stored == 0` means **"I have no ordering information"**, not "this delta is safe". With no prior peer install there is nothing to order, and refusing on gen-0 would break every legitimate first install and every legacy sender — which is precisely what the `gen == 0` arms exist for.

Ownership — *"may this peer touch a session this node owns and is forwarding for?"* — is a different question with different inputs, and it is answered one layer down in the helper, where local origin and local HA state both live. The issue's proposed fix (give the Go guards a local-ownership predicate) is at the wrong layer.

## The decisive check, resolved

> `synced_entry_allows_local_replace` may itself decline the replace; it is the one link in the trace not followed to ground.

**It declines — for INSTALL.** `upsert_synced_with_origin` (`session/install.rs:342`) refuses to clobber a local-origin entry when `allow_replace_local` is false, and that is false exactly when the incoming entry's owner RG is locally forwarding-active — the dual-primary case. So the headline claim is **refuted for the install half**.

## What survives: the DELETE half

`handle_delete_synced` called `sessions.delete(&key)` **unconditionally** — no origin check, no HA predicate. `SessionTable::delete` is a bare `remove_entry`.

| verb | ownership guard before this PR | dual-primary consequence |
|---|---|---|
| install | yes, and pinned by two cells | peer install refused, local session survives |
| delete | **none at any layer** | peer delete tears down a **live local** session mid-flight |

The asymmetry was invisible because the two verbs are guarded in different files at different layers — and delete is the **more damaging** half: a wrongful delete kills a live flow outright, where a wrongful install at least leaves a session installed.

## A claim my own mutation refuted before I published it

I searched for tests binding the install guard, found only positive `assert!(table.upsert_synced_with_origin(...))` call sites, and was about to report that the one mechanism preventing dual-primary overwrite was **unpinned**. Running the mutation instead of trusting the grep reds **two** cells — both assert on table state *after* the call, which a literal-only search of call lines cannot see. An absence claim from a grep needs a positive control; the mutation was it, and it cost 90 seconds to not publish a false claim.

## The fix

`handle_delete_synced` refuses when the existing entry is **local-origin AND** its owner RG is **locally forwarding-active** — the mirror of the install-side guard. `ha_state`/`now_secs` come from the dispatch arm, which already passes both to the sibling `UpsertSynced` arm.

Nothing below the guard runs on a refusal — not the NAT release, not the session-map delete, and **not** the `deleted_keys` record. #6457 records that key unconditionally so a stale flow-cache permit cannot outlive its table entry; here the entry *survives*, so the permit is still backed and invalidating it would be wrong in the one direction #6457 does not consider.

`PEER_DELETE_REFUSED_LOCAL_OWNED` → `ProcessStatus` → Go `PeerDeleteRefusedLocalOwned`. The refusal is silent by design (the condition produces one per closing flow, so a log line would be a storm exactly when the cluster is already in trouble), which makes the counter the **only** surface reporting it: nonzero means dual-primary. The helper's `UNSURFACED` allowlist (#6641/#7398) is what forced the field to be assigned rather than computed and dropped.

## Mutation matrix — each arm reds exactly its own cell

Each mutant `cargo build`-checked; restore verified byte-identical.

| # | Mutation | refusal | peer-synced arm | rg-inactive arm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | remove the guard | **FAIL** | ok | ok |
| M2 | drop the ORIGIN half | ok | **FAIL** | ok |
| M3 | drop the HA half | ok | ok | **FAIL** |
| M4 | drop the counter | **FAIL** | ok | ok |

M2 and M3 are the pair that matters — without them either half of the conjunction could be doing the other's work while the cell read as coverage.

## PR #9285 — logging: get syslog UDP and audit disk writes off the event reader (#9025) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9025-audit-write-offload`

Two synchronous, deadline-free I/O sites sat on the EventStream reader
goroutine. **That goroutine is not a logging goroutine** — the same `switch`
loop also carries `EventTypeSessionOpen/Update/Close` (**HA session sync**),
`EventTypeDrainComplete` (the **ISSU drain signal**) and `EventTypeFullResync`.

The contract was already in-tree and named this collateral by name.
`pkg/flowexport/routemask.go` (#3743) moved FIB lookups off this exact path
because they *"stall the event reader and every other callback behind it
(including the trace writer)"* — and **the trace writer it named as a victim was
itself still blocking.**

## Site 1 — the UDP exemption was a false comment

TCP/TLS armed a 4s deadline; UDP did a bare `conn.Write`, justified by a comment
repeated twice: *"UDP is connectionless and never blocks on Write."*

**This tree refutes that verbatim** in `pkg/flowexport/transport.go` (#4423 H07):
a connected-UDP Write *"can block indefinitely on a full socket send buffer"*.
Two modules, one syscall, opposite beliefs — and **UDP is the default protocol**,
so the unbounded path was the common one.

The comment was the proximate cause, not a footnote: a false rationale
re-justifies itself every time someone checks. Deleting it is as much of the fix
as arming the deadline.

`datagramWrite` is deliberately **separate** from `streamWrite` — they differ in
exactly what matters, partial writes. A stream write can leave a truncated
octet-counted frame that desyncs the collector (#3874's teardown); a datagram is
atomic. Sharing one function would carry that teardown into a path that cannot
need it.

A deadline expiry is **counted**: arming a deadline without counting trades a
silent stall for a silent drop, and a silent drop is worse — indistinguishable
from success. Only the timeout case is counted, so **#3478's accounting is
unchanged**, as the acceptance requires.

## Site 2 — audit disk writes ran inline

Both writers now hand off to a bounded queue drained by one dedicated goroutine,
dropping and counting on overflow — the #3478 shape, reused.

Three decisions worth flagging:

- **`LocalLogWriter.Send` was NOT made async.** Its error reports the write
  result, and #3478 M04 made that deliberate. That contract and "the write does
  not happen on your goroutine" cannot both hold. Existing cells red'd when I
  tried — a **prior decision speaking**, not stale tests — so only the event
  reader moved, via `SendFromEventReader`.
- **A retired writer REFUSES.** My first version regressed this: post-`Close`
  events were accepted into a channel with no reader and lost *with no drop

## PR #9286 — test/incus: attest BOTH cluster nodes, and say so when only one can be [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9044-exe-provenance-node1`

The harness executable-provenance readback read **node 0 only**, and the single-node assumption was written into the code as its own justification:

> And it reads NODE 0 only -- both nodes carry the same build after a `cluster-deploy`, so one readback is the attribution point for the run.

That is a property of one way of *invoking* the deploy, not of the system. `NODE ?= all` is a plain Makefile override and `cluster-setup.sh deploy` accepts `[0|1|all]`, so `make cluster-deploy NODE=0 && make test-failover` is two ordinary lines.

## Only one direction is dangerous

| Deploy scope | fw0 | fw1 | Row before this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NODE=1` | old | new | `MISMATCH` → VOID. **Fails safe.** |
| `NODE=0` | new | old | **clean `MATCH`** — for a gate that failed over onto the unattested node. |

An HA smoke **fails over by definition**, so the node a single-node attestation skips is the node the result depends on.

## Both of the issue's fix directions, because they answer different halves

- **Reading both nodes** is the *detector*, and it needs no cross-process state. A deploy-scope marker would have to be written at deploy time and read at gate time — it can go stale, and it only catches divergence a marker predicts, not a node manually restarted onto an old binary, a failed push, or a stale sbin symlink (#2162/#1917 shapes).
- **`exe_scope`** (`both` / `local-only` / `n/a`) is the *honesty* field, and it is what the issue rightly called the real gap: the row could not express *"I attested one of the two nodes this gate used"*. It matters exactly where the detector has nothing to say.

New fields: `node_peer`, `running_exe_sha256_peer`, `exe_scope`.

## The asymmetry inside the fix — the part to review

A peer running a **different** build → `MISMATCH` → VOID, same #2176 rule as a local mismatch.

A peer that is **unreadable** is **not** a void. `test-ha-crash`, `test-chained-crash` and `test-double-failover` force-stop a node and may legitimately leave it down when the gate ends, so voiding there would red exactly the gates whose job is to kill a node — the same mistake the existing exit-status rule refuses to make. That records `exe_scope=local-only` instead.

## Regression cells (hermetic)

The mock answers **per node** — the only shape in which a one-node and a two-node readback give different verdicts. A mock returning one sha for every node would pass under both the old and the new code.

- **10d** the finding: node 0 matches, peer differs → VOID + `MISMATCH`, peer sha on the row, void reason names the peer.
- **10e** the control that matters: both nodes on the build under test → still clean `MATCH`/`PASS`, `exe_scope=both`. *A guard that voided every cluster gate would satisfy 10d perfectly and be worthless.*
- **10f** peer unreadable → still `PASS`/`MATCH` with `exe_scope=local-only` — the arm proving the crash gates are not redded.
- **10g** `harness_exe_scope` as a table.

## Mutation matrix

Each mutant `bash -n`-checked; restore verified byte-identical.

| # | Mutation | Cells that red |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | never read the peer back | 10d (all four assertions) |
| M2 | never fold the peer into `exe_check` | 10d verdict + void reason |
| M3 | treat an UNREADABLE peer as a mismatch | 10f |
| M4 | `harness_exe_scope` always returns `both` | 10f + two 10g rows |

**M4 was first scored SURVIVED and that scoring was false** — the anchor never applied (shell quoting in my mutation helper), the assert failed, and the loop still printed a verdict for an unmutated file. That is "a mutation reported exit 0 and did nothing", in the *scoring harness* rather than the mutation. Re-run with the anchor verified (`grep -c MUTANT` = 1 before scoring), it kills three cells.

## PR #9287 — cluster: wait for the first heartbeat instead of sleeping for it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9110-flaky-timing`

## First: this PR fixes a REAL red on master, for every lane

`origin/master` carried an un-gofmt'd file — `pkg/logging/audit_write_offload_9025_test.go`, from `7d17fa542` — so **`TestTreeIsGofmtClean` (cmd/cli) failed on every repo-wide gate**.

It is the most flake-shaped red imaginable: an untouched package failing a gate. My own first reading was the wrong one (*"my edit raced the background gate in the same worktree"* — the self-inflicted shape #9110 describes), and I checked before claiming: `git show origin/master:<path> | gofmt -l` flags the **committed** content. The fix is pure alignment. Afterwards `gofmt -l ./pkg ./cmd ./test` is empty.

That #9110's own investigation turned up a real red being mistaken for noise is the issue's thesis demonstrated rather than argued.

## The reproduction the issue said nobody had run

| # | Load shape | Iterations | Failures |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | target test alone, 48 busy loops on 16 cores (3× oversubscription) | 20 each | **0** |
| 2 | target test alone, concurrent with a full repo-wide `go test ./...` | 60 cluster / 40 ra | **0** |
| 3 | **FULL package** binary, every test in normal order, 24 busy loops | 6 each | **0** |

~100+ iterations of each. **Neither flake reproduced.** Recorded as an unconfirmed hypothesis, explicitly *not* a clearance — the rate may be below 1-in-100. What it does mean is that a fix has to be justified by **reading** the test, not by inheriting "it's timing-sensitive".

### Two method errors, caught before they became claims

- Shapes 1 and 2 ran the target **alone**, next to load — which deletes the exact confound the difference is made of. "Passes alone / fails in suite" differs by *the rest of the package running first*, so an isolation re-run cannot see it by construction. Shape 3 is the corrected experiment.
- Shape 3's first attempt reported **96 failures** in `pkg/cluster`. All mine: a prebuilt test binary run from the repo root fails every AST/source-scanning cell, because `go test` sets CWD to the package directory and running the binary does not. Re-run with `cd pkg/cluster`: zero.

## What is fixed

```go
time.Sleep(2 * DefaultHeartbeatInterval)
if got := s.sent.Load(); got == 0 { t.Error("sender emitted no heartbeats") }
```

Nothing is waited **for**. The sleep is a guess at scheduler latency, and it silently converts the claim under test — *"a single StartHeartbeat leaves a LIVE sender"* — into *"the goroutine was scheduled AND emitted within 400 ms"*: a claim about the machine wearing the words of a claim about the code.

Now `waitForSenderProgress` — wait for the condition on a 30 s budget, and **dump every goroutine** when it expires. Same shape, budget and dump idiom as `waitForTeardownProgress` (#7970) already in this package, whose comment carries why the dump is not optional: the wait cannot separate a STARVED goroutine from a BLOCKED one, and the stack can. *Read the dump, do not re-run.*

Not weaker: it asserts liveness, which is what the test's name and body claim. Punctuality is a different assertion this test never actually made — it only appeared to.

**Mutation:** removing the sole `s.sent.Add(1)` call site reds the cell with its diagnostic and dump. The mutant **builds** (`go build`, not `go vet` — unreachable code is a vet diagnostic, and scoring a buildable mutant VOID silently drops matrix arms). Restore verified byte-identical.

## What is NOT fixed, deliberately

`TestRestartTimeoutNoGoodbyeNoReplacement` races a graceful `Withdraw` against a wedged restart **on purpose** — the race is the subject (#5094). A plausible mechanism is recorded (nothing orders the `Withdraw` against the 150 ms join timeout, and the test's own #8031 comment already notes the aggregate count cannot separate "the timeout path emitted" from "the reclaimer's legitimate goodbye observed early"), but **I did not observe it**. Rewriting a deliberate concurrency test against an unobserved mechanism is how a test gets narrowed into passing.

Item 2 of the issue (mark them known-flaky) is deliberately **not** done: a marker that lets a red be dismissed is a guard satisfiable by explaining reds away, which is the behaviour the issue exists to stop.

## Item 3, landed as documentation rather than left in the tracker

`docs/engineering-style.md` §"Time in tests" gains clause **4 — sleep-then-assert is clause 1 wearing clause 3's clothes** — and a new subsection **"Before you call a red a flake, DIFF — do not re-run"**: package-order (and the CWD trap that cost me 96 phantom failures), shared resources, unsound matches, the tree changing under a background gate, and the case the rule exists to prevent — *a red in a package your diff never touched can simply be REAL*.

Log: `docs/log/9110.md`.

## PR #9288 — nat: key the source-NAT flow and allocator on the routing domain (#9062) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9062-nat-routing-domain`

`SourceNatFlowKey` omitted the routing domain and `SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey`
omitted the routing instance, so two rule-sets scoped to **different** routing
instances referencing the **same** pool shared one flow-identity space and one
`PortAllocator`. `live_by_flow` then treated two distinct-VRF flows with an
identical 5-tuple as one flow and handed the second the first's translated tuple.

#7160 cannot recover it: the reverse index is inserted and probed with
`routing_domain: 0`, and the two-pass domain *preference* it uses has nothing to
prefer once both forward sessions carry the same reverse identity.

## The design constraint that decided the fix

My first attempt keyed on a **hash of the routing-instance name** — that name is
what `NatScopeCtx` carries, and the key is `Copy`. **It would have been wrong**,
for a reason found by reading the callers rather than the issue:

Three of the four sites that build this key — the release path, the HA-synced
reserve, the NAT64 arms — build it **from a `SessionKey`**, and `synced.rs` states
outright that its flow must be *"byte-identical to the active's SNAT-match
tuple"*. A scope derived differently at the match site would disagree, and **the
standby would fail to reserve the flow the active reserved** — turning a
cross-tenant collision into a sync defect.

So it is `SessionKey.routing_domain`, threaded through `NatScopeCtx`. Re-deriving
it at the match site is impossible anyway: `ingress_routing_domain` needs the
ingress VLAN id and the fabric-encoded zone, neither of which that site has.

## NAT64 pinned at 0, in both directions, through one constant

Its allocation path carries no routing domain. If its allocation and release
sites disagreed, **the release would silently stop matching and leak the pool
entry** — worse than the collision being fixed. Zero preserves today's behaviour
exactly; NAT64 pools are per-prefix, not the shared-pool multi-VRF shape.

`AddressOnlyReverseKey` is deliberately untouched: per #9075's calibration,
adding the domain there would **create** the cross-tenant hijack it prevents.

## The modularity gate, answered by splitting

The field pushed `source/mod.rs` from 1499 → 1534 LOC, past the 1500 [WATCH]
floor. `refactoring-audit-accepted.txt` would have been the cheap answer, but
that escape hatch is satisfiable by writing something false and there was a real
seam: the two keys move to `source/keys.rs` — **everything there is identity,
everything left behind is behaviour** — and the two keys this issue is about now
sit together, having had the same bug at two scopes. mod.rs is 1479.

## PR #9289 — config: read an elided routing-instance body instead of dropping it (#9055) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9055-routing-instance-keywords`

`compileRoutingInstances` hand-rolled a keyword switch implementing **three** of
the **eight** keywords its own admission helper names.

Shapes, dumped rather than inferred:

```
braced   [routing-instances] > [ri1] > [routing-options] > [static] > [route ...]
elided   [routing-instances] > [ri1 routing-options] > [static] > [route ...]
```

The keyword's **name** lands on the Keys tail and its **body** in Children — so
the property loop saw `static` / `ospf`, matched no case, and dropped it. Both
spellings are ACCEPTED through `configstore.CheckText`, no error, no warning:

| keyword | braced | elided |
|---|---|---|
| `routing-options` | `static=1` | **`static=0`** |
| `protocols` | `ospf=true` | **`ospf=false` AND `ifs=[ge-0/0/1.0]`** |

**The `protocols` row is not a plain drop — it is keyword theft.** The OSPF
area's interface token fell through to the `interface` case and was bound as a
VRF member. One accepted statement, two wrong outcomes: OSPF vanished *and* an
interface silently changed routing table — an **isolation** change, not only a
routing one.

## Re-dispatch, not a second reader

The elided body is wrapped in a synthesized node named after the keyword and fed
through the **existing** braced property loop. Adding elided cases instead is how
this defect started: #8787 created the hand-rolled loop and stopped at three of
eight. Two implementations of one keyword is how a switch drifts a second time.

## A guard that was inert, made exercisable rather than excused

A mutation making **every** keyword body-bearing **survived** the end-to-end
cells — inert for a specific reason: the Keys loop has already consumed a value
keyword's value before the property loop runs, and a value form carries no
Children to mis-route. It costs nothing today, and would cost something the
moment a value keyword could carry a body.

Rather than writing *"this mutation survives, correctly"* into the source, the
predicate is pinned as a unit where both directions can be driven. The mutant
dies there.

## Validation

Cells drive `configstore.CheckText` — the **commit gate** — never
`CompileConfig`: this is an operator-reachable divergence, and a `CompileConfig`
cell measures the tolerant Load/SyncApply channel while reporting on `commit`.

## PR #9290 — daemon: run the fail-closed shutdown actions before any blocking teardown [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9035-stop-budget`

## What must be true before the budget is gone

`TimeoutStopSec=20`, and systemd SIGKILLs there wherever the teardown has got to. Exactly **two** actions must have completed by then, because only they are FAIL-CLOSED:

1. **`rg_active` cleared** — this node stops forwarding.
2. **the Kea units stopped** (#6787) — it stops answering DHCP.

Everything else is best-effort cleanup whose loss costs telemetry, not correctness. Miss either and the peer promotes onto a segment this node is still serving: duplicate OFFERs from two lease databases, which is what #6787 exists to prevent.

## Why the ordering fix, and not the concurrency fix

The acceptance offered either. **Bounding the drain is necessary but not sufficient, and never could be** — it fixes the one subsystem that happened to be measured and leaves the next slow one to re-break the invariant.

The evidence is in the code's own history. The fail-closed block already carried the right intent in its comment — *"clear rg_active BEFORE stopping subsystems that may hang"* — but it was positioned relative only to the two subsystems anyone had worried about (VRRP, sync). So every teardown added **above** it over time — telemetry, feeds, RPM, SNMP, FRR, LLDP — silently moved ownership-release later in the budget, with nothing to notice. By `9bb0e8f11` it sat ~90 lines below the telemetry joins.

Both actions now run immediately after `stop(); wg.Wait()`, ahead of every teardown that can block. **That makes the invariant structural**: nothing added afterwards can push them past the budget, because they have already happened.

## The constraint that stops it moving even earlier

It cannot precede `stop(); wg.Wait()`. `desired = clusterPri || allVrrpMaster` (`rg_state.go`), so a live reconcile goroutine would re-drive `rg_active` back to TRUE after the clear — **#6530's retry doing exactly its job** against a clear it cannot distinguish from a spurious revert.

**Residual, stated rather than implied:** `wg.Wait()` is itself unbounded. Nothing in this issue's evidence points at it, and bounding a join whose goroutines are context-cancelled is a different change with a different risk.

## The drain is bounded too, because the two fail differently

Without the ordering, a bounded drain still delays ownership release by its bound × exporters. Without the bound, one wedged generation still burns the remainder of the budget *after* the fail-closed actions.

`telemetryDrainBudget` + `joinWithBudget` replace the untimed `flowWg.Wait()` / `ipfixWg.Wait()`. The constant is deliberately **not** tuned to today's cardinality — the acceptance rules that out ("a bare constant drifts the moment `collectorWriteTimeout` or the unit changes") — it is sized as the share of the budget telemetry may spend at most, which is what makes the drain **count-independent**.

## Mutation matrix, and the arm that SURVIVED first time

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | move the fail-closed block back below the telemetry joins | **FAIL** (ordering cell) |
| M2 | restore the unbounded `flowWg.Wait()` | **SURVIVED**, then FAIL — below |
| M3 | shrink the budget to 1 ns (instant give-up) | **FAIL** (bound + control) |
| M4 | unwire only the IPFIX leg | **FAIL** (call-site cell) |

**M2 survived its first scoring, and the reason is a rule I have applied all day and violated in my own cell.** `TestTelemetryJoinIsBounded9035` exercises `joinWithBudget` **directly**, so deleting the call site left it green — the cell still reached the helper by another route. *A bounded helper nothing calls is the same as no bound.* Fixed by adding `TestExporterTeardownsJoinThroughTheBudget9035`, which binds the **call sites**: both teardowns must join through the budget and neither may carry a bare `Wait()` on its generation WaitGroup. Re-scored, M2 reds with both messages; M4 then confirms the sibling leg is independently bound.

Every cell checks its **fixture** before asserting — a renamed teardown would otherwise make the ordering assertion vacuously true, which reads as a clean board for a file the guard never examined.

## Validation

- `go test ./...`: **73 packages, EXIT=0** (HA shutdown ordering has wide reach, so the full suite rather than a package list).
- `make cluster-deploy` + `make test-failover` — the smoke **reboots fw0**, so it exercises this shutdown path directly. Provenance read before the verdict: **`exe_check = MATCH`, `exe_scope = both`** (the peer-scope field added in #9044 earlier today), then **21 passed, 0 failed**.

## Not done

No cardinality cap and no parallel drain. The cap is what the acceptance warns about, and with the ordering in place neither is load-bearing for this failure — they would make the drain faster, not make the invariant hold.

## PR #9291 — routing: distinguish a whole-device VRF member from a unit-0 one (#9063) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9063-logical-unit-key`

A default-table IPv6 static route with a **link-local** next-hop silently failed
to install whenever its egress VLAN sub-unit shared a physical port with a
VRF-attached unit 0 — a routine dual-tenant trunk.

## The key is right; the consumers were wrong

`logicalUnitDeviceKey` collapses a unit with no vlan-id and unit number 0 to the
bare base — **correctly**: `ge-0-0-0` *is* the kernel device name for that unit.
What the key cannot express is:

```
interface ge-0/0/0;     # the PORT
interface ge-0/0/0.0;   # one UNIT
```

Both normalize to `ge-0-0-0`, and they mean different things to a base match. The
**raw reference** is where the distinction survives, and both consumers now read
it.

Consequence kept narrow, as the issue narrowed it: for a **global-unicast**
next-hop the missing entry is harmless (scopeless route, FRR resolves
recursively). Only a **link-local** next-hop is harmed — FRR rejects a scopeless
route, the static never installs, the prefix blackholes.

## Two sites, and the second is invisible from the first

`collectPrefixesForInterface` pulls prefixes **into** the VRF pool for the same
collapsed key. **A mutation reverting only that side survived every
default-table cell** — the tagged prefix is still in the default pool either way.
Observing it needs a **VRF-scoped** route: with the sibling wrongly in the pool
there are two link-local candidates, so the VRF's *own* static route stops
resolving too.

## Fixture notes, both of which cost a wrong result first

1. **A third IPv6 interface makes every arm read `""`** — the resolver returns
   nothing on an ambiguous link-local, so my first fixture failed its own positive
   control for a reason unrelated to the defect. One port, nothing else.
2. **The resolver keys VRF entries `vrf-blue`, not `blue`.** Filtering on the
   instance name returned nothing and read exactly like the defect.

Also: three probes produced no output because they did not compile (`Parse`
returns `[]ParseError`), and I read "no output" as "no result". **A build failure
and an empty result are different states.**

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| base match fires for any claim (the exclusion defect) | killed by 2 cells |
| inclusion side back to the normalized key | killed **by the VRF-scoped cell** |
| every claim recorded as whole-device | killed by 2 cells |

## PR #9292 — assurance: four gates that reported a clean board for unexamined subjects [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9052-assurance-gates`

Four gates, one acceptance criterion: **a gate that did not examine its subject must not report a clean board** — proved by mutating the production **subject**, not by deleting the gate.

All four claims re-verified at head first. Item 4's count had drifted 310 → **318**; the other three were exact.

## 1. `test-shim-run` was a prerequisite of nothing

The only behavioural coverage of the XDP shim's control flow was reachable solely by someone remembering its name — the #7766 shape.

**Not made a prerequisite of `make test`**, deliberately: it needs root, and a default gate that fails without privilege is unusable. The fix is a pair — `make test-root` as the named root-capable aggregate, **and** `make test` now printing what it did *not* examine. Silence was the defect. The announcement also states why the #1864 verifier gate is no substitute: two distinct WRONG fixes of #7494 both pass it.

## 2. cold-path-flooder, and a census blind by construction

44 tests reached by nothing — outside both cargo workspaces, no root `Cargo.toml`, `make test-rust` pinned elsewhere, undeclared in `HARNESSES.unreached`. Wired exactly like the sibling out-of-workspace crate `newflow-gen`, whose pattern already existed one target away. **43 passed, 1 ignored** on the first run: all green, and nobody could have known.

The Rust `#[ignore]` census could not see the crate **by construction** — `SCAN_DIRS` named only the two dataplane crates, so it reported a clean board over a population it had never looked at. Widened, **it immediately redded on the bare `#[ignore]` the issue predicted**. That red is the positive control for the widening; the marker is now declared.

## 3. A merge criterion citing CI that does not exist

*"Squash merge once CI is green"* was **vacuously satisfiable**: `.github/` holds only `instructions/`, and the Makefile says there is no CI twice. Replaced with the actual developer-invoked gate list and when to run each — including the two that get skipped and whose subjects nothing else examines (`sudo make test-root`, `make test-failover`). A criterion that cannot be unsatisfied is not a criterion.

## 4. The Go skip census — and what it found on its first run

`go test ./...` prints `ok` for a package whose cells all **skipped**; the summary for "everything passed" and "nothing ran" is byte-identical. 318 call sites, invisible to every gate, while censuses already existed for Rust, shell and python.

The privilege bucket is split by **direction**, and the split *is* the finding:

- **26** cells skip because privilege is **absent**
- **10** skip because it is **present**

**No single run examines all 36.** Running as root does not close the gap — it *swaps* which subjects go unexamined. A single "root-gated" total hides that, and makes the obvious remedy look like a fix when it is a trade.

**The load-bearing design decision is the `unparsed` bucket.** `t.SkipNow()` (no message by construction) and non-literal messages are **reported with their own floor**, not dropped. A census that silently drops what it cannot read is blind exactly where somebody wrote something unusual — and the failure mode is not a wrong number, it is a number that *looks complete*. This is the #9088 lesson applied ahead of time: `unmeasured` is not neutral, and neither is `unparsed`.

It deliberately does **not** judge whether a skip is justified. No marker convention exists on Go skips, so that verdict would be a guess off message prose, and a census whose verdict is a guess trains people to argue with it.

## Mutating the SUBJECT

| # | Mutation of the production subject | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | inject a new `t.Skip` into a real `pkg/config` test | **FAIL** — 318 → 319, delta named |
| M2 | remove "root" from an existing skip message | **FAIL twice** — one bucket shrank, another grew: the classifier is bound in both directions |
| M3 | widen the ignore-census scan to the flooder crate | **FAIL** on the bare `#[ignore]` — the census failing on a subject it had never examined |

## Three of my own errors, caught by the work

1. **My selftest's positive controls passed for the wrong reason.** `ROOT` resolved one directory short, the census script was missing, and every `rc != 0` control fired on the *missing file* — three false PASSes. The **message** assertions beside them caught it: an rc-only control cannot tell "the gate rejected the fixture" from "the gate never ran".
2. **The census silently read the wrong tree.** It hard-`cd`'d to its own repo root, so a fixture-directed run scanned the REAL tree and reported its 315 sites while the selftest asserted against a 5-site fixture. `GO_SKIP_ROOT` makes the scan root explicit.
3. **My selftest matched exact column spacing** — itself the unsound-match shape this census exists to find. Now whitespace-tolerant.

## PR #9293 — docs: correct two cost-path claims, and record why the #4800 run is blocked [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9053-flow-cost-bounds`

The cohort's requested outcome is **the measurement, not a fix**. Attempting it produced a more useful result than a number would have: it is **blocked**, for three specific reasons, none of which is the harness's wiring — and even unblocked it speaks to only **three of the seven** sites.

## The measurement is BLOCKED, and each blocker was read at source

Off-cluster everything passes: analyzer unit tests OK, `newflow-gen` 13/13, harness `--dry-run` resolves every host, target and analyzer. The blockers are all in the **shared cluster's committed state**.

1. **The client cannot source from the prefix the pool rule matches.** Committed `rule pool-snat` matches `source-address 10.0.61.240/28`; the LAN host is `10.0.61.102`, outside it — so its traffic takes the sibling interface-mode rule and the pool sees **zero allocations**, the harness's first named refusal. `newflow-gen` has no client source-address option: `--bind` (main.rs `:79`/`:341`) is the **sink's**, and the client calls `TcpStream::connect_timeout` (`:296`) with no local bind. Read at source — an absence claim from `--help` is a claim about the help text.
2. **The pool holds 1000 ports** (`172.16.80.7/32`, `range 30000 to 30999`) against a documented **5000–80000 flows/sec** sweep — two orders of magnitude short. Port exhaustion is another named refusal ("a capacity ceiling, not a lock ceiling"), so this refuses cells rather than corrupting a number. That is the failure mode to want, and it is why **no figure is quoted anywhere**.
3. **The default WAN target is not an instance on this cluster.** `172.16.80.200` answers from the wire (fw0 pings it) but is not an incus instance on `loss:`. Surmountable — `xpf-mouse-target` holds `172.16.80.201` on the same VLAN-80 subnet, and `TARGET_IP` is overridable.

**Blockers 1 and 2 need a change to the shared cluster's committed configuration** — a wider pool and a rule matching the generator's source — which affects every other lane's smokes. Reported rather than done unilaterally.

## Even unblocked, this harness attributes 3 of the 7 sites

Recorded because a run reported against all seven would be exactly the trap the harness's own header warns about.

| Site | This harness |
|---|---|
| NAT allocator `live` mutex | **attributed** |
| `replicate_session_upsert` | **attributed** |
| `publish_shared_session` | **attributed** |
| `publish_live_session_entry` (≤6 serial `bpf()`) | not attributed — no per-syscall counter |
| `remove_shared_session` (3 nested mutexes) | not attributed — CLOSE path; the sweep drives opens |
| `snapshot` + `replay_synced_sessions` | not attributed — a reconcile path the sweep never enters |
| source-NAT `matches` O(R) | not attributed — one rule-set of 2 rules; R is not varied |
| bulk HA import | not attributed — no peer bulk transfer during the sweep |

An unblocked run answers *which of three synchronization sites saturates first* — what #2852 Phase-2 is gated on — and nothing about the other five.

## The two doc defects, fixed

**A — a comment wrong twice.** The owner-RG bucket-walk comment said the walk runs *"on the control thread"* and that the bucket count *"is not enforced today"*. Both false at head: `remove_shared_session` runs from `session_delta.rs:520`/`:530`, **twice per Close delta on WORKER threads**, and **#8486 enforces the bound at the filing** with a counter for declined filings. A comment asserting a threading property that is false is how the next reader concludes a lock is uncontended and stops measuring it.

**B — a shipped signal called missing.** The proposed "O(1)-per-worker bulk-invalidation signal" is `SESSION_DELETE_DROP_EPOCH` (#8586), keyed on refused **deletes** rather than queue depth on purpose (depth-keyed pressure "would fire continuously through normal traffic and reconcile nothing"). No repo text called it missing, so the defect is **discoverability** — it lives only in source. Now named in the document a cost review reaches first, alongside `replicate_session_delete_repairing`'s measured 0 repaired-drops across 30,786 refusals.

## What landed instead of a number

- Both doc corrections.
- The blocked-attempt record replacing *"**Not yet performed.** The steps below are the owed procedure"* — which implied the only missing ingredient was someone's time.
- `HARNESSES.unreached` now names the blockers, so the census entry carries the reason rather than sending the next reader to rediscover it.
- **No per-connection figure**, which is that document's own standing rule.

Item 3 of the issue is gated on the measurement and stays closed.

Log: `docs/log/9053.md`.

Closes #9053

## PR #9294 — daemon: count an sshd validation failure on the retry path (#9073) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9073-sshd-validate-counter`

The `sshd -t` validation-failure arm logged and fell through **without touching
any counter**, so under a persistent validation failure the count stayed **flat**
while the retry owner ran and failed every pass — precisely the distinction the
counters were built to make. Their own contract, where they are declared:

> whether the retry owner is RUNNING and failing (count climbing) or wedged
> (count flat)

## The obvious fix was wrong, and an existing cell said so

My first version called `noteSSHDReloadResult(err)`. That red
`TestReassertRedrivesTheOwedSSHDReload6800`, which states its reason:

> a validation failure is not a reload ATTEMPT, so it must not inflate the reload
> failure count beyond the one the apply already recorded

**A prior decision speaking, and a correct one.** A failing *reload* means systemd
or sshd rejected a config that **passed** validation — a different fault from one
that never got that far. Folding them would have bought this issue's distinction
by **deleting** #6800's.

## Three states need three signals

| state | `sshd` | `sshd-validate` |
|---|---|---|
| wedged (owner not running) | flat | flat |
| reload failing | climbing | flat |
| validation failing | flat | **climbing** |

Exported as a new **series** on the existing per-service map rather than a new
accessor — the metric is per-service-labelled, so it reaches the same Prometheus
surface with no new plumbing.

It deliberately does **not** touch `sshdReload`: the debt is already outstanding
(this arm only runs when `sshdReloadOwed()` is true) and nothing was reloaded, so
nothing is paid and nothing needs re-latching. Purely the missing observation.

Severity stays **Low** as filed — the operator was not blind (the owed gauge stays
true, a WARN and an ERROR fire every pass). Only the metric channel was.

## A fixture note

All three cells failed on their first run — **including the two asserting
behaviour that already worked**, because `reassertServiceReloadDebtOnce` returns
early without an `applySem`. Those rows are what caught it; a cell testing only
the new thing would have read the early return as the fix not working.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| validation arm counts nothing (the original defect) | killed |

## PR #9295 — Refuse SYN-cookie replies to L2 group/broadcast frames [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9111-syn-cookie-l2-group-dst`

Closes #9111

## The defect

`write_reply_eth_header` copies the inbound L2 **destination** into the reply's own L2 **source** (`out[6..12] = frame[0..6]`), so a TCP reply built for a frame addressed to a multicast/broadcast MAC egresses with a group/broadcast **source** MAC. Switches learn that address against the firewall's port, or MAC-flap and err-disable it — a broadcast-domain-wide availability event any unauthenticated host on an attached segment can drive.

#3204 established exactly this and guarded **one** of three reply builders (`build_reject_rst_frame`), with a 12-line comment naming the hazard. `build_syn_cookie_syn_ack_frame` and `build_syn_cookie_ack_rst_frame` were never given it — and those two are armed precisely when SYN-flood cookies are on and the zone is over `attack-threshold`, i.e. during the DDoS the feature exists to survive.

## The guard moved to the choke point instead of being copied twice

A whole-tree census found `parse_tcp_reply_source` has exactly **three** non-test callers, and all three are the reply builders. Putting the refusal there means a fourth reply builder *inherits* it rather than having to remember it — which is the property the per-site version lacked, and the reason this defect existed at all. The old per-site check becomes a pointer note so #3204's history stays attached to the leg it was written for.

**The move was verified not to be a regression as well as a fix:** mutating the guard away reds the two **pre-existing** #3204 cells alongside the three new ones, so the original leg is still covered through the new location.

## Validation

Two complementary mutants, each verified to **build** before scoring, each restored by `cp` with the restore verified by reading the file back:

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | guard removed | reds **5** cells (2× #3204 + 3× #9111); both unicast controls stay green |
| M2 | guard fires on every frame | reds the two unicast **controls** and nothing else |

M2 is the one that matters. This defect is reachable only through the SYN-cookie challenge, so a guard that refused everything would "fix" the finding by disabling the feature — only the control row tells the two apart.

## HA wire

Nothing moves: no session key, no wire struct. This decides whether a synthesized reply frame is emitted at all.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` (5401-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed) **and** `go test ./...` whole-tree.

## PR #9296 — grpcapi: assert that ClearCounters is node-local by design (#9074) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9074-clear-counters-scope`

**No behaviour change.** The issue's own analysis is that the parity argument
does not carry, and it is right — so what was missing is the assertion, not a
fanout.

## Why no fanout

- **Sessions are REPLICATED**, so a local-only session clear is undone by sync —
  the stated reason for the session fanout (#2468). **Counters are not
  replicated**, so a node-local clear is self-consistent and complete. The two
  are not analogous.
- **The grammar already disclaims scope**, in both CLIs, byte-identically:
  *"takes no scope (per-scope clear is not supported)"*, and
  `ClearCountersRequest` has no node field.
- A fanout would require **widening `fabricAllowedUnaryMethods`** — which #9059
  has just argued must be done deliberately, per method, with its own rationale,
  not as a side effect. Trading a documented node-local scope for a wider fabric
  surface is a bad exchange for a behaviour nothing has asked for.

## What was actually missing

Behaviour and help text agree, and **nothing asserted the agreement** — so a
future "make it consistent with ClearSessions" change would have looked like a
tidy-up. The issue's acceptance asks for exactly this: *"a cell asserting the
documented scope, since today's behaviour and today's help text already agree."*

The cells assert the handler does not dial a peer (read from **source** — a
behavioural assertion would need a two-node harness to prove **nothing was
sent**, an absence a probe cannot establish), that both CLIs still disclaim
scope, and — the part that keeps the reasoning honest — that **ClearSessions
still does fan out**. If that stops, "sessions are replicated, counters are not"
no longer explains the asymmetry and this file is *wrong* rather than stale.

If node scoping is wanted later, the shape is `node <local|peer|both>` in the
grammar, not a silent fanout — and this cell should be updated in that change
rather than deleted.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| add a peer fanout to `ClearCounters` | killed |
| grammar drops the no-scope wording | killed |

Plus a positive control, so a stale source extraction fails rather than
reporting a clean board over an empty string.

`go test ./...` green.

Closes #9074

## PR #9299 — userspace-dp: carry the quoted GRE discriminator into embedded ICMP keys (#9031) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9031-embedded-gre-discriminator`

Every embedded-ICMP lookup key set `discriminator: Default::default()` —
`TunnelDiscriminator::None`. A live GRE session carries `Unkeyed`, `Keyed(k)` or
`Pptp(handle)`, and `SessionKey` derives `Hash/Eq` **including** that field
(#7188), so **every exact index probe for a GRE quote missed**.

An ICMP error for a translated accelerated GRE tunnel therefore found no NAT
state: the outer destination and quoted source could not be restored and no
usable signal reached the endpoint. GRE carries bulk payload, so small probes
stay healthy while large traffic **stalls after an MTU reduction**, and ordinary
unreachable/traceroute signalling is lost. HA-imported sessions inherit the same
mismatch, because sync correctly preserves the discriminator.

#8103 threaded the discriminator through the five *transform* helpers and pinned
them — those cover transforms of an existing key, not a key **produced from a
quote**, which is this gap.

## Fix

Both embedded parsers read it with `gre_transit_discriminator` — the **same
extractor the transit path uses**, reused rather than re-spelled, because a
second parser for one wire format is where two readings of the same bytes
silently diverge.

Bounded by the **quoted datagram's declared end**, not the backing frame (the
#2361 rule applied to the quote), and **fail-closed by construction**: every
failure path returns `Unparseable`, a class distinct from `Unkeyed` that equals
no live session's discriminator, so a malformed quote misses rather than
wildcarding across tunnels — met by the type, not by a check anyone could forget.

`nat64_match` is deliberately left at `None`, with the reason in-line: NAT64
translates the protocol across families, so a quoted GRE header on one side
names no tunnel identity the other side's session carries.

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutant | Result | Killed by |
|---|--------|--------|-----------|
| M1 | revert the v4 parser | **KILLED (8)** | eight parser cells |
| M2 | revert the v6 parser only | **KILLED** | the IPv6 PTB cell |

## PR #9300 — Recover a fragment's real protocol before the screens [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9114-fragment-protocol-sentinel`

Closes #9114

## The defect

`userspace-xdp` substitutes `PROTO_FRAGMENT_NO_L4` (255) for a non-first fragment's protocol before `parse_l4`, because such a fragment carries no L4 header. That sentinel rode `meta.protocol` into `extract_screen_info`, which seeded `info.protocol` from the caller and never re-derived it — so every protocol-keyed screen was evaluated against a protocol that was not the packet's.

## Miss, not over-match — censused before changing anything

Those are different defects with different fixes, so I enumerated all **eight** protocol-keyed sites first:

| behaviour on the sentinel | sites | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| tests for the real protocol → **never fires** | `check_icmp_fragment` (`stateless.rs:232`), `icmp-flood` (`zone.rs:297`), `udp-flood` (`zone.rs:305`) | **the defect** |
| `== PROTO_TCP` / `!= PROTO_TCP` → **declines** | `stateless.rs:46`, `mod.rs:846`, `:1127`, `:1263`, `extract.rs:425` | correct — no L4 header to screen |

Nothing over-matched; three screens silently did not run. (`check_tcp_flag_screens` also carries its own explicit non-first-fragment guard immediately below its protocol test.)

## The two halves need different sources

- **IPv4**: the protocol byte at header offset 9, already length-validated.
- **IPv6**: the walk `break`s out on a non-first fragment *before* it would assign `nexthdr`, so `nexthdr` is still 44 (Fragment). The real protocol is the **fragment header's own NextHdr** byte — present on every fragment, which is the field's purpose — and in bounds because the fragment offset at `offset + 2`/`+3` was just read.

Both are **gated on the sentinel**, so an ordinary packet is untouched and a caller that legitimately knows better (a decapsulated inner packet) is not overridden.

## Why the existing fixtures could not catch it

The pre-existing fragment cells pass the **real** protocol as the caller argument — a packet shape the shim never emits for a non-first fragment. The new cells pass the sentinel, as the shim does.

## Validation

Three mutants forming an **orthogonal matrix** — each kills exactly one cell and no other; each verified to *build* before scoring, each restore verified by reading the file back:

| # | mutation | reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | v4 recovery removed | v4 cell only |
| M2 | v6 recovery removed | v6 cell only |
| M3 | recovery ungated | pass-through control only |

## HA wire

Nothing moves — no session key, no wire struct. This corrects an input to the screen evaluators.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` (5404-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed) **and** `go test ./...` whole-tree.

## PR #9301 — daemon: absence of a fence barrier is not proof of fencing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9259-fence-verdict-typed`

#9036's chain was: *the barrier is gone → the wait returns nil → nil means applied.* PR #9247 removed **one** way for the barrier to be gone. The final link — **absence of a barrier read as proof of fencing** — was untouched, and two routes still reached it:

1. **NeverArmed** — a `(rgID, reqID)` for which no barrier was ever registered.
2. **VerdictConsumed** — the first waiter deletes the entry after reading it, deliberately, so a later wait cannot re-read a stale verdict (#6177). A second wait found an empty slot.

Both returned `nil`, and `sync_failover.go` sends `failoverAckApplied` **exactly when the wait returns nil**. The peer promoted on no evidence of a fence.

## The baseline was checked BEFORE the default was changed

`nil` → error is only safe if `b == nil` is not the normal path:

- `handleRemoteFailover` calls `WaitFailoverApplied` **only after** `OnRemoteFailover` returned nil — the error path acks and returns at `sync_failover.go:434`, so no wait runs.
- That handler **arms** the barrier before `ManualFailover` and disarms only on the error path, where it returns the error and again no wait runs.
- The supersede path deliberately leaves a **failed** barrier rather than none.

So on every path reaching the wait for a live request, a barrier is armed. The nil arm is reached only by the two abnormal routes.

## The fix

Both routes are errors now → the ack downgrades to `failed` → the peer **holds**. Asymmetric on purpose: holding costs a failover attempt; the previous default cost the one-owner-per-RG property (#5640).

They are **distinguished** (`ErrFailoverNeverArmed` vs `ErrFailoverVerdictConsumed`) because they send an operator to different places — a stale/duplicate request id versus a retry racing its own first attempt. That needs a consumed-request ledger, bounded with oldest-out eviction. **An eviction degrades the diagnostic, never the safety property**: an evicted key reports as never-armed — still an error, still a downgrade, and the more conservative reading. Pinned by its own cell, because a bounded structure silently changing an operator-facing reason is what gets discovered during an outage.

## Two existing cells redded, and neither was stale

Both were read before either was touched. In both, the property the cell actually pins **survives**; only an incidental half changed.

**`TestFailoverActuation_UnarmedRGIsNoop`** claimed *"resolving is a no-op **and** a wait returns immediately with no error"*, as if the second followed from the first. It does not — *"every ordinary demotion"* is true of **resolving** and false of **waiting**, since an ordinary local demotion never calls `waitFailoverActuated` at all. **Split**: the resolve-side no-op is kept and now asserted directly; the wait-side half is inverted into a named sibling with the reason attached.

**`TestFailoverActuationBarrier_DisarmedRequestReportsNoFence`** says in its own comment that *"the handler is not on the ack path here"*, and its subject is that the wait must return **immediately** rather than burn the timeout. `want nil` was incidental. **The timing assertion is kept verbatim**; only the value changed.

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutation | Cells that red |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | restore `return nil` on a nil barrier | **4** — both routes, the disarm cell, the ledger cell |
| M2 | drop the consumed-ledger note | **2** |
| M3 | remove the eviction bound | **1** |

Each mutant `go build`-checked; restore verified byte-identical.

## Validation

- `go test ./...`: **73 packages, EXIT=0**.
- `make cluster-deploy` + `make test-failover` — this changes the failover **ack path**, so the smoke exercises it directly. Provenance read before the verdict: **`exe_check = MATCH`, `exe_scope = both`**, then **21 passed, 0 failed**.

## Why I did this rather than reassigning it

It is the residual I split out of #9036 myself, and it stayed open across five status exchanges while I described it as "available to reassign" — **in messages, never on the artifact**. Same lesson #9036 taught: a statement that lives only in a message is not a statement about the work.

Branch: `fix/9067-ddns-ttl-compare`

Two defects with different permanence, both silent — no error, no warning, and
`show` reports the **configured** TTL throughout.

**Cloudflare (permanent).** `UpsertLease` returned on a CONTENT match alone, so a

explicit `request system dynamic-dns update` force latch — re-entered the same
early return. `cfRecord.TTL` was already parsed: the datum was available and
simply unread, while the Route 53 sibling has always compared both.

**Change detection (delay, every backend).** `changed := addr != rt.lastAddr` did
not treat a TTL edit as a change, so nothing republished promptly on ANY backend
— including Route 53, whose own comparison is correct. Convergence waited for the
24h forced-refresh floor.

Both defeat the same operator intent, which is what makes the delay a defect and
not just latency: a shorter TTL is bought precisely so a change propagates soon,
and the harm lands later — at the planned renumber it was bought for.

Eight backends; only **two** do a read-compare-skip at all:

- `backend_route53.go` — `live.found && live.ttl == ttl && sameValueSet(...)`. Correct.
- `backend_cloudflare.go` — content only. The defect.

The other six (`bind`, `duckdns`, `dyndns2`, `generic`, `http`, `rfc2136`) do no
live-state read before writing, so the TTL rides the wire op every time and none
can exhibit this. Checked by **reading each `UpsertLease`**, not inferred from TTL
mention counts — `rfc2136` mentions TTL fourteen times and always sends.

So the class has exactly two members and one was already right. The shape "three
do X and one does not" is not what this turned out to be.

**Cloudflare:** compare TTL alongside content. A content match with a differing
TTL PATCHes *that* row — falling through to the POST would create a **duplicate**
at the name, worse than the un-propagated TTL.

**Change detection:** `surfaceAState.lastTTL` records the last published TTL; a
delta marks the scope changed. Two details are load-bearing, and I got both wrong
first:

2. **Store the NORMALISED TTL.** `lastTTL == 0` means "not published in this

## PR #9303 — userspace-dp: bump the neighbour insert generation from the bulk paths (#9071) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9071-neighbor-generation`

The three per-key insert paths bumped `insert_generation`; the two **bulk** paths
bumped only the shard epoch. The consumer is #7156's poll-loop gate — a full
resolution pass runs only when `neigh_generation != binding.last_neigh_generation`
— so a neighbour learned by the netlink bulk sync or the #1787 RX source-MAC
transit learn never woke that pass, and its buffered packet waited for the ≤50 ms
recheck backstop.

**The epoch and the generation answer different questions.** The epoch
invalidates cached flows resolved to one shard; the generation tells the poll
loop a resolution pass is worth running at all. Neither substitutes for the other.

## The larger half is the false rationale

`neigh_schedule.rs` said the recheck covers *"**the one case** that gate cannot
see: the STATIC `forwarding.neighbors` map."* There were **two dynamic cases** it
also could not see. A reader tuning `RESOLUTION_RECHECK_INTERVAL_NS` upward on
the strength of that sentence would have converted a bounded 50 ms delay on two
live paths into a **real drop**.

Severity stays **Low** and the issue's refutations are kept, not quietly dropped:
the packet is **not** lost (`next_due_for_pending` arms every key at ≤50 ms
against an 800 ms–2 s pending timeout), and this is **not** the primary
resolution path.

## The gating condition took two attempts, and the wrong one was subtle

My first version reused the epoch's `changed_shards` set. **Wrong**:
`changed_shards` marks a key whose **MAC changed**, and a brand-new key has no
prior MAC to differ from — so a freshly resolved neighbour, *the exact case the
poll loop is waiting for*, would not have bumped.

Before that I bumped **unconditionally**, and the narrowness cell caught it: an
empty netlink sync would fire the gate every sweep — #7156's optimisation removed
while looking like a fix. **A counter that advances on every call carries the same
information as one that never advances.**

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| `bulk_replace_neighbors` stops bumping (the original defect) | killed by 3 cells |
| `learn_pair_if_changed` stops bumping | killed by 2 cells |
| bump unconditionally | killed by 2 cells |

Both cells carry a positive control establishing the counter moves at all, so a
flat reading is a property of the call under test rather than of the fixture.

Full `cargo test` green; `go test ./...` green.

Closes #9071

## PR #9304 — fsatomic: give rotation a persistence class, a primitive and a canary [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9057-rotate-durability`

Rotating a generation set (`x` → `x.1` → `x.2`) mutates the **directory**, not a file's contents, and none of the four sites that do it fsynced the containing directory.

**They did not get it wrong because four authors were careless.** The #1894 taxonomy defines three classes and every one is over *replace-a-file* writes; `pkg/fsatomic` exported no rotation primitive; and the canary that enforces the taxonomy only ever looked at `os.WriteFile`. That is what a missing class looks like from below — not one bug repeated four times, but **the same gap found four times**, two of them in no review report at all.

## Baseline verified before writing anything

- Canary: **0** occurrences of `Rename`, **8** of `WriteFile` (positive control — the file *is* being read).
- fsatomic's exported surface confirmed to contain **no rotation primitive**.
- All four sites present (line numbers had drifted from the issue).

## What landed

**The class** — a `DurableNamespace` row in `docs/engineering-style.md` and the fsatomic README, with the honest consequence bound: unclean shutdown only; lost is the newest seconds of lines plus possibly the generation numbering — **not** corruption, no file contents destroyed.

**The primitive** — `fsatomic.RenameDurable`, whose doc says when *not* to use it (a shift loop through it issues N fsyncs where one suffices) and which syncs **both** directories on a cross-directory move, because syncing one of two looks like a durable move and is half of one.

**The canary** — `TestNoUnsyncedRename`, keyed on the function's **behaviour**: a bare `os.Rename` is accepted in a function that also reaches `SyncDir`/`RenameDurable`, which is what a correct rotation looks like.

### Why behaviour and not a path allowlist — this paid immediately

My first allowlist guessed nine function names for the `pkg/upgrade` staged promotions. **The canary's own fixture check (`allowedHits == 0`) caught that every one was wrong**, and the sweep then showed it did not matter: those sites already call `SyncDir` in-function, so the behaviour rule passes them *because they are correct*. The allowlist shrank from nine invented entries to **two real ones**. A path allowlist would have been nine wrong entries that also silently stopped checking those functions.

**The two survivors, each with a real reason:**
- `configstore/journal::Journal.maybeRotateLocked` — the fsync is deliberately in the **caller** with `j.mu` released; doing it in-function reintroduces **#4829**, where a Tail reader blocks for the writer's whole fsync. Found by reading the code rather than assuming the canary was right.
- `ddns::quarantineBadState` — one-shot quarantine move, idempotent on retry.

**The four sites**, each with the error policy that site already uses: the two log writers count-and-log like their sibling shift failures; `monitor.go` returns, because every other rotation failure there returns and a caller writing onto an un-rotated file is what its rotate exists to prevent; `journal.go`'s `SyncDir` moves out from behind an early return on a file-sync failure — it *knew* about the helper and skipped it on an error path, and those are independent durability facts.

## The per-site cell needs a seam, and that is the point

> …*including* when the preceding file sync fails (that is the `journal.go` shape and an outcome-only assertion cannot see it)

**An fsync leaves no artifact.** You cannot inspect the filesystem afterwards and tell whether a directory was synced, so the only way to assert it ran is to observe the call — hence a `syncDir` seam mirroring the `syncFile` one beside it. The cell requires the dir sync to run **and** the file-sync error to still be reported (running it must not *swallow* the data-sync error). Its control requires the dir sync on the **healthy** path too, so a fix that ran it only on the error path fails.

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutation | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | drop `locallog.go`'s SyncDir | **FAIL** — canary names both renames in `LocalLogWriter.rotate` |
| M2 | drop `trace.go`'s SyncDir | **FAIL** — `TraceWriter.rotate` |
| M3 | drop `monitor.go`'s SyncDir | **FAIL** — `cli::rotateTraceFile` |
| M4 | restore `journal.go`'s early return | **FAIL** — the per-site cell, with its reason |

**M1–M3 scored VOID on the first attempt and that scoring was discarded, not banked** — deleting the call left two imports unused, so the mutant did not compile, and a mutant that does not build is not a survivor. Re-run with the imports referenced and the call removed, all three kill.

## Validation

`go test ./...`: **73 packages, EXIT=0**. `gofmt` clean. **No `make test-failover`** — nothing here touches cluster, VRRP, session-sync or failover; the changed packages are `fsatomic`, `logging`, `cli` and `configstore/journal`. Stated rather than silently skipped.

## PR #9305 — ipsec: feed the SA-listing parser stdout alone on both call paths (#9068) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9068-listsas-stdout-only`

Filed as **UNRESOLVED (reachability)**, not a confirmed defect. This closes it by
**removing the question rather than answering it** — which the issue itself names
as the cheaper and strictly better option.

## What was established

One parser, two exec channels. `GetSAStatus` used a stdout-only buffer with the
explicit comment *"the parser needs stdout alone"*. `liveConnNames` routed
through `CombinedOutput` — stderr folded in — on the security-critical
**teardown** path, justified in place by *"parseSAOutput ignores any unrecognized
stderr lines CombinedOutput may fold in"*. **Asserted, never tested.**

The issue's executed tolerance matrix: a whole stderr line before the header
preserves the name; a stderr line containing `": #"` yields a spurious extra name
(harmless); CRLF is tolerated; and a **mid-line splice into the IKE header LOSES
the real name** (`vpn-corp` → `vpn-cowarning`). True for whole lines, false in
the one direction that matters.

**A lost name is a fail-open.** `terminateRemovedConns` iterates
`for name := range live`, so a removed connection absent from `live` is neither
terminated nor entered into `pendingTerminate` — and `prevConnNames` has already
advanced past it, so the teardown-debt record #6542 exists to keep is never
created. A deleted VPN's SA keeps forwarding under an unloaded configuration,
with no retry and no debt.

## Which of the two was right

That was the question worth answering first, and the answer was already in the
code: `GetSAStatus`'s own comment. Whether swanctl can actually splice mid-line
on a *successful* listing remains unestablished — and the fix does not depend on
it.

`runSwanctlSplit` returns stdout and stderr separately; `liveConnNames` uses it
and puts **stderr alone** in its error, matching `GetSAStatus`. `GetSAStatus` is
refactored onto the same helper rather than keeping its inline copy — two
spellings of one exec discipline is how the divergence happened.

The **non-parsed** calls (`--load-all`, `--terminate --ike`) deliberately keep
`CombinedOutput`: their only consumer is an error message, and folding stderr in
is what makes it useful. The wiring guard asserts that split in both directions.

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutant | Result | Killed by |
|---|--------|--------|-----------|
| M1 | revert `liveConnNames` to the combined seam | **KILLED (3)** | ParsesStdoutOnly, ErrorCarriesStderr, wiring guard |
| M2 | `scSplit` folds stderr into stdout | **KILLED (2)** | ParsesStdoutOnly, ErrorCarriesStderr |
| M3 | drop the combined-seam fallback | **KILLED** | `…CombinedSeamStillFeedsTheParsedCall` |
| M4 | error carries stdout again | **KILLED** (void first) | `…ErrorCarriesStderr` |
| M5 | neuter the wiring guard's own scan | **KILLED** | its non-vacuity check |

## PR #9306 — ddns: compare Route 53 RRset values on a canonical key (#9147) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9147-route53-canonical-key`

The three RRset comparisons keyed on the **raw string**, so an AAAA written
expanded and the same address written compressed were two different values.

AWS's own *Supported DNS record types* page gives the AAAA example in the
**expanded** form — so an operator pre-seeding the FQDN by following that
documentation produces a string that can never byte-equal what xpf writes, and
`mergeUpsertValues` puts **both** into one ChangeBatch. Its own comment says
*"Route 53 rejects a duplicate value in one RRset"* — the publish 400s every tick
and the record never converges.

## Why this lands while the issue is UNRESOLVED

The issue is UNRESOLVED because whether Route 53 echoes AAAA values verbatim or
normalized **cannot be observed from inside the repo**, and it gated the fix on
that answer. **The fix does not depend on it:**

- Comparing IP **values** byte-exactly is wrong on its face — two spellings of one
  address are one address, whatever any server echoes.
- **The repo already holds this position.** `wireRRClaim` normalizes rdata through
  `netip` *"so the two ownership surfaces … compare EQUAL for the same address
  even if their textual forms differ (e.g. an IPv6 address written expanded vs
  compressed)"*. That is this exact argument, already shipped, on a path reaching
  the same data. This one did not use it. A cell now pins the two normalizations
  to **agree** — two that disagree would be worse than one that is missing.

If Route 53 *does* normalize on storage, this is **inert**, not wrong. The
unmeasurable premise decides whether the defect is **reachable today**, not
whether the comparison is **correct**.

## Key-only, deliberately

The normalized form is **never emitted** for a value xpf does not own —
rewriting a foreign member's spelling on write-back would edit someone else's
record to suit our comparison, the same sole-delete-authority boundary
`DeleteLease`'s doc draws. A cell asserts the **live** spelling survives a merge.
(The originating report normalized the output too; narrowed here.)

The report's *"stale AAAA leaked forever"* arm is **not** claimed — a leaked record
implies a successful publish, which implies xpf's canonical value is present and
`removeValue` finds it.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| key is the raw string again (the original defect) | killed by 4 cells |
| emit the NORMALIZED form (rewrites a foreign value) | killed |

The first was **VOID on its first attempt** — deleting the parse left two imports
unused, nothing compiled, no `--- FAIL` emitted, which reads exactly like a
survival.

## PR #9307 — cos: restore the flow-fair frontier on the demote FAILURE path too [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9066-cos-demote-frontier`

`demote_prepared_cos_queue_to_local` saved the MQFQ frontier before `drain_all` and restored it **only on the success path**. Both early returns dropped it, justified by:

> The failure-rollback path (`cos_queue_restore_front`) is round-trip neutral per #913 §3.7 and stays correct without snapshot/restore.

**True for a single bucket, false for several.** Three flows × two packets at vtime 5000, down the Local-head `else` arm:

| bucket | pre head | post head | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 6500 | 10700 | **+4200** |
| 1 | 5900 | 8600 | **+2700** |
| 2 | 6200 | 9500 | **+3300** |

Each bucket comes back inflated by the bytes of the *other* buckets drained ahead of its own last item.

## What it is, kept apart from what it is not

Not "corrupt scheduler state": vtime round-trips exactly and relative order among restored buckets survives. What it **is**: a new flow arriving right after a failed demote anchors at `vtime + bytes` and is served ahead of the entire restored backlog — **#926's temporal inversion**, fixed on the success path and left open on the failure one. Reachability is high: `cos_queue_accepts_prepared` refuses Prepared once the queue holds any Local item, so the first drained Local trips the `else` arm on every subsequent demote.

## Both halves fixed, per the standing rule

A corrected comment on uncorrected code would be the worse outcome, so:

- `restore_flow_fair_frontier` is **extracted and called on all three exits** rather than patched into two. Extraction is what stops them drifting again — the defect was precisely that two exits and one exit disagreed while a comment explained why that was fine.
- The comment is replaced **with the measurement that refutes it**, so the next reader inherits the number rather than a fresh assertion to trust.

## The cell, and why the existing one is blind to this

The failure-path sibling of the existing multi-bucket *success* cell, on the same fixture. Two deliberate choices:

- It triggers the failure with a **Local item in the queue** — the **common** trigger. The source finding named the rarer `clone_prepared_request_for_cos` failure and treated the Local-head arm as an aside; it is the other way round.
- It **asserts its own fixture before its subject**: the two flows must hash to distinct buckets (else it degenerates into the single-bucket case it exists to distinguish itself from), both buckets must carry a non-zero frontier (else the assertions compare zero to zero and pass whatever the code does), and the demote must actually **fail** (else everything below measures the success path that was already correct).

`mqfq_push_front_is_neutral_on_drained_bucket_round_trip` cannot see any of this by construction: with one bucket there are no others to drain ahead of it, so the neutrality it asserts is real *and irrelevant*.

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutation | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | drop the restore on the non-Prepared exit | **FAIL** — with the inflation message |
| M2 | neuter `restore_flow_fair_frontier` entirely | **FAIL** |

Both mutants build; restore verified byte-identical.

## Validation

Full Rust suite **rc=0**, 11 test binaries green. **No `make test-failover`, no `go test ./...`** — this is `userspace-dp` TX scheduling, touching no Go package and nothing in cluster, VRRP, session-sync or failover. Stated rather than silently skipped.

The issue suggests folding in GEMINI-050-013 (NAT64 ICMPv6 zero-checksum) as "a one-line consistency fix in the same subsystem family". Left alone: it has its own issue and its own acceptance, and bundling an unrelated one-liner into a fairness fix makes both harder to revert.
