## PR #9308 — Refuse a group or all-zero MAC on every neighbour-learn arm [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9115-neighbor-mac-learnable`

Closes #9115

## The defect

`outline_arp_reply_learn_and_program` and `outline_ndp_na_learn_and_program` gated on the **IP alone** (`neighbor_ip_is_learnable` + `!owns_configured_ip`), then inserted whatever hardware address the frame carried into `dynamic_neighbors` **and programmed it into the kernel**. The sibling RX-learn arm in `neighbor_dispatch.rs` had always refused a group or all-zero MAC — but *inline*, which is precisely the drift a shared predicate prevents. That inline test is now a call to the same function.

## What an attacker needs

L2 adjacency to an interface the firewall learns on, and the ability to emit **one** ARP reply or **one** NDP NA. No credentials, no prior state, no session. The victim IP only has to be learnable and not firewall-owned.

The result is a neighbour entry for the victim IP whose MAC is a group or broadcast address, in the userspace cache **and** in the kernel: traffic for that IP is then addressed to a group and reaches every station on the segment, and the firewall's own switch port can be MAC-flapped or err-disabled. That is a cache-poisoning primitive, not merely a wrong entry.

## The fix

One named predicate, `neighbor_mac_is_learnable`, beside the IP-side `neighbor_ip_is_learnable` it was always missing — called from all three arms so a fourth inherits it.

## A vacuous test caught mid-flight

The first NDP cells built a valid NA and rewrote the TLLA bytes in place. The builder stamps the **ICMPv6 checksum over the TLLA** and the NA parser is strict about it, so the edited frame failed to parse — and the cell passed because the NA was *malformed*, not because the guard refused it.

It looked green and proved nothing. The only reason it was caught is that the mutation removing the NDP guard **survived** with those cells in place. The builder is now parameterised on the TLLA MAC so the checksum covers the value under test, and the cell asserts `parse_ndp_neighbor_advert(&frame).is_some()` as an explicit precondition so the trap cannot recur silently.

## Validation

Four mutants, each verified to **build** before scoring, each restore verified by reading the file back:

| # | mutation | reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | ARP arm's guard removed | **only** the ARP refusal cell — predicate cell stays green, so this is a call-site binding |
| M4 | NDP arm's guard removed | **only** the NDP refusal cell |
| M2 | predicate accepts everything | both refusal cells + predicate cell |
| M3 | predicate refuses everything | both **controls** |

M3 matters: it stops a "refuse all" change from passing as a security improvement while breaking neighbour learning outright.

## HA wire

Nothing moves — no session key, no wire struct.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` (5424-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed) **and** `go test ./...` whole-tree, both re-run post-merge.

## PR #9309 — docs: correct the generic-XDP UMEM claim, mark the zero-copy one unverified (#9043) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9043-umem-readme-claims`

Two in-tree READMEs made **mutually inconsistent** claims about `XDP_PASS`
consuming UMEM frames, and one was steering the shim's non-IP design. One is
settleable from the tree; the other is not, and they get different treatment.

## Claim 1 — definitively wrong, and the tree says so

`userspace-dp/README.md`: *"Generic-XDP fallback consumes UMEM frames permanently
on mlx5"*. Wrong twice:

- A generic-XDP interface binds **`COPY_ONLY_BIND_FLAGS`** (`bind.rs`,
  `interface_uses_generic_xdp`; virtio_net is the one exception), and the umem
  README states copy mode's `XDP_PASS` *"operates on kernel DMA buffers, not UMEM
  frames"*. **The generic fallback cannot consume a UMEM frame at all.**
- *"on mlx5"* is incoherent besides — mlx5 supports native XDP and never takes
  the generic fallback.

Corrected, keeping the true half: the cpumap redirect is real and shipped.

## Claim 2 — cannot be settled here, so it is marked, not deleted

The umem README asserted **as fact** that zero-copy `XDP_PASS` on mlx5
permanently consumes a fill-ring frame. Nothing in the tree corroborates it and
**two independent readings contradict it** — `mlx5e_xsk_skb_from_cqe_linear`
copies into a fresh SKB and reuses the frame, and a verifier checking a
neighbouring claim reached the same conclusion by a different route.

It stays, marked **UNVERIFIED**, because the decisive check is outside the repo
(one flood test on a zero-copy mlx5 bind, or one read of the running kernel's
`mlx5e_xsk_*` path). **Deleting it would be as unfounded as asserting it** — I
have not measured it either.

The harm is not the mitigation, which is cheap and shipped either way. It is that
**a claim steering a design decision had never been measured and was written as
fact**, so the next decision made on its strength inherits the confidence without
the evidence.

## Why a cell for a documentation fix

The correction is now documentation, and *a documented fact with nothing
asserting it is how the wrong version got written*. The cell pins the bind
decision the corrected sentence rests on; if that stops being copy-only the
README becomes false and it fails. It carries a second assertion that AUTO and
COPY_ONLY actually **differ** — without which the first is vacuous.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| `COPY_ONLY_BIND_FLAGS` stops requesting copy mode | killed by 2 cells |

## PR #9310 — userspace-dp: route every NAT64 checksum arm through the zero-checksum SSOT (#9069) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9069-nat64-zero-checksum-ssot`

The `PROTO_ICMPV6` arm of `recompute_l4_checksum_after_nat64_v4_to_v6` wrote its
computed sum **raw**, while its own `PROTO_UDP` sibling ten lines above
canonicalised zero to `0xFFFF`, and while `adjust_zero_checksum_illegal` (#1839)
— this codebase's **declared SSOT** — says V6 zero is illegal for UDP *and
ICMPv6*. The afxdp-side `recompute_l4_checksum_ipv6` canonicalises its ICMPv6
arm. The translator diverged from the rule its sibling path enforces.

The zero is **producible**: a two-byte payload tail exists that folds the
pseudo-header checksum to zero.

## What this is NOT

The originating report cited RFC 4443 §2.3 and RFC 8200 §8.1 for a mandatory
all-ones substitution on ICMPv6. **That rule is UDP-specific in RFC 8200 §8.1,
and RFC 4443 §2.3 contains no such sentence.** A `0x0000` ICMPv6 checksum
verifies correctly at a compliant receiver — there is no "no checksum" sentinel
for ICMPv6 — so "dropped by compliant hosts" does not follow and is not claimed.

What survives is an internal SSOT divergence, which is a real contract
violation. Severity Low; the cells assert **consistency**, not wire correctness.
A fix justified by a non-existent RFC rule would be the same defect class as the
one it fixes.

## Fix — one rule, not a per-arm matrix

Per the issue's dedup note (this and its #8869 sibling should "ride on one fix
that routes every recompute arm through `adjust_zero_checksum_illegal` rather
than re-implementing the matrix per call site"):

`canonicalize_zero_checksum(sum, protocol, family)` consults the SSOT, and **all
four** NAT64 arms go through it. Both hand-rolled `if sum == 0 { 0xFFFF }`
fixups are gone.

`adjust_zero_checksum_illegal` and `ChecksumFamily` were
`pub(in crate::afxdp::frame)`. **That visibility is why a second implementation
grew outside the module and then drifted** — the rule was unreachable from the
translator, so the translator restated it, and a restatement is free to diverge.
Both are now `pub(crate)`.

Correctness of the uncovered pairs then *falls out of the rule* rather than being
re-argued: TCP in both families (a computed TCP `0x0000` is legal on the wire —
why the sibling finding GEMINI-050-009 was refuted) and V4 ICMP (no
pseudo-header, no sentinel).

## Mutation matrix

| # | Mutant | Result | Killed by |
|---|--------|--------|-----------|
| M1 | revert the ICMPv6 arm | **KILLED** | `…IcmpV6ChecksumIsCanonicalised` |
| M2 | canonicalise regardless of the SSOT | **KILLED (2)** | both over-apply cells |

## PR #9311 — test-failover: observe proxy-ARP ownership after every transition, not once [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9087-proxyarp-repeat`

## The leak is NOT fixed, and this PR does not close #9087

What it does is make the defect fail **within a single run** instead of only on the next one, and replace the issue's hypothesis with a measurement. Stated first because everything below reads better once that is clear.

## What the issue hypothesised vs. what is true

The issue proposed that "demotion does not remove the NTF_PROXY entry (or removes it late)", explicitly flagged as "a hypothesis, not a conclusion". Measured live, three ways:

1. **It is a permanent LEAK, not a 30-second window.** fw1 in `secondary-hold` held the entry across many re-assert cycles; sampled `1/1` at +20/+40/+60/+80s with this build deployed.
2. **The ownership decision is CORRECT; the sweep is what fails.** fw1 logs `proxy-arp: suppressing responder for an interface this node does not own` **every 30 seconds** while the kernel entry survives — so the defect is downstream of the gate, not in it.
3. **At the instant of failback the state is `fw0=0 fw1=1`.** The new owner has not installed and the old one has not cleared — for that window the *only* answerer is the wrong node. That is not the two-answerer shape the issue describes.

## The harness change — proven, and the acceptance's first bullet

The check is extracted into `check_proxy_arp_ownership <phase>` — body preserved **verbatim**, including its deliberate three-state reasoning and its "THIS BRANCH IS NOT LEFTOVER SCAFFOLDING / do not collapse it" comment — and called at the preflight **and** after the full crash-failover + manual-failback cycle.

**It caught the defect on the first run**, where that same run was previously green:

```
PASS  only the RG owner answers proxy-ARP for 172.16.80.7 (preflight, before any failover)
FAIL  the RG OWNER does not answer proxy-ARP for 172.16.80.7 after the crash
      failover AND the manual failback (fw0=0 fw1=1)
Failover test: 21 passed, 1 failed
```

`exe_check=MATCH exe_scope=both`. A defect that needed two runs and a cross-run comparison now fails once, in the run that caused it, naming **which** transition leaked.

## Two code changes, and neither is the fix

Labelled accurately rather than left to read as one.

1. **A misleading diagnostic.** `pkg/dataplane/proxyarp.go` logged `proxy-arp: interface not found` for an interface that *was* found and was deliberately suppressed by the #8297 gate. Verified fixed — the WARN is gone from fw1's log with the new binary, which also confirms the deployed build is this one.
2. **A one-shot sweep window.** `proxyARPIfaceMapFiltered`'s doc says a suppressed entry "must be actively torn down by the reconcile sweep rather than retained", and the sweep reaches only interfaces in `ifaceMap` or `priorIfaceMap`. A suppressed interface is in **neither** after the first suppressed pass, so the teardown had exactly one chance — during demotion, when `programRethMAC`'s link cycle makes the netdev hardest to resolve. `retainSuppressedProxySweepTargets` keeps it swept.

   Unit-pinned with a mutation, **deployed to the cluster, and the entry still did not clear** — so the gap is real and is *not* the cause.

## What the next person should measure

The gate fires and the entry survives, so the suspect is the delete: the entry is installed via `cfg.ResolveKernelIfName` (`reth0.80` → the local physical member's VLAN netdev) while the prior set is resolved by `ifaceIndexByName` on the **remembered Linux name**. If those disagree on the standby after a role change, the sweep manages an ifindex the entry is not on. That is a measurement, not another hypothesis.

## Validation

`go test ./...` 73 packages EXIT=0. Three unit cells for the retention, including the control that keeps it distinct from #6536's retention — which protects a **live** responder and is the opposite intent. Live run on a fresh deploy with `exe_check=MATCH exe_scope=both`.

## Why #9087 stays open

Acceptance bullet 1 is done and proven. Bullet 2 — "fix the demotion side if the hypothesis holds, with a cell that fails on revert" — is not: the hypothesis holds in *outcome* but not in *mechanism*. Closing on the harness half would retire the question while the defect ships, which is the #9052 shape this board just spent an issue on.

## PR #9312 — nftables: emit only the reachable rules of an lo0 reject pair (#9072) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9072-lo0-reject-dead-rule`

An `lo0` `reject` term with an **explicit** protocol emitted a dead rule.
`applyMatches` latches `l4Val` from the term's own protocol, so the following
`needL4proto(protoTCP)` saw `l4Val != 6` and appended a **second, contradictory**
`meta l4proto` compare — `l4proto==11 && l4proto==06`, which can never hold.

| term | r00 | r01 |
|---|---|---|
| no protocol | `==06` → tcp-reset | (bare) → icmpx *(both live)* |
| `protocol udp` | `==11 && ==06` → **dead** | `==11` → icmpx |
| `protocol tcp` | `==06` → tcp-reset | `==06` → icmpx, **unreachable** |
| `protocol icmp` | `==01 && ==06` → **dead** | `==01` → icmpx |
| `protocol [udp icmp]` | `set && ==06` → **dead** | `set` → icmpx |
| `protocol [tcp udp]` | `set && ==06` → correct | `set` → icmpx |

The dead rule **moves between the two positions** depending on the protocol — for
a TCP-only term it is the *icmpx* rule that is unreachable. Fixing only the
`needL4proto` end would have left that case untouched.

## Waste or shadow — the question asked at dispatch

**Waste**, and verified rather than taken on trust. The icmpx rule always carried
the correct family-agnostic reject for the specified protocols in every case,
including the mixed `[tcp udp]` one.

`TestRejectTermStillRejectsEveryNamedProtocol9072` asserts, per protocol case,
that a live reject **of the right kind** survives. That is the assertion a
dead-rule check cannot make, and the one a "fix" that simply emitted fewer rules
would fail.

Fixed anyway because the ruleset is operator-visible in `nft list ruleset`, where
a self-contradictory rule invites misdiagnosis.

## Fix

Emit by reachability: **tcp-reset** when TCP is among the protocols or none are
named; **icmpx** unless the term is TCP-only. The second arm is symmetric with
the first rather than an afterthought, precisely because the dead rule moves ends.

## The goldens were silent, not contrary

Checked for contrary evidence rather than assuming its absence:
`TestGoldenRejectTermPair` and the `reject-term` scenario both pin a term with
**no** `Protocols`; `netlink_lo0_proto_icmp_6806_test.go` never touches `reject`.
That case is byte-identical after the fix and is pinned again here — a behaviour
change smuggled in beside a cosmetic one is exactly what a low-severity cleanup
risks.

## PR #9313 — Segment a FIN-bearing oversized TCP frame [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9116-segment-fin-bearing`

Closes #9116

## The defect

Both segmentation admission gates read `(tcp_flags & (SYN | FIN | RST)) != 0 -> None`, so a FIN-bearing oversized datagram declined **both** builders and fell to `compute_forwarded_egress_ptb`. That returns PTB for IPv6 and for IPv4-with-DF, but **`Forward` for IPv4 with DF clear** — so the original oversized frame was submitted and dropped downstream, black-holing the connection close. There is no IPv4 transit fragmentation engine to catch it (the only fragmentation code in the dataplane is NAT64's).

SYN and RST still decline — a SYN carries no bulk payload and its options are per-connection, and a payload-bearing RST is exotic. FIN is different in kind: an ordinary data segment that also closes the sender's half.

## Admitting FIN is only half the fix

A FIN repeated on every segment would close the half-connection at the first one and leave the rest of the payload outside the sequence space the peer accepts. `finalize_tcp_segment_headers` — shared by both builders — now clears FIN on every non-last segment, beside the identical PSH rule already there.

The same rule went into the **property harness's shared flag oracle**, so every property that segments a FIN-bearing frame checks the placement, not just the cell that introduced it.

## An existing property test reddened — a prior decision speaking

`segmentation_declines_syn_fin_rst` **pinned the old contract** rather than detecting a defect. It's narrowed to `segmentation_declines_syn_rst` (reason recorded at the site), and the FIN case is replaced by a *stronger* property: the frame must segment, with flag placement delegated to the shared oracle. That fails both if FIN is declined (the defect) **and** if FIN is smeared across segments (the obvious wrong fix) — neither of which the deleted case could do.

## Two gates needed two bindings

A mutation restoring FIN to the **prepared-TX** gate compiled and survived the entire suite, because the property test only drives the copy-path builder. A dedicated cell now binds the twin.

| # | mutation | reds |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | FIN back in the copy-path decline set | FIN property |
| M2 | FIN not cleared on non-last segments | FIN property, different assertion |
| M3 | SYN/RST decline removed | narrowed decline property |
| M4 | FIN back in the prepared-TX decline set | the new prepared-TX cell, and nothing else |

Each verified to *build* before scoring; each restore verified by reading the file back.

## HA wire

Nothing moves — no session key, no wire struct.

Gates: full `cargo test` for `userspace-dp` (5435-cell bin suite plus every integration target, 0 failed) **and** `go test ./...` whole-tree, both re-run post-merge.

## PR #9314 — cos: exclude a mid-epoch newcomer instead of disarming the whole class [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9117-midepoch-fairshare`

A worker whose flow buckets were empty at one rotation has its fair share published as **0**. If it then goes active **mid-epoch** it demands and is granted — but carries no sample, because the sampler snapshot was taken at the rotation, before it woke. It tripped the `UnsampledActiveWorker` fail-open, and `fail_open` resets `valid_streak` and `smoothed_target_per_flow`, so with `EQUAL_FLOW_VALID_STREAK_REQUIRED = 2` **one activation suppressed enforcement for ~3 epochs across the whole class** (one lease serves every worker on it).

This is a **fourth shape**, absent from the module's own three-case enumeration: not *"a participant we failed to sample"* but *"a participant that did not exist yet"*.

## The issue located it one step downstream, and the probe proved it

> …IS admitted past the `prev_grants[id] == 0` skip at `:116`, reaches `:130`, and trips `UnsampledActiveWorker`.

I implemented the carve-out at that `prior_share == 0` check and the cell still failed:

```
reason=UnsampledActiveWorker excluded=0
```

`excluded=0` means **my branch never ran** — the class was already disarmed before that check was reached. The fail-open fires in the **first loop's participation arm**, not the second loop's share check.

## The fix

At the real site: a participant whose share was **published as 0** is excluded for one epoch — exactly what the idle-at-rotation case on the next line already does, and for the same reason: *a worker we cannot fairly compare is left out of the comparison rather than used to disarm it.* Its next epoch is fully sampled and it rejoins.

`None` vs `Some(0)` is now distinct where `unwrap_or(0)` collapsed them: a **missing** share is an inconsistency between the worker set and the share table and still fails open.

The exclusion is **counted** with an accessor rather than left as a local — a local assigned and never read is a claim in inert code, and a flat fail-open count beside a climbing exclusion count is what "the fix is working" looks like from outside.

**Deliberately NOT the reordering the originating report prescribed**: moving the share publication earlier would compare the just-ended epoch's grants against the *new* epoch's share and break the demand-saturation gate — the only consumer that pairing exists to feed.

## Mutation matrix, including the one that SURVIVED

| # | Mutation | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | restore the unconditional fail-open | **FAIL** |
| M2 | exclude EVERY unsampled participant, not just the newcomer | **SURVIVED** |

M2 is **recorded in the test file as a known coverage bound** rather than left to be rediscovered. It would delete the genuine case-2 safety fail-open, so the gap is real. The cell that closes it needs an **established** worker (non-zero share) that is **active but unsampled**, and that state is **not constructible through this API**: `rehydrate_worker_active_count(id, 0)` clears `active_by_worker` as well as the sampled count, so such a worker is skipped by the `!active_by_worker[id]` guard before reaching the arm — the attempt produced `reason=None` with enforcement ON, i.e. the shape never occurred. Closing it needs a seam that sets the sampled count independently of the active flag: a production-type change for a test's benefit, which I did not make unilaterally.

**The cell that could not construct its own precondition was deleted, not left green** — it would have asserted nothing while looking arranged.

## The pair, kept as a pair

The control is load-bearing: without it, "not enforced" is the state at every early epoch, so the subject would pass against code that never enforces at all. The subject also asserts its **precondition** directly — worker 1's published share is 0 while worker 0's is not — so a change that stops constructing the shape fails loudly rather than passing vacuously.

## Validation

Full Rust suite **rc=0**, 11 test binaries. No `go test ./...` and no `make test-failover`: this is `userspace-dp` CoS lease arithmetic, touching no Go package and nothing in cluster, VRRP, session-sync or failover.

Log: `docs/log/9117.md`.

Closes #9117

## PR #9315 — dhcpserver: refuse a narrowed DHCPv6 group instead of rendering it unselectable (#9122) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9122-v6-narrowed-group-refuse`

`generateKea6Config` states its own invariant and breaks it three lines later:

> Kea v6 subnet selection cannot fall back to address matching the way v4 can
> (clients talk from link-local source addresses), so subnet6 **REQUIRES** the
> interface selector.

It enforces that with `len(group.Interfaces) > 1`, then calls
`subnetInterface(group)` — which returns `""` **first** on `MembersFiltered`. A
group narrowed by the chassis-cluster master-RG filter presents a **singleton**
list, so the guard never trips and the subnet renders selector-less. Kea cannot
select it for a link-local SOLICIT: **a silent, total DHCPv6 outage for that
group, with no error anywhere.**

**It is the steady state, not a failover transient.**
`filterDHCPConfigForMasterRGs` runs on the 2 s periodic converger as well as on
RG edges, so a v6 group spanning two RGs in an active/active cluster renders this
way continuously on *both* nodes.

## Fix

Refuse the narrowed group — keeping #6520's do-not-cross-bind property by failing
**loud** on the family that has no address fallback.

**Its own message**, not folded into the existing multi-interface one. The two
are different states with different operator remedies: *"the runtime narrowed a
group you authored across RGs"* versus *"you authored this group too broadly"*.
That's your #9073 lesson — distinct states need distinct signals — and a mutant
that folds them reds.

**The originating report's proposed fix is HARMFUL and is pinned against.** It
returns `group.Interfaces[0]` for a narrowed singleton, binding the **removed**
member's pool to the **survivor's** interface: the #6520 cross-bind re-opened for
v6, where Kea would lease a foreign prefix on that link.
`TestV6FilteredGroupNeverCrossBindsToTheSurvivor9122` exists to make that loud.

**v4 is untouched** — #6520's address-fallback remedy is valid there and invalid
only for v6, and a cell pins it.

## PR #9316 — nat: report the deterministic unit prefix on a reverse NAT lookup (#9070) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9070-reverse-unit-prefix`

The deterministic-NAT reverse direction reconstructs the 32-bit subscriber
**word**, so its answer is the network base of a deterministic **unit**, not a
host. Rendered bare under `Internal host:` it read as an exact /128, and no
prefix length appeared on any surface.

## The obvious annotation is arithmetically wrong

Avoiding it is the substance of this change. The unit is the configured prefix
**plus** the reconstructed word: a /32-configured pool yields a **/64** unit, a
/64-configured pool yields a **/96**. So the value derives from `p.wordOffset` as
`(off + 4) * 8`, never from the configured prefix length — echoing the configured
value would replace an ambiguous answer with a **confidently wrong** one.

This is the two-similar-mechanisms shape: `detParamsForPool` already returns
something called `prefixLen` (32 or 64) a few dozen lines away — the *configured*
pool prefix, answering a similar-sounding question. **The two are never equal.**
The new field is `InternalPrefixLen` and its doc comment says outright that it is
not that value, so the next reader does not reuse the wrong one.

`ForwardResult.Render` is deliberately **not** changed. It shares the
`InternalHost` field name and an identical render line — the count assertion
caught it, because that line appears twice — but there the value is the exact
host the operator supplied, not a reconstructed base.

Carried onto all three surfaces: the `show` render becomes
`Internal prefix: <base>/<len>` for IPv6 reverse (keeping `Internal host:` for
IPv4), REST gains `internal_prefix_len`, and gRPC gains **proto field 14** —
added, never redefined, so a rolling upgrade reads it as absent rather than as
something else.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| echo the configured pool prefix (`off * 8`) | reds the /32 row at 32-want-64 |
| drop the computation (the original defect) | reds it at 0-want-64 |
| give IPv4 a prefix | reds the IPv4 control |

Each mutant verified to **build** before scoring, each restore verified by reading
the file back. The **/64-configured row is load-bearing**: an assertion that merely
checked "a prefix length is present" would pass the wrong value, so the cell
asserts `!= 64` with its own message before asserting `== 96`.

`docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md` gains the configured-prefix → unit table. It
described the subscriber word already but never said what granularity the reverse
answer has.

`go test ./...` green.

Closes #9070

## PR #9317 — nat: move the deterministic block probe off the allocator mutex (#9130) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9130-det-nat-lock-scope`

## Summary

- `allocate_deterministic_v4` / `allocate_deterministic_v6` took `lock_live()` first and held it across the whole linear CAS scan of the subscriber's port block, so the hold time was O(occupied prefix of the block). The documented example pool uses `block-size 2016`; every other flow through that pool serialized behind one subscriber's scan, worst-case exactly when a subscriber is near its own block budget.
- The sibling round-robin PAT path was deliberately restructured the other way in #4676 (claim lock-free on the CAS bitmap, mutex only for the tiny reuse/cap/insert section, GC moved off that section). #2852's and #4676's remedies reached `allocate_translation_inner` and never reached the deterministic arms. This applies that restructure to both.
- New order: probe lock-free → **no free port**: take the mutex once, O(1), and check idempotent re-entry BEFORE reporting the block full → **port claimed**: take the mutex once, O(1), for re-entry + flow-table cap + insert.
- Both refusals give the claimed port back with `free_no_recycle`, never `free_recycle` — a deterministic port is reusable via its occupancy bit alone and the deterministic path never drains the per-address recycle queue (#4559 / #5178).
- Docs: `docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md` gains an "Allocator lock discipline" subsection under the userspace-implementation section.

## The issue's stated fix direction is incomplete, in a way that drops packets

"Probe/claim the block without the mutex, then take `lock_live()` for the idempotency + cap check + insert" is right for a block with a free port and **wrong for a full one**. A live flow's own port is one of the occupied ones, so a re-entering flow on a full block finds nothing free and would be told `AllocatorExhausted` for a flow that already holds a translation — a working flow's second packet becomes a drop. Hence the O(1) re-entry check on the no-free-port arm.

An earlier draft instead kept the re-entry check under the mutex *before* the probe. That is correct, but it re-gates the probe on the mutex, so the defect is only half fixed. The new lock-scope cell went RED with that draft applied — the cell caught it, not the reasoning.

## Hot-path shape

Per deterministic allocation the mutex is taken **twice for O(1)** (re-entry, then insert) instead of **once for O(block occupancy)**. On the re-entry path a partially-full block now claims a port and gives it back (one CAS pair) rather than short-circuiting — the same trade `allocate_translation_inner` has made since #4676. No allocation, no new atomics beyond the existing `reuses_total` / `exhaustion_total` counters.

## Test plan

- [x] 6 new cells in `userspace-dp/src/nat/tests_det_lock_scope_9130.rs`
- [x] Full Rust dataplane suite: **5443 passed, 0 failed**
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` clean on every file this PR touches
- [ ] No cluster smoke: the loss userspace cluster carries no deterministic-NAT config, so this code has never been reached by a smoke run (the issue says the same). Nothing in this PR changes what the allocator returns, only when the mutex is held.

**How the lock scope is measured.** Hold time is not observable from a return value and a timing assertion would be flaky. The occupancy bitmap is CAS-based and lives outside the mutex, so one thread parks on `debug_live()` while an allocating worker runs: if the probe is inside the mutex the bit can never appear while the guard is held; if it is outside it must. The worker is joined at the end, so "still running" is excluded. A new test-only `debug_insert_live_locked` makes the insert-section idempotency race deterministic — without it that arm fires once in many runs and a mutation there scores as survived most of the time.

## PR #9318 — daemon: key the DHCP-route VRF map on the lease spelling, not the config token [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9135-dhcp-vrf-key-shape`

Closes #9135

## What was measured

The #8963 remedy tags each DHCP-learned route with the routing instance that owns the learning interface. Its lookup crosses a spelling boundary and keyed the wrong side of it.

- **Producer**: `RoutingInstance.Interfaces` — the compiler appends the config token VERBATIM, so the canonical Junos form carries slashes (`ge-0/0/1.0`).
- **Consumer**: `lease.Interface` = `config.DHCPLeaseIfName` — `LinuxIfName` unconditionally (dashes) plus `.<vlan-id>` for a tagged unit (`ge-0-0-1`, `ge-0-0-3.50`).

Reproduced by a cell driving `collectDHCPRoutes` (not a hand-built `frr.DHCPRoute`):

```
collectDHCPRoutes VRF for ge-0-0-1     = ""   want "tenant-a"   <-- slash-spelled member
collectDHCPRoutes VRF for ge-0-0-3.50  = ""   want "tenant-b"   <-- tagged unit
collectDHCPRoutes VRF for ge-0-0-2     = ""   want ""           control, green before and after
collectDHCPRoutes VRF for ge-0-0-4     = "tenant-c"             control, dash-spelled, green before
```

So the #8963 fix shipped INERT for the canonical spelling: every VRF-attached DHCP route fell back to `vrf == ""` and landed in the default FRR context — the exact behaviour #8963 was filed against.

The map's doc comment already claimed it was *"Keyed on the KERNEL/lease interface name"*, which the body did not do. Comment and code are corrected together.

## What changed

`dhcpLeaseKeysForMember` inserts each member under every spelling a lease can actually present, derived from the consumer's own rule (`config.DHCPLeaseIfName`) rather than hand-rolled. Three consequences of that being the rule shape the key set:

1. a lease key can never contain a slash, so the raw config token is not a candidate key at all and is no longer inserted;
2. a lease key never carries a unit NUMBER (`DHCPLeaseIfName` has no unit-number fallback), so `logicalUnitDeviceKey`'s `base.<unit>` arm — correct for the netdev-name family (#8321/#8597) — is wrong here;
3. a member naming the WHOLE DEVICE claims every unit on it (#9063's reading of the same list), and a tagged unit's lease key is `base.<vlan-id>`, which the device name alone cannot produce.

### Deviation from the issue's stated fix direction

The issue asks for `config.LinuxIfName(cfg.ResolveReth(member))`. **reth is deliberately not resolved.** `buildDHCPClientSpecs` keys the lease on the config interface name with **no** `ResolveReth`, so a reth client's lease is keyed `reth0` — already covered by the base spelling. Resolving would add a key no lease presents and could mis-attribute a lease genuinely learned on that physical member.

## Third-reader check

The issue's producer/consumer pair is the only reader of `dhcpRouteVRFMap` (single call site). The sibling lease consumers were audited: `managementVRFIfaceSet` already applies `LinuxIfName` correctly (it is the control showing the codebase knows the rule), and `daemon_neighbor.go` passes `lease.Interface` through `resolveJunosIfName` rather than a config-keyed map.

## Unguarded wiring found while fixing (not in the issue)

Replacing `DHCPRoutes: d.collectDHCPRoutes()` in `assembleFRRConfig` with `nil` killed **zero** tests in `pkg/daemon` — the entire DHCP-route contribution to FRR could be severed with the Go suite staying green. `TestAssembleFRRConfigCarriesDHCPRoutes9135` now binds it, asserting the route AND its VRF (a length check would let a MISSING→EMPTY regression pass).

## PR #9319 — daemon: gate RSS reshaping on capability, not on a driver name (#9040) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9040-rss-capability-probe`

The unconditional half of #9040 landed in #9262. What remained was recorded on
the issue as **a product decision** — widen the reshape to every driver, or
refuse the plan outright.

**I took neither arm**, because the issue's own *"what would settle it"* option 1
**dissolves the decision instead of making it**: a per-interface capability probe
turns "which global policy" into a per-interface answer that is *derived* rather
than chosen.

## The clamp was never the gap

`computeWeightVector` is already driver-generic — it clamps `active` to
`min(queues, BindingQueuesPerIface)` for anything it is called on. The gap was
one level up, in `applyRSSIndirection`, which matched the driver **name** and
skipped everything else, so a non-mlx5 NIC never reached the generic clamp and
transit on its unbound queues was dropped.

## Why a probe and not just a wider gate

`ethtool -X` support varies by driver — i40e/ice/bnxt accept the write,
virtio-net may not — and this path deliberately swallows its errors:

> Never returns a non-nil error — D3 regressions must not break interface bring-up.

So dropping the gate would produce a reshape that **silently succeeds on some
drivers and silently fails on others** — the same class of defect this issue is
about, re-created one layer up. Reading the table first identifies the
unsupported case **before** the write.

It costs nothing on the path it replaces: the idempotency check already read this
table, so a supported interface issues **exactly the same ethtool invocations as
before**.

## The asymmetry is the substance

**A restore fails open; a write fails closed.**

#5250 exists because an unreadable signal silently became *"do nothing"* and left
a concentrated table live. Probe-gating a restore re-creates that defect one
level up, so neither the unknown-queue-count restore nor the kill switch is
probe-gated. A wrongly attempted restore is a logged no-op; a wrongly attempted
reshape is a silent misconfiguration.

For the same reason the kill switch now sweeps **every allowlisted interface**:
**the restore set must equal the potential-apply set.** Keeping the driver gate on
the restore while widening apply would strand a concentrated table on exactly the
NICs the new apply path can write — reachable only by an operator backing out.

## PR #9320 — frr: render a DHCP route's vrf clause in the kernel namespace [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9136-dhcp-vrf-render-namespace`

Closes #9136

## What was measured

One `FullConfig`, three renderers side by side — the siblings are the evidence, not the absence:

```
renderDHCPDefaults (before):
    ip route 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.2.1 ge-0-0-1 200 vrf vr1
    ip route 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.3.1 ge-0-0-2 200 vrf fwd1
renderPreferredRoutes (SIBLING, same instances):
    ip route 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.2.1 1 vrf vrf-vr1
    ip route 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.3.1 1 table 4242
```

Two defects in one clause:

1. `vrf vr1` names a VRF that does not exist. A `virtual-router` instance is backed by the kernel device `vrf-vr1` (`pkg/routing/vrf.go`), which is what `InstanceConfig.VRFName` carries. The tenant's DHCP-learned default never reaches its table — the loss #8963 was filed against.
2. An `instance-type forwarding` instance has **no VRF device** (`daemon_ipmon.go` sets `VRFName=""`), so it was handed a `vrf` clause it can never have. Its routes belong in the instance's kernel table — the table the FBF `ip rule`s and the dataplane's `<ri>.inet.0` snapshot already target (#1827 PR-2).

## What changed

Rather than teach a third site the rule by hand, the resolution is **extracted** from `renderPreferredRoutes` as `instanceRouteTarget`, and both renderers call it. A lookup miss keeps the historical `vrf-<name>` fallback that `InstanceConfig.Name`'s own doc already specifies.

The extraction is load-bearing, not cosmetic: M2 and M3 below show a mutation in the shared resolver reds cells on **both** sides.

## Two existing cells red — a prior decision speaking

Exactly as the issue predicted. Both stated reasons were read before touching either:

| Cell | Its stated CLAIM | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `TestDHCPRouteCarriesItsVRF8963` | *"the DHCP route learned on an interface in `vrf1` was emitted without a `vrf` clause, so it lands in the DEFAULT routing table"* | claim is about **presence**, and is still true — kept verbatim |
| `TestDHCPDefaultSuppressionIsPerVRF8963` | *"a static default in the DEFAULT context suppressed a DHCP default belonging to `vrf1`"* | claim is about **suppression scope**, still true — kept verbatim |

Neither claim is about the SPELLING. The literal `vrf vrf1` was the #8963 author's assumption about the namespace — a positive control sharing the misconception it guarded, which is exactly why it could never fail on this. Both fixtures gain the `VRFName` a real instance has (they omitted it because the namespace was not the question they were asked) and the expected strings move. The prior decision was wrong here; the claims were right.

## Third state, third signal

`InstanceConfig` with neither a VRF device nor a table (`VRFName==""`, `TableID==0`) is a distinct state — `VRFName`'s doc calls it *"(and, historically, the master table)"*. It now has its own cell asserting no clause at all, so a future change cannot collapse it into the table arm and emit `table 0`, which is not a valid FRR operand and would fail the whole managed-section reload (#6795).

## Severity question the issue left open

The issue could not settle whether `% Can't find VRF` aborts the whole `vtysh` batch (High) or lands the route in an inert phantom VRF (Medium), and flagged it as needing a live FRR. **The fix removes the input either way** — no unknown VRF name is emitted — so the verdict does not gate the change. It is still worth settling for the general `sanitizeFRRValue`/render-belt reasoning, and is not settled here.

## PR #9329 — ipsec: resolve reth when zone-qualifying a link-local local_addrs [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9137-ipsec-linklocal-reth-zone`

Closes #9137

## What was measured

On a bondless-RETH cluster config (`reth0` over `ge-0/0/2` node-0 + `ge-7/0/2` node-1, `external-interface reth0.0`):

```
BEFORE  resolveConfiguredInterfaceAddress(reth0.0, 6) = "fe80::1%reth0"
        PrepareConfig -> gw1.LocalAddress            = "fe80::1%reth0"   (becomes swanctl local_addrs)
AFTER   node 0: "fe80::1%ge-0-0-2"   node 1: "fe80::1%ge-7-0-2"
CONTROL non-reth ge-0/0/3.0          = "fe80::1%ge-0-0-3"   (unchanged)
CONTROL global on the same reth      = "2001:db8::5"        (unzoned, as designed)
```

`reth0` is not a kernel netdev under bondless RETH — the shipped HA model. xpfd programs the VRRP VIP and per-node virtual MAC on the PHYSICAL member and creates no reth device; `pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go` skips reth for the same stated reason. charon cannot `if_nametoindex("reth0")`, so the IKE SA never binds and the tunnel never establishes — from a config that commits clean.

The asymmetry lived **inside one function pair**: the kernel-lookup fallback in `resolveInterfaceAddressFamily`, twenty lines above, has resolved reth since it was written.

## What changed

`zone := config.LinuxIfName(cfg.ResolveReth(base))`, guarded against an empty result. Both readers of the variable — the unit branch and the bare-ref fallback — are covered by the one assignment.

**The empty guard is not defensive noise.** A member carrying `RedundantParent` but no `Name` makes `RethToPhysical` map `reth0` to `""`, and `zoneQualify` with an empty interface returns the address **unqualified** — strictly worse than a wrong zone, because it loses the #2885 disambiguation that is the entire reason the zone exists. M2 in the table below is the mutation that removes the guard, and it is killed.

## A false doc corrected with the code

`pkg/ipsec/README.md` documented the OLD rule verbatim:

> using the kernel interface name it already has in scope (`config.LinuxIfName(base)` for the configured path, ...)

Left alone, that sentence becomes a false justification sitting next to corrected code, looking freshly confirmed by the edit beside it. It is rewritten in the same change, along with the finding's real bound: `selectFamilyAddress` is **global-wins**, so the link-local branch is reached only when the reth unit has no global IPv6 address. That bound is why the verified severity is Medium, not High, and it belongs in the doc rather than only in the issue.

## Both nodes, not one

The cells assert node 0 → `ge-0-0-2` **and** node 1 → `ge-7-0-2`. A fix proven on one node only would be consistent with a resolver that always returns a fixed member; `RethToPhysical` is node-local (it scores members by `SlotToNodeID`), and both readings are pinned.

The fixture self-checks that its reth binding actually formed (`ResolveReth("reth0")` neither unchanged nor empty) before any assertion runs, so a green cell cannot come from a config that models nothing.

## PR #9330 — nat: probe a sibling pool address for a fresh address-only lease (#9131) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9131-addr-only-persistent-sibling`

## Summary

- `reserve_address_only_persistent` returned `AllocatorExhausted` the moment the translated reverse identity it wanted was owned, without ever looking at another pool address. Its sibling `reserve_address_only_roundrobin` does `continue` on the identical condition, and #6226 exists precisely to have put it there.
- For a **port-less protocol** (GRE 47 / ESP 50 / ICMP) the identity degenerates to `(proto, translated_ip, 0, dst_ip, 0)`, so two tunnels from different subscribers to the same popular remote — a VPN concentrator, a cloud SASE endpoint — collide as soon as they land on one pool address, and the second was denied while other pool addresses sat idle.
- A **fresh** lease on a pool with `address-persistent` **off** now probes the remaining pool addresses and mints on the first whose identity is free.
- Docs: `docs/userspace-dataplane-architecture.md` (the sentence that said the #6041 branch "likewise single-probes" is now false and was corrected) and `docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md` (the #6041 row's collision paragraph).

## The refusal is not the defect

Only the missing retry was. The refusal is kept for the two PINNED cases:

- **`address-persistent`** — the address is `sticky_pool_index(src_ip)`, a pure function of the source. Rotating breaks the contract the operator configured; the round-robin sibling sets `address_attempts = 1` there for the same reason.
- **an EXISTING lease** — the address is pinned by `persistent-nat` for the permit scope's lifetime, and two flows sharing one public reverse identity are genuinely ambiguous on the return path. Admitting the second would be misdelivery.

## What the issue does not contain: the report's proposed fix reds shipped cells

The originating report asked for a **blanket** fallback. Applied as mutant N2 it does not merely over-reach in theory — it reds **three shipped #8132 HA cells** plus the two #6041 lease-reuse cells:

```
an_address_only_client_keeps_its_public_address_after_failover_8132
a_synced_address_only_flow_rejoining_an_idle_lease_leaves_the_expiry_index_8132
releasing_every_synced_address_only_flow_makes_the_lease_idle_8132
```

Those were already in the tree. Nobody had to write them for this.

## Reachability of the `reusing` + collision arm

Not obvious, and worth stating because it is what let the guard be a real cell rather than a comment. It needs two DIFFERENT flow keys producing the SAME reverse identity AND the SAME lease key. `AddressOnlyReverseKey` carries no routing scope and `PersistentSourceKey` carries none either, while `SourceNatFlowKey` does — so two flows identical except for `routing_scope` are exactly that shape.

## PR #9332 — dataplane: count auto-rebind give-ups, and split out the liveness masking (#9043) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9043-wedge-readiness-counter`

I closed #9043 earlier today on its **documentation** half and left its own
*"What IS confirmed, independent of the leak question"* section unaddressed —
two defects the issue states plainly are worth fixing **regardless** of how its
unresolvable kernel question resolves.

That is the failure mode where **a landed partial fix removes the reason anyone
would look again**: the tracker read as settled, so nothing would have led
anyone back to the confirmed half. Reopened, and this is item 2.

## The counter

The give-up arm of bounded auto-rebind had none, and its own message says why
that matters more here than almost anywhere else:

> the affected queues will not forward and **no readiness signal reports them**

Per #8384 binding readiness cannot see a bound-but-dead queue, so **once
automatic recovery gives up there is no other signal**. What existed was a single
`slog.Error`, emitted once per wedge by design — and a log line that fires once
is the hardest kind to alert on: gone from the ring buffer by the time anyone
looks, and its absence indistinguishable from a box that never wedged.

`binding_wedge_giveups_total` is incremented in the **same branch** as that
message so the two cannot drift — a counter keyed on a different condition than
the log beside it is worse than no counter, because the number then describes
something other than what the operator reads next to it.

Always emitted including at zero, per the #3464 convention and #8312's reason: a
counter that appears only once it fires cannot be alerted on, and cannot
distinguish "never happened" from "not scraped".

## Item 1 is filed, not fixed here — #9331

`xskLivenessProven` is **box-wide**, so one live queue disables wedge detection
for *every other queue*. The tree already says so in two files written for other
work (`metrics_dataplane_silent_skips_9019.go:31`, `process_napi.go:95`), and
combined with #8384 a masked queue has **no detection, no recovery and no
readiness signal**.

It needs a design change — per-binding liveness, with the idle-standby case
carried over and the rebind budget re-derived — and **#9043's title is about two
README claims and would never lead anyone to it**.

## The fixture caught itself

My first cell used a bare `&Manager{}` and measured **nothing**:
`hasBusyBindingsWedgeLocked` returns false on the nil proc, which *resets* the
attempt count and returns before the give-up branch. It failed loudly rather than
passing vacuously. The cell now asserts the wedge precondition explicitly, so a
fixture that stops reaching the branch says so instead of going green.

## PR #9334 — daemon: scope DHCP-learned DNS by routing instance [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9138-dhcp-dns-vrf-scope`

Closes #9138

## The security framing, stated plainly

**What an attacker needs:** the ability to answer DHCP on *any* segment where xpf runs a DHCP client. No credentials, no routing adjacency, no firewall-policy bypass — be the DHCP server, be faster than it, or spoof one on the wire. That includes a segment the operator deliberately isolated in a routing instance.

**What they get:** their nameserver IP appended to the firewall's `/etc/resolv.conf`, which is the whole resolver for this host (`systemd-resolved` is masked, so there is no second owner to fall back on).

**Blast radius:** everything the firewall host itself resolves — NTP peers, syslog and archival-transfer destinations, DDNS update servers, and the IPsec `dynamic-hostname` family hint. Redirecting archival transfer is the sharpest of those: it is where config archives go.

**Bounds, stated because the report's framing overreaches:**

1. Static `system name-server` entries are listed **first**, and glibc consults `nameserver` lines in order, so an operator with static DNS sees the leased server only on fallback.
2. The same vector exists with **no VRF at all** on any WAN DHCP link. That is a supported CPE deployment and matches Junos, where DHCP-learned DNS is global. **The VRF is not what enables the vector.**
3. The firewall does not resolve arbitrary user traffic. This is the host's own resolver, not a service.

**What the VRF actually adds** is the boundary crossing: a segment whose entire purpose is that it sits in a separate routing table nevertheless writes into the firewall's control-plane configuration. That is the part the operator did not consent to.

**And the claim that survives regardless of the security reading:** the host resolves from the **default** context, so a tenant-VRF nameserver is a **dead entry** — every lookup that reaches it burns a full resolver timeout before falling through.

## What was measured

`mergeDNSInput` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_dns.go`) walked every held lease with no interface, zone, VRF or trust filter. Its sibling lease consumer `collectDHCPRoutes` already filters. The module header and `docs/dns-ownership.md` documented the merge policy in detail and mentioned no scoping at all — **unconsidered, not rejected**.

## What changed

A lease whose interface belongs to a routing instance does not contribute nameservers. Three things are deliberately **not** excluded, each with its own control cell:

| Not excluded | Why |
|---|---|
| default-context WAN lease | the supported CPE deployment, matches Junos; dropping it breaks every standalone box |
| `fxp0`/`em*`/`fab*` | they live in the **synthesized** mgmt VRF, which is *not* a routing instance — a naive "exclude anything in a VRF" predicate would brick bootstrap DNS |
| static `system name-server` | authoritative, unconditional, and the escape hatch |

### Deviation from the issue's fix direction: no new config leaf

The issue suggests a `system services dhcp-client no-dns-update`-shaped leaf because this changes shipped behaviour on a documented policy. This lands **without** one, for two stated reasons:

1. The dimension was **unconsidered, not rejected** — the issue establishes this itself. An unconsidered dimension is a defect, not a policy.
2. The one deployment the change could regress (instance routes leaked into the default table, so the tenant resolver *is* reachable) has an existing, documented, one-line recovery: name it with `system name-server`, which is listed first and already authoritative. A new config-type field carries repo-wide blast radius; a knob is cheap to add later if an operator reports that case.

### Run against the shipped configs first

Before landing a blanket rule: the only DHCP client in `test/incus/xpf-test.conf` is `fxp0`, which is not in a routing instance. The routing-instance members are `gr-0/0/0.0` (`docs/ha-cluster-{loss,userspace}.conf`) and `ge-0/0/2` (test config, static addresses only). **The rule changes nothing in any shipped config.**

## Shared authority, not tidiness

The filter reads `dhcpLeaseRoutingInstances`, extracted from `dhcpRouteVRFMap` so both lease consumers answer the same question from one place. This is load-bearing: it makes the filter **inherit the #9135 lease-key-shape rule** rather than re-derive it. A filter keyed on the raw config token would be **inert for the canonical Junos slash spelling**, exactly as the #8963 remedy was. M4 below is that mutation, and it reds cells on both sides.

## PR #9336 — snmp: bound BER OID sub-identifiers to RFC 2578 at the decoder (#9133) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9133-ber-oid-subid-bound`

## Summary

- OID sub-identifiers were modelled as a platform-width **signed `int` with no bound**. Three symptoms follow from that one modelling choice, not from three defects: `berDecodeOID` accumulated over an unbounded continuation run and returned a NEGATIVE component with no error; `berEncodeSubID`'s `val < 0x80` fast path is true for every negative value and emitted a lone continuation octet; `oidCompare`'s signed `<` sorted a huge sub-id before 1.
- The fix is at the **decoder**, the only entry point from the wire: a `uint64` accumulator bounded by RFC 2578 §7.1.3's `0..4294967295` **before** each shift. No out-of-range component can then reach either of the other two sites.
- `berEncodeSubID`'s parameter becomes `uint32` — the standard's actual type — so the bad case is **unrepresentable at the call** rather than checked inside; `berEncodeOID` refuses an out-of-range component with its existing nil "not encodable" signal.
- `pkg/snmp/README.md` gains the rule, the exclusion, and the follow-up.

## `oidCompare` is deliberately unchanged, so the claim is tested

With the decoder bounded it only ever sees `0..4294967295` and its signed comparison is correct as written. `TestOIDOrderingHoldsOverTheWholeLegalRange9133` walks an ascending ladder across `math.MaxInt32` — the boundary a 32-bit `int` would wrap at — and then re-derives every rung through the codec, so the claim is about values the agent can actually hold rather than about literals. Mutant Q3 (bound set to `MaxInt32`) reds it.

## The "platform-width" half needed a compile-time guard

Components are carried as `[]int`. `const _ uint = uint(^uint(0)>>1) - maxOIDSubIdentifier` is a no-op on amd64/arm64 and a **compile error** on any 32-bit target, where `int(val)` would wrap every large sub-identifier negative — this defect restored by the back door.

## What is deliberately NOT bounded, and the mutant that justifies it

The **folded first two arcs**. X.690 §8.19.4 packs them into one octet and `berDecodeOID` reconstructs them as `data[0]/40` / `data[0]%40`, so a first octet above `0x77` yields a first arc above 2 — invalid ASN.1 that nonetheless round-trips byte for byte. Bounding it would replace a faithful echo of the client's own OID with an empty one. Mutant **Q7**, which adds that "obvious" extra hardening, reds a **shipped** cell (`TestWireVarbindByteFloors_6551`) as well as the guard written for it.

## Found while fixing, filed as #9333

`decodePDUFields` **skips** an undecodable varbind rather than failing the PDU. Measured: a two-varbind v1 GET with one bad OID gets a `noError` response carrying **one** varbind — an RFC 1157 §4.1.2 arity violation. It is **pre-existing**, and that is measured rather than argued: the pinning cell carries two vectors, and under the Q1 mutant (decoder bound removed) the `overflowing-subidentifier` sub-case reds while `truncated-continuation` stays green, because the latter reaches the same skip at master. Pinned here rather than fixed — the remedy is a decision about all five `continue` arms in that loop, not about OID bounds.

## Test plan

- [x] 8 new cells in `pkg/snmp/ber_oid_subid_bound_9133_test.go`
- [x] `go test ./pkg/snmp/` green (8.5s)
- [x] `gofmt` clean
- [x] `go test ./...` — green except one **pre-existing flake**, see below

**The one red in `go test ./...` is #9335, not this change.** `TestV2cTrapIsUnaffectedByTheTargetMove9123` asserts three independently-built v2c trap packets have equal length, but `buildLinkTrapV2` draws `rand.Int31()` and `berEncodeIntegerValue` emits the minimum octets, so the encoded request-id is 4 octets for a value ≥ 2^23 and shorter below. Diagnosed by mechanism rather than by re-running, then measured at 20,000 iterations in-tree: `MISMATCH 216/20000 = 1.080%`, lengths `{129: 2, 131: 215, 132: 59783}`. Nothing here touches `math/rand` or `berEncodeIntegerValue`, and the earlier `go test ./pkg/snmp/` run of this same tree was green. Filed as #9335.

## Mutation matrix

Each mutant confirmed BUILT and APPLIED before scoring.

| # | mutation | result | cells that fired |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | decoder bound removed — master body restored **verbatim** | KILLED (7) | both overflow vectors, the RFC-boundary cell, the end-to-end cell, and the arity pin's `overflowing-subidentifier` sub-case (its sibling stays green — that split is the "pre-existing" measurement) |
| Q2 | bound checked AFTER the shift instead of before | **SURVIVED** | — |
| Q3 | bound set to `MaxInt32` | KILLED (3) | RFC-boundary, round-trip, and ordering cells |
| Q4 | `berEncodeOID`'s range guard removed | KILLED (1) | `TestEncoderRefusesAnOutOfRangeComponent9133` |
| Q6 | **WIRING**: `decodePDUFields` ignores `berDecodeOID`'s error | KILLED (4) | end-to-end + both arity-pin sub-cases |
| Q7 | folded first arcs bounded too | KILLED (2) | its guard **and the shipped `TestWireVarbindByteFloors_6551`** |

**Q2 survived, and the honest reading is that my comment was overstated, not that the test is weak.** With a `uint64` accumulator a post-shift check is equally correct — seven more bits cannot wrap 64, so it fires at the fifth significant octet either way. The pre-shift form is still the one to keep (it bounds `val` below 2^25 so the shift cannot overflow *regardless* of the accumulator's width, removing a reasoning step rather than relying on it), and the comment now says that instead of claiming the post-shift form is wrong. Recorded rather than dropped from the matrix.

The compile-time `int`-width guard has no mutant: it either compiles or it does not, and there is no 32-bit target in the tree to build it against.

## PR #9338 — userspace-dp: carry the routing domain into the embedded-ICMP reply key [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9162-nat64-icmp-domain`

## What this fixes, and the regression it repairs

`icmp_embed::parse::embedded_reply_key` hardcoded `routing_domain: 0`, with a
comment citing the domain-agnostic convention in `session/key.rs`. **The
citation was the defect.** That convention governs the keys an INSTALLED session
is INDEXED under (`reverse_wire_key` / `reverse_canonical_key`, whose probes
`reverse_match_key` zeroes to match). It says nothing about a key a caller
builds and hands to a lookup, which is all `embedded_reply_key` produces.

**This also repairs a live regression from #9271 / #9033**, merged earlier
today. That PR was correct and its commit message states the right distinction —
the installed NAT64 reverse companion must carry the forward flow's domain, and
the `routing_domain: 0` convention belongs to the reverse-MATCH index, not to an
installed key. But the **lookup** side was never moved to match, which is exactly
the coupling #9162 was filed to prevent. #9271's own commit message recorded the
risk as "NOT REFUTED AND NOT CONFIRMED" and said whoever took #9162 should build
the combination. It is built here, and it confirms the risk.

## Consequence at `483badf39`

`nat64_match.rs` resolves an INSTALLED NAT64 session half through
`lookup_session_across_scopes`, whose four probes (`key_to_handle`,
`forward_wire_index` via the domain-preserving `forward_wire_key`, and the two
shared maps) are **every one domain-preserving** — and it has no second,
domain-agnostic arm. So a domain-0 probe could not reach a session in a routing
instance:

| arm | resolves | status before this PR |
|---|---|---|
| V6→V4 | the FORWARD session, domain-stamped since #7160 | dead in a VRF **since #7160** |
| V4→V6 | the v4 reverse companion | worked only because the companion was also installed at 0 — **#9271 correctly ended that accident** |

`forwards == 0` means the error is **dropped**, not forwarded untranslated:
PMTUD and traceroute across the NAT64 boundary were dead in **both directions**
for every flow in a non-default routing instance.

`nat64_match.rs` also contained **zero** `routing_domain` references while both
same-family siblings derived one via `ingress_routing_domain` — the asymmetry
#9162 named as its own positive control. The shared literal additionally
disabled the same-family **#6474 outbound-SNAT** arm in a VRF, where the quote's
reply key *is* the forward session's primary key, so the #5690 identity reversal
put the INTERNAL pre-NAT source on the wire.

## Two things measured, not assumed

The brief asked for these specifically, because a wrong answer to either trades
one broken tenant for another.

1. **All four probes behind `lookup_session_across_scopes` are
   domain-preserving.** Confirmed by reading each.

## PR #9339 — dataplane/routing: fan a bare routing-instance interface ref down to its units (#9132) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9132-bare-ri-iface-fandown`

## Summary

- `buildInterfaceRouteTables` and `buildInterfaceRoutingInstances` keyed a routing-instance interface reference on `config.CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef(ifname)` alone. For a **bare** `ge-0/0/0` that is the bare name, while the per-unit snapshot rows carrying the **addresses** are `ge-0/0/0.<unit>` — so the reference reached nothing addressed. The unit row fell back to `inet.0` with `RoutingInstance == ""`, which is exactly the field the Rust side derives the connected table from, so **#2388's table scoping was rendered inert rather than wrong**.
- The sibling binder in the same documented family — `CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef`'s own doc names all three — already fanned bare references down. Two of the three did not.
- The rule now lives in ONE place, `config.InterfaceUnitRefKeys`, which all three use.
- Docs: `docs/config-schema.md` (the #5878 Phase 2 routing-instance bullet) and `docs/userspace-dataplane-architecture.md` (the fan-down paragraph).

## It is NOT the #9063 collapse, and the difference decides the fix

I read #9063 first, as asked. It is **not** the same defect at a third consumer, and calling it that would have prescribed the wrong remedy.

| | #9063 | #9132 |
|---|---|---|
| mechanism | `logicalUnitDeviceKey` normalizes two DIFFERENT spellings onto ONE key | nothing collapses — `CanonicalInterfaceUnitRef` leaves `ge-0/0/0` and `ge-0/0/0.0` distinct (measured) |
| direction | **over**-match: the consumer cannot tell a whole-device reference from a unit-0 one | **under**-match: the bare key reaches no row at all |
| fix | read the RAW reference to recover the distinction | fan the bare reference DOWN to gain reach |

Same *class* — an interface reference whose key shape is held together by a note — opposite direction, opposite remedy.

## What did NOT move into the shared helper

The zone binder also fans a **unit** reference UP to the base key. That is right for zones (host-inbound on the physical interface must resolve) and **wrong for routing**: the base snapshot row inherits the kernel netdev's addresses, which belong to unit 0, so binding the base from a `ge-0/0/0.1` reference would move unit 0's prefix into unit 1's instance — #9063's hazard pointed the other way. Levelling the three to one behaviour would be consistency achieved in the wrong direction, so the fan-UP stays at the zone binder's own call site with a comment saying so.

The zone-binder refactor is a **proven no-op**: for each of the four reference shapes (bare, unit, `base.`, `.5`) the new loop writes the same keys in the same order as the loop it replaced, which matters because that map is first-writer-wins over sorted zone names. Mutants P4 and P5 confirm it empirically — they mutate only `InterfaceUnitRefKeys` and each reds ~20 cells written for the zone binder years ago.

## An ordering rule the fan-down forces someone to choose

Before this, a bare reference and an explicit unit reference could not collide. Now they can. `forEachRoutingInstanceInterfaceKey` walks twice — pass 0 binds the reference as written, pass 1 adds fanned units without overwriting — so the **explicit unit always wins**, whichever instance is authored first. Two properties fall out:

- **pass 0 is byte-for-byte the pre-#9132 loop, so the change is purely ADDITIVE on these maps.** `TestBareRefFanDownIsPurelyAdditive9132` asserts it against the old loop re-implemented verbatim as the oracle, so it cannot drift into agreeing with the new code by paraphrase.
- a single pass with plain assignment would have resolved a contradictory config by the order of `cfg.RoutingInstances` — deterministic (it is a slice, and **measured** to be in authoring order, not sorted by name) but not a rule anyone chose.

## The ordering cell was VACUOUS on its first form

Reported because the mutation matrix is the only reason I know. `TestExplicitUnitRefBeatsAFannedDownBareRef9132` originally varied the order of the two `set routing-instances <ri> interface …` lines and called them "authoring orders". They are not: an instance's position in `cfg.RoutingInstances` is fixed by its **first mention**, which is the `instance-type` line — identical in both sub-cases. Both produced the same slice order, and in that order (bare reference first) last-writer-wins happens to **agree** with the rule. **P3 survived.**

The cell now varies the `instance-type` order, **asserts** the resulting slice order so it cannot silently stop varying, and leads with the discriminating arrangement (the explicit unit reference in the *earlier* instance). P3 is then killed, and the `bare-instance-first` sub-case stays green — which is the point of keeping it.

## PR #9341 — snmp: make the v2c trap invariance cell immune to the random request-id (#9335) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9335-flaky-length-identity`

`TestV2cTrapIsUnaffectedByTheTargetMove9123` asserted that the v2c packet
**length** is identical across three targets. The v2c PDU carries a **randomized
request-id**, and a BER INTEGER is minimal-width — one that fits in a byte
encodes shorter than one needing three. The length varies **by chance**, with
nothing about the target having changed.

## The defect is mine, and it is the second instance of one error

The cell's own comment, three lines above it, reads:

> Byte-identity was my first attempt and it was simply wrong: the v2c PDU carries
> a RANDOMIZED request-id … It reported a difference for every target including
> the empty one, which is what showed it **was measuring the randomness rather
> than the change**.

**And then I asserted a length identity that measures exactly that same
randomness.** Writing the lesson down did not stop me reproducing it one level
lower, where the hit rate was low enough to survive review.

## Measured, with a positive control on the repair

| assertion | failures / 20,000 |
|---|---|
| length identity (as shipped) | **240 (1.2%)** |
| structural signature (this PR) | **0** |

Independently measured at 1.08% by another lane, which is how it surfaced.

**A low-rate flake is worse than a loud one.** At that rate it passes every time
its author runs it and fails for someone else, weeks later, in an unrelated
package — where the honest reading ("my change did this") is wrong and the cheap
reading ("re-run it") is how a suite stops being believed. It reds
`go test ./...` for every lane.

## What the replacement costs, stated rather than glossed

`berShape9335` renders the tag tree with every leaf's bytes included **except**
INTEGERs, whose value is discarded — that is where the randomness lives.
Discarding it is a real loss of strength, so
`TestTheShapeSignatureDiscriminates9335` pins that the signature still separates
linkUp from linkDown, and is stable across repeated builds of the same trap. **A
summarising comparison that discards too much passes trivially**, so the
discarding has to be shown to still discriminate.

The rule is not "avoid byte comparison": **any assertion over data containing a
random field is unsound unless it is invariant to that field — and a length is a
function of the field, not an escape from it.**

`go test ./...` green.

## PR #9342 — config: reject `then routing-instance` combined with `then next term` [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9140-routing-instance-next-term`

`then { routing-instance <x>; next term; }` committed cleanly and then rendered a
TERMINATING accept for the term's whole match set, making every later term in the
filter unreachable. On `lo0` — the host control-plane filter — an SSH deny written
after a PBR classification term was silently dead.

## Measured at `origin/master` (77240ec4e)

```
STRICT GATE ACCEPTED
term t1 Action="" NextTerm=true RoutingInstance="mgmt-vrf" TerminalActions=[]
term t2 Action="discard" NextTerm=false RoutingInstance="" TerminalActions=[discard]

nftRulesFromTerm(t1, ip) = [ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8 accept]      <-- TERMINATES
nftRulesFromTerm(t2, ip) = [meta l4proto 6 th dport 22 drop] <-- unreachable for 10/8
```

## The runtimes are not the bug

The source report claimed a boolean-precedence slip in the two Go renderers and
proposed loosening them to `if term.NextTerm || (term.Action == "" && term.RoutingInstance == "")`.
That is harmful. `then routing-instance` is a terminating filter-based-forwarding
action in **both** implementations, deliberately:

- `userspace-dp/src/filter/compiler.rs` — `continue_term: snap.action.is_empty() && snap.routing_instance.is_empty()`,
  with a comment saying a routing-instance term "takes its own routing decision and is
  NOT a fall-through even with an empty action"; `resolve_term_action` maps `""` to `Accept`.
- `pkg/daemon/daemon_nft_term_lower.go` / `pkg/nftables/netlink_lo0.go` — the
  fall-through arm is guarded by `RoutingInstance == ""` so the nft mirror matches.

Changing the Go side alone would make nft fall through while the Rust evaluator
terminates — a kernel-vs-userspace divergence on a shape the tolerant load /
peer-sync path can still deliver, against the mirror contract stated in
`daemon_nft_term_lower.go`. **Neither runtime is changed in this PR.**

## The fix: the missing commit gate

#5142 already rejects "terminating action + `next term`", but tested
`len(term.TerminalActions) > 0` — and `compileFilterThen` records the FBF steer on
`term.RoutingInstance`, because `TerminalActions` carries only the
`accept`/`reject`/`discard` keywords. `validateFilterTerminalConflictStrict` now
derives the terminating action from either field (explicit keyword first, so every
pre-existing error message is unchanged) and rejects the combination naming
`routing-instance <x>`. It already runs under `lenientFilterTerminalConflict`, so
the tolerant path inherits the #1960 downgrade to a warning.

Still legal, and covered by controls: a bare `then routing-instance <x>` (the FBF
case, #3427 M08), `then routing-instance <x>` + `then accept` (#3308), and a
modifier-only `then { count c; next term; }` fall-through (#2544/#3427).

## PR #9343 — logging: escape RFC 5424 SD-PARAM values in RT_FLOW records (#9321) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-06)

Branch: `fix/9321-sdparam-escape`

## Summary

- `formatStructuredMsg` built the Junos `[junos@2636.1.1.1.2.129 …]` SD element with `fmt.Sprintf` and interpolated seven operator-/config-derived values as `param="%s"` with **no RFC 5424 §6.3.3 escaping**. A policy named `p1" injected-param="1` forged a second SD-PARAM in every record shipped off-box; a `]` closed the element early so a strict collector read the remainder as MSG and lost the record.
- `escapeSDParamValue` escapes `"` (%d34), `\` (%d92) and `]` (%d93), applied **once per value** in `formatStructuredMsg` — after the empty-value fallbacks (a fallback is itself a param value) and before the type switch (`appName` is interpolated twice, as `service-name` and `application`).
- `pkg/logging/README.md` gains the rule, the two consequences, and why this is not a widening of #6585.

## I read #6585's reasoning first, and it rules out the obvious remedy

#6585's guard (`termsafe.SanitizeForDisplay` at `SyslogClient.Send`) is scoped to control bytes **on purpose**. Its third acceptance criterion is an explicit over-reach guard — *"ordinary multi-word and UTF-8 attribute values are unchanged on the wire"* — and it protects the RFC 3164 **frame**, which three printable bytes cannot damage. Widening it would mangle every other consumer of that sanitizer (gRPC show output, IPsec error text) for a property only the SD element has.

**#6585 closed frame integrity; this closes SD-element integrity.** Two boundaries; both needed. Nor is the remedy a commit-time reject: Junos permits these characters in a quoted name and the #1798 gate correctly accepts them, so rejecting would be a behaviour change on a supported spelling. The fix is at the render side, which is where `pkg/config/freetext.go`'s own three-layer doctrine puts it — that doctrine's layer-3 enumeration named `pkg/networkd`, `pkg/frr`, `pkg/ipsec`, and `pkg/logging` was a fourth interpolation sink outside it.

## A cell of mine was VACUOUS and the matrix found it

`TestARbracketInANameCannotTerminateTheElement9321` **passed under the identity mutant** — it was simply absent from R1's red list. The cause was my **oracle**, not the assertion: the first parser scanned a PARAM-VALUE only for `"` and `\`, so an unescaped `]` inside a quoted value read as ordinary content and the element never appeared to close early.

That is the *lenient* reading. §6.3.3 says the character MUST be escaped, so its presence is **malformed input**, and collectors differ in recovery (rsyslog terminates the element there). The oracle now does both — records the violation **and** ends the element — so the cell asserts the fact ("this record is malformed") without depending on a guess about any one collector.

The oracle is also deliberately **not** a reversal of the producer: it implements §6.3.3's *reading* rules, because a parser derived from the formatter agrees with it by construction and cannot fail.

## Hot-path shape

Allocation-free fast path (`strings.ContainsAny` then early return) for the already-clean case — every ordinary record — because this runs on the shared dataplane event path (#2283), once per firewall event per structured client. Byte-scan rather than rune-scan: all three characters are ASCII and every byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence is ≥ 0x80, so a byte scan can neither split a rune nor match inside one.

Address/port values are escaped too, and not out of paranoia: `splitAddrPort` returns its input **verbatim** when `net.SplitHostPort` fails, so "an address cannot contain a quote" is a claim about a parser, not about the data. The fast path makes the total rule and the cheap rule the same rule — and a total rule is the one a newly-added field inherits.

## Test plan

- [x] 6 new cells in `pkg/logging/sdparam_escape_9321_test.go`
- [x] `go test ./...` (not a package list)
- [x] `gofmt` clean
- [x] **Byte-identity** for ordinary records, pinned against goldens **captured** by running the unmodified formatter at `origin/master` (77240ec4e) in a throwaway worktree and pasting its stdout — a golden transcribed from the format strings would only prove my transcription agrees with itself
- [x] **Coverage by reflection**: every exported string field of `EventRecord` is poisoned in turn with `a"b\c]d`; the cell also asserts the poison actually **reached** an SD-PARAM (29 values across the three record types), because a reflection walk that reaches nothing is a green that asserts nothing

## Mutation matrix

Each mutant confirmed BUILT and APPLIED; the escape body is replaced **by span**, so a splice cannot land on a same-named site elsewhere.

| # | mutation | first oracle | strict oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | `escapeSDParamValue` is the identity (the shipped state) | KILLED (7) | **KILLED (11)** |
| R2 | `"` and `]` escaped, `\` not | KILLED (2) | KILLED (2) |
| R3 | wrong ORDER — `"` replaced before `\`, doubling the backslash just inserted | KILLED (7) | KILLED (7) |
| R4 | strip the three characters instead of escaping them | KILLED (11) | KILLED (11) |
| R5 | the two ZONE values left unescaped, everything else escaped | KILLED (1) | **KILLED (6)** |
| R6 | **WIRING / call site**: the `Format == "structured"` fanout emits the plain body | KILLED (3) | KILLED (3) |

**The two columns are the vacuity finding.** Same production code, same cells, different oracle. **R5 is the row that shows why it mattered**: a fix that escaped everything *except* the zone names scored one red with the lenient oracle and six with the strict one.

**R3** is why the helper is a single pass rather than three `ReplaceAll`s: escaping `"` first and `\` second doubles the backslash just inserted, so `a"b` emits `a\\"b` — which a conforming parser reads as a literal backslash followed by an *unescaped* quote, i.e. the injection restored through the fix.
