The issue is a validated external-review finding filed 26 commits behind. Both halves were re-measured before anything changed.

**V020 REPRODUCES, exactly as filed:**

```
CONTROL separate lines                err=<nil>  src="10.0.0.1" dst="10.0.0.2"
A untyped head swallows BOTH          err=<nil>  src=""         dst=""
B source own line, destination eaten  err=<nil>  src="10.0.0.1" dst=""
C destination own line, source eaten  err=<nil>  src=""         dst="10.0.0.2"
routing-instance head                 err=<nil>  src=""
typed head                            STRICT REJECT `tunnel destination: unknown modifier "keepalive-retry"`
```

**V021 DOES NOT — `d5b749b8a` (#8939) fixed it.** `compiler_security_flow.go` now calls `expandFlatRun(node.Children, securityFlowSchema8939())`, and all three packed spellings give `dns=true emb=true`. The issue's `dns=true emb=FALSE` transcript is a true record of a state the tree has left. Nothing was done for V021 beyond confirming it; the issue is corrected rather than closed over.

## V020: the remedy was measured, not picked by family

Three remedies exist in this tree and which one works depends on the shape `SetPath` built:

- **`packedStatements: true` is already declared on `tunnel`** and it still loses, because that flag splits a packed tail on ONE node's `Keys` and the flat-set form is a nested CHAIN — `[keepalive-retry 5] > [destination 10.0.0.2]`. The issue names this trap; it is real.
- **`expandFlatRun` alone** handles the chain and the packed tail but leaves a CONTAINER leaf's subtree alone, so `tunnel routing-instance destination VR1 source 10.0.0.1` would still lose the source two levels down.
- **`hoistAndSplitRun8939`** covers both, and lifts the nested `source` precisely because it is *unambiguously foreign* — legal in `tunnel`, illegal under `routing-instance`. That bound is what stops it turning a leaf's VALUE into a statement.

Mutant M3 is the measurement behind that choice: swapping in `expandFlatRun` kills **only** the routing-instance cell and leaves every other tunnel arm green.

## V020's second half is not a compiler change

The routing side and the dataplane side each had their own endpoint screen and they disagreed:

```
EmitTunnelEndpointNames (what the DATAPLANE learns)
  Mode != "wireguard" && (Source == "" || Destination == "")  -> skip

collectAppliedTunnels (what the ROUTING side creates)
  Source != "" || Mode == "wireguard"                          -> apply
  ...and its per-UNIT loop screened NOTHING AT ALL.
```

So variant B — source, no destination — passed the routing gate and failed the dataplane one: the TUN is created, brought up and given its configured addresses while the dataplane holds no endpoint for it. An operator can zone it, route into it, and every packet disappears.

`pkg/routing/tunnel.go` **has** a correct guard for exactly this (`localIP == nil || remoteIP == nil` → warn and refuse) and it is **dead code**: the daemon always sets AnchorOnly and `EffectiveType("")` is `TypeUserspace` on every box, so `Apply` always dispatches to `applyAnchorLocked`, which has no endpoint check at all.

`config.TunnelHasUsableEndpoints` is now the single predicate, used by the emitter and by both arms of `collectAppliedTunnels`, and the drop is WARNED rather than silent. It is deliberately the **stricter** of the two: creating a device the dataplane cannot forward through is the failure, not the remedy. WireGuard stays exempt (#1432/#1736). Checked against the shipped corpus — every in-tree tunnel writes both endpoints, so nothing stops being applied.

## PR #9396 — userspace-dp: count the oversized DF-clear IPv4 forward instead of booking it as a success [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9328-df-clear-oversize`

Closes #9328 (cheap half; the policy half is #9395)

## Re-derived, not inherited

The issue's `Executed` labels were not taken on trust.

**Positive-controlled grep for MF/offset WRITERS**: the only hits are `nat64.rs` (2477/3276/3853), which copy MF and offset **verbatim from an existing IPv6 Fragment Header** — none splits a datagram. Everything else is a reader or `GRE_FLAG_KEY`. The control matters: the grep demonstrably *can* find a writer, so finding none elsewhere is a result rather than a failed search.

**No generic MTU comparison in `tx/`**: only `tcp_segmentation.rs` (the TCP path) and a `_slow_path_mtu_exceeded` label. The only length guard on the forward path is `copy_frame_is_oversized`, which tests the **UMEM chunk (4096)**, not the egress MTU.

So an oversized DF-clear IPv4 datagram is submitted at full length and the NIC, switch or next hop drops it.

## The structural cause: the decision type lost the information

DF-clear-oversize returned the **same `EgressMtuDecision::Forward` value** as a frame that fits. Nothing downstream could tell them apart, so the oversize submission bumped `enqueue_ok`, `enqueue_copy`, `pending_copy_tx_packets` and `tx_bytes_total` and recorded no exception at all.

An operator debugging the downstream blackhole saw a **healthy counter — a wrong diagnostic, not a missing one.** The asymmetry is with the TCP arm of the identical outcome, which has recorded `tcp_segmentation_miss` since #1282.

`ForwardOversizeNoDf` now distinguishes it and the dispatcher records `egress_mtu_exceeded_forwarded_no_df`. **Behaviour is unchanged** — still forwarded, still no PTB (Fragmentation-Needed is meaningful only to a sender that set DF).

## The policy is deliberately not taken — #9395

Fragmenting per RFC 791, drop-and-count, or continuing to forward are all open, and **the wire-level fate of the oversize submission is unmeasured**. Option "drop" versus "keep forwarding" turns entirely on that: dropping a path that currently works would be a regression introduced by a fix. The counter is what makes the decision answerable, which is why it lands first.

## A prior decision spoke, and only half of it was a decision

`oversized_v4_without_df_forwards` went red, exactly as the issue predicted. Its stated reason:

> Oversized but DF clear: the downstream may fragment. Preserve the pre-#2301 forward behaviour rather than PTB-storming the flow.

That claim is **true and unchanged** — the frame still forwards and no PTB is sent. What the cell *also* pinned, silently, was that the outcome is **indistinguishable from a frame that fits**. That was not a decision anyone took; it was the absence of a distinction. The claim is kept verbatim, the expected value moves, and an in-MTU control is added so the new variant cannot leak the other way.

## Mutation table

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | revert to the indistinguishable `Forward` (**the defect**) | KILLED |
| M2 | in-MTU frames also flagged (**control**) | KILLED (6 cells) |
| M3 | sever the `record_exception` (**wiring**) | **SURVIVED** → KILLED |

**M3 is the fifth instance of this shape in the campaign**, and the sharpest here: the decision-level cell proves the value is distinguishable and says nothing about whether anything *acts* on it — a distinguishable decision that nothing records is exactly the silence being fixed. Bound by driving the real dispatcher harness (DF parameterised through it) and asserting the recorded reason, with an in-MTU control so an exception firing on every forward would not pass.

**3/3 killed** after that fix.

## Gates

- `go test ./...` — green.
- `cargo test` — green (**5471 passed**).
- No `cargo fmt` drift against master's own baseline.

## PR #9397 — nat: one pool is one allocator — revert #9062's routing-instance split (#9389) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9389-allocator-key-ri`

**#9062 was mine, and its rationale gave two reasons where only one was a defect:**

> a port handed to one tenant was unavailable to the other **and** — with the flow
> key also domain-blind — the second tenant's identical 5-tuple was answered with
> the first's translation.

- *"A port handed to one tenant was unavailable to the other"* is a **shared pool
  working correctly**. A pool is a finite set of wire identities; one
  `(address, port)` backs exactly one flow, whatever routing instance the traffic
  came from. "Unavailable to the other" is what a shared resource means.
- The **second** clause was the real defect, and `SourceNatFlowKey::routing_scope`
  closes it **alone** — two tenants with distinct flow keys hold two records and
  draw two *different* ports from the one allocator.

I fixed the second and also "fixed" the first, which needed no fixing.

## What the extra split cost

Two pointer-distinct `PortAllocator`s over identical addresses, either able to mint
the same `(addr, port)` for a different tenant. `same_allocator` is `Arc::ptr_eq`,
so the #6979/#8115 overlap index read them as **hostile peers** and refused every
mint whose candidate the other held — rolled back into a dropped packet. Measured:
**five consecutive refusals** on a pool with free capacity.

**The guard was right and the split was wrong.**

Nothing is lost by removing it: `pool_addresses_v4`/`_v6` were already in the key,
so two genuinely different pools sharing a NAME were always discriminated by their
addresses — pinned by a narrowness cell.

## The general shape

**A change that splits a shared object changes every identity test that object
participates in.** I reasoned about the key's *contents* and never about the
pointer identity of the thing now duplicated. `NatScopeCtx`'s own #9062 comment
draws the distinction I then failed to apply — *"the instance NAMES scope which
RULE matches; this scopes the flow's IDENTITY. They are different questions."* The
allocator is neither; it is the shared resource both are asked about.

## Two cells, and why neither caught it

`source_nat_allocator_key_separates_routing_instances_9062` asserted the split,
calling the shared-pool behaviour "a quieter defect". It is **inverted, not
deleted**, with the old wording quoted in place so the correction is legible; its
reference arm is kept verbatim. It did not catch the regression because **it was
the cell that encoded it**.

`two_rules_naming_one_pool_are_not_peers_6979` asserts exactly the invariant #9062
broke and **stayed green throughout** — its fixture leaves `from_routing_instance`

## PR #9398 — snmp/config: hoist the packed run at the SNMPv3 USM user level (#9155 R-02) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9155-r02-packed-authpriv`

```
set snmp v3 usm local-engine user alice \
    authentication-sha256 authentication-password A \
    privacy-aes128 privacy-password P
```

committed clean and compiled to `authProto="sha256" privProto=""`. **The operator
configured authPriv and the agent served authNoPriv.**

`SetPath` builds a flat-set line as a **nested chain**, not a packed run, so the
privacy stanza landed as a *grandchild* of the password node:

```
[user alice] > [authentication-sha256] > [authentication-password A]
                                          > [privacy-aes128 privacy-password P]
```

`compileSNMPv3Users` iterates the user's own children and never reached it.

## Why #9155's own gates could not catch it

Both read the **compiled config** and key on a protocol being NAMED. Neither can
fire when the privacy protocol was **discarded before the gate ran**.

> **A gate downstream of a dropping compiler is blind to exactly what it drops.**

Which is why this belongs in the compiler, not in a third validator.

## Three sites before the right one — two of which built cleanly

1. **`parseSNMPv3UserKeys`**, rewritten to walk a packed run. Plausible and
   wrong: this input is not a packed run. **Reverted rather than kept** — a change
   that fixes nothing still has to be maintained.
2. **`expandFlatRun`** — right family, wrong member. It leaves body-owning leaves
   alone *by design*, and `authentication-sha256` legitimately owns a body.
3. **`hoistAndSplitRun8939`** — the member that exists for exactly this shape.

The schema already declared every cut point, so no per-container shim was needed —
only the call. **I found the site by dumping the AST, after assuming it twice.**

## Behaviour change, stated because it is one

A config that compiled as authNoPriv now compiles as authPriv, so the #9155
runtime floor will refuse authNoPriv requests naming that user. **That is the
configured level being enforced, not a regression** — but a deployment polling
such a user at the wrong level will notice at upgrade.

## PR #9399 — config: stop a one-line login-user demotion from being silently dropped (and restore the leaf-run gate's second axis) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9391-login-user-class`

Row 1 of #9391, taken as security work. Also restores a change that #9394 said it landed and did not.

## The direction of failure, established before anything changed

The brief asked for this first. The answer is **both directions**, which is why "an empty class" was the wrong frame.

### Fresh user, no prior class — FAILS CLOSED

`PrincipalForUID` returns an UNRESOLVED principal for an empty class and `Authorize` denies on `p.Class == ""` before any permission is consulted. There is no default class anywhere on the path. Measured across all six permissions with a super-user control in the same run: every one denies, and the denial names the missing class.

**That direction is an availability bug, not an authorization one.** Saying so plainly, and downgrading it.

### An existing user being DEMOTED — FAILS OPEN. This is the finding.

The drop is one-directional. `class` is TYPED, so `class <c> uid <n>` is **rejected** at commit; only `uid <n> class <c>` is admitted. Losing the swallowed `class` does not produce an *empty* class when the user already has one — **it leaves the OLD class standing**:

```
set system login user admin class super-user          (earlier line)
set system login user admin uid 2001 class read-only

  one line   -> class="super-user"     THE DEMOTION IS DROPPED
  separate   -> class="read-only"      (the oracle)
```

Commit reports success. `show configuration | display set` renders the operator's own `read-only` line back. And:

- **`reconcileSudoers` keys the passwordless-root drop-in on `Class == "super-user"`**, so the demoted admin keeps the `xpf-admin` NOPASSWD grant. That is precisely the **#3889** defect — *"a demoted or deleted admin kept passwordless root sudo forever"* — reached through the config layer instead of through the missing revocation branch #3889 added.
- `pkg/authz` then evaluates the retained `super-user` class on every gRPC and REST call.

**Reachability: no attacker required.** An ordinary operator with `configure` permission, typing the idiomatic one-line `set`, silently fails to remove someone's root. The person who benefits is the one being demoted, and what they need to do is nothing. The braced spelling of the same demotion is rejected by #5180's duplicate-block guard, so this is **flat-set only** — the CLI-typed form.

## The fix

`expandFlatRun` over the user's children, computed **once** and read by both loops in the reader (the `authentication` probe and the property switch) so they cannot see different sets.

`expandFlatRun` rather than `hoistAndSplitRun8939` **deliberately**: the stronger helper descends into a container leaf's body, and `authentication` is one whose packed spelling the #6662 gate exists to REJECT. Lifting out of it would make the lenient path compile a shape the strict path refuses. A cell pins that an authored `authentication` block still reaches the reader.

`TestDemotionSpellingRevokesTheSudoersGrant9391` is the cell that matters. **Every cell #3889 wrote constructs `config.LoginUser` values directly and never goes through the compiler** — which is exactly why a compiler-layer drop could resurrect that defect with #3889's own suite green. This one drives the SPELLING end to end, with a genuine super-user as the control and the separate-lines demotion as the oracle.

## Second commit: a change #9394 claimed and did not land

Removing the now-fixed row from #9156's register made the ratchet report ONE stale entry where the totals demanded more. Chasing that arithmetic showed the two-axis gate change described in PR #9394 and commit `7a44a8cdc` **is not in the tree**:

- `gateCompileFlatSet9156` present with **zero call sites**;
- the gate comparing the **braced axis only**;
- the register holding the original 26 **unlabelled** rows.

### How

The mutation harness took a `cp` backup of the gate file at setup — *before* the two-axis work. A later mutant restore ran `cp <backup> <file>`, reverting it silently; the ratchet extraction was then re-applied on top of the reverted file.

## PR #9400 — feeds: redact the feed URL's credential in the stale-transition error (#9164) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9164-feed-credential-redaction`

`recordFailure` stored `ferr.Error()` verbatim and logged the error **object**. Go's
transport error quotes the URL it dialled:

```
fetch failed: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/list.txt?token=BEARER_TOKEN_ABC123": dial tcp ...
```

so a per-tenant bearer token reached journald and every support bundle. The repo
states outright that this is the common shape — *"dynamic-address feeds routinely
carry per-tenant bearer tokens in the URL"*. `config.RedactURL` was already called
two sites away and simply not here.

## Not the obvious fix

Wrapping `ferr.Error()` in `RedactURL` is what it looks like it wants, and it is
**wrong**: that helper is sound on *a URL*, not on arbitrary text, and an error
string is a prefix plus a quoted URL plus a trailing diagnostic. Redacting the URL
we already hold and substituting it is sound by construction — `fs.url` is the
operator's configured string, exactly the input `RedactURL` was written for.

## Two spellings, and that's a measurement

`net/http`'s `stripPassword` rewrites a basic-auth **password** to `***` before
formatting, so the error contains a string that is **not** `fs.url`. Replacing only
the raw URL misses every password case — and leaves the **username**, which
`stripPassword` doesn't touch. Replacing only the masked form misses the
query-token case, which is the one this product has.

## Two gaps in my own cells — both the lesson I've been giving other lanes

- **The wiring was unbound.** My first three cells drove the helper directly, and a
  mutant restoring the raw store *at the call site* **survived all of them**. A
  redaction helper nothing calls redacts nothing.
- **The journal was unbound, and it is the whole channel.** `LastError` has no
  operator-visible renderer — CLI and gRPC print only the already-redacted
  configured URL, Prometheus reads neither. What carries the secret off the box is
  the `slog.Warn`, and a mutant logging the raw `ferr` while the stored field
  stayed redacted survived *even the call-site cell*. **Storing and logging are two
  sinks; each needs its own binding.**

My wiring fixture was also wrong before it was right — it omitted `Manager.now`, so
`recordFailure` panicked on **unmutated** code, which made that mutant's score
meaningless: a cell failing for a fixture reason kills every mutant equally.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| sever the call site — store the raw error | applied (1→0), killed by 1 |
| log the raw `ferr` object (the journald half) | killed by 1 |
| drop the password-masked spelling | killed by 2 |
| always rewrite, even with no credential | **survives — EQUIVALENT** |

## PR #9402 — config: warn when a routing instance names a protocol nothing carries [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9374-inert-per-instance-protocols`

Closes #9374

## Measured at this head

```
routing-instances { V { instance-type vrf; protocols {
    router-advertisement { interface ge-0/0/0.0 { max-advertisement-interval 30; } } } } }
  -> STRICT COMMIT ACCEPTS      cfg.Warnings = 0
  -> ri.OSPF/OSPFv3/BGP/RIP/ISIS all nil
  -> cfg.Protocols.RouterAdvertisement empty
```

`compileRoutingInstances`' `case "protocols"` calls the shared `compileProtocols` and copies exactly five fields out of the result — OSPF, OSPFv3, BGP, RIP, ISIS. `router-advertisement` and `lldp` are compiled into the local `ProtocolsConfig` and go out of scope with it. **The stanza compiles to nothing, anywhere, and nothing says so.**

**This one is OPERATOR-REACHABLE** (`strictOK=true`), which is what separates it from the 25 lenient-only rows of #9391. Per-instance `router-advertisement` is a real Junos spelling, so an operator can reasonably write it, `show configuration` renders it back, and the box does not send RAs on that instance's interfaces.

## A warning, not a rejection

A new commit rejection has repo-wide blast radius and would refuse a config that boots and forwards today. #1960's doctrine is to keep it working and say so, so this warns through `cfg.Warnings` — the `show system commit warnings` channel.

## The set is DERIVED, not listed

It is every child of the per-instance `protocols` node that `schemaRoutingInstanceProtocols` does not declare — and that node's membership is bound to the compiler's copy set by `TestRoutingInstanceProtocolsShareTheGlobalGrammar9351`, which reads the `ri.X = proto.X` assignments out of the **source**.

So the chain is **compiler copy set → schema membership → this warning**, with no list anywhere that can fall out of date. Wiring a copy silences the warning; adding a protocol the compiler discards raises it.

A broken schema lookup returns **no** warnings rather than warning about everything — a lookup failure must not become a screen of warnings on every routing instance.

## Cells

`TestInertProtocolWarningIsDerivedNotListed9374` sweeps every child of the global `protocols` grammar and requires **warn IFF not-carried**, with a vacuity guard on both sides: **7 keywords, 5 carried, 2 warned**.

Three negative arms stop the whole thing being "warn about everything": a carried protocol, the global spelling, and an `apply-*` meta keyword must all stay silent.

## Mutation table — four, all killed

Backups from `git show HEAD:<file>`, restores verified with `git diff --quiet HEAD`.

| # | mutation | result | cells red |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | **wiring**: sever the call site in `compileRoutingInstances` | KILLED | both cells |
| M2 | drop the carried check — warn about everything | KILLED | both, via the negative arms |
| M3 | drop the `apply-*` meta exclusion | KILLED | the `apply-macro` arm |
| M4 | read the GLOBAL protocols node instead of the per-instance one | KILLED | both cells |

M2 and M3 are the arms that matter: **a warning that fires on everything is worse than none**, because it trains an operator to ignore the channel. M4 is the plausible wrong-node bug — reading `schemaProtocols` makes every keyword look declared and silences the warning entirely.

## PR #9418 — config: census the added9091 class, and make the #7484 coverage ratchet name the leaf that moved [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/ratchet-diff-census`

Census of the `added9091` class, prompted by PR #9399: a helper whose doc comment claimed to *"turn a bare count into something reviewable"* returned `blind[ceiling:]` — the **alphabetic tail** of a sorted slice. When two entries arrived it named two paths that had **not** moved and stayed silent about the two that had.

**Is that one bug, or a class?**

## Method — two AST passes, because grep cannot tell a call site from a helper body

**Pass A, the WRONG-diagnostic shape.** `added9091` was invisible at its call site: it appeared as `added9091(blind)` inside the failure message, and the positional-ness lived in the helper's **body**. So pass A collects every locally defined helper whose result is formatted into a member-naming failure, and classifies that helper's body — MEMBERSHIP (a containment test) vs POSITIONAL (returns a slice of its input).

**Pass B, the MISSING-diagnostic shape.** Test functions comparing against a **package-level** expectation identifier, classified by whether any failure message presents a non-numeric argument.

## Result

### Pass A — zero remaining instances

```
helpers whose result is presented as "what changed":  10
  MEMBERSHIP   1
  OTHER        8
  POSITIONAL   1   <- false positive: prop.Keys[1:], the skip-the-keyword
                      idiom, not a diff claim
```

**`added9091` was a single occurrence.** Its shape exists nowhere else in the tree. That is a smaller answer than the prompt assumed, and it is the answer.

### Pass B — 20 ratchets, 5 count-only, **all 5 correct**

```
epochClockSaneFloor      x3   a clock sanity floor                    SCALAR
bootEpoch*Budget              time budgets                            SCALAR
wantOptionsTemplateID         an IPFIX template id                    SCALAR
napiProbeFloor                historical probe count, a POSITIVE CONTROL   SCALAR
```

For a scalar threshold a count **is** the complete diagnostic — `got 30, want >= 40` names everything there is to name. None is a defect.

## What the census cannot see — stated, because a population an instrument produces is evidence about the instrument first

1. **Granularity.** Pass B's unit is the FUNCTION. A count-only assertion sitting in a function that names members for a *different* assertion reads as MEMBERS. **This blind spot hides the one real finding below**, which had to be reached by hand.
2. **Vocabulary.** Both passes key on message wording; a ratchet phrased differently is invisible.
3. **Indirection.** Pass A follows one level of helper.
4. **Data-file registries.** A `testdata/` expectation (#8921's shape) has no package-level identifier and is outside pass B. Those already do set-diff, so the omission is benign — but it is an omission, not a clean bill.

### Two false-positive modes, both caught by reading the members rather than by review

- Pass B first matched **function-local** `wantX` identifiers → population 169, dominated by ordinary tests where `got=3 want=4` is complete. Package scope only → **20**.
- Pass B read only single-literal format strings, while this repo **concatenates** them, so `t.Errorf("..."+"...", members)` parsed as having no format — mis-classifying 5 member-naming ratchets as count-only.

**The first number this census produced was wrong by 8x.**

## PR #9427 — runtime trust: refuse a group-writable runtime dir, verify the event-stream peer (#9171) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9171-runtime-trust-group-write`

Two bounded findings that were **each dismissed by assuming the other held**.

The trust check tested `S_IWOTH` only, so a root-owned but **group-writable**
runtime dir passed. And the helper's event-socket **client** was the one leg with
no peer verification. Together: a member of that group unlinks the socket, binds
their own, and the 100 ms reconnect loop delivers the live session-delta stream
plus `FullResync` — session table, addresses, ports, zone identity — and accepts
forged ACKs back.

## The issue's map was wrong; its finding was not

It cites `pkg/daemon/boot_probe.go`, which **does not exist**, and describes three
separately-checked Go dials — they share **one choke point**, `dialTrustedHelperSocket`,
which is why those legs were never the defective one. The coverage table was built
by enumerating the tree rather than transcribing the issue.

## Making the peer decision drivable

A refusal needs a peer running as a **different uid**, which needs a capability the
test binary lacks — so the arms were unreachable, and a mutation making the check
unreachable **survived every source-level assertion** because the checker's *name*
was still in the file. `peer_uid_refusal` is split from its syscall shell for the
same reason `runtimeDirTrustError` already is, and that function states the rule:
**a test needing a kernel capability stubs it rather than skipping**, since a skip
is indistinguishable from a pass in every summary line.

That still didn't bind the *wiring*, so a third cell asserts the defect's shape
directly: **no success path may return the stream without passing through the
check.**

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| drop the group-writable arm (the defect) | applied(1), killed by 2 |
| drop the root/own-group exemptions (over-refuse) | killed by 3 |
| checker present but unreachable | killed by 1 — **survived** until the success-path cell |

gid 0 and the daemon's own egid are exempt, mirroring the uid arm above; sticky and
group-*readable* have narrowness rows.

Three of my own errors are in the log: a table asserted against the issue's
citations and failed on a nonexistent file; a reuse cell matched `SO_PEERCRED` and
**tripped on my own doc comment**; and a splice left the loop body empty.

`go test ./...` green; full `cargo test` green.

Closes #9171

## PR #9429 — screen: key the SYN-cookie whitelist on the client, not the ephemeral port [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9419-syncookie-whitelist-key`

Closes #9419

## The defect

SYN-cookie protection uses challenge-and-reset. `docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md` step 6 is "client retransmits SYN -> passes as validated". **That step was unreachable.**

Step 5 sends a RST addressed to the client with `seq = parsed.ack` — the client's exact `RCV.NXT` — so RFC 5961 accepts it with no challenge ACK and the just-ESTABLISHED socket is aborted with `ECONNRESET`. No TCP stack retransmits a SYN from there; the application calls `connect()` again, on a **new ephemeral port**. The whitelist key carried that port (`SynCookieTuple`) and the lookup was a single-use `take`, so the reconnect missed, was challenged, and was reset again.

While an attacker held a zone above its SYN-flood attack threshold — the Junos default 200 SYN/s with no explicit `attack-threshold` (#3024) — every legitimate TCP client to that zone looped on `ECONNRESET`. Strictly worse than leaving the feature off, where an over-threshold zone merely drops SYNs.

**The RST is the documented design and is unchanged.** The defect is one layer down.

## The fix

Both halves were required; either alone still fails (the key alone still burns the entry on the first retry, the TTL alone still misses the new port).

- `SynCookieClientKey { src_ip, dst_ip, dst_port }` is the whitelist key. Deliberately distinct from `SynCookieTuple`, which stays the **cookie MAC** key — the MAC must bind the full 4-tuple; the whitelist must not. This restores the shape of the eBPF ancestor's `struct validated_client_key` (`git show 13fa1009ea:bpf/headers/xpf_common.h`).
- `take_valid` -> `contains_valid`, which peeks instead of consuming. Renamed rather than edited in place so any caller still assuming consume-on-hit fails to compile.

Bounds retained after removing the single-use bound: the one-cookie-epoch TTL (64 s, refreshed per validation) and the #2446 per-zone SYN-cookie profile generation. An expired entry is still reclaimed on the lookup that observes its expiry.

Also corrects `build_syn_cookie_ack_rst_frame`'s doc comment, which asserted a "mirrors the eBPF behavior" equivalence that did not hold while the key was narrower than the ancestor's, and documents the whitelist scope and lifetime in `docs/syn-cookie-flood-protection.md`.

## Cells re-anchored — prior decisions, not stale tests

Four shipped cells asserted the single-use property. Each is re-anchored with the reason recorded inline rather than deleted:

| Cell | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `syn_cookie_ack_validation_marks_next_syn_bypass_without_session_creation` | `len()==0`, "validated tuple is single-use" | `len()==1` |
| `syn_cookie_validated_syn_bypasses_flood_gate_and_passes` | `len()==0` | `len()==1` |
| `syn_cookie_validated_cache_hit_within_same_generation` | "Consumed exactly once", `len()==0` | `len()==1` |
| `session_miss_ack_stage_invokes_syn_cookie_runtime_validation` | "validated SYN-cookie bypass must be single-use" | the two claims that survive: the validated client's reconnect IS admitted, and a different source is still challenged. The assertion this cell actually exists for (the poll stage invokes cookie validation) is untouched. |

The unit-level cache cells got key distinctness from `src_port`. Under the new key that would insert the SAME entry N times and the cells would measure **nothing** — they now vary `dst_port`.

## New cells

- `syn_cookie_retry_from_new_ephemeral_port_bypasses_9419` — step 6 in the only shape it can occur in.
- `syn_cookie_repeated_reconnects_from_validated_client_bypass_9419` — five reconnects, each on its own port, all admitted within the TTL.
- `syn_cookie_whitelist_does_not_widen_past_the_validated_client_9419` — NEGATIVE CONTROL, with a positive control at the same instant so a challenge below reads as a real scope boundary rather than an empty whitelist. Without it, "always admit" passes the two cells above.
- `syn_cookie_whitelist_stops_bypassing_after_ttl_9419` — the TTL is what bounds the whitelist now.

## Validation

`cargo test --bins` in `userspace-dp/`: **5479 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored**. `go test ./...`: pass. `go build ./...`: clean.

## PR #9430 — config: normalise the screen family node's packed tail in both AST shapes [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9421-screen-family-packed-tail`

## What this fixes

`#6683` taught `compileScreen` to read the **ids-option** node's packed body and
stopped one level short. A screen **FAMILY** node — `icmp`, `ip`, `tcp`, `udp`,
`limit-session` — that carries its own body on its `Keys` arrives with ZERO
children, so every reader below it looped `node.Children` zero times: the check
compiled **DISABLED**, and nothing reached `ScreenProfile.UnknownLeaves`, so
`validateScreenUnknownStrict` (the #3318 gate, armed only from `UnknownLeaves`)
never fired either.

## Which channel does what — the part that makes this hard to notice

Four config channels exist and, on this input, they disagreed. Measured in an
owned worktree at the base revision `19b082fe8`:

| channel | hierarchical `ids-option P { icmp [ ping-death fragment ]; }` | flat `set … icmp [ ping-death fragment ]` |
|---|---|---|
| `config.SchemaValidate` | ACCEPT | ACCEPT |
| `config.CompileConfig` (strict) | **ACCEPT** | **REJECT** (#1960/#3318 message) |
| `config.CompileConfigLenient` | ACCEPT | ACCEPT (+ warning) |
| `configstore.CheckText` (operator commit) | **ACCEPT** | **REJECT** |

and the compiled result differed too:

| AST shape | `ICMP.PingDeath` | `UnknownLeaves` |
|---|---|---|
| hierarchical | `false` | `[]` |
| flat set | `true` | `[icmp ping-death fragment]` |

Three observables for **one statement**, split only by how it was typed. The
flat shape does not lose it because `SetPath` nests the tokens into a chain
before any compiler runs. **A gate that fires in one AST shape only is a
reachability defect in its own right**, separate from the value the other shape
lost — and it is the harder half to see, because the shape that rejects looks
like proof the gate works.

## The defect was wider than the reported case

Re-measured at the family depth, the hierarchical shape also lost:

| spelling | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `icmp ping-death;` | `PingDeath=false` | `true` |
| `ip tear-drop;` | `TearDrop=false` | `true` |
| `udp flood threshold 900;` | `0` | `900` |
| `icmp flood threshold 500;` | `0` | `500` |
| `tcp bogus-check;` | **ACCEPTED silently** | REJECTED, same message as flat |

## PR #9431 — nat: key source-NAT teardown and HA reserve on the post-DNAT port [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9388-snat-postdnat-port`

## The defect

#9034 moved the source-NAT match/allocate call site onto the **post-DNAT**
destination port — `poll_descriptor` builds `nat_match_flow` from
`policy_dst_port` = `pre_routing_dnat.rewrite_dst_port.unwrap_or(forward_key.dst_port)`
— so `live_by_flow` is now INSERTED under the translated port. The session is
installed under the *untranslated* `forward_key`, and every post-install site
rebuilds the allocation key from that installed `SessionKey`.

Both of those sites corrected the destination **address**
(`nat.rewrite_dst.unwrap_or(key.dst_ip)`) and left the destination **port** at
`key.dst_port`. On the ordinary port-translating VIP shape
(`198.51.100.7:443` -> `10.10.10.7:8443`) the allocation is recorded under 8443
and every teardown looks it up under 443.

#9034's own commit message reasons correctly about the in-invocation ROLLBACK,
which passes `source_nat_release_key` (already post-DNAT on both axes) and does
agree with the allocation. It is the other post-install callers that were left
behind — ordinary expiry/delete (`session_glue/mod.rs`, `promote.rs`,
`commands/delete_synced.rs`, `commands/upsert_synced.rs`), the worker sweep
(`worker/loop_body/mod.rs`), the HA import (`ha/session_import.rs`) — plus the
HA synced reserve, handed the peer's `entry.key`.

`live_by_flow` has exactly one removal site (`unlink_live_allocation_locked`).
`release_flow`, `rollback_flow` and `reserve_flow`'s stale-tuple eviction are
all keyed on the exact `SourceNatFlowKey` and therefore all miss, so a completed
twice-NAT flow permanently consumes a `(pool_addr, port)` and a `live_by_flow`
slot counted against `max_tracked_flows`. `free_translated_port` runs only on
those same unlink paths. On a `persistent-nat` rule the release-hit path is also
the only route to `complete_persistent_lease_locked`, so the lease and the pool
ADDRESS it pins are held too. The same `flow` binding drives the interface-mode
identity free 90 lines lower, so interface-mode SNAT leaks identically.

On the standby, `flow.dst_port` also feeds PASS 1's `matches_ignoring_scope`
filter, so the pre-translation port could select a rule the active never matched
when two rule-sets discriminate on `match destination-port`. The in-source
justification above that filter claimed the key carried *"original ports"* —
false since #9034, corrected here rather than left to look freshly confirmed by
the fix.

## Census of the shape — 4 sites, 2 fixed, 2 deliberately not

| site | domain | verdict |
|------|--------|---------|
| `nat/source/release.rs:211` | source NAT | **FIXED** |
| `nat/source/synced.rs:228` | source NAT | **FIXED** |
| `nat64.rs:1482` `release_nat64_allocation_with_mode` | NAT64 | correct as-is |
| `nat64.rs:1759` `reserve_synced_nat64_allocation_with_holder` | NAT64 | correct as-is |

## PR #9432 — frr: resolve protocol interface refs to kernel names [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9405-frr-iface-resolve`

Closes #9405

## The defect, re-measured at HEAD

The issue's evidence SHA was `0f665fa42`; this work is on `19b082fe8`. It reproduces unchanged.

A routing-protocol interface reference is stored by the compiler as the **authored Junos spelling** and was written into the FRR managed section verbatim. Linux `dev_valid_name()` forbids `/`, so `interface ge-0/0/1.0` could never bind a netdev: no OSPF / OSPFv3 / IS-IS / RIP adjacency formed, on a commit that succeeds with no warning anywhere.

Measured with a throwaway harness driving all four config channels plus a real `ApplyFull` against a temp `frr.conf`:

```
protocols { ospf { area 0.0.0.0 { interface ge-0/0/1.0; } } }
  configstore.CheckText        ACCEPT
  config.CompileConfig         ACCEPT
  config.CompileConfigLenient  ACCEPT
  config.SchemaValidate        ACCEPT
  compiled OSPF iface = "ge-0/0/1.0"
  rendered ->  interface ge-0/0/1.0
                ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
```

IS-IS rendered `interface ge-0/0/1.0`; RIP rendered ` network ge-0/0/1.0`; OSPFv3 rendered both ` interface ge-0/0/1.0 area 0.0.0.0` and its `interface` block; `interface all` rendered the literal operand `all`. The **dash-form control** (`interface ge-0-0-1`) rendered the real kernel name on the same four ACCEPTs — which is what makes this a spelling-dependent silent failure rather than a broken feature.

The injection half reproduced too: `interface "ge-0/0/1.0 zzz"` and `interface "ge-0/0/1.0; foo"` are ACCEPTED on all four channels and rendered raw.

## The fix

`FullConfig.IfNameResolver`, wired by `assembleFRRConfig` — the sole production `FullConfig` constructor — to `Config.ResolveKernelIfName`. `buildManagedSection` applies it once, for the global block and every routing instance.

- **Copies, never in place.** Those pointers are the daemon's active compiled config; a renderer that rewrites them is the #9141 defect. Every struct is copied by value, so a field added later to `OSPFInterface` / `ISISInterface` is carried through without an edit.
- **A nil resolver is identity.** `frr_test.go` alone holds 86 direct `generateProtocols` calls; the whole suite stays byte-identical.
- **The `validFRRInterfaceOperand` belt (#6795) now covers the protocol operands**, unconditionally. A failing reference is dropped with a warning rather than rendered — one malformed line fails the *whole* frr-reload (#1880/#2223), so rendering it turns one bad interface into a total routing outage.

## Two things the fix un-hid

**A collision the raw spelling was masking.** `generateInterfaceSettings` suppresses `ip ospf network point-to-point` when OSPF sets an explicit network-type, keying that on the OSPF interface NAME while `InterfacePointToPoint` is keyed by KERNEL name. With `ge-0/0/1.0` vs `ge-0-0-1` the two could never match, so the suppression was inert. Once both name `ge-0-0-1` it must actually fire, or one interface gets two conflicting `ip ospf network` lines — so that pass is fed the resolved OSPF set.

**A quadratic-compile guard caught my first draft.** The commit advisory originally called `ResolveKernelIfName` once per declared interface. `TestTunnelNameMapBuildsAreInputSizeIndependent8862` reddened immediately (`z=1:4 z=2:6 z=8:18 z=32:66 z=128:258`): that resolver rebuilds the tunnel-name map per call. The advisory now indexes declared interfaces by both spellings with no resolver call, and returns before touching the interface set when there are no protocol references.

## The advisory

`validateProtocolInterfaceRefWarnings` warns when a reference names no configured interface or unit, with a distinct message for `interface all` (legal Junos, unimplemented here). Advisory rather than gate per #1960. Silence is asserted for the canonical slash form, the dash form (#8829) and a RETH unit.

## Validation

`go test ./...` — full tree, green.

**Mutation: 9 applied, 9 KILLED, 0 escaped, 1 VOID-and-replaced.** Every mutant asserted APPLIED by occurrence count (1 → 0), non-building mutants scored VOID, every file restored from `git show HEAD:<file>` and verified with `git diff --quiet HEAD`.

## PR #9433 — daemon: compare IPsec SA loop identity, not context liveness (#9176) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9176-ipsec-loop-identity`

The shutdown guard's comment says it clears only *"if this loop is still the
registered one"*. Its condition was:

```go
if d.ipsecSASync.loopCancel != nil && loopCtx.Err() != nil {
```

`syncIPsecSAPeriodic` has exactly **one** return — `case <-ctx.Done()` — so the
error is **always** non-nil there. The guard reduced to **"always clear"**, the
opposite of what it promised.

A stop-then-restart while the old goroutine is still in flight had A's exit clear
B's cancel, leaving loop B **unregistered**: a later knob-OFF silently did nothing
(the publisher keeps advertising after the operator disabled it) and a later
knob-ON started a **second** publisher — the leak this file's own `launches`
counter exists to make observable.

A generation counter, not the cancel func: **Go cannot compare func values**, only
against nil — which is the comparison that was already there and already
insufficient.

## The sibling, with its exposure corrected

`stopClusterComms` had a DHCP reset and no IPsec one. Filed as needing a knob
toggle; **measured**, `daemon_apply_tail.go` calls `ensureIPsecSASyncLoop` on
*every* apply outside the transport-change branch, so recovery was bounded by
"until the next commit". The window is sub-millisecond unless blocked in a
strongSwan vici query.

## Extracted to avoid a flaky cell

The defect needs an **overlap**, and a *sequential* stop/restart passes on the
broken code. Racing a real goroutine would make the cell timing-dependent, and **a
low-rate flake is worse than no cell** — it passes for its author and fails for
someone else in an unrelated package.

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| restore the tautology (always clear) — the defect | killed by 2 |
| invert the identity test | killed by 3 |
| reset clears the pointer but doesn't invalidate the generation | applied (2→1), killed by 1 — **survived** until the fixture stopped masking it |

**My fixture masked the property it was testing.** Mutant C survived because the
cell bumped the generation *itself* after calling reset — with the fixture
supplying it, whether the code did changed nothing. **A cell that does the work
the code should do is testing its own arithmetic.**

C also failed to apply on its first run (a quoting error on "goroutine's"), and the
runner scored an **unmutated tree** as a survivor. Re-run with an occurrence-count

## PR #9434 — config: honour apply-groups-except instead of inheriting the excluded group [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9422-apply-groups-except`

## What this fixes

`apply-groups-except <group>` was **accepted by every config channel and
consulted by none**. `ConfigTree.expandGroups` collected only `apply-groups`;
there was no `apply-groups-except` branch anywhere in expansion, `mergeNodes`,
`walkGroupToContext` or `stripApplyGroups`. The five production references to
the keyword were all "skip this token so it is not misread as a sibling member"
(#7029) — none an exclusion.

Measured at the base revision, in BOTH AST shapes:

| channel | verdict |
|---|---|
| `config.SchemaValidate` | ACCEPT |
| `config.CompileConfig` (strict) | ACCEPT |
| `config.CompileConfigLenient` | ACCEPT |
| `configstore.CheckText` (operator commit) | ACCEPT |

```
groups { G { system { host-name FROM-GROUP; } } }
apply-groups G;
system { apply-groups-except G; domain-name example.com; }
  -> System.HostName = "FROM-GROUP",  Warnings = []
```

**The control is the finding: removing the `-except` line changed nothing.** The
token is absent from `setSchema`, so no channel could reject it either — the
#1960 shape, a knob accepted at commit that nothing enforces. An operator using
it to keep a permissive lab group off a production stanza got the permissive
config.

## Why IMPLEMENT and not the #1960 reject posture

The issue allows either. A refusal would reverse a landed decision:
`TestApplyMetaInZoneInterfaceMemberSlotCompiles_7029` exists specifically to
assert that a config carrying `apply-groups-except` **compiles**, on the ground
that it is legal Junos. When a fix would red an existing cell, that cell is a
prior decision speaking.

## Where the exclusion is enforced, and why there

In `mergeNodes`, not as a pre-prune of the group body, because mergeNodes is the
only place that already knows the **destination** each part of a group body
lands in. That matters for a `<*>` group key, which fans one source subtree out
into every matching destination container: two of those containers may disagree
about whether they exclude the group, and a decision taken once against the
group body cannot express that. `TestApplyGroupsExceptIsPerDestination9422`
pins it — one wildcard template, two interfaces, one excluding.

## PR #9435 — routing: scope next-table leak rules to their authoring instance [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9420-next-table-iif`

Closes #9420

## The defect

A `next-table` ip rule carried `Dst` + `Table` + `Priority` + `Family` and nothing else, at priority 100-199 — **ahead of the kernel's l3mdev rule at 1000**. A packet ingressing **any** other routing instance whose destination fell in the leaked prefix was routed out of the **target** instance's table, on the target instance's device, overriding the ingress instance's own routing.

This is the same defect **#5117** fixed for the PBR/FBF band **in the same file**, whose `PBRRule.IifName` comment names the harm word for word ("steered into the wrong VRF (cross-WAN / tenant route-leak)"). `nextTableManager.Apply` was not covered by that sweep. **#4073** closed the broad "VRF traffic is mis-routed" claim as a false positive, correctly, on the grounds that the rule is destination-scoped — an argument that holds for every packet *outside* the leaked prefix and says nothing about one inside it.

## Re-measured, not inherited

Executed in a private `unshare -rn` netns on this host (Linux 7.0.13) **before writing any code**, and now shipped as `TestNextTableIngressScopeOnRealKernel_9420`:

| Cell | Rule | Probe | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | none | `iif dumc` (VRF-C) | unreachable |
| B1 | `to 10.9.0.0/16 table 200 pref 100` | `iif dumc` | **`dev dumb table 200`** — diverted |
| B2 | same, VRF-C now HAS its own route | `iif dumc` | **still table 200** — VRF routing overridden |
| B3 | rule removed | `iif dumc` | unreachable (control) |
| F1a | `to 10.9.0.0/16 iif duma table 200` | `iif duma` | table 200 — intended leak preserved |
| F1b | same | `iif dumc` | unreachable — **no leak** |
| F1c | same, VRF-C has own route | `iif dumc` | `dev dumc table 300` |

The first probe shape tried (`from <a local address> iif <dev>`) returned `Invalid argument` on this kernel for **every** cell — a uniform null that reads exactly like "the defect does not reproduce". Using a non-local probe source made all eight cells resolve. Recorded in `docs/log/9420.md`.

## Designs measured and rejected

- **`goto` escape band** (keeps one rule per leak, so the #6467 kernel/FIB count agreement is untouched): the kernel requires the `goto` target to be a rule at that **exact** priority. With no rule at pref 200 it shows `[unresolved]` and is a silent **no-op** — every cell leaked again. A mechanism that fails open silently is the wrong shape here.
- **`iif <vrf-dev> lookup <vrf-table>` escape**: `iif <vrf-dev>` does match an enslaved-interface packet (measured), but the rule is not terminating — a VRF with no route for the prefix falls through and leaks. Fixes B2, not B1.
- **Including `lo`** to keep host-originated traffic on the leak: an `iif lo` rule was measured to hijack a socket bound to **another VRF** (`ip route get 10.9.0.1 oif vrf-c` → table 200) — the first exposed path the issue names.
- **Moving the band after l3mdev**: fixes B2 only.

## The fix — the #5117 shape

Emit `FRA_IIFNAME` on every rule, scoped to the ingress interfaces of the instance that authored the leak. `next-table` is only implemented for the global routing-options statics (per-instance `next-table` is hard-rejected at commit, #5830), so the authoring instance is always the default one, and the scoping set is every configured interface unit not claimed by a routing instance (`DefaultInstanceIngressIfaces`).

Three operator-visible consequences, all documented:

1. **One leak costs one rule per ingress interface**, so the 100-slot window is drawn down **leak-atomically** — a leak whose full expansion does not fit is dropped whole rather than installed on a subset of its interfaces (a partially-scoped leak works on some ingress interfaces and silently not on others). The overflow error names the multiplier.
2. **Fail closed**, matching `BuildPBRRules`: no resolvable ingress interface → install nothing, report degraded. The gate runs *after* `clear()` so a stale unscoped rule is still removed, and stays silent for a config with no eligible leak.
3. **Host-originated traffic no longer follows a `next-table` leak** — a deliberate, measured narrowing (see the `lo` row above).

The AF_XDP fast path was never exposed: the userspace FIB follows a `next_table` leak only when the route is found in the ingress instance's own table, so it is instance-scoped by construction.

Scorer given a two-direction control first (type error → `VOID(BUILD)`, assertion break → `KILLED`). Every mutant asserted APPLIED (removals 1 → 0) before scoring.

## PR #9436 — config: match a partial-glob group key instead of adopting it as an instance [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9423-partial-glob-group-key`

## What this fixes

A group key of the form `<ge-*>` did not match the target node. It was
materialised **verbatim as a phantom instance**: the compiled config gained an
interface literally named `<ge-*>` carrying the group's content, while the real
`ge-0/0/0` got none of it, and strict `CompileConfig` accepted that with an
empty `Warnings` slice.

```
pattern <*>        interfaces=[ge-0/0/0]            ge-0/0/0 description="FROM-GROUP"
pattern <ge-*>     interfaces=[ge-0/0/0 <ge-*>]     ge-0/0/0 description=""
pattern <*-0/0/0>  interfaces=[ge-0/0/0 <*-0/0/0>]  ge-0/0/0 description=""
```

The originating report claimed the group "matches nothing, leaving interfaces
unconfigured". The behaviour is worse: it does not merely fail to match, it
manufactures a config object the daemon then reconciles. xpfd owns every
interface on the box and reconciles the configured set against the kernel, and a
zone or policy can reference the phantom by name.

**Mechanism.** `keysContainWildcard` compared each key for exact equality with
the string `"<*>"`, so `<ge-*>` was not recognised as a wildcard at all. It fell
through to the ordinary container path in `mergeNodes`, matched no destination,
and was APPENDED. `keysMatchWildcard` itself was never broken — it is a correct
per-element matcher that only knows the whole-token form.

## Correction to the issue's channel claim

The issue was proposed NEG and flipped when a reviewer asked *what happens
instead*. Asking that one layer further down changes the finding again: the four
channels do **not** all accept, and they disagree by **slot**, not by pattern.

| slot | `CompileConfig` | `configstore.CheckText` (operator commit) |
|---|---|---|
| `interfaces <ge-*>` | ACCEPT + phantom | **REJECT** |
| `security-zone <tr*>` | ACCEPT + phantom | **ACCEPT** + a phantom zone named `<tr*>` |

`CheckText` caught the interfaces case only because the typed interface-name
validator refuses `<` as a NAME character — an incidental downstream refusal,
not the group matcher working. A slot whose instance name has no such validator
carried the phantom through the operator commit path with zero warnings. **A
probe on the issue's own example slot would have concluded the commit path was
already safe.**

## The change

`keysContainWildcard` now recognises any `<...>`-shaped key, so every
wildcard-shaped group key takes the **wildcard branch** — the branch that merges
into each matching destination and never appends. The phantom is therefore gone
**by construction**, independently of whether the pattern matches anything: a

## PR #9437 — dhcprelay: bind the kernel device, not the authored ref [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9406-dhcprelay-ifname`

Closes #9406

## Is this #4049 again? Same class, different remedy — and it is measurable

The brief asked whether #4049 (LLDP: `net.InterfaceByName` handed the Junos slash name) is this same defect and whether to reuse its remedy. **It is the same class. The remedy does not transfer**, and reusing it would have looked like a fix while still binding nothing. Measured at HEAD:

```
LinuxIfName("ge-0/0/0.0")          = "ge-0-0-0.0"    <- the #4049 remedy alone
ResolveKernelIfName("ge-0/0/0.0")  = "ge-0-0-0"      <- unit-0 collapse
ResolveKernelIfName("ge-0/0/0.80") = "ge-0-0-0.180"  <- .<vlan-id>, not .80
```

LLDP references are **physical** interfaces, so slash→dash sufficed there. A relay member is a **logical** interface, so it needs the unit-0 collapse and the vlan-id arm as well. The remedy is the canonical resolver.

## The defect, re-measured at HEAD

```
group g1 { active-server-group isp; interface ge-0/0/0.0; }
  config.CompileConfig         ACCEPT
  config.CompileConfigLenient  ACCEPT
  config.SchemaValidate        ACCEPT
  config.ValidateConfig        0 warnings
  computeDesired -> ifaceName "ge-0/0/0.0"   (raw — and this is what reached
                    net.InterfaceByName / SO_BINDTODEVICE)
```

Linux `dev_valid_name()` forbids `/` and a Junos unit suffix is not a device, so no listener bound, no giaddr resolved, and nothing was relayed — on a green commit.

## The fix, and the trap inside it

A relay now carries **two** names:

| | value | who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `ifaceName` | the authored reference (`ge-0/0/0.0`, `reth0.0`) | the #2348 Apply diff key, the Stats row, `shouldRelay` / the #2456 master gate, and `relayInterfaceRG`, which parses it as a **Junos unit ref** |
| `kernelName` | the Linux device (`ge-0-0-0.180`) | `SO_BINDTODEVICE`, the giaddr lookup, the #2347 ifindex drift check, the #2076 raw-L2 sender |

**Resolving the desired-set KEY is the tempting one-line fix and it silently breaks HA.** `relayInterfaceRG` looks the base name up in `cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces`, which is keyed by the authored name. A kernel name is not a key there → every RETH-owned segment resolves to RG 0 → the #2456 gate reads "not RG-owned, always relay" → **both** cluster nodes relay the same client broadcast upstream with different giaddrs. `TestDesiredSetResolvesBindNameKeepsIdentity9406` pins the identity for that reason.

`kernelName` is part of `relaySpec`, not a field beside it: a `vlan-id` retag changes the device to bind without changing any other field, and `relaySpec.equal` is the only thing that decides whether the reconcile rebinds.

## One call site, not two

Boot called `Manager.Apply` directly while the day-2 path went through `reconcileDHCPRelay` — two places to remember the resolver, and **boot is the one that matters**, since a box that boots with a relay already configured never sees a commit. Boot now routes through `reconcileDHCPRelay`, and a guard keeps it at one site.

## Loudness

The runtime cannot report this: `resolveGIAddrWithRetry` retries forever with no error, `"dhcp-relay: started"` is logged before any bind, and every `RelayStats` counter is a forwarding counter — a relay bound to nothing is indistinguishable from an idle segment. So `show services dhcp relay` prints the bound device beside the configured interface, and `validateDHCPRelayInterfaceRefWarnings` warns at commit when a member names no configured interface or unit (advisory, not a gate, per #1960). Its declared-interface index and unresolved-reference predicate are **shared** with the #9405 protocol advisory rather than written twice.

## PR #9438 — userspace: make the hybrid-apply guard see the secrets the helper receives [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9161-hybrid-guard-secret-blind`

`configsContentEqual` decided whether a published config differed from the one
the helper already holds by comparing `json.Marshal` output. `config.Secret`
fields render **REDACTED** in that encoding, so a WireGuard key rotation
marshalled to identical bytes and compared **EQUAL**.

That is not a missed diff, it is a false success: the #5680 hybrid-ACK refusal
never fired, the snapshot was marked applied, and the operator was told the
rotation had landed **while the tunnel kept running on the previous key
material**.

## The comment said not to do this, so its premise was checked

The function carried an explicit instruction not to restore the former
`DeepEqual`, justified by:

> the helper ALWAYS receives the redacted JSON encoding — it never sees raw
> secrets

That premise is false, and its own list gives the tell: it names strongSwan,
FRR, vrrp and cluster as the secret-bearing subsystems that apply on *separate
paths*, and WireGuard is not among them — because WireGuard does not apply on a
separate path. `protocol_tunnels.go` declares `WgLocalPrivkeyHex` and
`WgPresharedKeyHex` as plain `string` with json tags, and `tunnels.go:137,149`
fills them with `.Reveal()`.

## The fix

The coarsening is kept — the other half of that reasoning is still valid, and a
secret the helper cannot observe genuinely is not a route-overlay hybrid. Only
the secrets that demonstrably reach the helper are added back, via
`helperVisibleSecretDigest9161`, which walks `config.EmitTunnelEndpointNames` —
the same enumerator `buildTunnelEndpointSnapshots` uses, so the digest's
population *is* the snapshot's population by construction rather than a parallel
list that can drift — and sorts peers by public key as the snapshot builder
does.

The comment is rewritten rather than deleted: it records the refuted premise,
preserves the over-strictness reasoning, and forbids the new failure mode of
widening the digest to secrets the helper never receives.

## Acceptance table

Both controls the issue asked for, plus a precondition check that the two
rotation fixtures really are identical under the redacted marshal — without it
the cell could pass without exercising secret-blindness at all.

The peer-order cell drives the digest **directly**. Through
`configsContentEqual` it would be vacuous: the marshal comparison runs first and
already reports a reorder as a difference, so the digest is never consulted and
a mutation dropping the sort survives.

## PR #9439 — config: keep every address in a bracketed interface address list [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9424-bracketed-address-list`

## What this fixes

`set interfaces <if> unit <n> family inet address [ a/24 b/24 ]` compiled to
**one** address. The second and every further address was discarded with no
error and no warning, through **all four** config channels, in **both** AST
shapes, on **both** families. Nothing about the compiled unit says an address is
missing: the interface exists, `show configuration` renders what was typed, and
a lost service IP or routing-adjacency source address simply never comes up.

Measured at the base revision, `family inet address [ 10.0.0.1/24 10.0.0.2/24 ]`:

| | `SchemaValidate` | `CompileConfig` | `CompileConfigLenient` | `configstore.CheckText` | compiled |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| hierarchical | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | `[10.0.0.1/24]` |
| flat set | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | `[10.0.0.1/24]` |
| **control**: two `address` stanzas | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | ACCEPT | `[10.0.0.1/24 10.0.0.2/24]` |

Mechanism, the canonical #2419 shape: the lexer strips `[`/`]`, so the list
collapses onto one leaf's `Keys` hierarchically and into a CHAIN in the flat
shape, and `namedInstances` reads slot 0 only. **#6662 and #7653 both swept
`namedInstances` callers and did not reach this one.**

## ACCUMULATE, where the sibling class REFUSED

#8794 (`security-zone [ a b ]`), #9246 (a bracketed to-zone list) and #8810
(`device-map interface [ a b ]`) all refused. Each refused because **expanding
would invent a semantics the platform does not have** — one policy name living
in several zone-pair contexts, one device mapped twice. That argument does not
apply here: a logical unit with two addresses is ordinary, and the
two-separate-stanzas spelling compiles exactly it. That is both the argument for
accumulating and the positive control in every cell.

**The discriminator comes from the SCHEMA**, because the packed shape is
ambiguous with the brace-elided sub-statement spelling — `address a b;` and
`address a primary;` parse identically, so a detector keyed on "the node carries
extra `Keys`" refuses the legal spelling too (the false-positive shape #9246 hit
twice). A trailing token is an ADDRESS if the address node's own `keyValidator`
accepts it — the exact function the typed-leaf gate runs on the first address —
a SUB-STATEMENT if it names a declared child, and MALFORMED otherwise.

**The malformed arm is load-bearing.** The typed-leaf gate validates only the
FIRST key slot of an `address` leaf, so accumulating the valid extras while
discarding the invalid ones would leave this issue's own defect in place for the
case that matters most: `address [ 10.0.0.1/24 not-an-address ]` is accepted
today with the garbage dropped. Malformed tokens are recorded on
`InterfacesConfig.MalformedAddresses` (`json:"-"`) and refused by a strict gate
with the #1960 lenient downgrade — the `ScreenProfile.UnknownLeaves` /
`SecurityConfig.MalformedZonePairs` shape. The gate is appended at the **end** of
the uniform-gate phase because gate order is observable: the first failing gate
wins the strict error slot.

## PR #9440 — daemon: resolve Kea group interfaces with the canonical resolver [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9407-kea-ifname`

Closes #9407

## Re-measured at HEAD

```
Kea derivation  group untagged -> ["ge-0-0-1.0"]     <- not a device
Kea derivation  group tagged   -> ["ge-0-0-1.80"]    <- unit 80, vlan-id 180
ResolveKernelIfName(reth1.0 )  = "ge-0-0-1"
ResolveKernelIfName(reth1.80)  = "ge-0-0-1.180"
rethInterfacesMatchingRG(all)  = ["ge-0-0-1" "ge-0-0-1.180"]
```

The derivation was `LinuxIfName(ResolveReth(ref))` — the slash rewrite and the RETH member map, **two arms short** of `Config.ResolveKernelIfName`. Only the CLUSTER path papered over the first gap (`stripUntaggedUnitSuffix`, #4647), so the standalone builder named a phantom device on identical config.

## The consequence the report did not name, and it is the worse one

`filterDHCPConfigForMasterRGs` compares the group's resolved interface against `rethInterfacesMatchingRG`, which has **always** derived `<member>.<vlan-id>`. A tagged group resolved to `<member>.<unit>` matched neither `masterIfaces` nor `rgScoped`, so the #6520 arm *"not RG-scoped implies node-local, always keep"* kept it. Measured before the fix, on a Daemon mastering **no** redundancy group:

```
cluster filter  group tagged -> ["ge-0-0-1.80"]   (kept; should be dropped)
```

A redundancy-group-owned tagged segment served on the backup node — the exact failure #6520 exists to prevent, reached through a name mismatch instead of a mastership bug. Invisible to every existing cell because they all use untagged units, where the #4647 strip happens to paper over the difference.

`pkg/dhcpserver/README.md` carried the false half in prose: *"A TAGGED unit (`reth1.100` → `ge-0-0-1.100`) is left intact and still matches only its VLAN member."* It matched nothing. Corrected here.

## The test that pinned the defect needed TWO changes, not one

`dhcp_reth_resolve_nomutate_9141_test.go` asserted `"ge-0-0-1.0"` under the label *"Positive control: the resolution still happens"*. The issue is right that this pinned the buggy output. But the **fixture** was the deeper problem: `reth1` declared **no units**, so `ResolveKernelIfName` fell through to its verbatim arm and the cell could not tell the canonical resolver from the derivation it was pinning.

Observed directly: with the production fix applied and the fixture untouched, `go test ./...` was **green** — a test naming the exact function I had just changed could not see the change. Every config that can actually serve DHCP declares the unit; that is where the address lives. The fixture now declares `unit 0`, and the expectation is `ge-0-0-1`.

## The residual, said rather than guessed at

`ResolveKernelIfName` returns the ref verbatim when the unit is undeclared — it cannot know what device was meant. A blanket `.0` strip would close that **and** rewrite a legitimately dotted DECLARED interface name (#8994), so the residual is reported: `validateDHCPServerInterfaceRefWarnings` warns at commit for both families. A group whose unit is undeclared has no address either, so Kea could not have matched a subnet on it even with a perfect name — it is a broken config, and the operator should hear it at commit. Advisory, not a gate, per #1960. It reuses `declaredInterfaceIndex` / `unresolvedInterfaceRef`, introduced for #9405 and already shared with #9406.

## PR #9441 — screen: keep alarm-without-drop across substitution and inheritance [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9425-alarm-without-drop`

Closes #9425

## Are the two members one fix? No — checked before writing either

They share a theme and no code. Neither fix touches the other's path, and each is red under its own mutation with the other applied.

| | Member 1 | Member 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Zone state | **INERT** — no `ScreenState::zones` entry at all | **RESOLVED** — a live entry with inherited sub-state |
| Lost because | the flag never reaches the helper for that zone | the flag reaches it, but a latch set *before* the commit outranks it |
| Site | Go wire builder + `ScreenState::alarm_without_drop` | `ZoneScreenState::reconcile_substate` |
| Consequence | every substituted malformed-packet check hard-drops, indefinitely | session-miss ACKs hard-drop, bounded to 64 s |

## Member 1 — an inert zone hard-drops instead of alarming

An inert zone (profile DEFINED, zero checks enabled) gets no `screens` entry — `buildScreenSnapshots`' `enforcesAnyCheck` gate skips it — so `ScreenState::alarm_without_drop`'s `zones` lookup missed and returned false. Since **#7888** that zone *does* produce drop verdicts (`missing_profile_verdict` substitutes `conservative_default()`), so the lookup missed **exactly where a verdict existed to suppress**.

`set security screen ids-option p alarm-without-drop` and nothing else is both the canonical route into the inert state (`docs/feature-coverage.md:448` records that it passes STRICT commit with zero warnings) and an explicit request for audit mode. The operator got the exact inverse.

The flag now rides on `ScreenMissingProfileRef.AlarmWithoutDrop` — populated **only** for the inert set — decoded into a new `InertProfileRef` struct rather than a second parallel map (two structures keyed the same way can disagree silently), and `alarm_without_drop` falls back to it when the resolved lookup misses. That reuses the whole existing consumer path: the substituted checks still RUN, still count `substituted_default_drops`, still WARN, and the consumers turn the Drop into a log-only alarm + forward.

**#7888 is not contested.** It chose drop over PASS; this is drop over **ALARM**, for a zone that explicitly asked. An UNDEFINED reference is deliberately not covered — there is no profile that could have declared the modifier.

### Protocol version 10 → 11

The #8892 gate demanded it and the gate is right. *"Purely additive needs no bump"* is a **true rule that would have licensed this exact regression**: the acceptance gate is exact equality, so an unbumped field is silently **ignored** by an old helper rather than refused — and an old helper decoding `false` keeps hard-dropping, which **is** the defect. Both planes moved together, and the three version-*tracking* constants in the test tree moved with them.

## Member 2 — an enforce→audit commit keeps dropping for up to 64 s

`syn_cookie_active_until_secs` was inherited untouched by `reconcile_substate` (#4969 preserves per-zone state; #2446 invalidates only the cookie *generation*), and `validate_syn_cookie_ack_on_session_miss` checks `syn_cookie`, the threshold, the protocol and `locally_active` — **never** `alarm_without_drop`. So a zone latched cookie-active under a live flood kept dropping parse-valid session-miss ACKs as `Invalid` after the operator committed `alarm-without-drop` *to stop the drops*.

The freshly-configured-audit case was already guarded (`syn_cookie_alarm_without_drop_forwards_session_miss_ack_l10`) and is untouched — that guard *cannot reach* this transition, because the latch predates it. `reconcile_substate` now clears the latch when the new profile is in audit mode, which is idempotent with that guard (audit mode never sets the latch). A non-audit edit still inherits it.

## The load-bearing cell

`alarm_without_drop` returning true is **half a claim** — a guard whose name is in the file can be unreachable, and a state-level assertion cannot tell. `inert_zone_audit_mode_forwards_the_substituted_default_9425` drives the real consumers on BOTH the flow and flowless paths and asserts FORWARD + one alarm counted, **each leg carrying its own no-modifier baseline in the same run** — because "audit forwarded it" and "the substitution produced no verdict at all" otherwise read the same, and the second is the #7888 fail-open this must not reintroduce.

## Mutation matrix

Two-direction control first (type error → `VOID(BUILD)`, assertion break → `KILLED`). Every mutant asserted APPLIED (removals 1 → 0).

## PR #9442 — config: type ospf reference-bandwidth and convert its unit to FRR's [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9408-ospf-refbw`

## The defect

`protocols ospf reference-bandwidth` was declared `args: 1` with no `valueType`
and no `validator`, and the compiler stored the operator's token with a bare
`strconv.Atoi` **whose error was discarded**. Two silent failures, in opposite
directions:

- every **suffixed** spelling — `1g`, `100m`, the forms Junos documentation and
  every worked example use — failed `Atoi`, compiled to `0`, and rendered **no
  `auto-cost` line at all**. The cost basis silently stayed at FRR's default.
  `-5` behaved identically;
- the **bare-integer** spelling was passed through **verbatim** into
  `auto-cost reference-bandwidth`, whose unit is Mbps, while the Junos leaf's
  unit is bits/s.

| layer | unit | range |
|---|---|---|
| Junos `[edit protocols ospf] reference-bandwidth` | **bits per second** | 9 600 .. 100 000 000 000 000, default 100 Mbps |
| FRR `auto-cost reference-bandwidth` | **megabits per second** | 1 .. 4 294 967 |

## The fix

`ospfReferenceBandwidthMbps` is the SSOT for the parse, the conversion and the
range; the schema validator and `compileProtocols` both call it, so the gate and
the compiler cannot drift in either direction. The leaf is typed `ValueRate` —
whose own doc comment already said *"a Junos bandwidth value (bits/sec) with
k/m/g suffix"*; the type existed, the leaf had simply never adopted it. The
compiled field is renamed `ReferenceBandwidthMbps` so the unit boundary is named
rather than commented.

Accepted window = the intersection, in the leaf's own unit: a **whole number of
Mbps** in `1000000 .. 4294967000000` bits/s. A value Junos accepts but FRR cannot
express is REJECTED with a message naming the unit rather than truncated —
truncating 1.5 Mbps to 1 Mbps silently changes every interface cost, which is the
class of failure this leaf already had.

**Both channels, moving in opposite directions.** Strict commit / commit-check
rejects; the tolerant `Store.Load` / `Store.SyncApply` path downgrades that to a
warning — so unlike #9012 the **compiler must also fail safe**, leaving the field
at 0 (no `auto-cost` line, FRR's own default) rather than putting an
out-of-grammar number into the managed section.

**SEMANTIC CHANGE:** a bare integer now means bits per second.
`reference-bandwidth 10000` used to render 10000 Mbps and now names 10 kbps,
which is rejected at commit. Write `10g` or `10000000000`.

## The tree's own two cells concealed both halves

- `pkg/frr` pinned `ReferenceBandwidth: 10000` -> `"auto-cost
  reference-bandwidth 10000"` — int-in/int-out, silent about units;

## Half one — UDP write failures were not counted

The write-failure arm reached `noteDrop` only for stream protocols
(`if s.protocol != "udp"`), and **UDP is the documented default**. On a box
whose collector is down, `droppedWrites` stayed 0, the rate-limited
`slog.Warn("syslog message dropped")` never fired, and `show` still rendered the
collector as present — three instruments reading healthy at once while every
message went nowhere.

**Why it looked covered:** #9025 had added a UDP arm — for the *deadline expiry
it had itself introduced* (`if isTimeout(err)`). That is not the failure an
operator hits. A dead collector on a **connected** datagram socket (`dialUDP`)
surfaces as ECONNREFUSED from the ICMP port-unreachable, which is not a timeout,
so it fell straight through. Measured: 50/50 trials report the refusal.

Fixed at **both** sites — `Send` and `SendBinary`. The second carries the
RT_FLOW security log, so fixing only `Send` would leave the records an operator
most needs uncounted.

No reconnect arm was added: a datagram socket has no connection to
re-establish, so the message is still dropped and the error still returned.
**Only the accounting changed** — which is why the table asserts a UDP client
leaves `DroppedDials`/`DroppedCooldown` at zero.

## Half two — the counters had zero production readers

All three accessors had no non-test callers, so a counted drop reached an
operator through exactly one channel: the ≤1/s warning above. A warning already
rate-limited away leaves nothing behind, and a counter nobody reads is
indistinguishable from no counter.

`EventReader.SyslogDropStats` → `Daemon.syslogDropStats` →
`api.Config.SyslogDropsFn` → `xpf_syslog_messages_dropped_total{addr,protocol,reason}`,
emitted **before the dataplane gate** (the syslog clients run whether or not the
dataplane loaded, and a box that failed to load its dataplane is exactly the box
whose logs an operator needs). All three reasons emit even at zero — a series
that appears only once it is non-zero has no prior sample for `increase()`.

## The log-level half was NEG and was not touched

`ringbuf.go`'s `slog.Debug` sits in the per-event fan-out loop where CLAUDE.md
mandates Debug. Raising it would reintroduce the flood that rule exists to
prevent. Recorded so a later pass does not "fix" it.

## Acceptance

A real socket against a genuinely closed collector; a live collector as the
control, made non-vacuous by **reading a datagram back**; a cell per transport
