## PR #9445 — config: refuse protocols under instance-type forwarding [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9409-forwarding-instance-protocols`

Closes #9409

## Re-measured at HEAD — four channels plus the render

```
routing-instances { ISP-B { instance-type forwarding;
    protocols { ospf { area 0.0.0.0 { interface ge-0/0/1.0; } } } } }
  configstore.CheckText        ACCEPT
  config.CompileConfig         ACCEPT
  config.CompileConfigLenient  ACCEPT
  config.SchemaValidate        ACCEPT
  rendered -> TWO `router ospf` blocks, NEITHER with a `vrf` suffix

forwarding + isis -> a GLOBAL `router isis xpf`
forwarding + rip  -> a GLOBAL `router rip`
forwarding + bgp  -> ` neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65002` under a SECOND
                     `router bgp 65001` — it JOINS THE GLOBAL AS
CONTROL virtual-router + ospf -> `router ospf vrf vrf-ISP-B`   (correct)
```

`InstanceConfig.VRFName` is overloaded: `assembleFRRConfig` clears it for a forwarding instance — correct, because such an instance has no VRF device and its statics must render into `table <id>` (#1827 PR-2) — while `generateProtocols` reads an empty `VRFName` as *the global instance*.

The `virtual-router` control is load-bearing: this is specific to the forwarding **type**, not to per-instance protocols in general, so the remedy must not remove the feature.

## Severity: re-derived, and I agree with Medium

- **Reachability requires a non-Junos authoring act.** Junos `instance-type forwarding` takes `routing-options`, not `protocols` — a config migrated from a vSRX cannot contain it, because it would not have committed there.
- **No shipped or test config composes it.** `test/incus/fbf-two-upstream-config.set` is statics-only; `docs/multi-wan.md`'s recipe is statics-only.
- **The consequence when reached is genuinely bad** — an IGP running in the global routing context with its routes in the main table while the FBF table stays empty, and a BGP neighbor attached to the global AS, all silently.

Bad consequence × an authoring path the product's own documentation never describes = Medium. It would be High if any shipped config composed the two.

## The remedy is two halves, and the second is what makes the first safe

`validateForwardingInstanceProtocolsStrict` rejects at commit / commit-check, naming the instance **and** the protocol — mirroring the #5830 per-instance next-table rejection. `opts.lenientForwardingInstanceProtocols` downgrades it to a warning on the tolerant load / peer-sync paths so a box already carrying the config still boots (#1960).

That downgrade is only defensible because `assembleFRRConfig` now **NILs** a forwarding instance's protocol pointers. Every other lenient gate in that uniform block cites an "and the applier keeps it inert" clause; without the drop this one would have had none — the leniently-loaded config would boot and quietly rewrite the global routing table, which is the defect. `pkg/cli/apply.go`, which builds its own `InstanceConfig`, drops them too.

**The renderer is deliberately left alone.** Nothing in `pkg/frr` can distinguish "the master table" from "a forwarding instance's own table" through one empty string; the discriminator only exists at the assembler. And the compiler still *compiles* the protocols on the tolerant path — erasing them there would make `show configuration` disagree with what was committed.

## Validation

`go test ./...` — full tree, green.

**Mutation: 4 applied, 4 KILLED, 0 escaped.** Each asserted APPLIED by occurrence count (1 → 0); restored from `git show HEAD:<file>` and verified with `git diff --quiet HEAD`.

| # | mutant | result | killed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | sever the strict gate's call site | KILLED | all five `TestForwardingInstanceProtocolsRejected9409` subtests |
| Q2 | remove the assembler's protocol drop | KILLED | `TestAssemblerDropsForwardingInstanceProtocols9409` + `TestGlobalProtocolsRenderExactlyOnce9409` |

## PR #9448 — deploy: print the SIGNED install digest, not a re-hash of the public file (#9170) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9170-deploy-signed-digest`

## Summary

- `xpf-deploy.py fetch --no-import` / `--qcow2-only` printed a digest produced by
  `sign.sha256_file(qcow2_pub)` — a **second read of the public path, taken after
  the signature check had already finished**. The printed value bound "the bytes
  in `--out` at print time", not "the bytes that passed the signature".
- The correct value had already been computed and thrown away:
  `sign.verify_image_artifact` compares `sha256_file(path)` to the signed manifest
  entry and then returns a bare `True`. It now returns the signed digest, and
  `cmd_fetch` keeps what each verification established. **The second read is gone
  entirely, not merely moved.**
- The guard that was supposed to cover this asserted `assertIn("expected_sha",
  window)` under the message *"the digest must be computed from the verified
  file"*. The message named the property; the predicate was a substring the
  defective code satisfied. It was green over the defect for its whole life.
- The property is now driven end-to-end in a new hermetic file that swaps the
  public qcow2 the instant its signature check returns and reads what was
  printed. A source-text assertion cannot see where a value came from.
- `docs/distribution.md` records that the printed digest is the signed one and
  why the two importing paths do not need it.

## Why it matters

These two flags do not consume the image — they hand the operator a
`sha256sum -c … && sudo install …` one-liner to run **later** — so the gap
between the signature check and that install is unbounded, and `--out` stays
writable by any local process for all of it. `_verified_private_artifacts`'
docstring says so, three hundred lines up in the same file: *"The public `--out`
dir may be writable by another local process."* Between the verify read and the
digest read sit a full `verify_manifest_map` → `verify_and_read` →
`verify_signature` → `subprocess.run(minisign)`, two `mkdtemp`/`rmtree` cycles
and the watermark `os.replace`.

A process that wins that window gets its bytes installed **and** gets the
operator's own verification command to bless them. That is the last integrity
check before `sudo install` puts an image on a firewall.

## Test plan

New: `scripts/deploy/test_xpf_deploy_signed_digest_9170.py` (hermetic — throwaway
minisign keypair, `file://` base URL, private `XDG_STATE_HOME`, `incus` stubbed).

| cell | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| public qcow2 overwritten the instant its verify returns | FAIL (printed `sha256(EVIL)`) | pass |
| the operator's own `sha256sum -c` run on the swapped file | FAIL (rc 0 — **accepted**) | pass |
| public qcow2 **unlinked** after verify (nothing left to hash) | ERROR (`die`) | pass |
| `verify_image_artifact` returns the signed digest | FAIL (`True`) | pass |
| **LOAD-BEARING CONTROL** — untampered fetch, `sha256sum -c` run for real, must SUCCEED | pass | pass |
| `--qcow2-only` (fetches only the qcow2) | pass | pass |

## PR #9449 — screen: stop dropping a legal 1-7 byte last IP fragment as teardrop [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9426-teardrop-mf`

Closes #9426

## The defect

Every IP fragment except the **last** must be a multiple of 8 bytes; the last one may be any size. `check_teardrop` dropped **any** non-first fragment carrying 1-7 bytes, so an IPv4 datagram whose length mod 1480 lands in 1-7 produced a **legal** last fragment the firewall dropped — and the receiver's reassembly then times out, so the whole datagram is lost.

No attacker is required: any UDP application that fragments (DNS with large responses, IKE, RADIUS, NFS, VXLAN, GTP) emits one for ~0.5% of datagram sizes — deterministically per size, so an application with a fixed message size is either always broken or never affected. It compounds with `conservative_default()`, which enables `teardrop`, so a zone the operator never intended to enforce teardrop on could drop these tails (#7168/#7888).

The code comment called `< 8` "the classic overlapping-fragment signature". Wrong twice: a tiny tail is not an overlapping fragment (no overlap is computed anywhere here), and the heuristic it resembles is RFC 1858's, which applies to the **first** fragment. Juniper specifies `tear-drop` as overlap detection and says nothing about tiny tails.

The discriminator was already in the struct and unused — `ip_frag_off` is the raw field, so MF (v4 `0x2000`, v6 the Fragment header's low bit) is in hand. The `< 8` arm is now gated on MF=1. The zero/under-length arms stay **ungated**: a non-first fragment contributing no data is malformed whatever MF says, so #3027 and its IPv6 analogue are preserved — and M4/M5 below are the mutants that catch that over-correction.

## The shipped cell that pins the mistaken premise — re-anchored, not deleted

`teardrop_v6_tiny_non_first_fragment_drops` built an explicitly **trailing** (M=0) fragment carrying 4 bytes and asserted DROP, justifying it as "a tiny data contribution (< 8 bytes) **is** the IPv6 teardrop signature". That is a factual claim about IP, and it is false.

Reading its stated reason first, it splits cleanly:

- **#3119's actual claim — "the IPv6 arm exists at all"** (pre-#3119 the check was `AF_INET`-only) — is **still true** and still fail-on-revert: deleting the `AF_INET6` branch still reds this cell. **Kept verbatim.**
- **The fixture's `more: false`** is what was wrong. Corrected to `more: true` — a genuinely malformed non-last tiny fragment.

The legal case the old fixture actually described is now asserted, as a PASS, by `teardrop_v6_last_fragment_tiny_payload_passes_9426`. Nothing the cell established is lost.

### Five more cells red, and none of them is about the boundary

They use a teardrop fragment as a convenient **trigger** for something else. Each had its fixture's MF bit flipped with the reason recorded inline; every claim, assertion and message is unchanged.

| Cell | What it is actually about |
|---|---|
| `flowless_teardrop_fragment_dropped_3064` | the flowless screen path |
| `teardrop_still_screened_on_flowless_path` | the same, at the `ScreenState` level |
| `fabric_skip_flowless_still_runs_teardrop_4155` | the #4155 fabric rate-skip scope |
| `alarm_without_drop_forwards_but_alarms_l10` | audit-mode disposition |
| `inert_zone_audit_mode_forwards_the_substituted_default_9425` | the #9425 inert audit fix |

`flowless_teardrop_fragment_with_ihl_zero_is_still_dropped_8298` did **not** red — its drop comes from the #8298 `ihl < 5` fail-closed reject in `extract_screen_info`, not from `check_teardrop`, so the MF gate never runs. Its sibling control (payload exactly 8, MF=0) still passes; its comment now records that "the first size the `< 8` test admits" is only half the story after this change.

## Cells

- `teardrop_last_fragment_tiny_payload_passes_9426` / `..._v6_...` — **swept over 1..7**, not sampled.
- `teardrop_non_last_fragment_tiny_payload_still_drops_9426` / `..._v6_...` — the companion. Without the pair the fix is indistinguishable from deleting the `< 8` check outright.
- `teardrop_zero_payload_last_fragment_still_drops_9426` / `..._v6_...` — the #3027 arm must NOT be gated on MF.
- `teardrop_eight_byte_fragment_passes_either_way_9426` — the boundary control retained.
- `flowless_legal_last_fragment_tiny_payload_is_forwarded_9426` — **end to end** on the live flowless path, which IS the production path for a non-first fragment (#2344). Its two legs differ in ONE bit and the MF=1 leg is the positive control, so the MF=0 PASS is a real admission rather than a screen that stopped running.

## Mutation matrix

## PR #9450 — config: enumerate valueless brace-elision flags and normalize the security family (#9056) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9056-compact-flag-elision`

## Summary

- The #2419 compact/block census admits a site only when the folded token declares an `args` value or a wildcard. A **valueless boolean flag** (`args:0, wildcard:nil, children:nil`) satisfies none of the three arms, so it was never enumerated, appeared in **no skip bucket**, and its absence was indistinguishable from a clean verdict — the wrong-POPULATION failure, which no control at the census's own layer can reach.
- `collectCompactSites` gains a fourth arm and `compactSite` a `flag` field; the discriminator for a flag is **PRESENCE** (`stanza { flag; }` against `stanza { }`), which makes the existing vacuity guard read as "the presence of this flag is not observable in the typed config" — the same property it already asserts for a valued leaf.
- Measured at the widening: **511 flag sites, 93 divergent, 0 of them previously in the inventory.** The nineteen in the `security` subtree are normalized; the other 74 are recorded in the inventory with their drop shape and classified in the permanent-exclusion register.
- `security policies … then permit` / `then reject` are flags of the same shape and are **deliberately not admitted** — they are the family's negative control.

## The defect, per channel

Channels disagree, so each claim names its own.

| channel | verdict |
|---|---|
| `config.CompileConfigLenient` (the census's channel) | 93 flag sites diverge; the `security` nineteen all measure drop shape `empty` |
| `config.CompileConfig` (STRICT) | both spellings ACCEPTED for all nineteen, so the drop is silent on the operator's own commit path |
| `config.SchemaValidate` | not the discriminating layer here — these are declared leaves; the loss is the compiler reading `node.Children` |
| `configstore.CheckText` | the issue's original table; reproduced on `CompileConfig`, same verdicts |

```
security { flow { allow-dns-reply; allow-embedded-icmp; } }   dns=true  icmp=true
security { flow allow-dns-reply; flow allow-embedded-icmp; }  dns=false icmp=false
security { zones { security-zone z1 tcp-rst; } }              tcpRst=false  (braced: true)
security { flow { tcp-session no-syn-check; } }               noSynCheck=false (braced: true)
```

All accepted, no error, no warning, with `show configuration` rendering exactly what the operator typed.

**Two of the issue's claims are stale at this base and are recorded as such:** the `security screen ids-option <p> tcp land` family is no longer divergent (the screen subtree was normalized after the issue's verification SHA), and the count is 93, not 83.

**The premise carried into this work was refuted.** A prior lane reported that a valueless flag "cannot satisfy the `compactNormalizeInScope` table's admission precondition". Measured by running the pass with a recording predicate, `security { flow allow-dns-reply; }` asks `("flow", "allow-dns-reply")` and a scope entry for it converges the site. The blindness was the **census's**, not the scope table's — different mechanisms, and conflating them would have sent the fix at the wrong file.

## Why `synthPair` had to change too

An undeclared `valueType` is `ValueAny` — the zero value — so a flag fell through to the `ValueIdentifier, ValueAny` arm and got back `"xpfaaa"/"xpfbbb"`. The fixture built from that is `allow-dns-reply xpfaaa;`, which is not a spelling of anything: `FindChild` sees the leaf either way, both probes compile alike, the vacuity guard fires, and the site is recorded "leaf value not observable" — a verdict about the SYNTHESISER, not the leaf.

Refusing the shape is what keeps this a bounded change to a **shared traversal helper**: the other fourteen consumers of `collectCompactSites()` skip flags on `!ok` exactly as they did when the shape was outside the population, so none of their numbers move. One predicate, `isValuelessFlag9056`, is used by both the population and the refusal so they cannot drift.

## Collateral, named rather than absorbed

| guard | what changed | why it is not a weakening |
|---|---|---|
| `TestScopeWideningYieldsAdjudicatedSites8852` | 4 `zero-arg-leaf` registrations RETIRED | they were blind because the census could not enumerate the shape; it now adjudicates them. The `zero-arg-leaf` branch of the classifier is KEPT so a future re-narrowing is named rather than reported as "a reason this model does not explain" |
| `TestCompactDepth1AgreesWithTheBaseCensus7653` | flag branch added | depth 1 IS the base census's spelling, and the disagreement is what pointed here |
| `TestCompactNormalizeScopePreservesCompiledResult8690` | flag branch added | without it the guard that verifies admissions would have been GREEN AND SILENT about the nineteen this same change added. All nineteen now print `touched=1 passOFF=accepted passON=accepted` |
| `TestNormalizerScopeNeverCoversAPartialSite8690` | flag branch added | 5 of the 16 partial sites are now flags; the cell reconciles `examined == partials`, so it said so |
| `TestLeafRunDifferentialGate9156` | flags EXCLUDED from its population | population-preserving: every site it could previously see declared `args >= 1` or a wildcard. Admitting flags silently re-picked `heads[0]`/`tails[0]` and moved five recorded verdicts. Whether an argless head can carry a flat run is a real question on THAT gate's axis and a different one from this drop |
| `TestPackedOptInHoldsForEveryLeafPair8768` | fixture statements + reader fields for the three newly-admitted leaves under opted-in containers | the guard's own rule: an admitted leaf with no fixture is never compared |
| `TestMultisiteAdmissionsAreRecorded8921` | `gateway no-nat-traversal` recorded at its two declaring sites | it is the one pair in the family with more than one site, and both are asserted in the acceptance table rather than sampled |

## PR #9451 — config: bound `tunnel keepalive-retry` so dead-peer detection stays reachable (#9157) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9157-keepalive-retry`

## Summary

- `interfaces <*> tunnel keepalive-retry` declared **no `valueType` and no validator**, alone among the four leaves under `tunnel`. `key`, `ttl` and `keepalive` each carry `ValueInteger` plus an explicit `ValidateInteger` range; `schema_walk.go` builds a value checker exactly when `n.validator != nil`, so this leaf was walked and waved through.
- **The harm is REACHABILITY, not overflow.** `keepaliveTick` transitions the tunnel down at `state.Failures >= state.MaxRetries`, `Failures` increments once per probe tick, and `startKeepalive` normalizes only `<= 0 -> 3`. A large enough count makes that comparison unreachable: the tunnel is never declared down and routes over it keep forwarding into a dead peer, on a commit that reported success.
- Typed **1..255** (Junos's own range; default 3). `0` and negatives are rejected rather than silently meaning the runtime default, and `abc` is rejected rather than becoming 3 through the discarded `strconv.Atoi` error.
- Typing the leaf **removes an admission head**, which reds exactly one existing cell. That is handled deliberately, not absorbed — see below.

## Channel

The issue's table labelled its measurement "the strict commit gate"; the layer that actually discriminates is the typed-leaf schema walk. Re-measured at `566d132b0`:

| channel | `keepalive-retry 99999999999` | CONTROL `keepalive 99999999999` |
|---|---|---|
| `config.SchemaValidate` | **accepted** | **REJECTED** — `integer out of range [0..32767]` |
| `configstore.CheckText` (operator commit path — runs the walk via `compileTreeStrict`) | **accepted**, `kar=99999999999` | **REJECTED**, same message |
| `config.CompileConfig` (STRICT compiler gates) | accepted | **also accepted** |
| `config.CompileConfigLenient` | accepted | accepted |

So the claim is made on `SchemaValidate` / `CheckText`. Writing the table against `CompileConfig` would have been the wrong-instrument error: that layer accepts an out-of-range value for the ALREADY-BOUNDED sibling too, so the "control" would have agreed with the defect.

```
keepalive-retry 99999999999   accepted   -> KeepaliveRetry = 99999999999
keepalive-retry abc           accepted   -> 0, runtime-normalized to 3
keepalive-retry -5            accepted   -> -5, runtime-normalized to 3
```

## What typing it COST

`validateModifierChild` rejects a flat run whose head leaf is TYPED, so `keepalive-retry` was one of the `tunnel` container's two UNTYPED ADMISSION HEADS (#9156 V020):

```
set … tunnel keepalive-retry 5 source 10.0.0.1 destination 10.0.0.2
  before: accepted, and (since #9156) expanded correctly
  after : REJECTED — `tunnel keepalive-retry: unknown modifier "source"`
```

That is the only cell in the tree this reds: `TestTunnelFlatRunSurvivesAnUntypedHead9156`, all four arms.

**A prior decision is speaking there, so it was read before being touched.** #9156's rationale is that a run headed by an untyped leaf must EXPAND rather than be swallowed, and its own doc names `routing-instance` as the container's second untyped head. That head is still untyped and still admits a run — measured, all four arms pass unchanged with it — so the fixture was **re-pointed** rather than the arms deleted. Deleting them would have removed coverage while looking like a passing suite. The head that left is pinned in the other direction by `TestKeepaliveRetryHeadIsRejectedOnceTyped9157`, which also asserts the **surviving** head still works, so "the run is rejected" cannot be confused with "the expansion regressed".

The narrowing is defensible on its own terms: Junos does not accept several statements on one `set` line, and the typed-head order (`destination B keepalive-retry 5`) has always been refused here — so the two orders now agree instead of one being accepted and the other not.

## A stale premise corrected

The archived `fable-review-161` note in this tree says the keepalive engine is unreachable on the userspace dataplane, because the daemon sets `AnchorOnly` for every tunnel and `applyAnchorLocked` never consults `tc.Keepalive`. **#4071 ported the engine to the anchor path** (`pkg/routing/tunnel.go:444`, `startKeepalive` at `:591` and `:799`), so the consequence above is reachable on the production dataplane. Had that note still held, the severity would have been "an inert knob", which is a different issue.

## PR #9453 — daemon: distinguish a failed flow-exporter build from "not configured", and retry it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9166-flowexport-build-failed-visible`

A failed exporter build produced the **same observation as "flow export is not
configured"** on every surface:

- `FlowExportError()` had zero production readers;
- the `xpf_flow_export_collector_*` family is *"omitted entirely … when no flow
  export is configured (empty slice)"* — and an empty slice is exactly what a
  failed build produces;
- `show` renders the configuration as present, because the config **is** present.

The triggering fault is ordinary: a collector hostname unresolvable at boot, or
a pinned source-address bind attempted before the interface is up. NetFlow is
frequently the only record of what traversed the box, and its absence looks
exactly like a deployment where it was never turned on — which is why nobody
investigates.

## Half one — three distinguishable observations

`flowexport.BuildState{Family, ConfiguredGroups, BuildFailed}` →
`xpf_flowexport_configured_groups{family}` + `xpf_flowexport_build_failed{family}`,
for both families on every scrape, **including at zero**:

| observation | meaning |
|---|---|
| `configured=0, failed=0` | not configured |
| `configured>0, failed=0` | configured and healthy |
| `configured>0, failed=1` | configured, and the build FAILED |

Two decisions carry it. The configured count is recorded **before the hash
gate**, because the count of RUNNING exporters cannot stand in for it — on a
build failure with nothing previously running it is also 0, which is precisely
the not-configured reading. And emitting *only* the failure would not have
worked: it leaves not-configured and healthy both as "the series is absent", and
absence is also what a scrape that never reached the code looks like.

## Half two — nothing retried until the next commit

`reconcileFlowExporters` runs only from the apply tail and the boot block, so
the cadence was "the next commit", which on a stable box is never — while both
faults the #3742 design cites clear on their own minutes later. A single-flight
loop re-reconciles every 30s against the **live active config**, so a commit
that removes flow export converges it instead of resurrecting deleted config,
and it is cancelled and JOINED at shutdown under a bounded timeout.

## Not changed, deliberately

`d.flowHashSet = false` on the failure path. The finding narrates withholding
the hash as the defect; it is the **fix** — without it the next commit is
hash-gated into a permanently dead family. The #3742 build-before-swap and the
fatal dial error also stand: this makes that design observable and self-healing,
it does not weaken it.

## PR #9454 — cluster: close three bulk-session-sync gaps that let a stale peer frame complete or reset a bulk (#9174) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9174-bulk-sync-three-gaps`

## Summary

Three separate gaps in the HA bulk-session-sync protocol let a stale or mistimed
peer frame complete, reset or gut a bulk transfer. They share a file and a review
pass; they do **not** share a fix, so each arm has its own cells and each reds for
its own reason. All three end in the same place: a standby that believes it is
synced and is not — invisible until a failover, at which point every session
absent from the standby's table is a dropped flow.

### V013 — BulkEnd carried no incarnation

`BulkStart` has carried the sender's boot id since #5084; `BulkEnd` was matched on
the **epoch alone**. The epoch is `bulkSendNext.Add(1)`, and that counter
**restarts at zero when the peer reboots**, so an end marker buffered on a dead
boot's still-ESTABLISHED socket can carry the same epoch as the bulk the peer's
*replacement* has just started. Completing it reconciles the standby against a
partly-received table, latches `bulkEverCompleted` and releases the VRRP sync
hold: MASTER-eligible while forwarding with sessions it never received.

**ADD a field, never redefine one.** The payload grows 8 → 24 bytes as the same
length-gated trailing extension #2170 and #5084 use, so a mixed-version pair keeps
working through a rolling upgrade. The reader records the incarnation the accepted
`BulkStart` primed under and refuses an end marker from a different one, failing
open when either side is un-incarnated. Refusals are counted
(`BulkEndsDeadIncarnationDropped`) and rendered by `show chassis cluster`, because
a refusal that silently decides whether the sync hold is released must not itself
be silent.

### V015 — the #8966 guard could not fire between bulks

Its condition required `s.bulkInProgress`, and `reconcileStaleSessions` clears
that flag at `BulkEnd` while leaving `bulkRecvEpoch` standing. So between two
bulks any epoch was accepted: a stale full pair reordered off the other fabric
reopened a receive window for a transfer that had already finished, reset the
accumulators, and drove a reconcile against a set that was never received — a mass
delete followed by resurrection. Two consecutive bulks can pin different fabrics
(`BulkSync` pins `getActiveConn` once), so a reordered pair is the ordinary route.

The whole verdict moves into `bulkStartStaleLocked`. **Its between-bulks arm
requires an incarnation on the frame, and that is load-bearing rather than a
hedge:** within a bulk a wrong refusal costs one re-prime because a transfer is
already in flight, but between bulks nothing is in flight, so a wrong refusal is
terminal — and a rebooted peer legitimately restarts its counter lower (#2198 F2).
`switched` separates those two cases only when the peer sends an incarnation.

### V014 — `epochReboot` never armed `needColdPrime`

#7762 taught `installConn` to retire a dead incarnation on a raised boot epoch —
the evidence a replacement dialling the **empty alternate slot** leaves. That same

## PR #9455 — config: merge BGP neighbor AST nodes into one peer per (group, address) (#9192) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9192-bgp-neighbor-node-merge`

## Summary

- `compileBGP` appended one `*BGPNeighbor` **per AST NODE**, and one authored neighbor is not always one node. `SetPath` does not reuse a node it has already marked `IsLeaf`, so a bare declaration followed by a sub-leaf becomes two siblings — ordinary flat-set authoring, and the shape `pkg/config`'s own slot-escape fixtures use.
- Fixed by **find-or-create on `(GroupName, Address)`** within a BGP instance, the same shape as the #8436 OSPFv3 area-interface merge forty lines below it.
- The #5277 own-export/own-import flags move from **per-NODE locals to per-NEIGHBOR state**, or the second node's first `export` would wipe the first node's own list.
- Three boundaries measured and pinned: distinct addresses never fold, the #9007 cross-group case never folds, and the two-`group G`-blocks case does — reachable only on the lenient path, and pinned as a recorded decision.

## The defect

```
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2
set protocols bgp group G neighbor 10.0.2.2 import PS

AST:  [neighbor 10.0.2.2]
      [neighbor 10.0.2.2] > [import PS]

before:  neighbors=2   [0] import=[]   [1] import=[PS]
after:   neighbors=1   [0] import=[PS], peer-as=65001
```

Rendered:

```
-neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 10.0.2.2 remote-as 65001
  neighbor 10.0.2.2 activate
  neighbor 10.0.2.2 route-map PS in
```

**Channel.** Measured on `config.CompileConfigLenient`, the channel the issue used. Re-verified on `config.CompileConfig` (STRICT) with the policy-statement DEFINED — the issue's literal fixture is rejected by the undefined-policy gate for an unrelated reason — where it also gives `neighbors=2`. So the duplication is reachable through an ordinary commit, not only on the tolerant path. `config.SchemaValidate` returns `<nil>`: nothing here is a schema-shape error.

## Severity: low, and that is the point

The render was **redundant, not wrong** — FRR accepts a repeated `remote-as`, and the `activate` / route-map lines only entry `[1]` carried were still emitted. Nothing was broken for the operator, which is why nothing caught it.

What makes it worth fixing is that the duplication is invisible in the typed config's contract, so **anything reasoning over `BGP.Neighbors` as a set of peers is wrong by construction** and each new consumer has to rediscover it. Two already did, while #9007 was being fixed:

1. a duplicate-address check keyed on `Address` alone reported a peer as "configured in more than one group (**G and G**)" — the same group twice — and false-rejected a legitimate config;
2. a first-wins dedup at the renderer's `validNeighbors` silently dropped the policy-bearing entry, deleting the `activate` and `route-map … in` lines.

Both were caught by existing cells and reverted. `pkg/frr/README.md` now records the second so the next person reaching for it at that layer finds the reason first.

## The three boundaries

| shape | entries | why |
|---|---|---|
| one group, bare + extended node | **1** | the defect |
| one group, two distinct addresses | 2 | different key |
| TWO groups, one address (#9007) | 2 | genuinely ambiguous — divergent `peer-as`, timers, authentication keys; resolved by render order and rejected at commit by PR #9191. The key is the PAIR precisely so folding here cannot silently resolve an ambiguity the operator is meant to be told about |
| two `group G` BLOCKS, one address | **1**, lenient path only | shares the key. Rejected at strict commit by the #5180 duplicate-block gate, so reachable only via `Store.Load` / `SyncApply`. The merged neighbor keeps the FIRST block's group defaults and unions both blocks' per-neighbor statements, instead of two entries whose defaults disagree and which the renderer emits both of. A behaviour change, pinned by a cell that asserts the #5180 rejection FIRST so "lenient-only" is checked rather than claimed |

## PR #9456 — daemon: make the control-endpoint preflight total, so it refuses a deletion too [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-07)

Branch: `fix/9178-control-endpoint-deletion`

The #8965 preflight exists to stop an operator stranding a running cluster by
changing its control endpoint. It **passed the deletion case**:

```go
if want == "" || have == "" || want == have { return nil }
```

The comment's justification — *"unset on either side means there is no live
endpoint to strand"* — is true for `have == ""` (an **addition**, where the
heartbeat has not started) and **false** for `want == ""` (a **deletion**, where
the live endpoint being stranded is the one being removed). Two of the four
combinations were decided by a sentence that covered one of them.

## Severity is set by the fabric, not by the deletion

- **With a fabric configured**, `clusterSyncTransport` falls back to it, so the
  push still has a transport and the deletion propagates. The heartbeat dies on
  both nodes — what the operator asked for — and there is no partition. Admitted.
- **On a control-link-only cluster** (which the strict compiler gate accepts)
  there is no fallback: no heartbeat **and** no sync transport. That is exactly
  #8965's apply-then-push partition, durable because the peer never learns why.
  Reachable with `delete chassis cluster peer-address` + `commit`. Refused.

## The predicate mirrors the sync-START condition, not the transport label

`fabricFallbackConfigured9178` requires both fabric fields, which is the
condition `daemon_ha_sync.go` actually gates the sync goroutine on.

**The acceptance cell found that, not the reading.** Its first version derived
the runtime's answer from `clusterSyncTransport`'s *label* and RED on the
`FabricInterface == "", FabricPeerAddress != ""` row. The label is not the
answer: that function returns `"fabric"` whenever the control link is incomplete
— *including when the fabric is incomplete too* — so a gate reading it would
report a transport that never starts, and admit a deletion into a config with no
sync at all.

## Acceptance

`TestControlEndpointDecisionIsTotal9178` enumerates all four `(have, want)`
combinations × the two topology columns the issue asked for — ten rows. The
load-bearing rows are the ones that must still be **ALLOWED**; without them
"refuse every deletion" satisfies the refusal rows and breaks a legitimate
operation.

One row of the existing #8965 table is **corrected, not deleted**: it scored the
deletion as allowed, quoting the justification above. The rest of that table
stands, because the rest of its reasoning is correct.

## PR #9477 — userspace-dp: index the previous pool once instead of rescanning it per address [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9163-retained-pool-index-map`

The retained-pool index remap asked `prev.iter().position(|a| a == addr)` once
per NEW pool address. That is a nested linear scan — O(n·m) — over a quantity
the commit gate bounds at **1,048,576** addresses in one aggregate
(`MaxSourceNATAggregatePoolAddresses` = 16 × `MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS`), and a
single pool may hold the whole budget.

## Where it runs is what makes the cost matter

`reseed_retained_pool` is reached from `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous`
inside snapshot apply, under the same `state` mutex that serializes the control
socket. `update_ha_state` is the only refresher of the helper's 10 s per-RG
forwarding lease and is sent on a 3 s cadence, so it queues behind that apply,
and `is_forwarding_active` is consulted per packet. **A pool edit that holds the
mutex long enough expires the lease.**

Measured at `rustc -O`, n = m = 65,536 (one `MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS` prefix
member), every address retained and one added:

| | |
|---|---|
| nested scan | **1.22 s** |
| hash index | **0.018 s** |

## Implementation

`first_index_by_address` builds an `FxHashMap<Addr, usize>` over the previous
list once and the remap probes it.

`or_insert` is the whole of the equivalence with what it replaced: `position()`
returns the FIRST match, so a previous list holding one address twice always
resolved to its lower index. A bare `insert` would record the last occurrence
and quietly move which previous slot a duplicated address carries its live port
ownership from.

`retained_pool_index_map` now takes the previous address lists as **slices**
rather than a `&PreviousPool`. The NAT64 wrapper had been synthesising a whole
`PreviousPool` — cloning the previous address vector and constructing a
throwaway `PortAllocator` — to reach one formula that read neither. Slices also
make the v6 arm reachable from a test, which the module-private `PreviousPool`
shape did not.

## Validation

Five cells in `nat/tests_pool.rs`:

- **the BOUND**, at one `MAX_POOL_PREFIX_HOSTS` prefix member, with an in-cell
  **positive control**: a verbatim copy of the old loop is timed over the same
  inputs in the same run and must NOT satisfy the bound — so a machine fast
  enough to run the old shape inside 250 ms reports a vacuous green as a
  *failure* rather than a pass;

## PR #9479 — configstore: invalidate the applied-config marker when an apply fails [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9175-applied-digest-invalidate`

`appliedDigest` — the #4957 marker that lets a peer config-sync skip a redundant
re-apply — was stamped on success and **never invalidated**. `MarkActiveApplied`
and `MarkAppliedDigest` were its only writers, so it recorded a success and
nothing ever unrecorded one.

## The field comment's justification was half true

> the marker is keyed on the config text, so a stale value can only make the
> shortcut MORE conservative … never falsely converged

That holds for a **forward** sequence, where every promotion moves the active
text away from the stamped digest. It does not hold for **re-promotion** of a
text that already applied once in this process:

| step | `ActiveApplied()` |
|---|---|
| A applied | `true` |
| B promoted, apply FAILS | `false` — correct, the digest no longer matches |
| A re-promoted, apply FAILS | **`true`** — falsely converged |

At the third step the digest left over from the first still matches the active
text. `handleConfigSync` then takes its converged shortcut and returns nil, the
HA config high-water advances past a generation the dataplane never took, and the
standby reports the generation applied while holding an older one — the #4957
fail-open, re-entered through the remedy #4957 itself prescribed, and observable
only at failover.

## Where the clear goes, and why there

`applyConfigLocked` is the single choke point every apply in the daemon goes
through — boot/background, feed publication, commit, peer config-sync, and
commit-confirmed auto-rollback — so one clear covers all of them and every early
return inside it (the #2926 context abort, the factory-reset refusal, the test
seam) without a caller having to remember. Clearing at each caller's failure
branch would be four sites today and a fifth silently missing tomorrow.

The clear is **unconditional** rather than keyed to the failing text. The failing
path does not always hold a digest — a context abort bails before any capture —
and being wrong in that direction is the falsely-converged state this exists to
prevent, while being wrong in the other costs one idempotent re-apply.

## Validation

Five cells in `pkg/daemon` drive the **real** `applyConfigLocked` against a real
store, because the defect is that nothing *called* an invalidator: a cell that
calls the store method directly is green on a build where no production path
does.

Two are RED at the base commit, measured by neutralising the guard in place and
verifying the occurrence count round-trips 1 → 0 → 1.

## PR #9480 — netname: correct the false rationale defending the base-16 PCI function parse [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9458-netname-pci-function-rationale`

## What the tracker asked for, and why that is not what landed

#9458 says "#6204 still live on master (func parsed base-16); re-apply fix to
pkg/netname." Measured: **the base-16 parse is unobservable, so re-applying the
branch's fix would land the same no-op a third time.** What IS live is the FALSE
RATIONALE defending it, in three places on master — one of them a test row that
pins it.

## The measurement

Linux names a PCI device with

```c
dev_set_name(&dev->dev, "%04x:%02x:%02x.%d", pci_domain_nr(bus),
             bus->number, PCI_SLOT(devfn), PCI_FUNC(devfn));
```

and `PCI_FUNC(devfn)` is `devfn & 0x07` — bits 7:3 are the slot. The function
field is therefore **always 0-7**, ARI hardware included, and 0-7 parse
identically in base 10 and base 16.

```
$ for d in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/; do basename $d; done | sed 's/.*\.//' | sort -u
0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
```
175 devices, 46 ARI-enabled, max field 7 (at `0000:b7:0e.7`).

## The three false claims, and why the third is the worst

| Site | Claim | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg/netname/netname.go:127` | "an ARI device can carry functions above 9 (up to 255), which a base-10 parse rejects outright" | false — the field is 3 bits |
| `pkg/netname/README.md:79` | same, plus "Latent on the development host, whose maximum observed function is 7 — verified, not assumed" | reads a STRUCTURAL bound as sampling luck |
| `pkg/netname/netname_7426_test.go:78` | a test ROW pinning `FromPCIAddr("0000:b7:00.a") == "enp183s0f10"`, commented as ARI coverage | sysfs cannot emit `.a`; a red there reads as a guard working, which is what kept the wrong rationale alive through review |

The rationale points at the wrong mechanism for a **real** symptom. ARI does not
widen the field — it reinterprets slot and function together, which systemd
reconstructs as `func += slot << 3` when `ari_enabled` is set. That divergence is
#6677, fixed by reading the pre-rename name FROM THE KERNEL instead of deriving it
(PR #7420, `3c49cabd7`). #6204 and both its PRs (#6320, #6671) tried to reach that
gap by changing the parse base; a base change cannot reach it, and the owner closed
both as no-ops.

## What this PR does

**No behaviour change.** `FromPCIAddr` is byte-identical — deliberately, because a
third no-op change to the parse base would re-litigate a settled question.

- Corrects the rationale in `netname.go` and the README "Gotchas" bullet: states the
  structural bound, publishes the denominator, names the real ARI mechanism, and

## PR #9481 — userspace-dp: write the kernel RX drop counters the operator already reads [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9168-kernel-rx-counters`

`kernel_rx_dropped` and `kernel_rx_invalid_descs` were plumbed **end to end** —
`BindingLiveState` atomics, snapshot fields, wire encoding, Go decode, and the
`Kernel RX dropped:` / `Kernel RX invalid:` lines in `pkg/monitoriface/monitor.go`
— and **nothing ever wrote the producer end**. The worker loop sampled
`statistics_v2()` once per second per binding and stored exactly one of the six
counters it returns, discarding the rest.

So `show` / `monitor` reported a permanent hard **0** on both lines. That is the
observability form of a fail-open: 0 is the value an operator *wants* to see, and
it is what they saw while the NIC dropped every packet. It also disarms the
discriminating observation in the open zero-copy fill-ring question — a
measurement that reads those counters today can say nothing.

Re-verified at the base commit **with a positive control on the absence claim**:
grepping `userspace-dp/src` for a `.store(` / `.fetch_add(` on either atomic
exits 1, while the identical search shape finds the sibling
`rx_fill_ring_empty_descs` writer at `worker/loop_body/mod.rs`.

## Implementation

`BindingLiveState::publish_kernel_xdp_statistics` is now the one site that turns
a sample into atomics, and the worker loop hands it the whole
`XdpStatisticsV2` instead of picking a field out of it.

The publisher **destructures the struct exhaustively** rather than reading three
fields, because the defect was a field with a complete consumer and no producer
and nothing could have caught it: a consumer test passes on a hard zero, and a
producer that forgets a field compiles. With the exhaustive binding, a new kernel
counter is a **compile error** at the one site that could otherwise drop it
silently.

Fields deliberately left unpublished have no consumer, and a counter with no
reader is the same as no counter. They are named in
`UNPLUMBED_KERNEL_STAT_FIELDS` so the omission is **checked rather than
described**.

## Validation

Four cells in `binding_state/kernel_stats_9168_tests.rs`:

- **the PRODUCER cell** — distinct primes per field, so a cross-wire fails rather
  than passing on equal values, plus a second sample asserting `store()` and not
  `fetch_add()` (kernel counters are absolute per socket). RED on master, where
  nothing writes either atomic.
- **COMPLETENESS** — every declared `XdpStatisticsV2` field is named by the
  destructure, every bound name is actually stored, and every `_`-dropped name
  appears in `UNPLUMBED_KERNEL_STAT_FIELDS`.
- **the WIRING BIND**, which reads the sample site. The publisher-side cells prove
  the function behaves and say nothing about what its caller passes, and the
  original defect lived **entirely in the caller**.

## PR #9487 — cluster: move the bulk stat reset below the #8966 accept, and refuse a future-epoch BulkAck [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9177-bulk-stat-order-and-ack`

Closes #9177

Two small, **independent** defects in the same bulk-sync reader
(`pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go`). Unrelated edits, kept as separate cells, as
the issue's acceptance asks.

## V052 — the bulk stat reset ran ABOVE the #8966 accept

`syncMsgBulkStart` zeroed `stats.BulkSyncStartTime`, `BulkSyncEndTime` and
`BulkSyncSessions` **before** the `bulkMu` accept decision. So a **refused**
BulkStart — the reordered one #8966's own text calls *"the ordinary case"* with
two fabric streams — re-stamped the start time and zeroed the end time on its way
to being rejected. Two observable consequences:

- `show chassis cluster information` reported `Bulk sync in progress since …`
  **indefinitely**. Nothing could clear it: the BulkEnd that sets an end time
  belongs to a bulk that was never accepted.
- the session handlers decide "is this bulk traffic" with
  `BulkSyncStartTime > 0 && BulkSyncEndTime == 0`, which now read TRUE, so every
  subsequent **incremental** install was counted into `BulkSyncSessions`.

A statement-**ordering** defect, not an epoch-validation one: the accept itself is
correct and no incarnation rule fixes it. The #8966 author moved `resetRecvGen`
below the accept for exactly this reason and left these three where they were,
which is why they now sit beside it.

**The filed headline for V052 is refuted and is not fixed here.** The claim was
that the `len(payload) >= 8` read admits a malformed short frame. That read is the
deliberate #5084 legacy-compat path, and a short frame is taken as epoch 0 and
accepted only when no bulk is in progress — a state in which *any* epoch is
accepted, because the guard requires `bulkInProgress`. It grants nothing a
well-formed frame does not.

## V053 — BulkAck accepted a FUTURE epoch

`if pending == 0 || epoch < pending` becomes `epoch != pending`.

The authority here is **local**. `pendingBulkAckEpoch` is set by our own send path
under `bulkSendMu` (record-then-send) *before* the BulkEnd write, so it is by
construction the largest epoch this node has ever put on the wire. A conforming
peer cannot echo a larger one, so an ack for a future epoch is not an ack for
anything — yet accepting it cleared `pending`, latched `bulkEverCompleted` /
`outboundBulkAcked` and fired `OnBulkSyncAckReceived`, releasing the #3912
failover gate on a bulk that never completed and suppressing the #4090/#4360
stranded-bulk re-drive.

Reachability is honest: this needs a non-conforming or compromised peer past the
#5303 pre-auth admission, which is why it is Low rather than High. It is fixed
because the comparator has no reason to be loose, the tightening costs one
operator and needs no new input. #5272's `pending == 0` arm is unchanged.

## PR #9491 — coordinator: vacate a dead worker's CoS V_min slot in the existing sweep [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9367-vmin-dead-worker-vacate`

Closes #9367

## The defect, re-verified at the base commit

A worker that exits by **PANIC** never clears its `PaddedVtimeSlot`, and nothing
else does either.

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `types/shared_cos_lease/vtime.rs` | `participating_v_min_snapshot` counts every non-sentinel peer slot and takes the MIN. No TTL, generation, epoch or liveness input anywhere in the reduction |
| `grep -rn 'vacate()' userspace-dp/src` | exactly two production sites, BOTH executed by the owning worker: `cos/queue_ops/accounting.rs` (its last flow bucket drained) and `worker/cos/mod.rs` (binding reset / HA demotion) |
| `coordinator/supervisor.rs` | `spawn_supervised_worker` catches the unwind, records a message, sets `runtime_atomics.dead`, lets the thread exit. Nothing respawns it |
| `coordinator/cos_leases.rs` | the floor Arc SURVIVES — reuse filter is `f.slots.len() == num_workers`, and a panic does not change `num_workers` |
| `coordinator/status.rs` | `retire_worker_holders_where` already walks every `.dead` worker under a one-shot CAS, and reclaimed **NAT holder bits only** |

## Consequence, traced

`cos_queue_v_min_continue` compares `queue_vtime <= v_min + lag`. The dead
worker's `queue_vtime` is frozen while survivors' advance, so the check fails
permanently. The suspension window is restored to full **only on a PASSING
check** (the "#hb166 T-6(a)" decaying re-arm), so it decays
1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 64 and sticks. Steady state: **8 throttled + 64
suspended — the fairness brake off for 64/72 = 88.9% of drain opportunities** on
that shared_exact class, additive to the RX capacity the panic already cost.

Not "for the life of the process": a coordinator teardown discards the map, a
worker-count change fails the floor-reuse filter, and removing plus re-adding the
exact queue drops the key. Under unchanged operation none of those happen.

#4254 (R-7) closed the sibling **REJOIN** door by seeding a rebuilt worker to the
peer frontier. The never-returning door reaches the identical state and is not
closed by that fix.

## Why the sweep's author did not include this slot — the answer the issue asks for

Because including it is **not unconditionally safe**, and the unsafe case is the
sweep's own sibling. `retire_all_worker_holders` passes `|_| true`: it must name
every registered id for the #7092 teardown reclaim *before*
`workers.stop_and_clear` drops the records — and at that moment those workers are
**still running**. An ungated vacate there makes the coordinator a SECOND writer
to a slot whose documented contract is single-writer, racing a live `publish()`,
and buys nothing, because that same teardown stores an empty
`queue_vtime_floors` a few statements later.

So the vacate is gated on `atomics.dead`, not on the sweep's predicate. For a
worker the supervisor has already recorded `dead` the owning writer has exited
and this is the only writer left.

## PR #9492 — userspace-dp: revoke an established session on reject, not only on deny [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9381-reject-revoke`

## What

The #8356 established-session zone-policy re-derivation revoked only on `Deny`.
`PolicyAction` is three-valued, so a `Reject` verdict took the PERMIT exit: the
session kept its entry, its NAT translation and both directions of forwarding,
AND was stamped `policy_revalidated` for the generation so no later packet
re-asked. An operator narrowing a zone policy `permit` -> `reject` got the new
verdict for NEW flows only.

It was the **only** site in the crate collapsing the three actions. Admission
requires `Permit` (`poll_descriptor/mod.rs`, `flowless_verdict.rs`,
`host_inbound_policy.rs`, `forwarding/fabric.rs`), the first-packet path drops a
`Reject` (`reject_reply.rs`), and `policy.rs`'s own terminal-action test already
spells the pair `Deny | Reject`. `security policies policy-rematch` — the
commit-time mitigation — is **off by default**, so on a stock box nothing else
covered it.

## The fix

The predicate is spelled POSITIVELY, matching admission:
`if matches!(result.action, PolicyAction::Permit)`. A fourth action added later
then fails CLOSED here instead of inheriting the permit arm.

**A revoked-by-reject session tears down SILENTLY** — no ICMP unreachable, no
RST, no log, no counter, identical to `Deny`. That is a decision, written into
the module header: the derivation is side-effect-free by contract, and the
teardown evicts both flow-cache directions, so the next packet of the 5-tuple is
a session MISS that takes the full admission path and emits the reject reply +
RT_FLOW deny record from the one site that owns them.

## Acceptance (driven through the REAL poll body, `session_hit == 1` in every cell)

| `lan -> wan` rule | revoked | sessions left | base | branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| absent (shipped #8356 cell) | 1 | 0 | PASS | PASS |
| `permit` — **the load-bearing control** | 0 | 1 | PASS | PASS |
| `deny` | 1 | 0 | PASS | PASS |
| **`reject`** | **1** | **0** | **FAIL (left: 0, right: 1)** | PASS |

The `permit` control is what gives the reject cell its aim: "revoke on anything
not `Deny`" and "revoke unconditionally" both satisfy the reject cell and are
worse bugs than the one fixed.

Mutant = base tree + the new cells (the fix removed). Applied confirmed by
occurrence count in **both** directions (new spelling 1 -> 0, old spelling

## PR #9516 — nat: give the recycled-phase scan cost a production reader [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9392-recycle-scan-pops-signal`

Closes #9392

## The defect, re-verified at the base commit

```
$ grep -rn "recycle_scan_pops" userspace-dp/src/
allocator.rs:910    recycle_scan_pops: AtomicU64,     <- preceded by #[cfg(test)]
allocator.rs:928            recycle_scan_pops: AtomicU64::new(0),
allocator.rs:1100           self.recycle_scan_pops.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
allocator.rs:1633   pub(super) fn debug_recycle_scan_pops(...)
tests_pool.rs:      8 call sites, all tests

$ grep -rn "recycle_scan" pkg/
(nothing)
```

Every reference outside the declaration is a test. No Go consumer, no operator
surface, and a release build does not compile the counter at all.

What that costs: #9327 measured that the recycled phase of
`PortAllocator::claim` does **not** amortize — retained tokens go to the BACK of
the per-address FIFO, so K out-of-band-occupied tokens ahead of F free ones cost
`(K+F)/F` pops per claim, degrading to `K+1` as `F → 1`, i.e. **worst exactly as
an address approaches exhaustion**. It corrected the in-code "amortizes itself"
claim and deliberately did not bound the walk. It left the REACHABILITY question
open, and the counter that would answer it could not be asked.

## The remedy

1. `recycle_scan_pops` leaves `#[cfg(test)]`.
2. **A denominator comes with it.** The promoted counter alone answers nothing: a
   large cumulative pop count is equally consistent with a busy pool doing cheap
   walks and an idle one doing pathological ones, and *that distinction is the
   question*. `recycle_scan_walks` counts recycled-phase FIFO walks, incremented
   **after** the `occupied >= range` short-circuit — a short-circuited claim walks
   nothing, and counting it would add denominator without numerator, pulling
   pops/scan toward the healthy value on exactly the most exhausted pools.
3. Summed per POOL through `PortAllocatorSnapshot` → `SourceNatPoolStatus` → Go
   → `show security nat source pool <name>`:
   `Recycled-scan pops: 128 over 8 scans (16.00 per scan)`.
4. **ADD, never redefine** — two new keys, `serde(default)` / `omitempty`.

### Hot-path cost

The increment is **not** per pop. `claim` accumulates in a local `u64` and does
ONE `Relaxed` `fetch_add` after the walk, under the `recycle` mutex it already
holds. The pathological walk pays one RMW rather than K of them — strictly
cheaper than the `#[cfg(test)]` shape it replaces.

## PR #9518 — userspace-dp: re-derive policy on the POST-translation destination [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-09)

Branch: `fix/9382-post-translation-dst`

## What

Admission evaluates zone policy on the **post-translation** destination tuple
(#2345/#2358). The #8356 established-session re-derivation evaluated the **wire**
tuple, because the forward session is installed on the wire key. For any session
with an inbound destination translation the two sites asked different questions
about the same session.

**The dominant direction is fail-CLOSED and needs no crafted config.** A published
service whose permit names the real server is REVOKED and its packet dropped on
the first flow-cache miss, with the policy completely unchanged — the rule
admission matches (`dst 10.0.61.102`) is exactly the rule the re-derivation cannot
match against the VIP. Measured: *"the policy is identical to the admitting rule"*
and *"there is no rule at all"* were **indistinguishable**. The fail-OPEN
direction exists too: a deny narrowed against the real server was missed because
the VIP still matched a broader permit.

**The trigger is not an operator commit.** `PublishRouteOverlaySnapshot` bumps the
config generation for a ROUTE-ONLY publish and the rtnetlink route listener calls
it on kernel route changes, so ordinary BGP/OSPF churn invalidated every
flow-cache entry. Independently a session installs with
`policy_revalidated_gen: 0`, so an eviction alone sufficed.

## The fix

The destination comes from the entry's own `decision.nat`. Only `.resolution` is
re-resolved on a session hit, so `.nat` is the translation the flow was ADMITTED
with — the quantity admission folds into `policy_dst_ip` / `policy_dst_port`.
Verified equal per translation kind (DNAT/static-DNAT address **and** port, NPTv6
`rewrite_dst`, NAT64's extracted IPv4 target). With no destination translation both
`unwrap_or` arms collapse to the wire values, so non-translated sessions are
byte-identical. The SOURCE stays pre-translation in both places — Junos evaluates
after destination NAT and before source NAT.

## Acceptance — six two-phase cells through the real poll body

Phase 1 ADMITS the translated flow through the production path and is itself
asserted (`tx == 1`, 2 sessions) so no phase-2 assertion can be vacuous; phase 2
drives one more packet on a FRESH binding (an empty flow cache = what a generation
bump leaves behind). `session_hit == 1` in every cell.

| translation | phase-2 policy | expect | base | branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DNAT (`172.16.80.8:443`→`10.0.61.102:8443`) | **identical** to the admitting permit | revoked 0 | **FAIL (1)** | PASS |
| DNAT | permit names an unrelated host — **the load-bearing control** | revoked 1 | PASS | PASS |
| DNAT | DENY on the real server + permit-any | revoked 1 | **FAIL (0)** | PASS |
| DNAT | DENY on the VIP ONLY + permit real server | revoked 0 | **FAIL (1)** | PASS |
| NPTv6 | identical, names the INTERNAL prefix | revoked 0 | **FAIL (1)** | PASS |
| NAT64 | identical, **mixed-family** destination set | revoked 0 | **FAIL (1)** | PASS |

**Channel: `configstore.CheckText`** (`compileTreeStrict`) — the operator commit path, and the channel #9091's 102-container headline was measured on. Deliberately not the schema walk, because #9091's ratchet enumerates the schema-side set, which is a strict superset.

## The population number is attributed before it is touched

Filed against **156**; the shipped instrument reports **158** at this base. Two merges moved it, each documenting its own numbers:

| commit | effect |
|---|---|
| `5724b2442` make the per-instance protocols grammar the global one | blind 156 → 158, armed 7 → 8 |
| `f3605f099` (#9416) enforce the named client-list source restriction | armed 8 → 9 |

Neither is this work. My own enumeration was cross-checked against the shipped `instanceNameBlind9091()` before any number of mine was trusted — both report 158. **After this batch: blind 144, armed 23.**

## Three selection criteria, and the third was imposed by the test suite

1. **`closedWorld` INHERITS, so only ALL-TERMINAL containers are armed.** Measured precedent: the #9017 note records arming `firewall family` closing the whole filter grammar and rejecting `from source-prefix-list trusted`. 63 of the 158 declare only terminal children; this batch takes 14.
2. **Armed only where the container is fail-open END TO END.** `/snmp/trap-group` and `/system/ntp/server` are schema-blind but already refused downstream, so arming them spends the #1960 no-brick budget on paths that were never fail-open. Kept as `coveredDownstream` rows so the upper-bound evidence is asserted, not described.
3. **Arming must not change any SPELLING's acceptance, and the container must DECLARE every keyword it deliberately accepts.** This came from `go test ./...` rejecting a first pass that armed sixteen.

### Criterion 1 is necessary and NOT sufficient — the finding of this PR

Two containers were dropped:

- **`/snmp/community`** fails twice: #4306 S-5 deliberately ACCEPTS an undeclared `view` knob with an advisory, and #9416's supported packed spelling `community <c> client-list-name <n> authorization read-only` puts a legal *community-level* keyword under the **terminal** `client-list-name` leaf via the flat-set chain, where the inherited closed world refuses it.
- **`/protocols/router-advertisement/interface/prefix`**: `prefix <p> no-autonomous no-onlink` is accepted today; arming refuses it.

All-terminal stops arming from closing a declared sub-container, but a flat-set chain **nests the next statement under a terminal leaf**, and the inherited closed world then refuses a sibling that is legal one level up. Both dropped containers are all-terminal.

**My first acceptance fixture could not see it** — it used the braced spelling only, which is a silent claim about which question it answered. Every armed row now asserts the **packed** spelling too, as a fatal precondition, and both declined containers keep a row whose `packed` line is the fail-on-revert guard for the decline. Verified by re-arming `snmp community`: the cell reds.

## The acceptance row that matters is the one that must still COMMIT

"The container refuses an unknown keyword" is satisfiable by refusing *everything* — worse than the silent drop being closed, because a container that stops committing is an outage at the next commit and still **boots** under #1960, so the operator gets a config that loads, warns and truncates (#4191 class).

The verdict model is deliberately **three-state** (`armedClosed` / `coveredDownstream` / `stillFailOpen`): collapsing it would either score a still-open container as rejected (a false green) or drop it from the board, losing the only record that it is open.

Three first-pass fixtures were rejected for the *wrong* reason (two chassis-cluster ones needed `authentication-key`, the VRRP one a prefix length) — the `xpfarg` hazard, which under-reports blindness. The `clean` column **is** that control, asserted as a fatal precondition on every row.

## PR #9534 — config: stop telling operators policy-rematch is unenforced [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-10)

Branch: `fix/9387-policy-rematch-help`

## What

Config-mode `?` help described `security policies policy-rematch` as
**"(accepted-only; unenforced)"**. It is enforced: `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs`
(`pkg/daemon/daemon_policy_invalidate.go`) gates on
`newCfg.Security.PolicyRematch` and clears the sessions of every surviving policy
whose match or action changed — and with `extensive`, the sessions of an UNCHANGED
policy whose referenced object DEFINITION changed (#8993). The sub-token's own
`desc` denied that half too.

The doctrine was already written down in the very commit that REMOVED the matching
advisory (`compiler_validate_warn.go`): *"Leaving the old one would tell an
operator a capability is missing when it exists … and would do it in
operator-facing text rather than in a comment."* The advisory went under that rule;
the `?` help did not.

**Not cosmetic.** The knob is **off by default**, so on a stock box commit-time
invalidation does not run at all — and it is the only commit-time mitigation for
the #9381 `permit` → `reject` revocation gap. An operator told the knob does
nothing will not set it, and then has neither mechanism.

Two non-operator-facing comments in `types_security.go` carried the same stale
claim and are corrected.

## The guard, and why it is in `pkg/daemon`

One cell, **both halves**, because neither alone is the contract:

- **Half 1 (behavioural)**: `changedPolicyRuntimeIDs` really does report a policy
  whose action changed when the knob is SET, and nothing when it is UNSET. This is
  what makes "unenforced" false.
- **Half 2 (operator-facing)**: given half 1, neither the leaf's `?` help nor its
  `extensive` sub-token's may assert the capability is missing.

A guard in `pkg/config` could only assert the absence of a phrase — satisfiable by
rewording, and silent about whether the capability exists. Here, if the
enforcement is ever withdrawn, half 1 reds and says the help is now wrong in the
OTHER direction. The text is read through `config.CompleteSetPathWithValues` (the
function the CLI's `?` handler calls), so it reads the bytes an operator is shown;
a renamed leaf fails an explicit non-vacuity check, and an EMPTY desc fails too —
a guard against a false claim must not be satisfiable by saying nothing.

## PR #9535 — userspace-dp: key the zone ledger on the LOGICAL arrival ifindex [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-10)

Branch: `fix/9383-logical-ingress-zone`

## What

`ifindex_to_zone_id` deliberately PROPAGATES a zoned child unit's zone onto its
parent's ifindex (#921/#3618), so the RAW PHYSICAL key and the LOGICAL (VLAN unit)
key return **different answers** for the same frame — not two spellings of one
answer. Measured on a `build_forwarding_state` trunk (unit 42 in `wan`, unit 43
unzoned, both `parent_ifindex = 41`):

```
ifindex_to_zone_id[41]                       = Some(wan)
ifindex_to_zone_id[43]                       = None
resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex(41, vlan 80) = Some(43)
```

Three consumers used the physical key while every zone/filter/pre-routing-NAT
admission site resolves the logical unit first (#3021/#5802):

| site | cost |
| --- | --- |
| `session_glue/mod.rs` — the #7169 reverse-session synthesis | a wrong arrival zone MINTS a reverse session, and reverse entries are exempt from zone-policy re-derivation by design, so it then rides the established fast path unadjudicated |
| `poll_descriptor/mod.rs` — the fabric zone stamp | the id selects the **peer node's** ingress zone for a redirected packet |
| `forward_request.rs` — filter-log source-zone | found by the census this issue asked for; **forensic**, not enforcement, and fixed rather than filed because censusing a site and leaving it wrong removes the reason anyone looks again |

All three now use `resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex(...).unwrap_or(physical)`, the
established spelling. GRE/WireGuard decap is unaffected **by construction**:
`logical_ingress.rs` builds the inner meta with
`ingress_ifindex = logical_ifindex` / `ingress_vlan_id = 0`, and a tunnel row has no
parent so it keys itself.

## The guard PINNED the defect, and it was fixed first

`session_glue/tests.rs` asserted the literal source substring
`ifindex_to_zone_id.get(&ingress_ifindex)` — the raw physical key — saying that
without it "the reverse-canonical match is decided by tuple equality alone". So the
**correct fix reddened that cell with a message claiming the fix reopened the hole
it was closing.** A literal-source assertion only knows the bytes moved.

Re-anchored to the two properties that are invariant: `resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex(`
is called, **and** `ifindex_to_zone_id.get(&arrival_logical)` is what keys the ledger
— because resolving the logical index and then looking up the physical one anyway is
the defect with an extra line. Its doc comment's claim that a behavioural cell was
impractical was an argument for not writing the cell that mattered; it now points at
the one this adds.

## Acceptance — the pair differs in ONE byte of input

A first cell MEASURES THE PREMISE (a Go-shaped snapshot really can zone the parent
while the arrival unit has none), so the pair cannot pass for free.
`find_forward_nat_match(reply_key).is_some()` is asserted before each drive, so a
refusal is attributable to the zone check and not to an empty table.

## PR #9537 — ha: give LegacyDataPlaneAdapter the paged owner-RG export, so the cold prime runs [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-10)

Branch: `fix/9482-adapter-paged-owner-rg-export`

Closes #9482

The HA cold-prime bulk session sync **did not run at all**. On the loss userspace
cluster, both nodes logged this once a minute, indefinitely:

```
cluster sync: owed cold-prime re-drive failed, will retry
  err="bulk sync table-truth snapshot: dataplane does not export owner-RG sessions"
```

`doBulkSync` fails CLOSED — correctly, since a partial window is what #5085 turns
into deleted live sessions on the peer — so a rejoining node received **no bulk
window at all**, only whatever incremental deltas arrived afterwards.

## Reason

`userspaceBulkSnapshot` resolves its exporter by **runtime type assertion**.
`userspaceSessionExporter` names exactly one method, and #9344 changed *which* one
— from `ExportOwnerRGSessions(rgIDs, max)` to `ExportOwnerRGSessionsPaged(rgIDs)`
— adding the new method to `*dpuserspace.Manager`. But the daemon publishes
`*LegacyDataPlaneAdapter` (`Boot()` returns `NewLegacyDataPlaneAdapter(New())`),
which forwards a hand-written **subset**, and the new method was not added to it.

## PR #9538 — config: walk the flat-set chain at twelve lenient-path containers [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-10)

Branch: `fix/9235-lenient-flat-run-residue`

#8939 drove the operator-typed flat-run losses to zero. The residue was eighteen census rows at twelve containers — and **the channel is the whole finding, not a caveat on it**.

| channel | the packed spelling |
|---|---|
| `config.SchemaValidate` | REJECTS at ten of the twelve, so an operator cannot type it |
| `config.CompileConfig` (strict) | never sees the tree there — the schema gate ran first |
| `config.CompileConfigLenient` | **loses the value** — this is the defect's channel |
| `configstore.CheckText` | REJECTS (it is `compileTreeStrict`) |

The loss is reachable through `Store.Load` (boot from the persisted DB) and `Store.SyncApply` (HA config sync), which downgrade the gate to a `slog.Warn` under #1960. A warning on a booting firewall is not a channel anyone reads in time.

## The issue's first task: is that reach real? The code already answers it

Two **shipped** migrations exist for exactly this situation:

- `rewriteRetiredDataplaneType` (#1373/#1525) — *"a node may boot with `system dataplane-type ebpf` persisted from before the retirement-strict validator landed"*
- `SanitizeTreeControlChars` (#1798) — *"a persisted free-text value … committed before the strict commit-time gate landed"*

and `compileTreeLenient`'s own doc comment states both candidate mechanisms as design premises. The rows are reachable. Checking whether the code answered it was cheaper than measuring it.

## TWO of the eighteen rows are NOT lenient-only — the issue's premise is partly false

`protocols router-advertisement interface <if> prefix <p>` and `routing-options static route <r> qualified-next-hop <gw>` commit **clean** through `configstore.CheckText` and then enforce less than they say — the more severe #9088 class, not "a fidelity question, not a security one".

The census mislabelled them by the mechanism #9265 names: it synthesises the instance name as the literal token `arg1`, so `prefix arg1` fails the typed **key** validator and `flatSetAdmittedAnyOrder` reads any rejection as "the packed spelling is refused". **The row scored rejected because its NAME was invalid, not because its BODY was checked.** The channel is now recorded per row and asserted in both directions.

## Remedy

`hoistAndSplitRun8939`, not `expandFlatRun` — measured, not preferred. `SetPath` builds a flat-set line as a nested **chain**, so the trailing statements are not on the container's children at all; `expandFlatRun` splits a run on one node's Keys and cannot see the chain. Twelve call sites, each wrapped with its own schema resolver.

**Census: losers 19 → 1, walked 85 → 103** (+18 exactly). The survivor is the artifact the issue documents (`rpm probe … target [address | url]`, mutual alternatives). The fixture was **regenerated** with `UPDATE_8939=1` on a rebase conflict, never hand-merged, so it carries another lane's `unmeasured` 76 → 77 alongside mine.

## `unmeasured` is not a placeholder problem — correcting the scope comment

The scope correction says *"the answer is a better placeholder, not a smarter classifier"*. All 77 rows were diagnosed before being deprioritised: bucketed by the error that made each unmeasurable, the dominant causes are missing **cross-reference scaffolding** (a filter requiring a term, a CoS interface referencing an undefined scheduler-map, a policer requiring a positive rate) across 35 distinct buckets. The remedy is a per-container fixture **prelude**, a larger instrument rebuild than picking an acceptable value. `unmeasured` is unchanged, consistent with none of those rows being a flat-run question.

## Four existing cells went red, each a prior decision speaking

None was stale, and none was visible to a package-scoped run — only `go test ./...` found them.

1. **`TestBracedPackedUntouchedWithoutOptIn8886`** — there are **two** splitting mechanisms and the `packedStatements` opt-in governs only one. Measured on a never-opted container: `security flow tcp-session { closing-timeout 10 established-timeout 20; }` → `closing=10 established=20` with `packedStatements=false`. So `aging` was a valid subject only because it was un-opted **and** not reached by a compiler-read expansion; this change removes the second property, and the cell's own `t.Skip` anticipated it. Re-anchored onto `class-of-service schedulers <s>`, which has both properties, plus a positive control on the first statement.
2. **`TestLeafRunDifferentialGate9156`** — two DHCP `static-binding` rows no longer differ; removed, as the gate's own text prescribes. Its summary independently corroborates the channel finding: of the 21 still differing, 0 are operator-reachable.
3. **`TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate`** — the three `security flow aging` thresholds became **comparable for the first time** because the run that hid them is now expanded. Registered in `notAValueList` with the measurement its contract demands (`early-ageout 10 20` keeps 10 and discards 20; the schema walk rejects every multi-value spelling), following the #8939 `then`-actions precedent exactly.
4. **`TestSchemaSpellingGateCoverageIsGated_7484`** — that registration excludes them from the enumeration, so `compared` falls 743 → 740. Lowered with the argument that matters: the regression this floor catches is a leaf that **stopped compiling** and could still exhibit the #2419 class; these three cannot, because the class is about a two-element **list** and each is `args: 1` smallint.

A fifth red was **not** mine: `pkg/daemon/TestDeadResponderIsEvictedAndRestarted9237` is green at `-count=5` in isolation and green for the whole package on this branch, so it is flaky under full-tree parallelism. Recorded because the contrast matters — the same pair of controls run against the #9216 branch **failed** at package level, which is how that change was identified as a real regression.

## PR #9539 — userspace-dp: resolve the re-derivation's FROM-zone from the live arrival [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-10)

Branch: `fix/9384-live-from-zone`

## What

The #8356 re-derivation was handed `Some(metadata.ingress_zone)` as its from-zone
override. The override wins over the live ingress map, which also made the ifindex
argument beside it dead. So the to-zone was resolved LIVE and the from-zone came
from the session ENTRY — and the module header's claim that *"a commit that moves
an interface BETWEEN ZONES is caught"* was true of the **egress half only**.

An operator moving an interface OUT of a permitted zone to cut off access got the
new verdict for NEW flows, while every live session kept being judged under the
zone it was admitted in, was stamped fresh, and kept forwarding.

The generation is not what was missing: every commit bumps it unconditionally via
`m.bumpGeneration()`, so the re-derivation DID run — with the stale from-zone. Go's
commit-time invalidation cannot cover it either: it diffs policy text and
referenced-object fingerprints, never zone MEMBERSHIP.

## The two guards that keep this from being a revoke storm

1. **Fabric ingress keeps the entry's zone**, and the discriminator is the
   **packet's** fabric ingress (threaded from the call site), not the session's
   `metadata.fabric_ingress` — the latter says the session was *installed* from a
   punt, which says nothing about where *this* packet arrived.

   Load-bearing on the **shipped** config, not hypothetical:
   `docs/ha-cluster-userspace.conf` puts `fab0` in the `control` zone and the
   ledger propagates that onto `ge-0-0-0` (#921/#3618), so a live resolution there
   gives `control -> wan`, which nothing permits. Without the exemption, every
   established cross-chassis session is revoked on the first packet after any
   commit — TCP death on VRRP failback.
2. **#9383**: the live resolution goes through `resolve_ingress_logical_ifindex`.
   Keying the raw physical index here would turn a trunk mis-attribution into a
   *revocation*, which is why #9383 landed first.

**Residual, written down as a decision**: an arrival that resolves to NO zone
DECLINES via the pre-existing `from_id == 0` arm, because a lookup failure is not a
verdict. An interface moved out of every zone is not torn down. Pinned by a cell
that says it is a CHANGE DETECTOR, not a defect guard.

## Acceptance — two axes varied independently, `session_hit == 1` in every cell

| entry zone | live zone | permits | expect | base | branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lan` | **`dmz`** | `lan -> wan` | revoked 1 | **FAIL (0)** | PASS |
| `lan` | `dmz` | `dmz -> wan` — **disagreement control** | revoked 0 | **FAIL (1)** | PASS |
| `lan` | `lan` | `lan -> wan` — agree control | revoked 0 | PASS | PASS |
| `dmz` | `dmz` | `lan -> wan` — harness control | revoked 1 | PASS | PASS |
| `lan` | **no zone** | `lan -> wan` — residual pin | revoked 0 | PASS | PASS |
| fabric import | parent in `control` | `lan -> wan` — **cross-chassis control** | revoked 0 | PASS | PASS |
